text: Machine learning systems encounter difficulties in learning predictors that exhibit robustness to distribution shift. When evaluated on i.i.d data sampled from the training distribution, these systems can attain nearly perfect accuracy, even under regularization to prevent over-fitting. Nevertheless, performance may deteriorate to below-chance accuracy when the testing and training distributions differ even marginally \citep{goodfellow2015explaining,geirhos2020shortcut}. The field of Domain Generalization (DG) \cite{ganin2016domainadversarial, li2018domain} tackles this challenge by proposing robust methods that guarantee good test performance on distributions that differ from but are systematically related to the training distribution \citep{mansour2019robust}. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) \citep{arjovsky2019invariant} represents one of several recently successful approaches to Multi-Source Domain Generalization \citep{zhao2020multisource} which encourages models to learn predictors with invariant performance across different ``domains'', or ``environments'' \citep{peters2015causal, heinzedeml2018invariant}. Given $n$ different training environments, these models extract a set of predictors from the feature space such that the conditional distribution of the outcomes given the predictors remains invariant across all training environments. These predictors can therefore generalize effectively to all test out-of-distribution (OOD) environments which share this same invariance. Building on work in philosophy which characterizes causation as invariance \citep{cartwright2003two, mitchell2000dimensions}, existing invariance-based DG methods have been interpreted as a weak form of causal discovery whose returned predictors represent the causal factors underlying the phenomena we wish to predict. Fairness can often be characterized by robustness to changes in ``sensitive attributes'' \cite{arjovsky2019invariant}, particularly in the context of toxicity classification. Consider an automated moderation system employed by an online news platform to determine which comments on a news article are toxic to online discourse and should be censored. The performance of a fair system should remain unaffected by characteristics such as whether the comment concerns issues related to race, gender or other politically sensitive topics. Alternative definitions of distributive fairness vary in how the system's predictions should be invariant to changes in the sensitive attribute. For instance, statistical definitions such as Demographic Parity require that some conditional distribution of predictions given the sensitive attribute remains invariant to the sensitive attribute \citep{hardt2016equality}, and causal definitions such as counterfactual fairness \citep{kusner2018counterfactual} require that every individual's prediction remains invariant to counterfactual changes in that individual's sensitive attribute. There exist numerous ethical and legal criticisms to be levied against systems that predict based on sensitive group membership \citep{barocas2016big}. Furthermore, over-reliance on sensitive information could diminish robustness when the predictive performance of this information spuriously depends on the environmental context in which it is employed. Discussion about non-caucasian racial identities, for example, may be highly predictive of comment toxicity on white supremacist internet forums whose members routinely make discriminatory remarks about ethnic minorities. However, on other internet forums that are more welcoming of diversity the association between racial identity mention and toxicity would likely be considerably weaker. This brittleness of sensitive information has been identified as a key challenge that Perspective API, a Google-backed internet comment toxicity classifier, faced during implementation in real-world contexts \citep{borkan2019nuanced, jigsawmedium}, and has also been observed to cause bias in sentiment analysis \citep{kiritchenko2018examining} and facial detection \citep{buolamwini18a} tasks. Fair models, then, can perhaps be constructed by learning predictors whose performance remains invariant across a variety of different environments. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that Domain Generalization can be used to build fair machine learning systems by constructing models that are invariant to spurious correlations involving the sensitive attribute. Specifically, we assess the performance of IRM on a fair internet comment toxicity classification task derived from the Civil Comments Dataset. In this task, the model must generalize from biased training environments exhibiting a strong but spurious correlation between mention of a particular demographic identity and toxicity to a test environment in which this correlation is reversed. \footnote{\url{https://github.com/adragnar/irm-toxicity-classification}} Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We find that IRM outperforms ERM in both generalization accuracy and group fairness on this dataset, highlighting the alignment of robustness and fairness for the type of data bias studied; \item We examine the reason for this performance improvement via ablation studies: while sensitive information is marginally predictive, IRM exploits variation in this predictive power across environments to find an invariant (and thus more fair) solution; \item Examination of the IRM solution reveals that comment length is used as an invariant feature. While predicting from comment length may be more fair than predicting from sensitive group membership, IRM has still not found a truly ``causal'' feature. This highlights both a key limitation of IRM approach of treating invariance as a proxy for causality, and the importance of environment diversity as an inductive bias for this method. \end{itemize}

text: Reconfiguration problems comprise an extensive family of problems wherein we must provide a sequence of steps to transform one object into another. In this paper we consider the problem of reconfiguring a collection of modular robots in a lattice using some prespecified moves. Numerous variants of this problem have been investigated both in the robotics and in the computational geometry communities. In this paper we study the reconfiguration problem for (edge-)connected configurations of hexagons and of squares. As necessary for many applications, we require that (edge-)connectivity is maintained at all times (fulfilling the so-called \emph{single backbone condition}~\cite{Dumitrescu-Suzuki-Yamashita-2004}). The moves permitted are pivots: a module can rotate around vertices shared with other modules and at the end of a move the pivoting module must lie in a lattice cell. The interior of two modules can never intersect. Hexagons have only two types of pivoting moves, illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:hex_moves}. In a \emph{restricted} move a module $a$ adjacent to a module $s$ pivots around a vertex $v$ shared by $a$ and $s$ and ends the pivoting move in the other cell that has $v$ on the boundary. The \emph{restricted model} of pivoting only permits this move. In a \emph{monkey} move a module $a$ adjacent to a module $s$ starts pivoting around a vertex $v$ shared by $a$ and $s$ as in the restricted move, but halfway through the rotation another vertex $w$ of $a$ coincides with the vertex of a module $s'$. Then $a$ continues the move pivoting around $w$ in the same direction (clockwise or counterclockwise) as before until reaching a cell adjacent to~$s'$. The \emph{monkey model} of pivoting incorporates both the restricted move and the monkey move. Informally, the monkey move permits a module to keep pivoting in the same direction when a restricted move is not feasible. Further insights into the differences between both hexagonal models are presented in Section~\ref{sec:models}. {In the square grid two modules that share a vertex might not share an edge. Thus, for square modules there exists a greater variety of pivoting moves. The different three sets of moves are illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:square_moves}. The \emph{restricted model} incorporates only restricted moves, the \emph{leapfrog model} incorporates both restricted and leapfrog moves, and the \emph{monkey model} incorporates all moves. \ifabstract Section~\ref{sec_proto} contains a discussion of which of the above models have been actually implemented in practice. \fi } \later{ \iffull\paragraph*{Prototypes.} \fi \ifabstract

text: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) constitutes the art and science of automatically identifying speech patterns. Speech Command Recognition (SCR) represents a subcategory of ASR wherein machines identify brief spoken commands. It serves as a fundamental technology that enables machines to comprehend human instructions. Potential applications encompass smartphones equipped with mobile assistants, robots that execute human verbal instructions, and smart home assistants such as Amazon Echo and Google Home. These application types are progressively influencing human-machine interactions. There exist numerous use cases for this technology in both medical and educational domains, particularly for visually impaired or disabled individuals \cite{1998Single-surgeonThoracoscopicSurgeryWith,2014EducationalSystemForThe}. Since many such applications depend on compact devices with constrained computational capabilities, rapid and lightweight implementations are required to operate seamlessly in real-time \cite{2018FPGAImplementationOfConvolutional}. Traditional SCR methodologies depend on extracting discriminative features from raw speech signals. Frequency-domain features such as fast Fourier transforms constitute among the most extensively utilized features \cite{1989Speaker-independentPhoneRecognitionUsing,2013TechniquesForFeatureExtraction} for converting time-domain speech into frequency space. Following feature extraction, an acoustic model such as hidden Markov model (HMM) was traditionally employed to represent the sequence of words or phonemes \cite{2014SpeechAndLanguageProcessing.}. Combinations of neural networks and HMM-based methodologies have also been utilized for more than two decades \cite{2012ConnectionistSpeechRecognition:A,1986TheTRACEModelOf}. Recently, deep learning-based methodologies have achieved dominance, regarding performance accuracy, over conventional machine learning techniques for numerous applications \cite{2012DeepNeuralNetworksFor,2015DeepLearning,2016DeepLearning}. Neural networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) have elevated the accuracy of natural language processing systems beyond traditional methodologies \cite{1999LearningToForget:Continual,2016LSTM:ASearchSpace}. Additionally, neural network-based approaches have dominated the entire SCR field and have been recognized as the state-of-the-art tool by the speech recognition community \cite{2014Small-footprintKeywordSpottingUsing,2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Meanwhile, several distinct neural network architectures including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), LSTMs, and gated recurrent units (GRUs) have been successfully implemented for SCR \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Direct implementation of CNNs on raw audio has been investigated in \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw,2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith,2018End-to-endSpeechRecognitionFrom}. This occurs while the limited computational and memory capacities of embedded devices remain significant obstacles to fully exploiting the benefits of highly accurate complex deep networks. To address the computational complexity problem on embedded devices, two general approaches are typically employed. One can compress state-of-the-art deep models to reduce computational costs without severely compromising performance accuracy \cite{2019AnOptimizedRecurrentUnit,2020Small-FootprintOpen-VocabularyKeywordSpotting}. Alternatively, more efficient deep networks and methodologies can be utilized from the outset to achieve superior accuracy rates with reduced computational costs \cite{2019OperationalNeuralNetworks,2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks}. The second approach becomes particularly important when training examples are limited or the input signals possess low quality or resolution. Using either approach, one can implement a reasonable classifier on energy-constrained embedded devices. Numerous studies focus on compressing complex networks or constructing lightweight networks from the beginning. Progressive operational perceptrons (POPs)\cite{2017ProgressiveOperationalPerceptrons} attempt to generalize conventional multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) using generalized operational perceptrons (GOPs). GOPs possess a distinct set of operators to mimic the synaptic connections of biological neurons, which enables them to better learn the hidden semantics of data. PyGOP \cite{2019PyGOP:APythonLibrary} constitutes a library for implementing GOPs on both CPU and GPU. Authors in \cite{2020ProgressiveOperationalPerceptronsWith} accelerate the learning process in POPs by employing the concept of memory and information from previously learned layers. The concept of biologically inspired neurons is further explored in \cite{2019HeterogeneousMultilayerGeneralizedOperational}, where each neuron in the network can possess its distinct set of operators, resulting in a compact network. In \cite{2018ImprovingEfficiencyInConvolutional}, a generic neural network layer structure employing multi-linear projection is proposed, which requires several times less memory compared to traditional CNNs while achieving superior performance. Authors in \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting} utilized deep networks with dilated convolutions to achieve high accuracy with fewer parameters. SincNet Kernels \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith} at the first convolutional layer of a CNN represents another method to reduce the CNN by lowering the number of learnable parameters. This method is applied for speaker recognition in \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw} and subsequently for phoneme recognition \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith}. Depth-wise separable convolutions (DSCconvs) have also been introduced initially in the image processing field \cite{2017Xception:DeepLearningWith,2017Mobilenets:EfficientConvolutionalNeural} and later in SCR, keyword spotting \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting}, and machine translation \cite{2017DepthwiseSeparableConvolutionsFor} to reduce the amount of required computations. In this paper, we propose a novel network layer to enhance speech command recognition capability using a lightweight network. To this end, we employ a novel combination of self-organized operational neural networks (SelfONNs) \cite{2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks} and quadratic forms kernels \cite{2017Non-linearConvolutionFiltersFor}. The experiments on Google speech commands (GSC) \cite{2018SpeechCommands:ADataset} and synthetic speech commands (SSC) datasets\footnote{\url{https://kaggle.com/jbuchner/synthetic-speech-commands-dataset}} demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for recognizing speech commands particularly in lightweight networks. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a combination of SelfONNs and quadratic kernels to create a novel network layer type to enhance the performance of a lightweight CNN. We are also the first to apply concepts of SelfONN and quadratic kernels to the task of SCR. In the following, we describe the most relevant work in Section~II. The proposed quadratic SelfONN approach to the problem of SCR is introduced in Section~III, and the experiments are discussed in Section~IV. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section~V.

text: The utilization of robotic surgery has expanded in recent years. Robotic surgical consoles such as the da Vinci\textsuperscript{\textregistered} Surgical System~\cite{guthart2000intuitive} developed by Intuitive Surgical Inc. (Sunnyvale, CA). are being employed in lieu of conventional surgical instruments such as laparoscopes, with the objective of enhancing surgical quality and patient prognosis. These consoles alter the fundamental nature of the surgeon's interaction with the patient. Investigating human surgical performance within such a framework is therefore a highly compelling field of research that is essential for advancing our comprehension of surgeon-robot interaction as well as enhancing patient outcomes. The comprehensive and precise surgical data accessible in multiple modalities such as videos and kinematics can be utilized to achieve a holistic understanding of the surgery as well as examine human surgical performance closely and precisely. \\ Substantial recent work in this domain has concentrated on task-specific, supervised learning from a single modality. We contend that this approach possesses several limitations. For one, a task-specific learning paradigm (such as supervised skill detection, for example) facilitates a very constrained learning of the overall surgical process, providing very limited understanding beyond the specific training task. Furthermore, supervised learning imposes a dependence on expert annotations that are costly to acquire, subjective and potentially erroneous. Finally, disregarding multiple modalities of information (such as video and kinematics) can be detrimental to learning generalizable, feature-rich representations. \\ We contend that robotic surgery can be decomposed into a sequence of gestures or surgemes \cite{varadarajan2009data}. Thus, it is feasible to model a surgery analogously to language models \cite{mikolov2013distributed, devlin2018bert} over the vocabulary of the surgemes. In this work, we propose a self-supervised learning algorithm that learns task-agnostic surgical gesture representations from two modalities (viz. video and kinematics) that can generalize effectively across multiple tasks. \\ Our contributions in this paper are as follows: 1) we provide a deep-learning based architecture to learn self-supervised surgical gesture representations from video and kinematics, 2) we quantitatively demonstrate the utility of our representations across multiple tasks by achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in gesture recognition and high accuracy in skill recognition, 3) we qualitatively demonstrate the rich information stored in our representations by visualizing our representations forming semantically meaningful clusters.

text: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition has attracted considerable attention due to its fundamental importance in scene understanding. HOI recognition seeks to identify multiple \textit{$<$verb, object$>$} pairs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}. , ``hold, apple'') within images. Image-level HOI classification presents challenges for two primary reasons. First, the datasets \cite{hico15,vg17} exhibit long-tailed distributions and demonstrate severe class imbalance. Second, images contain multiple labels with unknown HOI positions. Most recent research emphasizes leveraging object and keypoint detection while neglecting the classifier. We find that the classifier plays a critical role in both HOI classification and detection. A fundamental difference between HOI recognition and traditional image classification lies in the fact that HOI classes represent combinations of verbs and objects, resulting in stronger semantic relationships between classes. For instance, the average number of classes sharing identical verbs is 5.1 in the HICO \cite{hico15} dataset, while the average number of classes sharing the same object category reaches 7.5. Nevertheless, the effective utilization of such semantic information remains underexplored in current methods. Several studies \cite{liao2020ppdm,uniondet20,sgg-imp17,atl21,scg20} classify objects and verbs separately. This approach substantially reduces the number of predicted classes but suffers from polysemy issues since identical verbs can convey different meanings across different HOIs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}. , ``{\em make}, pizza'', ``{\em make}, vase''). As an advancement, we employ language models to generate text embeddings of HOI classes and utilize them for initializing weight vectors in the linear classification layer. This method, subsequently termed \textit{Language Embedding Initialization}, demonstrates superior performance compared to commonly used Random Initialization approaches \cite{xavier10,kaiminginit15}, especially in few-shot scenarios. The underlying principle stems from the observation that weight vectors in the linear classifier can be interpreted as proxies (feature centers) for each class \cite{circleloss20,normface17}. When employing language embeddings for weight initialization, the initial proxy positions in the vector space are no longer random but are determined by their semantic structure. This arrangement facilitates the multi-label training process as vision features from the backbone are guided toward the semantic feature center, where HOIs that frequently co-occur in images also cluster closely (see \cref{fig:2_bert}). Moreover, language embeddings provide appropriate weight initialization for few-shot classes, whose weight vectors in the classifier cannot be adequately learned from limited samples. Previous studies \cite{transfer16,pairwise18} employ {\it weighted} sigmoid cross-entropy loss \cite{wbce15} to address positive/negative imbalance per class. This approach outperforms cross-entropy loss but proves less effective when classes are extremely imbalanced (20.1\% of HICO classes contain $\leq$ 5 positive samples). We introduce a novel loss function called Log-Sum-Exp Sign (\textit{LSE-Sign}) loss to improve multi-label learning scenarios on long-tailed datasets. We design the loss function such that its gradient form constitutes a softmax function of losses across all classes. The softmax function amplifies losses from poorly classified classes while suppressing losses from well-classified classes. This concept promotes multi-label learning and dynamically balances losses across all classes. Note that the LSE-Sign loss differs from focal loss \cite{lin2017focal} in two aspects: 1). it considers the {\em relative} difficulty among all classes whereas focal loss operates on individual classes, and 2) focal loss requires tuning two hyperparameters. Although a detection-free baseline using ImageNet-1K pre-trained ViT-B/32 as the backbone suffers significant performance degradation compared to detection-assisted state-of-the-art methods (from 47.1 to 37.8 mAP), Language Embedding Initialization using BERT successfully elevates it to 50.6 mAP. The applicability extends to other language model types, including SimCSE \cite{simcse21} and CLIP \cite{clip21}. LSE-Sign loss provides an average improvement of 3.1 mAP across eight experiments (\cref{tab:bce_vs_sign}). Building upon these two discoveries, we surpass existing detection-assisted approaches \cite{pairwise18,pastanet20,hake19} by substantial margins. With a ResNet101 backbone, our method achieves 53.6 mAP, exceeding the state-of-the-art \cite{hake19} that utilizes both object and human keypoint detections by 6.5 mAP. With a ViT-B/16 backbone, our method attains 65.6 mAP. On few-shot subsets, we achieve 52.7 mAP on 1-shot and 56.9 mAP on 5-shot classes. At the instance level, we decompose the HOI detection task into localization and regional HOI classification. The detection-free advantage enables us to apply the classification model to regional human-object box pairs generated by any off-the-shelf detector. With a vision transformer backbone, we transform bounding boxes into attention masks so that the CLS token can exclusively attend to the region of interest. Without additional training under instance-level supervision, it achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance (32.35 mAP) on the HICO-DET dataset, surpassing the SOTA \cite{cdn21} which is trained on HICO-DET.

text: Pretraining large neural networks with a language modeling objective has yielded substantial improvements across NLP \citep[][\emph{i.a.}]{peters2018deep,howard2018universal,radford2018improving,devlin2018bert,raffel2019exploring,brown2020language}. Additional improvements are frequently achievable by selecting a different pretraining objective that more closely aligns with the downstream task of interest. Examples include casing prediction for named entity recognition \citep{Mayhew_Nitish_Roth_2020}, gap sentence generation for summarization \citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and sentence unshuffling for discourse representations \citep{lee2020slm}. While such approaches can substantially reduce the quantity of training data required, they typically still do not perform well if only a handful of examples is available for the downstream task, which is a common scenario for many real-world applications of NLP. In such few-shot settings, however, substantial gains are achievable by reversing what is adapted to what: Instead of making pretraining more similar to a downstream task, we can reformulate the downstream task to make it more similar to the pretraining objective. For masked language models \citep[e.g.,][]{devlin2018bert,lewis2019bart}, one such reformulation technique is to convert inputs to cloze questions by adding a text snippet that contains some form of task description, often in the form of a short prompt \citep{radford2018language,schick2020exploiting}. Besides making pretraining and finetuning more similar, this approach has the compelling advantage of enabling users to \emph{explain} a task to a pretrained model, making it much easier for the model to comprehend the task. This is illustrated in Figure~\ref{figure:motivational-example}, where a pretrained language model is given the same input with different instructions and adapts its output accordingly. The idea of providing task descriptions even functions in an unsupervised setting \citep{radford2018language} or when examples are simply provided as additional context \citep{brown2020language}; however, it only realizes its full potential when combined with gradient-based training on a handful of labeled examples \citep{schick2020just}. Unfortunately, current approaches for doing so are limited to text \emph{classification} tasks \citep{schick2020exploiting}. Inspired by their success, we investigate whether the underlying idea can also be transferred to more challenging text-to-text tasks that require the \emph{generation} of text sequences given an input text, such as abstractive summarization. We introduce \textsc{genPet}{}, a novel method based on \textsc{Pet}{} \citep{schick2020exploiting}, that enables finetuning of generative language models using both instructions and labeled examples. We show that \textsc{genPet}{} is a highly data-efficient method that enables us to finetune a pretrained \textsc{Pegasus}{} model \citep{zhang2019pegasus} with as few as 10 or 100 training examples. We evaluate our approach on a diverse set of six English headline generation and text summarization tasks both in zero-shot and few-shot settings and show that \textsc{Pegasus}{} trained with \textsc{genPet}{} clearly outperforms regular finetuning. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[topsep=0.5em] 	\setlength\itemsep{-0.1em} 	\item We introduce \textsc{genPet}{}, a finetuning procedure for generative language models that achieves excellent data efficiency by using both textual instructions and training examples. 	\item We show that training \textsc{Pegasus}{} with \textsc{genPet}{} outperforms standard finetuning across a broad set of tasks and training set sizes. 	\item We analyze the factors contributing to \textsc{genPet}{}'s strong performance and quantify the impact of all its components. \end{itemize}

text: News curation represents the intricate process of selecting and prioritizing information according to specific relevance criteria and within temporal and spatial constraints. Although traditionally conducted within editorial offices of newspapers and media organizations, this curation is progressively executed by machine learning (ML) systems that assess content relevance~\cite{allcott2017social,eslami_i_2015}. This indicates that sophisticated, opaque ML systems shape the news consumption patterns of billions of users. The Pew Research Center determined that approximately half of U.S. adults utilizing Facebook (53\%) believe they lack understanding of why particular posts appear in their news feeds~\cite{pew_facebook_feed_2019}. This finding motivates our exploration of user perceptions regarding news recommendations and whether users can differentiate trustworthy from untrustworthy ML recommendations. We additionally investigate whether untrustworthy news content such as fake news gains credibility from trustworthy contexts, particularly when an ML system generates five stories comprising four trustworthy news articles and one fabricated news piece. We operationalized fake news as ``fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent''~\cite{lazer2018science}. Examining trust and fake news within algorithmic news curation contexts remains crucial since such algorithms constitute integral components of social media platforms like Facebook, which serve as primary vectors for fake news dissemination~\cite{allcott2017social}. Research into news trust and individuals' susceptibility to rumors possesses extensive historical foundations~\cite{allport1947psychology,allport1945wartime}. We concentrate on trust within news recommender systems, which relates to the work of O'Donovan et al. and Massa and Bhattacharjee \cite{massa2004using,o2005trust}. Unlike their approaches, our emphasis concerns not trust in individual items, but trust in the ML system and its recommendations. The study design reflects how users engage with machine learning systems. Participants evaluate their trust in machine learning system recommendations, specifically rating collections of news stories. Participants received explicit information that they were interacting with an ML system, meaning they were not merely evaluating content. We emphasize trust because succumbing to fake news transcends simple error. Fake news articles are deliberately crafted to deceive individuals by imitating news media content. Our framework connects to human-in-the-loop and active machine learning, where users engage with live systems that they enhance through their interactions \cite{rubens2015active,amershi2014power,Kulesza:2015:PED:2678025.2701399}. In such environments, improving news curation algorithms through individual item ratings would demand substantial time and effort from users. We therefore investigate explicit rating of ML recommendations collectively as a method for gathering feedback. An examination of how users perceive ML systems and their recommendations proves essential for those implementing algorithmic news curation and those seeking to enable users to identify algorithmic bias during usage. This relevance extends to all human-computer interaction designers who aim to facilitate user interaction with machine learning systems. This investigation also benefits ML practitioners seeking user feedback on system quality or practitioners pursuing crowdsourced training data collection for their machine learning models \cite{Gulla:2017:ADN:3106426.3109436,ozgobek,Russakovsky2015}. In our experiment, participants engaged with a straightforward algorithmic news curation system that delivered news recommendations resembling a collaborative filtering system~\cite{Resnick:1994:GOA:192844.192905,herlocker2000explaining}. We implemented a between-subjects study comprising two phases. Our participants were recruited from a vocational school. They possessed technical backgrounds and received briefings on ML system error types that can occur unexpectedly. During the first phase, participants assessed their trust in various news stories. This process generated a collection of news stories with trust ratings from our participants. Participants evaluated different news story subsets, meaning each news story in our investigation received ratings from some users while remaining unseen by others. In the second phase, the algorithmic news curation system combined previously unseen news stories for each user according to each story's median trust rating. text: Statistical power represents the quantitative probability of rejecting a null hypothesis. Consequently, it serves a fundamental role in detecting effects of hypothesized interest within any investigation. Historically, the most straightforward and direct approach to enhance power involves increasing the study's sample size, as mathematically, this yields the most substantial impact regarding factors under researcher control \cite{cohen1992things}. Nevertheless, practical constraints must be considered when expanding sample size. In rare disease investigations, the entire population may be limited, difficult to identify, and even more challenging to recruit, as observed in early- and late-stage neuro-genetic syndromes \cite{button2013power, szucs2017empirical}. Alternatively, access or funding limitations may restrict the number of participants a researcher can obtain. In this manuscript, we empirically demonstrate that adjusting model parameters (\emph{i.e.}, weights) can substantially alter the study's power. Therefore, modifications in model parameters can transform the investigation from a moderately-powered study to well-powered research even with constant sample size. Throughout the remainder of this manuscript, we assume that well-powered research achieves power exceeding \textit{0.8}. Fig.~\ref{fig:model-param-power} illustrates that even with fixed sample size, power can vary considerably due to changes in model parameters. In Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad} we calculate power \textit{gradients} by examining the directional difference between clusters obtained through KMeans, where power and the squared L2-norm of model parameters constitute the point coordinates. Consequently, generating such a manifold, as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad} can substantially assist researchers in identifying regions of elevated power. Providing access to these visualizations thus represents a straightforward method of reducing the \textit{ideal} sample size without compromising power. However, as outlined in Algorithm~\ref{algo:power}, computing power even once necessitates \textit{200-1000} simulations. Furthermore, the manifold parameter space, encompassing model weights, sample size, and additional hyperparameter selections, is extensive. For example, with a seven predictor model, featuring 11 options per predictor and 11 options for $N$, we obtain a parameter space of $11^{7 + 1}$. Computation across this vast space could require days. Therefore, in this investigation, we examine \textit{cheaper} alternatives to simulating the complete power manifold. We present three distinct contributions \begin{itemize} \item We develop a neural network-based methodology to predict power across a high-dimensional manifold for classification and regression applications. Such an approach delivers substantial performance with merely 10\% of the training data. \item We provide four baselines for alternatively predicting power and evaluate all our methodologies on three models-- regression, logistic and Repeated Measures ANOVA. \item To exploit the transfer of knowledge from one model's power manifold to another model's manifold, we initially demonstrate the rationale underlying such transfer. Subsequently, we show that such transfer can achieve equivalent or superior results in every instance. We structure the remainder of this manuscript as follows. We initially detail the pertinent literature and emphasize the background information necessary to construct our algorithm. We provide pseudocodes for the primary and auxiliary algorithms in this section. Subsequently, we present our empirical findings, highlight the significant achievements, and report the limitations. Finally, we also present potential future research. \end{itemize}

text: Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) methodologies furnish navigational charts that permit robots to autonomously investigate an environment, while emergent Semantic Mapping approaches incorporate semantic information regarding locations and objects within the environment. Semantic mapping permits robots to navigate according to a location's semantics rather than elementary geometric poses, and consequently enables the robot to deliberate about locations utilizing automated planning or through semantic interpretations of natural language instructions \cite{thomason2020jointly}. Semantic maps prove particularly beneficial for consumer-oriented robotic applications, including assisting visitors in navigating an unfamiliar structure \cite{Yedidsion_multi_robot} or object retrieval \cite{Jiang_Walker_Hart_Stone_2019}. Manual annotation of map semantics proves laborious or impractical for extensive maps. This research concentrates on the autonomous semantic annotation of a mapped environment. Buildings frequently exhibit signage that annotates crucial semantics for the advantage of human inhabitants, including the placards denoting office numbers. Previous research employed manually crafted detectors to identify door placards, record their position on a map, and transcribe their labels~\cite{Hart}~\cite{Case}. These approaches necessitate either the construction of a map preceding scanning for placards, or require a human to direct the robot while scanning for placards. One contribution of this research involves simultaneously exploring a novel environment and registering placards without human guidance through the utilization of an enhanced Frontier Exploration algorithm, termed Interruptable Frontier Exploration (IFE). Interruptable Frontier Exploration investigates the robot's environment, while an object detector searches for door placards. This procedure is designated as \emph{passive observation}. Upon detecting a sign, the exploration is interrupted and the robot executes an \emph{active observation}; wherein it moves into an optimal position to segment, transcribe, and register the sign's position on the robot's map. To demonstrate the effectiveness of IFE, we compare against a method which computes a robot motion trajectory to scan for placards along previously-identified sections of wall~\cite{Case}. We designate this procedure Wall-Scanning Discovery (WD). IFE requires substantially less time to execute than WD by conducting fewer active scans and not necessitating a complete map before scanning for placards.

text: Recommender systems fulfill a crucial function in the rapidly evolving Internet era, seeking to predict the most probable items that may capture users' interest. Collaborative filtering represents an effective and extensively employed methodology in recommendation, which endeavors to extract latent user and item characteristics from historical interactions. Foundational studies such as Matrix Factorization (MF)~\cite{koren2009matrix} factorize a rating matrix into user and item embeddings to extract implicit semantics. As the magnitude of users and items expands dramatically in recent years, additional deep learning models are developed based on collaborative filtering to characterize diverse user preferences across extensive item collections. For instance, ~\cite{berg2017graph} and~\cite{wang2019neural} construct user-item graphs to incorporate the multi-hop relationships of interactions.~\cite{liang2018variational} and~\cite{li2017collaborative} incorporate a variational auto-encoder framework into the model and derive the representation as a Gaussian distribution. 	 	Sequential recommendation constitutes a significant component within recommender systems. It characterizes user behaviors as a sequence of items rather than a collection of items. Markov Chain (MC)~\cite{cheng2013you} represents a classical approach, which characterizes short-term item transitions and forecasts the subsequent item a user may prefer. Factorized personalized Markov chain (FPMC)~\cite{rendle2010factorizing} integrates the markov chain and the conventional matrix factorization together to characterize user preferences. With the advancement of deep learning networks, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have attained success in sequential recommendation. For instance, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)~\cite{zhu2017next} constitutes a prevalent variation of RNN to strengthen model's capability of preserving sequential information through memory cells. GRU4Rec~\cite{chen2018sequential} employs Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) to session-based recommendation by incorporating session-parallel mini-batches. RNN-based approaches encounter the challenge of preserving long-range information. Subsequently self-attention network is employed to sequential recommendations recently to capture both long-term and short-term dependencies. SASRec and BERT4Rec both achieve favorable prediction results with attention mechanisms. SASRec~\cite{kang2018self} can capture long-term dependencies because it considers the influential weights of an entire historical sequence. BERT4Rec~\cite{sun2019bert4rec} utilizes a deep bidirectional self-attention network with Cloze tasks to enhance the efficiency of a transformer model. 	 	These preceding studies model user intentions with historical sequential interactions, neglecting dynamic underlying relationships behind items. The edges that connect pairwise items encompass abundant semantic information of factors explaining why and how users select one item after another. These underlying factors relate to real-world concepts, and one particular factor frequently assumes a dominant role in a single situation. For instance, suppose there are two users interacting with six items, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{intro}. The link graph demonstrates that item 2 is adjacent to all the other five items. However these edges are intuitively motivated by different factors. Item 2 is connected to items 1 and 4 because they share the same color, while it is connected to 5 and 6 because they possess short sleeves. Item 3 is linked to item 2 because it can function as a T-shirt jacket. These different factors demonstrate the intention transformation of user behaviors, and also disclose the shared characteristics of pairwise items. Therefore, recognizing and distinguishing the underlying item-link factors can enhance the expressive capability of models, and disentangled representation learning~\cite{locatello2019challenging} represents a common method proposed to accomplish this objective. 	 	Disentangled representation learning has gained considerable popularity in numerous fields such as Computer Vision~\cite{hsieh2018learning, mu2021disentangled}, and it has been applied to recommender systems recently. The general objective of disentangled representation learning is to separate the distinct and informative factors from the variations of data, where each unit relates to a single concept in the real world. A single modification of one factor will result in a change of the relevant unit. Numerous models have been demonstrated to possess the capability to learn disentangled representation and have been applied to accomplish realistic tasks. For instance, by learning disentangled representation of a face image, we can obtain independent representations of different characteristics of the face. Subsequently we can identify whether a person in a picture has bangs, is wearing glasses, is smiling, and so forth. Furthermore, we can modify these characteristics directionally by adjusting the values of the corresponding dimensions of these characteristics. Therefore, learning disentangled representation can enhance the interpretability and controllability of model. 	 	 	 	The most prominent networks to learn disentangled representation are $\beta$-VAE and InfoGAN. $\beta$-VAE~\cite{higgins2016beta} incorporates a coefficient hyperparameter $\beta$ to the KL-divergence term in the objective of variational auto-encoder to encourage more factorized latent representations. This additional hyperparameter imposes substantial pressure on the posterior distribution to match the factorized prior distribution~\cite{burgess2018understanding}. InfoGAN~\cite{chen2016infogan} maximizes the mutual information between a fixed small subset of the GAN's noise variables and observations. Regarding recommender systems, Macrid-VAE~\cite{ma2019learning} infers high-level concepts of user intentions at the macro level and applies VAE to enhance disentanglement at the micro level. The authors also propose a self-supervised seq2seq training strategy for sequential recommendation~\cite{ma2020disentangled}, which compares user intentions between sub-sequences generated by an intention disentangled encoder. DGCF~\cite{wang2020disentangled} designs intent-aware interaction graphs to distinguish user intentions over different items, focusing on user-item relationships. Nevertheless, these studies do not consider item-link relationship patterns, and fail to distinguish different user intentions behind sequences. Consequently, the sequential model will be sensitive to noisy data and hardly interpretable. 	 	In this paper, we propose an \textbf{E}dge-Enhanced \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{D}isentangled \textbf{G}raph \textbf{N}eural \textbf{N}etwork (EGD-GNN) model to capture the item-link information. We model item representations and user intentions from both the global and the local levels. At the global level, we construct a global item-link graph over all sequences, and each item-pair in the sequences is represented as an edge in the graph. Figure~\ref{intro} presents an example of the construction of a global graph over two sequences. We apply the channel-aware mechanism to decompose edges into several channels, where each channel corresponds to an influential factor. The channels extract features specifically to one of the disentangled factors from the neighbors and aggregate different factors jointly to the target item. At the local level, we model disentangled user-intention representation over the current sequence. We first infer the latent variation as a Gaussian distribution in order to enforce disentanglement from the statistical perspective of variational auto-encoder. Subsequently we use the channel-aware mechanism and aggregate item information through the edge channels from former items in the sequence. The aggregated item representation is utilized to express current user intention. We conduct experiments based on our proposed method on three real-world datasets and compare the predicting results with the state-of-art baselines. Results demonstrate that the EGD-GNN model not only outperforms the previous works in prediction tasks, but also compels the system to find good disentangled representations. 	 	The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 	 	\begin{itemize} 		\item To the best of our knowledge, it represents the first work to explore disentangled representation over the global and the local levels to learn factorized underlying factors of item relationships. 		 		\item We propose a disentangled graph neural network to infer the factors behind pairwise items which motivate user intentions. We apply the GNN model to the global graph and the local sequences to learn item link patterns, and employ variational auto-encoder leveraging its statistical property. 		 		\item We evaluate our model on three real-world datasets, and experimental results demonstrate our proposed model can achieve a good disentangled representation over sequences to indicate user intentions. 	\end{itemize} 	 	The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Initially, we review related works corresponding to our work in Section~\ref{related}. Subsequently we propose the problem formulation and definitions of our model

text: \IEEEPARstart{W}{ith} the escalating complexity of Information Technology (IT) operational environments, organizations have developed a requirement to sustain robust IT systems while simultaneously reducing operational costs, ticket volumes, and enhancing customer satisfaction. IT operations are administered through Incident, Problem and Change (IPC) ticketing systems wherein an issue is regarded as an IT Service Desk ticket~\cite{Jan2015}. In this manuscript, these challenges have been addressed through the utilization of structured and unstructured ticket information furnished by the Service Desk (SD). Cognitive computing provides the mechanisms to transform and scale IT Services Delivery by eliminating the necessity for repetitive training of service delivery competencies. The learning capability of the system furnishes a crucial differentiator enabling cognitive solutions to continuously enhance through ongoing interactions and adapt to evolving requirements. Furthermore, service quality can be enhanced by preventing omission errors as well as achieving faster problem resolution through automated comprehension and reasoning of the most appropriate solutions. The human component, while substantially diminished in effort, will nevertheless continue to fulfill a critical supervisory function to ensure uninterrupted user interaction. Overall, cognitive computing transformation delivers exceptional client experience and business competitiveness at operational efficiency and agility that have not previously been achievable. The SD receives tickets automatically generated by various device monitoring systems. Additionally, SD agents manually create tickets in response to user requests. Several analytical tools exist in the marketplace today that generate reports based exclusively on structured data attributes of historical ticket records. Some of these tools possess query capabilities to also provide the most frequently occurring keywords or specified patterns in the unstructured attributes of tickets. These reports are subsequently analyzed by specialized IT professionals with the goal to address those identified as the most prevalent topics. These tools certainly provide advantages but with several limitations such as capabilities to process extensive amounts of data, inability to reveal apparent and concealed issues, separate noise from text, and extract user sentiments related to key topics from Customer Satisfaction (CSat) surveys and social media data. Current surveys in the literature estimate that 80\% of information resides in unstructured data \cite{Rosu2012}. The proposed methodology is a solution that addresses all the aforementioned limitations. A key differentiator of the proposed methodology is the capability to extract meaning from fragmented sentences in the unstructured ticket description. Typically, this unstructured text exists in multiple languages which is detected using language identification and normalized into a common language, English, using machine translation techniques. Moreover, due to varying language skill levels of the globally sourced pool of agents, the grammar quality also varies. To develop a common baseline for the application of analytics, this solution initially translates all non-English text into English, utilizing statistical translation models. The use of a statistical versus a grammar-based model is necessitated due to the grammar quality of the input text. The statistical translation model introduces an additional level of complexity for a cognitive system. The system has enabled numerous clients to uncover patterns and trends for identification of contributing causes and prescription of precautions within minimal time, using data from hundreds of thousands of SD tickets. Typically these types of analyses would have required the SD support teams weeks or sometimes months. Therefore, the identification of contributing causes enables the support teams to leverage log analytics for root cause analysis. Additionally, this allows the team to adopt a proactive stance toward identifying opportunities to optimize IT operations and improve client satisfaction by demonstrating the following outcomes: \begin{itemize} \item Identification of contributing causes and actionable precautions from problem description and resolution. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise concealed behind volumes of unstructured data in tickets under different categories. \item Identification of emerging problems, trends and automated change point detection. \item Identification of patterns that can enable IT support teams to leverage real-time machine and data analytics to find the rapid root cause. \item Identification of self-service and automation opportunities, and transform operations from reactive to proactive. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise concealed behind volumes of unstructured text not captured in ticket categories. \item Sentiment analysis of the CSat survey comments to determine potential future dissatisfiers. \item Social Media and CSat sentiments correlation with IT and applications' issues to improve client experience. \item Predictive Analytics for improving resolution times by re-prioritization and routing of the tickets. \item Identification of skills and knowledge gaps derived from the analysis of first time resolution of failures, resolution time and agent performance differences. \end{itemize} The manuscript is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:Methodology} is devoted to an overview of the cognitive computing platform components and methodology of the overall system. Section \ref{sec:Algorithms} outlines key algorithms developed for this system. Section \ref{sec:Applications} describes various applications and use-cases whereas results of various experiments are presented in Section \ref{sec:Results}. The manuscript is concluded in Section \ref{sec:Conclusion}.

text: Recommender systems assist users in effortlessly discovering their preferred items from vast candidate pools. Typically, recommendation models, such as collaborative filtering~\cite{koren2009matrix} and DeepFM~\cite{10.5555/3172077.3172127}, utilize users' historical behaviors to learn user preferences for future recommendations. Recommender systems employing only exploitation models commonly experience closed-loop effects~\cite{jadidinejad2020using}: users predominantly interact solely with items recommended by the system; the system subsequently reinforces users' profiles through their interactions with items recommended by the deployed model. Consequently, over time, the system becomes biased toward a small, exposed set of interests for each user and continues recommending a limited range of items to the same user. Contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms, such as LinUCB~\cite{li2010contextual}, are classical approaches that utilize side information to provide an effective trade-off between exploration and exploitation, thereby mitigating the closed-loop effect. Items are regarded as arms and the recommender model is considered an agent. Fundamentally, at each round, the agent selects one arm with the greatest potential from $K$ arm candidates, then receives a corresponding reward based on user-item interaction. The objective is to maximize the cumulative reward over $T$ rounds. However, these algorithms maintain a premise that $K$ is small, making the enumeration of all arm candidates' scores and selection of the optimal one feasible. The premise holds for several scenarios where candidates are naturally limited, for instance, homepage breaking news ranking, advertisement creative ranking and online model selection. In general recommender system scenarios, to comprehensively explore users' potential interests and genuinely alleviate the closed-loop effect, the arm candidates constitute the entire item repository, which typically contains millions or even billions of items. Classical bandit methods become impractical due to the high computational cost of enumerating each of the arms. To address this challenge, we initially propose a generic hierarchical contextual bandit~ (\textbf{HCB}) algorithm to efficiently explore user interests for large-scale recommendation scenarios. Tree structures are extensively employed to partition the search space for reducing computational cost~\cite{jain2016extreme,prabhu2014fastxml,zhu2018learning,zhuo2020learning}. {HCB} employs a tree structure as the index for coarse-to-fine retrieval. For instance, in e-commerce scenarios, \textsl{``Apparel > Clothing > Women's Clothing > Dresses''} represents a path from general apparel to women's dresses. Rather than using the category taxonomy of items, we employ a bottom-up clustering method on item embeddings to organize items as a hierarchical tree, where each node contains a group of semantically similar items. Consequently, the number of items associated with each node on the hierarchy tree can be balanced, and users' collaborative behaviors (such as co-click relations) can be encoded to form the hierarchy tree. {HCB} leverages the hierarchical information and transforms the interest exploration problem into a series of decision-making problems. Beginning from the tree's root, on each non-leaf node, {HCB} performs a bandit algorithm among the children arms to select a child node until a leaf node is reached. Subsequently, another bandit algorithm is responsible for recommending an item from the leaf node to the user and collecting her feedback as reward. The reward will be back-propagated along the path to adjust the estimation of users' interest toward the hierarchy tree. The process of {HCB} resembles a depth-first search (DFS) approach. However, selecting a path in this DFS manner may introduce new uncertainties, particularly for a deep tree. First, if the selection of the parent node is misleading, all subsequent choices will be affected, which we term the \textsl{error propagation}. Second, since user interests are typically diverse, it is possible that the user is interested in many child nodes located in different parts of the tree. Therefore, we further propose a progressive {HCB} (\textbf{pHCB}) algorithm to reduce uncertainties and enhance recommendation capacity. Similar to the breadth-first search (BFS) process, {pHCB} explores items in an adaptive top-down manner. On one hand, it gradually maintains a limited number of nodes as a receptive field. If one node has been explored multiple times and the user's interest in this node has been verified, the node's children nodes will be included in the receptive field while the current node will be removed. On the other hand, {pHCB} learns user interests of different aspects by performing a bandit algorithm with visible nodes in the receptive field as arms. Consequently, the {pHCB} avoids greedily selecting only one node at each level to improve upon {HCB}. To summarize, we make the following contributions: \squishlist \item We emphasize the importance of exploring users' interests in the entire item space to genuinely alleviate the closed-loop effect in personalized recommender systems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to implement CB models on millions of items. \item Two simple yet effective algorithms, i.e. {HCB} and {pHCB}, are proposed to explore potential user interests efficiently through a hierarchical item tree. \item We conduct experiments on two large-scale recommendation datasets. Results demonstrate the superiority of {HCB} and {pHCB} over baselines, as well as the flexibility to integrate with different exploration methods such as LinUCB, Thompson Sampling and $\epsilon$-greedy. Additionally, we design an experiment to verify that thanks to the exploring mechanism, both {HCB} and {pHCB} can effectively alleviate the closed-loop effects in recommender systems and learn better user profiles in the long term. \squishend

In this case, the classic multi-armed bandit methods become impractical because of the high cost of searching through all the candidates. The HCH is a hierarchical learning method, which uses the tree structure as an index to search for coarse-grained information. It is a method for recursive learning, which uses the top-down clustering method to classify items, and organizes items into a tree of hierarchical structure, where each node contains a group of semantically similar items. The tree structure has been widely used to partition the search space and reduce the cost of searching, as in Jain 2016 Extreme, Prabhu 2014 Fast XML, Zhu 2018 Learning, and Zhuo 2012 Learning. For example, in an e-commerce scenario, the path from general clothing to women’s dresses is a “path”. Then, starting from the root node, the HCB uses the hierarchical information to transform the process of exploring interests into a series of decision-making problems. In this way, the number of items associated with each node of the hierarchy can be balanced, and the hierarchical tree can be formed from the number of items associated with each node and the interaction behavior of users (such as the inverse relationship of clicks). This heuristic classification process is very much like depth-first search. At each non-leaf node the bandit-algorithm selects one of its children until it reaches a leaf. At this point, another bandit-algorithm recommends an item from the leaf node to the user and receives a reward in response to this recommendation. But the process of a backward search introduces new uncertainties, especially for deep trees. To reduce uncertainty and increase recommendation capability, we have proposed an additional progressive HCB (pHCB) method. The reward is propagated backwards along the path to adjust the estimation of the interest of the tree in a particular node. The PHCB method acts in a top-down way, like breadth-first searching, and is inductive, in that, when a node has been visited several times and interest confirmed in it, its children are included in the receptive field and the node removed. The first point is that, if the choice of the parent node is wrong, it may affect the choices further down the line, and this is called "error propagation." The second is that the interests of the user are usually diverse, so that children on different branches may be of interest to the user. On the other hand, the bandit algorithm is run using nodes in the graph as arms. Therefore, the bandit is not used to select one node at each level, and HCB is improved. In summary, we propose the following: We believe that it is essential to explore the whole of the item space to truly reduce the closed-loop problem in personal recommender systems. As far as I know, this is the first time clustering has been applied to a million items. Two simple and effective clustering methods are proposed, namely HCB and pHCB, to explore the interests of users through the tree of hierarchical items. We have performed experiments on two large-scale recommender systems. The results show that HCB and pHCB outperform the standard methods, and can be effectively combined with different exploration methods such as UCB, Thompson sampling, and a-greedy. , Squishy Squishy Squishy. We have also confirmed in a long-term experiment that the exploration mechanism of HCB and pHCB can overcome the closed-loop effect in recommender systems and learn better in the long run.

text: In this paper we examine an evolutionary robot system where robot morphologies (bodies) and controllers (brains) undergo simultaneous evolution. Reproduction in such a system necessitates that a new body and a new brain are generated and combined to form the robot offspring. In the case of asexual reproduction one parent suffices and the new body and the new brain are obtained through random variation (mutation). For sexual reproduction (crossover) the bodies and the brains of the parents must be recombined and the offspring is composed of the resulting body, controlled by the resulting brain. Irrespective of the specific mode of reproduction, in general it cannot be presumed that the newly generated body and the newly generated brain constitute a good match. Although the parents might possess well-matched bodies and brains, recombination and mutation are stochastic operators and can reorganize the parental genomes such that the resulting body and brain do not form an effective combination. Therefore, the joint evolution of morphologies and controllers inherently gives rise to a potential body-brain mismatch. This problem has been originally identified by \citep{Eiben2013} and recently reexamined in \citep{Eiben2020}. The proposed solution is the incorporation of learning. In terms of the robotic life cycle this entails an extension of the straightforward two stages, the Morphogenesis Stage before 'birth' (when the robotic phenotype is constructed according to the instructions in the genotype) and the Operational Stage after 'birth' (when the robot is executing its task(s) and attempts to reproduce). The third stage is the so-called Infancy Stage, following Morphogenesis, when the 'newborn' robot is learning to optimize the control of the inherited body and achieve its maximum potential. The name Infancy is not merely metaphorical, it also signifies an important detail: during this stage the robot is not fertile, that is, not eligible for reproduction. Algorithmically, this means that the fitness of a new robot is only computed after the Infancy period, thus the robot can be subject to the (fitness based) mate selection procedure only after the learning is completed. This three-stage system architecture, termed The Triangle of Life, has been described in 2013, but to-date there are scarcely any studies into the functioning of such systems. One reason is that in general there are not many papers on the joint evolution of morphology and controller, the majority of work in evolutionary robotics considers the evolution of brains within a fixed body. Furthermore, the computational costs can be prohibitive, or at least discouraging. To illustrate the severity of this issue let us observe that the infant learning process is in fact a generate-and-test search process through the space of all possible controller configurations. Such a search algorithm will need to generate several new brains and test them all in the given body. This means several additional fitness evaluations\footnote{For the sake of simplicity, here we call all tests a fitness evaluation.} for each newborn robot. Providing newborn robots a learning budget of $N$ new controllers to be generated and tested during the Infancy stage implies that the total number of fitness evaluations will be $N$ times higher than evolving without learning. Of course, an appropriate value for $N$ depends on the system and the application at hand, but a few hundred or a few thousand learning trials seem common in the literature. The primary objective of this research is to investigate the effects of learning in morphologically evolving robots. To this end, we establish a system where (simulated) modular robots can reproduce and create offspring that inherit the parents' morphologies and controllers. Thus, in our system bodies and brains are both heritable and therefore evolvable. Additionally, we make the brains not only evolvable, but also learnable. We accomplish this by implementing a generic learning algorithm to optimize the inherited brain on any possible robot body. This system will be tested by providing it a problem to solve: developing robots for the task of targeted locomotion. This task will be interfaced to the evolutionary system by an appropriate fitness function that quantifies a robot's ability to move towards a pre-specified target. Applying mate selection and survivor selection mechanisms that are based on this notion of fitness will drive evolution towards robots whose body and brain are well-suited for the given task. In order to investigate the effects of learning we will execute the robot evolution process in two versions, one purely evolutionary and one where evolution and learning are combined. In the first one, the brain of a robot child is inherited from its parents and its fitness is established directly after 'birth'. In the second one, the inherited brain of a robot child is the starting point of a learning algorithm and the fitness of the robot will be based on its performance using the learned brain. Based on these experiments we address the issues of efficacy, efficiency, and the evolved morphologies. Regarding efficacy and efficiency, the main question is how the two algorithm variants compare in terms of the highest achieved performance and the time needed to achieve the best performance. Our underlying hypothesis is that in a real-world application learning constitutes a relatively fast and cheap way of reducing the number of slow and expensive evolutionary steps. To be specific, we can distinguish learning trials and evolutionary trials. An evolutionary trial equals producing, activating and testing a new robot, including the manufacturing of its body, while a learning trial means producing, activating and testing a new controller in a given robot. Because controllers are digital entities (i.e. lines of code), learning trials require much less time, effort and material resources than evolutionary trials \citep{Eiben2021}. For instance, if the time of manufacturing a new robot is 12 hours, the time needed for computing and installing a new controller to be tried is 10 seconds and the duration of one fitness evaluation is one minute, then 1,000 evolutionary trials need approximately 501 days, while 1,000 learning trials cost less than one day. Our corresponding research questions are the following. {\textbf{Research Question 1:}} How much 'savings' (in terms of evolutionary trials) can we achieve by adding infant learning as defined by the Triangle of Life architecture? The answer to this question will indicate whether it is preferable to spend all allowable fitness evaluations on evolutionary trials (creation of a new robot consisting of a new body and a new brain) or should they be divided between evolutionary trials and learning trials (creation of a new brain in an existing body). Concerning the morphologies, we will consider quantifiable morphological traits, e.g., size, symmetry, and compare the trends during the evolutionary process as well as the morphologies in the final populations. {\textbf{Research Question 2:}} Will the addition of learning lead to different evolved morphologies? Intuitively, one may expect no differences because learning is a process that only affects the brains, not the bodies. However, in the precursor of our current study we recently found that adding learning can lead to different morphologies \citep{Miras2020}. Additionally, we investigate the evolution of {\it morphological intelligence}, defined by the learning potential of a given body. The idea is to defer judgement about a newborn body and not judge it as-is right after birth with a semi-incidental controller, but to judge it as-it-can-be with a controller customized for that body through learning. Technically speaking we quantify morphological intelligence by what we call the {\it learning delta}, the performance difference between the inherited and the learned brain. Our definition and that of \citep{Gupta2021} are similar in spirit, but different in details. Specifically, \citep{Gupta2021} define morphological intelligence by the ability to learn novel tasks, whereas the notion based on \citep{Miras2020} relates it to the given task. {\textbf{Research Question 3:}} How does the morphological intelligence (measured by the learning delta) evolve over consecutive generations?

text: Document retrieval constitutes the task of identifying relevant documents within a large collection to address specific queries. This represents an important task in its own right and serves as a core component for solving many natural language processing~(NLP) problems, such as open domain question answering~\citep{chen2017reading} or fact checking~\citep{thorne2018fever}. Traditionally, retrieval systems, or retrievers, exploit lexical similarities to match queries and documents, employing, for instance, TF-IDF or BM25 weighting~\citep{robertson2009probabilistic}. These approaches, relying on near-exact matches between tokens of the queries and documents, suffer from the lexical gap and do not generalize effectively~\citep{berger2000bridging}. In contrast, approaches utilizing neural networks enable learning beyond lexical similarities, yielding state-of-the-art performance on question answering benchmarks, such as MS~MARCO~\citep{nguyen2016ms} or NaturalQuestions~\citep{kwiatkowski2019natural}. The robust retrieval results of neural networks have been achievable for domains and applications where large training datasets are accessible. In the case of retrieval, constructing these datasets requires manually matching queries to the relevant documents in the collection. This is scarcely feasible when the collection contains millions or billions of elements, resulting in many scenarios where only a few in-domain examples, if any, are accessible. A potential solution involves training a dense retriever on a large retrieval dataset such as MS~MARCO, and subsequently applying it to new domains, a setting termed \emph{zero-shot}. Unfortunately, in this setting, dense retrievers are frequently outperformed by classical methods based on term-frequency, which do not require supervision~\citep{thakur2021beir}. Furthermore large annotated datasets are typically not available in languages other than English. Thus, utilizing large collections of supervised data is not suitable for training multilingual retrieval systems. A natural alternative to transfer learning is unsupervised learning, which raises the following question: \emph{is it possible to train dense retrievers without supervision, and match the performance of BM25?} Training dense retrievers without supervision can be accomplished by employing an auxiliary task that approximates retrieval. Given a document, one can generate a synthetic query and subsequently train the network to retrieve the original document, among many others, given the query. The inverse Cloze task (ICT), proposed by \citet{lee2019latent} to pre-train retrievers, employs a given sentence as a query and predicts the context surrounding it. While demonstrating promising results as pre-training~\citep{chang2020pre,sachan2021endtoend}, this approach still lags behind BM25 when employed as a zero-shot retriever. ICT is strongly related to contrastive learning~\citep{wu2018unsupervised}, which has been extensively applied in computer vision~\citep{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}. In particular, computer vision models trained with the latest contrastive learning methods produced features well suited to retrieval~\citep{caron2021emerging}. We thus propose to revisit how effectively contrastive learning performs to train dense retrievers without supervision. In this paper, we make the following contributions. First, we demonstrate that contrastive learning can lead to robust unsupervised retrievers: our model achieves Recall@100 results competitive with BM25 on most of the BEIR benchmark. Second, in a few-shot setting, we demonstrate that our model benefits from few training examples, and obtains superior results than transferring models from large datasets such as MS~MARCO. Third, when employed as a pre-training method before fine-tuning on MS~MARCO, our technique leads to robust performance on the BEIR benchmark. We perform ablations to motivate our design choices, and demonstrate that cropping works better than the inverse Cloze task. Finally we train a multilingual dense retriever with contrastive learning and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code and pre-trained models are available here: \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/contriever}.

text: Contemporary years have witnessed an escalation of misinformation (and closely related phenomena, such as disinformation and fake news), and that such information can inflict serious societal harm. For instance, such detrimental effects encompass (among others) influencing voting decisions in an election, health care decisions during a pandemic, or stock prices\footnote{e.g., the GameStop incident in 2021: \url{https://reut.rs/3ra7stz }}. The emergence of misinformation has also stimulated a substantial body of work, particularly in natural language processing (NLP), on the automatic fact checking of claims \cite{fever,popat2018declare,multifc,hanselowski2019richly,wadden2020fact,xfact,covidfact}. Despite considerable progress, however, the task remains quite challenging.
