text: Contemporary commercial buildings constitute complex cyber-physical systems. They are progressively being outfitted with sensors and actuators, spanning from surveillance cameras and card readers for security and access control, to thermostats and air-quality sensors that feed into the Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system, which regulates the indoor environment while preserving occupant comfort~\cite{Haggerty13,ardakanian2018}. These buildings constitute significant financial investments and the administration of their security is considerably more critical relative to older buildings. Reasoning about and administering access to these buildings necessitate different access policies for different categories of users. For instance, as a standard practice, long-term building occupants such as employees who work in the building are granted access privileges to their offices and shared spaces, based on their organizational roles; conversely, facilities-management personnel typically possess access to the more restricted spaces where equipment is installed and also to the Building Management System (BMS) which enables them to monitor and control the equipment settings. Occupants may access the sensing and control devices, such as light switches and thermostats, in the spaces to which they have physical access even though these devices may impact building areas beyond the room in which they are physically located; for instance, a thermostat located in a room can determine the temperature setpoint of multiple adjacent rooms. Finally, visitors tend to have limited access, and are frequently required to be escorted by building occupants to the meeting rooms where their business is conducted; they might control equipment in these rooms, but only for the duration of their meeting. In large commercial buildings, this approach entails substantial administrative overhead and exposes the building infrastructure to various security threats. Ideally, an automated solution is required to efficiently administer the access privileges of a building's occupants. Traditional role-based access-control models adopted in existing access control systems are cumbersome, in that they necessitate the specification of all roles and their relative authority, which constitutes a challenge in large buildings occupied by multiple organizations, each one with their own distinct role hierarchy~\cite{Bindra19}. In this paper, we propose a methodology for managing building access control inspired by the concept of \emph{airline boarding-passes} and the workflows surrounding them. At any point in time, the airport is utilized by numerous airlines that manage their own flights at their corresponding gates and are responsible for issuing boarding passes to their passengers. Boarding passes become available shortly before passengers travel, enabling passengers to proceed through security, access their gate, and board their plane at the appropriate time. Each boarding pass is associated with an individual traveller, and is valid only during a brief period before the flight departure. During this period, security personnel are able to scan and verify the boarding pass. This methodology is envisioned to be implemented independent of any pre-existing access control delegation strategies, but still be co-existent with already implemented access control systems. Our methodology can flexibly and securely administer building access privileges for long-term occupants and short-term visitors alike, addressing the challenges and risks mentioned above. We establish a set of services for {\em fine-grained} decentralized management of people's access privileges within a commercial building. We use the term fine-grained to denote (a) person-centric instead of role-based, (b) tailored to different space/system granularities, and (c) spanning multiple timescales. The underlying intuition for this work is that {\em if a person is authorized to have physical access to a particular location in a building, then they also have access and opportunity to manipulate the sensors and control points in this space.} This is because, in most cases, there is no additional access-control beyond placing the equipment behind a locked door. Also by implication, {\em if a person should not have access to some control points, they should not be authorized to access the space where this equipment is located.} Our methodology relies on blockchain smart contracts to describe, grant, audit, and revoke fine-grained permissions for building occupants and visitors in a decentralized manner~\cite{andersen2018democratizing}. The smart contracts are specified through a process that leverages the information compiled from the BOT~\cite{Rasmussen17} and Brick~\cite{balaji2016brick} models of the building's spatial structure, equipment, and their relations. This information enables our methodology to grant an individual with precisely the appropriate access privileges to allow them to reach their destination within the building. We implement this intuition in the form of smart contracts, through which space-access privileges are granted to (and revoked from) individuals using an API that can be invoked by different software applications. The underlying \emph{access-control service} is responsible for accepting or rejecting individual access requests based on the currently valid smart contracts and their implications regarding access to sensors and actuators. We illustrate the proposed method through a typical use case in the context of a real building and we argue that it can substantially reduce the administration overhead, while simultaneously providing fine-grained, auditable access control. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides an overview of the context surrounding our work. Section~\ref{sec:method} describes in detail our methodology for smart-building access control using a graph model for reasoning, and blockchain smart contracts for managing access. Section~\ref{sec:implement} examines the implementation of the proposed work along with use cases in which the proposed solution can significantly enhance the authorization and access control procedures in a real building. Section~\ref{sec:perform} evaluates the performance of the proposed solution in terms of throughput and delay. Section~\ref{sec:system} presents practical considerations for utilizing blockchain-based access control. Section~\ref{sec:related} discusses related work on authorization and access-control solutions developed for the built environment. The paper concludes with an overview of the key contributions of our work and our plans for future work in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: Few-shot learning, which seeks to classify instances from unseen classes using only a limited number of training examples, has experienced rapid advancement in recent years. To enable swift adaptation to novel classes, considerable attention has been devoted to the meta-learning (or learning-to-learn) paradigm \cite{ren2018meta,snell2017prototypical,vinyals2016matching}. Meta-learning approaches established the necessity of organizing training data into {\em episodes}, thereby emulating the tasks that will be encountered during inference. However, despite the improvements achieved, several recent image classification studies \cite{boudiaf2020transductive,chen2018closer,dhillon2019baseline,GuoECCV20-DS,tian2020rethinking,zikolaplacian} have noted that meta-learning may possess limited generalization capability beyond the standard 1- or 5-shot classification benchmarks. For example, in more realistic scenarios involving domain shifts, simple classification baselines can surpass considerably more complex meta-learning approaches \cite{chen2018closer,GuoECCV20-DS}. Deep-learning based semantic segmentation has typically benefited from methodological developments in image classification. Few-shot segmentation, which has recently gained prominence \cite{gairola2020simpropnet,wei2019fss,liu2020crnet,nguyen2019feature,rakelly2018conditional,pfenet,wangfew,wang2019panet,rpmm,yang2020new,zhang2019canet,zhang2020sg}, represents no exception. In this framework, a deep segmentation model is initially pre-trained on {\em base} classes. Subsequently, model generalization is evaluated across few-shot {\em tasks} and novel classes not encountered during base training. Each task comprises an unlabeled test image, termed the {\em query}, alongside several labeled images (the {\em support} set). The contemporary literature in few-shot segmentation adheres to the learning-to-learn paradigm, and considerable research efforts have concentrated on designing specialized architectures and episodic-training schemes for base training. Nevertheless, i) episodic training inherently assumes that testing tasks possess a structure (e.g., the number of support shots) comparable to the tasks employed during the meta-training phase; and ii) base and novel classes are frequently assumed to be drawn from the same dataset. In practice, these assumptions may constrain the applicability of existing few-shot segmentation methods in realistic scenarios \cite{cao2019theoretical,chen2018closer}. Indeed, our experiments demonstrated consistency with findings in few-shot classification when extending beyond standard settings and benchmarks. Specifically, we observed among state-of-the-art methods a performance saturation \cite{cao2019theoretical} when increasing the number of labeled samples (See Table \ref{tab:n_shots_aggreg}). Furthermore, consistent with very recent observations in image classification \cite{chen2018closer}, existing meta-learning methods demonstrate reduced competitiveness in cross-domain scenarios (See Table \ref{tab:COCO2PASCAL_results_partial}). This raises questions regarding the viability of current few-shot segmentation benchmarks and datasets; and motivates reconsidering the relevance of the meta-learning paradigm, which has become the \textit{de facto} choice in the few-shot segmentation literature. \subsection*{Contributions} In this work, we abandon meta-learning, and reconsider simple cross-entropy supervision during training on the base classes for feature extraction. Additionally, we propose a \textit{transductive} inference that more effectively leverages the support-set supervision than existing methods. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We present a novel transductive inference--\textit{RePRI} (Region Proportion Regularized Inference)--for a given few-shot segmentation task. RePRI optimizes a loss incorporating three complementary terms: \textit{i)} a standard cross-entropy on the labeled pixels of the support images; \textit{ii)} the entropy of the posteriors on the query pixels of the test image; and \textit{iii)} a global KL divergence regularizer based on the proportion of the predicted foreground pixels within the test image. RePRI can be applied on top of any trained feature extractor, and utilizes precisely the same information as standard inductive methods for a given few-shot segmentation task. \item Although we employ basic cross-entropy training on the base classes, without complex meta-learning schemes, RePRI achieves highly competitive performance on the standard few-shot segmentation benchmarks, PASCAL-5$^i$ and COCO-20$^i$, with gains around $5\%$ and $6\%$ over the state-of-the-art in the 5- and 10-shot scenarios, respectively. \item We introduce a more realistic setting where, in addition to the usual shift on classes between training and testing data distributions, a shift on the images' feature distribution is also introduced. Our method attains the best performance in this scenario. \item We demonstrate that precise region-proportion information on the query object substantially improves the results, with an average gain of 13\% on both datasets. While assuming the availability of such information is not realistic, we show that imprecise estimates can still yield dramatic improvements, opening a highly promising direction for future research. \end{itemize}

text: Developing and evaluating recommenders to optimize business objectives represents one of the primary focuses within e-commerce machine learning. A fundamental discrepancy between business and machine learning domains is that target metrics, such as gross merchandise value (GMV), prove challenging to interpret as concrete learning objectives. Although several surrogate losses and evaluation metrics have demonstrated particular empirical success \cite{shani2011evaluating,herlocker2004evaluating}, online experimentation remains perhaps the sole reliable approach for assessing a candidate recommender's real-world performance. Specifically, there exists broad consensus regarding the various types of bias present in collected historical data \cite{chen2020bias}, which can induce the "feedback-loop effect" when empirical metrics are employed without correction \cite{gilotte2018offline}. Recently, there has emerged a surge of innovations in refining online A/B testing and correcting offline evaluation methodologies \cite{yin2019identification,lee2018winner,xie2018false,gilotte2018offline}. Nevertheless, they remain inadequate in specific applications where either the problem complexity outweighs their potential benefits, or their assumptions are not satisfied. Since our work addresses e-commerce recommendations primarily, we assume the online shopping context throughout this paper. Regarding A/B testing, there exists increasing demand for interleaving the tested recommenders and targeted customers due to growing interests in personalization \cite{schuth2015predicting}. The process of collecting sufficient observations and drawing inference with adequate power is often slow and expensive (in addition to the complication of defining buckets in advance), since the number of combinations can grow exponentially. Concerning recent advancements for offline A/B testing \cite{gilotte2018offline}, although certain unbiasedness and optimality results have been demonstrated theoretically, the real-world performance still depends on fundamental causal assumptions \cite{imbens2015causal}, e.g. unconfounding, overlap and identifiability, which are rarely satisfied in practice \cite{xu2020adversarial}. We emphasize that the role of both online and offline testing remains irreplaceable despite their drawbacks; however, the current issues motivate us to discover more efficient solutions that can better leverage the randomized design of traffic. The production scenario that motivates our work involves choosing from several candidate recommenders that have demonstrated comparable performances in offline evaluation. Through segment analysis, we find each recommender more favorable to specific customer groups, but again the conclusion cannot be drawn definitively due to exposure and selection bias in the historical data. In other words, while it is safe to deploy each candidate online, we still require randomized experiments to explore each candidate's real-world performance for different customer groups. We aim to design the experiment by accounting for customer features (e.g. their segmentation information) to minimize the cost of applying suboptimal recommenders to a customer group. Note that our objective deviates from traditional controlled experiments because we prioritize minimizing cost over drawing rigorous inference. In the sequel, we characterize our mission as a recommender-wise exploration-exploitation problem, a novel application to the best of our knowledge. Before proceeding, we illustrate the fundamental differences between our problem and learning ensembles of recommenders \cite{jahrer2010combining}. The business metrics, such as GMV, are random quantities that depend on the recommended content as well as the distributions governing customers' decision-making. Even if we have access to those distributions, we never know in advance the conditional distribution given the recommended content. Therefore, the problem cannot be appropriately described by any fixed objective for learning recommender ensembles. In our case, the exploration-exploitation strategy can be viewed as a sequential game between the developer and the customers. In each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, where the role of $n$ will be clarified later, the developer selects a recommender $a_t \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ that produces the content $c_t$, e.g. top-k recommendations, according to the front-end request $r_t$, e.g. customer id, user features, page type, etc. Then the customer reveals the \textsl{reward} $y_t$ such as click or not-click. The problem setting resembles that of \textsl{multi-armed bandits (MAB)} by viewing each recommender as the \emph{action} (\emph{arm}). The front-end request $r_t$, together with the recommended content $c_t = a_t(x_t)$, can be conceived as the \emph{context}. Obviously, the context is informative of the reward because the clicking will depend on how well the content matches the request. On the other hand, a (randomized) experiment design can be characterized by a distribution $\pi$ over the candidate recommenders, i.e. $0 < \pi_t(a) < 1$, $\sum_{i=1}^k \pi_t(i)=1$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. We note that a formal difference between our setting and classical \emph{contextual bandit} is that the context here depends on the candidate actions. Nevertheless, its impact becomes negligible if selecting the best set of contents remains equivalent to choosing the optimal action. Consequently, the goal of finding the optimal experimentation can be readily converted to optimizing $\pi_t$, which aligns with the bandit problems. The intuition is that by optimizing $\pi_t$, we refine the estimation of the structures between context and reward, e.g. via supervised learning, at a low exploration cost. The critical concern of conducting exploration in e-commerce, perhaps more concerning than in other domains, is that irrelevant recommendations can severely harm user experience and retention, which directly relates to GMV. Therefore, it is essential to leverage the problem-specific information, both the contextual structures and prior knowledge, to further design the randomized strategy for higher efficiency. We use the following toy example to illustrate our argument. \begin{example} Suppose that there are six items in total, and the front-end request consists of a uni-variate user feature $r_t \in \mathbb{R}$. The reward mechanism is given by the linear model: \[ Y_t = \theta_1 \cdot I_1 \times X_t + \ldots + \theta_6 \cdot I_6 \times X_t; \] where $I_j$ is the indicator variable on whether item $j$ is recommended. Consider the top-3 recommendation from four candidate recommenders as follows (in the format of one-hot encoding): \\ \begin{equation} \begin{split} a_1(r_t) = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]; \\ a_2(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]; \\ a_3(r_t) = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1]; \\ a_4(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]. \\ \end{split} \end{equation} If each recommender is explored with equal probability, the role of $a_1$ is underestimated since it is the only recommender that provides information about $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Also, $a_2$ and $a_4$ produce identical outputs, so their exploration probability should be discounted by half. Similarly, the information provided by $S_3$ can be recovered by $S_1$ and $S_4$ (or $S_2$) combined, so there exists a linear dependency structure we may leverage. \end{example} The example is representative of real-world scenarios, where the one-hot encodings and user features may simply be replaced by pre-trained embeddings. Thus far, we provide an intuitive understanding of the benefits from effective online experiment designs. In Section \ref{sec:background}, we introduce the notations and the formal background of bandit problems. We then summarize the relevant literature in Section \ref{sec:related}. In Section \ref{sec:method}, we present our optimal design methods and describe the corresponding online infrastructure. Both the simulation studies and real-world deployment analysis are provided in Section \ref{sec:experiment}. We summarize the major contributions as follows. \begin{itemize} \item We provide a novel setting for online recommender selection via the lens of exploration-exploitation. \item We present an optimal experiment approach and describe the infrastructure and implementation. \item We provide both open-source simulation studies and real-world deployment results to illustrate the efficiency of the approaches studied.

text: Semantic Segmentation seeks to accomplish dense prediction by labeling each pixel in an image according to the class that the pixel represents. Transformer-based vision networks \cite{vit,deit} have surpassed Convolutional Neural Networks on the image-classification task \cite{imagenet}. In contemporary research, transformer backbones have demonstrated remarkable performance when adapted to downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation \cite{beit, fapn, swin-T}. Most architectural designs in vision transformers address the problem through one of two approaches: (i) Employ an existing pretrained backbone as an encoder and adapt it to downstream tasks using pre-existing standard decoders such as Semantic FPN \cite{sem-fpn} or UperNet \cite{upernet}; OR (ii) construct a novel encoder-decoder network where the encoder is pretrained on ImageNet for the semantic segmentation task. Both approaches, as previously mentioned, require finetuning the encoder backbone on the segmentation task. Finetuning from a large-scale dataset enables early attention layers to integrate local information at lower layers of the transformers \cite{vit-cnn}. Nevertheless, it remains unable to leverage the semantic context during finetuning due to the relatively smaller dataset size and a shift in the number and nature of semantic classes from classification to the segmentation task. Hierarchical vision transformers \cite{segformer,swin-T} address the problem through progressive downsampling of features across the stages, though they still lack the semantic context of the image. Liu et al. \cite{swin-T} introduced the Swin Transformer, which builds hierarchical feature maps making it suitable as a general-purpose backbone for major downstream vision tasks. \cite{twins} proposed to employ two attention mechanisms: globally sub-sampled and locally sub-sampled on top of PVT \cite{pvt} and CPVT \cite{cpvt} for effective segmentation. Xie et al. \cite{segformer} further refined the hierarchical transformer encoder by eliminating positional-encoding and thus making it robust to different resolutions as commonly encountered in the segmentation task. All these works modified the encoders to enhance their performance for downstream tasks like segmentation and achieved success to an impressive degree. Nevertheless, they did not focus on capturing the semantic-level contextual information of the entire image. An absence of semantic contextual information results in sub-optimal segmentation performance, particularly in the case of small objects where they become merged with the boundaries of larger categories, resulting in incorrect predictions. Recently, \cite{segmenter} attempted to address this issue by designing a pure transformer-based decoder that jointly processes the patch and class embedding. However, it does not perform efficiently for tiny variants and fails with hierarchical architectures resulting in sub-optimal performance when employed with major transformer backbones like Swin \cite{swin-T}, and Twins \cite{twins} transformers. Jin et al. in \cite{isnet} proposed ISNet to model the image level contextual information alongside semantic level contextual information by introducing the SLCM and ILCM modules in the decoder structure. However there remains a limitation: ISNet is a CNN based method and only concentrates on the decoder part of the network, leaving the encoder unmodified. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose the SeMask framework that integrates semantic information into hierarchical vision transformer architectures and enhances the global feature information captured by the transformers with the semantic context. The existing frameworks formulate the architecture as an encoder-decoder structure with transformers pretrained on ImageNet \cite{imagenet} serving as the encoders and utilizing a specialized decoder for semantic segmentation. In contrast to directly employing the hierarchical transformers as a backbone, we insert a Semantic Layer after the Transformer Layer at each stage in the backbone, providing us the SeMask version of the backbone as illustrated in \cref{fig:intro}. We employ a lightweight semantic decoder to accumulate the semantic maps from all the stages, and a standard decoder like Semantic-FPN \cite{sem-fpn} for the main per-pixel prediction. The added semantic modeling with feature modeling throughout the encoder enables us to improve the performance of the semantic segmentation task. In \cref{sec:experiments}, we integrate the proposed SeMask block into the Swin Transformer \cite{swin-T} and Mix Transformer \cite{segformer} backbones. Our experimental results demonstrate considerable improvement in semantic segmentation for both backbones on two different datasets. To summarize, our contributions are threefold: \begin{itemize} \item To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the effect of adding semantic context to pretrained transformer backbones for the semantic segmentation task. Furthermore, we introduce a SeMask Block which can be integrated into any existing hierarchical vision transformer. We provide empirical evidence by incorporating SeMask into Swin-transformer~\cite{swin-T} and Mix-Transformer~\cite{segformer}, and achieving substantial performance improvement. \item We also propose to employ a simple semantic decoder for aggregating the semantic priors from different stages of the encoder. The semantic priors receive supervision from the ground truth using a per-pixel cross-entropy loss. \item Finally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the SeMask Block's effect on two different datasets: ADE20K and Cityscapes. We achieve the new state-of-the-art performance on the ADE20K dataset and an improvement above $3\%$ on the Cityscapes dataset. \end{itemize}

In contrast to those previous frameworks, which use directly hierarchical transformers as the main input, we introduce a SeMask layer after each transformer layer, which provides a SeMask version of the main input, as illustrated in Figure [f:intro]. This method is formulated as an encoder-decoder architecture, with the encoder being a transformer, trained on ImageNet, and a specialized decoder for semantic segmentation. This additional modeling along with the encoder allows us to improve the performance of the semantic segmentation task. In the experiments, we plugged the proposed SeMask block into the Swin-T [Swin-T] and Segformer [Segformer] cores. We use a lightweight semantic decoder to collect the semantic maps from all the stages, and a regular decoder such as Semantic FPN for the main per-pixel prediction. In addition, we present a new block, SeMask, which can be inserted into any existing hierarchical vision transformer. Our experimental results show a considerable improvement of the semantic segmentation in both backbones on two different datasets. We also present a simple semantic decoder, which combines the semantic priors from the different stages of the encoder. We show it in practice, by implementing it in Swin-T and Segformer and obtaining a significant improvement in performance. Finally, we analyze the effect of SeMask on two different datasets: ADE20K and Cityscapes. In conclusion, we make three contributions: We achieved a new state of the art on the ADE20K dataset and a 3.1 percent improvement on the Cityscapes dataset.

text: Image captioning, which seeks to automatically describe the visual content of an unlabeled image using natural language, has been extensively investigated~\cite{showandtell2015,bottomup2017,aoanet2019}. As a specialized branch, cross-lingual image captioning, possessing the capability to generate captions for a given image in a target language different from English, has garnered increasing interest within both multimedia and computer vision communities~\cite{icmr16-ch-cap,WeiyuLan2017,Jiuxiang2018,2019Improving,2019Unpaired,gao2020unsupervised}. Prior research in this domain focuses on innovative algorithms that efficiently learn image captioning models for the target language utilizing existing English datasets such as Flickr8k \cite{2015Framing}, Flickr30k \cite{2014From} and MS-COCO \cite{mscoco2014}. In \cite{icmr16-ch-cap}, for example, Li \emph{et al.~} employ machine translation to automatically convert English captions of Flickr8k into Chinese and then train a Show-Tell model~\cite{showandtell2015} on the translated dataset. Recognizing that machine-translated sentences may be incomprehensible, Lan \emph{et al.~} \cite{WeiyuLan2017} propose fluency-guided learning, where the significance of a training sentence is determined by its fluency score computed by a deep language model. Song \emph{et al.~} \cite{2019Unpaired} enhance \cite{WeiyuLan2017} by incorporating self-supervised reward considering both fluency and visual relevance. While such a training procedure requires only minimal (or zero) amounts of data in the target language, comprehensive evaluation of the resulting models typically necessitates thousands of test images paired with manually crafted captions, termed \textit{references}, in the corresponding language. Even with assistance from an interactive annotation system~\cite{icmr20-icap}, months of human effort are needed to re-annotate a medium-sized testset for each target language. In this paper we advance cross-lingual image captioning through a novel evaluation methodology. Specifically, we undertake an ambitious effort to eliminate the requirement for references in the target languages. We introduce three metrics that enable us to distinguish between high-performing and low-performing models, when a test image is accompanied by only one reference in English. Such a condition is reasonable, as prior work on cross-lingual image captioning has been conducted primarily on established English datasets. Our principal contributions are twofold: \begin{itemize} 	\item To our knowledge, this represents the first work on evaluating image captioning models in a cross-lingual context, without requiring any reference in the target language. To this end, we introduce three metrics, \emph{i.e.,~} WMDRel, CLinRel and CMedRel, that evaluate the semantic relevance of automatically generated captions with respect to the image content through different approaches. 	\item We have performed extensive experiments to assess the efficacy of the three proposed metrics. Given various combinations of image captioning networks, \emph{i.e.,~} Show-Tell~\cite{showandtell2015}, Up-Down~\cite{bottomup2017} and AoANet~\cite{aoanet2019} and datasets, \emph{i.e.,~} COCO-CN~\cite{cococn2019} and VATEX~\cite{2019VATEX}, we construct a collection of eight Chinese models for ranking. The combination of WMDRel, CLinRel and CMedRel achieves Spearman's rank correlation of 0.952 with the sum of the four standard metrics, \emph{i.e.,~} BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L and CIDEr. When no reference in the source language is provided, CMedRel alone achieves Spearman correlation of 0.881 with CIDEr. \end{itemize}

text: In recent years, the medical imaging community has experienced a rapid proliferation of image processing methodologies based on Deep Learning (DL). These innovative techniques have demonstrated exceptional performance across numerous tasks, including Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesion segmentation. Several automated algorithms have achieved human-level performance under controlled evaluation conditions (see \cite{carass2017longitudinal}). In contrast to over-controlled conditions where most DL approaches have been validated, real-world data demonstrate substantial diversity. Consequently, clinical application of MS lesion segmentation based on DL remains constrained primarily due to their inadequate generalization on novel data originating from medical sites not represented during training (unseen domains). This deficiency in generalization of DL methods may arise from multiple factors including the selected solution during optimization, the diversity of the training dataset, or the genericity of the extracted features. DL operates under the assumption that training and test data are independent yet originate from identical distributions. This assumption is typically violated in medical imaging data, particularly for Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) where acquisition protocols, MRI scanners, patient populations, and software processing may differ according to the clinical center or the cohort. As a consequence of these disparities in data distribution (covariate shift), a performance degradation is observed between the training data (source domain) and the test data derived from different distributions (target domain). This phenomenon is recognized as the domain shift. An intuitive approach to mitigate this problem involves training on a broader and more heterogeneous dataset (as demonstrated by \cite{maartensson2020reliability}). Nevertheless, this necessitates a large dataset annotated by experts, which is seldom available and laborious to generate. Some address this phenomenon by implementing extensive data augmentation (such as \cite{zhang2020generalizing}). Others utilize few available labeled images from the target domain to reduce the covariate shift, including few-shot and one-shot learning strategies (see \cite{snell2017prototypical,valverde2019one}). Furthermore, DL necessitates the tuning of numerous parameters relative to the number of training data samples. Consequently, it typically converges to one of many possible local minima rather than the theoretical optimal parameter configuration that yields the global minimum. Therefore, the generalization capability of the model depends upon the selected solution. The selection of the optimal generalizing local minimum remains an open question. On one hand, certain works have proposed selecting it using the local characteristics (\textit{e.g.}, flatness) of the loss function (see \cite{keskar2016large, wu2017towards} ). On the other hand, an alternative strategy involves combining multiple local minima to enhance the generalization capability of the method. This can be accomplished by averaging multiple local minima of one model (\textit{e.g.}, snapshot ensemble \cite{huang2017snapshot}) or by combining outputs of different models trained independently (\textit{e.g.}, classical ensemble \cite{zhang2019multiple} and spatially distributed networks \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d}). Unlike conventional methods that employ hand-crafted features, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) automatically extract the most appropriate set of features for a specific task. Although this strategy is highly effective for extracting relevant features for a particular source domain, this feature set may not generalize effectively to the target domain. Several works have proposed learning invariant features that exist across different source domains \cite{motiian2017unified,muandet2013domain,yang2013multi}. They attempted to apply regularization to learn an abstract representation of the specific computer vision task (\textit{i.e.}, similar to how humans comprehend high-level concepts). Indeed, the extraction of generalizing features exists between the freedom of the optimization process to identify the optimal combination from data, and the constraints employed for minimizing domain bias. The successful deployment of DL-based methods for MS lesion segmentation requires generalization capabilities that can ensure high performance for unseen domains. First, such methods should guarantee the convergence of the DL model to generalizing minima. Second, the training process should anticipate the reduction of the covariate shift. Moreover, the method should be constrained to learn MS lesion generalizing features from the source domain, to effectively delineate lesions despite the target domain distribution. Finally, this solution should not require additional annotation when processing unseen domains. Recently, numerous works have been proposed for MS lesion segmentation using CNNs.\\ First, \cite{brosch2016deep} proposed a deep 3D encoder-decoder network, with joint training of the encoder and the decoder. The authors employed shortcut connections between the two interconnected pathways for integrating high and low-level features. This pioneering work demonstrated the substantial potential of deep learning for MS lesion segmentation.\\ \cite{valverde2017improving} proposed a cascade of two patch-wise 3D CNNs, comprising a first sensitive network to identify potential lesion candidates followed by a second network to reduce misclassified voxels. This cascade enables refined segmentation but employs a small receptive field that prevents capturing the global context. Subsequently, the authors \cite{valverde2019one} enhanced their method by proposing a one-shot domain adaptation model which utilizes transfer learning and partial fine-tuning. However, this domain adaptation requires a labeled example from the new domain. Moreover, such strategies result in different versions of the method after each adaptation, leading to discrepancies in the segmentation. \\ \cite{hashemi2018asymmetric} addressed the problem of data imbalance (\textit{i.e.}, the under-sampling of the lesion class) by employing an asymmetric similarity loss function based on Tversky index to train a 3D CNN that performed superior to Dice or cross-entropy measures. This result suggests that additional work should be conducted on selecting appropriate loss functions. Although the proposed loss can be tuned for the optimal trade-off between precision and recall in a particular domain, the generalization to unseen domains must be demonstrated.\\ \cite{zhang2019multiple} employed a fully convolutional densely connected network for MS lesion segmentation. They stacked adjacent 2D slices of different modalities with channel-wise concatenation, before forwarding this stack through a 2D CNN. The final segmentation is based on majority voting along different orientations. While this method demonstrated competitive performance on a well-controlled challenge, the stacking using only the two directly adjacent slices provides limited insight into the 3D nature of the data. Moreover, 2D features may not be regarded as generalizing features when processing 3D volumes and can result in the constrained generalization of the method.\\ \cite{aslani2019multi} proposed an end-to-end encoder-decoder 2D network with multiple downsampling branches, one for each input modality, and a decoder component where features from the different modalities are combined at multiple scales. This separation in encoder branches enables the model to encode information efficiently from each modality, before integrating them in a subsequent stage. However, this 2D approach does not combine features based on axial, coronal, and sagittal orientations that may substantially reduce its generalization on 3D images.\\ \cite{feng2019self} addressed MRI modality unavailability during segmentation by introducing sequence dropout. This represents an important consideration since the availability of all modalities is not always guaranteed between datasets, which can significantly reduce the generalization capacity of a method. This framework randomly drops specific MRI sequences during training, with the intention to learn the intrinsic information of each sequence. This technique demonstrated it can produce acceptable segmentation even in the absence of one or two modalities. Nevertheless, it is less efficient than other state-of-the-art methods when all modalities are available (will be detailed in section \ref{same domain val}).\\ \cite{aslani2020scanner} addressed the problem of generalization to new domains by integrating a regularization network to the traditional encoder-decoder network. The regularizer penalizes the network when it learns features which enable the prediction of MRI scanning sites. However, \cite{li2018domain} have argued that such strategies suffer from overfitting, the obtained representation could generalize well for all the source domains but poorly for the unknown target domains. All the cited MS methods (\cite{brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,feng2019self,hashemi2018asymmetric,zhang2019multiple,aslani2019multi,feng2019self}) focused on achieving accurate segmentation within same-domain evaluation. However, the utilization of out-of-domain datasets is essential to ensure proper evaluation of the generalization capabilities of a method. This question is currently a prominent topic (see \cite{maartensson2020reliability}, and \cite{bron2020cross}) and an important recommendation from the clinical community (see \cite{omoumi2021buy

text: Anomaly Detection (AD) in remote sensing data analysis has been (and will continue to be) one of the principal important research topics for diverse applications~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. Anomaly determination is accomplished by analyzing the difference between the pixel under test (PUT) and the background. Numerous anomaly detectors have been proposed in the literature under several assumptions: 1) the selection of the background region and the distribution, 2) the method of calculating the distance between the PUT and the background statistics, and 3) the definition of the decision threshold or test statistic \cite{Matteoli2010}. Among the extensive variety of AD methods, the Reed-Xiaoli (RX) is widely utilized for its simplicity, favorable practical results and efficiency in operational settings~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. The RX algorithm, which is probably the most recognized AD method for hyperspectral images, is based on assuming a multivariate Gaussian distributed background and to address this, it employs the Mahalanobis distance between the PUT and the background~\cite{Reed90tassp}. Regarding the background region, there are two primary different approaches. In the global approach the entire image is defined as the background while in the local approach pixels surrounding the PUT are defined as the background through a sliding window or a segmentation based approach~\cite{Molero13jstars,Zhao15rs}. Additionally, potential anomalies can be censored to prevent degradation of the background statistics~\cite{Nar17dsp}. Although RX is computationally efficient and performs well for simple backgrounds (mostly linear), it cannot handle more complex, nonlinear and\slash or non-Gaussian backgrounds. To address its limitations, more powerful techniques such as kernel methods can be employed to handle non-Gaussian distributed data~\cite{CampsValls09wiley,Kwon07,Longbotham14}. Nevertheless, kernel RX is a computationally demanding method because it involves matrix inversion in the size of the sample count, e.g. for more than thousand pixels. In contrast, covariance matrix in RX has fixed size which is proportional to spectral dimension of the image, e.g. around ten for multispectral images and around hundred for hyperspectral images. Since AD is typically the first step in subsequent recognition tasks, the execution time is as (or even more) important as the detection accuracy \cite{Chen14taes}. text: We propose a Deep Interaction Prediction Network (\textsc{DIPN}\xspace) for learning object interactions directly from examples and utilizing the trained network for accurately predicting the poses of objects following an arbitrary push action (Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}). To demonstrate its efficacy, we integrate \textsc{DIPN}\xspace with a deep Grasp Network (\textsc{GN}\xspace) for completing challenging clutter removal manipulation tasks. Given grasp and push actions from which to choose, the objective is to remove all objects from the scene/workspace with a minimal number of actions. In an iteration of push/pick selection (Fig.~\ref{fig:system-architecture}), the system examines the scene and samples a large number of candidate grasp and push actions. Grasps are immediately scored by \textsc{GN}\xspace, whereas for each candidate push action, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace generates an image corresponding to the predicted outcome. In essence, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace ``imagines'' what occurs to the current scene if the robot executes a particular push. The predicted future images are also scored by \textsc{GN}\xspace; the action with the highest expected score, either a push or a grasp, is then executed. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace can accurately predict objects' poses following a push action with collisions, resulting in less than $10\%$ average single object pose error in terms of IoU (Intersection-over-Union), a significant improvement over the compared baselines. Push prediction by \textsc{DIPN}\xspace generates clear synthetic images that can be utilized by \textsc{GN}\xspace to evaluate grasp actions in future states. Together with \textsc{GN}\xspace, our entire pipeline achieves $34\%$ higher completion rate, $20.9\%$ higher grasp success rate, and $30.4\%$ higher action efficiency in comparison to~\cite{zeng2018learning} on challenging clutter removal scenarios. Moreover, experiments suggest that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace can learn from randomly generated scenarios with the learned policy maintaining high levels of performance on challenging tasks involving previously unseen objects. Remarkably, \textsc{DIPN+GN}\xspace achieves an even superior performance on real robotic hardware than it does in simulation, within which it was developed.

text: Inertial navigation represents a continuous pursuit to estimate the states ({\it i.e.,} \; position and orientation) of a moving entity ({\it e.g.,}\; pedestrian) by utilizing exclusively IMUs affixed to it. An IMU sensor, typically a combination of accelerometers and gyroscopes, assumes a critical role across diverse applications ranging from mobile devices to autonomous systems due to its exceptional energy efficiency, portability, and adaptability \cite{lymberopoulos2015realistic}. Nevertheless, conventional Newtonian-based inertial navigation methodologies exhibit not only suboptimal performance, but also necessitate impractical constraints that are incompatible with routine usage scenarios. For instance, strap-down inertial navigation systems (SINS) may derive erroneous sensor positions through double integration of IMU measurements, owing to exponential error propagation during integration \cite{titterton2004strapdown}. Step-based pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) methodologies can mitigate this accumulated error by exploiting prior knowledge of human locomotion patterns to predict trajectories \cite{tian2015enhanced}. However, an IMU must be mounted to a foot in the zero-velocity update \cite{foxlin2005pedestrian} or a subject must advance forward such that the motion direction remains constant in the body frame \cite{brajdic2013walk}. Additionally, inertial sensors are frequently integrated with supplementary sensors and models utilizing Extended Kalman Filter \cite{bloesch2015robust} to deliver more precise estimations, where the conventional sensors encompass WiFi \cite{ahmetovic2016navcog}, Bluetooth \cite{li2017indoor}, LiDAR \cite{zhang2014loam}, or camera sensors \cite{leutenegger2015keyframe}. Nevertheless, these combinations with supplementary sensors introduce novel challenges regarding instrument installations, energy efficiency, and data privacy. For example, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) significantly depends on environmental factors such as illumination conditions, signal quality, blurring effects \cite{usenko2016direct}. Recently, an increasing number of data-driven methodologies such as IONet \cite{chen2018ionet}, RoNIN \cite{herath2020ronin}, and IDOL \cite{sun2021idol} have demonstrated their capacity for utilizing well-trained neural networks to obtain precise estimates from IMU measurements with competitive performance relative to the aforementioned methods. However, substantial challenges persist when applying neural network techniques to IMU measurements: 1) most existing data-driven methodologies employ sequence-based models ({\it e.g.,}\; LSTM \cite{LSTM}) to learn temporal correlations but fail to capture spatial relationships between multivariate time-series. 2) There exists limited research work to explore rich {\it contextual} information among IMU measurements across spatial and temporal dimensions for inertial feature representation. 3) Typically, uncertainties of IMU measurements and model output are assumed to constitute a fixed covariance matrix in these pure and black-box neural inertial models, which introduces significant inaccuracy and considerably less robustness because they can fluctuate dramatically and unpredictably in nature. In response to the observations and concerns articulated above, a novel robust contextual Transformer network is proposed to regress velocity and predict trajectory from IMU measurements. Specifically, CTIN extends the concepts of ResNet-18 \cite{he2016deep} and Transformer \cite{vaswani2017attention} to exploit spatial and extended temporal information among IMU observations and subsequently employs the attention technique to fuse this information for inertial navigation. The primary contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Extending ResNet-18 with attention mechanisms serves to explore and encode spatial information of IMU samples. \item A novel self-attention mechanism is proposed to extract contextual features of IMU measurements. \item Multi-Task learning utilizing novel loss functions serves to improve learning efficiency and reduce models' uncertainty. \item Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative comparisons with existing baselines demonstrate that CTIN outperforms state-of-the-art models. \item A new IMU dataset with ground-truth trajectories under natural human motions is provided for future reference. \item To the best of our knowledge, CTIN represents the first Transformer-based model for inertial navigation. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec: background} provides background regarding inertial navigation and attention mechanism. Section \ref{sec: model} reviews architecture and workflow of CTIN. The evaluation and related work are discussed in Section \ref{sec: evaluation} and Section \ref{sec: related_work}. Section \ref{sec: conclusion} presents conclusion and future work.

text: Addressing math word problems (MWPs) presents distinctive challenges for comprehending natural-language problems and conducting arithmetic reasoning over quantities with commonsense knowledge. As demonstrated in \autoref{fig:example}, a typical MWP comprises a brief narrative describing a real-world situation and posing a question about an unknown quantity. To resolve the MWP in \autoref{fig:example}, a machine must extract essential quantities from the text, such as "100 kilometers" and "2 hours", and comprehend the relationships among them. General mathematical knowledge like "distance = velocity $\times$ time" is subsequently employed to compute the solution. Researchers have recently concentrated on addressing MWPs using neural-symbolic models~\cite{Ling2017ProgramIB, wang-etal-2017-deep, Huang2018NeuralMW, Wang2018TranslatingMW, Xie2019AGT}. These models typically comprise a neural perception module (\emph{i.e.}, Seq2Seq or Seq2Tree) that transforms the problem text into a solution expression or tree, and a symbolic module which executes the expression and produces the final answer. Training these models necessitates the complete supervision of the solution expressions. Nevertheless, these fully-supervised approaches possess three limitations. First, current MWP datasets only furnish one solution for each problem, while multiple solutions naturally exist that provide different paths for solving the same problem. For example, the problem in \autoref{fig:example} can be resolved by ``$(100/2) \times (2+3.5)$'' if we initially calculate the speed and subsequently multiply it by the total time; alternatively, we can solve it using ``$100 + 100/2 \times 3.5$'' by summing the distances of the first and second segments of the journey. The models trained with full supervision on current datasets are compelled to fit the given solution and cannot produce diverse solutions. Second, annotating the expressions for MWPs is labor-intensive. Nevertheless, a substantial amount of MWPs with their final answers can be extracted effortlessly from the internet (\emph{e.g.}, online forums). How to effectively utilize these partially-labeled data without the supervision of expressions remains an unresolved problem. Third, current supervised learning approaches suffer from the train-test discrepancy. The fully-supervised learning methods optimize expression accuracy rather than answer accuracy. However, the model is assessed by the answer accuracy on the test set, causing a natural performance gap. To address these challenges, we propose to solve the MWPs with \textit{weak supervision}, where only the problem texts and the final answers are required. By directly optimizing the answer accuracy rather than the expression accuracy, learning with weak supervision naturally resolves the train-test discrepancy. Our model comprises a tree-structured neural model similar to \citet{Xie2019AGT} to generate the solution tree and a symbolic execution module to compute the answer. However, the symbolic execution module for arithmetic expressions is non-differentiable with respect to the answer accuracy, making it impractical to use back-propagation to compute gradients. A straightforward approach is to employ policy gradient methods like REINFORCE~\cite{williams1992simple} to train the neural model. The policy gradient methods explore the solution space and update the policy based on generated solutions that happen to achieve the correct answer. Since the solution space is extensive and incorrect solutions are discarded with zero reward, these methods usually converge slowly or fail to converge. To enhance the efficiency of weakly-supervised learning, we propose a novel \textit{fixing} mechanism to learn from incorrect predictions, which is inspired by the human capacity to learn from failures via abductive reasoning~\cite{magnani2009abductive,Zhou2018AbductiveLT}. The fixing mechanism propagates the error from the root node to the leaf nodes in the solution tree and identifies the most probable \textit{fix} that can generate the desired answer. The fixed solution tree is further utilized as a pseudo label to train the neural model. \autoref{fig:framework} illustrates how the fixing mechanism corrects the erroneous solution tree by tracing the error in a top-down manner. Furthermore, we design two practical techniques to traverse the solution space and discover possible solutions efficiently. First, we observe a positive correlation between the number of quantities in the text and the size of the solution tree (the number of leaf nodes in the tree), and propose a \textit{tree regularization} technique based on this observation to constrain the range of possible tree sizes and reduce the solution space. Second, we adopt a \textit{memory buffer} to track and preserve the discovered fixes for each problem with the fixing mechanism. All memory buffer solutions are employed as pseudo labels to train the model, encouraging the model to generate more diverse solutions for a single problem. In summary, by combining the fixing mechanism and the above two techniques, the proposed \textbf{learning-by-fixing} (LBF) method contains an exploring stage and a learning stage in each iteration, as illustrated in \autoref{fig:framework}. We utilize the fixing mechanism and tree regularization to correct erroneous answers in the exploring stage and generate fixed expressions as pseudo labels. In the learning stage, we train the neural model using these pseudo labels. We conduct comprehensive experiments on the Math23K dataset~\cite{wang-etal-2017-deep}. The proposed LBF method significantly outperforms the reinforcement learning baselines in weakly-supervised learning and achieves comparable performance with several fully-supervised methods. Furthermore, our proposed method achieves significantly superior answer accuracies of all the top-3/5 answers than fully-supervised methods, illustrating its advantage in generating diverse solutions. The ablative experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of the designed algorithms, including the fixing mechanism, tree regularization, and memory buffer.

Second, they require a supervisory function of the entire solution expression. First, the current data only contains one solution to a given problem, whereas in reality there are many solutions to the same problem. The model trained with full supervision on the current data can only produce this solution and can’t produce different solutions. For example, the problem in the “Financial Times” section of the previous paragraph can be solved by “(100/2)*(2+3.25),” if you calculate the speed first and then multiply by the total time, or solved by “100+100/2*(3+2.25”), if you first calculate the distance of the first and second leg of the journey and then sum them up. Third, the current supervised learning methods are vulnerable to the training-test problem. It is difficult to collect a significant number of mWPs with their responses from the Internet (for example, from the Internet forums) in the form of answers. The implication of these difficulties is that the method for solving the Multi-Word Problem (MeWoP) should be a weakly supervised one, where only the questions and the final answers are needed. The fully supervised method optimizes for the precision of the evaluation rather than for the accuracy of the answers. How to effectively use the partial annotations without evaluations is still an unsolved problem. Most direct method is to use policy gradients like Xie et al. [Xie et al., 2019]. Compared with strong supervision learning, weak supervision learning directly optimizes the answer accuracy, which naturally solves the gap between training and test. However, the test accuracy of the model is evaluated by the model. In order to improve the efficiency of weakly supervised learning, we propose a novel learning mechanism based on repair. This mechanism is inspired by human heuristic learning and 'learning by doing,' and our method is as follows. Our model consists of a tree-like neural network similar to Xie et al.1 to generate the solution tree and a symbolic execution layer to calculate the solution. Since the symbolic execution of the arithmetic expression is not differentiable with respect to the accuracy of the solution, it is not possible to use back-propagation to estimate the gradient. Figure 3 shows how the repair mechanism corrects an error in the solution tree by tracing it from the top down. To facilitate the search, two practical techniques were devised. The repair mechanism propagates the error from the root node to the leaf nodes of the solution tree and identifies the most likely "textitfix" which will generate the desired solution. The repaired solution tree is used as a pseudo-label in training the neural network. In sum, our learning-by-fixing (LbF) method combines the fixing mechanism with these two methods, and each iteration comprises an exploration phase and a learning phase, as shown in Fig. 5. First, we observe that the number of words in a text and the size of a solution tree (number of leaves in the tree) are inversely related. Based on this observation, we introduce the regularization method for the solution tree, which limits the range of possible tree sizes and reduces the solution space. Second, we use a memory buffer for the solutions discovered by the textit-searching mechanism. The experiments were performed on the Math23k dataset. The correction mechanism and tree regularization are used to correct the incorrect responses during the exploration stage, and the correct responses are used as pseudo-labels. The entire solution memory is used as a pseudo-label for training, thereby enabling the model to learn more diverse solutions for the same problem. The experiments show that the proposed method is effective in its own way, including the mechanism of fixing the trees, the regularization of trees and the buffer memory. It also shows that the proposed method has a significantly higher accuracy of the top three answers than the full-supervised methods, which is an advantage in the diversity of solutions.

text: The goal of pattern mining is to identify a compact set of compelling patterns that collectively characterize a substantial portion of a dataset and can be readily interpreted and applied. Indeed, pattern mining encompasses a broad spectrum of algorithms in knowledge discovery and data mining designed to analyze datasets \citep{aggarwal2014frequent5interesting}. Current approaches in pattern mining focus on discovering an interesting \textit{pattern set} rather than a collection of individually interesting patterns, where pattern quality is assessed with respect to both the dataset and other patterns. One prevalent theoretical foundation for pattern set mining relies on the Minimum Description Length principle (MDL)~\citep{grunwald2007minimum}, which is applied to various types of patterns, e.g. itemsets~\citep{vreeken2011krimp}, patterns of arbitrary shapes in 2-dimensional data~\citep{faas2020vouw}, sequences~\citep{hinrichs2017characterising}, graphs~\citep{bariatti2020graphmdl}, etc. Despite recent advances in pattern mining, algorithms for mining numerical data appear to be inadequately explored. Currently, one of the most prevalent approaches to mine numerical pattern sets relies on the application of itemset mining to binarized datasets. This is discussed below in greater detail but beforehand we would like to mention an alternative to numeric pattern mining which is ``clustering''. In recent years, clustering algorithms have been extensively developed and numerous different and efficient approaches have been proposed \citep{Jain10,CraenendonckDB17,Jeantet0G20}. Nevertheless, there exists an important conceptual distinction between pattern mining and clustering. In pattern mining the \textit{description} takes precedence, while in clustering the primacy is accorded to the \textit{object similarity}. In other words, numerical pattern mining is more concerned with the characterization of a group of objects in terms of a set of attributes associated with these objects, while clustering emphasizes more the identification of these groups of objects based on their commonalities as measured by a similarity or a distance. The former entails certain requirements for the ease of interpretation, i.e., the resulting patterns should characterize a region in the ``attribute space'' that is readily interpretable. In contrast, in clustering, the emphasis is placed on groups of objects or instances. The clusters can be constrained to have specific shapes, e.g., spheres in \textsc{K-means} or \textsc{DBSCAN}, but still the similarity of objects remains the most crucial characteristic of clusters. For instance, clustering techniques such as agglomerative single-linkage clustering in a multidimensional space may yield clusters of very complex shapes. Typically no attention is devoted to these shapes while this is one of the most important concerns in numerical pattern mining. Consequently, in this paper, we propose an MDL-based approach to numerical pattern set mining called \textsc{Mint} for ``Mining INTeresting Numerical Pattern Sets''. \textsc{Mint} computes numerical patterns as $m$-dimensional hyper-rectangles which are products of $m$ intervals, where the intervals are associated with the attributes and their values. The primary benefits of the \textsc{Mint} approach are that (i) \textsc{Mint} does not need to explore the pattern space in advance as candidates to become optimal patterns are computed on the fly, (ii) the total number of explored patterns is at most cubic (and it is at most quadratic at each iteration) in the number of objects with distinct descriptions considered as vectors of attribute values, (iii) \textsc{Mint} is based on MDL and outputs a compact set of non-redundant informative patterns. Furthermore, a series of experiments demonstrates that \textsc{Mint} is efficient and outputs sets of patterns of high quality: the patterns characterize meaningful groups of objects with quite precise boundaries. Indeed, the \textsc{Mint} algorithm is capable of mining numerical patterns both on small and on large datasets, and it is most of the time more efficient and reliable than its competitors \textsc{Slim} and \textsc{RealKrimp}. The proposed encoding scheme is based on prequential plug-in codes, which have superior theoretical properties than the codes used in \textsc{Slim}, \textsc{RealKrimp} and an MDL-based method for discretization called \textsc{IPD}. The paper has the following structure. In Section~\ref{sec:related_work} we discuss the state-of-the art algorithms in itemset pattern mining for numerical data. Section~\ref{sec:basics} introduces the main concepts used in the paper while in Section~\ref{sec:method} we describe the foundations of proposed method. Next Section~\ref{sec:experiments} relates the experiments conducted for illustrating the favorable behavior and the strengths of \textsc{Mint}. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper with a discussion about the potential of \textsc{Mint} and some directions for future work.

text: \noindent In recent years, extensive research has been conducted on the application of deep learning models in computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) systems. These models have demonstrated promising diagnostic performance across numerous clinical domains, including fundoscopy \cite{asiri2019deep}, dermatology \cite{liu2020deep,esteva2017dermatologist}, and pulmonary disease diagnosis \cite{shoeibi2020automated,rajpurkar2017chexnet,gabruseva2020deep}. Given the global shortage of radiologists and increasing burnout rates \cite{wuni2020opportunities,ali2015diagnostic, kumamaru2018global,zha2018prevalence,rimmer2017radiologist}, the development of deep learning systems for chest radiography addresses a pressing clinical need. The task of chest radiography is particularly well-suited for supervised learning, as abundant chest radiographs with corresponding diagnostic labels are becoming available as training data for deep learning models. Chest radiograph data has been compiled into benchmark datasets for various diseases \cite{wang2017chestx,johnson2019mimic}, including COVID-19 most recently \cite{wang2020covid}. Deep learning models have demonstrated expert-level performance on these benchmark datasets \cite{rajpurkar2018deep,seyyed2020chexclusion}. Nevertheless, recent studies have revealed that even the highest-performing deep learning models may be vulnerable to adversarial attacks \cite{finlayson2019adversarial,han2020deep}. \citet{finlayson2018adversarial} argue that the substantial costs in the medical industry, combined with the foundation of pharmaceutical device and drug approvals on disease prevalence, may incentivize manipulation of disease detection systems. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item We explore backdoor attacks in-depth for medical imaging by focusing on chest radiography in the context of multi-label classification. Given that multiple diseases may be detected in a chest radiograph simultaneously, we propose an evaluation framework for multi-label classification tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time attention has been paid to backdoor attacks in the context of multi-label classification. \item We show how the trigger manifests in both low-level and high-level features learned by the model through Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), a weakly-supervised explainability technique \cite{selvaraju2017grad}. By showing how explainability can be used to identify the presence of a backdoor, we emphasize the role of explainability in investigating model robustness. \end{enumerate}

text: The PlatON network offers a platform for distributed transactions and computations~\cite{PlatON}. The network depends on the Giskard consensus protocol~\cite{Giskard} to achieve agreement among participating nodes concerning which transaction blocks to append to a distributed ledger (blockchain). The protocol accommodates up to one third of all participating nodes being Byzantine, meaning they may exhibit adversarial behavior~\cite{Byzantine}. In this paper, we present a rigorous specification of Giskard. In contrast to the protocol documentation~\cite{Giskard}, which provides an overview of the protocol and describes its general behavior, our objective is to specify the protocol with sufficient detail to serve as a guide for implementation and formal verification. To this end, we supply definitions of both protocol execution semantics and important protocol properties, and present proofs of its three key safety properties based on these definitions. Since our focus concerns protocol safety, we omit discussion of higher-level features of Giskard and only provide brief background; additional context and motivation can be found in the official documentation~\cite{Giskard}.

text: \xdef\@thefnmark{}\@footnotetext{$^*$Equal contribution. Correspondence to \email{alex@openai.com}, \email{prafulla@openai.com}, \email{aramesh@openai.com}} Visual content such as illustrations, paintings, and photographs can frequently be described with ease using textual descriptions, yet their creation often demands specialized expertise and substantial time investment. Consequently, a system capable of producing realistic imagery from natural language descriptions could enable individuals to generate rich and varied visual content with remarkable simplicity. The capability to modify images through natural language commands additionally enables iterative enhancement and precise control, both essential for practical applications. Contemporary text-conditional image generation models demonstrate the ability to synthesize images from open-ended textual prompts and can combine disparate objects in semantically coherent arrangements \citep{attngan,dmgan,dfgan,dalle,xmcgan}. Nevertheless, these models have not yet achieved the generation of photorealistic images that fully capture all elements specified in their corresponding textual descriptions. Conversely, unconditional image generation models can produce photorealistic imagery \cite{biggan,stylegan,stylegan2,vqvae2}, occasionally achieving sufficient quality that human observers cannot differentiate them from authentic photographs \cite{zhou2019hype}. Within this research domain, diffusion models \cite{dickstein,scorematching} have emerged as a compelling class of generative architectures, attaining state-of-the-art sample quality across multiple image generation benchmarks \citep{ddpm,sotapaper,cascaded}. To attain photorealism in class-conditional scenarios, \citet{sotapaper} enhanced diffusion models with \textit{classifier guidance}, a methodology that enables diffusion models to condition on classifier predictions. The classifier undergoes initial training on noise-corrupted images, and throughout the diffusion sampling procedure, classifier gradients direct the sample toward the target label. \citet{uncond} obtained comparable outcomes without requiring a separately trained classifier by employing \textit{classifier-free guidance}, a guidance approach that interpolates between predictions from diffusion models with and without conditioning labels. Inspired by the capacity of guided diffusion models to produce photorealistic samples and the ability of text-to-image models to process free-form prompts, we apply guided diffusion to text-conditional image synthesis. Initially, we train a 3.5~billion parameter diffusion model that employs a text encoder for conditioning on natural language descriptions. Subsequently, we evaluate two techniques for guiding diffusion models toward textual prompts: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. Through human and automated assessments, we determine that classifier-free guidance produces superior image quality. We observe that samples from our model generated using classifier-free guidance exhibit both photorealistic quality and demonstrate extensive world knowledge. When assessed by human evaluators, our samples receive preference over those from DALL-E \citep{dalle} in 87\% of cases for photorealism evaluation, and in 69\% of cases for caption similarity assessment. Although our model can render diverse textual prompts in a zero-shot manner, it may encounter difficulties generating realistic images for complex descriptions. Consequently, we equip our model with editing functionality alongside zero-shot generation, enabling users to iteratively refine model outputs until they align with more intricate prompts. Specifically, we fine-tune our model for image inpainting, discovering that it can perform realistic modifications to existing images using natural language instructions. Model-generated edits harmonize with the style and illumination of the surrounding context, including plausible shadows and reflections. Future implementations of these models could potentially assist individuals in creating compelling custom imagery with unprecedented efficiency and simplicity. We note that our resulting model could substantially reduce the effort necessary to generate convincing disinformation or deepfakes. To mitigate these potential applications while supporting future research endeavors, we release a smaller diffusion model and a noise-augmented CLIP model trained on filtered datasets. We designate our system as GLIDE{}, representing \textbf{G}uided \textbf{L}anguage to \textbf{I}mage \textbf{D}iffusion for Generation and \textbf{E}diting. We refer to our smaller filtered model as GLIDE{} (filtered).
