Our samples were preferred by human evaluators in 87.6% of the cases for photorealism and 69.3% of the cases for caption similarity. We rearranged our model in such a way that it was not only possible to make realistic changes to images by natural language instructions, but also that we could provide an editing function, which would allow the users to iteratively refine the resulting outputs to match the inputs. This was because we realized that our model could be used for image inpainting, and we found that it could also be used to make realistic changes to existing images using natural language commands. The model-generated changes were coherent with the surrounding context, style, illumination, and also had plausible shadows and reflections. The result of our study is that our model might significantly reduce the effort required to produce convincing fakes or disinformation. Future implementations of these models may help individuals to create compelling, bespoke images with unprecedented speed and simplicity. In order to mitigate the potential applications of our model, while facilitating further research, we release two smaller models, a noise-augmented clip model and a noise-augmented clip model trained on filtered data. We call our system GLIDE, for Guided Language Image Diffusion for Editing. We call our filtered model GLIDE-filtered.

text: \noindent Recent years have witnessed the rapid advancement of online recruitment platforms. With the increasing volume of online recruitment data, an expanding number of interview-related studies have emerged, including person-job (or talent-job) fit~\cite{shen2018joint, qin2018enhancing,luo2019resumegan, bian2019domain} and automatic analysis of asynchronous video interviews (AVIs)~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, hemamou2019slices,suen2019tensorflow}, which seek to enable automated job recommendation and candidate assessment. Among these investigations, person-job fit involves casting the task as a supervised text matching problem. Given a collection of labeled data (i.e., person-job match records), it seeks to predict the matching label between candidate resumes and job descriptions. More recently, deep learning has enhanced person-job fit methodologies by training more effective text matching or text representation models~\cite{xu2017measuring, jiang2019semantic}. AVI seeks to determine whether the candidate is hirable by evaluating responses to interview questions. In AVIs, an interview is typically considered as a sequence of questions and answers containing salient social signals. To evaluate candidates more comprehensively, AVI models extract features from video (or image), text, and voice modalities during the question-answering process. In this work, we focus on the scoring of multiple QA pairs, extracting only textual features and defining this task as scoring candidate competency rather than determining employment suitability. Based on the anatomy of human interviewers' evaluation processes, the solutions comprise two stages: (1) analyzing and evaluating individual QA pairs sequentially, then acquiring evaluation status, and (2) grading candidate competency based on the evaluation status of multiple QA pairs. \begin{comment} \end{comment} For the first stage, existing methodologies tend to employ text matching or attentional text matching algorithms to evaluate QA pairs~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, suen2019tensorflow}, which feed the concatenated representation of questions and answers to subsequent classifiers. As is well known, questions in asynchronous video interviews are not confined to specific domains. That is, candidates may answer questions according to their professional or academic experience. In this manner, candidates' responses will vary considerably, and it becomes challenging to evaluate answers accurately using text matching alone. Intuitively, it appears more reasonable to evaluate QA pairs through semantic interaction between questions and answers. A critical challenge along this direction is how to reveal latent relationships between each question and answer. Graph neural networks (GNNs, ~\cite{dai2016discriminative, yao2019graph, ghosal2019dialoguegcn}) can learn effective node representations by encoding local graph structures and node attributes. Due to model compactness and inductive learning capability, GNNs are widely utilized in modeling relational data~\cite{battaglia2018relational, schlichtkrull2018modeling, pan2020semantic} and logical reasoning~\cite{luo2019improving, jiang2020reasoning}. Recently, ~\citet{zhang2020efficient} proposed a GNN variant, named ExpressGNN, to achieve an optimal balance between representational power and model simplicity in probabilistic logic reasoning.~\citet{ghosal2019dialoguegcn} constructed DialogueGCN to address context propagation issues present in RNN-based methods. Specifically, they leverage self and inter-speaker dependencies of interlocutors to model conversational context for emotion recognition. Inspired by~\cite{ghosal2019dialoguegcn}, we present a sentence-level relational GCN to represent internal temporal and QA interaction dependencies during the question-answering process. For the second stage of candidate grading, based on QA pair representations, existing methods~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet,hemamou2019slices} prefer to encode question-answer pairs as sequences directly. However, such approaches result in insufficient interaction between semantic information of question and answer pairs. Therefore, it becomes difficult to ensure evaluation rationality and explainability. To mitigate this issue, in the first stage, we present a semantic-level graph attention network (GAT) to model interaction states of each QA session. To this end, we propose a Hierarchical Reasoning Graph Neural Network (HRGNN) for automatic scoring of answer transcriptions (ASAT) in job interviews. Specifically, the proposed sentence-level relational graph convolutional neural network (RGCN) is employed to capture contextual dependencies, and the semantic-level Reasoning graph attention network (RGAT) is applied to acquire latent interaction states. The contribution of our work can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a relational graph neural network to remedy the lack of QA interaction in previous assessment methodologies. Specifically, the relation of internal temporal dependency within each question/answer is beneficial for contextual understanding. The relation of QA interaction dependency can establish latent semantic interaction from question-to-answer and answer-to-question. \item To our knowledge, we are the first to construct a hierarchical graph neural network for ASAT to model relationships between sentences in questions and their corresponding answers, and interact and infer at the semantic level. Although we evaluate candidate competence solely on textual features, this greatly improves evaluation rationality and accuracy. \item Our model can outperform all existing benchmark approaches on a Chinese real-world dataset. Ablation studies and experimental results with 10 random seeds demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our models. \end{itemize}

text: With the advancement of intelligent technologies, individual robots have become increasingly powerful. Consequently, an expanding number of autonomous robots are being deployed to substitute human personnel in providing diverse services, including floor cleaning, surveillance through \emph{unmanned aerial vehicles} (UAVs), surgical procedures via surgical robots, and manufacturing operations using mechanical arms \cite{2020-liu}. Simultaneously, the volume of latency-sensitive and computation-intensive tasks executed by robots has substantially expanded. For example, in efforts to mitigate COVID-19 transmission, UAVs are tasked with monitoring social distancing among individuals \cite{20-chamola}, and search-and-rescue operations must be executed immediately following natural disasters. To tackle these challenges, \emph{multi-robot cooperation} (MRC) systems have garnered significant attention in recent years \cite{18-ismail}. Nevertheless, the battery constraints, limited sensing capabilities, and computational capacity of individual robots present obstacles to task completion \cite{18-bedi}. \emph{Mobile edge computing} (MEC) technology has emerged as a promising approach to facilitate task offloading through wireless communication, which aligns perfectly with MRC architectures. On one side, multiple robots must collaborate cooperatively to complete assignments under stringent time constraints. On the other side, efficient communication and task allocation are crucial for ensuring effective collaboration among robots. Therefore, in this work, we examine a MEC-based MRC system wherein an intelligent \emph{master robot} (MR) functioning as an edge server coordinates multiple \emph{slave robots} (SRs) to complete time-critical and computation-intensive tasks while minimizing and balancing the energy consumption of the robots. \subsection{Related Works} \subsubsection{Robot Cooperation Networks} In recent years, \emph{Artificial intelligence} (AI) applications have been extensively and effectively utilized to enhance robot capabilities in information processing due to their capacity to handle big data with high precision \cite{20-khan}. However, the implementation of AI technology generates enormous computational workloads \cite{17-kim}. In \cite{19-Alsamhi}, \emph{Machine learning} (ML) has been employed to enhance connection quality and efficient data collection in robots. Nevertheless, cooperation among robots was not addressed in this research. To accelerate time-critical robotic applications such as AI implementations and robot navigation utilizing \emph{Simultaneous Localization And Mapping} (SLAM) technology, numerous studies have focused on the following three domains \cite{18-ismail}: various robot types, control architectures, and communication technologies. In the robotics domain, Boston Dynamics has transformed people's perception of robotic capabilities \cite{19-guizzo}. However, depending on limited resources, it remains impossible for a single robot to accomplish large-scale, low-latency tasks. For instance, extensive environment sensing and surveillance represents a typical robotic application. To achieve accurate sensing and timely monitoring, robots must collect sufficient data, communicate with one another, and compute collaboratively in an efficient manner. MRC systems leverage cooperation to overcome the resource limitations of individual robots. First, the incorporation of controlled mobility has enabled sparse sensing applications in \cite{13-Mostofi}, which can be utilized for energy-efficient and non-redundant sensing in MRC networks. 	Second, the most significant benefit of such systems lies in robots' ability to share their collected information and resource management strategies with others through advanced wireless communication technologies. Thus, effective wireless communication among robots becomes one of the most critical components for facilitating cooperation among robots in MRC systems. In \cite{19-chen}, to achieve ultra-reliability and ultra-low latency, $p$-persistent real-time ALOHA has been proposed as the multiple access protocol for ad-hoc based MRC systems. With the advancement of wireless communication technologies, cloud robots have received particular attention \cite{15-kehoe}. In \cite{14-roazielo}, to reduce computational workload, a visual SLAM robotic system has been proposed utilizing a distributed framework where the cloud server handles map optimization and information storage. However, the data transmission latency required by cloud computing is unacceptable. Therefore, to reduce latency, the critical problem is to establish a communication paradigm that can facilitate cooperation among robots in the MRC system. MEC emerges as one of the key technologies of 5G and has become a viable solution for edge-enabled applications \cite{19-liu}. In the following subsection, we present the latest developments in MEC technology in detail. \subsubsection{Mobile edge computing} As a promising communication and computation offloading integration technology, MEC extends computation, communication, and storage resources toward the network edge. It possesses an interdisciplinary nature between computation offloading and wireless communication, which plays a crucial role in reducing energy consumption and latency \cite{20-Hai}. Therefore, MEC represents a natural choice for supporting cooperation among robots, as it can provide both efficient communications among robots and effective task assignment among robots. In \cite{15-chen}, to minimize task implementation latency and energy consumption, the authors have investigated a computing resource allocation scheme for mobile users and MEC servers. In \cite{17-wang}, by jointly considering computation offloading, resource allocation, and content caching strategy, an \emph{Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers} (ADMM)-based algorithm has been proposed to maximize the revenue of the \emph{MEC system operator} (MSO). In \cite{17-you}, an energy-efficient task offloading scheme for multiple devices has been proposed. To overcome network congestion and extended latency in cloud computing, a collaborative cloud and edge computing resource management algorithm has been developed in \cite{19-ren}. \subsubsection{MEC based Cooperative Communication} As an important technology for enabling cooperation among robots via mobile edge servers, it has been studied extensively to conserve computational resources of users in conventional wireless communication systems. When multiple edge servers serve multiple users, centralized and distributed methods have been proposed to solve the optimal task offloading problem in \cite{18-you} and \cite{16-chen}, respectively. Furthermore, a joint offloading and trajectory design scheme has been studied to minimize the sum of maximum delay in a MEC-based UAV system \cite{18-hu}. These works have considered cooperative MEC systems, but the users in such systems were not robots, so they did not consider unique characteristics of robotic systems, such as the capability to interact with the environment. \subsection{Our Contributions} This paper presents a MEC-based MRC system to accomplish computation-intensive and time-critical tasks while minimizing the energy consumption of robots to extend their operational time. In the studied scenario, the intelligent MR is modeled as an edge server to make decisions regarding the duration of environment sensing, the amount of data gathered by each SR, and the amount of data offloaded from each SR. The mobile SRs are primarily responsible for environment sensing and data collection. Subsequently, they can offload a certain amount of tasks to the MR to conserve energy consumption during data processing. Two resource management strategies are proposed to minimize and balance energy consumption among SRs while guaranteeing that tasks can be completed on time. The distinction is that the remaining energy at the SRs is considered to ensure that the SRs can process data locally without offloading in the second scheme. Therefore, it is more robust to unreliable wireless communication environments than the first scheme, but may consume more energy. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. \begin{enumerate} 	\item[$\bullet$] An implementation framework for computation-intensive and time-critical tasks in MEC-based MRC systems is proposed. The task implementation process is divided into three stages. In the first stage, the SRs perform environment sensing and data collection. In the second stage, the SRs may offload a certain amount of data to the MR and process the remaining data locally. 	In the third stage, the MR must process the data and may also upload a certain amount of data to the \emph{base station} (BS). 	The MR makes decisions regarding the time spent on sensing, data offloading, and power schemes at the SRs at the beginning of task implementation. 	\item[$\bullet$] Two resource management and offloading strategies are developed to ensure that tasks can be completed on time while minimizing the energy consumption of the robots. In the first scheme, the energy consumption of the SRs is minimized and balanced to enhance the operational time of the MRC systems. In the second scheme, the remaining energy of the SRs is also considered to address the variable wireless communication environment. As a result, each SR may process its entire collected data locally without offloading to the MR. The MEC is one of the pillars of 5G and provides a viable solution for applications at the edge. The latest developments in MEC are described below. The MEC (mobile edge computing) technology is a promising communication and computation offloading integration technology that extends the computation, communication, and storage resources to the network edge. Its interdisciplinary nature of offloading computation and wireless communication can be of great benefit in reducing energy consumption and latency. The critical problem for reducing latency is to ensure effective cooperation between robots in the MRC system. In, the authors proposed an energy-efficient task-offloading scheme for multiple devices. In, the authors investigated the calculation method for mobile terminals and MEC servers to minimize task execution time and energy consumption. It is therefore an ideal tool for supporting the cooperation of robots, because it allows for efficient communication between robots and a better task distribution between them. MEC is a basic technology for establishing cooperative interaction between robots through mobile edge servers. It is also a key technology for conserving the computational resources of mobile terminals in conventional wireless communication systems. By combining the computation off-loading, resource allocation and caching strategy, an ADMM-based heuristic was proposed to optimize the profit of MEC system operators. To overcome network congestion and delay in cloud computing, a unified method of resource allocation has been developed for cloud-edge computing. Then, the joint design of the offloading task and the trajectory has been studied in order to minimize the sum of the maximum delay in a MEC-based UAV system. The main task of the mobile swarm robots is to sense the environment and collect data, then offloading part of the data processing to the intelligent MR in order to save energy. The intelligent MR is modeled as an edge server that decides on the duration of the sensing time, the amount of data collected by each swarm robot, and the amount of data each swarm robot offloads. Finally, a joint offloading and trajectory design scheme is proposed to minimize the sum of the maximum delay of the UAV system. This article makes two main contributions. We propose a framework for the implementation of time-critical and computation-critical tasks in MEC-based MRC systems. In this paper, we propose two resource allocation strategies to minimize and balance the energy consumption of the swarm nodes while guaranteeing timely task completion. The difference between these two strategies is that the second strategy takes the residual energy of the swarm nodes into account, and therefore the second strategy is more robust to the unreliable wireless environment than the first strategy, but may consume more energy. The execution of the task is divided into three phases. First, the sensors must collect and collect data, then the MRs must process the data, and then the MRs can send a portion of the data to the base station. Two offloading and resource management strategies are developed to ensure that the task is completed on time, and at the same time reduce energy consumption. At the start of the task, the MR makes decisions on the duration of sensing, offloading and servo-powering time. In the first strategy, servos are operated with low energy and with balanced energy consumption to increase the operating time of the MR system. In the second scheme, the remaining energy of the sensors is taken into account in order to cope with the changing radio environment. This makes the second scheme more robust than the first, but it may require more energy. Each sensor can thus locally process the data it has gathered without transmitting it to the master. The MRC system is robust, as simulations show.

text: Clustering objects according to their mutual similarity constitutes a fundamental and pervasive task in machine learning. This similarity information among objects can be encoded in various forms, including pairwise distances between objects (where closer objects exhibit greater similarity) or similarity degrees between object pairs (where more similar objects possess higher similarity scores). \citet*{BBC04} introduced the Correlation Clustering problem, a flexible framework that elegantly formalizes this task of clustering objects based on similarity information. Since its inception, the correlation clustering problem has been applied across numerous domains, including co-reference resolution (see e.g., \citet*{Cohen01learningto, Cohen02learningto}), spam detection (see e.g., \citet{Ramachandran07filteringspam}, \citet{BonchiGL14}), image segmentation (see e.g., \citet{Wirth10}) and multi-person tracking (see e.g., \citet{tang2016multi, tang2017multiple}). In the Correlation Clustering problem, we receive a collection of objects accompanied by pairwise similarity information. Our objective is to partition these objects into clusters that conform to this information \textit{as much as possible}. The pairwise similarity information is provided as a weighted graph $G$ with edges classified as either ``positive/similar" or ``negative/dissimilar" by a noisy binary classifier. For a clustering $\mathcal{C}$, a positive edge conflicts with $\mathcal{C}$ if its endpoints reside in different clusters; and a negative edge conflicts with $\mathcal{C}$ if its endpoints reside in the same cluster. To evaluate the quality of the generated clustering, \citet{BBC04} examined the Correlation Clustering problem under two complementary objectives. Throughout the years, the objective that has garnered the most attention is finding a clustering that minimizes the total weight of conflicting edges. For complete unweighted graphs, \citet{BBC04} provided a constant factor approximation algorithm for this objective. \citet*{ACN08} enhanced the approximation ratio to $3$ by presenting a simple-yet-elegant combinatorial algorithm. They also developed a $2.5$-approximation algorithm based on Linear Programming (LP) rounding which was subsequently derandomized without approximation ratio degradation by~\citet*{vZHJW}. Finally, \citet*{CMSY15} provided an LP rounding algorithm which enhanced the approximation ratio to $2.06$. The standard LP was demonstrated to have an integrality gap of $2$ by \citet*{CGW03} for complete unweighted graphs. For general weighted graphs, \citet{CGW03} and \citet*{DEFI06} provided an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm. Define the disagreements vector as a vector indexed by the vertices of $G$. Given a clustering $\mathcal{P}$, $\operatorname{dis}(\mathcal{P}, E^+, E^-) \in \mathbb{R}^V$ is a $|V|$-dimensional vector where the $u$-th coordinate equals the weight of disagreements at $u$ with respect to $\mathcal{P}$. That is, $\operatorname{dis}_u(\mathcal{P}, E^+, E^-)= \sum\limits_{(u,v) \in E}w_{uv}\cdot \mathbf{1}\{(u,v)\text{ is in disagreement with }\mathcal{P}\}.$ Thus, minimizing the total weight of disagreements is equivalent to finding a clustering minimizing the $\ell_1$ norm of the disagreements vector. Another objective for Correlation Clustering that has received recent attention is minimizing the weight of disagreements at the most adversely affected vertex (also known as Min Max Correlation Clustering). This is equivalent to finding a clustering that minimizes the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm of the disagreements vector. Observe that minimizing the $\ell_1$ norm represents a global objective since the emphasis is on minimizing the total weight of disagreements. In contrast, for higher values of $p$ (particularly $p=\infty$), minimizing the $\ell_{p}$ norm becomes a more localized objective since the emphasis shifts toward minimizing the weight of disagreements at a single vertex. Minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of the disagreements vector can thus provide a balance between these global and local perspectives -- it considers the weight of disagreements at all vertices but penalizes vertices that are worse off more severely. The following scenario demonstrates that minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm might be a more appropriate objective than minimizing the $\ell_1$ norm. Consider a recommender system where the input is a bipartite graph with left and right sides representing customers and services, respectively. A positive edge indicates that a customer is satisfied with the service; whereas a negative edge indicates that they are dissatisfied with or have not utilized the service. We may be interested in grouping customers and services such that both the total and individual dissatisfaction of customers are minimized. \begin{definition}\textbf{(Local Correlation Clustering)} Given an instance of Correlation Clustering $G = (V, E = E^+ \cup E^-)$ and $p\geq 1$, the local objective is to find a partitioning $\mathcal{P}$ that minimizes the $\ell_p$ norm. \end{definition} We use the standard definition of the $\ell_p$ norm of a vector $x$: $\|x\|_p = \left(\sum_u |x_u|^p\right)^\frac{1}{p}$. Since its introduction by~\citet*{PueMil18}, local objectives for Correlation Clustering have been primarily studied under two models (see~\citet*{CharikarGS17}, \citet*{AhmadiKS19}, \citet*{KalhanMZ19}). We will refer to these models as (1) Correlation Clustering on Complete Graphs, and (2) Correlation Clustering with Noisy Partial Information. In the first model, the input graph $G$ is complete and unweighted. For this model, the first approximation algorithm was by~\citet{PueMil18} with an approximation factor of $48$ for minimizing the $\ell_p$ norm. This was subsequently improved to $7$ by~\citet{CharikarGS17}. Finally,~\citet{KalhanMZ19} provided a $5$ approximation algorithm. In the second model, $G$ is an arbitrary weighted graph with potentially missing edges. For minimizing the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm of the disagreements vector in this model, \citet{CharikarGS17} provided an $O(\sqrt{n})$ approximation. \citet{KalhanMZ19} gave an $O(n^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2p}}\cdot \log^{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2p}}n)$-approximation algorithm for minimizing the $\ell_p$ norm of the disagreements vector. We study local objectives in a different model -- Correlation Clustering with Asymmetric Classification Errors -- recently introduced by~\citet*{JafarovKMM20}. In this model, the input graph $G$ is complete and weighted. Furthermore, the ratio of the smallest edge weight to the largest positive edge weight is at least $\alpha\leq 1$. Thus, for some $\mathbf{w}>0$, each positive edge weight lies in the interval $[\alpha\mathbf{w},\mathbf{w}]$ and each negative edge weight is at least $\alpha\mathbf{w}$. This model better captures the nuances in real world instances than the standard models. Since real world instances rarely possess equal edge weights, assumptions in the Correlation Clustering on Complete Graphs model are too restrictive. text: Interactive media experiences provide individual audience members with content that is customized to their specific context, knowledge, or requirements. This differs from conventional media - where a single content version seeks to engage all audience members - by modifying either the information delivered or the manner of its delivery. The information utilized to determine the modification can originate from either (1) users interacting with the content during consumption; (2) gathering it from the user at the experience's onset (thus enabling a more `lean-back' consumption mode); (3) an existing `user profile', (4) through a combination. This paper concentrates on the first of these approaches. The interactive characteristics of these experiences render them more complex than conventional media forms. It is consequently essential for production teams to monitor their success or failure, enabling them to identify and address content issues, and learn to enhance user experience for future productions. A crucial metric for success is the degree to which audience members engaged with the experience. Nevertheless, user engagement is a complex, multidimensional phenomenon \cite{attfield2011towards} and since media is typically consumed by a geographically dispersed audience, across different contexts and devices, precise measurement presents both practical and methodological challenges. Interaction data have been employed in certain domains as an unobtrusive and scalable approach for monitoring engagement \cite{attfield2011towards,lehmann2012models,doherty2018engagement}; our research aims to understand whether it can also be applied in this domain. Given that interactive media experiences involve enhanced interactivity with content compared to traditional media, is it feasible to monitor these interactions and utilize them to infer engagement? This study explores and presents novel methods of information collection and analysis techniques that broadcasters could employ to better understand their audiences and their engagement with content; we are not evaluating an experience, we investigate whether interaction data might prove useful when measuring engagement. An additional rationale for measuring engagement through interaction data is that this could enable near real-time engagement monitoring. Consequently, not only would retrospective analysis to improve future work be possible, but it could also allow content to adapt dynamically. For instance, audience members who appear highly engaged might be offered supplementary material, while those who demonstrate low engagement levels might receive a shorter or simpler content conclusion. Designing successful interventions of this nature is clearly challenging, but could substantially enhance user experience and is only truly feasible if engagement can be monitored in real-time. Interaction data have been utilized successfully in other domains, specifically online news \cite{lagun2016understanding,grinberg2018identifying,lu2018between,constantinides2018framework} and search \cite{diriye2012leaving,kim2014modeling,zhuang2017understanding}. It has also been employed to extract user behaviors as proxies for engagement \cite{barbieri2016improving,arapakis2016predicting} and satisfaction \cite{chuklin2016incorporating,mehrotra2017user}. Since techniques and measures for engagement remain untested in this domain, we examine a production-quality and nationally broadcast interactive TV show where the audience receives control over presentation and their narrative path. We collected ground truth engagement metrics and user interactions (code and data are available: \cite{jonathan_carlton_2021_5137806}) from the live and in-the-wild interactive TV show to address the question: \begin{itemize} \item[\textit{(RQ)}] What behaviors can we infer from interaction metrics that assist in understanding how engaged an audience member is with an interactive media experience? \end{itemize} We extracted various metrics and examined how these correlate with engagement levels reported by audience members. To understand the relationships between metrics and engagement levels, we trained an interpretable model to predict engagement and derive feature importance using internal weights and a model-agnostic interpretation technique. We discovered that temporal metrics -- the time between events and the time an audience member requires to complete the story -- effectively distinguish, and are strongly correlated with, engagement levels. Our findings demonstrate the utility of interaction data for providing media creators insights into audience engagement and that it can be directly inferred from the data alone. Overall, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We confirm a connection between user engagement and interaction metrics collected from an interactive media experience; \item We demonstrate the feasibility of predicting engagement levels from user interactions; \item We establish, more broadly, the utility of collecting and analyzing user interactions from interactive media experiences and the potential insights about user engagement that can be obtained to inform the creative process. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:background} discusses related work. Section \ref{sec:methods} describes the study, and Section \ref{sec:results} presents the results. Section \ref{sec:discussion} discusses and contextualizes the findings and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} draws conclusions and considers future work.

The following is an answer to the question: “What metrics inferred from the audience’s interaction help us to understand how engaged they are with an interactive media experience?” We collected the ground truth engagement metrics and the users’ interactions (code and data available here: cite.db.proc.mc-sci.media.ccc.io_dlrc.org:10: jonathan_carlton_2021_5137806_dawn_msvc: ), and found that the time between events and the time an audience member takes to complete the story were effective in distinguishing different levels of engagement and were highly correlated with it. The authors also used interaction data successfully to extract proxies for engagement (e.g., Barbieri, 2016; Arapakis, 2016; et al., 2016; Chuklin, 2016; moreover, Mehta, 2017); and, as a result of the present work, have made a number of measurements of these data. - The paper is divided into the following sections: Section refsecbackground discusses previous research, Section refsecmethods describes the study, Section refsecresults presents the results, Section refsecdiscussion discusses and contextualizes the results, Section refsecconclusion draws conclusions and draws future work. Our results show that interaction data can provide media creators with insights into the audience's engagement and that these insights can be directly derived from the data. The results also show that temporal metrics, such as the time between events and the time an audience member takes to complete the story, can effectively distinguish between different levels of engagement and are strongly correlated with them.

text: \noindent Logo constitutes one of the fundamental elements of brand identity, and logo identification enables statistical analysis of brand exposure and influence across vast collections of images and videos (\citeauthor{gao2014brand} \citeyear{gao2014brand}). Given the design characteristics of logos: preference for concise symbols or textual elements (\citeauthor{ad2012logo}\citeyear{ad2012logo}), logos lack abundant information for representation; moreover, distinct logos may differ only by a single character or stroke, both factors rendering the learning of discriminative deep features extremely challenging. Logo recognition typically comprises two phases: localizing the bounding box and classifying the logo. Conventional logo recognition employs a closed-set methodology, with prevalent frameworks including Faster R-CNN (\citeauthor{ren2015faster} \citeyear{ren2015faster}), SSD (\citeauthor{liu2016ssd} \citeyear{liu2016ssd}), and YOLOv3 (\citeauthor{redmon2018yolov3} \citeyear{redmon2018yolov3}) among others. Nevertheless, closed-set approaches impose greater data requirements and cannot recognize logos absent from the training dataset. To address this limitation, open-set methodologies were introduced (\citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}; \citeauthor{bastan2019large} \citeyear{bastan2019large}; \citeauthor{fehervari2019scalable} \citeyear{fehervari2019scalable}), comprising two phases: detecting logo regions using class-agnostic binary detectors and identifying detected regions through classification or retrieval. The binary detection phase can directly utilize outputs from detection frameworks such as Faster R-CNN and YOLOv3. The identification phase can employ metric learning to measure distances in nonlinear data, thereby enabling straightforward comparison of complex data within the embedding space. In practical applications, we observed that when a low threshold is established, logo-like regions can be readily detected by class-agnostic binary detectors, yet determining whether a region constitutes a logo and its corresponding class remains extremely challenging, i.e., effectively mapping logos in the embedding space with similar classes clustered and dissimilar classes separated. Consequently, we contend that the primary challenge resides in the second phase of logo recognition, which constitutes our main focus in this investigation. The limitations of existing public logo datasets (Tab. \ref{table:1}) include: 1) insufficient logo classes, inadequately representing practical logo recognition challenges (\citeauthor{romberg2011scalable} \citeyear{romberg2011scalable}; \citeauthor{neumann2002integration} \citeyear{neumann2002integration}); 2) web-crawled origins where logos dominate images and scene complexity is diminished (\citeauthor{wang2020logodet} \citeyear{wang2020logodet}; \citeauthor{su2018open} \citeyear{su2018open}; \citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}); 3) image-level annotations (\citeauthor{su2018scalable} \citeyear{su2018scalable}), which cannot support logo recognition tasks. Therefore, we introduce Makeup216, whose advantages include: 1) specialization in the makeup domain, necessitating more robust recognition algorithms to distinguish logos due to minimal inter-class differences; 2) real-world capture where logos appear on actual products rather than advertisements, introducing various complex challenges including blur, occlusion, mirror reflection, and non-rigid deformation; 3) the highest object count per image among all datasets. These advantages of Makeup216 can substantially enhance the applicability of logo recognition models. We discovered that isolated logos possess limited visual fields and insufficient information for recognition, potentially leading to erroneous retrieval, as demonstrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a), where top-1 recalled logos are incorrect despite high similarity. However, incorporating broader external regions provides expanded visual context and contextual information. The products underlying logos and adjacent text or symbols can facilitate identification verification and prevent false recalls, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(b). Based on this observation, we propose a novel logo recognition framework incorporating an adversarial attention representation (AAR) module to leverage marginal background information. The framework can clarify its primary subject while maintaining auxiliary information for enhanced accuracy. We demonstrate that the issues presented in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a) can be resolved using our proposed framework, as detailed in the experimental section. To evaluate the noise robustness of logo recognition models, we constructed a distractor set for Makeup216 inspired by image retrieval datasets (\citeauthor{radenovic2018revisiting}\citeyear{radenovic2018revisiting}); consequently establishing two evaluation protocols, one excluding distractor samples and another including distractor samples. The proposed framework demonstrated superior performance when confronted with distractor samples. The primary contributions of this work are as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item A dataset specializing in the makeup domain is introduced. The logo diversity and scene complexity establish it as a challenging dataset for logo recognition; novel evaluation protocols are also constructed to assess logo recognition model robustness. Both the Makeup216 dataset and protocols will be publicly available. \item An adversarial attention representation (AAR) framework for logo recognition is proposed. The framework fully exploits marginal auxiliary information to enhance pure logo representation. The AAR can determine focal points and supplementary elements for improved accuracy. \item Our framework establishes a baseline for logo recognition, and comprehensive experiments on Makeup216 and LogoDet-3k demonstrate state-of-the-art performance achievement. \end{enumerate}

text: Lexical semantic change has recently attracted attention at the intersection of natural language processing and historical linguistics\footnote{see \url{https://languagechange.org/}}, consequently several datasets have been proposed for different languages \cite{schlechtweg2020semeval2020}. This work occurs within the context of DIACR-Ita \cite{diacrita_evalita2020} at EVALITA 2020 \cite{Evalita2020}, which establishes the task for the Italian language in a completely unsupervised manner. From DIACR-Ita we obtained 18 target words\footnote{'egemonizzare', 'lucciola', 'campanello', 'trasferibile', 'brama', 'polisportiva', 'palmare', 'processare', 'pilotato', 'cappuccio', 'pacchetto', 'ape', 'unico', 'discriminatorio', 'rampante', 'campionato', 'tac', 'piovra'}, and two time-specific and preprocessed Italian corpora, namely \textit{T0} and \textit{T1}, which contain part-of-speech tagging and lemmatization information. We present two perspectives for approaching the problem, concerning how we represent target words and estimate the lexical-semantic change across datasets. (1) utilizes the POS distribution of target words as representation, and employs an ensemble of distance measures for the estimation. (2) utilizes the target words neighbor similarities as representation and one (of two proposed) similarity measures for estimation. The following three sections describe the previous works, modeling, and results we obtained using these approaches. Subsequently, section \ref{discussion_section} (Discussion) focuses on examining the second approach to illustrate the impact of the $k$ parameter in similarity measures and the discriminatory performance of our embedding-based model.

text: \IEEEPARstart{A}{irborne} optical sectioning (AOS) \cite{Kurmi2018,Kurmi2019TAOS,Kurmi2019Sensor,Bimber2019IEEECGA,Kurmi2020GeoScience, David2020} constitutes an efficient aerial synthetic aperture imaging methodology for exposing artifacts that are otherwise concealed beneath dense forest canopy and remain imperceptible in individual images. For applications including search and rescue (SAR) \cite{Kurmi2019TAOS} and wildlife observation \cite{David2020}, % AOS captures the fractional thermal signal emitted from occluded targets as an unstructured thermal light-field recorded using a camera drone (Fig.~\ref{fig:Fig0CameraPose}). Recording across an extensive synthetic aperture area (30–100 m diameter) enables optical sectioning through image integration \cite{Kurmi2018}. \vspace{-1.5em} The integral images (representing the signal from a wide-aperture sensor measurement) are computed through registration and averaging of all individual image recordings with respect to the drone's three-dimensional poses and a specified synthetic focal plane. % RGB images in the visible waveband (Sony Alpha 6000 RGB camera) are acquired for drone pose estimation and thermal images (Flir Vue Pro; 7.5-13.5 $\mu m$ spectral band) for integration. Individual image recordings (both thermal and RGB) are stored on the camera's internal memory cards and are retrieved for subsequent processing following flights. Following integration, targets at the focal plane will appear crisp and sharp while occluders at greater distances will be severely blurred and disappear. Consequently, shifting focus by adjusting the focal plane interactively or automatically \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} toward its optimal position and orientation near the ground enables optical slicing through forest and the discovery and inspection of concealed targets, such as human bodies or animals. AOS necessitates precise measurements of the drone's pose for each captured thermal image. Currently it is implemented through applying state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms using general-purpose structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo pipeline \cite{schonberger2016sfm,schoenberger2016mvs} to the high resolution RGB images. However, a recent investigation \cite{Chin2018} has demonstrated that primarily estimating or fitting a model to data with outliers constitutes an NP-hard problem. Therefore, pose estimation remains error prone and resulting mis-registrations of individual recordings leads to defocus in AOS integral images. Note that, owing to their low resolution, high noise level, low contrast, and poor texture of natural scenes, thermal images do not provide usable image features for reliable pose estimation. Various approaches for correcting the remaining pose-errors have been proposed, such as optimizations with either imposing structural constraints \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018}, by utilizing localized depth maps \cite{Shin2018,Shamwell2019}, or by fusing different sensors \cite{Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018}. In this article, we present a different approach for reducing remaining pose errors by considering the underlying optimization as a focusing problem instead of solving the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem \cite{Chin2018}. PnP solutions \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018,Shin2018,Shamwell2019,Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018} require robust feature detection which is challenging in low-resolution thermal images and infeasible in the presence of strong occlusions. % Therefore, we solve the focusing problem by optimizing 3 or 6 pose parameters per image using simple gray level variance (GLV)\cite{Firestone1991} (which does not rely on any image features) as an error metric. % We have already demonstrated in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience}, that GLV is invariant to occlusion and is therefore (in contrast to traditional \mbox{gradient-,} Laplacian-, and wavelet-based metrics reviewed in \cite{Pertuz2013}) an ideal visibility metric for AOS thermal integral images. Figure \ref{fig:Fig1Completeresult} illustrates AOS results when the synthetic focal plane is globally optimized as presented in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} (focal plane), and the improved results when our new pose error reduction approach is applied to either 6D (brute force) or 3D (ours) pose parameters. For the latter, resulting integral images reveal more details as they are better focused and have a higher contrast. In the following sections, we will discuss effects of errors in different pose parameters and various integration strategies leading to our final optimization approach with reduced parameter search space and early stopping. We will demonstrate that our approach improves the quality of integral images (compared to state-of-the-art pose estimation methods) while also being significantly faster and more efficient than the brute force optimization of all pose parameters. \vspace{-0.8em}

text: Traditionally, recommendation algorithms were designed to maximize the accuracy of recommendations delivered to users. Nevertheless, as other scholars have observed, there exist additional important characteristics of recommendations that warrant consideration, including diversity, serendipity, novelty~\cite{Vargas:2011:RRN:2043932.2043955,ge2010beyond,castells2011novelty}, and fairness \cite{yao2017beyond}. These characteristics can exert substantial impacts on the utility of recommendations across all system stakeholders \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. In this paper, we concentrate on the problem of \textit{popularity bias}, the tendency of recommender systems to favor a small set of popular items in their recommendations, even beyond what their popularity would justify, and to disadvantage items that fall outside of this set, even when these items are preferred by a substantial number of interested users~\cite{park2008long,steck2011item,jannach2015recommenders}. Consider the distributions presented in Figure \ref{amplify_item_groups}. These four plots compare item popularity and recommendation popularity for four well-established recommendation algorithms (\textit{RankALS} \cite{takacs2012alternating}, \textit{Biased Matrix Factorization (Biased-MF)} \cite{koren2009matrix}, \textit{User-based Collaborative Filtering (User-CF)} \cite{aggarwal2016neighborhood}, and \textit{Item-based Collaborative Filtering (Item-CF)} \cite{sarwar2001item}) utilizing the MovieLens 1M \cite{movielens} data set (See section \ref{data_section} for additional details on this dataset). The x-axis represents the rank of each item when ordered from most popular to least popular. The black curve displays the cumulative frequency of the ratings for different items at a given rank. As we can observe, a few highly ranked items dominate the entire rating history. For example, only 111 items (less than 3\%) account for more than 20\% of the ratings. In many consumer preference domains, where recommender systems are commonly deployed, the same highly-skewed distribution of user interest is observed. A music catalog might contain artists whose songs have been played millions of times (Beyonc\'{e}, Ed Sheeran) and others whose songs have a much smaller audience (Iranian musician Kayhan Kalhor, for instance). These few popular items are referred to as the \textit{short-head} (shown by $H$ in the plots) in the literature which account for roughly 20\% of the ratings according to the Pareto Principle \cite{sanders1987pareto}. The remaining items in a long-tail distribution are typically divided into two other parts \cite{celma2008hits}: Tail items ($T$) are the larger number of less popular items which collectively account for roughly 20\% of the ratings\footnote{Tail items may also be new items that have yet to find their audience and will eventually become popular. In this way, popularity bias is related to the well-known item cold-start problem in recommendation.}, and \textit{Mid} items ($M$) include a larger number of items in between that receive around 60\% of the ratings, collectively. These three item groups are displayed on the top of each plot partitioning the items based on their popularity into the most popular items ($H$), items with medium popularity ($M$), and less popular items ($T$). The blue curves in each plot demonstrate popularity bias at work across the four algorithms. In the most extreme case (\textit{Item-CF}), almost no item beyond rank 111 is recommended. The head of the distribution constituting less than 3\% of the total items accounts for almost 100\% of the recommendations provided to the users. In \textit{User-CF} this number is 99\%. The other algorithms are only marginally better in this regard, with the \textit{H} items accounting for more than 64\% and 74\% of the recommendations in \textit{RankALS} and \textit{Biased-MF}, respectively. These plots provide an illustration of popularity bias in recommendation. Users' rating profiles exhibit skewed popularity distributions and recommendation algorithms tend to amplify this bias, producing a ``rich get richer'' dynamic. However, we contend that this aggregate view of recommendation frequency is an incomplete picture of the impact of popularity bias: our objective is to provide a more nuanced view informed by recent work in multistakeholder recommendation \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. Authors in \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020} distinguish among the main stakeholders in recommender systems: 1) users (those who receive the recommendations) and 2) suppliers (those who supply or, otherwise, stand behind the recommended items). The popularity bias affects both of these stakeholders as we observe in Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} (impact on users) and ~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} (impact on suppliers). The first plot in Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} displays the ratio of rated items for the three item groups $H$, $M$, and $T$ in the profiles of different users in the MovieLens 1M dataset. The interest of each user towards the three item groups is measured and the users are sorted from the highest interest towards popular items to the lowest based on the ratio of different item groups in their profile. Users are first sorted based on interest towards $H$ items and if there is a tie the interest towards $M$ will be considered and if still there is a tie, interest towards $T$ will be compared. Sorted users are divided into three equal-sized bins $G=\{G_1, G_2, G_3\}$ from most popularity-focused ($G_1$) to least ($G_3$). The y-axis displays the proportion of each user's profile devoted to different item groups. The narrow blue band shows the proportion of each users profile that consists of popular items ($H$), and its monotonic decrease reflects the way the users are ranked. Note, however, that all user groups, even $G_1$ have rated many items from the \textit{Mid} (green) and \textit{Tail} (red) parts of the distribution, and this makes sense: there are only a few really popular movies and even the most blockbuster-focused viewer will eventually exhaust them. Other plots in Figure~\ref{amplify_user_groups} also display users ordered by their popularity interest, but now the y-axis shows the proportion of recommended items delivered by different algorithms\footnote{The plots are ``banded'' because recommendation lists are of size 10 and there are only 10 possible ratio values for each item group.}. The difference with the original user profiles in rating data is stark, especially in the case of \textit{Item-CF} and \textit{User-CF} where the users' profiles are rich in diverse item groups, the generated recommendations are much less so. \textit{Tail} items do not appear at all, evidenced by the red line at the bottom of the plots. In \textit{Item-CF} almost 100\% of the recommendations are from the \textit{Head} category, even for the users with the most niche-oriented profiles. The ``head-focused'' $G_1$ users are receiving recommendations that are not well-matched to their interests in terms of item popularity, but the $G_3$ ``tail-focused'' users are quite poorly served, receiving a steady diet of popular movies in which they are less interested with none of their long-tail interests served. Thus, we observe that popularity bias has a differential impact across the user base: all are affected but some much more severely than others. Multistakeholder recommendation expands our view of those impacted by recommendations to also include \textit{suppliers}, individuals or entities that stand behind the recommended items. In this paper, we have considered the director of each movie as the supplier for that movie. Figure~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} examines popularity bias from the supplier-side of the recommendation interaction: the directors whose movies are being recommended. text: Reinforcement learning for control has demonstrated remarkable success across a diverse range of challenging sensory-motor control tasks, including agile drone flight~\cite{Kaufmann2018drone,Kaufmann2020drone,Loquercio2021drone}, deformable object manipulation~\cite{Wu2019deformable}, and quadruped locomotion~\cite{Hwangbo2019agile,Miki2022wild,Lee2020terrain,margonlis2022rapid}. Compared to their classical model-predictive control counterparts, reinforcement learning-based approaches enable the utilization of more realistic forward dynamics models in the form of physics simulators. Advances in rigid-body simulator technologies~\cite{Todorov2012mujoco, Makoviychuk2021Isaac} allow reinforcement learning algorithms to address their prohibitively high sample complexity by initially training in simulation and subsequently deploying directly on physical robots. Discrepancies, however, persist between what the controller encounters in the simulator and in the physical environment in the form of a \textit{sim-to-real gap}. Specifically, the capacity to generate visuomotor control policies that maintain robustness when perceptual conditions vary during deployment remains an open challenge. Consider the illustration in Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}. A prevalent approach to combat domain shift involves exposing the agent to extensive data variety during training with the expectation that the training distribution provides sufficient coverage over what the agent will encounter in practice. When the simulator is extensible, one can employ domain randomization to generate more diverse training data~\cite{tobin2017domain,active-domain-randomization}. Alternatively, one can utilize data augmentation mechanisms to enhance existing data~\cite{yarats2021drqv2,hansen2020deployment}. Both approaches seek to produce visual features that remain invariant to perceptual changes orthogonal to the task. Such invariance does not come without cost, however. Additional training reduces the wall-clock speed of the training process, while domain randomization necessitates manual tuning~\cite{Andrychowicz2020dexterous} and depends on the assumption that the policy network possesses sufficient capacity to manage the increased support of the input distribution. The added complexity can adversely impact model and policy performance~\cite{laskin2020reinforcement,hansen2020deployment}. Furthermore, concealed beneath lies the assumption that one must know approximately what types of perceptual shift will occur during deployment. Failure can arise when the target domain is not known \textit{a priori} and falls \textit{out-of-distribution}, resulting in a malfunctioning robot that cannot self-correct (see Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}). Distinct from these prior approaches that achieve invariance by memorizing what is irrelevant to the task during training, we consider a more demanding, yet also more realistic scenario in which the deployment specifics are not known in advance. This necessitates the agent to truly generalize \textit{out-of-distribution}, without prior knowledge of the target environment. We further assume that reward supervision is unavailable, so fine-tuning through reinforcement learning is not feasible. This might appear to be an intractable task, but it does implicitly assume that the \textit{same task} that the agent was optimized for during training remains well-defined in the target domain. This implies that the agent possesses \textit{some} notion of \textit{what it knows} despite the sudden emergence of many unknowns that are not required for the task of interest. Without additional assumptions or loss of generality, this \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization problem can be formulated as \textit{unsupervised policy adaptation} between two MDPs that share the same latent dynamics and reward structure, but with distinct pixel observations (See Figure~\ref{fig:graphicalmodels}). In this paper, we investigate methods to enhance generalization under this challenging scenario. Rather than combating domain shift by explicitly embedding perceptual invariance into the network during training, we demonstrate a method to produce feature invariance at deployment time by leveraging the fact that the task of interest remains the same, therefore what the agent experiences internally should remain consistent as well. We collect latent features gathered during training as examples of what the agent \textit{knows} about the task. On the target domain (see Figure~\ref{fig:latent-alignment}), the new latents are shifted from these prior distributions. Our objective in unsupervised policy adaptation is to align the distribution of these latent features on the target domain with those that appeared during training. This unsupervised learning objective, which we term \textit{latent alignment}, does not require paired image data between the source and the target, and can be applied to any agent without imposing specific requirements regarding how it is trained. To distinguish our approach from prior works that attempt to achieve generalization by embedding invariances into the policy at training time, we refer to our method as \textbf{\underline I}nvariance through \textbf{\underline L}atent \textbf{\underline A}lignment (\textbf{ILA}).

text: Ground-truth labels for healthcare data are both challenging and costly to obtain. Limited access to labelers (e.g., physicians) and patients failing to report symptoms constitute common sources of missing labels. Consequently, numerous healthcare datasets are partially or entirely unlabeled, with larger prospective studies frequently exhibiting proportionally fewer labels. This trade-off between study size and accuracy proves particularly acute in healthcare, though it appears in most real-world studies across domains. We focus on learning from person-generated activity time-series data that exhibits heavily imbalanced or missing labels. Since ground-truth labels constitute a requirement for supervised learning, we must examine alternative approaches to utilize the extensive information contained within the unlabeled data. One potential approach to address this need involves transfer learning, where a model receives initial training on a different but nearly identical population before the final task. Nevertheless, upon closer examination, this becomes challenging to implement in practice. First, study design critically influences the signals that link the observed data to the output labels. It proves impractical to expect access to a different dataset generated through identical study design. Second, when studying a rare disease, the low prevalence creates challenges in finding a large, separate initial training set. Thus, transfer learning alone fails to satisfy all our requirements. Self-supervised learning enables representation learning without defined labels. While the theoretical foundations of these methods remain undescribed, their empirical performance has been extensively documented. Most prominently in natural language processing \cite{brown2020language} and other syntactic tasks such as programming \cite{chen2021evaluating}, but also in image classification \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. The taxonomy of these models remains debated, with some researchers \cite{bommasani2021foundation} characterizing pre-trained, self-supervised, meta-learning models as \emph{Foundation Models}. A fundamental concept of self-supervised learning involves defining the objective as some function of the data itself. However, selecting an optimal self-supervised objective task proves non-trivial. Here, we investigate and compare three objective tasks and assess their performance on influenza-like illness (ILI) prediction with lab-validated ground-truth. We draw inspiration from natural language processing, where next-word prediction constitutes a task that enables learning rich representations \cite{brown2020language}. Our end-to-end transformer models initially learn through self-supervision to predict next-day activity levels using activity data from the preceding ten days in a large population. These models subsequently undergo fine-tuning on the ILI prediction task and receive evaluation on a small dataset with laboratory-confirmed ILI labels. Final evaluation on an ILI prediction task in a held-out testing set demonstrates that performance depends on the self-supervision task.

Adversarial examples represent a well-established critical security vulnerability of classification systems. Specifically, given a classifier $f$ and a test input $\mathbf{x}$, an adversary can meticulously construct a human-imperceptible perturbation $\delta$ such that $f(x)
eq f(x+\delta)$. The perturbation $\delta$ is termed an \emph{adversarial perturbation}, while the input $x+\delta$ is designated an \emph{adversarial example}. Numerous \emph{empirical} defenses~\citep{goodfellow2014explaining,na2017cascade,metzen2017detecting,svoboda2018peernets,buckman2018thermometer,ma2018characterizing,guo2018countering,dhillon2018stochastic,xie2018mitigating,song2018pixeldefend} have been developed to counter adversarial examples over recent years. Nevertheless, these empirical defenses were frequently circumvented by sophisticated adaptive adversaries~\citep{carlini2017adversarial,athalye2018obfuscated,uesato2018adversarial,athalye2018robustness}. To terminate this adversarial arms race, numerous \emph{certified} defenses~\citep{scheibler2015towards,carlini2017provably,ehlers2017formal,katz2017reluplex,cheng2017maximum,lomuscio2017approach,fischetti2018deep,bunel2018unified,wong2017provable,wong2018scaling,raghunathan2018certified,raghunathan2018semidefinite,dvijotham2018training,dvijotham2018dual,gehr2018ai2,mirman2018differentiable,singh2018fast,weng2018towards,zhang2018efficient,gowal2018effectiveness,wang2018formal,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,salman2019provably,wang2020certifying,jia2020certified,zhai2020macer} have been introduced. Specifically, a classifier $f$ is considered certifiably robust for an input $\mathbf{x}$ if it provably produces the same top-1 label (i.e.,$f(x)=f(x+\delta)$) when the adversarial perturbation $\delta$ is constrained, e.g., the $\ell_p$-norm of $\delta$ is below a threshold. This threshold is also termed the \emph{certified radius}. In this work, we concentrate on $\ell_0$-norm adversarial perturbations, which arbitrarily modify certain features of a test input and can be realized in physical environments. However, most existing certified defenses concentrate on top-1 predictions. In numerous applications, top-$k$ predictions that return the $k$ most probable labels are more pertinent. For example, when a classifier is deployed as a cloud service (also termed \emph{machine learning as a service})~\citep{Google_Cloud_Vision,microsoft_demo,amazon_demo,clarifai_demo}, top-$k$ labels for a test input are frequently returned to clients for more informed decision-making; in recommendation systems and web search, top-$k$ items/webpages are suggested to users. Despite the significance and relevance of top-$k$ predictions, their certified robustness against adversarial perturbations remains largely unexplored. One exception is the recent work by~\cite{jia2020certified}, which derived a tight $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. Such $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness can be converted to $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness via utilizing the inequality between $\ell_0$-norm and $\ell_2$-norm. However, the $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness derived from such transformations is suboptimal. \myparatight{Our work} We aim to develop $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness of top-$k$ predictions. Our approach is founded on \emph{randomized smoothing}~\citep{cao2017mitigating,liu2018towards,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,jia2020certified,levine2019robustness}, which can construct a certifiably robust classifier from any base classifier via input randomization. We adopt randomized smoothing because it is applicable to {any} classifier and scalable to large neural networks. Specifically, we employ a randomized smoothing method called \emph{randomized ablation}~\citep{levine2019robustness}, which achieves state-of-the-art $\ell_{0}$-norm certified robustness for top-1 predictions. Unlike other randomized smoothing methods~\citep{cao2017mitigating,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified} that randomize an input via adding \emph{additive} noise (e.g., Gaussian, Laplacian, or discrete noise) to it, randomized ablation randomizes an input via subsampling its features. Specifically, given an arbitrary classifier (called \emph{base classifier}) and a test input $\mathbf{x}$, randomized ablation creates an \emph{ablated input} via retaining some randomly selected features in $\mathbf{x}$ and setting the remaining features to a special value, e.g., median of the feature value, mean of the feature value, or a special symbol. When the test input is an image, the features are the image's pixels. Subsequently, we feed the ablated input to the base classifier. Since the ablated input is random, the output of the base classifier is also random. Specifically, we denote by $p_j$ the probability that the base classifier outputs a label $j$ for the random ablated input. The original randomized ablation method constructs a \emph{smoothed classifier} that outputs the label with the largest label probability $p_j$ for a test input $\mathbf{x}$. In our work, the smoothed classifier returns the $k$ labels with the largest label probabilities for $\mathbf{x}$. Our primary theoretical contribution is an almost tight $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantee of top-$k$ predictions for the smoothed classifier constructed by randomized ablation. Specifically, we first derive an $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantee of top-$k$ predictions for the smoothed classifier. Our results demonstrate that a label $l$ is provably among the top-$k$ labels predicted by the smoothed classifier for a test input $\mathbf{x}$ when the attacker arbitrarily perturbs at most $r_{l}$ features of $\mathbf{x}$, where $r_{l}$ is the $\ell_0$-norm {certified radius}. Moreover, we prove that our certified radius is \emph{tight} when $k=1$ and is \emph{almost tight} when $k>1$. eq 1)$. In other words, when an attacker manipulates at least $r_l+1+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$ features of a test input, there exists a base classifier from which the smoothed classifier's top-$k$ predicted labels do not include $l$ or there exist ties. Second, our certified radius is the same as or larger than that in \citet{levine2019robustness} for top-1 predictions, because we leverage the discrete property of the label probabilities to derive our certified radius. text: The individualization-refinement (IR) framework constitutes a general backtracking technique utilized by algorithms that solve tasks pertaining to the computation of symmetries of combinatorial objects~\cite{McKay201494}. These encompass algorithms that compute automorphism groups, isomorphism solvers, canonical labeling tools employed for computing normal forms, and to some degree recently also machine learning computations in convolutional neural networks~\cite{DBLP:conf/ijcai/AbboudCGL21,DBLP:conf/aaai/0001RFHLRG19}. In fact, all competitive graph isomorphism/automorphism solvers, specifically \textsc{nauty}/\textsc{Traces}~\cite{nautyTracesweb, McKay201494}, \textsc{bliss}~\cite{bliss:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/JunttilaK07}, \textsc{saucy}~\cite{saucy:webpage, Darga:2004:ESS:996566.996712}, \textsc{conauto}~\cite{conauto:webpage, DBLP:conf/wea/Lopez-PresaCA13}, and \textsc{dejavu}~\cite{dejavu:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21} operate within this framework. These tools alternate color-refinement techniques (such as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm) with backtracking steps. The latter execute artificial individualization of indistinguishable vertices. This results in recursive branching and overall in a tree of recursive function calls, the so-called IR-tree. Through clever invariants and heuristics, the tools succeed in pruning large portions of the IR-tree. Since the non-recursive work is quasi-linear, it has long been established that the number of traversed nodes of the IR-tree constitutes the determining factor in the running time for all the tools (see for example \cite[Theorem 9]{thesis} and \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-0804-4881}). And indeed, the running times of the various tools closely mirror this~\cite{McKay201494,DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}. Indeed, variation in the traversal strategies among the tools results in a different number of traversed nodes which in turn produces different running times. However, explicit bounds that rigorously demonstrate asymptotic advantages of randomized traversals over deterministic ones have only recently been established~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}. For this purpose, a specific problem --- a search problem in trees with symmetries -- is defined. It captures precisely the parameters within which IR-algorithms operate. While these results are quite general within an abstract model, the bounds proven in~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} apply to the search problem in arbitrary trees with symmetries, independent of whether they originate from actual IR-computations or not. Granted, the vast benchmark library of \textsc{Traces}{}~\cite{nautyTracesweb,McKay201494} demonstrates that IR-trees emerge in an abundance of forms and shapes. However, to date there have been no comprehensive results actually analyzing which trees can arise as an IR-tree. \xparagraph{Contribution.} In this paper we investigate which trees are IR-trees. Arising from a branching process, all IR-trees are rooted and all inner vertices have at least 2 children. Such trees are termed irreducible (or series reduced). Despite a vast variety of IR-trees arising from benchmark libraries, it emerges that not all irreducible trees are IR-trees. However, we can provide a complete, constructive characterization of IR-trees. \begin{theorem} An irreducible tree is an IR-tree if and only if there is no node that has exactly two children of which exactly one is a leaf. \end{theorem} To prove the theorem we first provide and justify necessary conditions for a tree to be an IR-tree. We then prove that, indeed, these conditions are sufficient by providing graphs on which the execution of an IR-algorithm yields the desired tree. In fact, our proof is constructive, meaning that we obtain an algorithm with the following property. Given a tree~$T$ satisfying the necessary conditions, the algorithm produces a graph whose IR-tree is~$T$. As we describe in our definition of IR-trees in Section~\ref{sec:ir}, the trees are naturally associated with a coloring of the vertices. This coloring constitutes a crucial component that is related to the automorphism group structure of the graph. Our characterization also fully describes how color classes may be distributed in a given tree. It emerges that there are several simple restrictions, in particular for vertices that have precisely two children, but apart from that all colorings can be realized and in particular any number of symmetries can be ensured (see Section~\ref{sec:graph:constr}). Our characterization provides a fundamental argument transferring the analysis of abstract tree traversal strategies performed in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} to backtracking trees of IR-algorithms on actual instances. Specifically, we may conclude that the abstract trees used for the lower bounds of probabilistic algorithms in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} indeed appear as IR-trees. However, interestingly, the abstract trees used for the lower bounds of deterministic algorithms (Theorem~13, \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}) are not IR-trees. In fact these trees have nodes with two children, one child that is a leaf and another that is not. This violates the necessary conditions as established by Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}. Fortunately, it also immediately follows from our results that a slight modification can rectify this: by simply replacing the respective leaves with inner nodes that have two attached leaves, the trees become actual IR-trees, due to our characterization.
