text: Deep Learning methodologies have delivered solutions, with remarkable performance, to general classification problems where abundant annotated data are available for training. Given that in real-world applications specific data are frequently scarce, extremely expensive to label, non-stationary, or streaming, novel and classical learning strategies have been integrated into the domain of Deep Learning to address these challenges \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Therefore, topics such as transfer learning \cite{wang2018deep}, reinforcement learning \cite{Ren2018DeepRL}, or incremental learning \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}, both supervised and unsupervised, have gained renewed momentum. Incremental learning is the capability of a classifier to evolve by continuously incorporating information from new instances and/or new classes, and without resorting to complete retraining \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Currently, incremental and online machine learning are receiving increasing attention particularly in the context of learning from real-time data streams \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online}. In particular, rehearsal-free continual learning techniques have also demonstrated their capabilities to extend the class-set of a classifier considering only labels from the new classes, while avoiding the problem of catastrophic forgetting \cite{tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. This is of particular interest when computational capacities do not permit complete retraining, or confidentiality issues prevent new access to old samples during the process of extending the class set. In contrast, less progress has been achieved in continual learning of a set of non-stationary classes, primarily when applied to tasks involving unsupervised streaming data. A paradigmatic example of the application of incremental learning, dealing with unsupervised, non-stationary and streaming data is the case of video-to-video face recognition (V2V-FR) in video surveillance \cite{huang2015cox}. Typically, video-frames are captured with a wide range of individual pose, camera position, resolution, and illumination, which often exceed the diversity available in datasets used to train deep networks (generally focused on web extracted images) \cite{guo2016mscleb1m}. Transfer learning to specific task domains in V2V-FR has proven to be challenging even for Deep Learning encoders \cite{gunther2016face,lopezlopez2019dataset} since image quality factors are still decisive for performance \cite{guo2019survey}. Besides, since the data are received continuously in a stream fashion, individual appearance could change when switching between different cameras, which could also operate in changing conditions over time \cite{ditzler2015learning,disabato2019learning}. While, in theory, all of these issues can be resolved with further labelling, the task of having addressed every possible variation in a training dataset is, in practical terms, infeasible \cite{he2020incremental}. Then, a more efficient and scalable approach is required \cite{maltoni2019continous,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. In this regard, what truly represents the context of application and the changes that appear over time is the actual data \textbf{incrementally} extracted during the operation of the system, and so \textbf{without labels}. Another characteristic of real-world applications of V2V-FR relates to their intrinsic open-set nature \cite{scheirer2013toward,gunther2017towards}. Take for example a practical case of an airport video-surveillance aimed to track some \emph{individuals of interest (IoI)} who have not been collaboratively enrolled in the system, e.g.\ those exhibiting suspicious behaviours, among a larger number of \emph{unknown} non-target identities, that should be identified as \emph{unknown} non-target identities. In this paper, we propose a novel incremental learning system, the Open-Set Dynamic Ensembles of SVM \ref{fig:illustrate}. Using deep feature encoder as a foundation, the system is capable of utilizing operational data to enhance and improve the recognition of target identities in an unsupervised manner. Additionally, guided by the real-world necessities, the system is designed to operate in a completely open set setting. Grounded on the power of a Deep features encoder, trained for the general face recognition problem, an incremental learning module, fed with stream data, simultaneously predicts and updates classifiers, while addressing catastrophic forgetting issues. The incremental module is based on dynamic ensembles of SVM classifiers, which from a single SVM built from a few labelled video-frames directly taken from the footage, can acquire and adapt to additional information by adding/removing classifiers to/from ensembles. It follows the self-training strategy \cite{yarowsky1995unsupervised} in which predictions also serve the role of pseudo-labels, which are used to update and improve the classifiers. Based on the modular nature of ensembles, adaptations consisting of either adding or removing classifiers. Contributions of this paper can be summarised as: \begin{itemize} \item An approach to unsupervised incremental learning designed to operate online with stream data. During its operation, predictions also serve the role of pseudo-labels. \item A strategy to address both catastrophic forgetting issues and the effect of mistaken pseudo-labels. \item An approach to instance-incremental learning in the open-set, which could be extended to cope with the class-incremental problem. \item A method for person re-identification based on face, which is not directly based on a reservoir of face images \end{itemize} The rest of the paper is organised as follows. First, in Sec.~\ref{sec:rel_work} we perform an extensive study of the existing literature related to the problem. After that, we move to present the proposed approach in Sec.~\ref{sec:desvm} and a set of experiments to study its behaviour, in Sec.~\ref{sec:experiments} and~\ref{sec:results}. Finally, in Sec.~\ref{sec:conclusion}, we reflect on the conclusions we can extract from the work.

text: Cancer is emerging as the primary cause of mortality and the most substantial barrier to extending life expectancy across numerous countries~\cite{world2020report}. Lung cancer, representing more than 11~\% of all newly diagnosed cases, constitutes the second most prevalent cancer and occupies the leading position in cancer-related deaths globally, comprising 18~\% of total cancer fatalities~\cite{Sung2021}. The most prevalent lung cancer therapeutic approaches encompass: surgical resection, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. Numerous of these interventions, along with successful diagnostic procedures utilizing bronchoscopy or computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy, rely upon precise localization, and frequently delineation (segmentation), of the tumor from healthy tissue in preoperative imaging, typically CT. Manual segmentation of lesions/tumors from preoperative CT represents a laborious and time-consuming procedure for oncologists, radiologists, and pulmonologists, which may result in treatment delays and reduced survival rates, particularly in clinics with limited resources. Furthermore, the quality of manual localization and segmentation depends upon prior knowledge and clinical expertise. Even with appropriate guidelines and standards, tumor segmentation frequently exhibits substantial inter- and intraobserver variability. Conversely, automatic segmentation techniques possess the potential to deliver efficient, consistent, and more precise outcomes. Automatic approaches can both reduce the time required for image interpretation and enable experts to dedicate their limited time to optimizing planning and treatment strategies. Historically, approaches such as thresholding~\cite{UZELALTINBULAT2017}, region growing~\cite{Adams1994,Dehmeshki2008}, and graph cuts~\cite{GU2013692} were frequently proposed for segmenting lung tumors from CT images. These algorithms are appropriate as semi-automatic approaches, but are not well-suited for lung tumor localization. Recent developments in deep learning facilitate automation of tasks that until recently were exclusively performed by trained specialists~\cite{ramanto2019,kim2019}. Advances in hardware have enabled development of larger and increasingly sophisticated models, but much of the enhancement stems from access to substantial amounts of annotated data. Currently, particularly following the introduction of the U-Net~\cite{ronneberger2015} architecture, deep learning approaches have dominated the domain of medical image segmentation~\cite{Du2020}. Nevertheless, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are memory intensive, especially for 3D volumes. It is therefore typical to train networks utilizing 2D or 2.5D input images~\cite{carvalho}, where the model processes one slice at a time, chunks of slices, or 3D patches, and then applied in a sliding window manner across the CT volume. Patching the 3D volume incurs a cost of reduced perception, and thus more efficient multi-scale 3D CNN architectures have been proposed, which enable the utilization of larger input volumes~\cite{Jiang2018}. An alternative strategy is to conduct segmentation in multiple stages, either employing multiple algorithms or a cascade of CNNs~\cite{Hossain2019,isensee,carvalho,gan2021}. To address the issue of insufficient training data, unsupervised approaches such as supervoxel have been proposed~\cite{Hansen2021}. To promote faster convergence and more precise results, multi-modality approaches that employ magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography (PET) scans in addition to CT have been suggested~\cite{fu2021,Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2}. Neural network architectures that can leverage multiple annotation types have also been proposed~\cite{Wang2019,Mlynarski2019}. A more recent strategy to address the shortage of training data is the teacher-student design, inspired by the concept of knowledge distillation~\cite{phuong19,furlanello18,hinton2015}. The teacher generates pseudo-annotations from suboptimal annotations to expand the dataset size for training the student. The teacher-student pattern can be applied to any type of network architecture, and does not constrain other hyperparameters or external configurations. A teacher-student design can be employed in various ways, from utilization of unlabeled data~\cite{caron2021,Xie2020,Li2020}, to exploitation of multiple modalities~\cite{Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2,Li2020}, and to usage of datasets with different annotation types~\cite{sun2020,Zhang2021}. Our approach differs from the previously mentioned methods applied to lung tumor segmentation by exploiting annotations of different supervision on the same modality, namely CT images. Since CT scanning is less invasive to the patient than the other modalities, it is an objective to efficiently segment tumors from CT-only examinations. Our method is inspired by Sun \textit{et al.}~\cite{sun2020} that demonstrates promising results using a teacher-student framework to segment liver and liver lesions given semantic and bounding box annotations. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to implement a similar teacher-student framework for CT images to perform semantic segmentation of lung tumors. text: While robot learning has achieved substantial progress, most algorithms are developed for robots operating in isolation. In practice, interaction with humans and other learning agents is unavoidable. Such interaction poses a substantial challenge for robot learning: the other agents will \textit{modify} their behavior in response to the robot, continuously altering the robot's learning environment. For instance, consider an autonomous vehicle that is learning to control the velocity of nearby human-driven vehicles so that it can safely decelerate those vehicles if there is congestion or construction ahead. The first time you encounter this autonomous vehicle, your intention is to behave cautiously: when the autonomous vehicle decelerates, you also reduce speed. But when it decelerated without any obvious reason, your strategy evolves: the next time you interact with this autonomous vehicle, you maneuver around it without any hesitation. The autonomous vehicle --- which initially believed it had learned the correct policy to decelerate your vehicle --- is left perplexed and frustrated by your modified behavior! To effectively \textit{co-adapt} alongside other agents, the robot must predict how the behavior of these other agents will evolve, and model how its own actions influence the hidden intentions of others. Previous works that examine these interactions impose restrictive assumptions about the other agents: treating the other agents as stationary~\cite{davison1998predicting,stone2000defining,mealing2015opponent,albrecht2015hba,grover2018learning}, sharing a learning procedure across other agents~\cite{foerster2016learning,lowe2017multi,foerster2018counterfactual}, directly accessing the underlying intentions and actions of other agents~\cite{albrecht2015hba,he2016opponent,hernandez2017efficiently, grover2018learning, foerster2018learning, everett2018learning}, or simplifying the space of intentions with hand-crafted features~\cite{kelley2008understanding,bandyopadhyay2013intention,bai2015intention,sadigh2016information,basu2019active, losey2019robots}. In contrast, we focus on general settings where the ego agent (e.g., a robot) repeatedly interacts with non-stationary, separately-controlled, and partially-observable agents. Humans effortlessly handle these scenarios on a daily basis (e.g., driving, walking), and they accomplish this without explicitly modeling every low-level aspect of each other's policy \cite{rubinstein1998modeling}. Motivated by humans, we recognize that: \begin{center} \vspace{-0.5em} \emph{The ego agent only observes the low-level actions of another agent, but --- just as in human-human interaction --- it is often adequate to maintain a high-level policy representation. We refer to this representation as the \emph{latent strategy}, and acknowledge that latent strategies can evolve over time.} \vspace{-0.5em} \end{center} Learning the other agent's strategy enables the robot to \textit{anticipate} how they will respond during the current interaction. Moreover, modeling how the latent strategy evolves over time --- i.e., the \textit{latent dynamics} --- allows the robot to predict how its own behavior will \textit{influence} the other agent's future intentions (see Fig.~\ref{fig:front}). Overall, we utilize latent representations of the other agent's policy to make the following contributions towards learning in non-stationary multi-agent interaction: \textbf{Learning Latent Representations.} We present an RL-based framework for multi-agent interaction that learns both latent strategies and policies for responding to these strategies. Our framework implicitly models how another agent's strategy evolves in response to the ego agent's behavior. \textbf{Influencing Other Agents.} Ego agents utilizing our proposed approach are encouraged to deliberately modify their policy to influence the latent strategies of other agents, particularly when certain strategies are better suited for co-adaptation than alternative strategies. \textbf{Testing in Multi-Agent Settings.} We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods across four simulated environments and a real robot experiment, where two $7$-DoF robot arms play air hockey. Our approach surpasses the alternatives, and also learns to influence the other agent.

text: Automatic language identification constitutes a challenging problem, and particularly the discrimination between closely related languages represents one of the primary bottlenecks of state-of-the-art language identification systems~\cite{DSL2014}. Language technology for Scandinavian languages remains in an emerging phase (e.g.~\newcite{kirkedal2019lacunae}). One challenge involves acquiring sufficient text with which to train e.g. large language models. High-quality language ID proves critical to this data sourcing, though leading models frequently confuse similar Nordic languages. This paper presents a machine learning approach for automatic language identification among six closely-related Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian (Nynorsk), Norwegian (Bokmål), Faroese and Icelandic. This paper investigates different methods of extracting features from a corpus of raw text data comprising Wikipedia summaries in respective languages and evaluates the performance of a selection of machine learning models. Specifically we will compare the performance of classical machine learning models such as Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support vector machine, and K nearest Neighbors with more contemporary neural network approaches such as Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Following evaluation of these models on the Wikipedia data set we will proceed to evaluate the best models on a data set from a different domain in order to investigate how effectively the models generalize when classifying sentences from a different domain.

text: Across diverse environments, including warehouses, manufacturing facilities, and residential settings, robots operate in shared workspaces alongside humans or other robotic systems. Although obstacle occupancy in such environments remains predominantly fixed or static, certain localized regions within these spaces may exhibit variable occupancy during operational periods. We classify such environments as \emph{semi-structured}. Furthermore, in these applications robots frequently execute repetitive tasks and demand rapid and dependable motion planning capabilities. Consider the scenario depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:cover}. The robot must retrieve the bowl while circumventing the pitchers, table and walls. The majority of the environment (e.g. table, walls, free space above the table etc.) can be presumed to be known, and given the repetitive nature of the task, certain information from prior planning queries can be reused to accelerate planning. Widely employed algorithms such as RRTs~\cite{lavalle1998rapidly,kuffner2000rrt} neither leverage the distinction between static and movable obstacles nor capitalize on the repetitive characteristics of planning problems to enhance planning speed. Roadmap-based approaches like Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRMs)~\cite{kavraki1996probabilistic} are either constrained to completely static environments or incur substantial overheads in repair operations which they necessitate to manage movable obstacles. Enhancements to PRM have reduced costly collision checks~\cite{kavraki2000path}, addressed dynamic environments~\cite{leven2002framework,yang2017hdrm}, and captured repetitive motions~\cite{lehner2018repetition}, but their performance can still fluctuate dramatically depending on a planning query. Rather than preprocessing collision information offline, another category of planners exploits prior experiences to accelerate search~\cite{Phillips-RSS-12,berenson2012robot,coleman2015experience}. Nevertheless, these experience degraded performance when past information is invalidated by environmental changes. All these methods consequently cannot provide fixed-time planning guarantees. Provably fixed-time planners were recently introduced in~\cite{islam2019provable,islam2020provably} for applications involving repetitive tasks. Given a start state, a goal region and known environmental model, they precompute a compressed set of paths that can be utilized online to plan to any goal within the goal region in constant or bounded time. These approaches have been previously employed for mail-sorting~\cite{islam2019provable} and for grasping objects moving along a conveyor belt~\cite{islam2020provably} While our approach APP draws inspiration from these works, we focus on enabling online obstacle avoidance by explicitly accounting for movable obstacles during the preprocessing phase by using the alternative paths planning approach. We extend these approaches to handle movable obstacles while still guaranteeing provably fixed-time planning via the \emph{Alternative Paths Planner (APP)}. The fundamental concept is to generate multiple alternative paths for each planning problem, such that for any configuration of movable obstacles, one path is guaranteed to be traversable. Our approach to accomplish this is to enforce that these paths are \emph{disjoint}: they are sufficiently separated that no single obstacle configuration can intersect two paths simultaneously. Handling $n$ movable obstacles requires generating only at most $n+1$ fully disjoint paths. Nevertheless, if the required number of disjoint paths cannot be found for the given problem, we find additional partially overlapping paths (that do not satisfy disjointness criterion) to provide the same guarantee. APP can be applied to performance-critical real-world applications such as mail-sorting, conveyor-belt picking, and shelving. For scenarios with multiple movable obstacles, we demonstrate microsecond-scale path-lookup times and achieve 100\% success rate. We include experimental results from three domains, compare with state-of-the-art existing approaches and validate our approach with a real-world case study.

text: Relational databases contain vast quantities of global data and are conventionally accessed through structured query languages such as SQL. A natural language interface to these databases (NLIDB) could substantially enhance the accessibility of this information by enabling users to retrieve and leverage data without requiring programming knowledge. Following the publication of large-scale datasets \cite{wikisql,DBLP:conf/acl/RadevKZZFRS18,spider}, this task has attracted considerable attention and has been extensively investigated in recent years. Previous research has predominantly concentrated on converting grammatical, complete sentences into queries. Nevertheless, an internal user survey conducted on the search service of a major customer relationship management (CRM) platform\footnote{\url{https://www.salesforce.com/} demonstrated that users exhibit a tendency to communicate using a colloquial format which may range from employing only keywords (``player 42'') to very brief phrases (``show player 42'') to complete sentences (``Who is the player who wears Jersey 42?''). Beyond stylistic variation, users omitting content words from their searches for the sake of conciseness also carries the potential consequence of rendering their questions ambiguous. This could make the task unsolvable even for models adapted to the NLS style of text. For instance, in Figure \ref{fig:example}, without the word ``Jersey'', it becomes impossible to determine which column's value (\texttt{Id} or \texttt{Jersey}) must equal 42. In this work, we demonstrate that Text2SQL systems trained exclusively on complete sentences encounter difficulties adapting to the noisy keyword/short phrasal style of questions. To address this challenge, we introduce various data augmentation strategies inspired by our user search patterns and style. \hide{ \todo{We have enough space, can you show 2-3 examples in this figure? No need to use a boxed layout, you can show a table. Also please use .pdf to save the figure, which has higher resolution.} } To address the resulting ambiguity, a potential solution involves utilizing the table content by enabling the model to scan the table for various terms present in the question and employ that information for disambiguation (If the token ``42'' was found exclusively in the \texttt{Jersey} column, then \texttt{Jersey} must be the column equal to 42). Although effective, this approach could become prohibitively costly (in terms of inference time or memory requirements) on large tables since the model would need to search through the entire table content for every question. We hypothesize that in most instances, the model requires only samples from the table content rather than the exact rows that match tokens in the NLS question to disambiguate columns. For example, if the \texttt{Id} column contained alpha-numeric IDs, \texttt{Player} and \texttt{Nationality} contained strings, and \texttt{Jersey} contained two digit numbers, then \texttt{Jersey} must be the column equal to 42. Sampling eliminates the necessity of a complete table scan for every question. The samples for each column could be generated offline and remain constant across questions or periodically updated (to reflect potential distribution shifts in the table or user queries), enabling adaptation and personalization without model retraining. Presently, a significant gap exists between how neural retrieval models process complete texts and the relevance labels that inform training, evaluation, and analysis. These labels, exemplified by those in the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 (TREC-DL) \cite{trec2019overview}, treat lengthy documents containing thousands of tokens as unified entities. For conventional models that reduce document statistics to bag-of-words representations, this labeling granularity proves adequate. Nevertheless, recently developed neural ranking models function at a more detailed level. They systematically construct their scores through interactions among all words to produce a singular score for the entire document \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir,zheng2019rltm,yilmaz2019}. Consequently, the objective of neural retrieval models evolves toward combining document-level relevance with word-level question answering or information extraction. These models must concurrently identify relevant information spans and, utilizing these spans, generate scoring decisions applicable for ranking numerous candidate documents. Nevertheless, a significant constraint in their advancement and assessment is the absence of datasets that address both sub-tasks with equal effectiveness. Existing datasets either emphasize retrieval outcomes with comprehensive judgments across ranked lists \cite{trec2019overview,hashemi2020antique}, or focus on question-answer selections within individual candidate texts that can subsequently be transformed into retrieval collections, yet result in incomplete retrieval judgments \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}. In this research, we introduce FiRA: a novel dataset of 	extbf{Fi}ne-grained 	extbf{R}elevance 	extbf{A}nnotations featuring word-level relevance selections and passage-level graded relevance labels for all relevant documents within the TREC 2019 Deep Learning Document dataset. We partition the documents into segments and present query-document segment pairs to annotators. In Figure ef{fig:fira-screenshot}, we demonstrate an example of an annotated document-segment. We maintain high quality through implementing at least 3-way majority voting for each candidate and continuous monitoring of quality metrics throughout our annotation process, including time expenditure per annotation. Additionally, by mandating annotators to identify relevant text spans, we minimize the likelihood of false-positive retrieval relevance labels. We executed our annotation process with 87 computer science students utilizing a specialized annotation tool that facilitates seamless workflow between selecting relevance labels and identifying relevant text spans. The FiRA dataset encompasses 
umprint{24199} query-document-segment pairs across all 
umprint{1990} relevant documents for the 
umprint{43} queries within TREC-DL. We selected to expand the TREC-DL document ranking test collection and utilize the ranked retrieval data as our foundation because 1) it enables us to focus our annotation task, given that fine-grained annotations require substantial time investment and 2) we can compare our non-expert annotators with TREC's expert annotators. FiRA remains model-agnostic while incorporating the complete pool of TREC annotations. Our innovative FiRA dataset facilitates various applications:  egin{itemize} \item 	extbf{Training:} FiRA supports both standalone and multi-task retrieval and QA fine-tuning. The density and coverage across query-document pairs enable detailed fine-tuning through word-level loss functions. \item 	extbf{Evaluation:} FiRA enhances TREC-DL evaluation with more detailed relevance labels and the capability to assess answer passages extracted from complete documents. Combined with the labeled non-relevant documents from TREC-DL, FiRA permits evaluation of both rankings and answer selections. \item 	extbf{Analysis:} Neural document ranking models that generate relevance scores for entire documents can undergo comprehensive analysis. Particularly, their intermediate results and attention regions can be quantitatively examined using FiRA. \end{itemize} The human subjectivity inherent in relevance tasks represents a persistent concern in IR research \cite{borlund2003concept}. When utilizing human-annotated datasets, understanding the noise and uncertainty introduced by varying human relevance judgments becomes crucial. For this purpose, we implement 3-way majority voting throughout our data collection process. Furthermore, we provide our FiRA dataset with a quantitative examination of the question:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ1}] What degree of subjectivity do our fine-grained relevance annotations demonstrate? \end{itemize} To address this, we selected 10 pairs for annotation by all our annotators, enabling us to examine their subjectivity through a dense distribution that minimizes outliers. We discovered that our annotators demonstrate strong agreement on a 2-level-graded relevance scale, while subjectivity increases for 4-level-graded relevance and text selections. We leverage our novel dataset and conduct a comprehensive investigation of positional bias in both relevance distribution across documents and within individual segments. By presenting annotators with segments in randomized order to eliminate attention bias toward the beginning, we seek to address our research question:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ2}] Does position-based relevance bias exist within lengthy documents? \end{itemize} Our FiRA annotations reveal that an increased probability of encountering relevant answers exists at document beginnings, though we also note that substantial numbers of relevant segments appear in later document sections. Additionally, we examined our annotators' behavior regarding relevant word selection within individual segments. An analysis of the MSMARCO-QA \cite{msmarco16} dataset revealed strong bias toward segment beginnings. Therefore, utilizing our FiRA annotations, we address the question:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ3}] Do annotators exhibit bias toward snippet beginnings? \end{itemize} For this investigation, we established a control group and a treatment group, rotating the first and second text halves. Neither group demonstrates positional bias toward the start. The rotation group actually emphasizes the significance of context surrounding relevant span selections, as divided sentences received fewer selections. To demonstrate FiRA's utility, we employ the fine-grained judgments to analyze how effectively the recently introduced state-of-the-art TKL neural document re-ranking model \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir} achieves its potential through TKL's interpretability functions. The TKL model provides information regarding which three 30-word regions within a document it utilizes to compute scores.  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ4}] How many of FiRA's relevant spans does the TKL model utilize for document score computation? \end{itemize} We determine that the TKL model trained on TREC-DL data \cite{trec2019overview} demonstrates disproportionate emphasis on document beginnings as ranking signals. The insights obtained through FiRA can inform the development of next-generation neural document ranking models. Our FiRA dataset, including raw annotations, documentation, and all accompanying utility scripts, is freely accessible at: \ 	extit{\url{https://github.com/sebastian-hofstaetter/fira-trec-19-dataset}}

text: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success across diverse tasks, including video game playing~\cite{dqn1, dqn2, starcraft2, a3c, a2c, ga3c, kf, pic, Jain19, JainECCV2020} and robotic control~\cite{Levine15, Gu17, Luo19}. Nevertheless, extended training duration represents a fundamental challenge preventing deep RL from scaling to increasingly complex tasks. To address the frequently excessive training duration, RL frameworks target two properties: (1) High throughput that ensures the framework gathers data at exceptionally high rates. (2) High sample efficiency that ensures the framework acquires the desired policy with reduced data requirements. To accomplish both objectives, synchronous and asynchronous parallel actor-learners have been developed that expedite RL training~\cite{a3c, a2c, impala, ga3c, seed_rl, ddppo, rlpyt, iswitch}. State-of-the-art synchronous approaches, such as synchronous advantage actor critic (A2C)~\cite{a3c, a2c} and related algorithms~\cite{ppo, trpo, acktr} are favored due to their \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}. Nevertheless, synchronous approaches experience idle time since all actors must complete experience collection before trainable parameters undergo updates. This becomes especially problematic when environment step duration exhibits significant variation. Consequently, existing synchronous approaches fail to scale to environments where step duration varies substantially due to computationally demanding 3D-rendering and (physics) simulation. \input{flow_time_fig} Conversely, asynchronous approaches, \eg, asynchronous advantage actor-critic on a GPU (GA3C)~\cite{ga3c} and importance weighted actor-learner architectures (IMPALA)~\cite{impala}, attain high throughput. Nevertheless, these approaches experience a stale-policy problem~\cite{ga3c, impala} since learning and data collection occur asynchronously. The policy employed for data collection (behavior policy) lags several updates behind the current policy (target policy) utilized for parameter updates. This delay produces noisy gradients and consequently reduced data efficiency. Therefore, asynchronous approaches sacrifice training stability for throughput. We demonstrate that this trade-off is unnecessary and propose High-Throughput Synchronous RL (HTS-RL), a technique that accomplishes both high throughput and high training stability. HTS-RL can be integrated with numerous off-the-shelf deep RL algorithms, such as A2C, proximal policy optimization (PPO)~\cite{ppo}, and actor-critic using Kronecker-factored trust region (ACKTR)~\cite{acktr}. HTS-RL is especially appropriate for environments with substantial step time variance: It executes concurrent learning and data collection, {which substantially enhances throughput.} Furthermore, actors interact with environment replicas asynchronously. The asynchronous interaction diminishes idle time. Finally, by executing batched synchronization, HTS-RL ensures that the lag between target and behavior policy equals one. Due to this constant latency, HTS-RL employs a `one step delayed-gradient' update that maintains the same convergence rate as a non-delayed variant. Consequently, HTS-RL preserves the advantages of synchronous RL, \ie, \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}, while achieving speedups, particularly in environments where step time varies. We demonstrate that HTS-RL enables acceleration of A2C and PPO on Atari environments~\cite{gym, atari} and the Google Research Football environment (GFootball)~\cite{gfootball}. Following the evaluation protocol of~\citet{Henderson17} and~\citet{Colas18}, we compare against the state-of-the-art, asynchronous method, IMPALA~\cite{impala}: our approach achieves {$3.7\times$} higher average episode reward on Atari games, and {$43\%$} higher average game scores in the GFootball environment. When compared against synchronous A2C and PPO, our approach attains a $2-6\times$ speedup. Code is available at~\url{https://github.com/IouJenLiu/HTS-RL}.

Using the evaluation protocol of Henderson and Cas, we compare our approach to the state-of-the-art asynchronous method, IMPALA, which obtains a reward per episode 3.7 times higher in the Atari environment, and a score per game 43% higher in the G-football environment. Compared with asynchronous A2C and PPO, our method is faster by 2-6 times. This enables HTS-RL to maintain the advantages of asynchronous policy, that is, high efficiency, stable learning, full determinism and reproducibility, while gaining speed. The code is available at https://github.com/IouJenLiu/HTS-RL.

text: The containment of the Covid-19 pandemic has necessitated the mobilization of the most extensive global public health response in decades \cite{fisher2020global}. Consequently, a broad spectrum of novel digital health strategies has been rapidly deployed at scale \cite{fagherazzi2020digital}; while this expedited deployment has been essential given the urgency of the circumstances, it remains crucial to responsibly examine the implications of these strategies \cite{ienca2020responsible}. We concentrate in this paper on the privacy implications of digital contact tracing smartphone applications \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}, also referred to as exposure notification applications \cite{Apple_Google}. It has been demonstrated that the Covid-19 virus is susceptible to presymptomatic and asymptomatic transmission \cite{Asymptomatic_transmission_1}, presenting a significant obstacle for containment because infected individuals can transmit the virus without manifesting any symptoms. Nevertheless, by identifying recent contacts of diagnosed individuals and convincing them to isolate, contact tracing can reduce the reproductive number. Contact-tracing efforts were originally manual; healthcare professionals gather information regarding recent contacts from patients and notify those contacts about their high-risk status and the subsequent steps to be undertaken \cite{Manual_contact_tracing}. Naturally, there are certain limitations to this approach, including the inability of patients to report contacts with strangers and the discomfort they may experience when disclosing information about contact identities and times to healthcare professionals \cite{Disclosure_discomfort}. On a broader scale, if infection rates persist in growing, the volume of patients may render manual contact tracing impractical \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. It is at this juncture that automated digital contact tracing/exposure notification applications enter the scenario \cite{kleinman2020digital, Apple_Google, Pan_European, bay2020bluetrace}, as they promise the capability to notify end-users of potential exposure to Covid-19 while diminishing the amount of manual labor required. By definition, contact tracing applications are designed to track colocation (though typically not directly the location) of application users, which raises substantial privacy concerns \cite{bengio2020need}. Consequently, a major focus of the design of contact tracing protocols is on privacy \cite{levine1988contact, cho2020contact, raskar2020apps, rivest2020pact, trieu2020epione, troncoso2020decentralized}. Many of the attempts to characterize and guarantee the privacy of contact-tracing applications have concentrated on the specific mechanisms they employ \cite{Mechanism_Privacy_1, MSB}; an optimal algorithm from a privacy-maximalist perspective leaks no information to any party other than that necessary to inform the end-user of an exposure. Indeed, the Google-Apple Exposure Notification framework \cite{Apple_Google}, which is currently the predominant protocol adopted by numerous national tracing applications, is designed to reveal only the minimal information necessary to inform the end-user that they were exposed, as well as some metadata about the individual exposure(s). This provides virtually no data to third parties (including unfortunately public health officials), but instead is capable of providing a robust guarantee of user privacy protection against all but their contacts. The security analyses for these mechanisms are generally predicated upon concealing everything except for the result of the query (in this case, determining the exposure(s)), usually by utilizing cryptography. However, the result of the query itself leaks information; indeed, in any digital contact tracing application without strong validation of user identities---which is naturally difficult when user privacy needs to be protected---it is possible using only logarithmically many identities for a user or other institution (such as a business) to infer details about their own exposure events. By combining that information with a record of other information about their contacts, this enables revealing the infection status of any of their contacts (or perhaps customers) using the exposure notification system \cite{Inherent_limitations}. This privacy leak is agnostic to the algorithm employed, and is instead 'inherent' to digital contact tracing, because it simply requires making repeated valid queries to the contact tracing system. Fortunately, there exists substantial work in the scientific literature that has grappled with controlling the leakage of information from the output of database queries, and we can frame contact tracing as a form of distributed database query on the part of the end-user. By utilizing results from the differential privacy and statistical database privacy literature \cite{differential_privacy}, we may hope to protect against information leakage due to the output of the query. Unfortunately, there is often some trade-off between utility and privacy, and there is some minimum threshold of added noise needed to guarantee any particular level of privacy, which may diminish the accuracy of contact tracing. In this paper, we recast the problem of contact tracing as a special case of two other database query settings. First, a contact-tracing application needs to determine which of a user's contacts have been exposed in order to alert them; this can be conceived as a query for the ones in a binary database containing COVID statuses of the user's contacts. Alternatively, users of a contact-tracing application can be conceived as nodes in a simple graph, with edges denoting contact events with diagnosed users. In this setting, alerting the user can be conceived as recommending one node to another, as in social recommendation algorithms \cite{social_recommendation_survey}. We thus translate two results from the mathematical privacy literature to inherent limitations of contact-tracing applications. The first, from statistical databases \cite{dinur_nissim}, is a lower bound on the error of queries for the number of diagnosed contacts in subsets of a user's contact database below which an adversary can almost completely reconstruct the database. The second, from graph-based social recommendation algorithms \cite{GRS}, is an explicit trade-off between the (differential) privacy and accuracy of alerting some target user about their high-risk contacts. We carefully adapt the settings of these results in their original forms to the setting of a contact-tracing application, which will allow us to deduce the conditions under which they apply to contact-tracing. We then use these conditions to re-state the results as inherent privacy/accuracy trade-offs for digital contact tracing. Finally, we use specific numerical examples as the foundation for a discussion of the results

text: Over recent decades, multi-class classification has found application across numerous domains, including image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar,deng2009imagenet, geusebroek2005amsterdam,Hsu02multisvm}, natural language processing~\cite{lang1995newsweeder,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2005-14165,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1801-06146}, among others. Loss functions have served a crucial role in multi-class classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/JanochaC17,kornblith2021why}. Within machine learning (ML), the most conventional loss functions encompass the cross-entropy (CE) loss and the Crammer-Singer (CS) Loss (also known as the SVM loss). Prior to the deep learning epoch, the CS loss had been extensively investigated and employed for training linear or kernelized models~\cite{10.5555/944790.944813}. Nevertheless, during the deep learning era, the CE loss appears to predominate over the CS loss in practical applications~\cite{he2016deep}. One explanation is that the CE loss maintains consistency for multi-class classification (i.e., producing Bayes optimal classifiers with unlimited samples), whereas the CS loss generally lacks consistency except under the exceptional circumstance that the maximum conditional probability of a class label given the input exceeds $0.5$~\cite{10.5555/1005332.1044701}, which may apply to straightforward tasks such as MNIST classification but is improbable for complex tasks, e.g., ImageNet classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2006-07159,tsipras2020imagenet}. Nonetheless, the CE loss has been discovered to be susceptible to label noise~\cite{ghosh2017robust,wang2019symmetric}. Consequently, efforts have been dedicated to robustifying the CE loss to render it noise-tolerant. A sufficient condition for a loss function to exhibit noise-tolerance is recognized as the symmetric property~\cite{ghosh2017robust}, i.e., the summation of losses across all possible class labels for a specified data point remains constant. Following the symmetric property, numerous variants of CE loss have been developed to possess the noise-tolerance characteristic. However, a symmetric loss alone typically proves insufficient for achieving satisfactory performance in practice due to slow convergence~\cite{zhang2018generalized,ma2020normalized}. Therefore, a loss that interpolates between the CE loss and a symmetric loss generally attains superior performance on real-world noisy datasets~\cite{wang2019symmetric,zhang2018generalized,englesson2021generalized,ma2020normalized}, e.g., on the WebVision dataset with 20\% noisy data~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-02862}. These established results can be interpreted through the uncertainty degree of the provided label information. When the provided label information of an instance is certain (e.g., MNIST data), the CS loss represents a favorable choice~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/Tang13}; when the provided label information exhibits slight uncertainty (e.g., ImageNet data), the CE loss constitutes a superior choice; when the provided label information demonstrates high uncertainty (e.g., WebVision data), a loss that interpolates between the CE loss and a symmetric loss prevails. While parameter tuning (e.g., the weights for combining the CE loss and a symmetric loss) can accomplish dataset adaptivity, an open question persists: "\textit{Can we formulate a loss to achieve instance adaptivity, i.e., adaptivity to the uncertainty degree of label information for each instance?}" To address this inquiry, this paper proposes capturing the uncertainty in the provided label information of each instance through the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework. For any instance, we assign each class label a distributional weight and formulate the loss in the worst-case scenario of the distributional weights appropriately regularized by a function, which is termed label distributionally robust (LDR) losses. The advantages of employing the DRO framework to model the uncertainty of the provided label information include: (i) it furnishes a unified framework for numerous existing loss functions, including the CE loss, the CS loss, and several of their variants, e.g., top-$k$ SVM loss. (ii) it encompasses an intriguing family of losses by selecting the regularization function of the distributional weights as Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, which is designated as LDR-KL loss for multi-class classification. The LDR-KL loss is closely associated with the temperature-scaled CE loss that has been extensively utilized in other contexts~\cite{HinVin15Distilling,chen2020simple}, where the temperature corresponds to the regularization parameter of the distributional weights. Hence, our theoretical analysis of LDR-KL loss can potentially illuminate the application of temperature-scaled CE loss in different scenarios. (iii) The LDR-KL loss can interpolate between the CS loss (at one extreme), the (margin-aware) CE loss (in between) and a symmetric loss (at the other extreme) by varying the regularization parameter, thereby providing enhanced flexibility for adapting to the noise level of provided label information. Our contributions are the following: \begin{itemize}[noitemsep,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] \item We establish strong consistency of the LDR-KL loss namely All-$k$ consistency that represents top-$k$ consistency (corresponding to the Bayes optimal top-$k$ error) for all $k\geq 1$, and a sufficient condition for the general family of LDR losses to be All-$k$ consistent. \item We demonstrate that an extreme case of the LDR-KL loss satisfies the symmetric property, rendering it tolerant to label noise. Additionally, we establish a negative result that a non-negative symmetric loss function cannot achieve top-$k$ consistency for $k=1$ and $k=2$ simultaneously. Hence, we conclude that existing top-$1$ consistent symmetric losses cannot be All-$k$ consistent. \item We propose an adaptive LDR-KL loss, which enables us to automatically learn the personalized temperature parameter of each instance adapting to its individual noise level. We develop an efficient algorithm for empirical risk minimization based on the adaptive LDR-KL loss without incurring substantial additional computational overhead. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets under various noisy label settings, and demonstrate the stable and competitive performance of the proposed adaptive LDR-KL loss across all settings. \end{itemize}

text: A completely automated system that generates realistic 3D human bodies approaching and grasping a target object in 3D space would prove valuable across numerous fields, from robotics and animation to computer vision. Although significant progress has been achieved in synthesizing realistic hand--object interactions, most existing approaches exclusively focus on hand pose generation without considering whole-body movements~\cite{GRAB:2020, GrapingField:3DV:2020, jiang2021graspTTA}. Meanwhile, whole-body motion generation~\cite{holden2016deep, martinez2017human, hernandez2019human, MOJO} predominantly ignores the presence of objects in the scene. Modeling and generating realistic whole-body grasping motions present significant challenges and remain unresolved due to several factors. Initially, whole-body grasping motions encompass both full-body dynamics and dexterous finger movements~\cite{GRAB:2020}, while the high-dimensional degrees of freedom render the generation of grasping motions complex. Additionally, a whole-body grasping sequence demonstrates intricate and frequent body--scene and hand--object contacts which prove challenging to generate in a perceptually realistic manner. % For instance, the hand's surface must conform naturally to the object and there must be no foot-skating artifacts in the whole-body motion. Furthermore, given solely a starting pose and a target object in 3D space, there could exist infinite approaches for the person to approach and grasp the object. The diversity of plausible grasping motions becomes further amplified by the substantial potential variation in object shape and pose. How to construct an effective generative model that can capture this diversity and generate diverse realistic motions to grasp various 3D objects remains an unresolved question. % To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{SAGA} (\textbf{S}toch\textbf{A}stic whole-body \textbf{G}rasping with cont\textbf{A}ct), a novel whole-body grasping generation framework that can generate stochastic motions of a 3D human body approaching and grasping 3D objects. Our solution comprises two components: (1) a novel 3D body generator that generates diverse static whole-body grasping end poses, and (2) a novel human motion generator that creates diverse and plausible motions between given start and end poses. We present two key insights regarding both components. First, rather than directly utilizing parametric body models (e.g.~SMPL~\cite{SMPL-X:2019}) to represent 3D bodies, we employ the markers-based representation~\cite{MOJO} which captures 3D human shape and pose information with a set of sparse markers on the human body surface. As demonstrated in~\cite{MOJO}, the markers-based representation proves easier for neural networks to learn than the latent parameters of the parametric body models, yielding more realistic motion. We demonstrate that the markers-based representation proves especially advantageous to the latent body parameters for learning whole-body grasping, as the accumulation of errors along the kinematic chain significantly impacts the physical plausibility of generated hand grasps, resulting in severe hand--object interpenetration. Second, {\it contact} plays a central role in our pipeline. As the human moves in 3D space and grasps a 3D object, physical contact proves key for modeling realistic motions and interactions. For both components of our method, we learn contact representations from data and use them to guide interaction generation, greatly improving the realism of the generated motion.% For the static grasping pose generation, we constructed a multi-task conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to jointly learn whole-body marker positions and fine-grained marker--object contact labels. During inference, given a target object in 3D space, our model jointly generates a diverse set of consistent full-body marker locations and the contact labels on both the body markers and the object surface. A contact-aware pose optimization module further recovers a parametric body mesh from the predicted markers, while explicitly enforcing the hand--object contact by leveraging the predicted contact labels. Next, given the generated static whole-body grasping pose as the end pose, and an initial pose as a start pose, we propose a novel generative motion infilling network to capture motion uncertainty and generate diverse motions in between. We design a CVAE-based architecture to generate both the diverse in-between motion trajectories and the diverse in-between local pose articulations. In addition, contacts between feet and the ground are also predicted as a multi-task learning objective to enforce better foot-ground interaction. Furthermore, leveraging the predicted human--object contacts, we design a contact-aware motion optimization module to produce realistic grasp-oriented whole-body motions from the generated marker sequences. By leveraging the GRAB~\cite{GRAB:2020} and AMASS~\cite{AMASS:ICCV:2019} datasets to learn our generative models, our method can successfully generate realistic and diverse whole-body grasping motion sequences for approaching and grasping a variety of 3D objects. \myparagraph{Contributions.} In summary, we provide (1) a novel generative framework to generate diverse and realistic whole-body motions approaching and grasping various unseen objects for 3D humans that exhibit various body shapes, (2) a novel multi-task learning model to jointly learn the static whole-body grasping poses and the body--object interactions, (3) a novel generative motion infilling model that can stochastically infill both the global trajectories and the local pose articulations, yielding diverse and realistic full-body motions between a start pose and end pose. We perform extensive experiments to validate technical contributions. Experimental results demonstrate both the efficacy of our full pipeline and the superiority of each component to existing solutions.

The input to the problem is a random graph $G(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices, where for every pair $\{u,v\}$ of distinct vertices, $(u,v)\in E$ independently with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. To streamline some of the terminology, we occasionally refer to a pair $\{u,v\}$ of distinct vertices as an edge, irrespective of whether $(u,v)\in E$, but if $(u,v)\in E$ we refer to it as a positive edge, and if $(u,v)\not\in E$ we refer to it as a negative edge. The objective of the algorithm is to identify in $G$ a clique (a complete subgraph) that is as large as possible. The algorithm can access $G$ through queries to the adjacency matrix of $G$, querying an edge $\{u,v\}$ and receiving in response its status, whether it is positive or negative. We may conceptualize these queries as queries to a random oracle, where for each new query (not previously posed), the oracle responds positively with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and negatively with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, independently of all previous responses. The constraining resource for the algorithm is the total number of queries $q$, whereas the running time of the algorithm may be unbounded (e.g., exponential in $n$). The sequence of queries posed by the algorithm may be adaptive, in the sense that the selection of the next query depends on answers to previous queries. The results of the $q$ queries induce a graph $G'(V,E')$, where the edges of $G'$ are those edges that were queried and received a positive answer. Since the algorithm is not bounded in its computation time, it can determine the maximum clique in $G'$. Hence the objective of the querying process is to generate a graph $G'$ in which the maximum clique is as large as possible. We denote this maximum clique by $K$ and its size by $k$. Note that for any nontrivial algorithm (for which $k > 1$), $K$ (and likewise $k$) is a random variable that will depend on the input graph $G$. Hence for a given algorithm, we shall consider $k$ as the median value of the size of the clique that the algorithm finds. For reasons that will become apparent later, if $k$ is even our results are somewhat simpler to express. Hence, we shall assume that $k$ is even (this has negligible effect on the results, a difference of at most~1 in the size of the clique found). text: Sparsification represents the fundamental principle of diminishing the size of a large graph $G$ while preserving essential properties of the graph. Significant examples encompass spanners \cite{Chew89}, which approximately maintain distances up to a multiplicative factor, or cut and spectral sparsifiers \cite{BK96,ST04}, which preserve the cuts and Laplacian spectrum of the graph up to a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor. These \emph{edge sparsifiers} enable one to reduce problems on dense graphs to sparse graphs at the expense of an approximation factor arising from the sparsification. Conversely, several methods such as elimination-based Laplacian solvers \cite{KLPSS16}, necessitate \emph{vertex sparsification}, that is, diminishing the number of vertices in the graph. In this work, the notion of vertex sparsification that we examine is \emph{cut sparsification}, introduced by \cite{HKNR98,Moitra09,LM10}. In this problem, we are provided a graph $G$ and a set of \emph{terminals} $\mathcal{T} \subseteq V(G)$. Our objective is to construct a smaller graph $G'$ that approximates the value of all cuts in $G$ between terminals up to a multiplicative factor $q$, termed the \emph{quality} of the sparsifier. Specifically, we seek to construct a graph $G'$ also containing the terminals $\mathcal{T}$ among its vertices, such that for any subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{T}$, the minimum cut in $G$ (respectively $G'$) between $S$ and its complement $\mathcal{T} \backslash S$ differ by at most the multiplicative approximation $q$. Desirable characteristics of an algorithm for producing vertex sparsifiers include achieving quality $q$ close to $1$, while maintaining that the graph $G'$ constructed has few vertices, ideally nearly linear in the number of terminals, which we denote as $k = |\mathcal{T}|$. Furthermore, for applications we also desire for the runtime of the vertex sparsification algorithm to be polynomial or even linear in the size of the original graph $G$. Previous results attain various subsets of these characteristics. In the setting where the sparsifier $G'$ has vertex set exactly $\mathcal{T}$, an upper bound quality $q = O(\log k / \log\log k)$ was achieved \cite{Moitra09,LM10,CLLM10,EGKRTT14}, and a polynomial runtime was achieved by \cite{MM10}. In the setting where the quality $q = 1$, upper bounds of $2^{2^k}$ \cite{HKNR98,KR14} and lower bounds of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KR13} were achieved. Furthermore, \cite{KW12} achieved a bound of size $O(Z^3)$ for quality $q = 1$ in polynomial time for graphs with integer capacities, where $Z$ is the total degree of all terminals. Nevertheless, it remains unknown whether quality $q = 1+\varepsilon$ sparsifiers with $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(k/\varepsilon))$ vertices exist except in special cases \cite{AGK14,ADKKP16}. In this paper we present a vertex sparsification algorithm for $c$-edge connectivity, a thresholded version of cut sparsification, which preserves all cuts of size at most $c$ exactly, has size linear in the number of terminals and polynomial in $c$, and runs in polynomial time for all $c$ (\cref{thm:main}). This notion, which we term a \emph{connectivity-$c$ mimicking network}, was introduced in \cite{CDL21} to study dynamic connectivity problems and parametrized complexity, and has yielded the first fully dynamic online algorithm for $c$-connectivities with almost constant update time for constant $c$ \cite{JS20}. Specifically, we say that graph $G'$ is a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for $G$ with terminals $\mathcal{T}$ if all cuts between terminals in $G$ with at most $c$ edges are preserved exactly in $G'$. The previous algorithm of \cite{CDL21} which constructs a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network with $O(kc^4)$ edges does not run in polynomial time because it employs the idea of a well-linked decomposition from \cite{Chu12}, which requires an exact solution to a restricted version of the sparsest cut problem. Consequently, the algorithm's runtime depended exponentially on $c$. Our main contribution is to open up the matroid-based cut covering lemmas of \cite{KW12}, and combine this with a much weaker notion of a well-linked decomposition. Specifically, we avoid performing a full well-linked decomposition, and instead just partition the graph $G$ into pieces whose ``expansion'' with respect to terminals is not too small, similar to an expander decomposition. text: Reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success across numerous challenging domains. Noteworthy achievements include DQN~\cite{mnih2015human}, AlphaGo~\cite{silver2016mastering} and OpenAI Five~\cite{berner2019dota}. Nevertheless, most of these accomplishments require an extensive number of environmental interactions. For instance, AlphaZero ~\cite{silver2017mastering} requires playing 21 million games during training. In contrast, a professional human player can typically play approximately 5 games per day, implying that a human player would require 11,500 years to accumulate equivalent experience. The sample complexity may present fewer concerns when deploying RL algorithms in simulated environments and games. Nevertheless, for real-world applications, including robotic manipulation, healthcare, and advertisement recommendation systems, attaining high performance while preserving low sample complexity represents the fundamental requirement for practical viability. Researchers have achieved substantial progress in sample efficient RL during recent years~\cite{chua2018deep, deisenroth2011pilco, srinivas2020curl, laskin2020reinforcement, kostrikov2020image, schwarzerdata, kaiser2019model}. Among these approaches, model-based methods have garnered considerable attention, since both data from actual environments and the ``imagined data'' from the model can be utilized to train the policy, rendering these methods particularly sample-efficient~\cite{chua2018deep,deisenroth2011pilco}. Nevertheless, most successes have occurred in state-based environments. In image-based environments, certain model-based methods such as MuZero~\cite{schrittwieser2020mastering} and Dreamer V2~\cite{hafner2020mastering} attain super-human performance, but they lack sample efficiency; other methods such as SimPLe~\cite{kaiser2019model} demonstrate reasonable efficiency but achieve suboptimal performance (0.144 human normalized median scores). Recently, data-augmented and self-supervised methods applied to model-free approaches have demonstrated greater success in the data-efficient regime~\cite{schwarzerdata}. However, they continue to fall short of achieving levels comparable to human performance. Consequently, for enhancing sample efficiency while maintaining superior performance, we identify the following three components as essential to the model-based visual RL agent: a self-supervised environment model, a mechanism to mitigate the model compounding error, and a method to address the off-policy issue. In this work, we propose EfficientZero, a model-based RL algorithm that attains high performance with constrained data. Our proposed method builds upon MuZero. We implement three critical modifications: (1) employ self-supervised learning to learn a temporally consistent environment model, (2) learn the \textit{value prefix} in an end-to-end manner, thereby helping to mitigate the compounding error in the model, (3) utilize the learned model to correct off-policy value targets. As demonstrated in Figure \ref{fig:compare}, our model attains state-of-the-art performance on the widely adopted Atari~\cite{bellemare2013arcade} 100k benchmark and it achieves super-human performance with merely 2 hours of real-time gameplay. More precisely, our model achieves 194.3\% mean human normalized performance and 109.0\% median human normalized performance. As a reference, DQN~\cite{mnih2015human} attains 220\% mean human normalized performance, and 96\% median human normalized performance, at the expense of 500 times more data (200 million frames). To further validate the effectiveness of EfficientZero, we conduct experiments on several simulated robotics environments of the DeepMind Control (DMControl) suite. It attains state-of-the-art performance and surpasses the state SAC which directly learns from the ground truth states. Our sample efficient and high-performance algorithm creates the possibility of achieving greater impact on numerous real-world problems.

text: Throughout recent years, \ac{NBR} has garnered substantial attention from the research community \citep{fpmc,dream,bai2018attribute}. Baskets, or collections of items that are acquired or utilized collectively, are ubiquitous across numerous real-world applications, with e-commerce and grocery retail serving as notable examples~\citep{hao, raeder}. Given a chronological sequence of baskets that a user has previously acquired or utilized, the objective of an \ac{NBR} system is to predict the basket of items that the user will likely acquire or utilize subsequently. Within each basket, items possess no chronological ordering and maintain equivalent significance. A fundamental distinction between \ac{NBR} and session-based or sequential item recommendation lies in the fact that \ac{NBR} systems must handle multiple items within a single collection. Consequently, models developed for item-based recommendation are inadequate for basket-based recommendation, and specialized \ac{NBR} approaches have been developed~\citep{tifuknn, recency, dream, beacon, intnet, clea, sets2sets, sun2020timestamp2}. \subsection{Types of recommendation methods} Throughout recent years, we have observed the emergence of an extensive array of recommendation approaches. \emph{Frequency-based} approaches remain significant as they can effectively capture global statistics regarding item popularity; this principle applies to both item-based recommendation contexts and \ac{NBR} contexts. Likewise, \emph{nearest neighbor-based} approaches have been extensively employed for both item-based and basket-based recommendation contexts. More recently, deep learning methodologies have been developed to tackle sequential item recommendation challenges, leveraging the ability of deep learning-based approaches to identify latent relationships and automatically derive representations~\citep{batmaz-2019-deep}. Recent developments have also witnessed contributions addressing various dimensions of the \ac{NBR} problem using deep learning-based approaches, e.g., item-to-item relationships~\citep{beacon}, cross-basket relationships~\citep{dnntsp}, and noise present within baskets~\citep{clea}. Recent investigations suggest that deep learning-based methodologies may not achieve optimal performance across all recommendation problems and under all circumstances~\citep{jannach-2020-why}. For the problem of producing a personalized ranked item list, linear models and nearest neighbor-based methodologies surpass deep learning-based approaches~\citep{dacrema-2021-troubling}. For sequential recommendation challenges, deep learning-based approaches may be exceeded by straightforward nearest neighbor or graph-based baselines~\citep{dacrema-2019-are}. What regarding the problem of \acl{NBR}? In this context, the retrieval unit --- a basket -- exhibits greater complexity than in the recommendation contexts examined in~\citep{dacrema-2019-are,dacrema-2021-troubling,jannach-2020-why}, featuring intricate dependencies among items and baskets across temporal dimensions, thereby establishing potential for advanced representation learning-based methodologies for \ac{NBR} to achieve performance improvements. In this study, we conduct a detailed examination of the field to determine whether this holds true. \subsection{A new analysis perspective} We identify significant gaps and limitations within the \ac{NBR} literature. These encompass inadequate or absent baselines, the utilization of distinct datasets across different studies, and the employment of non-standardized metrics. We assess the performance of three categories of state-of-the-art \ac{NBR} models (frequency-based, nearest neighbor-based, and deep learning-based), across three benchmark datasets, and discover that no \ac{NBR} approach consistently surpasses all alternative approaches across all configurations. As we demonstrate in Figure~\ref{fig:re-nbr}, baskets recommended within an \ac{NBR} context comprise \emph{repeat items} (items that the user has previously utilized, in earlier baskets) and \emph{explore items} (items that are novel to the user). The novelty of recommended items has been examined previously, and corresponding metrics have been introduced~\citep{epc-epd}, but novelty-focused metrics are not \ac{NBR} specific and exclusively address one dimension, i.e., assessing the novelty of the recommendation list. To enhance our comprehension of the comparative performance of \ac{NBR} models, particularly concerning repeat items and explore items, we present a collection of task-specific metrics for \ac{NBR}. Our newly introduced metrics enable us to understand which item types are included in the recommended basket and evaluate the performance of \ac{NBR} models when suggesting novel items versus previously-purchased items. \subsection{Main findings} Armed with our newly introduced metrics for \ac{NBR}, we conduct our comprehensive comparison of \ac{NBR} models and reach the following significant conclusions: \begin{itemize} \item No \ac{NBR} approach consistently surpasses all alternative approaches across different datasets. \item All published approaches are substantially biased towards either repetition or exploration relative to the ground-truth, which may impair long-term engagement. \item There exists a substantial \ac{NBR} performance disparity between repetition and exploration; repeat item recommendation is considerably easier. \item In numerous configurations, deep learning-based \ac{NBR} approaches are exceeded by frequency-based baselines that populate a basket with the most frequent items in a user's history, potentially supplemented with items that are most frequent across all users. \item A preference towards repeat items explains most of the performance improvements of recently published approaches, despite many sophisticated modules or strategies specifically targeting explore items. \item We introduce a novel protocol for evaluating \ac{NBR} approaches, featuring a new frequency-based \ac{NBR} baseline along with new metrics to evaluate the potential performance improvements of \ac{NBR} approaches. \item Existing \acs{NBR} approaches exhibit different treatment effects on user performance and item exposure for users with varying repetition ratios and items with different frequencies, respectively. \end{itemize} \noindent% Overall, our research illuminates the current state of \ac{NBR}, offers recommendations to enhance our evaluation methodology for \ac{NBR}, enables us to comprehend the underlying causes of performance differences, and provides insights to guide the development of future \ac{NBR} models.
