text: With the increasing complexity of machine learning models, particularly those employed in recommendation systems, effectively and efficiently handling abundant input features has become a critical challenge. For online recommendation systems in industrial environments, models are frequently trained on billion-scale sparse features utilizing one-hot encoding~\cite{cheng2016wide,zhou2018din,DBLP:conf/cikm/ShengZZDDLYLZDZ21}. Each feature can also be regarded as a unique identifier, which is typically mapped to a low-dimensional embedding prior to being input into the model. A straightforward approach to managing large-scale input involves treating each feature independently. Under this methodology, a DNN can be directly trained to estimate CTR based on the combination (e.g., concatenation) of features where feature interaction depends on the implicit modeling of fully connected layers. Nevertheless, features such as ``candidate item'' and ``user click history'' in recommendation systems are highly correlated~\cite{zhou2018din,zhou2019dien}, i.e., co-occurrence information exists. Another representative example is the narrative of ``Beer and Nappies''. This type of feature interaction is advantageous for better CTR estimation. As demonstrated in Fig.\ref{fig:coaction}, when no feature interaction is considered, the influences of features A and B toward the final label (click or not in CTR prediction) are modeled independently, as depicted by the blue lines. Feature interaction illustrated in the grey line explicitly establishes the correlations of feature pair (A, B) to the target label and provides more valuable information for the learning objective. We will examine this more thoroughly in Sec. \ref{sec:revisit}. To model feature interaction, the most straightforward method is utilizing cartesian product. Given two features A and B, once features A and B are selected, the co-occurrence <A, B> is treated as a novel feature and input into the model. Since the co-occurrence information is provided directly through additional input, the training process becomes more manageable. Although the cartesian product is simple and effective, it possesses some significant limitations, such as enormous parameter volume and feature space, inadequate generalization capability. Different from cartesian product that introduces supplementary input information, several research endeavors have been dedicated to modeling feature interaction through careful combinations of input features. The representative examples are factorization based methods~\cite{rendle2010factorization,qu2016product,WangFFW2017DCN,lian2018xdeepfm,xiao2017attentional,song2019autoint} which emphasize both low- and/or high-order feature interactions by directly combining feature embeddings in latent vector space with various operators. As these methods consider feature interaction from modeling perspective and the operators are well-designed, they are typically more deployment-friendly compared with cartesian product. However, they still possess some drawbacks that are non-negligible. Unfortunately, the shallow structures of some factorization based methods \cite{juan2016field,WangFFW2017DCN} constrain their representative power. More critically, the embeddings generated by their operators assume the responsibility of representation learning and feature interaction modeling simultaneously which may impede the training process. This type of combination diminishes the memory capability of feature interactions, thereby degrading the model capacity. \author{Weijie Bian$\dagger$, Kailun Wu$\dagger$, Lejian Ren$\dagger$, Qi Pi$\dagger$, Yujing Zhang$\dagger$, Can Xiao$\dagger$} \author{Xiang-Rong Sheng$\dagger$, Yong-Nan Zhu$\dagger$, Zhangming Chan$\dagger$, Na Mou$\dagger$, Xinchen Luo$\dagger$} \author{Shiming Xiang$\ddagger$, Guorui Zhou$\dagger$, Xiaoqiang Zhu$\dagger$, Hongbo Deng$\dagger$} \authornote{Hongbo Deng is the corresponding author (dhb167148@alibaba-inc.com).} \affiliation{% \institution{$\dagger$Alibaba Group\qquad \qquad \qquad$\ddagger$Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences} \city{Beijing} \country{China} } \email{{weijie.bwj,kailun.wukailun,lejian.rlj,dhb167148}@alibaba-inc.com} To address these issues, we propose \textbf{C}o-\textbf{A}ction \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{CAN}) that can capture feature interaction and utilize the mutual and common information of different feature pairs effectively. Specifically, for each feature pair, the embeddings of one side (induction feature) are employed to construct an MLP applied to the other side (feed feature) in the co-action unit. This paradigm of feature interaction modeling reduces the additional parameter from $O(N^2 \times D)$ to $O(N\times (D' + D))$ ($N$ is the number of features, $D$ and $D'$ are the dimensions of parameter used in co-action unit, $D < D' \ll N$) compared with cartesian product. Furthermore, CAN provides more powerful fitting capability and better non-linearity using MLP in the co-action unit compared with traditional factorization based methods. Additionally, CAN differentiates the parameter space for representation learning and feature interaction modeling to prevent mutual interference in training. Multi-order enhancement and multi-level independence are further utilized to enrich the expression capability in CAN. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item We investigate the effectiveness of cartesian product and identify the potential of implicit feature interaction modeling. Inspired by the independent coding of cartesian product, we design a novel feature interaction paradigm that has comparable performance compared with cartesian product yet has substantially less resource consumption. \item We propose Co-Action Network (CAN) to model feature interaction among raw features at the input stage. Each feature ID in CAN will be distributed to an individual micro-MLP to model the interaction with other features. In this manner, CAN improves the expressive capability of modeling feature interaction under limited parameters. The individual micro-MLP has a more powerful expressive capability than the ordinary operators utilized in factorization based methods. \item We conduct extensive experiments on both public and industrial datasets. The consistent superiority validates the effectiveness of CAN in modeling feature interaction compared with other state-of-the-art competitors. The deployment of CAN brings 12\% CTR and 8\% RPM lift in Alibaba's display advertisement system. \end{itemize}

text: {\bf Motivation}. Stack Overflow\footnote{https://stackoverflow.com/} represents one of the most widely utilized platforms for users to pose and respond to inquiries regarding software development topics. Since its establishment in 2008, the platform has been extensively employed by both professional software developers and dedicated programmers to exchange and enhance their knowledge. As of September 2019, Stack Overflow has garnered over 10.9M users and 18.1M questions. The platform's volume continues to expand with more than 150K new questions generated monthly\footnote{https://data.stackexchange.com/}. The accelerated expansion of the Stack Overflow platform presents challenges for content management and maintaining its appeal. Given its extensive dataset (in terms of questions), manual management proves highly expensive and burdensome for the platform's moderators \cite{moder2019, workload2019}. Consequently, there exists an urgent requirement for automated methods that facilitate effective management of the platform's content. This requirement has captured the interest of various researchers in recent years \cite{Ashton2012, anton2014, Sebastian2019}. Although numerous existing studies focus on Stack Overflow, only a limited number target automated management and data cleaning. Additionally, most previous research concentrates on detecting and filtering low-quality or duplicate questions \cite{Muhammad2016, denzil2013, Denzil14}. In this investigation, we propose that it becomes reasonable to discard even high-quality questions once they no longer align with users' collective information requirements, such as when the question pertains to an obsolete version of software or a library. Maintaining these irrelevant questions, on one hand, elevates the expense of data storage and retrieval while generating minimal or no value. On the other hand, the existence of superfluous information impacts user experience, potentially causing user dissatisfaction and driving them away from the platform. We introduce the concept of "forgetting" such unappealing questions, namely allowing them to recede from users' perception in a manner remarkably similar to how irrelevant memories fade away. As an initial step, in this study, we address the problem of identifying such quality-but-irrelevant content in Stack Overflow by examining the early identification of questions that are initially frequently encountered but will become less significant and diminish over time. Specifically, these comprise questions that were commonly asked and (1) extensively viewed recently by numerous users confronting similar issues, but then (2) will attract minimal views in the future. We designate these as \emph{forgotten questions}. We present an example of a forgotten question in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}. This question was established in 2008 and extensively viewed until late 2017. Particularly, it received 710 views in the final 6 months of 2017. However, it attracted only minimal views during the recent 6 months. {\bf Research Objectives}. Our analysis demonstrates that questions are not forgotten rapidly, but at a gradual pace. That is, in most instances, it requires years for a highly viewed question to become forgotten. Moreover, prediction for the distant future is neither accurate nor practical. We therefore concentrate on questions that are in the process of being forgotten in the immediate future. Specifically, given a question that is extensively viewed in the recent period, we aim to predict if the question's view count will decrease substantially in the subsequent period. For instance, in the example presented in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}, at time point 12/2017, where the question was extensively viewed, rather than predicting if the question will be forgotten after 2 years, we would prefer to predict if its view count will decline in the next 3 or 6 months. Our work here is inspired by the concept of managed forgetting~\cite{claudia2018}: items of diminishing importance are de-emphasized for enhancing focus on significant matters - remarkably similar to the function of forgetting in human cognitive processes~\cite{David2007}. Particularly, we seek to examine factors suggested by prior literature and general intuition that might influence the process of being forgotten of high-quality questions in Stack Overflow. Furthermore, we also develop a framework for early detection of such questions. This forgetting management framework can serve as an effective step to guide moderators to focus more attention and implement further actions for unnecessary content. It also assists in bringing more significant information to users and encouraging user engagement. For example, experienced developers would be more interested in recently highly viewed questions and are motivated to interact with them. Subsequently, this helps to enhance the ranking of these questions by search engines and makes it easier for users to search for information they currently require. It is crucial to emphasize that our problem differs from and complements other content-driven works such as \cite{Haoxiang2019}, which examines questions' answers for detecting obsolete content within questions. Such content is either no longer accurate at creation time or is becoming inaccurate in the near future. In contrast, the forgetting of questions can be triggered by numerous reasons, in which becoming incorrect or outdated is merely one of them. {\bf Contributions}. We summarize our primary contributions in this work as follows. \begin{itemize} \item We present the first study of forgetting management on Stack Overflow. We demonstrate that the forgetting process is prevalent among high-quality questions though at a rather gradual pace. \item We investigate a comprehensive range of factors that may influence questions being forgotten, and examine their capability as predictors for questions being forgotten. \item We examine the performance of several prediction models in identifying questions that are being forgotten. We identify some categories in which the questions being forgotten are more predictable though the prediction task is generally challenging. We also demonstrate the predictiveness of different feature groups and analyze their relative importance in those models. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 presents a description of the utilized Stack Overflow dataset as well as our study of forgotten questions. We then conduct experiments using a machine learning framework to predict forgotten questions on Stack Overflow in Section 4. We discuss some factors that can influence our forgetting prediction task in Section 5. Finally, we summarize our main contribution and discuss some promising directions for future work in Section 6.

text: A prevalent methodology for explanation generation in automated planning involves treating the problem as one of model reconciliation~\cite{chakraborti2017plan}. Through this approach, equilibrium can be achieved between generating explanations that revise the user's environmental model and selecting explicable action sequences, which require no additional explanation. Central to this methodology is an accurate user model, which proves impractical in numerous applications. An alternative perspective considers explanations within the broader framework of interaction. Humans employ a diverse array of communicative modalities during interaction, generating both deliberate and unconscious responses, while also utilizing various behavioral heuristics. To communicate effectively, an interactive agent must possess the capability to detect and interpret these signals or, ideally, anticipate them. Within this framework, we are developing a user study to examine human behavior and responses in collaborative task interaction with a plan-based agent. Although we anticipate this study will validate and expand upon prior research investigating collaborative task interaction, our primary objective centers on identifying how concepts associated with plan-based agents (e.g., plan generation, agent intention) can be leveraged to guide the agent's behavior. We have characterized plan-based agent behaviors that interface with fundamental aspects of collaborative task interaction (e.g., uncertainty and knowledge disparities). These behaviors have been employed to specify two distinct agents: a reactive agent, which embodies an initial interaction, e.g., where minimal information exists regarding the human's preferences and potentially the environment; and a partially predictive agent, which embodies a more knowledgeable agent that furnishes information proactively and endeavors to preemptively mitigate user uncertainty. Through collecting both quantitative and qualitative data from humans interacting with these agents, we aspire to develop enhanced understanding of how such agents could be engineered to achieve greater human acceptability. As part of this research, we have constructed a web-based user study that we are presently preparing to implement. The platform facilitates collaborative task interaction, where the human user must accomplish a task with assistance from an instruction/explanation providing virtual agent. In this paper, we describe the objectives of our user study, the scenarios that participants will experience and the research questions we are investigating. We also describe the agents that will be evaluated in the study and the dimensions of collaborative task interaction that they enable us to explore. While we do not yet possess results from users, we present an empirical analysis to contrast the strategies and explanations produced by each of the agent types. We initially present an overview of the collaborative task setting and the requisite planning background. We describe aspects of plan-based agent behavior that are pertinent to collaborative task interactions and subsequently utilize these to specify two distinct agents. We describe our proposed user study, an empirical analysis, related work and finally conclude.

text: \IEEEPARstart{C}ivil drones have constituted a prominent topic for a decade. Remarkably, this interest is distributed among industry, academia, business, and civil society. In May 2021, Morgan Stanley published their long-term forecast \cite{MS} indicating that by 2050 three decades from now) the aggregate market of urban air mobility (delivery, air taxi, patrolling drones, to name a few) will achieve \$9 tn (5-6\% of projected global GDP) or even \$19 tn (11-12\% of projected global GDP) in the "bull case". Technology giants like Amazon, Google, and Uber maintain projects devoted to drones. Aircraft manufacturers develop air taxis. Academia demonstrates considerable activity in this field: currently, approximately 300 000 research documents can be located in Scopus through a keyword search string comprising "drone" and its synonyms such as Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), Unmanned Aircraft, and Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS). Even when the scope is restricted to wireless communication, the interest remains substantial and is comprehensively summarized in several tutorial and survey papers \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} based on hundreds of selected research articles. Despite this enthusiasm from various stakeholders, drones are not integrated into our daily life. The prevailing opinion among industry and academia is that regulatory and certification constraints constitute the primary barriers. For instance, although articles \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} are technical, they emphasize this challenge. Furthermore, the authors of \cite{MS} assert that \textit{the regulatory requirements for aviation is one of the most underestimated risks}. Indeed, in 2021, Morgan Stanley reduced their estimation of the anticipated market size by 30\% compared to their previous Blue paper released in 2018. One of the principal reasons was "near-term hurdles related to regulation and certification". Conversely, we are far from considering that the regulatory bodies are malevolent. We recognize that managing and regulating technological innovation constitutes a complex undertaking since numerous stakeholders are involved: from civil society to security agencies, from university researchers to influential and resourceful companies. Partially, the restrictive policies address the public concerns regarding relatively low trust in the technology. Moreover, unmanned aviation represents a novel area with numerous uncertainties and knowledge gaps. Since academic researchers are frequently public servants, we should strive to close the pertinent gaps and address public concerns. By performing this work, we will assist policymakers while promoting balanced and harmonious technological development. Thus, the initial step is to identify the relevant problems and then appropriately resolve them. 300 000 published research items indicate that academia excels at identifying problems; the absence of drones around suggests that the problems are not always pertinent. This article aims at adopting a broader perspective on drone technology and evaluating the problems that are significant for all major stakeholders involved in the technology development. This work builds upon the accomplishments of Technology Assessment (TA). TA is an interdisciplinary research field aimed at providing knowledge for better-informed and well-reflected decisions concerning new technologies \cite{gw09}. It supplies information that could assist the stakeholders (policymakers, citizens, engineers, etc.) in developing their strategies and courses of action \cite{TA_toolkit_98}. TA can also be applied to specific technical products, processes, services, systems \cite{gw09}. It is utilized by various agencies and commissions of the European Union, the U.S. Government Accountability Office, national research councils. In China, New Zealand, Italy, Canada and numerous other countries, TA is extensively employed in sensitive areas such as healthcare. In this article, we employ TA to identify pertinent problems and evaluate the current solutions aimed at resolving those problems. Through this approach, we will indicate relevant research directions for the wireless communications community. Moreover, using TA, we provide tools for selecting appropriate research and development project scope and framework to enhance the project efficiency while considering the project nature, technology readiness, and other relevant factors.

text: COVID-19 has accelerated the widespread adoption of telehealth services \cite{Wosik2020}, resulting in increases exceeding 100\% for virtual urgent care consultations and surpassing 4000\% for virtual non-urgent care encounters \cite{telemedicine}. A conventional virtual consultation commences with patients articulating their reason for the encounter or visit (RFE) \cite{who}. Subsequently, utilizing the RFE as input, an automated history-taking algorithm collects additional information encompassing details regarding presenting symptoms, and ultimately patients are connected to practitioners via chat (video or text-based). This paper concentrates on an intermediate implicit phase of identifying symptoms within the patient's RFE, as this process constitutes the foundation for automated history collection. Note that this relates to the medical named entity recognition task wherein the objective has been extracting symptoms from clinical documentation in electronic health records (c.f.\cite{Baumel18} and references therein). In contrast, we concentrate on medical entity recognition from patient-generated text; because patient text (RFEs) exhibits less standardization and frequently expresses symptoms using colloquial language. Figure ~\ref{fig:ml4hp} displays several example RFEs from the dataset employed in our study. Developing a model for medical symptom recognition presents several challenges: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Access}: Since no publicly accessible dataset exists, any emerging telehealth platform seeking to construct its machine learning solution must commence with a limited set of labeled data points and rapidly expand the scope. This also indicates that as we augment the number of labeled data points, the system may require recognition of novel symptoms that were previously unidentified. \item \textbf{Multilabel distribution}: Multiple symptoms may exist within a given RFE, and \emph{all} symptoms must be extracted to enable proper execution of automated history taking. \item \textbf{Long-tailed distribution}: Certain symptoms are prevalent while numerous symptoms tend to co-occur. This implicitly creates asymmetry and long-tail characteristics in data distribution (Figure~\ref{fig:ml4hp}). This is further complicated by the distribution of patient populations on the telehealth platform. \end{enumerate} Considering these challenges, in this work, we propose a novel active learning algorithm for efficiently gathering data labels. The primary intuition underlying our algorithm is as follows: RFEs form distinctive clusters that are medically grounded through underlying health conditions. Therefore, the proposed algorithm selects informative examples by inducing clusterings within the latent space of unlabeled examples and choosing those that maximally encompass that clustering. By achieving the appropriate balance between selecting points proximate to cluster centroids and points distant from labeled RFEs, we can address the problem of long-tail distribution. Our experiments demonstrate that our model surpasses the state-of-the-art on multi-label classification tasks and can handle long-tailed distribution in our dataset. Ablation studies and qualitative analyses provide additional insight into the advantages of our approach. \subsection*{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} Deep learning has been implemented across various healthcare applications in recent years. One primary characteristic of utilizing deep learning for healthcare involves addressing the shortage of large annotated datasets. Collecting a large labeled dataset is typically expensive and time-intensive as annotations must be provided by healthcare professionals, and datasets cannot be readily shared between institutions when handling sensitive and high-risk data. Conversely, deep models generally require large datasets to perform accurately and robustly. Consequently, many AI applications in healthcare remain inaccessible, and substantial real-world impacts are postponed. Most previous research on active learning focuses on classification when the dataset maintains balance. However, in numerous healthcare applications, the dataset exhibits a long-tailed distribution, and the task involves identifying all correct labels (rather than the single correct class). Similarly, previous active learning strategies typically assume that only one label remains valid per data point. In our paper, we demonstrate the significance of ``multilabel'' classification - a data point can possess multiple correct labels. Equally important, for each data point, correctly identifying all labels and avoiding omissions is of critical importance for the subsequent task of history taking. In this work, we propose a novel algorithm for actively selecting the most informative examples to label for the multi-label classification task. Our method utilizes the latent space of the machine learning model to address the long-tailed distribution of data and to select a diverse set of data points covering an extensive range of inputs.

However, in a large number of medical applications, the distribution of the data is long-tailed, and the task is to find all the valid labels (not just the one that is correct). In our paper we illustrate the significance of multi-label classification: a single data point may have several correct labels. In the same way, for each data point, determining all labels and avoiding missing any is of paramount importance for the subsequent task of history taking. In this work we propose a novel approach to actively choosing the most informative examples to label for the multi-label classification task. The latent space of a machine-learning model is used to overcome the problem of the fat-tailed distribution of data by selecting a diverse set of data points covering a wide range of inputs.

text: Empowering autonomous robots to accomplish diverse and complex manipulation tasks has constituted a grand challenge for decades. In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches have achieved significant progress toward designing robot manipulation behaviors that are challenging to engineer manually~\cite{kalashnikov2018qtopt, openai2019learning,openai2019solving,kalashnikov2021mtopt}. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art DRL models demonstrate limitations in long-horizon tasks due to the exploration challenge --- the robot must explore a prohibitively large space of possible behaviors for task completion. To alleviate the exploration burden, prior DRL work has developed various temporal abstraction frameworks to exploit the hierarchical structure of manipulation tasks~\cite{coreyes18sectar,nachum2018hiro,bacon2016optioncritic,eysenbach2019sorb}. These methods learn low-level controllers, often modeled as \textit{skills} or \textit{options}, together with high-level controllers from trial-and-error. While they have demonstrated superior scalability compared to vanilla DRL methods, they often suffer from high sample complexity, lack of interpretability, and fragile generalization. Meanwhile, decades-long research in robotics has developed a rich repertoire of functional modules specialized for particular robot behaviors, such as grasping~\cite{bohg2014graspsurvey} and motion planning~\cite{karaman2011rrtstar,ijspeert2013dmps}. These pre-built functional modules, which we refer to as \emph{behavior primitives}, exhibit a high degree of robustness and reusability for achieving certain manipulation goals, such as picking up objects with the end-effector and moving the robot to a target configuration in a collision-free path. Despite their specialties, it remains challenging for DRL algorithms to utilize them as the building blocks to scaffold complex tasks. The challenge is primarily due to the fact that these behavior primitives are \textit{heterogeneous} by design. They accept non-uniform parameters as input, operate at varying temporal resolutions, and exhibit distinct behaviors. This thus requires an algorithm to reason about the temporal decomposition of a complex task and adaptively compose these behavior primitives accordingly. A variety of hierarchical modeling approaches in robotics have utilized behavior modules as low-level building blocks. Notably, task-and-motion planning~\cite{kaelbling2011hpn, garrett2020tamp, wang2021comptamp} and neural programming~\cite{xu2018neural, huang2019neural} methods have employed primitives such as motion planners and pick-and-place controllers to model manipulation tasks in a compositional fashion. They require well-specified domain knowledge to perform task planning or strong human supervision to train a high-level controller with ground-truth task decomposition. These assumptions limit the scalability of these methods in realistic tasks. In this work, we introduce MAPLE~(\textbf{Ma}nipulation \textbf{P}rimitive-augmented reinforcement \textbf{Le}arning), a general DRL algorithm that harnesses a set of pre-built behavior primitives for solving long-horizon manipulation tasks. To address the exploration challenge of DRL algorithms, our method employs a library of high-level behavior primitives (such as grasping or pushing objects) in conjunction with low-level motor actions to autonomously learn a hierarchical policy (see \cref{fig:overview}). Our algorithm models each behavior primitive as an implementation-agnostic controller that produces a temporally extended behavior. At a given state, our DRL policy invokes a behavior primitive (or an atomic motor action) and instantiates it with input parameters. For example, the input parameters to a 6-DoF grasping module can be the pre-grasp end-effector pose. The selected primitive interprets the input parameters and executes one or a sequence of motor actions to realize its specialized behavior. By integrating behavior primitives into DRL algorithms, MAPLE~abstracts away a substantial portion of complexity in manipulation planning, while preserving the flexibility for a generic reinforcement learning algorithm to discover the compositional structure of tasks without strong domain knowledge. Furthermore, by retaining low-level motor actions MAPLE~can rely on these actions for the stages of tasks where the finite library of behavior primitives is insufficient to express a desired behavior. We conduct an extensive set of experiments on a suite of eight manipulation tasks of varying complexities in the robosuite simulation framework~\cite{robosuite2020}. We compare our method to standard DRL approaches~\cite{haarnoja2018sac} that only utilize low-level motor actions, hierarchical DRL methods that learn options~\cite{zhang2019dac,nachum2018hiro,chitnis2020schema} or open-loop task schemas~\cite{chitnis2020schema}. MAPLE~achieves a $70\%$ increase in task success rate compared to using only atomic actions, becoming the only method that consistently solved all single-arm tasks in the standard robosuite benchmark. We also devise a data-driven metric to quantitatively examine the compositionality of manipulation tasks contingent on the available primitives, offering new insight into the challenges and opportunities of compositional modeling for realistic manipulation tasks. We highlight three contributions of this work: 1) We develop a novel method that augments standard DRL algorithms with pre-defined behavior primitives to reduce the exploration burden; 2) We validate the effectiveness of our method in solving diverse manipulation tasks and quantitatively analyze the compositional structure of these tasks; and 3) We demonstrate that the modularity and abstraction offered by the behavior primitives facilitate knowledge transfer of the learned policies to new task variants and physical hardware.

text: \input{images/figure1} Natural language processing (NLP) systems are available for only a small portion of the world's more than 6,000 living languages, with the primary constraint being the absence of resources necessary for training and evaluating models. Technological developments remain concentrated on languages with readily accessible data, while most other languages are neglected~\cite{joshi2020state}. This phenomenon is especially pronounced for endangered languages, namely languages at risk of extinction due to declining numbers of native speakers and younger generations transitioning to alternative languages. For the majority of endangered languages, locating \emph{any} data whatsoever presents significant challenges. In numerous instances, natural language text in these languages does exist. Nevertheless, it remains inaccessible in formats that are not machine-readable --- printed books, scanned images, and unstructured web pages. These encompass books from local publishing houses within communities that speak endangered languages, including educational or cultural materials. Furthermore, linguists documenting these languages also generate data such as word lists and interlinear glosses, frequently in the form of handwritten notes. Examples from such scanned documents are presented in~\autoref{fig:dataset_example}. Digitizing the textual data from these sources will not only facilitate NLP for endangered languages but also support linguistic documentation, preservation, and accessibility initiatives. In this work, we develop a benchmark dataset and propose a suite of methods to extract data from these resources, concentrating on scanned images of paper books containing endangered language text. Conventionally, this type of digitization requires an optical character recognition (OCR) system. However, the substantial amounts of textual data and transcribed images required to train state-of-the-art OCR models from scratch are unavailable in the endangered language context. Instead, we concentrate on \emph{post-correcting} the output of an off-the-shelf OCR tool that can process a variety of scripts. We demonstrate that targeted methods for post-correction can substantially improve performance on endangered languages. Although OCR post-correction is relatively well-established, most existing methods depend on considerable resources in the target language, including a substantial amount of textual data to train a language model~\cite{schnober-etal-2016-still,dong-smith-2018-multi,8978127} or to generate synthetic data~\cite{krishna-etal-2018-upcycle}. While readily accessible for high-resource languages, these resources are severely constrained in endangered languages, precluding the direct application of existing post-correction methods in our context. As an alternative, we present a method that builds upon previous models for OCR post-correction, implementing three improvements tailored to the data-scarce environment. First, we employ a \textbf{multi-source model} to incorporate information from the high-resource translations that commonly appear in endangered language books. These translations are typically in the \textit{lingua franca} of the region (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (a,b,c)) or the documentary linguist's primary language (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (d) from \citet{shangaji-elar}). Next, we introduce \textbf{structural biases} to facilitate learning from small amounts of data. Finally, we incorporate \textbf{pretraining methods} to utilize the limited unannotated data that exists in endangered languages. \medskip \noindent We summarize our main contributions as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt] \item A benchmark dataset for OCR post-correction on three critically endangered languages: Ainu, Griko, and Yakkha. \item A systematic analysis of a general-purpose OCR system, demonstrating that it lacks robustness in the data-scarce setting of endangered languages. \item An OCR post-correction method that adapts the standard neural encoder-decoder framework to the highly under-resourced endangered language setting, reducing both the character error rate and the word error rate by 34\% over a state-of-the-art general-purpose OCR system. \end{itemize}

text: Operating a vehicle in real-world environments, characterized by continuously evolving dynamics and populated with various actors (i.e., non-player characters or NPCs), constitutes an inherently hazardous undertaking. Every actor within the environment can substantially affect the driving decisions of the Ego actor\footnote{Actor that is being tested and is under the control of the tester.} and constrain the available options regarding navigation and safety planning. Under extreme circumstances, these actors, whether intentionally or inadvertently, may compromise the Ego actor's capacity to safely accomplish the designated task. Consequently, every actor present in the environment represents a potential risk to the Ego actor. In this work, we characterize the risk presented by an actor through estimating its influence on the Ego actor's decision-making process within a specified environment. Evidently, the risk constitutes a function of: \begin{enumerate*}[label=(\roman*)] \item the environment (i.e., driving scenario), and \item uncertainty associated with determining the future trajectories by the Ego actor. \end{enumerate*} \textbf{Driving scenario.} A driving scenario constitutes the specification of the Ego actor's initial position and the trajectories of NPCs. With every additional NPC present on the roadway, safe trajectories available to the Ego actor (i.e., the navigable space) may become substantially constrained. Likewise, particular locations within the environment present greater risk than others, as the navigable space may exhibit considerable variation from one location to another (e.g., operating within construction zones). This reduction in safe trajectories corresponds to increased risk because it demands more vigilant driving and diminishes the contingency options available to the Ego agent during unforeseen circumstances. This concept is illustrated in \cref{fig:motivation}(a). \textbf{Uncertainty.} Risk escalates when the future trajectory of NPCs cannot be accurately predicted by the Ego actor. Prediction accuracy deteriorates due to ambiguous intentions or abrupt changes in the intentions of other participants within the driving environment (e.g., a pedestrian suddenly deciding to halt or run, emergency braking or mechanical failure of other vehicles), measurement noise (e.g., resulting from adverse weather conditions), or imperfections in ML/AI models (e.g., failure to detect pedestrians). This phenomenon is illustrated in \cref{fig:motivation}(b) It should be noted that human drivers implicitly and continuously evaluate the risk associated with both the driving scenario and uncertainties in other actors' actions to maintain safe operation. Accidents occur when human drivers fail to properly assess risk, which may happen when (i) driving under the influence or otherwise distracted, (ii) involving less than fully competent drivers, and (iii) expectation mismatches occur because an actor violated traffic regulations or executed sudden actions (e.g., abrupt braking). It is unsurprising that risk becomes amplified in cases involving AI/ML-operated actors due to aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Therefore, it becomes critically important to develop methodologies and models for quantifying and characterizing this risk during runtime to not only ensure safety (through risk minimization) but also understand/identify situations where risk remains irreducible in order to prepare passengers for imminent collision through emergency braking or airbag deployment. In this work, we demonstrate the practical significance of risk metrics and their importance for ensuring safety. The primary contributions of this research lie in defining a novel risk metric and demonstrating the application of the proposed metric to quantify the relative risk associated with each actor within real-world driving scenarios. Although this paper focuses exclusively on self-driving cars as a use case, our framework remains general and can be applied to other autonomous systems such as aerial vehicles or ML-driven computer systems. \textbf{Related work.} There exist primarily two research directions associated with defensive driving: (i) identifying safe distances from other actors under the assumption that everyone adheres to ``duty-of-care'' policies, (ii) identifying out-of-training-distribution (OOD) scenarios to plan for worst-case collision avoidance. \textit{Duty-of-care approaches} such as Safety Force Field (SFF)~\cite{SafetyForceField} and Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS)~\cite{shalev2017formal} are designed to estimate safe distances from other actors assuming universal compliance with traffic regulations. Additionally, the objective involves identifying the responsible party in cases of safety hazards. \textit{OOD} models such as \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a} are designed to identify driving scenarios where the Ego actor's future trajectory (i.e., plan) exhibits significant variance. Such variance can be characterized through ensemble models or diverse datasets. Under conditions of high variance, the Ego actor selects the most conservative plan to avoid collisions. For instance, in \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a}, the Ego actor's plan is generated using a Bayesian imitative model, and the variance of the imitation prior relative to the model posterior serves as a proxy for identifying distribution shifts. Upon detecting distribution shift, the Ego actor may either plan for the worst-case model or the average model. Finally, in another research direction~\cite{Philion_2020_CVPR}, authors quantify the impact of uncertainty on driving performance, but do not assess the quality of the generated plan regarding its safety. In contrast, our objective is to (i) assign risk associated with an actor or driving scenario by characterizing its negative influence on the degree of freedom of the Ego actor's navigational choices, (ii) quantify the risk associated with the current plan and proactively mitigate safety hazards. This approach enables us to identify compelling driving scenarios in offline mode, and to select the safest plan to help the Ego actor operate defensively.

In extreme circumstances, the actor, whether deliberately or accidentally, may compromise the ego actor's ability to execute a task. Hence, every actor present in the environment represents a potential risk for the ego actor. The ego actor's risk is evidently a function of: i) the environment (the driving scenario) and ii) the uncertainty associated with determining the Ego Actor's future trajectories. A driving scenario is the specification of the Ego Actor's initial position and the trajectories of the NPCs. With every additional NPC present on the road, the safe trajectories available to the Ego-actor (i.e., the navigable space) may be greatly reduced. This reduction in the navigable space corresponds to increased risk because it requires more attentive driving and limits the ego-actor's opportunities for counter-measures in the event of unforeseen circumstances. In the same way, certain points in the environment can also be more dangerous than others, since the navigable space can vary considerably from one point to another (for example, the maneuvering in a construction area). Risk increases when the future course of NPCs is not accurately predicted by the Ego actor. This is illustrated in fig. (a). It is important to note that human drivers continuously evaluate the risk of their driving scenario and the uncertainties of the actions of other actors to ensure safe operation. Accidents occur when human drivers do not assess the risk properly, which can occur if they are driving under the influence of alcohol or other drugs, if they are driving in a less than perfect way, if their expectations are not in accordance with the traffic regulations (for example, if a pedestrian suddenly stops or runs, or if another vehicle suddenly brakes or breaks down) or if the predictions are deviated by the ambiguous intention or the sudden intention of other participants in the driving environment (e.g. a pedestrian suddenly decides to stop or run, or a car suddenly breaks down or is not able to stop), due to measurement noise (e.g. due to adverse weather conditions) or due to the shortcomings of ML/AI models (e.g. failure to detect pedestrians). This phenomenon is illustrated in figure (b). In this work we demonstrate the practical significance of risk metrics and their importance for ensuring safety. It is not surprising that risk becomes augmented in cases of AI/ML-controlled agents because of aleatory and epistemic uncertainty. It thus becomes extremely important to develop models and methods for analyzing and characterizing the risk during operation to not only ensure safety (through risk reduction) but also to understand and identify situations where the risk cannot be reduced and prepare the passengers for imminent collision by emergency braking or airbag deployment. The main contributions of this work consist in defining a novel risk metric and demonstrating the application of the proposed metric to quantify the relative risk associated with each actor in real-world driving scenarios. Although this paper focuses exclusively on self-driving cars as a use case, our framework remains general and can be applied to other autonomous systems such as unmanned aerial vehicles or Machine Learning-based systems. For a more in-depth look at our framework, please see our related work: Several approaches have been developed to ensure a 'duty of care', such as the Safety Force Field (SFF) and Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS), with the goal of establishing safe distances from other agents under the assumption of universal compliance with traffic regulations. These methods are designed to identify the liable party in cases of hazards. OOD models, such as [19] pmmr-v119-filos20a, are intended to detect driving situations where the Ego actor's future trajectory (i.e., plan) shows significant variability. This variability can be characterized through the use of ensembles or multiple datasets. Under conditions of high variability, the Ego actor selects the most conservative plan to avoid collisions. The authors, in another research direction, cited as Philipon_2020_CVPR,7 quantified the impact of uncertainty on the performance of the vehicle, but did not assess the quality of the generated plan with respect to its safety. For example, in the article pmlr-v119-filos20a,8 the plan of the Ego actor is generated by the Bayesian imitative model, and the variance of the imitative prior relative to the posterior serves as a proxy for detecting a distribution shift. Upon detecting the distribution shift, the Ego actor either plans for the worst-case model or for the average model. This approach allows us to identify the most attractive driving situation while in the off-line mode, and to choose the safest plan in order to help the ego-actor to operate defensively. Unlike the case of the “epistemic” method, our objective is to (i) assign a risk to a given actor or driving situation by characterizing its negative influence on the freedom of maneuver of the ego-actor, (ii) calculate the risk of the current plan, and proactively minimize the hazards of the latter.

text: Knowledge graphs~(KGs), which represent facts through semantic graph structures, have been utilized across multiple artificial intelligence tasks, e.g., recommendation~\cite{leiconversational,2021Learning}, dialogue generation~\cite{moon-etal-2019-opendialkg,leiinteractive}, and question answering~\cite{ChristmannRASW19,zhu2021retrieving}. Within KGs, facts are structured as triples, \texttt{(head~entity, relation, tail~entity)}, where the head entity connects to the tail entity through the relation. New knowledge continuously emerges, and consequently the incompleteness issue of KGs has stimulated extensive research interest in link prediction tasks, which involve predicting the missing links within KGs~\cite{simple}. The predominant link prediction models~\cite{bordes2013translating,Dettmers2018Convolutional} learn embeddings of entities and relations, and subsequently employ a score function to assess the validity of triples. Nevertheless, we contend that utilizing embedding learning for predominant link prediction models creates two fundamental problems: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Unbalanced relation distribution. } As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}, the relation distribution within an off-the-shelf KG learning resource~(i.e., FB15K-237~\cite{toutanova-chen-2015-observed}) exhibits considerable imbalance. For instance, { the frequencies of the two relations \texttt{/film/film/language} and \texttt{/film/film/edited} vary substantially.} Predominant link prediction models presume sufficient training instances for all relations and devote limited attention to few-shot relations, overlooking the fact that few-shot relation learning may significantly impact the learning performance. \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Existence of unseen relations. } Real-world KGs tend to be open and evolve rapidly, and consequently there exists a substantial number of zero-shot relations unseen in the off-the-shelf learning resources, for instance, the relation {\texttt{/film/film/sequel}} in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}. The unseen relations exceed the capability of predominant link prediction models, as no training instances exist to learn their embeddings. This limitation may constrain the application of these models in downstream tasks. \end{itemize} Recently, several efforts have been undertaken to address the aforementioned problems. \citet{Xiongoneshot}, \citet{shi2018open}, and \citet{ChenMeta} employed meta-learning or metric-based approaches to train on limited training samples and achieve rapid learning on new few-shot relations. These investigations demonstrate promise in few-shot relation learning, however they encounter difficulties in addressing unbalanced relation distributions, which is primarily attributed to the substantial time cost required for training numerous relations. More recently, \citet{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-08937}, \citet{Qin2020GenerativeAZ} predicted the unseen relations by extracting information from textual descriptions. They successfully accomplished the unseen relation prediction task. However, these models are unsuitable for link prediction tasks, since textual descriptions tend to be noisy and also fail to establish a bridge between seen and unseen relations. In general, an optimal link prediction model should be capable of jointly learning many-, few-, and zero- shot relations. Concerning the joint relation learning, we observed that semantic correlations, which represent the similarities of relations in semantics, can function as a bridge to connect the learning of many-, few-, and zero- shot relations. Consider Figure~\ref{fig:intro} as an example. The many-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/language}'', few-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/edited}'', and zero-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/sequel}'' are all associated with ``\texttt{film}''. Based on the assumption that semantically similar relations should be positioned near each other in embedding space~\cite{yang2014embedding}, it is reasonable to exploit semantic correlations, such as the one in the aforementioned example, to achieve the joint relation learning. Motivated by this, we propose a \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{R}elation \textbf{L}earning framework (abbreviated to GRL) based on learning semantic correlations. GRL can be integrated into a predominant link prediction model to make it (1) insensitive to unbalanced relation distributions and (2) capable of learning zero-shot relations. Specifically, GRL is integrated into a link prediction model following the embedding learning stage. To optimize the relation embedding, GRL extracts rich semantic correlations through an attention mechanism, fuses different relations, and minimizes the classification-aware loss to enable these implicitly embedded semantic correlations within the relation embeddings. Subsequently, the proximity of semantically similar relations in vector space and the discrimination of dissimilar relations can be enhanced. In this manner, few-shot relations can acquire knowledge from the semantically similar many-shot relations; for zero-shot relations, their most semantically similar relation can also be predicted. In our experiments, we enhance two base models (DistMult~\cite{yang2014embedding} and ConvE~\cite{Dettmers2018Convolutional}) by incorporating the proposed GRL framework across all relation classes, i.e., many, few, and zero-shot relations. Our work represents an important step towards a comprehensive understanding of KGs and a generalized solution of relation learning for the link prediction task. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] We carefully examine two fundamental problems of the embedding learning utilized by predominant link prediction models and we emphasize the necessity of jointly learning many-, few-, and zero- shot relations. \item[\small$\bullet$] We propose GRL framework by leveraging the rich semantic correlations between relations to make the link prediction models insensitive to unbalanced relation distributions and capable of learning zero-shot relations. \item[\small$\bullet$] We conduct experiments on six benchmarks to evaluate the link prediction capability of GRL, and demonstrate that GRL enables the base link prediction models to perform well across many-, few-, and zero- shot relations. \end{itemize}

text: Trajectory planning for autonomous agents frequently employs a receding time horizon approach. When functioning in environments with other agents, such as in autonomous driving scenarios, these plans must incorporate reasoning about predicted futures and accommodate properties like collision-avoidance through predictions of other agents' future actions. A challenge inherent in this methodology is that the resulting motion plans of the ``ego'' vehicle lack the capability to reason about other agents' reactions to its own decisions. A representative example of this limitation is an autonomous vehicle's inability to merge into dense traffic because it cannot anticipate that other agents will create space. Game-theoretic motion planners address these reactions by treating planning and prediction as coupled processes. Specifically, they represent the intentions of other agents in the scene as optimization problems that each agent attempts to solve, and compute an equilibrium solution. This equilibrium comprises a set of interacting trajectories for all agents; the ego agent can subsequently execute its own equilibrium trajectory. A significant limitation of game-theoretic planning is its assumption that other agents' intentions are known to the ego, and that agents behave rationally with respect to those intentions. In practice, beyond the scope of game-theoretic planning, these objectives and intents can be estimated online and incorporated as contingencies \cite{hardy2013contingency}. In this paper, we tackle this challenge within the framework of game-theoretic planning and introduce a multi-hypothesis approach that addresses this uncertainty and its associated coupling. Specifically, our methodology assumes the ego agent maintains a discrete collection of hypotheses concerning other agents' intentions. These hypotheses possess associated probabilities and capture uncertainties about intentions such as potential lane changes, nominal speeds, acceleration aversion, etc. Given uncertainty of this character, we propose constructing distinct optimization problems for each agent, which when solved, yield trajectories that are qualitatively representative of the different hypotheses. Replicas of each agent (one per hypothesis) are generated and assigned to the corresponding optimization problem. We introduce a novel formulation of the resulting dynamic game that enables the ego agent to reason about interactions with the replica agents based on their corresponding hypothesis probability. This formulation is essential for reasoning about collision-avoidance constraints in a probabilistic manner. Modeling the problem through this approach yields a pragmatic solution to this general category of motion-planning problems that autonomous vehicles must address. Our method produces interactive trajectories among multiple agents while explicitly incorporating uncertainty about others' intentions. We anticipate that our method will facilitate more practical application of game-theoretic planning for autonomous vehicles. This paper is structured as follows. \cref{sec:related_work} examines other approaches for multi-agent planning, including game-theoretic methods as well as methods utilizing derivatives of rational choice models, which address the uncertainty of other agents. \cref{sec:preliminaries} reviews concepts pertaining to game-theoretic planning necessary to formalize our method, which is presented in \cref{sec:methods}. In \cref{sec:results}, we present empirical results of our method on various realistic driving scenarios, and finally, we provide concluding remarks in \cref{sec:conclusion}.

text: The recognition of multi-party speech from an arbitrary number of speakers with naturally occurring speech overlap in far-field environments represents a challenging research problem that has received extensive investigation over many years \cite{Hain2007_AMI,fox13b_interspeech,Liu2016_SWC2,Barker_2018}. This problem is commonly referred to as the ``cocktail party problem''. Its resolution holds the key to the subsequent era of speech technology, establishing the foundation for natural human-device voice interactions. In such interactions, the speech agent on smart devices is expected to navigate multi-party conversations and provide necessary support. To enable real-time human-device interactions, the \ac{ASR} system must provide transcripts in a streaming manner for all speakers in the conversation. For enhanced privacy protection, the \ac{ASR} system design must accommodate local operation on device exclusively, which requires the model to be lightweight and robust against acoustic front-end limitations. All these factors emphasize the importance of streaming speech recognition for an arbitrary number of speakers with potential speech overlaps using only a single distant microphone. Traditionally, multi-speaker \ac{ASR} was addressed through cascaded modules such as speech separation and speech recognition \cite{Isik_2016, Menne_2019, Settle_2018, von_Neumann_2020, Neumann_2020}. Due to system complexity and technical limitations in certain modules, such systems are better suited for offline applications where the complete audio recording is available before the transcription task commences. In recent years, research progress has been achieved in training joint models that optimize multi-speaker ASR performance directly \cite{Yu_2017_icassp, Yu_2017_interspeech, Qian_2018, Seki_2018, Chang_2019, Tripathi_2020}. Recently, \cite{k2020serialized} proposed joint multi-speaker speech recognition and speaker change detection for any number of speakers via \ac{SOT}, demonstrating its effectiveness on simulated multi-speaker test sets of LibriSpeechMix. Subsequently \cite{kanda2021largescale} demonstrated that \ac{SOT} is also effective on real multi-speaker meeting corpora, and follow-up works \cite{kanda2020joint, kanda2021slt, kanda2021endtoend, kanda2021comparative} extended \ac{SOT} into speaker-attributed ASR that can transcribe ``who spoke what" in multi-speaker conversations with one integrated model. In parallel, recent research has also begun examining the maintenance of equivalent performance under streaming conditions. Two conceptually similar streaming multi-speaker ASR models based on \ac{RNN-T} \cite{graves2012sequence}, namely \ac{MS-RNN-T} \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} and \ac{SURT} \cite{Lu2021}, were concurrently proposed to enable time-synchronous decoding of partially overlapping speech, and \cite{Lu2021} was subsequently extended with speaker identification in \cite{lu2021streaming}. \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} conducted evaluations of \ac{MS-RNN-T} on single-speaker LibriSpeech and two-speaker LibriSpeechMix. It demonstrated that \ac{MS-RNN-T} achieves comparable performance with offline multi-speaker ASR systems on two-speaker test data and also enhances system robustness on noisy single-speaker test-other partition of LibriSpeech. This work builds upon \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021}, with the following contributions. First, we demonstrate the advantage of on-the-fly overlapping speech simulation over fixed pre-simulated data for training, resulting in a new low \ac{WER} on two-speaker partition of LibriSpeechMix with a streamable model architecture. Second, we address the primary limitation of \ac{MS-RNN-T}, namely the hard restriction on the maximum number of speakers in the audio. Assuming there are at most two speakers overlapping simultaneously, the proposed \ac{MT-RNN-T} model is capable of recognizing speech from an arbitrary number of speakers. text: \vspace{-0.2cm} Embedding models have served as the fundamental algorithms for numerous machine learning applications such as Information Retrieval (IR)~\citep{croft2010search,baeza1999modern} and Natural Language Processing (NLP)~\citep{word2vec, glove, attention, bert} throughout the past decade. Embedding models represent learned derivatives from low-rank approximation and Matrix Factorization techniques that previously dominated the recommendation systems domain before the advent of Deep Learning (DL). The fundamental objective of these models involves projecting a relatively straightforward and intuitive representation of an input into an abstract low-dimensional dense vector space. This projection facilitates two capabilities: 1) customizing the vectors for specific downstream applications and 2) preprocessing and storing documents or products as vectors, thereby rendering the retrieval process computationally efficient (typically matrix multiplication followed by sorting, which are well-suited to modern hardware such as GPUs). Beyond the computational benefits, embedding models capture the semantic relationships between queries and products. An exemplary case involves product prediction for a service such as Amazon. A user-generated query must be matched against millions of products and the optimal search results must be displayed within milliseconds. With raw product data, it would be infeasible to determine that products containing `aqua' in their titles are actually pertinent to the query `water'. Alternatively, if we can project all products to a dense low-dimensional vector space, a query can also be projected to the identical space and an inner product computation can be executed with all product vectors (typically a dot product). We can subsequently display the products with the highest inner product values. These projections can be learned to incorporate semantic information and can be continuously updated to reflect temporal variations in customer preferences. To our knowledge, embedding models represent the most widespread approaches in industry, particularly for product and advertisement recommendations (Amazon's - DSSM~\citep{dssm}, Facebook's DLRM~\citep{dlrm}). Nevertheless, the scale of these problems has expanded dramatically in recent years, prompting research in extreme classification tasks, where the number of classes reaches several million. Consequently, approaches such as Tree-based Models~\citep{prabhu2014fastxml,Pfastre,agrawal2013multi} and Sparse-linear Models~\citep{weston2013label,pdsparse,ppdsparse} have emerged as powerful alternatives. Specifically, Tree-based models are considerably faster to train and evaluate compared to other methods. However, most practical Information Retrieval systems possess dynamically changing output classes and all extreme classification models fail to generalize to novel classes with limited training data (\emph{e.g.}, new products being added to the catalogue daily). This has precipitated the resurgence of embedding models for large-scale Extreme Classification~\citep{bi2013efficient,annexml,sleec,chen2012feature}. {\bf Our Contributions:} In this paper, we present a novel, unique and compelling argument that sparse high-dimensional embeddings are superior to their dense low-dimensional counterparts. In this context, we make two noteworthy design choices: 1) We design the label embeddings (\emph{e.g.} products in the catalogue) to be high-dimensional, super-sparse, and orthogonal vectors. 2) We fix the label embeddings throughout the training process and learn only the input embeddings (one-sided learning), unlike conventional dense models, where both the input and label embeddings are learned. Since we employ a combination of {\bf S}parse, {\bf O}rthogonal, {\bf L}earned {\bf a}nd {\bf R}andom embeddings, we designate our method {\bf SOLAR}. We provide a theoretical foundation for SOLAR by demonstrating that one-sided and two-sided learning are mathematically equivalent. Our choices result in a four-fold advantage over prior methods: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep,nolistsep] \itemsep0em \item {\bf Matrix Multiplication to Inverted-Index Lookup:} Sparse high-dimensional embeddings can obtain a subset of labels using a simple inverted-index~\citep{croft2010search} lookup and restrict the computation and sorting to those labels. This enhances the inference speed by a substantial margin. \item {\bf Load-balanced Inverted Index:} By enforcing the label embeddings to be near-orthogonal and equally sparse (and fixing them), we ensure that all buckets in an inverted index are equally populated and we sample approximately the same number of labels for each input. This eliminates the well-known imbalanced buckets issue where we sub-sample nearly all the labels for popular inputs and end up compromising the inference speed. \item {\bf Learning to Hash:} An Inverted-Index can be conceptualized as a hash table where all the output classes are hashed into a few buckets~\citep{kulis2009learning, wang2017survey}. By fixing the label buckets and learning to map the inputs to the corresponding label buckets, we are performing a `partial learning to hash' task in retrospect (more on this in Appendix A). \item {\bf Zero-communication:} Our distinctive construction of label embeddings enables distributed training over multiple GPUs with zero-communication. Hence, we can afford to train on a 1.67 M book recommendation dataset and three largest extreme classification datasets and outperform the respective baselines on all 4 of them on both precision and speed. \end{itemize} \vspace{-0.5cm}

text: Within the knowledge economy, substantial volumes of data are gathered to facilitate decision-making, policy analytics, service delivery, and related functions. Nevertheless, the utility of these data is limited by the disclosure risks inherent in data processing generally and data sharing specifically. Among the essential tools employed to mitigate this risk is anonymisation. The Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework (ADF) operationalises the processes of functional anonymisation \cite{elliot2018functional}. This conceptualisation emerged from the work of the \textit{data environment analysis service} \cite{elliot2010data}; a support system for the 2011 UK census concentrated on data confidentiality and disclosure control \cite{willenborg2012elements,duncan2011concepts,hundepool2012SDC} and, specifically, re-identification risk assessment \cite {chen1998, skinner1998estimating,skinner2002measure}. The fundamental principle underlying this concept is that disclosure risk resides not within the data themselves but in the relationship between the data and their environment. Mackey and Elliot define the data environment as "the set of formal and informal structures, processes, mechanisms and agents that either: (i) act on data; (ii) provide interpretable context for those data or (iii) define, control and/ or interact with those data" \cite{mackey2013understanding}. Data environments manifest in numerous forms. For instance, the open data environment, an end-user license management data environment, restricted access secure data environments, and others. Despite this diversity, the ADF framework assumes that all data environments can be characterised through four descriptive features: other data, agents, infrastructure, and governance. It follows from the preceding discussion that to implement the appropriate anonymisation processes, one must consider both the data and their environment. Elliot et al. \cite{elliot2020anonymisation} developed the ADF to operationalise precisely such a process. The ADF emphasises that appropriate anonymisation decisions for a given dataset are only achievable by considering the relationship between the data and their environment(s) which they term the \textit{data situation}.\\ \vspace{-12pt} \textbf{\textit{Problem statement}.} \textit{Data situations are frequently dynamic in that data migrate between environments for both processing and utilisation. Therefore, understanding contextual risk, and how to manage that risk through anonymisation, requires an awareness of, and capacity to map, the data flows between environments.} Currently, capturing and mapping \textit{data situations} for analysis within the ADF framework is performed manually, which is labour intensive and error-prone. To automate this mapping, we propose the utilisation of data provenance - a concept that is already mentioned informally within the ADF. By integrating provenance with the ADF, we will be able to trace the flows of data and identify the upstream and downstream data situations - both existing and proposed. We note that data provenance has already been applied in modelling similar problems such as situation awareness and decision making \cite{baclawski2017framework}, controlling direct and indirect data flows \cite{rong2020provenance}, big data security and privacy \cite{gao2020big}. W3C PROV is a standard for provenance interoperability and for representing where data originated, and how it has been processed \cite{PROV-DM15,missier2013w3c}. PROV provides an abstract data model that includes agents, entities, activities, and relationship properties and which enables the representation of the provenance of data and systems. A critical element in the feasibility of linking provenance to the ADF is the representation of data environments. In the W3C PROV data model, two constructs \textit{bundles} and \textit{namespaces} might be considered as candidates for such representation. In this paper, we examine the potential value of both solutions. We also consider how the elements of PROV (i.e. Entity, Bundle, Agent, Activity) could be employed to represent data environment features (agents, other data, infrastructure, governance). We observe that there are limitations to representing data environments in this manner and suggest some modifications which would enable full capture of the desired features. The contributions of this work are as follows: \vspace{-12pt} \begin{enumerate} \item We outline -- using an ADF use case -- the requirements for provenance in the representation of data environments (in section \ref{sec:usecase}). \item Using these requirements, we propose four different approaches to apply and extend W3C PROV to enable the representation of data environments for machine-enabled reasoning (in section \ref{sec:impl}). \item We then analyse the four approaches (in section \ref{sec:analysis}) \end{enumerate}

text: The primary objective of this work is to develop a system for maintaining an \emph{audit trail} for the knowledge representation (KR) framework based on hierarchies of graphs presented in \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. We aim to utilize this system to record the history of predominantly small localized updates of a large knowledge corpus represented with graphs and graph hierarchies, where storing the corpus at each point in the history is not feasible. The aforementioned requirement for the transformations to be reversible in the context of our practical application does not constrain the set of operations that can be performed for updating a corpus, but rather introduces a reasonably small overhead on storing additional information that enables us to revert the applied transformations. Furthermore, we develop means for maintaining multiple versions of the corpus, essential when accommodating different versions of knowledge that, for example, correspond to different view-points of knowledge curators or some intrinsic knowledge conflicts (e.g. contradicting experimental results, alternative hypotheses). The primary use cases of audit trails for KRs based on hierarchies of graphs include version control for updates in schema-aware graph databases presented in \cite{bonifati2019schema} and updates to the knowledge corpora provided by the bio-curation framework KAMI \cite{harmer2019bio}. An audit trail system with the desired capabilities heavily depends on: (1) the existence of an \emph{efficient semantic representation of object transformations} (or deltas), which liberates us from the necessity to store the state of the object at each point of its transformation history; (2) the \emph{reversibility of transformations}, which ensures that any sequence of transformations can be `undone'; and (3) the existence of sound means for \emph{composing a pair of successive transformations}, which enables us to efficiently store and switch between different versions of the same object. text: Recently, numerous deep-learning-based point cloud generation and completion approaches have emerged utilizing autoencoder architectures. Approaches such as PointNet \cite{qi2016pointnet}, PointNet++ \cite{qi2017pointnetplusplus}, DGCNN \cite{dgcnn}, and Point Transformer \cite{zhao2020point} have examined encoders comprehensively to achieve superior point cloud representations. Numerous approaches have also investigated decoder design strategies. For instance, \cite{Fan_2017_CVPR, achlioptas2017latent_pc, yuan2018pcn, Yang_Wu_Zhang_Jin_2021} directly employ fully connected layers to produce coarse outputs. \cite{Yang_2018_CVPR, groueix2018, liu2019morphing, Wen_2020_CVPR} transform 2d squares into 3d surfaces. As illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(a), fully connected layers and folding operations constitute two prevalent approaches for transforming latent features into point clouds. Nevertheless, they fail to comprehensively investigate the transformation regarding point constraints, network parameters, data flow, and convergence speed. As demonstrated in the upper airplane in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b), point clouds produced by the FC-based approach typically exhibit outliers and irregular surfaces. This occurs because the generated points lack shared parameters, resulting in limited available parameters per point. When extended to multiple branches, the generated point clouds lack the self-clustering property. The self-clustering property indicates that points produced by each branch aggregate together, reflecting object locality. The lower airplane in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b) exemplifies a self-clustered point cloud. This issue arises because each generated point remains unconstrained and lacks centripetal constraint. Unlike the FC-based approach, the folding-based method employs significantly fewer parameters and utilizes grid priors to constrain generated points on smooth 2-manifolds. This constraint facilitates extension to multiple branches. However, its convergence rate is slow since deforming a 2d square into diverse 3d surfaces with limited parameters proves challenging. Simultaneously, 3d objects frequently possess non-smooth surfaces. Folding operations struggle with these scenarios since the generated surfaces originate from smooth 2-manifolds. To resolve these challenges, we propose an attention-based approach AXform for transforming latent features into point clouds. It initially employs a fully connected layer to generate points within an interim space. Subsequently, weighting operations are executed through an attention mechanism to aggregate target points within the interim space. Finally, these points are projected to 3d space, constituting the final point cloud. AXform offers four advantages. First, it requires fewer parameters compared to FC-based and folding-based methods, benefiting from shared network parameters. Second, its convergence rate exceeds these two methods. Third, points generated by AXform demonstrate greater concentration due to centripetal constraint. Therefore, AXform can be readily extended to multiple branches for local generations. Finally, as shown in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(c), our AXform with K branches exhibits space consistency properties, which further enables unsupervised semantic segmentation. Our primary contributions are the following: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel attention-based method for transforming latent features into point clouds. Extensive experiments demonstrate that it outperforms previous methods. \item The proposed AXform can be extended to multiple branches for local generations. It possesses self-clustering and space consistency properties, which enable unsupervised semantic segmentation on the generated point clouds. \item We apply AXform to point cloud completion, achieving state-of-the-art results on the PCN dataset. \end{itemize}
