text: \begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.45\textwidth} \vspace{-40pt} \begin{center} \end{center} \vspace{-0.5cm} \caption{Quantization intervals utilized in the proposed method and prior works.} \vspace{-0.7cm} \end{wrapfigure} In recent years, Federated Learning (FL)~\cite{mcmahan2017fl_google} has become a prominent paradigm for addressing stringent requirements regarding data privacy and computational resource constraints. This framework enables numerous edge devices, termed workers, to collaboratively train models while maintaining the confidentiality of their private data. Given the demonstrated efficacy of FL, it has been extensively deployed across various practical domains, including keyboard prediction~\cite{hard2018keyboard_prediction_fl, yang2018applied_keyboard} and privacy-critical applications~\cite{sheller2018multi_institutional,sheller2018multi_brain_fl,pokhrel2020fl_block_chain}. Nevertheless, FL model training necessitates frequent transmission of model weights and gradients between the central server and participating workers. With increasing model complexity, communication overhead inevitably emerges as the primary bottleneck constraining FL system performance. To address this challenge, numerous studies have endeavored to implement quantization techniques on model weights~\cite{yu2019double_quantization,tang2019doublesqueeze} or gradients~\cite{wen2017terngrad,alistarh2017qsgd} for reducing the payload size of model updates. While these approaches have demonstrated substantial advancement, they frequently fail to maintain model performance comparable to floating-point uncompressed training when aggressive compression is applied. Furthermore, we observe that low-bit quantization may compromise other commonly employed techniques (e.g., gradient sparsification~\cite{aji2017sparse_top_k,strom2015scalable_top_k}), thereby constraining additional cost reduction opportunities. In this study, we introduce a novel quantization methodology based on cosine functions, which is remarkably straightforward yet effective for quantizing model weights and gradients in bidirectional compression scenarios. Motivated by the fundamental insight that gradients and model weights with greater magnitudes convey more information than their smaller counterparts~\cite{han2015deep_compression,lin2018deep_gradient_compression,aji2017sparse_top_k}, we exploit the nonlinear characteristics of cosine functions to minimize quantization errors for extreme values, while most existing approaches~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd,han2015deep_compression} pursue the contrary objective as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}. Moreover, our methodology exhibits low temporal and spatial complexity, necessitates \textit{no} supplementary training, and incurs minimal additional overhead, rendering our approach particularly advantageous for federated learning systems where edge devices typically possess constrained hardware capabilities. We perform comprehensive experiments across diverse scenarios using CIFAR-10 for image classification tasks and the BraTS 2019 dataset for 3D volume segmentation applications. We summarize our contributions as follows: (a) As our primary contribution, we present a \textit{simple-yet-effective} cosine-based quantization framework that better maintains model performance, exhibits low temporal and spatial complexity, and requires no additional training, making it applicable to various distributed learning scenarios. (b) Our proposed quantization technique can be employed to compress both model weights and gradients, thereby reducing overall communication expenses in federated learning environments. (c) Our methodology demonstrates flexibility and compatibility with numerous existing beneficial techniques such as gradient sparsification. Through the integration of our quantization approach with complementary techniques, our system achieves model performance comparable to floating-point uncompressed training at exceptionally high compression ratios, while alternative quantization methods struggle to attain such results.

Motivated by the fundamental observation that the gradient and the weight of the greater magnitude contains more information than the smaller magnitude (refer to Han, 2015; Lin, 2018; Aji, 2017; Strom, 2015; Aji, 2017; Strom, 2015, Scalable-TOPT), whereas most existing methods (refer to Alistar, 2017QSGD, han, 2015, deep compression) pursue the opposite objective (see Fig. ). Strom, 2015Scalable_TOPT), thus limiting the potential for further reduction of cost. (a) We propose a simple-yet-effective cosine-based quantization scheme which keeps the performance of the model and is low in temporal and spatial complexity, does not require additional training, and can be used in many distributed learning applications. Our method is low in temporal and spatial complexity, does not require supplementary training, and has a low overhead. It is therefore suitable for federated learning systems with limited hardware resources at the edge nodes. (b) The proposed method is flexible and can be used with many existing useful methods such as sparse gradient. (c) Our method shows a great versatility and is compatible with many existing useful methods such as sparse gradient. Our method can be used to compress both the weights and the gradients, which reduces the overall communication costs of federated learning. The combination of our quantization method with supplementary techniques gives our system a similar performance to the uncompressed training at very high compression ratios, while most other quantization methods are unable to do so.

text: Numerous scenarios in software transformation and software security necessitate analyzing or operating on a given program binary. The most prevalent example occurs when we lack access to the source code of the binary. However, even when we possess it, we may lack access to the toolchain or the environment required to compile the transformed source, or we may be interested in analyses that depend on the actual machine code in the binary such as the amount of padding around functions or buffers. In these applications, the initial step of the analysis is typically to \emph{disassemble} the binary, which refers to the process of translating its machine code into assembly code. The study of \emph{disassembly} and the corresponding tool \emph{disassemblers} dates back to at least 1980~\cite{Horspool+Marovac:1980:AnApproach}. In recent years, the accuracy of numerous disassemblers is approaching or even exceeding $99\percent$ on many real-world binaries---see, e.g.,~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} and~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Unfortunately, due to well-known problems in binary analysis such as indirect jump resolution and % function start identification, % the proverbial ``last $1$\percent'' remains a challenge in disassembly. In response, our community has continued to devise innovative disassembly algorithms, with new work and improvements appearing frequently---see, e.g.,~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}, \cite{Miller+etal:2019:probabilistic}, and new releases of various existing disassemblers. Comparing highly-accurate disassemblers is challenging for two reasons. First, since different disassemblers may have different weaknesses, a small change to the set of binaries used to evaluate disassemblers may alter their accuracy ranking significantly. Unfortunately, thus far the publications in the disassembly literature tend to use different target sets; see, e.g., ~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} vs. \cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Second, since the accuracy of current disassemblers are exceeding $99\percent$ on many binaries, we need essentially $100\percent$-accurate ground truth to rank the disassemblers reliably. However, as this paper will demonstrate, while previous research tended not to discuss their ground truth generation methods at any length, our own experience suggests that accurate ground truth generation has considerable complexity and is thus not easy to reproduce without a detailed description. Due to the above reasons, we therefore believe it is appropriate time for our community to start standardizing on a set of community-accepted binaries for benchmarking disassemblers on their accuracy and, for the sake of practicality, their running time and memory usage. To help initiate this process, this paper presents a first version of our work-in-progress disassembly benchmark suite. We will discuss the design of our suite from two aspects: (a) the set of binaries included, and (b) our method to generate accurate disassembly ground truth on the instructions in these binaries. For aspect (a), we believe a good disassembly benchmark suite should have these properties: \begin{enumerate*}[(i)] \item The included binaries should be \emph{diverse} in size, type (e.g., editor vs. web server), compilers used, % and optimization settings used. % Achieving these would allow the binaries to better capture the complexities in real-world binaries. \item The number of included binaries should be \emph{moderate}, i.e., large enough but not excessively large. This would ensure the practicality of evaluating disassemblers over every included binary, whose number grows multiplicatively in the number of included compilers and optimization settings in each included ISA-OS pair. \end{enumerate*} At present, our benchmark suite is organized by a notion of ``project names'', which comprises an open-source project and a specific version (e.g., \verb!openssh-7.1p2!). For each project name, we specify a particular target binary inside (e.g., \verb!sshd!) and the set of ISA-OS pairs (e.g., \{x86-Linux, x64-Linux\}) that we include when building this project. In addition, for each ISA-OS pair, we specify the list of compiler-version pairs and the list of optimization settings we include during the build, which will be detailed in~\S\ref{sec:current-benchmark}. To encourage adoption, we maintain our benchmark suite openly on GitHub (\url{https://github.com/pangine/disasm-benchmark}), with the hope that it will evolve over time in ways similar to the SPEC CPU benchmark~\cite{misc:speccpu} due to community inputs and future investigations. For aspect (b), while one may believe that the generation of disassembly ground truth is simply a matter of having the compiler save the assembly code generated (e.g., \verb!gcc -S!), we find this to be an over-simplification in practice. First, even assuming we have all the generated assembly files, in reality the assembly statements (instructions/directives) in these files do \emph{not} form a complete description of the machine code in the binary because some assembly statements admit multiple machine code encodings. Second, during the development of our current benchmark suite, we had discovered numerous corner cases that needed to be handled when collecting the generated assembly files, % extracting information from them, % and representing such information. % In~\S\ref{sec:gt}, we will discuss these challenges and our solutions to them. Finally, using our work-in-progress benchmark suite and our (already mature) ground truth generator and disassembler evaluator, we will present in~\S\ref{sec:eval} our findings on four prominent open-source disassemblers: BAP~\cite{misc:bap}, Ghidra~\cite{misc:ghidra}, Radare2~\cite{misc:radaretwo}, and ROSE~\cite{misc:rose}. Our findings largely concur with~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth}: (i) function start identification remains a major issue that inhibits accurate disassembly, and (ii) linear-sweep disassembly~\cite{Schwarz+etal:2002:Disassembly} can be \emph{incidentally} highly accurate, even though it also has no hope of guaranteeing perfect accuracy and thus cannot be relied upon as a long-term solution. In summary, our contributions in this work are: \begin{enumerate*} \item We propose to start standardizing on a set of binaries from diverse projects compiled with multiple compilers and optimization settings for disassembler evaluation and present our work-in-progress suite as a starting point for community discussion. \item We developed a novel system based on a broadly-supported compiler toolchain feature known as ``listing files'' to generate accurate disassembly ground truth. We also developed support programs to evaluate four prominent open-source disassemblers against our ground truth and we present our findings. \item We open-source all our code and data to enable future studies and to encourage community adoption of and contribution to our system and our benchmark suite. \end{enumerate*}

text: Phishing websites represent a prominent social-engineering threat whose volume has substantially increased over recent years~\cite{phishincreasing:2020,data-breach:2020}. To counter these attacks, the security community has sustained prolonged efforts through automated tools employing sophisticated machine learning~\cite{sahingoz2019machine,rao2019detection,hassanpour2018phishing,abdelhamid2017phishing}, deep-learning~\cite{yang2019phishing,yi2018web,hassanpour2018phishing}, rule-based~\cite{moghimi2016new,sonowal2020phidma,tan2016phishwho,shirazi2018kn0w} and heuristic~\cite{nguyen2013detecting,babagoli2019heuristic,jeeva2016intelligent,sreedharan2016systems} methodologies. However, phishing websites exhibit highly elusive characteristics, frequently evolving to exploit various vulnerabilities and adversarial strategies to evade automated detection systems~\cite{liang2016cracking,rajivan2018creative,royremains,aleroud2020bypassing}. Consequently, domain hosting services, antiphishing tools and web-browsers frequently depend on one or more phishing feeds/blocklists, which constitute curated knowledge repositories containing regularly updated lists of phishing URLs that are incorporated either manually or through combined automated discovery/manual reporting with human verification. As observed by Oest et al.~\cite{oest2020phishtime}, phishing feeds exhibit \textit{reactive} characteristics, featuring substantial temporal gaps between website emergence and subsequent reporting. Nevertheless, these feeds typically undergo manual evaluation processes, theoretically rendering them less susceptible to errors than automated detection mechanisms. In this research, we examine phishing reports disseminated on Twitter~\cite{twitter:2021}, the prominent micro-blogging platform. To our knowledge, this investigation represents the inaugural study evaluating this resource as a substantial knowledge repository for identifying emerging phishing websites, and throughout this paper, we focus on determining its efficacy and comparing its characteristics and performance against two additional popular open source phishing feeds - PhishTank and OpenPhish. Specifically, this paper: (i) Establishes the reliability and information volume provided by these phishing reports, and their comparative performance against two alternative open source phishing feeds. (ii) Being hosted on Twitter, these reports can receive visible interactions from other platform users, a capability unavailable in the two other phishing feeds we examine. We therefore assess the frequency of these interactions, including those from domain registrars and organizations targeted by the reported phishing URLs, and investigate the effects of these interactions on the detection/removal of reported URLs. (iii) We additionally analyze the consequences of sharing these reports, specifically the duration URLs remain active following reporting, and the speed with which anti-phishing tools detect them. Both constitute factors that can safeguard users from inadvertently accessing threats. We collected and examined over 16k tweets containing 11k unique URLs during the period from 21st June to 17th August 2021. Employing combined automated and manual investigations, we continuously monitored numerous properties extracted from these posts including verifying URL activity, anti-phishing tool detection, information conveyed by these posts (including relevant hashtags, images, etc.), true positive rate (percentage of URLs representing legitimate phishing attacks), interactions with other users (likes, comments and replies). We also compared relevant statistics with two alternative phishing feeds- PhishTank and OpenPhish. In Section~\ref{datacollection}, we outline our collection methodology for phishing reports from Twitter, and characterize them according to their hosting domains. In Section~\ref{driveby}, we examine various drive-by download URLs also reported by these accounts, a characteristic absent from the two other feeds. In Section~\ref{comparison}, we assess the information provided by these phishing reports (\ref{content-shared-by-reporters}), alongside PhishTank (\ref{phishtank-share}) and OpenPhish (\ref{openphish-share}). We examine the information conveyed by these reports (including screenshots, IP addresses, targeted registrar/organization names, threat labeling, etc.), and their reliability and validity in Section~\ref{validity-url}. Our primary objective in this section involves evaluating how information shared by phishing reports on Twitter compares with offerings from PhishTank and OpenPhish, subsequently summarized in \textbf{Table~\ref{functionality}}. Unlike the two other phishing feeds, which typically prohibit user interaction, in Section~\ref{phishing-report-interactions}, we determine the interaction volume (favourites/retweets/comments) these reports receive on Twitter, and whether interaction from targeted domains/organizations impacts the removal speed of reported websites. We also qualitatively examine these interaction patterns (Fig~\ref{fig:interaction}) and assess the technological expertise of users typically engaging with these reports (\ref{followers}). Finally, in Section~\ref{activity-website}, we establish URL activity duration following reporting, and compare removal rates and pace with URLs posted on PhishTank and OpenPhish (Section~\ref{comparison}). We also verify phishing URL coverage by anti-phishing engines~\ref{virustotal-coverage}. Our principal findings can be summarized as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Twitter constitutes a viable candidate for utilization as a knowledge repository for phishing reports. During three months, users consistently shared over 16.4k such reports covering 11.1k unique URLs hosted across 203 unique registrars, targeting 146 different organizations. Unlike PhishTank and OpenPhish, these accounts also reported URLs distributing Drive-by downloads (7\%). \item The majority of URL reports obtained from Twitter contained more comprehensive information compared to PhishTank and OpenPhish, which can assist domain registrars and anti-phishing tools in expediting threat identification processes. \item The URLs shared in these reports demonstrate high true positive rates (87\%), with only one account contributing to the majority (11\%) of false positives in our dataset. \item These reports receive minimal engagement, with only 13.8\% of posts receiving at least one comment. The domain registrars and organizations targeted by reported URLs (referred to as \textit{targets} henceforth) contributed to merely 4\% of these comments. However, when they responded to these reports, the URLs became inactive more rapidly compared to URLs not receiving such interaction. Moreover, only 10.2\% of targets follow at least one such Phishing report account, indicating they are either unaware of these reporting accounts, or do not regard them as credible sources. \item 31\% of these reported URLs remain active even one week after their initial appearance in our dataset. Furthermore, anti-phishing tools consistently exhibit lower detection rates for at least 27\% of URLs when compared to URLs appearing in other phishing feeds. \end{enumerate} Therefore, our evaluation demonstrates that phishing reports shared on Twitter represent a reliable and efficient source for communicating information regarding emerging phishing websites. Utilizing these reports can assist domain registrars and anti-phishing tools in accelerating the identification process for newer phishing threats. Additionally, based on the information volume shared by these reports, it proves valuable for researchers constructing detailed ground truth datasets with reduced effort and enhanced efficiency compared to other open phishing feeds like PhishTank and OpenPhish. We explore our findings in greater detail from the subsequent section onwards.

Throughout this paper, we focus on evaluating its efficacy, comparing its characteristics and performance with two other open-source phishing feeds, PhishTank and OpenPhish. From 21 June to 17 August, we collected over 16,000 tweets, each with up to 11,000 unique URLs. Using a combination of automatic and manual methods, we monitor the properties of these posts, including the status of their associated URLs, the detection of anti-phishing tools, and the information contained in these posts (for example, the relevant hashtags, images, etc.). These measures can help prevent the unintentional exploitation of threats by users. In section [REF DATA COLLECTION] we describe how we gather phishing reports from Twitter and classify them by the domains they belong to. In section comparison we compare the information provided by these reports with that of the two phishing feeds PhishTank and OpenPhish. This section's main purpose is to compare the content of phishing reports on Twitter with the content of PhishTank and OpenPhish, which are later summarized in the Tables (ref). We examine the information in the reports (screenshots, IP addresses, registrars of the phished organizations, names of phished individuals, the name of the phish, etc.). In Section driveby, we examine some of the drive-by-download URLs reported by these accounts, which are not found in the other two feeds. In addition, in Section phishing-report-interactions we analyze the patterns of the interactions and the degree of the expertise of the users who usually intervene in these reports. Unlike the two other phishing feeds, which prevent user interaction, in Section phishing-report-interactions we examine the amount of interaction (favorited, retweeted, commented) that these reports receive on Twitter, and if this interaction by the target domains or organizations influences the speed of the reported phishing reports. The article shows that Twitter is a viable storage option for phishing reports. Finally, in the Section fig:fig:activity-website, we estimate the availability of the URL after the report and compare the speed and frequency of its removal to the URLs reported to PhishTank and OpenPhish (the Section fig:comparison). It regularly received 16,400 reports on 11,000 unique phishing URLs from 203 registrars, all targeted at 146 different organizations. Most of the URL reports obtained from Twitter contained more detailed information than those collected by PhishTank and OpenPhish, which can be useful for registrars and anti-phishing tools to identify phishing sites. These accounts also reported URLs spreading drive-by-downloads. The URLs shared in these reports have high true-positive rates (87 percent), and only one account is responsible for most of the dataset's false-positives (11 percent). Yet, only 4.2% of the comments were made by the registrars and organizations that were targeted by the URLs (hereafter referred to as the “Textra targets”), who by the way only 10.2% followed any of the accounts. This suggests that they were either unaware of the accounts' existence or did not consider them to be a credible source. Finally, only 31 percent of the reported URLs are still active after the week they first appeared in our data set. Moreover, phishing protection tools have consistently lower detection rates for at least 27 percent of these URLs compared to other phishing feeds. However, the URLs that did receive a response were much more active than those that did not receive a response. In summary, our evaluation shows that phishing reports shared on Twitter are a reliable and effective source of information about new phishing sites. By using these reports, domain registrars and anti-phishing tools can increase the detection of new phishing sites. We will present our results in more detail in the next section. The reports are a valuable resource for constructing detailed ground truths, with less effort and greater accuracy than with other open phishing data sources such as PhishTank and OpenPhish.

text: Image classification represents a fundamental yet crucial task with extensive applications including autonomous driving, industrial automation, medical diagnosis, and biometric identification~\cite{autonomous_driving, industrial_automation, medical_diagnosis, biometric_identification}. For addressing this task, supervised learning (SL) techniques have gained widespread adoption due to their demonstrated superiority~\cite{VGG, ResNet}. A well-recognized limitation of SL is its requirement for substantial training data across each class requiring identification. Regrettably, in numerous practical contexts, acquiring training data for specific classes proves challenging (e.g., endangered species and newly discovered species such as COVID-19 variants). When \textit{unseen} classes lack available training data, SL-based models exhibit bias toward \textit{seen} classes, thereby hindering the identification of unseen classes. Recently, to address this limitation, a technique for training classifiers using manually annotated attributes (e.g., color, size, and shape; see Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}) has been introduced~\cite{zsl_proposal, gzsl_intro}. The fundamental principle of this technique, termed generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL), involves learning the association between images and attributes from seen classes and subsequently applying the trained model for identifying unseen classes. In~\cite{ALE}, for instance, an approach for identifying unseen classes through measuring compatibility between image features and attributes has been introduced. In~\cite{CVAE-GZSL}, a network that synthesizes image features from attributes has been utilized to generate training data for unseen classes. For image feature extraction, networks trained on classification tasks (e.g., ResNet~\cite{ResNet}) have been commonly employed. A potential limitation of this extraction methodology is that image features may incorporate attribute-irrelevant information (e.g., human fingers in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), thereby interfering with the process of learning associations between images and attributes~\cite{DLFZRL, RFF-GZSL, Disentangled-VAE}. In this paper, we introduce a novel GZSL technique that eliminates interference arising from attribute-irrelevant information. The fundamental principle of the proposed methodology involves extracting the \textit{semantic feature}, which contains attribute-related information, from the image feature and subsequently utilizing it for learning associations between images and attributes. For semantic feature extraction, we employ a modified autoencoder comprising two encoders, namely, \textit{semantic} and \textit{residual} encoders (see Fig.~\ref{fig:SD}). Essentially, the semantic encoder captures all attribute-related information within the image feature while the residual encoder captures attribute-irrelevant information. In conventional autoencoders, only reconstruction loss (difference between input and reconstructed input) is utilized for training. In our methodology, to encourage the semantic encoder to capture exclusively attribute-related information, we employ two novel loss functions in addition to the reconstruction loss. First, we utilize mutual information (MI)-based loss to maximize (minimize) MI between the semantic (residual) encoder output and the attribute. Since MI serves as a metric for measuring dependency levels between two random variables, by leveraging the MI-based loss, we can encourage the semantic encoder to capture attribute-related information while simultaneously discouraging the residual encoder from capturing any attribute-related information. Consequently, all attribute-related information can be exclusively captured by the semantic encoder. Second, we employ similarity-based loss to prevent the semantic encoder from capturing any attribute-irrelevant information. For instance, when a bird image contains human fingers (see Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), we aim to exclude finger-related features from the semantic encoder output. To achieve this, we maximize similarity between semantic encoder outputs of images belonging to the same class (bird images in our example). Since attribute-irrelevant features are present only in limited image samples (e.g., human fingers appear in few bird images), by maximizing similarity between semantic encoder outputs of the same class, we can eliminate attribute-irrelevant information from the semantic encoder output. Through comprehensive experiments using various benchmark datasets (AwA1, AwA2, CUB, and SUN), we demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms conventional GZSL techniques. For instance, on the AwA2 and CUB datasets, our model achieves 2\% improvement in GZSL classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

text: Clique identification constitutes a thoroughly investigated subject within the graph theory community and possesses numerous compelling practical applications for community detection \cite{6249683, palla2005uncovering, 7117352, fang2019efficient} and social network analysis \cite{4811845, rossi2015parallel}. In recent years, the data mining community has integrated clique identification into deep learning classifiers to improve recommender systems in social networks \cite{dietrec, movierec}. Clique identification is employed prominently in bioinformatics, and researchers have utilized graph models to identify variants in gene sequences \cite{variant}, efficiently cluster related genes in a database \cite{database} and conduct protein structure analysis \cite{ppi}. The rapid expansion in the number of social media users and the substantial size of genome data has intensified the demand for high performance systems capable of analyzing these massive networks to count or enumerate their k-cliques. Clique identification represents merely a single problem in Graph Pattern Mining (GPM). Motifs constitute other general graph patterns that also attract researchers in this domain. Various GPM frameworks have been developed to count recurring instances of given patterns within the search graph. These include Pangolin \cite{chen2020pangolin}, Peregrine \cite{jamshidi2020peregrine}, Arabesque \cite{teixeira2015arabesque}, Fractal \cite{dias2019fractal}, and others. The aforementioned frameworks employ more generalized algorithms and provide their own APIs for counting instances of arbitrary, user-specified patterns. In contrast, there are also algorithms specialized for counting of k-cliques, such as kClist \cite{danisch2018listing}, Pivoter \cite{jain2020power}, and Arb-Count \cite{shi2021parallel}. By virtue of being custom designed to solve a specific problem, these algorithms generally perform superior to the general-purpose GPM frameworks. KClist~\cite{danisch2018listing} represents the current state-of-the-art clique counting algorithm, as it is algorithmically efficient and substantially outperforms prior work. However, when applied to large graphs, it exhibits poor parallel scalability, particularly for modest clique sizes. We carefully analyze kClist and identify scaling bottlenecks in both of its main phases: ordering \& counting. The ordering phase directionalizes the graph in order to avoid redundantly counting the same cliques multiple times in the subsequent counting phase. KClist employs a core ordering~\cite{matula1983smallest} to reduce the maximum degree in order to obtain the greatest reduction in the amount of algorithmic work in the counting phase. Since the ordering phase consumes a substantial portion of the execution time, and computing a core ordering is inherently sequential, it limits scalability due to Amdahl's Law. The parallel speedup of kClist's counting phase quickly saturates, and we observe speedups as poor as 5$\times$ on 24 cores for certain graphs. We find the counting phase is generally memory-bound due to poor locality and the substantial volume of memory traffic. We present CITRON (Clique Counting with Traffic Reducing Optimizations), a high performance clique counting algorithm. Due to its superior parallel scalability, it substantially outperforms kClist, particularly for modest clique sizes. We find the use of a core ordering unnecessary, and a parallelizable ordering such as a degree ordering not only greatly accelerates the ordering phase, but it also results in negligible slowdowns in the counting phase in practice. We accelerate the counting phase with our novel subgraph construction approach which materially reduces the amount of memory accesses and improves their spatial locality. We evaluate CITRON on a suite of real-world graphs and compare it to kClist and other prior works. For counting triangles, we achieve speedups of $18.16 - 208.27\times$ (Geometric Mean: $102.436\times$) in the ordering phase and speedups of $1.1-2.6\times$ (Geometric Mean: $1.798\times$) in the counting phase, resulting in total speedups of $14.37-39.37\times$ (Geometric Mean: $18.517\times$) over kClist. We have recently become aware of ArbCount \cite{shi2021parallel}, which outperforms us as demonstrated in Table \ref{table:3}. However, we believe that the analysis included in this paper will be beneficial for anyone who wishes to understand the performance characteristics of k-clique counting.

text: With the widespread deployment of mobile and edge devices, federated learning~\cite{konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication} has emerged as a paradigm for training machine learning models across geographically distributed and heterogeneous devices. In federated learning, a central server exists alongside numerous clients. The central server coordinates with the clients to train a machine learning model utilizing the local data maintained on the clients. Federated learning is frequently formulated as a distributed optimization problem~\cite{konevcny2016federatedoptimization, konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication, kairouz2019advances, wang2021field}. Let ${\mathcal{D}}$ be the complete dataset distributed across all $N$ clients/devices/workers/machines, where each client $i$ possesses a local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$. The objective is to solve the following optimization problem without sharing the local datasets with the central server: \begin{align} \min_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{ f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}) := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)\right\}, \end{align} where $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i) := \mathbb{E}_{d_i\sim{\mathcal{D}}_i} f({\bm{x}}; d_i)$. Here, ${\bm{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ represents the model, $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}})$, $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)$, and $f({\bm{x}}; d_{i})$ denote the loss function of the model ${\bm{x}}$ on the complete dataset ${\mathcal{D}}$, the local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$, and a random data sample $d_{i}$, respectively. \subsection{Communication efficiency} Communication between the central server and the clients constitutes a primary bottleneck for federated learning applications, particularly when the number of clients is substantial, the clients such as mobile phones possess limited bandwidth, and/or the machine learning model contains numerous parameters. Therefore, it is essential to design federated learning algorithms that reduce the overall communication cost, which considers both \emph{the number of communication rounds} and \emph{the communication cost per communication round} for achieving the desired accuracy. Based on these two quantities, there exist two lines of approaches for communication-efficient federated learning: 1) \emph{local methods}: in each communication round, clients execute multiple local update steps before communicating with the central server, aiming to reduce the number of communication rounds; 2) \emph{compressed methods}: clients transmit compressed communication messages to the central server, with the goal of reducing the communication cost per communication round. Both categories have attracted considerable attention. For local methods, a small sample of examples includes \algname{FedAvg}~\cite{mcmahan2017communication}, \algname{Local-SVRG}~\cite{gorbunov2020local}, \algname{SCAFFOLD}~\cite{karimireddy2020scaffold} and \algname{FedPAGE}~\cite{zhao2021fedpage}. Conversely, numerous compressed methods have been proposed, including but not limited to \cite{alistarh2017qsgd, khirirat2018distributed, mishchenko2019distributed, horvath2019stochastic, li2020acceleration, li2020unified, gorbunov2021marina, condat2021murana, li2021canita, richtarik20223pc, li2022soteriafl, zhao2022beer}. Specifically, the current state-of-the-art guarantees in convex and nonconvex settings are provided by \algname{CANITA}~\cite{li2021canita} and \algname{MARINA}~\cite{gorbunov2021marina}, respectively. In this paper, we concentrate on compression to enhance communication efficiency. See \Cref{sec:compression} for additional discussions. \subsection{Methods with variance reduction} Variance reduction, or \emph{data-variance} reduction represents a well-established technique in standard/centralized finite-sum optimization, which seeks to achieve a faster convergence rate. There exist many optimization algorithms employing the variance reduction technique, including \algname{SVRG}~\cite{johnson2013accelerating,reddi2016stochastic}, \algname{SAGA}~\cite{defazio2014saga}, \algname{SCSG}~\cite{lei2017less}, \algname{SARAH}~\cite{nguyen2017sarah}, \algname{SPIDER}~\cite{fang2018spider}, \algname{SSRGD}~\cite{li2019ssrgd,li2022simple}, and \algname{PAGE}~\cite{li2021page,li2021short}. These algorithms typically compute the stochastic gradients using a subset of data samples (obtain improved convergence results) and periodically compute the full gradient using all data samples (reduce data-variance). For instance, the convergence result for standard gradient descent (\algname{GD}) (which always computes full gradients) is $O(N/\epsilon^2)$ in the nonconvex setting, while the variance-reduced methods \algname{SARAH/SPIDER/PAGE} achieve much superior result $O(\sqrt{N}/\epsilon^2)$. In the federated learning setting, we decompose the \emph{data-variance} into two components: the \emph{client-variance} and the clients' \emph{local-variance}. The \emph{client-variance} captures the dissimilarity of data stored on different heterogeneous clients, i.e., the variance induced by different datasets ${\mathcal{D}}_i$ (see problem \eqref{eq:prob}), which represents the variance faced by the central server. The \emph{local-variance} or \emph{local-data-variance} is induced by the local data samples stored on each client, and it represents the data-variance faced by the local clients if they compute local \emph{stochastic gradients} not local \emph{full gradients}. We emphasize that the \emph{client-variance} constitutes the main issue for federated learning due to the data heterogeneity problem, and even if one can compute the local \emph{full gradients} using the entire local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$ on each client (i.e., eliminate the \emph{local-variance}), the \emph{client-variance} faced by the central server still persists. Furthermore, directly applying the variance reduction algorithms like \algname{SVRG/PAGE} in federated learning has the following limitations: (1) These variance-reduced methods typically need to periodically compute the full gradient using all data samples (reduce data-variance), which necessitates communication with all clients periodically in the federated learning setting. However, federated learning applications typically involve numerous clients, for example, Google Keyboard (Gboard)~\cite{hard2018federated,ramaswamy2019federated} involves billions of mobile phones, and thus it is impractical to communicate with all the clients in a communication round to reduce the \emph{client-variance}. (2) These variance-reduced algorithms do not utilize communication compression to further reduce the communication cost. Conversely, the existing communication compression algorithms typically need to communicate with all the clients in each communication round (see Tables~\ref{tab:results}). Among the compressed algorithms that support partial participation (PP) (do not need to communicate with all clients in each round), previous methods either need to communicate with all the clients (FP) using uncompressed messages periodically (\algname{PP-MARINA}~\cite{gorbunov2021marina}), or do not enjoy the faster convergence rate of variance reduction (\algname{FedGLOMO}~\cite{das2020improved}, \algname{EF21-PP}~\cite{fatkhullin2021ef21}). Therefore, we consider the following natural and important question:

text: Contemporary voice-controlled devices equipped with virtual assistants such as Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant have been increasingly integrated into numerous aspects of our daily activities, ranging from music playback to automotive navigation. Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) models that interpret the semantic content conveyed through a user's spoken utterance serve as the artificial intelligence foundation of these devices. The SLU task is typically decomposed into two sub-tasks: intent classification (IC), which determines the intent underlying a user's utterance; and slot filling (SF), which identifies semantic components within the utterance. Consider an annotated utterance from the ATIS dataset \cite{atis}: \begin{quote} \textbf{city}~~~~~~ [$_{\bf{O}}$~where] [$_{\bf{O}}$~is] [$_{\bf{B-airport\_code}}$~MCO] \end{quote} The SF sub-task should categorize ``where'' and ``is'' as ${\bf{O}}$ (i.e. Other); and ``MCO'' as ${\bf{B-airport\_code}}$, while the IC sub-task should recognize \textbf{city} as the intent. Contemporary state-of-the-art SLU models are predominantly DNN-based joint architectures for both sub-tasks \cite{Liu2016AttentionBasedRN,do19,chen19}. These architectures typically incorporate two separate decoders for detecting slot and intent labels above a shared encoder. As observed in numerous other NLP domains, the BERT encoder-decoder framework has demonstrated remarkable capability in capturing contextual information from data sources to enhance SLU performance \cite{chen19}. For standard SLU applications, the BERT encoder undergoes pre-training on extensive amounts of unlabeled text and subsequently fine-tuning on SLU training data. Given that the voice-controlled device market has been experiencing extraordinary growth worldwide, there exists an escalating demand for rapid language expansion in SLU models. Multilingual technology, which enables the creation of a unified model for multiple languages and facilitates knowledge transfer from one data resource to languages beyond its original scope, currently represents one of the most effective solutions to address this growing requirement. Conventionally, an SLU model undergoes training on supervised monolingual data, resulting in virtual assistants that typically operate using only one language during a working session. Conversely, a multilingual SLU model trained on supervised multilingual data can enable the virtual assistant to communicate in multiple languages during a single working session. Furthermore, from a developmental standpoint, multilingual modeling contributes not only to reducing the quantity of models requiring construction, but also to diminishing supervised data requirements through cross-linguistic knowledge transfer. Nevertheless, since languages exhibit differences across various dimensions from vocabulary to syntax, the cross-linguistic knowledge transfer of existing multilingual techniques may remain constrained. This generates the inquiries of: i) what constitutes an ideal cross-linguistic knowledge transfer; ii) what characterizes a naive cross-linguistic knowledge transfer; and iii) to what extent a multilingual model can facilitate knowledge transfer across languages. As one of the most effective multilingual techniques in recent years, multilingual BERT (mBERT) \cite{mBERT} is being employed with increasing frequency in natural language processing models across both zero-shot\footnote{The model is trained in one language and tested on another.} and multilingual\footnote{The model is trained on multiple languages.} contexts \cite{wu-dredze-2019-beto,multiatis++}. Since mBERT undergoes training without any cross-lingual objectives and does not utilize aligned data, its robust cross-lingual capabilities are remarkable and have, consequently, stimulated research endeavoring to comprehend why it can achieve them \cite{pires2019multilingual}. In this paper, we, nevertheless, concentrate on addressing the question of to what extent it can diminish language boundaries in the \textit{multilingual} SLU context by comparing its capacity to transfer knowledge across languages with the ideal and naive scenarios. Additionally, as mBERT is pre-trained for general purposes, we are also interested in how to enhance its multilinguality for the specific application of multilingual SLU. Our contribution in this paper is twofold: \textit{First}, through conducting an extensive range of experiments with bilingual and trilingual SLU models, we demonstrate that although mBERT is considerably effective in diminishing language boundaries even across distant language groups, a gap to the ideal multilingual performance persists. \textit{Second}, we propose a novel adversarial model architecture to learn language-shared and language-specific representations above mBERT representations during fine-tuning on SLU data. The experimental results establish that our proposed approach can reduce the gap to the ideal multilingual performance.

text: In recent years, micro-blogging has emerged as a source of current and topical news. Twitter\footnote{www.twitter.com} represents one of the most popular micro-blogging services that connects millions of users and enables the publication and exchange of short messages, known as \emph{tweets}. Twitter pioneered the provision of APIs for accessing public data since 2006\footnote{https://developer.twitter.com/en.html} and facilitated applications in retrieving tweets through a set of keywords. Nevertheless, no control exists over the retrieved tweets which are not consistently relevant. Obtaining relevant responses necessitates multiple calls and filtering of the retrieved results. Several research works exist that aim to search for relevant tweets according to a given query~\cite{gabielkov2014sampling,gouriten2014scalable,li2013towards,safran2012improving}. Researchers have attempted to enhance the methods based on features such as hashtags, retweets and mentions to retrieve the most relevant tweets from Twitter. For instance, one fundamental and straightforward method involves finding the frequency of a single query word across different Twitter features when the query contains only one word\cite{nazi2015walk}. Researchers have also attempted to utilize external information extracted from sources such as Wikipedia to enrich queries by identifying the most similar words to locate the most related results for the given query \cite{guisado2016enrich}. {In this paper, we exploited different external resources such as \textit{Wordnet}, \textit{Wordnik}, \textit{DBPedia}, and \textit{New York Times(NYT)} to obtain the most comprehensive set of keywords similar to the original query keywords. We also defined a smart crawling algorithm based on the tweet's features to reach the most relevant ones as early as possible and transcend Twitter limitations. More specifically, we define a novel crawling algorithm called \textbf{Smart Twitter Crawling} (STiC) by considering two distinct aspects: (i) Enriching the original query using external sources, (ii) crawling Twitter graph using a DFS search based on new scoring to reach the optimal nodes (tweets) related to the targeted topic. To measure the relevance of a tweet, the algorithm assigns a score to a tweet by considering its content, its hashtags and the user who maintains a relationship with it, such as posting, replying, being mentioned or retweeting. Given this score we can select highly related tweets in each iteration and continue by incorporating the related valuable tweets. Various experiments have been conducted on tweets collected for different types of query keywords to evaluate the precision of the STiC algorithm. Through our approach, compared to a simple BFS search, we enhanced the precision of related retrieved tweets up to 86\% for certain queries. Additionally regarding the number of retrieved results, we achieved significant improvement compared to the simple BFS model. In this paper, we first present related work in Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork}. Then, we present in detail our smart Twitter crawling approach including query enrichment and Twitter graph crawling in Section~\ref{sec:approach}. In section~\ref{sec:experiments}, we present and discuss our results using different queries. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} we provide our conclusions and perspectives.

text: Healthcare providers currently dedicate more time to documenting information in electronic health records (EHRs) than to patient communication, and the burden of utilizing inefficient EHRs is hypothesized to be a primary contributor to physician stress and burnout \citep{carayon15, gardner_burnout}. Physicians favor natural language and free-text documentation over restrictive structured formats \citep{khorana}, yet clinicians have adapted to time-consuming note composition by depending on overused acronyms and specialized terminology \citep{md_readability}. As an illustration, consider this sentence from an actual Emergency Department (ED) clinical note: \texttt{pt w/ h/o MS}. While \texttt{MS} might signify \texttt{mitral stenosis} to a cardiologist, it can also be employed to indicate \texttt{multiple sclerosis} to other specialists. To a layperson, the clinical note may be incomprehensible unless acronyms are expanded: \texttt{patient with a history of multiple sclerosis}. Therefore, medical documentation is frequently noisy, ambiguous, and incomplete. The absence of structure in notes further impedes comprehensibility for patients, other physicians, and machines \citep{Aljabri2018, patient_engagement, Koch-Weser_language2009}. The information contained within EHR notes remains largely underutilized and, currently, cannot be readily employed for downstream medical care or for machine learning models that depend on structured data. \paragraph{Statement of Contributions} We propose a method called \emph{contextual autocomplete}, which rapidly captures clinical concepts at the point-of-care through learned suggestions. To accomplish this, we construct a hierarchical language model for clinical concepts that can function in the noisy domain of ED notes. Our model is designed for deployment in a live hospital environment, with inputs restricted to the triage information and past medical notes available to a physician \emph{before} a note is composed. While these constraints render it impractical to construct a generative language model, we generalize to the task of \emph{autocompletion}, where we provide multiple suggestions for the next clinical concept to document and permit the clinician to determine the appropriate choice. Since all suggestions are mapped to standardized clinical vocabularies, we can simultaneously impose structure on notes as they are being composed, disambiguate between concepts, and accelerate documentation for clinicians in real-world hospital settings. \paragraph{Clinical Relevance} We present contextual autocompletion as the foundation of an intelligent EHR in Figure \ref{typing_readability}. The contextual autocompletion tool decreases the amount of text a clinician must type by suggesting relevant terms using a learned context. Tagged terms uniquely identify clinical concepts and can be linked with pertinent information from the medical record. Furthermore, these terms can facilitate widespread improvements in documentation and reduce overall cognitive burden on doctors. Once a term is tagged, it can be automatically inserted in multiple locations within the clinical note to limit the amount of redundant information a clinician types-- for instance, a tagged condition in an earlier section of a note can be automatically appended to the Past Medical History section that appears later on, as in the right panel of Figure \ref{typing_readability}. This alleviates the ``death by a thousand clicks" phenomenon that EHRs experience \citep{schulte_fry_2019}. Additionally, live-tagging clinical concepts can provide immediate benefits to physicians in the form of decision support; the captured structured data can then be utilized to build smarter EHR interfaces that enable contextual information retrieval about disease history and lab trends, without ever leaving the note interface. Finally, tagging clinical concepts with our system permits the translation of acronyms and domain-specific language to common names. By normalizing key clinical concepts from notes to a universal vocabulary (the Unified Medical Language System, or UMLS), notes written using our system are semi-structured and parseable. \FloatBarrier \paragraph{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} Previous research in clinical concept extraction attempts to retrospectively recover concepts from notes, but these methods often struggle to disambiguate between similar concepts, and suffer due to a scarcity of labeled data \citep{mcn}. Even for a human expert, it is challenging to reliably disambiguate between concepts when the clinical intention is unclear. Constructing a tool that enables clinicians to document terms on-the-fly not only reduces documentation burden, but also curates large-scale prospective datasets of labeled clinical concepts (e.g. conditions, symptoms, labs, and medications) in notes. These labels can be utilized to design robust medical knowledge graphs, develop better clinical entity extraction models, learn longitudinal patterns within disease history, and even build contextual representations of concepts. Learning relationships between clinical concepts, for instance, can inform and fill gaps in existing medical ontologies \citep{umls_missingness}. Moreover, this work demonstrates the power of combining varying noisy and possibly incomplete sources of a patient's medical record to create a context for the current clinical setting that enables us to accurately predict concepts relevant to a new medical event. \FloatBarrier

text: Hand dexterity constitutes a fundamental component of daily human activities, necessitating complex and precise control of finger movements. While most animals demonstrate fine-grained motor controls for locomotion and many exhibit elementary manipulation skills, the functionality and efficacy of human dexterity remains unmatched by others, endowing humans with the unique capability to execute highly sophisticated tasks with ease. Consequently, developing similarly-intelligent control strategies for robotic hands has been regarded as a holy grail for research on autonomous robots. Nevertheless, it represents an exceptionally challenging problem due to its high-dimensional action space and complex intermittent hand-object interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) has been gaining popularity for solving sensorimotor control tasks due to its capability to discover behaviors without laborious manual engineering~\cite{heess2017emergence,levine2016end}. Prior works have also demonstrated that with large-scale computation, RL policies can acquire useful skills to control dexterous hands from purely simulated experience and perform complex tasks in the real world, including in-hand rotation~\cite{andrychowicz2020learning} and solving Rubik's Cube~\cite{akkaya2019solving}. Nevertheless, the manipulation policies developed by these methods are typically only concerned with a single pre-determined object, rendering them impractical for real-world deployment. Since there are countless objects a robot may encounter in the real world, it is infeasible to develop an individual system for each of them. Consequently, it is imperative for a policy to exhibit strong robustness to object variations, preferably in a zero-shot manner as humans do. However, generalization to completely unseen and geometrically-diverse objects for dexterous manipulation policies has been under-explored in the community, primarily due to the specious belief that such generalization is beyond the reach of current RL algorithms. In this work, we demonstrate that with simple modifications, existing RL algorithms can produce strong and generalizable policies for a robotic hand with high degrees of freedom. First, we demonstrate that contrary to the common belief of the community, a multi-task jointly-trained policy does not necessarily lead to decreased performance compared to if it were to be trained on each task individually. In fact, we demonstrate that in the context of dexterous manipulation, a multi-task policy can be a \textit{generalist} that can match the performance of those single-task \textit{specialist} policies. Second, we demonstrate that with appropriate representation that can meaningfully associate the tasks, such a multi-task policy can even outperform the single-task \textit{specialists} on completely unseen objects, where the \textit{specialists} are trained on those objects. Furthermore, we demonstrate a linear scaling effect of better generalization when trained on more objects, revealing the possibility of future improvement. We hope that our work can serve as a key step towards building a general-purpose controller for dexterous hands. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We demonstrate that a multi-task policy trained on many objects can match the performance of the oracles, i.e. policies trained on those objects individually. \item We present a simple representation encoder that not only facilitates training but also leads to stronger zero-shot performance on unseen objects than what is achievable by the oracles of those objects. \item We provide detailed analysis of the potential scaling effect and the relevant design decisions of our method. \item We release a simulated benchmark, built upon OpenAI Gym~\cite{openaigym} and existing 3D object datasets, that contains over 100 geometrically-diverse real-world objects to encourage future studies of dexterous hand manipulation and generalization properties. \end{itemize}

text: Human modeling and rendering constitutes a fundamental technology required to facilitate applications in sports visualization, telepresence, shopping, and numerous other domains. Although substantial research has been conducted for calibrated data, such as multiview laboratory configurations \cite{shysheya2019textured, liu2019neural, liu2020neural}, synthesizing arbitrary individuals solely from data ``in the wild" remains challenging. Three-dimensional reconstruction methodologies necessitate training on synthetic, ground truth meshes, or 3D scans \cite{saito2019pifu, saito2020pifuhd, alldieck2019tex2shape, huang2020arch, lazova2019360, zhu2020reconstructing}, while image-to-image translation techniques concentrate exclusively on 2D synthesis \cite{chan2019everybody, wang2018video}. Our methodology addresses both challenges by reconstructing a volumetric representation of an individual that can be animated and rendered in arbitrary poses for any viewpoint. We utilize as input a video of the individual performing unconstrained activities, such as playing tennis or dancing. The fundamental observation is that image frames from a reasonably extended video (minutes to hours) of an individual provides abundant information regarding their appearance across different poses and viewpoints, even when each individual pose may occur only once, observed from a single direction. A significant contribution of our work is the design of a representation and a corresponding deep network that facilitate generalization to arbitrary poses and views given these images. Our contributions encompass a representation of an individual as an $RGB\alpha$ volume which can be reposed through a set of volumetric motion weights (adapting the work of~\cite{lombardi2019neural}), the design of a deep network that, following optimization over the video data, generates the person-specific volumes, a set of losses designed to match the output to both the pixel values and the qualitative appearance of the input frames, and finally, a system that integrates these components to enable fitting to unconstrained videos to produce reposable, free-viewpoint renderings of the individual. We demonstrate results on diverse video inputs, outperforming related methodologies and enabling applications such as motion re-targeting and bullet-time rendering. Our approach possesses certain limitations. We assume the appearance of the subject exhibits no view-dependence (no specular reflection) and, more significantly, that the appearance remains invariant with pose. The latter assumption implies that the results are most faithful to the original when the lighting is relatively diffuse and the shape, such as of clothing, does not vary substantially during movement. Additionally, the resolution of results is constrained by the voxel grid and by the inherent challenges of registering to, and recovering accurate body poses from, images in the wild. Despite these limitations, we demonstrate convincing results on a variety of sequences which, even when not physically exact, are plausible.

text: Autoencoders constitute a powerful class of Neural Networks capable of achieving compact data representations, and are frequently employed as a denoising technique \cite{autoencoders}. Building upon this concept, Quantum Autoencoders (QAEs) have recently emerged as a potential approach to address the debilitating quantum noise problem, which is pervasive in real-device quantum computations. Here, we elect to concentrate on QAEs as proposed in \cite{bondarenko2019quantum}, which facilitate an almost perfect reconstruction of Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states subjected to random bit-flips and small unitary noise. A $m$-qubit GHZ state is defined by \begin{align} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}( \ket{0}^{\bigotimes m}+\ket{1}^{\bigotimes m}). \end{align} Investigating GHZ states is of particular importance as they demonstrate long-range entanglement, and are utilized in a broad spectrum of applications. \medskip Notably, the circuit depth of the QAEs examined in this paper is very shallow (for example, the QAE denoising 3-qubit GHZ states only necessitates 4 qubits), rendering them straightforward to implement on currently available quantum devices. These QAEs depend on the Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) architecture described in \cite{beer2019efficient}, and are trained in an unsupervised learning manner \cite{sents2019unsupervised}. While \cite{beer2019efficient} already furnishes an implementation of QNNs in Matlab \cite{deepqnn}, we elect here to implement the QAEs in a pure quantum framework, utilizing the Qiskit \cite{qiskit} library. In this study, we propose an end-to-end quantum (circuit) encoding of all the algorithmic steps associated with QAEs training and testing. Furthermore, we discuss important implementation and training details accompanied by extended results of the QAEs. Finally, we perform a thorough mathematical analysis of the impact of noise in Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) and show how to counter it. Therefore, this work encompasses both theoretical and experimental aspects of QAEs. \medskip This paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{Implementation} addresses the theoretical background regarding the implementation and training of QAEs on quantum circuits. Section \ref{Results} presents numerical results concerning the performance of the QAEs when denoising corrupted states subjected to different kinds of noise. Finally, in section \ref{QSS} we discuss an application of QAEs in QSS, and demonstrate their significance in that context.

text: Environmental sound offers rich insights into the physical world. For instance, upon hearing: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash;} we can not only visualize concrete objects and actions that may have produced the auditory scene, but we can also infer plausible higher-level aspects, such as a child racing down a water slide at an aquatic facility, creating splashes in the water (see Figure~\ref{fig:image_pivot_idea}). Machines that can parse, represent, and describe environmental sound possess significant practical potential. For instance, based on the National Association of the Deaf's captioning guidelines, accessible audio caption generation systems must extend beyond speech recognition (i.e., identifying speakers and transcribing the explicit content of their utterances) and deliver textual descriptions of all sound effects, such as ``a large group of people talking excitedly at a party'', to convey the complete information present in that audio.\footnote{{\href{https://www.nad.org/resources/technology/captioning-for-access/what-is-captioning/}{nad.org's captioning guide}}; \citet{gernsbacher2015video} discusses the benefits of video captions beyond d/Deaf users.} The prevailing paradigm for investigating \emph{machine hearing}~\citep{lyon2010machine} has relied on human-annotated audio-text data, where text consists of either free-form audio descriptions (e.g., ``the sound of heavy rain'') or structured tagsets~\citep{US8K,audioset,audiocaps,audiocaps-clotho}. However, existing supervised audio-text resources remain constrained. Although some audio-text co-occurrences can be obtained from audio-tag associations~\citep{freesound} or video captioning datasets~\citep{rohrbach2015dataset,MSR-VTT,oncescu2021queryd}, they are either insufficiently related to environmental sound or restricted in scale and coverage. In this work, we investigate large-scale audio-text alignment without paired audio-text (AT) data. Drawing inspiration from pivot-based models for unsupervised machine translation~\citep{wu2007pivot,pivot-comparison-mt}, we propose \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, abbreviated for \modelnamelong. \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace employs images as a pivot modality to bridge audio and text. This approach mirrors our motivating example: upon hearing a sound, humans can visually \emph{imagine} the corresponding situation and verbally \emph{describe} it. Pivoting proves practically feasible because abundantly available image-text (VT) and video-audio (VA) co-occurrences exist on the web, from which bimodal correspondence models can be trained (see Figure~\ref{fig:keyidea}). By connecting audio and text implicitly through the combination of VT and VA models, we enable \emph{zero-resource} linkage between audio and text, meaning \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace can reason about audio-text connections without ever observing these modalities co-occur explicitly. We assess performance on zero-shot audio-text retrieval and zero-shot audio classification. On the Clotho caption retrieval task~\citep{audiocaps-clotho}, without any parallel AT data, \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace exceeds the supervised state of the art by 2.2\% R@1; on zero-shot audio classification tasks, it establishes new state-of-the-art results, achieving 57.1\% accuracy on ESC50~\citep{ESC50} and 44.7\% accuracy on US8K~\citep{US8K}. We also demonstrate that the zero-resource pivoting AT model \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace can be enhanced through: \begin{enumerate}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep \item[(1)] \emph{Unsupervised curation:} wherein noisy AT pairs are explicitly extracted from the pivoting model and function as additional training data (e.g., +5.7\% on ESC50 and +9.3\% on US8K); and \item[(2)] \emph{Few-shot curation:} wherein a limited number of human-annotated audio caption pairs are provided during training (e.g., several hundred pairs increase the zero-shot audio classification accuracy by 8\% on US8K). \end{enumerate} Nevertheless, for ESC-50, according to the empirical scaling relationship we discover, approximately $2^{21} \approx 2\text{M}$ aligned audio-text pairs would be required for the zero-shot model to achieve human parity on ESC50 under our configuration, representing an order-of-magnitude increase over the largest currently-available audio-text corpus from~\citet{audiocaps}. \begin{comment} Altogether, \yanpeng{this just duplicates the above para, maybe turn the above para into takeways?}: \begin{itemize}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep] \item[(1)] We introduce \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, a tri-modal pivoting model which learns strong \yanpeng{is "strong" too much?}\youngjae{then we can tone down a little, how about promising or robust/firm?} audio-text alignment without using any parallel audio-text pairs. \item[(2)] We investigate cases of minimum audio-text supervision and find that even un-aligned audio-text pairs help. \item[(3)] We study empirical scaling laws for \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace and find that filling the gap between zero-shot performance and supervised performance (e.g., on audio classification) would require a prohibitively large number of aligned audio-text pairs.\yanpeng{this finding is a bit strange, maybe it is because most of the newly added training samples have already been there in the training data.} \end{itemize} We believe that, by introducing the first tri-modal pivoting model and conducting comprehensive model analyses, our work will inspire future work on learning audio-text connections with little to no supervision. \end{comment}

text: The introduction of large pre-trained language models such as BERT~\cite{bert} has revolutionized Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. These models have demonstrated remarkable capability to adapt to diverse tasks through straightforward fine-tuning. In early 2019, \textit{Nogueira and Cho}~\cite{passage_ranking} attained state-of-the-art performance -- with substantial improvements -- on the MS MARCO passage re-ranking task, establishing the foundation for LM-based neural ranking models. Due to stringent efficiency constraints, these models have initially been employed as re-rankers within a two-stage ranking pipeline, where first-stage retrieval -- or candidate generation -- is performed using bag-of-words models (e.g. BM25) that utilize inverted indexes. While BOW models continue to serve as robust baselines~\cite{neural_hype}, they are affected by the persistent vocabulary mismatch problem, where relevant documents may lack terms that occur in the query. Consequently, there have been efforts to replace conventional BOW approaches with learned (neural) rankers. Developing such models presents multiple challenges concerning efficiency and scalability: thus there exists a requirement for methods where the majority of computation can be performed offline and online inference remains rapid. Dense retrieval using approximate nearest neighbors search has demonstrated remarkable performance~\cite{xiong2021approximate,qu-etal-2021-rocketqa,lin-etal-2021-batch,Hofstaetter2021_tasb_dense_retrieval}, but can still derive benefits from BOW models (e.g. through combining both signal types), owing to the lack of explicit term matching. Therefore, there has recently been increasing interest in learning \emph{sparse representations} for queries and documents~\cite{snrm, dai2019contextaware,nogueira2019document,zhao2020sparta,sparterm2020,gao-etal-2021-coil,10.1145/3404835.3463030,10.1145/3404835.3463098}. Through this approach, models can inherit the advantageous properties of BOW models such as exact-match of (potentially latent) terms, efficiency of inverted indexes and interpretability. Furthermore, by modeling implicit or explicit (latent, contextualized) \emph{expansion} mechanisms -- analogous to conventional expansion models in IR -- these models can mitigate the vocabulary mismatch. In this paper, we extend the SPLADE model~\cite{10.1145/3404835.3463098} and propose several enhancements/modifications that yield improvements in effectiveness or efficiency: \begin{enumerate*} \item through simply modifying SPLADE pooling mechanism, we achieve effectiveness increases by a substantial margin; \item simultaneously, we propose an extension of the model excluding query expansion. Such model is inherently more efficient, since everything can be pre-computed and indexed offline, while delivering results that remain competitive; \item finally, we employ distillation techniques~\cite{hofstatter2020improving} to enhance SPLADE performance, achieving near state-of-the-art results on the MS MARCO passage ranking task as well as the BEIR zero-shot evaluation benchmark~\cite{beir_2021}. \end{enumerate*}

text: Data sets and statistics concerning groups of individuals are increasingly gathered and disseminated, supplying numerous optimization and learning algorithms. In numerous instances, the disseminated data encompass sensitive information whose privacy is rigorously regulated. For instance, in the United States, census data is governed under Title 13 \cite{Title13}, which mandates that no individual be identifiable from any data release by the Census Bureau. In Europe, data dissemination is regulated according to the General Data Protection Regulation \cite{GDPR}, which governs the control and transfer of personal data. Consequently, statistical agencies disseminate privacy-preserving data and statistics that comply with these requirements. \emph{Differential Privacy} \cite{Dwork:06} is of particular significance to achieve this objective. Differential privacy constitutes a formal privacy definition that constrains the disclosure risk of any individual participating in a computation. It is regarded as the de-facto standard for privacy protection and has been adopted by various corporations \cite{erlingsson2014rappor,apple} and governmental agencies \cite{abowd2018us}. For data-release tasks, differentially private algorithms typically inject carefully calibrated noise into the data prior to release. Nevertheless, while this process guarantees privacy, it also compromises the fidelity of the released data. In particular, the injected noise frequently produces data sets that violate consistency constraints of the application domain. For instance, in census statistics, the number of individuals satisfying a property must be consistent within a geographical hierarchy, e.g., at the national, state, and county levels. The injection of independent noise, however, cannot ensure the consistency of these constraints. To address this limitation, the differentially private outputs can be \emph{post-processed} via data-independent functions that transform the noisy data to render it consistent with the domain constraints. The post-processing step is guaranteed to preserve differential privacy. Furthermore, when the feasible region is convex, a widely adopted class of post-processing functions, termed \emph{projections}, is guaranteed to enhance accuracy. Post-processing has been applied successfully in numerous applications, including census data \cite{abowd2018us}, energy systems \cite{fioretto:TSG20}, and mobility \cite{xi:15}. However, the effect of post-processing on the noise distribution is inadequately understood: It is frequently argued that it may introduce bias and/or increase variance. Figure \ref{fig:bias} illustrates this aspect on a census data-release problem, described subsequently in the paper. It depicts the distribution of the Laplacian residual $\tilde{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\bm{x}$ denotes the true data and $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ the noisy data, obtained by applying Laplacian noise to $\bm{x}$, as well as the post-processed residual $\hat{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\hat{\bm{x}}$ is the projection of $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ onto the feasible region. The results are presented for two counties, and, as can be observed, the post-processing introduces substantial bias on their associated privacy-preserving data. The primary contribution of this paper is to take an initial step towards understanding the properties of post-processing. Motivated by census applications, it examines the behavior of two widely adopted classes of post-processing functions, termed \emph{projections}, for domains where the feasibility space is specified by linear equations. The two classes differ by the presence of non-negativity constraints. The paper demonstrates that, when non-negativity constraints are absent, the projection does not introduce bias. When projections include non-negativity constraints, the paper presents an upper bound on the bias, which provides some insights regarding the type of problems for which the bias will be significant. Finally, the paper provides a detailed analysis of an important sub-problem used to satisfy hierarchical constraints in data-release tasks: It fully characterizes the residual distribution of the post-processed data, demonstrates that it converges towards the Laplace distribution, and sheds some interesting light on the effect of projections on the variance of the post-processed data, which may have strong implications with respect to group fairness.
