text: This work examines a perimeter defense problem within a conical environment where a single mobile vehicle attempts to intercept mobile intruders before they penetrate a designated region (termed the perimeter). This scenario emerges when a UAV must tag (or transmit critical information to) the intruders (targets) before they reach a particular region of interest. The intruders are spawned at the environment's boundary and advance radially inward with constant speed toward the perimeter. The vehicle, which possesses a finite capture radius, maneuvers with constrained speed (exceeding that of the intruders) with the objective of \textit{capturing} as many intruders as feasible before they reach the perimeter. This constitutes an online problem since the quantity and arrival location of intruders are progressively disclosed over time. Most previous works in the domain of perimeter defense have either concentrated on determining optimal strategies for a limited number of agents or examined a stochastic arrival process for the intruders~\cite{von2020multiple,macharet2020adaptive,ShivamDVR2019}. While these studies offer valuable insights, they fundamentally disregard the \emph{worst-case performance} where the intruders might coordinate their actions to overwhelm the defense \cite{von2021turret}. In this work, we employ a competitive analysis technique~\cite{sleator1985amortized} to evaluate online vehicle motion planning algorithms. In competitive analysis, we assess the performance of an online algorithm, $A$, utilizing the concept of \emph{competitive ratio}, i.e., the ratio of an optimal offline algorithm's performance divided by algorithm $A$'s performance for a worst-case input instance. Algorithm $A$ is $c$-competitive if its competitive ratio does not exceed $c$ which signifies its performance is guaranteed to remain within a factor, $c$, of the optimal for all input instances. In this work, the performance of an algorithm, whether online or offline, is quantified by the fraction of intruders captured. A related research area is vehicle routing with new inputs arriving over time. Introduced on graphs in~\cite{psaraftis1988dynamic}, a typical approach necessitates that the vehicle routes be re-planned as new information is revealed over time. We direct the reader to \cite{bullo2011dynamic} and the references therein for a review of this literature. In most vehicle routing problems, the input (known as \emph{demands}) are static, and thus, the problem involves finding the shortest route through the demands to minimize (maximize) the cost (reward); examples of such metrics would be the total service time or the number of inputs \emph{serviced}. Perimeter defense problems were initially introduced for a single vehicle and a single intruder in~\cite{isaacs1965differential}. Since then, perimeter defense has been predominantly formulated as a pursuit-evasion differential game. The multiplayer setting for the same has been studied extensively as a reach-avoid game in which the aim is to design control policies for the intruders and the defenders \cite{chen2016multiplayer,garcia2019strategies,davydov2020pursuer}. A typical approach requires computing solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation, which is generally only suitable for low dimensional state spaces and in simple environments \cite{margellos2011hamilton,chen2014path}. The key distinction of our current work from the past work is the geometry of the environment which produces novel results in terms of optimally positioning the vehicle, role of capture radius and additional conditions to guarantee competitiveness of the algorithms. A single vehicle having a finite capture radius $r$, maneuvers with maximum speed of unity with an aim to capture the intruders. Our main contributions are as follows. We first establish two necessary conditions in the parameter space for achieving a $c$-competitive algorithm with a finite $c$. Specifically, we characterize the parameter regime in which no online algorithm is $c$-competitive and a parameter regime in which no algorithm can be superior to $2$-competitive. Next, we design and analyze three classes of algorithms and establish their competitiveness. Specifically, we identify parameter regimes in which the first two algorithms are provably $1$ and $2$-competitive, respectively, and the third algorithm has a finite competitive ratio that varies with the problem parameters ($r,\rho,\theta$). Section \ref{sec:Fundamental_limits} establishes two necessary conditions; first on achieving a finite competitive ratio and second on achieving at best a competitive ratio of $2$. In section \ref{sec:Algorithms}, we design and analyze three algorithms and establish their competitive ratios, section \ref{sec:Results} provides additional insights through numerous parameter space plots and finally, section \ref{sec:Conclusion} summarizes this work and outlines directions for future works.

text: Semi-VOS tracks a target object across all frames within a video sequence given the ground truth mask of the initial frame. VOS categorizes each pixel as either background or part of a tracked object. This task exhibits broad applicability to numerous real-world applications including autonomous driving, surveillance, video editing, and the emerging category of augmented reality/mixed reality devices. VOS represents a challenging task since it must differentiate the target object from other similar objects within the scene even as the target's appearance evolves over time and through occlusions. Various methods have been proposed for addressing video object segmentation including online learning~\cite{robinson2020learning, maninis2018video}, mask propagation~\cite{lin2020flow, cheng2017segflow}, and template matching~\cite{wang2019fast, oh2019video}. A common characteristic across most of these prior methods is the utilization of information from previous frames -- either solely the first frame, some of the preceding frames (first and last being a popular choice) or all the previous frames -- to generate high quality segmentation masks. In this work, we pose a different question\\ \textbf{Q: Can we use temporal information to identify when the object appearance and position has not changed across frames?}\\ The rationale for doing so would be to bypass much of the expensive computation required to generate a high-quality mask for the current frame if that mask is nearly identical to the mask we computed in the previous frame. Instead, we can generate the current frame's mask using an inexpensive model that simply makes minor adjustments to the previous frame's features. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaserIntro2}(a), for a substantial fraction of the frames in the popular DAVIS and YouTube-VOS dataset, object masks are highly similar to their previous frame's masks (73.3\% of consecutive frames in DAVIS 17 dataset have IoU exceeding 0.7). We build upon the above observation by constructing an inexpensive temporal matching module to rapidly quantify the similarity of the current frame with the previous frame. We utilize the similarity to gate the computation of high-quality masks for the current frame -- if the similarity is high we reuse previous features with minor refinements and avoid the expensive mask generation step. This enables us to bypass the majority of computations for the current frame without compromising accuracy. Our approach complements the existing video object segmentation approaches and to demonstrate its generality, we integrate our proposal into multiple prior video object segmentation models -- FRTM~\cite{robinson2020learning} and TTVOS~\cite{park2020ttvos}. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose dynamically skipping computation of segmentation masks based on object movement. We believe this represents a significant contribution that will enable high-quality video object segmentation models to operate on mobile devices in real time with minimal battery impact. We make the following contributions in this paper: \begin{itemize} \item We make the case for exploiting temporal information to skip mask generation for frames with minimal or no movement. \item We develop a general framework to skip mask computation consisting of sub-networks to estimate movement across frames, dynamic selection between processing full-network or reusing previous frame's features for generating masks and a novel loss function to train this dynamic architecture. \item We evaluate our approach on multiple video object segmentation models (FRTM, TTVOS) as well as multiple challenging datasets (DAVIS 16, DAVIS 17, Youtube-VOS) and demonstrate that we can save up to $47.5\%$ computation and accelerate FPS by $1.45\times$ with minimal accuracy impact on DAVIS 16 (within approximately 0.4 $\%$ of baseline). \end{itemize}

text: Query attribute value extraction constitutes the joint task of detecting named entities in search queries as diverse surface form attribute values and normalizing them into canonical forms to address misspelling and abbreviation issues. These two sub-tasks are conventionally termed named entity recognition (NER)~\cite{chiu2016named} and attribute value normalization (AVN) ~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. As demonstrated in Figure~\ref{fig:framework}, we illustrate the procedure of optimal query attribute value extraction. When a user submits the query ``{\it MK tote for womans}'', we initially employ a NER model to identify the entity type ``brand'' for "{\it MK}", ``product type'' for "{\it tote}", and ``audience'' for ``{\it womans}''. These extracted named entities exist in the informal surface form of attribute values. Nevertheless, such informal surface forms are inconsistent with products indexed using canonical form attribute values in formal written style. Specifically, ``{\it MK}'' represents an abbreviation of brand ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' constitutes a hyponym of the product type "{\it handbag}", and ``{\it womans}'' contains a spelling error. This misalignment creates substantial challenges for the product search engine to retrieve relevant product items that users genuinely prefer. Consequently, the AVN module is equally crucial to transform the surface form for each attribute value into the canonical form, i.e., ``{\it MK}'' to ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' to ``{\it handbag}'' and ``{\it womans}'' to ``{\it women}''. In the E-commerce domain, extracting these attribute values from queries is essential to a broad range of product search applications, such as product retrieval~\cite{cheng2020end} and ranking~\cite{wen2019building}, and query rewriting~\cite{guisado2016enrich}. Unfortunately, existing works exclusively focus on surface form attribute value extraction based on NER while neglecting canonical form transformation, which is impractical in realistic scenarios~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. To address this gap, this paper proposes a unified query attribute value extraction system that encompasses both phases. By leveraging insights from large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data to reduce supervision costs, we further enhance extraction performance. Regarding the initial NER stage, recent advances in deep learning models (e.g., Bi-LSTM+CRF) have achieved promising results~\cite{huang2015bidirectional,raganato2017neural}. However, they heavily depend on massive labeled data, where manual labeling for token-level labels is particularly expensive and labor-intensive. To mitigate this issue in E-commerce, prior studies \cite{kozareva2016recognizing,cheng2020end,wen2019building} resort to utilizing large-scale behavior data from the product side as weak supervision for queries based on simple string matching strategies. Nevertheless, these weakly-supervised labels contain substantial noise due to partial or incomplete token labels based on exact string matching. For instance, as illustrated in Table~\ref{tab:ws_example} case\#1, when we utilize the attribute values of top-clicked product ``{LG 32-inch television}'', i.e., ``brand'' for ``{\it LG}'', ``size'' for ``{\it 32-inch}'', ``product type'' for ``{\it television}''as weak supervision to match the query ``{\it lg smart tv 32}'', it can only generate the label ``brand'' for ``{\it lg}'', concealing valuable knowledge for unannotated tokens. For this reason, weak supervision-based methods~\cite{shang2018learning,cheng2020end} typically perform poorly, even worse after powerful pre-trained language models (PLMs) (e.g., BERT~\cite{devlin2019bert} ) are introduced since PLMs are more susceptible to fitting noise. To address this issue, we consider a more reliable approach, which additionally incorporates strongly-labeled human annotated data to denoise the weak labels from distant supervision. As such, the NER model can be improved by making more effective use of both large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data and strongly-labeled human-annotated data. Regarding the second AVN phase, customers tend to employ diverse surface forms to mention each attribute value in search queries due to misspellings, spelling variants, or abbreviations. This circumstance occurs frequently in user queries and product titles of e-commerce. For example, eBay has observed that 20\% of product titles in the clothing and shoes category involve such surface form brands~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. Thus, normalizing these surface form attribute values derived from NER signals to a single normalized attribute value is critical. This aspect is typically overlooked by existing works~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. To reduce human annotation efforts, weakly-labeled behavior data can also contribute to AVN. For example, ``{\it MK tote for womans}'' mentioning the brand ``{\it MK}'' leads to clicks on product items associated with the brand ``{\it Michael Kors}''. We can reasonably infer a strong connection between the surface form value ``{\it MK}'' and the canonical form value ``{\it Michael Kors}'' if this association occurs across many queries. Motivated by these observations, we propose a unified \textbf{QUE}ry \textbf{A}ttribute Value Extraction in E\textbf{CO}mmerce (\textbf{QUEACO}) framework that efficiently utilizes large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data for both query NER and AVN. For query NER, QUEACO leverages strongly-labeled data to denoise weakly-labeled data based on a novel teacher-student network, where a teacher network trained on strongly-labeled data generates pseudo-labels to refine weakly-labeled data for teaching a student network. Unlike classic teacher-student networks that can only produce pseudo-labels from a fixed teacher, our pseudo-labeling process from the teacher is continuously and dynamically adapted by feedback from the student's performance on strongly-labeled data. This encourages the teacher network to generate superior pseudo-labels to teach the student, maximally mitigating error propagation from noisy weak labels. For query AVN, we utilize weakly-labeled query-to-attribute behavior data and QUEACO NER predictions to model associations between surface form and canonical form attribute values. As such, surface form attribute values from queries can be normalized to the most relevant canonical form attribute values from products. Empirically, extensive experiments on a real-world large-scale E-commerce dataset demonstrate that QUEACO NER can significantly outperform state-of-the-art semi-supervised and weakly-supervised methods. Moreover, we qualitatively demonstrate the effectiveness and necessity of QUEACO AVN. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first attempt to propose a unified query attribute value extraction system in E-commerce, incorporating both query NER and AVN. QUEACO can automatically identify product-related attributes from user queries and transform them into canonical forms, by leveraging weak supervision from large-scale behavior data; (2) Our QUEACO NER is also the first work that efficiently utilizes both human-annotated strongly-labeled data and large-scale weakly-labeled data from the query-product click graph. Moreover, the proposed QUEACO NER model can significantly outperform existing state-of-the-art baselines; (3) We propose the QUEACO AVN module that uses aggregated query-to-attribute behavioral data to build connections among queries, surface form attribute values, and canonical form values. The proposed QUEACO AVN module can effectively normalize surface form values with spelling errors, spelling variants, and abbreviation problems.

text: Manipulation seeks to achieve a relative arrangement of objects, frequently with a desired set of contacts between them. In structured environments, this desired contact can be attained with a specific robot pose, but as robots are deployed in less-structured environments, the required robot pose may vary. A robot that can robustly detect contact mode can enhance autonomy, for instance using online contact detection to switch the controller \cite{bledt2018} or to provide a reward signal to a learning process \cite{vecerik2018}. We define a {\it contact mode} as a constraint over generalized robot and environment position $q$, i.e. $\phi_i(q) = 0$ for the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ mode. This is frequently considered an infinitely stiff kinematic constraint in robotics, either eliminated or enforced with impulses in time-stepping approaches \cite{stewart2000}. Here, we consider a compliant contact model where forces are measured over position $q$ \cite{castro2020, minniti2021a}. Contact can also be described with an inequality $\phi_i(q) \geq 0$ to describe non-penetration of rigid bodies \cite{posa2014, stewart2000}, but we separate the contact conditions into discrete contact modes with equality constraints \cite{minniti2021a}. Contact mode can be utilized for task representation and planning. As the contact depends on surface geometry, contact modelling is more prevalent in locomotion where flat surfaces simplify the expression of $\phi(q)$ \cite{posa2014}. In manipulation, when constraints are simple and known in advance, a task can be represented as a sequence of contact modes \cite{fengpan2004}, which can then be employed for motion planning \cite{deschutter2007, polverini2019}. Contact geometry can also be demonstrated with specialized instruments \cite{meeussen2007}. Data-based methods have been utilized, learning contact geometry on simplified geometries \cite{pfrommer2020}, but not yet demonstrated on robotic manipulation. Offline contact models are not robust to variation in environmental objects \cite{rosell2000}, which can be enhanced with online detection of contact. Estimation of environment dynamics has been established, using a Kalman filter to estimate environment stiffness \cite{rovedaa} or impedance \cite{minniti2021a}. In locomotion, foot contact mode estimation has been proposed in a stochastic framework \cite{bledt2018}, demonstrated to improve robustness to unexpected changes in floor height. In manipulation, discrete contact mode estimation has been proposed through recursive Bayesian estimation \cite{jasim2014, ren2018, haninger2018} and support vector machines \cite{golz2015}. The capability to sense contact mode is influenced by the hardware design. Hardware design also affects peak collision force \cite{wensing2017, bicchi2004, haninger2019a}, and contact stability \cite{eppinger1992, pratt1995}. The location, degree and structure of compliance can be designed to improve energy efficiency \cite{bolivar-nieto2021, haddadin2018}, reduce the need for information \cite{haninger2021}, or reduce the problem dimension \cite{hamaya2020}. Compliance can have adverse effects, reducing the feasible feedback control gain \cite{tomei1991} and the effectiveness of feedforward control \cite{dellasantina2017}, limiting motion control performance. The contribution of this paper is a method to design compliance to enhance estimation of the contact mode. The estimation of contact mode is established \cite{bledt2018, jasim2014, ren2018, haninger2018}, but the impact of mechatronic design on this estimation is not yet investigated. Analytical rules for `distinguishability' of contact modes have been proposed \cite{debus2005}, but the approach here considers compliance and sensor noise. This paper first introduces the compliant contact models, then the information gain from position and force measurements in the fully- and partially-observed case. The information gain is written in closed form for a linear inertial system. text: Let $T$ be a weighted tree. The tree metric induced by $T$, denoted $M_T$, represents the complete graph on the vertices of $T$ where the weight of each edge $(u, v)$ equals the weight of the path connecting $u$ and $v$ in $T$. For $t\ge 1$, a $t$-spanner for a metric $(V, d)$ constitutes a subgraph $H$ of the complete graph on $V$ such that every pair of distinct points $u, v\in V$ is connected by a path in $H$ of total weight at most $t\cdot d(u, v)$. We designate such paths as $t$-spanner paths. A $t$-spanner possesses diameter $\Lambda$ if every pair of points is connected by a $t$-spanner path consisting of at most $\Lambda$ edges. Typically, $t$-spanners are constructed to be sparse, often with a linear number of edges. The lightness of a graph represents the ratio of its weight to the weight of its minimum spanning tree. Solomon and Elkin \cite{tree-spanner} establish a 1-spanner for tree metrics. Given an $n$ vertex weighted tree of maximum degree $\Delta$, the 1-spanner contains $O(n)$ edges, $O(\log n)$ diameter, $O(\log n)$ lightness and maximum degree bounded by $\Delta + O(1)$. While constituting an interesting construction in its own right, this tree metric 1-spanner has been employed in a series of papers as a tool for reducing the diameter of various Euclidean and doubling metric spanner constructions \cite{short-thin-lanky,doubling-spanner,optimal-euclidean-spanners,tree-spanner,partitions-to-covers}. Once a spanner has been constructed, it becomes crucial to find these short paths efficiently. A local routing algorithm for a weighted graph $G$ represents a method by which a message can be transmitted from any vertex in $G$ to a given destination vertex. The successor to each vertex $u$ on the path traversed by the routing algorithm must be determined using only knowledge of the destination vertex, the neighbourhood of $u$ and possibly some additional information stored at $u$. The efficiency of a routing algorithm is measured by the distance a message needs to traverse through a network before reaching its destination as well as by the storage requirements for each vertex. There exists a substantial body of work on local routing algorithms in the literature. The difficulty of designing an effective local routing algorithm clearly depends on the properties of the underlying network. Some authors have developed algorithms for very general classes of networks. For example, the algorithm of Chan et al. \cite{heirarchical-routing-in-doubling-metrics} operates in any network although its quality depends on the induced doubling dimension. Many authors have concentrated on highly efficient algorithms for specific classes of networks. For example, there has been a line of research into routing algorithms for various classes of planar graphs \cite{convex-subdivisions,routing-in-delaunay}. Support for efficient local routing algorithms constitutes a desirable feature in a spanner and in some recent papers, researchers have designed spanners which simultaneously achieve support for efficient local routing with other properties. See, for example, the work of Ashvinkumar et al. \cite{local-routing-in-sparse-and-light}. There appears to be limited work in the literature in designing spanners which achieve both support for local routing as well as low diameter. Given a spanner with diameter $\Lambda$, it is natural to require that a local routing algorithm on this spanner match this diameter, i.e., the algorithm should be guaranteed to terminate after at most $\Lambda$ hops. Abraham and Malkhi \cite{compact-routing-in-euclidean-metrics} provide a construction, for any $\epsilon > 0$, of a $(1+\epsilon)$-spanner for points in two dimensional Euclidean space with an accompanying routing algorithm. The diameter of the routing algorithm is $O(\log D)$ with high probability where $D$ represents the quotient of the largest and smallest inter-point distances. The routing algorithm achieves routing ratio $O(\log n)$, with high probability, for $n$ points on a uniform grid. In this paper, we demonstrate that the 1-spanner construction of Solomon and Elkin \cite{tree-spanner} supports a local routing algorithm with $O(\log n)$ diameter in the worst case. In Section~\ref{app:doubling}, we show that this routing algorithm can be adapted to a class of doubling metric $(1+\epsilon)$-spanners which employ the 1-spanner construction to achieve low diameter while maintaining low weight and low degree.

text: A text index constructed on a string $T$ of length~$n$ is a data structure that can respond to the following queries, for a given pattern~$P$ of length~$m$: \begin{description} \crampedItems \item[\functionname{exists}(P)]: does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \item[\functionname{count}(P)]: how often does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \item[\functionname{locate}(P)]: where does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \end{description} The responses are a boolean, a number, and a list of starting positions in the text, respectively. $\functionname{locate}(P)$ is the most powerful query since the cardinality of its returned set equals the return value of $\functionname{count}(P)$, while $\functionname{count}(P) > 0$ is a boolean statement equivalent to $\functionname{exists}(P)$. One prominent example of such a text index is the FM-index~\cite{ferragina00fmindex}. It comprises a wavelet tree~\cite{grossi03wavelet} constructed upon the BWT~\cite{burrows94bwt} of the text, and can respond to $\functionname{count}(P)$ in time linear to the length of $P$ multiplied by the operational cost of the wavelet tree, which can be logarithmic in the alphabet size and up to constant~\cite{belazzougui14index}. Given the BWT comprises $r$ maximal character runs, this data structure can be represented by two additional bit vectors~\cite[Thm.~3]{makinen05rle} of length~$n$ in $r \lg \sigma + \oh{r \lg \sigma} + \Oh{n}$ bits of space. This space can be further reduced with Huffman-shaped wavelet trees by exploiting the zeroth order empirical entropy on the string comprising the different letters of the runs in the BWT\@. For $\functionname{locate}$, the indexes based on the BWT are augmented by a sampling of the suffix array~\cite{manber93sa}, which requires $n \lg n$ bits in its plain form. In what follows, we do not address $\functionname{locate}$ since this augmentation can be performed orthogonal to our proposed data structure, and is left as future work. Although current approaches achieve \Oh{m} time for $\functionname{count}(P)$ with $|P| = m$, it involves $\Oh{m}$ queries to the underlying wavelet tree data structure, which is executed in a constant number of random accesses. Unfortunately, these random accesses make the FM-index rather slow in practice. The BWT constructed on a grammar compressed string allows us to match non-terminals in one backward search step, hence allowing us to \emph{jump over multiple characters} in one step. Consequently, we spend less time on the cache-unfriendly wavelet tree, but more time on extracting the grammar symbols stored in cache-friendly arrays. Our experiments reveal that this additional work pays off for the reduced usage of the wavelet tree regarding the time performance. Regarding the space, the grammar captures the compressibility far better than the run-length compression of the BWT constructed on the plain text. Here, we leverage certain properties of the GCIS (grammar compression by induced suffix sorting) grammar~\cite{nunes18grammar}, which have been discovered by~\citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms} for determining non-terminals of the text matching portions of the pattern. \paragraph{Our Contribution} To summarize, our contribution is that combining the BWT with a specific choice of grammar-based compression method achieves potentially better compression than the plain RLBWT, and at the same time reducing the memory accesses for count queries (heuristically). This comes at the expense of additional computation for constructing the grammar of the text during the construction and of the pattern during a query. \subsection*{Related Work} A lot of research effort has been invested in analyzing and improving \functionname{count}{} of the BWT (e.g., \cite{makinen05rle} and the references therein) and the sampling of the suffix array (e.g.,~\cite{gagie18bwt} and the references therein). Another line of research are grammar indexes, which usually enhance a grammar for \functionname{locate}{} queries. Although computing the smallest grammar is NP-complete~\cite{charikar05grammar}, there are grammars with a size of \Oh{r \log(n/r)}~\cite{gagie18bwt}, and some grammars are empirically much smaller than the RLBWT in practice. However, most indexes have a quadratic dependency on the pattern length for \functionname{locate}{}~\cite{claude12grammarindex,claude21grammarcompressed}, and are unable to provide improved query times independent of the number of occurrences of the pattern, when considering only \functionname{count}{}. A notable exception is the grammar index of \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}, which achieves \Oh{m + \log^{2+\epsilon} n} time for \functionname{count}{} with a space of $\Oh{\gamma \log(n/\gamma)}$, for $\gamma$ being the size of the smallest string attractor~\cite{kempa18stringattractors} of the input text. However, this approach seems to be rather impractical, and up to now nobody has considered implementing it. Related to our work is the grammar indexes of \citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms}, which are also based on the GCIS grammar, where the latter is based on results of \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}. They also use similar techniques for extracting non-terminals from the pattern grammar, for which they can be certain that these appear in the text grammar. However, they need to call \functionname{locate}{} for computing \functionname{count}{}, and thus their time complexity is dependent on the number of occurrences of a pattern. We are not aware of a combination of the BWT with grammar techniques, except for construction. Here, \citet{karkkainen12bwt} studied the construction of the BWT upon a grammar-compressed input. They applied a grammar compression merging frequent bigrams similar to Re-Pair~\cite{larsson99repair}, and empirically could improve the computation of the BWT as well as the reconstruction of the text from the BWT\@. With a similar target, \citet{diazdominguez21grammar,diaz21grammar} computed the extended BWT~\cite{mantaci07ebwt}, a BWT variant for multiple texts, from the GCIS grammar.

dipper: Introductory Chapter; The Problem; The Solution; The Solution; The Solution: Machine-learning (ML) systems have been widely adopted in mission-critical applications. Their effectiveness is fundamentally dependent on the quantity and quality of the training data, and on the assumption that the data distribution in the deployed system remains consistent and adequately represented by the training samples. However, this assumption cannot be guaranteed. Saria et al. (in Saria, 2019) classified limitations and failures of ML systems into multiple regimes: shifts in data distribution (from training to deployment), high variability of data (e.g., overlapping class labels near decision boundaries), and limitations of the model itself (e.g., using log-linear decision boundaries in the face of neural ML). In order to detect such risks and understand the underlying causes of failure, a trustworthy ML system requires models and tools for detecting failure risks and analyzing their underlying causes. This paper addresses the problem of predicting, analyzing and mitigating risks of system failure. Its aim is to equip the system with “uncertainty scores” for its predictions so as to be able to (a) reliably predict test-time inputs for which the system is likely to fail, and (b) identify the “type of uncertainty” that induces the risk, so that (c) appropriate actions can be taken. In the case of many production data out of distribution, collecting additional samples and retraining the system would be a remedy. The challenge is to decide which action is appropriate in which circumstances. For example, if an introspection component indicated that the ML system's output had a non-negligible probability of being wrong, the system could abstain and defer to a human expert rather than risk adverse consequences for human lives. The standard method for determining whether a model’s predictions are trustworthy is to use confidence scores based on the model’s predictive probabilities, such as the max-class probability in neural ML [16] or the distance from the decision boundary in SVMs [17, 18]. But such probabilities are unreliable estimates of a model’s uncertainty [18, 19]. Even if confidences are calibrated (e.g. Platt1999probabilistic, Guo2017calibration), they may still be unreliable because the ranking of the confidences can be unreliable. This is because calibration methods are focused on scaling the scores, that is, monotonic transformations with respect to the prediction scores, which do not change the ranking of the examples ranked as confident or uncertain. Figure ref: fig. (mnist-examples-a,b) presents two examples where a CNN model misclassifies handwritten digits from the MNIST dataset (a, b) while producing high confidence scores. Moreover, confidence scores do not reflect what the model does not know. Fig. 2 (c,d) shows two examples where a CNN model gives a higher confidence to a misclassified sample than to a correct one. Despite this, the CNN model predicts with high confidence (see Fig. In Fig. 1c, d) the Fashion MNIST data set contains many positive examples of shirts similar to (c), but few similar to (d). Here the training distribution is poorly adapted to the test distribution. However, the most important issue is that confidence scores are “one-dimensional” (ref:fig:mnist-examples). This limitation persists even in the state-of-the-art model Trust Score (cite:jiang2018trust), which serves as a major base line for this paper. Common methods for uncertainty estimation include Bayesian methods (Denker, 1990; Barber, 1998) or specialized changes to the learning algorithm (e.g., Gal, 2016; Depeweg, 2018; Lam, 2017; Shaker, 2020; Ustimenko, 2020). These methods are tightly coupled to the choice of the underlying classification model, and thus require special modifications to the ML pipeline. Hence, confidence scores from previous works have limited utility in identifying different mitigations that are appropriate. It is therefore unsuitable for a large number of black-box ML systems. This paper presents Risk Advisor, a general and versatile framework for estimating the risk of failure of any already trained black-box classification model. Risk Advisor consists of a post-hoc meta-learner for uncertainty estimation that is completely separate from the underlying ML system, and it can be incorporated without any changes to the underlying ML pipeline. Fig. 1 shows a schematic overview of our framework. The EM meta-learner is model-agnostic: it can be applied to any family of black-box classifiers (e.g., deep neural networks, decision trees, etc.). The method is based on the information-theoretic notions of “uncertainty of model”, “uncertainty of observation” and “uncertainty of inference”; these notions are well established, but to the best of our knowledge, have not yet been applied to the risk analysis of black-box ML systems. Besides a risk-score that is more reliable than that provided by previous work, Risk Advisor also provides a refined analysis of the underlying uncertainty that leads to the risks. text: The quantum community has achieved substantial progress in developing algorithms that demonstrate the potential for speedup relative to their classical counterparts. Nevertheless, implementing these algorithms into quantum circuits remains an outstanding challenge. Numerous research groups employ machine learning \cite{cincio2018learning, fosel2021quantum}, genetic algorithms \cite{lee07,rasconi2019an}, linear algebra techniques \cite{re:amy:phds,nam2018automated} to design circuits that implement either exactly or approximately quantum primitives that are fundamental to many quantum algorithms. Researchers are also developing optimization methods to efficiently map logical circuits to physical quantum machines \cite{itoko2020optimization,zulehner2018an}. In our work, we address the problem of generalizing the SWAP test to include an arbitrary number of overlapping states. Two-state SWAP tests are valuable primitives in quantum computing which rely on controlled-swap (CSWAP) gates and an ancillary qubit to estimate the inner product $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ between two pure quantum states $\phi$ and $\psi$ \cite{kopczyk2018quantum}, as well as to compute the overlap $\mathtt{Tr}(\rho \sigma)$ of two mixed states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. If $\rho=\sigma$, a SWAP test measures the purity of the quantum state $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. For two $q$-qubit states $\phi,\psi$, the cost of evaluating $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ on a classical computer scales exponentially with $q$, while the depth of the SWAP test circuit on a quantum machine scales linearly with $q$ \cite{garcia2013swap}, yielding an exponential speedup that provides a quantum advantage provided that error correction/mitigation is achievable. SWAP test appears in numerous applications that depend on estimation of state overlaps. It has been utilized in quantum state characterization, such as measurement of entanglement and indistinguishabiliy \cite{Foulds2021, garcia2013swap}. It is valuable for benchmarking on a quantum computer by monitoring the amount of decoherence that occurs through a circuit. It is also a key module in hybrid quantum machine learning algorithms. For instance, in quantum supervised learning \cite{kopczyk2018quantum,ciliberto2018quantum,havlicek2019supervised} and in particular in quantum support vector machines (SVM) \cite{rebentrost2014quantum, rudolph2020generation}, it is employed to measure pairwise distances at the stage of cluster assignment. While the question of improving the SWAP test for two high-dimensional states has been the subject of several studies \cite{cincio2018learning, garcia2013swap}, to date, with the exception of a 3-state model presented in \cite{Hai-Rui, Galvao2019}, SWAP tests have been only implemented between two quantum states at a time \cite{kathuria2020implementation}. We investigate how to extend the SWAP test to $m$ arbitrary pure quantum states $\ket{\phi_{1}...\phi_{m}}$ and compute $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ for all pairs $i\neq j$ using at most $O(\log{m})$ measurements. Our approach relies on a pairing unitary $\mathcal{U}_{m}$ composed of $O(m)$ CSWAP gates controlled by $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. The pairing operator applied to $m$ state registers produces a superposition state where all pairs $(\phi_{i}, \phi_{j})$ appear with positive probability on the first two state registers and are labeled with a basis state formed by the ancillaries. By applying a standard two-state SWAP test to the resulting superposition state, measurement on the ancillary qubits matches the probability of an ancillary basis state to the state overlap this ancillary basis state is assigned to label. First, we construct a unitary $\mathcal{U}_{4}$ for a 4-state input with three ancillaries and three CSWAP gates. We demonstrate that the resulting circuit is optimal with respect to the number of CSWAP gates when limiting the number of measurements to four. Then, we use our 4-state circuit as a building block to develop a recursive algorithm capable of producing an $m$-state circuit for which all overlaps $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ are measured on $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. We provide a formal analysis of its complexity and show that the resulting circuit relies on $c_m=O(m)$ CSWAP gates and $d_m=O(\log m)$ ancillaries. Since our estimates of state overlaps are probabilistic, we need to repeat our experiment to obtain an estimate of each state overlap with a mean squared error less than some precision $\epsilon$. We model these repeated experiments by assuming access to an oracle that constructs the states $\ket{\phi_{1}}, ..., \ket{\phi_{m}}$. We demonstrate that for arbitrary $m$, the constraint to limit the number of measurements to $O(\log m)$ is necessary to guarantee a polynomial number of calls to the oracle. Numerically, we implement a genetic procedure to search how to optimally apply CSWAP gates to maximize the number of pairs that appear on the two first registers of a quantum circuit. Our optimization procedure is motivated by the fact that genetic algorithms are well suited for optimization problems with complex parameter and energy landscapes. Genetic algorithms have been employed in a variety of applications including scheduling, building design, trajectory optimization \cite{Hart, Yu}. They are also successful in automating classical circuit design \cite{aly} and more recently, in designing quantum circuits \cite{Potocek}. For $m=8$ input states and six measurements, we demonstrate empirically that a genetic algorithm does not find circuits with fewer than nine CSWAP gates, which is the number of CSWAP gates we use in our recursive construction (see \ref{circuit: U3}). \begin{figure}[t] \centering \tikzset{every picture/.style={scale=3}}

text: With the rapid advancement of radiological imaging techniques, ophthalmic images are generated in continuously increasing volumes. Three common ophthalmic image modalities exist: (1) \textbf{Slit Lamp.} The slit lamp technique \cite{cheung2011validity} is typically employed to examine the anterior segment and the posterior segment of the human eye, including eyelid, sclera, conjunctiva, iris, crystalline lens, and cornea. (2) \textbf{Retinal Fundus.} The retinal fundus image represents a crucial eye image modality that has been employed to diagnose numerous ocular diseases \cite{fu2018joint,fu2018disc} by capturing the eye's inner lining and the structures of the posterior eye. (3) \textbf{ASOCT.} Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (ASOCT) is utilized for visualization and assessment of anterior segment ocular features, such as the tear film, cornea, conjunctiva, sclera, rectus muscles, anterior chamber angle structures, and lens \cite{hirnschall2017prediction}. In recent decades, motivated by pattern recognition and computer vision techniques, particularly deep learning methods \cite{litjens2017survey}, ophthalmic image processing assumes an increasingly significant role in assisting diagnosis and disease assessment. However, the objective interpretation of ophthalmic images is characterized by substantial inter-observer variability and limited reproducibility. To address the discrepancy between expert interpretations, prior cases with similar disease manifestations could be presented to establish a reference-based assessment through Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR). CBIR is employed for retrieving user-required images by indexing and mining visual features of image content (\textit{e.g.}, color, shape, texture) from large-scale image databases \cite{zhou2017recent}. Unlike classification and grading tasks that directly provide diagnostic results, the task of ophthalmic CBIR aims to enhance diagnosis with evidence-based support. For superior assistance in assessment, CBIR should incorporate numerous cases, which necessitates the retrieval algorithm to be both scalable and accurate. Toward this objective, hashing methods for CBIR emerge as a promising solution by representing a high-dimensional image as a compact hash-code due to their storage capacity and processing time efficiency \cite{conjeti2017deep,wu2019deep}. Recently, deep learning-based hashing methods have been extensively applied for medical image retrieval, such as deep multiple instances hashing for tumor assessment \cite{conjeti2017deep}, deep residual hashing for chest X-ray images \cite{conjeti2017hashing}, order-sensitive deep hashing method for multi-morbidity medical image retrieval \cite{chen2018order}, etc. Nevertheless, existing deep hashing methods do not fully exploit the learning capacity of the deep network to capture the features of salient regions specifically. The information from salient regions typically constitutes the primary clue for clinical diagnosis. Particularly in ophthalmology, different grades or classes of ophthalmic images may exhibit similar overall appearance but possess subtle differences that can be distinguished by mining salient regions. As Fig.\ref{fig1} demonstrates, the ophthalmic images (A) and (B) originate from ASOCT which represents a non-invasive high-resolution anterior segment imaging technique. Both (A) and (B) are cataract cases with similar overall appearance, but two types of salient regions exist to differentiate them: over-bright region (blue) and over-dark region (blue). Cataract grading depends substantially on detecting and observing the salient regions, so the representation of salient regions should be specifically considered in ophthalmic image retrieval. Conversely, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig1}, one retinal fundus image (C) contains three symptoms that can be diagnosed according to different salient regions (green rectangle). The pathological myopic eye is typically characterized by leopard fundus, the diagnosis of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) can depend on the spatial information of macular, and the large optic cup and abnormality of Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL), which represent typical symptoms of glaucoma. The information from these salient regions should be captured and mapped into the hash-code to achieve the effect of differentiating fundus images in the retrieval task. Inspired by the attention mechanism in deep networks \cite{woo2018cbam,chen2017sca}, to effectively mine salient regions of ophthalmic images, we propose a novel end-to-end network, named Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), to enhance the discriminative capability of the hash-code by exploiting salient regions. To comprehensively mine salient regions and effectively enlarge their proportion in the hashing space, we utilize a spatial-attention module to focus on capturing the information of salient regions in the complete ophthalmic image. For similarity preservation, with the input image pairs sharing weights, we apply the siamese structure \cite{bertinetto2016fully} to learn the pairwise loss in the objective function. The pairwise distance in the hashing space is desired to be smaller if the input image pairs are similar and vice versa. The primary contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item[1)] Different grades or classes of ophthalmic images may exhibit similar overall appearance but possess subtle differences that can be distinguished by mining salient regions. According to this issue, a novel end-to-end network, named Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), is proposed for ophthalmic image retrieval. \item[2)] With the assistance of a spatial-attention module, by focusing on salient regions in the complete ophthalmic image with an end-to-end manner, our ASH can enhance the representation of salient regions to maximize the discriminative capability of the hash-code. \item[3)] The experiments on two different modalities of ophthalmic image datasets demonstrate that our ASH can significantly improve the accuracy while achieving reasonable efficiency, compared to the state-of-the-art deep hashing methods. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2} introduces related works. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3} describes our methodology in detail. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4} extensively evaluates the proposed method on two ophthalmic images datasets. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral5} provides concluding remarks.

text: Robots are progressively navigating through densely populated environments and moving alongside human individuals. This phenomenon is evident for service robots deployed in airports, hotels, restaurants, delivery robots operating on sidewalks, mobile robots functioning in warehouses, and autonomous vehicles. For these robotic systems to be deployed securely, humans in their vicinity must comprehend their navigational intentions. HRI researchers have conventionally concentrated on arm movement intent \cite{gielniak2011generating,kwon2018expressing}, investigating eye gaze \cite{moon2014meet,admoni2017social} and other non-verbal modalities \cite{saunderson2019robots} for stationary robots to more effectively communicate such intent. Recently, nevertheless, HRI researchers have commenced exploring the externalization or visualization of robotic navigation intent (e.g. path plans) as well \cite{coovert2014spatial,szafir2015communicating,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi,blenk2021lane}, to enable more comprehensible robot navigation behaviors, thereby improving trust and acceptance. One approach for communicating navigation intent is through directional projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi} such as arrow projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}, where the robot is equipped with a projector and projects directional indicators signaling which direction the robot intends to move. These indicators can assume the forms of lines \cite{chadalavada2015s}, gradient bands \cite{watanabe2015communicating}, or arrows \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}. Compared to head-mounted see-through augmented reality \cite{williams2018virtual,williams2018augmented}, projector-based augmented reality does not require interactants to wear specialized hardware, enabling visualizations to be observed by multiple observers simultaneously, facilitating usability in group, team, or crowd contexts~\cite{chen2019crowd,sebo2020robots,oliveira2021human}. As we will discuss in Section~\ref{sec:related_work}, several human-subjects studies \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi} have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach \cite{watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}. In this work, we present a practical solution for robotic arrow projections, describe the characteristics of the implementation of this solution, and provide access to the code for that solution. Additionally, we provide a specific robot and off-the-shelf projector that we have successfully utilized, as well as a summary of a full-scale user study to provide additional empirical evidence. For the implementation, we employed the popular Robot Operating System (ROS) \cite{quigley2009ros} and its visualization tool, rviz \cite{gossow2011interactive}, for rendering the arrows. Using ROS made the implementation robot-agnostic, as most robots utilized in research and development have ROS support \cite{rosshowcase}. Even non-ROS frameworks \cite{kramer2007development,elkady2012robotics}, and cognitive architectures, such as DIARC~\cite{scheutz2019overview}, typically include bridges to ROS. Using rviz as the rendering engine eliminates the necessity for practitioners and researchers to learn a tool outside of the ROS ecosystem, such as Unity. Moreover, rviz has a GUI and does not require any computer graphics programming. Given the broad range of applications of arrow projection on different robots and its demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency, we believe our work is highly relevant and beneficial to the HRI community. The readily available implementation with step-by-step documentation also enables researchers to focus on other interesting and emerging issues under social navigation, e.g., human navigation modeling \cite{guy2010modeling,ratsamee2013social,ferrer2014proactive,che2018avoiding} and robot navigation that adheres to social or moral norms \cite{banisetty2021implicit,banisetty2021socially}. We welcome GitHub issues for questions and pull requests.

In comparison with the use of wearable glasses, the use of projection systems does not require the wearer of special equipment, thus making it suitable for multiple observations at once: for example, whereas a see-through augmented reality, which is based on the use of wearable glasses, does not require the observers to wear specialized equipment and allows them to observe the visualisations simultaneously, which is advantageous in group, team and crowd contexts. As we will explain in section, we will show how several human experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach. In this paper, we present a practical solution for arrow projection by a robot, describe the implementation details of this solution, and provide access to the code. In addition, we describe a specific robot and an off-the-shelf projector that we have successfully employed, and present the results of a large-scale human experiment that provides further evidence. In the implementation, we used the popular robot operating system, ROS, and its visualization tool, rviz (cf. Gossow, Interactive 2011). Using ROS makes the implementation robot agnostic, since most of the robots used in research and development have a ROS implementation (cf. ros-showcase). Even non-ROS robot frameworks such as DIARC (cf. Scheutz, Overview 2019) or the architecture for robots (KR1K, cf. kramer, 2007development, elkady, 2012robotics) often have a bridge to ROS. We chose rviz as a renderer to avoid the need for practitioners and researchers to learn a tool outside the ROS eco-system, such as Unity. Furthermore, rviz has a GUI and does not require any computer graphics knowledge. Given the wide range of applications for the projection of arrows onto various robots, and the demonstrated efficacy and efficiency of our method, we consider our work to be highly relevant and useful to the human-robot interaction community. It is also possible to use the availability of an implementation with detailed documentation to address other interesting and emerging problems in social navigation, for example human navigation modeling, see Guy (2010) modeling, Ratsamee (2013) social, Ferrer (2014) pro-active, and Che (2018) avoidance. We welcome GitHub issues for any questions or pull requests. “Banisetty 2023” is socially correct.

text: Multi-agent motion planning encompasses a broad spectrum of real-world applications, yet it remains notoriously challenging. Even guiding a single robot from an initial position to a target position while avoiding collisions with obstacles becomes exceptionally difficult in the presence of complex obstacles, high-dimensional state spaces, nonlinear nonholonomic dynamics, actuation constraints, and disturbances. The complexity escalates dramatically when such intricate robotic systems must interact within a shared environment, rendering the problem scale beyond the capabilities of most existing methodologies. In this paper, we introduce \underline{S}calable and \underline{S}afe \underline{M}ulti-agent \underline{M}otion (S2M2) planner, a novel multi-agent motion planning framework that can rapidly and effectively generate provably safe plans for agent models with high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics and bounded disturbances in continuous time and space. Rather than directly planning dynamically-feasible trajectories, which are computationally prohibitive, S2M2 leverages a separation-of-concerns methodology: We initially design piecewise linear (PWL) paths $S_i$ for each dynamical agent $\mathcal{A}_i$ to track, acknowledging that the agents cannot follow these PWL paths precisely. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that with appropriate tracking controllers, the actual trajectories of each agent under disturbances can converge to $S_i$ with guaranteed bounds on the spatial tracking error. More significantly, we establish that such error bounds can be pre-computed for any qualified PWL path. The key ingredient underlying S2M2's high efficiency is our ability to formulate the problem of finding PWL paths for a single agent as a Mixed Integer-Linear Program (MILP), which can be solved efficiently using commercial MILP solvers. To prevent inter-agent collisions, we integrate our single-agent motion planner with the priority-based search~\cite{ma2019searching} that explores the space of priority orderings through systematic search. When priorities are established, lower-priority agents replan their paths while treating higher-priority agents as moving obstacles. Combined with the MILP-based path planner and guaranteed tracking controller, S2M2 can efficiently discover plans that are provably safe and robust to disturbances during execution. Furthermore, by planning paths for multiple agents on a continuous map over continuous time, our approach identifies high-quality solutions with reduced flowtime (i.e., makespan sum of all single-agent plans). Consider an illustrative example of two disc-shaped vehicles executing u-turns, as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:uturn}. Given the partially known initial positions and bounded disturbances, we first calculate the spatial error bound of tracking a path segment, which is a line, and then consider this error together with the agent geometry to obtain the potential swept area of the path segment. The swept area of agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ during its second segment $(p_{12}, p_{13})$ is illustrated in light blue. We also consider the minimum duration for each segment such that the agent has sufficient time to adjust its position after turning, which is $3$ seconds in our example. When our single-agent motion planner generates such paths for the agents, the obstacles are inflated with respect to the spatial tracking error and the agent geometry, as shown in light red. The planner also constrains each segment to satisfy the minimum segment duration. As observed, when traversing the corridor, both agents decelerate and utilize this $3$ seconds to adjust their trajectories. After clearing the corridor, agent $\mathcal{A}_2$ employs its maximum speed to approach its goal position. When potential collisions are identified, some agents are assigned higher priorities and thus are treated as moving obstacles for others. In our example, agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ is assigned higher priority and thus traverses the corridor before agent $\mathcal{A}_2$. We evaluate the performance of S2M2 against ECBS-CT \cite{cohen2019optimal} and MAPF/C+POST \cite{honig2018trajectory} on 2D and 3D scenarios with ground vehicles and quadrotors, respectively. Results demonstrate that S2M2 outperforms both planners in terms of solution quality with $15\sim70\%$ reduction for most instances. Additionally, S2M2 requires several orders of magnitude less time for pre-processing and also exhibits competitive runtime performance compared to the other two planners.

text: Extracting the most significant directions or \emph{principal components} of a matrix from noisy observations constitutes a fundamental problem in both mathematical statistics and applications \cite{Rao-1964-PCA,Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA,Ringner-2008-PCA,AW-2010-PCA}. The theoretical asymptotics of this task have been extensively studied through the analysis of idealized \emph{spiked matrix models}. While the initial such models, introduced by Johnstone \cite{Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA}, addressed Gaussian observations from a covariance matrix perturbed by adding a rank-one ``spike,'' the following simpler \emph{Wigner spiked matrix model} captures much of the same phenomenology. We consider the following two probability distributions $\PP$ and $\QQ$ over $n \times n$ symmetric matrices. \begin{itemize} \item Under $\QQ = \QQ_n$, observe $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$ drawn from the \emph{Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)}, meaning $W_{ii} \sim \sN(0, \frac{1}{n})$ and $W_{ij} = W_{ji} \sim \sN(0, \frac{2}{n})$ for $i < j$ with all $\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ of these entries distributed independently. We also write $\QQ = \GOE(n)$ for this distribution. \item Under $\PP = \PP_n$, first draw $\bu \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$ for $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1} \subset \RR^n$ the sphere of unit radius, and then observe $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$ for $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and some fixed $\beta > 0$, held constant as $n \to \infty$. \end{itemize} Two natural statistical questions emerge: (1) \emph{detection} or \emph{testing}, where we observe $\bW$ drawn from $\PP$ or $\QQ$ and must determine which distribution $\bW$ was drawn from, and (2) \emph{recovery} or \emph{estimation}, where we observe $\bW \sim \PP$ and seek to produce a good estimate of $\bu$. In either case, the associated optimization problem of computing the largest eigenvalue is natural to consider: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\|\bx\|_2 = 1} \bx^{\top} \bW \bx. \end{equation} For recovery, computing the maximizer $\bx^{\star}$ (the top eigenvector of $\bW$) performs maximum likelihood estimation of $\bu$. For detection, computing and thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ itself constitutes a natural and often effective strategy. The optimal value and optimizer of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ can be approximated (to arbitrary accuracy) in time $\poly(n)$, so these correspond to efficient algorithms for recovery and detection, respectively. text: Estimating the distribution of a target value $y$ conditioned on an input $x$ constitutes the foundation of supervised learning tasks. When optimized using conventional losses such as Mean Square Error for regression or Cross-Entropy for classification, supervised methods are recognized to estimate the expected conditional distribution of the target given the input, namely, $\langle y|x \rangle$ \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}. This represents standard methodology when the target distribution exhibits unimodal characteristics and minor variations in the target value arise primarily from random noise. However, when the target distribution of a regression problem exhibits non-unimodal behavior, most machine learning methods fail to capture it accurately by predicting an averaged value. Indeed, a multimodal target distribution associates multiple plausible outcomes with a given input sample\revise{, and in this case one usually talks about solving a conditional density estimation problem.} To tackle this challenge, the Mixture Density Network (MDN) \cite{bishop_mixture_1994} was introduced to estimate arbitrarily complex conditional target distributions, and it finds application in robotics \cite{choi_uncertainty_2018}, epidemiology \cite{davis_use_2020} and finance \cite{schittenkopf_volatility_1998}, to name a few. \textsc{MDN}{}s were developed for input data of vectorial nature, but frequently real-world problems involve relational data where the structure significantly influences the possible outcomes. For example, this is particularly evident in epidemiology \cite{opuszko_impact_2013}. For over twenty years, researchers have devoted considerable effort to the adaptive processing of graphs (see recent surveys of \citet{bacciu_gentle_2020,wu_comprehensive_2020}). The objective is to derive the optimal representation of a structured sample for a given task through various neighborhood aggregation schemes, graph coarsening, and information propagation strategies. It is straightforward to identify applications that benefit from the adaptive processing of structured data, such as drug design \cite{podda_deep_2020}, classification in social networks \cite{yang_revisiting_2016}, and natural language processing \cite{beck_graph--sequence_2018}. Our primary contribution is the introduction of a hybrid approach to address multimodal target distributions within machine learning methods for graphs, termed Graph Mixture Density Network (\textsc{GMDN}{}). This model generates a multimodal distribution, conditioned on an input graph, for either the entire structure or its entities. \revise{For instance, given an observable input graph $x$, \textsc{GMDN}{} is trained to approximate the (possibly multimodal) distribution associated with the target random variable $y$ via maximum likelihood estimation. The likelihood is the usual metric to be optimized for density estimation tasks \cite{nowicki_estimation_2001}, and it tells us how well the model is fitting the empirical data distribution. Recall that, in general, it does not suffice to predict a single output value like in \quotes{standard} regression problems \cite{bishop_mixture_1994} to solve this kind of tasks; for this reason, \textsc{GMDN}{} extends the capabilities of deep learning models for graphs whose output is restricted to unimodal distributions.} We evaluate GMDN on a novel benchmark application presented in this paper, comprising large epidemiological simulations\footnote{\url{https://github.com/diningphil/graph-mixture-density-networks}} where both structure and multimodality serve an essential role in determining the outcome of an epidemic. Results demonstrate that \textsc{GMDN}{} yields a significantly enhanced likelihood. Subsequently, we assess our model on two real-world chemical graph regression tasks to demonstrate how \textsc{GMDN}{} can better characterize the uncertainty in the output prediction, i.e., the model reveals that there might be more than one admissible chemical property value associated with a given input molecule representation.

text: From delivery drones to autonomous electrical vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) passenger aircraft, contemporary unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) can execute numerous diverse tasks efficiently, including goods delivery, surveillance, public safety, weather monitoring, disaster relief, search and rescue, traffic monitoring, videography, and air transportation \citep{balakrishnan2018blueprint,kopardekar2016unmanned}. Urban air mobility (UAM) is anticipated to occur in urban areas proximate to buildings or airports. Therefore, it is expected that UAS can utilize onboard detect and avoid systems to avoid other traffic, hazardous weather, terrain, and man-made and natural obstacles without continuous human intervention \citep{kopardekar2016unmanned}. Numerous mathematical models for aircraft conflict resolution have been proposed in the literature. Research endeavors can be categorized into centralized algorithms and decentralized algorithms. Centralized approaches can be based on semidefinite programming \citep{frazzoli2001resolution}, nonlinear programming \citep{raghunathan2004dynamic,enright1992discrete}, mixed-integer linear programming \citep{schouwenaars2001mixed,richards2002aircraft,pallottino2002conflict,vela2009mixed}, mixed-integer quadratic programming \citep{mellinger2012mixed}, sequential convex programming \citep{augugliaro2012generation,morgan2014model}, second-order cone programming \citep{acikmese2007convex}, evolutionary techniques \citep{delahaye2010aircraft,cobano2011path}, and particle swarm optimization \citep{pontani2010particle}. These centralized approaches often pursue the global optimum for all the aircraft. Nevertheless, as the number of aircraft increases, the computational cost of these methods typically scales exponentially. Among the decentralized approaches, the conflict resolution problem can also be formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been demonstrated to be an effective solution to aircraft traffic management, but predominantly employs traditional algorithms \citep{sun2019reinforcement}. The next-generation airborne collision avoidance system (ACAS X) formulates the collision avoidance systems (CAS) problem as a partially observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and has been extended to unmanned aircraft, designated ACAS Xu \citep{kochenderfer2012next}. Both ACAS X and ACAS Xu employ Dynamic Programming (DP) to determine the expected cost of each action \citep{manfredi2016introduction, owen2019acas}. \cite{chryssanthacopoulos2012decomposition} integrated decomposition methods and DP for optimized collision avoidance with multiple threats. The traditional RL algorithms require a fine discretization scheme of state space and finite action space. Discretization potentially compromises safety by introducing discretization errors and cannot provide flexible maneuver guidance for UAS. Furthermore, discretizing large airspace implies a high computational demand and can be time-consuming. Tree search based algorithms \citep{yang2018autonomous,yang2020scalable} are also applied to CAS problems using MDP formulation which does not involve state discretization. However, they typically require high onboard computation time to accommodate the continuous state space. The large and continuous state and action spaces present a challenge for conflict resolution problems using reinforcement learning. Recently, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is investigated to address this challenge by applying the deep neural network to approximate the cost and the optimal policy functions. Development of DRL algorithms, such as Policy Gradient \citep{sutton2000policy}, Deep Q-Networks (DQN) \citep{mnih2013playing}, Double DQN \citep{van2016deep}, Dueling DQN \citep{wang2015dueling}, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) \citep{lillicrap2015continuous}, Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) \citep{mnih2016asynchronous}, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) \citep{ppo2} has enhanced the potential of automation. \cite{li2019optimizing} employed DQN to compute corrections for an existing collision avoidance approach to account for dense airspace. In \cite{yang2019real}, the feasibility of utilizing algorithms based on DQN in UAV obstacle avoidance is verified. \cite{wulfeuav} concluded that DQN can outperform value iteration both in terms of evaluation performance and solution speed when solving a UAV collision avoidance problem. The performance of the agent in avoiding single up to multiple aircraft by employing the DQN algorithm is investigated in \cite{keong2019reinforcement}. \cite{brittain2020deep} proposed a novel deep multi-agent reinforcement learning framework based on PPO to identify and resolve conflicts among a variable number of aircraft in a high-density, stochastic, and dynamic sector in en-route airspace. The DRL work mentioned above operates in continuous state and discrete action space. There has been limited progress on utilizing DRL to solve UAS conflict resolution with continuous control. \cite{pham2019machine} proposed a method inspired by Deep Q-learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithms and it can resolve conflicts, with a success rate exceeding 81 \%, in the presence of traffic and varying degrees of uncertainties. \cite{ma2018saliency} developed a generic framework that integrates an autonomous obstacle detection module and an actor-critic based reinforcement learning (RL) module to develop reactive obstacle avoidance behavior for a UAV. Experiments in \cite{ppo2} evaluate PPO on a collection of benchmark tasks, including simulated robotic locomotion and Atari game playing, and demonstrate that PPO outperforms other online policy gradient methods. PPO appears to represent a favorable balance between sample complexity, simplicity, and wall-time. Thus, a PPO-based conflict resolution model is highly valuable for UAS traffic management, which constitutes the primary motivation of this study. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to develop a DRL approach based on PPO algorithm to enable the UAS to navigate successfully in continuous state and action spaces. The advantage of calculating in continuous space is that there is no need to discretize the state space or smooth results for postprocessing results. The proposed model with the optimal policy after offline training can be utilized for UAS real-time online trajectory planning. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em} \item A PPO-based framework has been proposed for UAS to avoid both static and moving obstacles in continuous state and action spaces. \item A novel scenario state representation and reward function are developed and can effectively map the environment to maneuvers. The trained model can generate continuous heading angle commands and speed commands. \item We have evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed learning framework in the environment with static obstacles, the environment with static obstacles and UAS position uncertainty, and the deterministic and stochastic environments with moving obstacles. Results demonstrate that the proposed model can provide accurate and robust guidance and resolve conflict with a success rate exceeding 99\%. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. \cref{background} describes the backgrounds of Markov Decision Process and Deep Reinforcement Learning. \cref{mdp} presents the model formulation using Markov Decision Process for UAS conflict resolution in continuous action space. In \cref{result}, the numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach to enable the UAS to learn to avoid conflict. \cref{Conclusion} concludes this paper.

text: Frequently-Asked-Questions (FAQ) constitute a compilation of question-answer pairs that are either manually constructed or automatically extracted from pertinent documents. FAQ furnish users with a ``one-stop'' resource for the most pertinent or most frequently searched information concerning a product or service -- to facilitate immediate customer assistance for general inquiries. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Motivation.} FAQ retrieval systems offer a natural language interface for querying an FAQ collection, and are therefore increasingly gaining popularity with large-scale service-providing companies for presenting information to customers. Such systems deliver two-fold benefits: (i) automation of customer service tasks, e.g., intelligent chatbots~\cite{massaro2018,yan2016} and automated e-mail answering~\cite{karan2018,malik2007}, and (ii) facilitate efficient access to internal FAQ documents for customer service agents, enhancing the quality and efficiency. Moreover, with the emergence of personal assistants (like XiaoIce, Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant, etc.), these ``virtual agents'' can deliver answers to questions and assist users in solving routine tasks through an additional channel to FAQs, hotlines, and forums -- facilitating a natural interaction with users~\cite{lommatzsch2019,por2020}. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Challenges.} FAQ retrieval constitutes a challenging task, primarily attributed to the fact that the question-answer texts are brief, making it more difficult to bridge the {\em lexical and semantic gap} between a user query and the FAQ questions due to short span with limited context~\cite{karan2018,lee2008}. Furthermore, precise comprehension of user questions can be challenging due to informal representations, domain-specificity, abbreviations, and formal-colloquial term mismatches~\cite{lommatzsch2019}. For instance, consider the questions {\small{\tt ``How can I seal a hole in the gas tank of my car?''}} and {\small{\tt ``How to patch a leak in the fuel compartment of my van?''}} which are semantically equivalent but demonstrate low lexical overlap and formal-colloquial mismatch. Additionally, FAQ retrieval systems should be capable of handling both keyword as well as {\em short span} ``natural language'' questions. Given the predominantly ``customer-centric'' nature, such systems typically require higher precision and interpretability compared to traditional information retrieval methods. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Problem Statement.} The task of {\em FAQ Retrieval} involves the efficient ranking (in terms of relevance) of question-answer pairs of a collection, in response to a user input query. In other words, such retrieval engines endeavor to understand the underlying {\em intent} of users and retrieve the most related answers containing the correct information~\cite{kothari2009}. Formally, consider a pre-curated collection (or repository) of question-answer $(Q, A)$ pairs to comprise the FAQ $= \{(Q_1, A_1), \cdots, (Q_n, A_n)\}$, where $Q_i$ denotes a question related to the domain, and $A_i$ represents the corresponding answer. Given a user query $q$, the task then is to return an ordered list of FAQ $(Q, A)$ pairs, $\{(Q_1^q, A_1^q), \cdots, (Q_k^q, A_k^q)\}$, exhibiting high semantic and intent similarity with respect to the input user query $q$. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Contributions.} This work proposes {\em TI-S2S}, a novel keyword based supervised learning framework for efficient FAQ retrieval. Our approach utilizes {\em sequence-to-sequence} model to generate representative labels for user questions to compute query-question similarity. Additionally, a variant incorporating ``candidate'' identified using a deep learning architecture to guide the retrieval process is demonstrated to further enhance performance. We demonstrate that our proposed framework efficiently captures: (i) domain-specificity of the application, (ii) characteristic words and / or concepts to differentiate between questions, and (iii) semantic similarity for retrieving relevant QA pairs from the FAQ collection. Experiments on public FAQ dataset demonstrate our framework to outperform existing techniques in terms of accuracy, and also in robustness to limited training data. In effect, it implicitly considers both {\em document redundancy} and {\em query redundancy}~\cite{karan2018}.
