text: Extracting users' preferences from their historical data is crucial for generating effective recommendations, as both users' preferences and items' characteristics exhibit dynamic behavior. Additionally, users' preferences are heavily influenced by contextual factors (e.g., an individual is likely to show interest in purchasing a keyboard following the acquisition of a desktop). Consequently, sequential recommendation seeks to predict the subsequent set of items that users are likely to favor by leveraging their historical interactions. Numerous algorithms have been developed to enhance understanding of users' sequential history~\cite{SASRec, BERT4Rec, hidasi2018recurrent, CASER, M3, rendle2010factorizing, DIN, TRANSREC}. Despite their superior performance, the majority of these approaches disregard the timestamp values of interactions. Although recent studies such as TiSASRec~\cite{TISASRec} have successfully integrated temporal information, their utilization of time remained constrained to a singular embedding approach. Given that timestamp values contain abundant information, it would be advantageous to investigate various forms of temporal embeddings that can comprehensively extract diverse patterns, along with model architectures that can effectively exploit such diversity. In this work we introduce \textbf{MEANTIME} (\textbf{M}ixtur\textbf{E} of \textbf{A}tte\textbf{NTI}on mechanisms with \textbf{M}ulti-temporal \textbf{E}mbeddings) which incorporates multiple temporal embeddings to enhance the encoding of both absolute and relative positions of user-item interactions within a sequence. Furthermore, we utilize multiple self-attention heads that process each positional embedding independently. This approach proves advantageous as each head can function as a specialist that concentrates on a specific pattern of user behaviors. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that \textbf{MEANTIME} surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms on real-world datasets. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose diversifying the embedding schemes employed to encode the positions of user-item interactions within a sequence. This is accomplished by applying multiple kernels to positions/values of timestamps in a sequence to generate distinct embedding matrices. \item We additionally propose a novel model architecture that operates multiple self-attention heads concurrently, where each head specializes in extracting specific patterns from users' behaviors by utilizing one of the positional embeddings we propose above. \item We performed extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on real-world datasets. We also present a comprehensive ablation study that facilitates understanding of the impact of various components in our model. \end{itemize}

text: While deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved success across numerous computer vision and pattern recognition applications, various limitations have hindered their broader adoption. For instance, owing to the substantial computational demands for training and inference, deploying large DNN models on resource-constrained devices presents significant challenges \cite{wu2018deep}. The absence of interpretability renders DNNs inappropriate for real-world applications where decision-making transparency is essential. Given that DNNs fundamentally comprise repeatedly stacked basic computational units - perceptrons, it becomes natural to question whether substituting this fundamental component with alternative modules might yield beneficial outcomes. The decision tree is recognized for its model interpretability and computationally efficient training methodology. Is it feasible to construct a deep architecture that employs decision trees as fundamental computational components? This concept has been investigated in various recent studies and demonstrates initial promising results. \cite{zhou2017deep} introduced a deep random forest cascade, wherein each network layer consists of an ensemble comprising multiple random forests, and the concatenated outputs from current forests serve as input for the subsequent layer. \cite{miller2017forward} enhanced \cite{zhou2017deep} by utilizing a collection of decision trees per layer, while concatenating current layer outputs with the original input to generate new representations for the following layer. Both \cite{zhou2017deep} and \cite{miller2017forward} have documented comparable performance on the MNIST dataset relative to DNN models, along with substantial reductions in training duration and parameter complexity. Nevertheless, their architectures still require thousands of trees per layer, as the representational capacity of individual decision trees remains constrained. To overcome these limitations, we propose enhancing the existing deep forest framework across multiple dimensions. Initially, to enable end-to-end optimization, we substitute the hard splitting criterion in conventional decision trees with a \textit{soft routing} mechanism, wherein the routing criteria at each internal tree node employs a sigmoid function. The error signal can therefore be backpropagated through the tree structure via gradient descent. Additionally, we enable the tree to learn its structural topology globally by incorporating a \textit{leafness parameter} for each tree node. Consequently, every node can concurrently learn whether to function as a leaf or an internal node \cite{irsoy2014budding}.

text: Pre-training of language models has resulted in numerous breakthroughs within NLP (\cite{devlin2018bert}, \cite{brown2020language}, \cite{peters2018deep}, \cite{liu2019roberta} ) and has attained state-of-the-art performance across many challenging NLP tasks including question-answering and natural language inference. Within this problem space, the BERT model, founded upon the \cite{vaswani2017attention} architecture, has emerged as particularly prominent. The BERT model architecture comprises multiple bidirectional Transformer (\cite{vaswani2017attention}) encoder blocks arranged in a stacked configuration. BERT training involves initial pre-training on extensive corpora of unlabeled data, subsequently followed by fine-tuning on considerably smaller, task-specific datasets. Pre-training demands substantial computational resources and typically requires multiple days for completion, whereas fine-tuning can be accomplished within significantly shorter timeframes. BERT models possess substantial parameter counts and memory requirements, ranging from 110M (BERT\textsubscript{BASE}) to 340M (BERT\textsubscript{LARGE}) to 8.3B (Megatron \cite{shoeybi2019megatron}) parameters. In this investigation, we demonstrate reduced model size and diminished training time while maintaining negligible changes in fine-tuning accuracy. Although demonstrating reduced model size and diminished training time constitutes relevance to the field independently, we believe it remains equally important to furnish deeper comprehension of why our architectural modifications prove effective. Following the approach established in \cite{clark2019does}, we employ probing linear classifiers and centered kernel alignment (\cite{kornblith2019similarity}) to obtain insights into the improvements achieved through our architectural modifications.

Training BERT involves a preliminary pre-training on large, unlabeled data sets, followed by fine-tuning on smaller, task-related data sets. The pre-training requires significant computational resources and takes several days to complete, while fine-tuning can be completed in much shorter times. Although demonstrating that the reduced size of the model and the reduced training time constitutes a contribution to the field, it is also important to show why our architectural modifications have been effective. In this regard, we follow the methodology established in [Kornblith, Similarity], where we use probing with linear classifiers and centering with kernels to get insights into the improvements achieved by our architectural modifications.

text: A Recommender System~(RS)~\cite{rendle2009bpr,rendle2010factorization,he2017neural,wang19neural,zheng17joint,pinsage2018ying} can predict user preferences for items, where a typical approach involves modeling Collaborative Filtering~(CF) signals~\cite{wang19neural}. Under the assumption that similar users share relevant items, CF signals facilitate learning user and item embeddings from user-item interactions. One major challenge concerning CF methods is the cold-start problem~\cite{zheng2018spectral}, where embeddings of users or items with limited interactions are difficult to learn. To address this challenge, we can model \textit{high-order signals}~\cite{wang19neural} that propagate information from multiple hops away across the user-item bipartite graph. Recently, due to advances in Graph Neural Networks~(GNN)~\cite{kipf17semi,graphsage17hamilton,wu19simplifying}, we can readily propagate high-order signals by stacking multiple \textit{aggregation layers}. Consequently, users (items) can aggregate first-order signals from direct neighbors at the initial layer and high-order signals from indirect neighbors at deeper layers. Nevertheless, through experimental analyses on real-world datasets, we identify three common performance issues of existing GNNs on RS, which are designated as the \textbf{oscillation} problem, \textbf{varying locality} problem, and \textbf{fixed propagation pattern} problem in this work, respectively. Initially, stacking multiple layers causes the oscillation problem, which subsequently impedes information propagation. Before formal definition, intuitively, the oscillation problem arises when an information gap exists between successive hop propagations. This stems from the bipartite structure. As depicted in the left portion of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, the direct neighbors of users are exclusively items, while the 2-hop neighbors are exclusively users. This indicates that by aggregating direct neighbors, users only obtain information from items, and conversely. Consequently, information oscillates between users and items due to the bipartite graph structure. One immediate solution involves adding self-loops~\cite{kipf17semi,wang19neural} to disrupt the bipartite structure. However, we theoretically demonstrate that this cannot mitigate the oscillation problem. Furthermore, adding self-loops is equivalent to preventing information propagation, which actually aggravates the cold-start issue. Beyond the oscillation problem, the varying locality problem of bipartite graphs also constrains the propagation capability of multi-layer architectures~\cite{xu18jk}. This refers to the density of local structures across the bipartite graph. For instance, on the left side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, $u_4$ exhibits lower local density compared to $u_2$ since the former connects only to $i_4$ while the latter connects to $i_1$, $i_2$ and $i_3$. The $3$-hop propagation originating from $u_4$ (red edges in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}) encompasses only $3$ edges in the bipartite graph. Conversely, the $3$-hop propagation of $u_2$ (green edges in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}) spans nearly every edge in the bipartite graph. Specifically, we present the corresponding propagation trees of $u_2$ and $u_4$ on the right side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}. There exist fewer possible propagation paths for $u_4$ compared to $u_2$. Finally, the fixed propagation pattern across different layers of existing multi-layer RS models~\cite{he2020lightgcn,wang19neural,berg2017gcmc} generates redundant information propagation between layers. We illustrate an example of this redundancy as the yellow-shaded block on the right side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}. The first hop propagation distributes information from $u_2$ to $i_1$ and $i_2$. Subsequently, information from $i_1$ and $i_2$ is propagated to $u_1$ and $u_2$ at the second hop propagation, which is reversely propagated back at the third hop propagation. This occurs because the propagation pattern remains fixed across different layers. One potential solution involves sampling layer-dependent neighbors~\cite{zou2019layer}. However, the current sampling strategy requires additional computation and is non-differentiable, which compromises the training procedure. To address the aforementioned problems, we design a novel GNN framework specifically for bipartite graphs, termed deep \textbf{D}eoscillated Adaptive \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ollaborative \textbf{F}iltering~(DGCF). We propose a Cross-Hop Propagation~(CHP) layer that rectifies the bipartite propagation structure to resolve the oscillation problem. Compared to existing methods that aggregate only direct neighbors, the CHP layer also propagates information from cross-hop neighbors. As a result, users (items) can also receive information from cross-hop users (items). Additionally, we design a Locality-Adaptive~(LA) layer which regulates the amount of information to propagate. It learns an influence factor for each node, which adapts to the varying locality of the graph. Multiple CHP layers and LA layers constitute the DGCF model. It propagates high-order CF signals to train user embeddings and item embeddings, which adapts to the locality of nodes. The weights of LA layers and CHP layers differ from layer to layer, thus implementing a layer-wise propagation pattern. The contributions are: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Oscillation problem:} We formally define the graph oscillation problem and prove its existence and boundary in bipartite graphs. We also provide empirical evidence that oscillation occurs within a few layers. \item \textbf{Innovative layers:} We design two innovative layers, namely, CHP layer and LA layer. The CHP layer is designed to overcome the oscillation problem, while the LA layer addresses the varying locality problem. Stacking multiple LA layers resolves the fixed aggregation pattern problem. \item \textbf{Extensive experiments:} In addition to the overall comparison experiment, we conduct three types of detailed analyses regarding the three aforementioned problems. We examine the oscillation problem when stacking excessive layers. Additionally, we discuss the varying locality problem and how our model addresses it. Moreover, we observe the variations in the propagation pattern. \end{itemize}

text: Consider that we possess access to an image in a \textit{functional} form. Specifically, the image is represented as a function $f: \bm{p} \mapsto \bm{c}$ that accepts a pixel coordinate $\bm{p} = (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ as input and yields its corresponding RGB value $\bm{c} = (r, g, b) \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Such representations emerge, for instance, in differentiable rendering pipelines \cite{SynSin, SoftRasterizer} or implicit representations of images \cite{siren, fourier_inr, inr_gan, cips}. Now consider that we wish to generate a high-resolution raster image from this functional representation $f(\bm p)$. This requires that we evaluate $f(\bm p)$ at every coordinate location of an $H \times W$ grid to produce an $H \times W$ sized image. If evaluating $f(\bm p)$ is computationally expensive, then this becomes a laborious procedure. What alternatives exist? One approach would be to accelerate the inference for $f(\bm p)$. Another strategy is to generate a low-resolution version of an image and subsequently upsample it using one of the existing methods. Such upsampling methods assume that the points from which you are upsampling are positioned on a uniform grid, i.e., they maintain fixed equal horizontal and vertical spacing between each other, as illustrated in figure \ref{fig:uniform-interpolation}. However, in practice there occasionally arise situations when your points are positioned on a non-uniform grid, as shown in image \ref{fig:non-uniform-interpolation}, constraining the applicability of existing tools. To address this issue, we propose a novel interpolation method that enables reconstruction of an image from a subset of points that are arbitrarily scattered throughout the image. We accomplish this by representing each known color $c^{i}$ at location $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ as a 2D normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\bm \mu^{(i)}, \sigma^2 I)$ for $\bm\mu^{(i)} = (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ and some predefined variance $\sigma^2$. \input{figures/uniform-vs-non-uniform} To summarize, our contributions are the following: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel interpolation technique that is based on representing the known points as a GMM model and inferring the value for the unknown ones as an expectation. \item We develop an optimized CUDA kernel for both the forward and backward passes of the proposed interpolation procedure. \item We conduct experiments on the ImageNet dataset and demonstrate that our proposed interpolation technique outperforms 6 other standard interpolation methods in several scenarios based on reconstruction quality. \end{itemize}

text: The automated processing of textual content to extract insights has been extensively utilized across various industries. Such processing can be applied to analyze product or film reviews to determine overall sentiment. Additional applications encompass the examination of social media posts to assess brand perception or public opinion regarding particular subjects. These applications can fundamentally be reduced to classification or summarization problems. Contemporary state-of-the-art NLP methodologies demonstrate exceptional performance on these tasks when applied to monolingual texts. Nevertheless, these techniques may exhibit suboptimal performance on code-mixed content due to insufficient availability of annotated training data. Code-mixed text has gained prominence in recent years owing to the proliferation of various social media platforms \cite{gamback2016comparing} \cite{barman2014code}. The majority of these platforms establish English as the primary communication medium. In multilingual nations such as India, users frequently combine their native language with English when engaging on social media platforms. This phenomenon occurs because individuals feel more comfortable expressing themselves in their native languages. It is natural to describe indigenous terms or entities using local languages, which consequently results in code-mixing. Code-mixing fundamentally enables the borrowing of terms from various languages, thereby facilitating enhanced communication ease. A regional flavor can be imparted to film reviews, product evaluations, and commentary by incorporating details in the native language. These factors have collectively contributed to the increasing prevalence of code-mixed text \cite{khanuja2020gluecos}. To comprehend such code-mixed content, it becomes essential to identify the language employed in different textual segments, followed by language-specific processing \cite{das2015code}. In this research, we present various methodologies for language identification within code-mixed text. Within code-mixed text, languages can be interspersed in diverse patterns. One manifestation of code-mixing is illustrated in this example, \textit{"this is not union budget, ye to aam admi ka budget hai"} with language annotation as "eng eng eng eng eng hin hin hin hin hin hin hin". An alternative pattern can be observed as \textit{"maine aaj WhatsApp and Facebook uninstall kiya h"} annotated as "hin hin eng eng eng eng hin hin". Determining the language of individual tokens presents challenges since identical words may be utilized in both Hindi and English depending upon contextual factors. For instance, English terms such as \textit{"are"} and \textit{"maze"} can also function in Hindi contexts as \textit{"are mai ghar jaa raha hu"}, and \textit{"appke to maze hai"}. To further complicate matters, social media content typically contains noise where words are written in various forms merely for emphasis. For example, in the word \textit{"good"} the character \textit{'o'} may be repeated multiple times to generate different variants like \textit{"the movie was gooood"}. This necessitates the consideration of diverse input representations. Sentences can be processed on a word-by-word basis or character-by-character basis. The more contemporary representation approach involves sub-words where tokens are segmented into logical sub-word components \cite{kudo2018subword}. Character-based and sub-word-based representations demonstrate greater robustness to noisy textual variations compared to word-based representation, which treats each variant as a distinct token. Our work focuses on evaluating the performance of these input representations. This constitutes the first study to investigate sub-word-based representations for Hi-En language identification. The objective is to determine the language of each token within the sentence. This task is formulated as a token classification problem. Deep learning architectures based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks represent the most widely adopted techniques for token classification. We employ these straightforward models in conjunction with different input representations to assess their efficacy. These models are frequently combined with conditional random fields (CRF) to enhance performance. However, this work is constrained to simple architectures with emphasis on input representation. We demonstrate that sub-word-based representation combined with these simple models achieves superior performance compared to other complex architectures documented in the literature. Simple architectures are also advantageous as they reduce computational overhead and complexity. The language identification component should operate efficiently and rapidly since it will frequently precede other NLP modules. From this perspective, we conduct experiments with single-layer CNN and LSTM architectures. The experimental results indicate that these architectures are adequate to achieve desired accuracy thresholds. The primary contributions of this research are: \begin{itemize} \item The efficacy of character-based, sub-word-based, and word-based representations is evaluated for Hindi-English language identification tasks. \item The combinations of established model architectures and input representations are systematically compared. \end{itemize}

text: Evaluating classifier performance constitutes a fundamental task in machine learning. The computational time required by an algorithm that computes the measure assumes minimal importance in an offline context, for instance, when a researcher is developing the classifier. Nevertheless, the computational time becomes more critical if our objective is to monitor classifier performance over time where new data points may arrive at substantial velocity. For instance, consider a task of monitoring anomalous behavior in IT systems based on event logs. Here, the primary challenge is the enormous volume of event logs rendering manual monitoring infeasible. One approach involves employing a classifier to monitor for anomalous events and alert analysts for closer examination. Here, monitoring must be performed continuously to detect abnormalities rapidly. Furthermore, the classifier's performance should also be monitored continuously as the underlying distribution, and potentially the classifier's performance, may change due to modifications in the IT system. To detect recent changes in performance, we are frequently interested in the performance over the last $n$ data points. More broadly, we are interested in maintaining the measure under addition or deletion of data points. We investigate algorithms for maintaining two measures. The first measure is the area under the ROC curve (AUC), a classical technique for measuring classifier performance based on its ROC curve. We also investigate $H$-measure, an alternative measure proposed by~\citet{hand:09:alternative}. Roughly speaking, the measure is based on the minimum weighted loss, averaged over the cost ratio. A practical advantage of the $H$-measure over AUC is that it permits a natural approach for weighting classification errors. Both measures can be computed in $\bigO{n \log n}$ time from scratch, or in $\bigO{n}$ time if the data points are already sorted. In this paper we present 3 algorithms that enable us to maintain the measures in polylogarithmic time. The first algorithm maintains AUC under addition or deletion of data points. The approach is straightforward: we maintain the data points sorted in a self-balanced search tree. To update AUC we need to determine the ROC coordinates of the data point that we are modifying. Fortunately, this can be accomplished by modifying the search tree so that it maintains the cumulative counts of the labels in each subtree. Consequently, we can obtain the coordinates in $\bigO{\log n}$ time, which results in a total of $\bigO{\log n}$ maintenance time. Our subsequent two algorithms involve maintaining the $H$-measure. Computing the $H$-measure requires finding the convex hull of the ROC curve, and enumerating over the hull. First we demonstrate that we can employ a classic dynamic convex hull algorithm with some minor modifications to maintain the convex hull of the ROC curve. The modifications are necessary as we do not possess the ROC coordinates of individual data points, but we can use the same technique as when computing AUC to obtain the required coordinates. Then we demonstrate that if we estimate the class priors from the test data, we can decompose the $H$-measure into a sum over the points in the convex hull such that the $i$th term depends only on the difference between the $i$th and the $(i - 1)$st data points. This decomposition enables us to maintain the $H$-measure in $\bigO{\log^2 n}$ time. If the class priors are \emph{not} estimated from the test data, then we propose an estimation algorithm. Here the concept is to group points that are proximate in the convex hull together. Or in other words, if there are points in the convex hull that are close to each other, then we only utilize one data point from such group. The grouping is performed in a manner that we maintain $\epsilon$-approximation in $\bigO{(\log n + \epsilon^{-1}) \log n}$ time. \textbf{Structure:} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We present preliminary definitions in Section~\ref{sec:prel}. In Section~\ref{sec:auc} we demonstrate how to maintain AUC, and in Sections~\ref{sec:hexact}--\ref{sec:happrox} we demonstrate how to maintain the $H$-measure. We present the experimental evaluation in Section~\ref{sec:exp}, and conclude the paper with a discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

Video analytics applications, including those for urban mobility and autonomous vehicles \cite{bellevue-report}, are driven by deep neural network (DNN) models for object detection and classification, such as Yolo \cite{yolo9000-1}, ResNet \cite{deepresidual-2} and EfficientNet \cite{efficientnet-3}. Video analytics deployments transmit the videos to {\em edge servers} \cite{azure-ase, aws-outposts} deployed on-premise \cite{ieee-computer, edgevideo-1, edgevideo-2, getmobile}. Edge computation is favored for video analytics since it eliminates the need for costly network links to transmit videos to the cloud \cite{getmobile}, while simultaneously preserving video privacy (e.g., numerous European cities prohibit streaming their videos to the cloud \cite{sweden-data, azure-data}). Edge compute is provisioned with constrained resources (e.g., with limited GPUs \cite{aws-outposts, azure-ase}). This constraint is exacerbated by the disparity between the growth rate of model computational demands and processor compute cycles \cite{ion-blog, openai-blog}. Consequently, edge deployments depend on {\em model compression} \cite{compression-4, compression-5, compression-6}. The compressed DNNs are initially trained on representative data from each video stream, but during field deployment, they experience {\em data drift}, i.e., the live video data deviates substantially from the data utilized for training \cite{datadrift-7, datadrift-8, datadrift-a, datadrift-b}. Cameras in streets and autonomous vehicles encounter diverse scenes over time, e.g., illumination, crowd densities, and evolving object compositions. It is challenging to comprehensively encompass all these variations during training, particularly since even minor variations impact the accuracy. Consequently, there is a substantial decrease in the accuracy of edge DNNs due to data drift (by 22\%; \Sef{subsec:continuous-measurement}). Indeed, the reduced weights and shallower architectures of compressed DNNs frequently render them inadequate to deliver high accuracy when trained with extensive variations in the data 
oindent{ f Continuous model retraining.} A promising strategy to address data drift is continuous learning. The edge DNNs are incrementally {\em retrained} on the new video samples while preserving some knowledge from previous training \cite{compressiondrift-11, continuous-12}. Continuous learning techniques retrain the DNNs periodically \cite{distribution-20, mullapudi2019}; we designate the period between two retrainings as the ``retraining window'' and we utilize a sample of the data accumulated during each window for retraining. Such ongoing learning \cite{incremental-13, icarl-14, incremental-15} enables the compressed edge models to maintain high accuracy despite changing data characteristics. Edge servers utilize their GPUs \cite{azure-ase} for DNN inference on multiple live video streams (e.g., traffic cameras in a city). Incorporating continuous training into edge servers introduces a tradeoff between the live inference accuracy and accuracy degradation due to data drift. Allocating additional resources to the retraining job enables it to complete faster and deliver a more accurate model sooner. Simultaneously, during the retraining, diverting resources from the inference job reduces its accuracy (because it may need to sample the frames of the video being analyzed) Fundamental to the resource demand and accuracy of the jobs are their {\em configurations}. For retraining jobs, configurations denote the hyperparameters, e.g., number of training epochs, that significantly influence the resource demand and accuracies (\Sef{subsec:profiles}). The accuracy improvement due to retraining also depends on {\em how extensively} the characteristics of the live videos have changed. For inference jobs, configurations such as frame sampling and resolution affect the accuracy and resources required to maintain analysis of the live video \cite{chameleon, noscope}. 
oindent{ f Problem statement.} We make the following decisions for continuous retraining. ($1$) in each retraining window, determine which of the edge models to retrain; ($2$) allocate the edge server's GPU resources among the retraining and inference jobs, and ($3$) select the configurations of the retraining and inference jobs. We also constrain our decisions such that the inference accuracy {\em at any point in time} does not fall below a minimum value (so that the outputs continue to remain useful to the application). Our objective in making the above three decisions is to maximize the inference accuracy {\em averaged over the retraining window} (aggregating the accuracies during and after the retrainings) across all the videos analyzed on the edge server. Maximizing the inference accuracy over the retraining window creates novel challenges as it differs from $(i)$ video inference systems that optimize only the instantaneous accuracy \cite{videostorm, noscope, chameleon}, $(ii)$ model training systems that optimize only the final accuracy \cite{hyperparameter-16, DBLP:journals/jmlr/BergstraB12, DBLP:conf/nips/SnoekLA12, Swersky_scalablebayesian, DBLP:conf/osdi/XiaoBRSKHPPZZYZ18, DBLP:conf/eurosys/PengBCWG18} Addressing the fundamental tradeoff between the retrained model's accuracy and the inference accuracy is computationally challenging. First, the decision space is multi-dimensional comprising a diverse set of retraining and inference configurations, and choices of resource allocations over time. Second, it is difficult to determine the performance of different configurations (in resource usage and accuracy) as it requires actually retraining using different configurations. Data drift intensifies these challenges because a decision that performs well in a retraining window may not do so in the future. 
oindent{ f Solution components.} Our solution {{	t Ekya}\xspace} has two main components: a resource scheduler and a performance estimator. In each retraining window, the { f resource scheduler} makes the three decisions listed above in our problem statement. In its decisions, {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s scheduler prioritizes retraining the models of those video streams whose characteristics have changed the most because these models have been most impacted by data drift. The scheduler decides against retraining the models which do not enhance our target metric. To reduce the large decision space, the scheduler employs the following techniques. First, it simplifies the spatial complexity by considering GPU allocations only in coarse fractions (e.g., 10\%) that are sufficiently accurate for the scheduling decisions, while also being cognizant of the granularity achievable in modern GPUs \cite{nvidia-mps}. Second, it does not modify allocations to jobs {\em during the retraining}, thus largely avoiding the temporal complexity. Finally, our micro-profiler (described below) reduces the list of configurations to only the promising options. To make efficient choices of configurations, the resource scheduler relies on estimates of accuracy after the retraining and the resource demands. We have designed a { f micro-profiler} that observes the accuracy of the retraining configurations on a {\em small subset} of the training data in the retraining window with {\em just a few epochs}. It uses these observations to extrapolate the accuracies when retrained on a larger dataset for many more epochs. Furthermore, we restrict the micro-profiling to only a small set of {\em promising} retraining configurations. Together, these techniques result in {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s micro-profiler being nearly $100	imes$ more efficient than exhaustive profiling while still estimating accuracies with an error of $5.8\%$. To estimate the resource demands, the micro-profiler measures the retraining duration {\em per epoch} when $100\%$ of the GPU is allocated, and scales the training time for different allocations, number of epochs, and training data sizes. 
oindent{ f Implementation and Evaluation.} We have implemented and evaluated {{	t Ekya}\xspace} using a system deployment and trace-driven simulation. text: Deep-learning (DL) systems have demonstrated remarkable success in complex tasks such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012deep}, object detection, classification, tracking~\cite{geiger2012we, lillicrap2015continuous}, and so on. Extensive research, however, has revealed that DL systems are susceptible to {\em digital adversarial examples}, meticulously designed inputs intended to induce unintended behaviors. One approach for defending against these attacks involves detecting the attacks and enabling the system to formulate a new action based on the detection. Although numerous methods have been proposed for detecting adversarial examples~\cite{metzen2017detecting, grosse2017statistical} in the digital domain, these methods have proven to be ineffective against an adaptive attacker~\cite{carlini2017bypass} who targets a DL system to cause misclassification and evade detection. Expanding research demonstrates that similar vulnerabilities exist in the physical domain as well~\cite{lee2019physical,chou2018sentinet}. Physical adversarial attacks are designed to be robust to variance in scene and sensor factors such as lighting, rotation, and distance, rather than simply making them effective in a single example image. For instance, attackers can construct {\em adversarial patches} and position them anywhere within the field of view of an object detector to suppress object detection~\cite{lee2019physical}. This is accomplished through Expectation over Transformation (EOT)~\cite{athalye2017synthesizing}. EOT simulates a distribution of locations, orientations, and photometric properties of the patch, and then optimizes the attack across the dataset with the distribution applied. Unlike digital adversarial examples, adversarial patches must occupy a continuous area in input images. This property makes them easily detectable for humans, for example in the cases of toaster patches~\cite{brown2017adversarial} or printed t-shirts~\cite{xu2019adversarial}. Adversarial patches are inexpensive to construct, and unlike digital adversarial examples, can function in many scenarios. Adversarial patch attacks on time-sensitive safety-critical systems, such as a self-driving car, can endanger users as well as the general public. Detecting adversarial patch attacks, however, has received considerably less attention until recently. We observe that the only differences between the generation of adversarial patches and digital adversarial examples are that: i) adversarial patches are optimized over a distribution of input images rather than a single image, ii) adversarial patches are area constrained rather than norm constrained. We thus hypothesize that \emph{neural networks under attack by adversarial patches are behaviorally similar to neural networks under attack by digital adversarial examples, and methods to detect adversarial perturbations can be transferred over to detection of adversarial patches}. Intuitively, it should also be more straightforward to automate the detection of adversarial patches compared to digital adversarial examples, as humans can easily identify them. To the best of our knowledge, SentiNet~\cite{chou2018sentinet} is the only prior work conducted on detecting adversarial patches. SentiNet detects and segments adversarial objects from input by leveraging the high salience and scene-transferability of adversarial patches. In this paper, we adapt a mechanism originally proposed to detect digital adversarial perturbations~\cite{qin2019detecting} and empirically examine its effectiveness against simulated physical adversarial attacks. In particular, we examine the effectiveness of class-conditional reconstructions~\cite{qin2019detecting} -- which is inadequate in the digital domain -- against adversarial patches. We demonstrate that unlike digital adversarial examples, adaptive attacks using adversarial patches do not neutralize the detector. We have implemented the detection approach on a modified AlexNet as well as on a \emph{Capsule Network (CapsNet)}, a recently proposed and arguably powerful neural architecture~\cite{sabour2017dynamic,hinton2018matrix}. CapsNets utilize layers of vector- or matrix-valued capsules that represent the poses and probabilities of objects and can also represent part-whole relationships. Similar to how layers of neurons can represent the extraction of higher-level features from lower-level features in a standard neural network, layers of capsules can represent the extraction of higher-level objects from lower-level objects, shapes, or lines. In addition, we propose an improved CapsNet architecture incorporating {\em Dropout} and {\em Affine Voting} to enhance the test set classification performance. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{smitemize} \item We are the first to explore the effectiveness of a digital adversarial example detection method in the adversarial patch domain, and demonstrate it on three standard datasets: MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10. \item We are the first to show the effectiveness of CapNets to classify and detect adversarially patched input. \item We propose an improved Matrix Capsule Network with {\em capsule-dropout} and {affine voting} and empirically show their improved test accuracy on the smallNORB dataset. \end{smitemize}

text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) demonstrates considerable promise for recommendation systems, owing to its capacity to acquire optimal strategies through interactions for producing recommendations that optimally align with users' evolving preferences. DRL-based recommendation systems encompass three categories: deep Q-learning based methods, policy gradient based methods, and hybrid methods. Deep Q-learning seeks to identify the optimal step by maximizing a Q-value across all feasible actions. \citet{zheng2018drn} initially introduced DRL into recommendation systems for news recommendation; subsequently, \citet{chen2018stabilizing} presented a robust Q-learning approach to address dynamic environments for online recommendation. Nevertheless, Q-learning based methods encounter the \textit{agent stuck problem}, i.e., Q-learning necessitates the maximization operation across the action space, which becomes computationally intractable when the action space is exceptionally large. Policy gradient based methods can alleviate the agent stuck problem~\cite{chen2019large}. Such approaches employ average reward as the guiding principle yet they may misclassify poor actions as favorable actions, rendering the algorithm difficult to converge~\cite{pan2019policy}. In contrast, hybrid methods integrate the benefits of Q-learning and policy gradient. As a prevalent algorithm among hybrid methods, actor-critic network~\cite{konda2000actor} employs policy gradient on an actor network and Q-learning on a critic network to attain nash equilibrium across both networks. To date, actor-critic network has been extensively applied to DRL-based recommendation systems ~\cite{chen2019top,liu2020end,zhao2020leveraging,chen2020knowledge}. Despite variations, all existing DRL-based methods depend on carefully designed context-dependent reward functions, as illustrated in the general workflow of a DRL-based recommendation systems in Fig~\ref{fig:work} (a). Nevertheless, in numerous instances, the reward function cannot be readily defined, owing to dynamic environments and diverse factors that influence user's interest ~\cite{shang2019environment}. Consequently, the existing methods may experience limited generalization capability. Furthermore, they typically consider both user's preference and user's actions (e.g., click-through, rating or implicit feedback) in the reward function, under the assumptions that the reward is determined by the currently selected item and user's action remains uninfluenced by the recommended items. Such assumptions, however, no longer remain valid for online recommendation~\cite{shang2019environment}. Another challenge is that the utilization of reinforcement learning in discovering the recommendation policy from scratch might be computationally intensive~\cite{finn2016guided,levine2012continuous}. In a recommendation problem, the state space (i.e., all candidate items in which users might express interest) and action space (i.e., all the actions for candidate items) might be enormous, traditional reinforcement learning based methods iterate through all the possible combinations to determine the optimal policy which is laborious. Addressing the aforementioned challenges, we aim to enable the agent to deduce a reward function from user's behaviors via inverse reinforcement learning and acquire the recommendation policy directly from user behaviors in an efficient and adaptive manner, as demonstrated in Fig 1 (b). To this end, we propose a generative inverse reinforcement learning approach for adaptively inferring an implicit reward function from user behaviors. Specifically, the approach can evaluate the performance of the current recommendation policy and update the current policy with the expert policy in the discriminator, thereby mitigating the necessity of defining reward function for online recommendation. In particular, we transform inverse deep reinforcement learning (DRL) into a generator to augment a diverse collection of state-action pairs. Under this generative strategy, our method can achieve superior generalization capability under complex online recommendation conditions. In summary, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We propose generative inverse reinforcement learning to automatically learn reward function for online recommendation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to decouple the reward function and the agent for online recommendation. \item We design a novel actor-discriminator network module that takes a discriminator as the critic network and a novel actor-critic network as the actor network, to implement the proposed framework. The module is model-free and can be easily generalized to a variety of scenarios. \item We conduct experiments on a virtual online platform, VirtualTB, to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approach. Our proposed method achieves a higher click-through-rate that several state-of-the-art methods. \end{itemize}

text: Following the introduction of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)\cite{goodfellow2014generative} and diverse image forgery techniques~\cite{karras2017progressive,zakharov2019few,karras2019style,wu2019sliced}, numerous methods~\cite{karras2017progressive, karras2019style, wu2019sliced, choi2019stargan, karras2020analyzing, shaham2019singan} can generate highly realistic images containing human faces, scenery, and objects. Furthermore, recent approaches~\cite{zakharov2019few, sun2019meta} employing few-shot learning, a GAN-based technique, enable deep learning models to generate high-quality outputs using only limited training data. The generation of such images through few-shot learning can also be exploited for creating fraudulent images, where recent cases~\cite{cnn_business, yin_2019, deepnude} demonstrate the misuse of these images for malicious purposes. For detecting image forgeries, earlier research utilized metadata information or handcrafted image characteristics. However, the most recent AI methods, such as GANs, generate novel images along with metadata from scratch. Consequently, previous metadata-based detection approaches are neither practical nor effective against contemporary fake images generated by GANs. To address these challenges, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)-based binary classifiers such as \textit{ShallowNet}~\cite{tariq2019gan}, \textit{FakeTalkerDetect}~\cite{jeon2019faketalkerdetect}, \textit{FaceForensics++}~\cite{rossler2018faceforensics}, and \textit{Face X-ray}~\cite{li2020face} have been developed, training with extensive collections of real versus forged images. Additionally, other researchers~\cite{marra2019gans, zhang2019detecting, yu2019attributing} have demonstrated that detection performance can be enhanced by analyzing artifacts and patterns in underlying GAN-generated images. In this work, we propose~\textit{Dual Attention Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network} (\textit{DA-FDFtNet}), a fine-tuning neural network-based architecture for fake face image detection. ~DA-FDFtNet~integrates \textit{Fine-Tune Transformer} (FTT) and \textit{Channel attention modules} with a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) as a backbone, and \textit{MobileNet block V3} (MBblockV3) to differentiate between real and fake images. Figure~\ref{fig:overview_fdftnet}. presents an overview of our approach, where we implemented existing CNN architectures (pre-trained network)~\cite{simonyan2014very,szegedy2015going,he2016deep,iandola2014densenet,hu2018squeeze,howard2017mobilenets} and fine-tuned the pre-trained networks for fake image detection. Specifically, DA-FDFtNet~ extends the \textit{FDFtNet}~\cite{jeon2020fdftnet}, by implementing the FTT and MBblockV3 and an additional channel attention module to the final layer. In particular, FTT is designed to utilize different feature extraction from images using self-attention. Simultaneously, MBblockV3 extracts features using different convolution and structural techniques, and the channel attention module is employed to capture feature dependencies in the spatial and channel dimensions. Furthermore, various data augmentation methods have been applied to overcome the limitations of using a small dataset to fine-tune the baseline model and improve the overall performance across different types of fake images. We experiment with 4 different types of deepfakes (FaceSwap, DeepFakes, Face2Face, and NeuralTextures) as well as GAN-generated face images (StarGAN, PGGAN, StyleGAN, and StyleGAN2), and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across different domains. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose DA-FDFtNet, an extended neural network-based fake image detector, which achieves 97.02\% accuracy, improving the baseline model accuracy from 1\% to 47\% through our methods. \item We provide a novel fine-tuning neural network-based classifier that requires a small amount of data for fine-tuning, and can be easily integrated with popular existing CNN architectures. \item We perform an extensive evaluation on 8 different deepfake as well as GAN-generated fake image datasets, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across different domains. \end{itemize} We organized our paper as follows: In Section 2, we present an overview of fake image detection approaches and the novel approach we developed for our model. In Section 3, we present the details of the dataset and baseline models, and describe the architecture of~\textit{DA-FDFtNet}. In Section 4, we explain the training details for our experiment and show our experimental results. Finally, in Section 5, we offer our conclusion.

text: Machine learning models and automated decision-making procedures are becoming increasingly pervasive, thereby generating growing interest in the careful understanding of their behavior~\cite{surveyxaifosca, zehlike2021fairness}. A relevant step in explaining the outcomes of machine learning algorithms is the identification of data subgroups in which the considered algorithm may exhibit different, and potentially anomalous, behavior. The identification of peculiar behaviors within data subgroups finds important applications in the KDD pipeline, ranging from model validation and testing~\cite{ chung2019automated, wu2019errudite} to the evaluation of model fairness~\cite{chung2019automated, cabrera2019fairvis}. In particular, societal bias~\cite{barocas2016big} is becoming an increasing concern and researchers are progressively working on measuring and ensuring fairness in machine learning. To this end, human experts are frequently required to manually identify sensitive attributes (e.g., gender, ethnicity) or problematic data subgroups. The behavior of machine learning algorithms is frequently evaluated through global metrics, which consider the performance of the algorithm at a global level, for the entire dataset, or for specific class labels. In contrast, in this paper we propose the concept of \textit{divergence} as a measure of the difference in statistics (e.g., false positive rate) between the behavior of the machine learning algorithm on a data subgroup and on the entire dataset. Data subgroups exhibiting a significant deviation in their behavior are automatically identified by our approach, which characterizes data subgroups through a combination of attribute values, denoted in the paper as \textit{patterns}, or \textit{itemsets}. To illustrate the concept of divergence, consider the {\sc compas}\ dataset~\cite{angwin_2016}, in which a score measuring recidivism risk is assigned to criminal defendants by a proprietary algorithm. In this case, the positive class corresponds to high recidivism scores. Table~\ref{table-teaser} shows the false-positive (FPR) and false-negative (FNR) rates occurring in the entire dataset (first row) and in the data subgroups characterized by the highest FPR (second row) and FNR (third row) divergence. For instance, the pattern (\textit{age>45, charge=M, race=Cauc}) shows a high $\Delta_{FNR}$ divergence. Therefore, instances belonging to this data subgroup will be incorrectly assigned to the negative class with a higher rate compared to the entire dataset. We propose a general framework for divergence computation that allows the automatic identification of problematic data subgroups both in classification and ranking problems. Our approach builds upon well-established itemset mining algorithms (e.g., FP-growth~\cite{han2000mining}) and enables the efficient identification of all the problematic patterns above a (low) frequency threshold. Furthermore, given a specific pattern, we exploit the notion of Shapley value~\cite{shapley1953value} to quantify the contribution of each attribute value to the pattern divergence. For instance, as will be demonstrated in the following sections, the attribute value \textit {age>45} is contributing the most to the divergent behavior of the pattern discussed previously.

text: Robotic perception and manipulation of deformable objects constitutes a fundamental challenge. Given the object's intricate geometric configurations and stochastic deformations, a three-stage process is typically employed. The initial stage involves modeling the objects within a simulated environment \cite{Hess:2010:BFE:1893021,coumans2021} or utilizing finite element methods (FEM) \cite{doi:10.1143/JPSJ.66.367}. Subsequently, the second stage concerns learning deformations of the object within the simulated environment during object manipulation \cite{miller2012geometric,lin2015picking}. The concluding stage encompasses determining an optimized trajectory for object manipulation \cite{zaidi2017model,yamakawa2012simple}. Throughout these three stages, the challenge lies in learning the stress-strain relationship of these deformable objects \cite{courtney2005mechanical} which depends upon the physical properties of objects including stiffness, area weight and damping coefficients. Consequently, learning the physical properties of deformable objects is essential to enable robotic dexterous manipulation of deformable objects. Prior approaches for estimating material physics properties comprise either learning physics properties through alignment of simulated models with real objects \cite{9196770,arriola2017multimodal,wang2011data}, or learning physics properties from video sequences \cite{bouman2013estimating,yang2017learning,runia2020cloth}. The former approaches necessitate high precision in object alignment using finite element methods which is computationally demanding; whereas the latter approaches do not require simulated models that correspond to real objects. Consequently, learning from video sequences is computationally efficient and can be implemented in robotic systems where robots can exert external forces on deformable objects. In this paper, we therefore propose learning the fabric's dynamic characteristics. For this purpose, we have developed a Physics-Similarity Neural Network (PhySNet), as illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig:arch}, with the objective of predicting simulated and real fabric physics parameters. Our fundamental hypothesis in this work is that \textit{PhySNet can predict physics parameters of real fabrics and garments by learning physics similarities of simulated fabrics when a wind force field is applied to the fabric}. To validate our hypothesis, we construct a simulated fabric database to enable PhySNet to learn the physics similarity of simulated fabrics, and to generate a Physics Similarity Map (PSM) for a fabric. Following PhySNet training, a piece of real fabric and a simulated fabric with initialized physics parameters are input into PhySNet to obtain their Physics Similarity Distance (PSD). We subsequently input the PSD into a Bayesian optimizer, which outputs updated physical parameters. We input the updated physics parameters into the simulator to generate a new simulated fabric. This procedure iterates until stable parameters (Section \ref{sec:experiment-test_on_fabrics}) are obtained from the Bayesian optimizer.

text: PerceptIn was founded in 2016 to develop visual perception technologies for autonomous vehicles and robots. Since its establishment, PerceptIn has successfully secured over \$10 million in venture capital funding from Walden International, Matrix Partners, and Samsung Ventures \cite{liu2020critical}. PerceptIn is an international technology startup with operations in the U.S., Japan, Europe, and Asia. PerceptIn comprises over 30 researchers and engineers and 10 business professionals. The business professionals are accountable for business development across different markets and collect feedback for the company's R\&D efforts, while the engineers and researchers are responsible for developing cutting-edge autonomous driving technologies. In the past three years, PerceptIn has produced over 20 U.S. patents and over 100 international patents, as well as numerous research papers. In 2017, PerceptIn decided to develop low-speed autonomous vehicles to serve the micromobility market, as micromobility is an emerging transport mode wherein lightweight vehicles cover short trips that massive transit overlooks \cite{liu2020autonomous}. According to the US Department of Transportation, 60\% of vehicle traffic is attributed to trips under 5 miles \cite{santos2011summary}. Transportation needs for short trips are disproportionately under-served by current mass transit systems due to high cost, which affects society profoundly. Micromobility bridges transit services and communities' needs, driving the rise of Mobility-as-a-Service. Based on internal business analysis, if PerceptIn can provide low-speed autonomous vehicles under \$70,000 per unit, PerceptIn could generate a reasonable return-on-investment for PerceptIn's customers, the autonomous vehicle operators. However, the \$70,000 price point also imposes very strict and challenging constraints on the design of low-speed autonomous vehicles. In detail, we must break down the \$70,000 into Non-recurring engineering (NRE) cost such as research and development, recurring costs such as the cost of the chassis, the cost of drive-by-wire conversion (meaning to convert a traditional vehicle into one that can be controlled by computers), the cost of sensors, the cost of integration, the cost of customer service, and finally the cost of the computing system \cite{liu2020engineering}. As the on-vehicle computing system is a significant contributor to cost and power consumption, PerceptIn conducted a study on autonomous driving computing systems \cite{liu2017computer}\cite{liu2019edge}\cite{liu2020pirt}. PerceptIn concluded that computing is the bottleneck for the commercial deployment of autonomous vehicles, and PerceptIn required a computing system that is reliable, affordable, high-performance, and energy efficient. Most importantly, PerceptIn required a solution that is cost-effective and has a short time-to-market. PerceptIn faced several options: Option one, Optimization of commercial off-the-shelf mobile System-on-Chip (SoC) computing systems: This approach brings several benefits; first, since mobile SoCs have reached economies of scale, it would have been most beneficial for PerceptIn to build its technology stack on affordable, backward-compatible computing systems. Second, PerceptIn's vehicles target micromobility with limited speed, similar to mobile robots, for which mobile SoCs have been demonstrated previously. However, an extensive study is required to fully understand mobile SoCs' suitability for autonomous driving, which may delay PerceptIn's product launch by six months. Option two, Procurement of specialized autonomous driving computing systems: there were commercial computing platforms specialized for autonomous driving, such as those from NXP, MobilEye, and Nvidia. They are mostly Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) based chips that provide high performance at a much higher cost. For instance, the first-generation Nvidia PX2 system costs over \$10,000. Besides the cost issue, these computing systems mostly accelerate only the perception function in autonomous driving, whereas PerceptIn requires a system that optimizes the end-to-end performance. So we soon concluded that this option was not viable. Option three, Development of proprietary autonomous driving computing systems: developing a proprietary computing system guarantees that PerceptIn has the most suitable system for PerceptIn's customers and for its workloads, but also means that PerceptIn must invest a significant amount of financial and personnel resources in this project. Also, the investment does not guarantee the success of this project. It is a huge and risky bet for a startup like PerceptIn. After an unsuccessful exploration with option one, starting in early 2018, PerceptIn decided to move forward with option three and PerceptIn thus formed a team to develop the FPGA-based DragonFly computing system \cite{fang2018dragonfly+}\cite{fang2017fpga}\cite{liu2020pi}\cite{tang2018pi}\cite{yu2020building}. Option three was a tremendous success; today all autonomous vehicles shipped by PerceptIn are empowered by PerceptIn's proprietary DragonFly computing system. In this paper, from a technical perspective we explain how we designed PerceptIn's DragonFly computing systems, and the design trade-offs that we faced. For the rest of this paper, we first introduce the sensor suites of our vehicle (Sec. \ref{sec:veh}), and then present the end-to-end processing pipeline exercised by the on-vehicle computing systems (Sec. \ref{sec:alg}). Based on the processing pipeline, we then describe the on-vehicle computing system design (Sec. \ref{sec:sov}). To reduce the end-to-end computing latency, we offload the localization to an FPGA platform. Sec. \ref{sec:fpga} presents FPGA-based vSLAM (visual simultaneous localization and mapping) front-end and back-end systems designed for our vehicle.

text: Daily, millions of users worldwide engage with digitized public services. User authentication is frequently necessary to obtain access to the service. Users presumably trust that throughout this authentication procedure their personal data is handled privately and securely. Additionally, users desire interfaces that are rapid, well-designed, and intuitive; they can rapidly become frustrated or distrust services that are challenging to utilize. Eventually, they may eschew a service completely if the usability presents a substantial barrier to accomplishing their primary objective~\cite{Brostoff}. \subsection{Problem Statement} Currently widespread Identity Management Systems (IDMS) such as \textit{GOV.UK Verify} and the \textit{Federal Cloud Credential Exchange} (FCCX) have exhibited deficiencies concerning privacy and security~\cite{Brandao}. These concerns are amplified by the following two factors: \begin{enumerate} \item The expanding proliferation of systems, both regarding services and regarding users~\cite{ElMaliki2007}. \item Such systems implementing federated or centralized authentication systems. The establishment of such a central hub enables the aggregation and linking of a user's interactions with different service providers, as well as providing extensive access to personally identifiable information (PII). \end{enumerate} Additional users or additional linked services render a target more attractive for malicious attackers or malicious hub operators, and in the event of compromise by these actors, it becomes feasible to undetectably impersonate, profile, and target individual users~\cite{Brandao}, resulting in an erosion of public trust~\cite{Ohara} in the service. Regrettably, issues with privacy and security are not confined to government-operated services. Recently disclosed vulnerabilities or data breaches in platform services managed by Facebook and Google, which are frequently employed for user authentication to third-party services, are significant examples~\cite{fbreach, googlebreach}. Different use-cases possess different design requirements due to the particular needs of the system's stakeholders. Thorough analysis is consequently required to determine the specific considerations system implementers and users must consider, comprehend, and address. The subsequent section provides context for such a system and helps motivate their utility. Furthermore, it introduces terminology and possible competing solutions. Section~\ref{overview} describes the challenges in applying our proposed solution to Transport for London (TfL) and suggests possible extensions to address the limitations. Section~\ref{implementation} details the design specific choices in the implementation. Section~\ref{results} describes the testing approach, Section~\ref{analysis} discusses the results, and Section~\ref{conclusion} offers an analysis, with a view toward future work.

text: An estimated 276,480 women will receive breast cancer diagnoses in the U.S. during 2020, with 42,170 women anticipated to succumb to this disease \cite{Sieg20}. To inform clinical management, the majority of pathologists evaluate breast cancers using a standardized grading framework \cite{Bloo51, Elst91}, encompassing three components: 1) nuclear pleomorphism (or "atypia"), 2) degree of gland formation and 3) mitotic count. The assessment criteria for mitotic count and gland formation rely on quantitative measurements, while nuclear pleomorphism evaluation depends on qualitative examination of tumor nuclear morphology assessed microscopically on a 1 to 3 scale, indicating progressive morphological deviation from normal epithelium. The overall tumor grade derives from these three component scores. With expanding adoption of digital pathology, grading can now be performed on digitized histopathological images, achieving comparable concordance to light microscopy evaluation \cite{Gint20}. Furthermore, pathologists can increasingly receive support from Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in routine clinical practice \cite{Bera19, Niaz19, Bult20a, Rant20}. The predominant AI technology employed for medical image analysis comprises deep neural networks (deep learning; DL). Deep learning architectures consist of interconnected neurons that process input images and execute sequential operations on trainable network parameters to achieve learning objectives, including classification, regression and segmentation. These approaches have achieved remarkable success across multiple computer vision domains \cite{Kriz12, Le13, Silv16, Devl18} and more recently in digital pathology applications \cite{Jano16, Bejn17, Veta18, Nagp19, Bult20}. Specifically for breast cancer grading, automated mitosis detection represented an early DL application \cite{Cire13a, Veta15}, establishing its clinical and prognostic significance \cite{Tell18, Balk19, Balk19b}. Gland segmentation was conceptualized as sequential nuclei and gland detection, alongside segmentation tasks \cite{Nguy15, Lee18}, with extensions to clinical risk stratification \cite{Buch16} through deep learning implementation. In contrast to gland formation and mitotic count, nuclear pleomorphism lacks equivalent quantitative characteristics in its definition. Consequently, nuclear pleomorphism scoring represents the least reproducible among the three grading elements, thereby constraining its clinical utility \cite{Frie95, Meye05, Long05}. Research addressing automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring has remained limited, encompassing approaches utilizing manually engineered nuclear features \cite{Lu15, Gand19} combined with deep belief networks \cite{Maql16}, descriptor-based pixel-level image characteristics \cite{Khan15} or binary classification of high pleomorphism (score 3) employing simple convolutional neural networks on small image patches \cite{Noel15}. Supervised DL necessitates ground-truth labels corresponding to images for neural network training. Obtaining such labels presents substantial challenges for applications like pleomorphism scoring, involving discrete categories and inter-observer variability. Converting multiple observer scores into ground-truth labels (e.g. through majority vote or consensus) discards valuable information contained within individual expert score distributions. In this investigation, we therefore develop a novel DL approach to nuclear pleomorphism scoring by treating it as a continuous score, rather than categorizing it into three discrete classes. We reformulate the original three-category classification into a complete spectrum of continuous values spanning from minimal pleomorphism scores to the most severe. Our methodology primarily comprises two components. The first component involves an epithelial cell detection network developed previously \cite{Merc19}. This stage aims to restrict analysis to diagnostically relevant regions (i.e. invasive tumor) within whole slide images. In the second stage, a deep regression network predicts continuous nuclear pleomorphism scores on tumor regions. Training this network eliminates the requirement for detailed manual pathologist annotations, which represents a key limitation in computational pathology. This investigation presents the first end-to-end fully automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring in breast cancer utilizing DL. Additionally, we transform discrete classification into continuous regression to preserve valuable observer information not previously applied. The overview of our methodology, \AI, illustrating this two-stage nuclear pleomorphism scoring process is shown in Figure \ref{fig:introduction:overview_inference}. To develop and validate our methodology, we conducted two distinct studies, generating two separate datasets. The first study, designated as ROI-study, comprised $125$ tumor regions of interest (tumor ROIs) and an additional $79$ "normal appearing" epithelial regions of interest (normal ROIs) from $39$ whole slide images, carefully selected to encompass diverse tumor morphology in breast cancer histopathology. We recruited $10$ pathologists from $6$ countries to evaluate nuclear pleomorphism on tumor ROIs, each visually paired with a normal ROI from the same patient for pathologists to utilize as reference for scoring pleomorphism degree. We employed ROI-study results to train our \AI and evaluate its performance against the pathologist panel. In our automated methodology, we utilized averaged nuclear pleomorphism scores across the 10 pathologists as reference scores, representing their collective expertise rather than imposing discrete majority scores. The \AI was trained on diverse tumor morphology, utilizing reference scores to establish nuclear pleomorphism as a complete spectrum of tumor morphological variation. In the second study, designated as the slide-study, $118$ whole slide images of breast cancer resection tissue sections were employed for trained \AI evaluation. The slide distribution reflected case distributions in routine clinical practice. For the slide-study, we recruited $4$ pathologists to evaluate nuclear pleomorphism of slides, which were compared to our \AI for whole slide-level assessment. Additional details regarding the ROI-study and slide-study are provided in Section \ref{sec:methodology}.

text: Pose transfer, which involves applying the desired pose of a source mesh to a target mesh, represents a promising yet challenging task in 3D computer vision that can be extensively applied across various industrial domains. Nevertheless, existing methods ~\cite{NPT,LIMP,Unsupervised,AniFormer} can only achieve satisfactory performance within given datasets of synthesized or known pose and shape spaces, and fail to generalize to other unknown spaces with robust performance, which severely constrains their further real-world implementations. To achieve robust performance on unknown latent spaces and other domains as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:1}, we propose a novel Transformer network targeting generalized 3D mesh pose transfer. Specifically, a novel geometry-contrastive Transformer with geometrically structured encoders is designed that aims to enhance the identity mesh representation under the guidance of the pose mesh through their \emph{global geometric contrasts}. Locally, we introduce a novel central geodesic contrastive loss to improve the geometric representation by considering the \emph{regional contrast of all the geodesic directions} of each vertex as back-propagation gradients. Furthermore, we present a latent isometric regularization module to stabilize the unreliable performance of cross-dataset pose transfer problems. Moreover, we present a new 3D mesh dataset, namely SMG-3D, for quantitatively evaluating the 3D pose transfer with unknown spaces. The SMG-3D is based on daily spontaneously performed body gestures with more plausible and challenging body movements that differ from those well-performed poses \cite{AMASS,DFAUST}. We employ a semi-synthesis approach to construct the dataset to provide necessary GT meshes for training and validation. Our SMG-3D dataset can be jointly combined with other existing body mesh datasets for cross-dataset qualitative analysis. A natural question to pose is: why not simply use purely synthesized meshes to train and evaluate the model? The concise answer is that models trained on purely synthesized meshes will fail in the cross-dataset task. Indeed, utilizing mesh synthesizing models like the SMPL series~\cite{SMPL, SMAL, SMPLX} can synthesize unlimited poses that can cover the entire latent space, or a large-scale dataset AMASS \cite{AMASS} to eliminate the inconsistencies with unknown dataset space. However, in practice, even for a small dataset FAUST with only 10 pose categories, it requires more than 26 hours to train a model~\cite{LIMP} to fully learn the latent space. Thus, due to the staggering variability of poses and movements, it is not feasible to train the model with synthesized samples covering the entire pose space. It is desirable that a model can be directly generalized to unknown latent spaces in a more efficient manner. To this end, we propose the SMG-3D dataset to address the cross-dataset learning issue. It can provide challenging latent distribution allocated on natural and plausible body poses with occlusions and self-contacts instead of well-posed body moves like AMASS~\cite{AMASS}, which \textit{could advance the research to real-world scenarios one step further}. To summarize, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item A novel geometry-contrastive Transformer of positional embedding free architectures with state-of-the-art performance on the challenging 3D pose transfer task. \item A simple and efficient central geodesic contrastive loss that can further improve the geometric learning via preserving the directional gradient of the 3D vertices. \item A challenging 3D human body mesh dataset (namely SMG-3D) providing unknown space of naturally plausible body poses with challenging occlusions and self-contacts for the cross-dataset qualitative evaluation. \item A new latent isometric regularization module for adapting to challenging unknown spaces on cross-dataset tasks. \end{itemize}

text: Searcher struggle represents the phenomenon wherein a searcher ``makes strenuous efforts in the face of difficulties"\footnote{\url{merriam-webster.com}} throughout a search process. During a struggling moment, the user encounters negative emotions of feeling frustrated, upset, or annoyed by the search activity. Detecting searcher struggle constitutes an important task for Web search engines since it can alert the search engines to adjust their algorithms in a timely manner. Most existing struggle detection methods are classifiers utilizing features that quantify user efforts~\cite{Li:2009:GAM:1571941.1571951,Jiang:2015:UPG:2684822.2685319}. This occurs because struggling behaviors are frequently manifested through excessive repetitions of user actions. For example, when searching for ``curly hair dye", a user issued more than twenty queries and still could not locate a satisfactory result. It is intuitive to assume that a large number of user efforts indicate user struggles. Nevertheless, this conjecture does not always correspond with real-world observations. One observation is that non-struggling search tasks may also exhibit many user-issued queries and clicks. For example, a user searched for ``guy proposing ideas," and the log demonstrates that he browsed more than 900 search results and bookmarked 27; the user reported he enjoyed the search throughout the session. Recent laboratory studies have raised similar concerns. Edwards and Kelly \cite{Edwards:2017:EFD:3077136.3080818} noted that although an increase in user effort might help predict searcher struggle, such an increase can also indicate engagement or exploration. Without an effective mechanism, the discriminating power of effort-based features diminishes, making it challenging to separate a negative experience such as struggle from positive experiences such as engagement and thus difficult to improve Web user experiences. This paper references the psychology literature and proposes a novel feature modulation method for struggle detection. Our work is motivated by the Reversal Theory (RT)~\cite{gerrig2015psychology,apter2001motivation,personalitydynamics,APTER1984265,fourdomains}. RT is a ``mode-based" psychology theory that challenges some fundamental assumptions in the fields of motivation and personality. Rather than assuming static personality traits, RT focuses on the ``complexity, changeability, and dynamics of human motivation and personality"~\cite{APTER1984265}. Its key insight is that people change in the flow of everyday life, and their personalities and motivations can reverse~\cite{personalitydynamics}. RT suggests some counter-intuitive ideas, such as whether a user is conforming to rules or rebelling has minimal impact on his struggling behaviors, but whether she works on a serious or playful task would matter. We conducted statistical hypothesis tests on these arguments and confirmed them on commercial search logs. Furthermore, RT states that human motivations can be organized into several dimensions and each dimension consists of two opposing states. Within one dimension, a person can reverse between the pair of states but can be active at only one of them at any given moment, which indeed suggests a bi-modal distribution rather than a single-modal distribution. We leverage this insight in this paper and propose a novel and effective feature modulation method for struggle detection. We propose to (1) select features responsible for the related RT dimension, (2) moderate the selected features by reducing the bias between the two distributions in the bi-modal arousal model, and (3) send the modulated features to classifiers to identify if a search session has struggling moments. Our method can be used in combination with any feature-based struggle detection method. We evaluate our approach on one-week-long search logs collected from both mobile and PC platforms. The experimental results demonstrate that our method is highly effective; it can significantly improve several top-performing methods by $\sim$5\% accuracy and $\sim$9\% positive precision.
