text: The publication of the Bitcoin paper by~\cite{Satoshi2008} in 2008 has stimulated the investigation of blockchains and smart contracts in developing innovative applications. There exists a global consensus regarding the potential of smart contracts for constructing innovative applications across diverse sectors of industry and government~\cite{Hileman2017}. We concur with this perspective and consider that certain smart contract applications are appropriately implemented based on smart contracts deployed on--chain such as those on the Ethereum~\cite{Ethereum2017}, Hyperledger Fabric~\cite{HyperledgerHome} or Bitcoin~\cite{BitcoinHome} blockchains. Nevertheless, we believe that the potential of on--chain smart contracts has been overestimated. There exist applications where the utilization of on-blockchain smart contracts constitutes overkill and others where they produce a detrimental effect to the degree of rendering the application impractical or unimplementable~\cite{Morgen2018,Scriber2018,Valentina2018}. In these circumstances, developers should contemplate the utilization of smart contracts deployed on Trusted Third Parties. It appears that the confusion arises from the novelty of the technology and absence of global consensus regarding what smart contracts and blockchains represent. Before proceeding with the discussion we will present the definitions that will be followed in subsequent sections of this paper. \subsection{Blockchains} To software developers, a blockchain constitutes a piece of middle- ware that incorporates built--in services that can be utilized for the development of distributed applications without the involvement of a component (for instance, an authentication or a database server) functioning as a central control. The prominent services that blockchains can provide are indelible append--only storage, public--key--based access control to the execution of operations, public auditability of records and, notably, consensus services of some discipline (typically, eventual consensus). A substantial variety of applications can be constructed based on blockchains; smart contracts represent the best known but not the sole one. At an implementation level, a blockchain can be defined as a distributed data structure (known also as the ledger) composed of an ordered, back--linked list (chain) of blocks. Blocks are appended to the list following an append--only model, and only when a set of nodes that maintain local replicas of the current state of the blockchain achieve consensus regarding its next global state. The blocks are typically utilized for storing records of transactions executed by parties that do not necessarily trust each other and support the peer--to--peer execution model of the transactions. The transactions constitute operations aimed at modifying the current state of the blockchain and are not necessarily bank transactions. The construction and maintenance of a blockchain requires the combination of several technologies, consequently, different conceptual models have been proposed for modelling blockchains. For instance, in~\cite{KenjiSaito2016} a blockchain is regarded as a probabilistic state machine to emphasize the probabilistic nature of the consensus algorithms that are utilized in blockchains. \subsection{Smart contracts} Intuitively, a smart contract aims at being the digital version of a conventional commercial contract that is written in a human language, for instance, English. By digital we mean that the smart contract constitutes a piece of computer code that can be executed to monitor or enforce the clauses stipulated in the conventional contract, programmatically at run--time. For instance, a financial contract for a loan agreement between a borrower and lender might stipulate that at the request of the borrower, the lender will advance GBP 100.00 to the borrower within five days of receiving the request. Being an executable program, a smart contract is expected to be deployed on infrastructure that can provide it with a run--time environment, including, library support, facilities for managing the smart contract (initiate, stop, terminate, update, etc.) and databases for storing records regarding the inputs sent to the smart contracts and outputs produced by it. The primary responsibilities of the smart contract are i) to act as a contract monitor that observes the interaction between the contracting parties; ii) to determine whether each operation (for instance, request loan, honour loan request, decline loan request, etc.) that the contracting parties execute is compliant or non-compliant with the terms stipulated in the contract and in accordance with the rights and obligations inherent in the contract and iii) to produce a verdict. Notice that in some existing smart contract applications, the declaration of the verdict is directly and intricately associated with an action (e.g., collect payment) that is executed when the verdict is contract compliant. However, we believe that for the sake of modularity it makes sense to separate the two acts and focus on the verdict---the most fundamental operation that smart contracts need to perform. We regard the action as an arbitrary reaction that can be immediately or eventually executed by the smart contract itself or by a different component implemented in a different software layer. In many applications, the action consists of permitting the execution of the contractual operation when it is declared contract compliant or preventing its execution when the operation is declared non--contract compliant by the smart contract. In this approach, the smart contract functions as a contract enforcer. The question that emerges here is where to deploy the smart contract. \subsection{On--blockchain smart contracts} Smart contracts can be deployed on--chain. The term smart contract was coined by Szabo in 1997~\cite{Szabo1997} but it did not attract commercial interest until 2008 with the commercial success of Bitcoin as a cryptocurrency platform~\cite{Satoshi2008}. In Bitcoin~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2017}, smart contracts are implemented in an opcode stack--based script non--Turing complete language~\cite{BitcoinScript} and deployed on the Bitcoin blockchain. They were originally conceived for mediating the execution of payment operations in BTCs (Bitcoin's cryptocurrency). Ethereum~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2018}, currently a leading blockchain platform, extends the concept of Bitcoin's smart contracts and implements a blockchain that supports smart contracts written in Turing--complete languages, such as Solidity~\cite{Solidity2017}. As demonstrated by numerous Bitcoin and Ethereum use cases, in several situations, smart contracts can be conveniently deployed on--chain, but it is essential to appreciate that blockchains and smart contracts are two independent technologies. The deployment of smart contracts on--blockchain is only one out of several deployment alternatives. To appreciate the point, it is worth considering that smart contracts predate blockchains by several years. Research on smart contracts was pioneered by Minsky in the mid--80s~\cite{Minsky1985} and followed by Marshall~\cite{Lindsay1993}. In early works, smart contracts were referred to as electronic contracts, executable contracts, digital contracts and other similar names. Since the usage of the term smart contract is so widespread now, we will follow it in the rest of this document. \subsection{On--Trusted Third Parties smart contracts} Smart contracts can be deployed on--Trusted Third Parties (on--TTP). We define a TTP as an institution that in addition to possessing the technical infrastructure for hosting smart contracts, has earned trust, reputation and authority. E--commerce applications routinely utilize TTP services, examples include payment gateways, certification authorities, time--stamping services, custodian services, settlement services and various brokerage services~\cite{Mainelli2015}. In smart contract applications, a TTP is logically positioned between the two business partners and is trusted to host and run a single instance of the smart contract. The smart contract observes all the operations that the partners execute and maintains undeniable records regarding them. Pioneering work on smart contracts~\cite{Minsky1985,Lindsay1993} was primarily focused on on--TTP deployment. A strong assumption with a TTP--based deployment is that the TTP is trusted not to modify the code of the contract or abuse the sensitive data that the contractual parties expose to it. text: In recent years, we have observed the remarkable success of deep neural networks (DNNs) across diverse domains of artificial intelligence including computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{6296526}, and robot control~\cite{levine2018learning}. Despite their exceptional performance, DNNs have been demonstrated to be susceptible to adversarial attacks that introduce imperceptible perturbations to inputs~\cite{madry2017towards, goodfellow2014explaining,laidlaw2019functional, laidlaw2020perceptual, kang2019testing, dong2018boosting, carlini2017towards, chen2017ead, 7467366}. This presents a significant challenge for security-critical applications such as autonomous driving and medicine. To improve model robustness against adversarial attacks, numerous defense methods have been developed including empirical~\cite{madry2017towards,zhang2019theoretically, papernot2016distillation,lin2020dual, singla2021skew, Kannan2018AdversarialLP, wang2019improving} and certifiable defenses~\cite{raghunathan2018certified,cohen2019certified, levine2020randomized, levine2019certifiably, sinha2017certifying, levine2021improved}. Adversarial training (AT)~\cite{madry2017towards} is regarded as one of the most effective algorithms for adversarial defenses. Numerous works have focused on improving adversarial training through different loss functions, such as ALP~\cite{Kannan2018AdversarialLP}, TRADES~\cite{zhang2019theoretically}, and MART~\cite{wang2019improving}. However, they train only a single model without considering the synergy of a network ensemble. Additionally, most defense methods target a single perturbation type, which can be vulnerable to unseen perturbation types ~\cite{tramer2019adversarial, maini2020adversarial}. For instance, models adversarially trained on $l_\infty$-bounded adversarial examples can be vulnerable to $l_1$ and $l_2$-bounded attacks. Knowledge distillation (KD)~\cite{hinton2015distilling} is a well-established method for transferring knowledge learned by one model to another. There are numerous forms of KD~\cite{wang2020knowledge} including \textit{offline} KD, where the teacher models are pretrained and the students learn from static teachers\cite{hinton2015distilling}, and \textit{online} KD, where a group of student models learn from peers' predictions~\cite{zhang2018deep, guo2020online, song2018collaborative}. Several techniques based on KD have been developed for adversarial defenses~\cite{papernot2016distillation, goldblum2019adversarially, arani2020adversarial, chen2021robust}. ~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} demonstrates that robustness can be transferred among models through KD and~\cite{chen2021robust} shows that KD can help alleviate robust overfitting. Table~\ref{tab:kd} summarizes the differences among KD-based defenses. We contend that current KD-based defenses are suboptimal in terms of enhancing adversarial robustness. Defensive distillation (DD) trains a natural model with another natural model as the teacher, which cannot provide strong robustness as both the teacher and student are not adversarially trained, and it is compromised by~\cite{carlini2016defensive}. Adversarially robust distillation (ARD)~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} trains a robust model with another robust model as the teacher to distill the robustness of a large network onto a smaller student, which depends on the existence of strong teacher models, and the improvement of the student model is constrained as the teacher is fixed. Adversarial concurrent training (ACT)~\cite{arani2020adversarial} trains a natural and a robust model jointly in an online KD manner to align the feature space of both. However, since natural models and robust models learn fundamentally different features~\cite{tsipras2018robustness}, aligning the feature space of a robust model with a natural model may result in compromised robustness. In this paper, we propose Mutual Adversarial Training (MAT) that enables models to share their knowledge of adversarial robustness and teach each other to be more robust. Unlike previous KD-based defenses, we train a group of robust models simultaneously, and each network not only learns from ground-truth labels as in standard AT, but also the soft labels from peer networks that encode peers' knowledge for defending adversarial attacks to achieve enhanced robustness. The architecture of MAT is illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:mat}. MAT enhances model robustness through multiple aspects: 1) MAT inherits the benefits of KD, such as enhancing generalization~\cite{furlanello2018born} and reducing robust overfitting~\cite{chen2021robust}. 2) \textit{MAT creates a positive feedback loop of increasing model robustness}. Each network serves as a robust teacher to provide semantic-aware and discriminative soft labels to its peers. text: Android has progressively emerged as the most prevalent mobile operating system globally. Regrettably, owing to its widespread adoption, it has simultaneously become the primary target platform for malicious actors. Adversaries exploit Android to deploy millions of malicious applications that deceive victims into disclosing their confidential information or executing harmful operations, including surveillance of user activities, dissemination of spam, or deployment of unwanted advertisements. Concurrently, Android malware investigation, encompassing malware detection and classification, has evolved into an essential responsibility for security researchers in both commercial and academic sectors. Consequently, numerous research endeavors have sought to identify Android malware~\cite{canfora2015effectiveness,gascon2013structural,li2018android,mclaughlin2017deep,hybroid}. In recent years, a substantial proportion of the proposed methodologies exploits the contextual information of Android applications to detect and classify Android Malware, including permissions and sensitive application programming interfaces (APIs). For instance, Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} introduced a classifier employing the factorization machine (FM) architecture, wherein they extract diverse Android app characteristics (permissions, malicious APIs, etc.) from manifest files and source code. Likewise, Chen et al.~\cite{chen2018android} developed an approach that examines Android malware based on its static behavior involving the utilization of permissions, components, and sensitive API calls. Furthermore, several studies employ natural language processing(NLP)~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} based techniques to identify Android Malware, and these systems treat Android apps analogously to documents and instructions in Android apps as tokens. Consider ~\cite{kang2016n} as an illustration, which assesses the efficacy of uni-gram, bi-gram, and tri-gram with stacked generalization. Moreover, several existing studies rely on the Android network traffic pattern to identify the legitimate and malicious behaviors~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,xu2021hawkeye,xu2020manis,xu2021falcon}. Most of these approaches utilize manually specified rules and construct rule-based classifiers for detecting Android malware, such as CICAndMal2017~\cite{lashkari2018toward}, which employs third-party tools to extract nine features from the network PCAP (packet capture) file and identifies malware using those specific features. Zulkifli et al. ~\cite{zulkifli2018android} presents a decision tree algorithm on network traffic as dynamic characteristics of Android apps. Although the aforementioned methods provide the Android platform with an additional security layer, they possess limitations. On one hand, for instance, the contextual information of program code encounters difficulties against malware obfuscation procedures, such as ~\textit{identifier renaming}, ~\textit{string encryption}, ~\textit{dead-code insertion}, and ~\textit{instruction substitution}. These procedures induce modifications in the compiled code to circumvent detection effortlessly. For example, utilizing string encryption, the FM method in Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} would be affected because the system cannot extract the accessible permission information from the manifest file. Meanwhile, other NLP-based malware detection systems~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} are also impacted by certain obfuscation techniques. On the other hand, regarding the network traffic-based methods, the most significant issue is the code coverage problem~\cite{tazaki2013direct}. As one category of dynamic feature-based method, the network traffic only represents a limited portion of code functionality. Most of the code functionalities do not require or generate network traffic. Furthermore, most of the state-of-the-art network traffic-based malware detection systems are rule-based methods~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,hybroid} , which sophisticated attacks can readily circumvent since rule-based analysis depends on distinguishing expected versus anomalous behavior; these methods may encounter difficulties when malware is modified to conceal its footprints or behavior. Therefore, in this paper, we present a hybrid pattern malware detection and classification framework that integrates the network and program code features. First, we transform the network packets to the sequence of 2D gray images and utilize a convolution neural network (CNN) to pre-train the 2D gray images. We then employ a bi-directional LSTM network to process the continuous network traffic and perform the malware classification similar to the 2D image sequence classification task. Additionally, we design an NLP inspired-method for the program code pattern based on the graph neural network (GNN). It can identify obfuscated applications while maintaining excellent performance. In brief, we first design the \texttt{opcode2vec}, \texttt{function2vec}, and \texttt{graph2vec} components to represent instruction, function, and the whole program's information with vectors. After obtaining features both from the network traffic and program code, we then feed these vectors into the classifier and train it to distinguish between benign and malicious applications. Finally, \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace identifies the Android malware families and demonstrates that it outperforms most existing frameworks. We achieve 97.16\% accuracy for malware detection and 88.32\% accuracy for malware classification average. In this paper, we emphasize the novelty from two aspects. The first one is the bi-directional LSTM to process the 2D-image sequence. And the other is graph-based malware detection, which adopts natural language processing techniques as a node representation method. \bigskip \noindent In summary, we make the following main contributions: \begin{itemize} 	\item We introduce \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace, a hybrid pattern Android malware detection and categorization framework that combines the network traffic and program code features. 	\item We design a bidirectional LSTM network to accomplish 2D gray images sequence classification, which takes the network packets (converted to 2D images) as input. 	\item We create and release a dataset, \textit{AndroNetMnist}\xspace, which includes 3,255,391 2D gray images in five categories(Benign, Adware, Ransomware, Scareware and SMSmalware) for network traffic classification. 	\item We design and implement an NLP-inspired malware detection and categorization module for the program code that can process obfuscated programs. 	\item We evaluate the accuracy of our approach using real malicious and benign datasets. 	\item We release our work as an opensource project after the paper will be accepted. \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary developments in end-to-end neural network-based methodologies have demonstrated substantial success across diverse sequence generation applications: machine translation~\cite{sutskever2014sequence,luong2015effective}, dialogue systems~\cite{vinyals2015neural,serban2016building}, textual summarization~\cite{rush2015neural,nallapati2016abstractive,see2017get}, image/video captioning~\cite{bahdanau2014neural,venugopalan2015sequence,pasunuru2017multi}, question generation~\cite{du2017learning,du2018harvesting,zhang2019addressing}, etc. Across these applications, cross-entropy loss optimization has been extensively employed as the conventional optimization methodology~\cite{sutskever2014sequence}, yet this methodology encounters exposure-bias complications~\cite{ranzato2015sequence} and fails to optimize for non-differentiable automatic evaluation metrics that assess generated sequence quality. Contemporary introduction of policy gradient-based reinforcement learning methodologies addresses these complications for sequence generation applications by directly optimizing non-differentiable evaluation metrics~\cite{zaremba2015reinforcement,ranzato2015sequence,rennie2016self}. Nevertheless, optimizing for a specific metric/reward through policy gradient-based methodologies frequently results in improvement primarily in that particular metric, indicating that this methodology exploits the metrics~\cite{paulus2017deep}. The weighted combination of multiple metrics or surrogate rewards has been investigated~\cite{liu2017improved}, yet these methodologies must address identifying the optimal scale balance among different metrics. One may alternatively optimize multiple metrics through a mixing ratio~\cite{pasunuru2018multi}, yet this still requires careful tuning of the mixing ratio. Furthermore, all these reward methodologies are static and remain unchanged throughout training, and all metrics may not be significant across every training stage. Consequently, it may be beneficial to consider employing a dynamic combination of metrics, which rewards to utilize early versus later, or which rewards might be valuable to revisit later in training, and consider the context of the complete reward history, along with the model's current state and the metric's characteristics. Toward this objective, we introduce a multi-armed bandit methodology (which we designate the DORB{} framework) where the bandit's arms represent the choices of metrics that we aim to optimize as rewards. At each round, the bandit selects the subsequent possible metric to optimize based on its prior performance history across these metrics, thereby enabling automatic learning of an optimal reward curriculum. We investigate this methodology in the context of exploration versus exploitation through the Exp3 algorithm~\cite{auer2002nonstochastic} with two novel methodologies for bandit rewards: (1) Single Multi-reward Bandit (SM-Bandit); (2) Hierarchical Multi-reward Bandit (HM-Bandit). Initially, we introduce a reward scaling methodology to maintain the metric rewards range within $[0,1]$. Subsequently, we introduce our SM-Bandit, where at each round, the bandit's reward depends on performance improvement from multiple sources. Here, we employ the average of all scaled metric rewards from multiple sources as the final bandit reward. Finally, we introduce our HM-Bandit, which comprises a single first-level controller, along with $K$ second-level multi-armed bandits. The first-level controller's objective is to identify the under-performing reward metric, while the second-level bandits' objective is to activate the specific metric optimizer that will produce promising improvement in this particular metric. text: Object counting has gained increasing significance owing to its extensive range of applications including crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation and inventory management. Most existing counting methodologies~\cite{zhang2016single, ma2019bayesian, biswas2017automatic} concentrate on a \XP{specific,} single category. Nevertheless, when deployed to novel categories, their performance degrades catastrophically. Furthermore, it is \XP{exceptionally} challenging and expensive to collect all categories and annotate them for training purposes. For humans, the generalization capability enables them to acquire and handle diverse vision tasks without substantial prior knowledge and experience. We are fascinated by this extraordinary ability and in this work, we concentrate on this learning paradigm and develop a network to efficiently recognize and count novel categories given merely one example. We adopt the few-shot setting in ~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and adapt it to one-shot object counting. Specifically, the model receives an image with unseen novel categories and a supporting bounding box containing an exemplar instance of the desired category as input, and subsequently predicts the object count in the image. Nevertheless, there exist two primary challenges. \textbf{First}, the object counting task encompasses numerous different categories, and even multiple categories exist within a single image. Moreover in few-shot setting, these categories will not overlap between training and inference. This indicates that the model requires a robust distinguishing capability between features of different categories, and simultaneously, an effective associating capability among instances sharing the same category. \textbf{Second}, in one-shot counting, the model \XP{acquires knowledge} from merely one supporting instance. Much of the difficulty stems from the fact that the supporting sample may \XP{vary from other instances in, for instance, sizes and poses. Consequently, the model is required to be invariant towards these variations without observing the commonalities across different instances.} Therefore, in this paper, we propose an effective network named LaoNet for one-shot object counting. It comprises three main components: feature extraction, feature correlation and the density regressor, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:network}. The feature correlation model and the feature extraction model are carefully designed to address the aforementioned two challenges. We propose the feature correlation based on Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules to learn inner-relations and inter-relations respectively. The Self-Attention encourages the model to concentrate more on important features and their correlations, enhancing the efficiency of information refinement. Previous few-shot counting methods~\cite{ranjan2021learning, yang2021class} typically rely on a convolution operation to match the similarities between image features and supporting features. However, as the kernel is derived from supporting features with the default size and rotation angle, the convolution operation will greatly depend on the quality of supporting features and the consistency of physical properties among different instances. Instead, our designed feature correlation model benefits from two types of attention modules and addresses the aforementioned problem by considering all correlations. We further propose a Scale Aggregation mechanism in scale extraction to handle scale variations among different categories and different instances. By learning features from multi-subspace, the model aggregates diverse scale information while maintaining spatial consistency. To summarize, our contribution is threefold. \begin{itemize} \item We design a novel network named LaoNet (A network by which you only need to Look At One instance) for one-shot object counting. By combining Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules, LaoNet exploits the correlation among novel category objects with high accuracy and efficiency. 	\item We propose a Scale Aggregation mechanism to extract more comprehensive features and fuse multi-scale information from the supporting box. 	 	\item The experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art results with significant improvements on FSC-147~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft} datasets under the one-shot setting without fine-tuning. 	 	 \end{itemize}

text: Recommendation systems have been extensively deployed across online platforms today, including Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS} and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. Given the dynamic interactions between users and items, capturing evolving user interests from users' historical records becomes crucial. To accurately represent user interests and generate appropriate recommendations, substantial research efforts have focused on developing sequential recommendation methods \cite{Caser,sasrec,GRU4Rec,SR-GNN}. Typically, the sequential recommendation task seeks to characterize user representation from users' historical behaviors and predict the corresponding expected item. Considering the remarkable success of deep learning for sequential dependency modeling and representation learning, numerous methods based on deep neural networks \citep*{r1} have been introduced and developed to address this task, encompassing RNN-based frameworks~\cite{GRU4Rec,GRU4Rec+,STAMP}, various CNN blocks and architectures~\cite{Caser,3D_CNN}, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) \cite{SR-GNN,FGNN,GC-SAN}, and model variants \cite{sasrec,BERT4Rec,TiSASRec} that rely on the powerful multi-head self-attention \cite{atten}. Despite achieving strong performance, these methods may encounter the data sparsity problem \cite{Autoint,s3,sasrec} in sequential recommendation, particularly for models constructed on the multi-head self-attention mechanism, where only a single item prediction loss is employed to optimize the complete model parameters for capturing all potential correlations in input interaction sequences. To tackle the aforementioned challenge, various self-supervised learning strategies have been introduced~\cite{yao2020self,CLRec}. Among these approaches, the recently proposed contrastive learning (CL) objective~\cite{CL4SRec} demonstrates highly promising results. By combining effective data augmentation strategies and cooperating with the standard sequential prediction objective, the CL-based method can learn superior sequence-level user representations and improve the performance of sequential recommendations. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of CL-based approaches depends on the associated data augmentation methods, pretext tasks, efficient negative sampling, and hyper-parameter selection (e.g., the temperature in NCE and InfoNCE losses) \cite{jaiswal2021survey}. To address the aforementioned limitations, numerous efforts have been undertaken to simplify contrastive learning. \cite{gao2021simcse} propose a remarkably simple yet effective contrastive learning scheme that employs dropout noise as data augmentation to construct high-quality positive samples for sequence-level representation learning. While such a scheme proves effective for unsupervised representation learning, adapting it to the sequential recommendation task still encounters the dilemma where a higher proportion of CL objective in model training leads to superior representations that can easily distinguish positive and negative samples but may result in inferior item prediction performance and vice versa. In other words, there exists a notable gap between the discrimination of positive and negative samples and the task objective for sequential recommendation. Therefore, the key to obtaining superior user representations primarily for the item prediction task involves designing additional training strategies that can address the inherent issues of sequential recommendation models. Motivated by the recent observation on the multi-head attention model that a remarkably simple regularization strategy applied to the output space of supervised tasks yields substantial performance improvement~\cite{liang2021r} (achieving SOTA on numerous challenging tasks), we propose to comprehensively explore the effect of consistency training for the sequential recommendation task. We first introduce the simple bidirectional KL divergence regularization into the output space to constrain the inconsistency between two forward passes with different dropouts. Unlike previous machine translation, summarization, and natural language understanding tasks, we contend that the introduced consistency regularization solely in the output space is insufficient for the data sparsity setting of sequential recommendation. We subsequently design a novel and simple regularization objective in the representation space. Unlike previous studies that employ cosine \cite{gao2021simcse} and L2 \cite{ma2017dropout,zolna2018fraternal} distance to regularize the representation space, we propose to regularize the distributed probability of each user representation over others. Consequently, we can extend and leverage the effective bidirectional KL loss to regularize the representation inconsistency. Experiments on three public benchmarks and one newly collected large-scale corpus demonstrate that our proposed simple consistency training for sequential recommendation (CT4Rec) outperforms state-of-the-art methods based on contrastive learning by a substantial margin. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that our proposed consistency training can be readily extended to the data side. The Online A/B test also validates the effectiveness of our method. Additionally, we extend our consistency training method to the CTR prediction task, and experiments conducted on two newly constructed industrial datasets further confirm the effectiveness of our method. In summary, we primarily have the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a simple (with only two bidirectional KL losses) yet highly effective consistency training method for sequential recommendation systems. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to comprehensively study the effect of consistency training from different perspectives and with a unified training objective for the sequential recommendation task. \item Our proposed consistency training method can be readily extended to other inconsistency scenarios and tasks, e.g., data augmentation and CTR prediction. \item Extensive experiments on four offline datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed CT4Rec over SOTA models based on contrastive learning with substantially better performance and faster convergence time. The Online A/B test also shows significant improvement over the strong ensemble model. \end{itemize}

text: Security researchers consistently discover critical security vulnerabilities in essential components, including those subjected to extensive scrutiny and widespread deployment over many years. A promising direction in recent research has employed \textit{formal verification} methodologies to substantial real-world systems. Such certified systems are accompanied by machine-verifiable proofs demonstrating that the implementation satisfies the specification of ``correctness''. For instance, Project Everest~\cite{everest} established the correctness of a complete HTTPS stack by constructing and verifying not only the TLS implementation but also the underlying toolchain. In this research, we investigate secure file systems. Prior verified file systems~\cite{fscq,yggdrasil,cogent} have demonstrated their correctness regarding essential properties such as guaranteed recovery from arbitrary crashes. Nevertheless, none of these systems provide the capabilities typically associated with {\em cryptographic} file systems, which commonly employ cryptographic primitives to protect against integrity and/or confidentiality attacks, particularly under the ``evil maid'' threat model~\cite{evil_maid}, where an adversary obtains brief, physical access to the target disk, and can therefore execute arbitrary read and write operations to the raw storage device. Our file system, IFSCQ, developed as an extension to FSCQ~\cite{fscq}, represents the first file system that provides both proven consistency guarantees against crash failures and proven integrity guarantees against a compromised or malicious disk. At a high level, IFSCQ establishes a formal model of a malicious disk, and demonstrates that compromise of any data or metadata will be detected through cryptographic evidence. This is accomplished by constructing a traditional Merkle tree~\cite{merkle_tree} over every disk block. The root of the tree is stored in a modeled TPM (i.e., a small trusted storage where we can maintain a handful of Merkle tree root hashes), enabling us to store the majority of the Merkle tree on the potentially vulnerable disk, while verifying its correctness each time it is re-read. As we will demonstrate later, incorporating these integrity features into FSCQ necessitated various modifications in FSCQ's core logic, but all our changes continued to satisfy FSCQ's proof obligations as well as the additional integrity properties we formalized and verified. We maintain the same trusted computing base (TCB) from FSCQ: we rely on the Coq proof system, Haskell compiler and runtime, and Linux FUSE (user-space file system support). Our objective was not to minimize the TCB but to verify that our cryptographic file system is ``correct'', both regarding crash consistency and regarding the detection of disk tampering. We observe that numerous other research projects have explored how to verify an entire software stack~\cite{deepspec} or to generate C code with minimal runtime dependencies~\cite{cogent}. Such approaches would also be applicable to our work on IFSCQ if TCB minimization or full-stack verification were an objective. We note that the original FSCQ work is founded on the design of the Unix Version~6 filesystem; it was not designed with modern optimizations. Rather, it was intended to be simple, and to be subsequently extended for other requirements. Accordingly, IFSCQ is similarly not designed to achieve competitive performance with modern production filesystems. It is intended to demonstrate the feasibility of applying formal verification to important security properties. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Threat model.} We assume that the hardware and operating system are trusted but the disk can be malicious. We generalize the ``evil maid'' threat to a ``Byzantine disk,'' where adversaries can execute arbitrary writes at any time. Attacks could target specific file blocks, metadata blocks, or Merkle hash blocks, or they could roll back the complete state of the disk to a previously valid state. Consequently, we require some form of trusted ground truth to store and update the Merkle tree root. We adopt the term TPM (trusted platform module), included in many modern computers. We assume that our TPM provides us with a ``trusted boot'' facility, which most real TPMs support, but we diverge from real TPMs in several ways we will describe later. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} Overall, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item The design and implementation of a certified file system with cryptographic integrity that is proven to be both safe from crashes and to detect data tampering. \item A formal model of malicious storage systems, as well as desirable integrity properties a file system should provide against such attacks. \item A Merkle tree design, satisfying these integrity properties, which can protect all disk blocks (data blocks, inodes, and even unallocated blocks), while requiring only a small amount of trusted storage for root hashes. \item Evaluation results that demonstrate that our system runs with a reasonable overhead, and defends against a range of malicious attacks. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} describes the background needed to understand our system. Section~\ref{sec:design} describes the design of our system. Section~\ref{sec:proof} describes our proof engineering. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} describes our implementation. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents our evaluation results. Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork} summarizes other related work. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses possible improvements for IFSCQ, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

text: Robots are increasingly deployed in environments requiring human interaction, including collaborative grasping~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} and autonomous driving~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}. Consequently, substantial interest has emerged in developing planning and control algorithms for human-robot interaction. Guaranteeing safety for such robots remains critical given their potential to cause harm to humans~\cite{eder2014towards}. These concerns become particularly acute in contexts such as autonomous driving, where robots and humans may possess divergent or conflicting objectives---e.g., a self-driving vehicle executing an unprotected left turn~\cite{sadigh2016planning}. The fundamental challenge lies in defining safety for human-interactive robots. We might model the human as an adversary, yet this strategy proves typically overly conservative. An alternative strategy involves learning a model to predict human actions~\cite{ziebart2008maximum,fisac2018probabilistically,sadigh2019verifying}, and guaranteeing safety with respect to this model. If the model encompasses all actions demonstrated by humans, then this strategy ensures safety. Nevertheless, different humans may demonstrate vastly different behaviors~\cite{sadigh2016information}---e.g., individuals in a laboratory may behave differently than individuals on a street. Gathering data from all conceivable settings can prove extremely challenging. If a behavior is not demonstrated in the training data, then the model may fail to account for it. More fundamentally, even the most sophisticated machine learning models produce errors, which can correspond to actions overlooked by the model. Finally, \emph{responsibility sensitive safety (RSS)}~\cite{shalev2017formal} represents an approach that manually specifies the range of acceptable robot actions in various scenarios. That is, the designer of the robot controller bears responsibility for ensuring that acceptable actions only encompass safe actions. However, manually defining acceptable robot actions for all conceivable scenarios proves challenging, particularly for robots operating in open-world environments. For instance,~\cite{shalev2017formal} only formally defines acceptable actions for a restricted number of scenarios such as changing lanes. We propose a novel approach for guaranteeing safety in human-interactive systems that accounts for all human behaviors within some bounded set. Two challenges emerge: (i) how to define the set of human behaviors, and (ii) how to guarantee safety with respect to this set. We address these challenges as follows: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Bounding human behavior via backup actions:} Rather than specify the set of all actions the robot is \emph{permitted} to take (as in RSS), the designer specifies \emph{backup actions} that we believe the human always considers taking to prevent an accident (e.g., braking while steering in some direction). In particular, we assume the human may take any action in general, but that they take these actions when necessary to guarantee safety. \item {\bf Ensuring safety via abstract interpretation:} We employ \emph{abstract interpretation}~\cite{cousot1977abstract} to conservatively overapproximate the reachable set of the system for the above model of human behavior, and then guarantee safety with respect to this overapproximation. \end{itemize} First, our notion of backup actions captures the idea that we reasonably believe the human will execute a limited range of evasive maneuvers to prevent an accident---e.g., if the robot gradually decelerates to a stop, then we may expect the human to also decelerate to avoid rear-ending it.\footnote{We do not assume the human will execute evasive maneuvers such as swerving to prevent an accident (though can do so if it is safe). Also, we assume a reasonable amount of time for them to brake and come to a stop.} If the robot operates on a highway, coming to a stop becomes more dangerous, so we may require that the robot pull over to the shoulder before coming to a stop. Similarly, we may require that the robot avoid coming to a stop in an intersection. Specifying backup actions provides a method to define safety; we refer to such a safety constraint as \emph{safety modulo fault}.\footnote{The term ``fault'' is used simply to mean that safety ignores cases where the human does not act according to our model, not to blame an accident on the human driver. The controller designer bears responsibility for designing the backup actions to obtain a reasonable notion of safety.} At a high level, to instantiate our framework, the designer of the robot controller needs to design the following: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robot backup action:} An action the human anticipates the robot may execute to guarantee safety---e.g., brake without changing directions. It should be selected based on intuition about what actions the human driver anticipates the robot may execute (e.g., based on traffic rules). \item \textbf{Human backup action set:} A set of actions that includes \emph{at least one} action the human considers executing to guarantee safety---e.g., braking while steering in some direction. It should be selected based on intuition about safety maneuvers the human driver considers executing. \end{itemize} In particular, whereas RSS requires the control designer to specify the set of \emph{all} actions the robot is permitted to execute, we only require the designer to specify actions that they believe the human considers executing to prevent an accident. Next, we propose an algorithm for guaranteeing safety modulo fault. Our algorithm builds upon \emph{shielding}~\cite{akametalu2014reachability,alshiekh2018safe,wabersich2018linear,li2019robust}; in particular, rather than designing a specific controller, our algorithm accepts as input an arbitrary controller designed to achieve the goal, and then combines it with backup controller in a manner that attempts to use the given controller as frequently as possible while guaranteeing safety modulo fault. At a high level, it accomplishes this by employing on-the-fly verification based on abstract interpretation to determine whether it is safe modulo fault to use the given controller; if so, it employs the given controller, but otherwise, it employs a backup controller. Finally, we empirically evaluate our approach in a simulation, including both settings where the humans are simulated and settings where the human is controlled by a real person via keyboard inputs. We demonstrate that our MPS modulo fault algorithm enables the robot to prevent accidents both with real and simulated humans, even when combined with a na\"{i}ve controller that altogether ignores the humans. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} illustrates how our algorithm guarantees safety while interacting with a human driver without being overly cautious. It assumes that the human will at least slightly brake to prevent an accident (left). If it still cannot guarantee safety, then it permits the human to proceed first (right).

text: The Gaussian mechanism serves as the fundamental building block for numerous differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. Although sufficiently straightforward for mathematical analysis and privacy accounting procedures, its continuous characteristics introduce several practical complications. For instance, it cannot be precisely represented on finite computational systems, rendering it susceptible to numerical inaccuracies that may compromise its privacy assurances \cite{mironov2012significance}. Furthermore, it proves incompatible with distributed learning environments employing cryptographic multi-party computation primitives that utilize modular arithmetic, such as secure aggregation \cite{secagg, bell2020secagg}. To remedy these deficiencies, the binomial and (distributed) discrete Gaussian mechanisms have been recently proposed \cite{DworkKMMN06, agarwal2018cpsgd, CanonneKS20, ddg}. Regrettably, both exhibit distinct limitations: the privacy loss for the binomial mechanism may become infinite with non-zero probability, and the discrete Gaussian: (a) lacks closure under summation (i.e., the sum of discrete Gaussians does not yield a discrete Gaussian), thereby complicating analysis in distributed environments and resulting in performance inferior to continuous Gaussian in highly distributed, low-noise scenarios~\cite{ddg}; (b) necessitates a sampling algorithm absent from standard machine learning or data analysis software packages, creating implementation challenges for engineers in production environments (na\"ive implementations may result in catastrophic privacy violations). \textbf{Our contributions}\hspace{0.5em} To surmount these constraints, we present and examine the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism, a mechanism founded on incorporating noise distributed according to the difference between two independent Poisson random variables. The Skellam noise exhibits closure under summation (i.e., sums of Skellam random variables remain Skellam distributed) and permits straightforward sampling -- efficient Poisson samplers are readily accessible in numerical software packages. Its discrete nature also ensures compatibility with cryptographic protocols and may yield communication efficiencies. To examine the privacy guarantees of the Skellam mechanism and establish comparisons with alternative mechanisms, we present a numerical assessment of the privacy loss random variable and demonstrate a tight bound on the R\'enyi divergence between two shifted Skellam distributions. Our rigorous analysis demonstrates that for a multi-dimensional query function with $\ell_1$ sensitivity $\Delta_1$ and $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta_2$, the Skellam mechanism with variance $\mu$ attains $(\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))$ R\'enyi differential privacy (RDP) \cite{mironov2017renyi} for $\varepsilon(\alpha) \leq \frac{\alpha \Delta_{2}}{2 \mu}+\min \left(\frac{(2\alpha - 1) \Delta_{2}+6 \Delta_1}{4 \mu^2}, \frac{ 3\Delta_1}{2 \mu}\right)$ (see Theorem \ref{thm:mainSK}). This establishes that the RDP guarantees are at most $1 + O\left(1/{\mu}\right)$ times inferior to those of the Gaussian mechanism. To evaluate the performance of the Skellam mechanism in practical applications, we examine a differentially private and communication-constrained federated learning (FL) environment \cite{kairouz2019advances} where noise is incorporated locally to the $d$-dimensional discretized client updates that are subsequently aggregated securely through a cryptographic protocol, such as secure aggregation (SecAgg) \cite{bell2020secagg, secagg}. We present an end-to-end algorithm that suitably discretizes the data and implements the Skellam mechanism alongside modular arithmetic to constrain the data range and communication expenses prior to applying SecAgg. We demonstrate on distributed mean estimation and two benchmark FL datasets, Federated EMNIST~\cite{caldas2018leaf} and Stack Overflow~\cite{tffauthors2019}, that our approach can achieve performance comparable to the continuous Gaussian baseline under stringent privacy and communication constraints, despite employing generic RDP amplification via sampling~\cite{zhu2019poission} for our method and the precise RDP analysis for the subsampled Gaussian mechanism~\cite{mironov2019r}. Our method is implemented in TensorFlow Privacy~\cite{tf-privacy} and TensorFlow Federated~\cite{ingerman2019tff} and will be made open-source.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/google-research/federated/tree/master/distributed_dp}} While we primarily emphasize FL applications, the Skellam mechanism can also be employed in other learning and analytics contexts, including centralized environments. \textbf{Related work}\hspace{0.5em} The Skellam mechanism was initially introduced within the framework of computational differential privacy from lattice-based cryptography~\cite{valovich2017computational} and private Bayesian inference~\cite{schein2019locally}. However, the privacy analyses in previous work do not readily generalize to the multi-dimensional case, and they provide direct bounds for pure or approximate DP which renders only sophisticated composition theorems~\cite{kairouz2015composition, dwork2010boosting} directly applicable in learning environments where the mechanism is invoked repeatedly. For example, the guarantees from~\cite{valovich2017computational} yield suboptimal accuracy-privacy trade-offs as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:accounting-composition}. Moreover, we demonstrate in Section \ref{sec:skellam-pld} that extending the direct privacy analysis to the multi-dimensional setting is non-trivial because the worst-case neighboring dataset pair remains unknown in this scenario. For these reasons, our precise privacy analysis through a sharp RDP bound renders the Skellam mechanism practical for learning applications for the first time. These guarantees (nearly) match those of the Gaussian mechanism and enable us to employ generic RDP amplification via subsampling techniques \cite{zhu2019poission}. The mechanisms most similar to Skellam are the binomial \cite{agarwal2018cpsgd, DworkKMMN06} and the discrete Gaussian mechanisms \cite{CanonneKS20, ddg}. The binomial mechanism can (asymptotically) achieve performance comparable to the continuous Gaussian mechanism (when appropriately scaled). However, it does not satisfy R\'enyi or zero-concentrated DP \cite{mironov2017renyi, BunS16} and exhibits a privacy loss that can become infinite with non-zero probability, resulting in catastrophic privacy failures. The discrete Gaussian mechanism provides R\'enyi DP and can be implemented in distributed settings~\cite{ddg}, but it requires a sampling algorithm that remains unavailable in data analysis software packages despite being investigated in the lattice-based cryptography community (e.g.,~\cite{roy2013high, dwarakanath2014sampling, rossi2019simple}). The discrete Gaussian also lacks closure under summation and the divergence can be substantial in highly distributed low-noise settings (e.g. quantile estimation~\cite{andrew2019differentially} and federated analytics~\cite{fedanalytics}), which causes privacy deterioration. See the end of Section~\ref{sec:applying-skellam} for additional discussion.

text: Given that machine learning has attained super-human performance in image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and games \citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, the question emerges why we do not observe similar achievements in robotics. Several reasons account for this phenomenon. First, learning to operate in the physical world is orders of magnitude more challenging. While the data required by contemporary (deep) learning algorithms could be obtained directly on a real robot~\citep{Levine_Quillen_16}, this approach is too costly in terms of time and resources to scale effectively. Alternatively, the data can be produced in simulation more rapidly, economically, safely, and with unparalleled diversity. In pursuing this approach, we must address unavoidable approximation errors that arise when modeling reality. These errors, commonly termed the \enquote*{reality gap}, stem from omitting physical phenomena, imprecise parameter estimation, or the discretized numerical integration in conventional solvers. Exacerbating this problem, {state-of-the-art}\xspace (deep) learning methods are recognized to be fragile \citep{Szegedy_Fergus_13,Goodfellow_Szegedy_14,Huang_Abbeel_17}, that is, susceptible to shifts in their input domains. Furthermore, the learner is free to exploit the simulator, overfitting to characteristics which do not manifest in the real world. For instance, \citet{Baker_Mordatch_20} observed that the agents learned to exploit the physics engine to obtain an unexpected advantage. While this exploitation constitutes an intriguing observation for studies conducted entirely in simulation, it is highly undesirable in {sim-to-real}\xspace scenarios. In the optimal case, the reality gap manifests itself as a performance degradation, yielding a lower success rate or diminished tracking accuracy. More commonly, the learned policy is not transferable to the robot due to unknown physical effects. One effect that is challenging to model is friction, often resulting in an underestimation thereof in simulation, which can produce motor commands that are insufficiently strong to initiate robot movement. Another source of failure are parameter estimation errors, which can rapidly lead to unstable system dynamics. This scenario is particularly hazardous for the human and the robot. For these reasons, bridging the reality gap constitutes the essential step to endow robots with the capability to learn from simulated experience. There exists a consensus that further increasing the simulator's accuracy alone will not bridge this gap~\citep{Hofner_White_20}. Examining breakthroughs in machine learning, we observe that deep models in combination with large and diverse data sets yield better generalization~\citep{Russakovsky_etal_2015,Radford_etal_2019}. In a similar vein, a technique called domain randomization has recently gained momentum (Figure~\ref{fig_sota_collage_sim2real}). The common characteristic of such approaches is the perturbation of simulator parameters, state observations, or applied actions. Typical quantities to randomize encompass the bodies' inertia and geometry, the parameters of the friction and contact models, possible delays in the actuation, efficiency coefficients of motors, levels of sensor noise, as well as visual properties such as colors, illumination, position and orientation of a camera, or additional artifacts to the image (e.g., glare). Domain randomization can be viewed as a regularization method that prevents the learner from overfitting to individual simulation instances. From the Bayesian perspective, we can interpret the distribution over simulators as a representation of uncertainty. In this paper, we first present the necessary nomenclature and mathematical fundamentals for the problem (Section~\ref{sec_sota_mdp}). Next, we review early approaches for learning from randomized simulations, state the practical requirements, and describe measures for {sim-to-real}\xspace transferability (Section~\ref{sec_sota_simtoreal_foundations}). Subsequently, we discuss the connections between research on {sim-to-real}\xspace transfer and related fields (Section~\ref{sec_sota_related_fields}). Moreover, we introduce a taxonomy for domain randomization and categorize the current state of the art (Section~\ref{sec_sota_domain_randomization}). Finally, we conclude and outline potential future research directions (Section~\ref{sec_sota_discussion_and_outlook}). For those who wish to first become more familiar with robot policy learning as well as policy search, we recommend these surveys:~\citet{Kober_Peters_13}, \citet{Deisenroth_Peters_13}, and \citet{Chatzilygeroudis_Mouret_20}.

text: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly employed to generate predictions on privacy-sensitive data. In recent years, major technology corporations such as Google and Amazon have commenced offering machine learning as a service to the general public through their cloud platforms. Although these systems can produce novel and valuable insights across various domains, machine learning models trained on sensitive data also constitute a lucrative attack surface for adversaries. In a Membership Inference Attack (MIA)~\cite{shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy}, an adversary seeks to determine the data that was utilized to train an ML model (i.e., its members). Successful MIAs compromise the privacy of individuals and constitute a substantial threat to unprotected ML models~\cite{shokri2016membership}. Differentially private (DP) mechanisms can be incorporated into an ML model during the training process \cite{chaudhuri_differentially_nodate,Abadi_2016,beaulieujones2018privacypreserving, shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy, yu2019differentially} to constrain the influence that a single data point can exert on the model's output. Training ML models with DP mechanisms is becoming increasingly prevalent with popular libraries such as TensorFlow~\cite{tensorflow} and PyTorch~\cite{pytorch} providing several DP training algorithms. Previous research has furnished experimental and theoretical evidence of DP training as a defense against MIAs~\cite{li2013membership,yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,shokri2016membership}. Yeom et al.~\cite{yeom2017privacy} demonstrate that DP training algorithms ensure a \emph{theoretical upper bound} on the privacy leakage caused by MIAs. This bound, subsequently refined by Erlingsson et al.~\cite{jayaraman2020revisiting}, provides robust protection for high DP levels (corresponding to small values of the DP parameter $\epsilon$), but rapidly deteriorates for large $\epsilon$. Despite this, empirical assessments of MIAs against DP-trained models~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting} indicate that large values of $\epsilon$, theoretically considered as low-privacy settings, furnish adequate protection against MIAs in practice. Motivated by these observations, Murakonda and Shokri~\cite{murakonda2020ml} developed a tool for calibrating $\epsilon$ based exclusively on the empirical performance of MIAs, thereby enhancing the model's utility at the cost of theoretical privacy guarantees. In summary, this body of literature suggests that applying DP mechanisms to ML models, even in substantially weakened privacy regimes, provides adequate protection against known MIAs. These studies on membership inference all adhere to a similar evaluation methodology where members and non-members are sampled independently from the same distribution. However, this underlying assumption is not always representative of real data~\cite{Mohammad2020, arjovsky2021distribution, pmlr-v97-recht19a, Martensson2020, nagarajan2021understanding, pmlr-v119-sagawa20a, sagawa2020distributionally}. Furthermore, prior research has demonstrated that data dependencies can result in an overestimation of the privacy protection provided by DP~\cite{tschantz_sok_2020, kifer_no_2011, pufferfish, li2013membership, liu2016dependence}. Motivated by this, we conduct the first investigation of MIA performance on ML models trained with DP-SGD~\cite{Abadi_2016} \emph{under data dependencies}. We commence by examining the methodology from previous work on MIAs and identify the assumptions that underpin their theoretical findings~\cite{yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,nasr2021adversary}. Since there are no publicly documented instances of MIAs against ML models in practice, researchers are constrained to simulating attacks using theoretical games between the model owner and attacker called \emph{membership experiments}~\cite{yeom2017privacy}. We demonstrate that previous membership experiments assume independence between training samples, which might not represent many membership inference scenarios in practice. To address this, we propose a new membership experiment that relaxes the restrictive independence assumption. We establish that previous DP-based bounds on the adversary's success do not hold in this more general setting. We emphasize that this does not imply that DP is broken or flawed. Rather, the guarantees of DP mechanisms no longer apply when defining membership inference with data dependencies. Intuitively, this occurs because DP mechanisms limit the effect that a \emph{single} sample has on the output. However, when training samples exhibit dependencies, related samples can leak additional information about this single sample. Prior research has demonstrated the importance of studying MIA performance both theoretically and empirically~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting}. Thus, we also examine the effect of data dependencies on the \emph{empirical performance} of MIAs under different instantiations of our membership experiment. Using six real-world datasets, we assess the performance of off-the-shelf attacks. These attacks have black-box query access to the target model and are provided no additional background information about the data dependencies we consider. Using these attacks, we investigate three distinct types of data dependencies. First, to examine the extent to which data dependencies can affect MIAs, we artificially partition a dataset into members and non-members using a clustering algorithm. text: Confidence intervals constitute a standard instrument for summarizing the underlying distribution and for identifying outlier behavior. In this paper we shall examine the problem of computing confidence intervals for time series. \citet{korpela2014confidence} introduced a concept for computing confidence intervals: rather than computing point-wise confidence intervals, the authors propose computing confidence bands. More precisely, given $n$ time series $T$, we are asked to find $k$ time series $U \subseteq T$ that minimize the envelope area, that is, the sum $\sum_i \pr{\max_{t \in U} t(i)} - \pr{\min_{t \in U} t(i)}$. The advantage, as argued by \citet{korpela2014confidence}, of employing confidence bands instead of point-wise confidence intervals is superior family-wise error control: if we were to use point-wise intervals we can only state that a time series \emph{at some fixed point} is an outlier and require a correction for multiple testing (such as Bonferroni correction) if we want to assert with a certain probability that the \emph{whole} time series is normal. In this paper we examine the approximation algorithms for finding confidence bands. While \citet{korpela2014confidence} demonstrated that finding the optimal confidence band is an \textbf{NP}-hard problem, they did not provide any approximation algorithms nor any inapproximability results. We shall first demonstrate that despite being an \textbf{NP}-hard problem, we can solve the problem for \emph{some} $k$. We accomplish this by considering a different problem, where instead of having a hard constraint we have an objective function that favors selecting time series as long as they do not increase the envelope area too much. The objective depends on the parameter $\alpha$, larger values of $\alpha$ permit more increase in the envelope area. We shall demonstrate that this problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time and that each $\alpha$ corresponds to a certain value of $k$. We shall show that there are at most $n + 1$ of such bands, and that we can discover all of them in polynomial time by varying $\alpha$. Next, we provide a straightforward algorithm for approximating confidence bands by connecting the problem to the weighted $k$-\textsc{MinUnion}\xspace problem. We shall provide a variant of an algorithm by~\citet{chlamtac2018densest} that yields $\sqrt{n} + 1$ guarantee. We also argue that---under certain conjecture---we cannot approximate the problem better than $\bigO{n^{1/4}}$. Finally, we consider a variant of the problem where instead of minimizing the envelope area, we minimize the width of the envelope, that is, we minimize the maximum difference between the envelope boundaries. We demonstrate that a simple algorithm can achieve 2-approximation. This approximation provides interesting contrast to the inapproximability results when minimizing the envelope area. Surprisingly this guarantee is tight: we shall also demonstrate that there is no polynomial-time algorithm with smaller guarantee unless $\textbf{P}=\textbf{NP}$. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We define the optimization problems formally in Section~\ref{sec:prel}. We solve the regularized band problem in Section~\ref{sec:reg}, approximate minimization of envelope area in Section~\ref{sec:sum}, and approximate minimization of envelope width in Section~\ref{sec:max}. Section~\ref{sec:related} is devoted to the related work. We present our experiments in Section~\ref{sec:exp} and conclude with discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

text: As autonomous robotic systems become increasingly prevalent in our surroundings, controllers that drive these systems must demonstrate the sophistication necessary to function within our daily unstructured environments. Recent developments in reinforcement learning (RL) combined with deep neural networks as function approximators have demonstrated remarkable performance across various complex robotic control tasks including dexterous in-hand manipulation \cite{dexterous}, quadrupedal locomotion \cite{haarnoja2018learning}, and targeted throwing \cite{throwing}. However, the absence of \textit{safety} guarantees in deep RL-based controllers constrains their applicability for real-world robotics \cite{Ibarz_2021}. This limitation arises from the black-box characteristics of neural network policies and their unreliable handling of out-of-distribution states, particularly evident when simulation-trained models are deployed in real-world scenarios. Conversely, the classical robotics community has produced numerous controllers and algorithms for various real-world physical systems (from mobile robots to humanoids) that enable reliable and safe deployment of robotic agents in practical environments. These encompass classical feedback controllers \cite{maxwell1868governors}, trajectory generators \cite{ijspeert2008central} and behaviour trees \cite{colledanchise2016behavior}. This reliability stems from their explicit analytical derivation and established models, providing control theoretic guarantees that render them appropriate for real-world implementation. However, they can exhibit significant suboptimality when applied to complex tasks, owing to constraints in analytical modeling and approximations. A promising avenue for future robot control lies in merging the complementary advantages of these distinct control mechanisms to mitigate their individual limitations. Such methodologies have been documented in neuroscience as the fundamental control strategy employed by biological systems. The dual-process theory of decision making \cite{dickinson2002role} suggests that multiple distinct neural controllers participate in governing action selection within biological systems. \citet{lee2014neural} furnish evidence supporting this theory through human brain studies and demonstrate the presence of an arbitration mechanism that determines the degree to which different neural controllers influence behaviors. The arbitrator bases its decisions on specific performance metrics displayed by each controller, leveraging their respective capabilities in a particular state. We derive inspiration from this phenomenon and introduce Bayesian Controller Fusion (BCF), a hybrid control strategy that integrates the respective advantages of deep RL and traditional handcrafted controllers (\textit{control priors}) for secure real-world deployment. We formulate the final policy as a Bayesian composition of these two controllers, where the controller output for each system encodes their respective \textit{epistemic} uncertainty in a given state as illustrated in Figure \ref{front}. This enables BCF to naturally mediate control between the two systems based on their confidence to act. This has significant implications during real-world deployment, where we obtain the dexterity of the learned system in states to which it has generalized while depending on the risk-averse behaviors of the handcrafted system in out-of-distribution states for safe operation. Crucially, our method learns to control a real robot in joint space to accomplish a given task with no on-robot time (\textit{zero-shot}), despite the learned policy potentially not being perfectly transferable from simulation to the real world. We demonstrate our approach on two continuous control, robotic tasks involving reactive navigation on a mobile robot and a manipulability maximizing reacher on a robotic arm. We illustrate how BCF enables reliable transfer of a simulation trained policy to the real world while achieving substantial performance improvements from the RL component compared to the handcrafted system alone. We regard this as a promising and practical pathway to deploying simulation-trained RL controllers for safe operation in the real world.

text: With the increasing prevalence of open-access academic article repositories, such as arXiv or bioRxiv, the dissemination of novel research findings has become virtually effortless. Via these platforms, tens of thousands of scholarly papers are distributed by the research community each month\footnote{\url{https://arxiv.org/stats/monthly_submissions}}. Simultaneously, the non-peer-reviewed character of these repositories and the overwhelming volume of new publications has rendered it practically impossible to identify pertinent work and remain current with recent developments. Scientific paper summarization, a specialized task within automatic text summarization, seeks to support researchers in their endeavors by automatically condensing articles into concise, human-readable formats that retain only the most crucial information. In recent years, abstractive summarization, an approach wherein models are trained to produce fluent summaries through paraphrasing the source article, has demonstrated remarkable advancement. State-of-the-art methodologies exploit large, pre-trained models~\citep{raffel2019t5, lewis2020bart}, establish task-specific pre-training strategies~\citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and accommodate extended input sequences~\citep{zhao2020seal, zaheer2020bigbird}. Existing large-scale benchmark datasets, such as arXiv and PubMed~\citep{cohan2018discourse}, were automatically assembled from online archives and repurpose paper abstracts as reference summaries. Nevertheless, the current paradigm of scientific paper summarization wherein models are trained to produce paper abstracts has two limitations: 1) frequently, abstracts incorporate information that is not of primary significance, 2) the overwhelming majority of scientific articles include human-authored abstracts, rendering the generated summaries redundant. To remedy these deficiencies, we present the task of disentangled paper summarization. The novel task's objective is to produce two summaries concurrently, one strictly concentrated on the summarized article's innovations and contributions, the other presenting the context of the work and prior efforts. In this configuration, the generated summaries can address the requirements of diverse audiences: experienced researchers and domain experts who can benefit from examining the summarized contributions, and novices who can rapidly familiarize themselves with the complexities of the addressed problems by reviewing the context summary and obtain a perspective of the recent findings from the contribution summary. For this task, we present a novel large-scale dataset by augmenting the S2ORC~\citep{lo2020s2orc} corpus of scientific papers, which encompasses multiple scientific domains and provides extensive citation-related metadata. We structure and process the data, and augment it with automatically generated contribution and context reference summaries, to facilitate supervised model training. We also present three abstractive baseline approaches: 1) a unified, controllable model manipulated through descriptive control codes~\citep{fan2018controllable,keskar2019CTRL}, 2) a one-to-many sequence model featuring a branched decoder for multi-head generation~\citep{luong2016mtl, bansal2018mts}, and 3) an information-theoretic training strategy exploiting supervision derived from the citation metadata~\citep{peyrard2019simple}. To evaluate our models, we devise a comprehensive automatic evaluation protocol that assesses performance across three dimensions: relevance, novelty, and disentanglement. We rigorously evaluate and analyze the baseline models and examine the effects of the additional training objective on the model's performance. To demonstrate the utility of the newly introduced task, we conducted a human study involving human annotators in a simulated paper-reviewing scenario. The findings indicate disentangled summaries more beneficial in 79\% of cases compared to abstract-oriented outputs. Recent work has shown considerable progress in the development of abstractive summarization, whereby models are trained to produce fluent summaries by paraphrasing the source article. State-of-the-art methods exploit large, pre-trained models (raffel2019t5; lewis2020bart), develop task-related pre-training strategies (zhang2019pegasus; zaheer2020bigbird); and allow for long input sequences (zhao2020seal; zaheer2020bigbird).
