text: Advances in deep neural networks over the past decade have enabled models to begin addressing novel tasks requiring information from multiple modalities. The intersection of language and vision has emerged as a key research area, particularly visual question answering (VQA) \cite{Agrawal2015VQAVQ, Gupta2017SurveyOV} i.e. answering a question about an image (surveyed here \cite{Wu2017VisualQA, Srivastava2019VisualQA}). However, models addressing human tasks must look beyond the semantic information in text and visuals and demonstrate nuanced behavior: learning complex referential relations with numerous cases and exceptions (e.g. `green' may indicate a plant is healthy, or a person is ill, inexperienced, envious or recycling), or using one modality to overcome learned statistical biases in the other \cite{Agrawal2018DontJA, Cadne2019RUBiRU, Chen2020CounterfactualSS, goyal2017making, Ramakrishnan2018OvercomingLP} (`what colour is the banana?', we understand that typically they are yellow, but the one in a particular image may be pink). Representing such interactions presents a significant challenge in deep learning as it is not immediately clear how to optimally fuse feature tensors in a network. Early works employ vector concatenation to project different features into a new joint feature space \cite{Zhou2015SimpleBF, Lu2016HierarchicalQC}. Inspired by an earlier vision-only two-factor framework \cite{Tenenbaum:2000:SSC:1121517.1121518}, VQA models improved substantially by adopting a `pooled' bilinear representation (BLP) of vision and text features \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/GaoBZD15, DBLP:journals/corr/FukuiPYRDR16, DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block, Yu2018BeyondBG}. Research into BLP for VQA has concentrated on: developing more effective and less expensive bilinear representations \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block}, integrating BLP with attention mechanisms \cite{Kim2018BilinearAN, Yu2018BeyondBG, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471}, and recently analyzing and categorizing BLP (as a ``joint" representation) alongside other fusion techniques and models \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}. Despite achievements on VQA, BLP techniques have not yet been extensively applied to video-QA baselines \cite{MovieQA, pororoqa, jang-CVPR-2017, Fan_2019_ICCV, lei2018tvqa, Xu2017VideoQA}. In this paper, we begin addressing this research gap by applying BLP techniques to the TVQA \cite{lei2018tvqa}, TGIF-QA \cite{jang-CVPR-2017}, Ego-VQA \cite{Fan_2019_ICCV} and MSVD-QA \cite{Xu2017VideoQA} datasets. Our contributions include: \textbf{I)} Substituting concatenation with BLP techniques on the TVQA baseline model \cite{lei2018tvqa}, \textbf{II)} Experimenting with a modified version of the TVQA baseline to accommodate BLP we name the `dual-stream' model, \textbf{III)} Experiments substituting concatenation with BLP on the recently proposed heterogenous-memory-enhanced multimodal attention (HME) model \cite{Fan2019HeterogeneousME}, \textbf{IV)} Utilizing the TVQA dataset in our experiments on HME, \textbf{V)} An insight into the poor performance with respect to recent multimodal fusion taxonomies \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}, \textbf{VI)} Experiments on the TVQA baseline model augmented with deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) \cite{Andrew2013DeepCC} to contrast a `co-ordinated' representation with BLP's `joint' representation (as defined in \cite{8715409}), \textbf{VII)} Several additional best practices to consider when transitioning BLP from image-QA to video-QA, \textbf{VIII)} An overview of how bilinear representations compare and contrast with current psychological vision and perception models \cite{Goodale1992SeparateVP, milner2006visual, milner2008two, goodale2014and, Milner2017HowDT}. Notoriously, inconclusive or negative experimental results often remain unpublished, a practice that has been extensively criticized \cite{Mlinari2017DealingWT, Faschinger2019DoNH, Sandercock2012NegativeRW}. We wish to report our experimental results to expand the public experimental scope of multimodal fusion and encourage critical future research that may be able to build upon, contrast and critique our findings and speculations.

text: The question answering task has benefited substantially from advances in deep learning, particularly from pre-trained language models(LM)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}. While question answering over single passages (reading comprehension datasets) and over large-scale open-domain corpora~(open-domain QA) have gained considerably from these developments, the performance of QA over book stories (BookQA) remains inferior. For instance, the most representative benchmark in this area, the NarrativeQA~\cite{kovcisky2018narrativeqa} which was released three years ago - the current state-of-the-art methods demonstrate only modest improvement over the initial baselines. Several challenges in NarrativeQA impede research progress. First, the narrative stories introduce a novel writing style that differs from previous work on formal texts such as Wikipedia. Second, the lengthy inputs of books exceed the processing capacity of neural models, making evidence identification from an entire book crucial. Third, NarrativeQA constitutes a generative task, and numerous answers cannot be precisely matched in the original books. Therefore, generative QA models are necessary. Finally and most critically, the dataset lacks annotations of the supporting evidence. While this creates a realistic setting similar to open-domain QA, combined with the generative nature of the answers, it also complicates the inference of supporting evidence comparable to most extractive open-domain QA tasks. The requirements concerning evidence identification and the absent supporting evidence annotation render BookQA task analogous to open-domain QA. In this paper, we initially investigate whether the concepts employed in state-of-the-art open-domain QA systems can be extended to enhance BookQA including: (1) the neural ranker-reader pipeline~\cite{wang2018r}, where a neural ranker is utilized to select relevant passages (evidence) given a question from large candidate sets; (2) the application of pre-trained LMs as reader and ranker, such as GPT~\cite{radford2019language}, BERT~\cite{devlin2018bert} and their subsequent work; (3) the distantly supervised and unsupervised training techniques~\cite{wang2018r,Lee_2019orqa,min2019discrete,guu2020realm,karpukhin2020dense} that assist rankers in learning more from noisy gold data. By training a ranker-reader framework on BookQA, we successfully establish a new state-of-the-art on NarrativeQA using both generative and extractive readers. Based on these results and our analysis, we observe the following: \noindent$\bullet$ Employing the pre-trained LMs as the reader model, such as BERT and GPT, enhances the NarrativeQA performance. With the identical BM25 IR baseline, they provide 5-6\% improvement on Rouge-L over their non-pre-trained counterparts. \noindent$\bullet$ Our specifically designed distant supervision signals enhance the neural ranker significantly, but the improvement remains modest compared to the upper bound. Further analysis of the ranker module confirms the training difficulty, as the improvement from the pre-trained LM BERT is negligible in it.

text: Drones possess significant potential for revolutionizing urban logistics services. Through enabling rapid, adaptable, and efficient delivery operations, they can assist in addressing the rapidly expanding logistics and e-commerce demands of densely populated urban areas~\cite{chung2020optimization}. They can additionally diminish our dependence on conventional ground delivery services that contribute to traffic congestion~\cite{HolguinETAL18}. Nevertheless, operating package delivery services that depend exclusively on drones may prove infeasible due to their constrained flight range and payload capacity~\cite{SudburyETAL16}. To address these limitations, we investigate the problem of operating delivery drones in coordination with ground vehicles by permitting drones to travel on ground vehicles to preserve energy and extend effective flight range~\cite{choudhury2019dynamic,choudhury2021efficient}. Specifically, we concentrate on routing a team of drones and trucks across a shared road network, where drones can utilize trucks as transit in addition to flying. We formulate our setting as a \emph{coordinated} extension of the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) problem~\cite{stern2019multi}, which necessitates computing start-goal routes for all agents while seeking to minimize the total path cost incurred by the drones and trucks. The path cost can differ for the two agent types and can represent the energy consumed or the operational expense. As in the classical MAPF formulation, our problem setting requires satisfying inter-agent constraints, which in our case limits the maximum number of drones that can simultaneously utilize a truck. It also necessitates reasoning about the potential cost savings from coordinating trucks and drones to share trip segments. The characteristic of agents temporarily coordinating has not been investigated by the MAPF community thus far (to the best of our knowledge) and renders our problem significantly more challenging than the already difficult classical MAPF~\cite{yu2013structure, YuLaValle16}. Most state-of-the-art MAPF algorithms concentrate on preventing inter-agent collisions rather than optimizing coordination~\cite{felner2017search,stern2019multi}. Our recent work developed a MAPF solver for routing drones across transit networks~\cite{choudhury2021efficient} but assumed the transit vehicles follow predetermined and known routes and that drones were not required to fly across the road network. Another work examined MAPF problems with cooperation but only planned for predefined agent pairs to arrive at fixed meeting points~\cite{greshler2021cooperative}, rather than simultaneously traversing a route. The operations research community has investigated optimizing drones with trucks but their approaches only function for few agents on small abstract routing graphs~\cite{agatz2012optimization}. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} We develop an effective algorithmic approach for coordinated MAPF in the context of drones and ground trucks operating in tandem. Our key insight is to \textit{decompose our overall intractable MAPF problem into two distinct MAPF sub-problems that we can solve in stages} (\Cref{fig:approach}). In Stage 1, we compute truck routes that are likely to prove useful as transit options for drones. In Stage 2, we fix the truck routes, create a transit network based on them, and overlay this network on the road graph. We then compute drone routes across the composite road-and-transit network, where drones incur no cost on the segments where they utilize transit (subject to capacity constraints). As a post-processing step, we re-route trucks not utilized as transit to their shortest road network paths. We implement two variants of our approach that employ different MAPF solvers; the first utilizes Enhanced Conflict-Based Search~\cite{barer2014suboptimal} and the second utilizes Prioritized Planning~\cite{silver2005cooperative} for both stages. We evaluate our approach on a range of coordinated MAPF settings across the Manhattan road network, with nearly $4500$ vertices and $10000$ edges covering an area of nearly \SI{200}{\kilo\metre\squared}, and up to $20$ truck and $80$ drones. Our experiments demonstrate that coordinating drones and trucks can reduce more than $50\%$ of total vehicle distance traveled compared to no coordination. \textit{We refer to the sum of truck path distance and drone flight distance as vehicle distance traveled}, since drones incur no energy cost when traveling on a truck. For brevity and convenience, we will employ this phrase hereafter, with some abuse of terminology. Our approach plans paths for all settings within at most $5$ minutes of computation time on commodity hardware. We anticipate that our approach could serve as a building block in more complex problem settings where we also need to optimally allocate agents to tasks (i.e., package-delivery locations) and determine the order in which to execute them. For instance, in a manner similar to our previous work~\cite{choudhury2021efficient}, we could employ a bi-level approach where the upper layer allocates jobs to the agents and a lower-level planner---a coordinated MAPF solver in our case---executes the allocation in a receding-horizon fashion. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Layout.} In~\Cref{sec:related} we review prior related fundamental approaches and state-of-the-art applications. In~\Cref{sec:problem} we introduce basic notation and definitions and describe our problem setting of coordinated MAPF. In~\Cref{sec:approach} we describe our two-stage approach for coordinated MAPF in detail and discuss our extensive experimental results in~\Cref{sec:results}. We conclude by summarizing our work and outlining future research directions in~\Cref{sec:conclusion}.

In the related section, we review previous fundamental approaches and state-of-the-art applications. For example, following our previous work, we can use a bi-level approach where a higher level allocates jobs to agents and a lower level—a specialized MAPF solver in our case—executes the assignment with a receding horizon. Our approach takes five minutes at most to run on a commodity machine. In Crefsec:problem we introduce basic notations and definitions and our formulation of the coordinate MAPF problem. In Crefsec:related we review fundamental approaches and current applications. In Crefsec:approach we describe in detail our two-stage approach to the coordinate MAPF. In the section “Results” we present extensive experimental results, and in the section “Conclusions” we present our own work and future research directions.

In job scheduling contexts, the response time is alternatively termed the flow time. More precisely, for any schedule $\mathcal{S}$, let $c_i(\mathcal{S})$ denote the completion time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$ and $r_i$ represent the release time of $J_i$. text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has constituted an active research domain in robotics and computer vision throughout recent decades~\cite{cadena2016past,thrun2007simultaneous}. It addresses the estimation of a robot's instantaneous position through onboard sensory measurements, \emph{e.g.}, LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors, cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMU). SLAM proves particularly valuable in environments where GPS reception remains weak, such as indoor, urban, and underwater settings. Consequently, it has become an essential component in AR/VR~\cite{grasa2013visual}, autonomous driving~\cite{bresson2017simultaneous}, and GPS-denied robotics applications~\cite{weiss2011monocular}. Among existing systems, visual SLAM \cite{fuentes2015visual} attracts significant interest because cameras represent low-cost passive sensors that consume less energy compared to active alternatives such as sonar or LiDAR. Autonomous mobile robots operating outdoors derive substantial benefits from the low power consumption of cameras during long-term deployments. Visual SLAM systems can be classified into \emph{feature-based} methods and \emph{direct} methods. The feature-based methods~\cite{klein2007parallel, mur2015orb} detect and match features across frames, then estimate relative camera motion by minimizing reprojection error; whereas direct methods~\cite{engel2014lsd, engel2017direct} estimate camera motion by minimizing photometric error directly without requiring feature correspondences. The direct methods exhibit higher accuracy and robustness compared to feature-based methods, particularly in poorly-textured (less-textured or repetitively-textured) environments \cite{forster2016svo}. Since feature detection and matching algorithms are computationally expensive, sparse direct methods also possess the potential to operate much faster (\emph{e.g.}, $\geq300$ FPS for SVO \cite{forster2016svo}). Alternatively, visual SLAM systems can be classified into monocular systems and multi-camera systems. Monocular systems~\cite{klein2007parallel,engel2014lsd,mur2015orb,engel2017direct} cannot estimate the metric \textit{scale} of the environment, which multi-camera systems can accomplish. Multi-camera systems typically achieve higher accuracy and robustness; among these, stereo systems~\cite{mur2017orb,engel2015large,wang2017stereo} are particularly popular due to their simplicity and accessibility. Most existing stereo visual systems employ the standard \textit{stereo matching} algorithm~\cite{hartley2003multiple} to resolve the scale problem, which exhibits two major limitations. First, finding stereo correspondences by individually searching along respective epipolar lines proves computationally expensive. Second, when multiple points appear similar to the query point, selecting the correct one becomes challenging; this occurs when texture is repetitive (\emph{e.g.}, grass, sand). We address these two limitations in~\cite{mo2019extending}, where 3D points in the monocular system are projected into the second camera and the scale problem is resolved by minimizing photometric error. We demonstrate that such direct \textit{scale optimization} is computationally efficient and more robust to repetitive textures in visual scenes. However, even with metric scale, the global camera pose inevitably deviates from ground truth as the camera moves, since it is estimated by accumulating relative camera motions incrementally. The \textit{loop closure} introduces non-local pose constraints to optimize poses globally and address this issue. The conventional bag-of-word (BoW) approach detects loop closures by matching features from the current view to historical data. However, the BoW approach does not function out-of-the-box for direct SLAM systems since direct SLAM systems do not extract descriptors for features. Alternatively, we propose a \emph{LiDAR descriptor-based} place recognition method~\cite{mo2020fast} for urban driving scenarios. We assume the vehicle moves in the forward direction so that we can accumulate 3D points from the stereo direct SLAM system to simulate LiDAR scans, which are described by a LiDAR descriptor for place recognition. This enables significantly more efficient loop closure detection and ensures higher accuracy and robustness. In this paper, we systematically integrate scale optimization and the LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition approach into a fully-direct stereo SLAM system termed DSV-SLAM; we release an open-source implementation at {{\tt \url{https://github.com/IRVLab/direct_stereo_slam}}}. We conduct comprehensive experiments to validate its state-of-the-art accuracy, superior computational efficiency, and robustness in visually challenging scenarios. DSV-SLAM demonstrates the feasibility of a complete SLAM system without feature detection or matching. In DSV-SLAM, we adopt the state-of-the-art Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO)~\cite{engel2017direct} to track camera poses and estimate 3D points. Subsequently, we extend this to an efficient and accurate stereo visual odometry (VO) using scale optimization~\cite{mo2019extending}. Then, we employ the LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition approach~\cite{mo2020fast} to efficiently detect loop closures. The relative poses of potential loop closures are estimated through direct alignment and optionally, further refined by the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) method~\cite{besl1992method}. Finally, we compose and optimize a pose graph to further improve SLAM accuracy globally. Figure~\ref{fig:kitti00} shows the estimated trajectory and reconstructed environment by DSV-SLAM on sequence $00$ of the KITTI dataset~\cite{geiger2012we}.

text: Given the exponential expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, utilization of AI methodologies in structural engineering, analogous to numerous other fields, has experienced substantial growth in recent years. Multiple investigations have employed Machine Learning (ML) models to predict structural responses, fragility parameters, or performance limit states of steel and concrete moment frames, steel braced frames, and reinforced concrete walls \cite{ML1, ML2}. Additional investigations have utilized ML models to predict structural model parameter values (e.g., shear strength, drift capacity) from experimental data \cite{ML4, ML5}. Within the domain of image-based structural health monitoring, there has been considerable development of ML-based computer vision investigations to automatically detect damage from images \cite{ML7, ML8}. Further investigations have concentrated on AI-based damage detection, localization, and classification utilizing sensors positioned on structures \cite{ML10, ML11}. Natural hazards including earthquakes, tsunamis, and hurricanes possess the potential to cause fatalities and injuries in addition to damage to buildings and other infrastructure. Post-hazard reconnaissance is consequently crucial to enhance understanding of built environment performance, accelerate recovery, and make informed decisions regarding current and future hazards. While ML-based methodologies have been utilized in natural hazards reconnaissance, relatively limited investigations have examined techniques from natural language processing (NLP). NLP techniques can potentially result in substantial improvements in efficiency and accuracy for post-hazard reconnaissance evaluation. In one of the limited NLP-related investigations, \citet{ML13} trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for classifying building damage utilizing text-based natural language damage descriptions according to the green, yellow, and red tagging categories of ATC-20. Social media data including tweets have been employed in several investigations to train ML algorithms for direct eyewitness messages in disasters \cite{twitter1} and to identify themes in social media behavior during hazards \cite{twitter2}. In this paper, two applications of NLP are examined within the context of earthquake reconnaissance. The first is automatic generation of reconnaissance reports, which constitute an essential component of each field reconnaissance. Automatic report generation aims to reduce the time required to generate a report and enhance the accuracy and abundance of information by facilitating access to numerous identified resources that might be overlooked otherwise. The second application is the utilization of social media and crowd-sourcing to extract information related to earthquake consequences and resilience, including recovery time, which is challenging to obtain using alternative methods. Considering that this represents a novel unexplored application domain of AI, the preliminary investigation conducted herein is anticipated to initiate advances in this area. Subsequent sections of the paper are organized as follows: The automatic data collection approach utilized for both applications is described in Section \ref{sec:data}. Methodology and applications of automatic report generation and recovery time estimation are described in Sections \ref{sec:briefing} and \ref{sec:social-media}. Finally, concluding remarks and future directions are presented in the final section.

text: A fundamental challenge in machine learning involves constructing models that demonstrate reliability and safety in real-world applications. Beyond achieving strong performance on the training distribution, deployed models must exhibit robustness to distributional shifts, maintain consistency in their predictions, demonstrate resilience against adversarial attacks, provide calibrated uncertainty estimates, and possess the ability to identify anomalous inputs. Extensive prior research has addressed each of these challenges independently \cite{madry, hendrycks2019robustness, guo2017calibration, emmott2015meta}, yet they can be collectively categorized as different facets of ML Safety \cite{hendrycks2021unsolved}. Therefore, the aforementioned properties can be conceptualized as safety measures. Optimally, models deployed in practical environments would excel across multiple safety measures. Regrettably, previous research has demonstrated that optimizing for certain desirable properties frequently results in the degradation of others. For instance, adversarial training exclusively enhances adversarial robustness while compromising classification performance \cite{tsipras2018robustness}. Likewise, enforcing consistent predictions on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs appears to conflict with improved detection of these inputs, an intuition corroborated by recent research \cite{empiricalpaper} which demonstrates that existing approaches assist with certain safety metrics while deteriorating others. % This prompts the inquiry of whether enhancing all safety measures is achievable with a single model. While existing augmentation methods generate images that are distinct (e.g., translations) or more entropic (e.g., additive Gaussian noise), we contend that a significant underexplored dimension involves creating images that are more complex. In contrast to entropy or descriptive difficulty, which is maximized by pure noise distributions, structural complexity is frequently characterized in terms of the degree of organization \cite{lloyd2001measures}. A canonical example of structurally complex objects consists of fractals, which have recently demonstrated utility for pretraining image classifiers \cite{kataoka2020pre, Nakashima2021CanVT}. Therefore, an intriguing question concerns whether sources of structural complexity can be exploited to enhance safety through data augmentation techniques. We demonstrate that Pareto improvements are achievable with \textsc{PixMix}, a straightforward and effective data processing method that exploits pictures with complex structures and significantly improves all existing safety measures. \textsc{PixMix} comprises a novel data processing pipeline that integrates structurally complex ``dreamlike'' images. These dreamlike images encompass fractals and feature visualizations. We discover that feature visualizations constitute a suitable source of complexity, thereby establishing that they possess applications beyond interpretability. In comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that \textsc{PixMix} delivers substantial improvements on a wide range of existing safety measures, surpassing numerous previous methods. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}{\texttt{github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}}.

text: Due to the remarkable success of deep convolutional networks~\cite{he2016deep, chen2017deeplab, long2015fully}, object recognition tasks, including object detection and instance segmentation, have demonstrated substantial progress over the past decade. Predominant methods adhere to the "backbone with head" paradigm~\cite{he2017mask, chen2019hybrid, lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}. The backbone network~\cite{he2016deep}, pre-trained on ImageNet, extracts features from input images. Subsequently, the extracted features are fed into the head network to generate predictions for various recognition tasks, \textit{i.e.}, classification, box regression and mask segmentation. Most image/video instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask, huang2019mask, yang2019video, cao2020sipmask} and object detection methods~\cite{lin2017focal, tian2019fcos} employ similar designs for the head network. Specifically, four consecutive $3\times3$ convolutions are typically stacked in the head network to refine coarse instance features (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(a)) prior to the final prediction. Indeed, such explicit refinement design expands the receptive field and enhances the semantic level. However, simply stacking weight-independent convolutions has certain limitations. The receptive field obtained remains limited under the explicit setting since it has been demonstrated that the effective receptive field is typically much smaller compared to the theoretical receptive field. Additionally, such methods tend to lose the original instance signal, suffering from degraded performance and substantial parameter overhead as the number of convolutions increases. One question may emerge: is it feasible to replace such stacked $3\times3$ convolutions with a lightweight module while maintaining promising performance? One straightforward solution is to make these four convolutions weight-sharing (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(b)). To demonstrate this, we first provide an empirical comparison with the weight-sharing strategy. We discover that the widely-used four weight-independent $3\times3$ convolutions are not essential in the head network. In contrast, the weight-sharing design can achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters. To prevent the weight-sharing network from experiencing degraded performance, shortcut connections in ResNet~\cite{he2016deep} can be introduced (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(c)). The shortcut path can propagate the gradients smoothly and prevent the network from forgetting original instance features. While improving the overall segmentation performance, the weight-sharing strategy remains constrained by limited receptive field. Therefore, we explore a novel perspective: \textit{What if refining the instance features via a recursive network stacked with infinite blocks?} An intuitive idea is that we stack the weight-sharing blocks for infinite iterations. In this manner, we observe that the output of the refinement network will eventually converge to an equilibrium state as the number of blocks increases, which can be represented as: \begin{eqnarray} H^{\ast}=F_{\theta}(H^{\ast};X), \end{eqnarray} where $F_{\theta}$ represents the nonlinear transformation with parameters $\theta$. $H^{\ast}$ and $X$ are the equilibrium instance feature and original coarse instance feature, respectively. Inspired by DEQ~\cite{bai2019deep, bai2020multiscale}, we introduce the implicit feature refinement (IFR) to enhance feature representation via a simulated infinite-depth network, where the transformation $F_{\theta}$ is employed to construct the implicit model. Based on Eq.~\ref{eq1}, we can address the instance feature refinement as a fixed-point iteration problem. For the explicit design of transformation $F_{\theta}$, we simply adopt a single residual block with double residual connections to reduce the overall parameters of the mask head (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(d)). For the forward computation, several black-box Root-Find solvers (\textit{e.g.}, Broyden method~\cite{bai2020multiscale}) can be adopted to solve the root $H^{\ast}$ of the equilibrium equation presented in Eq.~\ref{eq1}. For the back-propagation, gradients are computed based on the equilibrium feature solved. Different from the explicitly stacked convolutions, IFR enjoys several advantages: 1) Simulates an infinite-depth feature refinement network using only parameters of a single residual block; 2) Produces the equilibrium instance features with large receptive field, which is beneficial to instance segmentation. It should be noted that IFR can be easily extended to the head network of most image/video instance segmentation frameworks, including both two-stage and one-stage approaches. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark~\cite{lin2014microsoft} demonstrate that our proposed IFR benefits most image instance segmentation frameworks. For instance, it improves the segmentation AP by 1.0\% on Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask} with ResNet-50-FPN backbone. Furthermore, it is also robust and flexible for video instance segmentation on the YouTube-VIS~\cite{yang2019video} benchmark, achieving promising improvements on state-of-the-art frameworks. Additionally, it can be applied to several one-stage object detectors with slight modifications. Our main contributions are summarized as: \begin{itemize} \item Empirical experiments are conducted to analyze the effect of multiple stacked convolutions on refining the instance features. \item Implicit feature refinement (IFR), which only requires parameters of a residual block, is proposed to produce high-level equilibrium instance features with global receptive field through fixed-point iteration. \item Double residual network is further introduced to prevent the network from experiencing degraded performance and propagate the gradients smoothly. \item The proposed IFR is precisely a general plug-and-play module that can be easily extended to most instance segmentation frameworks and serves as a strong alternative to explicitly stacked convolutions in the head network. \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary machine learning has attained remarkable accuracy across numerous computer vision tasks through training models exclusively on images. Extending these achievements and advancing three-dimensional object comprehension holds substantial potential for enabling a broader spectrum of applications, including augmented reality, robotics, autonomous systems, and image retrieval. Nevertheless, comprehending objects in three dimensions remains a formidable challenge owing to the scarcity of extensive real-world datasets relative to two-dimensional tasks (e.g., ImageNet~\cite{Deng:2009jn}, COCO~\cite{Lin:2014vm}, and Open Images~\cite{Kuznetsova:2020ff}). To facilitate the research community's continued progress in three-dimensional object understanding, there exists a compelling need for releasing object-centric video datasets that capture enhanced three-dimensional structural information of objects while conforming to the data format employed in numerous downstream vision tasks (i.e., video or camera streams), thereby supporting the training and evaluation of machine learning models. The object-centric methodology aligns with how human cognition processes novel objects as well. For instance, when children seek to comprehend a chair's geometry, they circumnavigate and observe the chair from various perspectives to acquire information. In essence, "We must also move in order to perceive"~\cite{Gibson:1979}\cite{Zamir:2018}. We introduce the Objectron dataset, a compilation of brief, object-centric video sequences capturing an extensive collection of common objects from diverse viewpoints. Each video sequence is accompanied by augmented reality (AR) session metadata encompassing camera poses, sparse point-clouds, and surface planes. The data additionally contains manually annotated three-dimensional bounding boxes for each object, which characterize the object's position, orientation, and dimensions. The dataset comprises $14,819$ annotated video sequences and $4M$ annotated images gathered from a geographically diverse sample (spanning ten countries across five continents). Figure~\ref{fig:example-seq} illustrates an exemplary video from our dataset. Several advantages emerge from utilizing the Objectron dataset compared to existing works: \begin{itemize} \item Videos encompass multiple perspectives of identical objects, facilitating numerous applications extending well beyond three-dimensional object detection. This encompasses multi-view geometric comprehension, view synthesis, three-dimensional shape reconstruction, etc. \item The three-dimensional bounding box persists throughout the entire video and maintains temporal consistency, thereby enabling three-dimensional tracking applications. \item Our dataset is gathered in natural environments to provide superior generalization for real-world scenarios in contrast to datasets collected under controlled conditions ~\cite{Hinterstoisser:2012ik}\cite{Calli:2017cd}. \item Each instance's translation and dimensions are preserved in metric scale, attributed to precise on-device AR tracking and provides sparse point clouds in three dimensions, enabling sparse depth estimation methodologies. The images are calibrated and camera parameters are furnished, enabling recovery of the object's actual scale. \item Our annotations are dense and continuous, unlike certain previous works~\cite{Savarese:2007by} where viewpoints have been discretized to conform to bins. \item Each object category encompasses hundreds of instances, collected from different locations across various countries under different illumination conditions. \end{itemize} We have performed experiments for three-dimensional object detection tasks utilizing our dataset. We proposed a novel approach to compute the precise three-dimensional IoU of oriented three-dimensional bounding boxes. These experiments can serve as baselines for future research.

text: Following its invention in 1972, \gls{ct} has rapidly gained recognition as an indispensable non-destructive modality for industrial inspection~\cite{de2014industrial}, medical diagnosis~\cite{maier2018medical}, and material sciences~\cite{withers2007x}. \gls{ct} exemplifies computational imaging, wherein a physical quantity is encoded within measured data through an image formation model and subsequently reconstructed by inverting this forward model. In X-ray \gls{ct}, an image representing the attenuation coefficient is reconstructed from projections obtained through circular acquisition. Under orthographic projection, this model reduces to the Radon transform. Discretized measurements of the Radon transform are termed sinograms, and their inversion has been extensively studied. The most prominent methodology is direct inversion utilizing a closed-form solution known as \gls{fbp}~\cite{maier2018medical}. Precise reconstruction using \gls{fbp} necessitates adequate angular sampling according to the Crowther criterion~\cite{crowther1970reconstruction}, which derives from the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem. When this criterion is violated, aliasing artifacts manifest as streak artifacts that severely compromise diagnostic quality. This scenario is designated as \gls{svct} and emerges in numerous practical applications, including motion compensation~\cite{enjilela2019cubic} and dose reduction~\cite{gao2014low,yu2009radiation}. Numerous approaches have been developed to address the ill-posed nature of \gls{svct} by incorporating prior knowledge into the reconstruction algorithm. text: Swarm intelligence has illuminated the collective behavior of autonomous entities governed by simple rules, including ants, boids, and particles. This concept has been applied to collections of robots, and swarm robotics has garnered significant attention over the past two decades. Each autonomous component of the system is termed a robot, module, agent, process, or sensor, and numerous swarm robot systems have been examined including the \emph{autonomous mobile robot system}~\cite{SY99}, the \emph{population protocol model}~\cite{AADFP04}, the \emph{programmable particles}~\cite{DDGRSS14}, \emph{Kilobot}~\cite{RCN14}, and \emph{3D Catoms}~\cite{TPB19}. Dumitrescu et al. introduced the \emph{metamorphic robotic system} (MRS), which comprises a collection of \emph{modules} within the infinite 2D square grid~\cite{DSY04a,DSY04b}. The modules are \emph{anonymous}, meaning they are indistinguishable. They are \emph{autonomous} and \emph{uniform}, such that each module independently determines its movement through a common algorithm. They are \emph{oblivious}, meaning each module retains no memory of the past. Therefore, each module determines its behavior by observing other modules in neighboring cells. Each module can execute a \emph{sliding} to a side-adjacent cell and a \emph{rotation} of $90$ degrees around a cell. The modules must maintain \emph{connectivity}, which is defined by side-adjacency of cells occupied by modules. The authors examined \emph{reconfiguration} of the MRS, which requires the MRS to transform the initial shape into a specified final shape~\cite{DSY04a}. They demonstrated that any horizontally convex connected initial shape of an MRS can be transformed into any convex final shape via a straight chain shape. Subsequently, Dumitrescu and Pach established that any connected initial shape can be transformed into any connected final shape via a straight chain shape~\cite{DP06}. In other words, the MRS possesses the capability of "universal reconfiguration." Reconfiguration can produce dynamic behavior of the MRS. Dumitrescu et al. showed that the MRS can advance forward by repeating a reconfiguration~\cite{DSY04b}. They presented a reconfiguration that achieves the fastest \emph{locomotion}. Doi et al. observed that the oblivious modules can utilize the shape of the MRS as global memory and the MRS can solve more complex problems as the number of modules increases. They investigated \emph{search} within a finite 2D square grid, which requires the MRS to locate a target cell in a finite rectangular \emph{field}~\cite{DYKY18}. Each module does not know the position of the target cell or the initial configuration of the MRS. They demonstrated that the MRS can locate the target cell by sweeping each row of the field without such prior knowledge. Specifically, if the modules agree on the cardinal directions (i.e., north, south, east and west), three modules are necessary and sufficient, otherwise five modules are necessary and sufficient. Nakamura et al. examined \emph{evacuation} of the MRS from a finite rectangular field in the 2D square grid~\cite{NSY20}. There exists a hole (i.e., two side-adjacent cells) on the boundary of the field, and the MRS is required to exit through it from an arbitrary initial position and arbitrary initial shape. They established that two modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules agree on the cardinal directions, otherwise four modules are necessary and sufficient. In this paper, we examine the effect of common knowledge on search by the MRS in the 3D cubic grid. We consider the following three cases: $(i)$ modules equipped with a common \emph{compass} (i.e., they agree on the direction and orientation of $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes). $(ii)$ modules equipped with a common vertical axis (i.e., they agree on the direction and orientation of $z$ axis), and $(iii)$ modules not equipped with a common compass (i.e., they have no agreement on directions and orientations). We establish that three modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules are equipped with a common compass and five modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules are not equipped with a common compass. The numbers of sufficient modules in the 3D cubic grid are identical to those in the 2D square grid~\cite{DYKY18} because the MRS has more states in the 3D cubic grid than in the 2D square grid. For the intermediate case with a common vertical axis, we establish that four modules are necessary and sufficient. Thus, our results in the 3D cubic grid reveal a smooth trade-off between the computational power of the MRS and common knowledge among modules, which the previous results in the 2D square grid could not demonstrate. We present search algorithms for these three settings and establish the necessity by examining the state transition graph of the MRS. \noindent{\bf Related work.}~Reconfiguration of swarm robot systems has been discussed for the MRS~\cite{DP06,DSY04a}, autonomous mobile robots~\cite{FYOKY15,SY99} and the programmable particles~\cite{DGRSS15,DFSVY20}. Michail et al. examined the \emph{programmable matter system}, which is similar to the MRS and investigated reconfiguration by rotations only and that by rotations and slidings~\cite{MSS19}. They demonstrated that the combination of rotations and slidings guarantees universal reconfiguration, while rotations alone cannot. They also presented an $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$-time reconfiguration algorithm by rotations and slidings. Almethen et al. examined reconfiguration by \emph{line-pushing}, where each module is equipped with the capability of pushing a line of modules~\cite{AMP20a}. They presented an $\mathrm{O}(n \log n)$-time universal reconfiguration algorithm that does not guarantee connectivity of intermediate shapes and an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time reconfiguration algorithm that transforms a diagonal line into a straight chain while preserving connectivity. The same authors subsequently demonstrated that their programmable matter system possesses the capability of universal reconfiguration and an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time reconfiguration algorithm together with an $\Omega(n \log n)$ lower bound~\cite{AMP20b}.

text: Self-modifying code constitutes a computer program that alters its own instructions during execution while maintaining overall functional integrity. Such modifications can be localized (impacting a limited code segment) or comprehensive (affecting the entire codebase), permanent (modifying the disk copy) or temporary (runtime patching). These alterations may occur during compilation, linking, post-processing phases, or at runtime. The code responsible for implementing modifications may operate as an independent process or constitute an integral component of the target program itself. Several self-modifying code implementations can be categorized into specialized cases as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Packers}: These represent the most straightforward implementations. Such programs contain the actual payload in compressed and/or encrypted format. The executable component is extracted from this format and executed entirely within memory. \item \textbf{Obfuscators}: These constitute tools that accept an executable file as input and generate a modified version as output. The resulting binary contains a distinct instruction set while preserving overall behavioral characteristics. The output executable does not incorporate additional functionality. \item \textbf{Self-injecting codes}: These applications inject supplementary code into their own process space (or spawned child process) and execute it within that context. The injected code may execute within the primary thread (effectively terminating the original code without deallocating associated memory and metadata) or within a newly instantiated thread. \item \textbf{Self-debugging codes}: These applications attach to themselves as debuggers or to a child instance of the identical process. Subsequently, the debugger process can manipulate the debuggee process, including but not restricted to overwriting executable code. A beneficial consequence is that dynamic analysis of these programs becomes significantly challenging. \item \textbf{Self-healing codes}: These applications can identify modifications (either in files or memory) and restore the original state by reversing the applied changes. \end{enumerate} We will examine self-debugging code comprehensively and introduce an additional technique that enables our malware to operate in forward execution mode (as conventional programs do) and reverse execution mode (instructions execute in inverted sequence). The malware exhibits distinct behaviors in both execution directions. The malicious functionality activates exclusively during reverse-direction execution, which facilitates evasion from various analytical approaches: \begin{enumerate} \item Analysis tools such as IDA Pro examine reverse-engineered assembly using a top-down methodology. Since our code demonstrates malicious behavior during bottom-up execution, this behavior remains obscured from immediate detection. \item Analysis tools including debuggers or sandboxes typically attach to processes using identical mechanisms employed in self-debugging. As a beneficial consequence, when such tools attach to our code, the self-debugging component fails to execute (since the operating system permits only one process to function as debugger for any given process), and the payload executes in top-down sequence, thereby concealing its malicious characteristics. \end{enumerate}

text: For a robot to intelligently interact with its environment, it must rapidly and precisely determine the relative position and orientation of neighboring robots, people, vehicles, and a variety of other static and dynamic obstacles in the scene. From drone racing~\cite{spica2018realtime} to pedestrian avoidance~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}, tasks depending on such estimates are numerous and are fundamental to creating truly autonomous robots. Nevertheless, the capability to track the six Degree of Freedom (6DoF) relative pose of a dynamic object in real-time, with onboard sensing and computation, is largely beyond the reach of existing robot perception frameworks. To address this need, we propose \textbf{M}onocular \textbf{S}equential \textbf{L}ightweight \textbf{R}otation \textbf{A}nd \textbf{P}osition \textbf{T}racking \textbf{O}n-\textbf{R}obots (MSL-RAPTOR), a lightweight, general-purpose robot perception module for tracking the 6DoF relative pose of a dynamic object using only an onboard monocular camera. MSL-RAPTOR performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches relying on more sensors (e.g. depth) and greater computation capability. text: Video analytics systems have achieved widespread adoption across various domains, spanning from computationally intensive tasks such as facial recognition for surveillance, to mobile applications such as object detection for mobile-based augmented reality (AR)~\cite{rohan2019convolutional, apicharttrisorn2019frugal, rao2017mobile}, and to real-time systems such as pedestrian and vehicle localization for autonomous driving~\cite{feng2020deep, arnold2019survey, li2019gs3d}. A fundamental capability shared by these applications is the capacity to detect objects in videos. There is an expanding number of use cases for performing such video object detection on {\em mobile devices}. These devices are increasingly equipped with mobile GPUs, although they are computationally much weaker than those on server-class machines. Nevertheless, there exists an imperative to perform the video processing in (near) real-time on the streaming (video) content, on the device itself\footnote{For convenience we will often use the shorthand ``device" to refer to a ``mobile device".}. This is required, for instance, to enhance the user's immersive experience ({e.g.,}\xspace in AR/VR games) or to provide high-confidence outputs from streaming videos ({e.g.,}\xspace for pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving). A typical operating point is processing each frame in 33 ms, which corresponds to the video stream rate of 30 frames per second (FPS). We observe empirically that state-of-the-art (SOTA) protocols (designed for servers) when executed on mobile platforms significantly exceed this latency margin. For example, MEGA~\cite{chen2020memory}, considered a SOTA solution, requires 253.4 msec per frame on NVIDIA AGX Xavier, when utilizing all computing resources. In response, a multitude of efficient models and systems have been proposed to enhance their efficiency or performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2, jiang2020learning, zhu2018towards, chen2018optimizing, liu2016ssd, redmon2018yolov3, zhang2018single}. \begin{comment} The existing research are mostly geared toward accuracy and may need to leverage server-class machines or cloud-enterprises~\cite{wu2019sequence, chen2020memory, sabater2020robust, zhu2017flow, deng2019relation}. However, mobile applications typically encounter limited energy or computational resources while still requiring strict latency guarantees. To improve the user's immersive experience ({e.g.,}\xspace in AR/VR games) or to give high-confidence outputs from streaming videos ({e.g.,}\xspace for pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving), such tasks must be performed in near real-time under stringent latency requirements of 33 msec (30 FPS) or lower. Even with advancements in mobile GPU devices, these devices lack the computation power that a server-class machine or a cloud enterprise provides. In response, efficient models and systems have been proposed to improve their efficiency or performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2}. \end{comment} Another approach to make the streaming analytics feasible on mobile devices is to utilize both object detection and tracking, which is captured by the technique ``\textit{tracking-by-detection}''~\cite{bae2014robust, muller2018trackingnet}. By interspersing multiple frames of tracking (lightweight compared to detection) with each frame where object detection is executed, the overall performance can be accelerated. The tracking-by-detection technique exposes several adaptation strategies. This can include selecting among a set of detectors and trackers and how to handle the trigger frequency between the detector and tracker. Empirically, we observe that the execution time of an object tracker is 10X lower than an object detector. A judicious choice of such adaptation strategies is required to satisfy the real-time requirements for energy, latency, and accuracy, especially on mobile devices. The stringent requirements on mobile devices at runtime expose another challenge for streaming video analytics: \textit{how to adapt (at runtime) to the dynamic user requirements and available resources on the device?} To address this problem, several recent works considered multi-branch solutions~\cite{fang2018nestdnn, xu2020approxdet, xu2019approxnet, lee2021benchmarking}. Such solutions include multiple execution kernels in a system and choose the optimal one {\em during runtime} to satisfy the user requirement of latency. Yet, omitting features that control energy consumption is a major limitation of all these approaches. Furthermore, compared to recent studies on efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, there have been limited studies and applications on efficient object detection solutions on embedded devices, along with the issue of using outdated feature extractors. In real applications, the change of video content, available resources on mobile devices, and manual control of the requirements make the dynamic adaptations even more challenging. The wide range of energy, latency, and accuracy requirement means the system needs to have the adaptability to a variety of scenarios. Thus, the design must satisfy the following prerequisites: (1) designing an execution kernel that is both energy and latency efficient for the mobile device, (2) analysis of the energy consumption and latency performance of all execution branches on mobile devices, and (3) an adaptive scheduler to make decisions at runtime to satisfy multiple requirements simultaneously. However, to our knowledge, no prior work has incorporated all of these design innovations. Another dimension that has been overlooked to date is how do these algorithms behave when there is resource contention on the device. Such resource contention can occur due to co-located applications running on the same device, an occurrence that is quite common because these are multi-purpose devices. Hence, for instance, when there is video detection occurring, another computationally intensive task such as speech recognition may also be executing on the device. No prior work has evaluated recent video object detection systems, under varying resource contention on leading GPU-enabled mobile devices. In this work, we present {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace\footnote{Just like a \name is a person who has exceptional skill, expertise, or talent at some endeavor, we believe our system demonstrates such skill in configuring streaming video object detection on embedded or mobile devices.\xspace}, which is customized for mobile devices under varying resource constraints, with additional efficiency knobs\footnote{We use the term ``efficiency knobs'' rather than the more common term ``tuning knobs'' as we are focusing on the performance metric of accuracy, normalized by latency or energy cost to achieve that accuracy, in other words, efficient accuracy.} for energy-aware adaptation. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace selects the most efficient baseline object detectors EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} and SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, enhances them by integrating object trackers, and provides 155 execution branches by exposing 8 efficiency knobs within one system. Moreover, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace has a scheduler that can select the optimal branch during runtime to satisfy the energy and latency requirements simultaneously, while maximizing the accuracy. We also evaluated a total of 15 baseline models on 3 different embedded boards under 2 resource contention levels to better understand the energy, latency, and accuracy performance of recent models for video object detection. We evaluate {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and the baselines using the ILSVRC 2015 VID datasets on 3 NVIDIA mobile GPUs of increasing compute capacity --- Jetson TX2, Xavier NX, and AGX Xavier, under 2 different power modes of AGX Xavier. On each board and under each power mode, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace is the optimal solution that can automatically choose the optimal branch to satisfy the energy and latency requirements, and maximize the accuracy performance. With the multi-branch execution kernel, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can adapt its energy efficiency within a wide range (span of 89X) and also latency in a wide range (span of 128X). Such wide ranges of energy efficiency and latency can satisfy various scenarios at runtime to optimize the functionality of our video object detection system. Given 1 J per frame energy requirement, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 52.0\% accuracy, and given 33.3 msec latency budget, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 60.1\% accuracy on an AGX Xavier board. This makes it difficult to satisfy the requirements for energy, speed, and accuracy simultaneously, and thus the design must be based on the following three requisites: (1) an energy-efficient and fast kernel for the mobile device; (2) an analysis of the energy consumption and the latency of the different branches of the mobile device; and (3) a run-time-adjustable scheduler, which can achieve both energy-efficiency and speed at run time. However, to our knowledge, no work has succeeded in satisfying all these requirements. In this paper we introduce the Virtuoso family of systems, which is especially designed for mobile devices with variable resource constraints, and is adapted to the energy constraints of the device. This resource competition may come from other applications running on the same device, which is very common, as these devices are often used for more than one task. For example, while the detection is being carried out, another very demanding application such as speech recognition may be running on the same device. This system has been designed to optimize object detection on mobile and embedded devices. The footnote of the title is a person who is highly skilled, talented or expert in a particular field or art; our system is considered to have such qualities when it comes to configuring object detection on mobile or embedded devices. The name knobs refers not to the tuning of the system, but to the energy consumption of the system, because we are primarily concerned with accuracy, normalized by the time or energy it costs to achieve accuracy, that is, efficiency accuracy. Xspace Virtuoso takes the two most efficient base object detection models, EfficientDet and SSD, and integrates them with object trackers for a total of 155 execution branches and exposes 8 efficiency controls. Thanks to this multi-branch kernel, Virtuoso's energy efficiency can be adapted over a wide range (up to 89x), and the latency can be adapted over a wide range (up to 128x). In addition, Xspace Virtuoso has a scheduler that at run-time selects the best execution branch to satisfy energy and latency requirements, while maximizing accuracy. The wide range of energy and latency can satisfy various requirements during the execution of a test, and thus optimize the performance of the system. Virtuoso and the reference models were tested on three NVIDIA mobile GPUs with an increasing degree of power, the Jetson TX2, the Xavier NX and the AGX Xavier, and on the two power modes available on the AGX Xavier. On each board and power mode, Virtuoso was the most effective solution, because it automatically chose the best branch to satisfy energy and latency requirements while giving the best performance. Given a frame energy budget of 1 j, VirtuosoXP reaches a resolution of 52%; given a latency budget of 33.3 ms, VirtuosoXP reaches a resolution of 61% on the Xavier.

text: Contemporary information is produced across multiple modalities, including text, images, audio, video, and others. Consequently, for a query expressed in one modality (e.g., text), the pertinent information may exist in an alternative modality (e.g., image). Cross-modal Information Retrieval (IR) algorithms are being developed to address such search requirements. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Need for Zero-shot Information Retrieval (ZSIR):} A train-test configuration of an IR task involves parameter learning for diverse classes or categories of queries. Conventional cross-modal retrieval methods require training data from all query classes to train the retrieval models. However, such methods may fail to retrieve data for queries from {\it novel} or {\it unseen} classes. For example, assume the retrieval model has been trained on images and textual descriptions of various vehicle classes, such as `car', `motorbike', `aeroplane', and others. Subsequently, given a query `bus', the model is expected to retrieve images and textual descriptions of buses (for which the model has not been trained). Such a scenario conforms to the ``zero-shot'' configuration~\cite{Larochelle:2008:ZLN:1620163.1620172,ZeroShotNIPS2009,ZeroShotNorouzi2013} which focuses on recognizing novel/unseen classes with limited training classes. Such scenarios are pertinent in any contemporary search system, where new events, hashtags, etc. emerge daily. Therefore, contrary to the traditional IR evaluation configuration, the zero-shot paradigm must be incorporated in an IR setting. Specifically, zero-shot cross-media retrieval aims to achieve retrieval across multiple modalities (e.g., images to be retrieved in response to a textual query) where there is no overlap between the query-classes in training and test data. Zero-Shot IR (ZSIR) is particularly challenging since models must handle not only different semantics across seen and unseen query-classes, but also the heterogeneous features of data across different modalities. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Present work and differences with prior works:} Although substantial research has been reported on general multimodal and cross-modal retrieval~\cite{cross-modal-ir-survey}, to our knowledge, only a few prior works have attempted cross-modal IR in a zero-shot setting~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797,AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020} (see Section~\ref{sec:related} and Section~\ref{sub:baselines} for details of these methods). Several of these prior works assume additional information about the class labels (e.g., a measure of semantic similarity between class labels) which may not always be available. In this paper, we propose a novel model for cross-modal IR in zero-shot setting, based on Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{mirza-conditional14}, that can retrieve {\it images} relevant to a given {\it textual} query. Our model -- which we name {\bf \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{}} (Zero-Shot Cross-modal Retrieval GAN) -- relies solely on the textual data to perform the retrieval, and {\it does not require additional information about class labels}. Although prior ZSIR models~\cite{ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797} also utilize GANs, the main novel contributions of the proposed model can be summarized as follows: (1)~We propose \textbf{use of wrong classes} to enable the generator to generate features that are unique to a specific class, by distinguishing it from other classes. (2)~We develop a \textbf{Common Space Embedding Mapper (CSEM)} to map both the image embeddings and the text embeddings to a common space where retrieval can be performed. {\it This is the key step that enables our model to perform retrieval without relying on additional semantic information of class labels.} (3)~We develop an {\bf Expectation-Maximization (E-M) based method} for efficiently training the retrieval model, where the GAN and the CSEM are trained alternately. We demonstrate that this E-M configuration enables better retrieval than jointly training the GAN and the CSEM. We experiment on several benchmark datasets for zero-shot retrieval -- (1)~the Caltech-UCSD Birds dataset, (2)~the Oxford Flowers-102 dataset, (3)~the North America Birds (NAB) dataset, (4)~the Wikipedia dataset, and (5)~the Animals With Attribute (AWA) dataset. Our proposed \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} substantially out-performs several strong and varied baselines on all the datasets, including ZSIR models~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,8643797,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018}, state-of-the-art Zero-Shot classification models~\cite{verma-cvpr18,xian2018feature_gen} suitably adapted for the Text-to-Image retrieval setting, as well as state-of-the-art Zero-Shot Hashing models~\cite{AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020,DCMH-AAAI17}. Also note that our proposed model can be utilized not only with textual queries, but also with other forms of queries such as attribute vectors, as demonstrated by its application on the AWA dataset. We make the implementation of \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ranarag/ZSCRGAN}.

text: Dense retrieval systems initially encode queries and documents into a dense embedding space and subsequently perform information retrieval by identifying a query's nearest neighbors within the embedding space~\cite{orqa, sentence-bert, dpr, ance}. Through the advancement of pre-trained language models~\cite{bert, lu2021less}, specialized training strategies~\cite{dpr, ance}, and efficient nearest neighbor search~\cite{faiss, scann}, dense retrieval systems have demonstrated effectiveness across a broad range of tasks, including web search~\cite{msmarco}, open domain question answering~\cite{naturalquestions}, and zero-shot IR~\cite{beir}. Retrieval using dense, fully-learned representations possesses the potential to address several fundamental challenges in sparse retrieval. For instance, vocabulary mismatch can be resolved \textit{if} the embeddings accurately capture the information need underlying a query and map it to relevant documents. Nevertheless, decades of IR research demonstrate that inferring a user's search intent from a concise and frequently ambiguous search query remains challenging~\cite{croft2010search}. Even with powerful pre-trained language models, it remains unrealistic to expect an encoder to perfectly embed the underlying information need from a limited number of query terms. A prevalent technique for improving query understanding in sparse retrieval systems is \textit{pseudo relevance feedback} (PRF)~\cite{croft2010search,PRF,rm12}, which utilizes the top retrieved documents from an initial search as supplementary information to enrich the query representation. Whether PRF information is employed via query expansion~\cite{PRF,trec2004} or query term reweighting~\cite{bendersky2011parameterized}, its effectiveness has been consistently observed across diverse search scenarios, making PRF a standard practice in numerous sparse retrieval systems. This work exploits PRF information to enhance query representations in dense retrieval. Given the top retrieved documents from a dense retrieval model, e.g., ANCE~\cite{ance}, we construct a PRF query encoder, ANCE-PRF, that employs a BERT encoder~\cite{bert} to process the query and the PRF documents to refine the query representation. ANCE-PRF is trained end-to-end using relevance labels and learns to optimize the query embeddings utilizing the rich information from PRF documents. It reuses the document index from ANCE to avoid duplicating index storage. In experiments on MS MARCO and TREC Deep Learning (DL) Track passage ranking benchmarks, ANCE-PRF demonstrates consistently higher accuracy than ANCE and several recent dense retrieval systems that employ more sophisticated models and training strategies~\cite{ltre,mebert}. We also observe substantial improvements on DL-HARD~\cite{dlhard} queries, a curated set designed to include complex search intents challenging for neural systems. To the best of our knowledge, ANCE-PRF ranks among the best performing first-stage retrieval systems on the highly competitive MARCO passage ranking leaderboard. Our studies confirm that the advantages of ANCE-PRF lie in its capacity to leverage the useful information from the PRF documents while disregarding the noise from irrelevant PRF documents. The PRF encoder allocates considerably more attention to terms from the relevant PRF documents, compared to those from the irrelevant documents. A case study demonstrates that the encoder focuses more on PRF terms that are complementary to the query terms in representing search intents. These factors help ANCE-PRF learn superior query embeddings that are closer to the relevant documents and improve the majority of testing queries.\footnote{Our code, checkpoints, and ranking results are open-sourced at \url{https://github.com/yuhongqian/ANCE-PRF}.}

text: Given the ubiquity and significance of smart devices in contemporary life, the capacity to comprehend and manipulate User Interfaces (UIs) has emerged as a crucial task for Artificial Intelligence. For example, a model capable of locating a UI component through its description could prove highly valuable for voice interfaces, while a model that can anticipate the expected outcome of button activation could facilitate page navigation. To effectively operate a UI, models must comprehend user tasks and intentions, along with the methods for executing these tasks within the provided UI. Nevertheless, UI understanding represents a challenging and under-explored domain. Initially, numerous tasks pertain to UI understanding. Typically, these tasks are cross-modal and cross-domain, such as activating a button via voice command and retrieving an icon through a semantically analogous one. Prior research in this domain generally focuses on individual tasks sequentially. Training distinct complex models for each task proves inefficient for on-device model deployment. Furthermore, models may experience overfitting when task-specific data remains limited. Pre-training models on extensive datasets for feature extraction has demonstrated substantial efficacy across multiple domains, such as ResNet \cite{he2016deep} in computer vision and BERT \cite{devlin2018bert} in natural language processing. No such universal feature representation exists for user interfaces, and whether a pre-trained feature extraction model can enhance multiple UI-related tasks remains unclear. Subsequently, the data sources and formats of UIs differ from natural image and language corpora. For instance, the View Hierarchy (VH) in mobile applications and Document Object Model (DOM) in web pages constitute tree structures representing UI layout. The VH and DOM encompass structural and semantic information regarding the UI; however, they remain generally invisible to users and contain brief phrases with functional hints. Effectively utilizing this domain-specific knowledge for comprehensive UI understanding constitutes an unresolved challenge. Additionally, comprehending UI functionality presents greater complexity than learning their visual appearance. UI elements with similar appearance commonly possess vastly different semantic meanings, and conversely. In the illustration shown in Figure \ref{fig:icon-semantic}, all icons appear similar to one another (``houses''), yet they possess distinct functionalities that can only be interpreted through additional context. In this paper, we present ActionBert, a pre-trained transformer-style \cite{vaswani2017attention} model that exploits sequential user action information for UI understanding. Our fundamental insight is that the semantic significance of a UI, along with the functionality of UI components, can be captured through user actions, such as a sequence of clicks and their effects on the UI. This model exploits the representational capacity of transformer models and incorporates domain-specific information including VH and user actions to construct embeddings reflecting the functionality of various UI elements. To our knowledge, this represents the initial attempt to establish a generic feature representation in this domain. Our primary contributions in this paper include: \begin{itemize} \item To our knowledge, we are the first to integrate powerful transformer models with domain-specific knowledge, such as VH and user actions, to enhance machines' comprehension of UIs. \item We present ActionBert, a transformer-style multi-modal model designed to capture the context and semantic significance of UI elements by introducing novel self-supervised pre-training tasks based on user actions and UI-specific features. \item We assess the proposed model across four categories of UI downstream tasks, encompassing various real-world use cases. We demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing models across all tasks. \end{itemize}
