text: Robots must execute fine manipulation, navigation, and target tracking tasks across diverse applications spanning from manufacturing automation to space exploration. For tasks requiring fine manipulation, integrating visual feedback proves advantageous when the robot end-effector operates in proximity to the manipulated object. For tasks such as landing a quadcopter from considerable distances, incorporating visual feedback becomes valuable when image features remain visible to an onboard camera sensor. When the object lies outside the field of view (FOV) of the camera or reliable features cannot be extracted or when feature loss occurs, learning-based motion generation methods such as dynamic movement primitives (DMP) can be employed to control the robot. For instance, in a wire pinning task for wire harness assembly, the robot grasping the wire must reach the pin by following a specific trajectory that avoids collision with the fixtures securing the pin. The pin may not consistently remain within the FOV of the camera mounted to the robot end-effector. In such scenarios, to insert the wire into the pin, a learned DMP can be utilized to generate the motion that brings the wire close to the pin before visual feedback of the pin becomes available \cite{Wirepinning}. Motivated by such examples and the necessity to ensure stable motion when transitioning between learned and vision-based controllers, a novel methodology that unifies DMP \cite{ijspeert2003learning} and Image-based Visual Servoing (IBVS)\cite{chaumette2006visual} is proposed in this paper. The proposed algorithm enables stable switching between DMP and IBVS controllers to reach the goal location from an initial location when visual feedback is not continuously available. The proposed switched system is designated as a DMP-IBVS switched system. Numerous approaches have been developed to design robot controllers using visual feedback that maintain objects within the FOV (see, e.g., \cite{lopez2009homography,gans2011keeping,Salehi2021ICRA}). A trajectory planning and tracking control approach for mobile robots is developed in \cite{Wang2021SMC} that employs virtual-goal-guided rapidly exploring random tree (RRT) for trajectory planning and IBVS with FOV constraints for tracking. A constrained IBVS approach for helicopter landing on a moving platform is proposed in \cite{Huang2021SMC} utilizing a control barrier function methodology to satisfy FOV constraints. A model predictive controller (MPC) for visual servoing of a mobile robot is developed in \cite{Ke2017SMC} which addresses visibility constraints for IBVS and velocity limits of the robot. In contrast, a learning-based robot motion generation using DMP is developed in this paper to generate robot control commands in the absence of visual feedback, and a switching control law is developed to transition to IBVS controller when visual feedback becomes available. It is established that switching arbitrarily between stable subsystems can result in instability\cite{liberzon2003switching,liberzon1999basic}. In \cite{hespanha1999stability}, an average dwell time condition based on multiple Lyapunov functions is developed for stabilizing switched systems. In \cite{daafouz2002stability}, the authors propose a linear matrix inequality-based condition to verify the existence of a quadratic Lyapunov function for proving asymptotic stability of a switched discrete system. In \cite{hespanha2004uniform}, LaSalle's invariance principle is extended to switched linear systems to establish asymptotic stability using multiple Lyapunov functions whose Lie derivatives are negative semidefinite. In \cite{lin2009stability}, a survey of results for stability of switched linear systems is presented, and the problem of stabilizability of switched systems is analyzed. Multiple Lyapunov functions for analyzing Lyapunov stability and iterated function systems as a tool for Lagrange stability are proposed in \cite{branicky1998multiple}. Invariance-like results for nonautonomous nonlinear switched systems are developed in \cite{kamalapurkar2018invariance}. Switched systems analysis of output feedback systems and observers have been investigated in the literature. The switching method in \cite{Astolfi2020_tac} analyzes switching between locally and globally converging observers with asymptotic stability. A composite output feedback control law is derived in \cite{Prieur2011_tac} that switches between locally and globally asymptotically stable output feedback controllers. Switched systems analysis has been applied to solve challenging problems in robotics, including visual servo control and vision-based trajectory tracking. In \cite{gans2007stable} an asymptotically stable hybrid switched systems visual servo controller is proposed, which switches between IBVS and position-based visual servo control (PBVS) based on multiple Lyapunov functions. The switching between IBVS-PBVS control is developed to switch between unstable systems and expand the region of stability. An estimator that switches between state predictor and image-based observer for object localization is presented in \cite{parikh2016switched} when image feedback is intermittently available. The stability of the switched system is established using a common Lyapunov function. An estimator for pose estimation of a moving target is developed in \cite{parikh2018target} when measurements are available intermittently by learning the motion model. In \cite{parikh2017switched,chen2019switched}, an observer-predictor framework is presented for target tracking and trajectory tracking in the presence of intermittent measurements by switching between a global uniformly ultimately bounded (GUUB) and an unstable system. The switched error system is demonstrated to be GUUB based on dwell time conditions. The approaches for image-based tracking utilize switching between systems primarily to accommodate feature track losses, occlusions, and limited camera field of view (FOV) of features. Switched systems analysis is also developed for target tracking in the presence of intermittent observations from a network of stationary cameras in \cite{harris2020target}. text: An emerging challenge in NLP is long-form question-answering (LFQA), wherein paragraph-length responses are generated to address open-ended questions. LFQA systems possess the potential to become a primary mechanism through which individuals acquire knowledge about the world, yet they currently fall short of human performance \citep{hurdles}. Existing research typically emphasizes two fundamental components of this task: information retrieval and synthesis. In this work we exploit existing solutions to these components: we delegate document retrieval to the Microsoft Bing Web Search API,\footnote{\url{https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/bing/apis/bing-web-search-api}} and employ unsupervised pre-training to attain high-quality synthesis through fine-tuning GPT-3 \citep{gpt3}. Rather than attempting to enhance these ingredients, we concentrate on integrating them using more faithful training objectives. Following \citet{summarization}, we employ human feedback to directly optimize answer quality, enabling us to achieve performance competitive with humans. We make two key contributions: \begin{itemize \item We construct a text-based web-browsing environment with which a fine-tuned language model can interact. This enables us to enhance both retrieval and synthesis in an end-to-end manner using general methods such as imitation learning and reinforcement learning. \item We produce answers \textit{with references}: passages extracted by the model from web pages during browsing. This is essential for enabling labelers to assess the factual accuracy of answers, without engaging in a challenging and subjective process of independent research. \end{itemize} Our models are trained primarily to respond to questions from ELI5 \citep{eli5}, a dataset of questions drawn from the ``Explain Like I'm Five'' subreddit. We collect two additional types of data: \textit{demonstrations} of humans utilizing our web-browsing environment to answer questions, and \textit{comparisons} between two model-generated answers to the same question (each accompanied by their own set of references). Answers are evaluated for their factual accuracy, coherence, and overall utility. We utilize this data in four principal ways: behavior cloning (i.e., supervised fine-tuning) using the demonstrations, reward modeling using the comparisons, reinforcement learning against the reward model, and rejection sampling against the reward model. Our optimal model employs a combination of behavior cloning and rejection sampling. We also discover reinforcement learning to provide some benefit when inference-time compute is more constrained. We assess our best model in three distinct ways. First, we compare our model's answers to answers written by our human demonstrators on a held-out set of questions. Our model's answers are preferred 56\% of the time, demonstrating human-level utilization of the text-based browser. Second, we compare our model's answers (with references removed, for fairness) to the highest-voted answer provided by the ELI5 dataset. Our model's answers are preferred 69\% of the time. Third, we evaluate our model on TruthfulQA \citep{truthfulqa}, an adversarial dataset of short-form questions. Our model's answers are accurate 75\% of the time, and are both accurate and informative 54\% of the time, surpassing our base model (GPT-3), but falling short of human performance. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item In Section \ref{section:environment}, we describe our text-based web-browsing environment and how our models interact with it. \item In Section \ref{section:methods}, we explain our data collection and training methods in more detail. \item In Section \ref{section:evaluation}, we evaluate our best-performing models (for different inference-time compute budgets) on ELI5 and TruthfulQA. \item In Section \ref{section:experiments}, we provide experimental results comparing our different methods and how they scale with dataset size, parameter count, and inference-time compute. \item In Section \ref{section:discussion}, we discuss the implications of our findings for training models to answer questions truthfully, and broader impacts. \end{itemize}

text: Autonomous driving in complex and dynamic traffic scenarios presents considerable challenges. On one hand, diverse road topologies and scenarios (e.g., roundabouts, multi-lane streets and intersections) must be considered\cite{Chen2019DeepIL}. On the other hand, the complex and coupled interactions among multiple road agents (e.g., pedestrians, bicyclists and vehicles) are difficult to model\cite{Chen2020RobotNI}. Additionally, various traffic regulations must be observed, such as traffic lights, lane markings and speed limits. Traditional decision and planning approaches are predominantly rule-based, and are challenging to generalize to novel scenarios. Consequently, they necessitate time-intensive and iterative manual tuning of rules and parameters to sustain performance\cite{Zeng2019EndToEndIN}. In recent years, as an alternative approach, deep learning has significantly advanced SDV technology. The capacity to \textit{learn and self-optimize} its behavior from data mitigates the laborious engineering maintenance for modeling all foreseeable scenarios, rendering a deep driving model well-suited to autonomous driving problems in high-dimensional, nonlinear and dynamic environments\cite{Cai2020ProbabilisticEV, Chen2019LearningBC,OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring, Tai2019VisualbasedAD}. Nevertheless, current learning-based models have not been adequately designed for scalable autonomous driving in a unified framework. Particularly, most studies only address isolated tasks such as conditional urban driving\cite{OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring,Chen2019LearningBC,Tai2019VisualbasedAD}, lane-following\cite{Xu2017EndtoEndLO}, lane-changing\cite{Wang2018ARL} or collision avoidance\cite{Porav2018ImminentCM, Woo2020CollisionAF}. In summary, high-performance scalable driving models that can manage extensive traffic scenarios remain elusive. To address this challenge, in this paper we propose a graph-based deep neural network \textit{DiGNet} (driving in graphs) for scalable autonomous driving. Specifically, we employ graph attention networks (GAT)\cite{velickovic2018graph} to model the complex interactions among traffic agents, utilize semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) images to model road topologies and traffic regulations, and adopt the variational auto-encoder (VAE)\cite{kingma2014autoencoding} to extract compact yet effective environmental features. The primary contributions of this paper are enumerated as follows: (1) We propose a specifically designed network architecture for autonomous driving in generic traffic scenarios. It considers both driving contexts and the interactions among dynamic road agents. (2) We demonstrate the scalable and safe autonomous driving performance of the proposed method through extensive closed-loop evaluation in both observed and unobserved urban/rural/highway environments.

text: Neural Networks (NNs) constitute computational models that comprise (potentially multiple) feature representation layer(s), along with a final linear learner. In recent years, deep NNs have substantially enhanced the state-of-the-art performances across numerous real applications, including image classification \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,he2016deep}, speech recognition \cite{hinton2012deep}, natural language processing \cite{bahdanau2014neural}, etc. Nevertheless, theoretical comprehension of these empirical successes for NNs remains limited. One primary conceptual challenge is the high non-convexity of these models, which implies that first-order algorithms such as gradient descent (GD) or stochastic gradient descent (SGD) may converge to poor local stationary points. Nevertheless, it is observed in practice that with the assistance of various techniques such as dropout \cite{SHKSS-dropout} and batch normalization \cite{ioffe15}, deep neural network (DNN) can be reliably trained from random initialization with reproducible outcomes. The solutions obtained through proper training procedures perform well and consistently. In other words, two distinct random initializations (employing the same initialization and training strategy) generally yield models that provide similar predictions on test data. Thus, we may conclude that appropriate neural network training leads to comparable solutions. This behavior resembles that of convex optimization, rather than generic non-convex optimization problems that tend to become trapped in suboptimal local stationary solutions. Because solutions from different random initializations are similar and reproducible, it can also be hypothesized that with proper training, deep neural networks can achieve solutions that are near globally optimal. These empirical observations appear to be quite mysterious, and they necessitate the development of new mathematical models for neural networks that can bridge the gap between non-convex and convex models to understand. In addition to the aforementioned empirical observations, it is also recognized by practitioners that overparameterized neural networks (NNs) with numerous hidden units are straightforward to learn \cite{zhang2016understanding}. They achieve superior and more consistent performance. Related to this empirical observation, it was noted in the 1990s that neural networks with infinitely many hidden units are more tractable to model and analyze theoretically \cite{Neal95-thesis,Williams97-nips}. In the past few years, there have been numerous significant theoretical developments in the analysis of overparameterized NNs with massive hidden units that approach infinity. Particularly, it was demonstrated that such systems behave like convex systems under various restricted settings. This provides theoretical justification of the empirical observations of the reproducibility of neural network training. { In this paper, we review some recently developed mathematical models for overparameterized NNs, with the focus on the {\em neural tangent kernel} (NTK) view and the {\em mean field} (MF) view. Section~\ref{sec:2two-levelNN} introduces the basic formulation for two-layer NNs and Section~\ref{sec:random} introduces a closely related learning model, random kitchen sinks \cite{rahimi2009weighted}. In Section \ref{sec:ntk}, we examine the NTK view for two-layer NNs, which demonstrates that a two-layer NN can be written equivalently as a linear model in the tangent space under some specialized conditions. Section \ref{sec:meanfield} considers the MF view for two-layer NNs. In this view, a continuous two-layer NN is regarded as a learned distribution over the weights, which leads to a more realistic mathematical model for analyzing practical behaviors of NNs. In Section \ref{sec:exp}, we compare the three models from the feature learning perspective. Section \ref{sec:deepnn} considers the possible extensions on deep NNs for NTK and MFs. In Section \ref{sec:complexity}, we introduce some basic complexity results for NTK. Section \ref{sec:othermodel} reviews some other mathematical models. Finally, we conclude the paper and outline active research directions in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}.} \IEEEpubidadjcol

text: With the exponential growth in the volume of scientific publications, researchers face increasing challenges in identifying papers worthy of examination from vast bodies of literature for rapid review or maintaining awareness of recent developments. When confronted with an unfamiliar research topic, a user might attempt to consult survey papers on the subject and reference their bibliographies to obtain additional details. Nevertheless, high-quality and current surveys are not consistently available for every research topic. A user might also employ academic search engines to discover relevant papers for reading. Current academic search engines typically return article lists by computing semantic similarity between the user's query and individual articles independently, disregarding prerequisite relationships among search results. Consequently, it would be extremely valuable to retrieve a list of core papers with a prescribed reading sequence for a given query to present users with a structured reading pathway. Through this approach, a user can follow the generated reading path and rapidly acquire familiarity with a new research domain. In recent years, research concerning scientific paper analysis has garnered considerable attention. Nevertheless, most existing studies concentrate on citation recommendation~\cite{zhou2008learning, tang2009discriminative, he2010context, ren2014cluscite, sun2017recommendation}, which seeks to recommend citations for given text. Another research category focuses on citation classification \cite{jurgens2016citation, teufel2006automatic, dong2011ensemble, zhao2019context, cohan2019structural, pride2020authoritative}, attempting to infer authors' intentions for citing papers. Research works also exist regarding the generation of reading lists for users. \cite{jardine2014automatically} proposed ThemedPageRank to construct reading lists by re-ranking topic-related papers. \cite{ekstrand2010automatically} developed a reading list for a given query set by exploring collaborative and content-based filtering techniques. However, these methods disregard prerequisite relationships among the returned papers. \cite{gordon2017structured} designed a concept graph-based approach to generate structured reading lists, which considers prerequisite concepts of the topic. Nevertheless, this method depends heavily on the quality of existing concept graphs. Previous research on reading list generation primarily addresses the problem of ``what to read" by producing paper lists for given research topics. However, to serve users unfamiliar with research fields, two critical problems are neglected by existing research: ``how to read" and ``how to understand". For the first problem, we must organize different research works in a structured fashion, enabling users to read papers according to structural paths and develop understanding of how research on specific topics evolves historically. Note that simply organizing papers by publication date is insufficient, as correlations between different research works are overlooked. For the second problem, we must include papers in our generated path that may not be directly related to the queried research topic, but are quite beneficial or essential for understanding the highly related papers in our generated list. Motivated by the above analysis, in this paper, we introduce a new task {\em Reading Path Generation (RPG)}, which seeks to automatically create a reading path for a given query. Our task is designed to assist researchers who are new to a field in conducting rapid surveys by addressing the two problems mentioned above. Specifically, we aim to retrieve a paper list that includes research works highly related to the given query, as well as prerequisite research works that are essential for understanding the highly related works. Furthermore, we organize these papers to form a reading path, which considers both chronological order and correlations between different research works. We hope that by reading the retrieved papers according to the reading path, a user can easily comprehend each research work, rapidly complete a survey and develop a comprehensive understanding of the research history of any topic. Due to the absence of benchmark datasets for evaluating Reading Path Generation, we further propose the {\em SurveyBank} dataset which is specifically designed for our newly proposed task. We create SurveyBank without human labeling based on two key insights. The first insight is that numerous existing high-quality survey papers are already available, and each is authored by professional researchers, encompassing highly valuable information about how to construct a survey on a research topic. Based on this observation, we utilize key phrases extracted from survey titles as inputs for the RPG task, and reading paths inferred from surveys' reference lists as ground truth labels. We initially collect $41,194$ surveys in the field of computer science from Google Scholar and S2ORC \cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc}. Subsequently, $9,321$ high quality surveys are selected to form SurveyBank. It encompasses 10 topics of computer science including Artificial Intelligence, Computer Network and Database. The second key insight is that citation relationships between different papers reflect coherence between different papers. Therefore, we construct a large-scale scientific citation graph with 6 million papers from S2ORC~\cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc} in the field of computer science through citation relationships, and this citation graph covers reference lists of each survey. To the best of our knowledge, SurveyBank is currently the largest survey dataset. Finally, we also propose and implement a Real-time Reading Path Generation System (RePaGer) which accepts key phrases as inputs and generates a reading path of papers for users to read. In RePaGer, we begin by retrieving top-$K$ articles called initial seed papers from Google Scholar. Subsequently, we re-allocate seeds by first capturing neighbors of initial seed papers as seed candidates and then selecting articles with high co-occurrence. We infer that these newly selected seeds are more likely to be prerequisite concepts of a topic since multiple articles directly relevant to the topic cite them in their papers. Finally we propose Node-Edge Weighted Steiner Tree (NWST), a graph optimization-based approach, to identify a reading path with prerequisite chains for a given query. Our model not only considers the importance of each paper in the entire citation network but also accounts for the relationships among them. We conduct extensive evaluations based on the SurveyBank dataset and compare our proposed approach for Reading Path Generation with existing academic search engines and baseline methods. The evaluation results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other baselines and can generate insightful reading paths for different research topics.

The first was that there are a great many excellent survey papers, each of which was written by a professional researcher, and contains highly valuable information about how to write a survey on a topic. It is our hope that by reading the articles in the reading paths, the reader can easily understand each of these papers, quickly assemble a review, and have a comprehensive understanding of the research history of any topic. From Google Scholar and S2ORC [S2ORC 98], we have collected 41,194 scholarly articles. The articles cover 10 topics in the field of computer science, including artificial intelligence, network and database, and are divided into 10 categories. We take advantage of this property to use the title of the paper as the input for the RPG task, and use the title of the reference as the ground truth. The second key insight is that the citation relations between different papers reflect the consistency of those papers. Then we selected 8,321 high-quality papers to build SurveyBank. To the best of our knowledge, SurveyBank is currently the largest collection of survey papers. In the RePaGer system, initial seeds are obtained by obtaining the first K papers from the search results of the Google Scholar search engine. Next, seeds are obtained by extracting the neighboring papers of the initial seeds as candidate seeds, and by selecting articles that have high co-occurrence. In this way, we have constructed a large-scale scientific citation network of 6 million papers from the field of computer science, and this network includes the references cited in each review article. Finally, we propose a graph-based method called NEWT (Node-Edge Weighted Steiner Tree), which enables us to find a reading path for a given query. Our model takes into account the importance of each paper in the citation network, but also the relationship between papers. Finally, we propose a real-time reading path generation system called RePaGer, which can generate a reading path for a given key phrase. Our evaluation based on the SurveyBank dataset shows that our method outperforms other methods and can produce useful reading lists for different topics. We infer that these newly selected seeds are more likely to be pre-requisite concepts for a topic since they are cited by several papers that are directly related to the topic.

text: Learning 3D-aware image synthesis has attracted considerable attention in recent years~\cite{graf, giraffe, pigan}. An emerging approach involves integrating a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)~\cite{nerf} within a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)~\cite{gan}. Specifically, the 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based generator is substituted with a generative implicit function, which transforms raw 3D coordinates to point-wise densities and colors conditioned on the provided latent code. Such an implicit function encodes the structure and texture of the output image within the 3D space. Nevertheless, two problems arise when directly utilizing NeRF~\cite{nerf} in the generator. On one hand, the implicit function in NeRF generates the color and density for each 3D point through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) network. With a highly local receptive field, it becomes challenging for the MLP to represent the underlying structure globally during image synthesis. Therefore, solely utilizing the 3D coordinates as inputs~\cite{graf, pigan, giraffe} lacks sufficient expressiveness to guide the generator with global structure. On the other hand, volume rendering produces the pixel values of the output image independently, which necessitates sampling numerous points along the camera ray for each pixel. The computational cost therefore increases substantially when the image size becomes larger. This may result in inadequate optimization during model training, and subsequently lead to unsatisfactory performance for high-resolution image generation. Previous work has demonstrated that 2D GANs benefit from meaningful representations learned by the generator~\cite{interfacegan, higan, xu2021generative}. Such generative representations characterize a synthesis with \textit{high-level features}. For instance, Xu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{xu2021generative} verify that a face synthesis model recognizes the landmark positions of the output face, and Yang~\textit{et al.}~\cite{higan} identify the multi-level variation factors emerging from generating bedroom images. These representative features encode abundant texture and structure information, thereby improving the synthesis quality~\cite{stylegan} and the controllability~\cite{interfacegan} of image GANs. In contrast, as noted above, existing 3D-aware generative models directly render the pixel values from coordinates~\cite{graf, pigan}, without learning explicit representations. In this work, we propose a novel generative model, termed \textbf{VolumeGAN}, which accomplishes 3D-aware image synthesis through \textit{explicitly learning a structural and a textural representation}. Rather than utilizing the 3D coordinates as inputs, we generate a feature volume using a 3D convolutional network, which encodes the relationships between various spatial regions and thus compensates for the limited receptive field caused by the MLP in NeRF. With the feature volume modeling the underlying structure, we query a coordinate descriptor from the feature volume to characterize the structural information for each 3D point. We then employ a NeRF-like model to construct a feature field, by taking the coordinate descriptor combined with the raw coordinate as the input. The feature field is subsequently accumulated into a 2D feature map as the textural representation, followed by a CNN with $1\times1$ kernel size to ultimately render the output image. In this manner, we separately model the structure and the texture with the 3D feature volume and the 2D feature map, enabling the disentangled control of the shape and the appearance. We evaluate our approach on various datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing alternatives. Regarding image quality, VolumeGAN achieves considerably better Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score~\cite{fid}. Taking the FFHQ dataset~\cite{stylegan} under $256\times256$ resolution as an example, we improve the FID from $36.7$ to $9.1$. We also enable 3D-aware image synthesis on the challenging indoor scene dataset, \textit{i.e.}, LSUN bedroom~\cite{lsun}. Our model also demonstrates stable control of the object pose and exhibits better consistency across different viewpoints, benefiting from the learned structural representation (\textit{i.e.}, the feature volume). Furthermore, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study on the learned structural and textural representations, and analyze the trade-off between the image quality and the 3D property.

text: Data minimisation constitutes a fundamental principle of the European Union's Data Protection Regulation~\citep{regulation2016regulation}, alongside data protection legislation in additional jurisdictions: \begin{quote} "Personal data shall be: [...] adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)" \end{quote} This requirement functions as guidance for respectful data processing practices. Contemporary empirical investigations have demonstrated that replicating the performance of data-driven systems using substantially reduced data quantities is feasible~\cite{biega2020dm, chow2013differential,vincent2019data, wen2018exploring}. These observations result from the diminishing returns that data collection demonstrates throughout various applications and domains~\cite{hestness1712deep, krause2010utility,tae2020slice}. Acknowledging that data limitation remains viable, legal frameworks indicate algorithmic approaches that might be integrated into minimization workflows, encompassing feature selection~\cite{icoDataMinimizationTechniques} or learning curve analysis~\cite{norwegianAuthorityArtificial}. Nevertheless, notwithstanding the availability of multiple algorithmic approaches that could be modified to conform with the minimization requirement, the data minimisation principle has garnered limited attention from the computer science community thus far. As observed by researchers reinvigorating discourse regarding the principle, an absence of concrete mathematical formulations and guidelines represents one of the primary factors impeding adoption~\cite{finckreviving}. Furthermore, qualitative investigations have revealed a deficiency in consistent data minimization standards or comprehension of the principle among software developers~\cite{senarath2018understanding}. Contemporary interpretations of data minimization suggest linking the data collection objective in data-driven systems to performance metrics, an interpretation designated \emph{performance-based data minimization}~\cite{finckreviving,biega2020dm}. Our investigation adheres to this interpretation, examining the question of \emph{how to proactively fulfill the performance-based data minimization principle in machine learning with personal data}. \\ \textbf{Contributions.} In this investigation, we introduce FIDO, a Framework for Inhibiting Data Overcollection, and illustrate how continuous personal data collection might be approached within the context of data minimization. FIDO's primary conceptual contribution involves \emph{adaptively learning an algorithm's performance curve} such that an \emph{appropriate data collection termination point} can be determined precisely. Through modeling the performance curve directly, the framework maintains flexibility across different underlying feature acquisition algorithms and performance definitions. Experiments utilizing multiple datasets within the recommender systems domain validate this flexibility and demonstrate FIDO's capacity to estimate algorithm performance given additional data accurately \emph{without} collecting additional data. The fundamental technical insight FIDO provides resides in its performance curve estimation methodology, which builds upon recent research in machine learning literature that recognizes three distinct phases in learning algorithm performance curves: the small data phase, the power law phase, and the diminishing returns phase \cite{hestness1712deep}. We establish that these performance phases can be observed within the context of user data collection and provide a technique to model the data collection phases directly through adaptively learning a piecewise power law curve. Empirical experiments reveal that alternative approaches to estimate performance curves systematically \emph{overestimate} the return on additional data. Modeling each phase directly enables FIDO to not only learn the performance curve more accurately as data is acquired but also satisfy practical constraints of data minimization. Finally, we investigate issues concerning user-level data minimization. We demonstrate the impacts that algorithmic components such as active feature acquisition (a technique to intelligently select which feature values to acquire) may have on minimization outcomes. We discover that active feature acquisition can result in unequal, concentrated data collection from a limited set of users, alongside decreased minimization performance for evolving user communities or when sensitive features are excluded from initial data collection. We also discover that user-specific performance curves exhibit high variability, where collecting additional data can frequently result in a \emph{decrease} in user-specific performance. This paper aims to provide a computational perspective on the GDPR's principle of data minimization, contributing insights to ongoing discussions regarding the technical implementation of this core data protection principle, and to offer recommendations to practitioners and scholars moving forward.

text: The \textit{Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch} (SCED) constitutes a fundamental optimization model for Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to clear real-time energy markets while ensuring reliable power grid operations \cite{conejo2018power}. In the US, TSOs such as MISO and PJM execute a SCED every five minutes, which necessitates that the optimization problem be solved within an even more restrictive time frame, i.e., well under a minute \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. Security constraints, which enforce robustness against the loss of any individual component, render SCED models particularly challenging for large systems \cite{Chiang2015_SolvingSCOPF,Wang2016_SolvingCorrectiveSCOPF,velloso2021exact} unless only a subset of contingencies is considered. With increasing distributed resources and heightened operational uncertainty, such computational bottlenecks will only become more critical \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. This paper is motivated by the expanding share of renewable generation, particularly wind, in the MISO system, which necessitates risk-aware market-clearing algorithms. One particular challenge is the requirement to perform risk analysis in real time, by solving a large number of scenarios for load and renewable production \cite{werho2021_ScenarioGenerationWind}. However, systematically solving numerous SCED instances is not practical given the stringent constraints of real-time operations. To overcome this computational challenge, this paper proposes to learn an optimization proxy for SCED, i.e., a Machine Learning (ML) model that can predict an optimal solution for SCED, within acceptable numerical tolerances and in milliseconds. It is important to emphasize that the present objective is not to replace optimization-based market-clearing tools. Instead, the proposed optimization proxy provides operators with an additional tool for risk assessment. This enables rapid evaluation of how the system would behave under various scenarios, without the need to run costly optimizations. In particular, because these predictions are combined into aggregated risk metrics, small prediction errors on individual instances are acceptable. \subsection{Related Literature and Challenges} The combination of ML and optimization for power systems has attracted increased attention in recent years. A first thread \cite{pan2019deepopf, fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high, lei2020data, chatzos2021spatial, velloso2020combining, zamzam2020learning, owerko2020optimal} employs ML models to predict an optimal solution to the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) problem. Pan et al. \cite{pan2019deepopf} train a Deep Neural Network (DNN) model to predict solutions to the security-constrained DC-OPFs, and report results on systems with no more than 300 buses. One common limitation of ML models, also noted in \cite{pan2019deepopf}, is that predictions are not guaranteed to satisfy the original problem's constraints. To address this limitation, recent efforts \cite{fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high} integrate Lagrangian duality into the training of DNNs in order to capture the physical and operational constraints of AC-OPFs. A similar approach is pursued in Velloso et al. \cite{velloso2020combining} in the context of preventive security-constrained DC-OPF. Namely, a DNN is trained using Lagrangian duality techniques, then employed as a proxy for the time-consuming master problem in a column-and-constraint generation algorithm. More recently, Chatzos et al. \cite{chatzos2021spatial} embed the Lagrangian duality framework in a two-stage learning that exploits a regional decomposition of the power network, enabling a more efficient distributed training. Another research thread is the integration of ML models within optimization algorithms, in order to improve runtime performance. For instance, a number of papers (e.g., \cite{deka2019learning,misra2021learning,xavier2021learning, yang2020fast,guha2019machine}) attempt to identify active constraints in order to reduce the problem complexity. In \cite{xavier2021learning}, the authors investigate learning feasible solutions to the unit commitment problem. Venzka el al. \cite{venzke2020neural} employ a DNN model to learn the feasible region of a dynamic SCOPF and transform the resulting DNN into a mixed-inter linear program. Existing research papers in ML for power systems typically suffer from two limitations. On the one hand, most papers report numerical results on small academic test systems, which are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than real transmission systems. This is especially concerning, as higher-dimensional data has an adverse impact on convergence and accuracy of machine-learning algorithms. On the other hand, almost all papers rely on artificially-generated data whose distribution does not capture the variability found in actual operations. For instance, only changes in load are considered, typically without capturing spatio-temporal correlations. Other sources of uncertainty, such as renewable production, are not considered, nor is the variability of economic bids. Finally, changes in commitment decisions throughout the day are rarely addressed, although they introduce non-trivial, combinatorial, distribution shifts. \subsection{Contributions and Outline} To address the above limitations, the paper proposes a novel ML pipeline that is grounded in the structure of real-world market operations. The approach leverages the TSO's forward knowledge of 1) commitment decisions and 2) day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable productions. Indeed, both are available by the time the day-ahead market has been executed. Furthermore, the paper presents an in-depth analysis of the real-time market behavior, which informs a novel ML architecture to better capture the nature of actual operations. The proposed learning pipeline is depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:learning_pipeline}. First, commitment decisions and day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable generation are gathered, following the clearing of the day-ahead market. Second, this information is employed to generate a training dataset of SCED instances, using classical data augmentation techniques. Third, specialized ML models are trained, ideally one for each hour of the operating day, thereby alleviating the combinatorial explosion of commitment decisions: each ML model only needs to consider one set of commitments and focus on load/renewable scenarios around the forecasts for that hour. Fourth, throughout the operating day, the trained models are employed in real time to evaluate a large number of scenarios. The entire data-generation and training procedure is completed in a few hours. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:opt_pipeline} describes the interplay between day-ahead and real-time markets in the MISO system, and provides an overview of the real-time SCED for MISO. Section \ref{sec:methodology} analyzes the behavior of the real-time market solutions, proposes a combined Classification-Then-Regression architecture, and presents the overall ML pipeline. Numerical experiments on a real-life system are reported in Section \ref{sec:results}

text: DNA sequencing seeks to determine the genetic composition of individuals. Without delving into specifics regarding the numerous distinct technologies, these procedures identify (fragments of) the genetic sequence. Typically, the primary data analysis comprises, among other procedures, of: 1) alignment against a reference genome, e.g., GRCh38 for human specimens, and 2) variant calling. The primary outcome is a catalog of variants, i.e., a collection of differences that is characteristic for the measured individual (sample), frequently documented in a tabular file such as the Variant Call Format~(VCF)~\cite{vcf}. These variants are utilized in subsequent applications spanning from fundamental and association research investigations to clinical diagnostics. It is beneficial to examine only differences (relative to some reference) since the genome is typically large~(ca.~$3 \cdot 10^9$ nucleotides for humans), while the individual differences between two genomes are comparatively small~(ca.~$0.6\%$~\cite{variation}). When variants are linked with phenotypic characteristics, they are documented in literature and archived with their annotation in (locus specific) databases. Typically, the representation of the variant in VCF is refined to a representation more appropriate for reporting. For this purpose, numerous (domain specific) languages exist. Most prominent are: \begin{itemize} \item Recommendations of the Human Genome Variation Society~(HGVS)~\cite{hgvs}; \item SPDI~\cite{spdi}, the internal data model for variants employed by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI); \item Variant Representation Specification~(VRS)~\cite{vrs}, developed by the Global Alliance for Genomic Health (GA4GH). \end{itemize} These languages endeavor to represent the observed differences in a human-comprehensible and/or machine interpretable fashion and, whereas VCF is implicitly linked to the tooling and configuration employed in the primary data analysis, these representations are process independent and universally interpretable. Within the domain of variant documentation, certain simplifications are common. First, small (local) variants on a single molecular sequence (part of the same haplotype) are documented separately, because this is convenient when storing large quantities of variants in databases. Phasing information, i.e., whether small variants are part of the same haplotype, is frequently lost or incomplete. This is partially a direct consequence of the sequencing technology and partially because this information is eliminated. Second, in certain representations (notably, HGVS) uncertainties might be expressed. Typically, the uncertainties relate to the positioning of the variant within the reference genome, but also the exact composition of larger insertions might be unknown. Finally, unchanged regions may be implicit. During primary data analysis, particularly the alignment step, the sequence from the reference genome is assumed to be present even when direct evidence, e.g., coverage information from the sequencing process, is absent. For the remainder of this paper, we adopt a rigorous view on the nature of variants: \begin{enumerate} \item A variant comprises deletions, insertions or a combination thereof with respect to a single molecular sequence. When these operations occur in combination, they are said to be phased, in cis or part of the same allele and can be documented as phase sets or allele descriptions. Many variant description languages have introduced higher-order operations such as single nucleotide variants (SNV) (termed substitutions in HGVS), multi-nucleotide variants (deletion/insertions), duplications, transpositions, inversions, repeats, etc. We consider all of these concepts to be special cases of the definition provided above. \item We consider only \emph{interpretable} variants, i.e., given a \emph{reference sequence}, there exists a deterministic and unambiguous method of ``applying'' the variants such that the result is the (originally) measured \emph{observed sequence}, cf. the Unix~\texttt{diff} and \texttt{patch} utilities. \end{enumerate} \noindent As is already recognized within the various variant representation languages, it is frequently possible to have multiple representations describing the same observed sequence. These possibilities can originate from the selection of ``operator'', e.g., an SNV can also be represented by a deletion of one nucleotide followed by an insertion of again one nucleotide. Another source contributing to the number of possibilities is the structure of the reference sequence. Consider the reference sequence~\texttt{ATTTA} and the observed sequence~\texttt{ATTA}. One of the symbols~\texttt{T} is eliminated; to specify which one precisely yields a number~($3$) of possibilities. To establish a universally accepted representation of a variant, most variant representation languages employ a \emph{normalization} procedure. Normalization selects a \emph{canonical} representation from the set of possibilities. Unfortunately, this procedure is not standardized across the various languages, e.g., the $3'$-rule in HGVS vs. the $5'$-rule in VCF. Within a particular language, however, proper normalization resolves the problem of identifying \emph{equivalent} variant representations. The implications of utilizing non-normalized variants representations have been reviewed in~\cite{variant_name, variant_calling, curation, litvar}. Solutions to this problem are presented in~\cite{unified, improved_vcf, vmc_spec, smash, plyranges, gql, ask2me, deletions}. Often dedicated tooling~\cite{varsome, validator, mutalyzer, vde} is required to rigorously apply the proposed normalization procedure. Normalized variant representations can be textually compared using standard string matching. \noindent Arguably, identification of equivalent variant representations, i.e., determining whether two variant descriptions yield the same observed sequence, is currently the most compelling query in the variant domain, as it enables the grouping and matching of equivalent variants and their annotations. With the emergence of long read single molecule sequencing technologies (provided by platforms such as those manufactured by Pacific Biosciences and Oxford Nanopore), which are capable of providing direct evidence of numerous small variants that are part of the same haplotype, a more comprehensive set of questions emerges. For example, identification of suballeles, which is of interest in the fields of molecular microbiology (strain typing) and pharmacogenomics (star allele calling), can be accomplished by determining whether the suballele of interest is contained within the observed allele. Minimal sequence level alignments, informally defined as sequences of deletions/insertions that transform one string into another, having shortest length possible, are employed to define relations between given variants of the same reference sequence. Figure~\ref{fig:example} shows an example. In Section~\ref{sec:formal} we precisely define how the relations depend on the set of all alignments between the two sequences. In the example situation the containment relation takes precedence over the overlap relation. In this paper we investigate the relations of variants in an exhaustive manner. In addition to the equivalence relation, we partition the domain of binary variant relations into Boolean relations: equivalence; containment, i.e., either a variant is fully contained in another or a variant fully contains another; overlap, i.e., two variants have (at least) one common element; and disjoint, i.e., no common elements. Due to this partitioning, exactly one of the aforementioned relations is true for every pair of variants. For determining the relation, we consider all (minimal) variant representations simultaneously.

text: The Tresillo constitutes a rhythm that originated in Africa and was transported to the Caribbean during the Atlantic Slave Trade period. Having gained popularity in Cuba, the rhythm subsequently disseminated worldwide from that location\cite{acquista2009tresillo, floyd1999black}, and can be encountered across numerous musical genres. \par While functioning as a primary rhythm independently, the Tresillo is also employed as a rhythmic pattern within other rhythms such as the Reggaeton rhythm or the Clave rhythm. Based on \cite {floyd1999black}, the Tresillo rhythm can be defined as follows (see Figure \ref{fig:tresillo}). The rhythmic pattern comprises a dotted eighth note, succeeded by a sixteenth note, an eighth rest and an eighth note and is reiterated twice within a 4/4 measure. When one incorporates a beat on all quarter notes to the rhythm, one derives the Reggaeton rhythm (see Figure \ref{fig:reggaeton}). By modifying the second half of the measure to an eighth rest, two eighth notes and another eighth rest, one generates the fundamental Clave rhythm pattern (see Figure \ref{fig:clave}). The Tresillo rhythm is frequently employed in Latin American music. Nevertheless, the utilization of this ``danceable Cuban Clave son"\cite{sethares2014geometry} is not confined to Latin American music exclusively, but has also penetrated the rhythmic sections of Western music \cite{sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic}. Notable contemporary examples include compositions such as ``Shape of you" by Ed Sheeran or ``Cheap Thrills" by Sia, both achieving top positions on the Billboard Charts. Additional examination of the pop charts by the authors through auditory analysis of the Billboard Charts validates the consistent employment of this rhythm in Pop Music. While the utilization, evolution and popularity of the Tresillo rhythm has been investigated in qualitative studies \cite{acquista2009tresillo, sandroni2001tresillo, sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic, floyd1999black}, the prevalence of this rhythm has not been examined quantitatively previously. In pursuit of a methodology to investigate the usage of this particular rhythm, we developed an approach to computationally represent the primary rhythm of a pop song and the Tresillo rhythm and compare both using different similarity measurements. Given these similarity measures, a distinctive temporal trend in Tresillo usage can be identified in the US Billboard Top 20 Charts of the past 20 years (1999-2019). \par This paper proceeds as follows: Initially, the secondary literature from several different fields, which are pertinent to this paper, will be examined. Subsequently, several assumptions necessary to conduct the presented analysis will be articulated in the problem statement section. The Data section discusses the selected data sources and data format for the analysis. In the method section, the final data representation, the proposed rhythm similarity measures and evaluation metrics are presented and explained. In the results section, the different rhythm similarity measures are evaluated and compared. The results section also encompasses a description and analysis of the temporal trend. The paper concludes with a discussion of the selected methods and obtained results. Furthermore, a potential interpretation of the generated results is presented. Finally, we propose possible extensions of the presented work.

text: Legged robots exhibit exceptional versatility and can be deployed across diverse application domains. However, robust locomotion remains a complex challenge requiring continued investigation. {Stability and safety} constitute fundamental prerequisites for robotic operation in real-world environments. The question arises: given legged robots' versatility, why do they not yet match human capabilities? To attain the intended versatility, we examined the fundamental aspects of learning balance recovery strategies. Humans employ multiple strategies (e.g., arm movement, ankle adjustment, hip positioning, stepping, etc.) to restore balance following external disturbances. They depend on prior experiences to refine their approaches. Furthermore, we examined existing bipedal robot locomotion frameworks. Although their stability has improved substantially, they remain insufficiently stable and safe for deployment in everyday environments. Multiple approaches for stabilizing bipedal robots have been proposed, which can be classified into three principal categories. Throughout the remainder of this section, these categories will be presented and recent contributions within each category will be concisely reviewed. \subsection{Analytical Approaches} The fundamental principle underlying approaches in this category involves utilizing a robot dynamics model and designing controller sets (e.g., force controller~\cite{mason2016balancing}, hybrid position/force~\cite{faraji2019bipedal}, admittance controller~\cite{caron2020icra}) based on specific criteria to minimize tracking error. The most extensively employed model in literature is the Linear Inverted Pendulum~(LIP) which abstracts the robot's overall dynamics as a single mass. It constrains the mass's vertical movement to provide a linear model that yields rapid solutions for real-time implementations. This model has been examined and extended over decades to design and analyze legged robot locomotion~\cite{takenaka2009real,englsberger2015three}. Takaneka et al.~\cite{takenaka2009real} introduced the Divergent Component of Motion~(DCM) concept that decomposes the LIP's dynamics into stable and unstable components, such that controlling the unstable component suffices for maintaining stability. In~\cite{englsberger2015three}, DCM was extended to 3D and multiple control approaches including classical feedback controllers~\cite{morisawa2014biped}, Linear Quadratic Regulator~(LQR)-based methods~\cite{faraji2019bipedal,8967778} and Model Predictive Control~(MPC)~\cite{ brasseur2015robust} have been proposed to formulate bipedal locomotion frameworks. All approaches attempt to compensate tracking error by employing a combination of three strategies: manipulating the Ground Reaction Force~(GRF) and modifying the position and timing of the subsequent step. Recently, researchers are exploring the relaxation of LIP assumptions (e.g., COM vertical motion and angular momentum) which necessitates addressing nonlinearities~\cite{caron2020icra, kajita2018biped, seyde2018inclusion}. \vspace{-2mm} \subsection{Machine Learning Approaches} The approaches within this category are designed to learn feasible policies through environmental interaction. Currently, Deep Reinforcement Learning~(DRL) has demonstrated its capability by solving complex locomotion and manipulation tasks, which typically comprise high-dimensional continuous observation and action spaces~\cite{gu2017deep,abreu2019learning}. Data augmentation in DRL is extensively utilized to enhance optimization performance; however, in this work, we limit the scope to symmetry-oriented solutions. The process of generating symmetric data from actual samples is employed to improve various robotic tasks~\cite{lin2020robotics}, including walking gaits of diverse humanoid models~\cite{abdolhosseini2019learning} and quadrupedal robots~\cite{mishra2019augmenting} (with multiple symmetry planes). Learning from scratch with DRL can achieve highly efficient behaviors, even in asymmetrical configurations~\cite{Abreu2019runfaster}. Nevertheless, if not regulated through model restrictions (e.g., symmetry, pattern generators), it can be challenging to produce human-like behaviors within reasonable timeframes. \subsection{Hybrid Approaches: combing analytical and learning} The approaches within this category focus on combining the potential of both aforementioned categories. To accomplish this, learning algorithms can be integrated with model-based gait pattern generators to predict parameters and learn residual dynamics (compensatory actions), which can yield remarkably accurate behaviors~\cite{koryakovskiy2018model,ahn2020data}. These frameworks typically comprise multiple layers connected in hierarchical structures. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2018learning} designed a hierarchical framework to ensure humanoid robot stability by learning motor skills. Their framework consisted of two independent layers: the high-level layer generates joint angle sets and the low-level layer translates those angles to joint torques using PD controller sets. Their reward function comprised six distinct terms primarily related to traditional push recovery strategies, and was obtained by summing all terms with different weights. \subsection{Overview of the Proposed Framework and Contributions} This work focuses on bipedal locomotion which represents the most challenging aspect in legged robotics. Particularly, we aim to address an intriguing question of whether a learning algorithm can learn to control and modulate a model-based control policy such as a gait pattern generator. Our contributions are the following: \textbf{(i)} we developed a locomotion framework for humanoid robots that integrates both analytical control and machine learning. An overview of this system is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:Cover}. Specifically, we employ an abstract dynamics model to analytically formulate closed-loop bipedal locomotion and recovery strategies as a kernel, and combine it with a symmetry-enhanced optimization framework using Proximal Policy Optimization~(PPO)~\cite{schulman2017ppo} to learn residual dynamics. The learned policy adjusts pattern generator parameter sets and generates compensatory actions as residual dynamics to regain stability; \textbf{(ii)} we proposed a learning method where data is only partially augmented, leveraging symmetry to improve learning time and human-likeness without restricting asymmetric movements, thus expanding the range of possible behaviors. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: In Section~\ref{sec:pattern}, the architecture of our fully parametric kernel pattern generator will be presented and each module will be explained. Subsequently, in Section~\ref{sec:learningResidual}, our learning framework will be introduced and we will explain how we augmented this framework with the kernel pattern generator to regulate kernel parameters and learn model-free skills~(generating compensatory joint positions). In Section~\ref{sec:simScenarios}, simulation scenario sets will be designed to validate the proposed framework's performance. Subsequently, in Section~\ref{sec:simulations}, extensive simulations will be conducted to provide assessments and analysis regarding overall performance, optimized policy behavior, symmetry, and robustness. Finally, conclusions and future research are presented in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: The objective of this paper is to examine the Parallel Drone Scheduling Traveling Salesman Problem (PDSTSP) defined as follows. We are provided with a complete undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ with the set of vertices $V=\{0,1,...,n, n+1\}$ and the set of edges $E=\{(i, j): i, j \in V, i < j\}$. Vertex 0 denotes the depot while vertex $n+1$ constitutes a copy of the depot vertex and is established for modeling purposes. The remaining vertices constitute the set of customers $V_c$. At the depot, there exists a truck and a set $D$ of $m$ drones available for delivery operations. Denote a subset of \textit{drone-eligible} customers $V_{d}\subseteq V_c$, whose distance from the depot and parcel weight can be accommodated by drones. The set of customers which must be served by the truck is represented by $V_{t}=V_c \setminus V_d$. The travel time from node $i$ to node $j$ of the truck is designated as $t_{ij}$. The time required by a drone to service customer $i$ is designated as $t'_i$, which is computed by doubling the time of flying from the depot to customer $i$. The PDSTSP involves constructing a set of routes for the truck and the fleet of drones such that: (i) every customer vertex is visited exactly once by either truck or drone; (ii) the truck route commences and terminates at the depot; (iii) the drone executes back-and-forth trips from the depot to serve several customers (one customer for each single trip); (iv) the completion time required to serve all customers and return all vehicles to the depot, is minimized. The PDSTSP has attracted considerable attention from the literature since its initial introduction in \citet*{murray2015flying}. The authors propose a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation to model the problem and design a simple heuristic. The latter method partitions the customers into two subsets, one for the truck and one for the drones. Two subproblems: the TSP and the Parallel Machine Scheduling (PMS) problem, defined on two customer sets, are independently solved to construct the truck tour and drone tours, respectively. Additionally, an improvement step is executed to reassign customers either to the drone set or to the truck to better balance the truck and drones' activities. The solution approaches are evaluated on small instances with up to 20 customers. Numerous attempts have been made to efficiently solve larger PDSTSP instances. \citet*{mbiadou2018iterative} propose the first metaheuristic, termed iterative two-step heuristic method. The first step constructs a customer sequence (also termed a giant or TSP tour) that visits all the customers. In the second step, dynamic programming is employed to split the giant tour into a truck tour and a set of trips for the drones, creating a complete PDSTSP solution. The method is evaluated on newly generated instances with up to 229 customers. \citet*{dell2020matheuristic} subsequently propose a matheuristic in which the authors employ the same concept as found in \cite*{mbiadou2018iterative}. However, instead of dynamic programming, a MILP approach is utilized to handle the second step. The obtained results demonstrate that the algorithm is slower but provides superior solutions than the heuristic of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. A nature-inspired algorithm termed Hybrid Ant Colony Optimization (HACO) is proposed in \citet*{Dinh2021}. The algorithm reuses the concept of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} that represents a PDSTSP solution as a permutation of all customers. However, the authors propose a novel dynamic programming with a controllable amount of states while exploring broader solution space to split the giant tour into a complete PDSTSP solution. Several problem-tailored components such as local search and solution construction also play crucial roles in improving the performance of the algorithm. When evaluated on benchmark instances from the literature, the HACO algorithm outperforms the two existing metaheuristics in terms of both running time and solution quality. The most recent metaheuristic for the PDSTSP is a Ruin-and-Recreate algorithm termed Slack Induction by String and Sweep Removals (SISSR) introduced in \cite{Nguyen2021}. Exploiting PDSTSP solution characteristics in an effective manner, the metaheuristic manages to introduce ``sufficient" space to a solution via new removal operators during the ruin phase. It is anticipated to enhance the possibilities for improving solutions later in the recreate phase. Also in \cite{Nguyen2021}, the authors introduce a novel variant of the PDSTSP termed PDSVRP in which they allow multiple trucks and consider the objective of minimizing the total transportation costs. \citet*{Raj2021} present a variant of the PDSVRP problem in which they consider the objective function that minimizes the completion time all the vehicles return to the depot. The authors propose three MILP formulations and develop a branch-and-price (BAP) algorithm and a BAP-based heuristic to solve the problem. The authors report that their exact methods can solve to optimality all the small PDSTSP instances of \cite{murray2015flying} and 3 instances with 52 customers of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. Most recently, \citet*{MBIADOUSALEU2021} generalize the PDSTSP problem in the same manner as the PDSVRP. The problem is termed the Parallel Drone Scheduling Multiple Traveling Salesman Problem. A hybrid Iterated Local Search is proposed. A MILP formulation and a simple branch-and-cut approach are also designed to solve small instances. As mentioned above, most approaches proposed to solve the PDSTSP belong to the class of heuristic methods. To the best of our knowledge, the results of exact algorithms for the problem are quite limited. Only optimal results obtained on small instances with no more than 20 customers and three instances with 52 customers are provided in \cite{murray2015flying, dell2020matheuristic, Raj2021}. Optimal solutions for 87 over 90 benchmark instances with up to 229 customers created by \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} have never been documented. The primary motivation of this paper is to address this methodological gap by proposing a simple, yet efficient exact branch-and-cut (B\&C) algorithm for the PDSTSP. The experimental results on the currently largest problem instances of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} demonstrate that the developed solution approach can solve all but two instances in reasonable running time. To provide more challenging instances to test solution methods in the future, we introduce a novel set of instances with up to 600 customers. We report the results of the state-of-the-art algorithms obtained on these instances to further investigate their performance. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec-formulation} describe our MILP formulation along with numerous valid inequalities, upon which the branch-and-cut algorithm is proposed in Section \ref{sec-method}. Section \ref{sec-experiment} reports experimental results and Section \ref{sec-conclusion} concludes our research.

text: In global endeavors toward addressing climate change and transitioning to sustainable energy sources, there has been substantial growth in developments and advancements of wind power systems in recent years \cite{darwish_al-dabbagh_2020}. Nevertheless, the complexity of environments in which wind turbines continue to be deployed, particularly offshore, regularly results in irregular loads, operational inconsistencies and failures in various electrical and mechanical sub-components within the turbine \cite{windenergy_journal}. Operations \& maintenance (O\&M) is essential to address such problems through fault detection and diagnosis \cite{ATTOUI201411}, and currently accounts for up to one-third of the total cost of energy generation \cite{seyr_muskulus_2019}. Condition-based monitoring (CBM) \cite{STETCO2019620} serves a crucial role in O\&M, by enabling monitoring of operational changes and anomalies in the turbine and its sub-components. In the past decade, there has been growing interest in utilizing signal-processing techniques and physics-based modeling for CBM. More recently, the wind industry has witnessed application of Artificial intelligence (AI) techniques toward data-driven decision making in O\&M, by utilizing the Supervisory Control \& Acquisition (SCADA) data generated by various sensors in the turbine at regular intervals. There have been some applications of Explainable AI (XAI) models \cite{BARREDOARRIETA202082,8329419,app10093258}, which can provide interpretations and reasoning behind predictions made by the conventionally black-box AI models during decision support, such as feature importances for SCADA parameters leading to faults \cite{windenergy_journal}. Such techniques have demonstrated immense success, particularly for anomaly prediction in turbine sub-components \cite{anomaly_paperhongshan,electronics9050751,Bo_2019}, wind resource assessment \cite{MURTHY20171320,DAI2017378} and forecasting vital operational parameters \cite{CHEN2018414,RePEc:eee:appene:v:241:y:2019:i:c:p:229-244,RePEc:eee:energy:v:201:y:2020:i:c:s0360544220308008} with high accuracy, which can be vital to improve the utilization efficiency of wind energy \cite{LIU2020113324}. However, they fail to provide contextualized information (e.g. in the form of comprehensive descriptions of failures and maintenance reports to fix/avert such inconsistencies), which is essential to achieve ambient intelligence during decision support. More importantly, these techniques do not present a concrete basis to serve as the generic foundation for critical concepts in the wind industry, pertaining to maintenance strategies and their relationship with other sources of heterogeneous information, such as SCADA data from sensors, alarm logs, images describing failures and prognostic actions etc. Knowledge bases (KBs) or knowledge graphs (KGs) serve an integral role in supporting effective and informed decision making, by interlinking heterogeneous entities (such as numerical data from sensors) with contextualized and semantic information \cite{amador-paper-kg}. KGs have been successfully utilized for optimal decision support in several safety-critical applications such as healthcare for clinical decision support \cite{health_semantic}, power systems for optimizing service processes \cite{Yuan_2018}, manufacturing for process safety management \cite{MAO2020107094}, finance for making business decisions \cite{kg_finance_yang} etc. Given the multidisciplinary nature of construction and management of wind farms as well as the presence of multiple sub-systems interacting with other sub-systems and various external components, a systematic organization of knowledge in the wind industry can serve an integral role in assisting developers, designers and researchers to utilize such domain-specific information for decision support \cite{wes-5-259-2020}. In comparison to other disciplines, the wind industry has witnessed very limited application of KGs for explainable decision support. In an early work in this area, Zhu et al. \cite{4470371} developed a wind power plant information model by utilizing the web ontology language (OWL) for systematic management of domain-specific information. The proposed ontology in the paper consists of conceptual information for wind power plant management with multiple classes based on different types of turbines, their functional parts etc., embedded as semantic information with corresponding OWL descriptions. While the paper demonstrates immense promise of graph databases for managing complex information in the wind industry through its conceptual overview, it does not provide a practical demonstration of the proposed ontology, including its use-cases in real-world information management in the wind energy domain. Moreover, there is no mention of the applicability of the proposed ontology for O\&M, particularly to facilitate decision support in real-world turbines. Küçük and Arslan \cite{KUCUK2014484} utilized web resources, specifically from Wikipedia, to develop a domain ontology for the wind energy sector. Their ontology is constructed semi-automatically and provides extensive coverage of the wind energy domain as a discipline, including terms like meteorological data, sub-components of the turbine, monitoring and control system etc. This can be useful for utilization in question-answering systems during information retrieval, wherein specific segments of natural language texts from the Wikipedia articles relevant to the end user can be accessed easily. While the semi-automatic construction of the ontology is less time consuming and a simpler process, it cannot provide low-level details pertaining to the wind industry and O\&M of turbines. Moreover, it lacks the ability to provide a coherent view on critical aspects in CBM, including the role of SCADA data for anomaly prediction and power forecasting, maintenance tasks for failures in the turbine and its sub-components and more comprehensive and technically detailed descriptions for engineers \& technicians beyond the Wikipedia articles. The role of the KG for utilization in real-world decision support systems is also not showcased in the paper. In another study, Quaeghebeur et al. \cite{wes-5-259-2020} proposed a graph database for the wind energy domain, consisting of a conceptual overview of several important terms and parameters in the wind energy sector, such as power curves, associated relationships between turbine sub-components, mathematical and statistical distributions for modeling vital parameters etc. The KG for this study was developed from the ground up by the authors, and provides a foundational ontology for the wind turbine as a system with a specific focus on offshore wind power. Similar to Zhu et al. \cite{4470371}, their focus is on developing knowledge representations and structured information pertaining to the wind industry. The paper provides significant information and descriptions which can be queried from the KG, being particularly beneficial for the purposes of education and training. However, the proposed KG does not contain any description of different types of faults which occur in real-world turbines, varieties of alarms and their relationship to turbine sub-components and maintenance action strategies to fix/avert the failures. More importantly, it does not demonstrate the applicability of the KG for O\&M, and its use-cases for explainable decision support in real-world practical scenarios. As evident, while these few existing studies have demonstrated the promise of utilizing KGs for systematically structuring conceptual information in the wind industry, they only serve as an endpoint \cite{amador-paper-kg} providing information for consultation without the ability to further reason over the data. Moreover, these ontologies need to be queried manually through specialized programming languages to extract relevant and meaningful information, which may not be easily accessible to turbine engineers \& technicians. The existing studies clearly do not focus on the critical aspects of O\&M, and their utility in decision-making systems for tasks such as recommendations and predictions. We believe that the optimal utility of KGs for decision support in the wind industry can only be realized by integrating conceptual information on O\&M with other heterogeneous data, such as SCADA parameters from sensors, alarm types, turbine sub-components preventive/predictive/corrective maintenance action strategies etc. and their associated relationships. In this paper, we propose the role of KGs for explainable decision support in the wind industry, and their utility in real-world applications for O\&M. We present a novel KG, \textit{XAI4Wind} and develop the domain-specific ontology for O\&M in the wind industry manually. The proposed KG currently contains 537 nodes and 1059 relationships (of 9 different types), and includes several types of heterogeneous data such as descriptions of various types of SCADA features, alarm types, turbine sub-components and maintenance action strategies. To demonstrate use-cases, we show that the KG can be queried interactively in Neo4j and graph data science algorithms can be applied to generate novel insights during O\&M. Notably, we utilize SCADA data from an operational turbine
