text: Video retrieval represents one of the most prominent and challenging problems in the contemporary digital landscape. It constitutes the task of ranking videos within a database according to their relevance to user-provided input queries. Although most practical applications utilize video metadata to transform the problem into a straightforward page ranking problem, extensive databases of videos exist without labeled metadata. User queries may assume multiple forms. The most prevalent form of input is textual input. One of the most widely available public applications of text-to-video retrieval is Google's video search. Its performance, however, is driven by the metadata of the videos within its search space. Some research has been published in recent years on video retrieval through text queries and the performance in this task has improved over the years. In this paper, we focus our efforts on video retrieval through image queries, where an even more limited degree of research has been conducted. There are also drawbacks in most methods proposed thus far and there are many challenges that any proposed method needs to overcome. The greatest of those challenges is to find an efficient method of storing the videos in your search database. The next significant challenge that has not been solved yet is to tap into the temporal information contained in video data. While image classification and object detection tasks in images have been demonstrated to work exceptionally well in recent years, simply searching for objects in the frames of a video would fail to utilize the temporal information contained in videos. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to solve this problem. We first preprocess a video database to extract key features from video frames. These features are clustered, such that similar frames end up in the same cluster. We generate the embeddings for these clusters by aggregating the embeddings of their constituent frames. To account for temporal information in videos, we model these clusters as nodes in a graph. Then, the cluster embeddings are augmented by incorporating neighboring cluster information. These augmented cluster embeddings are stored and used in our video ranking process. The proposed method was tested on the MSR-VTT dataset.

text: Next-generation cellular communication systems are anticipated to further enhance the diversity of applications delivered by 5G systems \cite{yazar6g}. These systems will offer a highly adaptable platform capable of providing features such as integrated sensing, flexible multi-band utilization, intelligent, sustainable and secure communications. In next-generation cellular communication, \ac{AI}, integrated sensing and communication are anticipated to serve as key enablers. \ac{V2X} or autonomous driving has already garnered significant attention in recent years and is anticipated to be utilized in next-generation communication systems. For instance, the convergence of \ac{MEC} and blockchain technologies for a novel robust, resilient, and reliable architecture for V2X communications is proposed in \cite{khan2021robust}. With the recent industrial achievements from Google's Waymo, Baidu's Apollo and Tesla's Autopilot technologies \cite{Cusumano}, full self-driving capabilities are feasible in the future. Nevertheless, the underlying secure communication technologies that support them remain in their infancy. In the security domain, quantum computers are gradually being developed by numerous prominent \ac{IT} and cloud companies (Google, IBM, Honeywell and Microsoft). In the long term, quantum computers are anticipated to achieve quantum supremacy and recent industrial work by Google has demonstrated that these claims are feasible \cite{arute2019quantum}. Devices and computers with quantum capabilities possess the ability to respond rapidly to complex problems by executing numerous operations simultaneously. Quantum-capable devices can also be employed to attack security protocols established between network devices (such as \ac{TLS}, \ac{DTLS}, \ac{IPSec}, etc.), compromise encryption schemes used in security protocols, and expose secure communications. In this scenario, algorithms resistant to quantum attacks in security protocols operated between mobile network devices must be utilized. Thus, secure communication can be established in the mobile network. \ac{NIST} is currently addressing this issue and has organized a competition to select the optimal algorithm that is resistant to quantum attacks. Algorithms such as NTRU, Saber and Kyber have already advanced to the final round of the \ac{NIST} competition \cite{NIST_comp}. After the \ac{NIST} competition concludes, one algorithm will be selected as the standard \ac{QRSA} and implemented in all devices as a consequence (such as \ac{AES}/\ac{DES}, which are the result of the previous \ac{NIST} competition and are widely used today). Currently, existing encryption algorithms can be implemented in software and hardware of mobile devices to ensure the operation of the security protocol. However, a significant problem emerges when implementing \glspl{QRSA}. This problem involves determining how to perform the computational processes within the algorithm. In the examination of existing \glspl{QRSA} such as NTRU, Saber, Kyber, the burden on the \ac{CPU} cores of the devices for computing mathematical operations with very high-order polynomials is substantial. The computational processes for existing encryption algorithms such as \ac{AES}, \ac{ECC} etc. are already in use and the existing hardware capabilities of the devices can support these types of operations. However for \glspl{QRSA}, we are addressing very high-degree polynomials. Therefore, the computational resources required for \glspl{QRSA} on the devices are greater than the resources required for the encryption algorithms already in use. For this reason, it is extremely challenging to perform computations for a \ac{QRSA} based on high-order polynomials with the currently available software and hardware. To address this problem, an efficient computation and orchestration framework is needed that is cognizant of the entire topological view of the mobile and \ac{V2X} network and can perform different computation methods for each \ac{QRSA}. To this end, the following contributions are made in this paper: \begin{itemize} \item We discuss key concepts and present the integration of post-quantum and mobile network connectivity through the \ac{SCO} framework with potential use cases. (Section \ref{Background} and \ref{frameworks}) \item We evaluate how post-quantum methods can be integrated into mobile networks via simulation analysis and discuss the evaluation results.(Section \ref{experiments}) \item From a standardization perspective, we describe current \glspl{SDO} efforts and their potential contributions to network management and orchestration and post-quantum technologies. (Section \ref{standardization}) \end{itemize}

Recent achievements in V2X include those of Waymo, Baidu Apollo and the Tesla AutoPilot. The technology for V2V communications, however, is still in its infancy. For example, a V2V architecture that uses both MEC and the Blockchain has been proposed. In the area of security, quantum computers are being developed in stages by some of the world's best-known cloud and IT companies, including Google, IBM, Honeywell, and Microsoft. In the long run, they are expected to achieve quantum supremacy, and recent industrial research by Google shows that such claims are possible. A device or a computer that can perform a series of operations simultaneously can quickly solve complex problems. In this case, the cellular network must employ encryption methods resistant to quantum attacks in its security protocols between its nodes. The devices and the computers whose functions can do so can resolve complex problems quickly by doing several things simultaneously. NIST has been working on this problem, and has organized a competition to find the best resistant to quantum attacks. One of them will be chosen as a standard, and implemented in all devices (like the AES/DES standard, which was a result of a previous NIST competition, and is now in use). Until the NIST competition is over, the NTRU, Saber, and Kyber algorithms can be used in both the hardware and the software of portable devices to guarantee the security protocol. The operation of the currently used encryptions like AES, ECC, etc., are already well-established, and the current capabilities of the devices are sufficient to support such operations. When it comes to QRSA, a major problem arises. The acCPU cores of the devices used to analyze the currently available QRSA like NTRU, Saber, and Kyber are overloaded to execute mathematical operations with very high-order polynomials. So the amount of calculation required for QRSA is much greater than for the resources needed for current encryption methods. For QRSA, the degree of polynomials is extremely high, so the amount of computation required is much greater than for current encryption methods. An efficient computing and synchronization framework is needed that is able to access the topology of the cellular and V2X network and execute the different methods of calculation for each QRSA. The following are the main contributions of this paper. I. The paper discusses the main concepts, and introduces the integration of mobile networks and post-quantum network, using the SCO framework, with the potential use cases. II. To solve the above problem, an efficient computing and orchestration framework is needed, which takes into account the topological structure of the mobile and V2X network and can be used for different calculations for each QRSA. II. We discuss the evaluation results from the simulation analysis. III. IV. (Section IV. Standardization.) We describe the current standardization efforts of GSDO, and the potential contribution of post-quantum technology to network management and orchestration.

text: In recommender systems, the user-item interactions and their associated side information can be modeled as a graph comprising a collection of objects~(nodes) and their relationships~(edges). Since these graphs inherently contain at least two distinct node types, namely user $u$ and item $v$, they constitute heterogeneous graphs (heterographs for brevity). Given the substantial expressive capacity of these graphs and the accelerated advancement of graph-based methodologies~\cite{kipf2016gcn, schlichtkrull2018rgcn, wu2019simplifying, chen2020simple}, graph-based recommendation approaches~\cite{wang2019ngcf, chen2020revisiting, he2020lightgcn, wang2018ripplenet, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat, fan2019graph, Liu2020Hetero} have garnered considerable attention in recent years. To obtain more effective representations, certain researchers attempt to leverage the structure of interaction graphs by propagating user and item embeddings across them. For instance, motivated by the graph convolutional network~(GCN)~\cite{kipf2016gcn}, Wang \emph{et al.} introduce NGCF (neural graph collaborative filtering)~\cite{wang2019ngcf} to generate more effective embeddings. Subsequently, both LR-GCCF (linear residual graph convolutional collaborative filtering)~\cite{chen2020revisiting} and LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} demonstrate that eliminating certain components from standard GCN (including non-linear activation and feature transformation) can produce superior performance for collaborative filtering (CF). Despite achieving notable progress, existing graph-based representation learning approaches continue to face the data sparsity challenge, which is prevalent in real-world recommendation scenarios. Since the aforementioned approaches are not specifically designed to tackle this challenge, they may experience substantial performance deterioration when confronted with it. One conventional solution to mitigate this challenge involves incorporating side information~\cite{GUO2017202}, which can augment indirect node connections or enrich node features. The recommendation-related textual information encompasses abundant side information, yet most existing efforts~\cite{Wang2019kgcn, fan2019graph, wang2019kgat} that incorporate side information disregard it, thereby constraining their performance. To mitigate the data sparsity challenge, similar to HGNR~(heterogeneous graph neural recommendation)~\cite{Liu2020Hetero}, based on the interaction graph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(a)), we incorporate description and comment nodes to construct our heterograph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(b)). However, it is noteworthy that merely adding these nodes cannot enhance indirect connections between users and items. Nonetheless, the text nodes themselves encompass abundant features, which are beneficial for adjusting the embeddings of users and items. Motivated by this observation, we employ advanced natural language processing~(NLP) techniques to initialize the embeddings of text nodes, thereby integrating semantics to enhance representational capacity. Through node information propagation, the embeddings of users and items will incorporate textual knowledge, which can effectively help mitigate the data sparsity challenge. HGNR employs standard GCN to learn embeddings on heterographs. In other words, it converts the heterogeneous learning process to a homogeneous one, which may result in unintended information loss and performance degradation. By iteratively applying the GCN framework across different relations, RGCN (Relational Graph Convolutional Network) has been demonstrated to be capable of handling the highly multi-relational data characteristics on heterographs~\cite{schlichtkrull2018rgcn}. In light of this, applying RGCN to propagate information on heterographs represents a superior choice. However, simply employing the standard RGCN is not optimal, since to distinguish different relations, the standard RGCN typically has a larger parameter scale than GCN on the same heterograph, which renders the training of RGCN-based models challenging and inefficient. To address this issue, we propose a modified RGCN to propagate information on heterographs in this work. First, it has been established in \cite{wu2019simplifying, he2020lightgcn} that feature transformation and non-linear activation of standard GCN contribute minimally to CF performance. Similarly, we discard these two components to simplify RGCN and consequently improve its performance and efficiency. Second, we adopt the weighted layer combination from LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} and the initial residual from GCNII~\cite{chen2020simple} to further modify RGCN for enhanced performance. The experimental results demonstrate that the aforementioned modifications to RGCN can significantly improve recommendation performance. After deriving efficient user and item embeddings through feature propagation of the modified RGCN, another crucial component of the recommender system is the matching function. Nearly all existing graph-based representation learning methods employ inner product as the matching function~\cite{wang2019ngcf, he2020lightgcn, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat}. However, in the heterographs constructed by us, both description and comment nodes contain rich semantics, and the simple linear inner product is inadequate for these complex features. To handle the semantic features learned by GNN from heterographs, GraphRec~\cite{fan2019graph} concatenated latent factors of users and items and employed an MLP (multi-layer perception) to predict ratings. Meanwhile, DeepCF~\cite{deng2019deepcf}, which applies MLP neural networks on user-item interaction matrices, combines the strengths of neural representation learning and neural matching function learning to overcome their respective limitations. Inspired by GraphRec and DeepCF, we design a predictive network that integrates graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning to better capture semantics. Specifically, the combination of graph-based representation learning and neural matching function learning can capture low-rank user-item relations and learn complex matching functions jointly. To summarize, the primary contributions of our work in this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We construct a heterograph and initialize the embeddings of text nodes with advanced NLP techniques to exploit knowledge in related textual information. Subsequently, by employing a modified RGCN, the semantics in these text nodes can be propagated to derive representations of users and items. \item Considering that inner product is inadequate for complex semantics, we propose a predictive framework that combines graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning for improved predictions. \item Extensive experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets, and the results verify the superior performance of our method compared to several baselines. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section~\ref{sec: relatedwork} discusses related work; Section~\ref{sec: method} details the proposed model; Section~\ref{sec: experiment} presents and analyzes the experimental results; Finally, Section~\ref{sec: conclusion} concludes this paper.

text: Atrial Fibrillation represents a cardiac condition that may remain undiagnosed for years unless a cardiac specialist examines the patient's ECG report. AF impacts approximately 1\% of the population \cite{zoni2014epidemiology}). Approximately 2.3 million cases exist in the United States. For early detection and reduction in case numbers, ECG signals can be analyzed utilizing advanced AI methodologies. ECG signals constitute time-series data that can be subjected to analysis. We can identify AF by detecting irregularities within the ECG signal. Figure 1 illustrates a normal ECG signal. The letters P, Q, R, S and T represent the distinct components of the heart: atria and ventricles through which electrical signals propagate.\\ The waveform characteristics for AF are distinguished by: \\ 1) Absence of p waves. \\ 2) The intervals between R points are not consistent throughout the signal.\\ Both of these characteristics can be observed in Figure 2 which illustrates the ECG signal for AF. The challenges in identifying AF through ECG analysis include:\\ 1) ECG signals contain random, low-frequency, and susceptible components, resulting in unstable diagnostic outcomes. \cite{wu2020study}.\\ 2) Manual interpretation of ECG signals is subjective and prone to inter-observer variability since non-AF signals may also demonstrate irregular RR intervals and absent P waves \cite{nurmaini2020robust}.

text: For autonomous vehicles to function effectively as traffic management systems \cite{wu2017flow}, secure navigation around human-operated vehicles on highways and in urban environments is essential. Nevertheless, secure navigation can be challenging to achieve because substantial uncertainty exists in actual driving scenarios that complicate the driving problem. Generally, Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis (HJI) can be employed to identify safe strategies around unknown components of a dynamical system \cite{bansal2017hamilton}. In prior work, researchers develop \cite{fisac2018general} a framework to safeguard a system against one known source of uncertainty using Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, with the objective of protecting the system from the worst-case scenario. Nevertheless, in actual driving scenarios, it may be essential to consider multiple sources of uncertainty. As illustrated in figure \ref{fig:sets} and \ref{fig:illustration}, extreme worst-case scenarios may never yield a feasible safety strategy, and it may be the case that establishing safety is infeasible. Consequently, in this work, we investigate the reduction of conservativeness in Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis by introducing structure into some or all of the human models. Particularly, we investigate a modeling strategy around the second disturbance that exploits the structure of human behavior in a manner that enables us to use differential game theory in more dense dynamic driving environments.

text: A collection of metrics designated NILC-Metrix was developed through funded projects involving multiple researchers, as well as through master's and doctoral projects at the Interinstitutional Center for Computational Linguistics --- NILC\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/}}, spanning from 2008 to 2021. The rationale for developing this comprehensive set of metrics, the stages of its development, and the re-implementations of certain metrics to standardize the use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools, are outlined below. The initial impetus for constructing a set of metrics for automatic assessment of textual complexity in BP originated in the PorSimples project, which focused on the Simplification of Portuguese Texts for Digital Inclusion and Accessibility \cite{candido-etal-2009-supporting,aluisio-gasperin-2010-fostering}. The target population of PorSimples comprises individuals with limited literacy, who seek to obtain information from web texts but encounter difficulties as they are literate at rudimentary and basic levels, according to the functional literacy indicator designated INAF\footnote{\url{https://ipm.org.br/inaf}}. In numerous projects within the reviewed literature, automatic text simplification is implemented as a process that diminishes the lexical and/or syntactic complexity of a text while attempting to preserve its meaning and information \cite{Carroll98practicalsimplification,Max2006,Shardlow2014}. Nevertheless, there exist simplification projects, for instance, the Terence project, in which the target audience also requires simplifications to enhance text comprehension both at the local level, facilitating connections between adjacent sentences and also at the global level of the text, assisting in the construction of a mental representation of the text \cite{terence_2014}. There are additional initiatives, such as the Newsela\footnote{\url{https://newsela.com/}} company, which conduct conceptual simplification, simplifying the content in addition to the form \cite{xu-etal-2015-problems}. Newsela also incorporates elaborations in the text to make certain concepts more explicit or the use of redundancies to emphasize important portions of the text. Furthermore, operations reduce and omit information that is not appropriate for a given target audience. Based on the aforementioned simplification projects, we recognized that textual complexity and textual simplification are strongly connected in the NLP domain. We also recognized that the type of simplification employed in the Terence project aims to enhance the coherence of a text, which leads the authors to characterize this type of simplification as being at the cognitive level. The simplification performed by Newsela is the most comprehensive in terms of different operations, although still without complete automation (but see the advances conducted by \cite{alva-manchego-etal-2017-learning}). During the PorSimples project, we implemented a system designated \textbf{Facilita} responsible for adapting web content for low-literacy readers by employing lexical elaboration and named entity labeling \cite{Watanabe2010}, and the simplification system was designated \textbf{Simplifica}. One of Simplifica's distinctive features was to conduct two levels of simplification, termed natural and strong, to assist people who are literate at basic and rudimentary levels, respectively. To analyze the textual complexity of the resulting text, and thus evaluate whether the simplification objective had been achieved, a multiclass predictor of textual complexity was constructed using traditional machine learning methods. This predictor required the extraction of a set of metrics that could evaluate the complexity of a text and compute proxies to assess the cohesion and coherence of the simplifications supported by Simplifica's automatic rules. In this context, the Coh-Metrix-Port \cite{Scarton2010a,Scarton2010b,Scarton2010c} project was established. At NILC, we had previously conducted a readability study before PorSimples aimed at adapting the Flesch Index to BP \cite{fleschport1996}, based on a corpus created to help identify the weights of the linear formula that evaluates word size and sentence size in texts of various text genres and sources. The Flesch Index \cite{flesch1948} is based on the theory that the shorter the words and sentences are, the easier a text is to read. Although it is highly practical, as it is a number indicative of the complexity of the text and can be associated with school grades, it does not inform which operations to perform in a given text to achieve the sizes of short sentences, for example. Additionally, it can lead us to make errors, because a short text is not the only characteristic of an easy-to-read text. One of the criticisms of the Flesch Index and other traditional readability formulas \cite{dalechall1948,gunning1952,fry1968,kincaidetal1975} is that they are often used to adapt instructional material as prescriptive guides and not as simple predictive tools for textual complexity \cite{crossley2008assessing}. These errors derive from the failure to understand that the traditional readability formulas were not designed to explain the reason for the difficulty of a text, as they are not based on theories of text comprehension. Instead these formulas were based on the statistical correlation of superficial measures of a text with its level of complexity, previously established by a linguist or specialist in education, for example. Once the limitations of traditional readability formulas at the beginning of the Coh-Metrix-Port project were understood, we selected the Coh-Metrix project as a foundation for the metrics to be developed in PorSimples. Coh-Metrix computes computational cohesion and coherence metrics for written and spoken texts \cite{Graesser2004,Coh-Metrix_2011,graesser2014coh} based on models of textual comprehension and cognitive models of reading \cite{kintsch1978toward,kintsch1973reading,kintsch1998comprehension} that explain: (i) how a reader interacts with a text, (ii) what types of memories are involved in reading, e.g., how the overload of working memory caused by using too many words before the main verb negatively influences the processing of sentences, (iii) the role of the propositional content of the discourse \cite{kintsch1998comprehension} which means that if the coherence of a text is improved, so will its comprehension \cite{crossley2007toward}, and (iv) how the mechanisms of cohesion, for example, discourse markers and repetition of entities, will help to create a coherent text. In summary, just as the Coh-Metrix tool\footnote {\url{http://cohmetrix.com/}} for the English language does, the textual complexity analysis planned in Coh-Metrix-Port employs a framework of multilevel analysis. Coh-Metrix-Port provided 48 metrics grouped into 10 classes. However, one of its requirements was the use of open-source NLP tools. Thus, many syntactic metrics were not implemented, given the absence of free parsers with good performance at the time. Then, the AIC tool (Automatic Analysis of the Intelligibility of the Corpus) was created \cite{maziero2008ferramenta} within the scope of PorSimples. AIC has 39 metrics (most of them are syntactic) based on the parser Palavras \cite{bick2000palavras} (see details in Section 2). After the conclusion of PorSimples, in 2010, new metrics were added to the list of the initial 48 of the Coh-Metrix-Port tool and the 39 of the AIC. This was the case of the 25 new metrics of the Coh-Metrix-Dementia \cite{CBMS_CMD_2015,Aluisio_Propor16}, developed in a master's dissertation. During the implementation of Coh-Metrix-Dementia, the first re-implementation of Coh-Metrix-Port was performed to standardize interfaces and the use of NLP tools. For example, the use of nlpnet PoS tagger \cite{evaluating_2015} was established as the default tagger, as Coh-Metrix-Dementia incorporates the Coh-Metrix-Port's 48 metrics. Several projects in the literature consulted on the subject of automatic text simplification implement it as a process that reduces the lexical and/or syntactic complexity of a text, trying to preserve its meaning and information (Carroll98PracticalSimplification, Max2006, Shardlow2014). However, there are simplification projects, for example, the Terence project, in which the simplifications are also intended to facilitate the comprehension of the text, both at the local level, facilitating the connection between the neighboring sentences, and at the global level, facilitating the construction of the mental representation of the text (terence_2014). There are also other initiatives, such as the Newsela company, which carries out a process of content simplification, simplifying the content as well as the form (footnote: url https://newsela.com/). Newsela also uses elaborations in the text to make certain concepts more explicit, and uses redundancies to emphasize important sections of the text. On the basis of these projects we recognized that the simplification of text and the textual complexity are closely linked in the NLP field. The simplification performed by Newsela is the most comprehensive in terms of different operations, though still not completely automatic (but see the progress made by Alva-Manchego et al., 2017). We also noticed that the type of simplification used by the Terence project tends to enhance the coherence of a text, which has led the authors to classify this type of simplification as being at the cognitve level. In the PorSimples project, a system was developed to adapt web content for low-literacy readers by means of lexical expansion and named entity labeling. It was called Facilita, and its simplification system was called Simplifica. One of Simplifica’s features was that it had two simplification modes: natural and strong, intended respectively for readers with elementary and poor literacy. To analyze the complexity of the resulting text and hence the degree of simplification achieved, we constructed a multiclass predictor of textual complexity using traditional machine learning methods. During the time PorSimples was being developed, the NILC had been conducting a readability study aimed at adapting the Flesch–Kincaid readability index to a broad range of text types and sources, using a corpus which was created in order to help identify the weights of the linear formula that estimates word and sentence size in texts of various genres and sources. For this predictor, we needed to extract a set of metrics that could evaluate the complexity of a text and produce proxies for assessing the cohesion and consistency of the simplifications performed by Simplifica. In this context, the Coh–Metrix–Port project was launched. The Flesch-Kincaid test, cited q. v. [Flesch, 1948], is based on the idea that the shorter the words and sentences are, the easier the text is to read. While this is a practical method because it is a numerical indicator of the difficulty of the text, and can be compared with school grades, it does not inform us about the operations that must be performed in a given text in order to achieve, for example, the size of the short sentences. Moreover, it can lead us to make mistakes, because the size of the text is not the only characteristic of a text that is easy to read. The Flesch-Kincaid and other readability formulas, cite dalechall1948, gunning1952, fry 1968, kincaid et al., are sometimes misused to adjust instruction, as a guide to modifying content, instead of merely as simple prediction tools of textual complexity, cite Crossley 2008. The reason for this misunderstanding is the failure to understand that these formulas were not designed to explain the reasons for the difficulty of a text, since they are not based on theories of the understanding of a text. Instead, they are based on the statistical correlation of the purely external measures of a text with its level of complexity, established, for example, by a linguist or a specialist in education. Assuming the limitations of readability formulas had been fully understood at the beginning of the Coh-Metrix-Port project, we chose to use Coh-Metrix as the basis for the metrics developed by PorSimples. As the Coh-Metrix tool for English does, the planned Coh-Metrix-Port analyzes the textual complexity in a framework of multilevel analysis. Coh-Metrix calculates the coherence and cohesion of written and spoken texts, based on models of textual comprehension and on the models of cognition, which explain: how a reader interacts with a text, what kind of memory is involved in reading (e.g. how overloading working memory by using too many words before the main verb negatively affects sentence comprehension), (ii) how the content of the text, e.g. the role of the propositional content, which means that if the coherence of a text is improved, so is its comprehension, cite: Crossley, and (iv) how the mechanisms of cohesion, for example, the use of discourse markers and the repetition of units, help to make the text coherent. One of its requirements was that the NLP tools be open source. This meant that a large number of syntactic metrics could not be implemented, as at that time there were no free, good-quality parsers. Coh-Metrix-Port provided forty-eight metrics grouped into ten classes. After the conclusion of PorSimples, in 2010, new metrics were added to the list of the original 48 metrics of Coh-Metrix-Port and the 39 metrics of AIC. AIC has 39 metrics, most of which are syntactic, based on the parser Palavras, cited as Bick, 2000, [cite: bick, 2000] (see details in section 2). While the implementation of Coh-Metrix-Dementia was under way, the first reimplementation of Coh-Metrix-Port was undertaken, in order to standardize the interfaces and the use of NLP tools. The use of the nlpnet PoS tagger, for example, was established as the default tagger, as Coh-Metrix-Dementia is based on the 48 metrics of Coh-Metrix-Port. This was the case, for example, of the 25 new metrics of Coh-Metrix-Dementia [CBMS_CMD_2015, Alusio_Propor16] developed in a master's thesis. A large lexical database with 26,874 words was annotated by an NILL student during her PhD in 2017. It was automatically annotated for the lexical characteristics of concreteness, age of acquisition, visual imageability, and subjective frequency (similar to familiarity).

text: This manuscript introduces a methodology for actively sampling individuals within a population to mitigate pandemic spread, specifically targeting diseases such as COVID-19. Sampling algorithms are frequently employed in machine learning for acquiring training data labels in classification tasks ("active learning" \cite{AL-MJ, pz2006}) and within bandit algorithms \cite{bandit-wolpert} to navigate complex search spaces through exploration and exploitation mechanisms. The methodology we introduce in this manuscript extends these concepts, applying them specifically to the context of epidemic containment within populations. The scholarly literature addressing disease spread management through active sampling concepts originates primarily from public health research. Two principal motivations drive this literature's consideration of sampling approaches, though these motivations often intersect within population surveillance contexts \cite{lee2010principles}. The initial motivation involves estimating actual disease incidence or transmission patterns, exemplified by HIV prevalence studies within populations. For HIV incidence estimation, approaches including population surveys and "sentinel surveillance" \cite{magnani2005review, fylkesnes_studying_1998} have demonstrated effectiveness. Population surveys within catchment areas (regions with probable disease presence) employ (stratified/cluster) random sampling methodologies, generally regarded as the gold standard while recognized as costly \cite{lee2010principles}. Sentinel surveillance, conversely, collects data from selected venues (the "sentinels", such as clinics) where disease-affected subsets likely seek treatment. Acknowledging that sensitive diseases like HIV may concentrate within hard-to-reach populations who remain concealed due to illegal or illicit activities (including sex workers, drug users), the literature \cite{magnani2005review, goel2010assessing} has rigorously examined alternative techniques including snowball sampling (initiating with disease-positive seeds who identify others potentially affected), respondent-driven sampling (resembling snowball methodology but employing longer chains with fewer referrals per seed), and time-location sampling (such as sampling users during nighttime hours in districts containing brothels). With sensor data availability, novel sampling forms are also emerging. Research has demonstrated, for example, that quantifying disease spread in livestock through sampling nodes (physical locations) with greatest movement can prove effective \cite{dawson2015sampling}. The secondary motivation for considering sampling strategies involves mitigating disease spread through proactive identification of individuals requiring quarantine or testing. One approach for achieving this, prevalent in public health literature, is contact-tracing \cite{PhysRevE.66.056115, eames2003contact, underwood_contact_2003}. The concept involves sampling contacts of known infected individuals for disease presence, and, combined with quarantine measures, constitutes the primary mechanism employed globally during the COVID-19 pandemic \cite{salathe2020covid, hellewell2020feasibility}. Traditional contact-tracing relies on questionnaire-based methods, though newer automated contact tracing utilizing cell phone proximity tracking has also been proposed \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. The SARS-Cov-2 pathogen and its transmission exhibit distinctive characteristics, however, that render none of these sampling methodologies individually sufficient. \begin{itemize} \item The potential for pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic transmission eliminates pure sentinel-based strategies that would test individuals reporting to clinics with symptoms. For identical reasons, contact tracing alone proves insufficient. This occurs because contact-tracing pursues exclusively contacts of those confirmed through positive testing. Asymptomatic carriers may have similarly transmitted the disease to their contacts, yet those contacts will not be actively pursued through this strategy. Consequently, random sampling also provides utility. \item The pathogen has demonstrated survival on surfaces or within air at specific locations for extended durations. Therefore, location-based sampling may also prove beneficial. \item Uncertainty exists regarding whether individuals develop durable immunity. Consequently, sampling strategies may require accommodation for repeated testing of identical individuals. \item Information concerning how covariates influence disease acquisition and disease impact continues evolving. For instance, while comorbidities and age are known to affect outcomes, uncertainty persists regarding whether this knowledge is comprehensive. Furthermore, how covariates might influence disease contraction remains uncertain. Within this environment, covariate-based sampling strategies alone might prove inadequate. Sampling strategies targeting specific \emph{individuals} for testing therefore becomes essential. \item The highly contagious nature of the pathogen and the scope of global spread have imposed constraints on testing capacities, necessitating test prioritization for utility in spread mitigation. \end{itemize} The methodology presented in this manuscript addresses all five aspects identified above. This manuscript introduces dynamic active sampling strategies based on multi-armed bandit algorithms that can optimally integrate different sampling concepts to generate real-time testing candidate lists. Bandit algorithms demonstrate particular effectiveness at combining exploration with exploitation and have achieved success across numerous scenarios where this combination proves important. This applies to SARS-Cov-2, where exploration (random sampling) must be effectively integrated with exploitation (contact-tracing, location-based sampling) dynamically based on available data. One key aspect of our work involves identifying specific individuals for testing/sampling, rather than criteria-based or covariate-based sampling strategies. Additionally, our algorithm functions within a high uncertainty network environment. Specifically, contacts between individuals are initially only partially observable and are revealed progressively through individual sampling. The bandit algorithm therefore initially employs the Thompson sampling strategy to balance expansion into unobserved nodes for identifying potential new hotspots versus densification on observed portions to utilize acquired knowledge for testing. When densification is selected, an inner level upper confidence bounding (UCB) policy is designed to balance between individuals having higher infection probability versus those having greater information uncertainty. To quantify individual proximity and infection risk, we construct heterogeneous network embedding to encode social interactions through continuous latent representation. To model how sampling affects, and is subsequently affected by, the underlying environment, we implement an agent-based model constructed from realistic New York City data. Several recent Covid-19 studies have concentrated on predicting and flattening disease spread through different intervention policy applications \cite{Keskinocak2020.07.22.20160036,Keskinocak2020.04.29.20084764, topirceanu2020centralized,atkeson2020will,ferguson2020report,chang2020modelling}. Among examined policies were case isolation, home quarantine, social distancing, air travel restrictions, and school closures and reopening. To assess restriction efficiency, most studies coupled S/I/R (representing susceptible/infected/recovered) diffusion modeling \cite{hethcote2000mathematics,cooper2020sir} with Agent Based simulation Model (ABM) \cite{perez2009agent} of infectious spread under different restriction scenarios. Among these studies, an ABM of Covid-19 spread in New York City under different quarantine policies was provided by \cite{hoertel2020facing}. This model serves as foundation for the ABM we developed in this work. Additionally, in contemporaneous work, \cite{grushka2020framework} present a framework utilizing historical data to construct a classifier computing a ``risk score'', which forms the basis for determining exploration and exploitation combination. While the concept of employing bandit-based algorithms for testing proves important, the challenge lies in developing specific methods addressing all previously noted complexities. Our work presents a specific method that is adaptive, dynamic, and comprehensive. Alongside questions of whom to sample for testing, similar questions arise regarding whom to vaccinate. \cite{chen2020allocation}, for example, present adaptive and dynamic covariate-based vaccination policies. Our framework permits vaccination incorporation into background dynamics to test combinational strategy effectiveness such as smart testing with vaccination. We make the following significant contributions. First, we present a novel active sampling algorithm for effectively managing pandemics such as COVID-19 (to our knowledge, no methods exist in the literature developed for this problem). We develop a general multi-armed bandit framework for this problem that (a) can leverage different information types such as individuals and locations, (b) can handle uncertainty in both underlying disease dynamics and information, and (c) is constructed to sample based on individuals rather than covariates. Second, we make several modeling contributions regarding how bandit-based algorithms can function in this setting. Specifically, we construct a heterogeneous network capturing social relations, neighborhood similarity, and community membership and demonstrate how this can drive a two-level active sampling strategy for individual sampling. The utilization of network embedding concepts within the heterogeneous network is novel. Third, we make important contributions to multi-armed bandit literature as well. Beyond classic bandit problems, limited literature exists on active search on graphs, with objectives of finding as many target nodes as possible with specific properties. Most existing work assumes complete network structure and underlying process knowledge beforehand. Very limited work addresses partially observed and dynamically changing networks and underlying (disease) dynamics. We model partially observed scenarios within this framework and demonstrate how networks can be strategically expanded over time to support active sampling strategies. \iffalse since we consider a scenario where the sampling is not independent of the environment, but itself affects the underlying mechanism

text: Identifying previously unseen novelties, or anomalies, constitutes a fundamental capability that humans employ to enhance awareness of emerging dangers and opportunities. Instances of such phenomena include recognizing novel behaviors in natural systems, identifying security threats, or discovering equipment failures. Although anomaly detection (AD) approaches targeting images \cite{reiss2021panda,hendrycks2019using,tack2020csi} typically encompass a broad spectrum of data domains, video AD has predominantly concentrated on surveillance footage. In such recordings \cite{luo2017revisit,mahadevan2010anomaly}, commonly captured by security cameras, conventional walking behavior is generally characterized as the normal class, while alternative behaviors (bicycle riding, crowd formation) are classified as anomalies. During recent years, numerous novel techniques have been proposed, advancing performance on such benchmarks \cite{georgescu2021anomaly,park2020learning}. However, alternative categories of video anomalies remain largely beyond the purview of contemporary research. In this investigation we examine different categories of anomalies, exploring various types of methodologies to address them. Our research focuses on physical abnormalities in the motion or trajectory of an object that have been substantially neglected and introduces a novel benchmark for video anomaly detection.

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance enhancements across diverse domains. Identifying an appropriate DNN architecture is essential for deploying a DNN to novel tasks and attaining superior performance. Nevertheless, since the architecture is characterized by a combination of dozens to hundreds of hyperparameters (convolutional layer filter dimensions, presence of inter-layer connections, etc.), optimizing such combinations demands substantial human effort and specialized expertise. Neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged as a promising methodology for automatically discovering sophisticated DNN architectures and addressing the challenges in deploying DNNs to previously unexplored tasks. Nevertheless, the substantial computational overhead (temporal and spatial complexity) of NAS constitutes a bottleneck in its deployment, particularly in commercial applications lacking access to multiple high-performance GPUs. Consequently, minimizing the computational overhead of NAS represents a crucial research trajectory. One-shot NAS diminishes the temporal complexity of NAS by concurrently optimizing the architecture and the parameters (weights) within a single training procedure or limited training procedures. It sustains a redundant deep learning model encompassing numerous layers and connections, termed the parent network, which can express all feasible architectures in the search space as its sub-network. All parameters necessitated by candidate architectures are contained within the parent network and distributed across different architectures. The quality of an architecture is assessed utilizing the shared parameters, which substantially diminishes the computational time for architecture search relative to conventional methodologies that necessitate parameter training from initialization for each candidate architecture evaluation. From the perspective of GPU memory utilization, one-shot NAS can be classified into dense propagation NAS (DP-NAS) and sparse propagation NAS (SP-NAS). DP-NAS necessitates the complete parent network to be loaded into GPU memory to execute forward and/or backward propagation, whereas SP-NAS requires only a sub-network to be loaded. DP-NAS is more prevalent due to the success of DARTS and its derivatives \cite{liu2018darts,xie2018snas,yao2020nasp}. Nevertheless, due to its substantial memory consumption, its search space remains constrained. SP-NAS addresses this limitation and provides more adaptable search spaces on standard GPUs with restricted memory. Therefore, we concentrate on SP-NAS in this investigation. To further diminish the computational overhead of one-shot SP-NAS, we propose a novel one-shot SP-NAS, specifically \emph{AdvantageNAS}. Although numerous factors influence NAS performance (performance estimation, search space, etc.) and state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance may necessitate searching for the optimal combination of these factors, this study concentrates on the search strategy. We emphasize that the objective of this investigation is not to achieve the SOTA architecture but to examine the efficiency of the search strategy. AdvantageNAS is a gradient-based SP-NAS.\footnote{The benefits of gradient-based approaches are as follows. Approaches utilizing evolutionary algorithms (e.g., \cite{real2017evo}) or progressive search methodologies (e.g., \cite{liu2018pnas}) must define a mutation or expansion strategy contingent on the search space. Such manual preparations dependent on the search space are not required in gradient-based methods. Another benefit of gradient-based methods is that they can be readily implemented in most contemporary deep learning frameworks, as they support automatic differentiation of deep neural networks.} This category of NAS encompasses ENAS \cite{pham2018enas}, ProxylessNAS \cite{cai2018proxylessnas}, PARSEC \cite{casale2019parsec}, and GDAS \cite{xuanyi2019gdas}. These methodologies introduce a family of parametric probability distributions from which an architecture is sampled, and the distribution parameter is updated with a gradient of the objective function estimated using the Monte Carlo method, which indirectly optimizes the architecture itself. Since the gradient is estimated, reducing the variance of the gradient estimate intuitively enhances the search effectiveness. Inspired by the actor-critic methodology \cite{konda2000ac}, we adopt the concept of \emph{advantage}, which has been introduced to address the well-established \emph{credit assignment} problem of policy gradients \cite{Minsky:1961:ire}. We examine AdvantageNAS both theoretically and empirically. Empirical investigations demonstrate that it performs effectively on different tasks with varying search spaces, whereas theoretical investigations guarantee its performance on empirically unforeseen tasks. Theoretical investigations are relatively limited in NAS research; however, they are crucial for examining search strategies for NAS. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel SP-NAS, specifically AdvantageNAS. Our analysis of a test scenario demonstrates that the estimation variance of the gradient is reduced compared to REINFORCE \cite{Williams1992}, which is a baseline search strategy for ENAS. \item The theoretical examination reveals that the estimated gradient in AdvantageNAS is an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the expected loss. From the unbiasedness, we establish that AdvantageNAS monotonically improves the expected loss and thus converges. Furthermore, we confirm that reducing the gradient variance contributes to an enhanced lower bound of the loss improvement in each iteration. \item We compared AdvantageNAS with various gradient-based NAS methods in three different configurations to demonstrate its efficacy on different search spaces. Our experiments were conducted on the same code base to compare the search strategies.\footnote{NAS approaches using different components such as search spaces and training protocols have been compared in the literature. However, it has been reported, e.g.,\ in \cite{Yang2020iclr}, that such differences in the components make it difficult to fairly compare the contributions of each component. Our code: \url{https://github.com/madoibito80/advantage-nas}.} The results demonstrated that AdvantageNAS converges more rapidly than existing SP-NAS approaches. \end{itemize}

The problem is formulated as follows. Consider that we possess a collection of data, expressed as $k$ discrete probability distributions $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given a set of non-negative weights $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$ that sum to $1$, and a class $\mathbb{P}$ of probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$, a Wasserstein barycenter under the $L_p$ objective for a parameter $p>0$ is a probability distribution $
u\in\mathbb{P}$ that minimizes  egin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_iW_p(\mu_i,
u)^p, \end{equation} where $W_p(\mu_i,
u)$ is the $p$-Wasserstein distance. The Wasserstein barycenter constitutes a natural quantity that encapsulates the geometric concept of centrality among point clouds, as it employs the optimal transport distance~\cite{bertsimas1997introduction} between multiple observed sets. Consequently, Wasserstein barycenters have been extensively utilized in machine learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, data sciences~\cite{ruschendorf2002n,elvander2020multi}, image processing~\cite{rubner1997earth}, computer graphics~\cite{pele2009fast}, and statistics~\cite{villani2008optimal}, with applications in constrained clustering~\cite{cuturi2014fast, ho2017multilevel}, Bayesian learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, texture mixing~\cite{rabin2011wasserstein}, and shape interpolation~\cite{solomon2015convolutional}. Regrettably, the problem is NP-hard to compute \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21} and numerous algorithms that even approximate the Wasserstein barycenter experience substantial running times, particularly when the datasets are high dimensional~\cite{MuzellecC19}. Indeed, \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein} recently provided an algorithm that computes the Wasserstein barycenter using runtime that depends exponentially on the dimension, thereby suffering the ``curse of dimensionality.'' To mitigate these computational limitations, we examine dimensionality reduction for computing the Wasserstein barycenter. Dimensionality reduction can be employed to enhance the performance of downstream algorithms on high dimensional datasets in numerous settings of interest, e.g., see the survey~\cite{cunningham2015linear}. text: Dhrupad represents one of the most ancient forms of North Indian classical vocal music. A conventional Dhrupad concert configuration features a solo vocalist or vocalist pair as the primary performer and a pakhawaj player providing percussive accompaniment, with a tanpura maintaining the harmonic drone in the background\cite{bonnie_wade}. A Dhrupad performance extends beyond an hour and encompasses an extensive, unaccompanied \textit{raga alap} followed by a composed work, the \textit{bandish}, executed alongside the percussion instrument. The bandish is not merely presented in its original form but also employed as a foundation for additional rhythmic improvisation (\textit{laykari}), wherein the vocalist articulates the syllables of the bandish text at varying rhythmic densities and in diverse patterns \cite[chapter~10]{clayton}. Throughout this process, the pakhawaj accompaniment either executes a fundamental pattern (\textit{theka}) of the metrical cycle (\textit{tala}), a rhythmic improvisation to complement the vocalist's improvisation, or an independent solo improvisation while the vocalist delivers the lines of fixed composition or the refrain \cite[p.~111]{clayton}. \\ Figure~\ref{fig:concert_structure} illustrates the structure of a bandish performance from the vocalist's perspective. The intermediate refrain segments constitute the non-improvised sections where the performer sings a line of the bandish or a portion thereof before returning to another episode of improvisation.\\ A fundamental distinction between Khyal and Dhrupad bandish performances lies in the relationship between the lead and accompanying percussion instrument's execution. In the former, performers typically alternate improvising while the other maintains the basic rhythm or the refrain, whereas in the latter, beyond this arrangement, there exist sections where both improvise simultaneously. A comprehensive segmentation of a Dhrupad bandish performance would therefore require providing rhythmic descriptions of non-improvised and improvised sections pertaining to each instrument - the vocals and the pakhawaj.\\ Several additional levels of segmentation could also be implemented for this musical form. One approach could target identifying sections of non-improvised and improvised music. Given that the bandish text itself comprises sections positioned in different portions of an octave, each containing several lines, another segmentation level could be based on which of these is being presented or improvised upon by the vocalist. While the former segmentation could, to some degree, be defined by variations in rhythmic attributes, the latter would rely more heavily on melodic characteristics. There could also be modifications in timbral attributes correlated with the nature of articulation accompanying the various rhythmic or melodic changes, which could assist with each type of segmentation.\\ The objective of this work is to develop automated methods for the structural segmentation of the Dhrupad bandish concert based exclusively on the tempo and the relationships of the rhythmic densities of the individual instruments. Given that vocal onsets are admittedly challenging to detect (even in isolated vocals due to the inherent diversity in singing), we resort to alternative methods for the direct estimation of the local rhythmic density. Developments in deep learning have resulted in the creation of methods that approach the estimation of the predominant tempo from the raw audio spectral representation as a classification task \cite{schreiber-ismir18,schreiber-smc19,mtl-beat-tempo-19}. We investigate a similar approach for our task of estimating the varying surface tempo or rhythmic density throughout a concert audio. In light of the substantial improvements reported in audio source separation in recent years, we also examine the use of source separation followed by tempo estimation for the constituent instruments (vocals and pakhawaj) to provide a more comprehensive description of each section.\\ The primary novel contributions of this work are as follows: (i) a dataset of tempo markings and rhythmic density based structural segmentation annotations for Dhrupad bandish concerts, (ii) adapting a state-of-the-art tempo estimation method to the task of estimating local surface tempo or rhythmic density of the polyphonic mix, and (iii) the utilization of source separation to extend this to each instrument(vocals and pakhawaj) to ultimately obtain a musically relevant segmentation of bandish concerts with section labels defined in terms of the rhythmic density inter-relationships.

text: Forecasting stock market returns and volatility has garnered considerable attention from both academic researchers and financial industry practitioners. However, can stock market prices and volatility be accurately predicted? Alternatively, can they be forecasted during certain specific periods? Quantifying sentiment extracted from online platforms such as Twitter or financial news articles may prove valuable for developing trading strategies. Furthermore, sentiment derived from financial news may possess predictive capabilities that can be leveraged by portfolio and risk management professionals. The findings and conclusions from our investigation can be categorized into three components. Initially, correlations between sentiment scores and stock market returns demonstrated statistical significance exclusively for our headline dataset. The findings reveal a statistically significant negative correlation between adverse news and the FTSE100 index closing price (returns). The most robust correlation between sentiment and volatility metrics was observed in our tweets dataset, whereas no correlation or minimal correlation was identified in headlines and news stories datasets. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that tweets tend to be more timely and responsive to diverse events, while article publication requires considerably more time, and markets operate according to the principle ``Buy on rumors, sell on news.'' This paper is organized as follows. In Section \ref{sec:related} we examine related research. In Section \ref{sec:data}, we describe data sources that have been utilized to compute sentiment scores: Thomson Reuters, RavenPack and Twitter. In Section \ref{sec:correlation} we perform a correlation analysis and Granger's causality test. In Section \ref{sec:lda}, we conduct additional experiments to evaluate whether topic modelling (or Latent Dirichlet Allocation) can be employed to improve the prediction accuracy of subsequent days' stock market directional volatility. In Section \ref{sec:results} and \ref{sec:conclusion} we present the analytical results and discuss future work.

But is it possible to predict them accurately, or only during specific periods? Our results show a significant negative correlation between the FTSE100 closing price and negative news. Moreover, the sentiment derived from financial news may have the power to predict and can be exploited by portfolio and risk management professionals. This article is organized as follows. First, we found that the correlations between the sentiments and the stock prices were significant only for the headlines. Then we looked at the correlation between the sentiments and the volatility metrics. We found the strongest correlation between the sentiments and the volatility metrics in the case of the Twitter dataset, while there was no or only a small correlation between the volatility metrics and the volatility metrics of the other two datasets. In the "Related Research" section, we review the existing studies. In the section "Data" we describe the data sources used for the calculation of sentiment indicators: Thomson Reuters, RavenPack and Twitter. In the section "Correlation" we perform a correlation analysis and Granger causality test. This phenomenon is a consequence of the fact that the twits are generally more timely and sensitive to various events, while the time required to publish articles is much longer, and the market works on the principle: "Buy on rumors, sell on news." In the sections “Results” and “Conclusions” the results of the statistical analysis are presented and further research is discussed. In the section “LDA” we conduct further experiments to see if the use of topic modeling (or Latent Dirichlet Allocation) can improve the accuracy of predictions for the next day's stock market volatility.

text: An expanding corpus of research has documented tools, utilized optimization techniques, or introduced novel algorithms to facilitate automated design and/or fabrication of robots (e.g.,~\citep{Luck-RSS-17,Schulz17,HoovFearing08,pervan2018low,zhang2020abstractions}). Significant among these approaches are algorithms that seek to manage or minimize resources (for example, see~\citep{censi17co}). Memory constitutes one resource of special interest to us, not because RAM is costly, but rather because when state requirements are diminished this frequently provides insight into the fundamental informational structure of specific robot tasks~(cf.~\citep{connell90,donald95information}). To this end, we concentrate on filter reduction, targeting combinatorial filters of the type advocated by LaValle~\citep{lavalle10sensing}. These filters are discrete variants of the probabilistic estimators prevalent in contemporary robotics, and they produce particularly elegant treatments for certain practical tasks (e.g, see \citep{tovar2014combinatorial}). The minimization problem for combinatorial filters is straightforward to state and simple to comprehend, but ongoing work on the topic~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial,rahmani2018relationship,zhang20cover,rahmani2020integer} demonstrates that it encompasses more than initially apparent. As a straightforward example to motivate filter minimization, consider the safari park with vehicle rental service depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_scenario}. The cars available for hire are each equipped with a compass and an intelligent gear shifting system. The compass measures the heading of the vehicle before and after its movement, e.g., `nw' indicates that the vehicle was heading north and then turned to face west. The intelligent gear shifting system receives the readings from the compass as input, and automatically shifts gears to comply with the speed limit. There are three categories of speed limits on roads: ($a$) between $15$ and $30$ (gray), ($b$) speeds below $30$ (brown), or ($c$) slower than $15$ (green). Every vehicle is capable of moving with a low gear to drive with a maximum speed $15$, and with a high gear to drive between speed $15$ and $30$. A na\"ive gear shifting system satisfying the speed limits is implemented by a filter shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}: each vertex represents a system state, each edge represents the state transition, with the label on the edges representing the readings from the compass. A vertex is colored gray if the system outputs high gear, colored green if it outputs low gear, or colored both colors if the system may use either gear (via, say, a nondeterministic choice). We are interested in discovering a minimal filter, such as the one shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_minimal}, that implements appropriate behavior but with fewest states. A natural approach is by first constructing a discrete state-transition system (such as in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}) using the problem description as a foundation. Then, the subsequent step is to apply some algorithm capable of compressing it. Despite the apparent similarity of combinatorial filter minimization to the problem of state minimization of deterministic automata, with Myhill--Nerode's celebrated and efficient reduction~\citep{hopcroft06introduction}, minimization of combinatorial filters is NP-complete~\citep{okane2013reduction}. One line of work investigates filter minimization based on merger operations. These algorithms reduce filter minimization to a graph coloring instance~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial} or integer linear programming~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Saberifar et. al.~\citep{saberifar2017combinatorial} examined special cases, approximation and parameterized complexity of filter minimization. Rahmani and O'Kane~\citep{rahmani2018relationship} demonstrated that the well-known notion of \emph{bisimulation} relation in general produces only sub-optimal solutions. They proposed three distinct integer linear programming formulations to search for the smallest equivalence relation~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Recent work demonstrates that both merge and split operations are necessary to find a minimal filter~\citep{zhang20cover}. It formalizes the problem as a clique cover problem subject to the constraint that the output filter should be deterministic and must simulate the output of the input filter. But both criteria involve constraints that are exponential in size, which is clearly computationally unattractive. In this paper, we propose a novel, competing formulation of the filter minimization problem with only a polynomial number of constraints and which produces a concise nonlinear integer programming formulation. Since utilizing nonlinear constraints is generally computationally inefficient, we `flatten' these nonlinear constraints leading to (1) an integer linear programming and (2) a Boolean satisfaction formalism---both involve expressions of constraints that are of comparable size. \gobble{But, unlike the one-shot optimization scheme used by both linear and nonlinear programming, Boolean satisfaction solves the problem by iteratively enumerating the integer values of the objective. Since the domain of the objective for filter minimization is small and the constraints in conjunctive normal form are relatively efficient to be exploited, Boolean satisfaction outperforms all other approaches in the experiment.} Examining the experimental results in depth, we observed that many constraints remain inactive during the iterative search for a minimal filter. To accelerate computation within the Boolean satisfaction formalism, we treat these constraints just-in-time: only introducing a constraint when we detect that some proposed variable assignment would violate it. Empirical results demonstrate that the speedup from this treatment can outweigh the overhead of detecting and dynamically introducing the constraints. After presenting the problem statement in Section~\ref{sec:prob}, we first formalize filter minimization as an integer nonlinear program in Section~\ref{sec:INP}. Based on that, we provide integer linear programming and Boolean satisfaction formulations in Section~\ref{sec:ILP_SAT}. Experimental results appear in Section~\ref{sec:expr}.

text: Ranking search results that correspond to a user query constitutes a fundamental component of information retrieval (IR) systems that support numerous popular websites. Generally, learning to rank (LTR) models are developed to score and order the results, and they are trained using labels derived from user engagement with results. Although pairwise or listwise loss functions are most frequently utilized in training LTR models, scoring the results during inference is typically performed in a unilateral manner. Such an approach of scoring results independently neglects to consider inter-document dependencies. Nevertheless, studies demonstrate that the perception of a search result is affected by other neighboring results \cite{agarwal2015constrained, neighbor_effect, wang2016beyond}. Such behavior is even more evident in domains like e-commerce search, where users commonly compare and contrast choices presented on a results page as part of their shopping process. Modeling such dependencies is essential within the top results (for example, results displayed on the first page), which users primarily engage with. Furthermore, in many real-world applications, there exists a requirement to ensure certain predetermined distributional criteria within results on a search results page. Managing the comprehensive composition of results within the page is crucial towards user perception of a website, and is frequently driven by business objectives or long-term goals aimed at objectives such as user retention. For example, ensuring that the spectrum of selection available for a query is represented within the top results is an important objective at eBay. Other examples of such business objectives include showcasing diversity in e-commerce inventory, mitigating bias in top results or personalization of results. Therefore, the constitution of an optimal set of top results (documents, or referred to as items in this paper) must consider any distributional criteria and inter-result dependencies, along with the individual quality of results. We refer to the top results for a search query, such as $k$ items displayed on the first page as perceived by the user (where $k \ll n$, $n$ is the number of results in the recall), as the slate. In this paper, we present a novel approach and an architecture to generate an optimal slate. An optimal slate is conceived as a slate that maximizes the probability of fulfilling search needs while satisfying predetermined query-specific distributional criteria. We jointly optimize for classical ranking metrics and adherence of the slate to distributional criteria, while modeling intra-slate dependencies. Various approaches have been presented by researchers to produce a set-aware ranking towards slate optimization. Heuristic methods such as Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) \cite{MMR}, IA-Select \cite{IA-Select}, and xQuAD \cite{xQuAD} aim to incorporate diversity into a slate or minimize user dissatisfaction as users browse the returned results. These approaches, however, tend to employ simpler heuristics that may lack the expressive power of the more complex models that are increasingly being used to capture inter-document dependencies. More recent models adopt set-aware ranking architectures \cite{group_wise_ranking,seq2slate}. By modeling a representation of the candidate set of documents and scoring documents cognizant of the candidate set, these approaches aim to produce an optimal slate in a set-aware fashion. For instance, groupwise scoring functions (GSF) \cite{group_wise_ranking} proposes multivariate scoring functions to jointly score documents and Seq2Slate \cite{seq2slate} adopts pointer networks to score documents sequentially. While these approaches are set-aware during inference, they are designed to optimize classic ranking metrics such as normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG). They do not explicitly model the additional distributional criteria, which is an important consideration in practice. To the best of our knowledge, there are no existing neural network based methods directly addressing this specific problem observed in search and specifically e-commerce. To that end, we propose conditional sequential slate optimization (CSSO), a novel framework that aims to address the slate optimization problem. It incorporates a sequential decoding approach built upon pointer network, that, during sequential decoding, manages the composition of the slate according to predetermined distributional criteria, while jointly optimizing traditional ranking metrics such as nDCG. This approach treats slate optimization problem as a re-ranking problem, where a \textit{base-ranker} produces a ranking based on a unilateral scoring of items, and the \textit{re-ranker} consumes a set of $n$ ranked items to produce a slate of size $k$, where $k \ll n$. We express query-specific distributional criteria with respect to the slate by means of representative or domain-specific features of the items being ranked. The hybrid optimization goal might lead to divergent optimization directions for each term as the model has to balance between ranking quality and all aspects within the predetermined distributional criteria set. Moreover, due to the existence of non-unique solutions and the non-convex nature of this problem, coupled with the non-differentiable nature of metrics like nDCG, it is difficult for traditional gradient based methods to find an optimal slate. To tackle this novel and challenging problem, we employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) for the training of CSSO. RL provides a systematic way to search in the feature space while progressively improving the non-differentiable optimization goal with the aid of policy gradient method. Simultaneously, with the exploration strategy in RL, the learned model is able to generalize better than traditional supervised method by efficiently learning the meaningful features from the rollouts. In the training, we utilize items' click-through data from IR systems as implicit relevance labels. Within the RL paradigm, a state is represented \textit{jointly} by the current items on the slate, the distance from the predetermined distribution, and the encoded candidate set. An action is equivalent to the item selection process in each step of decoding, and reward is determined based on the slate composition after the decoding process by considering both ranking quality and adherence to distributional criteria. The optimization problem, thus well defined, can be solved by policy gradient in the finite horizon with length $k$, and we adopt a baseline model to reduce the variance in training. The key contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item A framework to jointly optimize a slate for document relevance as well as adherence to a predetermined distribution, thus attempting to address an industry pain point of re-ranking to personalize, mitigate bias or introduce diversity in results. \item An enhancement to pointer network to include a conditional structure that facilitates representing slate composition during the decoding phase. \end{itemize} In experiments performed on public and proprietary e-commerce datasets, CSSO produces results with comparable ranking metrics and better distribution conformity when compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) slate optimization methods. On Yahoo \cite{yahoo_dataset} and Web30k \cite{LETOR} datasets with additional simulation for imitating users' real world behaviors, we demonstrate that both nDCG and GAP (distribution conformity metric which will be defined in the sections that follow) can be simultaneously optimized in the ranking task. Experiments on datasets from eBay.com search sessions show a significant improvement in GAP metrics and comparable ranking metrics to production ranker. In general, CSSO performs well with respect to both nDCG and GAP. We view CSSO as a practical approach to solve a very relevant industry problem of optimizing a slate for relevance and slate composition based on business objectives. We envision that the approach can be applied to solve problems such as ensuring diversity, mitigating bias, and adhering to business objectives across search and recommendation systems in various web domains including e-commerce, online media and web search.
