This approach considers the problem of ranking as a reranking problem, where the text base-ranker produces a ranking based on a single scoring of the items, and the text reranker consumes a set of n ranked items to produce a set of k ranked items, where k=n. The hybrid criterion may lead to the improvement of the ranking of each item in different directions, as the model must take into account the distribution of all the criteria. To solve this novel and difficult problem, we use reinforcement learning to train the cso. Within the framework of RL, each state is represented by the current items in the slate, their distance from the predetermined distribution, and their encoded candidate set. RL is a systematic way of searching the feature space, and by means of policy gradients, progressively improving the objective function. Also, the non-uniqueness of solutions and the non-convexity of the problem, as well as the non-differentiability of metrics like nDCG, makes it difficult for traditional gradient methods to find the optimum policy. The RL strategy learns more meaningful features from click-through data from IR systems than supervised learning. An action is equivalent to an item selection process at each step of decoding, and the reward is based on the composition of the list after decoding, which takes into account both the quality of the ranking and adherence to the distribution criteria. A framework for jointly optimising a list for document relevance as well as for adherence to a pre-specified distribution, which is able to address the industry-wide pain point of re-ranking results to personalise, mitigate bias or add diversity. In experiments on public and proprietary e-commerce datasets, CSSO shows comparable performance on metrics for ranking and better distribution conformity to that of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) tiling methods. The resulting optimization problem is solved by policy gradient on a finite horizon k, and we use a basic model to reduce the variance in training. In the decoding phase, a conditional structure is added to the pointer network to facilitate the composition of the tiling. We view the solution of the layered problem as a practical approach to the important industrial problem of balancing relevance with business objectives. In the ranking task, on the Yahoo! and Web30k data sets, which contain simulated users' actions, we demonstrate that nDCG and GAP (distribution conformity metric, which will be defined in the following sections) can be simultaneously improved. In experiments with eBay search sessions, we demonstrate significant improvements in GAP and similar ranking metrics compared to the production ranker. The proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of problems, including those relating to bias, diversity and commercial goals, and to many different Web domains, such as search, social media and commerce. Generally, it shows good performance in both nDCG and GAP.

text: The availability of computational resources has expanded exponentially since at least the 1970s, and all indications suggest that this resource will continue becoming more affordable and accessible well into the foreseeable future. Researchers have successfully leveraged the substantial computational power available to enhance control of robotic systems, and progress in computational capacity and algorithmic development continues to unlock new application domains. One promising manifestation of this trend is model-free reinforcement learning, a machine learning branch that enables an agent to interact with its environment and autonomously learn to maximize some reward measure. The potential here lies in allowing researchers to solve problems for systems that are difficult to model, and/or that the user lacks knowledge of how to solve directly. Recent examples within the robotics context include controlling a 47 DOF humanoid to navigate diverse obstacles \cite{heess_emergence_2017}, dexterously manipulating objects using a 24 DOF robotic hand \cite{openai_learning_2018}, and enabling a physical quadruped robot to run \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and recover from falls \cite{lee_robust_2019}. In this paper we examine legged locomotion. This problem class is notoriously challenging, and consequently reinforcement learning represents a popular tool to address it. We would contend that hand-designed, model-based control still constitutes the state of the art (exemplified by Boston Dynamics), but RL has proven a productive approach. There exist examples of learned policies surpassing hand-designed ones \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and there exists good reason to believe these learning methods will maintain their current trajectory of increasing performance gains and usability. But these algorithms possess a serious drawback in that they are predominantly black boxes. It remains an open challenge to determine what exactly your RL agent has learned. If all you know is that one of your agents attained very high reward, it remains unclear how to verify that this system is safe and reasonable in all state space regions it will visit during its lifetime. Nor can we necessarily make any claims about the stability or robustness properties of the system. Recent work ~\citep{Taleledeep} has employed so-called mesh-based tools to examine precisely these questions. However, the utility of any mesh-based tool to accurately discretize a state-space remains limited, due to the curse of dimensionality. In practice, these methods can only work on relatively high-dimensional systems if the reachable space grows at a rate that is substantially smaller than the exponential growth of the full state space within which it is embedded. To extend these methods to higher-dimensional systems, we will need to find ways to prevent the volume of visited states from expanding proportionally. One way to quantify this growth rate is by employing one of the several notions of "fractional dimensions" from fractal geometry. In this work, we discuss an efficient meshing algorithm, which we term box meshing. We demonstrate that this approach makes calculating the so-called mesh dimension feasible within the context of reinforcement learning. We also propose using other notions of fractional dimension from the literature as a proxy for the property we care about. We then demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents can be trained to reduce these measures by post-processing their reward function. We present the results of this training, and finally present some brief analysis of the resulting structure for selected policies.

text: Contemporary deep neural networks (DNNs) achieve remarkable breakthroughs across numerous domains including computer vision, speech recognition, and related fields. The capabilities of DNNs inspire boundless possibilities and speculation. Numerous significant and compelling investigations on DNNs continue to emerge. Various architectures of DNNs exist, including convolutional neural networks (e.g. LeNet \cite{45_lecun1998gradient}, AlexNet \cite{33_krizhevsky2012imagenet}, ResNet \cite{42_he2016deep}) and recurrent neural networks (e.g. LSTM \cite{46_olah2015understanding}). With the accelerated advancement of DNNs, increasing attention is directed toward the security aspects of DNNs. Specifically, generating adversarial examples and defending against adversarial attacks constitute fundamental techniques in DNN security. The vulnerability \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing} of DNNs has garnered substantial attention since its initial discovery. Extensive research has concentrated on this subject within the literature. These investigations can be broadly categorized into two primary areas: adversarial attacks \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,6_goodfellow2014explaining,7_kurakin2016adversarial,8_papernot2016limitations,9_moosavi2016deepfool,10_carlini2017towards,11_chen2017zoo,12_moosavi2017universal,13_su2019one,14_zhao2017generating,15_tabacof2016adversarial} and adversarial defenses \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,24_madry2017towards,43_tramer2017ensemble,44_papernot2016distillation,50_huang2015learning,51_cheng2020cat,52_song2018improving,53_zhang2019theoretically}. Adversarial attack methodologies consistently aim to generate adversarial examples capable of deceiving DNNs. Additionally, these adversarial examples are typically imperceptible to human observers. Conversely, adversarial defenses enhance DNN robustness against adversarial examples. The relationship between adversarial attacks and adversarial defenses resembles a zero-sum game. Numerous studies adhere to the definition that adversarial examples are nearly identical to original natural images while successfully deceiving DNNs \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing}. Within this definitional framework, an adversarial example remains imperceptible to humans (we term this an imperceptible adversarial example). Nevertheless, alternative forms of adversarial examples exist. For instance, certain research incorporates patches into original images to deceive DNNs \cite{16_brown2017adversarial,17_liu2018dpatch,18_karmon2018lavan,19_lee2019physical}. These examples are designated adversarial patches that successfully fool DNNs despite being perceptible to humans. Furthermore, adversarial noise images deliberately manipulated by humans can deceive DNNs \cite{4_nguyen2015deep}. Although these noise images are meaningless to humans, DNNs continue to classify them into specific classes with high confidence (we designate them as unrecognizable adversarial examples). It is noteworthy that the aforementioned works primarily concentrate on image perturbations designed to produce erroneous class labels. Consequently, Sabour et al. \cite{55_DBLP:journals/corr/SabourCFF15} focus on the hidden layers of DNN representations and propose a methodology to construct adversarial examples that are perceptually similar to one image, yet whose hidden layer representation appears remarkably similar to a different image from a distinct class. Their work raises questions regarding DNN representation and the interpretation of adversarial examples. Further investigation is warranted regarding how adversarial disturbances are represented in hidden layers and whether hidden layer information can be utilized to construct more robust adversarial defense strategies. Building upon the aforementioned works, in this paper, we analyze the characteristics of various types of adversarial examples. We discover that whether the sample constitutes an imperceptible adversarial example, an adversarial patch, or an unrecognizable adversarial example, uncertainty exists (correct or incorrect) in the machine's prediction results. However, for humans, provided the disturbance does not alter the original objective reality, human judgment remains fundamentally accurate. We emphasize that significant differences exist between human vision and DNNs in image recognition. Humans recognize images in pixel space while machines perform recognition in a specialized space (hidden layer) that constitutes a machine "vision" space. Therefore, we propose a conjecture that, without altering objective reality, the influence of adversarial disturbances on prediction results depends on whether the original characteristic semantics are modified during the hidden layer propagation process. Based on this assumption, we propose a defense mechanism that incorporates hidden layer representation to enhance the adversarial robustness of the model. Our defense strategy compresses input information and filters substantial portions of it, including adversarial perturbations. In fact, the proposed defense method can be regarded as an activation function that operates within the hidden layer of the neural network and contributes to improving the model's adversarial robustness. We theoretically certify the effectiveness of the defense under a simplified case. Additionally, we provide a specific defensive function and empirically verify the effectiveness of our defense mechanism. It is noteworthy that our defensive model achieves state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we discuss how to construct imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples by utilizing hidden layer representations. The contributions are listed as follows: \begin{enumerate} 	\item We discuss the characteristics of different types of adversarial examples (Imperceptible adversarial example, Adversarial patch and Unrecognizable adversarial example) and propose a conjecture that the representation of adversarial perturbation in hidden layer is much different with that of clean example. 	\item Based on this conjecture, we propose an effective and efficient defence method to improve the adversarial robustness of the model. The proposed defence strategy will compress the information of input and filter many of that, including the adversarial perturbation. This defense strategy is also regarded as an activation function, and we prove the effectiveness of this defense strategy theoretically. 	\item Incorporating the representation in hidden layer, we provide three types of adversarial attack to generate imperceptible adversarial examples, unrecognizable adversarial examples and adversarial patches, which are shown in Fig. \ref{overview_123}. 	\item Our defence method, which achieves state-of-the-art performance, has $97.09\%$ accuracy under CW on MNIST, $89.03\%$ accuracy under CW on CIFAR10 and $64.38\%$ under CW on ImageNet. \end{enumerate} In the remainder of this paper, Section \ref{section2} introduces the related work in the literature. In Section \ref{section3}, we discuss three types of adversarial examples and propose a conjecture. In Section \ref{section4}, we propose a defense strategy and a specific defense function (activation function). In Section \ref{section5}, incorporating the representation in hidden layers, we introduce three adversarial attacks to generate three types of adversarial examples, respectively. In Section \ref{experiment}, we conduct extensive experiments and confirm that our methods are effective. Finally, Section \ref{conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: Currently, cyber-attacks are typically executed by skilled hackers and are characterized by hybrid TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) and prolonged adversarial behaviors. Consequently, detecting them using conventional intrusion detection methods\cite{2018A,2020Preparing} proves extremely challenging, as these methods typically examine short-term behaviors while disregarding the abundant contextual information of the system. To address this challenge, we examine the findings of numerous existing studies and discover that provenance data represent the optimal approach for cyber-attack detection tasks\cite{2018Provenance,2017Applying,2020UNICORN}. Provenance data characterize system entities (e.g., processes, files, sockets) and interactions among these system entities (the interactions are typically represented as system events, e.g., read, write, fork). Initially, provenance data can characterize how system entities interact with one another and furnish comprehensive contextual information for each system entity\cite{2015Trustworthy}. Additionally, provenance data can link causally-related events even when these events are temporally separated by extended periods\cite{2020UNICORN}. Provenance data are typically gathered using OS audit logs (e.g., Linux Auditd\cite{LINUXAuditd}, Windows ETW\cite{ETW}). To execute cyber-attack detection tasks using provenance data, most existing approaches model the provenance data as a directed acyclic graph (termed a provenance graph), where nodes represent system entities and edges represent system events. Figure 1 illustrates an example of the provenance graph. Subsequently, most existing studies (e.g., SLEUTH\cite{2018SLEUTH}, HOLMES\cite{2019HOLMES}, CONAN\cite{0CONAN}) attempt to detect cyber-attacks by manually crafting various rules based on threat intelligence (e.g., kill chain\cite{2015Technical}, ATT\&CK\cite{ATT&CK}). Although rule-based detection strategies are efficient and have attained state-of-the-art performance, they still possess the following limitations. Initially, rule design constitutes an exceptionally challenging task, as it demands specialized domain expertise in cyber-attack strategies, operating systems, and computer networks. Additionally, rules lack generalization capability, as they are developed under specific macro environments (e.g., cyber-attack strategies, network environments). They readily become outdated and require adjustment or complete redesign when the macro environment evolves. Furthermore, rules are constrained by human experience and cannot address complex and latent patterns. Conversely, learning-based techniques have been extensively applied to cyber security tasks including intrusion detection\cite{2018A,2020Preparing}, malware detection\cite{2017Malware,2020Enhancing}, and fraud detection\cite{2018Online,2020Interleaved}. Compared to rule-based techniques, learning-based techniques offer the following advantages. Initially, learning-based techniques (particularly deep learning techniques) can extract latent patterns and construct detection models from training datasets with minimal domain knowledge. Additionally, the detection model can adapt to new macro environments through retraining or fine-tuning in an automated manner. Since provenance data are represented as provenance graphs, we utilize GNN (Graph Neural Network)\cite{2019Comprehensive} to construct the cyber-attack detection model. However, due to the complexity of cyber-attacks and system provenance, building cyber-attack detection models based on GNN remains a challenging endeavor. Initially, provenance graphs generated from OS audit logs are intricate. A provenance graph encompasses multiple node types (e.g., processes, files, sockets) and multiple edge types (e.g., read, write, and create). Furthermore, a node or edge can be characterized by additional attributes (e.g., a file can be characterized by attributes including source, file extension, and sensitivity level). Additionally, the nodes and edges of provenance graphs are specific instances of system entities and system events, which render the detection model nearly incapable of learning common patterns from these entirely distinct instances. Furthermore, cyber-attack detection constitutes a time-sensitive task. However, most GNNs incur high computational and space costs. Moreover, since cyber-attacks are typically persistent, provenance graphs continuously expand over time, causing GNN-based methods to inevitably encounter efficiency and memory challenges. Moreover, cyber-attacks are typically stealthy, making them extremely difficult to detect by examining individual system entities alone (e.g., an attack activity might be executed through collaboration among multiple processes and files). However, considering the entire provenance graph is also impractical, as it is typically too large and dominated by benign system entities. Finally, the detection model must continuously process new incoming system entities, while GNNs learn representations of new system entities by embedding them with existing nodes and edges in a shared space. However, rerunning the learning procedures whenever new system entities arrive is infeasible due to high computational complexity. To address the aforementioned challenges, this paper proposes an intelligent cyber-attack detection system based on heterogeneous provenance graph learning. For the first and second challenges, we adopt a heterogeneous graph\cite{0Mining} to represent the complex system entities and events in the provenance graph, and subsequently employ meta-path based approaches\cite{2017metapath2vec} to extract higher-level semantic interactions among system entities. For the third challenge, we utilize graph embedding techniques to learn low-dimensional vector representations for each node in the heterogeneous graph. Here, graph embedding can be executed as a pre-training step, and the vector representations are subsequently used to rapidly initialize the detection model. For the fourth and fifth challenges, we connect new incoming system entities to the existing heterogeneous graph and perform local graph sampling to incorporate the new incoming system entities and the most relevant existing nodes into a compact local graph. Subsequently, the detection model is constructed based on this local graph. In summary, the primary contributions of this paper are as follows. 1) We propose an intelligent cyber-attack detection system by leveraging GNNs. text: \vspace{-2mm} Our physical environment is three-dimensional, wherein the complete extent of objects -- their geometry and dynamics -- exists and persists within 3D space. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of visual predictive models presently employed in robotics, which forecast object motion under applied actions, remain constrained to predicting solely 2D motion (i.e\onedot} \def\Ie{I.e\onedot optical flow) of partial observations, e.g\onedot} \def\Eg{E.g\onedot forecasting the 2D flow of pixels \citep{vijayanarasimhan2017sfm,dosovitskiy2015flownet}, or predicting the 3D scene flow of visible points from a partial point cloud \citep{byravan2017se3,byravan2018se3}. Regrettably, modeling the motion of exclusively visible surfaces frequently results in data degeneration, wherein objects diminish and disappear from the representation as they become occluded. This phenomenon causes the predictive models to exhibit poor performance in cluttered environments, wherein objects regularly appear, disappear, then reappear within view as the robot manipulates them. In this work, we examine the advantages of learning a complete and persistent 3D scene representation for visual predictive modeling. We present \textbf{3D Dynamic Scene Representation\xspace (DSR)}: a 3D volumetric scene representation that concurrently discovers, tracks and reconstructs novel objects and predicts their motion under robotic interactions. Specifically, the representation encodes three object properties, all of which have been extensively argued as fundamental to human scene understanding~\cite{spelke2007core}. \begin{itemize} \vspace{-2mm} \item[\textbullet] \textbf{{Permanence}:} visual information is aggregated into a persistent 3D representation. This signifies that as objects vanish from view due to occlusion, they persist in the representation. This facilitates more precise predictions of object motion when displaced by other objects in occlusion, or when gradually reappearing in view. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Amodal completeness:} from partial observations of the scene, DSR infers complete 3D occupancy of each object, including regions that are not directly observed. This characteristic enables it to predict the rigid body motion of the entire object rather than solely visible surfaces. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Spatiotemporal continuity:} the representation identifies individual object instances and maintains their identity over time. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Interpretability:} DSR explicitly models object instances, geometry, and motion, rendering it readily applicable for high-level reasoning in robotic applications. \vspace{-2mm} \end{itemize} To learn this scene representation, we present DSR-Net\xspace, a 3D recurrent neural network that comprises two principal components: 1) a scene encoder that encodes visual observations (i.e\onedot} \def\Ie{I.e\onedot, depth images) into a volumetric 3D scene representation, and 2) a motion prediction network that accepts the 3D scene representation and an action to be executed by the robot and predicts volumetric scene flow. The scene flow is subsequently utilized to spatially warp the current scene representation before integrating it with the 3D scene representation of the subsequent time step. The warping operation enables the network to aggregate information over time in a spatially coherent manner. DSR-Net\xspace is trained end-to-end in simulation and subsequently evaluated in the real world with a robotic manipulator on a tabletop configuration. Our experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting the rigid body motion of novel objects under robotic interaction in unstructured cluttered environments. The contributions of our paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel 3D dynamic scene representation (DSR) that captures object permanence, amodal completeness, and continuity -- desirable properties as components of a perception stack for downstream robotic manipulation tasks. Second, we propose DSR-Net\xspace, an end-to-end framework that learns such 3D representations via 3D convolutions. Third, we construct a novel benchmark dataset with over 80,000 simulated interactions and 1,500 real-world interactions for learning and evaluating dynamic 3D scene representations. Our experiments in both simulation and the real world demonstrate that DSR-Net\xspace achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting 3D scene dynamics. Furthermore, it enables more precise action planning in manipulation tasks such as planar pushing. Please find additional results and videos in supplementary material.

text: Accurate box estimation is essential for successful tracking performance. Early trackers typically address this problem through multi-scale search~\cite{SiameseFC,ECO,DRT,unveiling} or sampling-then-regression approaches~\cite{SINT,MDNet}, which are imprecise and severely constrain tracker performance. To obtain more robust and accurate tracking results, numerous state-of-the-art trackers~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} employ a multi-stage tracking strategy, which incorporates additional tracking stages for enhanced box estimation precision. These trackers initially perform coarse target localization and subsequently refine the preliminary result in the additional tracking stages to achieve more accurate box prediction. Nevertheless, this box estimation remains improvable, even for state-of-the-art trackers. An oracle experiment confirms this assertion. We configure the tracker's search region to consistently center on the ground truth such that the performance becomes primarily determined by box estimation capability. Table~\ref{tab:oracle} demonstrates that under the aforementioned oracle configuration, state-of-the-art trackers' AUC scores remain substantially below perfection, indicating inadequate box estimation, despite some methods (\emph{e.g.} ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}) incorporating dedicated box estimation modules. Conversely, given the perfectly centered search region, the proposed Alpha-Refine attains significantly superior performance, demonstrating Alpha-Refine's excellence in box estimation. Furthermore, most refinement methods in existing trackers~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} exhibit limited transferability, since their training is integrated with other components. Additional retraining becomes necessary if these refinement modules are deployed to new base trackers. In contrast to these methods, Alpha-Refine is trained independently and can be directly deployed to any existing trackers in a plug-and-play manner, requiring no additional training or modification of the base tracker. In this work, various design alternatives are investigated and compared. Specifically, we evaluate multiple feature fusion modules and prediction heads. We also explore utilizing an auxiliary mask head, which incorporates pixel-level supervision into the training. We discover that extracting and preserving precise spatial information constitutes the key to accurate box estimation. To this end, we ultimately adopt pixel-wise correlation along with a key-point style prediction head for better preserving and exploiting the detailed spatial information. Additionally, an auxiliary mask head is employed, which encourages the network to extract more detailed spatial information, resulting in more precise box estimation. Furthermore, if we retain the mask head during the inference stage, Alpha-Refine will enable the base trackers to predict the object mask, accommodating scenarios where the mask is required. The design alternatives will be discussed in Section~\ref{sec:method} and validated in Section~\ref{sec:experiment}. To verify the effectiveness of our Alpha-Refine module, we select six prominent base trackers: ECO~\cite{ECO}, RT-MDNet~\cite{RTMDNet}, SiamRPNpp~\cite{SiamRPNplus}, ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}, and DiMPsuper~\cite{DiMP}, on multiple tracking benchmarks, namely, LaSOT~\cite{LaSOT}, GOT-10K~\cite{GOT10K}, TrackingNet~\cite{Trackingnet} and VOT2020~\cite{VOT2020}. Taking Fig.~\ref{LaSOT_Improvement} as an example, experimental results demonstrate that our proposed refinement module improves the base trackers' performance substantially. Compared with its competitors (\emph{i.e.} IoU-Net~\cite{ATOM,DiMP} and SiamMask~\cite{SiamMask}), Alpha-Refine's performance also exceeds them by a considerable margin. The proposed Alpha-Refine method yields a series of enhanced trackers, among which the ARSiamRPN (Alpha-Refine enhanced SiamRPNpp) and ARDiMP50 (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMP50) achieve favorable efficiency-precision trade-offs, while ARDiMPsuper (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMPsuper) achieves state-of-the-art performance at real-time speed on multiple benchmarks.

text: Learned index structures have emerged as an alternative to traditional database indexes in recent years since their potential was demonstrated by Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. The fundamental concept underlying learned indexes is that one can treat the index as a model that predicts the position of a given key within the dataset. A key advantage of this index type results from the reduced index size, which can achieve orders of magnitude reduction in memory footprint, since the trained model or the hierarchy of models in the index requires less space than storing actual data. Additionally, such indexes exchange increased computations for reduced memory accesses, which could enhance performance if the overall computation cycles are less expensive relative to memory access latency. Conversely, for such an index to be effective in its predictions, the index model must be trained on the target dataset prior to deployment, which constrains the dynamic nature of the index. There have been several proposals \cite{histtree, alex, pgmindex, fittingtree, shifttable, radixspline, learnedMultiDim} for learned index structures since the proposal from Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. These proposals and initial benchmarking efforts \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, benchmarkingSOSD} already compare learned indexes to index structures that are not based on learned models. However, these comparisons are conducted by primarily focusing on higher-level metrics such as throughput (requests completed per second), latency (average time to complete a request), index size, scalability with respect to number of threads utilized, etc. While these metrics are extremely important and necessary to understand the overall benefits and disadvantages of learned index structures, they represent one side of a coin, particularly for main-memory-optimized index structures. These metrics by themselves do not provide a detailed understanding of how learned indexes utilize the micro-architectural resources of a processor (e.g., utilization of the front-end resources and the different levels of the cache hierarchy). In this paper, our objective is to illuminate this other side of the coin. To achieve our objective, we focus on the learned index ALEX \cite{alex}, which is one of the first learned indexes that is designed from the ground up to enable efficient updates and inserts. We perform a micro-architectural analysis of ALEX, while comparing its behavior to two index structures that are not based on learned models; ART \cite{artpaper, artcode}, a trie-based index structure, and B+tree \cite{btreecode}, a tree-based index structure. The reason we select these two structures to compare against specifically is that ALEX is already compared against them in the original paper \cite{alex} and by other studies \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, histtree}. This would allow our results to be cross-validated. We create a benchmark driver \footnote{Will be made available once the paper is accepted.} that generates YCSB-like \cite{ycsbpaper} workloads. Using this driver, we generate four workloads with varying read-write intensities and two datasets of different sizes. We then report the breakdown of execution cycles into different micro-architectural components following Intel's Top-down Micro-architecture Analysis Method (TMAM) \cite{tmam}. Our study demonstrates the following: \begin{list}{\labelitemi}{\leftmargin=1.5em} \item{Similar to ART and B+Tree, ALEX spends the majority of its execution cycles in memory-bound stalls as a result of the long-latency data stalls from the last-level cache. In contrast to ART and B+Tree, in general, ALEX exhibits fewer stalls and spends fewer cycles per instruction across different workload patterns.} \item{On the other hand, inserts to the right-end of the tree (\textit{out-of-bound} keys) lead to an order of magnitude increase in the per-request instruction footprint of ALEX, while the impact for ART and B+Tree is not significant, due to model re-training. The instruction-level parallelism for such instructions, however, is quite high. Therefore, this increase in instruction footprint does not significantly impact the overall execution time for ALEX.} \end{list} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. First, \Cref{background} surveys related work and provides a brief summary of the index structures used in this study as well as the micro-architecture of a processor. Then, \Cref{setup} presents the experimental setup and methodology, and \Cref{results} presents and discusses the results of the analysis. Finally, \Cref{conclusion} concludes with a summary of our findings and outlines directions for future research.

text: Hardware developments in the past decade have brought multicore parallel machines into the mainstream. Although there exist multiple programming paradigms and tools to enable parallelism in multicore machines, the approach based on \defn{nested parallelism} with \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} is undoubtedly the most popular and widely adopted. The nested parallelism model and its variants have been supported by most parallel programming languages (e.g., Cilk, TBB, TPL, X10, Java Fork-join, and OpenMP), introduced in textbooks (e.g., Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein~\cite{CLRS}), and employed in a variety of research papers (to list a few: \cite{agrawal2014batching,blelloch2010low,BCGRCK08,BG04,Blelloch1998,blelloch1999pipelining,BlellochFiGi11,BST12,Cole17,BBFGGMS16,dinh2016extending,chowdhury2017provably,blelloch2018geometry,dhulipala2020semi,BBFGGMS18,Dhulipala2018,blelloch2020randomized,gu2021parallel,blelloch2016justjoin,sun2018pam,sun2019parallel,ptreedb}). At a high level, this model permits an algorithm to recursively and dynamically create (\emph{fork}) parallel tasks, which will be executed on $P$ processors by a dynamic scheduler. This nested (binary) fork-join provides an effective abstraction for shared-memory parallelism. From the user (algorithm designer or programmer) perspective, it represents a straightforward extension to the classic programming model with additional keywords for creating new tasks (e.g., \op{fork}) and synchronization (e.g., \op{join}) between tasks. The \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} plays a crucial role in this ecosystem. It automatically and dynamically maps a nested parallel algorithm to the hardware efficiently both in theory and in practice. In this paper, we study two important topics related to the RWS scheduler. First, we show a \defn{new, simplified, and classroom-ready version of analysis for the RWS scheduler}, which we believe is easier to understand than existing ones. Second, we provide some \defn{new analyses for parallel cache complexity} for nested-parallel algorithms based on the RWS scheduler. We provide a list of almost optimal bounds listed in \Cref{table:intro}, and more discussions will be given later. Our first contribution is a simplified analysis for the RWS scheduler. The theoretical efficiency of the RWS scheduler was first established by Blumofe and Leiserson~\cite{blumofe1999scheduling}, and is subsequently analyzed for a variety of settings (to list a few: \cite{Acar02,itpa,muller2016latency,acar2013scheduling,BBFGGMS16,singer2019proactive,Acar2016tapp,singer2020scheduling,arora2001thread}). Although these analyses fundamentally consider more complex settings (e.g., to also consider external I/Os), the analyses themselves are quite complicated. To the best of our knowledge, the details of the proofs are covered in very few courses related to parallelism, and in most cases, RWS is simply treated as a black box. Hence, we merely consider the goal of bounding the number of steals of the RWS scheduler, and we want to answer the question of what the simplest analysis for the RWS scheduler can be, or what is the most comprehensible version in education. This paper presents a simplified analysis in \Cref{sec:rws}. Unlike most of the existing analyses, our version does not rely on defining the potential function for a substructure of the computation, which we believe is easier to understand. Our analysis is inspired by a recent analysis~\cite{itpa} that is similar to~\cite{agrawal2008adaptive,suksompong2014bounds}. Our analysis differs from~\cite{itpa} in two aspects. First, unlike~\cite{itpa}, we do not assume all processors operate in lock-steps (the PRAM setting). Instead, we assume a highly asynchronous setting, which is more realistic for today's parallel machines. Second, we separate the mathematical calculation from the details of the RWS algorithm, which may be helpful for classroom teaching. Our second and main contribution of this paper is on the parallel cache complexity for algorithms using the RWS scheduler. On today's machines, the memory access cost typically dominates the running time of most combinatorial algorithms. To capture this, sequentially, Aggarwal and Vitter~\cite{AggarwalV88} first formalized the external-memory model to capture the I/O cost of an algorithm, which was refined by Frigo et al.~\cite{Frigo99} as the ideal-cache model. The cost measure is called \emph{I/O complexity}~\cite{AggarwalV88} (noted as $Q_1$) or \emph{cache complexity}~\cite{Frigo99} when specifying the communication cost between the cache and the main memory. While this model has achieved great success in the algorithm and database communities, so far, few results have extended it to the parallel (distributed cache) setting, which we summarize in \Cref{sec:cachebound}. Among them, Acar, Blelloch and Blumofe~\cite{Acar02} first defined and demonstrated that the parallel cache complexity $Q_P$ is at most $Q_1+O(PDM/B)$, where $P$, $D$, $M$ and $B$ are the number of processors, span (aka.\ depth, the longest critical path of dependences), cache size, and cache block size, respectively (definitions in \Cref{sec:prelim}). However, this bound is pessimistic and typically too loose. Frigo and Strumpen~\cite{frigo2009cache} and later work by Cole and Ramachandran~\cite{cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} demonstrated tighter parallel cache complexity for many cache-oblivious algorithms summarized \Cref{table:intro}. However, the bounds have a polynomial overhead\footnote{Such an overhead is usually $n^{a}$, where $a$ is a constant and $1/2\le a<1$.} on the input size when the span is polynomial to the input size. Such overhead can easily dominate the cache bound when plugging in the real-world input size, as discussed in the caption of \Cref{table:intro}. It remained an open question on how to close this gap. In this paper, we significantly close this gap for a variety of algorithms. The polynomial overhead in the previous analysis~\cite{Acar02,frigo2009cache,cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} is due to the high span of these algorithms (a polynomial of the algorithm's span appears in the bound). The key insight in our analysis is to break such polynomial correlation between the algorithm's span and the overhead for parallel cache complexity. Our new analysis is inspired by the abstraction of \kdgrid{} proposed recently by Blelloch and Gu~\cite{BG2020}, which was previously used to demonstrate sequential cache bounds. We extend the idea for analyzing parallel cache complexity. Our analysis directly examines the ``real'' dependencies in the computation structure of these algorithms, instead of those caused by parallelism. In particular, the core of our analysis is simply the \emph{recurrences} of these algorithms. As a result, the parallel dependency of the computation (the algorithm's span) does not appear in the analysis. This helps us avoid the complication of digging into the details of the scheduling algorithms in the analysis, and the analysis is no more complicated than simply solving recurrences. To accomplish this, we define the \dacrecur{}, which effectively models the pattern of recurrences of many classic algorithms, and show a general theorem, \Cref{thm:recur}, to solve these recurrences. By applying these results, we can achieve the new bounds in \Cref{table:intro}. The parallel overheads are polylogarithmic instead of polynomial to the input size, compared to the lower bounds by~\cite{ballard2014communication,BG2020}. We believe the methodology is of independent interest, and could be useful in analyzing other parallel or sequential algorithms. We leave this as future work. The contributions of this paper are as follows. \

text: When healthcare professionals (HCPs) utilize a treatment search engine to identify treatment options for their patients, they must develop sufficient trust in the system. While accuracy, performance, and design are fundamental for establishing such trust, additional measures may be necessary to achieve a threshold where HCPs trust the system sufficiently to employ it in critical scenarios, e.g., when a patient's life may be endangered. A search engine would conventionally deliver a ranked list of related items corresponding to a specific query. Nevertheless, absence of explanations could result in diminished user trust as they would fail to comprehend the underlying logic of retrieving an item in response to a query. In the medical domain, where the imperative to avoid errors is paramount, incorrectly attributing the cause of a mistake could prove fatal. Consequently, without the capacity to interpret the model, HCPs' confidence in the model diminishes and will, ultimately, refrain from using the model's outputs \cite{pu2006trust}. Furthermore, due to compliance regulations, most search engines in the medical domain deliver unordered lists of related items in response to a query, making it challenging for users to examine or distinguish the most relevant items for their requirements. As an example, treatment search engines such as clinicaltrials.gov do not provide relevance-based ranking of documents, partly because ranking in-criteria treatment options may be susceptible to favoritism, which is strictly prohibited for clinical trials \cite{Clinical58:online}. Moreover, for an efficient and comprehensive search, a status/date/title-based ordering may not always be the most practical for end users as they tend to disperse similar results from each other. A potential solution to deliver explanations is to employ current explainable methods. A class of such methods would furnish global explanations only so that we can assess the overall search engine as a whole, but cannot deliver appropriate explanations in response to each individual query \cite{dam2018explainable}. Another option is to utilize other methods for local explainability such as LIME \cite{das2020opportunities} and SHAP \cite{lundberg2017unified} as these explain how or why a specific result is delivered. However, these methods are designed for machine learning problems, such as classification and regression, but not for explaining search engine results. When local explanations were employed to explain search results, these were either based on one feature from the documents like word prominence \cite{verma2019lirme}, or not applicable to the clinical trials since they are based on user reviews for each document \cite{catherine2017explainable} (which are unavailable for clinical trials). Another major challenge is to furnish HCPs with user-friendly, reliable, and easy-to-understand explanations. A major limitation of current explainability techniques, such as LIME \cite{das2020opportunities}, is that these techniques tend to focus on assisting users with technical backgrounds to interpret the system. HCPs are not universally expected to comprehend the detailed workings of a complex retrieval model. Thus, HCPs require explanations that are high level and intuitive, while they do not necessarily need to reflect the exact inner workings of retrieval models. This opens up an opportunity in which explanation models can be constructed in a way that they are not sensitive to minor changes in the model of a search engine. For instance, with a treatment search engine, we may provide a local explanation such as "the queried disease is mentioned in the retrieved clinical trial's title", and as long as the retrieval model relies on this as a feature, we are employing a generic explanation method, and we can develop the search engine and explanation module fairly separately in practice. In this paper, an explainability method is developed which delivers tailored explanations to medical practitioners for retrieved items. To that end, meaningful features from clinical trials are extracted from different data sources, and preferences of different users are elicited by employing a crowdsourcing-based methodology. We then propose a method to translate preferences into importance level of features. Based on features' importance levels, tailored explanations are obtained for each specific query, according to which we develop a sentence template in order to present them to users. In addition, we introduce explainability scores, according to which we order retrieved items. The results suggest that the use of local explainability on clinical search engines enhances HCPs trust, search experience, and result ordering satisfaction.

text: Semantic segmentation aims to partition an image into segments with semantic categories. Although significant progress has been achieved~\cite{FCN,Deeplab,Deeplabv3Plus,pspnet,ocrnet,segformer}, contemporary semantic segmentation models are predominantly trained in a supervised fashion with a fixed set of predefined semantic categories, and typically require hundreds of samples for each class. In contrast, humans can differentiate at least 30,000 basic categories~\cite{biederman1987recognition,fu2017recent}, and identify novel categories merely from some \textit{high-level descriptions}. How to attain human-level capability to recognize stuff and things in images represents one of the fundamental objectives in computer vision. Recent studies on zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZS3)~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net} have indeed progressed towards that fundamental objective. Following the fully supervised semantic segmentation models~\cite{FCN,Deeplabv3Plus,Deeplab} and zero-shot classification models~\cite{lampert2013attribute,zhang2016zero,jayaraman2014zero,rohrbach2011evaluating,akata2015evaluation}, these works formulate zero-shot semantic segmentation as a \textit{pixel-level zero-shot classification problem}. {Although these investigations have reported promising results, two primary issues still require resolution : (1) They typically transfer knowledge from seen to unseen classes by \textit{language} models~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net,fasttext} pre-trained exclusively on texts, which constrains their performance on vision tasks. Although large-scale pre-trained \textit{vision-language} models (\eg CLIP~\cite{clip} and ALIGN~\cite{align}) have demonstrated potential on \textit{image-level} vision tasks, how to effectively integrate them into the \textit{pixel-level} ZS3 problem remains unknown. (2) They typically establish correlations between \textit{pixel-level} visual features and semantic features for knowledge transfer, which is \textit{not natural} since we humans often use \textit{words or texts} to describe \textit{objects/segments} instead of \textit{pixels} in images. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:confusion}, it is unsurprising to observe that the \textit{pixel-level} classification exhibits poor accuracy on \textit{unseen classes}, which consequently degrades the final segmentation quality. This phenomenon is particularly evident when the number of unseen categories is large (see Fig.~\ref{fig:visadeinfercoco}). } An intuitive observation is that, given an image for semantic segmentation, we humans can first \textit{group pixels into segments} and then perform a \textit{segment-level semantic labeling} process. For example, a child can easily group the pixels of an object, even though he/she does not know the name of the object. Therefore, we argue that {\em a human-like zero-shot semantic segmentation procedure should be decomposed into two sub-tasks}: \begin{itemize} \item[-] A {\em class-agnostic grouping} to group pixels into segments. This task is essentially a classical image partition/grouping problem~\cite{DDMCMC,NormalizeCUT,supervisedeval}, and can be revitalized via deep learning based methods~\cite{maskformer,KNet,panopticsegformer}. \item[-] A {\em segment-level zero-shot classification} to assign semantic labels either seen or unseen to segments. \end{itemize} As the grouping task does not involve the semantic categories, a grouping model learned from seen classes can be readily transferred to unseen classes. The segment-level zero-shot classification is robust on the unseen classes and provides a flexible approach to integrate the pre-trained large-scale vision-language models~\cite{clip} to the ZS3 problem. To instantiate the decomposition idea, we present a simple yet efficient {\em zero-shot semantic segmentation model with transformer}, named ZegFormer, which uses a transformer decoder to output \textit{segment-level} embeddings, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}. It is then followed by a \textit{mask projection} for \textit{class-agnostic grouping} (CAG) and a \textit{semantic projection} for \textit{segment-level zero-shot classification} (s-ZSC). The \textit{mask projection} maps each \textit{segment-level} embedding to a mask embedding, which can be used to obtain a binary mask prediction via a dot product with a high-resolution feature map. The \textit{semantic projection} establishes the correspondences between \textit{segment-level} embedding and semantic features of a pre-trained \textit{text encoder} for s-ZSC. While the steps mentioned above can constitute a standalone approach for ZS3, the model trained on a small dataset struggles to have strong generalization. Thanks to the decomposition formulation, it is also flexible to use an \textit{image encoder} of a vision-language model to generate image embeddings for zero-shot segment classification. As we empirically find that the segment classification scores with image embeddings and s-ZSC are complementary. We fuse them to achieve the final classification scores for segments. The proposed ZegFormer model has been extensively evaluated with experiments and demonstrated superiority on various commonly-used benchmarks for ZS3. It outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by \textbf{22 points} in terms of mIoU for unseen classes on the PASCAL VOC~\cite{voc}, and \textbf{3 points} on the COCO-Stuff~\cite{coco-stuff}. Based on the challenging ADE20k-Full dataset~\cite{ade20k}, we also create a new ZS3 benchmark with {\bf 275 unseen classes}, the number of unseen classes in which are substantially larger than those in PASCAL-VOC ($5$ unseen classes) and COCO-Stuff ($15$ unseen classes). On the ADE20k-Full ZS3 benchmark, our performance is comparable to MaskFormer~\cite{maskformer}, a fully supervised semantic segmentation model. Our contributions in this paper are three-fold: \begin{itemize} 	\item We propose a new formulation for the task of ZS3, by decomposing it into two sub-tasks, {\em a class-agnostic grouping} and {\em a segment-level zero-shot classification}, which provides a more natural and flexible approach to integrate the pre-trained large-scale vision-language models into ZS3. 	\item With the new formulation, we present a simple and effective ZegFormer model for ZS3, which uses a transformer decoder to generate \textit{segment-level} embeddings for grouping and zero-shot classification. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed ZegFormer is the first model taking full advantage of the pre-trained large-scale vision-language model (\eg CLIP~\cite{clip}) for ZS3. 	\item We achieved state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks for ZS3. The ablation and visualization analyses demonstrate that the decomposition formulation is superior to pixel-level zero-shot classification by a large margin. \end{itemize}

text: Despite recent advances in the field of autonomous driving, HD maps remain an essential component in contemporary systems as they provide detailed information regarding road infrastructure enabling various applications such as motion planning and enhanced perception. However, to utilize HD maps effectively, it is necessary to accurately determine the vehicle pose within the map. To address this localization task, high precision systems generally employ RTK-GNSS systems with integrated IMUs or vehicle odometry in a probabilistic fusion scheme~\cite{jo2011interacting,schreiber2016vehicle}. However, the high cost of equipment and limitations in dense urban environments render these methods restricted to research and data generation. Therefore, most deployed autonomous vehicles utilize an HD map that stores information about the environmental elements like lane topology, traffic signs, and traffic lights to localize. With the availability of this information, landmark-based localization has gained attention. Such methods consist of a perception module to extract the necessary features from the sensor readings and continuously match them to the available map elements to constrain the vehicle pose~\cite{caselitz2016monocular,cattaneo2019cmrnet}. Supported by the extensive research and advances in deep learning, the perception modules in contemporary systems typically consist of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract the necessary features from the environment~\cite{poggenhans2018precise},~\cite{pauls2020monocular}. Although state-of-the-art CNN architectures can provide a comprehensive understanding of the environment utilizing sensors such as cameras~\cite{porzi2019seamless,mohan2021efficientps} and LiDARs~\cite{sirohi2021efficientlps}, most CNNs cannot provide a reliable confidence estimate or are overconfident about their predictions. This can compromise a localization algorithm's robustness and accuracy. The task of uncertainty estimation with deep learning extends the standard neural network-based methods to additionally predict the associated uncertainty or confidence in the prediction. Popular uncertainty estimation methods primarily utilize the sampling-based methods~\cite{gal2016dropout}, which are computationally and time-intensive. While the research for sampling-free methods is gaining attention, current approaches focus on predicting the uncertainties for a single task like classification~\cite{sensoy2018evidential} or regression~\cite{amini2019deep}. In contrast, an overall perception system of autonomous vehicles consists of various tasks, such as segmentation and detection. In this paper, we aim to address the localization problem in challenging urban scenarios with a low-cost sensor setup and extremely sparse HD maps containing only lane borders and traffic lights. We present a novel monocular camera-based localization system that leverages the uncertainty estimations of our proposed multi-task perception module. The perception module simultaneously predicts the uncertainties associated with semantics of the lane and with bounding box parameters of the traffic lights in a single pass. The main contributions of this paper are: 1) a novel pose graph localization system robust in challenging scenarios by exploiting predicted uncertainties, 2) a multi-task uncertainty-aware perception module capable of simultaneously predicting semantic and regression uncertainties in a sampling free fashion, 3) a novel association-free and differentiable cost map generation module guided by prediction uncertainties. We demonstrate the performance gain by incorporating uncertainties in our localization method by evaluating on the challenging Lyft 5 dataset~\cite{kesten2019lyft}.

The aim of this paper is to deal with the problem of localization in a challenging urban environment with a cheap system of sensors and a sparse HD map consisting of lane boundaries and traffic lights. The perception system of an AV involves many different tasks such as object detection and feature extraction. Our perception system predicts the uncertainties associated with the semantics of the lanes and the bounding boxes of the traffic lights in a single pass. We present a novel monocular camera-based localization system that exploits the uncertainty estimation of our proposed multi-tasked perception module. The principal contribution of this paper is a new pose-graph localization system, robust to demanding environments, which exploits the uncertainty estimates of our proposed multi-task perception model. The performance improvement achieved by introducing uncertainty into the localization system is demonstrated by the experiments on the demanding Lyft5 data set.

text: \vspace{-8pt} Throughout the past eight years, deep generative models have exhibited remarkable performance in producing photorealistic images, substantially enhanced by the groundbreaking technique of generative adversarial networks (GANs)~\citep{gan14nips,radford2015dcgan,gulrajani2017wgan,miyato2018spectral,brock2018BigGAN,karras2017ProGAN,karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}. Nevertheless, as the gap between authentic and synthetic content narrows, numerous significant concerns emerge~\citep{harris2018deepfakes,chesney2019deepfakes,brundage2018malicious}: what happens when these models are exploited to deceive sensors, create deep fakes, and facilitate large-scale misinformation? Not only do humans struggle to differentiate deep fakes, but specialized research endeavors in deep fake detection~\citep{durall2019unmasking,zhang2019detecting,frank2020dct2d_detect,zhang2020not} and attribution~\citep{marra2019gans,ning2019iccv_gan_detection,wang2020cnn} also fail to maintain effectiveness against the advancement of generative models. For instance, researchers examine the mechanisms underlying deep fake detection and subsequently enhance generation techniques to better satisfy detection criteria~\citep{zhang2020not,margret2020upconvolution}. Fundamentally, any effective detector can serve as an auxiliary component to strengthen the discriminator in subsequent GAN iterations, thereby producing an even more powerful generator. The malicious potential of deep generative models impedes their commercialization process. For instance, during the commercialization of GPT-2~\citep{radford2019language} and GPT-3~\citep{brown2020language} models, OpenAI adopts a conservative approach by withholding open-source releases and instead providing only black-box APIs\footnote{\url{https://openai.com/blog/openai-api/}}. They employ costly human oversight to review user downloads and monitor API usage. Nevertheless, tracing accountability for downstream applications in an open-ended environment remains a challenging and industry-wide problem. \begin{wrapfigure}[13]{R}{0.6\textwidth} \centering \vspace{-8pt} \caption{The diagram of our fingerprinting mechanism for generators. See main text for descriptions. \vspace{-16pt} \end{wrapfigure} To address this challenge, we propose a model fingerprinting mechanism that facilitates responsible release and regulation of generative models. Specifically, we enable responsible model developers to fingerprint their generators and establish their accountability. Consequently, the generated samples embed fingerprints that can be precisely detected and traced to their origins. This is accomplished through efficient and scalable ad-hoc generation of numerous generator instances with unique fingerprints. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Middle. Similar to the principles of dynamic filter networks~\citep{jia2016dynamic} and style-based generator architectures~\citep{karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2} where network filters are conditioned on input rather than freely learned, we parameterize a unique fingerprint into the filters of each generator instance. The fundamental approach involves integrating a fingerprint auto-encoder into a GAN framework while maintaining original generation performance. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Left. Specifically, given a GAN backbone, we utilize the fingerprint embedding from the encoder to modulate each convolutional filter of the generator (Figure~\ref{fig:modulation}), and attempt to decode this fingerprint from the generated images. We jointly train the fingerprint auto-encoder and GAN using our fingerprint-related losses and the original adversarial loss. See Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline} for the diagram, and~\ref{sec:loss_design} for details. Following training, the responsible model developer can efficiently fingerprint and distribute different generator instances to various user downloads, which possess identical generation performance but distinct fingerprints. \ning{Each user download corresponds to a unique fingerprint, which is maintained by the inventor's database.} Therefore, when model misuse occurs, the model developer can employ the decoder to detect the fingerprint from the generated images, \ning{match it in the database,} and subsequently trace user responsibility. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Right. Through this form of responsible disclosure, responsible model developers, such as OpenAI, possess a method to mitigate adverse societal impacts when releasing powerful models, while simultaneously maintaining an automated approach to attribute misuses. Several key properties characterize our mechanism. The \textbf{efficiency} to instantiate a generator is inherently achieved because, after training, fingerprint encoding and filter modulation operate with minimal overhead. We assess the \textbf{effectiveness} of our fingerprinting and achieve nearly perfect fingerprint detection accuracy. We also demonstrate the \textbf{fidelity} with negligible impact on original generation quality. See Section~\ref{sec:effectiveness_fidelity}. Our recommended operating point employs a 128-bit fingerprint (Section~\ref{sec:capacity}) which theoretically yields a \textbf{capacity} exceeding $10^{38}$ identifiable generator instances. The \textbf{scalability} derives from the fact that fingerprints are randomly sampled dynamically during training so that fingerprint detection generalizes effectively across the entire fingerprint space. See Section~\ref{sec:scalability} for validation. Additionally, we validate in Section~\ref{sec:secrecy} the \textbf{secrecy} of fingerprint presence and value against shadow model attacks. We validate in Section~\ref{sec:robustness_immunizability} the \textbf{robustness} and \textbf{immunizability} against perturbations on generated images. To address the initial motivation, we transition deep fake detection and attribution solutions from \textit{passive} detectors to \textit{proactive} fingerprinting. We demonstrate in Section~\ref{sec:detection_attribution} optimal performance and advantages over two state-of-the-art discriminative methods~\citep{ning2019iccv_gan_detection,wang2020cnn} particularly in open-world scenarios. This occurs because, conditioned on user-specific fingerprint inputs, the presence of such fingerprints in generated images ensures the distinction between real and fake, and enables attribution and responsibility tracing of deep fakes to their sources. Our \textbf{contributions} encompass four areas: (1) We \revise{enhance} the concept of fingerprinting for generative models that enables responsible disclosure of state-of-the-art GAN models. (2) We pioneer the novel direction for efficient and scalable GAN fingerprinting mechanisms, i.e., only one generic GAN model requires training while more than $10^{38}$ fingerprinted generator instances can be obtained with minimal overhead during deployment. (3) We also validate several key properties of our fingerprinting, including effectiveness, fidelity, large capacity, scalability, secrecy, robustness, and immunizability. (4) Finally, for deep fake detection and attribution tasks, we transition the solution from \textit{passive} classifiers to \textit{proactive} fingerprinting, and validate its optimal performance and advantages. It renders our responsible disclosure independent of GAN technique evolution. \vspace{-8pt}

text: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) middleboxes are extensively deployed as components of contemporary network security infrastructures \cite{xu2016survey}. They are stateful, meaning they not only examine individual packets, but also reassemble them to construct stateful connections defined by a network protocol (e.g., TCP), based on a predefined state machine. To accomplish this, they (for ease of exposition we refer to these as DPIs) must incorporate a custom network protocol implementation that is frequently simplified compared to its counterpart on endpoint platforms (e.g. the OS kernel) due to limited computational capability, prohibitive overhead and occasionally the requirement to provide generality in the presence of ambiguous network protocol specifications. \point{Adversarial Packets} Since the emergence of DPI, there have been numerous attacks designed to circumvent them. These attacks exploit the discrepancies between the DPI's and the OS-level network protocol implementations, to construct subtle yet potent packets which trigger entirely different behaviors on the DPI and at the endpoint (e.g., server). For instance, such a packet may be constructed so as to cause the DPI to disregard it, while it still reaches and is processed by the server. Such packets can potentially carry malicious payloads, and yet successfully evade the detection of the DPI (because their contents would not be examined at all). Even more concerning, prior work demonstrates that in some cases, using only one such packet could cause the DPI to withdraw from monitoring of the associated connection, thereby permitting follow-up packets in the connection to pass through without triggering alerts. \point{Automated Discovery of Evasion Packets} In recent years, as network protocol stacks have become increasingly complex with newly introduced features \cite{ramaiah2010improving}, a growing number of vendor-specific implementations, and continuously evolving specifications, there is a surge in research \cite{li2017lib, bock2019geneva, wang2020symtcp} on automating the discovery of \textit{adversarial packets} as described above, to evade DPIs. By applying principled search \cite{li2017lib}, genetic mutation \cite{bock2019geneva}, or symbolic execution \cite{wang2020symtcp}, a vast array of adversarial packets can be discovered with minimal to no manual intervention. While this advances understanding of attackers, it presents a significant challenge from the defense perspective. As protocol stacks evolve and become more complex, the potential discrepancies that may be discovered with automation can grow theoretically, and it becomes prohibitive to manually analyze these subtle implementation issues and patch all of them in the code base; additionally it is challenging to generate new hardcoded DPI policies to keep pace with new discrepancies that may emerge given the rate of rapidly evolving implementations and protocol standards. \point{Existing Defenses} Given its difficulty, only a few limited countermeasures have been proposed against adversarial packets. Notably, \cite{kreibich2001network}, Kreibich et al., apply \textit{traffic normalization} to mitigate the threats of adversarial packets. Specifically, a so-called traffic normalizer is proposed, which functions as a network forwarding element preceding DPI middleboxes, and modifies/drops the packets passing through the latter according to a predefined set of rules. These rules are manually curated to describe the "normal traffic" (e.g., the IP header length field must never be smaller or greater than the actual header length). This countermeasure unfortunately, cannot scale in the presence of automation -- the achievable search space of all possible adversarial packets can become sufficiently large to make timely manual curation prohibitive. Moreover, the ever-evolving protocol standards introduce false positives -- a previously correct rule can later cause incorrect decisions (e.g. normal packets being dropped) because of updated implementations. It is also worth noting that as a normalizer, or more generally a \textit{traffic shaper}, \cite{kreibich2001network} provides no detection capability; rather, it blindly modifies the traffic stream. \point{Our Approach} Our objective in this paper is to design a practical defense to effectively detect evasion attempts on DPI middleboxes. Instead of relying on extensive manual curation/analysis, we propose a novel, fully-automated (with minimal feature engineering) Machine Learning (ML)-based approach called \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace (\textbf{C}ontext \textbf{L}earning based \textbf{A}dversarial \textbf{P}rotection). \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace learns the benign (what we call) \textit{context} from only normal traffic traces (i.e., unsupervised), and uses this learning to detect adversarial packets. In other words, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace determines whether the context of the unseen packets ``fit'' in the associated connection or not. Specifically, the context of a packet is composed of two types of sub-contexts to describe the aforementioned ``fitness'' of a given packet: \squishlist \item \textbf{Inter-packet context}, which captures the inter-relationships among different packets in the connection in terms of how their header fields change/evolve over the trace; these changes generally relate to the transitioning of states for a stateful network protocol (e.g., TCP); \item \textbf{Intra-packet context}, which captures the inter-relationships among different header fields in a given packet (in terms of the combinations of their values). \squishend By learning the joint distribution (i.e., the \textit{packet context}) of the two (sub-)contexts from benign traffic, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace automatically identifies violations thereof, caused by adversarial packets. \point{Motivating Example} To demonstrate the intuition behind how \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace works, we present a concrete attack and its detection with \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace. Bad-Checksum-RST is an attack that has been reported in \cite{wang2020symtcp, bock2019geneva} and shown to be effective against Great Fire Wall (GFW), a state-of-the-art DPI-based censorship system. It injects a malformed RST packet with a corrupted TCP checksum value after the three-way handshake. Since common endhost TCP implementations perform a rigorous checksum verification but the GFW does not, this injected RST packet is dropped by the endhost but not GFW. As a result, upon observing a RST packet, GFW would disengage its monitoring of the connection, while the communications between two endhosts would be permitted to continue. By learning the benign context from a large set of clean network traces, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace knows what requirements (inter- and intra-packet contexts) must be satisfied by a packet at its position in the connection (e.g., can it be a RST and if so, should its checksum be correct?); then, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace checks whether the packet conforms (fits in) to a benign packet context. In this case, the RST packet with a bad checksum value that appears after three-way handshake is determined as violating both the inter- (RST should not occur at this point) and intra-packet (checksum of RST packet should be correct) contexts (based on training) and thus, the evasion attempt is detected. \point{Contributions} In brief, our contributions in this paper are: \begin{enumerate} \item We are the first to propose a fully-automated unsupervised learning approach to detect adversarial packets that are crafted to elude DPI middleboxes. \item Our evaluations on 73 state-of-the-art DPI evasion attacks over realistic backbone traffic captures, show that by only learning from benign traffic, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace achieves an overall detection AUC-ROC of over \underline{\textbf{0.963}}\xspace, with an average EER of only \underline{\textbf{0.061}}\xspace (the two most commonly used evaluation metrics for ML-based IDSs \cite{mirsky2018kitsune,aqil2017jaal,marin2018rawpower,marin2019deepsec}). \item Our evaluations show that beyond detection, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$
