[Kreibich_2001_Network] applied traffic normalization to reduce the threat posed by the adversarial packets. Unfortunately, this countermeasure does not scale well in the presence of automation, since the search space for all possible adversarial packets can become so large that it becomes prohibitive to maintain the rule set by hand. As the protocol stack evolves and becomes more complex, the theoretical number of discrepancies that can be found by automation can theoretically increase, and it becomes prohibitive to analyze these subtle bugs and correct them all, or to create new hard-coded DPI policies to keep up with the rapidly evolving implementations and standards. This countermeasure consists in the introduction of a so-called traffic-normalizer as a network element before the DPI middlebox, which modifies or deletes the packets passing through it according to certain predetermined rules. It must be noted that a traffic-normalizer, or more generally a traffic-shaper, has no ability to detect anything, but simply blindly modifies the traffic stream. These rules are set by manual administration and describe "ordinary traffic" (the length field in the IP header must never be smaller or larger than the real length of the IP header). We aim in this paper to design a practical countermeasure that can effectively detect evasion attempts in DPI devices. Instead of relying on extensive manual curation and analysis, we propose a novel, fully-autonomous, machine-learning based (with minimum feature engineering) solution, called CLAP (C-learning based Adversarial Protection). Moreover, the ever-changing protocol standards can lead to false positives: a previously correct rule can lead to incorrect decisions (e.g., dropping normal packets) due to changes in implementations. The context of a packet is composed of two types of sub-contexts which describe the “fitness” of a packet to its associated connection: the first is the “inter-packet context,” which is a measure of the relationship between different packets in the same connection and the changes in their respective packet-header values throughout the course of the trace; the second is the “intra-packet context,” which is a measure of the relationship between the values of different fields in the same packet. The learning in CLAP is unsupervised—in other words, the system does not use supervised supervision—and uses this learning to detect unauthorized packets. To illustrate the intuition behind CLAP's workings, we will present an example of an attack that is detected by CLAP. Bad Checksum RST is an attack reported in Wang20 and Bock19 that is effective against the Great Firewall, a state-of-the-art deep packet inspection-based censorship system. By learning the distribution (that is, the “packet context”) of both (sub)contexts from normal traffic, CLAP is able to detect deviations caused by malicious packets. This attack involves sending a malformed RST packet after the three-way handshake with a corrupted TCP checksum value. Since most end-system TCP implementations rely strictly on checksums, while the GFW does not, the injected RST packet will be dropped by the end-system but not by the GFW. By learning the benign context from a large number of clean network traces, CLAP knows what kind of requirement (inside and outside) a packet in its position in the connection has to meet (for example, can it be a reset, and if so, whether its checksum is correct). In short, our contribution in this paper is: (1) First, we propose a fully-autonomous, unsupervised learning method to detect the attack packets against DPI middleboxes. After the three-way handshake, an RST packet with an incorrect checksum is deemed to violate both the external (RST shouldn't be emitted at this point) and the internal context (checksum of RST packet should be correct) contexts, and the attack is thus detected. The GFW, when it sees the RST packet, will stop monitoring the communication and let the two endpoints continue their communication. “Our tests have revealed that, in addition to achieving the same detection rates as the other machine-learning IDSs, CLAP has a false positive rate of 0.061 (according to the two most commonly used metrics cited by Mistsy, Kitsune, Aqil, Jaal and Marin—Raw Power, Deep Security).

text: Recently, a renaissance of contrastive learning (CL) \cite{DBLP:conf/nips/KhoslaTWSTIMLK20,jaiswal2021survey,liu2020self} has been observed in deep representation learning. Owing to its capacity to extract general features from massive unlabeled data and regularize representations in a self-supervised fashion, CL has yielded major breakthroughs in multiple research domains \cite{you2020graph,wujc2021self,chen2020simple,gao2021simcse}. Since data annotation is not required in CL, it serves as a natural remedy to the data sparsity problem in recommender systems \cite{sarwar2001sparsity,hao2021pre}. A growing number of very recent investigations \cite{wujc2021self,yu2021self,xia2020self,zhou2020s,zhou2021contrastive,yu2021socially} have attempted to leverage CL for enhancing recommendation performance and have demonstrated substantial improvements. A typical approach \cite{wujc2021self} to apply CL to recommendation involves first augmenting the user-item bipartite graph with structural perturbations (e.g., stochastic edge/node dropout at a specified ratio), and then maximizing the consistency of representations under different views learned via a graph encoder. In this configuration, the CL task serves as the auxiliary task, and is jointly optimized with the recommendation task (Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}). \par Despite the promising results achieved by CL, however, what underlies the performance improvements still remains unclear. Intuitively, we hypothesize that contrasting different graph augmentations can capture the essential information present in the original user-item interactions, by randomly eliminating the redundancy and impurity through edge/node dropout. Surprisingly, a few recent works \cite{yu2021socially,zhou2021selfcf,DBLP:conf/sigir/LeeKJPY21} have reported that even extremely sparse graph augmentations (with edge dropout rate 0.9) in CL can yield desired performance improvements. Such a phenomenon is quite puzzling and counter-intuitive because a large dropout rate will result in substantial loss of the raw information and a highly distorted graph structure. It naturally raises a meaningful question: \textit{Do we really need graph augmentations when integrating CL with recommendation?} \par To address this question, we first conduct experiments with and without the graph augmentations respectively for a performance comparison. The results demonstrate that when the graph augmentations are absent, the performance is also comparable to those with graph augmentations. We then examine the embedding space learned by non-CL and CL-based recommendation methods. By visualizing the distributions of the representations and correlating them with their performances, we discover that what truly matters for the recommendation performance is the CL loss, rather than the graph augmentation. Optimizing the contrastive loss InfoNCE \cite{oord2018representation} learns more uniformly distributed user/item representations regardless of whether graph augmentations are applied, which implicitly serves a role in alleviating the popularity bias \cite{chen2020bias}. Meanwhile, despite not as effective as anticipated, graph augmentations are not entirely useless in the sense that the appropriately perturbed versions of the original graph help learn representations invariant to the disturbance factors \cite{bachman2019learning,chen2020simple}. However, generating hand-crafted graph augmentations requires constant reconstruction of the graph adjacency matrix during training, which is quite time-consuming. Additionally, dropping a critical edge/node (e.g., a cut edge) may partition a connected graph into several disconnected components, at the risk of making the augmented graph and the original graph share minimal learnable invariance. In view of these limitations, a follow-up question then emerges: \textit{Are there more effective and efficient augmentation approaches?} \par In this paper, we provide an affirmative answer to the question. Based on our finding that the uniformity of the representation distribution is the key factor, we develop a graph-augmentation-free CL method in which the uniformity is more controllable. Technically, we follow the graph CL framework presented in Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}, but we discard the dropout-based graph augmentation and instead add random uniform noises to the original representations for a representation-level data augmentation. Imposing different random noises creates variance between contrastive views, while the learnable invariance is still preserved due to the controlled magnitude. Compared with the graph augmentation, the noise version directly regularizes the embedding space towards a more uniform distribution, which is easy-to-implement and far more efficient. \par The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] 	\item We experimentally reveal why CL can enhance recommendation performance and demonstrate that the InfoNCE loss, rather than the graph augmentation, is the decisive factor. 	\item We propose a simple yet effective graph-augmentation-free CL method for recommendation that can regulate the uniformity in a smooth manner. It can serve as an ideal alternative to cumbersome graph augmentation-based CL methods. 	\item We conduct a comprehensive experimental study on three benchmark datasets demonstrating that the proposed method has distinct advantages over its graph augmentation-based counterparts in terms of recommendation accuracy and model training efficiency. \end{itemize}

text: The contemporary state of data privacy may be characterized as the post-privacy era owing to the unintended ramifications of the big data revolution. The notorious Cambridge Analytica scandal \cite{berghel2018malice} exemplifies how re-identification can be accomplished through cross-analysis of extensive datasets containing personal information. The technological revolution that propelled us into post-privacy has not been halted by privacy legislation such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). We are presently experiencing another (r)evolution that may restore data privacy - blockchain technology. In 2018, The European Union established the GDPR \cite{EUdataregulations2018}, which governs the collection, processing and protection of personal data, including protected health information (PHI). Art. 4(15) of the EU GDPR defines health-related data as: "personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of healthcare services, which reveal information about his or her health status." The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) constitutes fundamental U.S. healthcare legislation and addresses primarily privacy rights and access rather than ownership of patient data \cite{annas2003hipaa}. Each state maintains ownership of patient data belonging to its residents, and such ownership is governed by respective state law in this instance. Given that there are 50 states, there exist 50 distinct laws, court decisions and interpretations regarding patient data ownership. New Hampshire stands as the sole state that has enacted legislation declaring that patient data ownership resides with the patient. How GDPR will interface and conform with U.S. state laws remains to be established. Blockchain, initially introduced with Bitcoin's launch in 2008, has become increasingly diluted in its definition, and there currently exists no fixed, universally accepted definition of the term blockchain. To clarify its application in this research, we have defined Blockchain as a distributed, decentralized and tamper-resistant ledger without centralized control. Blockchain technology and other Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT) could enhance our data privacy and empower individuals with control and access over their data, including health information. The objective of this study is twofold: (i) to analyze the various designs of blockchain and examine GDPR compliance for different components in established or proposed blockchain applications in the healthcare sector and, (ii) to provide future researchers with guidance on how to comply with GDPR when designing blockchain applications within the healthcare domain. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \textbf{Section II} provides a brief introduction to blockchain technology and outlines previous work addressing blockchain compliance with GDPR; \textbf{Section III} presents the research approach; \textbf{Section IV} describes four blockchain applications in healthcare identified through the literature; \textbf{Section V} presents our results and analysis; \textbf{Section VI} provides a discussion and conclusion to the work, and gives recommendations for future work.

text: Dependable identification of encrypted data fragments constitutes a crucial primitive with numerous applications in security and digital forensics. For example, ransomware detection algorithms utilize estimates of write-operations' data randomness to rapidly identify evidence of malicious encryption processes~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}. When conducting digital forensic analysis of hard drives and phones, it is frequently essential to identify encrypted archives~\cite{conti_automated_2010}. Additionally, encryption detection is extensively employed in network protocol analysis~\cite{de_carli_botnet_2017,dorfinger_real-time_2010}. A prevalent approach to address this challenge is to estimate the Shannon entropy of the sequence of interest using the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE): $\hat{H}_{MLE}$. This approach exploits the observation that the distribution of byte values in an encrypted stream closely approximates a uniform distribution; consequently, high entropy is employed as a proxy for randomness. This estimator possesses the advantage of being straightforward and computationally efficient. Since non-encrypted digital data is presumed to have low byte-level entropy, the estimator is anticipated to readily differentiate non-encrypted and encrypted content. Although this approach remains extensively utilized (e.g.,~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}), several works have emphasized its limitations. Contemporary applications tend to compress data prior to both storage and transmission. Prominent examples include the zip compressed file format, and HTTP compression~\cite{http-rfc} (both utilizing the DEFLATE algorithm). Since compression eliminates recurring patterns in data, compressed streams tend to exhibit high Shannon entropy. Consequently, compressed data exhibit values of $\hat{H}_{MLE}$ that are proximate and frequently overlapping with those obtained by encryption. In principle, compressed content can be identified by employing appropriate parsers. Nevertheless, many security-related applications, such as ransomware detection, traffic analysis and digital forensics, generally lack access to whole-file information, but rather operate at the level of \textit{fragments} of data. In these contexts, the metadata that is required by parsers is absent or incomplete~\cite{park_data_2008}. Given this challenge, numerous works have been investigating alternative tests to distinguish between encrypted and compressed content~\cite{malhotra_detection_2007,wang_using_2011,foresti_efficient_2016,lipmaa_data_2017,hahn2018detecting,casino_hedge_2019,choudhury_empirical_2020}. While these works possess the potential to be beneficial, there has been limited evaluation of their performance on a standardized dataset. Therefore, there is no clear understanding of how these approaches: (i) perform on a variety of compressed file formats and sizes, and (ii) compare to each other. The potential adverse implications are substantial: the use of ineffective techniques for identifying encrypted content can impede the effectiveness of ransomware detectors~\cite{gaspari2019}, and significantly constrain the capability of forensic tools. Our work compares selected state-of-the-art approaches on a large dataset of different data types and fragment sizes. We discover that, while more beneficial than entropy estimates, current approaches fail to achieve consistently high accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose \textsc{EnCoD} (\textbf{En}cription/\textbf{Co}mpression \textbf{D}istinguisher), a novel neural network-based approach. Our evaluation demonstrates that \textsc{EnCoD} outperforms existing approaches for most considered file types, across all considered fragment sizes. \textsc{EnCoD} can classify data fragments as small as $512B$ with $86\%$ accuracy, increasing to up to $~94\%$ for purely compressed data (i.e., zip, gzip) and up to $100\%$ for compressed application data fragments (e.g., pdf, jpeg, mp3) for $8KB$ fragment sizes. Overall, this paper makes the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We review and categorize existing literature on the topic of distinguishing compressed and encrypted data fragments. \item We systematically evaluate and compare state-of-the-art approaches on a large, standardized dataset including a variety of fragment formats and sizes. \item We propose a new neural-network based approach, which outperforms current state-of-the-art tests in distinguishing encrypted from compressed content for most considered formats, over all considered fragment sizes. \item We propose a new multi-class classifier that can label a fragment with high accuracy as encrypted data, general-purpose compressed data (zip/gzip/rar), or one of multiple application-specific compressed data (png, jpeg, pdf, mp3). \item We thoroughly discuss the implications of our findings, in terms of the applicability of the evaluated approaches. \end{itemize}

EnCoD can identify data fragments as small as 512 bytes with an accuracy of 86 per cent, which rises to 94 per cent for purely compressed data (e.g. from a ZIP file). We propose a new multiclass classifier that can, with high accuracy, classify a fragment as encrypted data, general purpose compressed data (zip, gzip, rar), or one of many application-specific compressed data (png, jpeg, pdf, mp3), based on the contents of a fragment of 8 kB. text: The brain represents one of the most complex and enigmatic tissues, governing the movement, perception, and emotion of animals (including humans). Nevertheless, the detailed brain architecture of most animals remains largely unexplored to this day due to its immense complexity. Our investigation concentrates on connectomics, which seeks to resolve the comprehensive connectivity networks in animal brains to illuminate the underlying mechanisms of intelligence and inspire improved treatments for neurological disorders. Recently, with the advancement of contemporary electron microscopy (EM) techniques, neuroscientists have been accumulating petabytes of volumetric images at {\em nanometer} resolution, facilitating the analysis of detailed neuronal connectivities and subcellular structures like synapses and mitochondria~\cite{kasthuri2015saturated,xu2020connectome,shapson2021connectomic}. Segmenting cellular and subcellular structures from microscopy images typically constitutes the initial step before structural~\cite{talwar2020topological} and functional~\cite{shapson2021connectomic} analysis. In computational terms, the segmentation tasks can be broadly classified into two categories, including {\em semantic} segmentation that assigns each pixel a class label and {\em instance} segmentation that additionally assigns each pixel an object index beyond the class label. Currently, deep learning has emerged as the {\em de facto} methodology for both semantic segmentation~\cite{chen2017deeplab} and instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask,ronneberger2015u}, which has attained state-of-the-art performance on most natural-scene and biomedical image datasets without employing hand-crafted features. Nevertheless, there exist several challenges when applying these automatic approaches to the segmentation of large-scale connectomics datasets. First, existing open-source segmentation packages are typically designed for standard benchmark datasets, which means adapting these tools to new data with different scales and formats requires substantial time in modifying hardware conditions and data pre-processing. Second, implementing specialized network architectures or different learning objectives for new tasks is often cumbersome in prevailing frameworks. Another layer of challenge is that most packages, despite having good performance on segmentation tasks, lack comprehensive tutorials and documentation, which adds additional learning burden for researchers without extensive experience in programming. To address these challenges, we present {\em PyTorch Connectomics} (PyTC), an open-source deep-learning framework for the semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy images. PyTC is constructed upon the state-of-the-art deep learning library PyTorch~\cite{NEURIPS2019_9015} and inherits its advantages in flexibility and simplicity for neural network implementation. Our framework is not designed for specific imaging modality, data scale, or model architecture but versatile for different types of datasets and segmentation tasks, which distinguishes us from previous works like flood-filling networks (FFN)~\cite{januszewski2018high} for neuron segmentation, StarDist~\cite{weigert2020star} for nuclei segmentation, and CleftNet~\cite{liu2021cleftnet} that only focuses on synapses. Similar to nnU-Net~\cite{isensee2021nnu}, we identify a set of components like data loaders, image augmentations, and optimizers that require minimal adaptation among different datasets and tasks. However, nnU-Net only handles semantic segmentation, while our framework can address both semantic and instance segmentation. Furthermore, our framework is considerably more customizable than nnU-Net to tackle unique challenges in different datasets and tasks, which helps us achieve substantially better performance (\eg, synaptic cleft segmentation). Several supported tasks of PyTC are demonstrated in Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}. Specifically, we design PyTC by identifying the primary requirements of connectomics researchers in different components of segmentation. For data loading, we handle large datasets by automatically partitioning them into manageable chunks, which is compatible with parallel and distributed processing and can readily be adapted to different hardware conditions. For modeling, researchers can customize 2D, 3D, or mixed architectures (for anisotropic images) and modify the number of layers and kernels based on data complexity. The model can also learn multiple targets with multiple losses for each target, facilitating hybrid-representation learning to fully exploit annotations. Besides, users can easily configure data-loading, model-building, optimization, and visualization by simply modifying a configuration file without coding. The design also ensures the reproducibility of experiments and is conducive for the development and maintenance of the package. Finally, we provide a comprehensive description of the design and usage of PyTC in our documentation and tutorials to accelerate the learning curve. To summarize, we present the {\em PyTorch Connectomics} framework for addressing challenges in volumetric microscopy image segmentation by achieving scalability and flexibility in data processing, modeling, and learning. We have been actively enhancing the framework with feedback from biomedical researchers and assistance from open-source contributors. We are incorporating recent machine learning techniques like semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to effectively utilize vast unlabeled data, which can better assist experts in connectomics research.

text: Evaluating the brain's structural organization is essential for advancing our comprehension of its typical and pathological operations. Recent developments in electron microscopy (EM) now enable three-dimensional (3D) imaging of tissue spanning hundreds of micrometers with nanometer-scale resolution, creating novel opportunities for investigating brain ultrastructural organization \cite{Phelps2021ReconstructionMicroscopy, Nahirney2021}. Quantitative examination of 3D-EM datasets, including morphological evaluation of ultrastructure, spatial arrangement or cellular connectivity, necessitates instance segmentation of discrete ultrastructural elements \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy, Kleinnijenhuis2020AMicroscopy, Yuan2021HIVE-Net:Images}. Executing this segmentation manually becomes laborious, if not impractical, given the substantial size and vast quantity of components in standard 3D-EM datasets. For instance, manual annotation of 215 neurites within a volume containing 500 million voxels demanded 1500 h \cite{Berning2015}, and \revised{we estimated that manual instance segmentation of axons in a white matter EM with 300 million voxels of the size $15 \times 15 \times 50 nm^3$ would require 2400 h} \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. Consequently, analyses of brain tissue 3D-EM datasets necessitate developing sophisticated software tools that enable neuroscientists to automatically visualize, segment, and extract geometric and topological characteristics of brain ultrastructures. Several software tools exist for analyzing 3D-EM datasets, including open source software packages such as Microscopy Image Browser (MIB) \cite{Belevich2016}, DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation}, Knossos \cite{Knossos}, \revised{webKnossos \cite{Boergens2017WebKnossos:Connectomics}}, AxonSeg \cite{Zaimi2016AxonSeg:Analysis}, AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks}, TrackEM2 \cite{Cardona2012}, CATMAID \cite{Saalfeld2009}, \revised{VAST \cite{Berger2018VASTStacks}, NeuroMorph \cite{Jorstad2018NeuroMorph:Connectivity}}, SegEM \cite{Berning2015}, Ilastik \cite{ilastik}, or MyelTracer \cite{Kaiser2021Myeltracer:Quantification}, and proprietary software such as Amira (Thermofisher Scientific$^{ TM }$, MA, \url{www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo}) or Imaris (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK, \url{www.imaris.oxinst.com}). Table \ref{tbl:software} summarizes the primary features of the \revised{open source} software packages. Nevertheless, the segmentation tools within these packages have predominantly been designed for manual or semi-automatic segmentation, rendering their usage highly labor-intensive for users. The supervised learning-based segmentation methods available in these packages, such as those in DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation} or AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks}, typically necessitate manually annotated training datasets, which can prove challenging and time-consuming to annotate. Furthermore, while certain packages possess excellent visualization capabilities, they are not optimized for interactive correction, proofreading, and validation of automatic segmentations. Within this framework, we developed a \textbf{G}raphical user interface for \textbf{A}utomati\textbf{C} \textbf{S}egmentation of ax\textbf{ON}s, designated gACSON, and axonal morphology analysis in extensive 3D-EM brain datasets. The \revised{Matlab-based} gACSON builds upon our previous pipelines ACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter} and DeepACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy} for 3D-EM segmentation and morphometrics and provides an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) and additional segmentation algorithms for myelin and the intra-axonal space of myelinated axons. The software enables automatic unsupervised segmentation that requires no manually annotated training datasets. While ACSON and DeepACSON constitute automated segmentation pipelines, gACSON represents an interactive tool, providing user-friendly tools to review and correct the segmentations. \revised{It} also permits segmentation of a subset of all myelinated axons so that users need not await completion of segmentation for all myelinated axons. More significantly, \revised{the software} provides instance segmentation of myelin that maps myelin sheaths to the corresponding intra-axonal space instance. This feature renders \revised{the new tool} unique compared to our existing ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. With the software, users can visualize and review the segmented ultrastructure or correct automated segmentation results by providing a dynamic environment for interactive merge or split operations on the segmented components. Like the ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines, gACSON extracts morphological parameters of segmented myelinated axons, such as axonal diameter or eccentricity, but extends the morphological parameters to measure myelin thickness and g-ratio by enabling instance segmentation of myelin. Moreover, visualization, segmentation evaluation, or correction of automatic segmentation results is not restricted to EM but can be applied to other biomedical imaging modalities, such as light microscopy images. The organization of this paper is as follows: Sections \ref{seg_pip} and \ref{morph_pip} present the gACSON segmentation and morphometry pipelines, respectively. Section \ref{visualization} introduces the GUI including the parameter settings and the tools for proofreading and correcting the automatic segmentation and evaluating the accuracy of the segmentation results. In Section 3, we demonstrate the software's application to segment a novel dataset of six serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM) volumes of rat somatosensory cortex. We further make these volumes and segmentations publicly available.

text: Contemporary developments in Supervised Re-Identification (re-ID) have achieved outstanding performance on extensively utilized public re-ID datasets (\cite{ye2021deep,ni2021adaptive}). Nevertheless, performance experiences a substantial decline when re-ID models undergo cross-dataset evaluation, i.e., on images from a target context distinct from the training context. In this pragmatic scenario, to circumvent expensive manual annotation of novel target datasets, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) has attracted attention among machine learning and computer vision researchers. The UDA objective is to transfer valuable knowledge of a re-ID model from a source domain to a target domain, without any additional identity (ID) label on the target domain. Unsupervised Domain Adaptive re-ID (UDA re-ID) methods have been developed to address the open-set nature of re-ID in which classes of individuals at test time differ from those observed during the training stage. An initial line of research in UDA re-ID examined \emph{Domain Translation}. This family of approaches seeks to bridge the gap between the source and target domains in the image space with style-transfer generative models (\cite{wei2018person, deng2018image, peng2019cross, zhong2018generalizing, qi2019novel}) or by constraining the feature space to learn a domain-invariant discriminative representation (\cite{chang2019disjoint, li2018adaptation, li2019cross, lin2018multi, mekhazni2020unsupervised}). Nonetheless, Domain Translation based approaches fail to learn target-specific discriminative features, thus limiting the re-ID performance achieved on the target domain.\\ Contemporary UDA re-ID approaches extensively rely on the utilization of \emph{pseudo-labels} for the target domain data (\cite{song2020unsupervised, zhang2019self, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep, ge2020mutual, zhai2020multiple, zhao2020unsupervised, zou2020joint,peng2020unsupervised, Zhang_2021_CVPR, Yang_2021_CVPR}). Indeed, learning with these target pseudo-labeled samples can lead to a superior identity-discriminative representation on the target domain. For this purpose, researchers developed a broad range of Pseudo-Labeling frameworks, based on a diverse variety of modeling choices. Consequently, various directions have been explored to enhance pseudo-label based UDA re-ID approaches: some works focus on improving the predicted pseudo-labels (\cite{jiattention,zhai2020ad, tang2019unsupervised, zou2020joint, Chen_2021_CVPR, Zheng_2021_CVPR, zheng2021online, Zhang_2021_CVPR}), others on reducing the impact of pseudo-label errors during training (\cite{ge2020mutual, zhao2020unsupervised, zhai2020multiple, jin2020global, liu2020domain, fu2019self, Xuan_2021_CVPR,lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, feng2021complementary, ge2020self}). These Pseudo-Labeling practices, integrated in specific Pseudo-Labeling methods, have been demonstrated experimentally to enhance the performance. However, there exists no general theoretical framework that can justify these practices, highlight the conditions for their effectiveness and explain how they improve the performance.\\ Furthermore, some of these practices are not universally accepted among Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID work: the most prevalent example is leveraging (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, Isobe_2021_ICCV, dubourvieux2021improving}) or alternatively discarding (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad}) the available ground-truth labeled source data to optimize the model jointly with the pseudo-labeled target data. Note that, the majority of Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID approaches do not utilize the available source training set (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad, song2020unsupervised, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep}) after having access to target pseudo-labels. However, some recent works (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, dubourvieux2021improving, Isobe_2021_ICCV}) demonstrate experimentally that the source data, continuously used in addition to the target pseudo-labeled data, can enhance re-ID performance on the target domain. Can the source data help to improve the cross-dataset re-ID performance of any Pseudo-Labeling approach? Are there some conditions under which any Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID method can benefit from the source data, after having access to target pseudo-labels? These questions are also left unanswered.\\ We believe the absence of general insight on these key UDA re-ID questions is due to the predominance of empirical-oriented works for UDA re-ID. Therefore this work seeks to answer these questions with a general theoretical framework, and to highlight good practices to design an effective Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID method. To this end, this work proposes three contributions that can be summarized as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Theoretical development to find a new upper-bound \item General good practices for Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID approaches, deduced from the theory, and therefore providing a better insight of their role in improving the cross-domain re-ID performance \item Experiments with different proposed implementations of these good practices, showing performance improvements of recent state-of-the-art methods by implementing the whole proposed good practices, on various person and vehicle cross-domain benchmarks \end{enumerate} The paper is structured as follows: in Sec.~\ref{sec:related}, the relevant existing work is reviewed. In Sec.~\ref{sec:theory}, notations, concepts and models on which our theoretical framework is based are introduced. Then in Sec.~\ref{sec:bound}, a new upper-bound on the target re-ID performance is constructed, taking into account the errors in the pseudo-labels, as well as the exploitation of the source data. In Sec.~\ref{sec:theory_to_practice}, insight and a set of general good practices for improving the UDA re-ID performance are derived from the theoretical bound. After introducing the experimental setting and proposed implementations for the good practices in Sec.~\ref{sec:experiments}, extensive experiments are conducted in Sec.~\ref{sec:results} on person and vehicle UDA re-ID benchmarks, and are discussed to validate the performance improvement obtained by following the good practices in a Pseudo-Labeling method.

text: This paper presents a policy learning methodology that exploits task-and-motion planning (TAMP) to train robotic manipulation policies for extended-horizon tasks. Contemporary policy learning methodologies can address robotic control problems using complex sensory inputs~\cite{Finn16, trpo, rubiks}, yet this achievement has been predominantly confined to brief-horizon tasks. Learning policies that execute extended sequences of manipulation operations remains an unresolved challenge~\cite{oneshothier, subpol}. Conversely, TAMP methodologies readily address problems requiring numerous abstract operations while satisfying intricate geometric constraints within high-dimensional configuration spaces~\cite{hiertamp, extendtamp}. Nevertheless, their deployment is frequently restricted to controlled environments since TAMP methodologies require reliable world state tracking and must allocate time for planning~\cite{garretttamp, householdmarathon}. To tackle these challenges, two research directions have developed. The initial direction employs machine learning to discover policies or heuristics that diminish planning duration~\cite{feasibletamp, scorespace, guidetamp, gripsqp, mctstamp, chitnis2016guided}. This broadens the domains where TAMP can be deployed, yet continues to depend on explicit state estimation. The alternative research direction learns policies that replicate the outputs of TAMP solvers. These methodologies decrease reliance on state estimation by, for instance, learning predictors to ground logical states~\cite{dpdl} or training recurrent models to predict task plan feasibility~\cite{geomlearn}. These learned policies function directly on perceptual data without requiring hand-crafted state estimation. Nevertheless, TAMP solvers establish a highly non-linear transformation from observations to controls, making imitation challenging. Moreover, the computational resources necessary for planning constrain the availability of training data for learning. In this paper, we expand upon both methodologies. We draw inspiration from guided expert imitation~\cite{GPS, grp} and train feed-forward policies to replicate TAMP. Our fundamental insight is that \citet{tamp2014}'s modular TAMP framework enables a distributed TAMP architecture that: 1) is optimized for throughput (rather than low latency, the conventional emphasis in TAMP research); 2) trains policies to replicate planner outputs; and 3) employs those policies to amortize planning across problems and diminish computational costs. The outcome is a beneficial cycle where learning expedites planning, and accelerated planning furnishes additional supervision. We propose a policy architecture that exploits the TAMP domain definition to enhance learning performance. Task plans from our system supervise a task-level model that learns to predict a parameterized operation. This output selects from and parameterizes a collection of control networks, one for each operation schema. We demonstrate that this architecture can execute manipulation skills in high-dimensional environments using complex sensory inputs. Consequently, our system can compile task and motion planning into a unified feed-forward policy. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1) we demonstrate a design for a distributed, asynchronous, high-throughput task and motion planning system that exploits policy learning to accelerate planning; 2) we propose a hierarchical policy architecture that exploits the TAMP problem specification; and 3) we implement and evaluate this methodology to demonstrate it can learn to accomplish multiple objectives over (comparatively) extended horizons with high-dimensional sensory data and action spaces. In a 2D pick-place task, we train policies that position 3 objects precisely onto targets 83\% of the time from RGB images. In the RoboSuite~\cite{robosuite2020} pick-place benchmark we train policies for 7-DoF joint control that position 4 objects $88\%$ of the time from object pose vectors. In the multitask RoboDesk benchmark, our learned policy achieves a 79\% success rate across 9 diverse tasks with 7-DoF joint control from RGB images.

text: It is a well-established and comprehensively understood phenomenon that humans can correlate voices and faces of individuals because the neuro-cognitive pathways for voices and faces share identical structure~\cite{kamachi2003putting,belin2004thinking}. Recently, Nagrani et al.~\cite{nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2017voxceleb} introduced the face-voice association task into the vision community with the development of a large-scale audio-visual dataset, comprising faces and voices of $1,251$ celebrities. Since then, the face-voice association task has attracted considerable research attention~\cite{horiguchi2018face,kim2018learning,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2018seeing,nawaz2019deep,wen2021seeking,wen2018disjoint}. Additionally, we are also observing the development of novel audio-visual datasets to investigate this emerging task. For instance, Nawaz et al.~\cite{nawaz2021cross} introduced a Multilingual Audio-Visual (\textit{MAV-Celeb}) dataset to examine the influence of language on face-voice association task; it comprises video and audio recordings of various celebrities speaking multiple languages. Most existing approaches ~\cite{kim2018learning,nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nawaz2021cross} address face-voice association as a cross-modal biometric task. The two primary challenges in developing an effective methodology for this task are learning of a common yet discriminative embedding space, where instances from two modalities are adequately aligned and instances of semantically similar identities are proximate. Often separate networks for face and voice modalities are utilized to obtain the respective feature embeddings and contrastive or triplet loss formulations are employed to construct this embedding space. Although demonstrating some efficacy in this task, such loss formulations, however, are restrictive in the following ways. First, they require tuning of a margin hyperparameter, which is challenging as the distances between instances can vary substantially during training. Secondly, the run-time training complexity for contrastive and triplet losses are $\mathcal{O} (n^2)$ and $\mathcal{O} (n^3)$, respectively, where $n$ is the number of available instances for a modality. Finally, to address the high run-time training complexity challenge, different variants of carefully designed negative mining strategies are employed, which are both time-consuming and performance sensitive. A few methodologies e.g., \cite{nawaz2019deep} have attempted to replace the contrastive/triplet loss formulations by utilizing auxiliary identity centroids~\cite{wen2016discriminative}. The training process alternates between the following two steps: 1) clustering embeddings around their identity centroids and pushing embeddings away from all other identity centroids, and 2) updating these centroids using the mini-batch instances. Such centroid based losses are employed with traditional classification loss (i.e. softmax cross-entropy (CE)). However, their co-existence is counterintuitive and ineffective because the former promotes margins in Euclidean space whereas the latter implicitly achieves separability in the angular domain. In this work, we hypothesize that an enriched unified feature representation, encompassing complementary cues from both modalities, alongside an effective yet efficient supervision formulation is essential towards realizing a discriminative joint embedding space for improved face-voice association. To this end, we propose a lightweight, plug-and-play mechanism that exploits the optimal characteristics in both modalities through fusion and semantically aligns fused embeddings with their identity labels via orthogonality constraints. We instantiate our proposed mechanism in the two-stream pipeline, which provides face and voice embeddings, and the resulting overall framework is an effective and efficient approach for face-voice matching and verification tasks. We summarize our key contributions as follows. 1) We propose to harness the complementary features from both modalities in forming enriched feature embeddings, that are consistent with semantics of identity, thereby enabling improved identity recognition. 2) We propose to impose orthogonality constraints on the fused embeddings. They are not only coherent with the angular characteristic of the commonly employed classification loss but are highly efficient as they operate directly on mini-batches. 3) Experimental results on large-scale VoxCeleb \cite{nagrani2017voxceleb} demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on both face-voice verification and matching tasks. Furthermore, we observe that our method performs favorably against the existing state-of-the-art methods. 4) We perform a comprehensive ablation study to analyze the impact of different components.

text: Edge-aware filters constitute some of the most frequently employed image processing operators across a broad spectrum of computational photography applications. Also termed \emph{edge-preserving smoothing} operators, they represent a fundamental component in numerous algorithms for image manipulation including tonemapping, image abstraction, detail enhancement, texture removal, and additional tasks. The widespread adoption of these operators can be ascribed to their apparent capacity to detect salient, structure-defining edges within an image and to handle them distinctly from other image details and discontinuities. Throughout the preceding decade, numerous edge-preserving smoothing operators have been presented in the literature, with some being explicitly developed for particular tasks, such as texture removal, or multiscale detail manipulation, while others lack an explicitly stated objective. We reference several specific examples in Section \ref{sec-smoothing-operators}. These operators vary from one another across multiple dimensions, including their visual characteristics, internal algorithmic approaches (e.g., local vs.~global operators), the quantity and scope of parameters (ranging from at least one to numerous), and computational complexity (spanning seconds to minutes). Such variations may not be immediately evident to a user with only superficial familiarity with these methods and, consequently, the task of selecting the appropriate operator for a particular purpose (or a particular image), along with determining its parameters, can prove quite demanding. When presenting a novel filter, researchers conventionally provide side-by-side visual comparisons of images processed using existing operators. For such a comparison to possess significance, an image must be processed by the various operators to an \emph{equivalent degree}. Nevertheless, each operator is governed by its distinct parameter(s), and no established consistent correspondence exists between the parameters of different operators. This situation is further compounded by the reality that even for each individual method the visual impact of its parameters on the outcome is frequently input-dependent, and the relationship among its parameters may fluctuate across different smoothing levels. Consequently, in practice, the parameters for each of the compared methods are selected subjectively by the authors, typically through trial-and-error. The selection of which methods to compare against is equally nontrivial. Optimally, one would prefer to incorporate in the comparison methods related in their methodology to the proposed one, together with ones representing entirely different approaches. It is also crucial to consider the primary intended application for which the competing methods were originally developed. Additionally, a common benchmark should be employed for all comparisons, but, in practice, no established benchmark exists; moreover, it is not uncommon to observe cases where a different image is selected to compare the proposed method against each of the existing competitors. In this paper, we present a novel methodology for evaluating and comparing edge-preserving smoothing operators in a more meaningful, objective, and quantitative manner. We propose a mechanism for achieving approximately equivalent smoothing degrees across different operators, which effectively establishes a correspondence between their primary governing parameters, on a per-image basis. Having established such a correspondence we can quantitatively assess various characteristics of different operators. This provides several insights regarding the operators' behavior, and enables conducting more meaningful comparisons, both visually and quantitatively. Finally, we are capable of clustering the different operators based on the similarity of their effects, using strictly empirical observations. Our observations concerning inherent method behavior suggest some specific recommendations for both developers and end-users of such operators. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section~\ref{sec-background} reviews existing approaches for comparing between tonemapping operators and several previous comparative surveys of edge-preserving filters. Section~\ref{sec-methods} first briefly enumerates the filters that we selected to demonstrate our methodology for comparing and evaluating smoothing operators, and then presents the methodology itself. Section~\ref{sec-results} demonstrates the application of our methodology on the selected set of operators. Section~\ref{sec-conclusions} provides a concluding discussion and offers some ideas for future research.

These operators differ on a number of dimensions such as their visual characteristics, internal mathematical approaches (e.g. local vs. global operators), the number and range of their parameters (from a minimum to many), and their time complexity (from seconds to minutes). We will cite some examples in Section ref.sec.smoothing-operators. When presenting a new operator, scientists generally present side-by-side visual comparisons of images processed by existing operators. For such a comparison to be meaningful, an image must be processed by the various operators to an equal degree. Such variations are not immediately obvious to a casual user with only a superficial knowledge of the operators, and therefore the task of selecting the appropriate operator for a particular purpose (or a particular image) and of determining its proper parameters can be quite difficult. However, each operator is governed by its own set of parameters, and no consistent relationship can be established between the parameters of different operators. Consequently, the authors of each compared method are generally obliged to select the parameters for each operator subjectively and by trial and error. This is complicated by the fact that the visual impact of the parameters on the outcome of a particular method is often dependent on the value of the inputs, and the relationship between the parameters themselves is often subject to different smoothing levels. Choosing which methods to compare is equally nontrivial. It is also necessary to consider the original purpose for which the methods were developed. Optimally, methods related to the methodology of the proposed method would be included in the comparison as well as methods representing a completely different approach. In this paper, we present a new method for evaluating and comparing edge-preserving smoothing operators in a more meaningful, objective, and quantitative manner. In addition, a common standard should be used for all comparisons; in practice, however, no such standard has been established, and it is not uncommon to see a different image chosen for each competitor. We propose a way to establish a correspondence between the primary governing parameters of different operators, which makes it possible to establish a degree of smoothing roughly equivalent across operators. Using this observation, we are able to establish the similarity of the effects of different operators, a purely empirical procedure. We can then establish the quantitative correspondence between various properties of the operators. This gives us a number of insights into the behavior of the operators and enables us to make more meaningful comparisons, both visual and quantitative. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: section reference-section-background reviews existing approaches to comparing tone-mapping operators and several previous comparative studies of edge-preserving filters; section reference-section-methods lists the filters we chose to illustrate our method for comparing and evaluating smoothing operators, and then presents the method itself. Our observations about the inherent behavior of the methods lead to specific recommendations for both the developer and the end-user. Section ref.sec-results. Section ref.sec-conclusions. Section ref.sec-conclusions.

text: Distribution shift poses a fundamental challenge for machine learning systems attempting to learn robust predictors. While these systems can achieve near-perfect accuracy on i.i.d test data from the training distribution—even with regularization to mitigate overfitting—their performance often deteriorates to below-chance levels when confronted with even minor differences between training and testing distributions \citep{goodfellow2015explaining,geirhos2020shortcut}. Domain Generalization (DG) \cite{ganin2016domainadversarial, li2018domain} tackles this problem by developing robust methodologies that maintain strong test performance across distributions that differ from, yet remain systematically connected to, the training distribution \citep{mansour2019robust}. Among the recent advances in Multi-Source Domain Generalization \citep{zhao2020multisource}, Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) \citep{arjovsky2019invariant} stands out as a particularly successful approach that promotes learning predictors with consistent performance across distinct ``domains'' or ``environments'' \citep{peters2015causal, heinzedeml2018invariant}. When provided with $n$ training environments, these models identify predictors within the feature space such that the conditional distribution of outcomes given these predictors remains invariant across all training environments. Such predictors can therefore generalize effectively to out-of-distribution (OOD) test environments that exhibit the same invariance property. Drawing from philosophical work that conceptualizes causation through invariance \citep{cartwright2003two, mitchell2000dimensions}, current invariance-based DG methods have been understood as implementing a form of weak causal discovery, where the identified predictors represent causal factors underlying the target phenomena. Robustness to variations in ``sensitive attributes'' frequently serves as a characterization of fairness \cite{arjovsky2019invariant}, particularly within toxicity classification contexts. Consider an automated moderation system deployed by an online news platform to identify toxic comments that warrant censorship from public discourse. A fair system's performance should remain unaffected by characteristics such as whether comments address race-related, gender-related, or other politically sensitive topics. Various distributive fairness definitions differ in specifying how system predictions should exhibit invariance to sensitive attribute changes. Statistical definitions like Demographic Parity mandate that certain conditional distributions of predictions given sensitive attributes remain invariant to those attributes \citep{hardt2016equality}, while causal definitions such as counterfactual fairness \citep{kusner2018counterfactual} require individual-level prediction invariance to counterfactual modifications of sensitive attributes. Systems that base predictions on sensitive group membership face substantial ethical and legal objections \citep{barocas2016big}. Furthermore, excessive dependence on sensitive information may compromise robustness when the predictive utility of such information spuriously varies across environmental contexts. For instance, discussions of non-caucasian racial identities might strongly predict comment toxicity on white supremacist forums where discriminatory remarks about ethnic minorities are commonplace. Conversely, on more diversity-welcoming forums, the association between racial identity mentions and toxicity would likely prove much weaker. This fragility of sensitive information emerged as a central challenge for Perspective API, Google's internet comment toxicity classifier, during real-world deployment \citep{borkan2019nuanced, jigsawmedium}, and has similarly caused bias in sentiment analysis \citep{kiritchenko2018examining} and facial detection \citep{buolamwini18a} applications. Consequently, fair models might be constructed by learning predictors that maintain invariant performance across diverse environments. This work empirically establishes that Domain Generalization can construct fair machine learning systems through models invariant to spurious correlations involving sensitive attributes. We specifically evaluate IRM's performance on a fair internet comment toxicity classification task derived from the Civil Comments Dataset. The task requires models to generalize from biased training environments displaying strong but spurious correlations between particular demographic identity mentions and toxicity to test environments where these correlations are reversed. \footnote{\url{https://github.com/adragnar/irm-toxicity-classification}} Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We demonstrate that IRM surpasses ERM in both generalization accuracy and group fairness on this dataset, illustrating the convergence of robustness and fairness for the examined data bias type; \item We investigate the mechanisms underlying this performance enhancement through ablation studies: although sensitive information provides marginal predictive value, IRM leverages cross-environment variation in this predictive capacity to identify invariant (and consequently more fair) solutions; \item Analysis of the IRM solution reveals reliance on comment length as an invariant feature. While length-based prediction may prove more fair than sensitive group membership-based prediction, IRM has not identified truly ``causal'' features. This underscores both a fundamental limitation of IRM's approach of treating invariance as a causality proxy and the critical importance of environment diversity as an inductive bias for this methodology. \end{itemize}

text: The broad family of reconfiguration problems requires providing step-by-step transformations to convert one object into another. This paper addresses the reconfiguration of modular robot collections within lattice structures through predetermined movement patterns. Both robotics and computational geometry communities have extensively investigated numerous problem variants. Our focus centers on reconfiguring (edge-)connected configurations composed of hexagonal and square modules. Following requirements essential for practical applications, we mandate continuous preservation of (edge-)connectivity throughout all transformations (satisfying the \emph{single backbone condition}~\cite{Dumitrescu-Suzuki-Yamashita-2004}). Permitted movements consist of pivots: modules rotate around vertices they share with neighboring modules, with each pivoting module concluding its movement within a lattice cell. Module interiors must never overlap. Figure~\ref{fig:hex_moves} demonstrates the two pivoting movement types available to hexagons. During a \emph{restricted} move, module $a$ neighboring module $s$ rotates around shared vertex $v$ between $a$ and $s$, concluding its pivot in the alternative cell bounded by $v$. The \emph{restricted model} permits exclusively this movement type. A \emph{monkey} move begins with module $a$ adjacent to module $s$ initiating rotation around shared vertex $v$ as in restricted moves, yet midway through rotation, another vertex $w$ of $a$ aligns with a vertex of module $s'$. Module $a$ then continues pivoting around $w$ maintaining identical rotational direction (clockwise or counterclockwise) until reaching a cell neighboring $s'$. The \emph{monkey model} encompasses both restricted and monkey movements. Essentially, monkey moves enable continued pivoting in consistent directions when restricted moves become impossible. Section~\ref{sec:models} provides additional analysis of distinctions between these hexagonal models. {Square grid configurations allow modules sharing vertices without sharing edges. Consequently, square modules possess expanded pivoting movement varieties. Figure~\ref{fig:square_moves} illustrates three distinct movement sets. The \emph{restricted model} incorporates solely restricted moves, the \emph{leapfrog model} combines restricted and leapfrog moves, while the \emph{monkey model} encompasses all movement types. \ifabstract Section~\ref{sec_proto} discusses which models have achieved practical implementation. \fi } \later{ \iffull\paragraph*{Prototypes.} \fi \ifabstract

text: The field of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) encompasses the scientific and technical endeavors aimed at enabling machines to automatically identify spoken language. Within this broader domain, Speech Commands Recognition (SCR) represents a specialized subset focused on the identification of brief, discrete vocal instructions. This technology serves as a fundamental bridge enabling seamless human-machine communication through natural speech interfaces. Contemporary applications span diverse domains, including mobile assistants integrated into smartphones, voice-controlled robotic systems that execute spoken directives, and intelligent home automation platforms such as Amazon Echo and Google Home. The proliferation of such applications has fundamentally transformed the landscape of human-computer interaction paradigms. Moreover, this technology demonstrates significant potential across medical and educational sectors, particularly in developing assistive solutions for visually impaired or physically disabled individuals \cite{1998Single-surgeonThoracoscopicSurgeryWith,2014EducationalSystemForThe}. Given that numerous applications operate on resource-constrained devices with inherent computational limitations, the development of efficient, lightweight implementations becomes crucial for achieving real-time performance \cite{2018FPGAImplementationOfConvolutional}. Traditional SCR methodologies fundamentally depend on the extraction of discriminative characteristics from raw speech signals. Among the most prevalent feature extraction techniques, frequency-domain transformations such as the fast Fourier transform have gained widespread adoption \cite{1989Speaker-independentPhoneRecognitionUsing,2013TechniquesForFeatureExtraction}, facilitating the conversion of temporal speech patterns into spectral representations. Following feature extraction, classical acoustic modeling approaches typically employed hidden Markov models (HMMs) to capture the sequential nature of phonemic or word-level structures \cite{2014SpeechAndLanguageProcessing.}. Hybrid architectures combining neural networks with HMM-based frameworks have maintained relevance for over two decades \cite{2012ConnectionistSpeechRecognition:A,1986TheTRACEModelOf}. The contemporary landscape has witnessed deep learning methodologies achieving unprecedented performance superiority across diverse application domains, consistently outperforming conventional machine learning approaches \cite{2012DeepNeuralNetworksFor,2015DeepLearning,2016DeepLearning}. Recurrent architectures, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have revolutionized natural language processing systems by surpassing traditional methodological boundaries \cite{1999LearningToForget:Continual,2016LSTM:ASearchSpace}. Neural network-based approaches have established dominance throughout SCR development and are now universally recognized as state-of-the-art solutions within the speech recognition community \cite{2014Small-footprintKeywordSpottingUsing,2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Concurrently, diverse neural architectures including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), LSTMs, and gated recurrent units (GRUs) have demonstrated successful SCR applications \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Research investigating direct CNN application to raw audio signals has been explored extensively \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw,2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith,2018End-to-endSpeechRecognitionFrom}. However, the constrained computational and memory resources of embedded systems continue to present significant obstacles in fully leveraging the capabilities of sophisticated, high-accuracy deep networks. Addressing computational complexity challenges on embedded platforms typically involves two primary strategies. The first approach focuses on compressing existing state-of-the-art deep models to minimize computational overhead while maintaining acceptable performance degradation \cite{2019AnOptimizedRecurrentUnit,2020Small-FootprintOpen-VocabularyKeywordSpotting}. Alternatively, the second strategy emphasizes developing inherently efficient deep architectures and methodologies from inception, targeting superior accuracy-to-computational-cost ratios \cite{2019OperationalNeuralNetworks,2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks}. This latter approach proves particularly valuable when dealing with limited training data or processing low-quality, low-resolution input signals. Both strategies enable the deployment of viable classification systems on energy-constrained embedded platforms. Extensive research has concentrated on either compressing complex networks or constructing lightweight architectures from the ground up. Progressive operational perceptrons (POPs)\cite{2017ProgressiveOperationalPerceptrons} extend conventional multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) through generalized operational perceptrons (GOPs). GOPs incorporate diverse operator sets that emulate biological synaptic connections, enhancing their capacity to learn underlying data semantics. PyGOP \cite{2019PyGOP:APythonLibrary} provides a comprehensive implementation library for GOPs across both CPU and GPU platforms. Research presented in \cite{2020ProgressiveOperationalPerceptronsWith} accelerates POP learning processes by incorporating memory concepts and leveraging information from previously trained layers. The exploration of biologically-inspired neurons continues in \cite{2019HeterogeneousMultilayerGeneralizedOperational}, where individual neurons possess distinct operator sets, resulting in more compact network architectures. Research in \cite{2018ImprovingEfficiencyInConvolutional} introduces a generic neural layer structure utilizing multi-linear projections, achieving substantial memory reduction compared to traditional CNNs while delivering enhanced performance. The work in \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting} employs deep networks with dilated convolutions to attain high accuracy using fewer parameters. SincNet Kernels \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith} applied to initial CNN convolutional layers represent another approach for reducing learnable parameters. This methodology has been successfully applied to speaker recognition \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw} and subsequently to phoneme recognition tasks \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith}. Depth-wise separable convolutions (DSCconvs), originally developed for image processing applications \cite{2017Xception:DeepLearningWith,2017Mobilenets:EfficientConvolutionalNeural}, have been successfully adapted to SCR, keyword spotting \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting}, and machine translation \cite{2017DepthwiseSeparableConvolutionsFor} to minimize computational requirements. This paper introduces a novel network layer designed to enhance speech command recognition performance within lightweight architectures. Our approach combines self-organized operational neural networks (SelfONNs) \cite{2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks} with quadratic forms kernels \cite{2017Non-linearConvolutionFiltersFor} in an innovative configuration. Experimental validation on Google speech commands (GSC) \cite{2018SpeechCommands:ADataset} and synthetic speech commands (SSC) datasets\footnote{\url{https://kaggle.com/jbuchner/synthetic-speech-commands-dataset}} demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed methodology for speech command recognition, particularly within lightweight network constraints. To our knowledge, this represents the first investigation combining SelfONNs with quadratic kernels to create a novel layer architecture for enhancing lightweight CNN performance. Additionally, we pioneer the application of SelfONN concepts and quadratic kernels specifically to SCR tasks. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~II presents the most relevant related work. Section~III introduces our proposed quadratic SelfONN approach for SCR. Section~IV discusses experimental results and analysis. Finally, Section~V concludes the paper.

text: Recent years have witnessed a substantial expansion in robotic surgery adoption. Systems like the da Vinci\textsuperscript{\textregistered} Surgical System~\cite{guthart2000intuitive} from Intuitive Surgical Inc. (Sunnyvale, CA) are increasingly replacing conventional surgical instruments such as laparoscopes, driven by objectives to enhance surgical precision and patient outcomes. These technological platforms fundamentally transform how surgeons interface with patients during procedures. Consequently, investigating human surgical performance within robotic environments represents a compelling research frontier that holds critical importance for advancing surgeon-robot interaction understanding and ultimately benefiting patient care. The comprehensive and precise surgical data captured across multiple modalities—including video recordings and kinematic measurements—offers opportunities to develop holistic surgical comprehension while enabling detailed and accurate analysis of human surgical performance. \\ Contemporary research in this field has predominantly concentrated on task-specific, supervised learning approaches utilizing single modalities. We contend that such methodologies present significant limitations. Task-specific learning paradigms, exemplified by supervised skill detection, facilitate only restricted understanding of comprehensive surgical processes, yielding minimal insights beyond the particular training objective. Additionally, supervised learning creates dependency on expert annotations that are costly to acquire, inherently subjective, and potentially error-prone. Moreover, disregarding multiple information modalities—such as video and kinematic data—can substantially impair the development of generalizable, feature-rich representations. \\ We propose that robotic surgery can be decomposed into sequential gestures or surgemes \cite{varadarajan2009data}. This decomposition enables surgical modeling analogous to language models \cite{mikolov2013distributed, devlin2018bert} operating over surgeme vocabularies. In this investigation, we introduce a self-supervised learning algorithm that acquires task-agnostic surgical gesture representations from dual modalities (specifically video and kinematics) with strong generalization capabilities across diverse tasks. \\ This paper presents the following contributions: 1) we introduce a deep-learning architecture for self-supervised surgical gesture representation learning from video and kinematic data, 2) we quantitatively validate our representations' effectiveness across multiple tasks by attaining state-of-the-art gesture recognition accuracy and achieving high skill recognition performance, 3) we qualitatively demonstrate the rich information encoded within our representations through visualization of semantically meaningful clustering patterns.

text: The field of Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition has garnered considerable attention due to its fundamental importance in scene understanding. The primary objective involves identifying multiple \textit{$<$verb, object$>$} pairs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}. , ``hold, apple'') within images. Two primary challenges complicate image-level HOI classification: datasets \cite{hico15,vg17} exhibit long-tailed distributions with severe class imbalances, and images contain multiple labels with unknown HOI positions. While recent approaches predominantly emphasize object and keypoint detection, they frequently neglect the classifier component. Our investigation reveals that the classifier plays a pivotal role in both HOI classification and detection tasks. The semantic correlation between HOI classes distinguishes this domain from conventional image classification, as HOI categories represent verb-object combinations. Within the HICO \cite{hico15} dataset, classes sharing identical verbs average 5.1, while those sharing object categories average 7.5. Despite this semantic richness, existing methods inadequately exploit such cues. Several approaches \cite{liao2020ppdm,uniondet20,sgg-imp17,atl21,scg20} independently classify objects and verbs, substantially reducing prediction complexity but introducing polysemy vulnerabilities—identical verbs may convey different meanings across HOIs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}. , ``{\em make}, pizza'', ``{\em make}, vase''). We advance beyond this limitation by employing language models to generate text embeddings for HOI classes, subsequently initializing linear classification layer weight vectors. This strategy, termed \textit{Language Embedding Initialization}, demonstrates superior performance over conventional Random Initialization approaches \cite{xavier10,kaiminginit15}, particularly in few-shot scenarios. Our approach leverages the conceptualization of weight vectors in linear classifiers as class proxies (feature centers) \cite{circleloss20,normface17}. Language embedding initialization positions these proxies according to semantic structure rather than random placement, facilitating multi-label training by guiding backbone vision features toward semantic centers where frequently co-occurring HOIs cluster spatially (see \cref{fig:2_bert}). Additionally, language embeddings provide appropriate weight initialization for few-shot classes, whose classifier weight vectors cannot be adequately learned from limited samples. Previous research \cite{transfer16,pairwise18} addresses positive/negative class imbalances using {\it weighted} sigmoid cross-entropy loss \cite{wbce15}, which outperforms standard cross-entropy but proves insufficient for extremely imbalanced classes (20.1\% of HICO classes contain $\leq$ 5 positive samples). We introduce Log-Sum-Exp Sign (\textit{LSE-Sign}) loss to enhance multi-label learning on long-tailed datasets. Our loss function's gradient takes the form of a softmax over all class losses, amplifying poorly classified classes while suppressing well-classified ones. This mechanism facilitates multi-label learning through dynamic loss balancing across classes. Notably, LSE-Sign loss differs from focal loss \cite{lin2017focal} in two key aspects: it considers {\em relative} difficulty across all classes rather than operating individually, and requires no hyperparameter tuning. A detection-free baseline employing ImageNet-1K pre-trained ViT-B/32 suffers significant performance degradation compared to detection-assisted state-of-the-art methods (declining from 47.1 to 37.8 mAP). However, Language Embedding Initialization with BERT elevates performance to 50.6 mAP. This improvement generalizes across language models, including SimCSE \cite{simcse21} and CLIP \cite{clip21}. LSE-Sign loss contributes an average 3.1 mAP improvement across eight experiments (\cref{tab:bce_vs_sign}). These innovations enable our method to substantially outperform existing detection-assisted approaches \cite{pairwise18,pastanet20,hake19}. Using ResNet101, we achieve 53.6 mAP, exceeding the state-of-the-art \cite{hake19} (which utilizes both object and human keypoint detection) by 6.5 mAP. With ViT-B/16, performance reaches 65.6 mAP. Few-shot evaluations yield 52.7 mAP on 1-shot and 56.9 mAP on 5-shot classes. For instance-level tasks, we decompose HOI detection into localization and regional HOI classification components. Our detection-free approach enables classification model application to regional human-object box pairs from any off-the-shelf detector. Using vision transformer backbones, we convert bounding boxes into attention masks, restricting CLS token attention to regions of interest. Without additional instance-level supervision training, this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance (32.35 mAP) on HICO-DET, surpassing the current SOTA \cite{cdn21} trained specifically on HICO-DET.
