text: The pretraining of large neural networks using language modeling objectives has yielded substantial advances across NLP \citep[][\emph{i.a.}]{peters2018deep,howard2018universal,radford2018improving,devlin2018bert,raffel2019exploring,brown2020language}. Additional gains frequently emerge when selecting pretraining objectives that align more closely with target downstream applications. Notable instances encompass casing prediction for named entity recognition \citep{Mayhew_Nitish_Roth_2020}, gap sentence generation for summarization \citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and sentence unshuffling for discourse representations \citep{lee2020slm}. Although these strategies can substantially decrease the volume of required training data, they generally exhibit poor performance when only limited examples exist for downstream tasks—a prevalent scenario in practical NLP applications. Nevertheless, few-shot contexts present opportunities for considerable improvements through a paradigm reversal: rather than adapting pretraining to resemble downstream tasks, we can restructure downstream tasks to mirror pretraining objectives. For masked language models \citep[e.g.,][]{devlin2018bert,lewis2019bart}, this reformulation involves converting inputs into cloze-style questions by incorporating textual snippets containing task descriptions, typically through concise prompts \citep{radford2018language,schick2020exploiting}. Beyond enhancing similarity between pretraining and finetuning phases, this methodology offers the attractive advantage of allowing users to \emph{explain} tasks to pretrained models, thereby facilitating task comprehension. Figure~\ref{figure:motivational-example} demonstrates this concept, showing how a pretrained language model receives identical input with varying instructions and modifies its output correspondingly. Task description provision proves effective even in unsupervised contexts \citep{radford2018language} or when examples serve as contextual information \citep{brown2020language}; nevertheless, its complete potential emerges when integrated with gradient-based training on limited labeled examples \citep{schick2020just}. Regrettably, existing methodologies remain confined to text \emph{classification} tasks \citep{schick2020exploiting}. Drawing inspiration from their achievements, we explore whether this fundamental concept extends to more complex text-to-text tasks requiring \emph{generation} of textual sequences from input text, including abstractive summarization. We present \textsc{genPet}{}, an innovative approach building upon \textsc{Pet}{} \citep{schick2020exploiting}, which enables finetuning of generative language models through combined instruction and labeled example utilization. Our findings demonstrate that \textsc{genPet}{} constitutes a highly data-efficient methodology, allowing finetuning of pretrained \textsc{Pegasus}{} models \citep{zhang2019pegasus} with merely 10 or 100 training instances. We assess our technique across six diverse English headline generation and text summarization tasks in both zero-shot and few-shot configurations, revealing that \textsc{Pegasus}{} trained via \textsc{genPet}{} substantially surpasses conventional finetuning approaches. Our principal contributions include: \begin{itemize}[topsep=0.5em] 	\setlength\itemsep{-0.1em} 	\item We present \textsc{genPet}{}, a finetuning methodology for generative language models that attains exceptional data efficiency through combined utilization of textual instructions and training examples. 	\item We demonstrate that \textsc{Pegasus}{} training with \textsc{genPet}{} surpasses standard finetuning across extensive task varieties and training set dimensions. 	\item We examine factors underlying \textsc{genPet}{}'s robust performance and measure the contribution of its constituent components. \end{itemize}

text: The intricate process of news curation involves selecting and prioritizing information according to specific relevance criteria while operating within temporal and spatial constraints. Once exclusively managed by editorial teams at newspapers and media organizations, this curatorial function has increasingly shifted to machine learning (ML) systems that algorithmically rank content relevance~\cite{allcott2017social,eslami_i_2015}. Consequently, opaque and sophisticated ML algorithms now shape the news consumption patterns of billions of users worldwide. Research by the Pew Research Center reveals that approximately 53\% of U.S. adults using Facebook lack understanding of the mechanisms determining their news feed content~\cite{pew_facebook_feed_2019}. These findings drive our investigation into user perceptions of news recommendations and their capacity to differentiate between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML-generated suggestions. Additionally, we investigate whether untrustworthy content, such as fake news, gains credibility when presented within a trustworthy context—for example, when an ML system generates five recommendations where four represent legitimate news stories and one constitutes fabricated content. Our operational definition of fake news follows Lazer et al.'s characterization: ``fabricated information that mimics news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent''~\cite{lazer2018science}. Examining trust and misinformation within algorithmic news curation frameworks proves crucial, as these algorithms form the backbone of social media platforms like Facebook, which serve as primary distribution channels for fake news~\cite{allcott2017social}. The scholarly examination of news credibility and rumor susceptibility has deep historical roots~\cite{allport1947psychology,allport1945wartime}. Our research centers on trust within news recommender systems, building upon foundational work by O'Donovan et al. and Massa and Bhattacharjee~\cite{massa2004using,o2005trust}. However, our approach diverges by examining trust in the ML system itself and its collective recommendations rather than evaluating individual content items. The experimental design reflects authentic user-ML system interactions, where participants assess their confidence in machine learning recommendations by evaluating clustered news stories. Participants received explicit notification that they were engaging with an ML system rather than merely evaluating content. Trust serves as our focal construct because susceptibility to fake news transcends simple error—fabricated news deliberately deceives by mimicking legitimate media formats. Our framework aligns with human-in-the-loop and active machine learning paradigms, where users engage with dynamic systems that evolve through user interactions~\cite{rubens2015active,amershi2014power,Kulesza:2015:PED:2678025.2701399}. Within such environments, enhancing news curation algorithms through individual item ratings would demand substantial user time and effort. Therefore, we investigate holistic evaluation of ML recommendations as an alternative feedback mechanism. Understanding user perceptions of ML systems and their outputs holds significance for practitioners implementing algorithmic news curation and those seeking to empower users in detecting algorithmic bias. This research benefits human-computer interaction designers developing ML system interfaces and ML practitioners collecting user feedback on system performance or crowdsourcing training data~\cite{Gulla:2017:ADN:3106426.3109436,ozgobek,Russakovsky2015}. Our experimental framework involved participants interacting with a streamlined algorithmic news curation system delivering recommendations comparable to collaborative filtering approaches~\cite{Resnick:1994:GOA:192844.192905,herlocker2000explaining}. We implemented a between-subjects design across two phases, recruiting participants from a vocational school with technical backgrounds who received briefings on potential ML system failures. The initial phase captured participant trust ratings for various news stories, establishing a rated story pool where different participant subsets evaluated different story collections—ensuring each story received ratings from some users while remaining unseen by others. During the second phase, the algorithmic curation system assembled previously unseen story combinations for each user based on median trust ratings from the first phase. This approach enabled investigation of how individual story trust influences group-level trust in ML-generated recommendations. We manipulated the ratio of trustworthy to untrustworthy stories within recommendations to examine their impact on 11-point scale trust ratings. Our primary objective involves understanding ML output trust ratings as a function of individual news item trustworthiness within machine learning systems. This paper addresses three specific research questions: \begin{itemize} \item Can users provide trust ratings for news recommendations of a machine learning system~(RQ1)? \item Do users distinguish trustworthy ML recommendations from untrustworthy ML recommendations~(RQ2)? \item Do users distinguish trustworthy ML recommendations from recommendations that include one individual untrustworthy news story~(RQ3)? \end{itemize} Our findings demonstrate that users can provide sophisticated ML recommendation ratings. Their trust assessments successfully differentiate between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML recommendations when all constituent stories share the same trustworthiness level. However, participants cannot distinguish trustworthy recommendations from those containing a single fake news story, despite their ability to differentiate other ML recommendation types from trustworthy ones.

text: The probability of rejecting a null hypothesis quantitatively defines statistical power, establishing its fundamental importance in detecting effects of theoretical interest across research domains. Traditionally, researchers have relied on sample size increases as the most straightforward approach to enhance power, given its substantial mathematical influence among controllable study parameters \cite{cohen1992things}. Nevertheless, practical constraints frequently limit this strategy's feasibility. Studies investigating rare diseases face inherent challenges: limited populations, difficult participant identification, and complex engagement processes, particularly evident in early- and late-stage neuro-genetic syndrome research \cite{button2013power, szucs2017empirical}. Additionally, access restrictions and funding limitations may constrain researchers' ability to recruit desired participant numbers. This article demonstrates empirically that adjusting model parameters (\emph{i.e.}, weights) can produce dramatic power variations. Such parameter modifications can transform mid-powered investigations into well-powered studies while maintaining constant sample sizes. Throughout this work, we define well-powered research as achieving power exceeding \textit{0.8}. Fig.~\ref{fig:model-param-power} illustrates how power can vary considerably across fixed sample sizes through model parameter adjustments. Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad} presents power \textit{gradients} calculated using directional differences between KMeans-derived clusters, with coordinates representing power and squared L2-norm of model parameters. Constructing manifolds like those in Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad} provides researchers exceptional assistance in locating high-power regions. Access to such visualizations offers a straightforward method for reducing \textit{ideal} sample sizes without compromising statistical power. However, Algorithm~\ref{algo:power} reveals that single power computations demand \textit{200-1000} simulations. Moreover, the manifold parameter space encompasses model weights, sample sizes, and additional hyperparameter selections, creating enormous computational demands. A seven-predictor model with 11 choices per predictor and 11 sample size options generates a parameter space of $11^{7 + 1}$, requiring potentially days of computation. Consequently, this investigation explores \textit{cheaper} alternatives to complete power manifold simulation. We present three distinct contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We develop a neural network-based approach to predict power over a high-dimensional manifold for classification and regression purposes. Such an approach provides significant performance with even 10\% of the training data. \item We provide four baselines for alternatively predicting power and test all our approaches on three models-= regression, logistic and Repeated Measures ANOVA. \item To leverage the transfer of knowledge from one model's power manifold to another model's manifold, we first demonstrate the intuition behind such a transfer. Next, we show that such a transfer can enable the same or better results in every case. The article's remaining sections follow this organization: we initially detail pertinent literature and essential background information for algorithm development. This section includes pseudocodes for primary and supporting algorithms. Subsequently, we present empirical findings, emphasize significant achievements, and document limitations. Finally, we outline potential future research directions. \end{itemize}

text: Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) methodologies generate navigational charts that empower robots to explore environments autonomously, while contemporary Semantic Mapping approaches incorporate semantic details regarding environmental locations and objects. Through semantic mapping, robots can navigate using location semantics instead of basic geometric coordinates, thereby enabling automated reasoning about spatial contexts via planning algorithms or semantic interpretation of natural language instructions \cite{thomason2020jointly}. Consumer-oriented robotic systems particularly benefit from semantic maps, whether assisting visitors with navigation in unfamiliar structures \cite{Yedidsion_multi_robot} or facilitating object retrieval tasks \cite{Jiang_Walker_Hart_Stone_2019}. Given that manual semantic annotation proves tedious and impractical for extensive maps, this research concentrates on autonomous semantic labeling within mapped environments. Architectural environments commonly display signage that conveys crucial semantic information for human inhabitants, exemplified by placards denoting office numbers. Previous research employed manually crafted detection systems to locate door placards, establish their map positions, and extract textual content~\cite{Hart}~\cite{Case}. Such approaches necessitate either pre-existing map construction before placard scanning or human supervision during the scanning process. A key contribution of our work involves simultaneous environmental exploration and placard registration without human intervention, achieved through an enhanced Frontier Exploration algorithm termed Interruptable Frontier Exploration (IFE). Interruptable Frontier Exploration conducts environmental exploration while object detection systems continuously scan for door placards through \emph{passive observation}. Upon sign detection, exploration halts and the robot executes \emph{active observation}, repositioning itself optimally to segment, transcribe, and map the sign's location. We evaluate IFE performance against a baseline method that computes robotic trajectories for placard scanning along previously-identified wall segments~\cite{Case}, designated as Wall-Scanning Discovery (WD). IFE demonstrates superior efficiency compared to WD through reduced active scanning requirements and elimination of complete mapping prerequisites before placard detection.

text: In the rapidly evolving Internet era, recommender systems serve a pivotal function by predicting items that users are most likely to find appealing. Collaborative filtering represents an effective and extensively adopted recommendation approach that focuses on extracting latent user and item characteristics from historical interaction data. Foundational methods such as Matrix Factorization (MF)~\cite{koren2009matrix} break down rating matrices into user and item embeddings to reveal implicit semantic patterns. With the exponential growth in user and item volumes in recent years, numerous deep learning architectures have emerged within the collaborative filtering paradigm to model diverse user preferences across extensive item catalogs. Notable examples include ~\cite{berg2017graph} and~\cite{wang2019neural}, which construct user-item graphs to capture multi-hop interaction relationships.~\cite{liang2018variational} and~\cite{li2017collaborative} incorporate variational auto-encoder frameworks into their models, representing embeddings as Gaussian distributions. 	 	Within recommender systems, sequential recommendation constitutes a crucial component that treats user behaviors as ordered item sequences rather than unordered sets. The Markov Chain (MC)~\cite{cheng2013you} serves as a classical approach, modeling short-term item transitions to predict subsequent user preferences. Factorized personalized Markov chain (FPMC)~\cite{rendle2010factorizing} merges markov chain principles with traditional matrix factorization to capture user preference patterns. The advancement of deep learning has enabled Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to achieve remarkable success in sequential recommendation tasks. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)~\cite{zhu2017next} exemplifies a popular RNN variant that strengthens the model's capacity to preserve sequential information through memory mechanisms. GRU4Rec~\cite{chen2018sequential} employs Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) for session-based recommendation by implementing session-parallel mini-batch processing. However, RNN-based approaches struggle with long-range information retention. Consequently, self-attention networks have recently been adopted in sequential recommendations to model both long-term and short-term dependencies effectively. Both SASRec and BERT4Rec demonstrate superior prediction performance through attention mechanisms. SASRec~\cite{kang2018self} successfully captures long-term dependencies by considering influential weights across entire historical sequences. BERT4Rec~\cite{sun2019bert4rec} utilizes a deep bidirectional self-attention network with Cloze tasks to enhance transformer model efficiency. 	 	While these existing approaches model user intentions through historical sequential interactions, they overlook the dynamic underlying relationships among items. The connections linking item pairs contain rich semantic information regarding the factors that drive users to select one item following another. These underlying factors correspond to real-world concepts, with specific factors typically dominating individual situations. Consider, for instance, two users interacting with six items as illustrated in Figure~\ref{intro}. The link graph reveals that item 2 connects to all other five items, yet these connections stem from distinct motivating factors. Item 2 links to items 1 and 4 due to shared color attributes, while connecting to items 5 and 6 because of their short sleeve characteristics. Item 3 relates to item 2 through its function as a T-shirt jacket. These varied factors demonstrate user behavioral intention transformations while revealing shared characteristics between item pairs. Consequently, identifying and differentiating these underlying item-link factors can significantly enhance model expressiveness, with disentangled representation learning~\cite{locatello2019challenging} providing a established methodology to accomplish this objective. 	 	Disentangled representation learning has gained substantial traction across multiple domains, including Computer Vision~\cite{hsieh2018learning, mu2021disentangled}, and has recently found application in recommender systems. The fundamental goal of disentangled representation learning involves separating distinct and informative factors from data variations, where individual units correspond to single real-world concepts. Modifying one factor results in changes to its associated unit. Numerous models have demonstrated the capability to learn disentangled representations and have been successfully applied to practical tasks. For instance, through disentangled representation learning of facial images, we can derive independent representations of various facial features. This enables identification of specific attributes such as the presence of bangs, glasses, or smiles. Furthermore, these features can be modified directionally by adjusting corresponding dimensional values. Therefore, disentangled representation learning enhances both model interpretability and controllability. 	 	 	 	The leading networks for disentangled representation learning include $\beta$-VAE and InfoGAN. $\beta$-VAE~\cite{higgins2016beta} introduces a coefficient hyperparameter $\beta$ to the KL-divergence term within the variational auto-encoder objective, promoting more factorized latent representations. This additional hyperparameter applies substantial pressure on the posterior distribution to align with the factorized prior distribution~\cite{burgess2018understanding}. InfoGAN~\cite{chen2016infogan} maximizes mutual information between a fixed subset of GAN noise variables and observations. In recommender systems, Macrid-VAE~\cite{ma2019learning} infers high-level user intention concepts at the macro level while applying VAE to strengthen micro-level disentanglement. The authors additionally propose a self-supervised seq2seq training strategy for sequential recommendation~\cite{ma2020disentangled}, comparing user intentions between sub-sequences generated by an intention disentangled encoder. DGCF~\cite{wang2020disentangled} develops intent-aware interaction graphs to differentiate user intentions across various items, emphasizing user-item relationships. Nevertheless, these studies neglect item-link relationship patterns and fail to distinguish different user intentions underlying sequences. Consequently, sequential models become susceptible to noisy data and lack interpretability. 	 	This paper introduces an \textbf{E}dge-Enhanced \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{D}isentangled \textbf{G}raph \textbf{N}eural \textbf{N}etwork (EGD-GNN) model to capture item-link information effectively. We model item representations and user intentions at both global and local levels. At the global level, we construct a comprehensive item-link graph spanning all sequences, where each item-pair within sequences represents a graph edge. Figure~\ref{intro} demonstrates the construction of a global graph from two sequences. We employ a channel-aware mechanism to decompose edges into multiple channels, with each channel corresponding to an influential factor. These channels extract features specific to individual disentangled factors from neighbors and jointly aggregate different factors to target items. At the local level, we model disentangled user-intention representations over current sequences. We initially infer latent variation as a Gaussian distribution to enforce disentanglement from the statistical perspective of variational auto-encoders. Subsequently, we utilize the channel-aware mechanism to aggregate item information through edge channels from preceding sequence items. The aggregated item representation expresses current user intention. We conduct experiments using our proposed method on three real-world datasets, comparing prediction results with state-of-the-art baselines. Results demonstrate that the EGD-GNN model not only surpasses previous works in prediction tasks but also compels the system to discover effective disentangled representations. 	 	This paper's major contributions are summarized as follows: 	 	\begin{itemize} 		\item To our knowledge, this represents the first work exploring disentangled representation across global and local levels to learn factorized underlying factors of item relationships. 		 		\item We propose a disentangled graph neural network to infer factors underlying pairwise items that motivate user intentions. We apply the GNN model to both global graphs and local sequences to learn item link patterns, employing variational auto-encoders to leverage their statistical properties. 		 		\item We evaluate our model on three real-world datasets, with experimental results demonstrating our proposed model's ability to achieve effective disentangled representation over sequences for indicating user intentions. 	\end{itemize} 	 	The remainder of this paper follows this organization: Section~\ref{related} reviews related works corresponding to our approach. Section~\ref{preliminary} presents problem formulation, model definitions, and preliminaries. Section~\ref{methodology} details our proposed model. Section~\ref{experiment} presents and visualizes experimental results, demonstrating our model's effectiveness. Finally, Section~\ref{conclusion} concludes the paper and outlines future work directions.

text: \IEEEPARstart{W}{ith} the escalating complexity of Information Technology (IT) operational landscapes, enterprises face mounting pressure to sustain robust IT infrastructures while simultaneously curtailing operational expenses, minimizing ticket volumes, and enhancing customer satisfaction metrics. IT operations management relies fundamentally on Incident, Problem and Change (IPC) ticketing frameworks, wherein each operational concern manifests as an IT Service Desk ticket~\cite{Jan2015}. This research addresses these operational imperatives through strategic exploitation of both structured and unstructured ticket data furnished by Service Desk (SD) systems. Cognitive computing presents transformative opportunities to revolutionize and scale IT Services Delivery by obviating repetitive skill training requirements across service delivery personnel. The inherent learning capabilities distinguish cognitive solutions by enabling continuous enhancement through ongoing operational interactions while dynamically adapting to evolving organizational requirements. Furthermore, service quality improvements emerge through elimination of oversight errors and accelerated problem resolution via automated comprehension and reasoning of optimal solution pathways. Although human involvement diminishes substantially in operational effort, personnel maintain critical supervisory functions ensuring seamless user experiences. Collectively, cognitive computing transformation delivers unprecedented client experiences and competitive advantages through operational efficiency and agility previously unattainable. SD systems receive tickets through automated generation from diverse device monitoring infrastructures alongside manual ticket creation by SD agents responding to user inquiries. Contemporary marketplace analytics tools predominantly generate reports utilizing exclusively structured data attributes from historical ticket repositories. Certain tools incorporate query functionalities enabling identification of frequently occurring keywords or specified patterns within unstructured ticket attributes. Specialized IT professionals subsequently analyze these reports targeting remediation of predominant identified topics. While these tools deliver measurable benefits, significant limitations persist including inadequate processing capabilities for massive data volumes, inability to reveal both apparent and concealed issues, insufficient noise segregation from textual content, and failure to extract user sentiments from key topics within Customer Satisfaction (CSat) surveys and social media datasets. Literature surveys indicate approximately 80\% of organizational information exists within unstructured formats \cite{Rosu2012}. Our proposed methodology comprehensively addresses these identified limitations. The distinguishing characteristic of our approach lies in extracting semantic meaning from fragmented sentences within unstructured ticket descriptions. This unstructured content typically spans multiple languages, requiring language identification followed by normalization into English through machine translation methodologies. Additionally, varying grammatical proficiency levels among globally distributed agent pools contribute to inconsistent grammar quality. To establish uniform analytical baselines, our solution initially translates non-English content into English utilizing statistical translation models. Statistical model selection over grammar-based alternatives becomes necessary due to input text grammatical inconsistencies. Statistical translation models introduce additional complexity layers for cognitive system implementation. The system has empowered multiple clients to rapidly uncover patterns and trends facilitating contributing cause identification and precautionary measure prescription using data from hundreds of thousands of SD tickets. Traditional analyses of this scope typically required SD support teams weeks or months to complete. Consequently, contributing cause identification enables support teams to leverage log analytics for comprehensive root cause analysis. This capability facilitates proactive operational optimization and client satisfaction enhancement through the following demonstrated outcomes: \begin{itemize} \item Identification of contributing causes and actionable precautions from problem description and resolution. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise hidden behind volumes of unstructured data in tickets under different categories. \item Identification of emerging problems, trends and automated change point detection. \item Identification of patterns that can enable IT support teams to leverage real-time machine and data analytics to find the rapid root cause. \item Identification of self-service and automation opportunities, and transform operations from reactive to proactive. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise hidden behind volumes of unstructured text not captured in ticket categories. \item Sentiment analysis of the CSat survey comments to determine potential future dissatisfiers. \item Social Media and CSat sentiments correlation with IT and applications' issues to improve client experience. \item Predictive Analytics for improving resolution times by re-prioritization and routing of the tickets. \item Identification of skills and knowledge gaps derived from the analysis of first time resolution of failures, resolution time and agent performance differences. \end{itemize} This manuscript follows the subsequent organizational structure. Section \ref{sec:Methodology} presents comprehensive cognitive computing platform component overviews and overall system methodology. Section \ref{sec:Algorithms} delineates critical algorithms developed for system implementation. Section \ref{sec:Applications} examines various applications and use-cases while Section \ref{sec:Results} presents experimental results from diverse investigations. Section \ref{sec:Conclusion} provides concluding remarks.

text: Recommender systems facilitate user discovery of preferred items within vast candidate pools. Traditional recommendation models, including collaborative filtering~\cite{koren2009matrix} and DeepFM~\cite{10.5555/3172077.3172127}, leverage historical user behaviors to model preferences for future suggestions. Systems relying solely on exploitation approaches frequently encounter closed-loop effects~\cite{jadidinejad2020using}: users predominantly engage with system-recommended items, while the system reinforces user profiles based on interactions with previously recommended content. This feedback loop progressively narrows the system's focus to a restricted set of exposed interests per user, perpetuating recommendations within increasingly limited item ranges. Classical contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms, exemplified by LinUCB~\cite{li2010contextual}, utilize auxiliary information to achieve effective exploration-exploitation balance, thereby mitigating closed-loop phenomena. These frameworks model items as arms and the recommendation system as an agent. During each round, the agent selects the most promising arm from $K$ candidates, subsequently receiving rewards based on user-item interactions. The objective involves maximizing cumulative rewards across $T$ rounds. Nevertheless, these approaches assume manageable values of $K$, making exhaustive enumeration of candidate arm scores computationally feasible. This assumption holds for specific scenarios with naturally constrained candidate sets, including homepage news ranking, advertisement creative selection, and online model optimization. Within general recommendation contexts, genuine exploration of user interests and meaningful closed-loop mitigation requires considering the complete item repository as arm candidates—typically encompassing millions or billions of items. Traditional bandit methods become computationally prohibitive when exhaustive arm enumeration is required. We address this computational challenge by introducing a generic hierarchical contextual bandit~ (\textbf{HCB}) algorithm designed for efficient interest exploration in large-scale recommendation environments. Tree structures have proven effective for search space partitioning to reduce computational overhead~\cite{jain2016extreme,prabhu2014fastxml,zhu2018learning,zhuo2020learning}. {HCB} employs hierarchical tree indexing for coarse-to-fine retrieval processes. Consider e-commerce taxonomies where \textsl{``Apparel > Clothing > Women's Clothing > Dresses''} represents a path from broad categories to specific items. Rather than relying on predefined item taxonomies, we implement bottom-up clustering on item embeddings to construct hierarchical trees where each node encompasses semantically related items. This approach ensures balanced item distribution across tree nodes while encoding collaborative user behaviors, such as co-click relationships, within the hierarchical structure. {HCB} exploits hierarchical organization by decomposing interest exploration into sequential decision-making processes. Beginning at the tree root, the algorithm applies bandit methods among child arms at each non-leaf node, selecting children until reaching leaf nodes. Subsequently, a secondary bandit algorithm recommends specific items from leaf nodes to users, collecting feedback as rewards. Rewards propagate backward along selected paths to refine user interest estimations throughout the hierarchy. The {HCB} process resembles depth-first search (DFS) traversal. However, path selection through DFS introduces additional uncertainties, particularly for deep trees. Misleading parent node selections impact all subsequent decisions—a phenomenon we term \textsl{error propagation}. Moreover, diverse user interests often span multiple child nodes across different tree regions. We therefore propose progressive {HCB} (\textbf{pHCB}) to reduce uncertainties and enhance recommendation capabilities. Following breadth-first search (BFS) principles, {pHCB} explores items through adaptive top-down strategies. The algorithm maintains limited node sets as receptive fields: when nodes undergo sufficient exploration and user interest verification, their children enter the receptive field while parent nodes are removed. Simultaneously, {pHCB} models diverse user interests by applying bandit algorithms with visible receptive field nodes as arms. This approach prevents greedy single-node selection at each level, improving upon {HCB} performance. Our contributions include: \squishlist \item We emphasize the critical importance of exploring user interests across complete item spaces to genuinely mitigate closed-loop effects in personalized recommendation systems. This represents the first attempt at implementing CB models across millions of items. \item We introduce two effective algorithms, {HCB} and {pHCB}, for efficient user interest exploration through hierarchical item trees. \item Experimental validation on two large-scale recommendation datasets demonstrates {HCB} and {pHCB} superiority over baseline methods, plus flexibility for integration with various exploration techniques including LinUCB, Thompson Sampling, and $\epsilon$-greedy. Additional experiments verify that exploration mechanisms enable both {HCB} and {pHCB} to effectively mitigate closed-loop effects while improving long-term user profile learning. \squishend

This is the first attempt to use the SquishList over millions of items. This prevents the greedy selection at each level, and improves the performance of the HCB. We emphasize the crucial importance of exploring the interest of the users in the entire item space to truly mitigate the closed-loop effect in personalization systems. Squishend: We propose two effective methods for exploring the item trees in the recommendation task: greedy and parallel greedy. An experimental evaluation on two large-scale recommendation datasets shows the superiority of greedy and parallel greedy over other baselines, and their ability to combine with a variety of exploration strategies such as greedy, LinUCB, and greedy.

text: This paper examines an evolutionary robotic system wherein morphologies (bodies) and controllers (brains) undergo simultaneous evolution. Creating offspring in such systems necessitates generating and combining new bodies with new brains to form complete robotic entities. Asexual reproduction relies on a single parent, with offspring bodies and brains derived through random variation (mutation). Sexual reproduction (crossover) demands recombination of parental bodies and brains, yielding offspring composed of the resulting body controlled by the resulting brain. Independent of the reproduction mechanism employed, newly generated bodies and brains cannot be presumed to form optimal pairings. While parents may possess well-matched body-brain combinations, the stochastic nature of recombination and mutation can disrupt parental genomes, producing poorly coordinated body-brain configurations. Consequently, co-evolving morphologies and controllers inherently generates potential body-brain mismatches. This challenge was initially identified by \citep{Eiben2013} and recently re-examined in \citep{Eiben2020}. The recommended solution involves incorporating learning mechanisms. Within the robotic lifecycle framework, this extends beyond the conventional two-stage model—the pre-birth Morphogenesis Stage (constructing robotic phenotypes from genotypic instructions) and the post-birth Operational Stage (task execution and reproduction attempts). A third component, the Infancy Stage, follows Morphogenesis, during which newborn robots learn to optimize control of their inherited bodies and achieve maximum potential. The Infancy designation carries both metaphorical and practical significance: robots remain infertile throughout this period, precluding reproduction eligibility. Algorithmically, fitness calculations occur only after the Infancy period concludes, enabling robots to participate in fitness-based mate selection exclusively following learning completion. This three-stage architectural framework, termed The Triangle of Life, was introduced in 2013, yet investigations into such systems remain scarce. Limited research on joint morphology-controller evolution partially explains this gap, as most evolutionary robotics work focuses on brain evolution within fixed bodies. Additionally, computational expenses can prove prohibitive or discouraging. The infant learning process essentially constitutes a generate-and-test search through all possible controller configurations, requiring generation and testing of multiple new brains within given bodies. This translates to several additional fitness evaluations\footnote{For simplicity, all tests are termed fitness evaluations here.} per newborn robot. Allocating newborn robots a learning budget of $N$ new controllers for generation and testing during Infancy implies total fitness evaluations will exceed non-learning evolution by a factor of $N$. While appropriate $N$ values depend on specific systems and applications, literature commonly reports hundreds to thousands of learning trials. Our research primarily aims to investigate learning effects in morphologically evolving robots. We establish a system where simulated modular robots reproduce and generate offspring inheriting parental morphologies and controllers. Both bodies and brains remain inheritable and thus evolvable within our framework. Furthermore, brains become not only evolvable but learnable through implementation of a generic learning algorithm optimizing inherited brains across any possible robot body. System testing involves presenting a targeted locomotion problem: developing robots capable of directed movement. This task interfaces with the evolutionary system through an appropriate fitness function quantifying robotic ability to approach pre-specified targets. Applying mate selection and survivor selection mechanisms based on this fitness concept drives evolution toward robots whose body-brain combinations suit the given task. To examine learning effects, we execute robot evolution in two variants: purely evolutionary and combined evolution-learning approaches. The first variant establishes robot child fitness directly after birth using inherited parental brains. The second variant treats inherited brains as learning algorithm starting points, basing robot fitness on performance using learned brains. These experiments address efficacy, efficiency, and evolved morphology questions. Regarding efficacy and efficiency, we compare algorithm variants in terms of peak performance achievement and required time. Our underlying hypothesis suggests that real-world learning provides relatively fast, inexpensive methods for reducing slow, expensive evolutionary steps. Specifically, we distinguish learning trials from evolutionary trials. Evolutionary trials involve producing, activating, and testing new robots, including body manufacturing, while learning trials involve producing, activating, and testing new controllers within existing robots. Since controllers represent digital entities (code lines), learning trials demand significantly fewer temporal, effort, and material resources than evolutionary trials \citep{Eiben2021}. For instance, if robot manufacturing requires 12 hours, new controller computation and installation takes 10 seconds, and fitness evaluation duration spans one minute, then 1,000 evolutionary trials require approximately 501 days, while 1,000 learning trials cost under one day. Our corresponding research questions follow. {\textbf{Research Question 1:}} What evolutionary trial 'savings' can be achieved by incorporating infant learning as defined by Triangle of Life architecture? This question's answer indicates whether all allowable fitness evaluations should focus on evolutionary trials (creating new robots with new bodies and brains) or should be distributed between evolutionary trials and learning trials (creating new brains in existing bodies). Regarding morphologies, we examine quantifiable morphological characteristics (size, symmetry) comparing evolutionary process trends and final population morphologies. {\textbf{Research Question 2:}} Does learning addition result in different evolved morphologies? Intuitively, differences seem unlikely since learning affects only brains, not bodies. However, our recent precursor study revealed that learning addition can produce different morphologies \citep{Miras2020}. We also investigate {\it morphological intelligence} evolution, defined by given body learning potential. Rather than immediately judging newborn bodies with semi-incidental controllers post-birth, we evaluate them as-they-can-be using controllers customized through learning. Technically, we quantify morphological intelligence through the {\it learning delta}—performance difference between inherited and learned brains. Our definition resembles \citep{Gupta2021} in spirit but differs in details. Specifically, \citep{Gupta2021} define morphological intelligence through novel task learning ability, whereas our \citep{Miras2020}-based notion relates to given tasks. {\textbf{Research Question 3:}} How does morphological intelligence (measured by learning delta) evolve across consecutive generations?

text: The fundamental challenge of document retrieval involves identifying relevant documents within extensive collections to address specific user queries. Beyond its intrinsic importance, this capability serves as a foundational element for numerous natural language processing~(NLP) applications, including open domain question answering~\citep{chen2017reading} and fact checking~\citep{thorne2018fever}. Classical retrieval systems, commonly termed retrievers, have historically relied on lexical similarity measures to establish correspondences between queries and documents, employing techniques such as TF-IDF or BM25 weighting~\citep{robertson2009probabilistic}. However, these token-based matching approaches encounter significant limitations due to the lexical gap phenomenon and demonstrate poor generalization capabilities~\citep{berger2000bridging}. Neural network-based methodologies, conversely, transcend lexical constraints by learning semantic representations, thereby achieving superior performance on established question answering benchmarks like MS~MARCO~\citep{nguyen2016ms} and NaturalQuestions~\citep{kwiatkowski2019natural}. The exceptional retrieval capabilities demonstrated by neural networks have emerged primarily in contexts where abundant training data exists. For retrieval tasks, dataset construction necessitates manual annotation linking queries to their corresponding relevant documents within the collection. Such annotation becomes impractical when collections encompass millions or billions of documents, creating numerous scenarios where minimal in-domain examples exist, if any are available at all. One potential approach involves training dense retrievers on extensive retrieval datasets like MS~MARCO, subsequently deploying them across novel domains—a paradigm known as \emph{zero-shot} transfer. Regrettably, dense retrievers frequently underperform compared to traditional term-frequency methods under these conditions, despite the latter requiring no supervision whatsoever~\citep{thakur2021beir}. Furthermore, comprehensive annotated datasets remain largely unavailable for non-English languages. Consequently, reliance on extensive supervised datasets proves inadequate for developing multilingual retrieval architectures. Unsupervised learning presents a compelling alternative to transfer-based approaches, prompting a crucial inquiry: \emph{can dense retrievers be trained without supervision while achieving performance comparable to BM25?} Supervision-free training of dense retrievers becomes feasible through auxiliary tasks that approximate the retrieval objective. By generating synthetic queries from documents and subsequently training networks to retrieve original documents from large candidate pools, one can establish effective learning signals. The inverse Cloze task (ICT), introduced by \citet{lee2019latent} for retriever pre-training, employs individual sentences as queries to predict their surrounding contextual information. Although demonstrating encouraging results in pre-training scenarios~\citep{chang2020pre,sachan2021endtoend}, this methodology continues to underperform relative to BM25 in zero-shot retrieval contexts. ICT exhibits strong connections to contrastive learning principles~\citep{wu2018unsupervised}, which have achieved remarkable success in computer vision applications~\citep{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}. Notably, computer vision models utilizing advanced contrastive learning techniques have produced representations particularly well-suited for retrieval tasks~\citep{caron2021emerging}. Therefore, we propose a comprehensive examination of contrastive learning's effectiveness for training supervision-free dense retrievers. Our work presents several key contributions. Initially, we demonstrate that contrastive learning enables the development of robust unsupervised retrievers: our approach achieves Recall@100 performance competitive with BM25 across the majority of BEIR benchmark tasks. Subsequently, within few-shot learning contexts, we establish that our model effectively leverages limited training examples, surpassing the performance of models transferred from large-scale datasets such as MS~MARCO. Additionally, when employed as a pre-training strategy prior to MS~MARCO fine-tuning, our technique delivers exceptional performance on the BEIR benchmark. Through comprehensive ablation studies, we validate our architectural decisions and demonstrate that cropping strategies outperform the inverse Cloze task approach. Finally, we develop a multilingual dense retriever using contrastive learning that establishes new state-of-the-art performance standards. Code and pre-trained models are available here: \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/contriever}.

text: The proliferation of misinformation—alongside related phenomena like disinformation and fake news—has emerged as a defining challenge of recent years, with documented capacity to inflict substantial societal damage. Such harmful consequences span multiple domains: electoral manipulation through voter influence, compromised healthcare choices amid pandemic conditions, and market volatility affecting stock valuations\footnote{e.g., the GameStop incident in 2021: \url{https://reut.rs/3ra7stz }}. This misinformation epidemic has catalyzed extensive research efforts, particularly within natural language processing (NLP), focused on developing automated fact-checking systems for claim verification \cite{fever,popat2018declare,multifc,hanselowski2019richly,wadden2020fact,xfact,covidfact}. While significant advances have been achieved, the fundamental challenge persists with considerable difficulty. Current state-of-the-art systems demonstrate performance below 50\% F1 on established natural claim datasets~\cite{Atanasova2020GeneratingFC,multifc,xfact}. Deeper examination of these datasets reveals substantial variation in verification difficulty across different claims—a phenomenon that has garnered minimal scholarly attention. {\bf Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy-examples}} presents multiple claims previously fact-checked by Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com}}. Contrasting claims 3 and 5 illuminates this difficulty spectrum: claim 3 permits straightforward verification through basic search queries yielding mainstream media coverage. Conversely, claim 5 lacks accessible direct evidence sources, whether digital or physical. Even expert historians, when eventually consulted, acknowledged the claim's fundamental uncertainty. Such examples demonstrate the extensive range of verification complexity inherent in different claims. We present the inaugural systematic investigation into the underlying factors that render certain claims more challenging to fact-check than others. Our analysis examines claims from Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com/}} previously incorporated into automated fact-checking datasets \cite{liar,liarplus,multifc}. Through this manual examination, we identify five discrete difficulty-contributing factors: claim ambiguity, source support, source readability, source trustworthiness, and inference requirements. The integration of claim difficulty considerations into fact-checking frameworks carries significant conceptual, practical, and research ramifications. Conceptually, existing research has addressed claim check-worthiness \cite{checkthat2020,nakov2021clef}, yet check-worthy claims may simultaneously prove extraordinarily difficult or impossible to verify. This distinction bears critical implications for practical fact-checking operations, where finite human resources demand strategic allocation, and for automated fact-checking dataset construction, where incorporating exceptionally difficult claims may yield minimal algorithmic comparison insights. Furthermore, automated claim difficulty prediction could substantially benefit fact-checking organizations' resource management strategies, despite the apparent absence of research addressing this prediction challenge. Although claim difficulty prediction represents a novel contribution within fact-checking contexts, the broader value of modeling and predicting task instance difficulty enjoys established recognition across diverse domains, including machine translation \cite{Mishra2013AutomaticallyPS,Li2015DetectingCS}, syntactic parsing \cite{Garrette2013LearningAP}, and search engine switching behaviors \cite{white2009characterizing}. From this established perspective, we contend that instance difficulty prediction offers comparable benefits to fact-checking applications.

text: Contemporary commercial buildings constitute intricate cyber-physical systems. These structures increasingly incorporate diverse sensors and actuators—from surveillance cameras and card readers supporting security and access management, to thermostats and air-quality monitors that interface with Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems for environmental control while ensuring occupant comfort~\cite{Haggerty13,ardakanian2018}. Given their substantial financial value, these buildings demand more rigorous security management than their traditional counterparts. Effective building access management necessitates differentiated policies tailored to distinct user categories. Standard practice grants long-term occupants, such as employees, access privileges to their workspaces and communal areas according to organizational hierarchies. Conversely, facilities-management staff typically receive broader access to restricted equipment areas and the Building Management System (BMS), enabling them to monitor and adjust equipment configurations. Occupants can interact with sensing and control devices—including light switches and thermostats—within their authorized spaces, despite these devices potentially affecting areas beyond their immediate location; for instance, a single thermostat may regulate temperature setpoints across multiple adjacent rooms. Visitors generally receive constrained access and often require escort by building occupants to designated meeting spaces, where they may operate equipment solely during their visit duration. This conventional approach generates considerable administrative burden in large commercial buildings while exposing infrastructure to diverse security vulnerabilities. An automated solution for efficiently managing occupant access privileges represents an ideal objective. Conventional role-based access-control models employed in current systems prove cumbersome, demanding comprehensive specification of all roles and their hierarchical relationships—a particularly challenging task in large buildings housing multiple organizations, each maintaining distinct role structures~\cite{Bindra19}. This paper introduces a methodology for building access control management inspired by \emph{airline boarding-passes} and their associated workflows. Airports simultaneously accommodate numerous airlines managing individual flights at designated gates while issuing boarding passes to their respective passengers. These passes become available shortly before travel, permitting passengers to navigate security, access gates, and board aircraft at appropriate times. Each boarding pass links to a specific traveler and maintains validity only during a brief pre-departure window, during which security personnel can scan and authenticate the document. This methodology operates independently of existing access control delegation strategies while maintaining compatibility with implemented systems. Our approach provides flexible and secure management of building access privileges for both permanent occupants and temporary visitors, addressing the aforementioned challenges and risks. We establish services for \emph{fine-grained} decentralized management of individual access privileges within commercial buildings. Fine-grained encompasses (a) person-centric rather than role-based authorization, (b) customization across different spatial and system granularities, and (c) operation across multiple temporal scales. The foundational principle underlying this work asserts that \emph{individuals authorized for physical access to specific building locations should correspondingly possess access and capability to manipulate sensors and control points within those spaces}. This principle reflects the reality that most equipment lacks additional access controls beyond physical barriers such as locked doors. Conversely, \emph{individuals who should not access certain control points should be denied authorization to spaces containing such equipment}. Our methodology employs blockchain smart contracts to describe, grant, audit, and revoke fine-grained permissions for building occupants and visitors through decentralized mechanisms~\cite{andersen2018democratizing}. Smart contract specification utilizes information compiled from BOT~\cite{Rasmussen17} and Brick~\cite{balaji2016brick} models describing building spatial structure, equipment, and their relationships. This information enables our methodology to provide individuals with precisely appropriate access privileges for reaching their building destinations. We implement this concept through smart contracts that grant and revoke space-access privileges via an API accessible to various software applications. The underlying \emph{access-control service} accepts or rejects individual access requests based on currently valid smart contracts and their implications regarding sensor and actuator access. We demonstrate the proposed method through typical use cases within a real building context, arguing that it significantly reduces administrative overhead while providing fine-grained, auditable access control. The paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} presents contextual background for our work. Section~\ref{sec:method} details our methodology for smart-building access control using graph models for reasoning and blockchain smart contracts for access management. Section~\ref{sec:implement} examines implementation alongside use cases demonstrating how the proposed solution enhances authorization and access control procedures in real buildings. Section~\ref{sec:perform} evaluates solution performance regarding throughput and delay. Section~\ref{sec:system} addresses practical considerations for blockchain-based access control deployment. Section~\ref{sec:related} discusses related authorization and access-control solutions for built environments. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with key contributions and future work directions.

text: The field of few-shot learning has experienced remarkable advancement in recent years, particularly in its pursuit of classifying instances from previously unseen classes using merely a small collection of training examples. The meta-learning paradigm (also known as learning-to-learn) has attracted considerable attention as a mechanism for rapid adaptation to novel classes \cite{ren2018meta,snell2017prototypical,vinyals2016matching}. This approach has popularized the concept of organizing training data into {\em episodes}, effectively mimicking the tasks that models will encounter during inference. However, despite notable achievements, multiple recent studies in image classification \cite{boudiaf2020transductive,chen2018closer,dhillon2019baseline,GuoECCV20-DS,tian2020rethinking,zikolaplacian} have revealed that meta-learning may exhibit constrained generalization capabilities when applied beyond conventional 1- or 5-shot classification benchmarks. When confronted with more realistic scenarios involving domain shifts, straightforward classification baselines can surpass significantly more sophisticated meta-learning approaches \cite{chen2018closer,GuoECCV20-DS}. Semantic segmentation based on deep learning has traditionally benefited from methodological innovations in image classification. The emerging field of few-shot segmentation \cite{gairola2020simpropnet,wei2019fss,liu2020crnet,nguyen2019feature,rakelly2018conditional,pfenet,wangfew,wang2019panet,rpmm,yang2020new,zhang2019canet,zhang2020sg}, which has recently gained considerable traction, follows this established pattern. Within this framework, a deep segmentation model undergoes initial pre-training on {\em base} classes, after which its generalization capabilities are evaluated through few-shot {\em tasks} involving novel classes that remained unseen during base training. Each task comprises an unlabeled test image (the {\em query}) accompanied by several labeled images (the {\em support} set). Contemporary few-shot segmentation literature adheres to the learning-to-learn paradigm, with significant research investments directed toward developing specialized architectures and episodic-training schemes for base training. Nevertheless, i) episodic training inherently presupposes that testing tasks possess structural similarities (such as support shot quantities) to meta-training stage tasks; and ii) base and novel classes are frequently assumed to originate from identical datasets. These assumptions may constrain the practical applicability of current few-shot segmentation methods in real-world scenarios \cite{cao2019theoretical,chen2018closer}. Indeed, our experimental findings align with observations from few-shot classification research when extending beyond standard settings and benchmarks. We specifically noted performance saturation among state-of-the-art methods \cite{cao2019theoretical} as the number of labeled samples increases (refer to Table \ref{tab:n_shots_aggreg}). Furthermore, consistent with recent image classification observations \cite{chen2018closer}, existing meta-learning methods demonstrate reduced competitiveness in cross-domain scenarios (see Table \ref{tab:COCO2PASCAL_results_partial}). These findings raise questions regarding the viability of current few-shot segmentation benchmarks and datasets, while motivating a reconsideration of the meta-learning paradigm's relevance—a paradigm that has become the \textit{de facto} standard in few-shot segmentation literature. \subsection*{Contributions} This work abandons meta-learning in favor of reconsidering straightforward cross-entropy supervision during base class training for feature extraction. Furthermore, we introduce a \textit{transductive} inference approach that more effectively exploits support-set supervision compared to existing methodologies. Our key contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a novel transductive inference method—\textit{RePRI} (Region Proportion Regularized Inference)—designed for few-shot segmentation tasks. RePRI optimizes a composite loss function incorporating three synergistic components: \textit{i)} standard cross-entropy applied to labeled pixels within support images; \textit{ii)} entropy of posterior distributions over query pixels in test images; and \textit{iii)} a global KL divergence regularizer derived from predicted foreground pixel proportions within test images. RePRI operates as a plug-in component for any trained feature extractor, utilizing identical information as conventional inductive methods for few-shot segmentation tasks. \item Despite employing basic cross-entropy training on base classes without sophisticated meta-learning schemes, RePRI demonstrates highly competitive performance on standard few-shot segmentation benchmarks—PASCAL-5$^i$ and COCO-20$^i$—achieving approximately $5\%$ and $6\%$ improvements over state-of-the-art methods in 5- and 10-shot scenarios, respectively. \item We establish a more realistic experimental setting that introduces feature distribution shifts in images alongside the conventional class distribution shifts between training and testing data. Our approach achieves superior performance under these conditions. \item We demonstrate that precise region-proportion information regarding query objects substantially enhances results, yielding average improvements of 13\% across both datasets. While assuming such information availability remains unrealistic, we establish that approximate estimates can still produce significant improvements, thereby opening promising avenues for future research. \end{itemize}

text: E-commerce machine learning primarily concentrates on developing and testing recommenders that optimize business objectives. A fundamental gap exists between business and machine learning domains: target metrics like gross merchandise value (GMV) resist straightforward translation into concrete learning objectives. Although specific surrogate losses and evaluation metrics have demonstrated empirical success \cite{shani2011evaluating,herlocker2004evaluating}, online experimentation remains the gold standard for assessing real-world recommender performance. The machine learning community widely acknowledges various biases present in historical data \cite{chen2020bias}, which can trigger "feedback-loop effects" when empirical metrics are applied without proper correction \cite{gilotte2018offline}. Recent innovations have refined online A/B testing methodologies and enhanced offline evaluation techniques \cite{yin2019identification,lee2018winner,xie2018false,gilotte2018offline}. Nevertheless, these approaches remain inadequate for specific applications where problem complexity exceeds their potential advantages or their underlying assumptions fail to hold. Given our focus on e-commerce recommendations, we maintain an online shopping context throughout this paper. A/B testing faces mounting pressure for interleaving tested recommenders with targeted customers, driven by increasing personalization demands \cite{schuth2015predicting}. Collecting sufficient observations and conducting inference with adequate statistical power proves both time-consuming and expensive—complications amplified by the need to predefine buckets—as combination numbers can expand exponentially. Recent offline A/B testing advances \cite{gilotte2018offline} have established theoretical unbiasedness and optimality results, yet real-world performance hinges on fundamental causal assumptions \cite{imbens2015causal} such as unconfounding, overlap, and identifiability, which rarely materialize in practice \cite{xu2020adversarial}. While both online and offline testing remain indispensable despite their limitations, current challenges compel us to seek more efficient solutions that better exploit randomized traffic design. Our work stems from a production scenario requiring selection among several candidate recommenders with comparable offline evaluation performance. Segment analysis reveals each recommender's preference for specific customer groups, though definitive conclusions remain elusive due to exposure and selection biases in historical data. While launching each candidate online appears safe, randomized experiments remain necessary to explore real-world performance across different customer segments. We design experiments that incorporate customer features (such as segmentation information) to minimize costs associated with deploying suboptimal recommenders on customer groups. Our objective diverges from traditional controlled experiments by prioritizing cost minimization over rigorous inference. We therefore frame our mission as a recommender-wise exploration-exploitation problem—a novel application to our knowledge. Before proceeding, we clarify fundamental distinctions between our problem and learning recommender ensembles \cite{jahrer2010combining}. Business metrics like GMV constitute random quantities dependent on recommended content and distributions governing customer decision-making. Even with access to these distributions, conditional distributions given recommended content remain unknown a priori. Consequently, no fixed objective can adequately describe the problem for learning recommender ensembles. We conceptualize the exploration-exploitation strategy as a sequential game between developers and customers. In each round $t=1,\ldots,n$ (where $n$'s role will be clarified later), developers select a recommender $a_t \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ that generates content $c_t$ (e.g., top-k recommendations) based on front-end request $r_t$ (e.g., customer ID, user features, page type). Customers then reveal \textsl{reward} $y_t$ such as clicks or non-clicks. This setting resembles \textsl{multi-armed bandits (MAB)} by treating each recommender as an \emph{action} (\emph{arm}). The front-end request $r_t$, combined with recommended content $c_t = a_t(x_t)$, functions as the \emph{context}. Context informativeness regarding reward is evident since clicking depends on content-request matching quality. A randomized experiment design can be characterized by distribution $\pi$ over candidate recommenders: $0 < \pi_t(a) < 1$, $\sum_{i=1}^k \pi_t(i)=1$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. Our setting formally differs from classical \emph{contextual bandits} in that context depends on candidate actions. However, this impact becomes negligible when selecting optimal content sets remains equivalent to choosing optimal actions. text: Dense prediction for pixel-level labeling constitutes the core objective of semantic segmentation, where each pixel receives classification according to its represented class. Vision networks built on transformer architectures \cite{vit,deit} have demonstrated superior performance compared to Convolutional Neural Networks in image classification tasks \cite{imagenet}. Contemporary research reveals that transformer backbones exhibit remarkable capabilities when adapted to downstream applications such as semantic segmentation \cite{beit, fapn, swin-T}. Vision transformer architectural designs typically address the challenge through two primary methodologies: (i) employing existing pretrained backbones as encoders while transferring them to downstream tasks via established standard decoders including Semantic FPN \cite{sem-fpn} or UperNet \cite{upernet}; OR (ii) constructing novel encoder-decoder networks where ImageNet-pretrained encoders serve the semantic segmentation objective. These approaches necessitate encoder backbone finetuning for segmentation tasks. Large-scale dataset finetuning enables early attention layers to integrate local information within transformer lower layers \cite{vit-cnn}. Nevertheless, semantic context remains underutilized during finetuning owing to dataset size limitations and the fundamental shift in semantic class quantity and characteristics between classification and segmentation tasks. Hierarchical vision transformers \cite{segformer,swin-T} address this challenge through progressive feature downsampling across stages, yet semantic image context remains inadequately captured. The Swin Transformer, introduced by Liu et al. \cite{swin-T}, constructs hierarchical feature representations that enable compatibility as a versatile backbone for primary downstream vision applications. \cite{twins} proposed dual attention mechanisms: globally sub-sampled and locally sub-sampled variants built upon PVT \cite{pvt} and CPVT \cite{cpvt} architectures for enhanced segmentation performance. Xie et al. \cite{segformer} further refined hierarchical transformer encoders by eliminating positional encoding dependencies, thereby achieving robustness across varying resolutions commonly encountered in segmentation scenarios. While these contributions successfully modified encoders for improved downstream task performance in segmentation, they overlooked comprehensive semantic-level contextual information capture. Insufficient semantic contextual information results in suboptimal segmentation outcomes, particularly affecting small objects that become merged with larger category boundaries, producing erroneous predictions. Recently, \cite{segmenter} attempted addressing this limitation through pure transformer-based decoder design that jointly processes patch and class embeddings. However, this approach demonstrates inefficiency for compact variants and fails with hierarchical architectures, yielding suboptimal performance when integrated with major transformer backbones such as Swin \cite{swin-T} and Twins \cite{twins} transformers. Jin et al. proposed ISNet in \cite{isnet} to model both image-level and semantic-level contextual information through SLCM and ILCM module integration within decoder structures. A significant limitation persists: ISNet represents a CNN-based methodology focusing exclusively on decoder components while maintaining unchanged encoder architectures. We propose the SeMask framework to address these limitations by incorporating semantic information into hierarchical vision transformer architectures and augmenting transformer-captured global feature information with semantic context. Existing frameworks adopt encoder-decoder structures utilizing ImageNet-pretrained transformers \cite{imagenet} as encoders alongside specialized segmentation decoders. Rather than directly employing hierarchical transformers as backbones, we insert Semantic Layers following Transformer Layers at each backbone stage, yielding SeMask backbone versions as demonstrated in \cref{fig:intro}. We employ lightweight semantic decoders for semantic map accumulation across all stages, complemented by standard decoders such as Semantic-FPN \cite{sem-fpn} for primary per-pixel prediction. Enhanced semantic modeling integrated with feature modeling throughout the encoder improves semantic segmentation task performance. In \cref{sec:experiments}, we integrate the proposed SeMask block into Swin Transformer \cite{swin-T} and Mix Transformer \cite{segformer} backbones. Experimental results demonstrate substantial semantic segmentation improvements for both backbones across two distinct datasets. Our contributions encompass three key aspects: \begin{itemize} \item We pioneer the investigation of semantic context integration effects within pretrained transformer backbones for semantic segmentation tasks. Additionally, we introduce the SeMask Block as a plug-in component compatible with existing hierarchical vision transformers. Empirical validation through SeMask integration into Swin-transformer~\cite{swin-T} and Mix-Transformer~\cite{segformer} demonstrates significant performance enhancements. \item We propose utilizing simple semantic decoders for semantic prior aggregation from various encoder stages. These semantic priors receive supervision from ground truth through per-pixel cross-entropy loss functions. \item We provide comprehensive analysis of SeMask Block effects across two datasets: ADE20K and Cityscapes. Our approach achieves new state-of-the-art performance on ADE20K dataset and exceeds $3\%$ improvement on Cityscapes dataset. \end{itemize}

text: The task of image captioning—automatically generating descriptive sentences for unlabeled images—has garnered substantial research attention~\cite{showandtell2015,bottomup2017,aoanet2019}. Within this domain, cross-lingual image captioning represents an emerging subtopic that focuses on producing captions in non-English target languages, drawing increasing interest from both multimedia and computer vision communities~\cite{icmr16-ch-cap,WeiyuLan2017,Jiuxiang2018,2019Improving,2019Unpaired,gao2020unsupervised}. Existing research in this area concentrates on developing sophisticated algorithms that can effectively adapt image captioning models to target languages using established English datasets like Flickr8k \cite{2015Framing}, Flickr30k \cite{2014From} and MS-COCO \cite{mscoco2014}. Li \emph{et al.~} \cite{icmr16-ch-cap} demonstrate one approach by employing machine translation to convert English captions from Flickr8k into Chinese, then training a Show-Tell model~\cite{showandtell2015} on this translated corpus. Recognizing that machine-translated sentences often suffer from readability issues, Lan \emph{et al.~} \cite{WeiyuLan2017} propose fluency-guided learning, which weights training sentences according to fluency scores derived from deep language models. Building upon this foundation, Song \emph{et al.~} \cite{2019Unpaired} enhance the approach by incorporating self-supervised rewards that consider both fluency and visual relevance. While these training methodologies require minimal (or zero) target language data, comprehensive evaluation of resulting models typically demands thousands of test images paired with human-authored captions—termed \textit{references}—in the target language. Despite assistance from interactive annotation systems~\cite{icmr20-icap}, creating medium-sized test sets for each target language necessitates months of intensive human effort. This paper advances cross-lingual image captioning through a novel evaluation methodology. Specifically, we boldly attempt to eliminate the dependency on target language references. We introduce three metrics capable of distinguishing high-performing from low-performing models when test images are accompanied solely by English references. This requirement remains reasonable since existing cross-lingual image captioning research predominantly utilizes established English datasets. Our primary contributions encompass two key aspects: \begin{itemize} 	\item We present the first evaluation framework for cross-lingual image captioning models that operates without target language references. We introduce three metrics—WMDRel, CLinRel and CMedRel—that evaluate semantic relevance between automatically generated captions and image content through diverse approaches. 	\item Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed metrics. Using various combinations of image captioning architectures—Show-Tell~\cite{showandtell2015}, Up-Down~\cite{bottomup2017} and AoANet~\cite{aoanet2019}—and datasets—COCO-CN~\cite{cococn2019} and VATEX~\cite{2019VATEX}—we construct eight Chinese models for ranking evaluation. The combined WMDRel, CLinRel and CMedRel metrics achieve a Spearman's rank correlation of 0.952 with the aggregate of four standard metrics: BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L and CIDEr. In scenarios lacking source language references, CMedRel independently achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.881 with CIDEr. \end{itemize}
