text: The medical imaging field has experienced an unprecedented surge in Deep Learning (DL)-based image processing methodologies in recent years. These innovative approaches have demonstrated exceptional capabilities across numerous applications, particularly in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesion segmentation tasks. Under carefully controlled evaluation scenarios, certain automated algorithms have achieved performance levels comparable to human experts (see \cite{carass2017longitudinal}). However, a significant gap exists between these controlled validation environments and real-world clinical data, which exhibits substantial heterogeneity. The clinical deployment of DL-based MS lesion segmentation remains constrained primarily due to inadequate generalization when encountering data from medical institutions not represented during the training phase (unseen domains). This generalization limitation in DL methodologies stems from multiple contributing factors, including the optimization solution selected, training dataset diversity, and the generality of learned feature representations. The foundational premise of DL assumes that training and testing datasets are statistically independent yet drawn from identical distributions. Medical imaging data, particularly Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), frequently violates this assumption due to variations in acquisition protocols, scanner specifications, patient demographics, and processing software across different clinical centers or research cohorts. These distributional discrepancies (covariate shift) manifest as performance degradation when models trained on source domain data encounter test data from different distributions (target domains)—a phenomenon termed domain shift. A straightforward approach to mitigate this challenge involves training on more comprehensive and heterogeneous datasets (as demonstrated by \cite{maartensson2020reliability}). Nevertheless, this strategy demands extensive expert-annotated datasets, which are seldom accessible and labor-intensive to generate. Alternative approaches address this phenomenon through aggressive data augmentation techniques (such as \cite{zhang2020generalizing}), while others leverage limited labeled samples from target domains to minimize covariate shift through few-shot and one-shot learning paradigms (see \cite{snell2017prototypical,valverde2019one}). Furthermore, DL necessitates optimizing numerous parameters relative to available training samples, typically converging to one among many possible local minima rather than the theoretically optimal global minimum configuration. The model's generalization capacity consequently depends on the selected solution, with the identification of optimally generalizing local minima remaining an active research question. Some investigations propose selection based on loss function local characteristics (\textit{e.g.}, flatness) (see \cite{keskar2016large, wu2017towards}). Alternatively, combining multiple local minima can enhance generalization through averaging several minima from a single model (\textit{e.g.}, snapshot ensemble \cite{huang2017snapshot}) or aggregating outputs from independently trained models (\textit{e.g.}, classical ensemble \cite{zhang2019multiple} and spatially distributed networks \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d}). While traditional methods employ manually crafted features, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) autonomously extract task-optimal feature sets. Although highly effective for extracting relevant features within specific source domains, these feature sets may demonstrate poor target domain generalization. Several studies propose learning invariant features that persist across diverse source domains \cite{motiian2017unified,muandet2013domain,yang2013multi}, applying regularization to learn abstract task representations (\textit{i.e.}, analogous to human high-level concept understanding). Effective generalizing feature extraction balances optimization freedom for discovering optimal data combinations against constraints that minimize domain bias. Successful clinical deployment of DL-based MS lesion segmentation demands generalization capabilities ensuring robust performance across unseen domains. Such methods must guarantee DL model convergence to generalizing minima while anticipating covariate shift reduction during training. Additionally, the approach should enforce learning of generalizing MS lesion features from source domains to effectively delineate lesions despite target domain distributional differences. Crucially, this solution should operate without requiring additional annotations when processing unseen domains. Numerous recent studies have addressed MS lesion segmentation using CNNs.\\ \cite{brosch2016deep} introduced a deep 3D encoder-decoder architecture with joint encoder-decoder training, incorporating shortcut connections between interconnected pathways to integrate multi-level features. This pioneering work established deep learning's substantial potential for MS lesion segmentation.\\ \cite{valverde2017improving} developed a cascaded approach using two patch-based 3D CNNs: an initial sensitive network identifying lesion candidates followed by a refinement network reducing false positives. While enabling refined segmentation, this cascade employs limited receptive fields that compromise global context capture. Subsequently, \cite{valverde2019one} enhanced their methodology through one-shot domain adaptation utilizing transfer learning and selective fine-tuning. However, this adaptation requires labeled target domain examples and generates method variations after each adaptation, introducing segmentation inconsistencies.\\ \cite{hashemi2018asymmetric} addressed data imbalance (\textit{i.e.}, lesion class under-representation) by implementing an asymmetric similarity loss based on Tversky index for 3D CNN training, outperforming Dice or cross-entropy measures. These findings suggest that loss function selection merits further investigation. Although the proposed loss enables precision-recall optimization within specific domains, generalization to unseen domains requires validation.\\ \cite{zhang2019multiple} employed fully convolutional densely connected networks for MS lesion segmentation, stacking adjacent 2D slices from different modalities through channel-wise concatenation before processing via 2D CNNs. Final segmentation utilized majority voting across orientations. Despite competitive performance in controlled challenges, utilizing only two adjacent slices provides limited 3D data insight. Additionally, 2D features may inadequately represent generalizing characteristics for 3D volume processing, potentially limiting method generalization.\\ \cite{aslani2019multi} proposed an end-to-end encoder-decoder 2D architecture featuring multiple downsampling branches for each input modality, with a decoder combining multi-modal features across scales. This encoder branch separation enables efficient modality-specific information encoding before subsequent combination. However, this 2D approach lacks axial, coronal, and sagittal orientation feature integration, potentially compromising 3D image generalization.\\ \cite{feng2019self} addressed MRI modality unavailability during segmentation by introducing sequence dropout, an important consideration since complete modality availability varies across datasets, significantly affecting method generalization capacity. This framework randomly omits specific MRI sequences during training to learn intrinsic sequence information, demonstrating acceptable segmentation despite missing modalities. Nevertheless, it underperforms compared to state-of-the-art methods when all modalities are available (detailed in section \ref{same domain val}).\\ \cite{aslani2020scanner} addressed domain generalization by integrating regularization networks into traditional encoder-decoder architectures. The regularizer penalizes networks learning features enabling MRI scanning site prediction. However, \cite{li2018domain} argued that such strategies suffer from overfitting, potentially generalizing well across source domains while performing poorly on unknown target domains. All cited MS methods (\cite{brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,feng2019self,hashemi2018asymmetric,zhang2019multiple,aslani2019multi,feng2019self}) prioritized achieving accurate same-domain evaluation segmentation. However, out-of-domain dataset evaluation is essential for assessing method generalization capabilities—currently a prominent research focus (see \cite{maartensson2020reliability}, and \cite{bron2020cross}) and critical clinical recommendation (see \cite{omoumi2021buy}). Same-domain training and testing experiments are inherently biased [\cite{omoumi2021buy}] and fail to ensure generalization. Therefore, clinically viable models should produce accurate segmentation for new domain images without requiring expert annotation-based retraining. This paper presents DeepLesionBrain (DLB), a novel MS lesion segmentation method robust to domain shift, validated through out-of-domain testing (cross-dataset evaluation).\\ Initially, we employ numerous compact 3D CNNs spatially distributed across the brain with overlapping regional receptive fields. text: Remote sensing data analysis has consistently identified Anomaly Detection (AD) as a fundamental research area with broad application significance~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. The anomaly detection process fundamentally relies on examining discrepancies between a pixel under test (PUT) and its surrounding background characteristics. The literature presents numerous anomaly detection algorithms, each built upon distinct foundational assumptions: 1) background region selection and distributional modeling, 2) distance computation methodologies between the PUT and background statistics, and 3) decision threshold formulation or test statistic definition \cite{Matteoli2010}. The Reed-Xiaoli (RX) detector stands out among the extensive collection of AD approaches due to its computational simplicity, robust practical performance, and operational efficiency~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. As arguably the most recognized AD technique for hyperspectral imagery, the RX algorithm operates under the assumption of multivariate Gaussian background distribution and employs Mahalanobis distance metrics to quantify separation between the PUT and background characteristics~\cite{Reed90tassp}. Background region definition follows two primary paradigms: the global strategy treats the entire image as background, whereas the local strategy defines background through pixels neighboring the PUT via sliding window techniques or segmentation-based methodologies~\cite{Molero13jstars,Zhao15rs}. Additionally, potential anomalies may undergo censoring procedures to preserve background statistical integrity~\cite{Nar17dsp}. While RX demonstrates computational efficiency and performs adequately for straightforward backgrounds (predominantly linear scenarios), it struggles with complex, nonlinear, and\slash or non-Gaussian background distributions. Addressing these constraints requires more sophisticated approaches such as kernel methods, which effectively handle non-Gaussian data distributions~\cite{CampsValls09wiley,Kwon07,Longbotham14}. Nevertheless, kernel RX presents significant computational challenges due to matrix inversion operations scaling with sample size, potentially involving thousands of pixels. Conversely, the RX covariance matrix maintains constant dimensions proportional to spectral bands—approximately ten for multispectral and one hundred for hyperspectral imagery. Given that AD typically serves as a preprocessing step for subsequent recognition tasks, execution efficiency becomes equally critical to detection performance \cite{Chen14taes}. Furthermore, operational constraints often limit available processing power (CPU or GPU), memory capacity, and computational budgets \cite{Molero13jstars}. Recent work by \cite{Zhao16rs} introduced a fast recursive kernel RX approach utilizing causal data processing. Despite improved speed, this method encounters threshold estimation difficulties for target decisions, as detection outcomes depend on PUT spatial positioning within the image. This work presents an alternative acceleration strategy for kernel RX while preserving detection accuracy: we approximate kernel functions using random Fourier features~\cite{Rahimi07nips} to transform data into nonlinear feature spaces where conventional, computationally efficient linear RX methods become directly applicable. Remote sensing applications have previously employed randomized approaches for classification and regression challenges~\cite{Valero15igarss,Perez17rks}. Our proposed randomized RX methodology achieves substantial reductions in both execution time and memory requirements compared to kernel RX implementations, while maintaining nearly equivalent detection performance. We provide empirical validation through synthetic and real-world remote sensing target detection scenarios. The paper structure proceeds as follows. Section \ref{sec:randomized_GRX} provides a concise review of our proposed methodology. Section \ref{sec:experiments} demonstrates the randomized RX method's performance characteristics. Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with summary observations and future research directions.

text: This work introduces a Deep Interaction Prediction Network (\textsc{DIPN}\xspace) that learns object interactions from training examples and employs the resulting model to precisely forecast object poses following arbitrary push actions (Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}). To validate this approach, we combine \textsc{DIPN}\xspace with a deep Grasp Network (\textsc{GN}\xspace) to tackle complex clutter removal manipulation challenges. The goal involves clearing all objects from the workspace while minimizing the total number of required actions, selecting between available grasp and push operations. During each push/pick selection cycle (Fig.~\ref{fig:system-architecture}), the system analyzes the current scene and generates numerous candidate grasp and push actions. While \textsc{GN}\xspace directly evaluates grasps, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace processes each potential push action by producing an image that depicts the anticipated result. Essentially, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace enables the robot to ``visualize'' the consequences of executing a specific push on the present scene. \textsc{GN}\xspace then scores these predicted future images, and the system executes whichever action—push or grasp—receives the highest expected evaluation. Through comprehensive evaluation, we show that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace achieves precise object pose prediction following push actions involving collisions, maintaining below $10\%$ average single object pose error measured by IoU (Intersection-over-Union), which represents a substantial advancement over baseline methods. The push predictions generated by \textsc{DIPN}\xspace produce high-quality synthetic images suitable for \textsc{GN}\xspace to assess grasp actions in projected future states. When integrated with \textsc{GN}\xspace, our complete system delivers $34\%$ improved completion rates, $20.9\%$ enhanced grasp success rates, and $30.4\%$ better action efficiency compared to~\cite{zeng2018learning} across demanding clutter removal scenarios. text: The perpetual challenge of inertial navigation centers on state estimation ({\it i.e.,} \; position and orientation) for moving entities ({\it e.g.,}\; pedestrians) utilizing exclusively IMU sensors mounted on the subject. IMU devices, typically integrating accelerometers and gyroscopes, serve critical functions across diverse applications spanning mobile platforms to autonomous systems, owing to their exceptional energy efficiency, portability, and adaptability \cite{lymberopoulos2015realistic}. However, traditional Newtonian-based inertial navigation approaches exhibit substantial limitations and impose impractical constraints that conflict with real-world deployment scenarios. Strap-down inertial navigation systems (SINS), for instance, frequently generate erroneous positional estimates through double integration of IMU data, resulting from exponential error accumulation inherent in the integration process \cite{titterton2004strapdown}. While step-based pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) methodologies can mitigate such cumulative errors by exploiting prior knowledge of human locomotion patterns for trajectory prediction \cite{tian2015enhanced}, they necessitate restrictive operational conditions. These include foot-mounted IMU placement for zero-velocity updates \cite{foxlin2005pedestrian} or maintaining forward walking motion to ensure consistent directional orientation within the body frame \cite{brajdic2013walk}. Furthermore, inertial sensors are frequently integrated with supplementary sensing modalities through Extended Kalman Filter frameworks \cite{bloesch2015robust} to enhance estimation accuracy, incorporating WiFi \cite{ahmetovic2016navcog}, Bluetooth \cite{li2017indoor}, LiDAR \cite{zhang2014loam}, or camera sensors \cite{leutenegger2015keyframe}. Nevertheless, such multi-sensor fusion introduces additional complexities regarding hardware deployment, power consumption, and privacy preservation. Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) systems, for example, exhibit strong dependencies on environmental variables including illumination conditions, signal integrity, and motion blur artifacts \cite{usenko2016direct}. Contemporary data-driven methodologies, including IONet \cite{chen2018ionet}, RoNIN \cite{herath2020ronin}, and IDOL \cite{sun2021idol}, have recently showcased the potential of neural networks to achieve precise IMU-based estimations with performance comparable to conventional approaches. Despite these advances, significant obstacles persist in applying neural network architectures to IMU data processing: 1) existing data-driven solutions predominantly employ sequence-based architectures ({\it e.g.,}\; LSTM \cite{LSTM}) that effectively model temporal dependencies while neglecting spatial correlations within multivariate time-series data. 2) Limited research has investigated the exploitation of rich {\it contextual} information embedded within IMU measurements across both spatial and temporal dimensions for enhanced inertial feature representation. 3) Current neural inertial models typically assume fixed covariance matrices for IMU measurement and output uncertainties, introducing substantial inaccuracies and reduced robustness due to the inherently dynamic and unpredictable nature of these uncertainties. Addressing these identified limitations and concerns, we introduce a novel robust contextual Transformer network designed for velocity regression and trajectory prediction from IMU measurements. Specifically, CTIN builds upon ResNet-18 \cite{he2016deep} and Transformer \cite{vaswani2017attention} architectures to leverage spatial and extended temporal information within IMU observations, subsequently employing attention mechanisms for information fusion in inertial navigation applications. The primary contributions of this work are outlined below: \begin{itemize} \item Extending ResNet-18 with attention mechanisms is to explore and encode spatial information of IMU samples. \item A novel self-attention mechanism is proposed to extract contextual features of IMU measurements. \item Multi-Task learning using novel loss functions is to improve learning efficiency and reduce models' uncertainty. \item Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative comparisons with the existing baselines indicate that CTIN outperforms state-of-the-art models. \item A new IMU dataset with ground-truth trajectories under natural human motions is provided for future reference. \item To the best of our knowledge, CTIN is the first Transformer-based model for inertial navigation. \end{itemize} The remainder of this manuscript follows this structure: Section \ref{sec: background} provides foundational knowledge regarding inertial navigation and attention mechanisms. Section \ref{sec: model} examines CTIN's architecture and operational workflow. Evaluation results and related research are presented in Section \ref{sec: evaluation} and Section \ref{sec: related_work}, respectively. Section \ref{sec: conclusion} concludes with findings and future research directions.

text: Mathematical word problems (MWPs) present distinctive challenges that require comprehending natural language descriptions and conducting arithmetic reasoning over numerical quantities using commonsense knowledge. As demonstrated in \autoref{fig:example}, a standard MWP features a brief narrative that depicts a real-world scenario and poses a question regarding an unknown quantity. To address the MWP shown in \autoref{fig:example}, a computational system must identify crucial numerical values from the text, including "100 kilometers" and "2 hours," while comprehending their interconnections. Subsequently, fundamental mathematical principles such as "distance = velocity $\times$ time" are applied to derive the solution. Recent research has concentrated on addressing MWPs through neural-symbolic architectures~\cite{Ling2017ProgramIB, wang-etal-2017-deep, Huang2018NeuralMW, Wang2018TranslatingMW, Xie2019AGT}. Such architectures typically incorporate a neural perception component (\emph{i.e.}, Seq2Seq or Seq2Tree) that transforms problem text into solution expressions or trees, coupled with a symbolic component that executes these expressions to produce final answers. Training such architectures necessitates complete supervision through solution expressions. Nevertheless, fully-supervised methodologies exhibit three significant limitations. Initially, existing MWP datasets supply only a single solution per problem, despite the natural existence of multiple solution paths for identical problems. Consider the problem illustrated in \autoref{fig:example}, which admits solution via ``$(100/2) \times (2+3.5)$'' through initial speed calculation followed by total time multiplication; alternatively, ``$100 + 100/2 \times 3.5$'' provides a solution by aggregating distances from both journey segments. Models receiving full supervision on current datasets become constrained to fit provided solutions, preventing diverse solution generation. Additionally, expression annotation for MWPs demands considerable time investment. Conversely, abundant MWPs with final answers can be readily extracted from internet sources (\emph{e.g.}, online forums). Efficiently leveraging such partially-labeled data without expression supervision remains unresolved. Finally, current supervised learning methodologies experience train-test misalignment. Fully-supervised approaches optimize expression accuracy instead of answer accuracy, yet model evaluation relies on answer accuracy during testing, creating an inherent performance disparity. We propose addressing these challenges through \textit{weak supervision} for MWP solving, requiring only problem texts and final answers. Direct optimization of answer accuracy rather than expression accuracy naturally resolves train-test misalignment through weak supervision learning. Our architecture employs a tree-structured neural model resembling \citet{Xie2019AGT} for solution tree generation, combined with a symbolic execution module for answer calculation. However, the symbolic execution module remains non-differentiable regarding answer accuracy, preventing backpropagation-based gradient computation. A direct approach involves employing policy gradient techniques such as REINFORCE~\cite{williams1992simple} for neural model training. Policy gradient methods explore solution spaces and update policies based on solutions that achieve correct answers. Given extensive solution spaces and zero rewards for incorrect solutions, these methods typically exhibit slow convergence or convergence failure. To enhance weakly-supervised learning efficiency, we introduce a novel \textit{fixing} mechanism that learns from incorrect predictions, drawing inspiration from human learning through failure via abductive reasoning~\cite{magnani2009abductive,Zhou2018AbductiveLT}. The fixing mechanism propagates errors from root to leaf nodes within solution trees, identifying the most probable \textit{fix} capable of generating desired answers. Fixed solution trees subsequently serve as pseudo labels for neural model training. \autoref{fig:framework} illustrates how the fixing mechanism corrects erroneous solution trees through top-down error tracing. Additionally, we develop two practical techniques for efficient solution space traversal and solution discovery. First, recognizing positive correlation between text quantity counts and solution tree sizes (leaf node numbers), we propose \textit{tree regularization} based on this observation to constrain possible tree size ranges and reduce solution spaces. Second, we implement a \textit{memory buffer} that tracks and stores discovered fixes for individual problems through the fixing mechanism. All memory buffer solutions function as pseudo labels for model training, promoting diverse solution generation for single problems. Through combining the fixing mechanism with these techniques, our proposed \textbf{learning-by-fixing} (LBF) method incorporates exploring and learning stages within each iteration, as depicted in \autoref{fig:framework}. We employ the fixing mechanism and tree regularization for wrong answer correction during exploration, generating fixed expressions as pseudo labels. During learning stages, we train neural models using these pseudo labels. Comprehensive experiments on the Math23K dataset~\cite{wang-etal-2017-deep} demonstrate that our proposed LBF method substantially surpasses reinforcement learning baselines in weakly-supervised learning while achieving performance comparable to several fully-supervised approaches. Moreover, our method attains significantly superior answer accuracies across all top-3/5 answers compared to fully-supervised methods, highlighting its advantage in diverse solution generation. Ablative experiments further confirm the effectiveness of designed algorithms, encompassing the fixing mechanism, tree regularization, and memory buffer.

text: Pattern mining seeks to uncover a compact collection of compelling patterns that collectively characterize substantial portions of datasets while maintaining interpretability and reusability. This field encompasses diverse algorithms within knowledge discovery and data mining for dataset analysis \citep{aggarwal2014frequent5interesting}. Contemporary pattern mining methodologies focus on identifying compelling \textit{pattern sets} instead of collections of individually noteworthy patterns, where pattern quality assessment considers both dataset characteristics and inter-pattern relationships. A prevalent theoretical foundation for pattern set mining employs the Minimum Description Length principle (MDL)~\citep{grunwald2007minimum}, which finds application across various pattern types including itemsets~\citep{vreeken2011krimp}, arbitrary-shaped patterns in 2-dimensional data~\citep{faas2020vouw}, sequences~\citep{hinrichs2017characterising}, and graphs~\citep{bariatti2020graphmdl}. Despite significant progress in pattern mining, numerical data mining algorithms remain inadequately investigated. Currently, the predominant approach for mining numerical pattern sets involves applying itemset mining techniques to binarized datasets. We elaborate on this approach subsequently, but first acknowledge clustering as an alternative to numeric pattern mining. Recent years have witnessed extensive clustering algorithm development, yielding numerous diverse and efficient methodologies \citep{Jain10,CraenendonckDB17,Jeantet0G20}. Nevertheless, a fundamental conceptual distinction exists between pattern mining and clustering. Pattern mining prioritizes \textit{description}, whereas clustering emphasizes \textit{object similarity}. Specifically, numerical pattern mining emphasizes describing object groups through attribute sets associated with these objects, while clustering concentrates on detecting object groups based on measured commonalities through similarity or distance metrics. The former necessitates interpretability requirements, meaning resulting patterns should describe easily interpretable regions within the ``attribute space''. Conversely, clustering emphasizes object or instance groups. Although clusters may be constrained to specific shapes (e.g., spheres in \textsc{K-means} or \textsc{DBSCAN}), object similarity remains the fundamental cluster characteristic. For instance, clustering techniques like agglomerative single-linkage clustering in multidimensional spaces may yield clusters with highly complex shapes. Typically, these shapes receive minimal attention, yet they constitute primary concerns in numerical pattern mining. Therefore, we present an MDL-based numerical pattern set mining approach termed \textsc{Mint} (``Mining INTeresting Numerical Pattern Sets''). \textsc{Mint} computes numerical patterns as $m$-dimensional hyper-rectangles representing products of $m$ intervals, where intervals correspond to attributes and their values. The primary advantages of the \textsc{Mint} approach include: (i) \textsc{Mint} eliminates the need for advance pattern space exploration since optimal pattern candidates are computed dynamically, (ii) the total explored pattern count remains at most cubic (and at most quadratic per iteration) relative to objects with distinct descriptions considered as attribute value vectors, (iii) \textsc{Mint} employs MDL principles and produces compact sets of non-redundant informative patterns. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate \textsc{Mint}'s efficiency and high-quality pattern set generation: patterns describe meaningful object groups with precise boundaries. The \textsc{Mint} algorithm successfully mines numerical patterns across both small and large datasets, typically outperforming competitors \textsc{Slim} and \textsc{RealKrimp} in efficiency and reliability. Our proposed encoding scheme utilizes prequential plug-in codes, which exhibit superior theoretical properties compared to codes employed in \textsc{Slim}, \textsc{RealKrimp}, and the MDL-based discretization method \textsc{IPD}. This paper follows the subsequent organization. Section~\ref{sec:related_work} examines state-of-the-art itemset pattern mining algorithms for numerical data. Section~\ref{sec:basics} presents fundamental concepts utilized throughout the paper, while Section~\ref{sec:method} describes our proposed method's foundations. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} details experiments conducted to demonstrate \textsc{Mint}'s favorable performance and strengths. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with discussions regarding \textsc{Mint}'s potential and future research directions.

text: \noindent The application of deep learning models within computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) systems has attracted substantial research attention in recent years. Across numerous clinical domains—including fundoscopy \cite{asiri2019deep}, dermatology \cite{liu2020deep,esteva2017dermatologist}, and pulmonary disease diagnosis \cite{shoeibi2020automated,rajpurkar2017chexnet,gabruseva2020deep}—these models have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance. Given the global shortage of radiologists and rising burnout rates \cite{wuni2020opportunities,ali2015diagnostic, kumamaru2018global,zha2018prevalence,rimmer2017radiologist}, developing deep learning systems for chest radiography addresses a pressing clinical need. The supervised learning paradigm proves particularly well-suited for chest radiography tasks, as extensive collections of chest radiographs paired with diagnostic labels provide abundant training data for deep learning architectures. Benchmark datasets encompassing various diseases have been assembled from chest radiograph collections \cite{wang2017chestx,johnson2019mimic}, with COVID-19 datasets emerging most recently \cite{wang2020covid}. On these benchmark datasets, deep learning models have achieved expert-level performance \cite{rajpurkar2018deep,seyyed2020chexclusion}. Nevertheless, recent investigations reveal that even top-performing deep learning models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks \cite{finlayson2019adversarial,han2020deep}. \citet{finlayson2018adversarial} argue that the medical industry's substantial costs, coupled with pharmaceutical device and drug approval processes based on disease prevalence, could incentivize the manipulation of disease detection systems. This paper makes the following primary contributions: \begin{enumerate} \item We conduct an in-depth exploration of backdoor attacks within medical imaging, specifically targeting chest radiography in multi-label classification scenarios. Since chest radiographs can simultaneously reveal multiple diseases, we introduce an evaluation framework tailored to multi-label classification tasks. To our knowledge, this represents the first investigation of backdoor attacks specifically within multi-label classification contexts. \item We demonstrate how triggers manifest across both low-level and high-level features that models learn, utilizing Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), a weakly-supervised explainability technique \cite{selvaraju2017grad}. Through illustrating how explainability methods can detect backdoor presence, we highlight explainability's crucial role in examining model robustness. \end{enumerate}

text: Distributed transactions and computations find their foundation in the PlatON network platform~\cite{PlatON}. Agreement among participating nodes concerning blockchain block additions relies on the Giskard consensus protocol~\cite{Giskard}, which maintains the distributed ledger's integrity. Byzantine fault tolerance characterizes the protocol's resilience, accommodating up to one-third adversarial node behavior~\cite{Byzantine}. This paper delivers a rigorous Giskard specification. While existing protocol documentation~\cite{Giskard} offers behavioral overviews and general descriptions, our specification targets implementation guidance and formal verification support through comprehensive detail. We establish protocol execution semantics alongside critical property definitions, subsequently demonstrating three fundamental safety properties through formal proofs grounded in these definitions. Given our safety-centric approach, we deliberately omit higher-level Giskard features and provide only essential background material; readers seeking broader context and motivational details should consult the official documentation~\cite{Giskard}.

Correspondence to \email{alex@openai.com}, \email{prafulla@openai.com}, \email{aramesh@openai.com}} While images—ranging from illustrations and paintings to photographs—can typically be described through natural language with relative ease, their creation demands specialized expertise and substantial time investment. Consequently, developing tools that can generate realistic imagery from textual descriptions would enable unprecedented accessibility in visual content creation, empowering users to produce rich and varied visual materials effortlessly. The capacity to modify images through natural language commands would further enable iterative enhancement and precise control, essential capabilities for practical deployment. Contemporary text-conditional image generation models demonstrate the ability to synthesize imagery from open-ended textual prompts and can meaningfully combine disparate objects in semantically coherent arrangements \citep{attngan,dmgan,dfgan,dalle,xmcgan}. Nevertheless, these systems fall short of producing photorealistic outputs that fully capture the nuanced details specified in their corresponding text descriptions. Conversely, unconditional generative models have achieved photorealistic image synthesis \cite{biggan,stylegan,stylegan2,vqvae2}, occasionally reaching fidelity levels that render human discrimination from authentic images challenging \cite{zhou2019hype}. Among these approaches, diffusion models \cite{dickstein,scorematching} have distinguished themselves as a particularly effective generative framework, establishing new benchmarks for sample quality across multiple image generation tasks \citep{ddpm,sotapaper,cascaded}. For achieving photorealism in class-conditional scenarios, \citet{sotapaper} enhanced diffusion models through \textit{classifier guidance}, enabling conditioning on classifier predictions. This approach involves training a classifier on noise-corrupted images, then leveraging classifier gradients during sampling to steer generation toward desired labels. Subsequently, \citet{uncond} demonstrated comparable performance without requiring separate classifier training via \textit{classifier-free guidance}, which interpolates between conditional and unconditional diffusion model predictions. Drawing inspiration from guided diffusion models' photorealistic generation capabilities and text-to-image models' flexibility with natural language inputs, we extend guided diffusion to text-conditional image synthesis. Our approach begins with training a 3.5~billion parameter diffusion model that incorporates a text encoder for natural language conditioning. We then evaluate two guidance strategies for steering diffusion models toward textual prompts: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. Through comprehensive human and automated assessment, we demonstrate that classifier-free guidance produces superior image quality. Our classifier-free guided model generates samples that exhibit both photorealistic quality and demonstrate extensive world knowledge. Human evaluators prefer our samples over DALL-E \citep{dalle} outputs in 87\% of photorealism comparisons and 69\% of caption similarity assessments. Although our model handles diverse text prompts in zero-shot settings, it encounters challenges with complex prompt specifications. To address this limitation, we augment our system with editing functionality beyond zero-shot generation, enabling users to iteratively refine outputs until they satisfy complex requirements. Through fine-tuning for image inpainting, our model achieves realistic modifications to existing images via natural language instructions. The resulting edits seamlessly integrate with surrounding visual context, producing convincing shadows and reflections that maintain stylistic consistency. Such capabilities could potentially revolutionize custom image creation by dramatically reducing time and effort requirements. We acknowledge that our model could substantially lower barriers to creating convincing disinformation or deepfake content. To mitigate these risks while supporting continued research, we provide access to a reduced-scale diffusion model and a noise-augmented CLIP model, both trained on curated datasets. Our system is designated GLIDE{}, representing \textbf{G}uided \textbf{L}anguage to \textbf{I}mage \textbf{D}iffusion for Generation and \textbf{E}diting. The constrained version is referred to as GLIDE{} (filtered).

text: \noindent The proliferation of online recruitment platforms has accelerated dramatically in recent years. As recruitment data volumes expand exponentially, numerous interview-focused research areas have emerged, including person-job (or talent-job) fit~\cite{shen2018joint, qin2018enhancing,luo2019resumegan, bian2019domain} and automated analysis of asynchronous video interviews (AVIs)~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, hemamou2019slices,suen2019tensorflow}, both targeting automated job recommendation and candidate evaluation systems. Person-job fit research typically frames the problem as supervised text matching, where labeled datasets (person-job match records) enable prediction of compatibility between candidate resumes and job descriptions. Deep learning approaches have recently strengthened person-job fit methodologies through enhanced text matching and representation models~\cite{xu2017measuring, jiang2019semantic}. AVI systems determine candidate hirability by analyzing responses to interview questions, treating interviews as sequential question-answer exchanges rich with social signals. Comprehensive candidate evaluation in AVIs involves extracting video (or image), textual, and vocal features during response generation. Our research concentrates on scoring multiple QA pairs, exclusively utilizing textual features while framing the task as competency assessment rather than binary hiring decisions. Human interviewer evaluation processes inform our two-stage solution architecture: (1) individual QA pair analysis and evaluation to determine assessment status, and (2) overall candidate competency scoring based on aggregated QA pair evaluations. \begin{comment} \end{comment} First-stage methodologies predominantly utilize text matching or attentional text matching algorithms for QA pair evaluation~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, suen2019tensorflow}, processing concatenated question-answer representations through subsequent classifiers. However, asynchronous video interview questions span diverse domains, enabling candidates to draw upon varied work or academic experiences in their responses. This variability renders accurate answer evaluation through text matching alone challenging. Semantic interaction analysis between questions and answers offers a more intuitive evaluation approach. The primary challenge involves uncovering latent question-answer relationships. Graph neural networks (GNNs, ~\cite{dai2016discriminative, yao2019graph, ghosal2019dialoguegcn}) excel at learning effective node representations by encoding local graph structures and node attributes. Their model compactness and inductive learning capabilities make GNNs valuable for relational data modeling~\cite{battaglia2018relational, schlichtkrull2018modeling, pan2020semantic} and logical reasoning~\cite{luo2019improving, jiang2020reasoning}. ~\citet{zhang2020efficient} introduced ExpressGNN, a GNN variant balancing representational power with model simplicity in probabilistic logic reasoning. ~\citet{ghosal2019dialoguegcn} developed DialogeGCN to address context propagation limitations in RNN-based approaches, leveraging self and inter-speaker dependencies for conversational context modeling in emotion recognition. Drawing inspiration from~\cite{ghosal2019dialoguegcn}, we introduce a sentence-level relational GCN capturing internal temporal and QA interaction dependencies during question-answering processes. Second-stage candidate grading approaches~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet,hemamou2019slices} typically encode question-answer pairs as direct sequences based on QA pair representations. Such methods inadequately capture semantic interactions between question-answer pairs, compromising evaluation rationality and explainability. Addressing this limitation, our first stage employs a semantic-level graph attention network (GAT) modeling interaction states within QA sessions. We present a Hierarchical Reasoning Graph Neural Network (HRGNN) for automatic scoring of answer transcriptions (ASAT) in job interviews. Our approach integrates a sentence-level relational graph convolutional neural network (RGCN) for contextual dependency capture with a semantic-level Reasoning graph attention network (RGAT) for latent interaction state acquisition. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a relational graph neural network addressing QA interaction deficiencies in existing assessment methodologies. Internal temporal dependency relations within questions/answers enhance contextual understanding, while QA interaction dependency relations establish latent semantic connections between question-to-answer and answer-to-question flows. \item We pioneer hierarchical graph neural network construction for ASAT, modeling sentence-level relationships between questions and corresponding answers while enabling semantic-level interaction and inference. Despite focusing solely on textual features for competency evaluation, our approach significantly enhances assessment rationality and accuracy. \item Our model surpasses all existing benchmark methods on a Chinese real-world dataset. Ablation studies and experimental validation across 10 random seeds demonstrate model effectiveness and stability. \end{itemize}

text: The advancement of intelligent technologies has significantly enhanced individual robot capabilities. text: Interactive media experiences deliver content that adapts to individual audience members based on their specific context, knowledge, or requirements. Unlike traditional media formats that present uniform content to all viewers, these experiences modify either the information delivered or its presentation format. The data driving these variations can originate from several sources: (1) real-time user interactions during content consumption; (2) information gathered at the experience's onset (enabling more passive consumption modes); (3) pre-existing user profiles; or (4) hybrid approaches combining these methods. This paper concentrates on the first category. The interactive complexity of such experiences surpasses that of conventional media formats. Consequently, production teams require effective monitoring systems to assess their success, enabling them to detect and address content issues while gaining insights for enhancing future user experiences. Audience engagement with the experience serves as a fundamental success indicator. Nevertheless, user engagement represents a multidimensional and intricate phenomenon \cite{attfield2011towards}. Given that media consumption occurs across geographically dispersed audiences using varied devices and contexts, precise measurement faces significant practical and methodological obstacles. Interaction data has emerged as an unobtrusive and scalable engagement monitoring approach in certain domains \cite{attfield2011towards,lehmann2012models,doherty2018engagement}; our investigation examines its applicability within this field. Since interactive media experiences feature enhanced content interactivity compared to traditional media, can these interactions be monitored and leveraged to deduce engagement levels? This study investigates and introduces novel information collection methods and analytical techniques that broadcasters might employ to better comprehend their audiences and their content engagement levels; rather than evaluating a specific experience, we examine whether interaction data proves valuable for engagement measurement. The capacity to measure engagement through interaction data offers an additional advantage: enabling near real-time engagement monitoring. This capability would facilitate not only retrospective analysis for future improvements but also dynamic content adaptation. For instance, highly engaged audience members might receive supplementary materials, while those displaying lower engagement could be presented with abbreviated or simplified content conclusions. Although designing effective interventions of this nature presents considerable challenges, such approaches could substantially improve user experiences and become feasible only through real-time engagement monitoring. Other domains have successfully employed interaction data, particularly online news \cite{lagun2016understanding,grinberg2018identifying,lu2018between,constantinides2018framework} and search \cite{diriye2012leaving,kim2014modeling,zhuang2017understanding}. These data have also enabled extraction of user behaviors serving as engagement proxies \cite{barbieri2016improving,arapakis2016predicting} and satisfaction indicators \cite{chuklin2016incorporating,mehrotra2017user}. Since engagement techniques and measures remain untested within this domain, we examined a production-quality, nationally broadcast interactive television program where audiences control presentation and narrative pathways. We gathered ground truth engagement metrics and user interactions (available code and data: \cite{jonathan_carlton_2021_5137806}) from this live, real-world interactive TV show to investigate: \begin{itemize} \item[\textit{(RQ)}] What behaviours can we infer from interaction metrics that help in understanding how engaged an audience member is with an interactive media experience? \end{itemize} We derived various metrics and examined their relationships with audience-reported engagement levels. To comprehend metric-engagement correlations, we developed an interpretable predictive model for engagement and determined feature importance through internal weights and model-agnostic interpretation methods. Our analysis revealed that temporal metrics—including inter-event intervals and story completion duration—effectively differentiate and strongly correlate with engagement levels. These findings establish the value of interaction data for providing media creators with audience engagement insights that can be directly extracted from the data itself. Our research delivers the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We establish a connection between user engagement and interaction metrics derived from interactive media experiences; \item We show the feasibility of predicting engagement levels through user interaction analysis; \item We validate, more broadly, the value of collecting and analyzing user interactions from interactive media experiences and the potential engagement insights available to inform creative processes. \end{itemize} The paper proceeds as follows: Section \ref{sec:background} examines related work. Section \ref{sec:methods} outlines the study methodology, while Section \ref{sec:results} presents our findings. Section \ref{sec:discussion} contextualizes and discusses the results, and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} provides conclusions and future work considerations.

text: \noindent As a fundamental element of brand identity, logos serve as critical indicators for statistical analysis of brand exposure and influence across vast collections of images and videos (\citeauthor{gao2014brand} \citeyear{gao2014brand}). The inherent design philosophy of logos—emphasizing minimalist symbols or textual elements (\citeauthor{ad2012logo}\citeyear{ad2012logo})—results in sparse representational information. Moreover, the subtle distinctions between different logos, often differing by merely a single character or stroke, present formidable challenges for learning discriminative deep features. The conventional logo recognition pipeline encompasses two sequential phases: bounding box localization followed by logo identification. Traditional closed-set approaches leverage established frameworks including Faster R-CNN (\citeauthor{ren2015faster} \citeyear{ren2015faster}), SSD (\citeauthor{liu2016ssd} \citeyear{liu2016ssd}), and YOLOv3 (\citeauthor{redmon2018yolov3} \citeyear{redmon2018yolov3}). Nevertheless, closed-set methodologies impose stringent data requirements while failing to recognize logos absent from training datasets. Addressing these limitations, open-set approaches have emerged (\citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}; \citeauthor{bastan2019large} \citeyear{bastan2019large}; \citeauthor{fehervari2019scalable} \citeyear{fehervari2019scalable}), employing a two-stage architecture: class-agnostic binary detection for logo localization, followed by classification or retrieval-based identification. While the detection stage can utilize existing frameworks like Faster R-CNN and YOLOv3, the identification phase employs metric learning to measure nonlinear data distances, facilitating complex data comparison within embedding spaces. Through practical deployment, we observed that while class-agnostic binary detectors can readily identify logo-like regions under low threshold settings, the subsequent challenge of determining logo authenticity and class assignment—effectively mapping logos within embedding spaces where similar classes cluster while different classes separate—proves considerably more demanding. Consequently, we identify the second stage as the primary bottleneck in logo recognition, forming the central focus of this investigation. Current public logo datasets exhibit several critical limitations (Tab. \ref{table:1}): 1) insufficient logo class diversity, inadequately representing real-world logo recognition challenges (\citeauthor{romberg2011scalable} \citeyear{romberg2011scalable}; \citeauthor{neumann2002integration} \citeyear{neumann2002integration}); 2) web-crawled images featuring overly prominent logos with diminished scene complexity (\citeauthor{wang2020logodet} \citeyear{wang2020logodet}; \citeauthor{su2018open} \citeyear{su2018open}; \citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}); 3) image-level annotations unsuitable for logo recognition tasks (\citeauthor{su2018scalable} \citeyear{su2018scalable}). To address these shortcomings, we present Makeup216, offering distinct advantages: 1) specialized focus on cosmetics domain, demanding sophisticated recognition algorithms due to minimal inter-logo variations; 2) real-world imagery capturing logos on actual products rather than promotional materials, introducing diverse complexities including blur, occlusion, mirror reflections, and non-rigid deformations; 3) highest object density per image among existing datasets. These characteristics substantially enhance logo recognition model applicability. Our analysis reveals that isolated logos provide limited visual information and narrow contextual scope, frequently resulting in erroneous retrievals. As demonstrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a), top-1 recalled logos exhibit high similarity despite incorrect matches. Conversely, incorporating extended peripheral regions provides broader visual context and supplementary information. Product backgrounds and adjacent textual/symbolic elements serve as verification mechanisms, mitigating false recalls as illustrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(b). Building upon this insight, we introduce a novel logo recognition framework incorporating an adversarial attention representation (AAR) module that leverages marginal background information. This framework simultaneously identifies primary subjects while preserving auxiliary information for enhanced accuracy. The experimental section demonstrates our framework's effectiveness in resolving the issues depicted in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a). To evaluate logo recognition model robustness against noise, we constructed a distractor set for Makeup216, drawing inspiration from image retrieval datasets (\citeauthor{radenovic2018revisiting}\citeyear{radenovic2018revisiting}). This enabled the development of dual evaluation protocols: one excluding distractor samples, another incorporating them. Our proposed framework demonstrates superior performance when confronted with distractor samples. This work's primary contributions include: \begin{enumerate} \item Introduction of a cosmetics-focused dataset featuring diverse logos and complex scenes, establishing a challenging benchmark for logo recognition. Novel evaluation protocols assess model robustness, with both Makeup216 dataset and protocols made publicly available. \item Development of an adversarial attention representation (AAR) framework that maximally exploits marginal auxiliary information to enhance pure logo representation. The AAR mechanism determines focal priorities while utilizing supplementary information for improved accuracy. \item Establishment of a logo recognition baseline through comprehensive experiments on Makeup216 and LogoDet-3k, achieving state-of-the-art performance. \end{enumerate}

text: The intersection of natural language processing and historical linguistics has witnessed growing attention toward lexical semantic change\footnote{see \url{https://languagechange.org/}}, prompting the development of multiple datasets across various languages \cite{schlechtweg2020semeval2020}. Our research operates within the framework of DIACR-Ita \cite{diacrita_evalita2020} at EVALITA 2020 \cite{Evalita2020}, which establishes an entirely unsupervised task for Italian. DIACR-Ita provided us with 18 target words\footnote{'egemonizzare', 'lucciola', 'campanello', 'trasferibile', 'brama', 'polisportiva', 'palmare', 'processare', 'pilotato', 'cappuccio', 'pacchetto', 'ape', 'unico', 'discriminatorio', 'rampante', 'campionato', 'tac', 'piovra'} alongside two temporally distinct, preprocessed Italian corpora designated as \textit{T0} and \textit{T1}, both enriched with part-of-speech tagging and lemmatization annotations. Our methodology encompasses two distinct perspectives for addressing this challenge, each differing in target word representation and lexical-semantic change estimation across datasets. The first approach (1) employs POS distributions of target words as representations while utilizing an ensemble of distance measures for estimation purposes. The second approach (2) leverages neighbor similarities of target words as representations, coupled with one of two proposed similarity measures for estimation. The subsequent three sections detail prior research, our modeling framework, and experimental outcomes derived from these methodologies. Section \ref{discussion_section} (Discussion) then examines the second approach in depth, highlighting the influence of the $k$ parameter on similarity measures and analyzing the discriminatory capabilities of our embedding-based model.

text: \IEEEPARstart{A}{irborne} optical sectioning (AOS) \cite{Kurmi2018,Kurmi2019TAOS,Kurmi2019Sensor,Bimber2019IEEECGA,Kurmi2020GeoScience, David2020} represents a powerful aerial synthetic aperture imaging methodology that reveals concealed artifacts beneath dense forest canopies, which would otherwise remain undetectable in conventional single-frame captures. This technique proves particularly valuable for search and rescue (SAR) operations \cite{Kurmi2019TAOS} and wildlife monitoring applications \cite{David2020}, % where AOS captures fractional thermal emissions from obscured targets as unstructured thermal light-field data via camera-equipped drones (Fig.~\ref{fig:Fig0CameraPose}). The method leverages extensive synthetic aperture coverage (spanning 30–100 m diameter) to enable optical sectioning through image integration processes \cite{Kurmi2018}. \vspace{-1.5em} Integral images—which represent wide-aperture sensor measurements—emerge through registration and averaging of individual image recordings relative to the drone's three-dimensional positioning and a predetermined synthetic focal plane. % The system employs RGB imagery in visible wavelengths (Sony Alpha 6000 RGB camera) for drone pose determination and thermal imagery (Flir Vue Pro; 7.5-13.5 $\mu m$ spectral band) for integration purposes. Both thermal and RGB recordings are preserved on internal camera storage and retrieved for post-flight processing. Following integration, targets positioned at the focal plane exhibit sharp clarity while occluding elements at greater distances undergo substantial blurring and eventual disappearance. Consequently, focus adjustment through interactive or automated focal plane positioning \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} toward optimal ground-level orientation enables optical penetration through forest layers and facilitates detection and examination of hidden targets, including human subjects or wildlife. Precise drone pose measurements for each thermal image capture constitute a fundamental AOS requirement. Current implementation relies on advanced computer vision algorithms employing general-purpose structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo frameworks \cite{schonberger2016sfm,schoenberger2016mvs} applied to high-resolution RGB imagery. Nevertheless, recent research \cite{Chin2018} demonstrates that model estimation or fitting procedures involving outlier-contaminated data represent NP-hard computational challenges. Consequently, pose estimation remains susceptible to errors, and resulting mis-registrations of individual recordings produce defocus artifacts in AOS integral images. Thermal images, characterized by limited resolution, elevated noise levels, reduced contrast, and inadequate natural scene texture, fail to provide reliable image features necessary for dependable pose estimation. Multiple methodologies for correcting residual pose errors have emerged, including optimization approaches that impose structural constraints \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018}, exploit localized depth mapping \cite{Shin2018,Shamwell2019}, or integrate multi-sensor fusion \cite{Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018}. This article introduces an alternative strategy for minimizing residual pose errors by reframing the underlying optimization as a focusing challenge rather than addressing the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem \cite{Chin2018}. PnP methodologies \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018,Shin2018,Shamwell2019,Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018} demand robust feature detection capabilities, which prove problematic for low-resolution thermal imagery and become impractical under severe occlusion conditions. % Our approach addresses the focusing problem through optimization of 3 or 6 pose parameters per image utilizing straightforward gray level variance (GLV)\cite{Firestone1991}—a feature-independent metric—as the error criterion. % Previous work \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} established GLV's occlusion invariance, making it superior to conventional \mbox{gradient-,} Laplacian-, and wavelet-based metrics surveyed in \cite{Pertuz2013} as a visibility measure for AOS thermal integral images. Figure \ref{fig:Fig1Completeresult} demonstrates AOS outcomes when synthetic focal plane undergoes global optimization as described in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} (focal plane), contrasted with enhanced results achieved through our novel pose error reduction methodology applied to either 6D (brute force) or 3D (ours) pose parameters. The latter approach yields integral images with superior detail revelation through improved focus and enhanced contrast. Subsequent sections examine pose parameter error effects and various integration strategies, culminating in our final optimization approach featuring reduced parameter search space and early termination mechanisms. We demonstrate that our methodology enhances integral image quality beyond state-of-the-art pose estimation techniques while achieving substantially greater speed and efficiency compared to brute force optimization across all pose parameters. \vspace{-0.8em}

text: Traditional recommendation algorithms prioritized maximizing accuracy in delivered recommendations. Yet as research has evolved, scholars have recognized additional crucial recommendation characteristics: diversity, serendipity, novelty~\cite{Vargas:2011:RRN:2043932.2043955,ge2010beyond,castells2011novelty}, and fairness \cite{yao2017beyond}. These dimensions profoundly influence recommendation utility across all system stakeholders \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. This work addresses \textit{popularity bias}—the systematic tendency for recommender systems to overemphasize a narrow set of popular items beyond what their actual popularity justifies, while simultaneously underrepresenting items outside this set, despite substantial user interest in these overlooked items~\cite{park2008long,steck2011item,jannach2015recommenders}. Figure \ref{amplify_item_groups} illustrates this phenomenon through distributions comparing item popularity against recommendation frequency across four established algorithms: \textit{RankALS} \cite{takacs2012alternating}, \textit{Biased Matrix Factorization (Biased-MF)} \cite{koren2009matrix}, \textit{User-based Collaborative Filtering (User-CF)} \cite{aggarwal2016neighborhood}, and \textit{Item-based Collaborative Filtering (Item-CF)} \cite{sarwar2001item}, evaluated on MovieLens 1M \cite{movielens} (detailed in section \ref{data_section}). Items are ranked by popularity along the x-axis, with the black curve depicting cumulative rating frequencies. The distribution reveals extreme concentration: merely 111 items (under 3\%) account for over 20\% of all ratings. This pattern mirrors consumer domains where recommender systems operate—music catalogs featuring artists with millions of plays (Beyonc\'{e}, Ed Sheeran) alongside those with smaller audiences (such as Iranian musician Kayhan Kalhor). Following established literature, we partition items into three categories based on the Pareto Principle \cite{sanders1987pareto}: \textit{short-head} items ($H$) comprise the most popular items capturing roughly 20\% of ratings; \textit{Mid} items ($M$) represent a larger collection of moderately popular items accounting for approximately 60\% of ratings; and \textit{Tail} items ($T$) encompass numerous less popular items collectively receiving around 20\% of ratings\footnote{Tail items may also be new items that have yet to find their audience and will eventually become popular. In this way, popularity bias is related to the well-known item cold-start problem in recommendation.}. These partitions appear at the top of each plot in \cite{celma2008hits}. The blue curves demonstrate popularity bias across algorithms. \textit{Item-CF} exhibits the most severe bias, recommending virtually no items beyond rank 111—the head items (under 3\% of the catalog) dominate nearly 100\% of recommendations. \textit{User-CF} shows similar concentration at 99\%. Other algorithms perform marginally better, with \textit{H} items capturing over 64\% and 74\% of recommendations in \textit{RankALS} and \textit{Biased-MF}, respectively. While these visualizations reveal popularity bias through a "rich get richer" amplification of skewed user preferences, we contend this aggregate perspective provides incomplete insight into bias impact. Drawing from multistakeholder recommendation research \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}, we examine two primary stakeholder groups: 1) users receiving recommendations and 2) suppliers providing recommended items. Popularity bias affects both stakeholders, as demonstrated in Figures ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} (user impact) and ~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} (supplier impact). Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} begins by showing item group ratios ($H$, $M$, $T$) across user profiles in MovieLens 1M. Users are ordered by their preference for popular items, measured through profile composition and divided into three equal bins $G=\{G_1, G_2, G_3\}$ from most popularity-focused ($G_1$) to least ($G_3$). The y-axis represents profile proportions devoted to each item group. While the blue band (popular items) decreases monotonically reflecting user ordering, all groups—even $G_1$—have rated substantial numbers of \textit{Mid} and \textit{Tail} items. This pattern reflects natural consumption: limited popular content forces even blockbuster-focused viewers toward diverse choices. Subsequent plots maintain user ordering but shift the y-axis to recommendation proportions from different algorithms\footnote{The plots are ``banded'' because recommendation lists are of size 10 and there are only 10 possible ratio values for each item group.}. The contrast with original user profiles is dramatic, particularly for \textit{Item-CF} and \textit{User-CF}. Despite users' diverse rating histories, recommendations become homogeneous. \textit{Tail} items vanish entirely (red line at plot bottom). \textit{Item-CF} delivers nearly 100\% \textit{Head} recommendations even to niche-oriented users. While head-focused $G_1$ users receive poorly matched recommendations regarding popularity preferences, tail-focused $G_3$ users suffer most severely—receiving exclusively popular movies despite minimal interest, with none of their long-tail preferences addressed. Popularity bias thus creates differential user impact: universal effects with disproportionate severity across segments. Multistakeholder analysis extends beyond users to include \textit{suppliers}—entities behind recommended items. Here, we consider movie directors as suppliers. Figure~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} examines popularity bias from the supplier perspective, paralleling Figure~\ref{amplify_item_groups} but focusing on director popularity. The distribution again shows extreme skew, with few popular directors' movies dominating ratings. We define three supplier groups by popularity $S=\{S_1, S_2, S_3\}$: $S_1$ represents few popular suppliers whose items capture 20\% of ratings; $S_2$ includes numerous medium-popularity suppliers accounting for 60\% of ratings; and $S_3$ encompasses less popular suppliers receiving 20\% of ratings\footnote{The popularity distribution of items and suppliers has a strong long-tail shape. Therefore, in order to create groups with different popularity values we cannot force the groups to have equal sizes as this would lead to groups with medium and extreme popularity to have very close average popularity.}. Algorithm results reveal popularity bias affects suppliers similarly. In \textit{Item-CF}, movies from merely 3 popular $S_1$ directors (under 0.4\%) constitute 50\% of recommendations, while $S_3$ items never appear. This pattern persists across algorithms. This analysis establishes popularity bias as a multistakeholder phenomenon severely impacting entities throughout the recommendation ecosystem, necessitating evaluation capturing diverse stakeholder perspectives. We propose an algorithmic solution based on \textit{popularity calibration}—ensuring recommendation lists match users' popularity profiles. Calibrated recommendations occur when item group ratios align with user profiles: if a user rates 20\% $H$, 40\% $M$, and 40\% $T$ items, calibrated recommendations maintain these proportions. Our approach delivers more calibrated user recommendations while improving supplier fairness. Notably, popularity calibration doesn't guarantee content preference matching. Documentary and film noir movies may both be unpopular, yet users might prefer one over the other. Our method calibrates recommendations by popularity rather than content characteristics. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Characterizing popularity bias through multistakeholder analysis as an ecosystem-wide problem, introducing impact quantification metrics. \item Demonstrating how existing popularity bias evaluation metrics often obscure crucial information about algorithmic bias control across stakeholders. \item Revealing state-of-the-art re-ranking algorithm weaknesses from multistakeholder perspectives. \item Proposing a novel, effective popularity calibration algorithm using re-ranking, applicable to any recommendation algorithm's output. \item Validating through music and movie datasets that our method surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in mitigating popularity bias impact across multiple stakeholders. \end{itemize}

text: Challenging sensory-motor control tasks have witnessed remarkable achievements through reinforcement learning approaches, spanning agile drone flight~\cite{Kaufmann2018drone,Kaufmann2020drone,Loquercio2021drone}, deformable object manipulation~\cite{Wu2019deformable}, and quadruped locomotion~\cite{Hwangbo2019agile,Miki2022wild,Lee2020terrain,margonlis2022rapid}. Unlike classical model-predictive control methods, reinforcement learning frameworks leverage more realistic forward dynamics through physics simulators. Advanced rigid-body simulation technologies~\cite{Todorov2012mujoco, Makoviychuk2021Isaac} enable reinforcement learning algorithms to circumvent their traditionally prohibitive sample complexity by conducting initial training in simulation before direct physical deployment. Nevertheless, a \textit{sim-to-real gap} persists between controller experiences in simulated versus physical environments. The challenge of developing visuomotor control policies that maintain robustness under varying perceptual conditions during deployment continues to pose significant difficulties. Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution} illustrates this challenge. Domain shift is commonly addressed by exposing agents to extensive data variety during training, hoping the training distribution adequately encompasses real-world experiences. Extensible simulators enable domain randomization for generating diverse training data~\cite{tobin2017domain,active-domain-randomization}. Data augmentation mechanisms can alternatively enhance existing datasets~\cite{yarats2021drqv2,hansen2020deployment}. Both strategies seek visual features invariant to task-orthogonal perceptual changes. However, such invariance carries costs. Extended training reduces wall-clock efficiency, domain randomization demands manual tuning~\cite{Andrychowicz2020dexterous}, and assumes sufficient policy network capacity for handling expanded input distributions. This added complexity can degrade model and policy performance~\cite{laskin2020reinforcement,hansen2020deployment}. Moreover, these approaches assume prior knowledge of deployment-time perceptual shifts. When target domains remain unknown \textit{a priori} and fall \textit{out-of-distribution}, failure occurs, resulting in malfunctioning robots unable to self-correct (see Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}). Rather than achieving invariance through memorizing task-irrelevant elements during training, we examine a more demanding yet realistic scenario where deployment specifics remain unknown beforehand. This necessitates genuine \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization without target environment knowledge. We assume reward supervision unavailability, precluding reinforcement learning fine-tuning. While seemingly impossible, this implicitly assumes the \textit{same task} optimized during training remains well-defined in target domains. Consequently, agents retain \textit{some} understanding of \textit{what they know} despite encountering numerous task-irrelevant unknowns. Without additional assumptions or generality loss, this \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization challenge becomes \textit{unsupervised policy adaptation} between MDPs sharing identical latent dynamics and reward structures but featuring distinct pixel observations (See Figure~\ref{fig:graphicalmodels}). This paper explores generalization improvement under these challenging conditions. Instead of combating domain shift through explicit perceptual invariance during training, we demonstrate feature invariance generation at deployment by exploiting task consistency—what agents experience internally should remain constant. We gather latent features from training as exemplars of agent task \textit{knowledge}. In target domains (see Figure~\ref{fig:latent-alignment}), new latents shift from these prior distributions. Our unsupervised policy adaptation objective matches target domain latent feature distributions with training-time distributions. This unsupervised learning goal, termed \textit{latent alignment}, requires no paired source-target image data and applies to any agent without specific training requirements. To differentiate from prior works that embed invariances into policies during training, we designate our method \textbf{\underline I}nvariance through \textbf{\underline L}atent \textbf{\underline A}lignment (\textbf{ILA}).

text: Obtaining ground-truth labels for healthcare datasets presents significant challenges in terms of both cost and feasibility. Missing labels frequently arise from limited access to qualified annotators (such as physicians) and from patients' failure to report their symptoms. Consequently, healthcare datasets often suffer from partial or complete absence of labels, with larger prospective investigations typically exhibiting proportionally lower labeling rates. While this tension between study scale and labeling accuracy is especially pronounced in healthcare contexts, it represents a widespread challenge across real-world research domains. Our focus centers on extracting insights from person-generated activity time-series data characterized by severely imbalanced or absent labels. Given that supervised learning fundamentally requires ground-truth labels, alternative methodologies must be explored to harness the substantial information embedded within unlabeled data. Transfer learning presents one viable approach, involving initial model training on a distinct yet closely related population before adaptation to the target task. Upon deeper examination, however, practical implementation proves challenging. Study design fundamentally influences the signal pathways linking observed data to target labels, making it unrealistic to assume availability of alternative datasets constructed under identical study protocols. Furthermore, when investigating rare diseases, low prevalence rates complicate the identification of sufficiently large, independent training datasets. Consequently, transfer learning alone fails to meet our comprehensive requirements. Self-supervised learning enables representation learning without requiring predefined labels. While the theoretical foundations underlying these approaches remain incompletely characterized, their empirical effectiveness has been extensively documented. Notable successes span natural language processing \cite{brown2020language} and related syntactic applications including programming \cite{chen2021evaluating}, as well as image classification tasks \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. The classification of these models remains contentious, with certain researchers \cite{bommasani2021foundation} categorizing pre-trained, self-supervised, meta-learning architectures as \emph{Foundation Models}. Central to self-supervised learning is the principle that objectives are formulated as functions of the data itself. Nevertheless, identifying optimal self-supervised objective tasks presents non-trivial challenges. In this work, we investigate and compare three distinct objective tasks, evaluating their effectiveness for influenza-like illness (ILI) prediction using laboratory-validated ground-truth data. Drawing inspiration from natural language processing, where next-word prediction facilitates the acquisition of rich representational knowledge \cite{brown2020language}, we develop end-to-end transformer architectures. These models initially undergo self-supervised training to predict subsequent-day activity patterns based on ten-day historical activity sequences across a large population. Subsequently, the models undergo fine-tuning for ILI prediction tasks and undergo evaluation using a smaller dataset containing laboratory-confirmed ILI annotations. Ultimate assessment through ILI prediction performance on held-out test data demonstrates that effectiveness varies significantly depending on the chosen self-supervision strategy.
