Classifiers face a critical security threat known as adversarial examples. When presented with a classifier $f$ and test input $\mathbf{x}$, an adversary can construct a nearly imperceptible perturbation $\delta$ that causes $f(x)
eq f(x+\delta)$. We term $\delta$ an \emph{adversarial perturbation} and $x+\delta$ an \emph{adversarial example}. Over recent years, numerous \emph{empirical} defenses~\citep{goodfellow2014explaining,na2017cascade,metzen2017detecting,svoboda2018peernets,buckman2018thermometer,ma2018characterizing,guo2018countering,dhillon2018stochastic,xie2018mitigating,song2018pixeldefend} have emerged to counter adversarial examples. Yet adaptive adversaries have consistently defeated these empirical approaches~\citep{carlini2017adversarial,athalye2018obfuscated,uesato2018adversarial,athalye2018robustness}. Breaking free from this adversarial arms race has motivated the development of \emph{certified} defenses~\citep{scheibler2015towards,carlini2017provably,ehlers2017formal,katz2017reluplex,cheng2017maximum,lomuscio2017approach,fischetti2018deep,bunel2018unified,wong2017provable,wong2018scaling,raghunathan2018certified,raghunathan2018semidefinite,dvijotham2018training,dvijotham2018dual,gehr2018ai2,mirman2018differentiable,singh2018fast,weng2018towards,zhang2018efficient,gowal2018effectiveness,wang2018formal,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,salman2019provably,wang2020certifying,jia2020certified,zhai2020macer}. A classifier $f$ achieves certifiable robustness for input $\mathbf{x}$ when it demonstrably maintains consistent top-1 predictions (i.e.,$f(x)=f(x+\delta)$) under bounded adversarial perturbations $\delta$, such as when $\delta$'s $\ell_p$-norm falls below a specified threshold. This threshold defines the \emph{certified radius}. Our investigation centers on $\ell_0$-norm adversarial perturbations, which modify arbitrary input features and enable practical physical-world attacks. Current certified defenses predominantly address top-1 predictions, yet top-$k$ predictions—returning the $k$ most probable labels—prove more practically relevant across many domains. Cloud-based classification services (\emph{machine learning as a service})~\citep{Google_Cloud_Vision,microsoft_demo,amazon_demo,clarifai_demo} typically provide customers with top-$k$ labels to support informed decision-making. Similarly, recommender systems and search engines present users with top-$k$ items or webpages. Despite this practical significance, certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions remains largely uncharted territory. A notable exception is recent work by~\cite{jia2020certified}, which established tight $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. While their $\ell_2$-norm guarantees can be converted to $\ell_0$-norm bounds using norm inequalities, this transformation yields suboptimal $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness. \myparatight{Our work} We develop $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantees for top-$k$ predictions. Our methodology builds upon \emph{randomized smoothing}~\citep{cao2017mitigating,liu2018towards,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,jia2020certified,levine2019robustness}, which constructs certifiably robust classifiers from arbitrary base classifiers through input randomization. We choose randomized smoothing for its universal applicability to {any} classifier and scalability to large neural networks. Specifically, we employ \emph{randomized ablation}~\citep{levine2019robustness}, which delivers state-of-the-art $\ell_{0}$-norm certified robustness for top-1 predictions. Randomized ablation differs fundamentally from other randomized smoothing approaches~\citep{cao2017mitigating,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified} that inject \emph{additive} noise (Gaussian, Laplacian, or discrete) into inputs. Instead, randomized ablation randomizes inputs through feature subsampling. Given any classifier (the \emph{base classifier}) and test input $\mathbf{x}$, randomized ablation generates an \emph{ablated input} by randomly retaining selected features from $\mathbf{x}$ while replacing remaining features with special values—such as feature medians, means, or designated symbols. For image inputs, features correspond to pixels. The ablated input then passes through the base classifier. Since ablation introduces randomness, classifier outputs become probabilistic. We denote $p_j$ as the probability that the base classifier assigns label $j$ to a random ablated input. The original randomized ablation constructs a \emph{smoothed classifier} that outputs the label with maximum probability $p_j$ for test input $\mathbf{x}$. Our extension modifies the smoothed classifier to return the $k$ labels with highest probabilities for $\mathbf{x}$. Our primary theoretical contribution establishes nearly tight $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantees for top-$k$ predictions using randomized ablation-based smoothed classifiers. We first derive $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness bounds for top-$k$ predictions from our smoothed classifier. Our analysis demonstrates that label $l$ provably appears among the top-$k$ predictions for test input $\mathbf{x}$ when attackers perturb at most $r_{l}$ features, where $r_{l}$ represents the $\ell_0$-norm {certified radius}. Furthermore, we establish that our certified radius achieves \emph{tightness} for $k=1$ and \emph{near-tightness} for $k>1$. Without base classifier assumptions, no method can achieve certified radius exceeding $r_{l}+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$. Consequently, when attackers manipulate at least $r_l+1+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$ input features, some base classifier exists where the smoothed classifier's top-$k$ predictions exclude $l$ or produce ties. Our approach presents several key technical distinctions from~\citet{levine2019robustness}. First, we establish $\ell_0$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions under randomized ablation, while \citet{levine2019robustness} addressed only top-1 predictions. Second, our certified radius equals or exceeds that of \citet{levine2019robustness} for top-1 cases, as we exploit discrete label probability properties in our derivation. Third, we prove (near-)tightness of our certified radius, which \citet{levine2019robustness} did not establish. Our work also differs substantially from~\citet{jia2020certified}, who derived tight $\ell_2$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions using Gaussian additive noise randomized smoothing. Their additive Gaussian noise creates continuous randomized input spaces, whereas our feature subsampling produces discrete ablated input spaces. text: Algorithms that solve computational problems involving symmetries of combinatorial objects commonly employ the individualization-refinement (IR) framework, a general backtracking technique~\cite{McKay201494}. This framework encompasses automorphism group computation algorithms, isomorphism solvers, canonical labeling tools for normal form computation, and has recently extended to machine learning applications in convolutional neural networks~\cite{DBLP:conf/ijcai/AbboudCGL21,DBLP:conf/aaai/0001RFHLRG19}. Every competitive graph isomorphism/automorphism solver operates within this framework, including \textsc{nauty}/\textsc{Traces}~\cite{nautyTracesweb, McKay201494}, \textsc{bliss}~\cite{bliss:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/JunttilaK07}, \textsc{saucy}~\cite{saucy:webpage, Darga:2004:ESS:996566.996712}, \textsc{conauto}~\cite{conauto:webpage, DBLP:conf/wea/Lopez-PresaCA13}, and \textsc{dejavu}~\cite{dejavu:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}. The framework operates by alternating between color-refinement techniques (including the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm) and backtracking steps that artificially individualize indistinguishable vertices. This process generates recursive branching, ultimately producing a tree of recursive function calls known as the IR-tree. Through sophisticated invariants and heuristics, these tools successfully prune substantial portions of the IR-tree. Given that non-recursive work requires only quasi-linear time, the number of traversed IR-tree nodes has long been recognized as the primary determinant of running time across all tools (see \cite[Theorem 9]{thesis} and \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-0804-4881}). The running times of different tools indeed closely mirror this relationship~\cite{McKay201494,DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}. Consequently, variations in traversal strategies among tools result in different numbers of traversed nodes, which directly translates to different running times. Nevertheless, rigorous bounds demonstrating asymptotic advantages of randomized over deterministic traversals have only recently emerged~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}. These results define a specific search problem in trees with symmetries that precisely captures the operational parameters of IR-algorithms. Although these findings are quite general within their abstract model, the bounds established in~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} address the search problem for arbitrary trees with symmetries, regardless of whether they originate from actual IR-computations. While the extensive benchmark library of \textsc{Traces}{}~\cite{nautyTracesweb,McKay201494} demonstrates that IR-trees exhibit tremendous diversity in form and structure, no comprehensive results have yet analyzed which trees can actually arise as IR-trees. \xparagraph{Contribution.} This paper investigates which trees qualify as IR-trees. Since IR-trees emerge from branching processes, they are inherently rooted with all inner vertices having at least 2 children—such trees are termed irreducible (or series reduced). Despite the remarkable variety of IR-trees found in benchmark libraries, not every irreducible tree constitutes an IR-tree. Nevertheless, we provide a complete, constructive characterization of IR-trees. \begin{theorem} An irreducible tree is an IR-tree if and only if there is no node that has exactly two children of which exactly one is a leaf. \end{theorem} Our proof strategy first establishes and justifies necessary conditions for IR-trees, then demonstrates that these conditions are indeed sufficient by constructing graphs whose IR-algorithm execution yields the desired tree. The proof is constructive, yielding an algorithm with the following property: given any tree~$T$ satisfying the necessary conditions, the algorithm constructs a graph whose IR-tree is~$T$. As detailed in our IR-tree definition in Section~\ref{sec:ir}, these trees naturally associate with vertex colorings. Such colorings constitute crucial components related to the graph's automorphism group structure. Our characterization completely describes how color classes may be distributed within any given tree. While several simple restrictions apply (particularly for vertices with exactly two children), all other colorings can be realized, and any number of symmetries can be ensured (see Section~\ref{sec:graph:constr}). Our characterization establishes a fundamental bridge, enabling the transfer of abstract tree traversal strategy analysis from \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} to backtracking trees of IR-algorithms on concrete instances. We can therefore conclude that the abstract trees used for probabilistic algorithm lower bounds in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} indeed appear as IR-trees. Interestingly, however, the abstract trees used for deterministic algorithm lower bounds (Theorem~13, \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}) are not IR-trees. These trees contain nodes with two children where exactly one child is a leaf and the other is not, violating the necessary conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}. Fortunately, our results immediately suggest a simple modification: replacing the respective leaves with inner nodes having two attached leaves transforms these trees into actual IR-trees, according to our characterization. We therefore establish that the lower bounds of \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} remain valid within the IR-paradigm. \xparagraph{Cell Selectors and Invariants.} The IR-paradigm formally permits various design choices in its components. For most components, competitive practical solvers make remarkably similar choices: refinement is invariably \emph{color refinement}, and solvers typically select the \emph{quotient graph} as their pruning invariant. Actual implementations differ from color refinement and quotient graphs primarily in minor details aimed at achieving practical speed-ups, resulting only in slightly weaker refinement and invariants in specific cases. This paper therefore adopts these common design choices. Numerous other design choices, such as IR-tree traversal methods, do not affect the characterization of IR-trees themselves. However, one integral design choice where competitive IR-solvers genuinely vary in ways that affect which trees are IR-trees concerns the so-called \emph{cell selectors}. We emphasize that Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient} only establishes that for trees satisfying the necessary conditions, some cell selector exists for which the graph is an IR-tree. We can also address specific cell selectors. When considering characterization for a \emph{given} cell selector, two possibilities emerge: either fewer trees qualify as IR-trees, or the same characterization applies. Our results enable us to argue that for certain practical cell selectors, our necessary conditions are sufficient, while for others they are not (see Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} for discussion). \xparagraph{Techniques.} Graph properties such as symmetries directly connect to properties of their IR-trees. When constructing a graph intended to produce a particular IR-tree, two major challenges emerge: \begin{enumerate} \item Color refinement effects on the graph must remain controllable. \item The IR-tree shape may require simultaneous symmetry representation across distinct graph regions. \end{enumerate} We address these challenges through various purpose-built gadget constructions. We introduce \emph{concealed edges}, enabling precise control over when the IR-process can observe specific edge sets and thus when color refinement takes effect (addressing issue (1)). By combining concealed edges with gadgets that enforce particular regular abelian automorphism groups, we can synchronize symmetries across multiple tree branches (addressing issue (2)). text: Deep Learning methodologies have delivered remarkable solutions to general classification challenges, achieving impressive performance when abundant annotated training data is available. However, real-world applications frequently encounter scenarios where specific datasets are scarce, prohibitively expensive to annotate, exhibit non-stationary characteristics, or arrive as continuous streams. To address these fundamental challenges, both novel and established learning paradigms have been integrated into Deep Learning frameworks \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Consequently, research areas including transfer learning \cite{wang2018deep}, reinforcement learning \cite{Ren2018DeepRL}, and incremental learning \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}—encompassing both supervised and unsupervised variants—have experienced renewed interest and significant advancement. The concept of incremental learning encompasses a classifier's capacity to evolve through continuous integration of information from novel instances and/or emerging classes, while circumventing the computational burden of complete retraining \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Contemporary research in incremental and online machine learning has garnered substantial attention, particularly within the framework of real-time data stream processing \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online}. Notably, rehearsal-free continual learning methodologies have demonstrated remarkable capability in expanding classifier class-sets using exclusively new class labels, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting phenomena \cite{tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. This approach proves particularly valuable when computational constraints prohibit full retraining or when confidentiality requirements prevent access to historical samples during class-set expansion procedures. Conversely, limited advancement has been achieved in continual learning for non-stationary class sets, especially when addressing tasks involving unsupervised streaming data. Video-to-video face recognition (V2V-FR) in surveillance applications exemplifies a paradigmatic case requiring incremental learning with unsupervised, non-stationary, and streaming data characteristics \cite{huang2015cox}. Video frames typically exhibit extensive variability in individual pose, camera positioning, resolution, and illumination conditions, often surpassing the diversity present in datasets employed for deep network training (which predominantly utilize web-extracted images) \cite{guo2016mscleb1m}. Transfer learning applications to specific V2V-FR task domains have proven challenging even for sophisticated Deep Learning encoders \cite{gunther2016face,lopezlopez2019dataset}, as image quality factors remain performance-critical determinants \cite{guo2019survey}. Furthermore, continuous data streaming introduces additional complexity: individual appearance may vary across different camera systems, which themselves may operate under temporally changing conditions \cite{ditzler2015learning,disabato2019learning}. Although theoretical solutions exist through extensive labeling, the practical task of addressing every conceivable variation within training datasets remains infeasible \cite{he2020incremental}. Therefore, more efficient and scalable methodologies are essential \cite{maltoni2019continous,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. In this context, the actual operational data extracted \textbf{incrementally} during system deployment—crucially \textbf{without labels}—authentically represents the application context and temporal variations. Real-world V2V-FR applications possess an additional characteristic: their inherently open-set nature \cite{scheirer2013toward,gunther2017towards}. Consider a practical airport surveillance scenario designed to track specific \emph{individuals of interest (IoI)} who have not undergone collaborative system enrollment, such as those displaying suspicious behaviors, while distinguishing them from numerous \emph{unknown} non-target identities that must be correctly classified as \emph{unknown} non-target entities. This paper introduces a novel incremental learning framework: the Open-Set Dynamic Ensembles of SVM \ref{fig:illustrate}. Built upon deep feature encoders, our system leverages operational data to enhance target identity recognition through unsupervised mechanisms. Additionally, responding to real-world requirements, the system operates within a completely open-set configuration. Grounded in the capabilities of Deep feature encoders trained for general face recognition tasks, an incremental learning module processes streaming data to simultaneously generate predictions and update classifiers while addressing catastrophic forgetting challenges. The incremental component employs dynamic SVM classifier ensembles that, beginning from a single SVM constructed using minimal labeled video frames extracted directly from footage, can acquire and adapt to supplementary information through ensemble classifier addition/removal operations. The approach follows self-training methodology \cite{yarowsky1995unsupervised}, wherein predictions simultaneously serve as pseudo-labels for classifier updating and improvement. Leveraging the modular ensemble architecture, adaptations involve strategic classifier addition or removal. This paper's contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item An unsupervised incremental learning approach engineered for online streaming data operation, where predictions simultaneously function as pseudo-labels during system operation. \item A comprehensive strategy addressing both catastrophic forgetting issues and erroneous pseudo-label effects. \item An instance-incremental learning methodology for open-set scenarios, with extensibility potential for class-incremental problems. \item A face-based person re-identification method that operates independently of face image reservoirs. \end{itemize} The manuscript organization proceeds as follows: Section~\ref{sec:rel_work} presents comprehensive literature analysis relevant to the addressed problem. Subsequently, Section~\ref{sec:desvm} details our proposed methodology, followed by experimental investigations examining system behavior in Sections~\ref{sec:experiments} and~\ref{sec:results}. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} provides concluding reflections and insights derived from this research.

text: Across numerous countries, cancer has emerged as the primary mortality cause and the most formidable barrier to extending life expectancy~\cite{world2020report}. Representing over 11~\% of all newly diagnosed cases, lung cancer stands as the second most prevalent malignancy globally while simultaneously claiming the highest cancer-related death toll at 18~\% of total cancer fatalities~\cite{Sung2021}. Contemporary lung cancer management encompasses surgical resection, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy approaches. The efficacy of these interventions, alongside successful diagnostic procedures involving bronchoscopy or computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy, fundamentally relies upon precise tumor localization and, frequently, accurate delineation (segmentation) from healthy tissue within preoperative imaging—predominantly CT scans. The manual delineation of lesions and tumors from preoperative CT represents an arduous, time-consuming undertaking for oncologists, radiologists, and pulmonologists. Such labor-intensive processes may precipitate treatment delays and compromise survival outcomes, particularly within resource-constrained clinical environments. Furthermore, manual localization and segmentation quality depends heavily upon accumulated knowledge and clinical proficiency. Despite established guidelines and standardized protocols, tumor segmentation remains susceptible to substantial inter- and intraobserver variation. Conversely, automated segmentation methodologies offer the promise of efficient, reproducible, and enhanced accuracy. These approaches can simultaneously reduce image interpretation time while enabling specialists to concentrate their expertise on optimizing therapeutic planning and treatment strategies. Traditional approaches including thresholding~\cite{UZELALTINBULAT2017}, region growing~\cite{Adams1994,Dehmeshki2008}, and graph cuts~\cite{GU2013692} have historically been employed for lung tumor segmentation in CT imaging. While these algorithms function adequately as semi-automated tools, they prove inadequate for lung tumor localization tasks. Contemporary deep learning breakthroughs have enabled the automation of procedures previously reserved for specialized practitioners~\cite{ramanto2019,kim2019}. Hardware developments have facilitated increasingly sophisticated and expansive models, though substantial improvements primarily stem from access to extensive annotated datasets. Following the U-Net~\cite{ronneberger2015} architecture's introduction, deep learning methodologies have achieved dominance within medical image segmentation~\cite{Du2020}. Nevertheless, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) demand considerable memory resources, particularly for volumetric 3D data. Consequently, networks commonly utilize 2D or 2.5D input configurations~\cite{carvalho}, processing individual slices, slice clusters, or 3D patches through sliding window techniques across CT volumes. This volumetric patching approach sacrifices perceptual scope, prompting the development of more efficient multi-scale 3D CNN architectures that accommodate larger input volumes~\cite{Jiang2018}. Alternative strategies employ multi-step segmentation through either multiple algorithms or cascaded CNN configurations~\cite{Hossain2019,isensee,carvalho,gan2021}. Addressing training data scarcity, unsupervised approaches such as supervoxel methods have been introduced~\cite{Hansen2021}. To enhance convergence speed and accuracy, multi-modal techniques incorporating magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography (PET) alongside CT have been developed~\cite{fu2021,Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2}. Additionally, neural architectures capable of leveraging diverse annotation formats have been proposed~\cite{Wang2019,Mlynarski2019}. The teacher-student framework represents a contemporary strategy for addressing limited training data availability, drawing inspiration from knowledge distillation principles~\cite{phuong19,furlanello18,hinton2015}. Within this paradigm, the teacher generates pseudo-annotations from suboptimal labels to expand the student's training dataset. This teacher-student methodology applies universally across network architectures without constraining hyperparameters or external configurations. Implementation variations range from unlabeled data utilization~\cite{caron2021,Xie2020,Li2020} and multi-modal exploitation~\cite{Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2,Li2020} to datasets incorporating heterogeneous annotation types~\cite{sun2020,Zhang2021}. Our methodology distinguishes itself from existing lung tumor segmentation approaches by exploiting annotations with varying supervision levels within the same modality—specifically CT imaging. Given that CT scanning imposes less patient burden compared to alternative modalities, efficient tumor segmentation from CT-exclusive examinations remains a priority objective. Our approach builds upon Sun \textit{et al.}'s~\cite{sun2020} promising results using teacher-student frameworks for liver and liver lesion segmentation with semantic and bounding box annotations. To our knowledge, we present the first implementation of a comparable teacher-student framework applied to CT images for lung tumor semantic segmentation. Our investigation demonstrates that despite limited semantic annotation datasets, students can attain state-of-the-art performance when provided with sufficiently large pseudo-annotated learning datasets.

text: While robot learning has achieved remarkable progress, the majority of algorithms assume robots operate in isolation. However, real-world scenarios inevitably involve interactions with humans and other learning agents. These interactions create substantial challenges for robot learning: other agents \textit{adapt} their behavior in response to the robot's actions, thereby continuously transforming the robot's learning environment. Consider an autonomous vehicle learning to modulate the velocity of surrounding human drivers to ensure safe deceleration when encountering traffic congestion or construction zones. During your initial encounter with this autonomous vehicle, you adopt a cautious approach: when it decelerates, you follow suit. However, after experiencing seemingly arbitrary slowdowns, your strategy evolves: in subsequent interactions with this autonomous vehicle, you bypass it without hesitation. The autonomous vehicle --- previously confident in its learned policy for influencing your driving behavior --- now faces confusion and failure due to your behavioral adaptation! For effective \textit{co-adaptation} with other agents, robots must predict how these agents' behaviors will evolve and understand how their own actions influence others' hidden intentions. Existing research addressing such interactions relies on limiting assumptions about other agents: modeling them as static entities~\cite{davison1998predicting,stone2000defining,mealing2015opponent,albrecht2015hba,grover2018learning}, assuming shared learning algorithms across agents~\cite{foerster2016learning,lowe2017multi,foerster2018counterfactual}, requiring direct access to other agents' underlying intentions and actions~\cite{albrecht2015hba,he2016opponent,hernandez2017efficiently, grover2018learning, foerster2018learning, everett2018learning}, or constraining the intention space through manually designed features~\cite{kelley2008understanding,bandyopadhyay2013intention,bai2015intention,sadigh2016information,basu2019active, losey2019robots}. In contrast, our work addresses general scenarios where the ego agent (e.g., a robot) engages in repeated interactions with non-stationary, independently-controlled, and partially-observable agents. Humans effortlessly navigate such situations daily (e.g., driving, pedestrian movement) without explicitly modeling every detailed aspect of others' policies \cite{rubinstein1998modeling}. Drawing inspiration from human behavior, we observe that: \begin{center} \vspace{-0.5em} \emph{While the ego agent can only observe another agent's low-level actions, maintaining a high-level policy representation --- similar to human-human interactions --- often proves sufficient. We term this representation the \emph{latent strategy} and acknowledge that these latent strategies evolve temporally.} \vspace{-0.5em} \end{center} By learning other agents' strategies, robots can \textit{anticipate} their responses during ongoing interactions. Additionally, modeling temporal changes in latent strategies --- the \textit{latent dynamics} --- empowers robots to predict how their own actions will \textit{shape} other agents' future intentions (see Fig.~\ref{fig:front}). Through latent representations of other agents' policies, we advance learning in non-stationary multi-agent interactions with the following contributions: \textbf{Learning Latent Representations.} We present an RL-based framework for multi-agent interaction that simultaneously learns latent strategies and corresponding response policies. Our framework implicitly captures how other agents' strategies evolve in reaction to the ego agent's behavior. \textbf{Influencing Other Agents.} Ego agents using our proposed method are incentivized to deliberately modify their policies to shape other agents' latent strategies, especially when certain strategies facilitate superior co-adaptation compared to alternatives. \textbf{Testing in Multi-Agent Settings.} We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods across four simulated environments and one real robot experiment featuring two $7$-DoF robot arms engaged in air hockey. Our approach demonstrates superior performance while successfully learning to influence other agents.

text: Discriminating between closely related languages represents one of the primary challenges facing contemporary automatic language identification systems, constituting a significant bottleneck in state-of-the-art approaches~\cite{DSL2014}. The development of language technology for Scandinavian languages remains in its early stages (e.g.~\newcite{kirkedal2019lacunae}). A fundamental obstacle involves obtaining sufficient textual data for training large-scale language models. While high-quality language identification proves essential for effective data collection, existing leading models frequently struggle to distinguish between similar Nordic languages. We present a machine learning methodology for automatic language identification across six closely-related Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian (Nynorsk), Norwegian (Bokmål), Faroese and Icelandic. Our investigation examines various feature extraction techniques applied to a corpus comprising Wikipedia summaries in the respective languages, while systematically evaluating the effectiveness of multiple machine learning architectures. Specifically, we conduct comparative performance analysis between traditional machine learning approaches—including Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support vector machine, and K nearest Neighbors—and modern neural network methodologies such as Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Following model evaluation on the Wikipedia dataset, we proceed to assess the top-performing models using data from an alternative domain, thereby examining their generalization capabilities when classifying sentences beyond their training distribution.

text: Robots frequently operate in shared workspaces alongside humans or other robotic systems across diverse settings—warehouses, manufacturing facilities, and domestic environments. These environments typically feature predominantly static obstacle configurations, though localized regions may experience dynamic occupancy changes throughout operation. We characterize such settings as \emph{semi-structured} environments. Furthermore, robots in these applications commonly execute repetitive tasks, necessitating motion planning capabilities that are both rapid and dependable. The scenario depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:cover} illustrates this challenge: the robot must retrieve the bowl while navigating around pitchers, table surfaces, and walls. The majority of environmental features (table structure, walls, overhead free space, etc.) remain predictable and known, while the repetitive task nature enables reuse of information from prior planning queries to accelerate subsequent planning operations. Standard algorithms like RRTs~\cite{lavalle1998rapidly,kuffner2000rrt} fail to leverage the fundamental distinction between static and movable obstacles, nor do they capitalize on the repetitive characteristics of planning problems for enhanced speed. Roadmap-based approaches such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRMs)~\cite{kavraki1996probabilistic} either restrict themselves to completely static environments or impose substantial computational overhead through repair operations needed to accommodate movable obstacles. Various PRM enhancements have reduced costly collision checking~\cite{kavraki2000path}, addressed dynamic environments~\cite{leven2002framework,yang2017hdrm}, and captured repetitive motion patterns~\cite{lehner2018repetition}, yet their performance remains highly variable across different planning queries. Rather than preprocessing collision information offline, alternative planners leverage prior experiences to accelerate search operations~\cite{Phillips-RSS-12,berenson2012robot,coleman2015experience}. Nevertheless, these methods experience performance degradation when environmental changes invalidate historical information. Consequently, none of these approaches can deliver fixed-time planning guarantees. Recent work introduced provably fixed-time planners~\cite{islam2019provable,islam2020provably} specifically designed for repetitive task applications. Given an initial state, target region, and known environmental model, these methods precompute a compressed path set that enables online planning to any goal within the target region in constant or bounded time. Previous applications include mail-sorting systems~\cite{islam2019provable} and conveyor belt object grasping~\cite{islam2020provably}. While our APP approach draws from these foundations, we specifically target online obstacle avoidance by explicitly incorporating movable obstacles during preprocessing through alternative paths planning methodology. Our work extends these methodologies to accommodate movable obstacles while preserving provably fixed-time planning guarantees through the \emph{Alternative Paths Planner (APP)}. The core concept involves generating multiple alternative paths for each planning problem such that at least one path remains traversable regardless of movable obstacle configurations. We achieve this by enforcing path \emph{disjointness}: paths maintain sufficient separation to prevent any single obstacle configuration from simultaneously intersecting multiple paths. Managing $n$ movable obstacles requires generating at most $n+1$ fully disjoint paths. When the required number of disjoint paths cannot be identified for a given problem, we supplement with additional partially overlapping paths (violating the disjointness criterion) to maintain the same guarantee. APP addresses performance-critical real-world applications including mail-sorting, conveyor-belt picking, and shelving operations. In multi-obstacle scenarios, we demonstrate microsecond-scale path-lookup performance with 100\% success rates. Our evaluation encompasses experimental results across three domains, comparisons with state-of-the-art existing methods, and validation through real-world case studies.

In the case of a multi-obstacle environment, we show microsecond scale path-finding with a success rate of 100 per cent. If the required number of disjoint paths cannot be identified for a particular problem, we complement the search with additional paths, which partially overlap and violate the disjointness criterion, in order to maintain the same guarantee. The evaluation of our approach is based on experimental results from three application domains, comparisons with existing methods and application of the results to real-world case studies.

text: The world's data repositories are predominantly housed in relational databases, which users typically query through structured languages such as SQL. Natural language interfaces to databases (NLIDB) hold tremendous potential for democratizing data access, enabling information retrieval without requiring programming knowledge from end users. Large-scale dataset releases \cite{wikisql,DBLP:conf/acl/RadevKZZFRS18,spider} have catalyzed widespread research interest in this domain over recent years. Most existing research concentrates on converting well-formed, grammatically complete sentences into database queries. Nevertheless, an internal user survey conducted on a major customer relationship management (CRM) platform's search service\footnote{\url{https://www.salesforce.com/}} uncovered that users predominantly communicate through colloquial expressions ranging from bare keywords (``player 42'') and terse phrases (``show player 42'') to full sentences (``Who is the player who wears Jersey 42?''). Beyond stylistic variations, users frequently omit content words for brevity, potentially introducing ambiguity that renders questions unsolvable even for models trained on natural language sentence (NLS) formats. Consider Figure \ref{fig:example}: without the term ``Jersey'', determining whether the \texttt{Id} or \texttt{Jersey} column should equal 42 becomes impossible. We demonstrate that Text2SQL systems trained exclusively on complete sentences fail to generalize to noisy keyword-based or short phrasal queries. To address this limitation, we develop data augmentation strategies that mirror observed user search behaviors and linguistic patterns. \hide{ \todo{We have enough space, can you show 2-3 examples in this figure? No need to use a boxed layout, you can show a table. Also please use .pdf to save the figure, which has higher resolution.} } One approach to resolving the resulting ambiguity involves leveraging table content by enabling models to scan tables for question terms and exploit this information for disambiguation (if token ``42'' appears exclusively in the \texttt{Jersey} column, then \texttt{Jersey} must equal 42). While effective, this strategy becomes computationally prohibitive for large tables, requiring exhaustive content searches for each query and consuming substantial inference time and memory. Our hypothesis posits that models typically require only representative samples from table content rather than exact matching rows to disambiguate columns effectively. For instance, if the \texttt{Id} column contains alphanumeric identifiers, \texttt{Player} and \texttt{Nationality} contain text strings, and \texttt{Jersey} contains two-digit integers, then \texttt{Jersey} must correspond to the column equaling 42. Sampling eliminates the necessity for comprehensive table scans per question. Column samples can be pre-computed offline and maintained across queries or periodically updated to capture table distribution shifts or evolving user query patterns, enabling adaptation and personalization without model retraining. Our contributions encompass the following: \begin{enumerate} \itemsep0em \item We augment the well-formed WikiSQL dataset with synthetic search-style questions to adapt to short, colloquial input. \item We propose new models which incorporate table content in a BERT encoder via two sampling strategies to handle ambiguous questions. \item We perform an in-depth qualitative and quantitative (accuracy, inference time, memory) analysis to show the efficacy of each content sampling strategy. \item We curate a dataset of 400 questions to benchmark performance of Text-to-SQL models in this setting. \end{enumerate} \hide{ \begin{enumerate} \item augmenting well-formed text with synthetic data to ensure robustness over NLS style questions \item incorporating table content to a BERT model via two sampling strategies to handle ambiguous questions \item an in-depth qualitative and quantitative (accuracy, inference time, memory) analysis showcasing the efficacy of both content sampling strategies \item a curated dataset to benchmark performance on short, ambiguous questions. \end{enumerate} } Beyond adapting to NLS-style queries, \textsc{ColloQL}\xspace establishes state-of-the-art performance on the original WikiSQL~\cite{wikisql} dataset, surpassing all baselines that exclude execution-guided decoding. While we build upon SQLova \cite{sqlova}, our methodologies generalize to alternative approaches\footnote{Our code and annotated data can be found at \\ \url{https://github.com/karthikradhakrishnan96/ColloQL}.}.

A significant gap exists between how neural retrieval models process complete texts and the relevance labels used for training, evaluation, and analysis. These labels—exemplified by the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 (TREC-DL) \cite{trec2019overview}—treat entire documents containing thousands of tokens as unified entities. While this coarse granularity suffices for traditional models that reduce documents to bag-of-words representations, it proves inadequate for contemporary neural ranking architectures. These modern systems operate through hierarchical mechanisms, constructing document-level scores from fine-grained word interactions \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir,zheng2019rltm,yilmaz2019}. Consequently, neural retrieval models must simultaneously perform document-level relevance assessment and word-level information extraction or question answering. They face the dual challenge of identifying pertinent information spans while generating scoring decisions suitable for ranking multiple candidate documents. A critical impediment to advancing these models lies in the scarcity of datasets that adequately address both subtasks. Existing collections either emphasize retrieval outcomes with comprehensive judgments across ranked lists \cite{trec2019overview,hashemi2020antique}, or focus on question-answer selection within individual texts that, when adapted for retrieval purposes, yield incomplete relevance assessments \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}. We introduce FiRA: a novel dataset providing 	extbf{Fi}ne-grained 	extbf{R}elevance 	extbf{A}nnotations through word-level relevance selections and passage-level graded relevance labels across all relevant documents from the TREC 2019 Deep Learning Document collection. Our methodology involves segmenting documents into discrete snippets and presenting query-snippet pairs to human annotators. Figure ef{fig:fira-screenshot} illustrates an annotated document snippet example. Quality assurance mechanisms include mandatory 3-way majority voting for each candidate and continuous monitoring of annotation quality metrics, including time expenditure per annotation. By mandating relevant text span selection, we minimize false-positive retrieval relevance assignments. Our annotation campaign engaged 87 computer science students through a purpose-built annotation platform that streamlines the workflow between relevance labeling and text span identification. FiRA encompasses 
umprint{24199} query-document-snippet pairs covering all 
umprint{1990} relevant documents across 
umprint{43} queries from TREC-DL. We selected the TREC-DL document ranking test collection as our foundation because: 1) it constrains our annotation scope, given the time-intensive nature of fine-grained annotations, and 2) it enables direct comparison between our non-expert annotators and TREC's expert assessors. FiRA maintains model-agnostic design while incorporating the complete TREC annotation pool. FiRA enables diverse research applications:  egin{itemize} \item 	extbf{Training:} FiRA supports both standalone and multi-task retrieval-QA fine-tuning approaches. The comprehensive coverage across query-document pairs facilitates granular optimization through word-level loss functions. \item 	extbf{Evaluation:} FiRA enhances TREC-DL evaluation through refined relevance labels and answer passage assessment capabilities within complete documents. When combined with TREC-DL's labeled non-relevant documents, FiRA enables comprehensive ranking and answer selection evaluation. \item 	extbf{Analysis:} Neural document ranking models producing document-level relevance scores can undergo detailed analysis. Their intermediate outputs and attention mechanisms become quantitatively assessable through FiRA. \end{itemize} Human subjectivity in relevance assessment represents a persistent challenge in information retrieval research \cite{borlund2003concept}. Understanding the noise and uncertainty inherent in human relevance judgments becomes crucial when utilizing human-annotated datasets. We address this through systematic 3-way majority voting throughout data collection. Additionally, FiRA includes quantitative analysis addressing:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ1}] What degree of subjectivity characterizes our fine-grained relevance annotations? \end{itemize} We selected 10 pairs for annotation by all participants, enabling subjectivity analysis through dense distributions that minimize outlier effects. Our findings reveal strong annotator agreement on binary relevance scales, while subjectivity increases for 4-level graded relevance and text selections. Leveraging our dataset, we conduct comprehensive analysis of positional bias in both document-level relevance and snippet-internal patterns. By presenting snippets in randomized order to eliminate attention bias toward document beginnings, we investigate:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ2}] Does position-based relevance bias exist within long documents? \end{itemize} FiRA annotations reveal heightened probability of relevant answers appearing at document beginnings, though substantial numbers of relevant snippets occur throughout later document sections. We examined annotator behavior regarding relevant word selection within individual snippets. Previous MSMARCO-QA \cite{msmarco16} analysis demonstrated strong bias toward snippet beginnings. Using FiRA annotations, we address:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ3}] Do annotators exhibit bias toward snippet beginnings? \end{itemize} We established control and treatment groups, rotating first and second text halves in the treatment condition. Neither group demonstrated positional bias toward beginnings. The rotation group actually emphasized contextual importance around relevant span selections, as fragmented sentences received fewer selections. Demonstrating FiRA's utility, we analyze the state-of-the-art TKL neural document re-ranking model \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir} using fine-grained judgments and TKL's interpretability features. TKL provides information about three 30-word document regions used for score computation.  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ4}] How many FiRA-identified relevant spans does TKL utilize for document scoring? \end{itemize} Analysis reveals that TKL models trained on TREC-DL data \cite{trec2019overview} demonstrate disproportionate focus on document beginnings as ranking signals. FiRA-derived insights can inform next-generation neural document ranking model development. The complete FiRA dataset, including raw annotations, documentation, and supporting scripts, is publicly available at: \ 	extit{\url{https://github.com/sebastian-hofstaetter/fira-trec-19-dataset}}

text: Across diverse domains—from video game mastery~\cite{dqn1, dqn2, starcraft2, a3c, a2c, ga3c, kf, pic, Jain19, JainECCV2020} to robotic manipulation~\cite{Levine15, Gu17, Luo19}—deep reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable achievements. Nevertheless, prohibitively long training durations remain a fundamental obstacle preventing deep RL from tackling increasingly sophisticated challenges. Addressing this computational bottleneck requires RL frameworks to exhibit two critical characteristics: (1) High throughput for rapid data acquisition rates, and (2) Superior sample efficiency enabling policy learning with minimal data requirements. The pursuit of these dual objectives has motivated the development of both synchronous and asynchronous parallel actor-learner architectures that substantially accelerate RL training processes~\cite{a3c, a2c, impala, ga3c, seed_rl, ddppo, rlpyt, iswitch}. Contemporary synchronous approaches, exemplified by synchronous advantage actor critic (A2C)~\cite{a3c, a2c} and its variants~\cite{ppo, trpo, acktr}, have gained widespread adoption due to their superior \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}. Yet synchronous frameworks inherently suffer from computational bottlenecks, as parameter updates cannot proceed until all actors complete their experience collection phases. This synchronization penalty becomes particularly severe when environment step durations exhibit substantial variability. Consequently, traditional synchronous approaches fail to scale effectively in environments characterized by highly variable step times—scenarios common in computationally demanding 3D rendering and physics simulation contexts. \input{flow_time_fig} Conversely, asynchronous methodologies such as asynchronous advantage actor-critic on a GPU (GA3C)~\cite{ga3c} and importance weighted actor-learner architectures (IMPALA)~\cite{impala} excel at achieving high throughput performance. These approaches, however, are plagued by the stale-policy problem~\cite{ga3c, impala}, wherein data collection and learning proceed independently. The resulting temporal gap between the behavior policy (used for data generation) and the target policy (employed for parameter updates) introduces gradient noise and diminishes data efficiency. This fundamental limitation forces asynchronous methods to sacrifice training stability in exchange for computational throughput. Our work demonstrates that this traditional trade-off is unnecessary by introducing High-Throughput Synchronous RL (HTS-RL), a novel technique that simultaneously achieves exceptional throughput and robust training stability. HTS-RL seamlessly integrates with established deep RL algorithms including A2C, proximal policy optimization (PPO)~\cite{ppo}, and actor-critic using Kronecker-factored trust region (ACKTR)~\cite{acktr}. The method proves especially advantageous for environments exhibiting significant step time variance: Through concurrent learning and data collection processes, {throughput increases dramatically.} Furthermore, actors engage with environment replicas asynchronously, substantially reducing idle periods. Most importantly, HTS-RL employs batched synchronization to maintain a constant lag of exactly one update between target and behavior policies. This controlled latency enables a 'one step delayed-gradient' update mechanism that preserves the convergence properties of non-delayed alternatives. Consequently, HTS-RL retains all benefits of synchronous RL—namely \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}—while delivering substantial speedups, particularly in variable step-time environments. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates HTS-RL's capacity to accelerate both A2C and PPO across Atari environments~\cite{gym, atari} and the Google Research Football environment (GFootball)~\cite{gfootball}. Adhering to rigorous evaluation protocols established by~\citet{Henderson17} and~\citet{Colas18}, we benchmark against the leading asynchronous method, IMPALA~\cite{impala}: our approach delivers {$3.7\times$} superior average episode rewards on Atari games and achieves {$43\%$} higher average scores in GFootball environments. Relative to conventional synchronous A2C and PPO implementations, our method realizes $2-6\times$ training acceleration. Implementation details are accessible at~\url{https://github.com/IouJenLiu/HTS-RL}.

text: Containing the Covid-19 pandemic necessitated mobilizing the most extensive global public health response in recent decades \cite{fisher2020global}. Consequently, numerous novel digital health strategies underwent rapid large-scale deployment \cite{fagherazzi2020digital}; although this swift implementation proved essential given the crisis's urgency, responsible examination of these strategies' implications remains crucial \cite{ienca2020responsible}. This paper examines the privacy ramifications of digital contact tracing smartphone applications \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}, alternatively termed exposure notification apps \cite{Apple_Google}. The Covid-19 virus demonstrates presymptomatic and asymptomatic transmission capabilities \cite{Asymptomatic_transmission_1}, creating substantial containment challenges since infected persons can transmit the virus while remaining symptom-free. Nevertheless, contact tracing can reduce the reproductive number by identifying recently diagnosed individuals' contacts and encouraging their isolation. Initial contact-tracing approaches relied on manual processes; healthcare workers gathered patient information regarding recent contacts and notified those contacts about their elevated risk status and recommended actions \cite{Manual_contact_tracing}. These methods face inherent constraints, notably patients' inability to identify stranger contacts and potential reluctance to disclose contact identities and interaction times to healthcare personnel \cite{Disclosure_discomfort}. At broader scales, escalating infection rates may overwhelm manual contact tracing capacity, rendering it impractical \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. Automated digital contact tracing and exposure notification applications emerge as solutions \cite{kleinman2020digital, Apple_Google, Pan_European, bay2020bluetrace}, offering end-user exposure notifications while minimizing manual intervention requirements. Contact tracing applications inherently monitor user colocation (though typically not direct location), generating substantial privacy concerns \cite{bengio2020need}. Consequently, privacy considerations dominate contact tracing protocol design \cite{levine1988contact, cho2020contact, raskar2020apps, rivest2020pact, trieu2020epione, troncoso2020decentralized}. Numerous efforts to characterize and ensure contact-tracing app privacy have concentrated on their specific operational mechanisms \cite{Mechanism_Privacy_1, MSB}; from a privacy-maximalist viewpoint, optimal algorithms leak exclusively information essential for exposure notification to end-users. The Google-Apple Exposure Notification framework \cite{Apple_Google}, currently the predominant protocol adopted by numerous national tracing applications, reveals only minimal information required to notify users of exposure, plus limited metadata regarding individual exposure events. While this approach provides minimal data to third parties (regrettably including public health officials), it delivers robust user privacy protection against all entities except their contacts. Security analyses for these mechanisms typically assume concealment of everything beyond query results (exposure determination), usually employing cryptographic techniques. However, query results themselves constitute information leakage; indeed, any digital contact tracing application lacking robust user identity validation---challenging when protecting user privacy---enables users or institutions (such as businesses) to infer exposure event details using only logarithmically many identities. Combining this information with contact records allows revelation of any contact's (or customer's) infection status through the exposure notification system \cite{Inherent_limitations}. This privacy vulnerability transcends algorithmic specifics, representing an 'inherent' digital contact tracing characteristic requiring only repeated valid system queries. Extensive scientific literature addresses controlling information leakage from database query outputs, enabling contact tracing conceptualization as distributed end-user database queries. Utilizing differential privacy and statistical database privacy research \cite{differential_privacy} may protect against query output information leakage. Unfortunately, utility-privacy trade-offs typically exist, with minimum noise thresholds required for specific privacy levels potentially reducing contact tracing accuracy. This paper reframes contact tracing as a specialized instance of two database query scenarios. Initially, contact-tracing applications must identify which user contacts have been exposed for notification purposes; this resembles querying binary databases containing users' contacts' COVID statuses. Alternatively, contact-tracing app users represent nodes in simple graphs, with edges denoting contact events involving diagnosed users. User alerting then resembles node-to-node recommendations, similar to social recommendation algorithms \cite{social_recommendation_survey}. We therefore adapt two mathematical privacy literature results to contact-tracing applications' inherent limitations. The first, from statistical databases \cite{dinur_nissim}, establishes error lower bounds for queries counting diagnosed contacts in user contact database subsets, below which adversaries can nearly reconstruct entire databases. The second, from graph-based social recommendation algorithms \cite{GRS}, presents explicit trade-offs between differential privacy and accuracy when alerting target users about high-risk contacts. We meticulously adapt these results' original settings to contact-tracing contexts, enabling deduction of their applicability conditions. These conditions allow restating results as inherent privacy-accuracy trade-offs for digital contact tracing. Finally, specific numerical examples provide discussion foundations for our findings.

text: Multi-class classification has found widespread application across diverse domains over recent decades, spanning image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar,deng2009imagenet, geusebroek2005amsterdam,Hsu02multisvm}, natural language processing~\cite{lang1995newsweeder,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2005-14165,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1801-06146}, and beyond. Central to multi-class classification success are loss functions~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/JanochaC17,kornblith2021why}, which fundamentally shape learning dynamics and performance outcomes. Within machine learning (ML), two classical loss functions stand prominent: cross-entropy (CE) loss and Crammer-Singer (CS) Loss (alternatively known as SVM loss). Prior to deep learning's emergence, CS loss received extensive investigation and deployment for linear or kernelized model learning~\cite{10.5555/944790.944813}. The deep learning revolution, however, witnessed CE loss achieving practical dominance over CS loss~\cite{he2016deep}. This shift stems from CE loss's consistency property for multi-class classification—ensuring Bayes optimal classifier convergence given infinite samples—whereas CS loss generally lacks consistency except when maximum conditional probability for any class label exceeds $0.5$~\cite{10.5555/1005332.1044701}. While this exceptional condition may apply to straightforward tasks like MNIST classification, it rarely holds for complex scenarios such as ImageNet classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2006-07159,tsipras2020imagenet}. Despite its theoretical advantages, CE loss exhibits vulnerability to label noise~\cite{ghosh2017robust,wang2019symmetric}. Consequently, substantial research efforts have focused on developing noise-tolerant CE loss variants. The symmetric property provides a sufficient condition for noise tolerance~\cite{ghosh2017robust}: loss summation across all possible class labels for any given data point remains constant. Leveraging this symmetric property, researchers have proposed numerous CE loss variants exhibiting noise-tolerance characteristics. However, symmetric losses alone typically yield suboptimal practical performance due to convergence limitations~\cite{zhang2018generalized,ma2020normalized}. Therefore, interpolated losses combining CE loss with symmetric losses generally achieve superior performance on real-world noisy datasets~\cite{wang2019symmetric,zhang2018generalized,englesson2021generalized,ma2020normalized}, exemplified by WebVision data containing 20\% noise~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-02862}. Label information uncertainty degree explains these empirical findings effectively. When label information exhibits high certainty (e.g., MNIST data), CS loss proves optimal~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/Tang13}; moderate uncertainty (e.g., ImageNet data) favors CE loss; high uncertainty (e.g., WebVision data) benefits from CE-symmetric loss interpolation. Although parameter tuning (such as weighting schemes for CE-symmetric loss combinations) enables dataset-level adaptivity, a fundamental question remains unresolved: "\textit{Can we construct a loss function achieving instance-level adaptivity—specifically, adaptation to individual instance label information uncertainty degrees?}" Addressing this challenge, we propose capturing label information uncertainty for each instance through distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework. Our approach assigns distributional weights to each class label per instance, defining loss under worst-case distributional weight scenarios with appropriate regularization—termed label distributionally robust (LDR) losses. The DRO framework for modeling label information uncertainty offers several advantages: (i) it unifies numerous existing loss functions, encompassing CE loss, CS loss, and variants like top-$k$ SVM loss; (ii) it introduces an intriguing loss family by selecting Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as distributional weight regularization, yielding LDR-KL loss for multi-class classification. LDR-KL loss connects closely to temperature-scaled CE loss prevalent in various applications~\cite{HinVin15Distilling,chen2020simple}, where temperature corresponds to distributional weight regularization parameters. Thus, our LDR-KL loss theoretical analysis potentially illuminates temperature-scaled CE loss applications across different contexts; (iii) LDR-KL loss interpolates between CS loss (one extreme), (margin-aware) CE loss (intermediate), and symmetric loss (opposite extreme) through regularization parameter variation, providing enhanced flexibility for adapting to label information noise levels. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize}[noitemsep,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] \item We demonstrate LDR-KL loss strong consistency through All-$k$ consistency—achieving top-$k$ consistency (corresponding to Bayes optimal top-$k$ error) for all $k\geq 1$—and establish sufficient conditions for general LDR loss families to achieve All-$k$ consistency. \item We prove that extreme LDR-KL loss cases satisfy symmetric properties, conferring label noise tolerance. Additionally, we establish that non-negative symmetric loss functions cannot simultaneously achieve top-$k$ consistency for $k=1$ and $k=2$. Consequently, existing top-$1$ consistent symmetric losses cannot achieve All-$k$ consistency. \item We introduce adaptive LDR-KL loss, enabling automatic learning of personalized temperature parameters for each instance based on individual noise characteristics. We develop efficient empirical risk minimization algorithms for adaptive LDR-KL loss without substantial computational overhead. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets under various noisy label conditions, demonstrating adaptive LDR-KL loss stable and competitive performance across all evaluated settings. \end{itemize}

text: Developing fully automated systems capable of synthesizing realistic 3D human bodies that approach and grasp target objects within three-dimensional environments holds significant value across diverse domains, spanning robotics and animation to computer vision applications. While substantial advances have emerged in realistic hand--object interaction synthesis, the majority of current approaches concentrate exclusively on hand pose generation, neglecting comprehensive whole-body movement patterns~\cite{GRAB:2020, GrapingField:3DV:2020, jiang2021graspTTA}. Conversely, existing whole-body motion synthesis methodologies~\cite{holden2016deep, martinez2017human, hernandez2019human, MOJO} predominantly disregard object presence within scene environments. The modeling and synthesis of realistic whole-body grasping motions present formidable challenges that persist as unresolved problems across multiple dimensions. Initially, whole-body grasping behaviors encompass both comprehensive full-body dynamics and intricate finger articulations~\cite{GRAB:2020}, where the substantial dimensional complexity of degrees of freedom significantly complicates motion synthesis processes. Additionally, complete whole-body grasping sequences demonstrate intricate and recurring body--scene alongside hand--object contact patterns that prove exceptionally difficult to synthesize with perceptual authenticity. % Consider, for instance, how hand surfaces must naturally conform to object geometries while simultaneously avoiding foot-skating artifacts throughout whole-body motion sequences. Furthermore, when provided solely with initial poses and target objects positioned in 3D space, countless approaches exist for individuals to navigate toward and grasp objects. This diversity of feasible grasping motions becomes exponentially amplified through extensive potential variations in object geometry and positioning. Constructing effective generative models capable of capturing such diversity while synthesizing varied realistic motions for grasping diverse 3D objects remains an unresolved challenge. % Addressing these fundamental challenges, we introduce \textbf{SAGA} (\textbf{S}toch\textbf{A}stic whole-body \textbf{G}rasping with cont\textbf{A}ct), an innovative whole-body grasping generation framework designed to synthesize stochastic motions of 3D human bodies approaching and grasping three-dimensional objects. Our approach incorporates two primary components: (1) an innovative 3D body generator synthesizing diverse static whole-body grasping terminal poses, and (2) a novel human motion generator creating diverse and plausible motions connecting specified initial and terminal poses. We present two fundamental insights regarding both components. Initially, rather than directly utilizing parametric body models (such as SMPL~\cite{SMPL-X:2019}) for 3D body representation, we implement markers-based representation~\cite{MOJO} that captures 3D human shape and pose information through sparse marker sets positioned on human body surfaces. Research in~\cite{MOJO} demonstrates that markers-based representation facilitates neural network learning more effectively than latent parameters of parametric body models, producing enhanced motion realism. We establish that markers-based representation proves particularly advantageous over latent body parameters for learning whole-body grasping, since error accumulation throughout kinematic chains significantly impacts physical plausibility of generated hand grasps, causing severe hand--object interpenetration issues. Subsequently, {\it contact} assumes a pivotal role throughout our pipeline. As humans navigate 3D space and grasp three-dimensional objects, physical contact becomes essential for modeling realistic motions and interactions. Across both method components, we learn contact representations from data and utilize them for guiding interaction synthesis, substantially enhancing generated motion realism.% Regarding static grasping pose generation, we constructed a multi-task conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) for jointly learning whole-body marker positions and detailed marker--object contact labels. During inference phases, given target objects in 3D space, our model simultaneously generates diverse sets of consistent full-body marker locations and contact labels on both body markers and object surfaces. A contact-aware pose optimization module subsequently recovers parametric body meshes from predicted markers while explicitly enforcing hand--object contact through leveraging predicted contact labels. Subsequently, utilizing generated static whole-body grasping poses as terminal poses and initial poses as starting positions, we propose an innovative generative motion infilling network for capturing motion uncertainty and generating diverse intermediate motions. We design CVAE-based architectures for generating both diverse intermediate motion trajectories and varied intermediate local pose articulations. Moreover, contacts between feet and ground surfaces are predicted as multi-task learning objectives to enforce superior foot-ground interactions. Additionally, leveraging predicted human--object contacts, we design contact-aware motion optimization modules for producing realistic grasp-oriented whole-body motions from generated marker sequences. Through leveraging GRAB~\cite{GRAB:2020} and AMASS~\cite{AMASS:ICCV:2019} datasets for training our generative models, our methodology successfully generates realistic and diverse whole-body grasping motion sequences for approaching and grasping various 3D objects. \myparagraph{Contributions.} In summary, we provide (1) an innovative generative framework synthesizing diverse and realistic whole-body motions approaching and grasping various unseen objects for 3D humans exhibiting varied body shapes, (2) an innovative multi-task learning model jointly learning static whole-body grasping poses and body--object interactions, (3) an innovative generative motion infilling model capable of stochastically infilling both global trajectories and local pose articulations, producing diverse and realistic full-body motions between initial and terminal poses. We conduct comprehensive experiments validating technical contributions. Experimental outcomes demonstrate both our complete pipeline's efficacy and each component's superiority over existing solutions.
dipper: The development of a fully automatic system for the synthesis of realistic 3D human bodies approaching and grasping target objects in three-dimensional environments is of fundamental importance for diverse applications, ranging from robots and animation to computer vision. To date, most of the available methods have concentrated on generating the hand poses and have ignored the comprehensive whole-body movement patterns, while the whole-body motion synthesis methods - cite: Grab, GrapingField:3DVision, JiangGraspTTA, - have mostly ignored the presence of objects in the scene. In fact, the modeling and synthesis of realistic whole-body grasping movements present formidable challenges that are still unresolved problems in many dimensions. First, whole-body grasping movements combine complex whole-body dynamics and complex finger articulations, whose substantial dimensional complexity greatly complicates the motion synthesis process. In addition, complete whole-body grasping sequences contain a complex and repeated body-object-hand contact pattern that is extremely difficult to animate with a high degree of perceptual realism. Moreover, given only initial poses and target objects positioned in three-dimensional space, there are countless approaches to navigating towards and grasping objects. This diversity of feasible grasping motions is further increased by the large number of possible variations in object geometry and location. Consider, for example, how hand surfaces must naturally conform to the geometry of the objects while avoiding the artifacts of skating the feet during whole-body movement sequences. At the same time as an effective generative model is needed that can produce realistic motions to grasp diverse 3D objects, a number of challenges remain unsolved. To address these fundamental challenges, we introduce SAGA (Stochastic Whole-Body Grasping with Contours), an innovative whole-body grasping generative framework designed to produce the random motions of 3D human bodies approaching and grasping 3D objects. Our approach is based on two main components: an innovative 3D body generator able to generate diverse static whole-body poses grasping objects, and a novel human motion generator able to produce diverse and plausible motions connecting initial and terminal poses. Firstly, instead of using directly parametric body models like SMPL, we implement markers-based 3D body representation which is capable of capturing 3D human shape and pose information by sparsely distributed markers positioned on the human body surfaces. The research of MOJO demonstrated that this markers-based representation facilitates neural network learning more effectively than the latent parameters of the parametric body models, thereby producing enhanced motion realism. As human beings navigate in 3D space and grasp 3D objects, physical contact becomes essential for modeling realistic motions and interactions. We demonstrate that markers-based representations are particularly advantageous over latent body parameters when learning whole-body grasping, as error accumulation in the kinematic chains severely hampers physical plausibility of the hand grasps, causing severe hand-object interpenetration issues. Considering the generation of static grasps, we have constructed a multi-task conditional variational autoencoder to learn marker positions on the whole body as well as detailed contact information between markers and objects. During the inference phase, given the positions of objects in 3D space, our model simultaneously generates different sets of consistent full-body marker locations and contact labels on both body markers and object surfaces. A contact-aware pose optimization component then recovers the body from these predicted markers, while requiring hand-object contact, using the predicted contact labels. Throughout both method components, we learn contact information from data and use it to guide interaction synthesis, thereby significantly enhancing the realism of generated motions. Then we designed a new architecture for generating both diverse intermediate motions and varied intermediate local postures. We then trained our network to predict the position of the foot as a multi-tasked learning objective to achieve better foot-ground interactions. Using the generated whole-body grasping poses as the final positions and the initial positions as the initial positions, we proposed a novel generative network of motion infilling to capture motion uncertainty and to generate diverse intermediate motions. By using the GRAB and AMASS datasets for training our generative models, we successfully generate realistic and diverse whole-body motions that can approach and grasp various 3D objects. We then use the predicted human-object contacts to design contact-aware motion optimizations that produce realistic whole-body motions oriented towards grasping from the generated marker sequences. Lastly, we provide extensive experiments validating our technical contribution. The results of the experiments show the efficacy of our overall pipeline and the superiority of each of the individual components over existing solutions. In summary, we propose: (1) an innovative framework to synthesize diverse and realistic whole-body motions, approaching and grasping various unseen objects, for 3D humans presenting different body shapes; (2) an innovative multi-tasked learning model, which combines the learning of static whole-body poses with the learning of body-object interactions; and (3) an innovative motion-synthesis model, which enables the generation of a whole-body motion by using a stodastic infill of both the global trajectories and local pose articulations.
