text: The fundamental goal of sparsification involves constructing a smaller graph $G'$ from a large graph $G$ while preserving crucial structural properties. Classical examples encompass spanners \cite{Chew89}, which maintain approximate distances within multiplicative bounds, alongside cut and spectral sparsifiers \cite{BK96,ST04}, which preserve graph cuts and Laplacian spectra up to $(1+\varepsilon)$ factors. Such \emph{edge sparsifiers} enable the reduction of dense graph problems to sparse counterparts, trading exact solutions for approximation guarantees inherent in the sparsification process. Conversely, certain approaches like elimination-based Laplacian solvers \cite{KLPSS16} necessitate \emph{vertex sparsification}—reducing the vertex count itself. This work focuses on \emph{cut sparsification} as our vertex sparsification paradigm, originally developed by \cite{HKNR98,Moitra09,LM10}. Given graph $G$ and terminal set $\mathcal{T} \subseteq V(G)$, we seek to construct a reduced graph $G'$ that maintains all terminal cuts within multiplicative factor $q$—the sparsifier's \emph{quality}. More precisely, $G'$ must contain terminals $\mathcal{T}$ such that for every subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{T}$, minimum cuts separating $S$ from $\mathcal{T} \backslash S$ in both $G$ and $G'$ differ by at most multiplicative approximation $q$. Optimal vertex sparsification algorithms should achieve quality $q$ approaching $1$ while ensuring $G'$ contains few vertices—ideally nearly linear in terminal count $k = |\mathcal{T}|$. Furthermore, practical applications demand polynomial or linear runtime in the original graph size. Prior work achieves various combinations of these objectives. When restricting sparsifier vertex sets to exactly $\mathcal{T}$, quality bounds of $q = O(\log k / \log\log k)$ were established \cite{Moitra09,LM10,CLLM10,EGKRTT14}, with polynomial-time construction demonstrated by \cite{MM10}. For perfect quality $q = 1$, size upper bounds of $2^{2^k}$ \cite{HKNR98,KR14} and lower bounds of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KR13} were proven. Additionally, \cite{KW12} achieved polynomial-time construction of quality-$1$ sparsifiers with $O(Z^3)$ size for integer-capacity graphs, where $Z$ represents total terminal degree. Nevertheless, the existence of quality-$(1+\varepsilon)$ sparsifiers with $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(k/\varepsilon))$ vertices remains unknown except in specialized cases \cite{AGK14,ADKKP16}. We present a vertex sparsification algorithm for $c$-edge connectivity—a thresholded cut sparsification variant that exactly preserves all cuts of size at most $c$, achieves linear terminal dependence and polynomial $c$ dependence, while running in polynomial time for arbitrary $c$ (\cref{thm:main}). This concept, termed \emph{connectivity-$c$ mimicking network}, was introduced by \cite{CDL21} for studying dynamic connectivity and parametrized complexity, yielding the first fully dynamic online algorithm for $c$-connectivities with nearly constant update time for fixed $c$ \cite{JS20}. Formally, graph $G'$ constitutes a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for $G$ with terminals $\mathcal{T}$ when all terminal cuts in $G$ containing at most $c$ edges are preserved exactly in $G'$. The prior algorithm from \cite{CDL21} constructing connectivity-$c$ mimicking networks with $O(kc^4)$ edges lacks polynomial runtime due to its reliance on well-linked decomposition from \cite{Chu12}, requiring exact solutions to restricted sparsest cut variants. Consequently, runtime scaled exponentially with $c$. Our primary contribution involves extending the matroid-based cut covering framework of \cite{KW12} while employing a significantly weaker well-linked decomposition notion. Rather than performing complete well-linked decomposition, we partition graph $G$ into components whose terminal ``expansion'' remains sufficiently large, resembling expander decomposition. Our central lemma (\cref{lemma:expanderc}), applying matroid theory and representative sets following \cite{KW12}, directly bounds connectivity-$c$ mimicking network sizes for these expander-like components based on expansion parameters. We then merge individual component mimicking networks to obtain the original graph's connectivity-$c$ mimicking network. This approach permits approximate sparsest cut algorithms (\cref{thm:sparsecut} \cite{ALN05}) with polynomial runtime. Unfortunately, we cannot achieve $O(m {\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ runtime due to expensive linear algebra required for matroid independent set computation. text: Reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable achievements across numerous challenging domains. Groundbreaking contributions include DQN~\cite{mnih2015human}, AlphaGo~\cite{silver2016mastering} and OpenAI Five~\cite{berner2019dota}. Nevertheless, these successes typically require extensive environmental interactions. Consider AlphaZero~\cite{silver2017mastering}, which necessitates 21 million training games. In contrast, professional human players manage approximately 5 games daily, implying that equivalent experience would demand 11,500 years of human gameplay. While sample complexity may pose fewer concerns in simulated environments and gaming contexts, real-world applications—including robotic manipulation, healthcare systems, and advertisement recommendation platforms—demand algorithms that simultaneously achieve superior performance and maintain minimal sample requirements for practical deployment. Substantial advances in sample-efficient RL have emerged over recent years~\cite{chua2018deep, deisenroth2011pilco, srinivas2020curl, laskin2020reinforcement, kostrikov2020image, schwarzerdata, kaiser2019model}. Model-based approaches have garnered considerable interest due to their capacity to leverage both authentic environmental data and synthetic ``imagined data'' generated by learned models for policy training, thereby enhancing sample efficiency~\cite{chua2018deep,deisenroth2011pilco}. However, these successes predominantly occur in state-based settings. Within image-based domains, certain model-based techniques like MuZero~\cite{schrittwieser2020mastering} and Dreamer V2~\cite{hafner2020mastering} demonstrate superhuman capabilities but lack sample efficiency; alternatively, methods such as SimPLe~\cite{kaiser2019model} exhibit efficiency yet deliver suboptimal performance (0.144 human normalized median scores). Recent developments in data augmentation and self-supervised learning applied to model-free approaches have shown greater promise in data-constrained scenarios~\cite{schwarzerdata}. Nevertheless, these methods remain unable to reach human-level expectations. Consequently, we identify three fundamental components crucial for enhancing both sample efficiency and maintaining exceptional performance in model-based visual RL agents: a self-supervised environment model, a mechanism for mitigating model compounding errors, and an approach for addressing off-policy complications. This work introduces EfficientZero, a model-based RL algorithm that delivers outstanding performance under data limitations. Our methodology builds upon MuZero while incorporating three pivotal modifications: (1) employing self-supervised learning to develop temporally consistent environment models, (2) learning the \textit{value prefix} through end-to-end training to reduce model compounding errors, (3) utilizing the learned model for correcting off-policy value targets. Figure \ref{fig:compare} demonstrates that our model establishes state-of-the-art performance on the established Atari~\cite{bellemare2013arcade} 100k benchmark, achieving superhuman performance within merely 2 hours of real-time gameplay. Specifically, our approach attains 194.3\% mean human normalized performance and 109.0\% median human normalized performance. For comparison, DQN~\cite{mnih2015human} reaches 220\% mean human normalized performance and 96\% median human normalized performance while requiring 500-fold more data (200 million frames). We further validate EfficientZero's effectiveness through experiments on simulated robotics environments within the DeepMind Control (DMControl) suite. The method achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing SAC performance despite the latter's direct access to ground truth states. Our sample-efficient, high-performance algorithm creates opportunities for substantial impact across diverse real-world applications.

text: The research community has devoted substantial attention to \ac{NBR} over recent years \citep{fpmc,dream,bai2018attribute}. Real-world services frequently encounter baskets—collections of items purchased or consumed simultaneously—with e-commerce platforms and grocery retail serving as notable examples~\citep{hao, raeder}. An \ac{NBR} system aims to predict the next basket of items a user will likely purchase or consume, based on their historical sequence of basket transactions. Items within any given basket lack temporal ordering and carry equal significance. The fundamental distinction between \ac{NBR} and session-based or sequential item recommendation lies in \ac{NBR}'s requirement to handle multiple items within a single set simultaneously. Consequently, models developed for individual item recommendation prove inadequate for basket-based scenarios, necessitating specialized \ac{NBR} approaches~\citep{tifuknn, recency, dream, beacon, intnet, clea, sets2sets, sun2020timestamp2}. \subsection{Types of recommendation methods} The evolution of recommendation methodologies has yielded diverse approaches across multiple decades. \emph{Frequency-based} methods maintain their significance by capturing global popularity statistics for items, proving valuable in both individual item and \ac{NBR} contexts. \emph{Nearest neighbor-based} approaches have similarly demonstrated enduring utility across item-based and basket-based recommendation scenarios. Deep learning techniques have emerged more recently to tackle sequential item recommendation challenges, leveraging their ability to model latent relationships and automatically derive representations~\citep{batmaz-2019-deep}. Contemporary research has introduced deep learning solutions targeting various \ac{NBR} dimensions, including item-to-item relationships~\citep{beacon}, cross-basket dependencies~\citep{dnntsp}, and intra-basket noise reduction~\citep{clea}. However, recent investigations suggest that deep learning approaches may not universally excel across all recommendation scenarios and conditions~\citep{jannach-2020-why}. When generating personalized item rankings, linear models and nearest neighbor techniques can surpass deep learning methods~\citep{dacrema-2021-troubling}. In sequential recommendation contexts, simple nearest neighbor or graph-based baselines may outperform sophisticated deep learning approaches~\citep{dacrema-2019-are}. This raises questions about \acl{NBR} performance: does the increased complexity of the retrieval unit—entire baskets rather than individual items—with intricate item-basket dependencies across temporal dimensions create opportunities for advanced representation learning methods to demonstrate superior \ac{NBR} performance? The present work examines this question through comprehensive empirical analysis. \subsection{A new analysis perspective} Our investigation reveals significant limitations and methodological issues within existing \ac{NBR} literature. These problems encompass inadequate baseline comparisons, inconsistent dataset usage across studies, and non-standardized evaluation metrics. text: As machine learning models grow increasingly complex, particularly within recommendation systems, efficiently managing vast input features has emerged as a critical challenge. Industrial online recommendation systems typically train on billion-scale sparse features using one-hot encoding~\cite{cheng2016wide,zhou2018din,DBLP:conf/cikm/ShengZZDDLYLZDZ21}. These features, essentially unique IDs, undergo mapping to low-dimensional embeddings prior to model input. A straightforward approach treats each feature independently, enabling direct DNN training for CTR estimation through feature combination (such as concatenation), where feature interactions depend on implicit modeling within fully connected layers. Nevertheless, recommendation system features like ``candidate item'' and ``user click history'' exhibit strong correlations~\cite{zhou2018din,zhou2019dien}, containing valuable co-occurrence patterns. The classic ``Beer and Nappies'' example exemplifies such relationships. Leveraging feature interactions proves beneficial for enhanced CTR estimation. Figure~\ref{fig:coaction} demonstrates this concept: without feature interaction consideration, features A and B influence the final label (click/no-click in CTR prediction) independently via blue pathways. The grey pathway represents explicit feature interaction, bridging correlations between feature pair (A, B) and the target label while providing additional learning information. Section~\ref{sec:revisit} explores this phenomenon in greater detail. Cartesian product offers the simplest feature interaction modeling approach. When features A and B are selected, their co-occurrence <A, B> becomes a new feature for model input. This direct provision of co-occurrence information as additional input simplifies training. Despite its simplicity and effectiveness, cartesian product suffers from significant limitations: excessive parameter volume, expanded feature space, and limited generalization capability. Unlike cartesian product's additional input strategy, numerous research initiatives focus on modeling feature interactions through sophisticated input feature combinations. Factorization-based methods~\cite{rendle2010factorization,qu2016product,WangFFW2017DCN,lian2018xdeepfm,xiao2017attentional,song2019autoint} exemplify this approach, emphasizing low- and/or high-order feature interactions by directly combining feature embeddings in latent vector space using diverse operators. These model-centric methods with well-designed operators typically offer superior deployment characteristics compared to cartesian product. However, they present notable disadvantages. Some factorization-based methods~\cite{juan2016field,WangFFW2017DCN} suffer from shallow structures that constrain representational power. More critically, their operator-generated embeddings simultaneously handle representation learning and feature interaction modeling, potentially impeding training effectiveness. This dual responsibility diminishes feature interaction memory capacity, thereby reducing overall model performance. \author{Weijie Bian$\dagger$, Kailun Wu$\dagger$, Lejian Ren$\dagger$, Qi Pi$\dagger$, Yujing Zhang$\dagger$, Can Xiao$\dagger$} \author{Xiang-Rong Sheng$\dagger$, Yong-Nan Zhu$\dagger$, Zhangming Chan$\dagger$, Na Mou$\dagger$, Xinchen Luo$\dagger$} \author{Shiming Xiang$\ddagger$, Guorui Zhou$\dagger$, Xiaoqiang Zhu$\dagger$, Hongbo Deng$\dagger$} \authornote{Hongbo Deng is the corresponding author (dhb167148@alibaba-inc.com).} \affiliation{% \institution{$\dagger$Alibaba Group\qquad \qquad \qquad$\ddagger$Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences} \city{Beijing} \country{China} } \email{{weijie.bwj,kailun.wukailun,lejian.rlj,dhb167148}@alibaba-inc.com} Addressing these challenges, we introduce \textbf{C}o-\textbf{A}ction \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{CAN}), designed to effectively capture feature interactions while leveraging mutual and shared information across different feature pairs. Within each feature pair, embeddings from one side (induction feature) construct an MLP applied to the opposite side (feed feature) through the co-action unit. This feature interaction modeling paradigm reduces additional parameters from $O(N^2 \times D)$ to $O(N\times (D' + D))$ (where $N$ represents feature count, $D$ and $D'$ denote co-action unit parameter dimensions, with $D < D' \ll N$) compared to cartesian product. Furthermore, CAN delivers enhanced fitting capability and superior non-linearity through MLP utilization in co-action units relative to traditional factorization-based approaches. Additionally, CAN separates parameter spaces for representation learning and feature interaction modeling, preventing mutual training interference. Multi-order enhancement and multi-level independence further enrich CAN's expressive capabilities. This work's primary contributions include: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item We examine cartesian product effectiveness and identify implicit feature interaction modeling potential. Drawing inspiration from cartesian product's independent coding, we develop a novel feature interaction paradigm achieving comparable performance with significantly reduced resource requirements. \item We present Co-Action Network (CAN) for modeling feature interactions among raw features at the input stage. CAN distributes each feature ID to individual micro-MLPs for interaction modeling with other features. This approach enhances feature interaction modeling expressiveness under parameter constraints. Individual micro-MLPs demonstrate superior expressive capabilities compared to conventional factorization-based operators. \item We perform comprehensive experiments across public and industrial datasets. Consistent superior performance validates CAN's effectiveness in feature interaction modeling against state-of-the-art competitors. CAN deployment achieves 12\% CTR and 8\% RPM improvements in Alibaba's display advertisement system. \end{itemize}

text: {\bf Motivation}. Stack Overflow\footnote{https://stackoverflow.com/} stands as one of the most widely-used platforms where users seek and provide answers to software development inquiries. Following its launch in 2008, the platform has become indispensable for professional developers and programming enthusiasts alike, serving as a hub for knowledge exchange and skill enhancement. By September 2019, Stack Overflow had amassed over 10.9M registered users and accumulated 18.1M questions. The platform continues its expansion, with more than 150K fresh questions emerging monthly\footnote{https://data.stackexchange.com/}. Such explosive growth presents significant challenges for content curation and platform appeal maintenance. The massive question repository renders manual oversight prohibitively expensive and overwhelming for site moderators \cite{moder2019, workload2019}. Consequently, automated approaches for efficient content management have become critically necessary. This pressing requirement has sparked considerable research interest in recent years \cite{Ashton2012, anton2014, Sebastian2019}. While numerous studies have examined Stack Overflow, relatively few address automated content management and data curation. Additionally, prior research predominantly concentrates on identifying and filtering poor-quality or duplicate questions \cite{Muhammad2016, denzil2013, Denzil14}. Our research advances the hypothesis that even high-quality questions merit removal when they no longer serve users' collective information requirements—for instance, when questions pertain to obsolete software versions or deprecated libraries. Retaining such irrelevant content not only inflates storage and retrieval expenses while generating minimal value, but also degrades user experience, potentially causing dissatisfaction and platform abandonment. We introduce the concept of "forgetting" such unappealing questions—allowing them to fade from user awareness much like irrelevant memories naturally disappear from human cognition. As an initial approach, this work tackles the challenge of identifying quality-but-irrelevant content on Stack Overflow by examining early detection of questions that initially garnered frequent attention but subsequently lose significance and fade over time. Specifically, we target questions that were commonly asked and (1) recently attracted substantial user views due to widespread similar issues, but (2) will generate minimal future interest. We term these \emph{forgotten questions}. Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample} illustrates such a question: created in 2008, it maintained high viewership until late 2017, accumulating 710 views during the final six months of 2017, yet attracted minimal attention during the most recent six-month period. {\bf Research Objectives}. Our investigation reveals that question forgetting occurs gradually rather than abruptly. Typically, years elapse before highly-viewed questions become forgotten. Furthermore, long-term predictions prove neither accurate nor practical. We therefore concentrate on questions undergoing near-term forgetting processes. Specifically, given a recently popular question, we aim to predict whether its viewership will decline substantially in the subsequent period. For the example in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}, at the December 2017 timepoint when the question enjoyed high visibility, rather than forecasting two-year abandonment, we seek to predict viewership drops within the following 3-6 months. Our approach draws inspiration from managed forgetting principles~\cite{claudia2018}: diminishing-importance items receive reduced emphasis to enhance focus on crucial matters—mirroring forgetting's role in human cognitive processes~\cite{David2007}. Particularly, we examine factors identified in prior literature and general intuition that potentially influence high-quality Stack Overflow questions' forgetting processes. Additionally, we develop a framework for early detection of such questions. This forgetting management system can guide moderators toward enhanced attention and appropriate actions regarding unnecessary content. It also elevates important information visibility for users and promotes engagement. For instance, seasoned developers would show greater interest in recently popular questions and feel motivated to interact with them. This subsequently improves search engine rankings for these questions and facilitates user access to currently relevant information. We emphasize that our problem differs from and complements content-focused works like \cite{Haoxiang2019}, which analyzes question responses to detect obsolete content within questions. Such content either lacks correctness at creation or becomes incorrect in the near future. Conversely, question forgetting can stem from various causes, where becoming incorrect or outdated represents merely one factor. {\bf Contributions}. Our primary contributions include the following: \begin{itemize} \item We present the inaugural forgetting management study on Stack Overflow, demonstrating that forgetting processes are widespread among high-quality questions, albeit occurring at relatively slow rates. \item We explore diverse factors potentially affecting question forgetting and assess their predictive capabilities for identifying forgotten questions. \item We evaluate multiple prediction models' performance in recognizing questions undergoing forgetting. We identify specific categories where forgotten questions show greater predictability despite the task's general difficulty. We also demonstrate various feature groups' predictive power and analyze their relative significance within these models. \end{itemize} The paper proceeds as follows: Section 2 examines related work. Section 3 describes our Stack Overflow dataset and presents our forgotten questions study. Section 4 implements machine learning experiments to predict forgotten questions on Stack Overflow. Section 5 discusses factors influencing our forgetting prediction task. Finally, Section 6 summarizes our main contributions and explores promising future research directions.

The platform continues to grow, with more than 150,000 new questions each month. This rapid growth presents a major challenge for content curation and maintaining the site’s appeal. And thus automatic solutions have become essential to ensure efficient content management. Many studies have investigated Stack Overflow, but very few have dealt with data management and data curation. The vast question bank makes the manual control of it prohibitively expensive and too demanding on the moderators [cite: moderator, workload, 2019], which makes automation an urgent requirement. This urgent need has aroused considerable research interest in recent years. This work addresses the problem of identifying high-quality, but irrelevant, content on Stack Overflow by focusing on the early detection of questions which initially are popular but then fade out. Most previous research has focused on identifying and filtering low-quality or duplicate questions, for example, questions about outdated software versions or deprecated libraries. Our research supports the hypothesis that even high-quality questions may be worth removing if they no longer serve the needs of the community, for example, questions about outdated software versions or deprecated libraries. In particular, we focus on questions that (1) have recently received a lot of attention because of a wide variety of similar problems, but (2) will receive little attention in the future. Keeping this kind of content increases storage and search costs while generating little value, but also makes the experience worse, causing dissatisfaction and potential withdrawal. We introduce the concept of forgetting such unattractive questions, which means making them disappear from the consciousness of users as irrelevant memories disappear from human consciousness. We call these questions "forgotten questions". The example in fig. [fig: ForgottenExample] shows a question which was created in 2008 and received significant attention from the users until the end of 2017, receiving 710 views in the last six months of the year, but received little attention in the last six months of the year. See the “Objectives of Research” section in the next chapter. Our research has shown that the process of forgetting is gradual, not abrupt. It takes several years for a question to be forgotten. Long-term forecasts are neither accurate nor practical. So we concentrate on questions that experience short-term memory loss. More specifically, we seek to predict whether a popular question will lose its popularity significantly in the next period. As an example, in the example of Figure 4, in December of 2017, when the question had a high visibility, instead of predicting a disappearance two years later, we try to predict a drop in popularity over the next three to six months. Our method is based on the principle of'managed forgetting': the memory for less important things is reduced to increase the memory for the most important things, in line with the role of forgetting in human memory. Specifically, we examine factors that the literature and our general intuition suggest to influence the forgetting process of high-quality Stack Overflow questions. We must stress that our work is distinct from, and complementary to, work that analyzes the responses to questions, such as that of Haoxiang and co., which analyzes the answers to questions to determine whether the question is obsolete. Management of oblivion helps moderators to focus less attention on unnecessary content, which will make the most important content more visible to users and thus encourage them to interact with it. In addition, we develop a framework for early detection of such questions. Contributions. For example, more experienced users will be interested in questions that have recently become popular and feel motivated to participate. This will improve the visibility of these questions in the search results and make it easier to find what is currently relevant. We present the first forgetting management study of Stack Overflow, which demonstrates that forgetting processes are widespread among high-quality questions, though they are slow. The content of the question either is incorrect when created or will be incorrect in the near future. On the other hand, forgetting can be caused by various factors, of which the question being incorrect or obsolete is only one. The structure of this paper is as follows. Item 1 - We test a number of prediction models to determine which questions are most likely to be forgotten. Item 2 - We test a number of other factors that may influence forgetting and their ability to predict forgotten questions. Section 2 examines previous research. We identify specific questions that are more predictable despite the general difficulty of the task. We also demonstrate the power of different features and their relative significance in these models. Section 3 describes the Stack Overflow dataset and our study of forgotten questions. Section 4 performs machine learning experiments to predict the forgotten questions on Stack Overflow. Section 5 discusses factors that may affect our forgetting task. Section 6 concludes by presenting the main contributions and by discussing promising future lines of research.

text: Model reconciliation has emerged as a prevalent framework for explanation generation in automated planning~\cite{chakraborti2017plan}. This paradigm seeks to balance two competing objectives: producing explanations that refine the user's environmental model and selecting inherently explicable action sequences that require minimal additional clarification. However, this approach fundamentally depends on maintaining an accurate user model—a requirement that proves impractical across numerous real-world applications. A more comprehensive perspective positions explanations within the broader landscape of interactive communication. During interaction, humans employ diverse communicative modalities, generating both deliberate and involuntary responses while leveraging various behavioral heuristics. Effective communication requires an interactive agent to not only detect and interpret these signals but ideally to anticipate them proactively. Given this interactive context, we are developing a user study designed to examine human behavioral patterns and responses during collaborative task execution with a plan-based agent. Although we anticipate this investigation will corroborate and expand upon existing research in joint task interaction, our primary objective centers on understanding how plan-based agent concepts (including plan generation and agent intention) can inform and enhance agent behavioral design. Our research has identified specific plan-based agent behaviors that intersect with fundamental elements of joint task interaction, particularly uncertainty management and knowledge asymmetries. These behavioral patterns have informed the development of two distinct agent architectures: a reactive agent that embodies initial interaction scenarios where human preferences and environmental knowledge remain limited; and a partially predictive agent that represents a more sophisticated system capable of providing anticipatory information while proactively mitigating user uncertainty. Through the collection of both quantitative and qualitative data from human-agent interactions, we aim to develop deeper insights into designing agents that achieve greater human acceptability. Our current work includes the development of a web-based experimental platform that we are preparing for deployment. This platform facilitates joint task interactions wherein human participants must accomplish objectives with assistance from a virtual agent that provides instructions and explanations. This paper outlines our user study objectives, describes the experimental scenarios participants will encounter, and articulates the research questions we seek to address. Additionally, we detail the agent architectures that will undergo comparative evaluation and examine the joint task interaction dimensions they enable us to investigate. While user data collection remains ongoing, we provide an empirical analysis comparing the strategies and explanations produced by each agent type. Our presentation begins with an overview of the joint task environment and requisite planning foundations. We then examine plan-based agent behavioral aspects relevant to collaborative interactions, utilizing these insights to characterize our two alternative agent designs. Subsequently, we describe our planned user study, present empirical analysis, review related work, and offer concluding remarks.

text: \IEEEPARstart{C}ivil drones have captured widespread attention across the past decade. This fascination spans industry, academia, business sectors, and civil society alike. Morgan Stanley's May 2021 long-term forecast \cite{MS} projected that urban air mobility markets (encompassing delivery services, air taxis, surveillance drones, among others) will achieve \$9 trillion by 2050—representing 5-6\% of anticipated global GDP—or potentially \$19 trillion (11-12\% of projected global GDP) under optimistic scenarios. Major technology corporations including Amazon, Google, and Uber maintain dedicated drone initiatives. Aircraft manufacturers are developing air taxi solutions. Academic engagement in this field has been equally robust: approximately 300,000 research documents emerge from Scopus searches using "drone" and related terminology such as Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), Unmanned Aircraft, and Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS). Even within the narrower domain of wireless communication, substantial interest persists, comprehensively documented in multiple tutorial and survey publications \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} drawing from hundreds of curated research articles. Yet despite this multi-stakeholder enthusiasm, drones remain absent from daily life. Industry and academic consensus identifies regulatory and certification barriers as primary impediments. Technical publications \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} emphasize these challenges, while \cite{MS} authors specifically note that \textit{the regulatory requirements for aviation is one of the most underestimated risks}. Indeed, Morgan Stanley reduced their 2021 market projections by 30\% compared to their 2018 Blue paper, citing "near-term hurdles related to regulation and certification" as a principal factor. However, we do not view regulatory bodies as adversarial. Managing technological innovation presents inherent complexity given the diverse stakeholder ecosystem: civil society, security agencies, university researchers, and influential corporations with substantial resources. Restrictive policies partially reflect public concerns and relatively limited technology trust. Additionally, unmanned aviation represents an emerging domain characterized by significant uncertainties and knowledge deficits. Academic researchers, often serving as public servants, should prioritize addressing relevant gaps and public concerns. This contribution assists policymakers while promoting balanced, harmonious technological advancement. The initial step involves identifying pertinent problems and developing appropriate solutions. While 300,000 published research items demonstrate academia's problem-identification capabilities, the continued absence of widespread drone deployment suggests these problems may not always address practical relevance. This article adopts a broader perspective on drone technology to evaluate problems significant for all major stakeholders in technology development. This work builds upon Technology Assessment (TA) achievements. TA constitutes an interdisciplinary research domain focused on generating knowledge for better-informed, well-considered decisions regarding emerging technologies \cite{gw09}. It delivers information supporting various actors (policymakers, citizens, engineers, etc.) in strategy development and action planning \cite{TA_toolkit_98}. TA methodology extends to specific technical products, processes, services, and systems \cite{gw09}. Various European Union agencies and commissions, the U.S. Government Accountability Office, and national research councils employ TA approaches. Countries including China, New Zealand, Italy, and Canada extensively utilize TA in sensitive domains such as healthcare. This article employs TA methodology to identify relevant problems and evaluate existing solutions targeting these challenges. Through this approach, we highlight pertinent research directions for the wireless communications community. Furthermore, utilizing TA principles, we provide frameworks for selecting appropriate research and development project scope and structure to enhance project efficiency while considering project characteristics, technology readiness levels, and additional relevant factors.

text: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated telehealth adoption at unprecedented rates \cite{Wosik2020}, driving virtual urgent care visits to surge by over 100\% and virtual non-urgent care visits to skyrocket by more than 4000\% \cite{telemedicine}. Virtual consultations typically commence when patients articulate their reason for encounter/visit (RFE) \cite{who}. Subsequently, leveraging the RFE, automated history-taking algorithms collect additional information regarding presenting symptoms before directing patients to practitioner consultations via chat, video, or text. Our work concentrates on an intermediary yet crucial implicit phase: symptom recognition within patient RFEs, which forms the foundation for automated history collection. While this relates to medical named entity recognition tasks that extract symptoms from clinical text in electronic health records (c.f.\cite{Baumel18} and references therein), our focus diverges toward medical entity recognition from patient-generated text. Patient text (RFEs) exhibits less standardization and frequently employs colloquial symptom descriptions. Figure ~\ref{fig:ml4hp} illustrates example RFEs from our dataset. Developing models for medical symptom recognition encounters several significant challenges: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Access}: Given the absence of publicly available datasets, telehealth platforms developing machine learning solutions must begin with limited labeled data and rapidly expand coverage. Consequently, as labeled data increases, systems must adapt to recognize previously unknown symptoms. \item \textbf{Multilabel distribution}: Individual RFEs may contain multiple symptoms, requiring comprehensive extraction of \emph{all} symptoms to enable proper automated history taking. \item \textbf{Long-tailed distribution}: While certain symptoms occur frequently, many symptoms demonstrate co-occurrence patterns. This inherently creates asymmetric and long-tailed data distributions (Figure~\ref{fig:ml4hp}), further complicated by telehealth platform patient demographics. \end{enumerate} Addressing these challenges, we introduce a novel active learning algorithm for efficient data labeling. Our algorithm's core insight recognizes that RFEs naturally cluster around medically-grounded underlying health conditions. The proposed approach selects informative examples by clustering unlabeled examples in latent space and choosing those providing maximal clustering coverage. Through optimal balance between selecting cluster-centroid-proximate points and points distant from labeled RFEs, we address long-tail distribution challenges. Experimental results demonstrate our model's superior performance over state-of-the-art multi-label classification approaches while effectively handling long-tailed distributions in our dataset. Ablation studies and qualitative analyses further illuminate our approach's advantages. \subsection*{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} Healthcare applications have increasingly embraced deep learning across diverse domains in recent years. A defining characteristic of healthcare deep learning involves managing scarce large annotated datasets. Collecting substantial labeled datasets proves costly and time-intensive, requiring healthcare professional annotations, while sensitive, high-risk data sharing between institutions remains challenging. Conversely, deep models typically demand extensive datasets for accurate, robust performance. Consequently, numerous healthcare AI applications remain inaccessible, delaying substantial real-world impact. Prior active learning research predominantly addresses balanced dataset classification scenarios. Nevertheless, healthcare applications frequently encounter long-tailed distributions where the objective involves identifying all correct labels rather than single correct classes. Similarly, conventional active learning strategies assume single-label validity per data point. Our paper demonstrates ``multilabel'' classification importance—individual data points may possess multiple correct labels. Crucially, comprehensive label identification without omissions proves paramount for subsequent history-taking tasks. We propose a novel algorithm for actively selecting maximally informative labeling examples in multi-label classification contexts. Our method leverages machine learning model latent space to overcome long-tailed data distributions while selecting diverse data points spanning broad input ranges.

text: The quest to develop autonomous robots capable of executing diverse and intricate manipulation tasks represents one of robotics' most enduring challenges. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have yielded significant progress in creating robot manipulation behaviors that resist traditional engineering approaches~\cite{kalashnikov2018qtopt, openai2019learning,openai2019solving,kalashnikov2021mtopt}. However, contemporary DRL models encounter substantial limitations when confronting long-horizon tasks, primarily due to exploration difficulties --- robots must navigate prohibitively vast behavioral spaces to accomplish their objectives. Various temporal abstraction frameworks have emerged within DRL research to address this exploration burden by leveraging the inherent hierarchical nature of manipulation tasks~\cite{coreyes18sectar,nachum2018hiro,bacon2016optioncritic,eysenbach2019sorb}. These approaches simultaneously learn low-level controllers, typically conceptualized as \textit{skills} or \textit{options}, alongside high-level controllers through trial-and-error processes. Although demonstrating superior scalability compared to conventional DRL methods, these techniques frequently exhibit high sample complexity, limited interpretability, and fragile generalization capabilities. Concurrently, decades of robotics research have cultivated an extensive collection of specialized functional modules targeting specific robot behaviors, including grasping~\cite{bohg2014graspsurvey} and motion planning~\cite{karaman2011rrtstar,ijspeert2013dmps}. These pre-constructed functional modules, termed \emph{behavior primitives}, demonstrate exceptional robustness and reusability for achieving particular manipulation objectives, such as object retrieval via end-effector manipulation and collision-free robot navigation to target configurations. Despite their specialized capabilities, integrating these primitives as foundational building blocks within DRL algorithms for complex task scaffolding remains challenging. This difficulty stems primarily from the inherently \textit{heterogeneous} nature of behavior primitives. They accept non-uniform input parameters, operate across varying temporal scales, and manifest distinct behavioral patterns. Consequently, algorithms must reason about temporal task decomposition while adaptively orchestrating these behavior primitives. Hierarchical modeling approaches in robotics have extensively utilized behavior modules as fundamental low-level components. Task-and-motion planning~\cite{kaelbling2011hpn, garrett2020tamp, wang2021comptamp} and neural programming~\cite{xu2018neural, huang2019neural} methodologies have employed primitives including motion planners and pick-and-place controllers for compositional manipulation task modeling. These approaches necessitate well-defined domain knowledge for task planning or substantial human supervision for training high-level controllers with ground-truth task decomposition. Such requirements constrain the scalability of these methods in practical applications. This work presents MAPLE~(\textbf{Ma}nipulation \textbf{P}rimitive-augmented reinforcement \textbf{Le}arning), a comprehensive DRL algorithm that exploits pre-built behavior primitive collections for long-horizon manipulation task resolution. To tackle DRL exploration challenges, our approach combines high-level behavior primitive libraries (encompassing grasping or object pushing) with low-level motor actions for autonomous hierarchical policy learning (see \cref{fig:overview}). Our algorithm treats each behavior primitive as an implementation-independent controller generating temporally extended behaviors. Given any state, our DRL policy selects a behavior primitive (or atomic motor action) and instantiates it with appropriate input parameters. For instance, a 6-DoF grasping module might receive pre-grasp end-effector pose parameters. The chosen primitive interprets these parameters and executes single or sequential motor actions to manifest its specialized behavior. Through behavior primitive integration into DRL algorithms, MAPLE~abstracts substantial manipulation planning complexity while preserving generic reinforcement learning algorithm flexibility to discover compositional task structures without extensive domain knowledge. Additionally, by maintaining low-level motor actions, MAPLE~can utilize these actions during task phases where finite behavior primitive libraries prove insufficient for expressing desired behaviors. text: \input{images/figure1} Among the world's more than 6,000 living languages, natural language processing (NLP) systems serve only a small subset, primarily due to insufficient resources for model training and evaluation. Technological progress remains concentrated on data-rich languages, systematically excluding most others~\cite{joshi2020state}. This exclusion proves especially acute for endangered languages—those facing extinction as native speaker populations decline and younger generations adopt alternative languages. Locating \emph{any} data for most endangered languages presents formidable challenges. Textual materials in these languages frequently exist but remain inaccessible in non-machine-readable formats: physical books, scanned images, and unstructured web content. Such materials encompass publications from community-based publishers serving endangered language speakers, including educational and cultural resources. Linguistic documentation efforts also generate valuable data—word inventories and interlinear glosses—typically preserved as handwritten records. \autoref{fig:dataset_example} illustrates examples from such scanned documents. Converting textual content from these sources into digital formats would simultaneously advance NLP capabilities for endangered languages and support documentation, preservation, and accessibility initiatives. We develop a benchmark dataset and introduce methodological approaches for data extraction from these resources, concentrating on scanned images of printed materials containing endangered language text. Such digitization typically demands optical character recognition (OCR) systems. Yet the extensive textual corpora and transcribed image collections required for training cutting-edge OCR models from inception remain unavailable for endangered languages. We therefore emphasize \emph{post-correcting} outputs from general-purpose OCR tools capable of processing diverse scripts. Our findings demonstrate that specialized post-correction techniques can substantially enhance performance for endangered languages. While OCR post-correction has received considerable research attention, existing approaches depend heavily on target language resources, requiring substantial textual corpora for language model training~\cite{schnober-etal-2016-still,dong-smith-2018-multi,8978127} or synthetic data generation~\cite{krishna-etal-2018-upcycle}. These resources, abundant for high-resource languages, remain severely constrained for endangered languages, precluding direct application of established post-correction methodologies. We propose an alternative approach that builds upon existing OCR post-correction models through three enhancements designed for data-scarce environments. Our \textbf{multi-source model} leverages information from high-resource translations frequently accompanying endangered language texts. These translations typically appear in regional \textit{lingua franca} languages (illustrated in \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (a,b,c)) or documentary linguists' primary languages (shown in \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (d) from \citet{shangaji-elar}). We incorporate \textbf{structural biases} to facilitate learning from limited data quantities. Additionally, we implement \textbf{pretraining methods} to exploit scarce unannotated endangered language data. \medskip \noindent Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt] \item A benchmark dataset for OCR post-correction across three critically endangered languages: Ainu, Griko, and Yakkha. \item Systematic evaluation of general-purpose OCR systems, revealing inadequate robustness in data-scarce endangered language contexts. \item An OCR post-correction methodology adapting standard neural encoder-decoder architectures to severely under-resourced endangered language environments, achieving 34\% reductions in both character error rates and word error rates compared to state-of-the-art general-purpose OCR systems. \end{itemize}

text: Navigating real-world environments presents inherent risks for autonomous vehicles, particularly when confronted with dynamic conditions and multiple actors (non-player characters or NPCs). The presence of each environmental actor substantially impacts the Ego actor's\footnote{Actor that is being tested and is under the control of the tester.} decision-making processes, constraining available navigation and safety planning options. Under extreme circumstances, these actors may—intentionally or inadvertently—compromise the Ego actor's capacity to accomplish tasks safely. Consequently, every environmental actor represents a potential risk source for the Ego actor. This work characterizes actor-associated risk through quantifying their influence on the Ego actor's decision-making within specific environments. Risk emerges as a function of two primary factors: \begin{enumerate*}[label=(\roman*)] \item the environment (i.e., driving scenario), and \item uncertainty associated with determining the future trajectories by the Ego actor. \end{enumerate*} \textbf{Driving scenario.} A driving scenario encompasses the Ego actor's initial positioning and NPC trajectory specifications. The introduction of additional NPCs progressively constrains the safe trajectory space available to the Ego actor (navigable space). Environmental locations exhibit varying risk levels, as navigable space fluctuates considerably across different areas (construction zones exemplify this phenomenon). The reduction in safe trajectory options correlates directly with increased risk, demanding heightened attention and diminishing contingency options for unforeseen circumstances. \cref{fig:motivation}(a) demonstrates this concept. \textbf{Uncertainty.} Inaccurate NPC trajectory prediction by the Ego actor amplifies risk levels. Prediction accuracy deteriorates through multiple mechanisms: ambiguous or abrupt intention changes among driving participants (pedestrians suddenly stopping or running, emergency braking, vehicle breakdowns), measurement noise from adverse weather conditions, or AI/ML model imperfections (undetected pedestrians). \cref{fig:motivation}(b) illustrates these uncertainty effects. Human drivers continuously perform implicit risk assessments encompassing both scenario-based risks and action uncertainty to maintain safe operation. Accidents manifest when risk assessment fails, occurring under conditions of (i) impaired or distracted driving, (ii) insufficient driver skill, and (iii) expectation mismatches from traffic rule violations or unexpected maneuvers (sudden braking). AI/ML-operated actors experience amplified risk due to aleatoric and epistemic noise sources. Developing runtime risk quantification and characterization methods becomes critically essential—not merely for safety assurance through risk minimization, but for identifying irreducible risk situations requiring passenger preparation through emergency braking or airbag deployment. This paper establishes the practical significance of risk metrics for safety assurance. Our primary contributions include defining a novel risk metric and demonstrating its application for quantifying relative actor-associated risks in real-world driving scenarios. While focusing on self-driving vehicles as our primary use case, the proposed framework maintains generalizability for other autonomous systems including aerial vehicles and ML-driven computational systems. \textbf{Related work.} Defensive driving research encompasses two principal directions: (i) safe distance identification assuming universal ``duty-of-care'' policy adherence, (ii) out-of-training-distribution (OOD) scenario identification for worst-case collision avoidance planning. \textit{Duty-of-care approaches} including Safety Force Field (SFF)~\cite{SafetyForceField} and Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS)~\cite{shalev2017formal} focus on safe distance estimation under universal traffic rule compliance assumptions. These methods additionally aim to identify culpability during safety hazards. \textit{OOD} models exemplified by \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a} target driving scenario identification where Ego actor trajectory planning exhibits significant variance. Ensemble models or diverse datasets can characterize such variance. Under high variance conditions, Ego actors adopt pessimistic planning strategies for collision avoidance. For instance, \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a} employs Bayesian imitative models for Ego actor planning, utilizing imitation prior variance relative to model posterior as a distribution shift proxy. Upon distribution shift detection, Ego actors can implement worst-case or average model planning. Additional research~\cite{Philion_2020_CVPR} quantifies uncertainty's impact on driving performance without addressing generated plan safety quality. Conversely, our objectives encompass (i) actor or scenario risk assignment through characterizing negative influence on Ego actor navigational freedom, (ii) current plan risk quantification with proactive safety hazard mitigation. This approach enables offline identification of compelling driving scenarios and optimal safe plan selection for defensive Ego actor operation.

text: Knowledge graphs~(KGs), which encode factual information through semantic graph structures, find extensive application across diverse artificial intelligence domains, including recommendation~\cite{leiconversational,2021Learning}, dialogue generation~\cite{moon-etal-2019-opendialkg,leiinteractive}, and question answering~\cite{ChristmannRASW19,zhu2021retrieving}. Within KGs, factual information manifests as triples of the form \texttt{(head~entity, relation, tail~entity)}, establishing connections between head and tail entities through specific relations. Given the continuous emergence of new knowledge, KG incompleteness has sparked considerable research attention toward link prediction, a task focused on inferring missing connections within KGs~\cite{simple}. Contemporary link prediction approaches~\cite{bordes2013translating,Dettmers2018Convolutional} typically learn entity and relation embeddings, subsequently employing scoring functions to assess triple validity. Nevertheless, we contend that embedding-based learning in current link prediction models introduces two fundamental challenges: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Unbalanced relation distribution. } Figure~\ref{fig:intro} demonstrates the highly skewed relation distribution characteristic of standard KG datasets~(e.g., FB15K-237~\cite{toutanova-chen-2015-observed}). Consider the stark frequency disparity between relations such as { \texttt{/film/film/language} and \texttt{/film/film/edited}.} Current link prediction models presuppose adequate training data across all relations while neglecting few-shot scenarios, overlooking how few-shot relation learning can significantly impact overall performance. \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Existence of unseen relations. } Real-world KGs exhibit openness and rapid evolution, consequently containing numerous zero-shot relations absent from standard training datasets, exemplified by {\texttt{/film/film/sequel}} in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}. Such unseen relations exceed the capabilities of conventional link prediction models, which lack training instances necessary for embedding learning. This limitation constrains model applicability in practical scenarios. \end{itemize} Recent research has attempted to address these challenges. \citet{Xiongoneshot}, \citet{shi2018open}, and \citet{ChenMeta} employed meta-learning and metric-based methodologies to enable rapid adaptation to few-shot relations using limited training data. While these approaches demonstrate potential for few-shot relation learning, they struggle with unbalanced relation distributions due primarily to the computational overhead of training across numerous relations. Subsequently, \citet{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-08937} and \citet{Qin2020GenerativeAZ} addressed unseen relation prediction through textual description analysis. Although successful in unseen relation prediction, these methods prove inadequate for general link prediction given the inherent noise in textual descriptions and their inability to establish connections between observed and unobserved relations. Ideally, link prediction models should seamlessly handle many-, few-, and zero-shot relations simultaneously. For joint relation learning, we observe that semantic correlations—representing relational semantic similarities—can bridge many-, few-, and zero-shot relation learning. Consider Figure~\ref{fig:intro}, where the many-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/language}'', few-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/edited}'', and zero-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/sequel}'' share semantic connections through ``\texttt{film}''. Given that semantically related relations should occupy proximate positions in embedding space~\cite{yang2014embedding}, leveraging semantic correlations like those illustrated above becomes crucial for unified relation learning. Building upon this insight, we introduce a \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{R}elation \textbf{L}earning framework (GRL) that exploits semantic correlations. GRL enhances mainstream link prediction models by rendering them (1) robust to unbalanced relation distributions and (2) capable of zero-shot relation learning. More precisely, GRL integrates with link prediction models following the embedding learning phase. For relation embedding optimization, GRL employs attention mechanisms to extract semantic correlations, performs relation fusion, and applies classification-aware loss to embed these semantic correlations within relation representations. This approach enhances the proximity of semantically related relations while improving discrimination between dissimilar ones. Consequently, few-shot relations benefit from knowledge transfer from semantically similar many-shot relations; zero-shot relations can be predicted through their closest semantic counterparts. Through experimentation, we enhance two baseline models (DistMult~\cite{yang2014embedding} and ConvE~\cite{Dettmers2018Convolutional}) via GRL integration across all relation categories: many-, few-, and zero-shot. This work advances comprehensive KG understanding and provides a unified relation learning solution for link prediction. text: Autonomous agents frequently employ receding horizon approaches for trajectory planning. In multi-agent environments such as autonomous driving, these planning algorithms must incorporate predictions of other agents' future behaviors while ensuring properties like collision avoidance through forecasts of neighboring agents' decisions. However, this methodology suffers from a fundamental limitation: the resulting motion plans for the ``ego'' vehicle fail to consider how other agents might react to its own actions. This shortcoming manifests clearly in scenarios where an autonomous vehicle cannot merge into heavy traffic, as it lacks the ability to anticipate that other agents might yield space in response to its intentions. Joint planning and prediction through game-theoretic motion planners addresses these reactive behaviors. These approaches model other agents' intentions as individual optimization problems that each agent attempts to solve, subsequently generating equilibrium solutions. Such equilibria comprise sets of interacting trajectories for all agents, enabling the ego agent to execute its corresponding equilibrium path. Game-theoretic planning faces a significant limitation: it presupposes that other agents' intentions are transparent to the ego agent and that all agents behave rationally according to those intentions. Beyond game-theoretic contexts, these objectives and intentions can be estimated dynamically and incorporated as contingencies \cite{hardy2013contingency}. We tackle this challenge within game-theoretic planning by introducing a multi-hypothesis framework that explicitly handles this uncertainty and its associated interdependencies. Our methodology operates under the assumption that the ego agent maintains a discrete collection of hypotheses concerning other agents' intentions. Each hypothesis carries an associated probability and captures uncertainties regarding intentions like prospective lane changes, preferred speeds, acceleration preferences, and similar behavioral factors. Under such uncertainty, we propose developing distinct optimization formulations for individual agents that, when solved, yield trajectories qualitatively reflecting different hypothetical behaviors. We generate replicas of each agent corresponding to each hypothesis and assign them to their respective optimization problems. We present a novel dynamic game formulation enabling the ego agent to reason about interactions with replica agents weighted by their hypothesis probabilities. This formulation proves essential for incorporating collision-avoidance constraints in a probabilistic manner. This problem formulation yields a practical methodology for the broader category of motion-planning challenges that autonomous vehicles encounter. Our approach produces interactive multi-agent trajectories while explicitly incorporating uncertainty regarding others' intentions. We anticipate that our method will facilitate more widespread adoption of game-theoretic planning in autonomous vehicle applications. The paper structure follows this organization. \cref{sec:related_work} examines alternative multi-agent planning approaches, encompassing game-theoretic methods and techniques utilizing rational choice model variants that address uncertainty in other agents' behaviors. \cref{sec:preliminaries} establishes game-theoretic planning concepts necessary for formalizing our approach, which we detail in \cref{sec:methods}. \cref{sec:results} demonstrates empirical validation of our method across various realistic driving scenarios, while \cref{sec:conclusion} provides concluding observations.

text: The challenge of recognizing multi-party speech from unlimited speakers in far-field environments, where natural speech overlap occurs, represents a complex research domain that has attracted sustained investigation over many years \cite{Hain2007_AMI,fox13b_interspeech,Liu2016_SWC2,Barker_2018}. This fundamental challenge is commonly known as the ``cocktail party problem''. Solving this problem will unlock the next generation of speech technology and establish the groundwork for seamless human-device voice communication. Within such communication paradigms, speech agents embedded in smart devices must effectively parse multi-party conversations while delivering appropriate assistance. To enable real-time human-device interaction, \ac{ASR} systems must generate streaming transcripts for all conversation participants. Enhanced privacy protection demands that \ac{ASR} systems operate exclusively on-device, necessitating lightweight models that remain robust despite acoustic front-end constraints. These requirements collectively underscore the critical need for streaming speech recognition capable of handling unlimited speakers with potential overlap using only a single distant microphone. Multi-speaker \ac{ASR} has traditionally relied on cascaded architectures incorporating speech separation and recognition modules \cite{Isik_2016, Menne_2019, Settle_2018, von_Neumann_2020, Neumann_2020}. Given their complexity and technical constraints within individual components, these systems are better suited for offline applications where complete audio recordings are accessible prior to transcription. Recent years have witnessed advances in joint model training that directly optimizes multi-speaker ASR performance \cite{Yu_2017_icassp, Yu_2017_interspeech, Qian_2018, Seki_2018, Chang_2019, Tripathi_2020}. The work by \cite{k2020serialized} introduced joint multi-speaker speech recognition with speaker change detection for unlimited speakers through \ac{SOT}, demonstrating effectiveness on simulated multi-speaker LibriSpeechMix test sets. Subsequently, \cite{kanda2021largescale} validated \ac{SOT} effectiveness on authentic multi-speaker meeting corpora, while follow-up studies \cite{kanda2020joint, kanda2021slt, kanda2021endtoend, kanda2021comparative} expanded \ac{SOT} into speaker-attributed ASR, enabling integrated ``who spoke what" transcription in multi-speaker conversations through unified modeling. Concurrently, emerging research has focused on preserving performance under streaming constraints. Two conceptually analogous streaming multi-speaker ASR architectures based on \ac{RNN-T} \cite{graves2012sequence}—namely \ac{MS-RNN-T} \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} and \ac{SURT} \cite{Lu2021}—were simultaneously developed to enable time-synchronous decoding of partially overlapping speech, with \cite{Lu2021} subsequently incorporating speaker identification capabilities in \cite{lu2021streaming}. Evaluation of \ac{MS-RNN-T} by \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} encompassed single-speaker LibriSpeech and two-speaker LibriSpeechMix datasets. Results demonstrated that \ac{MS-RNN-T} matches offline multi-speaker ASR system performance on two-speaker test data while enhancing system robustness on noisy single-speaker test-other LibriSpeech partitions. Building upon \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021}, this work presents several key contributions. We demonstrate the superiority of dynamic overlapping speech simulation during training over static pre-simulated datasets, achieving new low \ac{WER} results on two-speaker LibriSpeechMix partitions using streamable architectures. We address \ac{MS-RNN-T}'s primary constraint—the rigid limitation on maximum speaker count in audio. Under the assumption of at most two simultaneously overlapping speakers, our proposed \ac{MT-RNN-T} model achieves speech recognition for unlimited speakers. We also advance streaming rich transcription of multi-party speech through segmentation tag introduction. Finally, we provide comprehensive performance analysis using novel evaluation metrics—\ac{ORC} WER and turn counting accuracy—while outlining future research directions.

text: \vspace{-0.2cm} Over the past decade, embedding models have emerged as fundamental algorithms powering diverse machine learning applications, from Information Retrieval (IR)~\citep{croft2010search,baeza1999modern} to Natural Language Processing (NLP)~\citep{word2vec, glove, attention, bert}. These models represent evolutionary descendants of low-rank approximation and Matrix Factorization techniques that previously dominated recommendation systems before Deep Learning (DL) gained prominence. Their core objective involves transforming straightforward, intuitive input representations into abstract, low-dimensional dense vector spaces. Such transformations facilitate two critical capabilities: 1) customizing vectors for specific downstream tasks and 2) preprocessing and storing documents or products as vectors, thereby achieving computationally efficient retrieval (typically through matrix multiplication followed by sorting operations that leverage modern GPU architectures). Beyond computational benefits, embedding models excel at capturing semantic relationships between queries and products. Consider product prediction for platforms like Amazon: user queries must be matched against millions of products, with optimal search results delivered within milliseconds. Using raw product data, determining that items containing 'aqua' relate to 'water' queries would prove impossible. However, by projecting products into dense low-dimensional vector spaces and mapping queries to identical spaces, inner product computations (typically dot products) with all product vectors become feasible. Products achieving highest inner products can then be displayed. These projections learn to encode semantic information while continuously adapting to temporal shifts in customer preferences. To our knowledge, embedding models dominate industrial applications, especially for product and advertisement recommendations (Amazon's DSSM~\citep{dssm}, Facebook's DLRM~\citep{dlrm}). Nevertheless, problem scales have expanded dramatically in recent years, spurring research into extreme classification tasks involving millions of classes. Consequently, Tree-based Models~\citep{prabhu2014fastxml,Pfastre,agrawal2013multi} and Sparse-linear Models~\citep{weston2013label,pdsparse,ppdsparse} have emerged as formidable alternatives. Tree-based models particularly demonstrate superior training and evaluation speed compared to alternative approaches. However, most practical Information Retrieval systems feature dynamically evolving output classes, and existing extreme classification models struggle to generalize to novel classes with limited training data (\emph{e.g.}, daily catalog additions of new products). This limitation has triggered renewed interest in embedding models for large-scale Extreme Classification~\citep{bi2013efficient,annexml,sleec,chen2012feature}. {\bf Our Contributions:} This paper presents a novel, distinctive, and compelling argument that sparse high-dimensional embeddings outperform their dense low-dimensional counterparts. We introduce two innovative design decisions: 1) Label embeddings (\emph{e.g.} catalog products) are constructed as high-dimensional, super-sparse, orthogonal vectors. 2) Label embeddings remain fixed throughout training while only input embeddings are learned (one-sided learning), contrasting with conventional dense models where both input and label embeddings undergo learning. Given our utilization of {\bf S}parse, {\bf O}rthogonal, {\bf L}earned {\bf a}nd {\bf R}andom embeddings, we designate our approach {\bf SOLAR}. We establish theoretical foundations for SOLAR by demonstrating mathematical equivalence between one-sided and two-sided learning. Our design choices yield four-fold advantages over existing methods: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep,nolistsep] \itemsep0em \item {\bf Matrix Multiplication to Inverted-Index Lookup:} Sparse high-dimensional embeddings enable label subset retrieval through simple inverted-index~\citep{croft2010search} lookups, restricting computation and sorting to those labels. This substantially accelerates inference speed. \item {\bf Load-balanced Inverted Index:} Enforcing near-orthogonal, equally sparse label embeddings (while keeping them fixed) ensures uniform bucket filling in inverted indices and approximately equal label sampling per input. This eliminates the notorious imbalanced bucket problem where popular inputs trigger sub-sampling of nearly all labels, degrading inference performance. \item {\bf Learning to Hash:} Inverted-Indices function as hash tables where output classes are hashed into limited buckets~\citep{kulis2009learning, wang2017survey}. By fixing label buckets and learning input-to-label bucket mappings, we effectively perform 'partial learning to hash' tasks retrospectively (detailed in Appendix A). \item {\bf Zero-communication:} Our distinctive label embedding construction enables distributed multi-GPU training without communication overhead. Consequently, we can train on a 1.67M book recommendation dataset and three largest extreme classification datasets, surpassing respective baselines across all four datasets in both precision and speed metrics. \end{itemize} \vspace{-0.5cm}

text: Contemporary knowledge economies rely extensively on data collection to inform decision-making processes, policy development, and service provision. Nevertheless, disclosure risks inherent in data processing and sharing activities significantly limit the practical utility of these datasets. Anonymisation represents a crucial mechanism for risk mitigation in this context. The processes of functional anonymisation are operationalised through the Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework (ADF) \cite{elliot2018functional}. This framework emerged from research conducted by the \textit{data environment analysis service} \cite{elliot2010data}, which provided support infrastructure for the 2011 UK census with particular emphasis on data confidentiality and disclosure control \cite{willenborg2012elements,duncan2011concepts,hundepool2012SDC}, especially regarding re-identification risk assessment \cite {chen1998, skinner1998estimating,skinner2002measure}. The foundational principle of this approach recognises that disclosure risk originates not from datasets in isolation, but rather from the dynamic relationship between data and their operational context. Mackey and Elliot characterise the data environment as "the set of formal and informal structures, processes, mechanisms and agents that either: (i) act on data; (ii) provide interpretable context for those data or (iii) define, control and/ or interact with those data" \cite{mackey2013understanding}. Multiple categories of data environments exist, including open data environments, end-user license management systems, and restricted access secure facilities. Despite this diversity, the ADF framework posits that any data environment can be characterised using four fundamental descriptive dimensions: other data, agents, infrastructure, and governance. Consequently, effective anonymisation processes must account for both datasets and their environmental contexts. Elliot et al. \cite{elliot2020anonymisation} developed the ADF to operationalise precisely this integrated approach. The framework emphasises that appropriate anonymisation decisions for any given dataset can only emerge through careful consideration of the relationship between data and their environment(s), termed the \textit{data situation}.\\ \vspace{-12pt} \textbf{\textit{Problem statement}.} \textit{Data situations exhibit inherent dynamism as datasets migrate across environments during processing and utilisation phases. Therefore, comprehending contextual risk and implementing effective risk management through anonymisation necessitates both awareness of and capability to map inter-environmental data flows.} Present approaches to capturing and mapping \textit{data situations} for ADF analysis rely on manual processes, creating labour-intensive workflows susceptible to human error. To enable automated mapping capabilities, we propose leveraging data provenance—a concept already informally referenced within the ADF framework. Through provenance integration with the ADF, we can systematically track data flows while identifying both existing and proposed upstream and downstream data situations. Notably, data provenance has demonstrated effectiveness in addressing analogous challenges including situation awareness and decision-making \cite{baclawski2017framework}, direct and indirect data flow control \cite{rong2020provenance}, and big data security and privacy management \cite{gao2020big}. The W3C PROV standard facilitates provenance interoperability by providing standardised representations of data origins and processing histories \cite{PROV-DM15,missier2013w3c}. PROV offers an abstract data model encompassing agents, entities, activities, and relational properties, thereby enabling comprehensive representation of data and system provenance. The feasibility of connecting provenance to the ADF fundamentally depends on effective data environment representation. Within the W3C PROV data model, two constructs—\textit{bundles} and \textit{namespaces}—emerge as potential candidates for such representation. This paper evaluates the utility of both solutions while examining how PROV elements (Entity, Bundle, Agent, Activity) might represent data environment features (agents, other data, infrastructure, governance). We identify limitations in current representation approaches and propose modifications to enable comprehensive capture of required features. This work contributes the following: \vspace{-12pt} \begin{enumerate} \item We establish—through an ADF use case—the provenance requirements for data environment representation (in section \ref{sec:usecase}). \item Based on these requirements, we propose four distinct approaches for applying and extending W3C PROV to enable data environment representation suitable for machine-enabled reasoning (in section \ref{sec:impl}). \item We subsequently analyse these four approaches (in section \ref{sec:analysis}) \end{enumerate}
