text: This work aims to develop a system for maintaining an \emph{audit trail} within the knowledge representation (KR) framework utilizing hierarchies of graphs as presented in \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. Our objective centers on recording the evolutionary history of predominantly small, localized modifications to extensive knowledge corpora represented through graphs and graph hierarchies, particularly in scenarios where storing complete corpus snapshots at each historical point proves computationally infeasible. The requirement for transformation reversibility within our practical application context does not constrain the available operations for corpus updates; instead, it introduces a manageable overhead for storing supplementary information that enables the reversion of applied transformations. Additionally, we establish mechanisms for maintaining multiple corpus versions, which becomes essential when accommodating diverse knowledge iterations that may reflect varying perspectives of knowledge curators or inherent knowledge conflicts (such as contradictory experimental findings or competing hypotheses). Primary applications for audit trails in KRs based on graph hierarchies encompass version control for schema-aware graph database updates as described in \cite{bonifati2019schema} and modifications to knowledge corpora within the bio-curation framework KAMI \cite{harmer2019bio}. Constructing an audit trail system with these capabilities fundamentally depends on three components: (1) establishing an \emph{efficient semantic representation of object transformations} (or deltas), eliminating the need to store object states at every transformation point throughout history; (2) ensuring \emph{transformation reversibility}, guaranteeing that any transformation sequence can be systematically `undone'; and (3) developing robust methods for \emph{composing successive transformation pairs}, enabling efficient storage and version switching for identical objects. This work articulates these three essential components regarding both individual objects (Section \ref{s:preliminaries}), such as graphs, and object hierarchies (Section \ref{s:rulehierarchy}), while exploring how these components facilitate efficient audit trail construction (Section \ref{s:audit}). We introduce a mathematical framework for constructing traceable transformation histories utilizing the sesqui-pushout (SqPO) approach \cite{corradini2006sesqui}, which operates on individual objects and object hierarchies within appropriately structured categories. A transparent audit trail illuminates object transformation history while enabling reversion to any historical point. This capability proves invaluable when correcting erroneous transformations, for instance. Furthermore, such audit trails provide efficient mechanisms for accommodating multiple versions of identical objects that emerge from inconsistent transformations. \subsection*{Related work} SqPO rewriting extends both double (DPO) and single (SPO) pushout approaches to graph transformation by incorporating graph element cloning alongside conventional operations of adding, deleting, and merging graph elements. Although SqPO rewriting reversibility has received prior attention \cite{danos2014reversible}, the composition of consecutive (and not necessarily sequentially independent) SqPO rewrites remains less thoroughly developed. Such compositional constructions exist for the DPO approach (see D-concurrent productions in \cite{ehrig1991parallelism}) and for specific SqPO cases (involving linear rules \cite{behr2019sesqui} and scenarios where the first rule's right-hand side exactly matches the second rule's left-hand side \cite{lowe2015polymorphic}). We present such a construction for two consecutive general SqPO rule applications, requiring the first to be reversible. This approach draws inspiration from \cite{ehrig1991parallelism} and adapts it to SqPO rewriting. For well-defined composition, we require the underlying category to possess structure enabling well-behaved generalized object unions (formally, we require our category to be adhesive \cite{lack2005adhesive}). The concept of rule hierarchy and questions surrounding hierarchy rewrite reversibility and composition represent novel directions that extend SqPO rewriting from individual objects to object hierarchies \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. Our primary application of interest, transformation audit trails, closely relates to version control systems (VCSs) employed in software development. While such systems typically manage different software source code versions (represented as text files), our audit trail provides equivalent control for different graph or graph hierarchy versions. Like VCSs, transformation audit trails avoid maintaining object states at every transformation point by preserving only current states alongside compact transformation history representations. Moreover, through mechanisms resembling \emph{delta compression} in VCSs, such audit trails enable multiple version maintenance for identical objects and facilitate version switching. Diagram versioning for object-oriented data models in model-driven engineering domains closely relates to graph transformation audit trails since such model diagrams can be viewed as attributed graphs. However, work in this domain \cite{schneider2004coobra, barmpis2015towards} typically considers graph element addition and deletion operations (including attributes) to express data model changes, while largely excluding cloning and merging operations, as these prove difficult to interpret within data modeling contexts, whereas they hold significant interest for KR applications. Extensive research exists on database system versioning \cite{salzberg1999comparison}, including graph databases\footnote{Versioning for the Neo4j database \url{https://github.com/h-omer/neo4j-versioner-core}} \cite{castelltort2013representing, khurana2013efficient}. Such systems typically divide into snapshot- and delta-based categories (also termed copy and log), where the former stores complete database snapshots at different revision history points, while the latter preserves transformation logs. Within this context, our system occupies a hybrid category: although the audit trail stores transformation representations (logs), these logs themselves comprise subgraphs, i.e.\, graph patterns affected by transformations. An alternative classification for graph database versioning systems distinguishes between those providing revision history from individual node and edge (or relationship) perspectives and those employing graph-level perspectives \cite{castelltort2013representing}. While existing tools, including \texttt{neo4j-versioner-core} or the system presented in \cite{castelltort2013representing}, primarily address versioning from individual element viewpoints, our framework enables versioning of entire graphs and even graph hierarchies. Moreover, unlike model versioning approaches, existing database versioning techniques cannot record graph element cloning and merging operations.

text: Deep learning approaches for point cloud generation and completion have recently gained significant momentum, particularly those employing autoencoder architectures. Encoder design has been extensively investigated by methods including PointNet \cite{qi2016pointnet}, PointNet++ \cite{qi2017pointnetplusplus}, DGCNN \cite{dgcnn}, and Point Transformer \cite{zhao2020point}, all pursuing enhanced point cloud representations. Decoder architectures have similarly attracted substantial research attention. Several approaches, including \cite{Fan_2017_CVPR, achlioptas2017latent_pc, yuan2018pcn, Yang_Wu_Zhang_Jin_2021}, employ straightforward fully connected layers for coarse output generation. Alternative strategies \cite{Yang_2018_CVPR, groueix2018, liu2019morphing, Wen_2020_CVPR} transform 2D squares into 3D surfaces through deformation operations. Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(a) illustrates that fully connected layers and folding operations represent the two predominant approaches for converting latent features into point clouds. Nevertheless, these methods inadequately address the transformation process regarding point constraints, parameter efficiency, data flow optimization, and convergence characteristics. Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b) demonstrates that FC-based methods typically produce point clouds with outliers and irregular surfaces, as exemplified by the upper airplane. This limitation stems from the absence of parameter sharing among generated points, resulting in insufficient parameter allocation per point. Multi-branch extensions of these methods fail to exhibit self-clustering properties. Self-clustering refers to the tendency of points generated within each branch to form cohesive groups, thereby reflecting object locality. The lower airplane in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b) exemplifies proper self-clustering behavior. This deficiency arises because individual generated points operate independently without centripetal constraints. Folding-based approaches present a contrasting paradigm, utilizing significantly fewer parameters while employing grid priors to constrain generated points onto smooth 2-manifolds. Such constraints facilitate multi-branch expansion capabilities. However, these methods suffer from slow convergence due to the inherent difficulty of deforming 2D squares into diverse 3D surfaces using limited parameters. Additionally, real-world 3D objects frequently exhibit non-smooth surfaces. Folding operations struggle with such scenarios since they generate surfaces through smooth 2-manifold deformation. We introduce AXform, an attention-based approach that addresses these limitations in latent feature-to-point cloud transformation. Our method initially employs fully connected layers to generate points within an intermediate space. Subsequently, attention mechanisms perform weighting operations to aggregate target points from this interim space. These aggregated points are then projected into 3D space to form the final point cloud. AXform offers four key advantages. Parameter efficiency surpasses both FC-based and folding-based methods through shared network parameters. Convergence occurs more rapidly than existing approaches. Generated points demonstrate enhanced concentration through centripetal constraints. Consequently, AXform readily supports multi-branch expansion for localized generation tasks. Furthermore, Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(c) shows that our K-branch AXform variant exhibits space consistency properties, thereby enabling unsupervised semantic segmentation capabilities. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a novel attention-based transformation method for converting latent features to point clouds. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches. \item The proposed AXform supports multi-branch expansion for localized generation tasks. text: \begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.45\textwidth} \vspace{-40pt} \begin{center} \end{center} \vspace{-0.5cm} \caption{Quantization intervals utilized in the proposed method and prior works.} \vspace{-0.7cm} \end{wrapfigure} Federated Learning (FL)~\cite{mcmahan2017fl_google} has recently gained significant traction as a solution addressing stringent data privacy requirements and computational resource constraints. This paradigm enables numerous edge devices, termed workers, to collaboratively train models while maintaining data locality and privacy. Given FL's proven effectiveness, widespread adoption has occurred across diverse practical domains, including keyboard prediction~\cite{hard2018keyboard_prediction_fl, yang2018applied_keyboard} and privacy-critical applications~\cite{sheller2018multi_institutional,sheller2018multi_brain_fl,pokhrel2020fl_block_chain}. Nevertheless, FL model training necessitates frequent transmission of model weights and gradients between servers and workers. With increasing model complexity, communication overhead inevitably emerges as the primary system bottleneck. Addressing this challenge, numerous studies have explored quantization techniques applied to model weights~\cite{yu2019double_quantization,tang2019doublesqueeze} or gradients~\cite{wen2017terngrad,alistarh2017qsgd} for reducing update message sizes. Despite substantial advances, existing approaches frequently struggle to maintain model performance comparable to uncompressed float-based training under aggressive compression schemes. Furthermore, our observations indicate that low-bit quantization can degrade other established techniques (e.g., gradient sparsification~\cite{aji2017sparse_top_k,strom2015scalable_top_k}), thereby constraining additional cost reductions. We introduce a novel cosine function-based quantization methodology that, while conceptually straightforward, proves highly effective for round-trip compression of model weights and gradients. Drawing from the fundamental insight that gradients and weights with larger magnitudes carry greater information content than smaller counterparts~\cite{han2015deep_compression,lin2018deep_gradient_compression,aji2017sparse_top_k}, we exploit cosine function non-linearity to minimize quantization errors for extreme values. This approach contrasts with most existing methods~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd,han2015deep_compression} that pursue opposing objectives, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}. Moreover, our approach exhibits low computational and spatial complexity, eliminates additional training requirements, and imposes minimal overhead—characteristics particularly advantageous for federated learning environments where edge devices typically operate under resource constraints. Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse scenarios encompasses CIFAR-10 image classification and BraTS 2019 3D volume segmentation datasets. Our primary contributions include: (a) The central contribution presents a \textit{simple-yet-effective} cosine-based quantization framework that superior preserves model performance while maintaining low complexity and eliminating extra training needs, making it broadly applicable to distributed learning scenarios. (b) The proposed quantization technique addresses both model weight and gradient compression, thereby reducing aggregate communication costs in federated learning contexts. (c) Our methodology demonstrates flexibility and compatibility with existing beneficial techniques such as gradient sparsification. Through integration with complementary approaches, our system achieves model performance equivalent to uncompressed float-based training at exceptionally high compression ratios—a capability that remains challenging for alternative quantization methods.

text: Software transformation and security applications frequently demand analysis or manipulation of program binaries. The absence of source code represents the most prevalent scenario requiring such analysis. However, even with source availability, the necessary compilation toolchain or environment may be inaccessible, or the analysis may target machine-specific characteristics such as function padding or buffer spacing that depend on the actual binary representation. These applications typically commence with \emph{disassembly}---the conversion of machine code into its corresponding assembly representation. Research into \emph{disassembly} techniques and \emph{disassembler} tools traces back to at least 1980~\cite{Horspool+Marovac:1980:AnApproach}. Contemporary disassemblers achieve remarkable precision, with accuracy rates approaching or surpassing $99\percent$ on numerous real-world binaries---as demonstrated in studies such as~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} and~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Nevertheless, fundamental binary analysis challenges including indirect jump resolution and function boundary detection render the remaining ``$1$\percent'' particularly elusive. Consequently, researchers continue developing novel disassembly methodologies, with regular advances appearing in the literature---exemplified by~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}, \cite{Miller+etal:2019:probabilistic}, and ongoing improvements to established disassemblers. Evaluating high-precision disassemblers presents two fundamental difficulties. Given that disassemblers exhibit distinct vulnerabilities, minor modifications to evaluation datasets can substantially alter accuracy rankings. Regrettably, existing disassembly literature employs disparate target collections; contrast, for instance, ~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} with \cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Additionally, with current disassemblers exceeding $99\percent$ accuracy on numerous binaries, reliable ranking demands essentially perfect ground truth. Yet, as this work demonstrates, while prior research rarely elaborated on ground truth generation methodologies, our experience reveals that accurate ground truth creation involves substantial complexity and proves challenging to replicate without comprehensive documentation. These considerations motivate our belief that the community should establish standardized binary collections for benchmarking disassembler accuracy alongside practical metrics like execution time and memory consumption. To catalyze this standardization effort, we present an initial version of our evolving disassembly benchmark suite. Our suite design encompasses two primary dimensions: (a) the curated binary collection, and (b) our methodology for generating precise disassembly ground truth for instructions within these binaries. Regarding aspect (a), we contend that effective disassembly benchmarks should exhibit these characteristics: \begin{enumerate*}[(i)] \item Binary \emph{diversity} across multiple dimensions: size, application domain (e.g., text editor versus web server), compilation toolchains, % and optimization configurations. % Such diversity enables comprehensive coverage of real-world binary complexity. \item A \emph{manageable} binary count---sufficiently large yet bounded. This constraint ensures practical disassembler evaluation across all included binaries, whose total number scales multiplicatively with compiler and optimization combinations for each ISA-OS configuration. \end{enumerate*} Our current benchmark organization centers on ``project names''---specific open-source projects with designated versions (e.g., \verb!openssh-7.1p2!). Each project name specifies a target binary (e.g., \verb!sshd!) and the ISA-OS pair collection (e.g., \{x86-Linux, x64-Linux\}) included during compilation. Furthermore, each ISA-OS pair defines compiler-version combinations and optimization setting lists for the build process, detailed in~\S\ref{sec:current-benchmark}. To foster adoption, we maintain open access to our benchmark suite via GitHub (\url{https://github.com/pangine/disasm-benchmark}), anticipating community-driven evolution similar to the SPEC CPU benchmark~\cite{misc:speccpu} through collaborative input and ongoing research. For aspect (b), while disassembly ground truth generation might appear straightforward through compiler-generated assembly preservation (e.g., \verb!gcc -S!), practical implementation reveals significant complexity. Initially, even with complete assembly file access, the contained assembly statements (instructions/directives) provide incomplete machine code descriptions since certain statements permit multiple encoding variants. Furthermore, during benchmark development, we encountered numerous edge cases requiring careful handling during assembly file collection, % information extraction, % and data representation. % Section~\S\ref{sec:gt} explores these challenges alongside our solutions. Utilizing our developing benchmark suite and our mature ground truth generation and evaluation infrastructure, \S\ref{sec:eval} presents findings on four prominent open-source disassemblers: BAP~\cite{misc:bap}, Ghidra~\cite{misc:ghidra}, Radare2~\cite{misc:radaretwo}, and ROSE~\cite{misc:rose}. Our results corroborate~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} conclusions: (i) function boundary identification continues hindering accurate disassembly, and (ii) linear-sweep disassembly~\cite{Schwarz+etal:2002:Disassembly} can achieve \emph{surprisingly} high accuracy despite lacking theoretical guarantees and remaining unsuitable as a definitive solution. Our work contributes the following: \begin{enumerate*} \item We advocate for standardized binary collections spanning diverse projects with multiple compiler and optimization configurations for disassembler evaluation, offering our developing suite as a foundation for community discourse. \item We developed a novel system leveraging widely-supported compiler ``listing files'' to generate accurate disassembly ground truth. Additionally, we created evaluation tools for four major open-source disassemblers and present our comparative findings. \item We provide open access to all code and data, enabling future research and encouraging community adoption and contribution to both our system and benchmark suite. \end{enumerate*}

text: Social-engineering attacks through phishing websites represent a critical security threat that has witnessed dramatic escalation in recent years~\cite{phishincreasing:2020,data-breach:2020}. The security community has responded with sustained efforts to develop automated countermeasures employing advanced machine learning~\cite{sahingoz2019machine,rao2019detection,hassanpour2018phishing,abdelhamid2017phishing}, deep-learning~\cite{yang2019phishing,yi2018web,hassanpour2018phishing}, rule-based~\cite{moghimi2016new,sonowal2020phidma,tan2016phishwho,shirazi2018kn0w} and heuristic~\cite{nguyen2013detecting,babagoli2019heuristic,jeeva2016intelligent,sreedharan2016systems} methodologies. However, phishing campaigns demonstrate remarkable adaptability, continuously evolving through various exploits and adversarial strategies to evade automated detection mechanisms~\cite{liang2016cracking,rajivan2018creative,royremains,aleroud2020bypassing}. Consequently, domain hosting providers, anti-phishing solutions and web browsers frequently depend on phishing feeds or blocklists—curated knowledge repositories that maintain continuously updated collections of phishing URLs through manual addition or hybrid approaches combining automated discovery, community reporting, and human validation. Oest et al.~\cite{oest2020phishtime} emphasize that phishing feeds operate in a \textit{reactive} manner, creating substantial delays between a website's emergence and its eventual documentation. Nevertheless, these feeds typically undergo manual review processes, theoretically reducing error rates compared to fully automated detection approaches. This research examines phishing reports disseminated through Twitter~\cite{twitter:2021}, the widely-used microblogging service. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural investigation into evaluating this platform as a substantial knowledge repository for discovering emerging phishing websites. Throughout this study, we focus on assessing its efficacy while comparing its characteristics and performance against two established open-source phishing feeds: PhishTank and OpenPhish. Specifically, our research: (i) Assesses the credibility and information volume provided by these phishing reports, establishing comparisons with two alternative open-source phishing feeds. (ii) Given Twitter's hosting environment, these reports enable visible user interactions—a capability absent from the other feeds under examination. We therefore analyze interaction frequencies, including responses from domain registrars and organizations targeted by reported phishing URLs, while investigating how these interactions influence detection and removal of reported URLs. (iii) We examine post-sharing consequences, specifically URL persistence duration following reports and anti-phishing tool detection speed—both critical factors for preventing inadvertent user exposure to threats. Our analysis encompassed over 16k tweets containing 11k distinct URLs, collected between June 21st and August 17th, 2021. Through combined automated and manual investigation approaches, we continuously monitored numerous extracted properties from these posts, including URL activity verification, anti-phishing tool detection status, shared information content (hashtags, images, etc.), true positive rates (percentage of URLs representing genuine phishing attacks), and user interactions (likes, comments, replies). We additionally benchmarked relevant statistics against two alternative phishing feeds: PhishTank and OpenPhish. Section~\ref{datacollection} outlines our Twitter phishing report collection methodology and characterizes them according to hosting domains. Section~\ref{driveby} examines drive-by download URLs also reported by these accounts—a capability missing from the other two feeds. Section~\ref{comparison} evaluates information provided by these phishing reports (\ref{content-shared-by-reporters}), alongside PhishTank (\ref{phishtank-share}) and OpenPhish (\ref{openphish-share}). We examine shared information (screenshots, IP addresses, targeted registrar/organization names, threat classifications, etc.) and assess reliability and validity in Section~\ref{validity-url}. This section's primary objective involves comparing Twitter phishing report information against PhishTank and OpenPhish offerings, subsequently summarized in \textbf{Table~\ref{functionality}}. Unlike the other feeds that typically prohibit user interaction, Section~\ref{phishing-report-interactions} quantifies interaction volumes (favorites/retweets/comments) these reports receive on Twitter, investigating whether targeted domain/organization interactions impact reported website removal speed. We qualitatively examine interaction characteristics (Fig~\ref{fig:interaction}) and assess technological expertise of users typically engaging with these reports (\ref{followers}). Finally, Section~\ref{activity-website} determines URL persistence duration post-reporting and compares removal rates and timing with URLs posted on PhishTank and OpenPhish (Section~\ref{comparison}). We also examine anti-phishing engine coverage of phishing URLs~\ref{virustotal-coverage}. Our principal findings include: \begin{enumerate} \item Twitter demonstrates viability as a phishing report knowledge repository. During three months, users consistently shared over 16.4k reports covering 11.1k unique URLs across 203 distinct registrars, targeting 146 different organizations. Unlike PhishTank and OpenPhish, these accounts additionally reported drive-by download URLs (7\%). \item Most Twitter URL reports contained superior information compared to PhishTank and OpenPhish, potentially enabling domain registrars and anti-phishing tools to accelerate threat identification processes. \item URLs shared in these reports demonstrate high true positive rates (87%), with a single account responsible for most false positives (11%) in our dataset. \item These reports generate minimal engagement, with only 13.8\% receiving at least one comment. Domain registrars and targeted organizations (hereafter termed \textit{targets}) contributed merely 4\% of comments. However, when they responded to reports, URLs became inactive more rapidly compared to URLs without such interaction. text: The task of image classification, while long-established, remains critically important across diverse application domains including autonomous driving, industrial automation, medical diagnosis, and biometric identification~\cite{autonomous_driving, industrial_automation, medical_diagnosis, biometric_identification}. Supervised learning (SL) approaches have gained widespread adoption for addressing this challenge due to their demonstrated effectiveness~\cite{VGG, ResNet}. However, SL methods suffer from a fundamental limitation: they demand substantial training data volumes for each target class. This requirement proves problematic in numerous real-world scenarios where collecting training samples for specific classes becomes challenging (e.g., endangered species or newly emerging variants such as COVID-19 strains). The presence of \textit{unseen} classes—those lacking training data—causes SL-based models to exhibit bias toward \textit{seen} classes, thereby hindering accurate identification of novel categories. To address this limitation, researchers have developed techniques that leverage manually annotated attributes (such as color, size, and shape; illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}) for classifier training~\cite{zsl_proposal, gzsl_intro}. This approach, known as generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL), operates on the principle of learning image-attribute relationships from seen classes, then applying this knowledge to identify unseen categories. For instance, ~\cite{ALE} introduces a method that identifies unseen classes through compatibility measurement between image features and attributes. Meanwhile, ~\cite{CVAE-GZSL} employs a network that synthesizes image features from attributes to generate training data for unseen classes. Image feature extraction typically relies on networks trained for classification tasks (such as ResNet~\cite{ResNet}). However, this extraction approach suffers from a significant drawback: the resulting image features may incorporate attribute-irrelevant information (exemplified by human fingers in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), which interferes with the learning process of image-attribute relationships~\cite{DLFZRL, RFF-GZSL, Disentangled-VAE}. This paper introduces a novel GZSL technique designed to eliminate interference from attribute-irrelevant information. Our approach centers on extracting \textit{semantic features}—features that encapsulate attribute-related information—from image features, subsequently utilizing these for learning image-attribute relationships. The semantic feature extraction process employs a modified autoencoder architecture comprising two distinct encoders: \textit{semantic} and \textit{residual} encoders (depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:SD}). Essentially, the semantic encoder captures all attribute-related information within the image feature, while the residual encoder handles attribute-irrelevant components. Traditional autoencoders rely solely on reconstruction loss (the discrepancy between input and reconstructed input) for training purposes. Our methodology introduces two innovative loss functions alongside reconstruction loss to ensure the semantic encoder exclusively captures attribute-related information. Initially, we implement a mutual information (MI)-based loss that maximizes (minimizes) MI between the semantic (residual) encoder output and attributes. Given that MI quantifies dependency levels between random variables, this MI-based loss encourages attribute-related information capture by the semantic encoder while simultaneously preventing the residual encoder from capturing such information. Consequently, the semantic encoder becomes the sole repository for attribute-related information. Additionally, we incorporate a similarity-based loss that prevents the semantic encoder from capturing attribute-irrelevant information. Consider a scenario where bird images contain human fingers (as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB})—we aim to exclude finger-related features from the semantic encoder output. This objective is achieved by maximizing similarity between semantic encoder outputs from images within the same class (bird images in this example). Since attribute-irrelevant features appear in only limited image samples (e.g., human fingers in select bird images), maximizing intra-class similarity of semantic encoder outputs effectively eliminates attribute-irrelevant information. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets (AwA1, AwA2, CUB, and SUN) demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing GZSL techniques. Specifically, our model achieves 2\% improvement in GZSL classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods on both AwA2 and CUB datasets.

text: The graph community has extensively studied clique finding, which serves numerous practical applications including community detection \cite{6249683, palla2005uncovering, 7117352, fang2019efficient} and social network analysis \cite{4811845, rossi2015parallel}. Recently, the data mining community has integrated clique finding into deep learning classifiers to improve recommender systems for social networks \cite{dietrec, movierec}. Bioinformatics represents another prominent application domain, where researchers employ graph models to identify gene sequence variants \cite{variant}, efficiently cluster related genes within databases \cite{database}, and conduct protein structure analysis \cite{ppi}. The exponential growth of social media users and the expanding scale of genomic data have intensified demands for high-performance systems that can analyze massive networks to count or enumerate k-cliques. Within Graph Pattern Mining (GPM), clique finding constitutes just one problem among many. Motifs represent additional general graph patterns that attract significant research interest. Several GPM frameworks have emerged to count recurring instances of specified patterns within target graphs, including Pangolin \cite{chen2020pangolin}, Peregrine \cite{jamshidi2020peregrine}, Arabesque \cite{teixeira2015arabesque}, Fractal \cite{dias2019fractal}, and others. These frameworks employ generalized algorithms and offer APIs for counting instances of arbitrary, user-specified patterns. Conversely, specialized algorithms target k-clique counting specifically, such as kClist \cite{danisch2018listing}, Pivoter \cite{jain2020power}, and Arb-Count \cite{shi2021parallel}. These custom-designed solutions typically outperform general-purpose GPM frameworks due to their problem-specific optimizations. KClist~\cite{danisch2018listing} currently represents the state-of-the-art in clique counting algorithms, demonstrating algorithmic efficiency and substantially outperforming previous approaches. Nevertheless, when processing large graphs, it exhibits limited parallel scalability, particularly for modest clique sizes. Through careful analysis of kClist, we identify scaling bottlenecks within both primary phases: ordering and counting. The ordering phase directionalizes the graph to prevent redundant counting of identical cliques during the subsequent counting phase. KClist employs core ordering~\cite{matula1983smallest} to minimize maximum degree, thereby achieving maximum reduction in algorithmic work during counting. However, since the ordering phase consumes considerable execution time and core ordering computation is inherently sequential, scalability becomes limited by Amdahl's Law. The counting phase's parallel speedup saturates rapidly, yielding speedups as low as 5$\times$ on 24 cores for certain graphs. We determine that the counting phase typically becomes memory-bound due to poor locality and excessive memory traffic volume. We introduce CITRON (Clique Counting with Traffic Reducing Optimizations), a high-performance clique counting algorithm. Through superior parallel scalability, it substantially outperforms kClist, especially for modest clique sizes. We demonstrate that core ordering is unnecessary, and that parallelizable orderings such as degree ordering not only dramatically accelerate the ordering phase but also produce negligible counting phase slowdowns in practice. We enhance the counting phase through our novel subgraph construction approach, which significantly reduces memory accesses while improving spatial locality. Our evaluation of CITRON employs a comprehensive suite of real-world graphs, comparing performance against kClist and other prior works. For triangle counting, we achieve ordering phase speedups of $18.16 - 208.27\times$ (Geometric Mean: $102.436\times$) and counting phase speedups of $1.1-2.6\times$ (Geometric Mean: $1.798\times$), yielding total speedups of $14.37-39.37\times$ (Geometric Mean: $18.517\times$) over kClist. We have recently discovered ArbCount \cite{shi2021parallel}, which demonstrates superior performance as shown in Table \ref{table:3}. Nevertheless, we believe this paper's analysis will prove valuable for understanding k-clique counting performance characteristics.

text: The widespread adoption of mobile and edge devices has positioned federated learning~\cite{konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication} as a prominent framework for training machine learning models across geographically distributed and heterogeneous devices. This paradigm involves a central server coordinating with numerous clients to collaboratively train models using locally stored data without direct data sharing. The federated learning framework is commonly formulated as a distributed optimization challenge~\cite{konevcny2016federatedoptimization, konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication, kairouz2019advances, wang2021field}. Consider the entire dataset ${\mathcal{D}}$ partitioned across $N$ clients/devices/workers/machines, where client $i$ maintains local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$. The objective involves solving the following optimization problem while preserving data locality: \begin{align} \min_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{ f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}) := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)\right\}, \end{align} where $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i) := \mathbb{E}_{d_i\sim{\mathcal{D}}_i} f({\bm{x}}; d_i)$. The model parameter ${\bm{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ minimizes loss functions $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}})$, $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)$, and $f({\bm{x}}; d_{i})$ corresponding to the global dataset ${\mathcal{D}}$, local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$, and individual data sample $d_{i}$, respectively. \subsection{Communication efficiency} Communication overhead between the central server and clients represents a critical bottleneck in federated learning deployments, particularly when dealing with numerous clients, bandwidth-constrained devices like mobile phones, and parameter-rich machine learning models. Consequently, developing federated learning algorithms that minimize overall communication costs becomes essential, considering both \emph{the number of communication rounds} and \emph{the communication cost per communication round} required to achieve target accuracy. Two primary research directions address communication-efficient federated learning: 1) \emph{local methods}: clients perform multiple local update iterations before server communication, aiming to reduce total communication rounds; 2) \emph{compressed methods}: clients transmit compressed messages to reduce per-round communication overhead. Both research directions have attracted substantial interest. Local methods encompass algorithms such as \algname{FedAvg}~\cite{mcmahan2017communication}, \algname{Local-SVRG}~\cite{gorbunov2020local}, \algname{SCAFFOLD}~\cite{karimireddy2020scaffold} and \algname{FedPAGE}~\cite{zhao2021fedpage}. Compressed methods include numerous proposals~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd, khirirat2018distributed, mishchenko2019distributed, horvath2019stochastic, li2020acceleration, li2020unified, gorbunov2021marina, condat2021murana, li2021canita, richtarik20223pc, li2022soteriafl, zhao2022beer}. Current state-of-the-art theoretical guarantees for convex and nonconvex scenarios are established by \algname{CANITA}~\cite{li2021canita} and \algname{MARINA}~\cite{gorbunov2021marina}, respectively. This work concentrates on compression techniques for enhanced communication efficiency. Additional discussion appears in \Cref{sec:compression}. \subsection{Methods with variance reduction} Variance reduction, specifically \emph{data-variance} reduction, constitutes a well-established technique in centralized finite-sum optimization for accelerating convergence rates. Numerous optimization algorithms leverage variance reduction, including \algname{SVRG}~\cite{johnson2013accelerating,reddi2016stochastic}, \algname{SAGA}~\cite{defazio2014saga}, \algname{SCSG}~\cite{lei2017less}, \algname{SARAH}~\cite{nguyen2017sarah}, \algname{SPIDER}~\cite{fang2018spider}, \algname{SSRGD}~\cite{li2019ssrgd,li2022simple}, and \algname{PAGE}~\cite{li2021page,li2021short}. These methods typically compute stochastic gradients using data subsets (achieving improved convergence) while periodically calculating full gradients across all samples (reducing data-variance). For instance, standard gradient descent (\algname{GD}) achieves $O(N/\epsilon^2)$ convergence in nonconvex settings, whereas variance-reduced approaches \algname{SARAH/SPIDER/PAGE} attain superior $O(\sqrt{N}/\epsilon^2)$ rates. Notably, \emph{client-variance} poses the primary challenge in federated learning due to data heterogeneity, persisting even when computing local \emph{full gradients} using complete local datasets ${\mathcal{D}}_i$. text: Virtual assistants such as Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant have rapidly integrated into countless aspects of daily life, spanning from music playback to automotive navigation through voice-controlled devices. At the core of these systems lie Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) models, which serve as the artificial intelligence engines responsible for interpreting the semantic content embedded within users' spoken commands. SLU typically encompasses two fundamental sub-tasks: intent classification (IC), which determines the user's intended action from their utterance, and slot filling (SF), which identifies and extracts semantic elements within the spoken input. An illustrative example from the ATIS dataset \cite{atis} demonstrates this dual functionality: \begin{quote} \textbf{city}~~~~~~ [$_{\bf{O}}$~where] [$_{\bf{O}}$~is] [$_{\bf{B-airport\_code}}$~MCO] \end{quote} Here, the SF component must label "where" and "is" as ${\bf{O}}$ (Other), while categorizing "MCO" as ${\bf{B-airport\_code}}$, and the IC component should recognize \textbf{city} as the underlying intent. Contemporary leading SLU architectures predominantly employ DNN-based joint modeling approaches for these interconnected sub-tasks \cite{Liu2016AttentionBasedRN,do19,chen19}. Such frameworks typically incorporate dual specialized decoders for slot and intent prediction, built upon a unified encoder foundation. Following trends across numerous NLP domains, BERT-based encoder-decoder configurations have demonstrated exceptional capability in extracting contextual information, thereby enhancing SLU system performance \cite{chen19}. In standard SLU applications, BERT encoders undergo pre-training on extensive unlabeled text corpora before undergoing fine-tuning with domain-specific SLU datasets. The explosive global growth of voice-controlled device markets has created urgent demands for rapid language expansion capabilities in SLU systems. Multilingual approaches, enabling single-model deployment across multiple languages while facilitating knowledge transfer from resource-rich to resource-poor languages, represent the most promising solution to address these escalating requirements. Traditional SLU development relies on supervised monolingual datasets, constraining virtual assistants to operate within single-language sessions. Conversely, multilingual SLU models trained on diverse supervised multilingual corpora enable assistants to seamlessly handle multiple languages within individual sessions. Beyond user experience benefits, multilingual modeling offers significant developmental advantages by reducing both model complexity and supervised data requirements through cross-linguistic knowledge sharing. Nevertheless, given the substantial linguistic variations spanning lexical, syntactic, and semantic dimensions, current multilingual techniques may face inherent limitations in cross-language knowledge transfer effectiveness. This limitation prompts critical inquiries: i) what constitutes optimal cross-language knowledge transfer; ii) what represents baseline cross-language knowledge transfer; and iii) how effectively can multilingual models achieve cross-linguistic knowledge propagation. Multilingual BERT (mBERT) \cite{mBERT} has emerged as one of the most impactful multilingual technologies, gaining widespread adoption across natural language processing applications in both zero-shot\footnote{The model is trained in one language and tested on another.} and multilingual\footnote{The model is trained on multiple languages.} contexts \cite{wu-dredze-2019-beto,multiatis++}. Given that mBERT training excludes explicit cross-lingual objectives and avoids aligned datasets, its remarkable cross-lingual capabilities appear counterintuitive and have consequently motivated extensive research investigating the underlying mechanisms enabling such performance \cite{pires2019multilingual}. This work, however, concentrates on quantifying mBERT's capacity to transcend language boundaries within \textit{multilingual} SLU contexts by benchmarking its cross-linguistic knowledge transfer against both optimal and baseline scenarios. Additionally, since mBERT undergoes general-purpose pre-training, we investigate enhancement strategies for improving its multilingual effectiveness specifically for SLU applications. This paper presents two primary contributions: \textit{First}, through comprehensive experimentation with bilingual and trilingual SLU configurations, we demonstrate that while mBERT exhibits considerable proficiency in bridging language gaps across distant language families, a performance gap persists relative to ideal multilingual benchmarks. \textit{Second}, we introduce a novel adversarial architecture designed to learn both language-invariant and language-specific representations layered upon mBERT embeddings during SLU fine-tuning phases. Experimental validation confirms that our proposed methodology effectively reduces the gap toward ideal multilingual performance.

text: In recent years, micro-blogging platforms have emerged as vital sources for current and topical news dissemination. Twitter\footnote{www.twitter.com} stands as one of the most prominent micro-blogging services, connecting millions of users worldwide and facilitating the publication and exchange of brief messages known as \emph{tweets}. Since 2006, Twitter has pioneered the provision of APIs for accessing public data\footnote{https://developer.twitter.com/en.html}, enabling applications to retrieve tweets through keyword-based queries. Nevertheless, the absence of control mechanisms over retrieved tweets often results in irrelevant content. Obtaining pertinent responses necessitates multiple API calls and subsequent filtering of results. Numerous research endeavors have focused on retrieving relevant tweets based on specific queries~\cite{gabielkov2014sampling,gouriten2014scalable,li2013towards,safran2012improving}. Scholars have attempted to enhance retrieval methods by leveraging Twitter-specific features including hashtags, retweets, and mentions to identify the most pertinent tweets. A fundamental approach involves analyzing single-word queries by calculating word frequency across various Twitter features\cite{nazi2015walk}. Additionally, researchers have incorporated external information from sources like Wikipedia to augment queries by identifying semantically similar terms, thereby improving result relevance for given queries \cite{guisado2016enrich}. {This paper leverages diverse external resources including \textit{Wordnet}, \textit{Wordnik}, \textit{DBPedia}, and \textit{New York Times(NYT)} to construct comprehensive keyword sets that are semantically similar to original query terms. We additionally propose an intelligent crawling algorithm that utilizes tweet features to efficiently identify highly relevant content while circumventing Twitter's inherent limitations. Specifically, we introduce a novel crawling algorithm termed \textbf{Smart Twitter Crawling} (STiC) that addresses two key dimensions: (i) Query enhancement through external resource utilization, (ii) Twitter graph traversal employing DFS search with innovative scoring mechanisms to identify optimal nodes (tweets) pertaining to target topics. The algorithm evaluates tweet relevance by assigning scores based on multiple factors including content analysis, hashtag presence, and user interactions such as posting, replying, mentioning, or retweeting. This scoring framework enables the selection of highly relevant tweets during each iteration while continuously incorporating additional valuable related content. Comprehensive experiments were conducted using tweets collected across various query keyword categories to assess STiC algorithm precision. Our methodology demonstrates substantial improvements over simple BFS search approaches, achieving precision increases of up to 86\% for certain queries. Furthermore, we observed significant enhancements in the quantity of relevant retrieved results compared to conventional BFS models. This paper begins with related work presentation in Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork}. Subsequently, Section~\ref{sec:approach} provides detailed exposition of our smart Twitter crawling methodology, encompassing query enrichment and Twitter graph traversal techniques. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents and analyzes experimental results across different query types. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} offers conclusions and future research directions.

Section Experimental presents and analyzes the results of experiments with various types of questions. Moreover, an increase in the number of relevant retrieved documents over the usual BFS models was observed. Section Conclusions gives some conclusions and suggestions for further study. text: Electronic health records (EHRs) now consume more of clinicians' time than direct patient interaction, with inefficient documentation systems identified as a primary driver of physician stress and burnout \citep{carayon15, gardner_burnout}. While physicians favor natural language and free-text documentation over rigid structured formats \citep{khorana}, the time pressures of clinical practice have led to widespread adoption of dense acronyms and specialized jargon \citep{md_readability}. Consider this authentic Emergency Department (ED) note excerpt: \texttt{pt w/ h/o MS}. The abbreviation \texttt{MS} could signify \texttt{mitral stenosis} in cardiology contexts or \texttt{multiple sclerosis} across other specialties. Without acronym expansion, such documentation remains opaque to laypeople: \texttt{patient with a history of multiple sclerosis}. This documentation approach yields medical records that are frequently noisy, ambiguous, and fragmented. The absence of structural organization compounds comprehension difficulties for patients, fellow physicians, and computational systems \citep{Aljabri2018, patient_engagement, Koch-Weser_language2009}. Valuable clinical information embedded within EHR notes thus remains largely inaccessible and cannot readily support downstream medical care or machine learning applications requiring structured inputs. \paragraph{Statement of Contributions} We introduce \emph{contextual autocomplete}, a methodology for rapidly capturing clinical concepts during point-of-care documentation through intelligent suggestions. Our approach employs a hierarchical language model tailored for clinical concepts within the challenging domain of ED notes. The model architecture accommodates real-world hospital deployment constraints, utilizing only triage data and historical medical records accessible to physicians \emph{before} note composition begins. Rather than pursuing generative language modeling—rendered impractical by these constraints—we address the \emph{autocompletion} challenge by generating multiple suggestions for subsequent clinical concepts, enabling clinicians to select appropriate options. Since all suggestions map to standardized clinical vocabularies, our system simultaneously structures notes during composition, disambiguates concepts, and accelerates documentation workflows in operational hospital environments. \paragraph{Clinical Relevance} Contextual autocompletion serves as the foundation for intelligent EHR systems, as illustrated in Figure \ref{typing_readability}. This tool diminishes typing requirements by proposing contextually relevant terms through learned associations. Tagged terminology provides unique clinical concept identification and enables linkage with pertinent medical record information. Furthermore, these tagged elements can drive comprehensive documentation improvements while reducing physicians' cognitive burden. Tagged terms support automatic insertion across multiple note sections, minimizing redundant data entry—for instance, a tagged condition from an early note section can populate the Past Medical History section automatically, as demonstrated in Figure \ref{typing_readability}'s right panel. This approach addresses the "death by a thousand clicks" challenge plaguing current EHR systems \citep{schulte_fry_2019}. Real-time clinical concept tagging delivers immediate physician benefits through decision support capabilities; the resulting structured data enables sophisticated EHR interfaces supporting contextual information retrieval for disease histories and laboratory trends without departing from the documentation interface. Additionally, our system's clinical concept tagging facilitates translation of acronyms and specialized terminology into accessible language. Through normalization of key clinical concepts to universal vocabularies (the Unified Medical Language System, or UMLS), notes produced via our system achieve semi-structured, machine-parseable formats. \FloatBarrier \paragraph{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} Existing clinical concept extraction research attempts retrospective concept recovery from completed notes, yet these approaches frequently fail at disambiguating similar concepts and suffer from limited labeled training data \citep{mcn}. Even expert clinicians struggle with reliable concept disambiguation when clinical intent remains unclear. Developing tools that enable real-time clinical term documentation not only reduces documentation overhead but also generates large-scale prospective datasets containing labeled clinical concepts (conditions, symptoms, laboratory results, medications) within notes. These labels support robust medical knowledge graph construction, enhanced clinical entity extraction model development, longitudinal disease pattern analysis, and contextual concept representation learning. Clinical concept relationship modeling can inform and address gaps in established medical ontologies \citep{umls_missingness}. Moreover, this research demonstrates how combining diverse, noisy, and potentially incomplete patient medical record sources can establish clinical context for current settings, enabling accurate prediction of concepts relevant to emerging medical events. \FloatBarrier

text: Complex and precise finger movement control lies at the heart of human hand dexterity, which proves essential for countless daily activities. Although many animals demonstrate fine-grained motor control capabilities and basic manipulation skills, human dexterity remains unmatched in both functionality and efficacy, granting humans the distinctive capacity to execute highly sophisticated tasks effortlessly. Consequently, creating comparably intelligent control strategies for robotic hands has emerged as a holy grail within autonomous robotics research. Nevertheless, this represents an extraordinarily demanding challenge due to the high-dimensional action space and intricate intermittent interactions between hand and object. The growing popularity of reinforcement learning (RL) for addressing sensorimotor control tasks stems from its ability to discover behaviors without requiring laborious manual engineering~\cite{heess2017emergence,levine2016end}. Previous research has also shown that when equipped with large-scale computational resources, RL policies can develop valuable skills for controlling dexterous hands through purely simulated experience, subsequently performing complex real-world tasks such as in-hand rotation~\cite{andrychowicz2020learning} and Rubik's Cube solving~\cite{akkaya2019solving}. Nevertheless, manipulation policies produced by these approaches typically focus exclusively on a single predetermined object, which severely limits their practical applicability. Given the countless objects that robots may encounter in real-world scenarios, developing individual systems for each object becomes infeasible. Consequently, policies must demonstrate robust performance across object variations, ideally achieving zero-shot generalization as humans naturally do. Yet the community has largely overlooked generalization to completely novel and geometrically diverse objects for dexterous manipulation policies, primarily due to the widespread assumption that current RL algorithms cannot achieve such generalization. This work demonstrates that existing RL algorithms can generate robust and generalizable policies for high-degree-of-freedom robotic hands through straightforward modifications. Initially, we challenge the community's prevailing assumption by showing that multi-task jointly-trained policies do not inevitably underperform compared to individually trained task-specific policies. We actually demonstrate that within dexterous manipulation contexts, multi-task policies can function as \textit{generalists} capable of matching single-task \textit{specialist} policy performance. Additionally, we establish that when equipped with suitable representations that meaningfully connect tasks, such multi-task policies can even surpass single-task \textit{specialists} on entirely novel objects, despite the \textit{specialists} being trained specifically on those objects. Moreover, we reveal a linear scaling relationship between training object diversity and improved generalization, suggesting substantial potential for future advancement. We anticipate that our work will constitute a crucial step toward developing general-purpose dexterous hand controllers. Our key contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We demonstrate that multi-task policies trained across numerous objects can achieve performance parity with oracle policies trained individually on those same objects. \item We introduce a straightforward representation encoder that both enhances training efficiency and delivers superior zero-shot performance on novel objects compared to object-specific oracles. \item We conduct comprehensive analysis of potential scaling effects and relevant design choices within our methodology. \item We provide a simulated benchmark constructed using OpenAI Gym~\cite{openaigym} and existing 3D object datasets, featuring over 100 geometrically diverse real-world objects to promote future research in dexterous hand manipulation and generalization capabilities. \end{itemize}

text: Human modeling and rendering represents fundamental technology for enabling diverse applications across sports visualization, telepresence, shopping platforms, and numerous other domains. Although substantial research progress has emerged for calibrated datasets—particularly multiview laboratory configurations \cite{shysheya2019textured, liu2019neural, liu2020neural}—synthesizing arbitrary individuals from unconstrained "in the wild" data remains challenging. Existing 3D reconstruction methodologies necessitate training on synthetic ground truth meshes or 3D scan data \cite{saito2019pifu, saito2020pifuhd, alldieck2019tex2shape, huang2020arch, lazova2019360, zhu2020reconstructing}, while image-to-image translation techniques concentrate exclusively on 2D synthesis \cite{chan2019everybody, wang2018video}. We address these dual challenges through reconstructing volumetric human representations that support animation and rendering across arbitrary poses and viewpoints. Our input consists of video sequences capturing individuals engaged in unconstrained activities—tennis playing, dancing, and similar motions. The fundamental insight driving our approach recognizes that image frames extracted from sufficiently lengthy videos (spanning minutes to hours) provide rich information regarding appearance across diverse poses and viewpoints, despite individual poses potentially occurring only once from singular viewing directions. A primary contribution involves designing both a representation framework and corresponding deep network architecture that facilitate generalization to arbitrary poses and views given these image collections. Our technical contributions encompass several key elements: a human representation utilizing $RGB\alpha$ volumes that enable reposing through volumetric motion weights (building upon \cite{lombardi2019neural}), a deep network architecture that generates person-specific volumes following optimization over video data, specialized loss functions designed to match both pixel-level values and qualitative appearance characteristics of input frames, and an integrated system combining these components to enable fitting on unconstrained videos while producing reposable, free-viewpoint human renderings. We demonstrate results across varied video inputs, achieving superior performance compared to related approaches and enabling applications including motion re-targeting and bullet-time rendering effects. Our methodology acknowledges certain limitations. We assume subject appearance remains view-independent (excluding specular reflections) and, more critically, that appearance characteristics remain consistent across pose variations. This latter constraint implies optimal results when lighting conditions are relatively diffuse and shape characteristics—particularly clothing deformation—exhibit minimal variation during movement. Additionally, result resolution faces constraints from voxel grid limitations and inherent challenges associated with registering and recovering accurate body poses from uncontrolled imagery. Nevertheless, despite these constraints, we demonstrate compelling results across various sequences that, while potentially not physically precise, maintain visual plausibility.

Existing methods require ground truth meshes or 3D scan data (see for example   Pifu  Pifu HD) and image-to-image techniques are limited to synthesis of two-dimensional images (see for example   AllPeople  Wang  Video ). Our approach to these two challenges is to construct a volumetric human model that supports animation and rendering from any position and any perspective. Our input consists of a series of digitized human figures - dancing, playing tennis, etc. The basic idea is that images extracted from sufficiently long videos (minutes to hours) contain a wealth of information about the appearance of the underlying skeletal motions, despite the fact that each skeletal motion is only captured once, from a particular view. The main contribution is the construction of a framework and a deep network architecture which allows generalization to arbitrary poses and views given an annotated image collection. Our method is subject to certain restrictions. Our work introduces several major technical contributions, such as a representation of the human body in terms of RGBA volumes which enables pose-to-pose matching through the motion-weights of volumes (cite lombardi_neural), a deep architecture that can generate person- and view-dependent volumes after training on a set of annotated videos, specialized loss functions aimed at obtaining both the pixel-level values and the appearance of the input frames, and an integrated system which combines these components to produce an unconstrained and pose-able rendering of a human being. The result, given the resolution limits and the inherent difficulties in registering and reproducing body positions from images taken from the outside, is that we can obtain, for different sequences, which are perhaps not physically precise, but are visually plausible. We assume that the appearance of the subject remains view-independent (apart from the specula) and, more importantly, that the characteristics of this appearance are constant with the changes in pose. This last constraint leads to better results when the lighting is rather diffuse and the morphology of the subject—especially its clothing—does not change much during movement.

text: Neural Networks of the autoencoder variety represent a potent architecture capable of learning compressed data representations, frequently employed for denoising applications \cite{autoencoders}. Building upon this foundation, Quantum Autoencoders (QAEs) have recently surfaced as a promising approach to address the pervasive quantum noise challenge that plagues practical quantum computing implementations. Our investigation centers on the QAE framework introduced in \cite{bondarenko2019quantum}, which demonstrates near-perfect recovery of Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states corrupted by random bit-flip errors and minor unitary perturbations. The $m$-qubit GHZ state takes the form \begin{align} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}( \ket{0}^{\bigotimes m}+\ket{1}^{\bigotimes m}). \end{align} The investigation of GHZ states holds special significance due to their manifestation of long-range entanglement properties and their widespread utility across diverse quantum applications. \medskip A particularly noteworthy characteristic of the QAEs examined in this work is their remarkably shallow circuit architecture (the QAE for denoising 3-qubit GHZ states, for example, operates with merely 4 qubits), rendering them readily implementable on contemporary quantum hardware platforms. The QAE implementation leverages the Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) framework detailed in \cite{beer2019efficient}, employing unsupervised learning methodologies \cite{sents2019unsupervised}. Although \cite{beer2019efficient} presents a Matlab-based QNN implementation \cite{deepqnn}, our approach develops QAEs within a purely quantum computational paradigm utilizing the Qiskit \cite{qiskit} framework. This investigation presents a comprehensive quantum circuit-based encoding encompassing all algorithmic components involved in QAE training and evaluation procedures. Additionally, we examine crucial implementation considerations and training methodologies, supplemented by extensive QAE performance analyses. Finally, we conduct a rigorous mathematical investigation of noise effects in Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) protocols and demonstrate mitigation strategies. Consequently, our work encompasses both theoretical foundations and experimental validations of QAE systems. \medskip The manuscript structure proceeds as follows. Section \ref{Implementation} examines the theoretical foundations underlying QAE implementation and training within quantum circuit frameworks. Section \ref{Results} delivers numerical analyses characterizing QAE performance in denoising corrupted states under various noise conditions. Finally, section \ref{QSS} explores QAE applications within QSS protocols, establishing their practical importance in this domain.

text: Environmental sound offers profound insights into the physical world around us. Consider hearing: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash;} Beyond visualizing the concrete objects and actions that could generate such an audio scene, we can infer plausible higher-level scenarios—perhaps a child racing down a water slide at an amusement park, creating splashes as they hit the water (see Figure~\ref{fig:image_pivot_idea}). Machines that can parse, represent, and articulate environmental sound carry significant practical value. The National Association of the Deaf's captioning guidelines, for instance, specify that accessible audio caption systems must extend beyond speech recognition (identifying speakers and transcribing spoken content) to include textual descriptions of all sound effects, such as ``a large group of people talking excitedly at a party'', thereby conveying the complete auditory information.\footnote{{\href{https://www.nad.org/resources/technology/captioning-for-access/what-is-captioning/}{nad.org's captioning guide}}; \citet{gernsbacher2015video} discusses the benefits of video captions beyond d/Deaf users.} Research in \emph{machine hearing}~\citep{lyon2010machine} has predominantly relied on human-annotated audio-text datasets, where text takes the form of either free-form audio descriptions (such as ``the sound of heavy rain'') or structured tagsets~\citep{US8K,audioset,audiocaps,audiocaps-clotho}. Yet current supervised audio-text resources face substantial limitations. Although audio-text co-occurrences can be extracted from audio-tag associations~\citep{freesound} or video captioning datasets~\citep{rohrbach2015dataset,MSR-VTT,oncescu2021queryd}, these sources either lack sufficient relevance to environmental sound or suffer from restricted scale and coverage. This paper investigates large-scale audio-text alignment in the absence of paired audio-text (AT) data. Drawing inspiration from pivot-based approaches in unsupervised machine translation~\citep{wu2007pivot,pivot-comparison-mt}, we introduce \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, an acronym for \modelnamelong. \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace employs images as a pivot modality to bridge audio and text. This approach mirrors our opening example: upon hearing a sound, humans can mentally \emph{visualize} the corresponding situation and subsequently \emph{articulate} it. The pivoting strategy proves practically feasible given the abundant availability of image-text (VT) and video-audio (VA) co-occurrences online, from which bimodal correspondence models can be trained (see Figure~\ref{fig:keyidea}). Through implicit linking of audio and text via combined VT and VA models, we achieve \emph{zero-resource} audio-text connection—\merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace can establish audio-text relationships without ever observing explicit co-occurrence between these modalities. Our evaluation encompasses zero-shot audio-text retrieval and zero-shot audio classification. On the Clotho caption retrieval benchmark~\citep{audiocaps-clotho}, \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace exceeds the supervised state of the art by 2.2\% R@1 without utilizing any parallel AT data; for zero-shot audio classification tasks, it sets new state-of-the-art results, attaining 57.1\% accuracy on ESC50~\citep{ESC50} and 44.7\% accuracy on US8K~\citep{US8K}. We demonstrate that the zero-resource pivoting AT model \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace can be enhanced through: \begin{enumerate}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep \item[(1)] \emph{Unsupervised curation:} where noisy AT pairs are explicitly extracted from the pivoting model to serve as supplementary training data (yielding improvements of +5.7\% on ESC50 and +9.3\% on US8K); and \item[(2)] \emph{Few-shot curation:} where a limited set of human-annotated audio caption pairs becomes available during training (for example, several hundred pairs boost zero-shot audio classification accuracy by 8\% on US8K). \end{enumerate} Nevertheless, for ESC-50, our empirical scaling analysis reveals that approximately $2^{21} \approx 2\text{M}$ aligned audio-text pairs would be required for the zero-shot model to achieve human parity on ESC50 within our framework—representing an order-of-magnitude increase over the largest currently available audio-text corpus from~\citet{audiocaps}. \begin{comment} Altogether, \yanpeng{this just duplicates the above para, maybe turn the above para into takeways?}: \begin{itemize}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep] \item[(1)] We introduce \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, a tri-modal pivoting model which learns strong \yanpeng{is "strong" too much?}\youngjae{then we can tone down a little, how about promising or robust/firm?} audio-text alignment without using any parallel audio-text pairs. \item[(2)] We investigate cases of minimum audio-text supervision and find that even un-aligned audio-text pairs help. \item[(3)] We study empirical scaling laws for \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace and find that filling the gap between zero-shot performance and supervised performance (e.g., on audio classification) would require a prohibitively large number of aligned audio-text pairs.\yanpeng{this finding is a bit strange, maybe it is because most of the newly added training samples have already been there in the training data.} \end{itemize} We believe that, by introducing the first tri-modal pivoting model and conducting comprehensive model analyses, our work will inspire future work on learning audio-text connections with little to no supervision. \end{comment}

text: The advent of large pre-trained language models such as BERT~\cite{bert} has fundamentally transformed Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. Through straightforward fine-tuning procedures, these models demonstrate remarkable adaptability across diverse tasks. Early in 2019, \textit{Nogueira and Cho}~\cite{passage_ranking} established new state-of-the-art performance -- with substantial improvements -- on the MS MARCO passage re-ranking task, thereby establishing the foundation for LM-based neural ranking architectures. Given stringent efficiency constraints, initial deployments of these models focused on re-ranking within two-stage ranking pipelines, where candidate generation relies on bag-of-words models (e.g. BM25) utilizing inverted indexes for first-stage retrieval. Although BOW models maintain their status as robust baselines~\cite{neural_hype}, they encounter the persistent vocabulary mismatch challenge, wherein relevant documents may lack query terms. Consequently, efforts have emerged to replace conventional BOW approaches with learned (neural) ranking systems. Such model design presents multiple efficiency and scalability obstacles: thus requiring methodologies that enable offline computation of most processing while maintaining rapid online inference. Dense retrieval employing approximate nearest neighbors search demonstrates remarkable performance~\cite{xiong2021approximate,qu-etal-2021-rocketqa,lin-etal-2021-batch,Hofstaetter2021_tasb_dense_retrieval}, yet continues to benefit from BOW models (e.g. through signal combination), given the lack of explicit term matching. Accordingly, recent research has increasingly focused on learning \emph{sparse representations} for both queries and documents~\cite{snrm, dai2019contextaware,nogueira2019document,zhao2020sparta,sparterm2020,gao-etal-2021-coil,10.1145/3404835.3463030,10.1145/3404835.3463098}. This approach enables models to leverage advantageous BOW characteristics including exact matching of (potentially latent) terms, inverted index efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, through modeling implicit or explicit (latent, contextualized) \emph{expansion} mechanisms -- analogous to conventional IR expansion models -- these approaches can mitigate vocabulary mismatch issues. Building upon the SPLADE model~\cite{10.1145/3404835.3463098}, this paper introduces multiple enhancements and modifications that yield effectiveness or efficiency improvements: \begin{enumerate*} \item through straightforward modifications to SPLADE's pooling mechanism, we achieve substantial effectiveness gains; \item simultaneously, we present a model extension eliminating query expansion. This variant offers inherent efficiency advantages through complete offline pre-computation and indexing, while maintaining competitive performance; \item ultimately, we employ distillation techniques~\cite{hofstatter2020improving} to enhance SPLADE performance, achieving near state-of-the-art results on both the MS MARCO passage ranking task and the BEIR zero-shot evaluation benchmark~\cite{beir_2021}. \end{enumerate*}
