text: Statistical agencies and organizations increasingly gather and disseminate datasets containing information about individual groups, which subsequently power numerous optimization and machine learning algorithms. These released datasets frequently encompass sensitive information subject to stringent privacy regulations. For instance, U.S. census data falls under Title 13 regulations \cite{Title13}, mandating that the Census Bureau's data releases prevent individual identification. Similarly, European data releases must comply with the General Data Protection Regulation \cite{GDPR}, governing personal data control and transfer. Consequently, statistical agencies must publish privacy-preserving data and statistics that satisfy these regulatory frameworks. \emph{Differential Privacy} \cite{Dwork:06} has emerged as a particularly compelling approach for achieving this objective. This formal privacy framework establishes bounds on disclosure risk for any individual participating in computational processes. Recognized as the gold standard for privacy protection, differential privacy has gained widespread adoption across major corporations \cite{erlingsson2014rappor,apple} and government agencies \cite{abowd2018us}. For data release applications, differentially private mechanisms typically introduce precisely calibrated noise into datasets prior to publication. While this approach ensures privacy guarantees, it simultaneously compromises the fidelity of released data. Specifically, the noise injection process frequently generates datasets that violate domain-specific consistency constraints. Consider census statistics, where population counts satisfying particular properties must maintain consistency across geographical hierarchies—from national to state to county levels. Independent noise injection cannot preserve such constraint consistency. Addressing this challenge requires \emph{post-processing} the differentially private outputs through data-independent transformations that restore consistency with domain constraints. This post-processing stage preserves differential privacy guarantees. Furthermore, when feasible regions exhibit convexity, a widely employed class of post-processing functions known as \emph{projections} demonstrably enhances accuracy. Post-processing has achieved notable success across diverse applications, spanning census data \cite{abowd2018us}, energy systems \cite{fioretto:TSG20}, and mobility analysis \cite{xi:15}. Nevertheless, post-processing's impact on noise distributions remains poorly characterized: common arguments suggest it may introduce bias and elevate variance. Figure \ref{fig:bias} demonstrates this phenomenon using a census data-release scenario detailed subsequently. The figure contrasts the Laplacian residual distribution $\tilde{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\bm{x}$ represents true data and $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ denotes data with applied Laplacian noise, against the post-processed residual $\hat{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\hat{\bm{x}}$ represents $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ projected onto the feasible region. Results from two counties reveal that post-processing introduces substantial bias in their corresponding privacy-preserving data. This paper's primary contribution involves establishing foundational understanding of post-processing properties. Drawing motivation from census applications, we examine the behavior of two prevalent post-processing function classes—\emph{projections}—within domains where feasibility spaces are defined by linear equations. These classes are distinguished by non-negativity constraint presence. Our analysis demonstrates that projections without non-negativity constraints introduce no bias. For projections incorporating non-negativity constraints, we establish bias upper bounds that illuminate problem types where bias becomes significant. Additionally, we provide comprehensive analysis of a crucial sub-problem addressing hierarchical constraints in data-release tasks: we fully characterize post-processed data's residual distribution, demonstrate its convergence toward Laplace distribution, and illuminate projection effects on post-processed data variance, potentially carrying substantial group fairness implications.

text: We examine a perimeter defense scenario within a conical environment where a single mobile vehicle attempts to intercept mobile intruders before they breach a designated region (the perimeter). Such situations emerge when UAVs must tag intruders or transmit crucial information to them prior to their arrival at a critical zone. Intruders spawn at the environment's boundary and advance radially inward at constant velocity toward the perimeter. The defending vehicle, equipped with a finite capture radius, operates at bounded speed (exceeding that of intruders) while striving to \textit{capture} the maximum number of intruders before perimeter breach. Since intruder quantity and arrival positions are progressively disclosed, this constitutes an online optimization problem. Previous perimeter defense research has predominantly concentrated on optimal strategies for limited agent numbers or examined stochastic intruder arrival processes~\cite{von2020multiple,macharet2020adaptive,ShivamDVR2019}. While these investigations yield valuable understanding, they fundamentally neglect \emph{worst-case performance} scenarios where intruders might coordinate strategically to overwhelm defensive capabilities \cite{von2021turret}. We employ competitive analysis techniques~\cite{sleator1985amortized} for evaluating online vehicle motion planning algorithms. Competitive analysis quantifies online algorithm $A$ performance through the \emph{competitive ratio} concept—the quotient of optimal offline algorithm performance divided by algorithm $A$ performance under worst-case input conditions. Algorithm $A$ achieves $c$-competitiveness when its competitive ratio remains bounded by $c$, ensuring performance within factor $c$ of optimality across all input instances. Here, algorithm performance—whether online or offline—is quantified by the captured intruder fraction. Vehicle routing with dynamically arriving inputs represents a related research domain. Originally formulated on graphs in~\cite{psaraftis1988dynamic}, conventional approaches necessitate route re-planning as new information emerges. For comprehensive literature review, we direct readers to \cite{bullo2011dynamic} and associated references. Traditional vehicle routing problems feature static input (\emph{demands}), focusing on shortest route identification through demands to optimize cost-reward metrics; examples include total service duration or \emph{serviced} input quantity. Perimeter defense scenarios involve dynamic input (intruders) advancing toward specified regions, creating greater complexity than static counterparts. Our earlier investigations introduced perimeter defense problems in circular and rectangular environments with stochastic input generation \cite{ShivamDVR2019,Smith2009translating}. The current work's primary distinction lies in \emph{competitiveness} characterization for worst-case rather than average-case inputs. Single-vehicle, single-intruder perimeter defense problems originated in~\cite{isaacs1965differential}. Subsequently, perimeter defense has been predominantly formulated as pursuit-evasion differential games. Multiplayer variants have received extensive study as reach-avoid games, emphasizing control policy design for both intruders and defenders \cite{chen2016multiplayer,garcia2019strategies,davydov2020pursuer}. Standard approaches require Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation solutions, typically suitable only for low-dimensional state spaces within simple environments \cite{margellos2011hamilton,chen2014path}. Contemporary research includes \cite{yan2019matchingbased, shishika2019perimeter,velhal2021decentralized,lee2021guarding}. The authors of \cite{yan2019matchingbased} propose maximum matching-based receding horizon strategies, while \cite{ shishika2019perimeter,velhal2021decentralized} examine scenarios constraining defenders to perimeter positions and \cite{lee2021guarding} extends reach-avoid games to $n$-dimensional Euclidean spaces. We previously introduced competitive analysis-based perimeter defense for linear environments \cite{bajaj2021competitive}. Our current work's key differentiation involves environmental geometry, yielding novel insights regarding optimal vehicle placement, capture radius significance, and additional competitiveness guarantee conditions. This paper's general contribution addresses conical environments with unit radius and angle $2\theta$, where arbitrary intruder numbers are released at circumferential positions during arbitrary time instances. Upon release, intruders advance radially inward at fixed speed $v<1$, targeting a conical perimeter of radius $\rho<1$ and angle $2\theta$. A single vehicle with finite capture radius $r$ operates at maximum unit speed to capture intruders. Our primary contributions follow. We establish two necessary parameter space conditions for achieving $c$-competitive algorithms with finite $c$. Specifically, we characterize parameter regimes where no online algorithm achieves $c$-competitiveness and regimes where no algorithm can exceed $2$-competitiveness. Subsequently, we design and analyze three algorithm classes, establishing their competitiveness properties. We identify parameter regimes where the first two algorithms achieve provable $1$ and $2$-competitiveness, respectively, while the third algorithm maintains finite competitive ratios varying with problem parameters ($r,\rho,\theta$). The paper organization proceeds as follows. Section \ref{sec:Problem} formally describes our problem and defines competitive ratios for online algorithms. Section \ref{sec:Fundamental_limits} establishes two necessary conditions: first regarding finite competitive ratio achievement and second concerning optimal $2$-competitive ratio bounds. Section \ref{sec:Algorithms} designs and analyzes three algorithms while establishing their competitive ratios, section \ref{sec:Results} provides additional insights through extensive parameter space visualizations, and finally, section \ref{sec:Conclusion} summarizes this work while outlining future research directions.

text: Given the ground truth mask of the initial frame, Semi-VOS performs object tracking across all subsequent video frames. Each pixel receives classification as either background or tracked object in VOS. Real-world applications spanning autonomous driving, surveillance, video editing, and emerging augmented reality/mixed reality devices demonstrate the broad utility of this task. The challenge in VOS stems from the need to differentiate the target object from visually similar objects while accommodating temporal appearance variations and occlusions. Video object segmentation has motivated diverse methodological approaches, including online learning~\cite{robinson2020learning, maninis2018video}, mask propagation~\cite{lin2020flow, cheng2017segflow}, and template matching~\cite{wang2019fast, oh2019video}. These previous methods share a common strategy: leveraging temporal information from preceding frames—whether exclusively the first frame, selected previous frames (commonly first and last), or the complete frame history—to generate high-quality segmentation masks. Our work poses a fundamentally different question\\ \textbf{Q: Can we use temporal information to identify when the object appearance and position has not changed across frames?}\\ Such capability would enable bypassing computationally expensive mask generation for frames where the result closely resembles the previous frame's mask. A lightweight model could instead generate the current frame's mask through minor modifications to previous frame features. Fig.~\ref{fig:teaserIntro2}(a) reveals that consecutive frames in popular DAVIS and YouTube-VOS datasets frequently exhibit highly similar object masks (73.3\% of consecutive frames in DAVIS 17 achieve IoU exceeding 0.7). This observation motivates our construction of an efficient temporal matching module that rapidly quantifies inter-frame similarity. The similarity metric gates expensive mask computation—high similarity triggers feature reuse with minimal refinements, bypassing costly mask generation. This strategy eliminates the majority of current frame computations while preserving accuracy. Our approach enhances existing video object segmentation methods, and we demonstrate its versatility by integrating our framework into multiple established models—FRTM~\cite{robinson2020learning} and TTVOS~\cite{park2020ttvos}. We pioneer the dynamic skipping of segmentation mask computation based on object movement patterns. This contribution represents a significant advancement toward enabling high-quality video object segmentation on mobile devices with real-time performance and minimal battery consumption. This paper presents the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We establish the case for leveraging temporal information to bypass mask generation during frames exhibiting minimal movement. \item We develop a comprehensive framework for computational skipping, incorporating sub-networks for inter-frame movement estimation, dynamic selection between full-network processing and previous frame feature reuse, and a novel loss function for training this dynamic architecture. \item We validate our approach across multiple video object segmentation models (FRTM, TTVOS) and challenging datasets (DAVIS 16, DAVIS 17, Youtube-VOS), achieving up to $47.5\%$ computational savings and $1.45\times$ FPS improvement while maintaining accuracy within approximately 0.4 $\%$ of baseline performance on DAVIS 16. \end{itemize}

text: The joint task of query attribute value extraction encompasses two critical components: identifying named entities within search queries that represent diverse surface forms of attribute values, and normalizing these entities into canonical representations to address issues of misspelling and abbreviation. These complementary sub-tasks are conventionally termed named entity recognition (NER)~\cite{chiu2016named} and attribute value normalization (AVN)~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. Figure~\ref{fig:framework} demonstrates the workflow of optimal query attribute value extraction. Consider a user query ``{\it MK tote for womans}''—a NER model first identifies entity types: ``brand'' for "{\it MK}", ``product type'' for "{\it tote}", and ``audience'' for ``{\it womans}''. While these extracted entities represent informal surface forms of attribute values, they fail to align with the canonical attribute values used to index products in formal written style. The abbreviation ``{\it MK}'' represents the brand ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' serves as a hyponym for the product type "{\it handbag}", and ``{\it womans}'' contains a spelling error. Such misalignment creates substantial obstacles for product search engines attempting to retrieve relevant items that match user preferences. Consequently, the AVN module becomes equally crucial, transforming surface forms into canonical representations: ``{\it MK}'' becomes ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' becomes ``{\it handbag}'', and ``{\it womans}'' becomes ``{\it women}''. Within E-commerce environments, extracting these attribute values from queries proves essential for numerous product search applications, including product retrieval~\cite{cheng2020end}, ranking~\cite{wen2019building}, and query rewriting~\cite{guisado2016enrich}. Current research predominantly concentrates on surface form attribute value extraction through NER while neglecting canonical form transformation, rendering these approaches impractical for real-world scenarios~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. To address this limitation, we propose a unified query attribute value extraction system encompassing both phases. We enhance extraction performance by leveraging large-scale weakly-labeled behavioral data to reduce supervision costs. Regarding the initial NER stage, recent deep learning advances (such as Bi-LSTM+CRF) have demonstrated promising outcomes~\cite{huang2015bidirectional,raganato2017neural}. Nevertheless, these models depend heavily on extensive labeled datasets, where manual token-level annotation proves particularly expensive and labor-intensive. Previous E-commerce studies~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing,cheng2020end,wen2019building} have attempted to mitigate this challenge by utilizing large-scale behavioral data from products as weak supervision for queries through simple string matching strategies. However, these weakly-supervised labels introduce substantial noise due to partial or incomplete token labels derived from exact string matching. Table~\ref{tab:ws_example} case\#1 illustrates this issue: when using attribute values from the top-clicked product ``{LG 32-inch television}''—``brand'' for ``{\it LG}'', ``size'' for ``{\it 32-inch}'', ``product type'' for ``{\it television}''—as weak supervision to match query ``{\it lg smart tv 32}'', only the ``brand'' label for ``{\it lg}'' can be generated, obscuring valuable knowledge for unannotated tokens. Consequently, weak supervision-based methods~\cite{shang2018learning,cheng2020end} typically exhibit poor performance, deteriorating further when powerful pre-trained language models (PLMs) like BERT~\cite{devlin2019bert} are introduced, as PLMs readily overfit to noise. We address this challenge through a more robust approach that incorporates strongly-labeled human-annotated data to denoise weak labels from distant supervision. This strategy enables the NER model to leverage both large-scale weakly-labeled behavioral data and strongly-labeled human-annotated data more effectively. Concerning the second AVN phase, customers frequently employ diverse surface forms when referencing attribute values in search queries due to misspellings, spelling variants, or abbreviations. This phenomenon appears regularly in user queries and product titles across e-commerce platforms. eBay reports that 20\% of product titles in clothing and shoes categories contain such surface form brands~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. Therefore, normalizing surface form attribute values derived from NER signals into unified normalized attribute values becomes critical—a aspect typically overlooked by existing research~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. Weakly-labeled behavioral data can also support AVN while reducing human annotation requirements. For instance, the query ``{\it MK tote for womans}'' mentioning brand ``{\it MK}'' generates clicks on products associated with brand ``{\it Michael Kors}''. We can reasonably infer strong connections between surface form value ``{\it MK}'' and canonical form value ``{\it Michael Kors}'' when this association appears across multiple queries. Based on these insights, we introduce a unified \textbf{QUE}ry \textbf{A}ttribute Value Extraction in E\textbf{CO}mmerce (\textbf{QUEACO}) framework that efficiently exploits large-scale weakly-labeled behavioral data for both query NER and AVN. For query NER, QUEACO employs strongly-labeled data to denoise weakly-labeled data through a novel teacher-student network, where a teacher network trained on strongly-labeled data generates pseudo-labels to refine weakly-labeled data for instructing a student network. Unlike conventional teacher-student networks that produce pseudo-labels from fixed teachers, our pseudo-labeling process continuously and dynamically adapts based on student performance feedback on strongly-labeled data. This approach encourages the teacher network to generate superior pseudo-labels for student instruction, maximally reducing error propagation from noisy weak labels. For query AVN, we utilize weakly-labeled query-to-attribute behavioral data and QUEACO NER predictions to model associations between surface form and canonical form attribute values. This enables normalization of surface form attribute values from queries to the most relevant canonical form attribute values from products. Extensive experiments on a real-world large-scale E-commerce dataset empirically demonstrate that QUEACO NER significantly surpasses state-of-the-art semi-supervised and weakly-supervised methods. Additionally, we qualitatively establish the effectiveness and necessity of QUEACO AVN. Our contributions include: (1) To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt at proposing a unified query attribute value extraction system in E-commerce, incorporating both query NER and AVN. QUEACO automatically identifies product-related attributes from user queries and transforms them into canonical forms by leveraging weak supervision from large-scale behavioral data; (2) Our QUEACO NER constitutes the first work efficiently utilizing both human-annotated strongly-labeled data and large-scale weakly-labeled data from query-product click graphs. The proposed QUEACO NER model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines; (3) We introduce the QUEACO AVN module that employs aggregated query-to-attribute behavioral data to establish connections among queries, surface form attribute values, and canonical form values. The proposed QUEACO AVN module effectively normalizes surface form values affected by spelling errors, spelling variants, and abbreviation issues.

text: Manipulation seeks to establish specific spatial relationships between objects, typically requiring precise contact configurations. While structured environments allow robots to achieve desired contact through predetermined poses, unstructured settings demand adaptable positioning strategies. Robots equipped with robust contact mode detection capabilities can enhance autonomous operation by leveraging real-time contact information for controller transitions \cite{bledt2018} or as feedback signals in learning frameworks \cite{vecerik2018}. A {\it contact mode} represents a constraint imposed on the combined generalized coordinates $q$ of robot and environment, expressed as $\phi_i(q) = 0$ for mode $i$. Traditional robotics often treats this as an infinitely rigid kinematic constraint, either eliminated or managed through impulsive forces in time-stepping methodologies \cite{stewart2000}. Our approach adopts a compliant contact framework where forces correlate with position $q$ \cite{castro2020, minniti2021a}. While contact can alternatively be characterized through inequality constraints $\phi_i(q) \geq 0$ to prevent rigid body interpenetration \cite{posa2014, stewart2000}, we decompose contact conditions into distinct modes governed by equality constraints \cite{minniti2021a}. Task representation and planning benefit significantly from contact mode characterization. Since contact behavior depends on surface geometry, contact modeling finds particular application in locomotion where planar surfaces simplify $\phi(q)$ expressions \cite{posa2014}. For manipulation tasks with predetermined simple constraints, sequential contact modes can encode task structure \cite{fengpan2004}, enabling systematic motion planning \cite{deschutter2007, polverini2019}. Specialized instrumentation can demonstrate contact geometry \cite{meeussen2007}, while data-driven approaches have explored learning contact geometry on simplified forms \cite{pfrommer2020}, though robotic manipulation applications remain limited. Environmental object variations compromise offline contact models \cite{rosell2000}, necessitating online contact detection for improved robustness. Environment dynamics estimation has matured through Kalman filtering approaches for stiffness \cite{rovedaa} or impedance estimation \cite{minniti2021a}. Locomotion research has advanced stochastic foot contact mode estimation \cite{bledt2018}, demonstrating enhanced resilience to unexpected terrain variations. Manipulation applications have explored discrete contact mode estimation via recursive Bayesian methods \cite{jasim2014, ren2018, haninger2018} and support vector machine approaches \cite{golz2015}. Contact mode sensing capabilities depend critically on hardware architecture. Design choices influence peak collision forces \cite{wensing2017, bicchi2004, haninger2019a} and contact stability characteristics \cite{eppinger1992, pratt1995}. Strategic compliance placement, magnitude, and structure can optimize energy efficiency \cite{bolivar-nieto2021, haddadin2018}, minimize information requirements \cite{haninger2021}, or reduce problem dimensionality \cite{hamaya2020}. However, compliance introduces trade-offs, constraining feasible feedback gains \cite{tomei1991} and diminishing feedforward control effectiveness \cite{dellasantina2017}, thereby limiting motion control performance. This paper contributes a systematic approach for designing compliance to enhance contact mode estimation. While contact mode estimation techniques are well-established \cite{bledt2018, jasim2014, ren2018, haninger2018}, the influence of mechatronic design on estimation performance remains unexplored. Previous analytical frameworks for contact mode `distinguishability' exist \cite{debus2005}, but our methodology incorporates compliance effects and sensor noise considerations. We begin by presenting compliant contact models, followed by information gain analysis for position and force measurements under complete and partial observability conditions. Closed-form information gain expressions are derived for linear inertial systems. Experimental validation demonstrates that information gain metrics predict both certainty and convergence speed in assembly monitoring and collision detection scenarios, where compliance location and magnitude are systematically varied. \subsubsection*{Notation} Boldface notation denotes random variables ${\bf n} \sim p(n)$. text: Consider a weighted tree $T$ and its induced tree metric $M_T$, which forms a complete graph on $T$'s vertices where each edge $(u, v)$ carries weight equal to the path weight connecting $u$ and $v$ in $T$. For any $t\ge 1$, a $t$-spanner of a metric $(V, d)$ constitutes a subgraph $H$ of the complete graph on $V$ such that each distinct pair $u, v\in V$ connects via some path in $H$ with total weight bounded by $t\cdot d(u, v)$. Such connecting paths are termed $t$-spanner paths. When every point pair connects through a $t$-spanner path containing at most $\Lambda$ edges, the $t$-spanner possesses diameter $\Lambda$. Sparsity represents a typical design goal for $t$-spanners, frequently targeting linear edge counts. Graph lightness measures the ratio between a graph's weight and its minimum spanning tree weight. Solomon and Elkin \cite{tree-spanner} present a 1-spanner construction for tree metrics. Their construction, applied to an $n$-vertex weighted tree with maximum degree $\Delta$, yields a 1-spanner containing $O(n)$ edges, exhibiting $O(\log n)$ diameter and $O(\log n)$ lightness, while maintaining maximum degree within $\Delta + O(1)$. Beyond its intrinsic interest, this tree metric 1-spanner serves as a fundamental tool across multiple works for diameter reduction in various Euclidean and doubling metric spanner constructions \cite{short-thin-lanky,doubling-spanner,optimal-euclidean-spanners,tree-spanner,partitions-to-covers}. Following spanner construction, efficient path discovery becomes crucial. Local routing algorithms for weighted graphs $G$ enable message transmission from any vertex to specified destinations. At each vertex $u$ along the routing path, the successor selection relies solely on destination knowledge, $u$'s neighborhood information, and potentially additional data stored at $u$. Routing algorithm efficiency encompasses both the travel distance required for message delivery and per-vertex storage demands. Extensive literature addresses local routing algorithms, with design complexity clearly correlating to underlying network properties. Some researchers target very general network classes—for instance, Chan et al.'s algorithm \cite{heirarchical-routing-in-doubling-metrics} operates on arbitrary networks, though performance depends on induced doubling dimension. Others pursue highly efficient algorithms for specific network classes, exemplified by research into routing algorithms for planar graph varieties \cite{convex-subdivisions,routing-in-delaunay}. Efficient local routing support represents a desirable spanner characteristic, prompting recent research into spanners that simultaneously achieve routing efficiency alongside other properties, as demonstrated by Ashvinkumar et al. \cite{local-routing-in-sparse-and-light}. Literature appears sparse regarding spanners achieving both local routing support and low diameter. Given a spanner with diameter $\Lambda$, natural requirements dictate that local routing algorithms should match this diameter—guaranteeing termination within $\Lambda$ hops. Abraham and Malkhi \cite{compact-routing-in-euclidean-metrics} provide a construction yielding $(1+\epsilon)$-spanners for two-dimensional Euclidean points (any $\epsilon > 0$) with accompanying routing algorithms. Their routing algorithm achieves $O(\log D)$ diameter with high probability, where $D$ represents the ratio between maximum and minimum inter-point distances. For $n$ points on uniform grids, the routing algorithm demonstrates $O(\log n)$ routing ratio with high probability. This paper establishes that Solomon and Elkin's 1-spanner construction \cite{tree-spanner} supports local routing algorithms achieving worst-case $O(\log n)$ diameter. Section~\ref{app:doubling} demonstrates how this routing algorithm adapts to doubling metric $(1+\epsilon)$-spanners that employ the 1-spanner construction for low diameter achievement while preserving low weight and degree properties.

text: For a string $T$ of length~$n$, a text index constitutes a data structure capable of responding to the subsequent queries when given a pattern~$P$ of length~$m$: \begin{description} \crampedItems \item[\functionname{exists}(P)]: does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \item[\functionname{count}(P)]: how often does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \item[\functionname{locate}(P)]: where does the pattern~$P$ occur in $T$? \end{description} These queries yield a boolean value, a numeric count, and a collection of starting positions within the text, respectively. Since the cardinality of the set returned by $\functionname{locate}(P)$ equals the result of $\functionname{count}(P)$, and since $\functionname{count}(P) > 0$ represents a boolean expression equivalent to $\functionname{exists}(P)$, $\functionname{locate}(P)$ stands as the most comprehensive query type. The FM-index~\cite{ferragina00fmindex} exemplifies such text indexing structures prominently. This index comprises a wavelet tree~\cite{grossi03wavelet} constructed over the BWT~\cite{burrows94bwt} of the input text, enabling $\functionname{count}(P)$ responses in time proportional to $P$'s length multiplied by the wavelet tree's operational overhead, which ranges from logarithmic in alphabet size to constant time~\cite{belazzougui14index}. When the BWT contains $r$ maximal character runs, the structure admits representation through two supplementary bit vectors~\cite[Thm.~3]{makinen05rle} of length~$n$, requiring $r \lg \sigma + \oh{r \lg \sigma} + \Oh{n}$ bits of storage. Huffman-shaped wavelet trees can further compress this space by exploiting zeroth-order empirical entropy on the string formed by distinct run letters in the BWT\@. For $\functionname{locate}$ functionality, BWT-based indexes incorporate suffix array sampling~\cite{manber93sa}, demanding $n \lg n$ bits in uncompressed form. Since this augmentation operates orthogonally to our proposed structure, we defer $\functionname{locate}$ considerations to future investigations. Nevertheless, the translation of these algorithms into implementable quantum circuits presents ongoing challenges. Numerous research groups employ machine learning \cite{cincio2018learning, fosel2021quantum}, genetic algorithms \cite{lee07,rasconi2019an}, and linear algebra methodologies \cite{re:amy:phds,nam2018automated} to construct circuits implementing quantum primitives—either exactly or approximately—that serve as fundamental components in quantum algorithms. Parallel efforts focus on developing optimization strategies for efficient mapping between logical circuits and physical quantum hardware \cite{itoko2020optimization,zulehner2018an}. Our investigation addresses the extension of SWAP tests to encompass arbitrary numbers of overlapping quantum states. Traditional two-state SWAP tests constitute valuable quantum computing primitives, utilizing controlled-swap (CSWAP) gates alongside ancillary qubits to estimate inner products $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ between pure quantum states $\phi$ and $\psi$ \cite{kopczyk2018quantum}, and to evaluate overlaps $\mathtt{Tr}(\rho \sigma)$ for mixed states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. When $\rho=\sigma$, SWAP tests quantify the purity of quantum state $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. While classical evaluation of $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ for two $q$-qubit states exhibits exponential scaling in $q$, quantum SWAP test circuits demonstrate linear depth scaling \cite{garcia2013swap}, yielding exponential speedups that confer quantum advantage when error correction or mitigation becomes feasible. State overlap estimation through SWAP tests finds application across diverse quantum computing domains. These tests facilitate quantum state characterization, including entanglement and indistinguishability measurements \cite{Foulds2021, garcia2013swap}. They provide benchmarking capabilities for quantum computers through decoherence monitoring throughout circuit execution. Additionally, SWAP tests serve as essential components in hybrid quantum machine learning frameworks. Quantum supervised learning applications \cite{kopczyk2018quantum,ciliberto2018quantum,havlicek2019supervised}, particularly quantum support vector machines (SVM) \cite{rebentrost2014quantum, rudolph2020generation}, leverage these tests for pairwise distance measurements during cluster assignment phases. Although improvements to two-state SWAP tests for high-dimensional systems have received considerable attention \cite{cincio2018learning, garcia2013swap}, implementations have historically been restricted to pairwise quantum state comparisons \cite{kathuria2020implementation}, with the notable exception of a three-state model described in \cite{Hai-Rui, Galvao2019}. We investigate extensions of SWAP tests to $m$ arbitrary pure quantum states $\ket{\phi_{1}...\phi_{m}}$, enabling computation of $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ across all pairs $i\neq j$ through at most $O(\log{m})$ measurements. Our methodology employs a pairing unitary $\mathcal{U}_{m}$ constructed from $O(m)$ CSWAP gates controlled by $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. This pairing operator transforms $m$ state registers into superposition states where all pairs $(\phi_{i}, \phi_{j})$ manifest with positive probability on the initial two state registers, labeled by basis states formed through ancillary qubits. Standard two-state SWAP tests applied to resulting superposition states enable measurements on ancillary qubits, matching ancillary basis state probabilities to corresponding state overlaps. For arbitrary $m$, constraining measurements to $O(\log m)$ proves essential for guaranteeing polynomial oracle calls. Numerically, we implement genetic procedures searching optimal CSWAP gate applications to maximize pair appearances on quantum circuit's first two registers. text: The exponential growth in radiological imaging capabilities has led to unprecedented volumes of ophthalmic image data. Three primary modalities dominate ophthalmic imaging: (1) \textbf{Slit Lamp.} This technique \cite{cheung2011validity} enables comprehensive examination of both anterior and posterior eye segments, encompassing the eyelid, sclera, conjunctiva, iris, crystalline lens, and cornea. (2) \textbf{Retinal Fundus.} As a crucial imaging modality, retinal fundus photography facilitates the diagnosis of numerous ocular pathologies \cite{fu2018joint,fu2018disc} through detailed visualization of the eye's inner lining and posterior structures. (3) \textbf{ASOCT.} Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography provides high-resolution visualization and quantitative assessment of anterior ocular structures, including the tear film, cornea, conjunctiva, sclera, rectus muscles, anterior chamber angle, and lens \cite{hirnschall2017prediction}. The convergence of pattern recognition, computer vision, and particularly deep learning methodologies \cite{litjens2017survey} has revolutionized ophthalmic image analysis, establishing it as a cornerstone of diagnostic assistance and disease assessment. Nevertheless, subjective interpretation of ophthalmic imagery suffers from substantial inter-observer variability and compromised reproducibility. Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) offers a compelling solution by presenting reference cases with analogous disease presentations, thereby enabling evidence-based assessment that mitigates interpretive discrepancies. CBIR systems retrieve relevant images by indexing and extracting visual characteristics (\textit{e.g.}, color, shape, texture) from extensive image repositories \cite{zhou2017recent}. Rather than providing direct diagnostic classifications, ophthalmic CBIR enhances diagnostic confidence through evidence-based support. Effective clinical implementation demands CBIR systems capable of handling vast case volumes while maintaining both scalability and precision. Hashing methodologies have emerged as particularly promising for CBIR applications, offering compact hash-code representations of high-dimensional images that excel in storage efficiency and computational speed \cite{conjeti2017deep,wu2019deep}. Deep learning-based hashing approaches have gained widespread adoption in medical image retrieval applications, including deep multiple instance hashing for tumor evaluation \cite{conjeti2017deep}, deep residual hashing for chest radiographs \cite{conjeti2017hashing}, and order-sensitive deep hashing for multi-morbidity medical image retrieval \cite{chen2018order}. However, current deep hashing methodologies fail to fully leverage deep networks' capacity for targeted salient region feature extraction. Salient region information typically provides the primary diagnostic evidence in clinical practice. This limitation is particularly pronounced in ophthalmology, where different disease grades or classifications may exhibit similar global appearances while harboring subtle distinctions detectable only through salient region analysis. Figure \ref{fig1} illustrates this phenomenon with ASOCT images (A) and (B), both representing cataract cases with comparable overall presentations. Despite their similarity, two distinct salient region types differentiate them: over-bright regions (blue) and over-dark regions (blue). Accurate cataract grading fundamentally depends on salient region detection and characterization, necessitating specialized consideration of salient region representation in ophthalmic image retrieval systems. Additionally, as demonstrated in Figure \ref{fig1}, a single retinal fundus image (C) may contain three distinct pathological indicators identifiable through different salient regions (green rectangles). Pathological myopia typically manifests as leopard fundus patterns, Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) diagnosis relies on macular spatial information, while glaucoma presents with enlarged optic cups and Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) abnormalities. Effective hash-code mapping must capture and preserve this salient region information to enable accurate fundus image differentiation during retrieval. Drawing inspiration from deep network attention mechanisms \cite{woo2018cbam,chen2017sca}, we introduce Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), a novel end-to-end architecture designed to enhance hash-code discriminative power through effective salient region exploitation in ophthalmic images. Our approach employs a spatial-attention module to comprehensively mine salient regions and amplify their representation within the hashing space. To preserve similarity relationships, we implement a siamese architecture \cite{bertinetto2016fully} with shared weights for input image pairs, enabling pairwise loss optimization in the objective function. The resulting hashing space maintains smaller pairwise distances for similar image pairs while maximizing distances for dissimilar pairs. This paper's primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item[1)] Recognition that ophthalmic images of different grades or classes may exhibit similar global characteristics while containing subtle salient region differences, leading to the development of Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), a novel end-to-end network for ophthalmic image retrieval. \item[2)] Integration of a spatial-attention module that enhances salient region representation through end-to-end learning, thereby maximizing hash-code discriminative capability by focusing on critical image regions. \item[3)] Comprehensive experimental validation on dual-modality ophthalmic image datasets demonstrating ASH's superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art deep hashing methods while maintaining computational efficiency. \end{itemize} This manuscript proceeds as follows: Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2} reviews relevant literature. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3} provides detailed methodology description. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4} presents comprehensive experimental evaluation on two ophthalmic image datasets. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral5} concludes with final remarks.

text: As robots become more prevalent in densely populated environments, they increasingly share spaces with humans—from service robots operating in airports, hotels, and restaurants, to delivery robots traversing sidewalks, warehouse mobile units, and autonomous vehicles. Safe deployment of these systems requires that nearby humans comprehend their navigational intentions. While HRI research has traditionally concentrated on communicating arm movement intentions \cite{gielniak2011generating,kwon2018expressing}, investigating eye gaze \cite{moon2014meet,admoni2017social} and additional non-verbal communication methods \cite{saunderson2019robots} for stationary robots, recent work has shifted toward externalizing or visualizing robotic navigation intent (including path plans) \cite{coovert2014spatial,szafir2015communicating,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi,blenk2021lane}. This approach aims to enhance the interpretability of robot navigation behaviors, thereby fostering greater trust and acceptance. Directional projections represent one approach for communicating navigation intent \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}, including arrow-based projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi} where robots utilize onboard projectors to display directional indicators showing intended movement directions. These visual cues may appear as lines \cite{chadalavada2015s}, gradient bands \cite{watanabe2015communicating}, or arrows \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}. Unlike head-mounted see-through augmented reality systems \cite{williams2018virtual,williams2018augmented}, projector-based augmented reality eliminates the need for specialized hardware worn by users, enabling simultaneous visualization for multiple observers and enhancing applicability in group, team, or crowd scenarios~\cite{chen2019crowd,sebo2020robots,oliveira2021human}. Multiple human-subjects studies \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi} have demonstrated this approach's effectiveness \cite{watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}, as detailed in Section~\ref{sec:related_work}. This paper presents a practical implementation for robotic arrow projections, details the solution's technical characteristics, and provides open-source code access. We specify a particular robot platform and commercial projector that have proven successful in our implementation, alongside results from a comprehensive user study offering additional empirical validation. Our implementation leverages the widely-adopted Robot Operating System (ROS) \cite{quigley2009ros} and its visualization framework, rviz \cite{gossow2011interactive}, for arrow rendering. The ROS foundation ensures robot-agnostic compatibility, given that most research and development robots support ROS \cite{rosshowcase}. Non-ROS frameworks \cite{kramer2007development,elkady2012robotics} and cognitive architectures like DIARC~\cite{scheutz2019overview} typically maintain ROS bridges. Employing rviz as the rendering engine removes the necessity for practitioners and researchers to master external tools like Unity, while rviz's graphical interface eliminates computer graphics programming requirements. Considering arrow projection's broad applicability across diverse robotic platforms and its demonstrated effectiveness, we believe this contribution significantly benefits the HRI community. Our readily deployable implementation with comprehensive documentation enables researchers to concentrate on other compelling social navigation challenges, including human navigation modeling \cite{guy2010modeling,ratsamee2013social,ferrer2014proactive,che2018avoiding} and socially or morally compliant robot navigation \cite{banisetty2021implicit,banisetty2021socially}. We encourage GitHub issues for inquiries and welcome pull requests.

text: Real-world applications of multi-agent motion planning are abundant, yet the computational challenges remain formidable. The task of guiding even a single robot from its starting position to a target destination while avoiding obstacle collisions becomes extraordinarily complex when confronted with dense obstacle fields, high-dimensional state spaces, nonlinear and nonholonomic dynamics, actuator constraints, and environmental disturbances. When multiple such sophisticated robotic systems must operate within a shared workspace and potentially interfere with one another, the problem complexity escalates far beyond what most current methodologies can handle. This work introduces the \underline{S}calable and \underline{S}afe \underline{M}ulti-agent \underline{M}otion (S2M2) planner, an innovative approach to multi-agent motion planning that rapidly generates provably safe trajectories for agent models characterized by high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics and bounded disturbances operating in continuous spatiotemporal domains. Rather than pursuing the computationally prohibitive direct generation of dynamically-feasible trajectories, S2M2 employs a separation-of-concerns methodology: We initially construct piecewise linear (PWL) paths $S_i$ for each dynamic agent $\mathcal{A}_i$ to track, acknowledging that perfect path following is unattainable. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that through suitable tracking controllers, the actual agent trajectories under disturbances will converge toward $S_i$ with guaranteed spatial tracking error bounds. Crucially, we establish that these error bounds can be computed a priori for any admissible PWL path. The computational efficiency of S2M2 stems from our ability to cast the single-agent PWL path generation problem as a Mixed Integer-Linear Program (MILP), enabling efficient solution via commercial MILP solvers. Inter-agent collision avoidance is achieved by embedding our single-agent motion planner within the priority-based search framework~\cite{ma2019searching}, which systematically explores priority ordering spaces. Under specified priority assignments, lower-priority agents recompute their paths while treating higher-priority agents as dynamic obstacles. The integration of MILP-based path planning with guaranteed tracking control enables S2M2 to efficiently discover plans that are both provably safe and robust against execution disturbances. Furthermore, by planning agent paths on continuous maps over continuous time domains, our approach yields high-quality solutions with reduced flowtime (the aggregate makespan across all single-agent plans). Figure~\ref{fig:uturn} illustrates a representative scenario involving two disc-shaped vehicles executing u-turn maneuvers. Given partially known initial positions and bounded disturbances, we first determine the spatial error bounds for tracking individual path segments (lines), then combine this error analysis with agent geometry to establish the potential swept regions for each segment. The swept region for agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ during its second segment $(p_{12}, p_{13})$ appears in light blue. We additionally enforce minimum segment durations to ensure agents have sufficient time for positional adjustments following turns—three seconds in this example. During single-agent path planning, obstacles undergo bloating to account for both spatial tracking errors and agent dimensions, as depicted in light red. The planner enforces minimum segment duration constraints throughout. Notably, both agents decelerate when traversing the corridor, utilizing the three-second interval for trajectory adjustment. Beyond the corridor, agent $\mathcal{A}_2$ accelerates to maximum velocity toward its destination. Upon collision detection, priority assignments designate certain agents as moving obstacles for others. Here, agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ receives higher priority, enabling corridor passage before agent $\mathcal{A}_2$. Performance evaluations compare S2M2 against ECBS-CT \cite{cohen2019optimal} and MAPF/C+POST \cite{honig2018trajectory} across 2D and 3D scenarios featuring ground vehicles and quadrotors, respectively. Results demonstrate S2M2's superior solution quality, achieving $15\sim70\%$ improvements across most test instances. Additionally, S2M2 exhibits orders-of-magnitude reductions in preprocessing time while maintaining competitive runtime performance relative to alternative planners.

text: The extraction of \emph{principal components} or most significant directions from matrices corrupted by noise represents a cornerstone problem spanning mathematical statistics and diverse applications \cite{Rao-1964-PCA,Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA,Ringner-2008-PCA,AW-2010-PCA}. Theoretical understanding of this task's asymptotic behavior has emerged through extensive analysis of idealized \emph{spiked matrix models}. Beginning with Johnstone's pioneering models \cite{Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA} involving Gaussian observations from covariance matrices perturbed by rank-one ``spikes,'' researchers have developed the simpler yet equally illuminating \emph{Wigner spiked matrix model} that exhibits comparable phenomenology. Our focus centers on two probability distributions $\PP$ and $\QQ$ defined over $n \times n$ symmetric matrices. \begin{itemize} \item The distribution $\QQ = \QQ_n$ generates $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$ from the \emph{Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)}, where diagonal entries satisfy $W_{ii} \sim \sN(0, \frac{1}{n})$ while off-diagonal entries follow $W_{ij} = W_{ji} \sim \sN(0, \frac{2}{n})$ for $i < j$, with independence across all $\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ entries. This distribution is denoted $\QQ = \GOE(n)$. \item The distribution $\PP = \PP_n$ first samples $\bu \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$ from the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1} \subset \RR^n$, then produces $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$ where $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and $\beta > 0$ remains fixed as $n \to \infty$. \end{itemize} These models naturally give rise to two fundamental statistical challenges: (1) \emph{detection} or \emph{testing}, requiring determination of whether observed $\bW$ originates from $\PP$ or $\QQ$, and (2) \emph{recovery} or \emph{estimation}, demanding accurate estimation of $\bu$ given $\bW \sim \PP$. Both problems connect naturally to the optimization of the largest eigenvalue: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\|\bx\|_2 = 1} \bx^{\top} \bW \bx. \end{equation} The maximizer $\bx^{\star}$ (top eigenvector of $\bW$) provides maximum likelihood estimation of $\bu$ for recovery tasks. text: Supervised learning fundamentally centers on approximating the conditional distribution of a target value $y$ given an input $x$. Standard training procedures employing losses like Mean Square Error for regression or Cross-Entropy for classification yield methods that approximate the expected conditional distribution $\langle y|x \rangle$ \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}. Such approaches prove adequate when target distributions exhibit unimodal characteristics and variations in target values primarily stem from random noise. However, regression problems featuring non-unimodal target distributions expose critical limitations in most machine learning approaches, which typically fail by producing averaged predictions. Multimodal target distributions inherently link multiple plausible outcomes to individual input samples\revise{, leading to what is commonly termed conditional density estimation.} The Mixture Density Network (MDN) \cite{bishop_mixture_1994} emerged as a solution for approximating arbitrarily complex conditional target distributions, with successful deployments spanning robotics \cite{choi_uncertainty_2018}, epidemiology \cite{davis_use_2020}, and finance \cite{schittenkopf_volatility_1998}. While \textsc{MDN}{}s target vectorial input data, numerous real-world scenarios involve relational data where structural properties fundamentally influence potential outcomes—a phenomenon particularly pronounced in epidemiological contexts \cite{opuszko_impact_2013}. Graph processing research has flourished over two decades, as evidenced by comprehensive surveys from \citet{bacciu_gentle_2020,wu_comprehensive_2020}. The field pursues optimal structured sample representations through diverse neighborhood aggregation mechanisms, graph coarsening techniques, and information propagation strategies. Applications leveraging adaptive structured data processing proliferate across domains including drug design \cite{podda_deep_2020}, social network classification \cite{yang_revisiting_2016}, and natural language processing \cite{beck_graph--sequence_2018}. We introduce Graph Mixture Density Network (\textsc{GMDN}{}), a hybrid methodology addressing multimodal target distributions in graph-based machine learning. This architecture generates multimodal distributions conditioned on input graphs, applicable to entire structures or constituent entities. \revise{\textsc{GMDN}{} approximates the potentially multimodal distribution of target random variable $y$ given observable input graph $x$ through maximum likelihood estimation. Likelihood optimization serves as the standard metric for density estimation tasks \cite{nowicki_estimation_2001}, quantifying model adherence to empirical data distributions. Unlike \quotes{standard} regression approaches that suffice with single output predictions \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}, such tasks demand more sophisticated handling; consequently, \textsc{GMDN}{} transcends the unimodal distribution constraints inherent in existing deep learning graph models.} Our evaluation employs a novel benchmark featuring extensive epidemiological simulations\footnote{\url{https://github.com/diningphil/graph-mixture-density-networks}} where structural and multimodal factors critically determine epidemic outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate \textsc{GMDN}{}'s substantial likelihood improvements. Additionally, we assess our model on two real-world chemical graph regression tasks, illustrating \textsc{GMDN}{}'s enhanced uncertainty modeling capabilities—specifically, its ability to reveal multiple admissible chemical property values for given molecular representations.

text: Contemporary unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) demonstrate remarkable versatility across diverse operational domains, spanning from delivery drones to autonomous electrical vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) passenger aircraft. These systems efficiently execute numerous missions including goods delivery, surveillance, public safety, weather monitoring, disaster relief, search and rescue, traffic monitoring, videography, and air transportation \citep{balakrishnan2018blueprint,kopardekar2016unmanned}. Given that Urban air mobility (UAM) operations will predominantly occur within urban environments proximate to buildings and airports, UAS must incorporate sophisticated onboard detect and avoid systems. Such systems enable autonomous navigation around other traffic, hazardous weather conditions, terrain features, and both artificial and natural obstacles while minimizing reliance on continuous human oversight \citep{kopardekar2016unmanned}. The literature presents extensive mathematical frameworks addressing aircraft conflict resolution, broadly categorized into centralized and decentralized algorithmic approaches. Centralized methodologies encompass semidefinite programming \citep{frazzoli2001resolution}, nonlinear programming \citep{raghunathan2004dynamic,enright1992discrete}, mixed-integer linear programming \citep{schouwenaars2001mixed,richards2002aircraft,pallottino2002conflict,vela2009mixed}, mixed-integer quadratic programming \citep{mellinger2012mixed}, sequential convex programming \citep{augugliaro2012generation,morgan2014model}, second-order cone programming \citep{acikmese2007convex}, evolutionary techniques \citep{delahaye2010aircraft,cobano2011path}, and particle swarm optimization \citep{pontani2010particle}. While these centralized approaches typically seek global optimization across all aircraft, their computational complexity generally exhibits exponential scaling with increasing aircraft numbers. Within decentralized frameworks, conflict resolution can be formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated effectiveness in aircraft traffic management, implementations predominantly utilize conventional algorithms \citep{sun2019reinforcement}. The next-generation airborne collision avoidance system (ACAS X) conceptualizes collision avoidance systems (CAS) as a partially observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), with its unmanned aircraft extension termed ACAS Xu \citep{kochenderfer2012next}. Both ACAS X and ACAS Xu employ Dynamic Programming (DP) for determining expected action costs \citep{manfredi2016introduction, owen2019acas}. \cite{chryssanthacopoulos2012decomposition} integrated decomposition methods with DP to achieve optimized collision avoidance against multiple threats. Traditional RL algorithms necessitate fine state space discretization and finite action spaces. Such discretization potentially compromises safety through discretization errors while failing to provide flexible maneuvering guidance for UAS. Furthermore, discretizing extensive airspace demands substantial computational resources and proves time-intensive. Tree search algorithms \citep{yang2018autonomous,yang2020scalable} address CAS problems through MDP formulations without state discretization, yet typically require significant onboard computation time to handle continuous state spaces. Continuous state and action spaces pose significant challenges for reinforcement learning-based conflict resolution. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged to address these challenges by employing deep neural networks to approximate cost and optimal policy functions. The evolution of DRL algorithms—including Policy Gradient \citep{sutton2000policy}, Deep Q-Networks (DQN) \citep{mnih2013playing}, Double DQN \citep{van2016deep}, Dueling DQN \citep{wang2015dueling}, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) \citep{lillicrap2015continuous}, Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) \citep{mnih2016asynchronous}, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) \citep{ppo2}—has substantially enhanced automation potential. \cite{li2019optimizing} applied DQN to compute corrections for existing collision avoidance approaches in dense airspace scenarios. \cite{yang2019real} validated the feasibility of DQN-based algorithms for UAV obstacle avoidance. \cite{wulfeuav} demonstrated that DQN surpasses value iteration in both evaluation performance and solution speed for UAV collision avoidance problems. \cite{keong2019reinforcement} investigated agent performance in avoiding single and multiple aircraft using DQN algorithms. \cite{brittain2020deep} introduced a novel deep multi-agent reinforcement learning framework utilizing PPO to identify and resolve conflicts among variable aircraft numbers in high-density, stochastic, and dynamic en-route airspace sectors. The aforementioned DRL research operates within continuous state and discrete action spaces. Limited progress exists in applying DRL to UAS conflict resolution with continuous control. \cite{pham2019machine} developed a method combining Deep Q-learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithms, achieving over 81\% success rates in conflict resolution under traffic and varying uncertainty conditions. \cite{ma2018saliency} created a comprehensive framework integrating autonomous obstacle detection with actor-critic based reinforcement learning modules to develop reactive UAV obstacle avoidance behaviors. \cite{ppo2} demonstrated PPO's superior performance across benchmark tasks including simulated robotic locomotion and Atari gameplay, showing advantages over other online policy gradient methods. PPO achieves favorable balance among sample complexity, simplicity, and computational efficiency. Consequently, PPO-based conflict resolution models offer significant value for UAS traffic management, constituting this study's primary motivation. To our knowledge, this represents the first investigation developing a DRL approach utilizing PPO algorithms for UAS navigation in continuous state and action spaces. Continuous space computation eliminates state space discretization requirements and post-processing smoothing needs. The proposed model, featuring optimal policies from offline training, enables real-time online UAS trajectory planning. This paper's primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em} \item Development of a PPO-based framework enabling UAS avoidance of both static and moving obstacles within continuous state and action spaces. \item Creation of novel scenario state representations and reward functions that effectively map environmental conditions to maneuvers, with trained models generating continuous heading angle and speed commands. \item Comprehensive testing of the proposed learning framework across environments containing static obstacles, static obstacles with UAS position uncertainty, and deterministic/stochastic environments with moving obstacles, demonstrating accurate and robust guidance with over 99\% conflict resolution success rates. \end{itemize} This paper's organization proceeds as follows. \cref{background} establishes Markov Decision Process and Deep Reinforcement Learning foundations. \cref{mdp} presents model formulation using Markov Decision Process for UAS conflict resolution in continuous action space. \cref{result} provides numerical experiments demonstrating the proposed approach's capability for UAS conflict avoidance learning. \cref{Conclusion} presents concluding remarks.

They also demonstrate that PPO is superior to other online policy gradient methods on the two test tasks, simulated robot locomotion and Atari game playing. This is, to our knowledge, the first investigation of a DRL approach using PPOs for unmanned aerial vehicle navigation in continuous state and action spaces. The continuous space computation eliminates the need for state space discretization and post-processing smoothing. As such, PPO-based conflict resolution models are of significant value to UAS traffic management and constitute the main motivation of this study. This paper's primary contributions are:  the development of a framework for avoiding both moving and stationary obstacles in the continuous state and action spaces.  the construction of novel scenario state representations and reward functions, which effectively map the environment into maneuvers, with the trained model generating continuous heading angles and speeds. The proposed model, which is trained in the offline mode, enables the real-time control of the unmanned aerial system. This paper is organized as follows: 1. Introduction. The Markov Decision Process and Deep Reinforcement Learning foundations. 2. A comprehensive experimental evaluation in environments with static obstacles, static obstacles with the position of the UAS uncertain, and deterministic/stochastic environments with moving obstacles, demonstrating accurate and robust guidance with over 99.9% conflict resolution success rate. Presents a summary of the results of the experiments. Presents a formulation of the model using Markov decision process for the resolution of UAS conflict in the continuous action space. Presents numerical experiments demonstrating the ability of the proposed approach to learn avoidance of UASs.

text: Collections of question-answer pairs, known as Frequently-Asked-Questions (FAQ), emerge through manual curation or automated extraction from pertinent documentation. These repositories serve as centralized hubs delivering the most pertinent or commonly sought information about products and services, thereby facilitating rapid customer assistance for routine inquiries. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Motivation.} Natural language interfaces for querying FAQ collections are realized through FAQ retrieval systems, which have gained substantial traction among large-scale service providers as information delivery mechanisms for customers. These systems offer dual benefits: (i) they automate customer service operations, including intelligent chatbots~\cite{massaro2018,yan2016} and automated e-mail responses~\cite{karan2018,malik2007}, and (ii) they facilitate streamlined access to internal FAQ repositories for customer service representatives, thereby enhancing both service quality and operational efficiency. Moreover, the emergence of personal assistants (such as XiaoIce, Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant, etc.) has enabled these ``virtual agents'' to deliver question responses and assist users with routine tasks through an additional pathway complementing FAQs, hotlines, and forums -- thus fostering natural user interactions~\cite{lommatzsch2019,por2020}. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Challenges.} The task of FAQ retrieval presents significant difficulties, primarily stemming from the brevity of question-answer content, which complicates efforts to overcome the {\em lexical and semantic gap} between user queries and FAQ questions due to limited contextual information within short spans~\cite{karan2018,lee2008}. Additionally, accurate interpretation of user questions becomes problematic when confronted with informal language, domain-specific terminology, abbreviations, and disparities between formal and colloquial expressions~\cite{lommatzsch2019}. Consider, for instance, the questions {\small{\tt ``How can I seal a hole in the gas tank of my car?''}} and {\small{\tt ``How to patch a leak in the fuel compartment of my van?''}} which demonstrate semantic equivalence despite minimal lexical similarity and formal-colloquial discrepancies. Furthermore, FAQ retrieval systems must accommodate both keyword-based searches and {\em short span} ``natural language'' inquiries. Given their inherently ``customer-centric'' orientation, such systems typically require enhanced precision and interpretability relative to conventional information retrieval approaches. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Problem Statement.} {\em FAQ Retrieval} encompasses the effective ranking of question-answer pairs within a collection based on their relevance to user input queries. Such retrieval mechanisms strive to comprehend users' underlying {\em intent} and locate the most pertinent answers containing accurate information~\cite{kothari2009}. More precisely, given a pre-established collection (or repository) of question-answer $(Q, A)$ pairs constituting the FAQ $= \{(Q_1, A_1), \cdots, (Q_n, A_n)\}$, where $Q_i$ represents a domain-related question and $A_i$ denotes its corresponding answer, the objective becomes returning a ranked list of FAQ $(Q, A)$ pairs, $\{(Q_1^q, A_1^q), \cdots, (Q_k^q, A_k^q)\}$, that exhibit substantial semantic and intent alignment with the input user query $q$. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Contributions.} We introduce {\em TI-S2S}, an innovative keyword-driven supervised learning framework designed for effective FAQ retrieval. Our methodology employs a {\em sequence-to-sequence} model to produce representative labels for user questions, enabling query-question similarity computation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a variant incorporating ``candidates'' identified through deep learning architecture to direct the retrieval process yields additional performance improvements. Our proposed framework effectively captures: (i) application domain-specificity, (ii) distinctive words and concepts for question differentiation, and (iii) semantic similarity for retrieving pertinent QA pairs from FAQ collections. Public FAQ dataset experiments demonstrate our framework's superiority over existing methods in accuracy metrics and robustness when training data is limited. Consequently, it implicitly addresses both {\em document redundancy} and {\em query redundancy}~\cite{karan2018}.

dipper_dipper: Introduction – – – – – – – – – – Natural-language access to FAQ collections is provided by a set of retrieval systems, such as are used by many large companies to answer customer questions. These question-and-answer pairs, called frequently asked questions (FAQ), are created by manual or automatic extraction of relevant documentation and serve as central information sources for the most relevant and most frequently sought information about products and services, allowing for quick and efficient customer support in the face of routine inquiries. The appearance of personal assistants (e.g., Xiaoice, Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant) has also increased the demand for such systems... They have two advantages: (i) they automate the service of customers, generating emails through intelligent chatbots (e.g., Massaro, Yan, and Malik); (ii) they facilitate access to internal FAQ for customer service representatives, thereby improving the quality of service and the efficiency of operation. V-space* — The task of providing answers to questions in the form of virtual assistants, which are an addition to the already existing FAQs, helplines, and discussion boards, has been facilitated by the development of a “natural language processing” method... In view of the difficulties of the task of answering the questions, it is necessary to overcome the “lexical and semantic gap” between the question asked and the answer given, the narrow context of which in short texts makes it difficult to overcome. For example, if a person asks, “How to plug a hole in the tank of my car?,” or “How to plug a leak in a tank of a truck? With their inherent “customer-oriented” orientation, such systems require more precision and accuracy of interpretation than conventional systems. It is also a problem to interpret questions correctly in the presence of slang, special terminology, abbreviations, and differences between formal and informal expressions. The “FAQ retrieval” is the ranking of questions and answers from a collection based on their relevance to the input query. The corresponding mechanisms have to try to understand the underlying intent and find the most relevant questions and answers. In particular, they must be able to handle both keywords and natural language queries, which may have semantic equivalence, despite the low degree of lexical similarity and the formal-casual differences. The question and the answer are the mainstay of all search systems. Our system introduces a novel method for determining the effectiveness of search systems: the supervised learning system, in which the answers to the questions are ranked by semantic similarity. Our system effectively captures application-dependent features, and the unique words and concepts that make up the questions, and the semantic similarity of questions and answers to find relevant questions from the question and answer collections. In a word, the method implicitly handles both “document redundancy” and “query redundancy” (Karan et al., 2018). Our method is based on a sequence-to-sequence model that obtains a representative label of the question and the answer and thus makes it possible to calculate the semantic similarity between the question and the answer. We also demonstrate that a variant which introduces “candidates” into the retrieval process obtains an additional improvement. We have tested our framework on a public Q&A dataset, and the results show that it outperforms the existing methods in accuracy metrics and in robustness to the lack of training data.
