The 	extit{gradient} has emerged as a cornerstone in deep learning optimization, spanning from G. Hinton's Turing-award-winning 	extit{backpropagation} research in 1986 \cite{Rumelhart1986LearningRB} to contemporary optimizers embedded within mainstream frameworks such as Google's Tensorflow \cite{Abadi2016TensorFlowAS} and Facebook's PyTorch\cite{NEURIPS2019_9015}. Consider image classification as an illustrative example: gradients furnish classifiers with optimal parameter adjustment directions, systematically reducing discrepancies (captured by the 	extit{loss function}) between model predictions and ground-truth labels. Through iterative parameter updates opposing gradient directions across diverse training samples, loss functions progressively diminish while model accuracy correspondingly improves. Nevertheless, this fundamental gradient dependency harbors an inherent vulnerability. Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad} illustrates a conventional face recognition pipeline where training image batches feed into neural network classifiers. These classifiers generate label predictions, compute average loss functions, and employ back-propagation to derive gradients as parameter derivatives of average loss. Since gradients explicitly originate from data inputs and labels, adversaries reasonably anticipate that gradients expose sensitive information regarding original training data. The proliferation of distributed learning paradigms \cite{yang2019FL,Chen2020NebulaAS} has catalyzed research investigating gradient-based inference of data properties \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF}, membership status \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF, Nasr2019ComprehensivePA}, class representatives \cite{Hitaj2017DeepMU, Wang2019BeyondIC}, or raw data inputs\cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG} from gradients potentially accessible to man-in-the-middle attackers or honest-but-curious servers \cite{Lyu2020,Kairouz2021AdvancesAO}. While gradient-based privacy attacks demonstrate feasibility, prior research consistently encounters an enigmatic performance bottleneck affecting privacy leakage effectiveness. Melis et al. \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF} document precision degradation exceeding $30\%$ for sensitive word inference when batch sizes increase $8	imes$. Nasr et al. \cite{Nasr2019ComprehensivePA} observe reduced membership information leakage in shallower neural architectures. Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} report $10	imes$ iteration increases for training batch reverse engineering when batch sizes expand from $1$ to $8$, with attack failure rates rising for shallow networks. These findings suggest information leakage diminishes with larger training batches and shallower network architectures. However, whether this phenomenon stems from a unified root cause intertwined with deep learning's underlying mechanisms remains unexplored in existing literature. 
oindent	extbf{Our Work.} We address this fundamental question by analyzing 	extit{data reconstruction attacks}\cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG}, an emerging privacy threat exploiting leaked average gradients to reverse engineer corresponding training batches. Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad}'s right panel demonstrates how data reconstruction attacks target training sample recovery from gradients, severely threatening private training data confidentiality. Among pioneering reconstruction attacks, Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} introduce a learning-based methodology treating unknown training batches as learnable variables (	extit{dummy data}). Through L2 distance minimization between dummy data gradients and ground-truth gradients (	extit{gradient matching}), they achieve reconstruction feasibility for batch sizes up to $8$ on CIFAR-100 \cite{Krizhevsky2009LearningML}, though reconstruction quality exhibits instability across trials and relatively small victim models. Subsequent works \cite{Zhao2020iDLGID,Geiping2020InvertingG} propose technical refinements to \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF}'s learning framework while encountering similar reconstruction bottlenecks. Due to limited interpretability, previous research fails to characterize 	extit{why, when and how gradient-based data reconstruction succeeds}, which we consider crucial for understanding and enhancing gradient privacy properties. We present the inaugural analytical investigation of data reconstruction attack security boundaries on fully-connected neural networks (FCNs) with rectified linear units (ReLUs \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}), a fundamental architecture commonly employed for demonstrating attack and defense innovations \cite{Jagielski2020HighAA,Tramr2016StealingML,Rolnick2020ReverseengineeringDR}. As deep learning's most prevalent activation function \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}, ReLUs transmit nonnegative inputs unchanged while blocking negative inputs. This distinctive gate-like ReLU behavior enables individual input samples to maintain unique 	extit{activation paths} constituting their 	extit{activation patterns} \cite{Montfar2014OnTN, Laurent2018TheMS}. We develop deterministic algorithms decoding hidden average gradient information to determine individual sample activation patterns, a crucial step transforming the highly nonlinear gradient-matching problem into linear equation systems concerning inputs for enhanced analytical tractability. By investigating conditions enabling activation pattern reconstruction from gradients, we contribute the following key insights: 
oindent	extbf{(1) Neuron Exclusivity State Analysis.} We introduce 	extit{neuron exclusivity state}, quantified by 	extit{	extbf{Ex}clusively 	extbf{A}ctivated 	extbf{N}eurons} (ExANs, i.e., ReLUs activated by single batch samples during forward passes), as critical for data reconstruction attack feasibility. We characterize boundary conditions governing training batch neuron exclusivity states under attack scenarios. 
oindent	extbf{(2) Boundary of Insecure Exclusivity States.} We establish 	extit{sufficient exclusivity} conditions—when batch samples possess at least $2$ ExANs at final ReLU layers and $1$ at remaining layers—as strong indicators of insecure neuron exclusivity states (Section ef{sec:atk_case_a}). We demonstrate deterministic attack algorithms with guaranteed reconstruction accuracy (Theorem ef{col:optim_bound_mult}) for training batches satisfying sufficient exclusivity conditions. Evaluations across $5$ real-world scenarios encompassing medical, face recognition, and visual datasets with diverse FCN depths and widths show our attacks consistently surpass previous methods in reconstruction recognizability while achieving $100\%$ label inference accuracy (Section ef{sec:evaluation}). We extend attack algorithms to convolutional neural network (CNN) classifiers by combining analytical and optimization-based techniques. 
oindent	extbf{(3) Boundary of Secure Exclusivity States.} Through remaining exclusivity state space analysis, we identify 	extit{lack of exclusivity} conditions—when samples have $0$ ExANs at first ReLU layers—as indicators of unique reconstruction impossibility (Section ef{sec:def_case_b}). For these states, we prove infinitely many artifact batches always exist yielding identical gradients to victim ground-truth batches, deriving lower bounds for maximum distances between artifact and ground-truth batches (Theorem ef{thm:impossible_reconstr}). This observation motivates our exclusivity reduction strategy, replacing first ReLU layers with linear layers to enhance arbitrary training batch privacy when batch sizes exceed first layer neuron counts, with negligible model performance degradation. For analytical completeness, Section ef{sec:discussion} presents preliminary experimental results empirically analyzing data reconstruction performance on remaining states.

text: Effective recommendation systems fundamentally depend on extracting user preferences from behavioral history, particularly given the dynamic nature of both user inclinations and item attributes. Context plays a crucial role in shaping preferences—for instance, purchasing a desktop computer naturally increases the likelihood of subsequent keyboard interest. Sequential recommendation therefore seeks to leverage historical patterns to predict the next items users will likely favor. Numerous algorithms have emerged to decode users' sequential behavioral patterns~\cite{SASRec, BERT4Rec, hidasi2018recurrent, CASER, M3, rendle2010factorizing, DIN, TRANSREC}. While these methods demonstrate strong performance, they predominantly overlook temporal information embedded in interaction timestamps. Although recent advances like TiSASRec~\cite{TISASRec} have begun incorporating temporal signals, their approach remains constrained to singular embedding strategies. Given the rich information contained within timestamp data, exploring diverse temporal embedding approaches alongside architectures capable of harnessing such variety presents significant opportunities. We introduce \textbf{MEANTIME} (\textbf{M}ixtur\textbf{E} of \textbf{A}tte\textbf{NTI}on mechanisms with \textbf{M}ulti-temporal \textbf{E}mbeddings), which leverages multiple temporal embeddings to capture both absolute and relative positional information of user-item interactions within sequences. Our approach employs specialized self-attention heads, each processing distinct positional embeddings independently. This design proves advantageous as individual heads function as experts, concentrating on specific behavioral patterns. Real-world dataset experiments demonstrate \textbf{MEANTIME}'s superior performance against state-of-the-art methods. We contribute the following: \begin{itemize} \item We diversify positional encoding schemes for user-item interactions by applying multiple kernels to timestamp positions and values, generating distinct embedding matrices for sequence representation. \item We introduce a novel architecture operating multiple specialized self-attention heads concurrently, where each head extracts specific behavioral patterns using dedicated positional embeddings from our proposed framework. \item We present comprehensive experimental validation demonstrating our method's effectiveness on real-world datasets, accompanied by detailed ablation studies elucidating individual component contributions within our model. \end{itemize}

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous computer vision and pattern recognition applications, yet fundamental limitations continue to constrain their broader adoption. The substantial computational demands for both training and inference create significant barriers when deploying large DNN architectures on resource-constrained devices \cite{wu2018deep}. Moreover, the inherent lack of interpretability renders DNNs inappropriate for real-world scenarios requiring transparent decision-making processes. Given that DNNs fundamentally comprise stacked perceptrons as basic computational units, a compelling question emerges: could substituting these atomic components with alternative modules yield beneficial outcomes? Decision trees offer notable advantages through their inherent model transparency and computationally efficient training procedures. This naturally leads to the question of whether deep architectures can be constructed using decision trees as fundamental computational building blocks. Recent research has investigated this concept with encouraging preliminary results. Zhou et al. \cite{zhou2017deep} introduced a deep random forest cascade architecture, wherein each network layer consists of an ensemble containing multiple random forests, with the concatenated outputs from current forests serving as input to subsequent layers. Miller et al. \cite{miller2017forward} enhanced this approach by employing decision tree sets per layer while concatenating current layer outputs with original inputs to generate new representations for following layers. Both studies \cite{zhou2017deep,miller2017forward} demonstrated performance comparable to DNN models on the MNIST dataset, achieving substantial reductions in training time alongside lighter parameter requirements. Nevertheless, these approaches still necessitate thousands of trees per layer due to the inherently limited expressive capacity of individual decision trees. We propose advancing existing deep forest architectures through several key innovations to overcome these limitations. First, we introduce a \textit{soft routing} mechanism that replaces traditional hard splitting criteria in classical decision trees, employing sigmoid functions as routing criteria at internal tree nodes to enable end-to-end optimization through gradient-based error propagation. Second, we enable global topology learning by incorporating a \textit{leafness parameter} for each tree node, allowing nodes to simultaneously determine whether to function as leaves or internal nodes \cite{irsoy2014budding}.

text: The advent of language model pre-training has catalyzed numerous breakthroughs across NLP domains (\cite{devlin2018bert}, \cite{brown2020language}, \cite{peters2018deep}, \cite{liu2019roberta}), establishing state-of-the-art performance on challenging tasks including question-answering and natural language inference. Within this landscape, the BERT model has emerged as a dominant force, leveraging the \cite{vaswani2017attention} architecture as its foundation. BERT's architecture comprises multiple stacked bidirectional Transformer (\cite{vaswani2017attention}) encoder blocks. The training paradigm involves initial pre-training on extensive unlabeled corpora, subsequently followed by fine-tuning on considerably smaller, task-specific datasets. While pre-training demands substantial computational resources and typically spans several days, fine-tuning can be accomplished within significantly reduced timeframes. Contemporary BERT variants exhibit substantial parameter counts and memory requirements, ranging from 110M parameters (BERT\textsubscript{BASE}) through 340M (BERT\textsubscript{LARGE}) to 8.3B parameters (Megatron \cite{shoeybi2019megatron}). Our work establishes that model size and training duration can be substantially reduced while maintaining negligible impact on fine-tuning accuracy. Beyond demonstrating these practical improvements in efficiency, we emphasize the critical importance of elucidating the underlying mechanisms that render our architectural modifications effective. Following methodologies established in \cite{clark2019does}, we employ probing linear classifiers alongside centered kernel alignment (\cite{kornblith2019similarity}) to illuminate the nature of improvements achieved through our architectural innovations.

text: Recommender Systems~(RS)~\cite{rendle2009bpr,rendle2010factorization,he2017neural,wang19neural,zheng17joint,pinsage2018ying} predict user preferences for items by modeling Collaborative Filtering~(CF) signals~\cite{wang19neural}. CF methods leverage the assumption that users with similar preferences interact with related items, enabling the learning of user and item embeddings from interaction patterns. The cold-start problem~\cite{zheng2018spectral} represents a fundamental challenge in CF approaches, as users or items with sparse interactions yield poorly learned embeddings. \textit{High-order signals}~\cite{wang19neural} offer a solution by propagating information across multiple hops in the user-item bipartite graph. Graph Neural Networks~(GNNs)~\cite{kipf17semi,graphsage17hamilton,wu19simplifying} facilitate this propagation through stacked \textit{aggregation layers}, allowing users (items) to gather first-order signals from direct neighbors in initial layers and high-order signals from distant neighbors in deeper layers. Through empirical analysis on real-world datasets, we identify three critical performance limitations in existing GNN-based RS approaches: the \textbf{oscillation} problem, the \textbf{varying locality} problem, and the \textbf{fixed propagation pattern} problem. The oscillation problem emerges when stacking multiple layers impedes effective information propagation. This phenomenon manifests as information gaps between successive propagation hops, stemming directly from bipartite graph structure. Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci} (left) demonstrates that users' direct neighbors consist exclusively of items, while their 2-hop neighbors comprise only users. Consequently, user aggregation receives information solely from items, and vice versa. This bipartite structure forces information to oscillate between user and item domains. While adding self-loops~\cite{kipf17semi,wang19neural} appears to address bipartite constraints, our theoretical analysis proves this approach fails to resolve oscillation issues. Furthermore, self-loops effectively prevent information propagation, thereby worsening cold-start problems. The varying locality problem further constrains multi-layer propagation capabilities~\cite{xu18jk} through heterogeneous local structure densities across the bipartite graph. Consider Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci} (left): $u_4$ exhibits lower local density than $u_2$, connecting only to $i_4$ versus $u_2$'s connections to $i_1$, $i_2$, and $i_3$. Three-hop propagation from $u_4$ (red edges) encompasses merely $3$ graph edges, while equivalent propagation from $u_2$ (green edges) spans nearly all edges. The corresponding propagation trees (Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, right) reveal significantly fewer propagation paths available to $u_4$ compared to $u_2$. Finally, existing multi-layer RS models~\cite{he2020lightgcn,wang19neural,berg2017gcmc} employ fixed propagation patterns across layers, generating redundant information flow. The yellow-shaded region in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci} (right) exemplifies this redundancy: first-hop propagation distributes $u_2$'s information to $i_1$ and $i_2$, second-hop propagation forwards this information to $u_1$ and $u_2$, and third-hop propagation reverses the flow. Layer-dependent neighbor sampling~\cite{zou2019layer} represents a potential solution, yet current sampling strategies demand additional computation and lack differentiability, compromising training efficiency. We introduce deep \textbf{D}eoscillated Adaptive \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ollaborative \textbf{F}iltering~(DGCF), a novel GNN framework designed specifically for bipartite graphs to address these challenges. Our Cross-Hop Propagation~(CHP) layer modifies bipartite propagation structure to eliminate oscillation by enabling information flow from cross-hop neighbors alongside direct neighbors. This allows users (items) to receive information from cross-hop users (items). Additionally, our Locality-Adaptive~(LA) layer controls propagation volume through node-specific influencing factors that adapt to local graph structure variations. DGCF combines multiple CHP and LA layers to propagate high-order CF signals while adapting to node locality. Layer-specific weights in LA and CHP components create dynamic propagation patterns that vary across network depth. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Oscillation problem:} We provide formal definition and theoretical proof of graph oscillation existence and boundaries in bipartite graphs, supported by empirical evidence of oscillation onset in shallow networks. \item \textbf{Innovative layers:} We introduce two novel components: CHP layers address oscillation issues while LA layers handle varying locality problems. Stacked LA layers resolve fixed aggregation pattern limitations. \item \textbf{Extensive experiments:} Beyond comprehensive performance comparisons, we conduct detailed analyses of all three identified problems, examining oscillation effects in deep networks, varying locality resolution, and propagation pattern adaptations. \end{itemize}

text: Consider having access to an image represented in \textit{functional} form. Here, the image exists as a function $f: \bm{p} \mapsto \bm{c}$ that maps pixel coordinates $\bm{p} = (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ to their corresponding RGB values $\bm{c} = (r, g, b) \in \mathbb{R}^3$. These functional representations emerge naturally in contexts such as differentiable rendering pipelines \cite{SynSin, SoftRasterizer} and implicit image representations \cite{siren, fourier_inr, inr_gan, cips}. Consider further the task of generating a high-resolution raster image from this functional representation $f(\bm p)$. This requires evaluating $f(\bm p)$ at every coordinate within an $H \times W$ grid to produce an image of size $H \times W$. When $f(\bm p)$ evaluation proves computationally expensive, this process becomes prohibitively slow. What solutions exist? One strategy involves accelerating the inference of $f(\bm p)$. Alternatively, one could generate a low-resolution image version and subsequently upsample it using established methods. text: Industry applications have extensively leveraged automatic text processing to extract meaningful insights. Such processing enables sentiment derivation from product or movie reviews, while other use cases encompass tweet analysis for brand perception assessment or public opinion mining on particular subjects. These diverse applications fundamentally reduce to classification or summarization challenges. Contemporary NLP methodologies demonstrate exceptional performance on monolingual texts for such tasks. Nevertheless, code-mixed content presents significant challenges due to insufficient labeled training data. Social media platforms have elevated the relevance of code-mixed text in recent years \cite{gamback2016comparing} \cite{barman2014code}. English serves as the predominant communication medium across most platforms. Within multilingual societies such as India, users frequently blend local languages with English during social media interactions, driven by greater comfort with native languages. Local terminology and entities naturally emerge in regional languages, fostering code-mixing phenomena. This linguistic borrowing mechanism facilitates communication by incorporating terms from multiple languages. Movie reviews, product evaluations, and user comments acquire local authenticity through regional language integration. These dynamics have propelled code-mixed text popularity \cite{khanuja2020gluecos}. Comprehending such multilingual content necessitates identifying languages within different text segments, followed by language-specific processing \cite{das2015code}. This research presents various methodologies for language identification within code-mixed contexts. Code-mixed texts exhibit diverse interleaving patterns across languages. One manifestation appears in this example: \textit{"this is not union budget, ye to aam admi ka budget hai"} with corresponding language tags "eng eng eng eng eng hin hin hin hin hin hin hin". Alternative patterns emerge as \textit{"maine aaj WhatsApp and Facebook uninstall kiya h"} tagged "hin hin eng eng eng eng hin hin". Individual word language determination poses challenges since identical words may function in both Hindi and English contextually. English terms like \textit{"are"} and \textit{"maze"} demonstrate Hindi usage in \textit{"are mai ghar jaa raha hu"} and \textit{"appke to maze hai"}. Social media text introduces additional complexity through noisy variations where words undergo deliberate modifications for emphasis. The word \textit{"good"} exemplifies this through repeated letters creating variations like \textit{"the movie was gooood"}. These factors underscore the importance of diverse input representation strategies. Sentences may undergo word-level, character-level, or sub-word processing. Sub-word representation constitutes a contemporary approach involving logical sub-word unit decomposition \cite{kudo2018subword}. Character and sub-word representations demonstrate superior resilience to noisy text variations compared to word-based approaches that treat each variation as distinct tokens. Our research evaluates these input representation performances. This represents the inaugural exploration of sub-word representations for Hi-En language identification. The objective involves determining individual word languages within sentences, formulated as token classification. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks constitute prevalent deep learning approaches for token classification tasks. We employ these fundamental models with various input representations to assess effectiveness. Conditional random fields (CRFs) often enhance these models' performance. However, our investigation focuses on simple architectures emphasizing input representation analysis. We demonstrate that sub-word representations combined with elementary models surpass complex architectures documented in existing literature. Simple architectures offer advantages through reduced runtime and computational complexity. Language identification modules require efficiency and speed since they typically precede additional NLP components. From this perspective, we experiment with single-layer CNN and LSTM configurations. Experimental results indicate these architectures achieve satisfactory accuracy levels. This work's primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Evaluation of character, sub-word, and word-based representation effectiveness for Hindi-English language identification tasks. \item Comparative analysis of popular model architecture and input representation combinations. \end{itemize}

text: Evaluating classifier performance constitutes a fundamental challenge in machine learning. While computational efficiency of performance measurement algorithms remains relatively unimportant in offline scenarios—such as during model development by researchers—runtime considerations become critical when continuously monitoring classifier behavior as new data arrives at high velocity. Consider the challenge of detecting anomalous behavior in IT systems through event log analysis. The overwhelming volume of generated logs renders manual monitoring infeasible. A viable solution involves deploying classifiers to identify abnormal events and trigger alerts for analyst investigation. Such monitoring requires continuous operation to enable rapid anomaly detection. Additionally, classifier performance itself demands ongoing surveillance, as both underlying data distributions and model effectiveness may shift due to evolving IT system characteristics. To identify recent performance degradation, practitioners typically focus on metrics computed over the most recent $n$ observations. More broadly, the challenge involves efficiently maintaining performance measures as data points are dynamically added or removed. This work examines algorithms for maintaining two distinct measures. Our primary focus addresses the area under the ROC curve (AUC), a well-established metric for classifier evaluation based on receiver operating characteristic analysis. We additionally investigate the $H$-measure, an alternative metric introduced by~\citet{hand:09:alternative}. This measure fundamentally relies on minimum weighted loss computations, averaged across cost ratios. The $H$-measure offers a practical advantage over AUC by naturally accommodating weighted classification errors. Computing either measure from scratch requires $\bigO{n \log n}$ time, reducing to $\bigO{n}$ when data points are pre-sorted. We present 3 algorithms enabling polylogarithmic-time maintenance of these measures. Our initial algorithm maintains AUC during data point additions or deletions. The strategy is direct: we preserve sorted data points within a self-balancing search tree. AUC updates require determining ROC coordinates for modified data points. This computation becomes feasible by augmenting the search tree to track cumulative label counts across subtrees. The resulting coordinate retrieval operates in $\bigO{\log n}$ time, yielding overall $\bigO{\log n}$ maintenance complexity. The subsequent two algorithms address $H$-measure maintenance. Since $H$-measure computation requires identifying the ROC curve's convex hull and iterating over hull points, we demonstrate that classical dynamic convex hull algorithms can maintain ROC curve hulls with minimal modifications. These adaptations become necessary because individual data point ROC coordinates are unavailable, though the coordinate computation technique from AUC maintenance applies here as well. We then establish that when class priors are estimated from test data, the $H$-measure decomposes into a hull point summation where each $i$th term depends exclusively on differences between consecutive hull points $i$ and $(i-1)$. This decomposition enables $\bigO{\log^2 n}$ time $H$-measure maintenance. When class priors are \emph{not} derived from test data, we introduce an approximation algorithm. The core concept involves clustering proximate convex hull points together. Specifically, when hull points exhibit spatial similarity, we retain only a single representative from each cluster. This clustering strategy maintains $\epsilon$-approximation guarantees within $\bigO{(\log n + \epsilon^{-1}) \log n}$ time complexity. \textbf{Structure:} The remainder of this paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{sec:prel} establishes preliminary definitions. Section~\ref{sec:auc} presents our AUC maintenance approach, while Sections~\ref{sec:hexact}--\ref{sec:happrox} detail $H$-measure maintenance techniques. Section~\ref{sec:exp} provides experimental evaluation, with Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} offering concluding discussion.

Deep neural network (DNN) models for object detection and classification—including Yolo \cite{yolo9000-1}, ResNet \cite{deepresidual-2} and EfficientNet \cite{efficientnet-3}—now drive video analytics applications spanning urban mobility and smart cars \cite{bellevue-report}. These deployments typically stream video data to {\em edge servers} \cite{azure-ase, aws-outposts} positioned on-premise \cite{ieee-computer, edgevideo-1, edgevideo-2, getmobile}. Edge computation offers compelling advantages for video analytics: it eliminates costly network links required for cloud streaming \cite{getmobile} and preserves video privacy (particularly important given European cities' mandates against cloud-based video streaming \cite{sweden-data, azure-data}). However, edge compute environments operate under severe resource constraints, often equipped with weak GPUs \cite{aws-outposts, azure-ase}. The growing disparity between model computational demands and processor capabilities \cite{ion-blog, openai-blog} further exacerbates these limitations. Consequently, edge deployments must rely heavily on {\em model compression} \cite{compression-4, compression-5, compression-6}. Although compressed DNNs undergo initial training on representative data from each video stream, field deployment exposes them to {\em data drift}—the phenomenon where live video data diverges substantially from training data \cite{datadrift-7, datadrift-8, datadrift-a, datadrift-b}. Street cameras and smart car systems encounter dynamic environmental conditions: fluctuating lighting, variable crowd densities, and evolving object compositions. Exhaustively capturing these variations during training proves challenging, as even minor changes can significantly impact accuracy. Consequently, edge DNNs experience substantial accuracy degradation due to data drift (22% reduction; \Sef{subsec:continuous-measurement}). Moreover, compressed DNNs, with their reduced weights and simplified architectures, often struggle to maintain high accuracy when trained across diverse data variations. 
oindent{ f Continuous model retraining.} Continuous learning emerges as a promising strategy for mitigating data drift. Edge DNNs undergo incremental {\em retraining} on fresh video samples while preserving previously acquired knowledge \cite{compressiondrift-11, continuous-12}. These continuous learning approaches perform periodic DNN retraining \cite{distribution-20, mullapudi2019}; we define the interval between consecutive retraining cycles as the ``retraining window'' and utilize accumulated data samples from each window for retraining. This ongoing learning paradigm \cite{incremental-13, icarl-14, incremental-15} enables compressed edge models to sustain high accuracy despite evolving data characteristics. Edge servers deploy their GPUs \cite{azure-ase} for DNN inference across multiple concurrent video streams (such as citywide traffic cameras). Incorporating continuous training into edge servers creates a fundamental tradeoff between live inference accuracy and accuracy loss from data drift. Increased resource allocation to retraining jobs accelerates completion and delivers improved models sooner. Conversely, diverting resources from inference during retraining degrades its accuracy (potentially requiring frame sampling for video analysis). The resource requirements and accuracy of these jobs fundamentally depend on their {\em configurations}. Retraining job configurations encompass hyperparameters such as training epochs, which significantly influence both resource consumption and accuracy outcomes (\Sef{subsec:profiles}). The magnitude of accuracy improvement from retraining correlates with {\em the extent} of change in live video characteristics. For inference jobs, configuration parameters like frame sampling rates and resolution directly affect both accuracy and computational resources required for real-time video analysis \cite{chameleon, noscope}. 
oindent{ f Problem statement.} Our continuous retraining framework addresses the following decisions: ($1$) determining which edge models require retraining within each retraining window; ($2$) distributing the edge server's GPU resources between retraining and inference tasks; and ($3$) optimizing configurations for both retraining and inference jobs. We impose the constraint that inference accuracy {\em must never fall} below a minimum threshold (ensuring application outputs remain viable). Our optimization objective involves maximizing inference accuracy {\em averaged across the retraining window} (incorporating accuracies during and following retraining cycles) for all videos processed on the edge server. This retraining window accuracy maximization introduces novel challenges distinct from $(i)$ video inference systems focused solely on instantaneous accuracy optimization \cite{videostorm, noscope, chameleon}, and $(ii)$ model training systems targeting only final accuracy \cite{hyperparameter-16, DBLP:journals/jmlr/BergstraB12, DBLP:conf/nips/SnoekLA12, Swersky_scalablebayesian, DBLP:conf/osdi/XiaoBRSKHPPZZYZ18, DBLP:conf/eurosys/PengBCWG18}. Resolving the core tradeoff between retrained model accuracy and inference performance presents significant computational complexity. Initially, the decision space spans multiple dimensions encompassing diverse retraining and inference configurations alongside temporal resource allocation choices. Additionally, determining configuration performance (resource utilization and accuracy) requires actual retraining experiments across different configurations. Data drift compounds these challenges since effective decisions in one retraining window may prove inadequate in subsequent periods. 
oindent{ f Solution components.} Our {{	t Ekya}\xspace} solution comprises two primary components: a resource scheduler and a performance estimator. The { f resource scheduler} executes the three decisions outlined in our problem statement within each retraining window. {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s scheduler prioritizes retraining models from video streams exhibiting the greatest characteristic changes, as these models suffer most severely from data drift. The scheduler excludes models whose retraining would not enhance our target metric. Several techniques enable decision space pruning. First, spatial complexity reduction occurs through coarse GPU allocation fractions (e.g., 10\%) that provide sufficient accuracy for scheduling decisions while respecting modern GPU granularity constraints \cite{nvidia-mps}. Second, resource allocations remain static {\em throughout retraining}, effectively avoiding temporal complexity. Finally, our micro-profiler (detailed below) filters configurations to retain only promising candidates. The resource scheduler depends on accuracy estimates following retraining and resource demand predictions for efficient configuration selection. Our { f micro-profiler} design observes retraining configuration accuracy on {\em small training data subsets} using {\em minimal epochs}. These observations enable extrapolation to accuracies achieved through extensive dataset retraining over numerous epochs. Furthermore, micro-profiling targets only a limited set of {\em promising} retraining configurations. These combined techniques make {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s micro-profiler approximately $100	imes$ more efficient than exhaustive profiling while maintaining accuracy estimation errors within $5.8\%$. For resource demand estimation, the micro-profiler measures retraining duration {\em per epoch} under full GPU allocation, then scales training time across different allocations, epoch counts, and training data volumes. 
oindent{ f Implementation and Evaluation.} We implemented and evaluated {{	t Ekya}\xspace} through system deployment and trace-driven simulation. Our evaluation utilized video workloads from smart car dashboard cameras (Waymo \cite{waymo} and Cityscapes \cite{cityscapes}) and statically mounted traffic and building cameras across 24-hour periods. {{	t Ekya}\xspace} achieves $29\%$ higher accuracy compared to competing baselines. Regarding {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s efficiency, baseline approaches require $4	imes$ additional GPU resources on edge servers to match {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s accuracy performance. 
oindent{ f Contributions:} This work delivers the following contributions. 
oindent{1)} We establish the {\em inference accuracy averaged over the retraining window} metric for continuous training systems. 
oindent{2)} We develop an {\em efficient micro-profiler for estimating} the benefits and costs associated with edge DNN model retraining. 
oindent{3)} We create a scalable resource scheduler enabling {\em joint retraining and inference} operations on edge servers. 
oindent{ f This work does not raise any ethical issues.}

text: Complex tasks including image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012deep}, object detection, classification, and tracking~\cite{geiger2012we, lillicrap2015continuous} have witnessed remarkable achievements through deep-learning (DL) systems. Nevertheless, extensive research has demonstrated that these DL systems remain susceptible to {\em digital adversarial examples}—meticulously designed inputs that trigger unintended system behaviors. Attack detection represents one defensive strategy, enabling systems to reformulate actions upon identifying malicious inputs. While numerous detection methods for adversarial examples~\cite{metzen2017detecting, grosse2017statistical} have emerged in the digital realm, these approaches prove inadequate against adaptive attackers~\cite{carlini2017bypass} who simultaneously target DL systems for misclassification while circumventing detection mechanisms. Emerging research demonstrates that analogous vulnerabilities manifest in physical environments as well~\cite{lee2019physical,chou2018sentinet}. Rather than optimizing effectiveness for isolated image instances, physical adversarial attacks achieve robustness against variations in environmental and sensor conditions including illumination, rotation, and distance. Attackers can deploy {\em adversarial patches} strategically positioned within object detector fields of view to suppress detection capabilities~\cite{lee2019physical}. This robustness emerges through Expectation over Transformation (EOT)~\cite{athalye2017synthesizing}, which models distributions of patch locations, orientations, and photometric characteristics, subsequently optimizing attacks across datasets with applied distributional variations. Adversarial patches differ from digital adversarial examples by requiring continuous spatial regions within input images. This spatial constraint renders them conspicuous to human observers, exemplified by toaster patches~\cite{brown2017adversarial} or printed t-shirts~\cite{xu2019adversarial}. While adversarial patches offer cost-effective generation and multi-scenario applicability unlike digital adversarial examples, their deployment against time-critical safety systems such as autonomous vehicles poses risks to users and the broader public. Despite these concerns, adversarial patch detection has garnered limited research attention until recently. We observe that adversarial patch generation differs from digital adversarial example creation in merely two aspects: i) optimization occurs across input image distributions rather than individual images, ii) area constraints replace norm constraints. This observation leads to our hypothesis that \emph{neural networks experiencing adversarial patch attacks exhibit behavioral patterns similar to those under digital adversarial example attacks, enabling the transfer of digital adversarial perturbation detection methods to adversarial patch detection}. Automated adversarial patch detection should theoretically surpass digital adversarial example detection in feasibility, given human visual recognition capabilities. To our knowledge, SentiNet~\cite{chou2018sentinet} represents the sole prior investigation into adversarial patch detection, leveraging the high salience and scene-transferability characteristics of adversarial patches for detection and segmentation. This paper adapts a mechanism initially designed for digital adversarial perturbation detection~\cite{qin2019detecting} and empirically evaluates its performance against simulated physical adversarial attacks. Specifically, we investigate class-conditional reconstructions~\cite{qin2019detecting}—which demonstrate limited effectiveness in digital domains—against adversarial patches. Our findings reveal that unlike digital adversarial examples, adaptive attacks employing adversarial patches fail to neutralize the detector. We implement this detection approach on modified AlexNet architecture and on \emph{Capsule Networks (CapsNets)}, a recently introduced and potentially powerful neural architecture~\cite{sabour2017dynamic,hinton2018matrix}. CapsNets employ vector- or matrix-valued capsule layers representing object poses and probabilities while capturing part-whole relationships. Analogous to how neuron layers extract higher-level features from lower-level features in conventional neural networks, capsule layers extract higher-level objects from lower-level objects, shapes, or lines. Additionally, we introduce an enhanced CapsNet architecture incorporating {\em Dropout} and {\em Affine Voting} to improve test set classification performance. Our contributions encompass the following: \begin{smitemize} \item We pioneer the exploration of digital adversarial example detection method effectiveness within adversarial patch domains, demonstrating results across three standard datasets: MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10. \item We establish the first demonstration of CapsNet effectiveness for classifying and detecting adversarially patched inputs. \item We introduce an enhanced Matrix Capsule Network featuring {\em capsule-dropout} and {affine voting}, empirically demonstrating improved test accuracy on the smallNORB dataset. \end{smitemize}

text: Recommendation systems stand to benefit significantly from deep reinforcement learning (DRL), which excels at discovering optimal strategies through interactive learning to generate recommendations aligned with users' evolving preferences. Three primary categories characterize DRL-based recommendation approaches: methods grounded in deep Q-learning, those utilizing policy gradients, and hybrid techniques. The objective of deep Q-learning centers on identifying optimal actions by maximizing Q-values across all feasible choices. \citet{zheng2018drn} pioneered the integration of DRL into recommendation systems for news applications, while \citet{chen2018stabilizing} subsequently developed robust Q-learning techniques to address dynamic online recommendation environments. Nevertheless, Q-learning approaches encounter the \textit{agent stuck problem}—the requirement for maximization operations over action spaces becomes computationally prohibitive when dealing with extremely large action domains. The agent stuck problem finds mitigation through policy gradient methodologies~\cite{chen2019large}. While these approaches employ average rewards as optimization criteria, they may misclassify poor actions as beneficial ones, creating convergence difficulties~\cite{pan2019policy}. Hybrid methodologies offer superior performance by synthesizing Q-learning and policy gradient advantages. Actor-critic networks~\cite{konda2000actor} exemplify popular hybrid algorithms, employing policy gradients within actor networks while utilizing Q-learning in critic networks to establish Nash equilibrium across both components. Contemporary DRL-based recommendation systems extensively leverage actor-critic architectures~\cite{chen2019top,liu2020end,zhao2020leveraging,chen2020knowledge}. All current DRL-based approaches, regardless of their distinctions, depend fundamentally on carefully crafted context-dependent reward functions, as illustrated in Fig~\ref{fig:work} (a) depicting the standard DRL-based recommendation workflow. Nevertheless, reward function specification often proves challenging due to dynamic environmental conditions and the multitude of factors influencing user interests~\cite{shang2019environment}. Consequently, existing methodologies may exhibit constrained generalization capabilities. Furthermore, these approaches typically incorporate both user preferences and user actions (including click-through rates, ratings, or implicit feedback) within reward functions, operating under assumptions that rewards depend solely on currently selected items and that user actions remain independent of recommended items. Online recommendation scenarios, however, invalidate these assumptions~\cite{shang2019environment}. An additional obstacle emerges from the computational intensity of reinforcement learning when deriving recommendation policies from initial conditions~\cite{finn2016guided,levine2012continuous}. Recommendation problems involve massive state spaces (encompassing all candidate items potentially interesting to users) and action spaces (covering all possible actions for candidate items), requiring traditional reinforcement learning methods to exhaustively explore combinations for optimal policy identification—a computationally demanding process. Addressing these challenges, we seek to enable agents to derive reward functions from user behaviors through inverse reinforcement learning while efficiently and adaptively learning recommendation policies directly from behavioral data, as demonstrated in Fig 1 (b). We therefore introduce a generative inverse reinforcement learning framework for adaptively inferring implicit reward functions from user behaviors. This approach evaluates current recommendation policy performance and updates existing policies using expert policies within the discriminator, thereby reducing the necessity for explicit reward function definition in online recommendation contexts. We specifically reformulate inverse deep reinforcement learning (DRL) as a generator for augmenting diverse state-action pair collections. This generative strategy enables our method to achieve enhanced generalization under complex online recommendation scenarios. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce generative inverse reinforcement learning for automatic reward function learning in online recommendation contexts. This represents the first work to decouple reward functions from agents in online recommendation systems. \item We develop an innovative actor-discriminator network module incorporating a discriminator as the critic network and a novel actor-critic network as the actor network for framework implementation. This module operates model-free and generalizes readily across diverse scenarios. \item We evaluate our approach through experiments on VirtualTB, a virtual online platform, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed method. Our technique achieves superior click-through rates compared to several state-of-the-art approaches. \end{itemize}

This is the first work that decouples reward functions from agents in the context of online recommendations. We introduce a generative method for learning reward functions in an online setting. This generative strategy allows our method to generalize better to complex online recommendation situations. Our technique has superior click-through rates compared to several state-of-the-art approaches. We evaluate our method through experiments on VirtualTB, a virtual platform for a simulation game, and demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our method. We develop a new actor-discriminator network that combines a discriminator as a critic and a novel actor-critic network as an actor for the implementation of the framework, which is model-free and easily generalized to various simulations.

text: The emergence of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)\cite{goodfellow2014generative} alongside diverse image forgery techniques~\cite{karras2017progressive,zakharov2019few,karras2019style,wu2019sliced} has enabled numerous methodologies~\cite{karras2017progressive, karras2019style, wu2019sliced, choi2019stargan, karras2020analyzing, shaham2019singan} to generate remarkably realistic imagery featuring human faces, landscapes, and various objects. Additionally, contemporary approaches~\cite{zakharov2019few, sun2019meta} employing few-shot learning—a GAN-based technique—enable deep learning frameworks to achieve high-quality outputs using minimal training data. The capability to generate such imagery through few-shot learning presents opportunities for creating deceptive content, as evidenced by recent incidents~\cite{cnn_business, yin_2019, deepnude} showcasing malicious exploitation of these technologies. Traditional image forgery detection relied on metadata analysis or manually crafted image features. Nevertheless, cutting-edge AI methodologies like GANs synthesize both novel images and corresponding metadata entirely from scratch. Consequently, conventional metadata-dependent detection strategies prove ineffective against contemporary GAN-generated fake imagery. To tackle these challenges, researchers have developed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based binary classification systems including \textit{ShallowNet}~\cite{tariq2019gan}, \textit{FakeTalkerDetect}~\cite{jeon2019faketalkerdetect}, \textit{FaceForensics++}~\cite{rossler2018faceforensics}, and \textit{Face X-ray}~\cite{li2020face}, which undergo training using extensive collections of authentic versus fabricated images. Additionally, investigations by other scholars~\cite{marra2019gans, zhang2019detecting, yu2019attributing} have demonstrated enhanced detection capabilities through examination of artifacts and distinctive patterns inherent in GAN-generated imagery. This research introduces~\textit{Dual Attention Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network} (\textit{DA-FDFtNet}), a fine-tuning neural architecture designed for detecting fabricated facial imagery. ~DA-FDFtNet~integrates \textit{Fine-Tune Transformer} (FTT) and \textit{Channel attention modules} with pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) backbones, incorporating \textit{MobileNet block V3} (MBblockV3) for distinguishing authentic from synthetic images. An architectural overview appears in Figure~\ref{fig:overview_fdftnet}, illustrating our implementation of established CNN frameworks (pre-trained networks)~\cite{simonyan2014very,szegedy2015going,he2016deep,iandola2014densenet,hu2018squeeze,howard2017mobilenets} with fine-tuning adaptations for fake image detection. Notably, DA-FDFtNet~ builds upon \textit{FDFtNet}~\cite{jeon2020fdftnet} by incorporating FTT and MBblockV3 components alongside an additional channel attention module in the final layer. The FTT component leverages self-attention mechanisms for diverse feature extraction from input images. Simultaneously, MBblockV3 employs varied convolution and structural approaches for feature extraction, while the channel attention module captures feature dependencies across spatial and channel dimensions. Furthermore, we employ diverse data augmentation strategies to address constraints associated with limited dataset sizes during baseline model fine-tuning, thereby enhancing overall performance across various fake image categories. Our experimental evaluation encompasses 4 distinct deepfake variants (FaceSwap, DeepFakes, Face2Face, and NeuralTextures) along with GAN-synthesized facial images (StarGAN, PGGAN, StyleGAN, and StyleGAN2), establishing our approach's effectiveness across multiple domains. The primary contributions of this work include: \begin{itemize} \item We propose DA-FDFtNet, an enhanced neural network-based fake image detection system achieving 97.02\% accuracy while improving baseline model performance by 1\% to 47\% through our methodological innovations. \item We present a novel fine-tuning neural network-based classification framework requiring minimal data for fine-tuning and offering seamless integration with established CNN architectures. \item We conduct comprehensive evaluations across 8 different deepfake and GAN-generated fake image datasets, validating our approach's effectiveness across diverse domains. \end{itemize} The paper structure proceeds as follows: Section 2 surveys fake image detection methodologies and details our novel model approach. Section 3 presents dataset specifications, baseline models, and~\textit{DA-FDFtNet} architectural details. Section 4 outlines experimental training procedures and presents results. Section 5 concludes our findings.

text: The proliferation of machine learning models and automated decision-making systems has sparked considerable interest in comprehensively understanding their operational characteristics~\cite{surveyxaifosca, zehlike2021fairness}. A critical component in elucidating machine learning algorithm outcomes involves detecting data subgroups where these algorithms may exhibit distinct, potentially aberrant behaviors. Discovering unusual behavioral patterns within data subgroups serves crucial functions throughout the KDD pipeline, encompassing model validation and testing~\cite{ chung2019automated, wu2019errudite} as well as fairness assessment~\cite{chung2019automated, cabrera2019fairvis}. Societal bias~\cite{barocas2016big} has emerged as an escalating concern, prompting researchers to intensify efforts toward measuring and guaranteeing fairness in machine learning systems. This objective typically necessitates human experts to manually pinpoint sensitive attributes (such as gender or ethnicity) or identify problematic data subgroups. Machine learning algorithm performance is conventionally assessed through global metrics that examine algorithmic behavior across entire datasets or specific class labels at an aggregate level. In contrast, this paper introduces the notion of \textit{divergence} to quantify statistical differences (such as false positive rates) between machine learning algorithm behavior on particular data subgroups versus the complete dataset. Our methodology automatically detects data subgroups exhibiting substantial behavioral deviations, characterizing these subgroups through combinations of attribute values, referred to throughout this work as \textit{patterns} or \textit{itemsets}. The divergence concept can be demonstrated using the {\sc compas}\ dataset~\cite{angwin_2016}, where a proprietary algorithm assigns recidivism risk scores to criminal defendants, with the positive class representing high recidivism scores. Table~\ref{table-teaser} presents false-positive (FPR) and false-negative (FNR) rates for the complete dataset (first row) alongside data subgroups exhibiting the highest FPR (second row) and FNR (third row) divergence values. The pattern (\textit{age>45, charge=M, race=Cauc}) demonstrates elevated $\Delta_{FNR}$ divergence, indicating that instances within this subgroup experience incorrect negative class assignments at rates exceeding those of the overall dataset. We present a comprehensive framework for divergence computation that enables automatic identification of problematic data subgroups in both classification and ranking scenarios. Our methodology leverages established itemset mining algorithms (such as FP-growth~\cite{han2000mining}) to efficiently discover all problematic patterns exceeding a minimal frequency threshold. Additionally, for any given pattern, we employ Shapley values~\cite{shapley1953value} to measure individual attribute value contributions to pattern divergence. As demonstrated in subsequent sections, the attribute value \textit{age>45} contributes most significantly to the divergent behavior observed in the previously discussed pattern.

text: The perception and manipulation of deformable objects by robots continues to present significant challenges. Given the intricate geometric configurations and unpredictable deformations inherent to such objects, researchers typically employ a three-stage methodology. Initially, objects undergo modeling within simulated environments \cite{Hess:2010:BFE:1893021,coumans2021} or through finite element methods (FEM) \cite{doi:10.1143/JPSJ.66.367}. Subsequently, the learning phase focuses on understanding object deformations during manipulation within the simulated environment \cite{miller2012geometric,lin2015picking}. The concluding stage involves determining optimal manipulation trajectories \cite{zaidi2017model,yamakawa2012simple}. Throughout this three-stage process, the primary challenge lies in acquiring knowledge of the stress-strain relationships characterizing these deformable objects \cite{courtney2005mechanical}, which fundamentally depend on physical properties including stiffness, area weight, and damping coefficients. Consequently, understanding the physical properties of deformable objects becomes essential for enabling robots to execute sophisticated manipulation tasks. Existing methodologies for estimating material physics properties fall into two categories: approaches that learn physical properties through alignment between simulated models and real objects \cite{9196770,arriola2017multimodal,wang2011data}, and techniques that extract physics properties directly from video sequences \cite{bouman2013estimating,yang2017learning,runia2020cloth}. While the alignment-based methods demand precise object matching using finite element techniques—a computationally intensive process—video-based approaches eliminate the need for simulated models that correspond to real objects. Consequently, video sequence learning offers computational efficiency and practical deployment potential in robotic systems where robots can exert external forces on deformable objects. This paper therefore introduces a method for learning fabric dynamic characteristics. We present a Physics-Similarity Neural Network (PhySNet), illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig:arch}, designed to predict physics parameters for both simulated and real fabrics. Our central hypothesis posits that \textit{PhySNet can accurately predict physics parameters of real fabrics and garments through learning physics similarities of simulated fabrics under wind force field conditions}. To validate this hypothesis, we construct a comprehensive simulated fabric database enabling PhySNet to learn physics similarities among simulated fabrics and generate Physics Similarity Maps (PSM) for individual fabrics. Following PhySNet training, we input both real fabric samples and simulated fabrics with initialized physics parameters to obtain their Physics Similarity Distance (PSD). The PSD then feeds into a Bayesian optimizer that produces updated physical parameters. These refined physics parameters drive the simulator to generate new simulated fabric instances. This iterative process continues until the Bayesian optimizer converges on stable parameters (Section \ref{sec:experiment-test_on_fabrics}).

text: Founded in 2016, PerceptIn emerged as a developer of visual perception technologies targeting autonomous vehicles and robotics applications. The company has secured more than \$10 million in venture capital from prominent investors including Walden International, Matrix Partners, and Samsung Ventures \cite{liu2020critical}. Operating as a global technology startup, PerceptIn maintains a presence across the U.S., Japan, Europe, and Asia. The organization comprises over 30 researchers and engineers alongside 10 business professionals. While business professionals focus on market development and collect feedback to inform R\&D initiatives, the engineering and research teams concentrate on advancing autonomous driving technologies. Over the past three years, the company has produced more than 20 U.S. patents, over 100 international patents, and numerous research publications. PerceptIn pivoted toward developing low-speed autonomous vehicles for the micromobility sector in 2017, recognizing micromobility as an emerging transportation paradigm where lightweight vehicles address short-distance travel needs that conventional mass transit overlooks \cite{liu2020autonomous}. The US Department of Transportation reports that trips under 5 miles account for 60\% of vehicle traffic \cite{santos2011summary}. Current mass transit systems inadequately serve short-trip transportation requirements due to prohibitive costs, creating significant societal impacts. Micromobility fills this gap between transit services and community requirements, catalyzing the growth of Mobility-as-a-Service. Internal business analysis revealed that PerceptIn could deliver reasonable return-on-investment to customers—autonomous vehicle operators—by providing low-speed autonomous vehicles priced below \$70,000 per unit. This \$70,000 target, however, creates exceptionally stringent design constraints for low-speed autonomous vehicles. The budget must accommodate Non-recurring engineering (NRE) expenses including research and development, alongside recurring costs encompassing chassis, drive-by-wire conversion (transforming traditional vehicles into computer-controllable systems), sensors, integration, customer service, and computing systems \cite{liu2020engineering}. Given that on-vehicle computing systems represent a major cost and power consumption factor, PerceptIn investigated autonomous driving computing architectures \cite{liu2017computer}\cite{liu2019edge}\cite{liu2020pirt}. The analysis determined that computing constitutes the primary bottleneck for commercial autonomous vehicle deployment, necessitating a computing solution that delivers reliability, affordability, high performance, and energy efficiency. Critical requirements included cost-effectiveness and rapid time-to-market. PerceptIn evaluated several alternatives: The first option involved optimizing commercial off-the-shelf mobile System-on-Chip (SoC) computing platforms. This approach offered notable advantages: mobile SoCs benefit from economies of scale, making them ideal foundations for affordable, backward-compatible computing architectures. Additionally, PerceptIn's vehicles target micromobility applications with constrained speeds, resembling mobile robots where mobile SoCs have proven successful. Nevertheless, comprehensive evaluation of mobile SoCs' autonomous driving suitability would require extensive research, potentially delaying product launch by six months. The second option considered procuring specialized autonomous driving computing platforms from vendors like NXP, MobilEye, and Nvidia. text: Across the globe, millions of individuals engage daily with digitized public services. Access to these platforms typically necessitates user authentication procedures. During such processes, users reasonably expect their personal data to receive private and secure handling. Furthermore, users demand interfaces that are efficient, thoughtfully designed, and intuitive; services that prove cumbersome to navigate can rapidly generate user frustration and erode confidence. When usability barriers significantly impede users from accomplishing their primary objectives, complete service abandonment may result~\cite{Brostoff}. \subsection{Problem Statement} Prevalent Identity Management Systems (IDMS) including \textit{GOV.UK Verify} and the \textit{Federal Cloud Credential Exchange} (FCCX) exhibit notable privacy and security deficiencies~\cite{Brandao}. Two critical factors amplify these vulnerabilities: \begin{enumerate} \item Rapid expansion of these systems across both service offerings and user populations~\cite{ElMaliki2007}. \item Implementation of federated or centralized authentication architectures. Central hub deployment enables aggregation and correlation of user activities across multiple service providers while providing extensive access to personally identifiable information (PII). \end{enumerate} Increased user bases or expanded service linkages create more attractive targets for malicious actors or compromised hub operators. When such breaches occur, undetectable user impersonation, profiling, and targeting become feasible~\cite{Brandao}, ultimately undermining public confidence~\cite{Ohara} in these services. Privacy and security challenges extend beyond government-operated platforms. Recent vulnerability disclosures and data breaches affecting Facebook and Google platforms—frequently employed for third-party service authentication—exemplify these widespread concerns~\cite{fbreach, googlebreach}. Addressing these challenges through privacy-by-design principles, researchers have developed privacy-enhancing identity and credential management systems~\cite{Goodell2019, Idemix, UPort, Chainspace, AnonCredLight}. While each system tackles specific privacy and security concerns with distinct advantages, privacy characteristics, compromises, and limitations~\cite{Goodell2019}, the complex relationships between these systems' strengths and constraints within practical deployment scenarios remain poorly understood. Varying use-cases impose different design constraints based on stakeholder requirements. Consequently, thorough analysis becomes essential for identifying specific considerations that system implementers and users must recognize, comprehend, and resolve. Additional research is needed to evaluate whether current privacy-enhancing identity and credential management systems can realistically compete with existing enterprise and government deployments. \subsection{Research Objectives} This chapter examines the viability and efficacy of deploying privacy-enhancing identity management within large-scale public transport payment infrastructures. We constrain our investigation to three specific questions regarding the protocol developed by Goodell et al~\cite{Goodell2019}, which we term the \textit{Distributed Digital Identity Architecture} (DigID): \begin{enumerate} \item How does the DigID address the key privacy and security requirements of modern public transport payment systems compared to current centralized solutions? \item What are the technical, operational, and user experience trade-offs when implementing DigID in a large-scale public transport network? \item To what extent can DigID meet or exceed the performance requirements of Transport for London's existing payment infrastructure? \end{enumerate} London serves as our case study given its operational scale, complex fare structure, and accessible public datasets that enable comparative analysis. \subsection{Chapter Structure} The following sections proceed systematically. We first establish contextual background for such systems while demonstrating their practical value. This section also introduces essential terminology and examines alternative solutions. Section~\ref{overview} explores implementation challenges specific to Transport for London (TfL) while proposing potential extensions to overcome identified limitations. Section~\ref{implementation} elaborates on specific design decisions within our implementation. Section~\ref{results} outlines our testing methodology, Section~\ref{analysis} examines the findings, and Section~\ref{conclusion} provides comprehensive analysis alongside future research directions.

text: Breast cancer will affect an estimated 276,480 women in the U.S. during 2020, with 42,170 anticipated deaths from this disease \cite{Sieg20}. Most pathologists employ a standardized grading framework to inform treatment decisions \cite{Bloo51, Elst91}, evaluating three distinct characteristics: 1) nuclear pleomorphism (termed "atypia"), 2) gland formation extent, and 3) mitotic activity. While mitotic count and gland formation rely on quantitative assessment criteria, nuclear pleomorphism evaluation depends on qualitative microscopic analysis of tumor nuclear morphology, scored from 1 to 3 based on progressive deviation from normal epithelial appearance. These three component scores combine to determine the final tumor grade. Digital pathology's expanding adoption enables grading through digitized histopathological images, achieving comparable inter-observer agreement to traditional light microscopy \cite{Gint20}. Furthermore, Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support pathologists in clinical workflows \cite{Bera19, Niaz19, Bult20a, Rant20}. Deep neural networks (deep learning; DL) represent the predominant AI approach for medical image analysis. These architectures utilize interconnected neurons that process input images through sequential operations on trainable network parameters to execute learning objectives including classification, regression, and segmentation. Their remarkable achievements span computer vision domains \cite{Kriz12, Le13, Silv16, Devl18} and extend to recent digital pathology breakthroughs \cite{Jano16, Bejn17, Veta18, Nagp19, Bult20}. Within breast cancer grading specifically, automated mitosis detection emerged as an early DL application \cite{Cire13a, Veta15}, establishing clinical and prognostic significance \cite{Tell18, Balk19, Balk19b}. Researchers approached gland segmentation through nuclei and gland detection combined with segmentation methodologies \cite{Nguy15, Lee18}, extending to clinical risk stratification \cite{Buch16} via deep learning implementations. However, nuclear pleomorphism lacks the quantitative foundation characterizing gland formation and mitotic count. Consequently, nuclear pleomorphism assessment exhibits the poorest reproducibility among the three grading elements, constraining its clinical value \cite{Frie95, Meye05, Long05}. Previous automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring efforts remain sparse, encompassing manually engineered nuclear features \cite{Lu15, Gand19} paired with deep belief networks \cite{Maql16}, descriptor-based pixel-level image characteristics \cite{Khan15}, or binary high pleomorphism (score 3) classification using basic convolutional neural networks on limited image patches \cite{Noel15}. Supervised DL necessitates ground-truth annotations paired with training images for neural network optimization. Obtaining reliable annotations presents substantial challenges for applications like pleomorphism scoring, characterized by discrete categories and significant observer variation. Converting multiple observer scores into single ground-truth labels (through majority voting or consensus) eliminates crucial information embedded within individual expert score distributions. Therefore, we propose a novel DL methodology for nuclear pleomorphism scoring by conceptualizing it as continuous scoring rather than discrete three-category classification. We transform the conventional three-class classification framework into a comprehensive continuous spectrum spanning minimal to maximal pleomorphism severity. Our methodology comprises two primary components. Initially, we employ a previously developed epithelial cell detection network \cite{Merc19}. This stage restricts analysis to diagnostically significant regions (invasive tumor areas) within whole slide images. Subsequently, a deep regression network generates continuous nuclear pleomorphism scores for tumor regions. Network training circumvents detailed manual pathologist annotations, addressing a fundamental computational pathology bottleneck. This represents the inaugural end-to-end fully automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring system for breast cancer utilizing DL. Additionally, we pioneer the transformation of discrete classification into continuous regression to preserve valuable observer information previously unexploited. Figure \ref{fig:introduction:overview_inference} illustrates our \AI approach, depicting this two-stage nuclear pleomorphism scoring methodology. We conducted two distinct studies with corresponding datasets to develop and validate our approach. The ROI-study encompassed $125$ tumor regions of interest (tumor ROIs) plus $79$ "normal appearing" epithelial regions of interest (normal ROIs) extracted from $39$ whole slide images, deliberately selected to represent diverse breast cancer histopathological tumor morphologies. Ten pathologists from $6$ countries evaluated nuclear pleomorphism on tumor ROIs, with each tumor ROI visually paired with a normal ROI from the identical patient to provide pleomorphism scoring reference standards. ROI-study results facilitated \AI training and performance evaluation against the pathologist panel. Our automated methodology utilized averaged nuclear pleomorphism scores across all 10 pathologists as reference standards, capturing their collective expertise rather than imposing discrete majority classifications. The \AI trained on diverse tumor morphologies, leveraging reference scores to establish nuclear pleomorphism as a comprehensive tumor morphology change spectrum. The slide-study utilized $118$ whole slide images from breast cancer resection specimens for trained \AI evaluation. Slide distribution mirrored routine clinical practice case patterns. Four pathologists scored nuclear pleomorphism for slide-study images, enabling whole slide-level \AI performance comparison. Section \ref{sec:methodology} provides comprehensive ROI-study and slide-study details.

text: The task of pose transfer—wherein a desired pose from a source mesh is applied to a target mesh—represents both a compelling opportunity and formidable challenge within 3D computer vision, offering broad applicability across numerous industrial domains. Nevertheless, current approaches ~\cite{NPT,LIMP,Unsupervised,AniFormer} demonstrate satisfactory performance solely within constrained datasets featuring synthesized or familiar pose and shape spaces, yet exhibit poor generalization when confronted with unknown spaces, thereby substantially constraining their practical real-world deployment. We introduce a novel Transformer architecture designed for generalized 3D mesh pose transfer that achieves robust performance across unknown latent spaces and diverse domains, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:1}. Our approach centers on a geometry-contrastive Transformer incorporating geometrically structured encoders, which strengthens identity mesh representation through pose mesh guidance via \emph{global geometric contrasts}. At the local level, we develop a central geodesic contrastive loss that enhances geometric representation by leveraging the \emph{regional contrast of all geodesic directions} for each vertex during back-propagation. Additionally, we incorporate a latent isometric regularization module that addresses performance instabilities inherent in cross-dataset pose transfer scenarios.
