text: Searcher struggle represents the phenomenon where a searcher ``makes strenuous efforts in the face of difficulties"\footnote{\url{merriam-webster.com}} throughout their search journey. During such episodes, users encounter negative emotional states characterized by frustration, upset feelings, or annoyance with the search activity. The detection of searcher struggle constitutes a critical task for Web search engines, as it enables these systems to receive timely alerts for algorithmic adjustments. Contemporary struggle detection approaches predominantly employ classifiers that utilize features quantifying user efforts~\cite{Li:2009:GAM:1571941.1571951,Jiang:2015:UPG:2684822.2685319}. This approach stems from the observation that struggling behaviors frequently manifest through excessive repetitions of user actions. Consider, for example, a user searching for ``curly hair dye" who generated over twenty queries yet failed to locate satisfactory results. The assumption that substantial user efforts indicate struggle appears intuitive. Nevertheless, this assumption frequently diverges from real-world observations. One notable finding reveals that non-struggling search tasks can equally exhibit numerous user-generated queries and clicks. To illustrate, a user investigating ``guy proposing ideas" browsed over 900 search results and bookmarked 27 items; this user subsequently reported enjoying the entire search session. Contemporary laboratory studies have echoed these concerns. Edwards and Kelly \cite{Edwards:2017:EFD:3077136.3080818} emphasized that while increased user effort may facilitate struggle prediction, such increases can equally indicate engagement or exploration. In the absence of effective discriminatory mechanisms, effort-based features lose their distinguishing capacity, creating difficulties in separating negative experiences like struggle from positive experiences such as engagement, thereby complicating Web user experience improvements. This paper draws upon psychological literature to introduce a novel feature modulation approach for struggle detection. Our research finds motivation in Reversal Theory (RT)~\cite{gerrig2015psychology,apter2001motivation,personalitydynamics,APTER1984265,fourdomains}. RT constitutes a ``mode-based" psychological framework that challenges fundamental assumptions within motivation and personality domains. Instead of presuming static personality characteristics, RT emphasizes the ``complexity, changeability, and dynamics of human motivation and personality"~\cite{APTER1984265}. The theory's central insight recognizes that individuals undergo changes during everyday life experiences, with their personalities and motivations capable of reversal~\cite{personalitydynamics}. RT proposes counter-intuitive concepts, suggesting that whether users conform to rules or rebel bears minimal impact on struggling behaviors, while the serious or playful nature of their tasks proves significant. We performed statistical hypothesis testing on these propositions and validated them using commercial search logs. Furthermore, RT posits that human motivations organize into several dimensions, each comprising two opposing states. Within any dimension, individuals can reverse between state pairs but remain active in only one state at any given moment, suggesting bi-modal rather than single-modal distributions. We harness this insight to propose a novel and effective feature modulation method for struggle detection. Our approach involves (1) selecting features corresponding to relevant RT dimensions, (2) moderating chosen features through bias reduction between the two distributions in the bi-modal arousal model, and (3) transmitting modulated features to classifiers for identifying struggling moments within search sessions. Our methodology integrates with any feature-based struggle detection approach. We assess our technique using week-long search logs gathered from both mobile and PC platforms. Experimental findings demonstrate our method's high effectiveness; it achieves significant improvements in several top-performing methods by $\sim$5\% accuracy and $\sim$9\% positive precision.

text: The emergence of Bitcoin through~\cite{Satoshi2008} in 2008 sparked widespread investigation into blockchain technology and smart contracts for developing novel applications. A worldwide consensus recognizes smart contracts' transformative potential across diverse industrial and governmental domains~\cite{Hileman2017}. While we share this perspective and acknowledge that certain smart contract applications benefit from on-chain deployment—such as those operating on Ethereum~\cite{Ethereum2017}, Hyperledger Fabric~\cite{HyperledgerHome}, or Bitcoin~\cite{BitcoinHome} blockchains—we contend that on-chain smart contracts' capabilities have been excessively emphasized. Numerous applications exist where blockchain-based smart contracts represent excessive complexity, while others suffer such detrimental effects that implementation becomes impractical or impossible~\cite{Morgen2018,Scriber2018,Valentina2018}. Under these circumstances, developers ought to explore smart contracts deployed on Trusted Third Parties. This confusion appears to stem from technological novelty and the absence of universal agreement regarding smart contract and blockchain definitions. We shall establish the definitions that guide our subsequent discussion. \subsection{Blockchains} From a software development perspective, blockchains constitute middleware incorporating integrated services for building distributed applications without requiring centralized control components (such as authentication or database servers). Key blockchain services include immutable append-only storage, public-key-based operation access control, public record auditability, and notably, consensus services following specific protocols (typically eventual consensus). While smart contracts represent the most recognized blockchain application, numerous other applications can be constructed using this foundation. Technically, blockchains are distributed data structures (also termed ledgers) comprising ordered, back-linked block chains. New blocks join the chain exclusively through append-only operations, occurring only when consensus emerges among nodes maintaining local blockchain state replicas regarding the next global state. These blocks typically store transaction records executed by mutually distrusting parties, supporting peer-to-peer transaction execution models. Transactions represent state-altering operations and need not involve monetary exchanges. Blockchain construction and maintenance demands multiple technological components, leading to various conceptual modeling approaches. For instance,~\cite{KenjiSaito2016} characterizes blockchains as probabilistic state machines, emphasizing the probabilistic nature of blockchain consensus algorithms. \subsection{Smart contracts} Conceptually, smart contracts represent digital equivalents of traditional commercial contracts written in human languages like English. The digital aspect means smart contracts are executable computer code capable of monitoring or enforcing conventional contract clauses programmatically during runtime. Consider a financial loan agreement between borrower and lender stipulating that upon borrower request, the lender must advance GBP 100.00 within five days. As executable programs, smart contracts require deployment infrastructure providing runtime environments, including library support, management facilities (initiation, termination, updates), and databases for storing input/output records. Smart contracts bear three primary responsibilities: i) serving as contract monitors observing contracting party interactions; ii) determining operation compliance (loan requests, approvals, rejections) with contractual terms and inherent rights/obligations; and iii) producing verdicts. While existing smart contract applications often directly link verdict declarations with actions (payment collection) executed upon compliance determination, we advocate separating these functions for modularity purposes, focusing on verdicts as smart contracts' fundamental operation. Actions represent arbitrary reactions executed immediately or eventually by smart contracts themselves or different software layer components. Many applications involve permitting compliant contractual operations or preventing non-compliant ones, positioning smart contracts as contract enforcers. This raises the deployment location question. \subsection{On--blockchain smart contracts} On-chain smart contract deployment represents one viable option. Although Szabo coined "smart contract" in 1997~\cite{Szabo1997}, commercial interest emerged only after Bitcoin's 2008 cryptocurrency success~\cite{Satoshi2008}. Bitcoin~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2017} implements smart contracts using opcode stack-based, non-Turing complete scripting languages~\cite{BitcoinScript} deployed on Bitcoin's blockchain, originally designed for mediating BTC payment operations. Ethereum~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2018}, currently a leading blockchain platform, extends Bitcoin's smart contract concept by supporting Turing-complete languages like Solidity~\cite{Solidity2017}. Numerous Bitcoin and Ethereum use cases demonstrate situations where on-chain smart contract deployment proves convenient, yet recognizing blockchains and smart contracts as independent technologies remains crucial. On-blockchain deployment represents merely one among several alternatives. Notably, smart contracts preceded blockchains by years—Minsky pioneered smart contract research in the mid-1980s~\cite{Minsky1985}, followed by Marshall~\cite{Lindsay1993}. Early research employed terms like electronic contracts, executable contracts, and digital contracts. Given widespread "smart contract" usage, we maintain this terminology throughout. \subsection{On--Trusted Third Parties smart contracts} Alternative deployment involves Trusted Third Parties (on-TTP). We define TTPs as institutions possessing both technical smart contract hosting infrastructure and established trust, reputation, and authority. E-commerce applications regularly utilize TTP services, including payment gateways, certification authorities, timestamping services, custodian services, settlement services, and various brokerage offerings~\cite{Mainelli2015}. In smart contract applications, TTPs occupy logical positions between business partners, trusted to host and execute single smart contract instances. Smart contracts observe all partner operations while maintaining undeniable records. Pioneering smart contract research~\cite{Minsky1985,Lindsay1993} primarily emphasized on-TTP deployment. TTP-based deployment assumes TTPs won't alter contract code or misuse sensitive contractual party data. Emerging trusted hardware technologies like Intel SGX~\cite{VictorCostan2016} and ARM TrustZone~\cite{Sandro2019} address this concern. This approach deploys contract code within trusted hardware environments (SGX enclaves, TrustZone trusted worlds). Trusted hardware prevents TTPs from compromising contract code integrity or accessing sensitive data. \subsection{Contributions of this paper} Following Bitcoin's publication~\cite{Satoshi2008}, smart contract discussions have predominantly occurred within blockchain contexts, creating apparent intrinsic associations. Consequently, Trusted Third Party smart contract potential and practicality have been significantly undervalued. This paper aims to restore balance by examining on-blockchain and on-TTP smart contract advantages and disadvantages. Our arguments derive from practical experience: as developers advising on smart contract technology selection for car insurance applications, we conducted exploratory implementations using both on-chain and on-TTP approaches. We share our experiences and insights regarding encountered technical challenges, discovering that on-TTP smart contracts sometimes offer superior solutions compared to on-chain alternatives. While acknowledging on-TTP smart contracts' notable disadvantage—single TTP dependence, considered undesirable and avoidable through blockchains—we argue that where TTP inconveniences prove tolerable, on-TTP smart contracts may surpass their on-chain counterparts. This paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{motivatingscenario} introduces our hypothetical car insurance application use case requiring smart contract implementation. Section~\ref{centralisedanddecentralised} explains centralized versus decentralized smart contract implementation architectures. Section~\ref{onblockchainimplementation} discusses our experience implementing the car insurance application using on-chain smart contracts in Solidity for Ethereum deployment. Section~\ref{onTTPimplementation} presents complementary arguments from on-TTP smart contract implementation. Section~\ref{discussion} expresses our personal smart contract perspectives and identifies open research questions. Section~\ref{relatedwork} contextualizes this article within broader smart contract literature, covering pioneering works and recent related publications. Finally, Section~\ref{conclusions} presents our conclusions.

On-chain deployment of smart contracts is one viable option. Many examples of this exist. In the case of smart contracts, the scripting languages deployed on the block-chain of the Bitcoin network, originally devised to mediate Bitcoin transactions, are not Turing complete. But in the case of the current most important platform for the blockchain, the idea of smart contracts is extended by the support of Turing complete languages like the solidity language. A quick word of explanation: smart contracts predate the invention of the blockchain by many years; Minsky started his research in the mid-80s, followed by Marshall in the early 90s. The first articles used terms like “electronic contracts”, “executable contracts” and “digital contracts”. Putting them on a blockchain is only one of several possible deployment methods. Trusted third parties are an alternative to a trust-free smart contract. Using the current terminology "smart contract", we use this terminology throughout. We define TTP as a company that has both the technical smart contract hosting and a reputation for trust, reliability and authority. E-commerce applications commonly use TTSs such as payment gateways, certification authorities, time stamping services, custodial services, settlement services, and different brokerage services (Mainelli, 2015). In smart contract applications, TTSs occupy the logical place between the business partners, being trusted to host and execute single smart contract instances. They monitor the activity of both parties while maintaining an undisputed record. Early smart contract research, for example Minsky ’85 and Lindsay ’93,1 emphasized the importance of using trusted third parties to deploy smart contracts. The reliance on a trusted third party for the deployment of smart contracts relies on the assumption that the third party will not alter the code or misuse the private data of the parties. Trusted hardware technologies like Intel SGX and ARM TrustZone can address this concern. - Since the first paper on Bitcoin (Satoshi, 2008), smart contracts have been discussed mostly in the context of the blockchain, thus creating an alleged inherent connection between the two. This paper aims to remedy this imbalance by comparing the relative advantages and disadvantages of smart contracts deployed on the public chain and on the trusted third party. It proposes to deploy smart contracts in trusted hardware environments (SGX enclaves, TrustZone trusted worlds). So far the potential and practicality of smart contracts in the TTP system has been greatly underestimated. Our statements are based on practical experience. As a smart contract technology advisor to the automobile insurance industry, we have conducted experiments in which the smart contract was implemented both on the public chain and in the TTP. This article is as follows. We share our experiences and insights on the encountered technical difficulties and find that on-TTP smart contracts can sometimes offer a better solution than on-chain smart contracts. Although we recognize that the main disadvantage of on-TTP smart contracts is their dependence on a single TTP, which is considered as unwise and can be avoided using a blockchain, we argue that on-TTP smart contracts can provide a better solution than on-chain smart contracts when the inconvenience of TTPs is bearable. Section refmotivatingscenario introduces a fictitious car insurance application, which requires the implementation of smart contracts. Section refonblockchainimplementation describes our experience with the implementation of the car insurance application using smart contracts in the language of the Ethereum network. Section refcentralisedanddecentralised explains the centralized and decentralized architectures of smart contract implementation. Section ref: relatedwork places the article in the context of the smart contract literature, citing both pioneering work and recent publications. Section ref: onTTPimplementation presents additional arguments from a smart contract implementation on TTP. Section ref: discussion discusses our personal views on smart contracts and identifies further research questions. The conclusion is finally given in the section entitled Conclusion.

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse artificial intelligence domains, spanning computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{6296526}, and robot control~\cite{levine2018learning}. However, despite their exceptional performance, these networks exhibit critical vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks—subtle input perturbations that remain imperceptible yet cause misclassification~\cite{madry2017towards, goodfellow2014explaining,laidlaw2019functional, laidlaw2020perceptual, kang2019testing, dong2018boosting, carlini2017towards, chen2017ead, 7467366}. Such vulnerabilities present significant security risks in mission-critical applications, particularly autonomous driving and medical diagnosis systems. Numerous defense strategies have emerged to strengthen model resilience against adversarial threats, encompassing both empirical~\cite{madry2017towards,zhang2019theoretically, papernot2016distillation,lin2020dual, singla2021skew, Kannan2018AdversarialLP, wang2019improving} and certifiable approaches~\cite{raghunathan2018certified,cohen2019certified, levine2020randomized, levine2019certifiably, sinha2017certifying, levine2021improved}. Among these, adversarial training (AT)~\cite{madry2017towards} stands as one of the most potent defense mechanisms. Various enhancements to AT have been developed through alternative loss formulations, including ALP~\cite{Kannan2018AdversarialLP}, TRADES~\cite{zhang2019theoretically}, and MART~\cite{wang2019improving}. Nevertheless, these approaches train individual models in isolation, overlooking potential synergistic benefits from network ensembles. Furthermore, most defenses target single perturbation types, leaving models susceptible to novel attack variants~\cite{tramer2019adversarial, maini2020adversarial}. Models trained against $l_\infty$-bounded perturbations, for instance, often fail against $l_1$ and $l_2$-bounded attacks. Knowledge distillation (KD)~\cite{hinton2015distilling} provides a powerful framework for knowledge transfer between models. The KD paradigm encompasses multiple variants~\cite{wang2020knowledge}, including \textit{offline} approaches where students learn from pre-trained static teachers~\cite{hinton2015distilling}, and \textit{online} methods enabling peer-to-peer learning among student cohorts~\cite{zhang2018deep, guo2020online, song2018collaborative}. Several KD-based adversarial defenses have emerged~\cite{papernot2016distillation, goldblum2019adversarially, arani2020adversarial, chen2021robust}, with~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} demonstrating robustness transferability through KD and~\cite{chen2021robust} showing KD's effectiveness in mitigating robust overfitting. Table~\ref{tab:kd} contrasts existing KD-based defense approaches. Current KD-based defenses exhibit suboptimal adversarial robustness enhancement. Defensive distillation (DD) employs natural models as both teachers and students, failing to provide substantial robustness since neither undergoes adversarial training—an approach subsequently compromised by~\cite{carlini2016defensive}. Adversarially robust distillation (ARD)~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} transfers robustness from larger to smaller networks using robust teacher models, but depends on pre-existing strong teachers and achieves limited student improvement due to static teacher constraints. Adversarial concurrent training (ACT)~\cite{arani2020adversarial} jointly trains natural and robust models through online KD to align feature representations. However, given the fundamental differences in features learned by natural versus robust models~\cite{tsipras2018robustness}, such alignment may compromise robustness. We introduce Mutual Adversarial Training (MAT), enabling models to collaboratively share adversarial robustness knowledge and mutually enhance defensive capabilities. Diverging from previous KD-based defenses, our approach simultaneously trains multiple robust models where each network learns not only from ground-truth labels as in standard AT, but also from peer-generated soft labels encoding collective adversarial defense knowledge for superior robustness. Figure~\ref{fig:mat} illustrates the MAT architecture. MAT enhances model robustness through multiple mechanisms: 1) MAT leverages inherent KD advantages, including improved generalization~\cite{furlanello2018born} and reduced robust overfitting~\cite{chen2021robust}. 2) \textit{MAT establishes a positive feedback cycle for escalating model robustness}. Each network functions as a robust teacher, providing semantically-aware and discriminative soft labels to peers. Through learning from strong peers, networks achieve enhanced robustness, subsequently improving peer performance. 3) \textit{MAT enables robust models to collectively explore expanded adversarial sample spaces and jointly discover more resilient feature representations and decision boundaries}. Each model's adversarial examples constitute a subspace within the broader adversarial input domain~\cite{tramer2017space}, with model predictions encoding decision boundary and adversarial subspace information. In MAT, models learn not only from their own adversarial examples but also receive peer adversarial information through soft labels. This approach requires each model to consider enlarged adversarial spaces and identify feature representations and decision boundaries effective across both personal and peer adversarial examples, promoting more robust and generalizable solutions. This paper presents MAT, a novel KD-based adversarial training framework for enhancing network robustness without requiring strong teacher models. We extend MAT to defend against multiple perturbation types (MAT-MP) by leveraging adversarial robustness transferability, proposing specialized training strategies for MAT-MP implementation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MAT significantly improves AT baseline robustness and surpasses state-of-the-art methods for both single and multiple perturbation scenarios.

text: Android has emerged as the world's dominant mobile operating system. This widespread adoption has simultaneously made it an attractive target for malicious actors. Adversaries exploit Android's popularity by deploying millions of malicious applications designed to extract private user data or execute harmful operations—including surveillance activities, spam distribution, and unwanted advertisement delivery. Consequently, Android malware investigation, encompassing both detection and categorization tasks, has become essential for security researchers across industry and academic domains. This critical need has spawned numerous research initiatives focused on Android malware detection~\cite{canfora2015effectiveness,gascon2013structural,li2018android,mclaughlin2017deep,hybroid}. Contemporary approaches increasingly exploit contextual information from Android applications for malware detection and categorization, particularly leveraging permissions and sensitive application programming interfaces (APIs). Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} developed a factorization machine (FM) architecture-based classifier that extracts diverse Android application features—including permissions and malicious APIs—from manifest files and source code. Chen et al.~\cite{chen2018android} introduced a static behavior analysis approach examining permissions, components, and sensitive API calls. Concurrently, natural language processing (NLP) methodologies~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} have been applied to Android malware detection, treating applications as documents and instructions as words. Kang et al.~\cite{kang2016n} exemplify this approach by evaluating uni-gram, bi-gram, and tri-gram effectiveness using stacked generalization. Network traffic pattern analysis represents another significant research direction for distinguishing legitimate from malicious behaviors~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,xu2021hawkeye,xu2020manis,xu2021falcon}. These approaches predominantly employ manually-defined rules to construct rule-based classifiers. CICAndMal2017~\cite{lashkari2018toward} utilizes third-party tools to extract nine features from network PCAP (packet capture) files for malware detection. Zulkifli et al.~\cite{zulkifli2018android} implement decision tree algorithms on network traffic as dynamic Android application features. Despite providing additional security layers for Android platforms, these methodologies exhibit significant limitations. Contextual program code information proves vulnerable to malware obfuscation techniques, including ~\textit{identifier renaming}, ~\textit{string encryption}, ~\textit{dead-code insertion}, and ~\textit{instruction substitution}. Such procedures modify compiled code to facilitate detection evasion. String encryption, for instance, compromises the FM method of Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} by preventing permission information extraction from manifest files. Similarly, NLP-based malware detection systems~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} suffer degradation from various obfuscation techniques. Network traffic-based methods face the fundamental challenge of code coverage limitations~\cite{tazaki2013direct}. As dynamic feature-based approaches, network traffic represents only limited code functionality, since most code operations neither require nor generate network traffic. Furthermore, state-of-the-art network traffic-based malware detection systems predominantly employ rule-based methodologies~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,hybroid}, which sophisticated attacks can readily circumvent. Rule-based analysis depends on distinguishing expected from anomalous behavior, making these methods vulnerable when malware is modified to conceal its footprints or behavioral patterns. This paper introduces a hybrid pattern malware detection and categorization framework combining network and program code features. We transform network packets into 2D grayscale image sequences and employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for pre-training these images. Subsequently, bi-directional LSTM networks process continuous network traffic for malware classification, treating it as a 2D image sequence classification problem. We develop an NLP-inspired methodology for program code pattern analysis based on graph neural networks (GNNs), capable of detecting obfuscated applications while maintaining superior performance. Our approach incorporates \texttt{opcode2vec}, \texttt{function2vec}, and \texttt{graph2vec} components to represent instruction, function, and complete program information as vectors. After extracting features from both network traffic and program code, we feed these vectors into classifiers trained to distinguish benign from malicious applications. \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace ultimately identifies Android malware families, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing frameworks. We achieve 97.16\% accuracy for malware detection and 88.32\% average accuracy for malware categorization. Our novelty encompasses two primary contributions: bi-directional LSTM processing of 2D-image sequences and graph-based malware detection employing natural language processing techniques for node representation. \bigskip \noindent In summary, we make the following main contributions: \begin{itemize} 	\item We introduce \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace, a hybrid pattern Android malware detection and categorization framework that combines the network traffic and program code features. 	\item We design a bidirectional LSTM network to accomplish 2D gray images sequence classification, which takes the network packets (converted to 2D images) as input. 	\item We create and release a dataset, \textit{AndroNetMnist}\xspace, which includes 3,255,391 2D gray images in five categories(Benign, Adware, Ransomware, Scareware and SMSmalware) for network traffic classification. 	\item We design and implement an NLP-inspired malware detection and categorization module for the program code that can process obfuscated programs. 	\item We evaluate the accuracy of our approach using real malicious and benign datasets. 	\item We release our work as an opensource project after the paper will be accepted. \end{itemize}

text: End-to-end neural network architectures have demonstrated remarkable success across diverse sequence generation domains, including machine translation~\cite{sutskever2014sequence,luong2015effective}, dialogue systems~\cite{vinyals2015neural,serban2016building}, textual summarization~\cite{rush2015neural,nallapati2016abstractive,see2017get}, image/video captioning~\cite{bahdanau2014neural,venugopalan2015sequence,pasunuru2017multi}, and question generation~\cite{du2017learning,du2018harvesting,zhang2019addressing}. While cross-entropy loss optimization remains the predominant training paradigm~\cite{sutskever2014sequence}, this conventional approach encounters significant limitations: exposure bias during inference~\cite{ranzato2015sequence} and inability to directly optimize non-differentiable automatic evaluation metrics that assess generation quality. Policy gradient-based reinforcement learning methods have emerged to tackle these challenges by enabling direct optimization of non-differentiable evaluation metrics~\cite{zaremba2015reinforcement,ranzato2015sequence,rennie2016self}. Nevertheless, policy gradient optimization targeting individual metrics frequently yields improvements concentrated primarily within that specific metric, indicating potential metric gaming behavior~\cite{paulus2017deep}. While researchers have investigated weighted combinations of multiple metrics or surrogate rewards~\cite{liu2017improved}, such strategies require careful calibration of optimal scaling factors across different metrics. Alternative approaches utilizing mixing ratios for multi-metric optimization~\cite{pasunuru2018multi} similarly demand meticulous ratio tuning. Furthermore, these reward formulations remain static throughout training, despite the likelihood that different metrics carry varying importance across training phases. Consequently, a dynamic metric combination strategy could prove beneficial—one that determines which rewards to emphasize during early versus late training stages, identifies when to revisit specific rewards, and considers the complete reward history alongside the model's current state and metric characteristics. We introduce a multi-armed bandit framework (termed DORB{}) wherein bandit arms represent selectable optimization metrics serving as rewards. During each training round, the bandit selects the subsequent metric for optimization based on historical performance across all metrics, thereby enabling automatic discovery of an optimal reward curriculum. Our exploration employs the Exp3 algorithm~\cite{auer2002nonstochastic} for exploration-exploitation balance, incorporating two innovative bandit reward mechanisms: (1) Single Multi-reward Bandit (SM-Bandit); (2) Hierarchical Multi-reward Bandit (HM-Bandit). We begin by introducing a reward scaling methodology that constrains metric rewards within $[0,1]$. Subsequently, we detail our SM-Bandit approach, where each round's bandit reward derives from performance improvements across multiple sources, utilizing averaged scaled metric rewards from all sources as the final bandit reward. Finally, we describe our HM-Bandit architecture, featuring a primary first-level controller alongside $K$ secondary multi-armed bandits. The first-level controller identifies underperforming reward metrics, while second-level bandits activate specific metric optimizers that promise substantial improvements for targeted metrics. We demonstrate our approaches' effectiveness across two critical generation tasks: question generation and data-to-text generation (incorporating unseen-test transfer evaluation) through comprehensive automatic metrics and human assessment. Question generation experiments utilize the SQuAD QG dataset~\cite{du2017learning}, while data-to-text natural language generation employs the WebNLG dataset~\cite{gardent2017webnlg}. Our results establish that bandit-based methods achieve statistically significant improvements (validated through human evaluation) over robust single-reward reinforcement learning models and non-bandit multi-reward approaches such as the multi-task framework by~\newcite{pasunuru2018multi}. Additionally, we provide comprehensive interpretable analyses examining bandit progression and learned reward curricula across different bandit configurations.

text: The significance of object counting has grown substantially across diverse applications including crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation, and inventory management. Conventional counting approaches~\cite{zhang2016single, ma2019bayesian, biswas2017automatic} typically concentrate on \XP{particular,} individual categories. Nevertheless, when deployed on novel categories, these methods experience dramatic performance degradation. Simultaneously, acquiring comprehensive category datasets with proper annotations remains \XP{extremely} challenging and expensive. Human cognitive abilities demonstrate remarkable generalization, enabling adaptation to diverse visual tasks with minimal prior knowledge or experience. Inspired by this extraordinary capability, our work explores this learning paradigm by developing a network that efficiently recognizes and counts novel categories using a single exemplar. We adopt the few-shot framework from ~\cite{ranjan2021learning}, adapting it for one-shot object counting scenarios. Specifically, our model processes an image containing unseen novel categories alongside a supporting bounding box that provides one example instance of the target category, subsequently generating object count predictions for the image. Two primary challenges emerge in this context. \textbf{First}, object counting encompasses numerous diverse categories, with multiple categories potentially coexisting within individual images. Under few-shot conditions, training and inference categories remain completely disjoint. Consequently, models must exhibit robust discriminative capabilities for distinguishing features across different categories while maintaining effective associative abilities for instances within identical categories. \textbf{Second}, one-shot counting requires models to \XP{learn} from a single supporting instance. The primary difficulty stems from potential variations between the supporting sample and other instances, including \XP{differences in scale, orientation, and appearance. Models must therefore achieve invariance to such variations without observing commonalities across multiple instances.} This paper introduces LaoNet, an effective network architecture for one-shot object counting. The system comprises three core components: feature extraction, feature correlation, and density regression, illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:network}. Both the feature correlation and feature extraction modules are specifically engineered to tackle the aforementioned challenges. Our feature correlation approach employs Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules to capture inner-relations and inter-relations respectively. Self-Attention enables the model to emphasize critical features and their correlations, enhancing information refinement efficiency. Existing few-shot counting methodologies~\cite{ranjan2021learning, yang2021class} typically employ convolution operations for matching similarities between image features and supporting features. However, since kernels derive from supporting features with fixed dimensions and orientations, convolution operations become heavily dependent on supporting feature quality and physical property consistency across instances. Our feature correlation design overcomes these limitations through dual attention mechanisms that consider comprehensive correlations. Additionally, we introduce a Scale Aggregation mechanism within feature extraction to handle scale variations across categories and instances. Through multi-subspace feature learning, the model aggregates diverse scale information while preserving spatial consistency. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce LaoNet (A network by which you only need to Look At One instance), a novel architecture for one-shot object counting. Through the integration of Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules, LaoNet effectively exploits correlations among novel category objects with superior accuracy and efficiency. 	\item We develop a Scale Aggregation mechanism that extracts comprehensive features and integrates multi-scale information from supporting boxes. 	 	\item Experimental validation demonstrates that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance with substantial improvements on FSC-147~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft} datasets under one-shot conditions without requiring fine-tuning. 	 	 \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary online platforms extensively deploy recommendation systems, including Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS} and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. Given the dynamic nature of user-item interactions, capturing the evolution of user preferences from historical activity records becomes crucial. Substantial research efforts have focused on sequential recommendation methodologies \cite{Caser,sasrec,GRU4Rec,SR-GNN} to achieve accurate user interest representation and deliver appropriate recommendations. The sequential recommendation paradigm fundamentally seeks to model user representations through historical behavioral patterns and subsequently predict target items. Leveraging deep learning's remarkable achievements in sequential dependency modeling and representation learning, numerous deep neural network approaches \citep*{r1} have emerged to tackle this challenge. These encompass RNN-based architectures~\cite{GRU4Rec,GRU4Rec+,STAMP}, diverse CNN configurations~\cite{Caser,3D_CNN}, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) \cite{SR-GNN,FGNN,GC-SAN}, and variants \cite{sasrec,BERT4Rec,TiSASRec} leveraging multi-head self-attention mechanisms \cite{atten}. Despite their effectiveness, these approaches often encounter data sparsity challenges \cite{Autoint,s3,sasrec} in sequential recommendation scenarios, particularly models utilizing multi-head self-attention, where a single item prediction loss optimizes the entire parameter space to capture all potential correlations within input interaction sequences. Self-supervised learning strategies have been introduced to tackle this limitation~\cite{yao2020self,CLRec}. Notably, contrastive learning (CL) objectives~\cite{CL4SRec} have demonstrated exceptional performance. By integrating effective data augmentation techniques with conventional sequential prediction objectives, CL-based methods learn superior sequence-level user representations, thereby improving sequential recommendation performance. Nevertheless, CL-based approaches depend heavily on correlated data augmentation techniques, pretext task design, efficient negative sampling strategies, and hyperparameter tuning (such as temperature parameters in NCE and InfoNCE losses) \cite{jaiswal2021survey}. Numerous studies have attempted to streamline contrastive learning to address these limitations. \cite{gao2021simcse} introduced an elegantly simple contrastive learning framework employing dropout noise as data augmentation to generate high-quality positive samples for sequence-level representation learning. While this approach proves effective for unsupervised representation learning, its adaptation to sequential recommendation tasks creates a fundamental trade-off: increasing the CL objective's proportion during training yields better representations that effectively distinguish positive and negative samples, yet potentially degrades item prediction performance, and conversely. This reveals a significant disconnect between positive-negative sample discrimination and the core sequential recommendation objective. Consequently, developing superior user representations for item prediction requires training strategies that address the fundamental challenges inherent in sequential recommendation models. Recent findings regarding multi-head attention models demonstrate that simple regularization strategies applied to supervised task output spaces yield remarkable performance improvements~\cite{liang2021r} (achieving state-of-the-art results across numerous challenging tasks). This observation motivates our comprehensive exploration of consistency training effects in sequential recommendation contexts. We initially incorporate simple bidirectional KL divergence regularization into the output space, constraining inconsistencies between two forward passes utilizing different dropout configurations. Unlike prior work in machine translation, summarization, and natural language understanding, we contend that output space consistency regularization alone proves insufficient for sequential recommendation's data-sparse environment. We subsequently develop a novel, straightforward regularization objective targeting the representation space. Departing from previous approaches that employ cosine \cite{gao2021simcse} and L2 \cite{ma2017dropout,zolna2018fraternal} distance metrics for representation space regularization, we propose regularizing the distributed probability of individual user representations relative to others. This enables us to extend and utilize effective bidirectional KL loss for representation inconsistency regularization. Experimental validation across three public benchmarks and one newly assembled large-scale corpus demonstrates that our proposed simple consistency training for sequential recommendation (CT4Rec) substantially outperforms state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods. Comprehensive experiments further establish that our consistency training approach readily extends to data-side applications. Online A/B testing confirms our method's practical effectiveness. Additionally, we extend our consistency training methodology to CTR prediction tasks, with experiments on two newly constructed industrial datasets providing further validation. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a simple (requiring only two bidirectional KL losses) yet highly effective consistency training methodology for sequential recommendation systems. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive investigation of consistency training effects from multiple perspectives using a unified training objective for sequential recommendation tasks. \item Our consistency training approach easily generalizes to alternative inconsistency scenarios and tasks, including data augmentation and CTR prediction. \item Comprehensive experiments across four offline datasets demonstrate CT4Rec's effectiveness compared to state-of-the-art contrastive learning models, achieving superior performance with accelerated convergence. Online A/B testing reveals significant improvements over robust ensemble models. \end{itemize}

text: Critical system components continue to harbor severe security vulnerabilities despite extensive scrutiny and widespread deployment across years of operation. Recent research has increasingly turned to \textit{formal verification} methodologies for analyzing substantial real-world systems. These certified implementations provide machine-verifiable proofs demonstrating adherence to specified correctness properties. Project Everest~\cite{everest}, for instance, established correctness guarantees for an entire HTTPS stack through comprehensive verification of both the TLS implementation and its supporting toolchain. This paper focuses on secure file systems. While existing verified file systems~\cite{fscq,yggdrasil,cogent} have established correctness regarding crucial properties such as guaranteed recovery following arbitrary system crashes, they lack features characteristic of {\em cryptographic} file systems. Such systems typically employ cryptographic primitives to counter integrity and confidentiality threats, especially within the ``evil maid'' threat model~\cite{evil_maid}. This scenario involves an adversary obtaining temporary physical access to target storage, enabling arbitrary read and write operations on raw storage devices. IFSCQ, our file system developed as an FSCQ~\cite{fscq} extension, represents the first implementation providing both proven crash consistency guarantees and verified integrity protection against compromised or malicious storage. IFSCQ establishes a formal malicious disk model and demonstrates that any data or metadata compromise will be cryptographically detectable. This protection mechanism employs a conventional Merkle tree~\cite{merkle_tree} structure encompassing all disk blocks. Tree roots are maintained within a modeled TPM—a small trusted storage repository for Merkle tree root hashes—enabling bulk tree storage on potentially compromised disks while ensuring correctness verification upon each read operation. Integrating these integrity capabilities into FSCQ necessitated substantial modifications to its core logic. Nevertheless, all modifications satisfy both FSCQ's existing proof obligations and the additional integrity properties we formalized and verified. Our trusted computing base (TCB) mirrors FSCQ's dependencies: the Coq proof system, Haskell compiler and runtime, and Linux FUSE user-space file system support. Rather than pursuing TCB minimization, our objective centers on verifying cryptographic file system correctness regarding both crash consistency and disk tampering detection. While other research initiatives have explored complete software stack verification~\cite{deepspec} or minimal runtime dependency C code generation~\cite{cogent}, such approaches could complement IFSCQ development if TCB reduction or comprehensive stack verification became priorities. The original FSCQ design derives from the Unix Version~6 filesystem architecture, prioritizing simplicity over modern optimizations to facilitate future extensions. Consequently, IFSCQ similarly avoids competing with contemporary production filesystem performance, instead demonstrating formal verification feasibility for critical security properties. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Threat model.} Our security model assumes trusted hardware and operating systems while treating storage as potentially malicious. We extend the ``evil maid'' concept to encompass ``Byzantine disk'' scenarios where adversaries execute arbitrary writes continuously. Attack vectors may target individual file blocks, metadata structures, Merkle hash blocks, or implement complete disk state rollbacks to previously valid configurations. Consequently, trusted ground truth storage becomes essential for Merkle tree root maintenance and updates. We adopt TPM (trusted platform module) terminology, reflecting components present in numerous modern systems. While assuming TPM-provided ``trusted boot'' functionality—supported by most actual TPMs—our implementation diverges from real TPM specifications in several aspects detailed subsequently. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} This work delivers the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item Design and implementation of a certified cryptographic integrity file system with proven crash safety and data tampering detection capabilities. \item Formal malicious storage system modeling alongside desirable integrity properties for file system protection against such threats. \item Merkle tree architecture satisfying integrity requirements while protecting all disk blocks (data, inodes, and unallocated blocks) through minimal trusted storage requirements for root hash maintenance. \item Evaluation demonstrating reasonable system overhead and effective defense against diverse malicious attack scenarios. \end{itemize} The paper proceeds as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} establishes necessary background for understanding our approach. Section~\ref{sec:design} details system design principles. Section~\ref{sec:proof} examines our proof engineering methodology. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} covers implementation specifics. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} analyzes evaluation outcomes. Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork} surveys related research. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} explores potential IFSCQ enhancements, while Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} provides concluding remarks.

text: As robots increasingly deploy in human-populated environments—from collaborative manipulation tasks~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} to autonomous vehicles~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}—the design of planning and control algorithms for human-robot interaction has garnered substantial attention. Given the potential for physical harm to humans~\cite{eder2014towards}, safety assurance becomes critical for such systems. These concerns prove especially acute in scenarios like autonomous driving, where robots and humans may pursue conflicting objectives—consider, for instance, a self-driving vehicle attempting an unprotected left turn~\cite{sadigh2016planning}. Defining safety for human-interactive robots presents a fundamental challenge. While modeling humans as adversaries offers one approach, such strategies typically yield excessive conservatism. Alternatively, learning-based methods predict human actions~\cite{ziebart2008maximum,fisac2018probabilistically,sadigh2019verifying} and guarantee safety relative to these models. This approach succeeds when models capture all human behaviors, yet humans exhibit remarkable behavioral diversity~\cite{sadigh2016information}—laboratory subjects may behave quite differently from street pedestrians. Comprehensive data collection across all possible contexts remains prohibitively difficult. When training data lacks certain behaviors, models fail to account for them. Moreover, even sophisticated machine learning models produce errors, potentially missing critical human actions. \emph{Responsibility sensitive safety (RSS)}~\cite{shalev2017formal} offers another paradigm, manually specifying acceptable robot actions across various scenarios. Here, the controller designer bears responsibility for ensuring that permissible actions remain safe. Yet manually defining acceptable robot behaviors for all conceivable scenarios proves challenging, particularly for robots in open-world environments. Indeed,~\cite{shalev2017formal} formally addresses only limited scenarios such as lane changes. Our work introduces a novel safety framework for human-interactive systems that accommodates all human behaviors within specified bounded sets. Two primary challenges emerge: (i) characterizing the human behavior set, and (ii) guaranteeing safety with respect to this set. We address these challenges through: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Bounding human behavior via backup actions:} Instead of specifying all \emph{permissible} robot actions (as RSS does), designers specify \emph{backup actions} that humans presumably always consider when avoiding accidents (e.g., braking while steering). Specifically, we assume humans may execute arbitrary actions generally, but will employ these backup actions when safety demands it. \item {\bf Ensuring safety via abstract interpretation:} We employ \emph{abstract interpretation}~\cite{cousot1977abstract} to conservatively overapproximate system reachable sets under our human behavior model, then guarantee safety relative to this overapproximation. \end{itemize} Our backup action concept captures the reasonable expectation that humans will execute limited evasive maneuvers to prevent accidents—for example, if the robot gradually decelerates to a stop, we anticipate the human will also decelerate to avoid rear-ending.\footnote{We do not assume humans will take evasive maneuvers such as swerving to avoid an accident (though can do so if it is safe). Also, we assume a reasonable amount of time for them to brake and come to a stop.} Highway scenarios may render stopping more hazardous, potentially requiring robots to reach the shoulder before stopping. Similarly, robots should avoid stopping within intersections. Backup action specification provides a safety definition mechanism; we term such constraints \emph{safety modulo fault}.\footnote{The term ``fault'' is used simply to mean that safety ignores cases where the human does not act according to our model, not to blame an accident on the human driver. The controller designer is responsible for designing the backup actions to obtain a reasonable notion of safety.} To instantiate our framework, robot controller designers must specify: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robot backup action:} An action humans expect the robot might execute for safety—e.g., braking without directional changes. Selection should reflect intuitions about human driver expectations regarding robot actions (e.g., based on traffic regulations). \item \textbf{Human backup action set:} A set containing \emph{at least one} action humans consider for safety—e.g., braking while steering in various directions. Selection should reflect intuitions about safety maneuvers human drivers contemplate. \end{itemize} Notably, while RSS requires control designers to specify \emph{all} permissible robot actions, we require only actions designers believe humans consider for accident avoidance. We subsequently propose an algorithm for guaranteeing safety modulo fault. Our approach builds upon \emph{shielding}~\cite{akametalu2014reachability,alshiekh2018safe,wabersich2018linear,li2019robust}; rather than designing specific controllers, our algorithm accepts arbitrary goal-achieving controllers as input, then combines them with backup controllers to maximize given controller usage while ensuring safety modulo fault. The algorithm employs on-the-fly verification through abstract interpretation to assess whether the given controller can safely operate modulo fault; when safe, it employs the given controller, otherwise switching to backup control. We empirically evaluate our approach through simulations encompassing both simulated humans and real human participants using keyboard controls. Results demonstrate that our MPS modulo fault algorithm enables robots to avoid accidents with both real and simulated humans, even when paired with na\"{i}ve controllers that completely ignore human presence. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} illustrates how our algorithm maintains safety during human driver interactions without excessive caution. The system assumes humans will minimally brake to prevent accidents (left). When safety cannot be guaranteed, the algorithm yields to human drivers (right).

text: Differentially private learning algorithms rely extensively on the Gaussian mechanism as their fundamental building block \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. Despite its mathematical tractability and amenability to privacy accounting, the continuous nature of Gaussian noise creates substantial practical obstacles. Finite computational representations cannot capture it exactly, introducing numerical errors that may compromise privacy guarantees \cite{mironov2012significance}. Furthermore, distributed learning environments employing cryptographic multi-party computation with modular arithmetic—such as secure aggregation protocols \cite{secagg, bell2020secagg}—cannot accommodate continuous distributions. Recent efforts to address these limitations have yielded the binomial and (distributed) discrete Gaussian mechanisms \cite{DworkKMMN06, agarwal2018cpsgd, CanonneKS20, ddg}. However, these alternatives introduce their own complications: binomial mechanisms may exhibit infinite privacy loss with positive probability, while discrete Gaussian mechanisms suffer from: (a) lack of closure under summation, which complicates distributed analysis and degrades performance relative to continuous Gaussian in highly distributed, low-noise scenarios~\cite{ddg}; (b) dependence on specialized sampling algorithms absent from standard machine learning and data analysis libraries, creating implementation barriers that may result in severe privacy violations when handled improperly. \textbf{Our contributions}\hspace{0.5em} We present the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism to address these challenges, leveraging noise from the difference between two independent Poisson random variables. This approach maintains closure under summation—sums of Skellam variables remain Skellam distributed—while enabling straightforward sampling through widely available Poisson generators in numerical software. Its discrete structure naturally integrates with cryptographic protocols and enables communication efficiency gains. We establish privacy guarantees through numerical evaluation of the privacy loss random variable and derive tight R\'enyi divergence bounds for shifted Skellam distributions. Our analysis demonstrates that for multi-dimensional queries with $\ell_1$ sensitivity $\Delta_1$ and $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta_2$, the Skellam mechanism with variance $\mu$ satisfies $(\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))$ R\'enyi differential privacy (RDP) \cite{mironov2017renyi} where $\varepsilon(\alpha) \leq \frac{\alpha \Delta_{2}}{2 \mu}+\min \left(\frac{(2\alpha - 1) \Delta_{2}+6 \Delta_1}{4 \mu^2}, \frac{ 3\Delta_1}{2 \mu}\right)$ (Theorem \ref{thm:mainSK}). These RDP guarantees exceed Gaussian mechanism performance by at most $1 + O\left(1/{\mu}\right)$. We evaluate practical performance in differentially private, communication-constrained federated learning (FL) \cite{kairouz2019advances}, where local noise addition to discretized $d$-dimensional client updates precedes secure summation via cryptographic protocols like secure aggregation (SecAgg) \cite{bell2020secagg, secagg}. Our end-to-end algorithm handles data discretization and applies Skellam noise with modular arithmetic to constrain data ranges and communication overhead before SecAgg deployment. Experiments on distributed mean estimation and benchmark FL datasets—Federated EMNIST~\cite{caldas2018leaf} and Stack Overflow~\cite{tffauthors2019}—demonstrate performance matching continuous Gaussian baselines under stringent privacy and communication constraints. This occurs despite our reliance on generic RDP amplification via sampling~\cite{zhu2019poission} versus the precise RDP analysis available for subsampled Gaussian mechanisms~\cite{mironov2019r}. Implementation in TensorFlow Privacy~\cite{tf-privacy} and TensorFlow Federated~\cite{ingerman2019tff} will be publicly released.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/google-research/federated/tree/master/distributed_dp}} Though we emphasize FL applications, the Skellam mechanism applies broadly across learning and analytics contexts, including centralized scenarios. \textbf{Related work}\hspace{0.5em} Prior introduction of the Skellam mechanism occurred within computational differential privacy from lattice-based cryptography~\cite{valovich2017computational} and private Bayesian inference~\cite{schein2019locally}. However, existing privacy analyses do not extend naturally to multi-dimensional cases and provide only direct pure or approximate DP bounds, limiting applicability to learning scenarios requiring repeated mechanism application to advanced composition theorems~\cite{kairouz2015composition, dwork2010boosting}. The guarantees from~\cite{valovich2017computational} yield poor accuracy-privacy trade-offs, as Fig.~\ref{fig:accounting-composition} illustrates. Section \ref{sec:skellam-pld} reveals that extending direct privacy analysis to multi-dimensional settings proves non-trivial due to unknown worst-case neighboring dataset pairs. Our tight RDP-based privacy analysis therefore enables practical Skellam mechanism deployment in learning applications for the first time. These guarantees nearly match Gaussian mechanism performance while supporting generic RDP amplification through subsampling techniques \cite{zhu2019poission}. The binomial \cite{agarwal2018cpsgd, DworkKMMN06} and discrete Gaussian mechanisms \cite{CanonneKS20, ddg} represent the closest alternatives to Skellam. Properly scaled binomial mechanisms can asymptotically match continuous Gaussian performance but fail to achieve R\'enyi or zero-concentrated DP \cite{mironov2017renyi, BunS16}, with privacy loss potentially infinite at positive probability, creating catastrophic privacy failures. Discrete Gaussian mechanisms provide R\'enyi DP and support distributed applications~\cite{ddg}, yet require sampling algorithms unavailable in standard data analysis packages despite exploration in lattice-based cryptography (e.g.,~\cite{roy2013high, dwarakanath2014sampling, rossi2019simple}). Additionally, discrete Gaussian lacks closure under summation, with large divergence in highly distributed low-noise settings (e.g., quantile estimation~\cite{andrew2019differentially} and federated analytics~\cite{fedanalytics}), causing privacy degradation. Section~\ref{sec:applying-skellam} provides extended discussion.

text: Machine learning has demonstrated superhuman capabilities in image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and strategic games \citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, yet comparable achievements remain elusive in robotics applications. Multiple factors contribute to this disparity. Physical world interaction presents exponentially greater complexity than these domains. Although modern deep learning algorithms could theoretically acquire necessary data through direct robot interaction~\citep{Levine_Quillen_16}, such approaches prove prohibitively expensive regarding temporal and resource requirements for meaningful scaling. Simulation offers an attractive alternative, enabling faster, more economical, safer data generation with unprecedented diversity. However, this approach necessitates confronting inevitable approximation errors inherent in reality modeling. These discrepancies, collectively termed the \enquote*{reality gap}, emerge from neglected physical phenomena, imprecise parameter estimation, and discretized numerical integration within conventional solvers. This challenge intensifies given that {state-of-the-art}\xspace deep learning methods exhibit notable brittleness \citep{Szegedy_Fergus_13,Goodfellow_Szegedy_14,Huang_Abbeel_17}—demonstrating pronounced sensitivity to input domain variations. Furthermore, learning algorithms may exploit simulator-specific characteristics, overfitting to artifacts absent in physical reality. \citet{Baker_Mordatch_20} documented instances where agents manipulated physics engines for unintended advantages. While such exploitation provides fascinating insights for purely simulated studies, it proves highly detrimental for {sim-to-real}\xspace applications. Optimistically, reality gaps manifest as performance degradation—reduced success rates or diminished tracking precision. More commonly, learned policies fail entirely during real-world deployment due to unmodeled physical phenomena. Friction exemplifies such modeling difficulties, frequently underestimated in simulation, resulting in insufficient motor commands for robot actuation. Parameter estimation inaccuracies represent another failure mode, potentially destabilizing system dynamics. Such instabilities pose significant safety risks to both humans and robotic systems. Consequently, bridging the reality gap constitutes the fundamental prerequisite for enabling robots to leverage simulated learning experiences. Consensus indicates that merely enhancing simulator fidelity cannot resolve this gap~\citep{Hofner_White_20}. Machine learning breakthroughs demonstrate that deep architectures combined with extensive, diverse datasets yield superior generalization~\citep{Russakovsky_etal_2015,Radford_etal_2019}. Following this principle, domain randomization techniques have gained considerable traction (Figure~\ref{fig_sota_collage_sim2real}). These approaches share a fundamental characteristic: systematic perturbation of simulator parameters, state observations, or action executions. Common randomization targets encompass body inertia and geometry, friction and contact model parameters, actuation delays, motor efficiency coefficients, sensor noise levels, and visual attributes including colors, illumination, camera positioning and orientation, plus image artifacts such as glare effects. Domain randomization functions as a regularization mechanism, preventing learner overfitting to specific simulation instances. Through a Bayesian lens, simulator distributions represent uncertainty quantification. This paper begins by establishing essential terminology and mathematical foundations (Section~\ref{sec_sota_mdp}). We subsequently examine early randomized simulation learning approaches, articulate practical requirements, and characterize {sim-to-real}\xspace transferability metrics (Section~\ref{sec_sota_simtoreal_foundations}). Following this, we explore connections between {sim-to-real}\xspace transfer research and adjacent fields (Section~\ref{sec_sota_related_fields}). We then present a domain randomization taxonomy and systematically categorize existing literature (Section~\ref{sec_sota_domain_randomization}). Finally, we synthesize conclusions and delineate prospective research trajectories (Section~\ref{sec_sota_discussion_and_outlook}). Readers seeking foundational knowledge in robot policy learning and policy search should consult these comprehensive surveys:~\citet{Kober_Peters_13}, \citet{Deisenroth_Peters_13}, and \citet{Chatzilygeroudis_Mouret_20}.

text: Privacy-sensitive data increasingly serves as the foundation for machine learning (ML) predictions. Major technology corporations including Google and Amazon now provide machine learning services to the public via cloud-based platforms. While these systems generate valuable insights across diverse domains, ML models trained on sensitive information create attractive targets for malicious actors. Through Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs)~\cite{shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy}, adversaries seek to determine which specific data points were used during model training (i.e., identifying members). When MIAs succeed, they compromise individual privacy and represent substantial risks to vulnerable ML systems~\cite{shokri2016membership}. During the learning phase, differentially private (DP) mechanisms can be integrated into ML models \cite{chaudhuri_differentially_nodate,Abadi_2016,beaulieujones2018privacypreserving, shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy, yu2019differentially} to constrain how much influence any individual data point exerts on model outputs. The adoption of DP-based ML training continues expanding, with established libraries like TensorFlow~\cite{tensorflow} and PyTorch~\cite{pytorch} incorporating multiple DP training algorithms. Existing research has established both experimental and theoretical support for DP training as an MIA defense~\cite{li2013membership,yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,shokri2016membership}. Yeom et al.~\cite{yeom2017privacy} demonstrate that DP training algorithms guarantee a \emph{theoretical upper bound} on privacy leakage from MIAs. Although Erlingsson et al.~\cite{jayaraman2020revisiting} subsequently refined this bound, it provides robust protection only under high DP levels (small $\epsilon$ values), deteriorating rapidly as $\epsilon$ increases. Nevertheless, empirical MIA assessments against DP-trained models~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting} indicate that even large $\epsilon$ values—theoretically considered low-privacy configurations—offer adequate real-world MIA protection. Building on these observations, Murakonda and Shokri~\cite{murakonda2020ml} created a tool that tunes $\epsilon$ based exclusively on empirical MIA performance, thereby enhancing model utility while sacrificing theoretical privacy assurances. Collectively, this research indicates that DP mechanisms applied to ML models provide adequate protection against established MIAs, even under substantially weakened privacy conditions. All prior membership inference studies employ similar evaluation frameworks where members and non-members are independently sampled from identical distributions. Yet this fundamental assumption fails to capture real-world data characteristics~\cite{Mohammad2020, arjovsky2021distribution, pmlr-v97-recht19a, Martensson2020, nagarajan2021understanding, pmlr-v119-sagawa20a, sagawa2020distributionally}. Moreover, existing research demonstrates that data dependencies can cause overestimation of DP's privacy protection~\cite{tschantz_sok_2020, kifer_no_2011, pufferfish, li2013membership, liu2016dependence}. This motivates our investigation—the first examination of MIA performance against DP-SGD-trained ML models~\cite{Abadi_2016} \emph{under data dependencies}. Our analysis begins by examining methodologies from previous MIA research and identifying assumptions underlying their theoretical results~\cite{yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,nasr2021adversary}. Since no documented instances of real-world MIAs against ML models exist, researchers must simulate attacks through theoretical frameworks called \emph{membership experiments}~\cite{yeom2017privacy} that model interactions between model owners and attackers. We demonstrate that existing membership experiments presuppose training sample independence, potentially misrepresenting numerous practical membership inference scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel membership experiment that relaxes the restrictive independence assumption. We establish that existing DP-based bounds on adversarial success fail under this generalized framework. Importantly, this does not indicate that DP itself is fundamentally flawed. Instead, DP mechanism guarantees become inapplicable when membership inference incorporates data dependencies. The underlying reason is that DP mechanisms constrain the influence of \emph{individual} samples on outputs. When training samples exhibit dependencies, however, related samples can reveal additional information about any single sample. Given that prior research emphasizes the importance of examining MIA performance through both theoretical and empirical lenses~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting}, we also investigate how data dependencies affect the \emph{empirical performance} of MIAs across different instantiations of our membership experiment. Across six real-world datasets, we assess the effectiveness of standard attacks. These attacks operate with black-box query access to target models without additional background knowledge about the data dependencies we examine. Through these attacks, we explore three distinct categories of data dependencies. Initially, to assess the maximum impact of data dependencies on MIAs, we artificially partition datasets into members and non-members via clustering algorithms. Our findings reveal that data dependencies can enable perfect membership inference despite DP training. Subsequently, we examine how explicit attribute biases in training sets affect performance. Specifically, we introduce gender and education biases into training sets, observing that MIA effectiveness generally increases with more pronounced training set biases. Finally, we analyze MIA performance across various real-world data dependency examples that emerge during data collection. For instance, we examine scenarios where all members originate from a particular health region (or hospital) while non-members come from other regions. We also evaluate MIA performance when members and non-members derive from identical sources (the US Census) but undergo curation by different researchers. Across all evaluations involving statistical dependencies among training samples, we observe substantial increases in MIA performance compared to related work assuming Independent and Identically Distributed (IID) samples~\cite{shokri2016membership,jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting, yeom2017privacy,jagielski2020auditing, nasr2021adversary}. This demonstrates that assuming data independence among training samples leads to underestimating attack effectiveness. Our empirical results produce attack performance exceeding DP bounds, confirming that established DP bounds become inapplicable under dependent data conditions, and thus DP mechanisms cannot serve as universal solutions for membership inference. These findings underscore the critical importance of incorporating data dependencies into future MIA evaluations and call for new research developing improved defenses alongside more realistic theoretical bounds on MIA performance.

text: Time series analysis frequently employs confidence intervals as fundamental tools for characterizing underlying distributions and identifying anomalous behavior. This work examines the computational challenges associated with constructing confidence intervals specifically for temporal data sequences. The concept of confidence bands, as introduced by \citet{korpela2014confidence}, represents a departure from traditional point-wise confidence interval computation. Rather than calculating intervals at individual time points, this approach seeks confidence bands across entire series. The formal problem requires selecting $k$ time series $U \subseteq T$ from a collection of $n$ time series $T$ such that the envelope area—defined as $\sum_i \pr{\max_{t \in U} t(i)} - \pr{\min_{t \in U} t(i)}$—is minimized. \citet{korpela2014confidence} demonstrated that confidence bands offer superior family-wise error control compared to point-wise intervals. While point-wise methods can only identify outliers \emph{at specific temporal locations} and necessitate multiple testing corrections (e.g., Bonferroni) to make probabilistic statements about \emph{entire} time series normality, confidence bands avoid these complications. This paper focuses on approximation algorithms for confidence band discovery. Although \citet{korpela2014confidence} established the \textbf{NP}-hardness of optimal confidence band identification, neither approximation schemes nor inapproximability bounds were provided in their work. Our first contribution demonstrates that polynomial-time solutions exist for \emph{certain} values of $k$, despite the problem's \textbf{NP}-hard nature. We achieve this by reformulating the hard constraint as a regularized objective function that balances time series selection against envelope area growth. This objective incorporates a parameter $\alpha$—higher $\alpha$ values permit greater envelope expansion. We establish that this regularized variant admits exact polynomial-time solutions, with each $\alpha$ value corresponding to a specific $k$. Furthermore, we prove that at most $n + 1$ distinct bands exist and present a polynomial-time algorithm for discovering all such bands through $\alpha$ variation. Our second contribution provides a straightforward approximation algorithm by establishing connections to the weighted $k$-\textsc{MinUnion}\xspace problem. We adapt techniques from~\citet{chlamtac2018densest} to achieve a $\sqrt{n} + 1$ approximation guarantee. Additionally, we present evidence suggesting that—under certain complexity-theoretic assumptions—no algorithm can achieve better than $\bigO{n^{1/4}}$ approximation. Finally, we investigate an alternative formulation that minimizes envelope width rather than area—specifically, minimizing the maximum difference between envelope boundaries. We demonstrate that a straightforward algorithm achieves 2-approximation for this variant. This result provides compelling contrast to the inapproximability findings for area minimization. Remarkably, this guarantee is optimal: we prove that no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve better approximation ratios unless $\textbf{P}=\textbf{NP}$. The paper proceeds as follows: Section~\ref{sec:prel} provides formal problem definitions, Section~\ref{sec:reg} addresses the regularized band problem, Section~\ref{sec:sum} covers envelope area approximation, and Section~\ref{sec:max} examines envelope width approximation. Section~\ref{sec:related} surveys related work, Section~\ref{sec:exp} presents experimental results, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} offers concluding remarks.
