text: The proliferation of autonomous robotic systems in everyday environments demands controllers capable of sophisticated operation within unstructured settings. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) with neural network function approximators has demonstrated remarkable success across challenging robotic control domains, including dexterous in-hand manipulation \cite{dexterous}, quadrupedal locomotion \cite{haarnoja2018learning}, and targeted throwing \cite{throwing}. However, deep RL-based controllers suffer from a critical limitation: the absence of \textit{safety} guarantees that restricts their practical deployment in real-world robotics \cite{Ibarz_2021}. This limitation stems from the opaque nature of neural network policies and their unreliable performance when encountering out-of-distribution states—a phenomenon particularly pronounced during sim-to-real transfer. Classical robotics, conversely, has produced a wealth of controllers and algorithms for diverse physical systems (spanning mobile robots to humanoids) that enable reliable and safe real-world deployment. These encompass classical feedback controllers \cite{maxwell1868governors}, trajectory generators \cite{ijspeert2008central}, and behaviour trees \cite{colledanchise2016behavior}. Their explicit analytical foundations and well-understood models provide control-theoretic guarantees that ensure real-world suitability. However, these approaches often yield highly suboptimal performance on complex tasks due to analytical modeling constraints and necessary approximations. The future of robot control lies in synthesizing the complementary advantages of these disparate control paradigms to overcome their individual shortcomings. Such hybrid approaches mirror strategies observed in neuroscience, where biological systems employ multiple control mechanisms. The dual-process theory of decision making \cite{dickinson2002role} suggests that distinct neural controllers participate in action selection within biological systems. \citet{lee2014neural} substantiate this theory through human brain studies, demonstrating an arbitration mechanism that modulates the influence of different neural controllers based on their performance characteristics, thereby leveraging their respective capabilities in specific states. Drawing from this biological insight, we introduce Bayesian Controller Fusion (BCF), a hybrid control framework that synthesizes the strengths of deep RL with traditional handcrafted controllers (\textit{control priors}) for safe real-world operation. Our approach formulates the final policy as a Bayesian composition of these controllers, where each system's output encodes its \textit{epistemic} uncertainty for a given state, as illustrated in Figure \ref{front}. This formulation enables BCF to naturally arbitrate control based on each system's confidence, yielding crucial benefits during real-world deployment: we harness the learned system's dexterity in familiar states while relying on the handcrafted system's risk-averse behavior in out-of-distribution scenarios for safe operation. Crucially, our method achieves real robot control in joint space for task completion without requiring on-robot training time (\textit{zero-shot}), despite potential imperfections in sim-to-real policy transfer. Our evaluation encompasses two continuous control robotic tasks: reactive navigation on a mobile robot and manipulability-maximizing reaching on a robotic arm. We demonstrate that BCF enables reliable sim-to-real policy transfer while achieving substantial performance gains from the RL component compared to using handcrafted systems alone. This work represents a promising and practical pathway toward deploying simulation-trained RL controllers safely in real-world environments.

text: The proliferation of open-access academic repositories like arXiv and bioRxiv has revolutionized how research findings reach the scientific community. These platforms facilitate the monthly distribution of tens of thousands of scholarly articles across diverse research domains\footnote{\url{https://arxiv.org/stats/monthly_submissions}}. However, the unprecedented volume of unreviewed publications has created significant challenges for researchers attempting to navigate relevant literature and maintain awareness of cutting-edge developments. Automatic text summarization addresses these challenges through scientific paper summarization, which seeks to distill lengthy articles into concise, accessible formats containing crucial information. Recent advances in abstractive summarization have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, with models generating coherent summaries through sophisticated paraphrasing of source materials. Contemporary approaches exploit large-scale pre-trained architectures~\citep{raffel2019t5, lewis2020bart}, implement domain-specific pre-training methodologies~\citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and accommodate extended input sequences~\citep{zhao2020seal, zaheer2020bigbird}. Existing benchmark datasets like arXiv and PubMed~\citep{cohan2018discourse} utilize automatically harvested content from digital archives, treating original abstracts as gold-standard reference summaries. Nevertheless, conventional scientific summarization approaches that train models to reproduce paper abstracts suffer from two fundamental limitations: 1) abstracts frequently emphasize secondary rather than primary contributions, and 2) most scholarly articles already include human-authored abstracts, rendering generated summaries redundant. We propose disentangled paper summarization as a solution to these limitations. This novel task requires simultaneous generation of two distinct summaries: one concentrating exclusively on the paper's innovations and contributions, while the other establishes contextual background and reviews prior research. Such differentiated summaries serve heterogeneous readership requirements: experienced researchers and domain specialists can efficiently access contribution-focused content, whereas newcomers can rapidly acquire domain knowledge through contextual summaries before engaging with novel findings. We present a comprehensive large-scale dataset constructed by augmenting the S2ORC~\citep{lo2020s2orc} corpus, which encompasses multiple scientific disciplines and provides extensive citation metadata. Our data processing pipeline generates automated contribution and context reference summaries to support supervised learning paradigms. We establish three abstractive baseline methodologies: 1) a unified controllable architecture utilizing descriptive control tokens~\citep{fan2018controllable,keskar2019CTRL}, 2) a one-to-many sequence framework employing branched decoders for multi-target generation~\citep{luong2016mtl, bansal2018mts}, and 3) an information-theoretic training approach incorporating citation metadata supervision~\citep{peyrard2019simple}. Our evaluation framework encompasses automatic assessment across three dimensions: relevance, novelty, and disentanglement quality. We conduct extensive baseline analysis and examine how auxiliary training objectives influence model performance characteristics. A human evaluation study simulating paper review scenarios demonstrates that disentangled summaries prove more beneficial than abstract-focused alternatives in 79\% of evaluated cases. Implementation code, trained model parameters, and data preprocessing utilities are publicly accessible at~\url{https://github.com/salesforce/disentangled-sum}.

text: The past decade's breakthroughs in deep neural networks have enabled models to tackle novel tasks that demand integration across multiple modalities. Research at the intersection of language and vision has emerged as a pivotal area, with visual question answering (VQA) \cite{Agrawal2015VQAVQ, Gupta2017SurveyOV}—answering questions about images—receiving particular attention (comprehensive surveys available in \cite{Wu2017VisualQA, Srivastava2019VisualQA}). Nevertheless, models addressing human-level tasks must transcend mere semantic processing of textual and visual content, demonstrating sophisticated behavioral patterns: mastering intricate referential relationships with numerous cases and exceptions (for instance, 'green' might indicate plant health, human illness, inexperience, envy, or environmental consciousness), or leveraging one modality to overcome statistical biases learned from another \cite{Agrawal2018DontJA, Cadne2019RUBiRU, Chen2020CounterfactualSS, goyal2017making, Ramakrishnan2018OvercomingLP} (when asked 'what colour is the banana?', we recognize the typical yellow expectation while acknowledging that a specific image might show a pink specimen). Modeling such cross-modal interactions presents formidable challenges in deep learning, as optimal strategies for fusing feature tensors within networks remain unclear. Initial approaches employed vector concatenation to map disparate features into unified joint spaces \cite{Zhou2015SimpleBF, Lu2016HierarchicalQC}. Drawing inspiration from earlier vision-centric two-factor frameworks \cite{Tenenbaum:2000:SSC:1121517.1121518}, VQA models achieved substantial improvements through 'pooled' bilinear representation (BLP) of visual and textual features \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/GaoBZD15, DBLP:journals/corr/FukuiPYRDR16, DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block, Yu2018BeyondBG}. VQA-focused BLP research has concentrated on three primary directions: developing more efficient and computationally economical bilinear representations \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block}, incorporating BLP with attention mechanisms \cite{Kim2018BilinearAN, Yu2018BeyondBG, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471}, and recently analyzing and categorizing BLP (as "joint" representation) alongside alternative fusion approaches and architectures \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}. Although BLP techniques have demonstrated success in VQA contexts, their adoption in video-QA baselines remains limited \cite{MovieQA, pororoqa, jang-CVPR-2017, Fan_2019_ICCV, lei2018tvqa, Xu2017VideoQA}. This work addresses this research gap by implementing BLP techniques across TVQA \cite{lei2018tvqa}, TGIF-QA \cite{jang-CVPR-2017}, Ego-VQA \cite{Fan_2019_ICCV}, and MSVD-QA \cite{Xu2017VideoQA} datasets. We present eight key contributions: \textbf{I)} Substituting concatenation with BLP techniques in the TVQA baseline model \cite{lei2018tvqa}, \textbf{II)} Developing and testing a modified TVQA baseline variant—termed the 'dual-stream' model—designed to accommodate BLP, \textbf{III)} Implementing BLP replacements for concatenation in the recently introduced heterogenous-memory-enhanced multimodal attention (HME) model \cite{Fan2019HeterogeneousME}, \textbf{IV)} Applying the TVQA dataset within HME experimental frameworks, \textbf{V)} Providing insights into suboptimal performance through the lens of contemporary multimodal fusion taxonomies \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}, \textbf{VI)} Conducting experiments on TVQA baseline models enhanced with deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) \cite{Andrew2013DeepCC} to compare 'co-ordinated' representations against BLP's 'joint' representations (following definitions in \cite{8715409}), \textbf{VII)} Identifying additional best practices for transitioning BLP from image-QA to video-QA applications, \textbf{VIII)} Examining how bilinear representations align with contemporary psychological models of vision and perception \cite{Goodale1992SeparateVP, milner2006visual, milner2008two, goodale2014and, Milner2017HowDT}. The academic community has long criticized the tendency to suppress inconclusive or negative experimental results \cite{Mlinari2017DealingWT, Faschinger2019DoNH, Sandercock2012NegativeRW}. We therefore present our experimental findings to broaden the publicly available scope of multimodal fusion research and stimulate critical future investigations that may build upon, contrast with, or challenge our observations and hypotheses.

text: Deep learning advances, particularly pre-trained language models (LM)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}, have substantially enhanced question answering capabilities. Although reading comprehension datasets (single passage QA) and open-domain QA over large-scale corpora have experienced significant improvements from these developments, question answering over book stories (BookQA) continues to underperform. Consider NarrativeQA~\cite{kovcisky2018narrativeqa}, the most prominent benchmark in this area released three years ago—current state-of-the-art approaches demonstrate only modest gains beyond initial baseline methods. NarrativeQA presents multiple obstacles that impede research advancement. The narrative format introduces distinctive stylistic elements that contrast sharply with formal texts such as Wikipedia articles used in prior studies. Additionally, books' extensive length exceeds neural models' processing capabilities, making evidence identification across entire volumes essential. The generative nature of NarrativeQA compounds these difficulties, as numerous answers lack exact textual matches within source books, necessitating generative QA architectures. Most critically, the dataset lacks supporting evidence annotations—while this creates realistic conditions similar to open-domain QA, it simultaneously complicates evidence inference when combined with generative answer requirements, unlike predominantly extractive open-domain QA approaches. These evidence identification demands and absent supporting annotations establish parallels between BookQA and open-domain QA tasks. We investigate whether successful open-domain QA methodologies can enhance BookQA performance, examining: (1) neural ranker-reader pipelines~\cite{wang2018r} that employ neural rankers for selecting relevant passages (evidence) from extensive candidate collections given questions; (2) pre-trained LM integration as readers and rankers, including GPT~\cite{radford2019language}, BERT~\cite{devlin2018bert}, and subsequent developments; (3) distantly supervised and unsupervised training approaches~\cite{wang2018r,Lee_2019orqa,min2019discrete,guu2020realm,karpukhin2020dense} enabling rankers to extract greater value from noisy gold standard data. Through ranker-reader framework training on BookQA, we establish new state-of-the-art NarrativeQA results using both generative and extractive readers. Our findings and subsequent analysis reveal: \noindent$\bullet$ Pre-trained LM readers, including BERT and GPT, enhance NarrativeQA performance substantially. Compared to non-pre-trained equivalents using identical BM25 IR baselines, they deliver 5-6\% Rouge-L improvements. \noindent$\bullet$ Our custom distant supervision signals provide notable neural ranker enhancements, though improvements remain modest relative to upper bounds. Ranker module analysis confirms training complexity, evidenced by BERT's minimal pre-trained LM contributions in this component.

text: Urban logistics services stand to be revolutionized by drone technology. These aerial vehicles offer rapid, adaptable, and streamlined delivery capabilities that can meet the escalating logistical and e-commerce demands of densely populated metropolitan areas~\cite{chung2020optimization}. Furthermore, they present an opportunity to diminish dependence on conventional ground-based delivery systems that exacerbate urban traffic congestion~\cite{HolguinETAL18}. Nevertheless, establishing package delivery operations that depend exclusively on drones presents feasibility challenges stemming from their constrained flight endurance and payload limitations~\cite{SudburyETAL16}. To address these constraints, we investigate the coordination of delivery drones with ground vehicles, enabling drones to utilize ground vehicles as mobile platforms for energy conservation and extended operational range~\cite{choudhury2019dynamic,choudhury2021efficient}. Specifically, we examine the routing of combined drone and truck fleets across shared road networks, where drones can leverage trucks for transportation alongside autonomous flight capabilities. We conceptualize this scenario as a \emph{coordinated} variant of the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) problem~\cite{stern2019multi}, necessitating the computation of origin-destination routes for all agents while seeking to minimize aggregate path costs across both drones and trucks. Path costs may vary between agent categories and can represent energy expenditure or operational overhead. Consistent with traditional MAPF formulations, our problem framework incorporates inter-agent constraints that limit the maximum drone capacity per truck simultaneously. Additionally, it demands consideration of potential cost reductions achievable through coordinated truck-drone operations sharing route segments. The concept of temporary agent coordination remains unexplored within the MAPF research community (to our knowledge) and significantly increases the complexity beyond the already challenging classical MAPF~\cite{yu2013structure, YuLaValle16}. Contemporary state-of-the-art MAPF algorithms prioritize collision avoidance between agents rather than coordination optimization~\cite{felner2017search,stern2019multi}. Our previous research introduced a MAPF solver for drone routing across transit networks~\cite{choudhury2021efficient} but operated under assumptions of fixed, predetermined transit vehicle routes and eliminated requirements for drones to navigate road networks. Alternative research examined cooperative MAPF problems but focused exclusively on predetermined agent pairs converging at designated meeting locations~\cite{greshler2021cooperative}, rather than simultaneous route traversal. The operations research field has addressed drone-truck optimization, though their methodologies are limited to small-scale scenarios with few agents on simplified routing graphs~\cite{agatz2012optimization}. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} We present a robust algorithmic framework for coordinated MAPF addressing drone-truck tandem operations. Our fundamental approach involves \textit{decomposing the computationally intractable overall MAPF problem into two manageable MAPF sub-problems solved sequentially} (\Cref{fig:approach}). Stage 1 determines truck routes with high potential utility as drone transit options. Stage 2 fixes these truck routes, constructs a transit network based on them, and superimposes this network onto the road graph. Subsequently, we compute drone routes across the hybrid road-and-transit network, where drones experience zero cost on transit segments (subject to capacity limitations). Post-processing involves re-routing unused transit trucks to their optimal road network paths. We implement dual variants of our methodology employing different MAPF solvers; one utilizes Enhanced Conflict-Based Search~\cite{barer2014suboptimal} while the other employs Prioritized Planning~\cite{silver2005cooperative} across both stages. We assess our approach across diverse coordinated MAPF scenarios using the Manhattan road network, encompassing approximately $4500$ vertices and $10000$ edges across nearly \SI{200}{\kilo\metre\squared}, with configurations up to $20$ trucks and $80$ drones. Experimental results demonstrate that drone-truck coordination achieves over $50\%$ reduction in total vehicle distance traveled relative to uncoordinated operations. \textit{We define vehicle distance traveled as the combined truck path distance and drone flight distance}, since drones consume no energy while transported by trucks. For conciseness and clarity, we employ this terminology throughout, acknowledging some terminological imprecision. Our approach successfully plans paths for all tested configurations within maximum $5$-minute computation times on standard hardware. We anticipate our approach will function as a foundational component in more sophisticated problem domains requiring optimal agent-task allocation (i.e., package-delivery destinations) and execution sequencing. For example, following our prior work~\cite{choudhury2021efficient}, we could implement a hierarchical approach where upper-level job allocation to agents combines with lower-level planning---coordinated MAPF solving in this context---executed through receding-horizon methodology. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Layout.} \Cref{sec:related} examines prior foundational approaches and cutting-edge applications. \Cref{sec:problem} establishes fundamental notation and definitions while describing our coordinated MAPF problem framework. \Cref{sec:approach} details our two-stage coordinated MAPF methodology, with comprehensive experimental analysis presented in~\Cref{sec:results}. We conclude in~\Cref{sec:conclusion} by synthesizing our contributions and identifying future research trajectories.

text: Within server systems, the Quality of Service (QoS) for any job is typically quantified through its response time—the duration spanning from job release to job completion. This metric is alternatively termed flow time in job scheduling contexts. For a given schedule $\mathcal{S}$, we denote the completion time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$ as $c_i(\mathcal{S})$ and its release time as $r_i$. The flow time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$, represented as $f_i(\mathcal{S})$, is thus expressed as \[ f_i(\mathcal{S}) = c_i(\mathcal{S}) - r_i. \] Server systems commonly pursue two fundamental QoS objectives: minimizing the average (equivalently, the $\ell_1$ norm) of job flow times, and minimizing the maximum (or $\ell_{\infty}$ norm) of job flow times. The Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) algorithm, which optimizes average flow time, is notorious for potentially causing prolonged and inequitable flow times for certain jobs (job starvation). Conversely, First-Come-First-Served (FCFS), which optimizes the maximum flow time~\cite{10.5555/314613.314715}, can significantly compromise average flow time performance. \begin{example} Consider Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, where jobs $J_1$ and $J_2$ arrive at time 1, each requiring 2 units of processing time. The remaining jobs $J_i$ arrive at time $i$ and demand unit processing times. When SRPT prioritizes $J_1$ for execution, job $J_2$ experiences starvation, waiting until all subsequent jobs complete before receiving service. Under FCFS, conversely, each job achieves a flow time of merely $O(1)$. \end{example} \begin{example} Examine Fig.~\ref{fig: ex2}. Here, unlike Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, jobs $J_1$ and $J_2$ require processing times of $n$ units each. FCFS yields flow times of $\Theta(n)$ for every job, resulting in an average flow time of $\Theta(n)$. SRPT, however, maintains an average flow time of merely $O(1)$. \end{example} The conventional strategy for balancing the $\ell_1$ and $\ell_{\infty}$ norms of flow time involves optimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. The $\ell_2$ norm of flow time for schedule $\mathcal{S}$ is defined as \[ \sqrt{f_1(\mathcal{S})^2 + f_2(\mathcal{S})^2 + \cdots + f_n(\mathcal{S})^2}, \] where $n$ represents the total number of jobs. This paper focuses on online minimization of the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time on a single machine. Existing analyses of online $\ell_2$ norm flow time minimization have examined conventional algorithms such as SRPT, Shortest Job First (SJF), Shortest Elapsed Time First (SETF), and Round Robin (RR), under the assumption of machines with augmented speed~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. Nevertheless, SRPT, SJF, and SETF are susceptible to job starvation, while FCFS and RR can severely compromise average flow time performance. These limitations adversely impact the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time (detailed in Appendix~\ref{sec: cr}). The scenarios depicted in Figs.~\ref{fig: ex1} and \ref{fig: ex2}, for instance, establish that both FCFS and SRPT exhibit $\Omega(n^{1/2})$-competitive ratios for $\ell_2$ norm flow time minimization. Our approach employs FCFS to address SRPT-induced starvation. The proposed algorithm initially follows SRPT scheduling. When a job remains in the system excessively long while possessing sufficiently small remaining processing time, it transitions to starving status. A job $J_i$ becomes starving at time $t$ when \[ \frac{t-r_i}{\text{remaining processing time of } J_i} \geq \theta, \] where $\theta$ represents the \textit{starvation threshold}. Upon detecting starving jobs, the algorithm prioritizes the job that first achieved starving status. We denote this algorithm as $BAL(\theta)$ when the starvation threshold equals $\theta$. Note that $BAL(0)$ reduces to FCFS while $BAL(\infty)$ reduces to SRPT. \subsection{Our Result} Our competitive ratio analysis of $BAL(\theta)$ indicates that $\theta = n^{\frac{2}{3}}$ represents the optimal starvation threshold. Among the standard scheduling algorithms mentioned previously, both SRPT and FCFS attain the best known competitive ratio of $O(n^{\frac{1}{2}})$ for $\ell_2$ norm flow time minimization (see Appendix~\ref{sec: cr}). We demonstrate that $BAL(n^{\frac{2}{3}})$, which combines SRPT and FCFS principles, achieves a substantially improved competitive ratio of $O(n^{\frac{1}{3}})$. Practical implementations can only approximate $n$. During peak hours, when job scheduling becomes critical, job arrival processes are typically modeled as Poisson processes. Consequently, multiplying the job arrival rate by the peak hour duration provides a reasonable estimate of $n$. However, this study makes no assumptions regarding the job arrival process or estimation methodology. We assume availability of an estimate $\tilde{n}$ of $n$ with bounded error. text: Over recent decades, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has emerged as a central research challenge in robotics and computer vision~\cite{cadena2016past,thrun2007simultaneous}. The fundamental problem involves determining a robot's real-time position through onboard sensor data, including LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) devices, cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMU). SLAM proves indispensable in environments where GPS signals are compromised—indoor spaces, dense urban areas, and underwater settings. Consequently, it serves as a cornerstone technology for AR/VR applications~\cite{grasa2013visual}, autonomous vehicle navigation~\cite{bresson2017simultaneous}, and GPS-denied robotic operations~\cite{weiss2011monocular}. Within the spectrum of available systems, visual SLAM \cite{fuentes2015visual} attracts considerable attention due to cameras being cost-effective passive sensors that demand minimal energy compared to active alternatives like sonar or LiDAR. For autonomous mobile robots in outdoor environments, cameras' energy efficiency proves crucial during extended operational periods. Visual SLAM architectures divide into two primary categories: \emph{feature-based} approaches and \emph{direct} methodologies. Feature-based techniques~\cite{klein2007parallel, mur2015orb} identify and correlate features between consecutive frames, subsequently determining relative camera movement through reprojection error minimization. Conversely, direct approaches~\cite{engel2014lsd, engel2017direct} bypass feature correspondence entirely, estimating camera motion via direct photometric error minimization. Direct methods exhibit superior accuracy and resilience compared to feature-based alternatives, particularly within poorly-textured environments (characterized by minimal or repetitive texturing) \cite{forster2016svo}. Since feature detection and matching procedures impose significant computational overhead, sparse direct methods offer substantial speed advantages (\emph{e.g.}, achieving $\geq300$ FPS with SVO \cite{forster2016svo}). Additionally, visual SLAM systems can be distinguished as either monocular or multi-camera configurations. While monocular implementations~\cite{klein2007parallel,engel2014lsd,mur2015orb,engel2017direct} cannot determine environmental metric \textit{scale}, multi-camera systems possess this capability. Multi-camera configurations typically deliver enhanced accuracy and robustness, with stereo systems~\cite{mur2017orb,engel2015large,wang2017stereo} gaining widespread adoption due to their straightforward implementation and broad accessibility. The majority of existing stereo visual systems employ conventional \textit{stereo matching} algorithms~\cite{hartley2003multiple} to resolve scale ambiguity, yet this approach suffers from two significant drawbacks. Primarily, establishing stereo correspondences through individual epipolar line searches demands substantial computational resources. Additionally, when multiple points exhibit visual similarity to the query point, selecting the correct correspondence becomes problematic—a frequent occurrence in repetitively textured environments (\emph{e.g.}, grasslands, sandy terrain). Our previous work~\cite{mo2019extending} addresses these constraints by projecting 3D points from the monocular system into the secondary camera and resolving scale through photometric error minimization. This direct \textit{scale optimization} approach demonstrates computational efficiency while providing enhanced robustness against repetitive visual textures. Nevertheless, despite metric scale availability, global camera pose estimation inevitably diverges from ground truth as the camera progresses, since poses are computed through incremental accumulation of relative motions. \textit{Loop closure} detection introduces non-local pose constraints that enable global pose optimization to mitigate this drift. Traditional bag-of-words (BoW) methods identify loop closures by matching current view features against historical data. However, BoW approaches prove incompatible with direct SLAM systems since these systems avoid feature descriptor extraction. As an alternative, we developed a \emph{LiDAR descriptor-based} place recognition technique~\cite{mo2020fast} specifically for urban driving scenarios. Under the assumption of forward vehicle motion, we accumulate 3D points from the stereo direct SLAM system to simulate LiDAR scans, which are then characterized using LiDAR descriptors for place recognition. This strategy enables substantially more efficient loop closure detection while maintaining superior accuracy and robustness. This paper presents a systematic integration of scale optimization and LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition into a comprehensive fully-direct stereo SLAM system designated DSV-SLAM; our open-source implementation is available at {{\tt \url{https://github.com/IRVLab/direct_stereo_slam}}}. Through extensive experimental validation, we demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy, exceptional computational efficiency, and robustness under visually challenging conditions. DSV-SLAM establishes the viability of complete SLAM systems operating without feature detection or matching procedures. Our implementation leverages the advanced Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO)~\cite{engel2017direct} framework for camera pose tracking and 3D point estimation. We then extend this foundation to create efficient and accurate stereo visual odometry (VO) through scale optimization~\cite{mo2019extending}. Subsequently, our LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition method~\cite{mo2020fast} enables efficient loop closure detection. Relative poses for potential loop closures are determined through direct alignment, with optional refinement via the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm~\cite{besl1992method}. Finally, we construct and optimize a pose graph to achieve global SLAM accuracy improvements. Figure~\ref{fig:kitti00} illustrates the trajectory estimation and environmental reconstruction achieved by DSV-SLAM on sequence $00$ from the KITTI dataset~\cite{geiger2012we}.

text: The exponential expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has driven a substantial surge in AI applications within structural engineering, mirroring trends across numerous disciplines in recent years. Machine Learning (ML) models have been extensively deployed to forecast structural responses, fragility parameters, and performance limit states across various systems including steel and concrete moment frames, steel braced frames, and reinforced concrete walls \cite{ML1, ML2}. Additional research has leveraged ML approaches to estimate structural model parameters such as shear strength and drift capacity directly from experimental datasets \cite{ML4, ML5}. Within image-based structural health monitoring, a considerable body of ML-driven computer vision research has emerged to enable automated damage detection from visual data \cite{ML7, ML8}. Complementary investigations have concentrated on AI-powered damage detection, localization, and classification through sensor networks deployed on structural systems \cite{ML10, ML11}. Catastrophic natural events including earthquakes, tsunamis, and hurricanes pose severe threats, potentially resulting in human casualties and extensive infrastructure damage. Post-event reconnaissance thus plays a critical role in advancing our comprehension of built environment performance, accelerating recovery processes, and informing evidence-based decisions for current and future hazard mitigation. While ML-based approaches have found application in natural hazard reconnaissance, limited research has investigated natural language processing (NLP) methodologies. NLP techniques offer substantial potential for enhancing both efficiency and precision in post-hazard reconnaissance assessments. Among the scarce NLP-related investigations, \citet{ML13} developed a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to classify building damage using textual natural language damage descriptions aligned with ATC-20's green, yellow, and red tagging framework. Social media platforms, particularly Twitter, have served as data sources in select studies for training ML algorithms to process direct eyewitness disaster accounts \cite{twitter1} and to extract thematic patterns from social media activity during hazardous events \cite{twitter2}. This research investigates two NLP applications within earthquake reconnaissance contexts. The first involves automated reconnaissance report generation, a fundamental component of field reconnaissance activities. Automated report generation seeks to reduce report preparation time while enhancing information accuracy and comprehensiveness by enabling access to numerous identified resources that might otherwise be overlooked. The second application employs social media and crowd-sourcing platforms to extract earthquake-related information concerning consequences and resilience metrics, particularly recovery timeframes, which prove challenging to obtain through conventional methods. Given that this represents an unexplored AI application domain, this preliminary investigation aims to catalyze future developments in this emerging field. The paper's subsequent sections follow this organization: Section \ref{sec:data} presents the automatic data collection methodology employed across both applications. Sections \ref{sec:briefing} and \ref{sec:social-media} detail the methodologies and applications for automatic report generation and recovery time estimation, respectively. The final section provides concluding observations and outlines future research directions.

text: Machine learning faces a fundamental challenge: developing models that operate reliably and safely in real-world environments. Beyond achieving strong performance on training distributions, deployed systems must exhibit robustness against distribution shifts, maintain prediction consistency, withstand adversarial attacks, provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, and detect anomalous inputs effectively. While extensive research has addressed these challenges individually \cite{madry, hendrycks2019robustness, guo2017calibration, emmott2015meta}, they collectively constitute different facets of ML Safety \cite{hendrycks2021unsolved}. These characteristics can therefore be conceptualized as safety measures. Real-world model deployment would ideally achieve excellence across multiple safety measures simultaneously. However, existing research demonstrates that optimizing certain desirable properties frequently undermines others. Adversarial training exemplifies this trade-off, enhancing adversarial robustness while simultaneously degrading standard classification accuracy \cite{tsipras2018robustness}. A similar tension emerges between enforcing prediction consistency on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and effectively detecting such inputs—an observation corroborated by recent findings \cite{empiricalpaper} showing that current approaches benefit certain safety metrics while compromising others. % This evidence prompts a critical question: can a single model achieve improvements across all safety measures? Traditional augmentation techniques generate images that differ spatially (such as translations) or exhibit higher entropy (like additive Gaussian noise). We contend that a crucial yet underexplored dimension involves creating images with enhanced structural complexity. Unlike entropy or descriptive difficulty—which reaches its maximum in pure noise distributions—structural complexity typically reflects organizational sophistication \cite{lloyd2001measures}. Fractals represent a canonical example of structurally complex entities and have recently demonstrated value in pretraining image classifiers \cite{kataoka2020pre, Nakashima2021CanVT}. This observation raises an intriguing possibility: can sources of structural complexity be harnessed to enhance safety through data augmentation strategies? Our work demonstrates that Pareto improvements are achievable through \textsc{PixMix}, an elegant and powerful data processing approach that exploits structurally complex imagery to deliver substantial enhancements across all established safety measures. \textsc{PixMix} introduces a novel data processing pipeline incorporating structurally complex ``dreamlike'' images, including fractals and feature visualizations. Our investigation reveals that feature visualizations serve as an excellent complexity source, establishing their utility beyond interpretability applications. Through comprehensive experimentation, we demonstrate that \textsc{PixMix} delivers significant improvements across diverse safety measures, surpassing numerous existing methodologies. Implementation details are accessible at \href{https://github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}{\texttt{github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}}.

text: The remarkable achievements of deep convolutional networks~\cite{he2016deep, chen2017deeplab, long2015fully} have propelled object recognition tasks—including object detection and instance segmentation—to unprecedented levels of performance over the past decade. Contemporary approaches predominantly adopt the "backbone with head" paradigm~\cite{he2017mask, chen2019hybrid, lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}, wherein a backbone network~\cite{he2016deep}, typically pretrained on ImageNet, performs feature extraction from input images. Subsequently, these extracted features are processed through a head network that generates task-specific predictions for classification, bounding box regression, and mask segmentation. The head network architecture remains remarkably consistent across most image/video instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask, huang2019mask, yang2019video, cao2020sipmask} and object detection methodologies~\cite{lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}. The conventional approach involves stacking four consecutive $3\times3$ convolutions within the head network to refine coarse instance features (illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig1}(a)) prior to final prediction generation. While this explicit refinement strategy effectively expands the receptive field and enhances semantic representation, the simple stacking of weight-independent convolutions presents notable limitations. The achievable receptive field remains constrained under explicit configurations, as empirical evidence demonstrates that effective receptive fields are substantially smaller than their theoretical counterparts. Moreover, this approach exhibits a tendency to lose original instance signals, resulting in performance degradation and increased parameter overhead as convolution layers accumulate. This raises a fundamental question: can we substitute these stacked $3\times3$ convolutions with a lightweight module while maintaining competitive performance? A straightforward approach involves implementing weight-sharing across the four convolutions (depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig1}(b)). Our empirical analysis of this weight-sharing strategy reveals that the conventional four weight-independent $3\times3$ convolutions are unnecessary within the head network. Conversely, weight-sharing designs achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced parameters. To mitigate potential performance degradation in weight-sharing networks, we incorporate shortcut connections inspired by ResNet~\cite{he2016deep} (shown in Fig.~\ref{fig1}(c)). These shortcut pathways facilitate smooth gradient propagation and preserve original instance features. Although weight-sharing improves overall segmentation performance, it remains constrained by limited receptive fields. This motivates our exploration of a novel perspective: \textit{What if instance features were refined through a recursive network comprising infinite blocks?} Conceptually, we envision stacking weight-sharing blocks infinitely. Under such conditions, the refinement network output converges to an equilibrium state as block count increases, mathematically expressed as: \begin{eqnarray} H^{\ast}=F_{\theta}(H^{\ast};X), \end{eqnarray} where $F_{\theta}$ denotes the nonlinear transformation parameterized by $\theta$, while $H^{\ast}$ and $X$ represent the equilibrium instance feature and original coarse instance feature, respectively. Drawing inspiration from DEQ~\cite{bai2019deep, bai2020multiscale}, we present implicit feature refinement (IFR) to enhance feature representation through simulated infinite-depth networks, utilizing transformation $F_{\theta}$ for implicit model construction. Following Eq.~\ref{eq1}, we reformulate instance feature refinement as a fixed-point iteration problem. For the explicit design of transformation $F_{\theta}$, we employ a single residual block with dual residual connections to minimize mask head parameters (illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig1}(d)). Forward computation leverages black-box root-finding solvers (\textit{e.g.}, Broyden method~\cite{bai2020multiscale}) to determine the equilibrium equation root $H^{\ast}$ from Eq.~\ref{eq1}. Backpropagation computes gradients based on the resolved equilibrium features. Unlike explicitly stacked convolutions, IFR offers several distinct advantages: 1) It simulates infinite-depth feature refinement networks using only single residual block parameters; 2) It generates equilibrium instance features with expansive receptive fields, benefiting instance segmentation tasks. Notably, IFR integrates seamlessly into most image/video instance segmentation frameworks, encompassing both two-stage and one-stage approaches. Comprehensive experiments on the COCO benchmark~\cite{lin2014microsoft} validate IFR's effectiveness across various image instance segmentation frameworks. For instance, it enhances Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask} with ResNet-50-FPN backbone by 1.0\% segmentation AP. Additionally, it demonstrates robustness and flexibility for video instance segmentation on the YouTube-VIS~\cite{yang2019video} benchmark, delivering substantial improvements on state-of-the-art frameworks. With minor modifications, it also applies to several one-stage object detectors. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Empirical investigation of multiple stacked convolutions' impact on instance feature refinement. \item Introduction of implicit feature refinement (IFR), requiring only residual block parameters to generate high-level equilibrium instance features with global receptive fields through fixed-point iteration. \item Development of double residual networks to prevent performance degradation and ensure smooth gradient propagation. \item Demonstration that IFR serves as a versatile plug-and-play module, easily integrated into most instance segmentation frameworks as a robust alternative to explicitly stacked convolutions in head networks. \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary machine learning has demonstrated remarkable performance across numerous computer vision tasks through image-based model training alone. Extending these achievements to advance 3D object comprehension holds immense promise for enabling diverse applications including augmented reality, robotics, autonomous systems, and image retrieval. However, 3D object understanding presents significant challenges primarily due to the scarcity of extensive real-world datasets when compared to their 2D counterparts (such as ImageNet~\cite{Deng:2009jn}, COCO~\cite{Lin:2014vm}, and Open Images~\cite{Kuznetsova:2020ff}). To facilitate continued progress in 3D object understanding within the research community, there exists a compelling need for object-centric video datasets that capture richer 3D structural information while maintaining compatibility with standard data formats used in downstream vision tasks (namely video or camera streams), thereby supporting both training and evaluation of machine learning models. This object-centric methodology aligns with human perceptual processes as well. Consider how children learn object shapes—they naturally circumnavigate a chair, observing it from various perspectives to gather comprehensive information. This reflects the principle that "We must also move in order to perceive"~\cite{Gibson:1979}\cite{Zamir:2018}. We introduce Objectron, a comprehensive dataset comprising brief, object-focused video sequences that capture diverse common objects from multiple viewpoints. Each sequence includes augmented reality (AR) session metadata encompassing camera poses, sparse point-clouds, and surface planes. Additionally, the data features manually annotated 3D bounding boxes for every object, specifying position, orientation, and dimensional properties. The complete dataset encompasses $14,819$ annotated video sequences and $4M$ annotated images sourced from geographically diverse locations spanning ten countries across five continents. An exemplary video from our collection is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:example-seq}. The Objectron dataset offers numerous advantages compared to existing alternatives: \begin{itemize} \item Video sequences provide multi-perspective views of identical objects, facilitating applications far beyond 3D object detection, including multi-view geometric analysis, view synthesis, and 3D shape reconstruction. \item 3D bounding boxes maintain temporal consistency throughout entire videos, thereby supporting 3D tracking applications. \item Data collection occurs in natural environments, enhancing real-world generalization capabilities compared to datasets acquired under controlled conditions~\cite{Hinterstoisser:2012ik}\cite{Calli:2017cd}. \item Instance translations and dimensions are recorded at metric scale through precise on-device AR tracking, providing 3D sparse point clouds that enable sparse depth estimation methods. Calibrated images with provided camera parameters allow recovery of true object scale. \item Our annotations maintain density and continuity, contrasting with previous approaches~\cite{Savarese:2007by} where viewpoints were discretized into categorical bins. \item Every object category includes hundreds of instances gathered from diverse global locations under varying illumination conditions. \end{itemize} We have performed experimental evaluations for 3D object detection using our dataset and introduced a novel approach for computing accurate 3D IoU of oriented 3D bounding boxes. These experimental results serve as benchmarks for subsequent research endeavors.

text: Following its invention in 1972, \gls{ct} rapidly emerged as a fundamental non-destructive technique across industrial inspection~\cite{de2014industrial}, medical diagnosis~\cite{maier2018medical}, and material sciences~\cite{withers2007x}. As a quintessential example of computational imaging, \gls{ct} operates by encoding physical quantities within measured data through an image formation model, subsequently reconstructing them via forward model inversion. For X-ray \gls{ct}, attenuation coefficient images are reconstructed from projections obtained through circular acquisition geometry. When orthographic projection conditions apply, this model reduces to the Radon transform. The discrete measurements of this transform, termed sinograms, present a well-established inversion problem. The predominant solution employs direct inversion through a closed-form approach known as \gls{fbp}~\cite{maier2018medical}. Reliable \gls{fbp} reconstruction demands adequate angular sampling that satisfies the Crowther criterion~\cite{crowther1970reconstruction}, which derives from Shannon-Nyquist sampling principles. When this criterion fails, aliasing manifests as streak artifacts that severely compromise diagnostic quality. This scenario defines \gls{svct}, which frequently occurs in practical contexts involving motion compensation~\cite{enjilela2019cubic} or radiation dose reduction~\cite{gao2014low,yu2009radiation}. Various methodologies have emerged to address \gls{svct}'s ill-posed nature through prior knowledge integration within reconstruction algorithms. Conventional \gls{ir} techniques optimize data-fidelity terms combined with suitable priors~\cite{kudo2013image,zhu2013improved,vandeghinste2011split}. The widely-adopted \gls{tv} prior, for instance, assumes piecewise constant object characteristics in \gls{ct}~\cite{sidky2008image}. More recently, learning-based reconstruction approaches have gained substantial momentum~\cite{adler2017solving}. Notable implementations include \gls{cnn}-based architectures for reconstruction-domain artifact removal~\cite{kofler2018u} and unrolled networks that emulate data-fidelity-driven \gls{ir}~\cite{ongie2020deep}. An alternative perspective frames \gls{svct} as either super-resolution or inpainting, wherein missing information undergoes interpolation between sparse projections. Sparse-view sinograms accommodate both inpainting and 1D super-resolution approaches. Regardless of the specific technique, 1D sinogram upsampling presents greater constraints than 2D natural image super-resolution~\cite{katsaggelos2007super}, given the smooth angular variation inherent in sinogram data~\cite{helgason}. Similar formulations characterize other tomographic challenges, including metal artifact reduction and limited-angle tomography, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:superres_vs_inpainting}. Despite its potential, sinogram inpainting has received limited attention relative to iterative methodologies. This stems from the extraordinary difficulty of capturing sinogram representations' intricate characteristics~\cite{li2012strategy,tovey2019directional,kostler2006adaptive}. Nevertheless, rapid deep learning advancement now facilitates efficient low-dimensional data representation capture across diverse imaging domains. These technological developments inspire exploration of learning-based super-resolution for \gls{svct} applications. We specifically advocate and will demonstrate that measurement-domain image processing surpasses post-reconstruction approaches. Sinogram-based methods prevent streak artifact generation, which proves challenging for local processing techniques (such as CNNs) due to their widespread distribution throughout the image domain. Our proposed architecture employs a two-stage design that learns sinogram-domain super-resolution followed by image-domain residual artifact removal. Figure~\ref{fig:abstract} illustrates this core concept. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item A novel dual-domain reconstruction framework operating in both measurement and image spaces, ensuring superior detail preservation compared to single-stage networks. \item An innovative domain-specific, lightweight perceptual loss that surpasses VGG-based perceptual loss~\cite{johnson2016perceptual} in accuracy, memory efficiency, and computational speed. \item Specialized loss functions and submodules designed for sinogram-domain applications, accompanied by comprehensive ablation studies examining each proposed component's effectiveness. \item Demonstration of precise reconstructions at high compression ratios while achieving substantial performance improvements (exceeding $4$ dB PSNR) over state-of-the-art methods. \end{itemize}

text: The phenomenon of swarm intelligence illuminates how autonomous entities following elementary behavioral rules—including ants, boids, and particles—exhibit sophisticated collective dynamics. This paradigm has been successfully extended to robotic systems, with swarm robotics emerging as a prominent research domain over the past twenty years. Within these systems, individual autonomous components may be designated as robots, modules, agents, processes, or sensors, leading to diverse swarm robotic architectures including the \emph{autonomous mobile robot system}~\cite{SY99}, the \emph{population protocol model}~\cite{AADFP04}, \emph{programmable particles}~\cite{DDGRSS14}, \emph{Kilobot}~\cite{RCN14}, and \emph{3D Catoms}~\cite{TPB19}. The \emph{metamorphic robotic system} (MRS) introduced by Dumitrescu et al. comprises a collection of \emph{modules} operating within an infinite 2D square grid~\cite{DSY04a,DSY04b}. These modules exhibit several key properties: they are \emph{anonymous} (mutually indistinguishable), \emph{autonomous} and \emph{uniform} (each executes identical algorithms for independent decision-making), and \emph{oblivious} (lacking historical memory). Consequently, module behavior depends entirely on real-time observations of neighboring modules in adjacent cells. The operational repertoire includes \emph{sliding} movements to side-adjacent cells and $90$-degree \emph{rotations} around cells, with the critical constraint that \emph{connectivity}—defined through side-adjacency of module-occupied cells—must be preserved throughout operations. The fundamental challenge of \emph{reconfiguration} requires transforming an MRS from its initial configuration into a designated target shape~\cite{DSY04a}. Initial investigations demonstrated that any horizontally convex connected configuration can be reconfigured into any convex target shape via intermediate straight chain formations. Dynamic MRS behavior emerges through iterative reconfiguration processes. Their investigation of \emph{search} within finite 2D square grids required locating target cells within rectangular \emph{fields} without prior knowledge of target positions or initial configurations~\cite{DYKY18}. They proved that systematic row-by-row field sweeping enables target discovery, with three modules being necessary and sufficient when cardinal directions are mutually agreed upon, and five modules required otherwise. text: Computer programs that alter their own instructions during execution while maintaining overall functionality are known as self-modifying code. Such modifications can be categorized as local (targeting specific code segments) or global (encompassing entire codebases), and may persist (modifying disk copies) or remain temporary (runtime patching). These alterations occur across various stages: compile-time, link-time, post-processing, or runtime. The modification logic may reside within the target code itself or operate as an independent process. Self-modifying code encompasses several specialized categories: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Packers}: Representing the most straightforward variant, these programs encapsulate their actual payload in compressed and/or encrypted formats. The executable content is extracted and executed entirely within memory. \item \textbf{Obfuscators}: These utilities transform executable files by generating output binaries with altered instruction sets while preserving behavioral equivalence. The resulting binaries maintain identical functionality without introducing additional features. \item \textbf{Self-injecting codes}: Such programs introduce supplementary code into their own process space (or spawned child processes) for execution. The injected code may execute within the primary thread (effectively replacing the original code while retaining associated memory and metadata) or within newly instantiated threads. \item \textbf{Self-debugging codes}: These applications establish debugger relationships with themselves or child process copies. The debugger process gains comprehensive control over the debuggee, including the capability to overwrite executable instructions. This approach significantly complicates dynamic analysis efforts. \item \textbf{Self-healing codes}: These programs possess the ability to detect modifications (whether file-based or memory-resident) and restore themselves to their original state through patch reversion. \end{enumerate} Our focus centers on self-debugging code, alongside introducing a novel technique enabling malware to operate in both forward execution mode (conventional program flow) and reverse execution mode (instructions executed in inverted sequence). The malware exhibits distinct behaviors depending on execution direction. Malicious functionality activates exclusively during reverse-direction execution, facilitating evasion of numerous analysis methodologies: \begin{enumerate} \item Reverse engineering tools such as IDA Pro employ top-down analysis approaches for disassembled code. Since our implementation demonstrates malicious behavior through bottom-up execution, the threatening nature remains concealed from immediate detection. \item Analysis tools including debuggers and sandboxes typically establish process connections using identical mechanisms employed in self-debugging. Consequently, when such tools attach to our code, the self-debugging component fails to execute (since operating systems permit only single debugger attachment per process), resulting in top-down execution that conceals malicious behavior. \end{enumerate}

text: Intelligent environmental interaction requires robots to rapidly and precisely establish the relative position and orientation of surrounding entities—neighboring robots, humans, vehicles, and diverse static or dynamic obstacles within the scene. Such estimations underpin countless applications, from drone racing~\cite{spica2018realtime} to pedestrian avoidance~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}, forming the cornerstone of genuinely autonomous robotic systems. Nevertheless, real-time tracking of six Degree of Freedom (6DoF) relative pose for dynamic objects using onboard sensing and computation remains largely unattainable with current robot perception frameworks. Addressing this gap, we introduce \textbf{M}onocular \textbf{S}equential \textbf{L}ightweight \textbf{R}otation \textbf{A}nd \textbf{P}osition \textbf{T}racking \textbf{O}n-\textbf{R}obots (MSL-RAPTOR), a lightweight, versatile robot perception module that tracks dynamic object 6DoF relative pose using solely an onboard monocular camera. MSL-RAPTOR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches that depend on additional sensors (e.g., depth) and enhanced computational resources. Vision-based 6DoF relative pose estimation methods fall into three categories: model-based, deep learning-based, and hybrid approaches. Model-based techniques match object views against template databases or visual feature collections. However, these approaches struggle with low-texture scenes or varying conditions and prove unusable without prior 3D object models \cite{schmidt2014dart,andriluka2010humantracking}. Deep learning methods like PoseCNN~\cite{xiang2017posecnn} and LieNets~\cite{do2018lienets} circumvent these limitations by directly estimating relative pose from images, learning the inverse mapping through extensive training data. Hybrid approaches merge deep neural networks with model-based techniques. Methods such as BB8~\cite{rad2017bb8}, SSD-6D~\cite{kehl2017ssd}, and SingleShotPose~\cite{tekin2018ssp} (SSP) employ deep neural networks to estimate 2D projections of 3D bounding boxes encompassing objects. These projections subsequently solve the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem for pose estimation~\cite{lepetit2009epnp}. NOCS~\cite{wang2019normalized}, another hybrid method, estimates pose through pixel correspondences and depth data using category-level canonical representations. Nevertheless, these deep and hybrid methods neglect temporal correlations across multiple frames for object tracking enhancement. Conversely, 6-PACK~\cite{wang20196sixpack} exploits temporal consistency by learning object representations through keypoints matched between frames. While demonstrating impressive pose estimation performance, these methods prove either too slow, computationally intensive, or require excessive prior model knowledge for practical onboard relative pose perception on resource-constrained robots. Self-driving car pose tracking approaches suffer identical limitations, where tracking methods constitute system-critical components~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}. These approaches depend on sophisticated sensors and/or advanced computational capabilities for online performance, often assuming planar constraints when handling exclusively ground-based objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles), thus functioning as SE(2) trackers with 3DoF (e.g.,~\cite{cho2014multi, buyval2018realtime}). \textbf{Contribution.} Considering onboard robotic perception requirements, we propose MSL-RAPTOR, which combines optimal aspects of deep learning-based and model-based perception paradigms. MSL-RAPTOR processes raw image data through a dual deep neural network architecture front-end that generates and tracks angled 2D bounding boxes around scene objects. Since a single 2D bounding box provides insufficient information for pose determination (see Fig.~\ref{fig:pose_ambiguity-a}), this semantically labeled bounding box feeds into a model-based Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)~\cite{julier2000ukf, wan2000ukf} back-end that fuses temporal measurements and produces Bayesian relative pose estimates for objects. The deep front-end employs a YOLOv3 network~\cite{redmon2018yolov3}, retrained on robot-specific object classes for initial detection and labeling, alongside a SiamMask network~\cite{wang2019siammask} for rapid frame-to-frame 2D object bounding box tracking following detection. Bounding box corners and semantic object labels (e.g., "person," "UAV," "car," "tree") then transfer to the UKF back-end. The back-end treats bounding box corners as pseudo-measurements, fusing them temporally to infer complete 6DoF object relative pose. The UKF propagates target motion using label-specific motion models (since humans, cars, and UAVs exhibit distinct movement patterns). We establish back-end to front-end loop closure through a re-detection trigger. When Mahalanobis distance between measurement and posterior exceeds a threshold or pose estimates approach field-of-view edges (assessed via z-test based on covariance), the target is deemed lost, re-triggering YOLO target detection on the front-end. This framework enables object tracking through occlusions and temporary field-of-view absences. MSL-RAPTOR currently handles single objects but extends straightforwardly to multiple objects and classes. We demonstrate MSL-RAPTOR operating on a Jetson TX2 aboard a standard quadrotor UAV platform while tracking another UAV at 8.7 frames per second. This achieves 3× faster performance than the fastest comparable state-of-the-art method, SSP~\cite{tekin2018ssp}, while producing pose estimates with 66\% and 23\% lower translation and rotation median errors, respectively. We also benchmark performance against several state-of-the-art deep learning methods for 6DoF pose tracking using depth cameras. Standard dataset evaluations demonstrate that MSL-RAPTOR performs comparably to existing methods despite utilizing only monocular cameras without depth information.

If the Mahalanobis distance between the measurement and the posterior exceeds a certain threshold or if the poses of the model are close to the limits of the field of view (based on a z-test on the covariance), the target is lost, and the YOLO target detection system is activated again. The MSL-RAPTOR system, despite the use of monocular cameras without depth information, achieves a similar level of performance to other methods. It is three times as fast as the best existing method, the SSP, and has a mean translation error and a mean rotation error that are both 23% lower.

text: Across diverse domains, video analytic systems have achieved remarkable success, spanning computationally intensive surveillance applications that recognize faces, mobile augmented reality (AR) systems that detect objects~\cite{rohan2019convolutional, apicharttrisorn2019frugal, rao2017mobile}, and real-time autonomous driving platforms that localize pedestrians and vehicles~\cite{feng2020deep, arnold2019survey, li2019gs3d}. Central to these applications lies a fundamental capability: video object detection. An increasing array of use cases demands video object detection directly on {\em mobile devices}. While these devices now feature mobile GPUs, their computational power remains substantially weaker than server-class hardware. Despite these limitations, there exists compelling motivation to execute video processing in (near) real-time on streaming content locally on the device itself\footnote{For convenience we will often use the shorthand ``device" to refer to a ``mobile device".}. Such local processing becomes essential for enhancing immersive user experiences ({e.g.,}\xspace AR/VR gaming) or delivering high-confidence outputs from video streams ({e.g.,}\xspace pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving). The standard operational target involves processing individual frames within 33 ms, corresponding to 30 frames per second (FPS) video stream rates. Our empirical analysis reveals that state-of-the-art (SOTA) protocols, originally designed for servers, substantially exceed this latency threshold when deployed on mobile platforms. As an illustration, MEGA~\cite{chen2020memory}, recognized as a SOTA solution, requires 253.4 msec per frame on NVIDIA AGX Xavier while utilizing all available computing resources. Consequently, researchers have developed numerous efficient models and systems to enhance performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2, jiang2020learning, zhu2018towards, chen2018optimizing, liu2016ssd, redmon2018yolov3, zhang2018single}. \begin{comment} The existing research are mostly geared toward accuracy and may need to leverage server-class machines or cloud-enterprises~\cite{wu2019sequence, chen2020memory, sabater2020robust, zhu2017flow, deng2019relation}. However, mobile applications typically encounter limited energy or computational resources while still requiring strict latency guarantees. To improve the user's immersive experience ({e.g.,}\xspace in AR/VR games) or to give high-confidence outputs from streaming videos ({e.g.,}\xspace for pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving), such tasks must be performed in near real-time under stringent latency requirements of 33 msec (30 FPS) or lower. Even with advancements in mobile GPU devices, these devices lack the computation power that a server-class machine or a cloud enterprise provides. In response, efficient models and systems have been proposed to improve their efficiency or performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2}. \end{comment} An alternative strategy for enabling feasible streaming analytics on mobile devices involves combining object detection with tracking, embodied in the ``\textit{tracking-by-detection}'' methodology~\cite{bae2014robust, muller2018trackingnet}. Through interleaving multiple lightweight tracking frames with periodic object detection execution, overall system performance can be significantly accelerated. The tracking-by-detection approach reveals multiple adaptation strategies, encompassing detector and tracker selection alongside trigger frequency management between detection and tracking components. Our empirical findings demonstrate that object tracker execution time is 10X lower than object detector execution time. Careful selection of these adaptation strategies becomes crucial for meeting real-time energy, latency, and accuracy requirements on mobile devices. Mobile devices' stringent runtime requirements present an additional challenge for streaming video analytics: \textit{how can systems adapt dynamically to evolving user requirements and device resource availability?} Recent research has explored multi-branch solutions to address this challenge~\cite{fang2018nestdnn, xu2020approxdet, xu2019approxnet, lee2021benchmarking}. These solutions incorporate multiple execution kernels within a system, selecting the optimal kernel {\em during runtime} to meet user latency requirements. However, all these approaches suffer from a significant limitation: they neglect energy consumption control features. Moreover, compared to recent advances in efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, research on efficient object detection solutions for embedded devices remains limited, compounded by the use of outdated feature extractors. Real-world applications face even greater adaptation challenges due to dynamic video content, fluctuating mobile device resources, and manual requirement adjustments. The broad spectrum of energy, latency, and accuracy requirements necessitates system adaptability across diverse scenarios. Consequently, the design must fulfill these essential prerequisites: (1) developing execution kernels that optimize both energy and latency efficiency for mobile devices, (2) analyzing energy consumption and latency performance across all execution branches on mobile platforms, and (3) implementing an adaptive scheduler for runtime decision-making that simultaneously satisfies multiple requirements. To our knowledge, no existing work incorporates all these design innovations. A previously overlooked dimension concerns algorithm behavior under device resource contention. Such contention frequently occurs when co-located applications execute on the same device—a common scenario given these devices' multi-purpose nature. For instance, while video detection operates, another computationally intensive task like speech recognition may simultaneously execute on the device. No prior research has assessed recent video object detection systems under varying resource contention on leading GPU-enabled mobile devices. This work introduces {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace\footnote{Just like a \name is a person who has exceptional skill, expertise, or talent at some endeavor, we believe our system demonstrates such skill in configuring streaming video object detection on embedded or mobile devices.\xspace}, specifically customized for mobile devices operating under variable resource constraints, featuring additional efficiency knobs\footnote{We use the term ``efficiency knobs'' rather than the more common term ``tuning knobs'' as we are focusing on the performance metric of accuracy, normalized by latency or energy cost to achieve that accuracy, in other words, efficient accuracy.} for energy-aware adaptation. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace selects highly efficient baseline object detectors EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} and SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, enhances them through object tracker integration, and delivers 155 execution branches by exposing 8 efficiency knobs within a unified system. Additionally, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace incorporates a scheduler that selects optimal branches during runtime to simultaneously satisfy energy and latency requirements while maximizing accuracy. We comprehensively evaluated 15 baseline models across 3 different embedded boards under 2 resource contention levels to better understand energy, latency, and accuracy performance of current video object detection models. Our evaluation of {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and baselines utilizes ILSVRC 2015 VID datasets across 3 NVIDIA mobile GPUs with increasing computational capacity—Jetson TX2, Xavier NX, and AGX Xavier—under 2 different AGX Xavier power modes. Across each board and power mode, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace emerges as the superior solution, automatically selecting optimal branches to satisfy energy and latency requirements while maximizing accuracy performance. Through its multi-branch execution kernel, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace adapts energy efficiency across an extensive range (89X span) and latency across an equally broad range (128X span). These wide-ranging energy efficiency and latency capabilities enable diverse runtime scenarios to optimize video object detection system functionality. Under a 1 J per frame energy constraint, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace achieves 52.0\% accuracy, while under a 33.3 msec latency budget, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace attains 60.1\% accuracy on AGX Xavier boards. Furthermore, when energy and latency constraints are relaxed, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace reaches 63.9\% accuracy, exceeding baseline models by more than 10\%. \begin{comment} From the benchmark results, we learned some valuable lessons, including the following: tracking-by-detection is the most efficient way to decrease energy consumption for video object detection; accuracy is mostly determined by the selection of object detector as the tracker will use the detection results from the detector for its initialization; the majority of energy consumption comes from GPU module on mobile devices. \end{comment} Our contributions in this paper include the following. \vspace{-3pt} \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1

text: Contemporary information manifests across diverse modalities—text, images, audio, video, and beyond. Consequently, when users submit queries in one modality (such as text), the most pertinent information might reside in an entirely different modality (such as images). Cross-modal Information Retrieval (IR) systems are emerging to address these heterogeneous search demands. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Need for Zero-shot Information Retrieval (ZSIR):} Traditional IR frameworks operate through train-test configurations where parameters are learned across various query classes and categories. Conventional cross-modal retrieval approaches necessitate comprehensive training data spanning all potential query classes to develop effective retrieval models. However, these methodologies encounter significant limitations when confronted with queries from {\it novel} or {\it previously unseen} classes. Consider a scenario where a retrieval system has been trained using images and textual descriptions across multiple vehicle categories—`car', `motorbike', `aeroplane', among others. When presented with a `bus' query, the system must successfully retrieve relevant bus images and descriptions despite lacking explicit training on this category. This challenge exemplifies the ``zero-shot'' paradigm~\cite{Larochelle:2008:ZLN:1620163.1620172,ZeroShotNIPS2009,ZeroShotNorouzi2013}, which emphasizes recognizing novel classes using only limited training categories. Modern search ecosystems continuously encounter such scenarios as new events, trending hashtags, and emerging concepts proliferate daily. Therefore, unlike traditional IR evaluation frameworks, contemporary systems must integrate zero-shot capabilities. Zero-shot cross-media retrieval specifically targets cross-modal retrieval scenarios (such as retrieving images for textual queries) where training and testing query-classes remain completely disjoint. Zero-Shot IR (ZSIR) presents exceptional complexity since models must simultaneously navigate semantic disparities between seen and unseen query-classes while managing heterogeneous feature representations across distinct modalities. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Present work and differences with prior works:} While extensive research has explored general multimodal and cross-modal retrieval~\cite{cross-modal-ir-survey}, remarkably few investigations have tackled cross-modal IR within zero-shot frameworks~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797,AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020} (detailed analysis appears in Section~\ref{sec:related} and Section~\ref{sub:baselines}). Several existing approaches require supplementary class label information (such as semantic similarity metrics between class labels), which frequently remains unavailable in practical applications. We introduce a novel cross-modal IR model for zero-shot settings, leveraging Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{mirza-conditional14} to retrieve {\it images} corresponding to {\it textual} queries. Our approach—designated {\bf \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{}} (Zero-Shot Cross-modal Retrieval GAN)—operates exclusively on textual data for retrieval tasks, {\it eliminating dependencies on supplementary class label information}. Although previous ZSIR models~\cite{ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797} incorporate GANs, our proposed model introduces several key innovations: (1)~We introduce \textbf{wrong class utilization} to enable generators to produce class-specific features through explicit differentiation from alternative classes. (2)~We design a \textbf{Common Space Embedding Mapper (CSEM)} that projects both image and text embeddings into a unified space conducive to retrieval operations. {\it This mechanism represents the critical component enabling retrieval without additional semantic class label dependencies.} (3)~We establish an {\bf Expectation-Maximization (E-M) training methodology} for efficient retrieval model optimization, alternating between GAN and CSEM training phases. Our analysis demonstrates superior retrieval performance compared to joint GAN-CSEM training approaches. Comprehensive experiments span multiple zero-shot retrieval benchmark datasets: (1)~Caltech-UCSD Birds, (2)~Oxford Flowers-102, (3)~North America Birds (NAB), (4)~Wikipedia, and (5)~Animals With Attribute (AWA). Our \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} consistently surpasses numerous robust baselines across all datasets, including established ZSIR models~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,8643797,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018}, leading Zero-Shot classification approaches~\cite{verma-cvpr18,xian2018feature_gen} adapted for Text-to-Image retrieval contexts, and cutting-edge Zero-Shot Hashing techniques~\cite{AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020,DCMH-AAAI17}. Additionally, our model extends beyond textual queries to accommodate alternative query formats including attribute vectors, as evidenced through AWA dataset applications. The \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} implementation is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ranarag/ZSCRGAN}.
