text: Information retrieval systems employing dense representations operate by encoding both queries and documents within a shared embedding space, subsequently retrieving information through nearest neighbor search in this space~\cite{orqa, sentence-bert, dpr, ance}. The convergence of advances in pre-trained language models~\cite{bert, lu2021less}, specialized training methodologies~\cite{dpr, ance}, and scalable nearest neighbor algorithms~\cite{faiss, scann} has established the effectiveness of dense retrieval across diverse applications, spanning web search~\cite{msmarco}, open-domain question answering~\cite{naturalquestions}, and zero-shot information retrieval~\cite{beir}. The adoption of dense, fully-learned representations in retrieval offers promising solutions to longstanding limitations inherent in sparse retrieval approaches. Notably, the vocabulary mismatch problem could be resolved \textit{if} embeddings successfully capture the underlying information need expressed in queries and establish meaningful connections to relevant documents. Nevertheless, extensive information retrieval research has established that extracting user search intent from brief and frequently ambiguous queries presents substantial difficulties~\cite{croft2010search}. Despite the capabilities of modern pre-trained language models, expecting encoders to flawlessly embed complex information needs from limited query terms remains unrealistic. \textit{Pseudo relevance feedback} (PRF)~\cite{croft2010search,PRF,rm12} represents a well-established approach for enhancing query understanding in sparse retrieval, utilizing top-ranked documents from initial searches to provide supplementary context for query representation enrichment. The effectiveness of PRF information—whether applied through query expansion~\cite{PRF,trec2004} or term reweighting strategies~\cite{bendersky2011parameterized}—has been demonstrated consistently across diverse search contexts, establishing PRF as fundamental practice in numerous sparse retrieval implementations. This research applies PRF principles to enhance query representations within dense retrieval frameworks. Utilizing top-retrieved documents from dense retrieval models such as ANCE~\cite{ance}, we develop ANCE-PRF, a PRF-enhanced query encoder that employs BERT~\cite{bert} to process queries alongside PRF documents for query representation refinement. Through end-to-end training with relevance labels, ANCE-PRF learns to optimize query embeddings by exploiting rich contextual information from PRF documents while maintaining compatibility with existing ANCE document indices, eliminating storage duplication requirements. Experimental evaluation on MS MARCO and TREC Deep Learning (DL) Track passage ranking datasets demonstrates that ANCE-PRF consistently outperforms ANCE and several state-of-the-art dense retrieval systems employing more complex architectures and training procedures~\cite{ltre,mebert}. Particularly notable improvements emerge on DL-HARD~\cite{dlhard} queries—a challenging collection designed to test neural systems on complex search scenarios. ANCE-PRF achieves performance levels placing it among the top-performing first-stage retrieval systems on the competitive MARCO passage ranking leaderboard. Analysis reveals that ANCE-PRF's effectiveness stems from its capacity to extract valuable information from PRF documents while filtering noise from irrelevant sources. The PRF encoder demonstrates significantly higher attention allocation to terms from relevant PRF documents compared to irrelevant ones. Case study examination shows the encoder's preference for PRF terms that complement query terms in representing search intentions. These mechanisms enable ANCE-PRF to generate superior query embeddings with enhanced proximity to relevant documents, benefiting the majority of test queries.\footnote{Our code, checkpoints, and ranking results are open-sourced at \url{https://github.com/yuhongqian/ANCE-PRF}.}

text: Smart devices have become ubiquitous in contemporary life, making the capacity to comprehend and manipulate User Interfaces (UIs) a critical challenge for Artificial Intelligence systems. Consider how a model capable of locating UI components through natural language descriptions could revolutionize voice-driven interfaces, or how predicting button-click outcomes could streamline page navigation workflows. Successful UI operation demands that models grasp both user intentions and the procedural knowledge required to execute tasks within specific interface contexts. Nevertheless, UI understanding remains a formidable and underexplored research domain. The landscape encompasses diverse task categories that are inherently cross-modal and cross-domain—ranging from voice-activated button interactions to icon retrieval based on semantic similarity. Existing research typically addresses individual tasks in isolation, making the deployment of multiple specialized models inefficient for on-device applications. Furthermore, when task-specific datasets are scarce, models become susceptible to overfitting. Large-scale pre-training for feature extraction has demonstrated remarkable success across domains, exemplified by ResNet \cite{he2016deep} in computer vision and BERT \cite{devlin2018bert} in natural language processing. Yet no comparable generic feature representation exists for user interfaces, leaving uncertain whether pre-trained models could enhance performance across multiple UI-related tasks. The data characteristics and structural formats of UIs diverge significantly from conventional image and text corpora. Mobile applications utilize View Hierarchy (VH) structures while web pages employ Document Object Model (DOM) representations—both forming tree-based layouts that encode UI organization. Although VH and DOM capture structural and semantic UI information, they remain invisible to end users while containing abbreviated functional descriptors. Leveraging such domain-specific knowledge for comprehensive UI understanding constitutes an unresolved challenge. Understanding UI functionality presents greater complexity than analyzing visual appearance alone. UI elements with similar visual characteristics frequently serve disparate semantic purposes, and conversely, functionally equivalent elements may appear visually distinct. Figure \ref{fig:icon-semantic} illustrates this phenomenon: despite their visual similarity as "house" icons, these elements serve different functional roles that become interpretable only through contextual information. We introduce ActionBert, a pre-trained transformer-based \cite{vaswani2017attention} architecture that harnesses sequential user interaction data for UI comprehension. Our central hypothesis posits that UI semantic meaning and component functionality can be effectively captured through user behavioral patterns—specifically, click sequences and their resulting interface modifications. This approach exploits transformer models' representational capabilities while incorporating domain-specific elements such as VH structures and user actions to generate embeddings that reflect UI element functionality. This represents the inaugural effort to establish generic feature representations within this research area. Our primary contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We pioneer the integration of powerful transformer architectures with domain-specific knowledge sources, including VH structures and user actions, to enhance machine comprehension of user interfaces. \item We present ActionBert, a transformer-based multi-modal architecture that captures UI element context and semantic significance through novel self-supervised pre-training objectives grounded in user actions and UI-specific characteristics. \item We conduct comprehensive evaluation across four distinct UI downstream task categories, encompassing diverse real-world application scenarios. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches across all evaluated tasks. \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary robotics applications spanning manufacturing automation to space exploration demand robots capable of executing fine manipulation, navigation, and target tracking tasks. Visual feedback integration proves advantageous for fine manipulation tasks when the robot end-effector operates in proximity to the manipulated object. Similarly, for tasks such as quadcopter landing from extended distances, visual feedback becomes valuable when image features remain visible to onboard camera sensors. However, when objects fall outside the camera's field of view (FOV), when reliable feature extraction becomes impossible, or when feature loss occurs, learning-based motion generation approaches like dynamic movement primitives (DMP) can assume robot control responsibilities. Consider wire pinning tasks in wire harness assembly: the robot must guide the wire to the pin following a collision-free trajectory that avoids fixture interference. Since the pin may not consistently remain within the end-effector-mounted camera's FOV, a learned DMP can generate motion bringing the wire near the pin before visual pin feedback becomes available \cite{Wirepinning}. Such scenarios, combined with the necessity for stable motion during transitions between learned and vision-based controllers, motivate this paper's novel methodology unifying DMP \cite{ijspeert2003learning} and Image-based Visual Servoing (IBVS)\cite{chaumette2006visual}. Our proposed algorithm facilitates stable switching between DMP and IBVS controllers for goal location achievement from initial positions when visual feedback remains intermittently unavailable. We term this approach the DMP-IBVS switched system. Numerous methodologies have emerged for designing robot controllers using visual feedback while maintaining objects within the FOV (see, e.g., \cite{lopez2009homography,gans2011keeping,Salehi2021ICRA}). Wang et al. \cite{Wang2021SMC} developed trajectory planning and tracking control for mobile robots employing virtual-goal-guided rapidly exploring random tree (RRT) for planning and IBVS with FOV constraints for tracking. Huang et al. \cite{Huang2021SMC} proposed constrained IBVS for helicopter landing on moving platforms using control barrier function methodology to satisfy FOV constraints. Ke et al. \cite{Ke2017SMC} developed model predictive control (MPC) for mobile robot visual servoing, handling visibility constraints for IBVS and robot velocity limits. Our approach contrasts by developing learning-based robot motion generation through DMP for control command generation during visual feedback absence, coupled with switching control law development for IBVS controller activation when visual feedback becomes available. Arbitrary switching between stable subsystems can induce instability\cite{liberzon2003switching,liberzon1999basic}. Hespanha and Morse \cite{hespanha1999stability} developed average dwell time conditions based on multiple Lyapunov functions for switched system stabilization. Daafouz et al. \cite{daafouz2002stability} proposed linear matrix inequality-based conditions for quadratic Lyapunov function existence to prove asymptotic stability in switched discrete systems. Hespanha \cite{hespanha2004uniform} extended LaSalle's invariance principle to switched linear systems, deducing asymptotic stability through multiple Lyapunov functions with negative semidefinite Lie derivatives. Lin and Antsaklis \cite{lin2009stability} surveyed switched linear system stability results and analyzed switched system stabilizability problems. Branicky \cite{branicky1998multiple} proposed multiple Lyapunov functions for Lyapunov stability analysis and iterated function systems as Lagrange stability tools. Kamalapurkar et al. \cite{kamalapurkar2018invariance} developed invariance-like results for nonautonomous nonlinear switched systems. Output feedback systems and observer switching have received literature attention. Astolfi et al. \cite{Astolfi2020_tac} analyzed switching between locally and globally converging observers with asymptotic stability. Prieur et al. \cite{Prieur2011_tac} derived composite output feedback control laws switching between locally and globally asymptotically stable output feedback controllers. Robotics applications have leveraged switched systems analysis for challenging problems including visual servo control and vision-based trajectory tracking. Gans and Hutchinson \cite{gans2007stable} proposed asymptotically stable hybrid switched systems visual servo controllers switching between IBVS and position-based visual servo control (PBVS) using multiple Lyapunov functions. IBVS-PBVS switching development addressed unstable system switching and stability region enhancement. Parikh et al. \cite{parikh2016switched} presented estimators switching between state predictors and image-based observers for object localization during intermittent image feedback, establishing switched system stability through common Lyapunov functions. The same authors \cite{parikh2018target} developed pose estimation for moving targets during intermittent measurements by learning motion models. In \cite{parikh2017switched,chen2019switched}, observer-predictor frameworks addressed target tracking and trajectory tracking with intermittent measurements by switching between globally uniformly ultimately bounded (GUUB) and unstable systems, demonstrating GUUB switched error systems based on dwell time conditions. Image-based tracking approaches primarily employ switching to accommodate feature track losses, occlusions, and limited camera FOV. Harris et al. \cite{harris2020target} developed switched systems analysis for target tracking with intermittent observations from stationary camera networks. Zegers et al. \cite{zegers2019switched} developed consensus protocols for distributed multi-agent systems using switched systems analysis where leaders provide intermittent follower information. Veer and Poulakakis \cite{veer2019switched} applied switched systems to biped locomotion, proving boundedness of input-to-state (ISS) stable switched systems with multiple equilibria. These switched system results typically switch between globally stable or locally stable systems. Unlike switched systems approaches addressing feature track losses, occlusions in object tracking and localization, and IBVS-PBVS stability improvement methods, this paper develops novel methodology switching between image-based control and learning-based control during image-feedback unavailability, including limited camera FOV, occlusions, and feature losses. We present new switched systems analysis for systems transitioning between locally stable (IBVS system) \textit{and} globally stable (DMP system) modes. Our objective involves camera pose regulation relative to targets. IBVS controllers generate camera accelerations when visual feedback is available. During visual feedback absence, DMP generates camera accelerations. DMP implementation involves online end-effector acceleration control with weights trained using pose regulation task demonstration data. This methodology proves useful for robotic tasks where robot arms with eye-in-hand configurations utilize DMP and IBVS controllers for precision achievement, or when ground robots employ robot-mounted cameras with image and non-image feedback. This paper's technical contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Novel common state-space representation development for switched system stability analysis of IBVS and DMP acceleration controllers. \item New IBVS acceleration control law development with corresponding closed-loop dynamics proven UUB when initial states remain sufficiently close to goal states. \item Combined position and orientation DMP presentation with corresponding dynamics proven globally asymptotically stable. \item Switching analysis between locally stable IBVS controllers and globally stable DMP using multiple Lyapunov functions, proving switched system dynamics converge asymptotically to bounds with derived analytical expressions. text: Long-form question-answering (LFQA) represents an emerging frontier in NLP, where systems must generate paragraph-length responses to open-ended queries. While LFQA systems hold promise as primary vehicles for knowledge acquisition, their performance remains substantially below human standards \citep{hurdles}. Prior research has predominantly concentrated on two fundamental task components: information retrieval and content synthesis. Rather than attempting to enhance these individual components, our approach leverages established solutions—delegating document retrieval to the Microsoft Bing Web Search API\footnote{\url{https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/bing/apis/bing-web-search-api}} and employing unsupervised pre-training for high-quality synthesis through GPT-3 fine-tuning \citep{gpt3}. Our primary focus centers on integrating these elements through more faithful training objectives. Drawing inspiration from \citet{summarization}, we employ human feedback to directly optimize answer quality, enabling us to achieve human-competitive performance. Our work presents two principal contributions: \begin{itemize \item We develop a text-based web-browsing environment enabling fine-tuned language model interaction. This framework facilitates end-to-end improvement of both retrieval and synthesis through general methodologies including imitation learning and reinforcement learning. \item We produce answers \textit{with references}: model-extracted passages from web pages during browsing sessions. This capability proves essential for enabling labelers to assess factual accuracy without requiring difficult and subjective independent research processes. \end{itemize} Training occurs primarily on ELI5 questions \citep{eli5}, sourced from the ``Explain Like I'm Five'' subreddit. We gather two supplementary data types: \textit{demonstrations} showing humans utilizing our web-browsing environment for question-answering, and \textit{comparisons} between paired model-generated responses to identical questions (each accompanied by distinct reference sets). Answer evaluation considers factual accuracy, coherence, and overall utility. This data supports four primary applications: behavior cloning (supervised fine-tuning) from demonstrations, reward modeling from comparisons, reinforcement learning against the reward model, and rejection sampling against the reward model. Our optimal model combines behavior cloning with rejection sampling. Reinforcement learning additionally benefits scenarios with constrained inference-time computation. Our evaluation employs three distinct approaches for our best-performing model. Initially, we contrast our model's responses with human demonstrator answers on held-out questions. Our model achieves 56\% preference rates, indicating human-level text-based browser utilization. Subsequently, we compare our model's answers (references removed for fairness) against top-voted ELI5 dataset responses. Our model garners 69\% preference rates. Finally, we assess performance on TruthfulQA \citep{truthfulqa}, an adversarial short-form question dataset. Our model produces truthful answers 75\% of the time and both truthful and informative responses 54\% of the time, surpassing our base model (GPT-3) while remaining below human performance levels. The paper proceeds as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Section \ref{section:environment} details our text-based web-browsing environment and model interaction mechanisms. \item Section \ref{section:methods} elaborates on data collection procedures and training methodologies. \item Section \ref{section:evaluation} assesses our top-performing models (across varying inference-time compute budgets) using ELI5 and TruthfulQA. \item Section \ref{section:experiments} presents experimental comparisons of different methods and their scaling behavior across dataset size, parameter count, and inference-time computation. \item Section \ref{section:discussion} examines implications for truthful question-answering model training and broader societal impacts. \end{itemize}

text: Autonomous navigation through complex and dynamic traffic environments presents formidable challenges. The diversity of road topologies and scenarios—including roundabouts, multi-lane arterials, and intersections—creates substantial complexity\cite{Chen2019DeepIL}. Moreover, modeling the intricate and interdependent interactions among heterogeneous road agents such as pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles remains exceptionally difficult\cite{Chen2020RobotNI}. Additionally, adherence to various traffic regulations, including signal compliance, lane boundary respect, and speed limit enforcement, must be ensured. Traditional decision-making and planning approaches rely predominantly on rule-based frameworks, which exhibit poor generalization capabilities across novel scenarios. Consequently, these methods demand extensive and iterative manual calibration of rules and parameters to sustain adequate performance\cite{Zeng2019EndToEndIN}. Recently, deep learning has emerged as a promising alternative, significantly advancing self-driving vehicle (SDV) technology. The capacity to \textit{learn and self-optimize} behavioral patterns from data substantially reduces the burdensome engineering overhead required to model all conceivable scenarios, rendering deep driving models particularly well-suited for autonomous navigation in high-dimensional, nonlinear, and dynamic environments\cite{Cai2020ProbabilisticEV, Chen2019LearningBC,OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring, Tai2019VisualbasedAD}. Nevertheless, existing learning-based approaches lack proper design for scalable autonomous driving within unified frameworks. Most research efforts concentrate on isolated tasks, including conditional urban navigation\cite{OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring,Chen2019LearningBC,Tai2019VisualbasedAD}, lane-following behavior\cite{Xu2017EndtoEndLO}, lane-changing maneuvers\cite{Wang2018ARL}, or collision avoidance strategies\cite{Porav2018ImminentCM, Woo2020CollisionAF}. Consequently, high-performance scalable driving models capable of managing diverse traffic scenarios remain elusive. To address this limitation, we introduce a graph-based deep neural network architecture termed \textit{DiGNet} (driving in graphs) for scalable autonomous driving. Our approach employs graph attention networks (GAT)\cite{velickovic2018graph} to capture complex inter-agent interactions, utilizes semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) representations to encode road topologies and traffic regulations, and leverages variational auto-encoders (VAE)\cite{kingma2014autoencoding} to extract compact yet informative environmental features. This paper's primary contributions include: (1) A purpose-built network architecture for autonomous driving across generic traffic scenarios, incorporating both contextual driving information and dynamic agent interactions. (2) Comprehensive demonstration of the proposed method's scalable and safe driving performance through extensive closed-loop evaluations in both familiar and novel urban, rural, and highway environments.

text: Neural Networks (NNs) constitute computational architectures featuring one or more feature representation layers coupled with a terminal linear classifier. Over recent years, deep NNs have dramatically advanced state-of-the-art performance across diverse real-world applications, including image classification \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,he2016deep}, speech recognition \cite{hinton2012deep}, natural language processing \cite{bahdanau2014neural}, among others. Nevertheless, theoretical comprehension of these empirical achievements in NNs remains constrained. A primary conceptual challenge stems from the pronounced non-convexity inherent in these models, which implies that first-order optimization methods like gradient descent (GD) or stochastic gradient descent (SGD) might settle at inferior local stationary points. Nevertheless, practical experience reveals that through various techniques including dropout \cite{SHKSS-dropout} and batch normalization \cite{ioffe15}, deep neural networks (DNNs) can be dependably trained from random initialization while yielding reproducible outcomes. Models obtained through appropriate training protocols demonstrate robust and consistent behavior. Put differently, distinct random initializations (employing identical initialization and training protocols) typically produce models that yield comparable predictions on test datasets. Consequently, we can infer that appropriate neural network training converges to similar solutions. This phenomenon mirrors convex optimization behavior, rather than typical non-convex optimization scenarios that become trapped in suboptimal local stationary solutions. Since solutions from varying random initializations exhibit similarity and reproducibility, one might hypothesize that through proper training, deep neural networks can attain solutions approaching global optimality. These empirical phenomena appear quite enigmatic, necessitating the development of novel mathematical frameworks for neural networks that can reconcile the divide between non-convex and convex models for understanding. Beyond these empirical findings, practitioners also recognize that overparameterized neural networks (NNs) containing numerous hidden units facilitate learning \cite{zhang2016understanding}. Such networks deliver superior and more reliable performance. Connected to this empirical insight, researchers observed in the 1990s that neural networks possessing infinitely many hidden units become more tractable for theoretical modeling and analysis \cite{Neal95-thesis,Williams97-nips}. Throughout recent years, substantial theoretical progress has emerged in analyzing overparameterized NNs with extensive hidden units approaching infinity. Particularly, research demonstrated that such systems exhibit convex-like behavior under various constrained conditions. This offers theoretical validation for the empirical observations regarding neural network training reproducibility. { This paper surveys recently developed mathematical frameworks for overparameterized NNs, emphasizing the {\em neural tangent kernel} (NTK) perspective and the {\em mean field} (MF) perspective. Section~\ref{sec:2two-levelNN} presents the fundamental formulation for two-layer NNs while Section~\ref{sec:random} introduces a related learning framework, random kitchen sinks \cite{rahimi2009weighted}. Section \ref{sec:ntk} explores the NTK perspective for two-layer NNs, demonstrating that a two-layer NN can be equivalently expressed as a linear model within the tangent space under specific conditions. Section \ref{sec:meanfield} examines the MF perspective for two-layer NNs. This viewpoint treats a continuous two-layer NN as a learned distribution over weights, yielding a more realistic mathematical framework for analyzing practical NN behaviors. Section \ref{sec:exp} contrasts these three models through a feature learning lens. Section \ref{sec:deepnn} explores potential extensions to deep NNs for NTK and MFs. Section \ref{sec:complexity} presents fundamental complexity results for NTK. Section \ref{sec:othermodel} surveys additional mathematical models. Finally, we conclude and outline active research directions in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}.} \IEEEpubidadjcol

text: The exponential growth in scientific literature presents researchers with an increasingly daunting challenge: identifying valuable papers from vast collections for efficient literature review or staying current with emerging developments. When encountering unfamiliar research domains, researchers typically consult survey papers and explore their reference lists for deeper insights. Yet comprehensive, current surveys remain unavailable for many research areas. Alternatively, researchers turn to academic search engines to discover relevant publications. Current academic search platforms typically return article lists by computing semantic similarity between user queries and individual papers in isolation, neglecting prerequisite dependencies among search results. Consequently, tremendous value would emerge from retrieving core paper collections with prescribed reading sequences for given queries, providing users with structured learning pathways. Such an approach would enable researchers to navigate generated reading paths and rapidly familiarize themselves with novel research domains. Scientific paper analysis has garnered substantial research interest recently. Nevertheless, existing efforts predominantly address citation recommendation~\cite{zhou2008learning, tang2009discriminative, he2010context, ren2014cluscite, sun2017recommendation}, seeking to suggest citations for given texts. A second research stream examines citation classification \cite{jurgens2016citation, teufel2006automatic, dong2011ensemble, zhao2019context, cohan2019structural, pride2020authoritative}, attempting to decode authors' citation motivations. Additional studies have explored reading list generation for users. \cite{jardine2014automatically} introduced ThemedPageRank for creating reading lists through topic-related paper re-ranking. \cite{ekstrand2010automatically} constructed query-based reading lists using collaborative and content-based filtering approaches. These methodologies, however, disregard prerequisite relationships among returned papers. \cite{gordon2017structured} developed a concept graph-based framework for structured reading list generation, incorporating prerequisite topic concepts. This approach, though, depends heavily on existing concept graph quality. Prior reading list generation research primarily addresses the question of ``what to read" by producing paper collections for specified research topics. However, for users unfamiliar with research fields, two essential problems remain unaddressed: ``how to read" and ``how to understand". The first challenge requires organizing diverse research works structurally, enabling users to follow structured pathways while comprehending how specific topic research has evolved historically. Merely chronological paper organization proves insufficient, as it overlooks inter-research correlations. The second challenge demands including papers that may not directly relate to queried research topics but prove valuable or essential for understanding highly relevant papers in generated lists. Drawing from this analysis, we introduce a novel task termed {\em Reading Path Generation (RPG)}, which automatically constructs reading paths for given queries. This task assists field newcomers in conducting rapid surveys by addressing both aforementioned challenges. Specifically, we aim to retrieve paper collections encompassing research works highly relevant to given queries, alongside prerequisite research essential for understanding highly relevant works. Moreover, we organize these papers into reading paths that consider both chronological ordering and inter-research correlations. We anticipate that following retrieved papers according to reading paths will enable users to comprehend individual research works easily, complete surveys efficiently, and develop comprehensive research history landscapes for any topic. Given the absence of benchmark datasets for Reading Path Generation evaluation, we propose the {\em SurveyBank} dataset, specifically designed for our novel task. SurveyBank creation requires no human annotation, building upon two fundamental insights. First, numerous existing high-quality survey papers, authored by professional researchers, contain invaluable information about research topic survey formation. Based on this observation, we employ key phrases extracted from survey titles as RPG task inputs, with reading paths inferred from survey reference lists serving as ground truth labels. We initially gathered $41,194$ computer science surveys from Google Scholar and S2ORC \cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc}. Subsequently, $9,321$ high-quality surveys were selected to constitute SurveyBank. The dataset spans 10 computer science topics including Artificial Intelligence, Computer Networks, and Databases. The second insight recognizes that citation relationships between papers reflect inter-paper coherence. Accordingly, we constructed a large-scale scientific citation graph containing 6 million S2ORC~\cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc} computer science papers through citation relationships, with this citation graph encompassing each survey's reference lists. To our knowledge, SurveyBank represents the currently largest survey dataset. Finally, we propose and implement a Real-time Reading Path Generation System (RePaGer) that accepts key phrases as inputs and generates paper reading paths for users. RePaGer begins by retrieving top-$K$ articles termed initial seed papers from Google Scholar. Subsequently, we reallocate seeds by first capturing initial seed paper neighbors as seed candidates, then selecting articles with high co-occurrence. We hypothesize these newly selected seeds more likely represent topic prerequisite concepts, as multiple topic-relevant articles cite them. Finally, we propose Node-Edge Weighted Steiner Tree (NWST), a graph optimization-based approach, for identifying reading paths with prerequisite chains for given queries. Our model considers both individual paper importance within entire citation networks and inter-paper relationships. We conduct comprehensive evaluations using the SurveyBank dataset, comparing our proposed Reading Path Generation approach against existing academic search engines and baseline methods. Evaluation results demonstrate our approach's superiority over other baselines and its capability to generate insightful reading paths for diverse research topics.

text: The field of 3D-aware image synthesis has garnered significant attention in recent years~\cite{graf, giraffe, pigan}. A promising approach involves incorporating Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~\cite{nerf} within Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{gan}. This methodology substitutes traditional 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) generators with generative implicit functions that transform raw 3D coordinates into point-specific densities and colors, conditioned on provided latent codes. These implicit functions encode both structural and textural information of output images within 3D space. Nevertheless, directly incorporating NeRF~\cite{nerf} into generators presents two significant challenges. First, NeRF's implicit function generates color and density values for individual 3D points through Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) networks. Given the highly localized receptive field of MLPs, global structural representation becomes problematic during image synthesis. Consequently, relying solely on 3D coordinates as inputs~\cite{graf, pigan, giraffe} provides insufficient expressiveness for guiding generators with global structural information. Second, volume rendering computes pixel values independently for output images, necessitating extensive point sampling along camera rays for each pixel. This dramatically escalates computational demands as image resolution increases. Such computational burden may result in suboptimal model training and consequently diminished performance in high-resolution image generation. Previous research has established that 2D GANs derive substantial benefits from meaningful representations learned by generators~\cite{interfacegan, higan, xu2021generative}. These generative representations characterize synthesis through \textit{high-level features}. For instance, Xu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{xu2021generative} demonstrate that face synthesis models maintain awareness of landmark positions in generated faces, while Yang~\textit{et al.}~\cite{higan} identify multi-level variation factors emerging from bedroom image generation. Such representative features encapsulate rich textural and structural information, thereby improving both synthesis quality~\cite{stylegan} and controllability~\cite{interfacegan} in image GANs. Conversely, existing 3D-aware generative models directly render pixel values from coordinates~\cite{graf, pigan} without acquiring explicit representations. This work introduces a novel generative model, designated \textbf{VolumeGAN}, which accomplishes 3D-aware image synthesis by \textit{explicitly learning structural and textural representations}. Rather than utilizing 3D coordinates as direct inputs, we generate feature volumes through 3D convolutional networks, encoding spatial relationships between various regions and compensating for MLP receptive field limitations inherent in NeRF. With feature volumes modeling underlying structure, we extract coordinate descriptors from these volumes to characterize structural information for individual 3D points. Subsequently, we deploy NeRF-like models to construct feature fields by incorporating coordinate descriptors alongside raw coordinates as inputs. These feature fields accumulate into 2D feature maps serving as textural representations, followed by CNNs with $1\times1$ kernels for final image rendering. This approach separately models structure and texture through 3D feature volumes and 2D feature maps, enabling disentangled control over shape and appearance. We assess our methodology across diverse datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing alternatives. Regarding image quality, VolumeGAN achieves markedly improved Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores~\cite{fid}. For the FFHQ dataset~\cite{stylegan} at $256\times256$ resolution, we enhance FID from $36.7$ to $9.1$. We additionally enable 3D-aware image synthesis on challenging indoor scene datasets, specifically LSUN bedroom~\cite{lsun}. Our model exhibits stable object pose control and demonstrates enhanced consistency across varying viewpoints, benefiting from learned structural representations (\textit{i.e.}, feature volumes). Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies on learned structural and textural representations, analyzing trade-offs between image quality and 3D properties.

text: The European Union's Data Protection Regulation~\citep{regulation2016regulation} establishes data minimisation as a fundamental principle, mirrored in data protection frameworks across multiple jurisdictions: \begin{quote} "Personal data shall be: [...] adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)" \end{quote} This requirement establishes a framework for ethical data processing practices. Contemporary empirical investigations demonstrate that data-driven systems can maintain equivalent performance levels while operating on substantially reduced datasets~\cite{biega2020dm, chow2013differential,vincent2019data, wen2018exploring}. Such outcomes reflect the phenomenon of diminishing returns inherent in data collection across diverse applications and domains~\cite{hestness1712deep, krause2010utility,tae2020slice}. Given the feasibility of data limitation, regulatory frameworks identify specific algorithmic approaches suitable for integration into minimization workflows, such as feature selection~\cite{icoDataMinimizationTechniques} and learning curve analysis~\cite{norwegianAuthorityArtificial}. However, the computer science community has devoted minimal attention to the data minimisation principle, despite the availability of various algorithmic techniques adaptable for compliance purposes. Scholars advocating for renewed focus on this principle identify the absence of precise mathematical formulations and implementation guidelines as a primary barrier to widespread adoption~\cite{finckreviving}. Qualitative investigations reveal inconsistent data minimization practices and limited comprehension of the principle among software development professionals~\cite{senarath2018understanding}. Contemporary interpretations of data minimization advocate linking data collection objectives in data-driven systems to performance indicators, an approach designated as \emph{performance-based data minimization}~\cite{finckreviving,biega2020dm}. This work adopts this interpretation, examining \emph{methods for proactively implementing performance-based data minimization principles in machine learning applications involving personal data}. \\ \textbf{Contributions.} We introduce FIDO, a Framework for Inhibiting Data Overcollection, illustrating how continuous personal data acquisition can be managed within data minimization frameworks. FIDO's fundamental conceptual innovation involves \emph{adaptive learning of algorithmic performance curves} to enable precise determination of \emph{optimal data collection termination points}. Through direct performance curve modeling, the framework maintains adaptability across diverse feature acquisition algorithms and performance definitions. Validation experiments across multiple recommender systems datasets confirm this adaptability and establish FIDO's capability to predict algorithmic performance under additional data scenarios accurately \emph{without} requiring actual data expansion. FIDO's primary technical contribution centers on its performance curve estimation methodology, which leverages recent machine learning research identifying three characteristic phases in algorithmic performance curves: the small data phase, the power law phase, and the diminishing returns phase \cite{hestness1712deep}. We establish that these performance phases manifest within user data collection contexts and present a technique for direct modeling of data collection phases through adaptive piecewise power law curve learning. Empirical evaluations reveal that alternative performance curve estimation methods consistently \emph{overestimate} returns from additional data. Direct phase modeling enables FIDO to achieve superior performance curve learning accuracy during data acquisition while meeting practical data minimization requirements. Additionally, we investigate user-level data minimization challenges. We analyze how algorithmic components like active feature acquisition (a method for intelligent selection of feature values for collection) influence minimization outcomes. Our findings indicate that active feature acquisition generates unequal, concentrated data collection patterns focused on limited user subsets, while reducing minimization effectiveness for dynamic user communities and scenarios excluding sensitive features from initial collection. We also observe high variability in user-specific performance curves, where additional data collection frequently produces \emph{decreased} user-specific performance. This research provides a computational framework for understanding the GDPR's data minimization principle, contributing to ongoing technical implementation discussions of this essential data protection concept, while offering guidance for practitioners and researchers in future work.

FIDO's main technical contribution is the performance curve estimation, which uses the knowledge derived from the recent study of the three characteristic phases of the performance curve of the learning models: the small data phase, the power law phase and the phase of diminishing returns. The main conceptual innovation of FIDO is its adjustment to the performance curve of its algorithms, which enables the precise determination of the “optimal” data collection points. We establish that performance phases are connected with the data collection and we present a technique for direct modeling of these phases through the adaptation of a piecewise power-law learning. By directly modeling the performance curve, the framework retains its adaptability to the extraction strategies and the performance metrics and confirms the accuracy of predicting the performance of the learning models under additional data without actual data expansion. At the level of the individual users, we also study the difficulties of data minimization. The direct phase modeling of FIDO allows it to acquire superior learning performance while satisfying practical data constraints. We analyze how the use of the active acquisition method for selecting features affects the minimization. This work offers a computational framework for understanding the data minimization principle of the GDPR, and contributes to ongoing technical discussions about the implementation of this essential data protection concept, guiding the work of practitioners and scholars. We also find a high degree of variability in the performance curves of individual users, where an increase in data collection often results in a decrease in the performance of the individual users. Our results show that this method produces a disproportionately uneven and highly focused collection pattern for small subsets of users, and that it can compromise the effectiveness of minimization for dynamically evolving communities of users and in cases where sensitive features are excluded from the start.

text: Transmission System Operators (TSOs) rely on the \textit{Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch} (SCED) as a cornerstone optimization framework for clearing real-time energy markets while maintaining power grid reliability \cite{conejo2018power}. TSOs such as MISO and PJM in the United States execute SCED algorithms every five minutes, necessitating solution times well under one minute to meet operational deadlines \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. The incorporation of security constraints—which guarantee system robustness against single-component failures—creates substantial computational challenges for large-scale systems \cite{Chiang2015_SolvingSCOPF,Wang2016_SolvingCorrectiveSCOPF,velloso2021exact}, particularly when comprehensive contingency sets are analyzed. These computational bottlenecks will intensify as distributed resources proliferate and operational uncertainty increases \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. The increasing penetration of renewable generation, particularly wind power within the MISO system, drives our motivation to develop risk-aware market-clearing methodologies. A critical operational challenge involves conducting real-time risk analysis through the evaluation of numerous scenarios encompassing load variations and renewable production uncertainty \cite{werho2021_ScenarioGenerationWind}. Nevertheless, the systematic solution of multiple SCED instances remains impractical under real-time operational constraints. We address this computational barrier by proposing an optimization proxy for SCED—a Machine Learning (ML) model capable of predicting optimal SCED solutions within acceptable numerical tolerances and millisecond timeframes. We emphasize that our objective does not involve replacing existing optimization-based market-clearing infrastructure. Rather, the proposed optimization proxy serves as a complementary risk assessment tool for system operators. This capability enables rapid evaluation of system behavior across diverse scenarios without requiring computationally expensive optimizations. Since these predictions contribute to aggregated risk metrics, individual instance prediction errors remain tolerable. \subsection{Related Literature and Challenges} Recent years have witnessed growing interest in combining ML and optimization techniques for power system applications. One research direction \cite{pan2019deepopf, fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high, lei2020data, chatzos2021spatial, velloso2020combining, zamzam2020learning, owerko2020optimal} employs ML models to predict optimal Optimal Power Flow (OPF) solutions. Pan et al. \cite{pan2019deepopf} developed a Deep Neural Network (DNN) approach for predicting security-constrained DC-OPF solutions, demonstrating results on systems containing up to 300 buses. A prevalent limitation of ML approaches, acknowledged in \cite{pan2019deepopf}, concerns the absence of constraint satisfaction guarantees for predicted solutions. Recent investigations \cite{fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high} incorporate Lagrangian duality principles into DNN training procedures to capture AC-OPF physical and operational constraints. Velloso et al. \cite{velloso2020combining} adopt similar methodologies for preventive security-constrained DC-OPF contexts. Their approach trains DNNs using Lagrangian duality techniques, subsequently employing them as proxies for computationally intensive master problems within column-and-constraint generation algorithms. Chatzos et al. \cite{chatzos2021spatial} recently embedded Lagrangian duality frameworks within two-stage learning architectures that exploit regional power network decomposition, facilitating more efficient distributed training. A parallel research direction integrates ML models within optimization algorithms to enhance computational performance. Multiple studies (e.g., \cite{deka2019learning,misra2021learning,xavier2021learning, yang2020fast,guha2019machine}) focus on active constraint identification to reduce problem complexity. Xavier et al. \cite{xavier2021learning} explore learning approaches for unit commitment feasible solutions. Venzka et al. \cite{venzke2020neural} employ DNN models to learn dynamic SCOPF feasible regions, subsequently transforming these networks into mixed-integer linear programs. Current ML research for power systems exhibits two significant limitations. First, most studies present numerical results on small academic test systems that are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than actual transmission networks. This scale disparity raises concerns, as higher-dimensional data adversely affects machine-learning algorithm convergence and accuracy. Second, nearly all studies utilize artificially-generated datasets whose distributions fail to capture operational variability. For example, investigations typically consider only load variations without accounting for spatio-temporal correlations. Additional uncertainty sources, including renewable production and economic bid variability, remain unaddressed. Moreover, daily commitment decision changes are seldom examined, despite introducing significant combinatorial distribution shifts. \subsection{Contributions and Outline} We propose a novel ML pipeline grounded in real-world market operation structures to address these limitations. Our approach exploits TSO forward knowledge of 1) commitment decisions and 2) day-ahead load and renewable production forecasts. Both information sources become available following day-ahead market execution. Additionally, we present comprehensive real-time market behavior analysis that informs a novel ML architecture designed to better capture actual operational characteristics. Figure~\ref{fig:learning_pipeline} illustrates our proposed learning pipeline. Initially, commitment decisions and day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable generation are collected following day-ahead market clearing. Subsequently, this information generates SCED instance training datasets using classical data augmentation techniques. Third, specialized ML models undergo training, ideally one per operating hour, thereby mitigating commitment decision combinatorial explosion: each ML model considers only one commitment set while focusing on load/renewable scenarios surrounding hourly forecasts. Fourth, trained models evaluate numerous scenarios in real time throughout the operating day. The complete data-generation and training procedure requires only a few hours. The paper proceeds as follows. Section \ref{sec:opt_pipeline} describes day-ahead and real-time market interactions within the MISO system and provides a real-time SCED overview for MISO. Section \ref{sec:methodology} analyzes real-time market solution behavior, proposes a combined Classification-Then-Regression architecture, and presents the comprehensive ML pipeline. Section \ref{sec:results} reports numerical experiments on real-world systems.

text: The fundamental goal of DNA-sequencing is to characterize the genetic composition of individual organisms. While numerous technological approaches exist, these methodologies collectively determine genetic sequence fragments or complete sequences. Standard primary data analysis workflows typically encompass several key stages: 1) sequence alignment to a reference genome (such as GRCh38 for human specimens), and 2) identification of genetic variants. The principal output comprises a catalog of variants—essentially a collection of sequence differences unique to the analyzed sample—frequently documented in structured formats such as the Variant Call Format~(VCF)~\cite{vcf}. These identified variants serve as foundational data for diverse downstream applications, spanning basic research investigations and association studies to clinical diagnostic procedures. Focusing exclusively on genomic differences relative to a reference proves computationally efficient, given that complete genomes are substantial~(approximately~$3 \cdot 10^9$ nucleotides in humans), while inter-individual genomic variation remains relatively modest~(roughly~$0.6\%$~\cite{variation}). Literature documentation and database storage of variants associated with phenotypic characteristics typically involves transforming VCF representations into formats better suited for scientific reporting. Multiple domain-specific representation languages have emerged to address this need. The most prominent include: \begin{itemize} \item Human Genome Variation Society~(HGVS) recommendations~\cite{hgvs}; \item SPDI~\cite{spdi}, which serves as the internal variant data model for the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI); \item Variant Representation Specification~(VRS)~\cite{vrs}, created by the Global Alliance for Genomic Health (GA4GH). \end{itemize} These representation systems strive to encode observed genomic differences in formats that are both human-comprehensible and computationally interpretable. Unlike VCF, which remains intrinsically linked to specific analytical pipelines and configuration parameters, these alternative representations maintain process independence and universal interpretability. Several conventional simplifications characterize variant documentation practices. Initially, discrete small variants occurring on individual molecular sequences (within identical haplotypes) receive separate documentation, facilitating efficient database storage of extensive variant collections. Phasing information—indicating whether multiple small variants belong to the same haplotype—frequently becomes lost or remains incomplete. This information loss stems partly from inherent sequencing technology limitations and partly from deliberate data processing decisions. Additionally, certain representation systems (particularly HGVS) accommodate uncertainty expression. Such uncertainties typically concern variant positioning within reference genomes, though the precise composition of larger insertions may also remain undetermined. Finally, unchanged genomic regions often remain implicit. Primary data analysis, especially alignment procedures, assumes reference genome sequence presence even when direct supporting evidence, such as sequencing coverage data, is absent. Throughout this manuscript, we maintain a rigorous perspective on variant characteristics: \begin{enumerate} \item Variants comprise deletions, insertions, or combinations thereof relative to individual molecular sequences. Combined operations are considered phased, occurring in cis, or belonging to identical alleles, expressible as phase sets or allele descriptions. Numerous variant description languages have introduced specialized operations including single nucleotide variants (SNV) (termed substitutions in HGVS), multi-nucleotide variants (deletion/insertions), duplications, transpositions, inversions, repeats, and others. We regard all such concepts as specific instances of our general definition. \item We exclusively consider \emph{interpretable} variants, meaning that given a \emph{reference sequence}, a deterministic and unambiguous method exists for ``applying'' variants to yield the originally measured \emph{observed sequence}, analogous to Unix~\texttt{diff} and \texttt{patch} utilities. \end{enumerate} \noindent Various variant representation languages have recognized that multiple representations can describe identical observed sequences. These representational alternatives may arise from operator selection choices—for instance, an SNV can alternatively be expressed as a single nucleotide deletion followed by a single nucleotide insertion. Reference sequence structure provides another source of representational multiplicity. Consider reference sequence~\texttt{ATTTA} and observed sequence~\texttt{ATTA}. Removing one~\texttt{T} symbol generates multiple~($3$) possible specifications for which symbol was deleted. Most variant representation languages implement \emph{normalization} procedures to establish universally accepted variant representations. Normalization selects a \emph{canonical} representation from available alternatives. Unfortunately, standardization of this procedure remains incomplete across different languages—exemplified by HGVS's $3'$-rule versus VCF's $5'$-rule. Within individual languages, however, appropriate normalization resolves the challenge of identifying \emph{equivalent} variant representations. The consequences of employing non-normalized variant representations have been extensively examined in~\cite{variant_name, variant_calling, curation, litvar}. Proposed solutions appear in~\cite{unified, improved_vcf, vmc_spec, smash, plyranges, gql, ask2me, deletions}. Rigorous application of normalization procedures frequently requires specialized software tools~\cite{varsome, validator, mutalyzer, vde}. Normalized variant representations enable direct textual comparison through standard string matching algorithms. \noindent Currently, identifying equivalent variant representations—determining whether two variant descriptions produce identical observed sequences—represents the most significant query in variant analysis, enabling variant grouping and annotation matching. The emergence of long-read single-molecule sequencing technologies (from manufacturers like Pacific Biosciences and Oxford Nanopore), capable of providing direct evidence for numerous small variants within identical haplotypes, introduces more sophisticated analytical questions. For example, suballele identification, valuable in molecular microbiology (strain typing) and pharmacogenomics (star allele calling), can be accomplished by determining whether specific suballeles are contained within observed alleles. We employ minimal sequence-level alignments—informally characterized as deletion/insertion sequences that transform one string into another with minimum possible length—to define relationships between variants sharing identical reference sequences. Figure~\ref{fig:example} illustrates this concept. Section~\ref{sec:formal} provides precise definitions of how these relationships depend on complete alignment sets between sequence pairs. In the example scenario, the containment relationship takes precedence over overlap relationships. This paper comprehensively explores variant relationships. Beyond equivalence relations, we partition the binary variant relationship domain into Boolean relations: equivalence; containment (where one variant is fully contained within another or completely contains another); overlap (where variants share at least one common element); and disjoint (where no common elements exist). This partitioning ensures that exactly one relationship holds true for every variant pair. Relationship determination considers all (minimal) variant representations simultaneously.

Apart from the relation of equivalence, the relationship domain is divided into boolean relations: equivalence, containment (when a variant is either fully within or completely contained by another variant), overlap (when two variants have at least one common element), and disjoint (when there is no common element). This partitioning ensures that there is exactly one relation between any two variants. The relationship determination takes into account all (minimal) variant representations.

text: Originating from African musical traditions, the Tresillo rhythm arrived in the Caribbean through the Atlantic Slave Trade. Cuba served as the primary catalyst for its global dissemination\cite{acquista2009tresillo, floyd1999black}, subsequently embedding itself across diverse musical genres worldwide. \par Beyond functioning as a standalone rhythmic foundation, the Tresillo serves as a structural component within more complex rhythmic frameworks, including Reggaeton and Clave patterns. Following the framework established by \cite {floyd1999black}, we define the Tresillo rhythm as shown in Figure \ref{fig:tresillo}. This rhythmic structure features a dotted eighth note succeeded by a sixteenth note, an eighth rest, and an eighth note, with this sequence repeating twice within a 4/4 measure. Adding beats on every fourth count transforms this pattern into the Reggaeton rhythm (see Figure \ref{fig:reggaeton}). Alternatively, modifying the bar's second half to include an eighth rest, two eighth notes, and another eighth rest yields the fundamental Clave rhythm (see Figure \ref{fig:clave}). Latin American musical traditions extensively employ the Tresillo rhythm. Nevertheless, this \textit{``danceable Cuban Clave son"}\cite{sethares2014geometry} transcends Latin American boundaries, permeating Western musical arrangements \cite{sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic}. Contemporary mainstream examples encompass Ed Sheeran's ``Shape of you" and Sia's ``Cheap Thrills," both achieving Billboard Chart dominance. Our preliminary examination of pop charts through Billboard Chart analysis reveals consistent Tresillo integration in popular music. Although qualitative research has extensively documented the Tresillo rhythm's usage, evolution, and cultural significance \cite{acquista2009tresillo, sandroni2001tresillo, sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic, floyd1999black}, quantitative analysis of its prevalence remains unexplored. To address this research gap, we developed computational methods for representing both pop song rhythmic structures and the Tresillo pattern, enabling comparative analysis through various similarity metrics. These measurements reveal a discernible temporal trend in Tresillo utilization within US Billboard Top 20 Charts spanning two decades (1999-2019). \par Our investigation unfolds systematically: We begin by examining relevant interdisciplinary literature, followed by establishing analytical assumptions in our problem statement. The Data section outlines our selected sources and formatting approaches. Our methodology section details the final data representation, proposed rhythm similarity measures, and evaluation frameworks. Results encompass both similarity measure assessment and temporal trend analysis. We conclude by discussing methodological choices and findings, offering interpretive frameworks for our results, and proposing future research directions.

text: Legged robots demonstrate remarkable versatility across diverse applications, yet achieving robust locomotion remains a challenging research frontier requiring continued investigation. {Stability and safety} constitute fundamental prerequisites for robots operating in real-world environments. This raises a compelling question: given their inherent versatility, what prevents legged robots from matching human capabilities? In pursuit of this intended versatility, we examined the fundamental principles underlying balance recovery strategy learning. Humans employ multiple coordinated strategies—including arm movements, ankle adjustments, hip positioning, stepping responses, and others—to restore equilibrium following external perturbations. These responses improve through accumulated experience and adaptive learning. Additionally, we analyzed contemporary biped robot locomotion frameworks. While stability improvements have been substantial, current systems lack the robustness and safety necessary for deployment in everyday environments. Various biped robot stabilization approaches have emerged, which can be organized into three primary categories. The following subsections introduce these categories and provide brief reviews of recent developments within each. \subsection{Analytical Approaches} Approaches within this category utilize robot dynamics models to design controller sets (such as force controllers~\cite{mason2016balancing}, hybrid position/force systems~\cite{faraji2019bipedal}, and admittance controllers~\cite{caron2020icra}) based on specific criteria for minimizing tracking errors. The Linear Inverted Pendulum~(LIP) model, which abstracts robot dynamics as a single mass, represents the most prevalent approach in literature. By constraining vertical mass movement, this model provides linear dynamics enabling rapid real-time solutions. Decades of research have investigated and extended this model for legged robot locomotion design and analysis~\cite{takenaka2009real,englsberger2015three}. The Divergent Component of Motion~(DCM) concept, proposed by Takaneka et al.~\cite{takenaka2009real}, decomposes LIP dynamics into stable and unstable components, requiring only unstable part control for stability maintenance. Englsberger et al.~\cite{englsberger2015three} extended DCM to three dimensions, leading to various control approaches including classical feedback controllers~\cite{morisawa2014biped}, Linear Quadratic Regulator~(LQR)-based methods~\cite{faraji2019bipedal,8967778}, and Model Predictive Control~(MPC)~\cite{ brasseur2015robust} for biped locomotion framework formulation. These approaches compensate tracking errors through three combined strategies: Ground Reaction Force~(GRF) manipulation, next step position modification, and step timing adjustment. Current research explores relaxing LIP assumptions (including COM vertical motion and angular momentum constraints), necessitating nonlinear dynamics handling~\cite{caron2020icra, kajita2018biped, seyde2018inclusion}. \vspace{-2mm} \subsection{Machine Learning Approaches} This category encompasses approaches designed to learn feasible policies through environmental interaction. Deep Reinforcement Learning~(DRL) has demonstrated remarkable capability in solving complex locomotion and manipulation tasks characterized by high-dimensional continuous observation and action spaces~\cite{gu2017deep,abreu2019learning}. While DRL data augmentation techniques are extensively employed for optimization performance enhancement, this work focuses specifically on symmetry-oriented solutions. Symmetric data generation from actual samples has improved various robotic tasks~\cite{lin2020robotics}, including walking gaits for diverse humanoid models~\cite{abdolhosseini2019learning} and quadruped robots~\cite{mishra2019augmenting} (featuring multiple symmetry planes). DRL learning from scratch can achieve highly efficient behaviors, even in asymmetrical configurations~\cite{Abreu2019runfaster}. However, without model restrictions (such as symmetry constraints or pattern generators), producing human-like behaviors within reasonable timeframes becomes challenging. \subsection{Hybrid Approaches: combing analytical and learning} This category focuses on harnessing the combined potential of both previously mentioned approaches. Learning algorithms can integrate with model-based gait pattern generators to predict parameters and learn residual dynamics (compensatory actions), resulting in remarkably accurate behaviors~\cite{koryakovskiy2018model,ahn2020data}. These frameworks typically comprise interconnected layers organized in hierarchical structures. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2018learning} developed a hierarchical framework ensuring humanoid robot stability through motor skill learning. Their system features two independent layers: a high-level layer generating joint angle sets and a low-level layer translating these angles into joint torques via PD controllers. Their reward function incorporated six distinct terms primarily related to traditional push recovery strategies, combined through weighted summation. \subsection{Overview of the Proposed Framework and Contributions} This research concentrates on bipedal locomotion, representing the most challenging aspect of legged robotics. We specifically address whether learning algorithms can effectively control and modulate model-based control policies such as gait pattern generators. Our contributions include: \textbf{(i)} development of a humanoid robot locomotion framework integrating analytical control with machine learning. Figure~\ref{fig:Cover} provides a system overview. We employ an abstract dynamics model to analytically formulate closed-loop biped locomotion and recovery strategies as a kernel, combined with symmetry-enhanced optimization using Proximal Policy Optimisation~(PPO)~\cite{schulman2017ppo} for residual dynamics learning. The learned policy adjusts pattern generator parameters and generates compensatory actions as residual dynamics for stability recovery; \textbf{(ii)} proposal of a learning method utilizing partial data augmentation, leveraging symmetry to improve learning efficiency and human-likeness while preserving asymmetric movement capabilities, thereby expanding possible behavior ranges. This paper proceeds as follows: Section~\ref{sec:pattern} presents our fully parametric kernel pattern generator architecture with detailed module explanations. Section~\ref{sec:learningResidual} introduces our learning framework, explaining the kernel pattern generator augmentation for parameter regulation and model-free skill learning~(compensatory joint position generation). Section~\ref{sec:simScenarios} designs simulation scenarios validating the proposed framework performance. Section~\ref{sec:simulations} conducts comprehensive simulations providing assessments and analyses of overall performance, optimized policy behavior, symmetry, and robustness. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} presents conclusions and future research directions.

text: This paper investigates the Parallel Drone Scheduling Traveling Salesman Problem (PDSTSP), which we define as follows. Consider a complete undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ where $V=\{0,1,...,n, n+1\}$ represents the vertex set and $E=\{(i, j): i, j \in V, i < j\}$ denotes the edge set. The depot is represented by vertex 0, while vertex $n+1$ serves as a depot copy introduced for modeling convenience. The customer set $V_c$ comprises the remaining vertices. A truck and a fleet $D$ of $m$ drones are stationed at the depot for delivery operations. We define $V_{d}\subseteq V_c$ as the subset of \textit{drone-eligible} customers whose depot distance and parcel weight constraints allow drone service. Customers requiring truck service form the set $V_{t}=V_c \setminus V_d$. The truck's travel time between nodes $i$ and $j$ is denoted $t_{ij}$, while $t'_i$ represents the drone service time for customer $i$, computed as twice the flight time from depot to customer $i$. The PDSTSP seeks to construct vehicle routes satisfying: (i) each customer receives exactly one visit from either truck or drone; (ii) the truck route originates and terminates at the depot; (iii) drones execute round-trip journeys from the depot, serving one customer per trip; (iv) the total completion time for serving all customers and returning all vehicles to the depot is minimized. Since its initial presentation by \citet*{murray2015flying}, the PDSTSP has garnered substantial research interest. These authors developed a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation and designed a straightforward heuristic approach. Their method partitions customers into truck and drone subsets, then independently solves the resulting TSP and Parallel Machine Scheduling (PMS) subproblems to generate truck and drone routes, respectively. A refinement phase reassigns customers between vehicle types to achieve better workload balance. Testing was conducted on small instances containing at most 20 customers. Subsequent research has focused on efficiently handling larger PDSTSP instances. \citet*{mbiadou2018iterative} introduced the first metaheuristic approach, termed the iterative two-step heuristic method. This approach initially constructs a customer sequence (termed a giant or TSP tour) encompassing all customers, then employs dynamic programming to decompose this giant tour into truck routes and drone trips, yielding a complete PDSTSP solution. Evaluation was performed on newly generated instances containing up to 229 customers. \citet*{dell2020matheuristic} subsequently developed a matheuristic adopting the same conceptual framework as \cite*{mbiadou2018iterative}. Their approach substitutes the dynamic programming component with a MILP-based method for the decomposition step. Results demonstrated that while this algorithm requires longer computation times, it produces superior solutions compared to \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}'s heuristic. \citet*{Dinh2021} developed a nature-inspired Hybrid Ant Colony Optimization (HACO) algorithm. This method adopts \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}'s representation of PDSTSP solutions as customer permutations but introduces an enhanced dynamic programming approach with controllable state space while exploring broader solution regions for giant tour decomposition. Problem-specific components including local search and solution construction mechanisms significantly contribute to algorithmic performance. Benchmark testing revealed that HACO surpasses existing metaheuristics in both computational efficiency and solution quality. The most recent metaheuristic development is the Slack Induction by String and Sweep Removals (SISSR) Ruin-and-Recreate algorithm presented by \cite{Nguyen2021}. By effectively leveraging PDSTSP solution characteristics, this metaheuristic generates ``sufficient" solution flexibility through novel removal operators during the ruin phase, thereby enhancing improvement opportunities in the subsequent recreate phase. \cite{Nguyen2021} also introduced the PDSVRP variant, which incorporates multiple trucks and adopts a total transportation cost minimization objective. \citet*{Raj2021} examined a PDSVRP variant targeting completion time minimization for all vehicles returning to the depot. Their contribution includes three MILP formulations alongside a branch-and-price (BAP) algorithm and BAP-based heuristic. Their exact methods achieved optimal solutions for all small PDSTSP instances from \cite{murray2015flying} and three 52-customer instances from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. More recently, \citet*{MBIADOUSALEU2021} generalized the PDSTSP following the PDSVRP framework, creating the Parallel Drone Scheduling Multiple Traveling Salesman Problem. They proposed a hybrid Iterated Local Search method and developed both MILP formulation and branch-and-cut approaches for small instance resolution. The literature reveals that PDSTSP solution approaches predominantly fall within the heuristic method category. Exact algorithm results remain severely limited, with optimal solutions reported only for small instances (maximum 20 customers) and three 52-customer instances in \cite{murray2015flying, dell2020matheuristic, Raj2021}. Notably, optimal solutions for 87 of the 90 benchmark instances (up to 229 customers) created by \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} remain unreported. This methodological gap motivates our paper's primary contribution: developing a straightforward yet efficient exact branch-and-cut (B\&C) algorithm for the PDSTSP. Experimental evaluation on the largest available problem instances from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} demonstrates that our solution approach resolves all but two instances within reasonable computational time. To provide more challenging test cases for future method development, we introduce a new instance set containing up to 600 customers. We present state-of-the-art algorithm results on these instances to further examine their performance characteristics. The paper organization proceeds as follows: Section \ref{sec-formulation} presents our MILP formulation with numerous valid inequalities, forming the foundation for the branch-and-cut algorithm described in Section \ref{sec-method}. Section \ref{sec-experiment} provides experimental results, while Section \ref{sec-conclusion} concludes our research.
