The set of customers that can be served by truck is denoted by $V_t=V_c – V_d$, where V_d is the time taken by the truck to travel from the depot to node $i$ or node $j$, and $t_i$ is the time taken by the drone to service customer $i$, and we denote by $t'$ the time it takes to fly from the depot to node $i$. Testing was performed on instances containing a maximum of twenty customers. The method is to divide the customers into truck and drone sets, then separately solve the travelling salesman problem and the parallel machine scheduler problem to obtain truck and drone routes, respectively. A final step allocates the customers to different vehicle classes to optimize the work distribution. Then Citetmbiadou-iterative* presented the first meta-heuristic, called the iterative two-stage method, which first determines the sequence of the customers (the giant tour, TSP), then, using dynamic programming, decomposes this giant tour into truck routes and drone flights, and thus produces a complete solution to the PDSTSP. Tests were carried out on new instances of up to 229 customers. Subsequent work has been devoted to the problem of obtaining efficient solutions to large PDSTSPs. The authors have based their ant-inspired hybrid ant-colony optimization (HACO) on the representation of the PDSTSP solution in terms of permutations of customers, similar to the one used in, but the state space is more manageable and the solution space for the giant tour decomposition is more comprehensive. The problem-related features of the HACO method, such as local search and solution building, play an important role in the performance of the method. By adopting the same conceptual framework as that of, dell'Allegro '20 developed a matheuristic which, although requiring longer computing times, proved to yield superior results to those obtained by MBIADOU's iterative method. Nguyen and Raj also studied a PDSVRP variant involving multiple trucks with the aim of reducing the total transport costs. The latest metaheuristic development is the String and Sweep Reduction (SISR) Ruin-and-Recreate method presented by Nguyen et al., which, by judiciously exploiting the characteristics of the PDSTSP, provides sufficient flexibility through novel removal operators during the Ruin-phase to enhance the improvement opportunities during the subsequent Recreate-Phase. Benchmarking revealed that SISSR outperforms other metaheuristics in both efficiency and solution quality. In more recent work, Bibi Doussan and her colleagues have generalized the PDSTSP, by using the framework of the PDSVRP, and have thus created the PDSTSP: PDSTSP. They contributed three MILP formulations, as well as a branch-and-price (BAP) and a BAP-based heuristic. The literature on the problem of the PDS-TSP problem is largely of a heuristic nature and only a few exact solutions exist, mainly on small problems with up to twenty clients and three problems with up to fifty-two clients in [1,2]. They have proposed a hybrid iterative local search method and have developed an MILP formulation as well as a branch and cut method for the small problems. Their exact methods have provided the best solution to all small PDSTSP problems in [1] and to three problems with 52 clients in [2]. Experimental evaluations of the largest available instances from the Iterative method (Mbiadou, 2018) have shown that our solution procedure resolves all but two instances within a reasonable time. Specifically, of the 87 instances created by Mbiadou, the solutions of 87 are still unknown. Considering the need for more demanding test cases for future developments, we introduce a new set of instances which contain up to 600 clients. The structure of the paper is as follows: the section entitled “Formulation” presents the MILP formulation and a series of valid inequalities which are the basis of the branch-and-cut method presented in the section entitled “Methods”. The section entitled “Experiments” presents the experimental results; the section entitled “Conclusions” summarizes the work. We also show the performance of the best state-of-the-art methods on these instances. This motivates our main contribution, which is to develop a simple and efficient branch-and-cut (B&C)-based exact solution for the problem of solving the partitioning problem for a sequence of tasks.

text: Recent years have witnessed unprecedented growth in wind power system development and advancement as part of global initiatives to combat climate change and achieve sustainable energy transitions \cite{darwish_al-dabbagh_2020}. Nevertheless, the challenging environments where wind turbines are increasingly deployed—particularly in offshore locations—consistently generate irregular loading conditions, operational inconsistencies, and component failures across various electrical and mechanical subsystems \cite{windenergy_journal}. Operations \& maintenance (O\&M) serves as a critical mechanism for addressing these challenges through comprehensive fault detection and diagnosis \cite{ATTOUI201411}, currently representing up to one-third of total energy generation costs \cite{seyr_muskulus_2019}. Condition-based monitoring (CBM) \cite{STETCO2019620} constitutes a fundamental component of O\&M by enabling continuous surveillance of operational variations and anomalies within turbines and their subsystems. The past decade has experienced growing adoption of signal-processing methodologies and physics-based modeling approaches for CBM applications. Recently, the wind energy sector has embraced Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for data-driven O\&M decision-making, leveraging Supervisory Control \& Acquisition (SCADA) data continuously generated by turbine sensor networks. Several implementations of Explainable AI (XAI) models \cite{BARREDOARRIETA202082,8329419,app10093258} have emerged, offering interpretations and rationale for predictions typically generated by black-box AI systems during decision support processes, including feature importance rankings for SCADA parameters associated with fault conditions \cite{windenergy_journal}. These methodologies have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness, particularly in turbine subsystem anomaly prediction \cite{anomaly_paperhongshan,electronics9050751,Bo_2019}, wind resource evaluation \cite{MURTHY20171320,DAI2017378}, and forecasting critical operational parameters \cite{CHEN2018414,RePEc:eee:appene:v:241:y:2019:i:c:p:229-244,RePEc:eee:energy:v:201:y:2020:i:c:s0360544220308008} with exceptional accuracy, potentially enhancing wind energy utilization efficiency \cite{LIU2020113324}. However, these approaches cannot deliver contextualized information—such as comprehensive failure descriptions and maintenance reports for addressing or preventing operational inconsistencies—which remains essential for achieving ambient intelligence in decision support frameworks. Furthermore, these techniques lack concrete foundations to serve as universal building blocks for fundamental wind industry concepts, particularly maintenance strategies and their interconnections with diverse heterogeneous information sources including sensor SCADA data, alarm logs, failure imagery, and prognostic actions. Knowledge bases (KBs) or knowledge graphs (KGs) serve fundamental roles in supporting effective, informed decision-making by interconnecting heterogeneous entities (including numerical sensor data) with contextualized, semantic information \cite{amador-paper-kg}. KGs have achieved successful implementation for optimal decision support across numerous safety-critical domains: healthcare clinical decision support \cite{health_semantic}, power system service process optimization \cite{Yuan_2018}, manufacturing process safety management \cite{MAO2020107094}, and financial business decision-making \cite{kg_finance_yang}. Considering the multidisciplinary characteristics of wind farm construction and management, along with multiple subsystem interactions with other subsystems and external components, systematic knowledge organization within the wind industry could serve crucial roles in assisting developers, designers, and researchers to leverage domain-specific information for decision support \cite{wes-5-259-2020}. Compared to other disciplines, the wind industry has experienced extremely limited KG applications for explainable decision support. In pioneering work within this domain, Zhu et al. \cite{4470371} constructed a wind power plant information model using web ontology language (OWL) for systematic domain-specific information management. Their proposed ontology encompasses conceptual information for wind power plant management through multiple classes representing different turbine types, functional components, etc., embedded as semantic information with corresponding OWL descriptions. Although this work demonstrates tremendous potential for graph databases in managing complex wind industry information through conceptual frameworks, it lacks practical demonstration of the proposed ontology, including real-world information management use-cases within the wind energy domain. Additionally, the ontology's applicability to O\&M—particularly for facilitating decision support in operational turbines—remains unaddressed. Küçük and Arslan \cite{KUCUK2014484} leveraged web resources, particularly Wikipedia, to construct a domain ontology for the wind energy sector. Their semi-automatically constructed ontology provides extensive wind energy domain coverage, incorporating terms such as meteorological data, turbine subcomponents, monitoring and control systems. This approach proves valuable for question-answering systems during information retrieval, enabling easy access to specific natural language text segments from Wikipedia articles relevant to end users. While semi-automatic ontology construction offers reduced time consumption and simplified processes, it cannot deliver detailed wind industry and turbine O\&M specifics. Moreover, it lacks capability to provide coherent perspectives on critical CBM aspects, including SCADA data roles in anomaly prediction and power forecasting, maintenance tasks for turbine and subcomponent failures, and comprehensive technical descriptions for engineers and technicians beyond Wikipedia content. The paper also fails to demonstrate KG utilization in real-world decision support systems. In separate research, Quaeghebeur et al. \cite{wes-5-259-2020} developed a wind energy domain graph database containing conceptual overviews of important wind energy sector terms and parameters, including power curves, turbine subcomponent relationships, and mathematical/statistical distributions for modeling vital parameters. Their KG was developed from scratch by the authors, providing foundational ontology for wind turbines as systems with specific offshore wind power focus. Similar to Zhu et al. \cite{4470371}, their emphasis centers on developing knowledge representations and structured wind industry information. This work provides substantial information and descriptions queryable from the KG, offering particular benefits for education and training purposes. However, their proposed KG lacks descriptions of real-world turbine fault types, alarm varieties and their relationships to turbine subcomponents, and maintenance action strategies for addressing or preventing failures. Most importantly, it fails to demonstrate KG applicability for O\&M and its use-cases for explainable decision support in practical scenarios. Evidently, while these limited existing studies have shown promise for utilizing KGs to systematically structure conceptual wind industry information, they function merely as endpoints \cite{amador-paper-kg} providing consultative information without further data reasoning capabilities. Furthermore, these ontologies require manual querying through specialized programming languages to extract relevant, meaningful information, which may remain inaccessible to turbine engineers and technicians. Existing studies clearly neglect critical O\&M aspects and their utility in decision-making systems for tasks including recommendations and predictions. We believe optimal KG utility for wind industry decision support can only be achieved by integrating conceptual O\&M information with other heterogeneous data sources, such as sensor SCADA parameters, alarm types, turbine subcomponents, preventive/predictive/corrective maintenance action strategies, and their associated relationships. This paper proposes KG roles for explainable decision support in the wind industry and their utility in real-world O\&M applications. We present a novel KG, \textit{XAI4Wind}, and manually develop the domain-specific ontology for wind industry O\&M. Our proposed KG currently contains 537 nodes and 1059 relationships (across 9 different types), incorporating various heterogeneous data types including SCADA feature descriptions, alarm types, turbine subcomponents, and maintenance action strategies. To demonstrate use-cases, we show that the KG enables interactive querying in Neo4j and supports graph data science algorithm applications for generating novel O\&M insights. Notably, we utilize operational turbine SCADA data and demonstrate its interfacing with an Explainable AI (XAI) model. We illustrate the intrinsic role our proposed KG can fulfill in decision support during various turbine failures predicted by the XAI model, providing comprehensive fault condition descriptions and maintenance actions required for addressing or preventing failures. Unlike existing studies, our proposed KG supports both manual querying (through relevant syntactic programming commands) and automatic querying (through XAI model integration), thereby establishing pathways toward autonomous decision-making for the wind energy sector that can serve as complementary resources for assisting engineer and technician decisions. Figure ~\ref{intro_kgfig} presents our proposed KG overview and applications demonstrated in this paper. text: Among the most prominent and formidable challenges in today's digital landscape stands video retrieval. This task involves ranking videos within databases according to their relevance to user-provided queries. Although most practical implementations rely on video metadata to transform this into a conventional page ranking challenge, extensive video repositories exist without any labeled metadata. User queries manifest in various formats, with textual input representing the predominant approach. Google's video search exemplifies one of the most widely accessible text-to-video retrieval applications available to the public. Nevertheless, its effectiveness depends heavily on the metadata associated with videos within its search domain. Recent years have witnessed published research on text-based video retrieval, demonstrating progressive performance improvements in this domain. Our paper concentrates on video retrieval using image queries, an area where significantly less research has been conducted. Most methods proposed to date suffer from notable limitations, and numerous challenges must be addressed by any viable approach. Chief among these challenges is developing an efficient storage mechanism for videos within search databases. Another substantial challenge that remains unresolved involves leveraging the temporal information inherent in video data. Although image classification and object detection tasks have demonstrated remarkable success in recent years, merely searching for objects within video frames fails to exploit the temporal information that videos contain. We present a novel approach to address this problem. Our method begins by preprocessing video databases to extract key features from video frames. These features undergo clustering to group similar frames together. Cluster embeddings are generated through aggregation of their constituent frame embeddings. To incorporate temporal information from videos, we model these clusters as graph nodes. Subsequently, cluster embeddings are enhanced by incorporating information from neighboring clusters. These augmented cluster embeddings are stored and utilized in our video ranking procedure. We evaluated the proposed method using the MSR-VTT dataset.

text: Future cellular communication systems are anticipated to expand significantly beyond the application diversity already established by 5G networks \cite{yazar6g}. These systems will constitute a highly adaptable platform capable of delivering integrated sensing capabilities, flexible multi-band utilization, and intelligent, environmentally sustainable, secure communications. Within next-generation cellular frameworks, \ac{AI}, combined sensing and communication functionalities are projected to serve as fundamental enablers. \ac{V2X} communications and autonomous vehicle technologies have garnered substantial interest recently and are anticipated for deployment in future communication infrastructures. For instance, \cite{khan2021robust} proposes merging \ac{MEC} with blockchain technologies to create a novel robust, resilient, and reliable V2X communication architecture. Given recent industrial progress from Google's Waymo, Baidu's Apollo, and Tesla's Autopilot systems \cite{Cusumano}, complete autonomous driving capabilities may become reality. Nevertheless, the foundational secure communication technologies supporting these advances remain in early developmental stages. Within cybersecurity domains, quantum computing development is progressing through major \ac{IT} and cloud corporations including Google, IBM, Honeywell, and Microsoft. Long-term projections suggest quantum computers will attain quantum supremacy, with recent Google industrial research demonstrating the feasibility of such achievements \cite{arute2019quantum}. Quantum-enabled devices and systems possess capabilities for rapid responses to complex computational challenges through simultaneous operation execution. These quantum-capable systems can potentially compromise security protocols established among network devices (including \ac{TLS}, \ac{DTLS}, \ac{IPSec}, and others), defeat encryption schemes within security protocols, and compromise secure communications. Consequently, quantum-resistant algorithms must be deployed within security protocols operating among mobile network devices to establish secure mobile network communications. \ac{NIST} currently addresses this challenge through a competitive process designed to identify optimal quantum-attack-resistant algorithms. Algorithms including NTRU, Saber, and Kyber have advanced to the \ac{NIST} competition's final phase \cite{NIST_comp}. Upon competition completion, a single algorithm will be designated as the standard \ac{QRSA} for universal device implementation, similar to \ac{AES}/\ac{DES} algorithms resulting from previous \ac{NIST} competitions and achieving widespread contemporary usage. Contemporary encryption algorithms can be deployed through software and hardware implementations within mobile devices to enable security protocol operations. However, \glspl{QRSA} implementation presents significant challenges, particularly regarding computational process execution within algorithmic frameworks. Analysis of existing \glspl{QRSA} including NTRU, Saber, and Kyber reveals extremely high \ac{CPU} core loads when computing mathematical operations involving very high-degree polynomials. Computational processes for established encryption algorithms such as \ac{AES} and \ac{ECC} are already operational, with existing device hardware capabilities supporting these operation types. Conversely, \glspl{QRSA} involve extremely high-degree polynomial computations. Therefore, device computational resource requirements for \glspl{QRSA} exceed those needed for currently deployed encryption algorithms. Consequently, performing \ac{QRSA} computations based on high-degree polynomials proves extremely challenging using currently available software and hardware resources. Addressing this challenge requires an efficient computation and orchestration framework with comprehensive topological awareness of mobile and \ac{V2X} networks, capable of executing diverse computational methods for each \ac{QRSA}. Accordingly, this paper provides the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We discuss key concepts and present the integration of post-quantum and mobile network connectivity through the \ac{SCO} framework with potential use cases. (Section \ref{Background} and \ref{frameworks}) \item We evaluate how post-quantum methods can be integrated into mobile networks via simulation analysis and discuss the evaluation results.(Section \ref{experiments}) \item From a standardization perspective, we describe current \glspl{SDO} efforts and their potential contributions to network management and orchestration and post-quantum technologies. (Section \ref{standardization}) \end{itemize}

text: Recommender systems naturally lend themselves to graph-based representations, where user-item interactions and associated side information form networks comprising objects~(nodes) and their relationships~(edges). Since these networks inherently contain multiple node types—minimally users $u$ and items $v$—they constitute heterogeneous graphs (heterographs for short). The exceptional expressive capacity of such graphs, combined with rapid advances in graph-based methodologies~\cite{kipf2016gcn, schlichtkrull2018rgcn, wu2019simplifying, chen2020simple}, has sparked considerable interest in graph-based recommendation approaches~\cite{wang2019ngcf, chen2020revisiting, he2020lightgcn, wang2018ripplenet, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat, fan2019graph, Liu2020Hetero} over recent years. To derive more powerful representations, researchers have explored leveraging interaction graph structure through embedding propagation mechanisms. Drawing inspiration from graph convolutional networks~(GCN)~\cite{kipf2016gcn}, Wang \emph{et al.} introduced NGCF (neural graph collaborative filtering)~\cite{wang2019ngcf} for enhanced embedding generation. Subsequently, LR-GCCF (linear residual graph convolutional collaborative filtering)~\cite{chen2020revisiting} and LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} demonstrated that removing certain standard GCN components (including non-linear activations and feature transformations) actually improves collaborative filtering (CF) performance. Despite these notable advances, current graph-based representation learning approaches remain vulnerable to data sparsity—a pervasive challenge in real-world recommendation scenarios. Since existing methods lack explicit mechanisms to address this limitation, they experience substantial performance deterioration under sparse conditions. A prevalent strategy for mitigating sparsity involves incorporating side information~\cite{GUO2017202}, which enriches node features or establishes additional indirect connections. While recommendation-related textual content offers abundant side information, most current approaches~\cite{Wang2019kgcn, fan2019graph, wang2019kgat} that integrate side information overlook this resource, thereby constraining their effectiveness. Following HGNR~(heterogeneous graph neural recommendation)~\cite{Liu2020Hetero}, we address data sparsity by extending the basic interaction graph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(a)) with description and comment nodes to form our heterograph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(b)). However, merely incorporating these nodes fails to establish additional indirect user-item connections. Instead, text nodes inherently possess rich features that can effectively refine user and item embeddings. Leveraging this insight, we employ state-of-the-art natural language processing~(NLP) techniques for text node embedding initialization, thereby integrating semantic knowledge to strengthen representational capacity. Through node information propagation, user and item embeddings acquire textual knowledge, effectively mitigating data sparsity challenges. HGNR employs standard GCN for heterograph embedding learning, essentially converting heterogeneous learning into a homogeneous process—potentially causing information loss and performance degradation. RGCN (Relational Graph Convolutional Network) demonstrates superior capability for handling highly multi-relational heterograph data through iterative GCN framework application across different relations~\cite{schlichtkrull2018rgcn}. Consequently, RGCN represents a more suitable choice for heterograph information propagation. Nevertheless, standard RGCN implementation proves suboptimal due to its larger parameter scale compared to GCN on equivalent heterographs—a consequence of relation differentiation requirements that complicates training and reduces efficiency. We propose a modified RGCN to address these limitations. First, following evidence from \cite{wu2019simplifying, he2020lightgcn} that feature transformation and non-linear activation contribute minimally to CF performance, we eliminate these components to simplify RGCN while enhancing performance and efficiency. Second, we incorporate weighted layer combination from LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} and initial residual connections from GCNII~\cite{chen2020simple} to further optimize RGCN performance. Experimental results demonstrate that these RGCN modifications yield significant recommendation performance improvements. Beyond efficient user and item embedding generation through modified RGCN feature propagation, matching functions constitute another critical recommender system component. Virtually all existing graph-based representation learning methods employ inner product matching functions~\cite{wang2019ngcf, he2020lightgcn, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat}. However, within our constructed heterographs, description and comment nodes contain rich semantics that simple linear inner products cannot effectively capture. GraphRec~\cite{fan2019graph} addressed semantic features learned by GNNs from heterographs by concatenating user and item latent factors and employing MLP (multi-layer perception) for rating prediction. Similarly, DeepCF~\cite{deng2019deepcf} applies MLP neural networks to user-item interaction matrices, combining neural representation learning strengths with neural matching function learning to overcome individual limitations. Drawing inspiration from GraphRec and DeepCF, we develop a predictive network that integrates graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning for improved semantic handling. Specifically, this combination captures low-rank user-item relations while jointly learning complex matching functions. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We construct a heterograph and leverage advanced NLP techniques for text node embedding initialization to exploit textual information knowledge. Subsequently, through modified RGCN utilization, semantics from text nodes propagate to generate user and item representations. \item Recognizing inner product limitations for complex semantics, we propose a predictive framework combining graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning for enhanced prediction accuracy. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments across three benchmark datasets, with results confirming our method's superior performance relative to several baseline approaches. \end{itemize} This paper proceeds as follows: Section~\ref{sec: relatedwork} examines related work; Section~\ref{sec: method} presents our proposed model in detail; Section~\ref{sec: experiment} discusses experimental results and analysis; Section~\ref{sec: conclusion} provides concluding remarks.

text: Atrial Fibrillation represents a cardiac pathology that frequently remains undiagnosed for extended periods, requiring specialized cardiological evaluation of electrocardiographic recordings for proper identification. This condition impacts approximately 1\% of the global population \cite{zoni2014epidemiology}, with the United States alone documenting roughly 2.3 million documented cases. Advanced artificial intelligence methodologies applied to electrocardiographic signal analysis offer promising avenues for enhanced early detection capabilities and subsequent reduction in disease prevalence. Since electrocardiographic recordings constitute time-series datasets amenable to computational analysis, atrial fibrillation identification becomes feasible through systematic detection of signal irregularities. Figure 1 illustrates characteristic features of normal electrocardiographic patterns, where the alphabetic designations P, Q, R, S, and T represent distinct cardiac anatomical regions—specifically the atrial and ventricular chambers—through which electrical impulses propagate.\\ Atrial fibrillation manifests distinctive waveform characteristics including: \\ 1) Complete absence of discernible P-wave components. \\ 2) Irregular R-R interval spacing throughout the recorded signal.\\ Figure 2 demonstrates these pathognomonic features within an atrial fibrillation electrocardiographic trace. Electrocardiographic-based atrial fibrillation detection encounters several analytical obstacles:\\ 1) Electrocardiographic recordings contain inherent noise components, low-frequency artifacts, and signal vulnerability, compromising diagnostic reliability \cite{wu2020study}.\\ 2) Human interpretation of electrocardiographic data introduces subjective bias and inter-observer variability, particularly since non-atrial fibrillation conditions may also present irregular R-R intervals and P-wave absence \cite{nurmaini2020robust}.

text: The deployment of autonomous vehicles as traffic management systems \cite{wu2017flow} necessitates robust safety guarantees when navigating alongside human-operated vehicles in both highway and urban environments. Yet achieving such safety assurances proves challenging due to the substantial uncertainty inherent in real-world driving contexts, which significantly complicates the navigation problem. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis (HJI) typically offers a powerful approach for deriving safe strategies when confronting unknown elements within dynamical systems \cite{bansal2017hamilton}. Prior research has established \cite{fisac2018general} a comprehensive framework that leverages Hamilton-Jacobi reachability to safeguard systems against a single identified uncertainty source, with the primary objective of ensuring protection under worst-case conditions. Nevertheless, realistic driving environments often demand consideration of multiple uncertainty sources simultaneously. As illustrated in figures \ref{fig:sets} and \ref{fig:illustration}, scenarios involving extreme worst-case assumptions may fail to yield any viable safety strategy, potentially rendering safety establishment fundamentally impossible. Consequently, this work investigates methods for reducing conservativeness within Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis through the incorporation of structural assumptions into partial or complete human behavioral models. Our approach focuses specifically on a modeling framework for the secondary disturbance that exploits inherent patterns in human driving behavior, thereby enabling the application of differential game theory within more densely populated dynamic driving scenarios.

text: The NILC-Metrix metric collection emerged from collaborative research spanning 2008 to 2021, encompassing funded initiatives with multiple investigators alongside graduate dissertations and doctoral studies at the Interinstitutional Center for Computational Linguistics --- NILC\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/}}. Below we outline the driving forces behind this comprehensive metric suite, its developmental trajectory, and the strategic re-implementations undertaken to standardize Natural Language Processing (NLP) tool integration. The foundational impetus for constructing automated textual complexity evaluation metrics for Brazilian Portuguese (BP) originated within the PorSimples project, which focused on Portuguese Text Simplification for Digital Inclusion and Accessibility \cite{candido-etal-2009-supporting,aluisio-gasperin-2010-fostering}. PorSimples targeted individuals with limited literacy skills who seek information from web-based texts but encounter comprehension barriers due to their rudimentary and basic literacy levels, as classified by the INAF functional literacy indicator\footnote{\url{https://ipm.org.br/inaf}}. Conventional automatic text simplification approaches, as documented in the literature, typically implement processes that diminish lexical and syntactic complexity while preserving semantic content and informational integrity \cite{Carroll98practicalsimplification,Max2006,Shardlow2014}. Nevertheless, certain simplification initiatives—exemplified by the Terence project—address target populations requiring enhancements to textual comprehension at both local levels (facilitating inter-sentential connections) and global levels (supporting mental text representation construction) \cite{terence_2014}. Additional approaches, such as those employed by Newsela\footnote{\url{https://newsela.com/}}, incorporate conceptual simplification that addresses content alongside form \cite{xu-etal-2015-problems}. Newsela's methodology includes textual elaborations to clarify concepts and strategic redundancies to emphasize critical information, while simultaneously reducing or omitting content inappropriate for specific audiences. These diverse simplification frameworks revealed the intimate relationship between textual complexity and simplification within NLP research. Furthermore, we recognized that Terence-style simplification enhances textual coherence, leading researchers to characterize this approach as cognitive-level simplification. Newsela's comprehensive operational framework represents the most complete simplification methodology, despite lacking full automation (though significant progress has been achieved by \cite{alva-manchego-etal-2017-learning}). Throughout PorSimples development, we constructed \textbf{Facilita}, a system designed to adapt web content for low-literacy audiences through lexical elaboration and named entity labeling \cite{Watanabe2010}, alongside the \textbf{Simplifica} simplification system. Simplifica's distinctive feature involved implementing dual simplification levels—natural and strong—targeting individuals at basic and rudimentary literacy levels, respectively. To evaluate the textual complexity of processed outputs and determine simplification effectiveness, we developed a multiclass textual complexity predictor using traditional machine learning approaches. This predictor necessitated extracting metrics capable of assessing textual complexity and computing proxies for evaluating cohesion and coherence in Simplifica's rule-based simplifications. This context gave rise to the Coh-Metrix-Port project \cite{Scarton2010a,Scarton2010b,Scarton2010c}. Prior to PorSimples, NILC had conducted readability research aimed at adapting the Flesch Index for BP \cite{fleschport1996}, utilizing a corpus designed to identify linear formula weights for evaluating word and sentence lengths across diverse textual genres and sources. The Flesch Index \cite{flesch1948} operates on the principle that shorter words and sentences correlate with enhanced readability. text: We introduce a methodology for strategic individual sampling within populations to curtail pandemic transmission, exemplified by COVID-19. While sampling algorithms have established utility in machine learning for active learning applications \cite{AL-MJ, pz2006} and in bandit frameworks \cite{bandit-wolpert} for navigating complex search landscapes through balanced exploration-exploitation, our approach extends these principles to epidemic containment within population dynamics. Public health literature addressing disease spread management through active sampling frameworks encompasses two primary motivations, often interconnected within population surveillance contexts \cite{lee2010principles}. Disease incidence estimation represents the first application domain, particularly for conditions like HIV prevalence assessment. HIV incidence estimation employs methodologies including population surveys and sentinel surveillance \cite{magnani2005review, fylkesnes_studying_1998}, both demonstrating effectiveness. Population surveys within catchment areas utilize stratified or cluster random sampling, establishing the methodological gold standard despite recognized cost barriers \cite{lee2010principles}. Sentinel surveillance alternatively collects data from strategic venue subsets—the "sentinels" such as clinical facilities—where affected populations likely seek treatment. Acknowledging that sensitive diseases like HIV may concentrate within hard-to-reach populations engaging in illegal or illicit activities (sex workers, substance users), researchers \cite{magnani2005review, goel2010assessing} have examined alternative approaches: snowball sampling (initiating with disease-positive seeds who identify additional candidates), respondent-driven sampling (extending snowball methodology through longer chains with reduced per-seed referrals), and time-location sampling (targeting users during specific times in relevant districts). Sensor-based data has enabled emerging sampling forms, with livestock disease quantification demonstrating effectiveness through sampling nodes with maximal movement patterns \cite{dawson2015sampling}. Disease spread mitigation through proactive identification of quarantine or testing candidates constitutes the second sampling rationale. Contact-tracing represents a prevalent public health approach \cite{PhysRevE.66.056115, eames2003contact, underwood_contact_2003}, sampling contacts of confirmed infected individuals for disease presence. Combined with quarantine measures, contact-tracing serves as the primary mechanism deployed globally throughout the COVID-19 pandemic \cite{salathe2020covid, hellewell2020feasibility}. Traditional questionnaire-based contact-tracing has evolved to include automated proximity tracking through cell phone data \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. SARS-CoV-2 pathogen characteristics and transmission patterns, however, render these individual sampling methodologies insufficient when applied independently. \begin{itemize} \item Pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic transmission possibilities eliminate pure sentinel-based strategies targeting symptomatic clinic presentations. Contact tracing alone proves inadequate for identical reasons, pursuing only contacts of confirmed positive cases while overlooking asymptomatic carriers who may transmit to their contacts undetected. Random sampling therefore provides essential complementary value. \item Extended pathogen survival on surfaces and in air within specific locations necessitates location-based sampling approaches. \item Uncertainty regarding long-lasting immunity development requires sampling strategies accommodating repeated individual re-testing. \item Evolving understanding of covariate influences on disease acquisition and severity creates limitations for covariate-based sampling strategies alone. While comorbidities and age affect outcomes, knowledge completeness remains uncertain, and covariate effects on disease contraction remain unclear. This environment demands sampling strategies targeting specific \emph{individuals} for testing. \item The pathogen's highly infectious nature and extensive global spread have constrained testing capacities, requiring test prioritization for effective spread mitigation. \end{itemize} Our methodology addresses these five considerations comprehensively. We present dynamic active sampling strategies utilizing multi-armed bandit algorithms that optimally integrate diverse sampling approaches, generating real-time individual sampling lists. Bandit algorithms excel at exploration-exploitation balance, demonstrating success across scenarios requiring this combination. SARS-CoV-2 contexts demand effective integration of exploration (random sampling) with exploitation (contact-tracing, location-based sampling) through data-driven dynamic approaches. Our work's distinguishing feature involves identifying specific individuals for testing/sampling rather than employing criteria or covariate-based sampling strategies. Our algorithm operates within high-uncertainty network environments where individual contacts remain initially partially observable, revealing gradually through individual sampling. The bandit algorithm employs Thompson sampling strategy to balance expansion into unobserved nodes for potential hotspot identification against densification within observed portions to leverage acquired knowledge for testing. When densification is selected, an inner-level upper confidence bounding (UCB) policy balances individuals with higher infection probabilities against those with greater information uncertainty. We construct heterogeneous network embedding to quantify individual closeness and infection risk, encoding social interactions through continuous latent representation. To model sampling effects on and responses to the underlying environment, we implement an agent-based model using realistic New York City data. Recent COVID-19 studies have examined disease spread prediction and flattening through various intervention policies \cite{Keskinocak2020.07.22.20160036,Keskinocak2020.04.29.20084764, topirceanu2020centralized,atkeson2020will,ferguson2020report,chang2020modelling}, including case isolation, home quarantine, social distancing, air travel restrictions, and school closures/reopening. Restriction efficiency assessment typically couples S/I/R (susceptible/infected/recovered) diffusion modeling \cite{hethcote2000mathematics,cooper2020sir} with Agent Based simulation Models (ABM) \cite{perez2009agent} of infectious spread under different restriction scenarios. \cite{hoertel2020facing} developed a COVID-19 spread ABM for New York City under various quarantine policies, serving as our ABM foundation. In contemporaneous work, \cite{grushka2020framework} present a framework using historical data to build classifiers computing "risk scores" for exploration-exploitation combination determination. While bandit-based testing algorithms show importance, the challenge lies in developing specific methods addressing all previously noted complexities. Our work presents a specific methodology that is adaptive, dynamic, and comprehensive. Parallel to testing sampling questions, vaccination targeting presents similar considerations. \cite{chen2020allocation} present adaptive and dynamic covariate-based vaccination policies. Our framework incorporates vaccination into background dynamics to test combinational strategy effectiveness such as smart testing with vaccination. We contribute the following important advances. First, we present a novel active sampling algorithm for effective pandemic management such as COVID-19 (to our knowledge, no existing literature methods address this problem). We develop a general multi-armed bandit framework that (a) leverages diverse information types including individuals and locations, (b) handles uncertainty in both underlying disease dynamics and information, and (c) samples based on individuals rather than covariates. Second, we make several modeling contributions regarding bandit-based algorithm operation in this setting. We construct a heterogeneous network capturing social relations, neighborhood similarity, and community membership, demonstrating how this drives a two-level active sampling strategy for individual sampling. Network embedding integration within heterogeneous networks represents a novel approach. Third, we contribute importantly to multi-armed bandit literature. Beyond classic bandit problems, limited literature exists on active graph search with objectives of finding maximum target nodes possessing specific properties. Most existing work assumes complete network structure and underlying process knowledge beforehand. Minimal work addresses partially observed and dynamically changing networks and underlying (disease) dynamics. text: The capacity to identify unprecedented novelties—anomalies—represents a fundamental human skill for recognizing emerging threats and opportunities. This ability manifests in diverse contexts: identifying novel patterns in natural phenomena, recognizing security vulnerabilities, or discovering equipment failures. Contemporary anomaly detection (AD) approaches for images \cite{reiss2021panda,hendrycks2019using,tack2020csi} typically encompass broad data domains, yet video AD research has concentrated predominantly on surveillance footage. Such surveillance datasets \cite{luo2017revisit,mahadevan2010anomaly}, captured through security camera systems, conventionally establish standard pedestrian movement as the baseline normal class, while alternative activities (bicycle riding, crowd formation) constitute anomalous behavior. Recent advances have introduced numerous innovative methodologies, advancing benchmark performance significantly \cite{georgescu2021anomaly,park2020learning}. However, alternative categories of video anomalies have remained largely peripheral to current research efforts. This investigation examines diverse anomaly types through various methodological approaches. We focus on physical irregularities in object motion and trajectories—aspects that have received insufficient attention—while introducing novel benchmarks for video anomaly detection.

text: Across diverse domains, deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated extraordinary performance gains. The selection of an appropriate DNN architecture represents a crucial factor when deploying DNNs for novel tasks and maximizing their effectiveness. Nevertheless, since architectures emerge from combinations involving dozens to hundreds of hyperparameters—including convolutional layer filter dimensions, inter-layer connectivity patterns, and similar elements—optimizing these combinations demands substantial human expertise and considerable effort. As a promising solution for automatically discovering sophisticated DNN architectures, neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged to address the challenges inherent in adapting DNNs to unexplored tasks. Nevertheless, NAS applications face a significant obstacle: the substantial computational demands (encompassing both temporal and spatial complexity), particularly within commercial contexts lacking access to multiple high-performance GPUs. Consequently, minimizing NAS computational requirements constitutes a vital research priority. Through simultaneous optimization of both architectural configurations and parameter weights within a unified training framework or limited training cycles, one-shot NAS achieves dramatic reductions in temporal complexity. This approach maintains an overparameterized deep learning structure containing extensive layers and connections—termed the parent network—capable of encoding all feasible architectures within the search domain as constituent sub-networks. The parent network encompasses all parameters necessary for candidate architectures, enabling parameter sharing across different architectural configurations. Architecture quality assessment utilizes these shared parameters, dramatically accelerating the search process compared to traditional methods requiring parameter training from initialization for each architectural candidate evaluation. Regarding GPU memory utilization, one-shot NAS methodologies divide into dense propagation NAS (DP-NAS) and sparse propagation NAS (SP-NAS) categories. While DP-NAS necessitates loading the complete parent network into GPU memory for forward and/or backward propagation operations, SP-NAS requires only sub-network loading. The success of DARTS and subsequent developments \cite{liu2018darts,xie2018snas,yao2020nasp} has established DP-NAS as the predominant approach. Nevertheless, its substantial memory requirements constrain the available search space. SP-NAS addresses this constraint, enabling more versatile search spaces on standard GPUs with memory limitations. Therefore, our investigation concentrates on SP-NAS methodologies. We introduce \emph{AdvantageNAS}, a novel one-shot SP-NAS approach designed to further minimize computational costs in one-shot SP-NAS. While numerous factors influence NAS performance—including performance estimation techniques, search space design, and others—and state-of-the-art (SOTA) results may necessitate optimizing combinations of these elements, our research emphasizes search strategy development. We clarify that achieving SOTA architectures is not our primary objective; rather, we investigate search strategy efficiency. AdvantageNAS represents a gradient-based SP-NAS methodology.\footnote{Gradient-based approaches offer several benefits. Methods employing evolutionary algorithms (e.g., \cite{real2017evo}) or progressive search techniques (e.g., \cite{liu2018pnas}) require defining mutation or expansion strategies specific to the search space. Gradient-based methods eliminate such manual, search-space-dependent preparations. Additionally, gradient-based methods integrate seamlessly with most contemporary deep learning frameworks through their automatic differentiation capabilities for deep neural networks.} This NAS category encompasses ENAS \cite{pham2018enas}, ProxylessNAS \cite{cai2018proxylessnas}, PARSEC \cite{casale2019parsec}, and GDAS \cite{xuanyi2019gdas}. These approaches establish parametric probability distribution families for architecture sampling, with distribution parameters updated via objective function gradients estimated through Monte Carlo methods, thereby indirectly optimizing the architecture. Since gradient estimation occurs, intuitively, reducing gradient estimate variance should enhance search effectiveness. Drawing inspiration from actor-critic methodologies \cite{konda2000ac}, we incorporate the \emph{advantage} concept, originally developed to address the notorious \emph{credit assignment} challenge in policy gradients \cite{Minsky:1961:ire}. Both theoretical and empirical investigations of AdvantageNAS are presented. While empirical studies demonstrate strong performance across various tasks and search spaces, theoretical analyses provide performance guarantees for empirically unexplored scenarios. Although theoretical studies remain relatively uncommon in NAS research, they provide essential insights for investigating NAS search strategies. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We present AdvantageNAS, a novel SP-NAS approach. Through test scenario analysis, we demonstrate reduced gradient estimation variance compared to REINFORCE \cite{Williams1992}, which serves as the baseline search strategy for ENAS. \item Theoretical analysis establishes that AdvantageNAS gradient estimates constitute unbiased estimators of expected loss gradients. This unbiasedness property ensures monotonic expected loss improvement and convergence in AdvantageNAS. Additionally, we verify that gradient variance reduction contributes to enhanced lower bounds for per-iteration loss improvement. \item We evaluated AdvantageNAS against various gradient-based NAS methods across three distinct configurations to establish its effectiveness across different search spaces. Experiments utilized identical codebases for fair search strategy comparison.\footnote{Literature comparisons of NAS approaches using different components like search spaces and training protocols exist. However, as noted in \cite{Yang2020iclr}, such component differences complicate fair assessment of individual component contributions. Our code: \url{https://github.com/madoibito80/advantage-nas}.} Results indicate that AdvantageNAS achieves faster convergence than existing SP-NAS approaches. \end{itemize}

In statistics and machine learning, the Wasserstein barycenter (WB) serves as a prominent technique for aggregating data from multiple sources while preserving their geometric structure~\cite{martial11}. We formulate this problem as follows. Consider a collection of $k$ discrete probability distributions $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given non-negative weights $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$ summing to unity, and a class $\mathbb{P}$ of probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$, the Wasserstein barycenter under the $L_p$ objective with parameter $p>0$ corresponds to a probability distribution $
u\in\mathbb{P}$ minimizing  egin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_iW_p(\mu_i,
u)^p, \end{equation} where $W_p(\mu_i,
u)$ denotes the $p$-Wasserstein distance. By leveraging optimal transport distances~\cite{bertsimas1997introduction} between observed sets, the Wasserstein barycenter provides a natural geometric interpretation of centrality among point clouds. Consequently, Wasserstein barycenters find extensive applications across machine learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, data sciences~\cite{ruschendorf2002n,elvander2020multi}, image processing~\cite{rubner1997earth}, computer graphics~\cite{pele2009fast}, and statistics~\cite{villani2008optimal}, with specific uses in constrained clustering~\cite{cuturi2014fast, ho2017multilevel}, Bayesian learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, texture mixing~\cite{rabin2011wasserstein}, and shape interpolation~\cite{solomon2015convolutional}. However, computing this problem remains NP-hard \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21}, and algorithms that approximate the Wasserstein barycenter typically exhibit prohibitive computational costs, particularly for high-dimensional datasets~\cite{MuzellecC19}. Recent work by \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein} demonstrates that Wasserstein barycenter computation requires runtime exponential in dimension, highlighting the ``curse of dimensionality.'' We address these computational limitations by investigating dimensionality reduction for Wasserstein barycenter computation. Dimensionality reduction enhances downstream algorithm performance on high-dimensional datasets across numerous applications, as surveyed in~\cite{cunningham2015linear}. For Wasserstein barycenters specifically, dimensionality reduction offers multiple advantages: reduced storage requirements, accelerated distance computations, and versatility as a preprocessing technique compatible with \emph{any} Wasserstein barycenter algorithm. \subsection{Our Results} We examine dimensionality reduction methods for computing Wasserstein barycenters of discrete probability distributions. Our primary contributions demonstrate that distributions can be projected into low dimensions while provably maintaining barycenter quality. The foundational Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma~\cite{johnson1984extensions} establishes that projecting $N$ points into approximately $O(\log N)$ dimensions suffices to preserve all pairwise distances. Applying the JL lemma, we initially establish that distributions can be embedded in $O(\log(nk))$ dimensions, where $k$ represents the number of input distributions, $n$ denotes the barycenter support size, and each input distribution has support size $\poly(n)$. Our bound follows naturally since the union of all distributions contains $k \cdot \poly(n)$ total point masses, requiring projection into $O(\log( k \poly(n))) = O(\log(nk))$ dimensions to preserve all pairwise distances. text: Among the most ancient forms of North Indian classical vocal music stands Dhrupad. The conventional concert arrangement features either a single vocalist or vocal pair as the primary performer, accompanied by a pakhawaj for percussive support, while a tanpura provides the harmonic drone backdrop\cite{bonnie_wade}. Extending beyond an hour in duration, a Dhrupad performance unfolds through an extensive, unaccompanied \textit{raga alap}, subsequently transitioning to a composed section known as the \textit{bandish}, which incorporates the percussion instrument. Rather than merely presenting the bandish in its original form, performers utilize it as a foundation for additional rhythmic exploration (\textit{laykari}), wherein vocalists articulate the bandish text syllables across varying rhythmic densities and diverse patterns \cite[chapter~10]{clayton}. Throughout this process, the pakhawaj accompaniment alternates between executing a fundamental pattern (\textit{theka}) of the metric cycle (\textit{tala}), developing rhythmic improvisations that complement the vocalist's creativity, or delivering independent solo improvisations during the vocalist's presentation of fixed compositional lines or refrains \cite[p.~111]{clayton}. \\ The bandish performance structure from the vocalist's viewpoint is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:concert_structure}. The intervening refrain segments represent non-improvised portions where performers deliver a bandish line or fragment before returning to subsequent improvisational episodes.\\ The relationship between lead and accompanying percussion instruments distinguishes Dhrupad from Khyal bandish performances fundamentally. While the former typically involves artists alternating improvisational roles as the other maintains basic rhythm or refrain, the latter additionally incorporates sections featuring simultaneous improvisation by both performers. Comprehensive segmentation of a Dhrupad bandish performance therefore necessitates rhythmic characterization of both non-improvised and improvised sections for each component—vocals and pakhawaj.\\ Additional segmentation levels could be applied to this musical form. One approach might focus on distinguishing non-improvised from improvised musical sections. Given that the bandish text comprises sections positioned across different octave portions, each containing several lines, another segmentation level could identify which specific section the vocalist is presenting or elaborating upon. While the former segmentation might be partially defined through rhythmic attribute changes, the latter would rely more heavily on melodic characteristics. Timbral attribute variations correlated with articulation styles accompanying various rhythmic or melodic transformations could also facilitate each segmentation type.\\ This work aims to develop automatic methods for structural segmentation of Dhrupad bandish concerts using exclusively tempo and rhythmic density relationships of individual instruments. Recognizing the acknowledged difficulty of vocal onset detection (even in isolated vocals due to singing's inherent diversity), we pursue alternative approaches for direct local rhythmic density estimation. Deep learning advances have enabled methods treating predominant tempo estimation from raw audio spectral representations as classification tasks \cite{schreiber-ismir18,schreiber-smc19,mtl-beat-tempo-19}. We investigate a comparable approach for estimating changing surface tempo or rhythmic density throughout concert audio. Considering the substantial improvements reported in audio source separation recently, we also examine source separation followed by tempo estimation for constituent instruments (vocals and pakhawaj) to provide more comprehensive section descriptions.\\ This work's primary novel contributions include: (i) a dataset containing tempo markings and rhythmic density-based structural segmentation annotations for Dhrupad bandish concerts, (ii) adaptation of state-of-the-art tempo estimation methodology for local surface tempo or rhythmic density estimation in polyphonic mixtures, and (iii) source separation implementation extending this approach to individual instruments (vocals and pakhawaj) to ultimately achieve musically meaningful bandish concert segmentation with section labels defined through rhythmic density interrelationships.

The first division could be partly determined by the rhythmic attributes, the second by the melodic features. text: The prediction of stock market returns and volatility has garnered significant interest from both academic researchers and financial industry practitioners. Yet fundamental questions persist: are stock market prices and volatility truly predictable? More precisely, can predictability be achieved during specific temporal windows? Sentiment analysis derived from online platforms like Twitter and financial news articles offers considerable potential for enhancing trading strategy development. Furthermore, sentiment extracted from financial news sources may possess predictive capabilities that portfolio and risk managers can effectively exploit. Our analytical findings can be organized into three distinct categories. Initially, we observed statistically significant correlations between sentiment metrics and stock market returns exclusively within our headline dataset. These findings reveal a statistically significant inverse relationship between negative news sentiment and FTSE100 index closing prices (returns). The most robust correlation between sentiment indicators and volatility metrics emerged from our Twitter dataset, whereas the headlines and news stories datasets exhibited either negligible or weak correlations. This phenomenon can be attributed to Twitter's inherently timely and reactive nature regarding various market events, contrasting with the extended publication timelines of traditional articles, while markets operate under the established principle of ``Buy on rumors, sell on news.'' The paper follows this organizational structure. Section \ref{sec:related} examines relevant prior research. Section \ref{sec:data} details the data sources employed for sentiment score computation: Thomson Reuters, RavenPack, and Twitter. Section \ref{sec:correlation} presents our correlation analysis alongside Granger's causality testing. Section \ref{sec:lda} explores supplementary experiments investigating whether topic modeling (specifically Latent Dirichlet Allocation) can improve prediction accuracy for next-day stock market directional volatility. Sections \ref{sec:results} and \ref{sec:conclusion} deliver our analytical results and explore future research directions.

text: Recent research has increasingly focused on developing tools, optimization techniques, and novel algorithms to automate robotic design and fabrication processes (e.g.,~\citep{Luck-RSS-17,Schulz17,HoovFearing08,pervan2018low,zhang2020abstractions}). Among these approaches, algorithms targeting resource management and minimization hold particular significance (for instance, see~\citep{censi17co}). Memory represents a resource of special interest to our work—not due to RAM costs, but because reducing state requirements frequently reveals insights about the fundamental informational architecture underlying specific robotic tasks~(cf.~\citep{connell90,donald95information}). We therefore concentrate on filter reduction, specifically targeting combinatorial filters in the tradition established by LaValle~\citep{lavalle10sensing}. These filters constitute discrete counterparts to the probabilistic estimators prevalent throughout contemporary robotics, offering particularly elegant solutions for certain practical applications (e.g, see \citep{tovar2014combinatorial}). While the minimization problem for combinatorial filters appears straightforward to articulate and comprehend, ongoing research efforts~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial,rahmani2018relationship,zhang20cover,rahmani2020integer} demonstrate that the problem encompasses greater complexity than initially apparent. To illustrate the motivation behind filter minimization, we present the safari park vehicle rental scenario depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_scenario}. Each rental vehicle features both a compass and an intelligent transmission system. The compass records vehicle heading before and after movement—for example, `nw' indicates the vehicle initially faced north before turning westward. The intelligent transmission receives compass data as input and automatically selects appropriate gears to maintain speed limit compliance. Three distinct speed limit categories govern the roads: ($a$) speeds ranging from $15$ to $30$ (gray), ($b$) speeds not exceeding $30$ (brown), or ($c$) speeds under $15$ (green). Each vehicle operates in either low gear (maximum speed $15$) or high gear (speeds between $15$ and $30$). Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input} presents a na\"ive transmission system that satisfies speed requirements through a filter implementation: vertices denote system states, edges represent state transitions, and edge labels correspond to compass readings. Gray vertices indicate high gear output, green vertices signify low gear output, while vertices displaying both colors permit either gear selection through nondeterministic choice. Our objective involves discovering a minimal filter, such as the one illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_minimal}, that maintains appropriate functionality while utilizing the fewest possible states. The conventional approach begins by constructing a discrete state-transition system (exemplified in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}) based on the problem specification. Subsequently, a compression algorithm is applied to reduce the system. Although combinatorial filter minimization superficially resembles deterministic automata state minimization—which benefits from Myhill--Nerode's renowned and efficient reduction~\citep{hopcroft06introduction}—combinatorial filter minimization proves to be NP-complete~\citep{okane2013reduction}. One research direction investigates filter minimization through merger operations. These algorithms transform filter minimization into graph coloring problems~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial} or integer linear programming formulations~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Saberifar et. al.~\citep{saberifar2017combinatorial} explored special cases, approximation strategies, and parameterized complexity aspects of filter minimization. Rahmani and O'Kane~\citep{rahmani2018relationship} demonstrated that the established concept of \emph{bisimulation} relations generally produces only suboptimal solutions. They introduced three distinct integer linear programming formulations to identify the smallest equivalence relation~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Recent investigations reveal that achieving minimal filters requires both merge and split operations~\citep{zhang20cover}. This work formalizes the problem as clique cover optimization subject to constraints ensuring the output filter remains deterministic and simulates the input filter's behavior. However, both requirements involve exponentially-sized constraints, creating obvious computational disadvantages. This paper introduces a novel, alternative formulation of the filter minimization problem featuring only polynomial constraint complexity, resulting in a compact nonlinear integer programming framework. Given the computational inefficiency typically associated with nonlinear constraints, we `linearize' these nonlinear constraints, producing (1) an integer linear programming formulation and (2) a Boolean satisfiability approach—both incorporating constraint expressions of comparable magnitude. Examining experimental results thoroughly, we observed that numerous constraints remain inactive throughout the iterative search for minimal filters. To accelerate computation within the Boolean satisfiability framework, we implement just-in-time constraint handling: introducing constraints only when detecting that proposed variable assignments would violate them. Empirical findings demonstrate that speedup gains from this approach can exceed the overhead costs associated with constraint detection and dynamic introduction. Following the problem statement presentation in Section~\ref{sec:prob}, we formalize filter minimization as an integer nonlinear program in Section~\ref{sec:INP}. Building upon this foundation, we develop integer linear programming and Boolean satisfiability formulations in Section~\ref{sec:ILP_SAT}. Section~\ref{sec:expr} contains experimental results.

text: Information retrieval (IR) systems powering popular websites rely critically on ranking search results that correspond to user queries. Learning to rank (LTR) models typically handle the scoring and sorting of these results, with training based on labels derived from user engagement patterns. Although pairwise or listwise loss functions dominate LTR model training, inference commonly employs unilateral scoring approaches. This independent result scoring methodology overlooks inter-document dependencies, yet research demonstrates that neighboring results significantly influence how users perceive individual search outcomes \cite{agarwal2015constrained, neighbor_effect, wang2016beyond}. E-commerce search domains particularly exhibit this phenomenon, as users routinely compare and contrast options presented on results pages during their shopping journey. Modeling these dependencies becomes essential within top results—specifically those displayed on the first page—where user engagement concentrates. Additionally, real-world applications frequently demand adherence to specific distributional criteria across search result pages. The holistic composition of page results critically shapes user website perception and typically aligns with business objectives or long-term goals targeting user retention. At eBay, for instance, ensuring comprehensive query spectrum representation within top results constitutes a key objective. Similar business goals encompass showcasing e-commerce inventory diversity, mitigating top result bias, and personalizing outcomes. Consequently, optimal top result sets (documents, termed items herein) must account for distributional criteria and inter-result dependencies alongside individual result quality. We define the slate as the top results for search queries—such as $k$ items appearing on the first user-perceived page (where $k \ll n$, with $n$ representing total recall results). This paper introduces a novel approach and architecture for generating optimal slates. An optimal slate maximizes search need fulfillment likelihood while satisfying predetermined query-specific distributional criteria. Our method jointly optimizes classical ranking metrics and slate adherence to distributional criteria while modeling intra-slate dependencies. Researchers have proposed various set-aware ranking approaches for slate optimization. Heuristic methods including Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) \cite{MMR}, IA-Select \cite{IA-Select}, and xQuAD \cite{xQuAD} incorporate slate diversity or minimize user dissatisfaction during result browsing. However, these approaches employ simpler heuristics potentially lacking the expressive capacity of complex models increasingly used for capturing inter-document dependencies. Recent models adopt set-aware ranking architectures \cite{group_wise_ranking,seq2slate}. Through candidate document set representation modeling and set-cognizant document scoring, these approaches generate optimal slates in set-aware fashion. Groupwise scoring functions (GSF) \cite{group_wise_ranking} propose multivariate scoring functions for joint document scoring, while Seq2Slate \cite{seq2slate} employs pointer networks for sequential document scoring. Although these approaches maintain set-awareness during inference, they target classic ranking metrics like normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) optimization. They lack explicit modeling of additional distributional criteria—a crucial practical consideration. To our knowledge, no existing neural network-based methods directly address this specific search problem, particularly in e-commerce contexts. We therefore propose conditional sequential slate optimization (CSSO), a novel framework addressing slate optimization challenges. It incorporates sequential decoding built upon pointer networks that manages slate composition according to predetermined distributional criteria during sequential decoding, while jointly optimizing traditional ranking metrics such as nDCG. This approach frames slate optimization as re-ranking, where a \textit{base-ranker} generates rankings through unilateral item scoring, and a \textit{re-ranker} processes $n$ ranked items to produce size-$k$ slates, with $k \ll n$. We express query-specific distributional criteria through representative or domain-specific features of ranked items. The hybrid optimization objective may generate divergent optimization directions for each term, as models must balance ranking quality against all predetermined distributional criteria aspects. Furthermore, non-unique solutions and non-convex problem nature, combined with non-differentiable metrics like nDCG, challenge traditional gradient-based methods in finding optimal slates. To address this novel, challenging problem, we employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) for CSSO training. RL provides systematic feature space search while progressively improving non-differentiable optimization goals through policy gradient methods. Simultaneously, RL exploration strategies enable better model generalization than traditional supervised methods by efficiently learning meaningful features from rollouts. During training, we utilize item click-through data from IR systems as implicit relevance labels. Within the RL paradigm, states are represented \textit{jointly} by current slate items, predetermined distribution distance, and encoded candidate sets. Actions correspond to item selection processes during each decoding step, while rewards depend on post-decoding slate composition considering both ranking quality and distributional criteria adherence. This well-defined optimization problem can be solved through policy gradient in finite horizon with length $k$, employing baseline models for training variance reduction. Our work's key contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item A framework jointly optimizing slates for document relevance and predetermined distribution adherence, addressing industry re-ranking challenges for personalization, bias mitigation, and result diversification. \item Pointer network enhancement incorporating conditional structure facilitating slate composition representation during decoding phases. \end{itemize} Experiments on public and proprietary e-commerce datasets demonstrate CSSO's comparable ranking metrics and superior distribution conformity versus state-of-the-art (SOTA) slate optimization methods. On Yahoo \cite{yahoo_dataset} and Web30k \cite{LETOR} datasets with additional simulation mimicking real-world user behaviors, we show simultaneous nDCG and GAP (distribution conformity metric defined in subsequent sections) optimization in ranking tasks. eBay.com search session dataset experiments reveal significant GAP metric improvements and comparable ranking metrics to production rankers. Generally, CSSO performs well regarding both nDCG and GAP. We view CSSO as a practical solution for the highly relevant industry problem of optimizing slates for relevance and composition based on business objectives. We envision this approach's applicability to problems including diversity assurance, bias mitigation, and business objective adherence across search and recommendation systems in various web domains encompassing e-commerce, online media, and web search.

text: Since the 1970s, computational resources have expanded exponentially, with strong indicators suggesting this trend will persist far into the foreseeable future. This computational abundance has enabled researchers to achieve superior robotic system control, while ongoing advances in both processing power and algorithmic innovation continuously unlock new application domains. Model-free reinforcement learning exemplifies this promising development—a machine learning paradigm enabling agents to interact with their environments and autonomously discover reward-maximizing strategies. This approach offers particular value for systems that resist modeling or present challenges beyond the user's direct problem-solving capabilities. Recent robotic applications demonstrate this potential: controlling 47-DOF humanoids through complex obstacle courses \cite{heess_emergence_2017}, achieving dexterous manipulation with 24-DOF robotic hands \cite{openai_learning_2018}, enabling quadruped locomotion \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and implementing fall recovery mechanisms \cite{lee_robust_2019}. Our investigation centers on legged locomotion, a notoriously challenging problem domain that has made reinforcement learning a popular solution approach. While we contend that hand-designed, model-based control methods (exemplified by Boston Dynamics) still define the state of the art, RL has proven remarkably productive. Evidence shows learned policies surpassing hand-designed alternatives \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and compelling reasons suggest these learning methodologies will maintain their trajectory toward enhanced performance and usability. Nevertheless, these algorithms suffer from a critical limitation: their black-box nature. Determining precisely what an RL agent has learned remains an open challenge. When an agent achieves exceptional reward performance, verifying system safety and sensibility across all state-space regions it will encounter during operation becomes unclear. Similarly, we cannot necessarily characterize the system's stability or robustness properties. Recent investigations ~\citep{Taleledeep} have employed mesh-based tools to address exactly these concerns. Nevertheless, mesh-based tools face inherent limitations in accurately discretizing state spaces due to the curse of dimensionality. These methods prove practical for relatively high-dimensional systems only when reachable space growth rates remain substantially below the exponential expansion characteristic of the full embedded state space. Extending these approaches to higher-dimensional systems requires strategies to prevent visited state volumes from expanding proportionally. Fractional dimension concepts from fractal geometry provide one quantification method for this growth rate. This work introduces an efficient meshing algorithm termed box meshing, demonstrating how this approach renders mesh dimension calculations feasible within reinforcement learning contexts. We further propose employing alternative fractional dimension concepts from existing literature as proxies for our target property. Subsequently, we demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents can be trained to minimize these measures through reward function post-processing. We present training results and conclude with brief structural analysis of selected policies.
