text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across diverse domains including computer vision and speech recognition. The transformative capabilities of DNNs have sparked widespread fascination and generated numerous significant research contributions. Various DNN architectures have emerged, including convolutional neural networks (exemplified by LeNet \cite{45_lecun1998gradient}, AlexNet \cite{33_krizhevsky2012imagenet}, and ResNet \cite{42_he2016deep}) and recurrent neural networks (such as LSTM \cite{46_olah2015understanding}). As DNNs continue their rapid evolution, the security aspects of these networks have garnered increasing attention. Particularly critical are the techniques for generating adversarial examples and developing defenses against adversarial attacks. Since the discovery of DNN vulnerability \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing}, this phenomenon has attracted substantial research interest. The literature broadly categorizes these investigations into two main areas: adversarial attacks \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,6_goodfellow2014explaining,7_kurakin2016adversarial,8_papernot2016limitations,9_moosavi2016deepfool,10_carlini2017towards,11_chen2017zoo,12_moosavi2017universal,13_su2019one,14_zhao2017generating,15_tabacof2016adversarial} and adversarial defenses \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,24_madry2017towards,43_tramer2017ensemble,44_papernot2016distillation,50_huang2015learning,51_cheng2020cat,52_song2018improving,53_zhang2019theoretically}. Adversarial attack methodologies aim to craft adversarial examples capable of deceiving DNNs, typically while remaining imperceptible to human observers. Conversely, adversarial defense strategies enhance DNN robustness against such malicious inputs. This dynamic resembles a zero-sum game between attackers and defenders. Conventional adversarial examples are defined as inputs that closely resemble natural images yet successfully mislead DNNs \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing}. Under this framework, adversarial examples remain imperceptible to humans (termed imperceptible adversarial examples). Nevertheless, alternative forms of adversarial examples exist. Some research incorporates visible patches into original images to deceive DNNs \cite{16_brown2017adversarial,17_liu2018dpatch,18_karmon2018lavan,19_lee2019physical}. These adversarial patches successfully fool DNNs despite being perceptible to humans. Additionally, deliberately manipulated noise images can mislead DNNs \cite{4_nguyen2015deep}. Although these noise patterns appear meaningless to humans, DNNs classify them with high confidence into specific categories (designated as unrecognizable adversarial examples). Notably, the aforementioned research primarily targets image perturbations designed to induce misclassification. Sabour et al. \cite{55_DBLP:journals/corr/SabourCFF15} examined DNN hidden layer representations, proposing methods to construct adversarial examples that appear perceptually similar to one image while their hidden representations closely resemble a different class. Their work raises fundamental questions about DNN representations and adversarial example interpretations. Further investigation is warranted regarding how adversarial perturbations manifest in hidden layers and whether hidden layer information can inform more robust defense strategies. Building upon existing research, we analyze the characteristics of various adversarial example types. Our findings reveal that regardless of whether samples are imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, or unrecognizable adversarial examples, machine predictions exhibit uncertainty (correct or incorrect outcomes). However, human judgment remains largely accurate provided perturbations do not alter the underlying objective reality. We emphasize the fundamental difference between human vision and DNN image recognition processes. Humans recognize images in pixel space, whereas machines operate in specialized hidden layer spaces representing machine "vision." Consequently, we propose that adversarial perturbations influence prediction outcomes by altering original semantic characteristics during hidden layer propagation, without modifying objective reality. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce a defense mechanism incorporating hidden layer representations to enhance model adversarial robustness. Our defense strategy compresses input information while filtering various components, including adversarial perturbations. The proposed method functions as an activation function operating within neural network hidden layers to improve adversarial robustness. We provide theoretical certification of defense effectiveness under simplified conditions. Additionally, we present a specific defensive function and empirically validate our mechanism's effectiveness. Notably, our defensive model achieves state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we discuss constructing imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples using hidden layer representations. The contributions are listed as below: \begin{enumerate} 	\item We discuss the characteristics of different types of adversarial examples (Imperceptible adversarial example, Adversarial patch and Unrecognizable adversarial example) and propose a conjecture that the representation of adversarial perturbation in hidden layer is much different with that of clean example. 	\item Based on this conjecture, we propose an effective and efficient defence method to improve the adversarial robustness of the model. The proposed defence strategy will compress the information of input and filter many of that, including the adversarial perturbation. This defense strategy is also regarded as an activation function, and we prove the effectiveness of this defense strategy theoretically. 	\item Incorporating the representation in hidden layer, we provide three types of adversarial attack to generate imperceptible adversarial examples, unrecognizable adversarial examples and adversarial patches, which are shown in Fig. \ref{overview_123}. 	\item Our defence method, which achieves state-of-the-art performance, has $97.09\%$ accuracy under CW on MNIST, $89.03\%$ accuracy under CW on CIFAR10 and $64.38\%$ under CW on ImageNet. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{section2} reviews related literature. Section \ref{section3} examines three adversarial example types and presents our conjecture. Section \ref{section4} introduces our defense strategy and specific defensive function (activation function). Section \ref{section5} presents three adversarial attacks incorporating hidden layer representations to generate respective adversarial example types. Section \ref{experiment} provides comprehensive experimental validation of our methods' effectiveness. Section \ref{conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: Contemporary cyber-attacks typically originate from sophisticated adversaries employing hybrid TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) alongside persistent adversarial campaigns. Consequently, conventional intrusion detection approaches\cite{2018A,2020Preparing} prove inadequate for identifying such threats, as they predominantly examine short-term behavioral patterns while disregarding the comprehensive contextual information inherent in system operations. To address this challenge, our investigation of existing research reveals that provenance data represents the optimal foundation for cyber-attack detection tasks\cite{2018Provenance,2017Applying,2020UNICORN}. Such data characterize system entities (including processes, files, and sockets) along with their interconnections (typically manifested as system events such as read, write, and fork operations). Provenance data offer two critical advantages: they illuminate the interaction mechanisms between system entities while furnishing extensive contextual information for each component\cite{2015Trustworthy}, and they establish causal relationships between events despite temporal separation\cite{2020UNICORN}. Collection of provenance data typically relies on OS audit logs (such as Linux Auditd\cite{LINUXAuditd} and Windows ETW\cite{ETW}). For cyber-attack detection utilizing provenance data, prevailing methodologies represent such data as directed acyclic graphs (termed provenance graphs), wherein nodes denote system entities and edges signify system events. Figure 1 illustrates a representative provenance graph. Subsequently, established approaches (including SLEUTH\cite{2018SLEUTH}, HOLMES\cite{2019HOLMES}, and CONAN\cite{0CONAN}) attempt attack detection through manual rule construction based on threat intelligence (such as kill chain\cite{2015Technical} and ATT\&CK\cite{ATT&CK}). While rule-based detection strategies demonstrate efficiency and achieve state-of-the-art performance, they exhibit several critical limitations. Rule design presents extraordinary complexity, demanding specialized expertise across cyber-attack methodologies, operating systems, and network architectures. Furthermore, rules demonstrate limited generalization capabilities, being tailored to specific environmental conditions (including attack strategies and network configurations), becoming obsolete as environments evolve and requiring adjustment or complete redesign. Additionally, rules remain constrained by human experience and cannot accommodate complex, latent patterns. Conversely, learning-based methodologies have established extensive applications in cybersecurity domains, including intrusion detection\cite{2018A,2020Preparing}, malware identification\cite{2017Malware,2020Enhancing}, and fraud detection\cite{2018Online,2020Interleaved}. Compared to rule-based approaches, learning-based techniques offer distinct advantages. They can extract latent patterns and construct detection models from training datasets with minimal domain expertise, particularly through deep learning methodologies. Moreover, detection models can automatically adapt to evolving environments through retraining or fine-tuning procedures. Given that provenance data manifests as provenance graphs, we leverage GNN (Graph Neural Network)\cite{2019Comprehensive} architectures for cyber-attack detection model development. However, constructing GNN-based cyber-attack detection models remains challenging due to the inherent complexity of cyber-attacks and system provenance. Provenance graphs derived from OS audit logs exhibit substantial complexity, incorporating multiple node types (processes, files, sockets) and diverse edge types (read, write, create operations). Additionally, nodes and edges possess supplementary attributes (for instance, files characterized by source, extension, and sensitivity level attributes). The nodes and edges within provenance graphs represent specific instances of system entities and events, rendering pattern learning from these distinct instances nearly impossible for detection models. Cyber-attack detection demands time-sensitive processing, yet most GNNs impose significant computational and spatial overhead. Since cyber-attacks typically persist over extended periods, provenance graphs continuously expand, inevitably causing efficiency and memory constraints for GNN-based approaches. Cyber-attacks maintain stealth characteristics, making detection through individual system entity analysis extremely challenging (attack activities often require coordination among multiple processes and files). However, considering entire provenance graphs proves impractical due to their excessive size and predominance of benign system entities. Detection models must continuously process newly arriving system entities, while GNNs learn representations for new entities by embedding them within shared spaces alongside existing nodes and edges. Rerunning learning procedures upon each new entity arrival becomes computationally prohibitive. Addressing these challenges, this paper introduces an intelligent cyber-attack detection system utilizing heterogeneous provenance graph learning. For the initial two challenges, we employ heterogeneous graphs\cite{0Mining} to represent complex system entities and events within provenance graphs, subsequently applying meta-path based methodologies\cite{2017metapath2vec} to extract higher-level semantic interactions among system entities. Regarding the third challenge, we utilize graph embedding techniques to derive low-dimensional vector representations for each heterogeneous graph node. Graph embedding operates as a pre-training phase, with vector representations subsequently enabling rapid detection model initialization. For the fourth and fifth challenges, we connect newly arriving system entities to existing heterogeneous graphs and execute local graph sampling to incorporate new entities with the most relevant existing nodes into compact local graphs. Detection models are then constructed based on these local graphs. The primary contributions of this paper include: 1) We introduce an intelligent cyber-attack detection system leveraging GNNs that automatically learns patterns from provenance data for cyber-attack detection without requiring domain expertise. 2) We develop a heterogeneous graph-based methodology for provenance data modeling and semantic vector representation learning for diverse system entities. 3) We present a local graph sampling-based approach for cyber-attack detection on newly arriving system entities lacking pre-learned vector representations. 4) We perform comprehensive experiments using datasets generated through simulated cyber-attacks on actual hosts. Experimental results demonstrate that our methodology surpasses existing machine learning-based cyber-attack detection approaches and achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art rule-based cyber-attack detection systems built upon extensive domain knowledge.

The detection model has to constantly process new system entities. The GNNs learn the representations of the new nodes and edges in the shared space between the nodes and edges. Analyzing the entire network of events is not practical because of its size and because of the majority of the system elements that are harmless. To run the learning process each time a new entity arrives is a huge computational cost. For the first two issues, we use heterogeneous graphs to represent complex system entities and events in the provenance graphs, and then we apply meta-graph-based methodology to extract higher-level semantic relationships among system entities. We present an intelligent cyber attack detection system that learns patterns from the network provenance without requiring any domain knowledge. To address the third challenge, we use graph embedding to extract low-dimensional features from each node of the heterogeneous graph, which serve as a pre-training phase, enabling rapid initialization of detection models. To address the fourth and fifth challenges, we connect the new entities to the existing heterogeneous graphs and execute a local graph sampling, whereby the new entities are grouped with the most relevant existing nodes into small local graphs. 3) We present a local graph sampling approach to detect cyber attacks on new entities without any pre-learned representation. Secondly, we develop a heterogeneous graph-based methodology to model the provenance data and learn the semantic representation of various system entities. Detection models are built from these local graphs. We performed extensive experiments with data collected from simulated cyber attacks against real hosts. Our method outperforms existing machine learning-based attack detection methods, and is as good as methods based on a deep understanding of attacks.

text: \vspace{-2mm} The three-dimensional nature of our physical world means that objects possess complete shape and exhibit motion throughout 3D space. However, most visual predictive models employed in robotics today are constrained to forecasting 2D motion patterns (such as optical flow) from incomplete observations. These approaches typically predict pixel-level 2D flow \citep{vijayanarasimhan2017sfm,dosovitskiy2015flownet} or estimate 3D scene flow for visible point cloud regions \citep{byravan2017se3,byravan2018se3}. Such surface-only motion modeling suffers from significant data degeneration: objects progressively disappear from the representation when occluded, causing predictive models to fail in cluttered scenarios where objects continuously enter and exit the field of view during robotic manipulation. This work explores the advantages of learning comprehensive and persistent 3D scene representations for visual prediction. We introduce \textbf{3D Dynamic Scene Representation\xspace (DSR)}: a volumetric 3D scene representation that concurrently discovers, tracks, and reconstructs novel objects while predicting their motion during robotic interactions. Our representation encodes three fundamental object properties that cognitive science has long identified as essential for human scene understanding~\cite{spelke2007core}. \begin{itemize} \vspace{-2mm} \item[\textbullet] \textbf{{Permanence}:} visual information accumulates into a persistent 3D representation where occluded objects maintain their presence. This persistence enables accurate motion prediction when objects are manipulated behind occlusions or gradually re-enter the visual field. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Amodal completeness:} DSR reconstructs complete 3D occupancy for each object from partial scene observations, including unobserved regions. This completeness allows prediction of full rigid body motion rather than merely visible surface dynamics. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Spatiotemporal continuity:} the representation maintains individual object identity tracking across temporal sequences. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Interpretability:} by explicitly modeling object instances, geometry, and motion, DSR provides ready-to-use components for high-level robotic reasoning applications. \vspace{-2mm} \end{itemize} We develop DSR-Net\xspace, a 3D recurrent neural network architecture, to learn this scene representation through two primary components: 1) a scene encoder that transforms visual observations (i.e\onedot} \def\Ie{I.e\onedot, depth images) into volumetric 3D scene representations, and 2) a motion prediction network that processes the 3D scene representation alongside robotic actions to generate volumetric scene flow predictions. This predicted scene flow spatially warps the current scene representation before integration with the subsequent timestep's 3D scene representation. Through this warping mechanism, DSR-Net\xspace aggregates temporal information while maintaining spatial coherence. We train DSR-Net\xspace end-to-end in simulation before deploying it on real-world robotic manipulation tasks using a tabletop setup. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance for predicting rigid body motion of novel objects during robotic interactions in unstructured, cluttered environments. Our contributions are threefold. We first present a novel 3D dynamic scene representation (DSR) that embodies object permanence, amodal completeness, and continuity—properties that are highly valuable for perception systems supporting downstream robotic manipulation. We then propose DSR-Net\xspace, an end-to-end learning framework that acquires such 3D representations through 3D convolutional operations. Finally, we construct a comprehensive benchmark dataset containing over 80,000 simulated interactions and 1,500 real-world interactions for training and evaluating dynamic 3D scene representations. Both simulated and real-world experiments confirm that DSR-Net\xspace delivers state-of-the-art 3D scene dynamics prediction performance while enabling improved action planning for manipulation tasks like planar pushing. Additional results and demonstration videos are available in the supplementary material.

text: Accurate bounding box estimation constitutes a fundamental requirement for effective tracking systems. Traditional tracking approaches typically address this challenge through multi-scale search strategies~\cite{SiameseFC,ECO,DRT,unveiling} or sampling-followed-by-regression methodologies~\cite{SINT,MDNet}, both of which exhibit limited accuracy and substantially constrain tracker performance. To achieve more robust and precise tracking outcomes, numerous state-of-the-art methods~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} employ multi-stage tracking frameworks that incorporate supplementary stages dedicated to enhanced box estimation precision. These approaches initially perform coarse target localization, subsequently refining preliminary results through additional tracking stages to obtain improved bounding box predictions. Nevertheless, even contemporary state-of-the-art trackers demonstrate potential for enhanced box estimation accuracy. This assertion finds support through an oracle-based experimental validation. By constraining the tracker's search region to remain consistently centered on ground truth annotations, performance becomes predominantly governed by box estimation capabilities. Results presented in Table~\ref{tab:oracle} reveal that under these oracle conditions, leading trackers' AUC scores remain substantially below optimal levels, exposing inadequate box estimation performance despite certain methods (\emph{e.g.} ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}) incorporating dedicated box estimation components. Conversely, when provided with perfectly centered search regions, our proposed Alpha-Refine demonstrates markedly superior performance, establishing Alpha-Refine's excellence in box estimation tasks. Furthermore, refinement approaches employed by existing trackers~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} exhibit limited transferability, as their training procedures remain tightly integrated with other system components. Applying these refinement modules to novel base trackers necessitates additional retraining efforts. In contrast to such approaches, Alpha-Refine undergoes independent training and enables direct application to arbitrary existing trackers through plug-and-play integration, eliminating requirements for supplementary training or base tracker modifications. This investigation examines and compares various design alternatives. We evaluate multiple feature fusion architectures and prediction head configurations. Additionally, we investigate incorporating an auxiliary mask head that introduces pixel-level supervision during training. Our findings indicate that extracting and preserving precise spatial information represents the critical factor for accurate box estimation. Consequently, we adopt pixel-wise correlation alongside a keypoint-style prediction head to better preserve and exploit detailed spatial information. Furthermore, an auxiliary mask head provides encouragement for the network to extract finer spatial details, resulting in enhanced box estimation precision. Additionally, retaining the mask head during inference enables Alpha-Refine to provide object mask predictions for base trackers, accommodating scenarios requiring mask outputs. These design choices receive detailed discussion in Section~\ref{sec:method} and experimental validation in Section~\ref{sec:experiment}. To demonstrate our Alpha-Refine module's effectiveness, we select six prominent base trackers: ECO~\cite{ECO}, RT-MDNet~\cite{RTMDNet}, SiamRPNpp~\cite{SiamRPNplus}, ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}, and DiMPsuper~\cite{DiMP}, evaluating performance across multiple tracking benchmarks including LaSOT~\cite{LaSOT}, GOT-10K~\cite{GOT10K}, TrackingNet~\cite{Trackingnet} and VOT2020~\cite{VOT2020}. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{LaSOT_Improvement}, experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed refinement module yields substantial performance improvements for base trackers. When compared against competing methods (\emph{i.e.} IoU-Net~\cite{ATOM,DiMP} and SiamMask~\cite{SiamMask}), Alpha-Refine achieves significantly superior performance margins. Our proposed Alpha-Refine methodology generates multiple enhanced tracker variants, where ARSiamRPN (Alpha-Refine enhanced SiamRPNpp) and ARDiMP50 (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMP50) deliver favorable efficiency-precision balance, while ARDiMPsuper (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMPsuper) attains state-of-the-art performance while maintaining real-time processing speeds across multiple benchmarks.

text: In recent years, learned index structures have gained prominence as compelling alternatives to conventional database indexing approaches, particularly following the groundbreaking work of Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. At its core, the learned indexing paradigm conceptualizes an index as a predictive model that estimates the position of a specified key within the underlying dataset. This approach offers significant advantages through dramatic reductions in index size—often achieving memory footprint reductions spanning multiple orders of magnitude—since trained models or model hierarchies require substantially less storage than maintaining the actual data structures. Furthermore, these indexes implement a strategic trade-off, exchanging increased computational overhead for reduced memory access patterns, potentially delivering performance improvements when computation cycles prove more economical than memory access latencies. However, the effectiveness of such predictive indexing depends critically on model training using the target dataset before deployment, thereby constraining the index's adaptability to dynamic scenarios. Following Kraska et al.'s seminal contribution \cite{originalLearnedIndex}, numerous learned index architectures have been proposed \cite{histtree, alex, pgmindex, fittingtree, shifttable, radixspline, learnedMultiDim}. Existing evaluation efforts \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, benchmarkingSOSD} have established comparative baselines between these learned approaches and traditional non-learned index structures. Nevertheless, such evaluations predominantly emphasize high-level performance indicators including throughput (requests processed per second), latency (mean request completion time), memory consumption, and multi-threading scalability characteristics. Although these metrics provide essential insights into the overall advantages and limitations of learned indexing, they represent merely one perspective—particularly for main-memory-optimized structures. These aggregate measures fail to illuminate how learned indexes exploit processor micro-architectural resources, including front-end resource utilization and cache hierarchy interactions across different levels. This paper aims to illuminate this complementary analytical dimension. Our investigation centers on ALEX \cite{alex}, among the pioneering learned indexes architected specifically for efficient update and insertion operations. We conduct comprehensive micro-architectural profiling of ALEX while benchmarking its behavior against two non-learned index implementations: ART \cite{artpaper, artcode}, representing trie-based indexing, and B+tree \cite{btreecode}, exemplifying tree-based approaches. These particular structures were selected because ALEX has been previously evaluated against them in its original publication \cite{alex} and subsequent comparative studies \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, histtree}, enabling cross-validation of our findings. Our evaluation framework employs a custom benchmark driver \footnote{Will be made available once the paper is accepted.} generating YCSB-compatible \cite{ycsbpaper} workload patterns. Through this infrastructure, we synthesize four distinct workloads exhibiting varied read-write characteristics across two dataset scales. Performance analysis follows Intel's Top-down Micro-architecture Analysis Method (TMAM) \cite{tmam}, decomposing execution cycles into constituent micro-architectural components. Our investigation reveals the following key insights: \begin{list}{\labelitemi}{\leftmargin=1.5em} \item{Like ART and B+Tree, ALEX dedicates the majority of execution cycles to memory-bound stalls resulting from high-latency data dependencies originating from last-level cache misses. However, ALEX generally demonstrates reduced stall frequencies and lower cycles-per-instruction metrics across diverse workload configurations compared to ART and B+Tree.} \item{Conversely, insertions targeting the tree's right boundary (\textit{out-of-bound} keys) trigger order-of-magnitude increases in ALEX's per-request instruction count due to model retraining requirements, while ART and B+Tree exhibit minimal impact from such operations. Despite this instruction footprint expansion, high instruction-level parallelism characteristics ensure that overall execution time remains largely unaffected for ALEX.} \end{list} The paper proceeds as follows. \Cref{background} examines related research and provides essential background on the index structures analyzed in this study alongside processor micro-architectural fundamentals. \Cref{setup} details our experimental methodology and configuration, while \Cref{results} presents and analyzes our findings. \Cref{conclusion} synthesizes our discoveries and outlines promising avenues for future investigation.

text: The proliferation of multicore parallel machines over the past decade has fundamentally transformed mainstream computing. Among the various programming paradigms and tools designed to harness parallelism in multicore architectures, the approach based on \defn{nested parallelism} with \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} has emerged as the most prevalent and extensively adopted solution. This nested parallelism model, along with its variants, enjoys widespread support across numerous parallel programming languages (including Cilk, TBB, TPL, X10, Java Fork-join, and OpenMP), features prominently in educational materials (such as Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein~\cite{CLRS}), and serves as the foundation for extensive research endeavors (exemplified by: \cite{agrawal2014batching,blelloch2010low,BCGRCK08,BG04,Blelloch1998,blelloch1999pipelining,BlellochFiGi11,BST12,Cole17,BBFGGMS16,dinh2016extending,chowdhury2017provably,blelloch2018geometry,dhulipala2020semi,BBFGGMS18,Dhulipala2018,blelloch2020randomized,gu2021parallel,blelloch2016justjoin,sun2018pam,sun2019parallel,ptreedb}). Conceptually, this model enables algorithms to recursively and dynamically spawn (\emph{fork}) parallel tasks, which are subsequently executed across $P$ processors through dynamic scheduling mechanisms. Such nested (binary) fork-join constructs offer an elegant abstraction for shared-memory parallelism. From the perspective of users—whether algorithm designers or programmers—this represents a straightforward extension of traditional programming models, requiring only additional keywords for task creation (such as \op{fork}) and inter-task synchronization (such as \op{join}). Within this ecosystem, the \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} serves a pivotal function by automatically and dynamically mapping nested parallel algorithms to hardware resources with both theoretical and practical efficiency. This paper investigates two significant aspects of the RWS scheduler. Initially, we present a \defn{new, simplified, and classroom-ready version of analysis for the RWS scheduler}, which we contend offers superior comprehensibility compared to existing approaches. Subsequently, we contribute \defn{new analyses for parallel cache complexity} applicable to nested-parallel algorithms utilizing the RWS scheduler. We establish a collection of nearly optimal bounds enumerated in \Cref{table:intro}, with detailed discussions provided in subsequent sections. Our primary contribution involves a streamlined analysis of the RWS scheduler. While Blumofe and Leiserson~\cite{blumofe1999scheduling} initially established the theoretical efficiency of the RWS scheduler, subsequent analyses have addressed various configurations (including: \cite{Acar02,itpa,muller2016latency,acar2013scheduling,BBFGGMS16,singer2019proactive,Acar2016tapp,singer2020scheduling,arora2001thread}). Despite these analyses fundamentally addressing more sophisticated scenarios (such as incorporating external I/Os), the analytical frameworks themselves exhibit considerable complexity. To our knowledge, detailed proofs rarely appear in parallelism-focused curricula, with RWS typically treated as an opaque component. Consequently, we focus specifically on bounding the number of steals in the RWS scheduler, seeking to determine the most elementary analysis possible for the RWS scheduler and identify the most pedagogically accessible version. \Cref{sec:rws} presents our simplified analysis. In contrast to most existing approaches, our version eschews reliance on potential function definitions for computation substructures, thereby enhancing comprehensibility. Our analysis draws inspiration from recent work~\cite{itpa} that shares similarities with~\cite{agrawal2008adaptive,suksompong2014bounds}. Our approach diverges from~\cite{itpa} in two fundamental ways. First, rather than assuming processor synchronization in lock-step fashion (the PRAM setting), we adopt a highly asynchronous framework that better reflects contemporary parallel machine realities. Second, we decouple mathematical calculations from RWS algorithm specifics, potentially facilitating classroom instruction. Our secondary and principal contribution addresses parallel cache complexity for algorithms employing the RWS scheduler. In contemporary computing environments, memory access costs typically dominate execution times for most combinatorial algorithms. To address this phenomenon, Aggarwal and Vitter~\cite{AggarwalV88} initially formalized the external-memory model for capturing algorithmic I/O costs, subsequently refined by Frigo et al.~\cite{Frigo99} as the ideal-cache model. This cost metric is termed \emph{I/O complexity}~\cite{AggarwalV88} (denoted as $Q_1$) or \emph{cache complexity}~\cite{Frigo99} when quantifying communication costs between cache and main memory. Although this model has achieved remarkable success within algorithm and database communities, limited results have extended it to parallel (distributed cache) settings, which we summarize in \Cref{sec:cachebound}. Notably, Acar, Blelloch and Blumofe~\cite{Acar02} initially defined and demonstrated that parallel cache complexity $Q_P$ is bounded by $Q_1+O(PDM/B)$, where $P$, $D$, $M$ and $B$ represent processor count, span (depth, the longest critical dependency path), cache size, and cache block size, respectively (formal definitions in \Cref{sec:prelim}). Nevertheless, this bound proves pessimistic and typically overly loose. Frigo and Strumpen~\cite{frigo2009cache} and subsequent work by Cole and Ramachandran~\cite{cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} established tighter parallel cache complexity bounds for numerous cache-oblivious algorithms, summarized in \Cref{table:intro}. However, these bounds incorporate polynomial overhead\footnote{Such overhead typically takes the form $n^{a}$, where $a$ represents a constant with $1/2\le a<1$.} relative to input size when span exhibits polynomial dependence on input size. This overhead can readily dominate cache bounds when applied to real-world input sizes, as elaborated in \Cref{table:intro}'s caption. Closing this gap remained an outstanding open problem. This paper substantially narrows this gap across various algorithms. The polynomial overhead in previous analyses~\cite{Acar02,frigo2009cache,cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} stems from these algorithms' high span (with polynomial span terms appearing in bounds). Our analytical breakthrough involves severing the polynomial correlation between algorithmic span and parallel cache complexity overhead. Our novel analysis leverages the \kdgrid{} abstraction recently proposed by Blelloch and Gu~\cite{BG2020}, previously employed for sequential cache bound analysis. We extend this concept to parallel cache complexity analysis. Our approach directly examines ``genuine'' dependencies within these algorithms' computational structures, rather than those induced by parallelism. Specifically, our analysis centers on the \emph{recurrences} characterizing these algorithms. Consequently, computational parallel dependencies (algorithmic span) are eliminated from the analysis. This enables us to circumvent the complexity of incorporating scheduling algorithm details into the analysis, rendering the analysis no more complex than recurrence solving. To achieve this, we define the \dacrecur{}, which effectively captures the recurrence patterns of numerous classical algorithms, and establish a general theorem, \Cref{thm:recur}, for solving these recurrences. Through application of these results, we attain the new bounds presented in \Cref{table:intro}. The parallel overheads exhibit polylogarithmic rather than polynomial scaling with input size, approaching the lower bounds established by~\cite{ballard2014communication,BG2020}. We believe this methodology possesses independent significance and could prove valuable for analyzing additional parallel or sequential algorithms. We reserve this exploration for future investigation. text: Healthcare professionals (HCPs) require substantial trust in treatment search engines when seeking therapeutic options for their patients. Beyond fundamental requirements like accuracy, performance, and interface design, additional measures become necessary to establish sufficient confidence for deployment in high-stakes scenarios where patient lives hang in the balance. Traditional search engines deliver ranked lists of relevant items corresponding to specific queries. The absence of explanatory mechanisms, however, undermines user trust by obscuring the retrieval logic that connects queries to results. Within medical contexts, where error tolerance approaches zero, misattributing causality in diagnostic or treatment decisions can prove catastrophic. Consequently, without interpretable models, HCPs lose confidence in system outputs and ultimately abandon their use \cite{pu2006trust}. Compounding this challenge, regulatory compliance requirements force most medical search engines to present unordered result lists, complicating users' ability to identify the most pertinent items. Treatment search platforms like clinicaltrials.gov exemplify this limitation by avoiding relevance-based ranking, partly because prioritizing qualifying treatments risks introducing favoritism—a practice strictly forbidden in clinical trial contexts \cite{Clinical58:online}. Furthermore, conventional ordering schemes based on status, date, or title often prove impractical for comprehensive searches, as they disperse related results across the interface. Current explainable methods offer one potential avenue for providing explanations. Global explanation techniques enable overall search engine evaluation but fail to address individual query responses adequately \cite{dam2018explainable}. Local explainability approaches like LIME \cite{das2020opportunities} and SHAP \cite{lundberg2017unified} explain specific result generation mechanisms. Nevertheless, these methods target machine learning applications such as classification and regression rather than search result interpretation. Previous attempts to apply local explanations to search results either relied on single document features like term prominence \cite{verma2019lirme} or required user review data unavailable for clinical trials \cite{catherine2017explainable}. Delivering user-friendly, dependable, and comprehensible explanations to HCPs presents another significant obstacle. Existing explainability techniques like LIME \cite{das2020opportunities} primarily serve users with technical expertise in system interpretation. Since HCPs cannot universally be expected to grasp complex retrieval model mechanics, they require high-level, intuitive explanations that need not mirror exact internal operations. This constraint creates opportunities for developing explanation models resilient to minor search engine modifications. For treatment search engines, local explanations such as "the queried disease appears in the retrieved clinical trial's title" remain valid provided the retrieval model incorporates this feature, enabling relatively independent development of search and explanation components. This paper presents an explainability method delivering customized explanations to medical practitioners for retrieved items. We extract meaningful clinical trial features from diverse data sources and elicit user preferences through crowdsourcing methodologies. Subsequently, we propose a framework for converting preferences into feature importance rankings. Using these importance levels, we generate tailored explanations for specific queries and develop sentence templates for user presentation. Additionally, we introduce explainability scores for ordering retrieved items. Results demonstrate that local explainability in clinical search engines enhances HCP trust, search experience, and result ordering satisfaction.

text: The objective of semantic segmentation is to partition images into semantically meaningful segments. Despite significant advances~\cite{FCN,Deeplab,Deeplabv3Plus,pspnet,ocrnet,segformer}, contemporary semantic segmentation approaches predominantly rely on supervised learning with predefined category sets, typically demanding hundreds of training examples per class. Conversely, human visual cognition can differentiate among approximately 30,000 fundamental categories~\cite{biederman1987recognition,fu2017recent} and identify novel categories using merely \textit{high-level descriptions}. Achieving this human-level capacity for recognizing objects and regions in visual scenes represents a fundamental aspiration in computer vision. Zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZS3) research~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net} has begun advancing toward this ambitious objective. Drawing inspiration from fully supervised segmentation frameworks~\cite{FCN,Deeplabv3Plus,Deeplab} and zero-shot classification methodologies~\cite{lampert2013attribute,zhang2016zero,jayaraman2014zero,rohrbach2011evaluating,akata2015evaluation}, existing approaches conceptualize zero-shot semantic segmentation as a \textit{pixel-level zero-shot classification problem}. {While these investigations have yielded encouraging outcomes, two critical limitations persist: (1) Knowledge transfer from seen to unseen categories typically relies on \textit{language} models~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net,fasttext} trained exclusively on textual data, constraining their effectiveness for visual tasks. Although large-scale pre-trained \textit{vision-language} models (\eg CLIP~\cite{clip} and ALIGN~\cite{align}) have shown promise for \textit{image-level} vision applications, their efficient integration into \textit{pixel-level} ZS3 remains unexplored. (2) Current methods establish connections between \textit{pixel-level} visual representations and semantic features for knowledge transfer, which appears \textit{unnatural} given that humans typically employ \textit{words or texts} to characterize \textit{objects/segments} rather than individual \textit{pixels} within images. Fig.~\ref{fig:confusion} illustrates that \textit{pixel-level} classification exhibits poor accuracy on \textit{unseen classes}, consequently compromising overall segmentation performance. This degradation becomes particularly pronounced when dealing with numerous unseen categories (see Fig.~\ref{fig:visadeinfercoco}). } A fundamental insight emerges from human visual processing: when performing semantic segmentation on images, humans naturally \textit{group pixels into coherent segments} before conducting \textit{segment-level semantic labeling}. Consider how children can effortlessly cluster object pixels despite lacking knowledge of the object's name. Consequently, we propose that {\em human-inspired zero-shot semantic segmentation should decompose into two distinct sub-tasks}: \begin{itemize} \item[-] {\em Class-agnostic grouping} for clustering pixels into coherent segments. This constitutes a classical image partitioning problem~\cite{DDMCMC,NormalizeCUT,supervisedeval}, recently revitalized through deep learning approaches~\cite{maskformer,KNet,panopticsegformer}. \item[-] {\em Segment-level zero-shot classification} for assigning semantic labels (both seen and unseen) to segments. \end{itemize} Since grouping operates independently of semantic categories, models trained on seen classes transfer seamlessly to unseen categories. Segment-level zero-shot classification demonstrates robustness on unseen classes while enabling flexible integration of pre-trained large-scale vision-language models~\cite{clip} into the ZS3 framework. We instantiate this decoupling concept through ZegFormer, a {\em zero-shot semantic segmentation model with transformer} that employs a transformer decoder to generate \textit{segment-level} embeddings, as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}. The architecture incorporates a \textit{mask projection} for \textit{class-agnostic grouping} (CAG) and a \textit{semantic projection} for \textit{segment-level zero-shot classification} (s-ZSC). The \textit{mask projection} transforms each \textit{segment-level} embedding into a mask embedding, enabling binary mask prediction through dot product operations with high-resolution feature maps. The \textit{semantic projection} creates correspondences between \textit{segment-level} embeddings and semantic features from a pre-trained \textit{text encoder} for s-ZSC. Although these components constitute a complete ZS3 approach, models trained on limited datasets struggle with robust generalization. Our decoupling formulation facilitates the incorporation of \textit{image encoders} from vision-language models to generate image embeddings for zero-shot segment classification. Empirical analysis reveals that segment classification scores from image embeddings and s-ZSC exhibit complementary characteristics. We combine these scores to produce final segment classifications. Extensive experimental evaluation demonstrates ZegFormer's superiority across standard ZS3 benchmarks. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches by \textbf{22 points} in mIoU for unseen classes on PASCAL VOC~\cite{voc} and \textbf{3 points} on COCO-Stuff~\cite{coco-stuff}. Using the challenging ADE20k-Full dataset~\cite{ade20k}, we establish a novel ZS3 benchmark featuring {\bf 275 unseen classes}, substantially exceeding the unseen class counts in PASCAL-VOC ($5$ unseen classes) and COCO-Stuff ($15$ unseen classes). On this ADE20k-Full ZS3 benchmark, our performance matches MaskFormer~\cite{maskformer}, a fully supervised semantic segmentation model. This paper presents three primary contributions: \begin{itemize} 	\item We introduce a novel ZS3 formulation that decomposes the task into {\em class-agnostic grouping} and {\em segment-level zero-shot classification}, offering a more intuitive and adaptable framework for incorporating pre-trained large-scale vision-language models into ZS3. 	\item Through this formulation, we develop ZegFormer, an effective ZS3 model utilizing transformer decoders to produce \textit{segment-level} embeddings for both grouping and zero-shot classification. To our knowledge, ZegFormer represents the first approach to fully leverage pre-trained large-scale vision-language models (\eg CLIP~\cite{clip}) for ZS3. 	\item We establish new state-of-the-art performance on standard ZS3 benchmarks. Ablation studies and visualization analyses confirm that our decoupling formulation substantially outperforms pixel-level zero-shot classification approaches. \end{itemize}

text: While autonomous driving has witnessed remarkable progress recently, HD maps continue to serve as fundamental components in contemporary systems, furnishing comprehensive road infrastructure details that enable diverse applications including motion planning and perception enhancement. Nevertheless, leveraging HD maps necessitates precise determination of vehicle pose within the mapping framework. Contemporary high-precision localization solutions typically deploy RTK-GNSS systems coupled with IMUs or vehicle odometry through probabilistic fusion frameworks~\cite{jo2011interacting,schreiber2016vehicle}. Yet the substantial equipment costs and operational constraints in densely populated urban areas restrict these approaches primarily to research contexts and data collection purposes. Consequently, most operational autonomous vehicles rely on HD maps containing environmental element information—including lane topology, traffic signage, and traffic light configurations—for localization purposes. Given such information availability, landmark-based localization approaches have attracted considerable attention. These methodologies incorporate perception modules that extract requisite features from sensor data and perform continuous matching against available map elements to constrain vehicle pose estimation~\cite{caselitz2016monocular,cattaneo2019cmrnet}. Driven by substantial deep learning research and technological advancement, contemporary perception modules predominantly employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for environmental feature extraction~\cite{poggenhans2018precise},~\cite{pauls2020monocular}. While cutting-edge CNN architectures demonstrate comprehensive environmental understanding through various sensors including cameras~\cite{porzi2019seamless,mohan2021efficientps} and LiDARs~\cite{sirohi2021efficientlps}, most CNNs fail to provide dependable confidence estimates or exhibit overconfidence in their predictions. Such limitations can undermine localization algorithm robustness and precision. Deep learning-based uncertainty estimation extends conventional neural network methodologies by additionally predicting associated uncertainty or confidence levels in predictions. Prevalent uncertainty estimation techniques primarily employ sampling-based approaches~\cite{gal2016dropout}, which demand significant computational resources and processing time. Although sampling-free method research is gaining momentum, existing approaches concentrate on uncertainty prediction for individual tasks such as classification~\cite{sensoy2018evidential} or regression~\cite{amini2019deep}. Conversely, comprehensive autonomous vehicle perception systems encompass multiple tasks including segmentation and detection. This paper addresses the localization challenge in demanding urban environments using cost-effective sensor configurations and highly sparse HD maps containing exclusively lane boundaries and traffic lights. We introduce an innovative monocular camera-based localization system that exploits uncertainty estimates from our proposed multi-task perception module. Our perception module concurrently predicts uncertainties related to lane semantics and traffic light bounding box parameters through a single forward pass. This paper's primary contributions include: 1) an innovative pose graph localization system demonstrating robustness in challenging scenarios through predicted uncertainty exploitation, 2) a multi-task uncertainty-aware perception module enabling simultaneous semantic and regression uncertainty prediction without sampling requirements, 3) a novel association-free and differentiable cost map generation module directed by prediction uncertainties. We validate the performance improvements achieved by incorporating uncertainties into our localization methodology through evaluation on the demanding Lyft 5 dataset~\cite{kesten2019lyft}.

text: \vspace{-8pt} The past eight years have witnessed remarkable advances in deep generative models, which now produce photorealistic images with unprecedented quality. This progress has been largely driven by the groundbreaking development of generative adversarial networks (GANs)~\citep{gan14nips,radford2015dcgan,gulrajani2017wgan,miyato2018spectral,brock2018BigGAN,karras2017ProGAN,karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}. As the gap between synthetic and authentic content continues to narrow, significant societal concerns have emerged~\citep{harris2018deepfakes,chesney2019deepfakes,brundage2018malicious}: what happens when these powerful models are exploited for sensor spoofing, deepfake creation, or large-scale misinformation campaigns? The challenge extends beyond human perception—even specialized research in deepfake detection~\citep{durall2019unmasking,zhang2019detecting,frank2020dct2d_detect,zhang2020not} and attribution~\citep{marra2019gans,ning2019iccv_gan_detection,wang2020cnn} struggles to keep pace with generative model evolution. This creates an adversarial cycle: researchers analyze detection mechanisms in detail, then leverage these insights to enhance generation techniques that circumvent detection criteria~\citep{zhang2020not,margret2020upconvolution}. Fundamentally, any effective detector can serve as an auxiliary discriminator component in subsequent GAN iterations, ultimately producing even more sophisticated generators. These concerning implications have significantly hindered the commercialization of deep generative models. OpenAI's approach to GPT-2~\citep{radford2019language} and GPT-3~\citep{brown2020language} exemplifies this caution—rather than open-sourcing these models, they provide only black-box API access\footnote{\url{https://openai.com/blog/openai-api/}}. Their deployment strategy requires costly human oversight for user approval and API usage monitoring. Nevertheless, establishing accountability for downstream applications in an open-ended ecosystem remains an industry-wide challenge. \begin{wrapfigure}[13]{R}{0.6\textwidth} \centering \vspace{-8pt} \caption{The diagram of our fingerprinting mechanism for generators. See main text for descriptions. \vspace{-16pt} \end{wrapfigure} We introduce a novel model fingerprinting framework that facilitates responsible deployment and governance of generative models. Our approach enables conscientious model developers to embed unique fingerprints within their generators while maintaining full accountability. Generated samples thus carry detectable fingerprints that enable precise source attribution. This capability emerges from an efficient, scalable system for creating numerous generator instances, each bearing distinct fingerprints. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Middle. Drawing inspiration from dynamic filter networks~\citep{jia2016dynamic} and style-based generator architectures~\citep{karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}—where network filters are conditioned on inputs rather than learned independently—we parameterize unique fingerprints directly into each generator instance's filters. Our key insight involves integrating a fingerprint auto-encoder within the GAN framework while preserving original generation capabilities. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Left. Specifically, given a GAN backbone, fingerprint embeddings from our encoder modulate every convolutional filter in the generator (Figure~\ref{fig:modulation}), while we simultaneously decode these fingerprints from generated images. Joint training combines fingerprint-specific losses with standard adversarial objectives. See Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline} for the complete pipeline and~\ref{sec:loss_design} for implementation details. Following training, responsible model developers can efficiently fingerprint and distribute distinct generator instances to different users, each maintaining identical generation performance while carrying unique identifiers. \ning{Every user download corresponds to a specific fingerprint, tracked within the developer's database.} When model misuse occurs, developers can employ the decoder to extract fingerprints from generated images, \ning{cross-reference the database,} and establish user accountability. See Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} Right. This responsible disclosure framework provides organizations like OpenAI with mechanisms to mitigate societal risks when releasing powerful models, while enabling automated misuse attribution. Our mechanism exhibits several critical properties. \textbf{Efficiency} in generator instantiation is inherent—post-training fingerprint encoding and filter modulation incur minimal computational overhead. We demonstrate \textbf{effectiveness} through near-perfect fingerprint detection accuracy. \textbf{Fidelity} is preserved with negligible impact on original generation quality. See Section~\ref{sec:effectiveness_fidelity}. Our recommended configuration employs 128-bit fingerprints (Section~\ref{sec:capacity}), theoretically supporting over $10^{38}$ identifiable generator instances—ensuring substantial \textbf{capacity}. \textbf{Scalability} derives from random fingerprint sampling during training, enabling detection generalization across the entire fingerprint space. See Section~\ref{sec:scalability} for empirical validation. Additionally, we verify fingerprint \textbf{secrecy} against shadow model attacks in Section~\ref{sec:secrecy}, and establish \textbf{robustness} and \textbf{immunizability} against image perturbations in Section~\ref{sec:robustness_immunizability}. Addressing our core motivation, we transform deepfake detection and attribution from \textit{passive} detection paradigms to \textit{proactive} fingerprinting approaches. Section~\ref{sec:detection_attribution} demonstrates superior performance compared to two state-of-the-art discriminative methods~\citep{ning2019iccv_gan_detection,wang2020cnn}, particularly in open-world scenarios. User-specific fingerprint conditioning ensures reliable margins between authentic and synthetic content, enabling robust attribution and responsibility tracing for deepfakes to their origins. Our \textbf{contributions} span four key areas: (1) We \revise{enhance} the fingerprinting concept for generative models, enabling responsible disclosure of state-of-the-art GAN architectures. (2) We pioneer efficient, scalable GAN fingerprinting—training a single generic model while generating over $10^{38}$ fingerprinted instances with minimal deployment overhead. (3) We establish multiple critical fingerprinting properties: effectiveness, fidelity, large capacity, scalability, secrecy, robustness, and immunizability. (4) For deepfake detection and attribution, we shift from \textit{passive} classification to \textit{proactive} fingerprinting, demonstrating superior performance and advantages. This approach makes responsible disclosure independent of GAN technique evolution. \vspace{-8pt}

text: Modern network security infrastructures extensively incorporate Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) middleboxes as fundamental components \cite{xu2016survey}. These systems operate with statefulness, meaning they examine not merely isolated packets but reconstruct them into coherent stateful connections according to network protocol definitions (such as TCP), utilizing predetermined state machines. Consequently, DPIs must incorporate specialized network protocol implementations that typically exhibit simplification relative to their endpoint counterparts (such as OS kernels) due to limited computational resources, excessive overhead concerns, and occasionally the necessity to maintain generality when confronting ambiguous network protocol specifications. \point{Adversarial Packets} From DPI's emergence, numerous circumvention attacks have materialized. These exploits leverage implementation disparities between DPI systems and OS-level network protocol stacks, engineering sophisticated packets that induce divergent behaviors across DPI and endpoint systems (such as servers). Consider a packet engineered to prompt DPI dismissal while successfully reaching and gaining server acceptance. Such packets may harbor malicious content yet successfully evade DPI detection entirely (since their payloads remain uninspected). More alarmingly, previous research demonstrates that a single strategically crafted packet can force DPI disengagement from connection monitoring, permitting subsequent connection packets to traverse undetected without triggering security alerts. \point{Automated Discovery of Evasion Packets} Recent years have witnessed network protocol stacks evolving into increasingly intricate systems featuring novel capabilities \cite{ramaiah2010improving}, expanding vendor-specific implementations, and continuously developing specifications. This complexity has sparked research momentum \cite{li2017lib, bock2019geneva, wang2020symtcp} toward automating \textit{adversarial packet} discovery for DPI evasion. Through systematic search methodologies \cite{li2017lib}, genetic mutation techniques \cite{bock2019geneva}, or symbolic execution approaches \cite{wang2020symtcp}, extensive adversarial packet collections emerge with minimal manual oversight. While advancing attacker comprehension, this automation presents formidable defensive challenges. Protocol stack evolution and increasing complexity theoretically expand discoverable discrepancies through automation, making manual analysis of implementation subtleties and comprehensive codebase patching prohibitively expensive. Additionally, generating novel hardcoded DPI policies to address emerging discrepancies becomes impractical given rapidly evolving implementations and protocol standards. \point{Existing Defenses} Considering this complexity, adversarial packet countermeasures remain remarkably limited. Notably, Kreibich et al. \cite{kreibich2001network} employ \textit{traffic normalization} for adversarial packet threat mitigation. Their approach introduces traffic normalizers functioning as network forwarding elements positioned before DPI middleboxes, modifying or discarding packets according to predefined rule sets. These manually curated rules characterize "normal traffic" patterns (such as requiring IP header length fields to match actual header lengths precisely). Unfortunately, this countermeasure fails to scale against automation—achievable adversarial packet search spaces can expand sufficiently to render timely manual curation impossible. Furthermore, evolving protocol standards generate false positives—previously valid rules may subsequently cause erroneous decisions (including normal packet drops) due to implementation updates. Additionally, as normalizers or more broadly \textit{traffic shapers}, \cite{kreibich2001network} lacks detection capabilities, instead blindly modifying traffic streams. \point{Our Approach} This paper aims to develop practical defenses for effectively detecting DPI middlebox evasion attempts. Consider a packet engineered to cause DPI to reject it while it successfully reaches and is accepted by the endpoint. text: Deep representation learning has recently experienced a remarkable revival of contrastive learning (CL) \cite{DBLP:conf/nips/KhoslaTWSTIMLK20,jaiswal2021survey,liu2020self}. Through its capacity to extract generalizable features from vast unlabeled datasets while providing self-supervised regularization of representations, CL has catalyzed breakthrough advances across diverse research domains \cite{you2020graph,wujc2021self,chen2020simple,gao2021simcse}. Given that CL operates without requiring data annotation, it presents an ideal solution to address data sparsity challenges inherent in recommender systems \cite{sarwar2001sparsity,hao2021pre}. A growing body of contemporary research \cite{wujc2021self,yu2021self,xia2020self,zhou2020s,zhou2021contrastive,yu2021socially} has explored leveraging CL to enhance recommendation performance, yielding substantial improvements. The conventional approach \cite{wujc2021self} for incorporating CL into recommendation involves first augmenting the user-item bipartite graph through structural perturbations (such as stochastic edge/node dropout at specified ratios), then maximizing representational consistency across different views learned through a graph encoder. Within this framework, the CL task serves as an auxiliary objective, jointly optimized alongside the primary recommendation task (Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}). \par While CL has produced promising results, the underlying mechanisms driving these performance improvements remain poorly understood. Our intuitive hypothesis suggests that contrasting various graph augmentations enables the capture of essential information embedded within original user-item interactions by stochastically eliminating redundancy and noise through edge/node dropout. Surprisingly, several recent investigations \cite{yu2021socially,zhou2021selfcf,DBLP:conf/sigir/LeeKJPY21} have documented that even extremely sparse graph augmentations (employing edge dropout rates of 0.9) within CL frameworks can yield substantial performance benefits. This phenomenon appears both puzzling and counterintuitive, as excessive dropout rates inevitably cause significant raw information loss and severely distorted graph structures. This observation naturally prompts a critical inquiry: \textit{Do we really need graph augmentations when integrating CL with recommendation?} \par We address this question by conducting comparative experiments with and without graph augmentations to evaluate performance differences. Our findings reveal that performance remains comparable even when graph augmentations are eliminated entirely. Subsequently, we examine the embedding spaces produced by non-CL and CL-based recommendation approaches. Through visualization of representational distributions and their correlation with performance metrics, we discover that recommendation performance hinges primarily on the CL loss itself, not on graph augmentation strategies. Optimizing the contrastive InfoNCE loss \cite{oord2018representation} produces more uniformly distributed user/item representations regardless of graph augmentation application, implicitly serving to alleviate popularity bias \cite{chen2020bias}. Although graph augmentations prove less effective than anticipated, they retain some utility by helping learn representations that remain invariant to disturbance factors through properly perturbed versions of the original graph \cite{bachman2019learning,chen2020simple}. Nevertheless, generating handcrafted graph augmentations necessitates continuous reconstruction of graph adjacency matrices during training, creating substantial computational overhead. Furthermore, dropping critical edges/nodes (such as cut edges) risks fragmenting connected graphs into disconnected components, potentially eliminating learnable invariance between augmented and original graphs. These limitations raise a subsequent question: \textit{Are there more effective and efficient augmentation approaches?} \par This paper provides an affirmative response to that question. Building upon our discovery that representational distribution uniformity constitutes the crucial factor, we develop a graph-augmentation-free CL method offering enhanced uniformity control. Our technical approach follows the graph CL framework illustrated in Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}, but eliminates dropout-based graph augmentation in favor of adding random uniform noise to original representations for representation-level data augmentation. Applying different random noise patterns creates variance between contrastive views while preserving learnable invariance through controlled magnitude. Unlike graph augmentation, our noise-based approach directly regularizes the embedding space toward more uniform distribution, offering straightforward implementation and superior efficiency. \par This paper's primary contributions are summarized below: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] 	\item We experimentally reveal the mechanisms by which CL enhances recommendation performance and demonstrate that the InfoNCE loss, not graph augmentation, serves as the determining factor. 	\item We introduce a simple yet powerful graph-augmentation-free CL method for recommendation that smoothly regulates uniformity, providing an optimal alternative to complex graph augmentation-based CL approaches. 	\item We present comprehensive experimental analysis across three benchmark datasets demonstrating our proposed method's superior performance compared to graph augmentation-based counterparts in both recommendation accuracy and training efficiency. \end{itemize}

text: Contemporary data privacy landscapes can be characterized as existing within a post-privacy epoch, largely attributable to unforeseen ramifications stemming from the big data paradigm shift. The notorious Cambridge Analytica affair \cite{berghel2018malice} exemplifies how re-identification processes can be executed through cross-referential analysis of extensive datasets harboring sensitive personal information. Despite privacy legislation such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the technological transformation propelling society toward post-privacy conditions persists unabated. Nevertheless, we find ourselves amid another transformative wave—blockchain technology—that possesses the potential to reinstate data privacy protections. The European Union established GDPR in 2018 \cite{EUdataregulations2018}, creating comprehensive frameworks governing personal data collection, processing, and protection, with particular emphasis on protected health information (PHI). According to Art. 4(15) of EU GDPR, health-related data encompasses: "personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of healthcare services, which reveal information about his or her health status." Within the United States healthcare framework, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPPA) serves as fundamental legislation primarily addressing privacy rights and data access rather than establishing patient data ownership \cite{annas2003hipaa}. Patient data ownership for citizens falls under individual state jurisdiction, governed by respective state legislation. Consequently, fifty distinct legal frameworks, judicial precedents, and interpretative approaches to patient data ownership exist across states. New Hampshire stands alone in enacting legislation explicitly designating patients as owners of their health data. The intersection and compliance mechanisms between GDPR and U.S. state legislation remain undetermined. Since Bitcoin's introduction in 2008, blockchain terminology has experienced conceptual dilution, lacking universally accepted definitional consensus. For this research's purposes, we establish blockchain as a distributed, decentralized, and tamper-resistant ledger operating without centralized governance. Blockchain technology, alongside other Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT), presents opportunities to enhance data privacy while empowering individuals with greater control and access over personal information, particularly health-related data. This study pursues dual objectives: (i) examining diverse blockchain architectural designs and investigating GDPR compliance across various components within existing or proposed healthcare blockchain applications, and (ii) furnishing future researchers with comprehensive guidance for achieving GDPR compliance when developing blockchain applications within healthcare domains. The paper's structure proceeds as follows: \textbf{Section II} delivers concise blockchain technology introduction while outlining prior research addressing blockchain-GDPR compliance; \textbf{Section III} details our research methodology; \textbf{Section IV} characterizes four healthcare blockchain applications identified through literature review; \textbf{Section V} presents analytical results and findings; \textbf{Section VI} offers discussion, conclusions, and recommendations for future research directions.

text: The ability to reliably identify encrypted data fragments represents a fundamental primitive with broad applications across security and digital forensics domains. Ransomware detection systems, for example, leverage assessments of data randomness in write operations to rapidly pinpoint evidence of malicious encryption activities~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}. Digital forensic investigations of storage devices and mobile phones frequently require the identification of encrypted archives~\cite{conti_automated_2010}. Network protocol analysis also extensively employs encryption detection techniques~\cite{de_carli_botnet_2017,dorfinger_real-time_2010}. A prevalent methodology for tackling this challenge involves estimating Shannon entropy of target sequences through the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE): $\hat{H}_{MLE}$. This technique exploits the principle that byte value distributions in encrypted streams approximate uniform distributions, making high entropy a reliable indicator of randomness. The estimator offers computational efficiency and implementation simplicity. Given that non-encrypted digital content typically exhibits low byte-level entropy, this approach should theoretically provide clear differentiation between encrypted and unencrypted material. Despite its continued widespread adoption (e.g.,~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}), several studies have exposed significant limitations in this methodology. Contemporary applications routinely compress data before storage and transmission operations. Notable instances include zip compressed formats and HTTP compression~\cite{http-rfc}, both utilizing the DEFLATE algorithm. Since compression eliminates repetitive data patterns, compressed streams naturally demonstrate elevated Shannon entropy levels. Consequently, compressed data produces $\hat{H}_{MLE}$ values that closely approximate, and frequently overlap with, those generated by encryption processes. While appropriate parsers can theoretically identify compressed content, numerous security applications—including ransomware detection, traffic analysis, and digital forensics—operate exclusively on data \textit{fragments} rather than complete files. Under these constraints, the metadata essential for parser functionality remains unavailable or incomplete~\cite{park_data_2008}. Addressing this fundamental limitation, various research efforts have explored alternative methodologies for distinguishing encrypted from compressed content~\cite{malhotra_detection_2007,wang_using_2011,foresti_efficient_2016,lipmaa_data_2017,hahn2018detecting,casino_hedge_2019,choudhury_empirical_2020}. Although these approaches demonstrate potential utility, their evaluation against standardized datasets remains limited. This gap prevents comprehensive understanding of how these techniques: (i) perform across diverse compressed file formats and sizes, and (ii) compare against one another. The implications of this knowledge deficit are substantial: deploying ineffective encrypted content identification methods can compromise ransomware detector performance~\cite{gaspari2019} and severely constrain forensic tool capabilities. This work presents a comparative analysis of leading state-of-the-art approaches using an extensive dataset encompassing various data types and fragment dimensions. Our findings reveal that while current methods surpass entropy-based estimates, they fail to deliver consistently high accuracy levels. We therefore introduce \textsc{EnCoD} (\textbf{En}cription/\textbf{Co}mpression \textbf{D}istinguisher), an innovative neural network-based solution. Evaluation results demonstrate \textsc{EnCoD}'s superior performance over existing approaches across most examined file types and all considered fragment sizes. \textsc{EnCoD} achieves $86\%$ accuracy for data fragments as small as $512B$, with performance increasing to approximately $94\%$ for pure compressed data (zip, gzip) and reaching $100\%$ for compressed application data fragments (pdf, jpeg, mp3) at $8KB$ fragment sizes. This paper delivers the following key contributions: \begin{itemize} \item A comprehensive review and categorization of existing literature addressing compressed versus encrypted data fragment discrimination. \item Systematic evaluation and comparison of state-of-the-art methodologies using a large, standardized dataset incorporating diverse fragment formats and sizes. \item Introduction of a novel neural network-based approach that surpasses current leading techniques in distinguishing encrypted from compressed content across most examined formats and all considered fragment sizes. \item Development of a multi-class classifier capable of accurately labeling fragments as encrypted data, general-purpose compressed data (zip/gzip/rar), or specific application-compressed data types (png, jpeg, pdf, mp3). \item Comprehensive discussion of findings' implications regarding the practical applicability of evaluated approaches. \end{itemize}
