text: Among the most enigmatic and complex tissues, the brain governs animal motion, perception, and emotion—including our own human experiences. Despite this fundamental role, the intricate structural organization of most animal brains remains largely unexplored due to overwhelming complexity. Connectomics represents our research focus, seeking to map comprehensive connectivity networks within animal brains and thereby illuminate intelligence mechanisms while inspiring enhanced treatments for neurological disorders. Modern electron microscopy (EM) advances have recently enabled neuroscientists to acquire petabyte-scale volumetric imagery at {\em nanometer} resolution, facilitating detailed analysis of neuronal connections and subcellular components such as synapses and mitochondria~\cite{kasthuri2015saturated,xu2020connectome,shapson2021connectomic}. Microscopy image segmentation of cellular and subcellular structures typically precedes both structural~\cite{talwar2020topological} and functional~\cite{shapson2021connectomic} analyses. Computationally, segmentation tasks divide into two primary categories: {\em semantic} segmentation, which assigns class labels to individual pixels, and {\em instance} segmentation, which additionally provides object indices alongside class labels. Deep learning has emerged as the {\em de facto} standard for both semantic segmentation~\cite{chen2017deeplab} and instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask,ronneberger2015u}, delivering state-of-the-art results across natural-scene and biomedical image datasets without requiring hand-crafted features. Nevertheless, applying automated approaches to large-scale connectomics dataset segmentation presents multiple obstacles. Existing open-source segmentation tools typically target standard benchmark datasets, making adaptation to novel data with varying scales and formats time-intensive due to hardware modifications and data preprocessing requirements. Additionally, implementing specialized network architectures or alternative learning objectives for emerging tasks proves cumbersome within established frameworks. A further complication arises from most packages lacking comprehensive tutorials and documentation despite strong segmentation performance, thereby increasing the learning burden for researchers with limited programming expertise. Addressing these obstacles, we introduce {\em PyTorch Connectomics} (PyTC), an open-source deep-learning framework designed for semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy images. Built upon PyTorch~\cite{NEURIPS2019_9015}, PyTC inherits the flexibility and simplicity advantages of this state-of-the-art deep learning library. Rather than targeting specific imaging modalities, data scales, or model architectures, our framework provides versatility across diverse datasets and segmentation tasks, distinguishing it from previous specialized works such as flood-filling networks (FFN)~\cite{januszewski2018high} for neurons, StarDist~\cite{weigert2020star} for nuclei, and CleftNet~\cite{liu2021cleftnet} exclusively for synapses. Like nnU-Net~\cite{isensee2021nnu}, we identify component sets including data loaders, image augmentations, and optimizers requiring minimal cross-dataset adaptation. However, while nnU-Net addresses only semantic segmentation, our framework handles both semantic and instance segmentation. Moreover, PyTC offers substantially greater customizability than nnU-Net for addressing unique dataset and task challenges, enabling significantly superior performance (\eg, synaptic cleft segmentation). Figure~\ref{fig:teaser} demonstrates several PyTC-supported tasks. PyTC design stems from identifying connectomics researchers' primary segmentation component requirements. For data loading, we manage large datasets through automatic splitting into manageable chunks, supporting parallel and distributed processing while adapting easily to varying hardware conditions. Modeling-wise, researchers can customize 2D, 3D, or mixed architectures (for anisotropic images) and modify layer and kernel numbers based on data complexity. Models can learn multiple targets with corresponding multiple losses, enabling hybrid-representation learning to maximize annotation utilization. Furthermore, users configure data-loading, model-building, optimization, and visualization simply by modifying configuration files without coding. This design ensures experimental reproducibility while maintaining package development and maintenance friendliness. Finally, we provide comprehensive PyTC design and usage descriptions through documentation and tutorials to minimize learning curves. In summary, we present the {\em PyTorch Connectomics} framework to address volumetric microscopy image segmentation challenges through scalable and flexible data processing, modeling, and learning capabilities. We continuously enhance the framework incorporating biomedical researcher feedback and open-source contributor assistance. Current efforts integrate recent machine learning techniques including semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to effectively leverage vast unlabeled data, better supporting connectomics research experts.

And yet, the application of the method to the segmentation of large-scale connectomic data raises several problems. Existing open-source tools are usually targeted to standard benchmarks and the time-consuming adaptation to new data of varying formats and scales, because of the required hardware and the preprocessing of the data, is very costly. Despite excellent segmentation performance, most packages have no documentation or tutorials, increasing the learning curve for the researcher with little coding experience. Like nnU-Net, we identify the components of our system, which are the loaders, augmentations and optimizer, which require minimal adaptation between data. The PyTC framework, built on PyTorch, inherits the flexibility and simplicity advantages of this state-of-the-art deep learning library. Figure 2 shows several examples of tasks that can be supported by PyTc. However, while nnU-Net is only able to address the semantic task, our system also handles the instance task, allowing for far superior performance (e.g., for segmenting a synaptic cleft). PytConnect is designed on the basis of the primary needs of the segmentation required by the connectomics researcher. The architecture of the model can be adapted to 2D, 3D or hybrid images (for anisotropic images) by changing the layer and kernel numbers depending on the complexity of the data. The loading of large data can be performed by automatic splitting of the data into manageable pieces, parallel and distributed processing, easily adaptable to changing hardware conditions. Moreover, the user can easily change the configuration files of data loading, model building, optimization, and visualization without coding, which can ensure the reproducibility of experiments and ensure the convenience of developing and maintaining packages. In short, we present the PyTorch Connectomics framework which addresses the volumetric microscopy image segmentation challenge through scalable and flexible data processing, modeling, and learning capabilities. We constantly improve the framework, integrating biomedical researcher feedback and open-source contributor assistance. We provide extensive PyTC documentation and tutorials to minimize learning curves. Efforts are now under way to make the most of the enormous unlabeled data available, and to make better use of machine learning tools such as semi-supervised learning and self-supervised learning.

text: Understanding brain structure remains fundamental for elucidating both normal and pathological neural function. Recent electron microscopy (EM) developments enable three-dimensional (3D) imaging across hundreds of micrometers of tissue at nanometer resolution, opening unprecedented avenues for investigating brain ultrastructure \cite{Phelps2021ReconstructionMicroscopy, Nahirney2021}. Quantitative 3D-EM analysis—encompassing morphological ultrastructure assessment, cellular spatial distribution, and connectivity mapping—necessitates instance segmentation of individual ultrastructural elements \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy, Kleinnijenhuis2020AMicroscopy, Yuan2021HIVE-Net:Images}. Manual segmentation proves prohibitively laborious given the vast scale and component density characteristic of typical 3D-EM datasets. Manual annotation of merely 215 neurites within 500 million voxels demanded 1500 hours \cite{Berning2015}, while \revised{our estimates indicate that manual instance segmentation of axons in white matter EM containing 300 million voxels at $15 \times 15 \times 50 nm^3$ resolution would require 2400 hours} \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. Consequently, 3D-EM brain tissue analysis demands sophisticated software solutions enabling automated visualization, segmentation, and geometric-topological feature extraction of neural ultrastructures. Multiple software platforms exist for 3D-EM analysis, encompassing open-source packages like Microscopy Image Browser (MIB) \cite{Belevich2016}, DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation}, Knossos \cite{Knossos}, \revised{webKnossos \cite{Boergens2017WebKnossos:Connectomics}}, AxonSeg \cite{Zaimi2016AxonSeg:Analysis}, AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks}, TrackEM2 \cite{Cardona2012}, CATMAID \cite{Saalfeld2009}, \revised{VAST \cite{Berger2018VASTStacks}, NeuroMorph \cite{Jorstad2018NeuroMorph:Connectivity}}, SegEM \cite{Berning2015}, Ilastik \cite{ilastik}, MyelTracer \cite{Kaiser2021Myeltracer:Quantification}, alongside proprietary solutions including Amira (Thermofisher Scientific$^{ TM }$, MA, \url{www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo}) and Imaris (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK, \url{www.imaris.oxinst.com}). Table \ref{tbl:software} outlines key features of these \revised{open source} packages. Nevertheless, their segmentation capabilities primarily target manual or semi-automatic approaches, imposing substantial user workload. Supervised learning-based segmentation methods within packages like DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation} or AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks} typically demand manually annotated training datasets, creating laborious annotation requirements. Furthermore, despite excellent visualization features in some packages, they lack optimization for interactive correction, proofreading, and automatic segmentation validation. Addressing these limitations, we present a \textbf{G}raphical user interface for \textbf{A}utomati\textbf{C} \textbf{S}egmentation of ax\textbf{ON}s, termed gACSON, designed for axonal morphology analysis within large-scale 3D-EM brain datasets. This \revised{Matlab-based} platform extends our established ACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter} and DeepACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy} pipelines for 3D-EM segmentation and morphometrics, incorporating an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) alongside novel segmentation algorithms targeting myelin and intra-axonal spaces of myelinated axons. The software enables fully automatic unsupervised segmentation without requiring manually annotated training datasets. While ACSON and DeepACSON function as automated segmentation pipelines, gACSON operates as an interactive platform, offering user-friendly segmentation review and correction capabilities. \revised{The system} permits selective myelinated axon segmentation, eliminating user wait times for complete dataset processing. Crucially, \revised{this software} delivers instance segmentation of myelin with proper mapping between myelin sheaths and corresponding intra-axonal space instances. This functionality distinguishes \revised{our new platform} from existing ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. Users can visualize and review segmented ultrastructures or refine automated segmentation results through dynamic interactive merge-split operations on segmented components. Like ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines, gACSON extracts morphological parameters from segmented myelinated axons—including axonal diameter and eccentricity—while expanding morphological measurements to encompass myelin thickness and g-ratio through myelin instance segmentation. Additionally, visualization, segmentation evaluation, and automatic segmentation correction capabilities extend beyond EM to other biomedical imaging modalities, including light microscopy. This paper organization proceeds as follows: Sections \ref{seg_pip} and \ref{morph_pip} detail gACSON segmentation and morphometry pipelines, respectively. Section \ref{visualization} presents the GUI framework, including parameter configuration and tools for automatic segmentation proofreading, correction, and accuracy evaluation. Section 3 demonstrates software application for segmenting novel serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM) datasets comprising six rat somatosensory cortex volumes. These volumes and corresponding segmentations are made publicly accessible.

text: Contemporary developments in Supervised Re-Identification (re-ID) have achieved remarkable results across established public re-ID benchmarks (\cite{ye2021deep,ni2021adaptive}). Nevertheless, these models experience substantial performance degradation when evaluated cross-dataset—specifically, when applied to target contexts that differ from their training environments. Within such practical scenarios, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) has emerged as a compelling research direction for machine learning and computer vision communities, offering an alternative to expensive manual annotation of novel target datasets. The fundamental objective of UDA involves transferring learned knowledge from a source domain re-ID model to a target domain while eliminating the need for additional identity (ID) labels within the target domain. Unsupervised Domain Adaptive re-ID (UDA re-ID) methodologies address the inherent open-set characteristics of re-ID, where test-time individual classes differ from those encountered during training phases. Initial UDA re-ID research explored \emph{Domain Translation} approaches. These methodologies attempt to minimize source-target domain disparities within image space through style-transfer generative architectures (\cite{wei2018person, deng2018image, peng2019cross, zhong2018generalizing, qi2019novel}) or by imposing constraints on feature spaces to develop domain-invariant discriminative representations (\cite{chang2019disjoint, li2018adaptation, li2019cross, lin2018multi, mekhazni2020unsupervised}). However, Domain Translation-based strategies demonstrate limitations in acquiring target-specific discriminative features, thereby constraining achievable re-ID performance within target domains.\\ Contemporary UDA re-ID methodologies predominantly employ \emph{pseudo-labels} for target domain data (\cite{song2020unsupervised, zhang2019self, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep, ge2020mutual, zhai2020multiple, zhao2020unsupervised, zou2020joint,peng2020unsupervised, Zhang_2021_CVPR, Yang_2021_CVPR}). Training with target pseudo-labeled samples enables enhanced identity-discriminative representation learning within target domains. Consequently, researchers have developed diverse Pseudo-Labeling frameworks incorporating varied modeling strategies. Multiple research directions have emerged to enhance pseudo-label-based UDA re-ID approaches: certain investigations concentrate on refining predicted pseudo-labels (\cite{jiattention,zhai2020ad, tang2019unsupervised, zou2020joint, Chen_2021_CVPR, Zheng_2021_CVPR, zheng2021online, Zhang_2021_CVPR}), while others focus on mitigating pseudo-label error impacts during training phases (\cite{ge2020mutual, zhao2020unsupervised, zhai2020multiple, jin2020global, liu2020domain, fu2019self, Xuan_2021_CVPR,lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, feng2021complementary, ge2020self}). While these Pseudo-Labeling practices, embedded within specialized Pseudo-Labeling methods, demonstrate experimental performance improvements, no comprehensive theoretical framework exists to justify these practices, establish effectiveness conditions, or explain their performance enhancement mechanisms.\\ Furthermore, consensus remains elusive regarding certain practices within Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID research: a prominent example involves either leveraging (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, Isobe_2021_ICCV, dubourvieux2021improving}) or discarding (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad}) available ground-truth labeled source data for joint optimization with pseudo-labeled target data. Notably, most Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID approaches abandon source training sets (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad, song2020unsupervised, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep}) following target pseudo-label acquisition. Conversely, recent investigations (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, dubourvieux2021improving, Isobe_2021_ICCV}) demonstrate experimentally that continuous source data utilization alongside target pseudo-labeled data can enhance target domain re-ID performance. Critical questions emerge: Can source data universally improve cross-dataset re-ID performance across Pseudo-Labeling approaches? Do specific conditions exist under which Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID methods benefit from source data following target pseudo-label access? These fundamental questions remain unresolved.\\ The absence of comprehensive insights regarding these pivotal UDA re-ID questions stems from the field's predominant emphasis on empirical-oriented research. Consequently, this work addresses these questions through a comprehensive theoretical framework while identifying effective practices for designing robust Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID methods. This investigation presents three primary contributions: \begin{enumerate} \item Theoretical development to find a new upper-bound \item General good practices for Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID approaches, deduced from the theory, and therefore providing a better insight of their role in improving the cross-domain re-ID performance \item Experiments with different proposed implementations of these good practices, showing performance improvements of recent state-of-the-art methods by implementing the whole proposed good practices, on various person and vehicle cross-domain benchmarks \end{enumerate} The manuscript organization follows this structure: Sec.~\ref{sec:related} examines relevant existing literature. Sec.~\ref{sec:theory} establishes notations, concepts, and models underlying our theoretical framework. Subsequently, Sec.~\ref{sec:bound} constructs a novel upper-bound for target re-ID performance, incorporating pseudo-label errors and source data exploitation. Sec.~\ref{sec:theory_to_practice} derives insights and comprehensive good practices for enhancing UDA re-ID performance from theoretical bounds. Following experimental setting introduction and proposed good practice implementations in Sec.~\ref{sec:experiments}, Sec.~\ref{sec:results} presents extensive experiments across person and vehicle UDA re-ID benchmarks, with discussions validating performance improvements achieved through good practice implementation within Pseudo-Labeling methodologies.

text: This paper presents a policy learning framework that harnesses task-and-motion planning (TAMP) for training robot manipulation policies capable of executing long-horizon tasks. While contemporary policy learning methods demonstrate remarkable success in solving robotic control problems from complex sensory observations~\cite{Finn16, trpo, rubiks}, their effectiveness remains predominantly confined to short-horizon scenarios. The challenge of learning policies that can execute extended sequences of manipulation actions continues to pose significant difficulties~\cite{oneshothier, subpol}. In stark contrast, TAMP approaches excel at solving problems demanding dozens of abstract actions while satisfying intricate geometric constraints within high-dimensional configuration spaces~\cite{hiertamp, extendtamp}. Nevertheless, their practical deployment often faces restrictions to controlled environments, as TAMP methods require robust world state tracking and must allocate computational time for planning~\cite{garretttamp, householdmarathon}. Two distinct research directions have emerged to tackle these limitations. The first direction employs machine learning to discover policies or heuristics that minimize planning computational overhead~\cite{feasibletamp, scorespace, guidetamp, gripsqp, mctstamp, chitnis2016guided}. While this approach broadens TAMP's applicable domains, it maintains reliance on explicit state estimation mechanisms. The second research trajectory focuses on learning policies that replicate TAMP solver outputs. These methods diminish state estimation dependencies through techniques such as learning predictors for logical state grounding~\cite{dpdl} or training recurrent architectures to assess task plan feasibility~\cite{geomlearn}. Such learned policies process perceptual data directly, eliminating the need for manually engineered state estimation. However, TAMP solvers establish highly non-linear mappings between observations and controls, creating substantial imitation learning challenges. Additionally, the computational demands of planning constrain the volume of training data available for learning algorithms. Our work synthesizes insights from both research directions. Drawing inspiration from guided expert imitation methodologies~\cite{GPS, grp}, we develop feed-forward policies that imitate TAMP behavior. Our central contribution lies in recognizing that \citet{tamp2014}'s modular TAMP framework enables a distributed TAMP architecture featuring three key properties: 1) optimization for throughput rather than low latency (the conventional emphasis in TAMP research); 2) policy training to replicate planner outputs; and 3) utilization of these policies to amortize planning costs across multiple problems. This creates a beneficial feedback loop wherein learning accelerates planning performance, while enhanced planning speed generates additional supervisory signals. We introduce a policy architecture that exploits TAMP domain definitions to enhance learning effectiveness. Our system's task plans provide supervision for a task-level model that learns to predict parameterized actions. This output mechanism selects from and configures a collection of control networks, with each network corresponding to a specific action schema. We demonstrate that this architecture successfully executes manipulation skills within high-dimensional environments using complex sensory inputs. Consequently, our approach compiles task and motion planning into a unified feed-forward policy. This work makes three primary contributions: 1) we present a distributed, asynchronous, high-throughput task and motion planning system design that exploits policy learning to accelerate planning; 2) we propose a hierarchical policy architecture that capitalizes on TAMP problem specifications; and 3) we implement and evaluate this methodology, demonstrating its capacity to learn multi-goal accomplishment over extended horizons using high-dimensional sensory data and action spaces. In a 2D pick-place domain, our trained policies achieve precise placement of 3 objects onto targets with 83\% success from RGB imagery. Within the RoboSuite~\cite{robosuite2020} pick-place benchmark, we train policies for 7-DoF joint control that successfully place 4 objects 88\% of the time using object pose vectors. In the multitask RoboDesk benchmark, our learned policy maintains a 79\% average success rate across 9 diverse tasks employing 7-DoF joint control from RGB observations.

text: The neurological basis for human ability to link voices with faces stems from shared neuro-cognitive pathways that process both modalities using identical structural frameworks~\cite{kamachi2003putting,belin2004thinking}. This well-established phenomenon inspired Nagrani et al.~\cite{nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2017voxceleb} to pioneer the face-voice association challenge within computer vision, developing a comprehensive audio-visual dataset containing faces and voices from $1,251$ celebrities. This foundational work has catalyzed substantial research momentum in face-voice association~\cite{horiguchi2018face,kim2018learning,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2018seeing,nawaz2019deep,wen2021seeking,wen2018disjoint}, while simultaneously spurring development of specialized audio-visual datasets. Notably, Nawaz et al.~\cite{nawaz2021cross} constructed the Multilingual Audio-Visual (\textit{MAV-Celeb}) dataset to investigate linguistic influences on face-voice matching, incorporating multilingual recordings from various celebrities. Contemporary approaches~\cite{kim2018learning,nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nawaz2021cross} predominantly frame face-voice association as cross-modal biometric identification. Two fundamental obstacles emerge when developing robust methodologies: establishing a unified discriminative embedding space where cross-modal instances achieve proper alignment while maintaining proximity for semantically related identities. Standard practice employs dedicated networks for each modality to extract feature representations, subsequently applying contrastive or triplet loss functions to construct the embedding space. Despite demonstrating reasonable performance, these loss formulations impose several limitations. Margin hyperparameter tuning proves challenging since inter-instance distances fluctuate dramatically throughout training. Additionally, computational complexity scales poorly—contrastive losses require $\mathcal{O} (n^2)$ operations while triplet losses demand $\mathcal{O} (n^3)$ complexity, where $n$ represents the instance count per modality. Addressing these computational burdens necessitates sophisticated negative mining strategies that consume significant time while remaining highly sensitive to performance variations. Alternative approaches, exemplified by \cite{nawaz2019deep}, substitute contrastive/triplet formulations with auxiliary identity centroids~\cite{wen2016discriminative}. Training alternates between two phases: clustering embeddings around corresponding identity centroids while repelling them from competing centroids, then updating centroids using mini-batch samples. These centroid-based losses typically combine with conventional classification objectives (softmax cross-entropy). Nevertheless, this combination lacks theoretical coherence since centroid methods enforce Euclidean margins while classification losses implicitly achieve angular separability. We propose that constructing discriminative joint embedding spaces for enhanced face-voice association requires enriched unified representations that capture complementary information across modalities, paired with computationally efficient supervision mechanisms. Our approach introduces a lightweight, modular component that leverages cross-modal strengths through fusion while semantically aligning merged embeddings with identity labels using orthogonality constraints. This mechanism integrates seamlessly into two-stream architectures that generate face and voice embeddings, yielding an effective framework for face-voice matching and verification applications. Our primary contributions include: 1) Exploiting complementary cross-modal features to construct enriched embeddings that maintain semantic consistency with identity information, enabling superior identity recognition performance. 2) Introducing orthogonality constraints for fused embeddings that align naturally with angular properties of standard classification losses while maintaining computational efficiency through direct mini-batch operations. 3) Demonstrating superior performance on large-scale VoxCeleb~\cite{nagrani2017voxceleb} across face-voice verification and matching benchmarks, with favorable comparisons against existing state-of-the-art approaches. 4) Conducting comprehensive ablation studies examining individual component contributions.

text: Among the most prevalent image processing operators across computational photography applications are edge-aware filters. These \emph{edge-preserving smoothing} operators constitute a fundamental component in numerous image manipulation algorithms, spanning tonemapping, image abstraction, detail enhancement, texture removal, and beyond. Their widespread adoption stems from their apparent capacity to distinguish salient, structure-defining edges within images and handle them distinctly from other image details and discontinuities. The literature has witnessed the introduction of numerous edge-preserving smoothing operators throughout the past decade. While some target specific applications—such as texture removal or multiscale detail manipulation—others lack explicitly stated objectives. Section \ref{sec-smoothing-operators} provides concrete examples of these methods. These operators exhibit considerable variation across multiple dimensions: visual aesthetics, algorithmic foundations (including local versus global approaches), parameter complexity (ranging from single to multiple parameters), and computational demands (spanning seconds to minutes). Such distinctions may remain obscure to users with limited familiarity with these techniques, rendering the selection of appropriate operators for particular purposes or images—along with parameter tuning—remarkably challenging. Researchers introducing novel filters conventionally present side-by-side visual comparisons with existing operators. For meaningful comparison, images must undergo processing to an \emph{equivalent degree} across different operators. Nevertheless, each operator employs distinct parameters, and no standardized parameter mapping exists between methods. This challenge intensifies because parameter effects on results often depend on input characteristics, and parameter relationships may shift across smoothing intensities within individual methods. Consequently, authors typically select parameters subjectively through trial-and-error processes. Selecting comparison methods presents additional complexity. Optimal comparisons should encompass methods both algorithmically related to the proposed approach and representing fundamentally different paradigms. The primary intended applications of competing methods warrant consideration. While universal benchmarks would benefit all comparisons, none exist in practice; moreover, different images are frequently employed when comparing proposed methods against distinct existing competitors. This paper introduces a novel methodology for evaluating and comparing edge-preserving smoothing operators through more meaningful, objective, and quantitative approaches. We present a mechanism for achieving approximately equivalent smoothing intensities across different operators, effectively establishing per-image parameter mappings between their primary controlling parameters. With such mappings established, we can quantitatively assess various operator characteristics. This framework yields insights into operator behavior patterns and enables more meaningful comparisons, both visual and quantitative. Additionally, we demonstrate operator clustering based on effect similarity using purely empirical observations. Our findings regarding intrinsic method behaviors inform specific recommendations for both developers and end-users of such operators. The paper proceeds as follows: Section~\ref{sec-background} examines existing approaches for tonemapping operator comparison and previous comparative surveys of edge-preserving filters. Section~\ref{sec-methods} initially catalogs the filters selected to demonstrate our comparative methodology for smoothing operators, then presents the methodology itself. Section~\ref{sec-results} illustrates our methodology's application to the chosen operator set. Section~\ref{sec-conclusions} concludes with discussion and future research directions.

text: Machine learning systems struggle to learn predictors that are robust to distribution shift. This fundamental challenge arises because traditional machine learning algorithms are designed to minimize empirical risk on training data, under the implicit assumption that test data will be drawn from the same distribution. However, in real-world deployments, this assumption frequently fails due to various factors including temporal changes, geographical variations, population shifts, and differences in data collection procedures \cite{quinonero2009dataset, koh2021wilds}. The problem of distribution shift manifests in multiple forms. \textit{Covariate shift} occurs when the marginal distribution of input features changes while the conditional distribution of labels given features remains constant \cite{shimodaira2000improving}. \textit{Label shift} involves changes in the label distribution while maintaining constant feature distributions within each class \cite{zhang2013domain}. More challenging is \textit{concept drift}, where the fundamental relationship between inputs and outputs evolves over time \cite{webb2016characterizing}. Additionally, \textit{subpopulation shift} emerges when the relative proportions of different subgroups in the data change, potentially exposing models to previously underrepresented populations \cite{sagawa2019distributionally}. Recent empirical studies have demonstrated the pervasiveness and severity of this issue across diverse domains. In computer vision, models trained on standard benchmarks like ImageNet exhibit substantial performance degradation when evaluated on natural distribution shifts such as changes in lighting conditions, camera angles, or image corruption \cite{hendrycks2019benchmarking, recht2019imagenet}. Similarly, natural language processing models show brittleness when deployed on text from different domains, time periods, or demographic groups than those represented in training data \cite{blitzer2006domain, koh2021wilds}. The healthcare domain presents particularly concerning examples of distribution shift vulnerabilities. Medical imaging models trained on data from specific hospitals or patient populations often fail to generalize to new clinical settings, potentially leading to misdiagnoses and compromised patient safety \cite{zech2018variable, larrazabal2020gender}. These failures highlight the critical need for robust machine learning approaches that can maintain reliable performance across diverse deployment scenarios. Traditional approaches to addressing distribution shift have focused on domain adaptation and transfer learning techniques \cite{pan2009survey}. These methods typically assume access to unlabeled data from the target distribution during training, enabling algorithms to learn domain-invariant representations or adapt existing models to new domains. However, such approaches have limited applicability when target distributions are unknown at training time or when multiple potential shifts may occur during deployment. More recent work has explored distributionally robust optimization (DRO) as a principled framework for learning models that perform well across a family of related distributions \cite{ben2013robust, duchi2021statistics}. DRO formulations seek to minimize the worst-case expected loss over an uncertainty set of distributions, providing theoretical guarantees on out-of-distribution performance. However, the choice of uncertainty set and the computational complexity of solving DRO problems remain significant challenges in practice. Invariant risk minimization (IRM) represents another promising direction, aiming to learn predictors that rely only on stable, causal relationships between features and labels \cite{arjovsky2019invariant}. The core insight is that truly causal relationships should remain invariant across different environments, while spurious correlations may vary. By encouraging models to learn invariant predictors across multiple training environments, IRM seeks to improve generalization to unseen distributions. Data augmentation strategies have also gained attention as a means of improving robustness to distribution shift. Techniques such as adversarial training \cite{goodfellow2014explaining}, mixup \cite{zhang2017mixup}, and domain randomization \cite{tobin2017domain} artificially expand the training distribution to cover a broader range of potential test conditions. While these approaches can improve robustness in some settings, they require careful design of augmentation strategies and may not capture all relevant forms of distribution shift. Ensemble methods offer another avenue for enhancing robustness by combining predictions from multiple diverse models \cite{lakshminarayanan2017simple}. The intuition is that different models may capture complementary aspects of the underlying relationship between inputs and outputs, leading to more reliable predictions when combined. Deep ensembles, in particular, have shown promise in improving both predictive performance and uncertainty estimation under distribution shift \cite{ovadia2019can}. The field has also witnessed growing interest in meta-learning approaches that explicitly optimize for adaptation to new distributions \cite{finn2017model, nichol2018first}. These methods learn initialization parameters or update rules that enable rapid adaptation to new tasks or domains with minimal additional data. While primarily developed for few-shot learning scenarios, meta-learning techniques show potential for addressing certain types of distribution shift. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in developing truly robust machine learning systems. The fundamental tension between fitting training data well and generalizing to shifted distributions continues to pose difficulties. Moreover, the evaluation of robustness methods remains challenging due to the difficulty of characterizing all possible distribution shifts that may occur in practice. Recent benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols have begun to address this challenge by providing standardized testbeds for distribution shift \cite{koh2021wilds, gulrajani2020search}. These resources enable systematic comparison of different approaches and highlight the gap between current methods and the level of robustness required for reliable real-world deployment. The importance of this research area continues to grow as machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications where robustness to distribution shift is crucial for safety, fairness, and reliability. Understanding and addressing these challenges remains one of the most pressing problems in modern machine learning research.

text: Reconfiguration problems encompass a large family of problems in which we need to provide a sequence of steps to transform one object into another. These problems have gained significant attention in recent years due to their theoretical richness and practical applications across various domains, including robotics, computational geometry, and algorithm design \cite{nishimura2018introduction}. In the context of reconfiguration, we typically consider a \emph{configuration space} consisting of all valid states or arrangements of a given system, along with a set of \emph{reconfiguration rules} that define which transitions between configurations are permissible. The fundamental question is whether there exists a sequence of valid moves that transforms an initial configuration into a target configuration, and if so, to find such a sequence efficiently. One of the most well-studied reconfiguration problems is the \emph{Token Swapping} problem, where we have a set of tokens placed on vertices of a graph, and we want to rearrange them to achieve a desired configuration by swapping adjacent tokens \cite{yamanaka2019swapping}. Another prominent example is \emph{Graph Coloring Reconfiguration}, where we seek to transform one proper coloring of a graph into another through a sequence of recoloring operations that maintain the validity of the coloring at each step \cite{bonamy2012recoloring}. The complexity landscape of reconfiguration problems is remarkably diverse. While some instances admit polynomial-time algorithms, many variants are PSPACE-complete, reflecting the inherent difficulty of reasoning about exponentially long sequences of moves \cite{hearn2009pspace}. This complexity often arises from the need to explore large state spaces while ensuring that intermediate configurations satisfy all required constraints. Reconfiguration problems also exhibit fascinating connections to other areas of theoretical computer science. For instance, the reachability question in configuration spaces relates closely to problems in computational topology and homotopy theory \cite{farber2003topological}. Moreover, these problems have inspired the development of new algorithmic techniques, including specialized graph algorithms for exploring reconfiguration graphs and approximation methods for handling intractable instances. From a practical perspective, reconfiguration problems model real-world scenarios such as robot motion planning, where a robot must navigate from one position to another while avoiding obstacles and satisfying kinematic constraints \cite{lavalle2006planning}. Similarly, in network optimization, reconfiguration techniques help in dynamically adjusting network topologies to maintain connectivity while optimizing performance metrics. The study of reconfiguration has also led to the identification of important structural properties that influence problem difficulty. Parameters such as the diameter of the reconfiguration graph, the presence of forbidden substructures, and the connectivity properties of the configuration space all play crucial roles in determining algorithmic approaches and complexity bounds \cite{ito2011complexity}. Recent research has focused on parameterized complexity analysis, seeking to identify problem parameters that allow for fixed-parameter tractable algorithms. This approach has proven particularly fruitful for problems where the solution length or certain graph parameters can be bounded \cite{mouawad2017graph}.

text: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) is the art and science of automatic identification of speech. Speech commands recognition (SCR) is a specialized subset of ASR that focuses on recognizing and interpreting specific spoken commands or keywords rather than continuous speech transcription. Unlike traditional ASR systems that aim to convert entire spoken utterances into text, SCR systems are designed to detect predefined voice commands that can trigger specific actions or responses in various applications \cite{hinton2012deep, graves2013speech}. The fundamental distinction between general ASR and SCR lies in their operational scope and accuracy requirements. While ASR systems must handle diverse vocabularies, complex sentence structures, and natural language variations, SCR systems typically operate with a limited set of predetermined commands, allowing for more focused optimization and higher accuracy within their constrained domain \cite{yu2016automatic, li2017jasper}. This specialization makes SCR particularly suitable for applications such as voice-controlled smart devices, automotive systems, and hands-free computing interfaces where reliability and low-latency response are critical. Modern SCR systems face several significant challenges that distinguish them from their ASR counterparts. First, the need for real-time processing with minimal computational overhead is paramount, as many SCR applications run on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones, embedded systems, or Internet of Things (IoT) devices \cite{chen2014small, sainath2015learning}. Second, robustness to environmental noise, speaker variability, and acoustic conditions is essential since voice commands are often issued in uncontrolled environments. Third, the system must maintain high precision to minimize false activations while ensuring sufficient recall to capture legitimate commands reliably. The evolution of SCR technology has been closely intertwined with advances in machine learning and signal processing. Early SCR systems relied heavily on traditional pattern recognition techniques, including Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), combined with hand-crafted acoustic features such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) \cite{rabiner1989tutorial, reynolds1995robust}. These approaches, while effective for simple command sets, struggled with speaker variability and environmental robustness. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized SCR systems, enabling more sophisticated feature learning and pattern recognition capabilities. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have proven particularly effective for SCR tasks due to their ability to capture local temporal and spectral patterns in audio signals \cite{abdel2014convolutional, sainath2013deep}. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architectures, have demonstrated superior performance in modeling temporal dependencies inherent in speech signals \cite{graves2005framewise, chung2014empirical}. Recent developments have introduced attention mechanisms and transformer architectures to SCR, allowing models to focus selectively on relevant portions of the input signal and capture long-range dependencies more effectively \cite{vaswani2017attention, dong2018speech}. These architectural innovations have led to significant improvements in recognition accuracy and robustness across diverse acoustic conditions. One of the most critical aspects of SCR system design is the trade-off between model complexity and computational efficiency. Many SCR applications require real-time operation on devices with limited processing power and memory constraints. This has driven research into model compression techniques, including knowledge distillation, pruning, and quantization, which aim to maintain recognition performance while reducing computational requirements \cite{hinton2015distilling, han2015deep}. Additionally, specialized architectures designed specifically for edge computing, such as MobileNets and EfficientNets, have been adapted for SCR applications \cite{howard2017mobilenets, tan2019efficientnet}. The evaluation of SCR systems presents unique challenges compared to traditional ASR evaluation. Standard metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, but SCR-specific considerations such as false wake-up rates, response latency, and robustness to out-of-vocabulary utterances are equally important \cite{warden2018speech}. Furthermore, the evaluation must account for real-world deployment scenarios, including varying noise conditions, speaker demographics, and acoustic environments. Dataset availability and quality significantly impact SCR system development. While large-scale ASR datasets like LibriSpeech and Common Voice provide extensive training data for general speech recognition, SCR-specific datasets are often smaller and more specialized \cite{panayotov2015librispeech, ardila2019common}. Notable SCR datasets include the Google Speech Commands dataset, which contains short utterances of common commands, and various wake word detection datasets that focus on specific activation phrases \cite{warden2018speech}. The integration of SCR systems into practical applications introduces additional considerations beyond core recognition performance. Privacy concerns have become increasingly important as voice-controlled devices become ubiquitous in homes and workplaces. This has led to the development of on-device processing capabilities and federated learning approaches that minimize the transmission of sensitive audio data to cloud servers \cite{mcmahan2017communication, hard2018federated}. Another emerging area of research focuses on personalization and adaptation of SCR systems to individual users. Speaker adaptation techniques allow systems to improve performance for specific users over time, while multi-speaker models aim to maintain consistent performance across diverse user populations \cite{li2010comparison, senior2014improving}. These approaches must balance personalization benefits with privacy protection and system complexity. The future of SCR technology is being shaped by several key trends and research directions. Multimodal approaches that combine audio with visual or contextual information promise to improve robustness and accuracy \cite{ngiam2011multimodal}. Edge AI developments are enabling more sophisticated processing capabilities on resource-constrained devices, while advances in self-supervised learning are reducing dependence on large labeled datasets \cite{oord2018representation, baevski2020wav2vec}. As SCR systems become increasingly prevalent in everyday applications, ensuring fairness and inclusivity across diverse user populations has become a critical research priority. This includes addressing performance disparities across different accents, languages, age groups, and speech characteristics to ensure equitable access to voice-controlled technologies \cite{tatman2017gender, koenecke2020racial}.

text: The use of robotic surgery has increased in the recent years. Robotic surgical consoles such as the da Vinci\textsuperscript{\textregistered} Surgical System~\cite{guthart2000intuitive} developed by Intuitive Surgical Inc. have revolutionized minimally invasive surgery by providing surgeons with enhanced precision, dexterity, and visualization capabilities. These systems offer three-dimensional high-definition vision, tremor filtration, and intuitive hand-eye coordination through master-slave manipulation~\cite{lanfranco2004robotic}. The da Vinci system has been successfully implemented across various surgical specialties, including urology, gynecology, cardiothoracic surgery, and general surgery~\cite{ruurda2002robot}. Despite the significant advantages offered by robotic surgical platforms, several challenges persist in their widespread adoption and optimization. One primary concern is the steep learning curve associated with robotic surgery training~\cite{hernandez2004learning}. Surgeons must acquire new skills to effectively operate through the robotic interface, which differs substantially from traditional laparoscopic or open surgical techniques. The haptic feedback limitations in current robotic systems also present challenges, as surgeons rely heavily on visual cues rather than tactile sensation during procedures~\cite{okamura2004haptic}. Furthermore, the economic implications of robotic surgery implementation remain a subject of ongoing debate. The initial capital investment for robotic surgical systems is substantial, with costs exceeding \$2 million per unit, in addition to ongoing maintenance expenses and specialized instrument costs~\cite{barbash2010new}. Healthcare institutions must carefully evaluate the cost-effectiveness of robotic surgery programs while considering patient outcomes, surgical efficiency, and long-term financial sustainability. Recent technological advances have focused on addressing these limitations through improved training simulators, enhanced haptic feedback systems, and the development of next-generation robotic platforms. Virtual reality-based training modules have shown promise in accelerating the learning process for novice robotic surgeons~\cite{seymour2002virtual}. Additionally, research into force feedback mechanisms and tactile sensing technologies aims to restore the sense of touch that is crucial for delicate surgical maneuvers~\cite{bethea2004application}. The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms into robotic surgical systems represents an emerging frontier with significant potential for improving surgical outcomes~\cite{shademan2016supervised}. These technologies may enable autonomous suturing, tissue recognition, and real-time surgical guidance, ultimately enhancing the precision and safety of robotic procedures.

text: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition has drawn significant interest for its essential role in scene understanding. HOI recognition aims to retrieve multiple \textit{$<$verb, object$>$} pairs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}. , ``hold, apple'') from a single image containing human subjects. This task is fundamental to comprehensive scene understanding and has numerous applications in robotics, autonomous systems, surveillance, and human-computer interaction. Traditional approaches to HOI recognition have primarily relied on hand-crafted features and conventional machine learning techniques \cite{chao2015hico, gkioxari2018detecting}. These methods typically decompose the problem into multiple stages: human detection, object detection, and interaction classification. However, such pipeline-based approaches suffer from error propagation, where mistakes in early stages compound throughout the system, leading to suboptimal performance. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized HOI recognition by enabling end-to-end learning frameworks that can jointly optimize all components of the recognition pipeline \cite{li2019transferable, wang2020learning}. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in capturing spatial relationships between humans and objects, while recent transformer-based architectures have shown promise in modeling long-range dependencies and complex interactions \cite{kim2020hotr, chen2021qpic}. Despite these advances, HOI recognition remains challenging due to several inherent difficulties. First, the combinatorial nature of human-object interactions leads to an exponentially large space of possible \textit{$<$human, verb, object$>$} triplets. Second, visual ambiguity often exists where similar poses or spatial configurations can correspond to different interactions depending on context. For instance, a person near a bicycle could be ``riding,'' ``pushing,'' or ``repairing'' it, requiring sophisticated reasoning beyond mere spatial proximity. Furthermore, the distribution of HOI instances in real-world datasets is heavily imbalanced, with common interactions like ``hold person'' or ``sit chair'' appearing frequently while rare interactions such as ``cut cake'' or ``fly kite'' occur infrequently \cite{chao2018learning}. This imbalance poses significant challenges for training robust models that can generalize to uncommon but important interactions. Recent research has explored various strategies to address these challenges. Graph-based methods model the relationships between humans, objects, and their interactions as structured representations, enabling more sophisticated reasoning about complex scenes \cite{qi2018learning, ulutan2020vsgnet}. Attention mechanisms have been employed to focus on relevant image regions and filter out irrelevant background information \cite{gao2018ican, wang2019deep}. Additionally, multi-scale feature fusion approaches attempt to capture interactions at different levels of granularity, from fine-grained hand-object contacts to broader spatial arrangements \cite{liao2020ppdm, zhang2021spatially}. The evaluation of HOI recognition systems typically employs mean Average Precision (mAP) metrics computed over different interaction categories. Standard benchmarks such as HICO-DET \cite{chao2015hico} and V-COCO \cite{gupta2015visual} provide comprehensive evaluation protocols, though they also highlight the performance gaps that exist between current methods and human-level understanding. Context modeling has emerged as a crucial component for improving HOI recognition accuracy. Environmental context, such as scene type and object co-occurrence patterns, provides valuable cues for disambiguation. For example, the presence of a kitchen setting increases the likelihood of food-related interactions, while outdoor scenes may favor sports or recreational activities \cite{mallya2016learning, bansal2020detecting}. Another significant research direction involves leveraging external knowledge sources to enhance interaction understanding. Knowledge graphs and semantic embeddings can provide prior information about plausible human-object interactions, helping models reason about unseen or rare combinations \cite{shen2018scaling, peyre2019detecting}. This approach is particularly valuable for zero-shot and few-shot learning scenarios where training data for specific interactions may be limited. The integration of temporal information has also gained attention, particularly for video-based HOI recognition. Sequential modeling allows systems to capture the dynamics of interactions over time, providing richer understanding than single-frame analysis \cite{girdhar2018better, ji2020action}. However, this introduces additional computational complexity and requires careful design of temporal aggregation mechanisms. Current state-of-the-art methods increasingly adopt unified frameworks that jointly address human detection, object detection, and interaction classification within a single neural network architecture. These end-to-end approaches have demonstrated superior performance compared to multi-stage pipelines, though they require careful design of loss functions and training strategies to balance the different subtasks effectively \cite{liao2022gen}.

text: Pretraining large neural networks with a language modeling objective has led to significant improvements throughout NLP \citep[][\emph{i.a.}]{peters2018deep,howard2018universal,radford2018improving,devlin2018bert,raffel2019exploring,brown2020language}. These models, commonly referred to as foundation models or large language models (LLMs), have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks including text classification, question answering, machine translation, and text generation \citep{bommasani2021opportunities,qiu2020pre}. The success of these approaches has fundamentally shifted the paradigm in natural language processing from task-specific architectures to general-purpose models that can be fine-tuned or prompted for downstream applications. The transformer architecture \citep{vaswani2017attention} has emerged as the dominant framework for these large-scale models, with variants such as BERT \citep{devlin2018bert} employing bidirectional encoding for understanding tasks, and GPT-style models \citep{radford2018improving,radford2019language,brown2020language} utilizing autoregressive generation for both understanding and generation capabilities. More recent developments have explored unified architectures that combine the strengths of both approaches \citep{raffel2019exploring,lewis2019bart}. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges remain in the development and deployment of large language models. First, the computational requirements for training these models have grown exponentially, with state-of-the-art models requiring thousands of GPUs and enormous datasets \citep{kaplan2020scaling,hoffmann2022training}. This has led to concerns about the environmental impact and accessibility of such models \citep{strubell2019energy,bender2021dangers}. Second, while these models demonstrate impressive performance on many benchmarks, they often exhibit concerning behaviors including factual inconsistencies, reasoning failures, and the generation of biased or harmful content \citep{bender2021dangers,bommasani2021opportunities}. Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying the success of large-scale pretraining remain poorly understood. text: News curation is the complex activity of selecting and prioritizing information based on some criteria of relevance and in regards to limitations of time and space. Traditional news curation has been the domain of professional journalists and editors who apply their expertise, editorial judgment, and understanding of audience needs to filter the vast stream of information into coherent, digestible narratives \cite{Gans1979, Tuchman1978}. However, the digital revolution has fundamentally transformed this landscape, introducing new actors, mechanisms, and challenges that reshape how news is selected, prioritized, and distributed to audiences worldwide. The emergence of social media platforms, algorithmic recommendation systems, and user-generated content has democratized the curation process while simultaneously complicating it \cite{Hermida2010, Bruns2018}. Where once a relatively small number of gatekeepers controlled information flow, we now witness a complex ecosystem where algorithms, social networks, and individual users all participate in determining what information reaches public attention \cite{Bozdag2013, Gillespie2014}. This shift has created unprecedented opportunities for diverse voices and perspectives to emerge, but it has also introduced new forms of bias, misinformation, and information fragmentation \cite{Pariser2011, Sunstein2017}. Contemporary news curation operates within multiple interconnected layers of selection and filtering. At the production level, journalists and news organizations continue to make editorial decisions about which stories to cover and how to frame them \cite{McCombs2014}. However, these decisions are increasingly influenced by metrics of audience engagement, social media virality, and algorithmic optimization rather than traditional newsworthiness criteria \cite{Tandoc2017, Carlson2018}. The temporal constraints of the digital news cycle have intensified, with organizations facing pressure to publish rapidly and continuously update their coverage to maintain relevance in an attention economy \cite{Rosenberg2009, Usher2014}. Algorithmic curation represents a particularly significant development in this evolution. Platforms such as Google News, Facebook, and Twitter employ sophisticated machine learning algorithms to personalize news feeds based on user behavior, preferences, and social connections \cite{Diakopoulos2015, Thurman2019}. These systems can process vast quantities of information and identify patterns that human curators might miss, potentially improving the relevance and timeliness of news delivery \cite{Monzer2020}. However, algorithmic curation also raises concerns about transparency, accountability, and the potential for creating filter bubbles that limit exposure to diverse viewpoints \cite{Zuiderveen2016, Haim2018}. The criteria for relevance in news curation have become increasingly complex and context-dependent. Traditional factors such as proximity, timeliness, prominence, and human interest remain important, but they now compete with metrics derived from user engagement, social sharing patterns, and algorithmic predictions of reader interest \cite{Harcup2017, Welbers2016}. This multiplicity of relevance criteria can lead to tensions between professional journalistic values and audience-driven metrics, potentially affecting the quality and diversity of news coverage \cite{Ferrer2019, Vos2018}. Spatial and temporal limitations continue to shape curation decisions, though their nature has evolved significantly. While digital platforms theoretically offer unlimited space for content, practical constraints emerge from attention economics and interface design \cite{Webster2014}. The challenge is no longer simply fitting stories into a fixed newspaper layout or broadcast schedule, but rather competing for user attention in an environment of information abundance \cite{Simon1971, Lanham2006}. Temporal constraints have intensified with the expectation of real-time updates and continuous news cycles, forcing curators to make rapid decisions with potentially incomplete information \cite{Lewis2013, Eldridge2019}. The democratization of curation through social media has introduced new dynamics where ordinary users become active participants in the news selection process. Through sharing, commenting, and engaging with content, audiences collectively influence which stories gain prominence and how they are interpreted \cite{Hermida2014, Papacharissi2015}. This participatory dimension of curation can enhance democratic discourse by amplifying marginalized voices and enabling grassroots agenda-setting, but it can also facilitate the spread of misinformation and contribute to polarization \cite{Benkler2018, Tucker2018}. Cross-platform curation presents additional challenges as news organizations must adapt their content for multiple channels with different affordances, audience expectations, and algorithmic requirements \cite{Molyneux2018, Tandoc2018}. A story that performs well on Twitter may require different framing for Facebook or LinkedIn, leading to questions about editorial consistency and the fragmentation of news narratives across platforms \cite{Duffy2018, Caplan2018}. The international dimension of news curation has also been transformed by digital technologies. Global events can now be covered and curated by local actors worldwide, challenging traditional hierarchies of international news flow \cite{Archetti2008, Cottle2009}. However, this globalization of curation also raises questions about cultural sensitivity, local context, and the potential for misinterpretation when stories cross cultural and linguistic boundaries \cite{Robertson2015, Paterson2011}. Quality assessment in contemporary news curation involves balancing multiple, sometimes competing objectives: accuracy, timeliness, relevance, diversity, and engagement \cite{Christians2009, Kovach2007}. The speed of digital publishing can compromise fact-checking and verification processes, while the pressure for engagement may incentivize sensationalism over substantive reporting \cite{Karlsson2011, Phillips2015}. These tensions highlight the ongoing importance of professional editorial judgment even in an increasingly automated media landscape.

text: Statistical power is quantitatively equal to the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis. Statistical power is quantitatively equal to the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis when it is indeed false, representing one of the most fundamental concepts in inferential statistics \cite{cohen1988statistical}. This probability, typically denoted as $1-\beta$ where $\beta$ represents the Type II error rate, serves as a critical measure for evaluating the effectiveness of statistical tests and experimental designs \cite{neyman1933problem}. The concept of statistical power emerged from the foundational work of Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in the 1920s and 1930s, who developed the theoretical framework for hypothesis testing that remains central to modern statistical practice \cite{neyman1928use}. Their contributions established the dual nature of statistical inference errors: Type I errors ($\alpha$), representing false positives, and Type II errors ($\beta$), representing false negatives. The complement of the Type II error rate, $1-\beta$, thus defines the power of a statistical test. Mathematically, statistical power can be expressed as: \begin{equation} \text{Power} = P(\text{Reject } H_0 | H_1 \text{ is true}) = 1 - \beta \end{equation} where $H_0$ denotes the null hypothesis and $H_1$ represents the alternative hypothesis \cite{lehmann2005testing}. This formulation highlights that power is inherently conditional on the truth of the alternative hypothesis, making it a function of the actual effect size present in the population. The importance of statistical power extends beyond theoretical considerations to practical research applications. Adequate power ensures that studies can detect meaningful effects when they exist, thereby reducing the likelihood of false negative conclusions that may impede scientific progress \cite{button2013power}. Conversely, underpowered studies contribute to the replication crisis in various fields by failing to detect true effects, leading to inconsistent findings across research endeavors \cite{ioannidis2005most}. Several factors influence statistical power, creating a complex interplay that researchers must navigate when designing studies. The primary determinants include: (1) the effect size, representing the magnitude of the difference or relationship being investigated; (2) the sample size, which directly affects the precision of statistical estimates; (3) the significance level ($\alpha$), typically set at 0.05 in most research contexts; and (4) the variability in the data, often measured through standard deviations or error terms \cite{faul2007gpower}. The relationship between these factors can be expressed through power functions specific to different statistical tests. For a two-sample t-test, power is given by: \begin{equation} \text{Power} = \Phi\left(\frac{\delta\sqrt{n/2} - z_{\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{1}}\right) \end{equation} where $\Phi$ represents the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution, $\delta$ is the standardized effect size, $n$ is the total sample size, and $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the critical value for the chosen significance level \cite{cohen1977statistical}. Contemporary research increasingly emphasizes the importance of conducting power analyses both prospectively and retrospectively. Prospective power analysis, performed during the study design phase, helps determine appropriate sample sizes to achieve desired power levels, typically 0.80 or higher \cite{cohen1992quantitative}. This approach ensures that studies are adequately equipped to detect effects of practical significance while optimizing resource allocation. Retrospective power analysis, while more controversial, involves calculating the power of completed studies based on observed effect sizes \cite{hoenig2001abuse}. Critics argue that such analyses can be misleading since they are inherently tied to the statistical significance of results, potentially creating circular reasoning. Nevertheless, retrospective power calculations can provide valuable insights into the interpretability of null findings and inform future research directions. The advent of sophisticated statistical software has democratized power analysis, making complex calculations accessible to researchers across disciplines. Programs such as G*Power \cite{faul2009statistical}, R packages like \texttt{pwr} \cite{champely2020pwr}, and specialized modules in comprehensive statistical suites enable researchers to conduct detailed power analyses for various experimental designs and statistical tests. Modern applications of power analysis extend beyond traditional null hypothesis significance testing to encompass Bayesian approaches, equivalence testing, and meta-analytic frameworks \cite{kruschke2018bayesian}. These developments reflect the evolving landscape of statistical methodology and the growing recognition that different research questions may require different approaches to power consideration.

text: Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) techniques provide navigational maps that enable robots to autonomously explore an environment, while emerging Semantic Mapping techniques add semantic information about locations and objects within these environments. Traditional SLAM approaches focus primarily on geometric reconstruction, creating metric maps that represent the spatial structure of the environment through point clouds, occupancy grids, or feature-based representations \cite{durrant2006simultaneous, thrun2002robotic}. However, these geometric maps lack the semantic understanding necessary for high-level robot reasoning and human-robot interaction. Semantic mapping extends traditional SLAM by incorporating object recognition, scene understanding, and semantic labeling into the mapping process \cite{kostavelis2015semantic, cadena2016past}. This integration enables robots to not only understand where they are and what the environment looks like geometrically, but also to comprehend what objects are present, their semantic categories, and their functional relationships within the environment. Such semantic understanding is crucial for applications ranging from domestic service robots to autonomous vehicles operating in complex urban environments. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures, have significantly enhanced the capability of semantic mapping systems \cite{mccormac2017semanticfusion, bowman2017probabilistic}. These methods can simultaneously perform dense semantic segmentation while maintaining real-time performance requirements for robotic applications. The integration of RGB-D sensors has further accelerated progress by providing both visual and depth information, enabling more robust semantic understanding and geometric reconstruction \cite{hermans2014dense, mccormac2017semanticfusion}. Contemporary semantic SLAM systems face several key challenges. First, the computational complexity of real-time semantic segmentation can limit system performance, particularly on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Second, maintaining consistency between semantic labels and geometric representations over time remains difficult, especially in dynamic environments where objects may move or change. Third, handling semantic ambiguity and uncertainty in object recognition while maintaining map coherence presents ongoing research challenges \cite{sünderhauf2017limits, lianos2018vso}. The emergence of neural implicit representations, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and their variants, has opened new possibilities for semantic mapping by enabling continuous, differentiable representations of both geometry and semantics \cite{mildenhall2020nerf, zhi2021place}. These approaches promise to address some limitations of traditional discrete representations while providing novel capabilities for view synthesis and semantic understanding. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of semantic mapping techniques, analyzing the evolution from early geometric SLAM systems to modern neural approaches, and identifying key research directions for future development in this rapidly advancing field.
