text: Recommender systems play a critical role in the fast-developing Internet age, aiming to predict the most likely items which users may be interested in. These systems have become indispensable components of modern digital platforms, from e-commerce websites like Amazon and eBay to streaming services such as Netflix and Spotify, fundamentally transforming how users discover and interact with content \cite{ricci2015recommender}. The exponential growth of available information and products online has created an information overload problem, making it increasingly difficult for users to find relevant items without intelligent filtering mechanisms \cite{adomavicius2005toward}. The fundamental challenge in recommender systems lies in accurately modeling user preferences and item characteristics to generate personalized recommendations that enhance user satisfaction and engagement \cite{lu2015recommender}. Traditional approaches have evolved from simple content-based filtering, which relies on item features and user profiles, to collaborative filtering methods that leverage the wisdom of crowds by analyzing user-item interaction patterns \cite{su2009survey}. However, these conventional techniques often struggle with several inherent limitations, including the cold-start problem for new users and items, data sparsity issues in large-scale systems, and scalability challenges as the number of users and items grows exponentially \cite{schein2002methods}. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized the field of recommender systems, offering sophisticated solutions to overcome these traditional limitations \cite{zhang2019deep}. Deep neural networks excel at learning complex, non-linear relationships between users and items from high-dimensional, heterogeneous data sources, enabling more accurate preference modeling and recommendation generation \cite{covington2016deep}. These models can effectively capture intricate patterns in user behavior, temporal dynamics, and contextual information that were previously difficult to model using conventional machine learning approaches \cite{hidasi2015session}. Matrix factorization techniques, particularly those enhanced with deep learning components, have emerged as powerful tools for collaborative filtering \cite{koren2009matrix}. These methods decompose the user-item interaction matrix into lower-dimensional latent factor representations, capturing underlying preferences and item characteristics in a continuous vector space \cite{mnih2007probabilistic}. The integration of neural networks with matrix factorization has led to more flexible and expressive models capable of learning non-linear transformations and incorporating additional side information \cite{he2017neural}. Graph-based recommender systems have gained significant attention due to their ability to model complex relationships between users, items, and various contextual entities \cite{wang2019neural}. Graph neural networks (GNNs) provide a natural framework for leveraging the rich structural information inherent in recommendation scenarios, enabling the propagation of preference signals through multi-hop connections in the user-item graph \cite{wu2022graph}. These approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in capturing high-order collaborative signals and improving recommendation accuracy, particularly in scenarios with sparse interaction data \cite{wang2019neural}. The incorporation of contextual information has become increasingly important in modern recommender systems, as user preferences often vary significantly depending on temporal, spatial, and situational factors \cite{adomavicius2011context}. Context-aware recommendation models attempt to capture these dynamic aspects of user behavior by incorporating features such as time of day, location, weather conditions, and social context into the recommendation process \cite{baltrunas2011incarmusic}. Deep learning architectures, with their ability to process heterogeneous input modalities, have proven particularly effective at integrating diverse contextual signals \cite{cheng2016wide}. Sequential recommendation represents another crucial aspect of modern recommender systems, focusing on modeling the temporal evolution of user preferences and predicting the next item a user might interact with \cite{quadrana2018sequence}. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), have been widely adopted for capturing sequential patterns in user behavior \cite{hidasi2015session}. More recently, attention mechanisms and transformer architectures have shown superior performance in modeling long-range dependencies and complex sequential relationships \cite{kang2018self}. The evaluation of recommender systems presents unique challenges, as traditional accuracy metrics may not fully capture the user experience and business objectives \cite{herlocker2004evaluating}. Beyond prediction accuracy, modern evaluation frameworks consider factors such as diversity, novelty, serendipity, and fairness to provide a more comprehensive assessment of recommendation quality \cite{kaminskas2016diversity}. The development of robust evaluation methodologies remains an active area of research, particularly in addressing issues related to selection bias, temporal effects, and the gap between offline and online performance \cite{schnabel2016recommendations}. Fairness and bias mitigation have emerged as critical considerations in recommender system design, as these systems can inadvertently perpetuate or amplify existing societal biases \cite{chen2023bias}. Research in this area focuses on developing algorithms that provide equitable recommendations across different demographic groups while maintaining overall system performance \cite{burke2018balanced}. Techniques such as adversarial training, fairness constraints, and bias-aware sampling strategies have been proposed to address these challenges \cite{beutel2017data}. The scalability requirements of modern recommender systems, which must handle millions of users and items with real-time response constraints, have driven the development of efficient algorithms and distributed computing frameworks \cite{linden2003amazon}. Techniques such as approximate nearest neighbor search, sampling-based methods, and hierarchical clustering have been employed to reduce computational complexity while maintaining recommendation quality \cite{bachrach2014speeding}. The integration of recommender systems with cloud computing platforms and edge computing architectures has further enabled the deployment of sophisticated models at scale \cite{shi2014collaborative}. Privacy preservation has become increasingly important as recommender systems collect and process vast amounts of personal data \cite{friedman2016privacy}. Differential privacy, federated learning, and homomorphic encryption techniques have been explored as potential solutions for protecting user privacy while maintaining recommendation effectiveness \cite{mcsherry2009differentially}. The challenge lies in finding the optimal balance between personalization accuracy and privacy protection, particularly in light of evolving regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) \cite{wang2018privacy}. The integration of multi-modal data sources, including text, images, audio, and video content, has opened new possibilities for enhancing recommendation accuracy and user experience \cite{deldjoo2021multimedia}. Deep learning models excel at processing and fusing information from these diverse modalities, enabling more comprehensive item representations and user preference modeling \cite{zhang2018explainable}. Computer vision techniques for analyzing product images, natural language processing for understanding reviews and descriptions, and audio analysis for music recommendation have all contributed to the advancement of multi-modal recommender systems \cite{chen2017joint}.

text: \IEEEPARstart{W}{ith} the increasing complexity of Information Technology's (IT) operational environments, organizations have build a need to maintain healthy IT systems while reducing operational cost, ticket volume and improving customer satisfaction. Traditional reactive approaches to IT service management, where issues are addressed only after they occur, have proven insufficient for modern enterprise requirements. This paradigm shift has led to the emergence of proactive IT operations management, emphasizing predictive analytics, automated monitoring, and intelligent incident prevention strategies. The evolution of IT infrastructure has introduced unprecedented complexity through cloud computing, microservices architectures, containerization, and hybrid environments. These technological advances, while offering enhanced scalability and flexibility, have simultaneously increased the challenge of maintaining system reliability and performance. Modern IT ecosystems typically comprise hundreds or thousands of interconnected components, each potentially contributing to system failures or performance degradation. Consequently, organizations require sophisticated monitoring and management solutions capable of handling this complexity while ensuring optimal service delivery. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies have emerged as transformative solutions for addressing these challenges in IT operations, commonly referred to as AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations). AIOps platforms leverage advanced algorithms to analyze vast amounts of operational data, identify patterns, predict potential issues, and automate remediation processes \cite{gartner2019aiops}. These systems can process structured and unstructured data from multiple sources, including log files, performance metrics, network traffic, and user behavior patterns, to provide comprehensive insights into system health and performance. The implementation of AIOps solutions offers several key benefits for modern organizations. First, predictive analytics capabilities enable early detection of potential system failures, allowing IT teams to address issues before they impact end users. This proactive approach significantly reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) and improves overall system availability \cite{chen2020predictive}. Second, intelligent automation reduces the manual effort required for routine monitoring and incident response tasks, allowing IT professionals to focus on strategic initiatives rather than reactive firefighting. Third, advanced correlation algorithms can identify root causes of complex issues that span multiple system components, reducing the time and expertise required for troubleshooting \cite{zhang2021correlation}. However, the adoption of AIOps technologies is not without challenges. Organizations must address concerns related to data quality, algorithm transparency, integration complexity, and skill gaps within their IT teams. The effectiveness of AI-driven solutions heavily depends on the quality and completeness of input data, requiring organizations to establish robust data governance practices and ensure comprehensive monitoring coverage across their IT infrastructure \cite{liu2020data}. Additionally, the "black box" nature of many machine learning algorithms can create challenges for IT professionals who need to understand and trust the recommendations provided by AIOps platforms. The current landscape of IT operations management is characterized by increasing adoption of cloud-native technologies, DevOps practices, and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines. These trends have accelerated the pace of change in IT environments while simultaneously increasing the volume and velocity of operational data generated. Traditional monitoring tools and manual processes are increasingly inadequate for managing this complexity, creating a compelling business case for AI-driven solutions that can adapt to dynamic environments and scale with organizational growth. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated digital transformation initiatives across industries, leading to rapid expansion of remote work capabilities and increased reliance on digital services. This shift has placed additional pressure on IT organizations to ensure reliable service delivery while managing distributed workforces and evolving security requirements. AIOps technologies have proven particularly valuable during this transition, providing the visibility and automation capabilities necessary to maintain service quality in rapidly changing environments \cite{smith2021covid}. The integration of AIOps capabilities with existing IT service management (ITSM) frameworks represents a critical success factor for organizations seeking to modernize their operations. Effective integration requires careful consideration of workflow automation, alert correlation, and incident management processes to ensure that AI-driven insights translate into actionable improvements in service delivery. Organizations must also develop appropriate governance frameworks to ensure that automated decision-making aligns with business objectives and regulatory requirements. As organizations continue to embrace digital transformation and adopt increasingly complex IT architectures, the importance of intelligent operations management will only continue to grow. The ability to leverage AI and machine learning technologies effectively will become a key differentiator for organizations seeking to maintain competitive advantage through superior IT service delivery and operational efficiency.

text: Recommender systems help users to easily find their favorite items from massive candidates. Typically, recommender models, such as collaborative filtering~\cite{koren2009matrix} and matrix factorization~\cite{mnih2008probabilistic}, learn user preferences from historical interactions to predict future user behaviors. With the rapid development of deep learning, neural collaborative filtering~\cite{he2017neural} and various deep learning-based approaches~\cite{cheng2016wide,guo2017deepfm,wang2017deep} have achieved remarkable success in recommendation tasks by capturing complex user-item relationships and non-linear patterns. However, traditional recommender systems face significant challenges when dealing with new users or items that have limited or no historical interaction data, commonly known as the cold-start problem~\cite{schein2002methods}. This issue is particularly prevalent in real-world scenarios where new users continuously join the platform and new items are frequently added to the catalog. For new users, the system lacks sufficient behavioral data to understand their preferences, while for new items, there is insufficient user feedback to assess their appeal to different user segments. To address the cold-start problem, various approaches have been proposed. Content-based methods~\cite{pazzani2007content} leverage item features and user profiles to make recommendations, but they often suffer from limited content information and the inability to capture collaborative signals. Demographic-based approaches~\cite{krulwich1997lifestyle} utilize user demographic information, yet they may lead to stereotypical recommendations and privacy concerns. Knowledge graph-based methods~\cite{wang2018dkn,wang2019kgat} incorporate external knowledge to enrich item representations, but they require extensive domain knowledge and may not be applicable across different domains. Meta-learning, also known as "learning to learn"~\cite{finn2017model}, has emerged as a promising paradigm for addressing the cold-start problem in recommender systems. The core idea of meta-learning is to train models that can quickly adapt to new tasks with minimal training examples. In the context of recommendation, meta-learning enables the system to rapidly learn user preferences from a few interactions or quickly understand new item characteristics from limited feedback data. Recent advances in meta-learning for recommendations have shown encouraging results. Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML)~\cite{finn2017model} provides a general framework for learning good parameter initializations that can be fine-tuned for new tasks with gradient descent. MeLU~\cite{lee2019melu} applies meta-learning to collaborative filtering by treating each user as a separate task and learning to quickly adapt to new users' preferences. MetaHIN~\cite{lu2020meta} leverages heterogeneous information networks with meta-learning to handle cold-start recommendations in multi-domain scenarios. Despite these advances, existing meta-learning approaches for recommendation still face several limitations. First, most methods focus primarily on the user cold-start problem while neglecting the equally important item cold-start scenario. Second, many approaches require extensive computational resources during the meta-training phase, making them less practical for large-scale applications. Third, existing methods often fail to effectively leverage both collaborative and content information simultaneously, limiting their ability to capture comprehensive user-item relationships. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of user preferences and item popularity poses additional challenges for meta-learning-based recommender systems. Users' tastes may evolve over time, and new trends in item preferences can emerge rapidly. Traditional meta-learning approaches often assume stationary task distributions, which may not hold in real-world recommendation scenarios where user behaviors and item characteristics continuously change. Another critical challenge is the heterogeneity of interaction patterns across different domains and platforms. Users may exhibit different behaviors when interacting with movies, books, or music, and the same user might have varying engagement patterns on different platforms. This heterogeneity requires meta-learning models to be flexible enough to adapt to diverse interaction patterns while maintaining the ability to transfer knowledge across related domains. The evaluation of meta-learning approaches in recommendation also presents unique challenges. Traditional recommendation metrics may not adequately capture the quick adaptation capability that meta-learning aims to achieve. New evaluation protocols and metrics are needed to properly assess how well these methods perform in few-shot learning scenarios and their ability to generalize to unseen users and items. In this work, we propose a novel meta-learning framework that addresses these limitations by incorporating both user and item cold-start scenarios within a unified model. Our approach leverages advanced attention mechanisms to dynamically weight the importance of different types of information during the adaptation process. We introduce a dual-level meta-learning strategy that operates at both the user and item levels, enabling the model to quickly adapt to new users while simultaneously handling new items effectively. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive analysis of the cold-start problem in modern recommender systems and identify key limitations of existing meta-learning approaches. (2) We propose a novel dual-level meta-learning framework that simultaneously addresses user and item cold-start problems through adaptive attention mechanisms. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to state-of-the-art baselines. (4) We provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence showing the superior adaptation capability and computational efficiency of our proposed method.

text: In this paper we investigate an evolutionary robot system where robot morphologies (bodies) and controllers (brains) are evolved simultaneously. The simultaneous evolution of robot morphologies and controllers represents a fundamental paradigm shift in robotics, moving away from traditional approaches where hardware design and control algorithms are developed separately. This co-evolutionary framework, often referred to as evolutionary robotics \cite{nolfi2000evolutionary}, enables the discovery of novel robot designs that would be difficult or impossible to conceive through conventional engineering methods. The motivation for this research stems from biological systems, where form and function have co-evolved over millions of years to produce remarkably efficient and adaptable organisms. In nature, the morphology of an organism is intimately linked to its behavioral capabilities and environmental niche. For instance, the streamlined body of a dolphin is perfectly suited for aquatic locomotion, while the wing structure of a bird enables efficient flight. This tight coupling between physical structure and behavioral control suggests that artificial systems could benefit from similar co-evolutionary processes \cite{pfeifer2007body}. Traditional robotics approaches typically follow a sequential design methodology: first, engineers design the mechanical structure based on anticipated tasks and environmental constraints, then develop control algorithms to operate within the constraints of that fixed morphology. This approach, while systematic, may lead to suboptimal solutions because the morphology and controller are not optimized together. The resulting systems may exhibit limited adaptability and may not fully exploit the potential synergies between physical design and control strategies. Evolutionary approaches to robot design offer several compelling advantages. First, they can explore vast design spaces that would be computationally intractable for human designers to navigate systematically. Second, they can discover counterintuitive solutions that challenge conventional engineering wisdom. Third, they provide a principled framework for handling the complex interactions between morphological and behavioral parameters. Finally, evolutionary methods can potentially produce robots that are more robust and adaptable to environmental variations \cite{lipson2000automatic}. The field of evolutionary robotics has witnessed significant developments since its inception in the 1990s. Early pioneering work by researchers such as Floreano and Mondada \cite{floreano1994evolution} demonstrated the feasibility of evolving neural network controllers for simple robotic tasks. Subsequently, researchers began exploring the evolution of morphologies, initially focusing on relatively simple structural parameters such as leg lengths or sensor placements \cite{sims1994evolving}. More recent advances have enabled the evolution of increasingly complex morphological features. The development of sophisticated simulation environments has been crucial in this progress, allowing researchers to evaluate thousands of candidate designs efficiently without the prohibitive costs of physical prototyping. Notable simulation platforms include physics engines such as ODE (Open Dynamics Engine), Bullet Physics, and more recently, specialized frameworks designed specifically for evolutionary robotics research \cite{hupkes2018evolving}. One of the key challenges in evolutionary robotics is the reality gap—the discrepancy between simulated and real-world performance. Robots that perform well in simulation may fail when deployed in physical environments due to factors such as sensor noise, actuator dynamics, material properties, and environmental uncertainties that are difficult to model accurately. Researchers have developed various strategies to address this challenge, including domain randomization, robust control techniques, and incremental evolution approaches that gradually increase the complexity of the simulated environment \cite{jakobi1995noise}. The representation of robot morphologies poses another significant challenge. Unlike controller parameters, which can often be represented as real-valued vectors, morphological features involve discrete structural choices, topological relationships, and geometric constraints. Various encoding schemes have been proposed, including direct encoding methods that explicitly represent morphological parameters, and indirect encoding approaches such as developmental systems and generative grammars that can produce complex structures from compact genetic representations \cite{stanley2007compositional}. Neural networks have emerged as a popular choice for robot controllers in evolutionary systems due to their flexibility and the availability of well-established evolutionary algorithms for optimizing network architectures and parameters. Neuroevolution techniques can simultaneously optimize network topology and connection weights, potentially discovering control architectures that are well-matched to the evolved morphologies \cite{stanley2002evolving}. The fitness evaluation process in evolutionary robotics typically involves simulating robots performing specific tasks over predetermined time periods. Common benchmark tasks include locomotion (maximizing distance traveled), navigation (reaching target locations), manipulation (moving objects), and more complex behaviors such as foraging or predator avoidance. The choice of fitness function significantly influences the evolutionary trajectory and can lead to unexpected emergent behaviors \cite{lehman2011abandoning}. Recent work has also explored open-ended evolution, where the goal is not to optimize performance on a specific task but rather to continuously generate novel and increasingly complex behaviors. This approach is inspired by biological evolution, which has produced an extraordinary diversity of life forms without any predetermined objectives. Open-ended evolutionary systems pose unique challenges, including the need for novelty metrics, diversity preservation mechanisms, and scalable computational architectures \cite{stanley2017open}. The integration of machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning, has opened new avenues for evolutionary robotics research. Deep neural networks can serve as powerful function approximators for both morphological generators and control policies. Additionally, techniques such as reinforcement learning can be combined with evolutionary methods to create hybrid approaches that leverage the strengths of both paradigms \cite{such2017deep}. Multi-objective optimization represents another important consideration in evolutionary robotics. Real-world robot applications typically involve trade-offs between multiple competing objectives, such as speed versus energy efficiency, or robustness versus performance. Evolutionary algorithms are well-suited to handle multi-objective problems, potentially discovering Pareto-optimal solutions that represent different trade-offs between conflicting goals \cite{deb2002fast}. The scalability of evolutionary approaches remains an active area of research. As the complexity of robot morphologies and behaviors increases, the computational requirements for fitness evaluation can become prohibitive. Researchers have explored various strategies to address scalability challenges, including hierarchical evolution, modular approaches, and distributed computing frameworks that can leverage parallel processing capabilities \cite{clune2013evolutionary}. This paper contributes to the field by presenting a comprehensive investigation of simultaneous morphological and controller evolution, addressing several key research questions regarding the effectiveness of co-evolutionary approaches, the impact of different representation schemes, and the role of environmental complexity in shaping evolutionary outcomes.

text: Document retrieval is the task of finding relevant documents in a large collection to answer specific queries. Traditional approaches to document retrieval have relied heavily on lexical matching techniques, such as TF-IDF and BM25, which identify relevant documents based on exact term matches between queries and document content \cite{robertson2009probabilistic}. While these methods have proven effective for many applications, they suffer from fundamental limitations in capturing semantic relationships and handling vocabulary mismatch problems \cite{manning2008introduction}. The advent of dense retrieval methods has revolutionized the field by leveraging neural networks to encode both queries and documents into high-dimensional vector representations \cite{karpukhin2020dense}. These dense embeddings enable semantic matching that goes beyond exact keyword overlap, allowing systems to identify relevant documents even when they use different terminology to express similar concepts \cite{reimers2019sentence}. Models such as Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) \cite{karpukhin2020dense} and ColBERT \cite{khattab2020colbert} have demonstrated significant improvements over traditional sparse retrieval methods across various benchmarks. However, dense retrieval systems face several challenges that limit their practical deployment. First, the computational requirements for encoding large document collections and performing similarity searches at scale can be prohibitive \cite{johnson2019billion}. Second, these systems often struggle with out-of-domain generalization, performing poorly when applied to domains or query types different from their training data \cite{thakur2021beir}. Third, the interpretability of dense retrieval results remains limited, making it difficult to understand why certain documents are ranked higher than others \cite{hofstatter2021efficiently}. Recent research has explored hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of both sparse and dense retrieval methods \cite{lin2021few}. These hybrid systems typically employ sparse retrieval as an efficient first-stage filter, followed by dense retrieval for more sophisticated reranking \cite{xiong2020approximate}. Additionally, advances in approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms and specialized hardware have made dense retrieval more computationally feasible for large-scale applications \cite{malkov2018efficient}. The evaluation of document retrieval systems has traditionally relied on metrics such as precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) \cite{jarvelin2002cumulated}. However, these metrics may not fully capture the user experience in real-world scenarios, leading to increased interest in user-centric evaluation approaches \cite{azzopardi2021measuring}. Furthermore, the quality and coverage of relevance judgments in standard benchmarks have come under scrutiny, with researchers highlighting the need for more comprehensive evaluation methodologies \cite{voorhees2005trec}. Contemporary challenges in document retrieval extend beyond technical performance metrics to include fairness, bias, and robustness considerations \cite{rekabsaz2021societal}. Retrieval systems may inadvertently amplify existing biases present in training data or exhibit unfair treatment of certain demographic groups \cite{chen2021towards}. Additionally, adversarial attacks on retrieval systems have emerged as a concern, where malicious actors attempt to manipulate rankings through carefully crafted content \cite{song2020adversarial}. This work addresses these challenges by proposing novel methodologies that enhance both the effectiveness and efficiency of document retrieval systems while maintaining interpretability and fairness. Our contributions span theoretical foundations, algorithmic innovations, and comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse domains and use cases.

Such systems as DPR (Dense Passage Retrieval) and ColBERT (Khattab et al., 2002) have shown a marked improvement over sparse methods in several standard tests, but dense systems have some difficulties that hinder their use. In the new system of search, both the documents and the queries are represented by high-dimensional n-dimensional vectors, which has proved excellent in the various standard tests. In recent research, hybrid methods which combine the advantages of sparse and dense IR have been developed. Firstly, the complexity of encoding large collections of documents and of searching at large scale for similarities may be prohibitive. Secondly, they are subject to generalization problems, performing poorly on domains or types of queries that are different from those used in training. The evaluation of retrieval systems has so far relied on measures such as precision, recall and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG). These hybrid systems typically use sparse retrieval as an efficient first-stage filter, followed by dense retrieval for a more sophisticated re-ranking (citation: lin-2012few). Third, the interpretability of the dense retrieval results remains limited, making it difficult to understand why certain documents are ranked higher than others (citation: hofstatter-2012-efficiently). But these metrics may not fully capture the end-user experience in real-world use cases, resulting in an increased interest in more end-user oriented evaluation methods (cf. Azzopardi, 2001; Jarvelin, 2002). Modern challenges in information retrieval are not only in technical performance metrics but also in the considerations of fairness, bias and robustness (cf. Rekabsaz and colleagues). Furthermore, advances in approximate nearest neighbor searching algorithms and specialized hardware have made dense searching more efficient for large-scale applications (see Malkov, 2018). Besides the problem of efficiency, this paper addresses the problem of effectiveness by proposing novel methods for increasing the effectiveness and efficiency of document retrieval systems while preserving their interpretability and fairness. The quality and coverage of relevance judgments in standard evaluations has also been questioned, and it has been argued that more comprehensive evaluation methods are needed (see Voorhees, 2005). In this paper we present new theoretical foundations, new algorithms and extensive empirical evaluations in diverse domains and use cases.

text: Recent years have seen a surge of misinformation (and closely related phenomena, such as disinformation and fake news), and that such information can cause serious societal harm. The proliferation of misinformation has been amplified by the widespread adoption of social media platforms and digital communication channels, which enable rapid dissemination of unverified or deliberately false information to vast audiences \cite{vosoughi2018spread, lazer2018science}. This phenomenon has manifested across numerous domains, including public health, political discourse, climate science, and emergency response situations, often undermining evidence-based decision-making and eroding public trust in authoritative institutions \cite{lewandowsky2012misinformation, pennycook2021psychology}. The COVID-19 pandemic exemplified the devastating potential of misinformation, with false claims about treatments, prevention measures, and vaccine safety leading to preventable deaths and reduced compliance with public health guidelines \cite{brennen2020types, roozenbeek2020susceptibility}. Similarly, misinformation surrounding electoral processes has threatened democratic institutions and civic engagement, while climate misinformation has hindered collective action on environmental challenges \cite{cook2017consensus, van2017inoculation}. Traditional approaches to combating misinformation have primarily focused on post-hoc fact-checking and content moderation strategies \cite{graves2018understanding, clayton2019real}. However, these reactive measures often prove insufficient, as false information can spread faster than corrections and may continue to influence beliefs even after debunking \cite{nyhan2010corrections, walter2020fact}. The "continued influence effect" demonstrates that misinformation can persist in memory and continue shaping judgments despite explicit correction \cite{johnson1994sources, ecker2022psychological}. Consequently, researchers have increasingly turned their attention to proactive approaches that aim to prevent misinformation from taking hold in the first place. Among these preventive strategies, psychological inoculation has emerged as a particularly promising framework \cite{mcguire1964inducing, compton2013inoculation}. Drawing from medical immunization principles, inoculation theory suggests that exposing individuals to weakened forms of persuasive attacks, along with refutational preemption, can build resistance to subsequent misinformation \cite{mcguire1961effectiveness, banas2011meta}. Recent empirical investigations have demonstrated the efficacy of inoculation-based interventions across various contexts and populations \cite{roozenbeek2020breaking, maertens2021long}. These studies have shown that brief exposure to educational content highlighting common misinformation techniques can significantly reduce susceptibility to false claims, with effects persisting over time and generalizing across different topics \cite{basol2020good, cook2017neutralizing}. The present research contributes to this growing body of literature by examining the mechanisms underlying inoculation effectiveness and exploring optimal implementation strategies for large-scale deployment.

text: Modern commercial buildings are complex cyber-physical systems. They are increasingly being equipped with sensors and actuators, ranging from surveillance cameras and card readers for security and access control, to temperature sensors, humidity monitors, and HVAC control systems for environmental management. These interconnected devices form sophisticated Building Automation Systems (BAS) that enable centralized monitoring and control of various building functions \cite{kastner2005communication, granzer2010security}. The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices within commercial buildings has created unprecedented opportunities for energy optimization, occupant comfort enhancement, and operational efficiency improvements \cite{minoli2017iot, li2017internet}. However, this technological advancement has simultaneously introduced significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that pose serious threats to building operations, occupant safety, and data privacy \cite{mundt2016cyber, wang2018security}. Unlike traditional IT systems that primarily handle data processing and storage, building automation systems directly control physical infrastructure, making security breaches potentially catastrophic. A successful cyberattack on a building's control systems could result in HVAC system manipulation leading to unsafe temperature conditions, lighting system disruption affecting occupant safety during emergencies, or elevator control compromise endangering lives \cite{zetter2016inside, case2016analysis}. The cybersecurity landscape for commercial buildings is further complicated by several inherent characteristics of building automation systems. First, these systems often employ legacy protocols and devices that were designed with functionality and reliability as primary concerns, with minimal consideration for security \cite{holmberg2003building, granzer2006security}. Many building control protocols, such as BACnet, LonWorks, and Modbus, were developed decades ago when cybersecurity threats were not as prevalent or sophisticated as they are today \cite{newman2017bacnet, echelon2019lonworks}. Second, building systems typically have extended operational lifespans, often remaining in service for 15-20 years or more, making security updates and patches challenging to implement \cite{eisenhauer2001introduction}. The convergence of Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) in modern buildings has created additional attack vectors. While IT systems focus on data confidentiality, integrity, and availability, OT systems prioritize availability, safety, and reliability \cite{stouffer2011guide}. This fundamental difference in security priorities creates gaps that malicious actors can exploit. Furthermore, the increasing connectivity of building systems to corporate networks and the internet has expanded the attack surface, enabling remote attacks that were previously impossible \cite{formby2016mixed}. Recent high-profile incidents have demonstrated the real-world impact of cybersecurity vulnerabilities in building systems. The 2013 Target data breach, which originated from compromised HVAC system credentials, highlighted how building systems can serve as entry points for broader network infiltration \cite{krebs2014target}. Similarly, the 2016 attack on a Ukrainian power grid involved manipulation of SCADA systems, demonstrating the potential for cyber-physical attacks to cause widespread disruption \cite{liang2017review}. These incidents underscore the critical need for comprehensive cybersecurity frameworks specifically designed for building automation systems. The unique operational requirements of commercial buildings present additional challenges for cybersecurity implementation. Building systems must maintain continuous operation to ensure occupant comfort and safety, making traditional security measures such as system shutdowns for patching or updates problematic \cite{cardenas2008challenges}. Additionally, building operators often lack specialized cybersecurity expertise, as their primary focus is on mechanical and electrical systems rather than information security \cite{wang2018security}. Current cybersecurity approaches for building systems often rely on adaptations of traditional IT security measures, which may not adequately address the specific requirements and constraints of cyber-physical systems \cite{humayed2017cyber}. Generic security frameworks typically fail to account for the real-time operational requirements, safety-critical functions, and physical constraints inherent in building automation systems. This gap necessitates the development of specialized security frameworks that balance cybersecurity requirements with operational needs. The regulatory landscape for building cybersecurity is also evolving rapidly. Various standards and guidelines, including NIST Cybersecurity Framework, IEC 62443, and ASHRAE/NIST cybersecurity guidelines, provide recommendations for securing industrial control systems and building automation systems \cite{nist2018framework, iec2018security, ashrae2019cybersecurity}. However, the implementation of these standards in practice remains challenging due to the diversity of building systems, varying organizational capabilities, and cost considerations. This research addresses the critical gap between existing cybersecurity frameworks and the specific needs of commercial building systems. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a comprehensive, practical cybersecurity framework specifically tailored for commercial building automation systems. Our framework considers the unique characteristics of building systems, including their cyber-physical nature, operational requirements, and resource constraints, while providing actionable guidance for implementation across diverse building types and organizational contexts. The proposed framework integrates multiple security dimensions, including network security, device security, data protection, access control, and incident response, within a cohesive structure that acknowledges the interdependencies between building systems and their operational requirements. Unlike existing approaches that often focus on individual security components, our framework provides a holistic view of building cybersecurity that enables systematic risk assessment, security planning, and implementation.

text: Few-shot learning, which aims at classifying instances from unseen classes given only a handful of training examples, has witnessed a rapid progress in the recent years. The paradigm has emerged as a critical research direction due to its potential to address the data scarcity problem that plagues many real-world applications, where collecting large amounts of labeled data is either prohibitively expensive or practically infeasible \cite{wang2020generalizing, chen2019closer}. Traditional deep learning approaches typically require thousands or even millions of labeled examples to achieve satisfactory performance \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet, he2016deep}. However, this requirement becomes a significant bottleneck in domains such as medical imaging, where expert annotations are scarce and costly \cite{litjens2017survey}, or in natural language processing tasks for low-resource languages \cite{hedderich2021survey}. Few-shot learning addresses this limitation by enabling models to generalize to new classes with minimal supervision, mimicking the human ability to learn new concepts from just a few examples \cite{lake2015human}. The few-shot learning problem is typically formulated within the episodic training framework, where the model is trained on a series of episodes, each containing a support set with a few labeled examples and a query set for evaluation \cite{vinyals2016matching}. This meta-learning approach allows the model to learn how to learn, developing strategies that can be quickly adapted to new tasks \cite{finn2017model}. The most common benchmark scenarios include 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot classification, where the model must distinguish between 5 classes given either 1 or 5 examples per class, respectively \cite{ravi2016optimization}. Several methodological approaches have been developed to tackle the few-shot learning challenge. Metric-learning based methods focus on learning an appropriate distance metric in an embedding space where examples from the same class are close together while examples from different classes are far apart \cite{snell2017prototypical, sung2018learning}. These approaches typically employ techniques such as prototypical networks, which represent each class by the mean of its support examples in the embedding space \cite{snell2017prototypical}, or relation networks that learn to compare query examples with support examples through a learnable similarity function \cite{sung2018learning}. Optimization-based approaches, on the other hand, focus on learning good initialization parameters that can be quickly fine-tuned to new tasks with gradient descent \cite{finn2017model}. Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) exemplifies this approach by learning initial parameters that are sensitive to changes in the task, enabling rapid adaptation through a few gradient steps \cite{finn2017model}. Variants of MAML have been proposed to address computational efficiency and stability issues, including First-Order MAML (FOMAML) and Reptile \cite{nichol2018first}. Data augmentation strategies have also proven effective in few-shot scenarios, where the limited training data can be artificially expanded through various transformations \cite{wang2020instance}. Techniques such as mixup, cutmix, and more sophisticated generative approaches have been employed to create additional training examples while preserving class semantics \cite{zhang2017mixup, yun2019cutmix}. These methods are particularly valuable in few-shot learning where every additional example can significantly impact performance. Recent advances have also explored the integration of self-supervised learning with few-shot classification \cite{gidaris2019boosting}. By pre-training models on large-scale unlabeled datasets using self-supervised objectives, these approaches learn rich feature representations that transfer well to few-shot scenarios \cite{chen2020simple}. The combination of contrastive learning and few-shot learning has shown particularly promising results, as the learned representations naturally cluster similar examples together \cite{khosla2020supervised}. Transformer architectures have recently been adapted for few-shot learning, leveraging their attention mechanisms to model relationships between support and query examples \cite{ye2020few}. These attention-based approaches can dynamically focus on relevant parts of the support set when making predictions for query examples, leading to improved performance across various benchmarks \cite{li2019finding}. Despite significant progress, several challenges remain in few-shot learning. Domain shift between training and testing scenarios continues to be a major issue, as models often struggle to generalize when the distribution of test classes differs significantly from training classes \cite{chen2019closer}. Additionally, the evaluation protocols and benchmarks used in few-shot learning research have been subject to criticism, with concerns about the artificial nature of episodic evaluation and the limited diversity of existing datasets \cite{triantafillou2019meta}. The field has also grappled with the question of what constitutes a fair comparison between different approaches, particularly when considering the amount of prior knowledge and data used during pre-training \cite{chen2019closer}. Some recent work has emphasized the importance of strong baselines and proper experimental design to ensure meaningful comparisons between methods \cite{wang2020instance}. Furthermore, the scalability of few-shot learning methods to real-world applications remains an open question. While laboratory benchmarks provide controlled environments for evaluation, the transition to practical applications often reveals additional challenges related to class imbalance, noisy labels, and computational constraints \cite{triantafillou2019meta}.

While controlled experiments like LibSVM provide a controlled environment for evaluation, the transition to practical applications often reveals additional challenges in the form of class imbalance, noisy annotations and computational constraints. Several recent works have emphasized the importance of strong heuristics and good experimental design to ensure meaningful comparisons between methods.

text: Developing and testing recommenders to optimize business goals are among the primary focuses of e-commerce machine learning. However, traditional recommender systems often face significant challenges when deployed in real-world e-commerce environments. These systems typically rely on historical user-item interaction data to predict future preferences, but they struggle with several critical limitations that can severely impact business performance. One of the most pressing challenges is the cold start problem, which manifests in multiple forms within e-commerce platforms. New users entering the system have no historical interaction data, making it difficult to provide personalized recommendations immediately. Similarly, new products lack sufficient user feedback to be effectively recommended to potential customers. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem where new items struggle to gain visibility, potentially leading to reduced sales and inventory turnover issues. The temporal aspect of this challenge is particularly acute in fast-moving e-commerce environments where product catalogs change rapidly and user preferences evolve continuously. Another fundamental limitation lies in the inherent feedback sparsity that characterizes most e-commerce datasets. Users typically interact with only a small fraction of available products, resulting in extremely sparse user-item interaction matrices. This sparsity makes it challenging for collaborative filtering approaches to identify meaningful patterns and relationships between users and items. Moreover, the majority of user feedback is implicit (clicks, views, purchases) rather than explicit ratings, introducing additional noise and ambiguity in preference inference. The long-tail distribution of product popularity further exacerbates this issue, where a small number of popular items receive the majority of interactions while numerous niche products remain largely unnoticed. The dynamic nature of e-commerce environments presents additional complexities that traditional recommender systems struggle to address effectively. User preferences shift over time due to seasonal trends, life events, changing needs, and evolving tastes. Product catalogs are continuously updated with new arrivals, discontinued items, and varying availability across different regions. Market conditions, promotional campaigns, and competitive dynamics introduce external factors that influence purchasing behavior but are often not captured by conventional recommendation algorithms. These temporal dynamics require recommender systems to be adaptive and responsive to change, rather than relying solely on static historical patterns. Furthermore, e-commerce platforms must balance multiple, often conflicting business objectives beyond simple accuracy metrics. While maximizing user satisfaction through relevant recommendations remains important, businesses also need to consider factors such as profit margins, inventory management, supplier relationships, and strategic product positioning. For instance, recommending high-margin items or promoting new product launches may be more valuable than suggesting items with the highest predicted user preference scores. This multi-objective optimization challenge requires sophisticated approaches that can incorporate business constraints and priorities into the recommendation process. The scalability requirements of modern e-commerce platforms add another layer of complexity to recommender system design. Large-scale platforms must handle millions of users, products, and interactions while providing real-time recommendations with minimal latency. Traditional collaborative filtering approaches often struggle with computational efficiency when dealing with such massive datasets, particularly when frequent model updates are required to maintain recommendation quality. The need for real-time personalization during user sessions further constrains the computational budget available for recommendation generation. Privacy and regulatory considerations have become increasingly important factors in recommender system development. With growing awareness of data privacy rights and the implementation of regulations such as GDPR and CCPA, e-commerce platforms must carefully balance personalization capabilities with user privacy protection. This includes considerations around data collection, storage, processing, and the ability to provide users with control over their personal information. The challenge extends to developing recommendation algorithms that can operate effectively with limited or anonymized data while still delivering valuable personalization. The evaluation of recommender systems in e-commerce contexts presents unique challenges that differ significantly from traditional academic settings. While offline evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, and RMSE provide useful insights, they often fail to capture the full complexity of real-world performance. Online A/B testing remains the gold standard for evaluating recommender systems in production, but it requires careful experimental design to account for factors such as seasonality, user learning effects, and the potential impact of recommendations on long-term user behavior. The business impact of recommendations extends beyond immediate click-through or conversion rates to include metrics such as customer lifetime value, revenue per user, and overall platform engagement. Recent advances in deep learning and machine learning have opened new possibilities for addressing these challenges in e-commerce recommendation systems. Neural collaborative filtering approaches can capture complex non-linear relationships between users and items that traditional matrix factorization methods might miss. Recurrent neural networks and attention mechanisms enable better modeling of sequential user behavior and temporal dynamics. Multi-task learning frameworks allow simultaneous optimization of multiple business objectives, while reinforcement learning approaches can optimize for long-term user engagement rather than immediate rewards. The integration of contextual information has emerged as a crucial factor in improving recommendation quality and business relevance. This includes incorporating user demographics, device information, time of day, seasonal patterns, and browsing context into the recommendation process. Content-based features such as product descriptions, images, categories, and attributes can help address cold start problems and improve recommendation explainability. Social signals and collaborative information from user networks can provide additional insights into preference patterns and trending items. Hybrid approaches that combine multiple recommendation techniques have shown promise in addressing the limitations of individual methods. These systems can leverage the strengths of different algorithms while mitigating their respective weaknesses. For example, combining collaborative filtering with content-based methods can help address both the cold start problem and the need for diverse recommendations. Ensemble methods can improve robustness and reduce the risk of poor performance due to data quality issues or algorithmic biases. The importance of recommendation diversity and serendipity in e-commerce has gained increased recognition as a factor that influences both user satisfaction and business outcomes. While accuracy remains important, users also value discovering new and unexpected items that align with their interests. Diversity in recommendations can help users explore different product categories, discover new brands, and avoid the filter bubble effect that can limit their exposure to the full product catalog. From a business perspective, diverse recommendations can help promote a wider range of products, reduce inventory concentration, and potentially increase average order values.

text: Semantic Segmentation aims to perform dense prediction for labeling each pixel in an image corresponding to the class that the pixel represents. Transformer-based vision networks \cite{vit,deit} have revolutionized computer vision tasks by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies and global contextual information. Following the success of Vision Transformer (ViT) \cite{vit} in image classification, numerous transformer-based architectures have been proposed for semantic segmentation, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) \cite{fcn,unet,deeplabv3}. The fundamental challenge in semantic segmentation lies in achieving accurate pixel-level classification while maintaining spatial resolution and preserving fine-grained details. Traditional CNN-based approaches \cite{fcn,segnet,pspnet} have dominated this field for years, utilizing hierarchical feature extraction through convolutional operations and pooling layers. However, these methods suffer from limited receptive fields and struggle to capture global context effectively, particularly in complex scenes with multiple objects and varying scales. Transformer architectures address these limitations by employing self-attention mechanisms that enable direct modeling of relationships between all spatial locations in an image. The self-attention operation computes attention weights for each pixel with respect to all other pixels, allowing the model to capture long-range dependencies and global context information. This capability is particularly beneficial for semantic segmentation tasks where understanding the relationship between distant objects and regions is crucial for accurate classification. Recent developments in transformer-based segmentation models \cite{setr,segmenter,segformer} have demonstrated significant improvements over CNN-based methods on benchmark datasets such as ADE20K \cite{ade20k}, Cityscapes \cite{cityscapes}, and PASCAL VOC \cite{pascalvoc}. These models typically follow an encoder-decoder architecture where the transformer encoder extracts hierarchical features from input images, and the decoder reconstructs high-resolution segmentation maps. The SETR \cite{setr} model pioneered the application of pure transformers to semantic segmentation by treating images as sequences of patches and applying standard transformer blocks for feature extraction. However, pure transformer architectures face several challenges when applied to dense prediction tasks. First, the computational complexity of self-attention scales quadratically with the number of input tokens, making it computationally expensive for high-resolution images. Second, transformers lack the inherent inductive biases of CNNs, such as translation invariance and locality, which are beneficial for visual tasks. Third, the patch-based tokenization used in vision transformers may lose fine-grained spatial information, leading to reduced accuracy in boundary regions. To address these challenges, hybrid architectures that combine the strengths of both transformers and CNNs have emerged as a promising direction \cite{pyramid_vision_transformer,twins,segformer}. These models leverage CNN backbones for efficient feature extraction while incorporating transformer blocks to capture global dependencies. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) \cite{pyramid_vision_transformer} introduces a hierarchical transformer architecture that generates multi-scale features similar to CNN backbones, making it suitable for dense prediction tasks. Another significant advancement is the development of efficient attention mechanisms that reduce computational complexity while maintaining performance. Linear attention \cite{linear_attention}, sparse attention \cite{sparse_attention}, and window-based attention \cite{swin_transformer} have been proposed to make transformer-based segmentation models more practical for real-world applications. The Swin Transformer \cite{swin_transformer} introduces shifted window attention that computes self-attention within local windows, achieving linear computational complexity with respect to image size. The integration of multi-scale feature fusion has also proven crucial for semantic segmentation performance. Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) \cite{fpn} and similar architectures enable models to leverage features at different scales, improving the detection and segmentation of objects with varying sizes. Transformer-based models have adopted similar strategies, incorporating multi-scale attention mechanisms and hierarchical feature representations to enhance segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, the advent of large-scale pre-training has significantly boosted the performance of transformer-based segmentation models. Pre-training on large datasets such as ImageNet-21K \cite{imagenet21k} or using self-supervised learning methods \cite{mae,simclr} provides models with rich visual representations that transfer effectively to downstream segmentation tasks. This pre-training paradigm has become a standard practice in developing state-of-the-art segmentation models. Despite these advances, several open challenges remain in transformer-based semantic segmentation. The trade-off between computational efficiency and model performance continues to be a critical consideration, particularly for real-time applications. Additionally, the interpretability of transformer models and their decision-making processes require further investigation to build trust in critical applications such as autonomous driving and medical imaging. The field continues to evolve rapidly with ongoing research focusing on architectural innovations, efficient training strategies, and novel attention mechanisms. Recent work explores the integration of knowledge distillation \cite{knowledge_distillation}, neural architecture search \cite{nas}, and domain adaptation techniques to further improve the performance and applicability of transformer-based segmentation models across diverse scenarios and datasets.

text: Image captioning, which aims to automatically describe the pictorial content of an unlabeled image with a sentence, is being actively studied~\cite{showandtell2015,bottomup2017,aoanet2019}. This task bridges computer vision and natural language processing, requiring models to not only recognize objects and their spatial relationships within images but also generate coherent and grammatically correct descriptions that capture the essential semantic content~\cite{vinyals2015show,xu2015show}. Early approaches to image captioning relied on template-based methods that combined object detection with predefined sentence structures~\cite{farhadi2010every,kulkarni2013babytalk}. However, these methods were limited by their rigid templates and inability to generate diverse, natural descriptions. The breakthrough came with the introduction of encoder-decoder architectures that leverage deep neural networks~\cite{vinyals2015show,donahue2015long}. These models typically employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) as an encoder to extract visual features from input images, followed by a recurrent neural network (RNN) decoder that generates word sequences conditioned on the visual representations. The attention mechanism has emerged as a crucial component in modern image captioning systems~\cite{xu2015show,lu2017knowing}. By allowing the decoder to focus on different regions of the image while generating each word, attention-based models can produce more accurate and contextually relevant descriptions. This has led to significant improvements in both the quality and interpretability of generated captions, as the attention weights provide insights into which image regions influence specific words in the output sequence. Recent advances have explored various architectural innovations to further enhance captioning performance. Transformer-based models have gained popularity due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and parallel processing capabilities~\cite{vaswani2017attention,cornia2020meshed}. These models replace traditional RNN decoders with self-attention mechanisms, enabling more efficient training and often superior performance. Additionally, the integration of object detection frameworks has proven beneficial, as explicit object-level features can provide richer semantic information compared to global image features~\cite{anderson2018bottom,jiang2018recurrent}. Graph-based approaches represent another promising direction, modeling images as scene graphs that explicitly capture object relationships and spatial configurations~\cite{yao2018exploring,yang2019auto}. These methods aim to generate more structured and detailed captions by leveraging the hierarchical nature of visual scenes. Furthermore, the incorporation of external knowledge bases and commonsense reasoning has shown potential for generating more informative and contextually aware descriptions~\cite{wu2022human,li2022comprehensive}. Despite these advances, image captioning still faces several challenges. The evaluation of generated captions remains problematic, as traditional metrics like BLEU and CIDEr may not fully capture semantic correctness or human preferences~\cite{vedantam2015cider,kilickaya2017re}. The diversity-accuracy trade-off is another persistent issue, where models often generate safe but generic descriptions rather than detailed and specific ones~\cite{vijayakumar2018diverse,wang2019describing}. Additionally, bias and fairness concerns have emerged, as models may perpetuate stereotypes present in training data~\cite{hendricks2018women,zhao2017men}. Current research directions include developing more sophisticated evaluation metrics that better align with human judgment, exploring few-shot and zero-shot learning scenarios to reduce dependence on large annotated datasets, and investigating multimodal pretraining strategies that leverage vast amounts of image-text pairs from the web~\cite{radford2021learning,li2021align}. The field continues to evolve rapidly, with ongoing efforts to create more robust, fair, and generalizable image captioning systems.

text: In recent years, the medical imaging community has witnessed a rapid increase in image processing methods based on Deep Learning (DL). These methods have demonstrated remarkable success across various medical imaging tasks, including image segmentation, classification, reconstruction, and enhancement \cite{litjens2017survey, shen2017deep}. The adoption of DL techniques in medical imaging has been particularly transformative due to their ability to automatically learn complex patterns and features from large datasets without requiring explicit feature engineering \cite{lecun2015deep}. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as the predominant architecture for medical image analysis, owing to their inherent ability to capture spatial hierarchies and local patterns that are crucial for understanding anatomical structures \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}. The success of CNNs in natural image processing has been successfully translated to medical imaging domains, where they have achieved state-of-the-art performance in tasks such as diabetic retinopathy detection \cite{gulshan2016development}, skin cancer classification \cite{esteva2017dermatologist}, and chest X-ray analysis \cite{rajpurkar2017chexnet}. However, the application of DL methods to medical imaging presents unique challenges that distinguish it from conventional computer vision tasks. Medical images often exhibit high variability in acquisition protocols, imaging modalities, and anatomical variations across different patient populations \cite{chen2020deep}. Furthermore, medical datasets are typically characterized by limited sample sizes, class imbalances, and the requirement for expert annotations, which can be both time-consuming and expensive to obtain \cite{ker2017deep}. These constraints necessitate the development of specialized approaches that can effectively leverage the available data while maintaining clinical relevance and reliability. The interpretability of DL models represents another critical concern in medical imaging applications. Unlike natural image classification tasks, medical diagnosis requires not only accurate predictions but also explanations that can be understood and validated by healthcare professionals \cite{arrieta2020explainable}. The "black box" nature of many DL models has raised concerns about their clinical adoption, leading to increased research focus on developing interpretable and explainable AI methods for medical imaging \cite{holzinger2019causability}. Transfer learning has emerged as a particularly effective strategy for addressing the data scarcity issues commonly encountered in medical imaging \cite{tajbakhsh2016convolutional}. By leveraging pre-trained models developed on large-scale natural image datasets such as ImageNet, researchers have demonstrated significant improvements in performance when fine-tuning these models for specific medical imaging tasks \cite{shin2016deep}. This approach has proven especially valuable for rare disease detection and analysis of small medical datasets where training deep networks from scratch would be impractical. The integration of multi-modal imaging data represents another frontier in medical DL applications. Modern medical practice often involves the acquisition of multiple imaging modalities for comprehensive patient assessment, such as combining MRI, CT, and PET scans for cancer diagnosis and staging \cite{zhou2019review}. DL methods have shown promise in effectively fusing information from multiple modalities to improve diagnostic accuracy and provide more comprehensive clinical insights \cite{wang2020multi}. Recent advances in generative models, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), have opened new possibilities for medical image synthesis and augmentation \cite{yi2019generative}. These techniques address the data scarcity problem by generating synthetic medical images that can augment training datasets while preserving important anatomical and pathological features \cite{frid2018gan}. Additionally, generative models have shown potential for cross-modal image translation, enabling the synthesis of one imaging modality from another, which can be valuable when certain imaging sequences are unavailable or contraindicated \cite{wolterink2017mr}. The emergence of federated learning has introduced new opportunities for collaborative medical imaging research while addressing privacy and data sharing concerns \cite{li2020federated}. This paradigm allows multiple institutions to collaboratively train DL models without sharing sensitive patient data, potentially enabling the development of more robust and generalizable models across diverse patient populations and imaging protocols \cite{sheller2020federated}. Attention mechanisms and transformer architectures, which have revolutionized natural language processing, are increasingly being adapted for medical imaging applications \cite{vaswani2017attention}. These architectures excel at capturing long-range dependencies and have shown promise in medical image analysis tasks that require understanding of global context and spatial relationships \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. Vision transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated competitive performance with CNNs in various medical imaging tasks while offering improved interpretability through attention visualization \cite{matsoukas2021time}. The development of uncertainty quantification methods for medical DL applications has gained significant attention as a means to enhance clinical trust and safety \cite{begoli2019need}. Bayesian deep learning and ensemble methods provide mechanisms for estimating prediction uncertainty, which is crucial for clinical decision-making and identifying cases that may require additional expert review \cite{gal2016dropout}. These approaches help bridge the gap between algorithmic predictions and clinical practice by providing confidence measures that can guide appropriate use of AI-assisted diagnosis. Domain adaptation techniques have become increasingly important for addressing the distribution shifts commonly encountered when deploying medical DL models across different institutions, populations, or imaging equipment \cite{kamnitsas2017unsupervised}. These methods aim to improve model generalizability by adapting models trained on source domains to perform well on target domains with different characteristics, thereby reducing the need for extensive retraining and annotation efforts. The integration of prior medical knowledge into DL architectures represents an active area of research aimed at improving model performance and interpretability \cite{zhang2019deep}. Physics-informed neural networks and anatomically-constrained models incorporate domain-specific knowledge about imaging physics, anatomy, and pathophysiology to guide the learning process and improve model reliability \cite{raissi2019physics}. Quality assurance and validation of medical DL systems require rigorous evaluation protocols that go beyond traditional machine learning metrics \cite{park2018methodological}. Clinical validation studies, external validation across multiple sites, and assessment of model performance across different demographic groups are essential for ensuring the safe and effective deployment of DL methods in clinical practice \cite{nagendran2020artificial}. The regulatory landscape for medical AI continues to evolve, with agencies such as the FDA developing frameworks for the approval and monitoring of AI-based medical devices \cite{muehlematter2021approval}. Understanding these regulatory requirements and incorporating appropriate validation and documentation practices is crucial for translating research developments into clinically deployable solutions. This comprehensive overview of the current state and challenges in medical imaging DL sets the foundation for examining specific methodological advances and their clinical applications in the subsequent sections of this work.
