text: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been impressively successful on a wide variety of tasks, including playing of video games~\cite{dqn1, dqn2, starcraft2, a3c, a2c, ga3c, kf, pic, Jain19, JainECCV2020} , robotic control~\cite{ddpg, td3, sac, ppo}, and strategic board games~\cite{alphago, alphazero, muzero}. However, despite these successes, deep RL algorithms often suffer from significant sample inefficiency, requiring millions of environment interactions to learn effective policies~\cite{rainbow, dreamer, curl}. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in real-world applications where data collection is expensive, time-consuming, or potentially dangerous~\cite{safe_rl, real_world_rl}. One promising approach to address sample inefficiency is through the use of auxiliary tasks that provide additional learning signals beyond the primary reward~\cite{unreal, impala, auxiliary_tasks}. These auxiliary objectives can help agents learn more robust and generalizable representations by encouraging the discovery of useful features that may not be directly optimized by the main task reward~\cite{curl, drq, rad}. Common auxiliary tasks include predicting future observations~\cite{world_models, dreamer}, learning inverse dynamics models~\cite{icm, curiosity}, and reconstructing input observations~\cite{ae_rl, beta_vae}. Another critical challenge in deep RL is the problem of catastrophic forgetting, where agents lose previously acquired knowledge when learning new tasks or adapting to environmental changes~\cite{catastrophic_forgetting, ewc, packnet}. This issue is particularly pronounced in continual learning scenarios where agents must sequentially learn multiple tasks without access to previous task data~\cite{continual_rl, clear, packnet_rl}. Traditional deep RL algorithms typically employ experience replay buffers~\cite{dqn1, rainbow} to mitigate this problem, but these approaches have limited capacity and may not scale effectively to long-term learning scenarios~\cite{gem, agem}. The intersection of representation learning and reinforcement learning has emerged as a crucial research area, with growing evidence that learning good representations is fundamental to sample-efficient RL~\cite{bisim, curl, drq}. Recent work has shown that incorporating techniques from self-supervised learning can significantly improve the data efficiency of RL algorithms~\cite{simclr_rl, moco_rl, byol_rl}. These approaches typically involve learning representations that capture task-relevant information while being invariant to task-irrelevant variations in the input~\cite{data_aug_rl, rad, drq}. Furthermore, the challenge of generalization remains a significant obstacle in deep RL, where agents often fail to transfer learned behaviors to slightly modified environments or unseen scenarios~\cite{generalization_rl, procgen, coinrun}. This limitation highlights the need for learning algorithms that can extract and utilize transferable knowledge across different but related tasks~\cite{meta_learning_rl, maml, reptile}. Recent advances in contrastive learning have shown remarkable success in computer vision and natural language processing~\cite{simclr, moco, clip}, leading researchers to explore their application in reinforcement learning contexts~\cite{curl, drq, proto_rl}. Contrastive methods learn representations by maximizing agreement between differently augmented views of the same data while minimizing agreement between views of different data points~\cite{contrastive_survey, simclr}. This approach has proven particularly effective for learning robust visual representations that generalize well across different domains~\cite{domain_adaptation, transfer_learning}. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines contrastive representation learning with auxiliary task objectives to improve sample efficiency and generalization in deep reinforcement learning. Our approach leverages the complementary strengths of these techniques to learn rich, transferable representations that accelerate learning across multiple tasks and environments.

To counter this problem, deep RL algorithms usually use experience replay buffers (see DQN, Rainbow), which have a limited capacity and might not scale to long-term learning. “The challenge of generalization is still a major obstacle in deep learning, where agents often fail to transfer the actions they have learned to slightly altered or new environments. Recent studies have shown that this can significantly improve the efficiency of RL methods. These methods typically learn representations which are invariant to task-irrelevant changes in the input (cf. data_aug_rl, rad, drq). The problem has become so important recently that learning methods have been needed that would be able to extract and use transferable knowledge from one task to another task. In recent years, contrastive learning has proved to be a great success in vision and natural language processing. Contrastive methods learn representations by maximizing the agreement between differently augmented views of the same data, and by reducing the agreement between views of different data. The recent success of contrastive learning has encouraged the investigation of its application in the context of reinforcement learning (drq, curly, proto_rl). In the present work, we propose a new method which combines representation learning by contrastive methods with auxiliary objectives, for the purpose of improving efficiency and generalization in deep reinforcement learning. This method combines the complementary advantages of the two methods, and so acquires rich and transferable representations, which permit better learning of the tasks and the environments. This method has been particularly successful in learning robust visual representations which generalize well to different domains, adaptation and transfer.

text: The containment of the Covid-19 pandemic has required the mobilization of the largest global public health response in decades \cite{fisher2020global}. Governments worldwide have implemented unprecedented measures ranging from border closures and travel restrictions to mandatory quarantines and nationwide lockdowns \cite{hale2021global, chinazzi2020effect}. These interventions, while necessary to mitigate virus transmission, have generated substantial economic and social costs that continue to reverberate across societies \cite{nicola2020socioeconomic, guerrieri2022macroeconomic}. The economic impact of pandemic containment measures has been profound and multifaceted. Initial estimates suggested that the global economy contracted by approximately 3.1\% in 2020, representing the worst recession since the Great Depression \cite{imf2021world}. However, the distribution of these economic costs has been highly uneven across sectors, regions, and demographic groups \cite{bartik2020impact, chetty2020economic}. Service industries, particularly hospitality, tourism, and retail, experienced disproportionate disruptions due to social distancing requirements and mobility restrictions \cite{goolsbee2021fear, baker2020covid}. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) faced acute liquidity challenges, with many unable to sustain operations during extended periods of reduced revenue \cite{fairlie2020impact, humphries2020does}. Labor markets have undergone dramatic transformations as a result of pandemic-related policies. Unemployment rates surged to levels not seen since the 1930s in many developed economies, with the United States experiencing peak unemployment of 14.8\% in April 2020 \cite{bls2021employment}. The burden of job losses fell disproportionately on workers in contact-intensive occupations, those with lower educational attainment, and historically disadvantaged groups including women and minorities \cite{mongey2021workers, alon2020impact}. The shift toward remote work arrangements, while enabling business continuity for some sectors, has exacerbated existing inequalities between workers who can perform their duties remotely and those whose jobs require physical presence \cite{dingel2020many, brynjolfsson2020covid}. Beyond immediate economic disruptions, the pandemic has accelerated structural changes in how societies organize work, education, and social interactions. The rapid adoption of digital technologies has fundamentally altered patterns of consumption, production, and service delivery \cite{brynjolfsson2020covid, bartik2021labor}. Educational institutions have been forced to transition to remote learning modalities, raising concerns about learning losses and widening achievement gaps \cite{engzell2021learning, maldonado2022educational}. Healthcare systems have faced unprecedented strain while simultaneously adapting to new protocols for infection control and patient care \cite{rosenbaum2020facing, mehrotra2020rapidly}. The social consequences of containment measures have been equally significant. Social isolation and reduced mobility have contributed to increased rates of mental health disorders, domestic violence, and substance abuse \cite{pfefferbaum2020mental, bradbury2020covid}. Vulnerable populations, including the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and those experiencing homelessness, have faced heightened risks and reduced access to essential services \cite{armitage2020covid, tsai2020covid}. The disruption of routine healthcare services has led to delayed diagnoses and treatments for non-COVID conditions, potentially resulting in long-term health consequences \cite{czeisler2020delay, santoli2020effects}. Policymakers have responded to these challenges through an array of fiscal and monetary interventions aimed at supporting households, businesses, and financial markets. Government spending programs have included direct cash transfers to individuals, enhanced unemployment benefits, and loans or grants to businesses \cite{blanchard2021defense, yagan2021employment}. Central banks have implemented aggressive monetary accommodation, including near-zero interest rates and quantitative easing programs \cite{bernanke2022monetary, yellen2021federal}. While these measures have provided crucial support during the acute phase of the crisis, they have also raised concerns about fiscal sustainability, inflation risks, and potential asset price bubbles \cite{summers2021biden, krugman2021arguing}. The heterogeneous nature of pandemic impacts has highlighted and, in many cases, exacerbated existing inequalities within and across countries. Developing nations have faced particular challenges due to limited fiscal capacity, weaker healthcare systems, and greater reliance on sectors vulnerable to pandemic disruptions \cite{loayza2020costs, aspachs2021real}. Within countries, the pandemic has disproportionately affected low-income communities, which often have higher rates of essential worker employment, limited ability to work from home, and reduced access to quality healthcare \cite{chetty2020economic, chen2021socioeconomic}. As the immediate health crisis has evolved with the development and distribution of vaccines, attention has increasingly turned to understanding the longer-term implications of pandemic-era policies and their effectiveness in achieving public health objectives while minimizing collateral damage. The experience has revealed both the capabilities and limitations of existing institutional frameworks for crisis response, highlighting areas where reforms may be necessary to enhance resilience against future shocks \cite{bavel2020using, haushofer2020both}. This unprecedented global experiment in public health intervention provides a unique opportunity to examine the complex tradeoffs inherent in pandemic response policies. Understanding these tradeoffs is essential for informing future preparedness efforts and developing more targeted approaches that can achieve public health goals while minimizing adverse economic and social consequences. The lessons learned from this experience will undoubtedly shape how societies prepare for and respond to future health emergencies, making rigorous analysis of pandemic containment measures and their multifaceted impacts a critical priority for researchers and policymakers alike.

text: In the past decades, multi-class classification has been used in a variety of areas, including image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar,deng2009imagenet, geusebroek2005amsterdam,Hsu02multisvm}, natural language processing~\cite{lang1995newsweeder,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2005-14165,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1801-06146}, etc. The success of multi-class classification algorithms depends heavily on their ability to handle complex decision boundaries and scale effectively with increasing numbers of classes. Traditional binary classification methods, while well-established, face significant challenges when extended to multi-class scenarios. The most common approaches include one-versus-one (OVO) and one-versus-all (OVA) strategies~\cite{rifkin2004defense,hsu2002comparison}, which decompose the multi-class problem into multiple binary classification tasks. One-versus-all methods train $k$ binary classifiers for $k$ classes, where each classifier distinguishes one class from all others. Despite their computational efficiency, OVA approaches often suffer from class imbalance issues, particularly when dealing with datasets where class distributions are highly skewed~\cite{krawczyk2016learning}. The decision boundaries learned by individual binary classifiers may not be optimal for the overall multi-class problem, leading to regions of ambiguity where multiple classifiers provide conflicting predictions. In contrast, one-versus-one strategies construct $\binom{k}{2}$ binary classifiers, each trained to distinguish between pairs of classes. While this approach typically yields better classification performance due to more balanced training sets for each binary problem, the computational complexity grows quadratically with the number of classes~\cite{platt1999large}. The final prediction requires a voting mechanism among all pairwise classifiers, which can be computationally expensive and may introduce additional sources of error. Support Vector Machines (SVMs) have emerged as particularly effective tools for multi-class classification due to their strong theoretical foundations and ability to handle high-dimensional feature spaces~\cite{cortes1995support,vapnik1998statistical}. The extension of SVMs to multi-class problems has been approached through various methodologies. Direct multi-class SVM formulations, such as those proposed by Crammer and Singer~\cite{crammer2001algorithmic} and Weston and Watkins~\cite{weston1999support}, attempt to solve the multi-class problem in a single optimization step. These methods formulate the problem as: \begin{equation} \min_{w,\xi} \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|w_i\|^2 + C\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j \end{equation} subject to the constraints: \begin{equation} w_{y_j}^T\phi(x_j) - w_i^T\phi(x_j) \geq 1 - \xi_j, \quad \forall i \neq y_j \end{equation} where $w_i$ represents the weight vector for class $i$, $\phi(x_j)$ denotes the feature mapping of sample $x_j$, and $\xi_j$ are slack variables allowing for misclassification. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized multi-class classification, particularly in domains with large-scale datasets and complex feature representations~\cite{lecun2015deep,goodfellow2016deep}. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in image classification tasks, achieving human-level performance on benchmark datasets such as ImageNet~\cite{he2016deep,simonyan2014very}. The ability of deep networks to automatically learn hierarchical feature representations has proven invaluable for handling the complexity inherent in multi-class problems. However, deep learning approaches face their own set of challenges in multi-class scenarios. The softmax activation function, commonly used in the output layer, can suffer from numerical instability when dealing with a large number of classes~\cite{bridle1990probabilistic}. Additionally, the class imbalance problem becomes more pronounced in deep networks, where minority classes may be overshadowed during the training process~\cite{johnson2019survey}. Recent advances have focused on addressing these limitations through various techniques. Hierarchical classification methods organize classes into tree-like structures, enabling more efficient training and prediction~\cite{silla2011survey}. These approaches are particularly beneficial when natural hierarchies exist among classes, such as in taxonomic classification or product categorization tasks. Ensemble methods have also gained significant attention for multi-class classification. Random forests~\cite{breiman2001random} and gradient boosting~\cite{friedman2001greedy} naturally extend to multi-class problems and often provide robust performance across diverse domains. The combination of multiple weak learners helps mitigate overfitting and improves generalization, particularly when dealing with noisy or limited training data. The evaluation of multi-class classification systems requires careful consideration of appropriate metrics. While overall accuracy provides a general measure of performance, it can be misleading in the presence of class imbalance. Metrics such as macro-averaged and micro-averaged F1-scores~\cite{sokolova2009systematic} offer more nuanced views of classifier performance across different classes. The confusion matrix remains an essential tool for understanding classification errors and identifying classes that are frequently confused with one another. Contemporary research continues to explore novel approaches to multi-class classification challenges. Few-shot learning~\cite{vinyals2016matching} addresses scenarios where only limited training examples are available for some classes, while zero-shot learning~\cite{xian2018zero} attempts to classify instances of classes not seen during training. These paradigms are particularly relevant in applications where obtaining labeled data for all classes is expensive or impractical. The integration of attention mechanisms~\cite{vaswani2017attention} and transformer architectures~\cite{devlin2018bert} has opened new avenues for multi-class classification, especially in natural language processing tasks. These models' ability to capture long-range dependencies and contextual relationships has proven valuable for document classification~\cite{adhikari2019docbert} and sentiment analysis applications.

text: A fully automated system that synthesizes realistic 3D human bodies approaching and grasping a target object in 3D space will be valuable in various fields, from robotics and computer vision to animation and virtual reality. Such systems require sophisticated understanding of human motion dynamics, spatial reasoning, and object interaction patterns. The challenge lies in generating natural, physically plausible movements that account for both the geometric constraints of the environment and the biomechanical limitations of human anatomy. Traditional approaches to human motion synthesis have relied heavily on motion capture data and database-driven methods \cite{kovar2002motion, arikan2002interactive}. While these techniques can produce high-quality results, they are fundamentally limited by the scope and diversity of the captured motion sequences. When faced with novel scenarios or target objects not present in the training data, such methods often fail to generalize effectively. Moreover, the discrete nature of motion databases makes it challenging to generate smooth transitions between different movement patterns or adapt to varying environmental constraints. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in deep generative models and reinforcement learning, have opened new avenues for addressing these limitations \cite{holden2017phase, peng2018deepmimic}. Neural network-based approaches can learn continuous representations of human motion and demonstrate improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional methods. However, most existing learning-based techniques focus on either locomotion or manipulation tasks in isolation, rather than addressing the integrated challenge of approach-and-grasp behaviors. The synthesis of realistic approach-and-grasp motions presents several interconnected challenges. First, the system must generate plausible approach trajectories that account for obstacles, workspace constraints, and the geometric properties of both the human body and the target object \cite{yamane2004planning}. Second, the transition from approach to grasping must be seamless, requiring careful coordination between whole-body motion and fine-grained hand movements. Third, the generated motions must satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously, including collision avoidance, joint limits, balance maintenance, and task completion. Existing work in human motion synthesis can be broadly categorized into several approaches. Physics-based simulation methods leverage biomechanical models and control theory to generate motions that satisfy physical constraints \cite{liu2005sampling, mordatch2012discovery}. While these approaches can produce physically consistent results, they often require extensive parameter tuning and may struggle to capture the nuanced characteristics of natural human movement. Data-driven methods, on the other hand, learn motion patterns directly from captured human demonstrations \cite{brand2000style, li2017auto}. These techniques excel at reproducing the statistical properties of training data but may lack the flexibility needed for novel scenarios. More recently, hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of physics-based simulation and data-driven learning have gained attention \cite{peng2021amp, won2021physics}. These methods use neural networks to learn control policies that operate within physics simulators, potentially achieving both physical realism and natural motion characteristics. However, the application of such techniques to complex manipulation tasks involving whole-body coordination remains an active area of research. The problem of grasp synthesis itself has been extensively studied in robotics literature \cite{sahbani2012overview, bohg2014data}. Traditional approaches focus on identifying stable grasp configurations based on geometric and force analysis. While effective for robotic applications, these methods often produce grasps that appear unnatural when applied to human hand models. Recent work has explored learning-based approaches to generate more human-like grasps \cite{brahmbhatt2019contactgrasp, taheri2020grab}, but these methods typically assume the hand is already positioned near the target object, neglecting the approach phase. The integration of approach and grasping behaviors requires addressing the coupling between global body motion and local hand control. During the approach phase, the entire body must be coordinated to position the hand appropriately while maintaining balance and avoiding obstacles. As the hand nears the target, the motion transitions to a more precise manipulation phase where finger positioning becomes critical. This transition must be smooth and natural, avoiding abrupt changes in motion characteristics that would appear unrealistic. Environmental awareness represents another crucial aspect of the problem. Real-world scenarios involve complex 3D environments with obstacles, varying surface heights, and spatial constraints that influence both approach trajectories and grasping strategies. The system must be capable of reasoning about these environmental factors and adapting the generated motion accordingly. This requires sophisticated spatial understanding and the ability to perform collision detection and avoidance in real-time. Furthermore, the diversity of human motion patterns presents both an opportunity and a challenge. Different individuals exhibit varying movement styles, preferences, and physical capabilities. A robust motion synthesis system should be able to capture this diversity while still producing motions that appear natural and task-appropriate. This requires learning representations that can encode both the common principles of human movement and the individual variations that make each person's motion unique. The evaluation of synthesized human motion presents its own set of challenges. Traditional metrics based on joint angle errors or trajectory deviations may not adequately capture the perceptual quality of generated motions. More sophisticated evaluation approaches that consider biomechanical plausibility, task success, and visual naturalness are needed to properly assess the quality of synthesized approach-and-grasp behaviors. In this work, we propose a novel framework for synthesizing realistic 3D human approach-and-grasp motions that addresses many of these challenges through a unified learning-based approach.

text: We consider a problem introduced by Feige, Gamarnik, Neeman, Rácz and Tetali \cite{feige2020finding}, that of finding a large clique in a random graph $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$, where the graph $G$ has been modified by planting a clique of size $k$ on a random subset of vertices. This problem serves as a fundamental example in the study of computational-statistical gaps in random structures, where information-theoretic detection is possible but efficient algorithms may fail. More precisely, we study the following planted clique model: Let $G \sim G(n, \frac{1}{2})$ be an Erdős-Rényi random graph on $n$ vertices where each edge appears independently with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. We then plant a clique of size $k$ by selecting a random subset $S \subseteq [n]$ of size $|S| = k$ and adding all edges within $S$ to form a complete subgraph. The resulting graph $G'$ contains this planted clique, and our goal is to recover $S$ (or a large subset of $S$) efficiently. The planted clique problem exhibits a rich phase transition structure that has been extensively studied in the literature \cite{jerrum1992large, kucera1995expected, alon1998finding}. When $k = \Omega(\sqrt{n \log n})$, spectral methods and semidefinite programming approaches can successfully recover the planted clique in polynomial time \cite{alon1998finding, feige2001finding}. However, for smaller values of $k$, no polynomial-time algorithm is known to succeed, despite the fact that information-theoretic detection remains possible for $k = \Omega(\log n)$. The computational hardness of the planted clique problem for intermediate values of $k$ has profound implications for understanding the limits of efficient computation in random structures. This problem has served as a testing ground for various algorithmic techniques, including spectral methods \cite{mcsherry2001spectral}, semidefinite programming relaxations \cite{feige2001finding}, and more recently, sum-of-squares hierarchies \cite{barak2016nearly, hopkins2017efficient}. In this work, we focus on the regime where $k = o(\sqrt{n})$, which lies in the conjectured computationally hard phase. Our main contribution is to analyze the performance of a natural greedy algorithm that iteratively builds a large clique by selecting vertices with the highest degree within the current candidate set. While such greedy approaches have been studied in various contexts \cite{karp1976probabilistic, bollobas1985random}, their analysis in the planted clique setting requires careful handling of the interplay between the random background graph and the planted structure. The greedy algorithm we analyze proceeds as follows: Starting from the full vertex set $V$, we iteratively remove the vertex with the smallest degree in the induced subgraph until we obtain a clique. At each step, we maintain a subset $T \subseteq V$ and remove the vertex $v \in T$ that minimizes the number of neighbors of $v$ within $T$. This process continues until the induced subgraph $G'[T]$ forms a clique. Our main theoretical result establishes that with high probability, this greedy algorithm recovers a clique of size $\Theta(k)$ when applied to a graph with a planted clique of size $k$. More specifically, we prove that for $k = \omega(\log n)$ and $k = o(\sqrt{n})$, the greedy algorithm finds a clique of size at least $ck$ for some absolute constant $c > 0$. \begin{theorem} Let $G'$ be a graph obtained by planting a clique of size $k$ in $G \sim G(n, \frac{1}{2})$. If $k \geq C \log n$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$, then with probability $1 - o(1)$, the greedy algorithm finds a clique of size at least $\frac{k}{4}$. \end{theorem} The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main} relies on a careful analysis of the degree sequence evolution during the greedy process. We show that vertices in the planted clique tend to have higher degrees than vertices outside the planted clique at each step of the algorithm, making them less likely to be removed. This bias accumulates over the course of the algorithm, leading to the recovery of a substantial fraction of the planted clique. Our analysis technique builds upon concentration inequalities for random graphs and careful tracking of the degree distributions. A key technical challenge is to control the correlation between the degrees of different vertices as the algorithm progresses, since the removal of vertices affects the degrees of their neighbors in a complex manner. The study of greedy algorithms for clique finding is motivated by their simplicity and practical appeal. While spectral and semidefinite programming methods achieve better theoretical guarantees, they are often more complex to implement and may be less suitable for very large graphs. Greedy algorithms, on the other hand, are straightforward to implement and have low computational overhead, making them attractive for practical applications. Furthermore, our analysis contributes to the broader understanding of how local search heuristics perform on random instances with planted structure. The planted clique problem serves as a canonical example where such methods can be rigorously analyzed, providing insights that may extend to other combinatorial optimization problems on random graphs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide necessary background on random graphs and concentration inequalities. Section 3 contains the detailed analysis of the greedy algorithm, including the proof of our main theorem. In Section 4, we discuss extensions and variations of our results, including the performance of the algorithm on graphs with multiple planted cliques and modifications of the greedy strategy. Finally, Section 5 concludes with open questions and directions for future research. Our results complement the existing literature on planted clique algorithms by providing a rigorous analysis of a natural and practical approach. While the greedy method does not achieve the optimal information-theoretic threshold, it offers a compelling trade-off between simplicity and performance in the regime where more sophisticated algorithms are not known to succeed.

text: Sparsification is the fundamental concept of reducing the size of a large graph $G$ while still maintaining essential properties of the graph. This process has become increasingly important in modern computational settings where graphs can contain millions or billions of vertices and edges, making direct analysis computationally prohibitive. The primary goal of sparsification is to construct a smaller graph $H$ that approximates $G$ in some well-defined sense, enabling efficient algorithms to operate on $H$ while providing meaningful insights about the original graph $G$. The theoretical foundations of graph sparsification can be traced back to the seminal work of Benczúr and Karger \cite{benczur1996approximating}, who introduced the concept of cut sparsifiers. A cut sparsifier is a weighted subgraph that preserves the value of all cuts in the original graph up to a multiplicative factor of $(1 \pm \epsilon)$ for some small $\epsilon > 0$. This breakthrough established that any graph with $n$ vertices admits a cut sparsifier with $O(n \log n / \epsilon^2)$ edges, representing a significant reduction from the potentially $O(n^2)$ edges in dense graphs. Building upon this foundational work, Spielman and Teng \cite{spielman2011spectral} introduced spectral sparsifiers, which preserve the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian matrix. A spectral sparsifier $H$ of graph $G$ satisfies the condition that for all vectors $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$: \begin{equation} (1-\epsilon) x^T L_G x \leq x^T L_H x \leq (1+\epsilon) x^T L_G x \end{equation} where $L_G$ and $L_H$ denote the Laplacian matrices of graphs $G$ and $H$, respectively. This spectral preservation property ensures that many important graph algorithms, including those for solving linear systems, computing effective resistances, and approximating eigenvalues, can be efficiently executed on the sparsifier with performance guarantees that translate back to the original graph. The construction of effective sparsifiers has evolved through several algorithmic paradigms. Early approaches relied on random sampling techniques, where edges are sampled with probabilities proportional to their effective resistances \cite{spielman2011graph}. The effective resistance of an edge $e = (u,v)$ in graph $G$ is defined as $R_{eff}(u,v) = (e_u - e_v)^T L_G^{\dagger} (e_u - e_v)$, where $e_u$ and $e_v$ are standard basis vectors and $L_G^{\dagger}$ represents the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the Laplacian matrix. This quantity captures the electrical resistance between vertices $u$ and $v$ when the graph is viewed as an electrical network, providing a natural measure of edge importance. However, computing effective resistances exactly requires expensive matrix operations, leading to the development of more practical algorithms. Koutis, Miller, and Peng \cite{koutis2014approaching} proposed nearly-linear time algorithms for constructing spectral sparsifiers by employing sophisticated techniques from algebraic graph theory and numerical linear algebra. Their approach achieves a running time of $\tilde{O}(m)$ where $m$ is the number of edges in the original graph, making sparsification practical for large-scale applications. Recent advances have focused on improving the quality-size trade-offs of sparsifiers and developing specialized variants for specific applications. Batson, Spielman, and Srivastava \cite{batson2012twice} proved the existence of spectral sparsifiers with only $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges, which is optimal up to constant factors. Their constructive proof, based on the method of interlacing polynomials, provides a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for constructing such optimal sparsifiers, though the running time remains impractical for very large graphs. The applications of graph sparsification extend far beyond theoretical computer science into numerous practical domains. In machine learning, sparsifiers enable efficient processing of large-scale similarity graphs arising in clustering, semi-supervised learning, and dimensionality reduction \cite{chen2015fast}. The preservation of spectral properties ensures that algorithms like spectral clustering maintain their approximation guarantees when applied to sparsified graphs, while achieving significant computational speedups. In network analysis, sparsification techniques facilitate the study of large social networks, biological networks, and infrastructure networks. For instance, analyzing the connectivity structure of the internet graph or understanding protein-protein interaction networks becomes computationally feasible through appropriate sparsification \cite{leskovec2008statistical}. The key insight is that many network properties of interest, such as conductance, mixing times of random walks, and community structure, are preserved under spectral sparsification. The field has also witnessed the development of specialized sparsification techniques tailored to specific graph classes and applications. For planar graphs, Batson et al. \cite{batson2013spectral} showed that linear-sized spectral sparsifiers exist, leveraging the special structure of planar graphs to achieve better bounds than the general case. Similarly, for graphs with bounded treewidth or other structural constraints, improved sparsification results have been established. Dynamic sparsification represents another active research direction, addressing scenarios where the underlying graph changes over time through edge insertions and deletions. Maintaining a high-quality sparsifier in a dynamic setting poses unique challenges, as naive reconstruction after each update would be computationally expensive. Recent work by Kapron, King, and Mountjoy \cite{kapron2013dynamic} and others has developed data structures that can maintain approximate sparsifiers with polylogarithmic update times. The theoretical analysis of sparsification algorithms often relies on sophisticated probabilistic techniques and concentration inequalities. Matrix concentration inequalities, particularly those developed by Tropp \cite{tropp2012user}, provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing the spectral properties of randomly constructed sparsifiers. These tools enable precise characterization of the trade-offs between sparsifier size, approximation quality, and failure probability. Furthermore, the connection between sparsification and other fundamental problems in theoretical computer science has led to cross-pollination of ideas. text: Social networks are used not only to stay in touch with friends and family, but also to spread and receive information on specific products and services. The proliferation of social media platforms has fundamentally transformed how consumers discover, evaluate, and share information about products and services \cite{kietzmann2011social}. This transformation has created unprecedented opportunities for businesses to engage with their target audiences while simultaneously presenting new challenges in understanding and managing online consumer behavior \cite{kaplan2010users}. Traditional marketing paradigms relied heavily on one-way communication channels, where companies broadcast messages to passive consumers through television, radio, and print media \cite{kotler2016marketing}. However, the emergence of social networks has democratized information sharing, enabling consumers to become active participants in brand conversations and influence networks \cite{mangold2009social}. This shift has profound implications for how products and services gain market traction, as peer-to-peer recommendations now carry significantly more weight than traditional advertising messages \cite{trusov2009effects}. The architecture of social networks facilitates rapid information diffusion through interconnected user relationships, creating what researchers term "viral marketing" effects \cite{watts2007viral}. When users share positive experiences with products or services, this information can cascade through their social connections, potentially reaching audiences far beyond the original poster's immediate network \cite{kempe2003maximizing}. This phenomenon has led to the emergence of influencer marketing, where individuals with large followings can significantly impact consumer purchasing decisions through product endorsements and reviews \cite{freberg2011who}. Moreover, social networks have become critical platforms for customer service and brand reputation management. Consumers increasingly turn to social media to voice complaints, seek support, and share both positive and negative experiences with brands \cite{kiron2013social}. Companies must now monitor multiple social channels simultaneously to respond promptly to customer inquiries and address potential reputation threats before they escalate \cite{aral2013creating}. The data generated through social network interactions provides valuable insights into consumer preferences, sentiment, and behavior patterns. Advanced analytics techniques, including natural language processing and machine learning algorithms, enable businesses to extract actionable intelligence from social media conversations \cite{he2013social}. This capability allows for more targeted marketing campaigns, improved product development decisions, and enhanced customer segmentation strategies \cite{chen2012business}. However, the use of social networks for commercial purposes also raises significant privacy and ethical concerns. The collection and utilization of personal data for targeted advertising has sparked debates about user consent, data ownership, and the potential for manipulation \cite{tufekci2014engineering}. Regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) have emerged to address these concerns, requiring businesses to adopt more transparent data practices \cite{regulation2016general}. The effectiveness of social network marketing varies considerably across different product categories and demographic segments. Research indicates that products with high social visibility, such as fashion items and consumer electronics, tend to benefit more from social media promotion than utilitarian products with lower social significance \cite{berger2013word}. Similarly, younger demographics, who are more active on social platforms, show greater susceptibility to social influence in their purchasing decisions \cite{smith2012social}. The global reach of social networks has also enabled small businesses and entrepreneurs to access international markets previously dominated by large corporations with substantial marketing budgets \cite{quinton2013digital}. Platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter provide cost-effective advertising options that allow businesses to target specific geographic regions, interests, and demographic characteristics with precision \cite{tuten2017social}. Furthermore, the real-time nature of social media communication has compressed the product lifecycle, accelerating both the adoption and abandonment of trends. Products can achieve viral status overnight, leading to sudden spikes in demand, while negative sentiment can equally quickly damage brand reputation and sales \cite{godes2004using}. This dynamic environment requires businesses to be more agile in their marketing strategies and responsive to changing consumer sentiment \cite{kietzmann2011social}. The integration of e-commerce functionality within social platforms has further blurred the lines between social interaction and commercial transaction. Features such as Instagram Shopping and Facebook Marketplace enable users to discover and purchase products without leaving the social environment, creating seamless shopping experiences that capitalize on impulse buying behavior \cite{zhang2014understanding}. As artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies continue to evolve, social networks are becoming increasingly sophisticated in their ability to predict user preferences and deliver personalized content and advertisements. This technological advancement promises to make social media marketing even more effective while raising additional questions about privacy and the potential for algorithmic bias \cite{barocas2016big}. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of social media for business purposes, as physical distancing measures forced companies to rely more heavily on digital channels for customer engagement and sales \cite{he2020covid}. This shift has permanently altered consumer expectations regarding online interaction with brands and has established social media as an essential component of any comprehensive marketing strategy. Understanding the complex dynamics of how information spreads through social networks, the factors that influence user engagement, and the mechanisms that drive purchasing decisions has become crucial for businesses seeking to leverage these platforms effectively. This understanding requires interdisciplinary approaches that combine insights from marketing, psychology, sociology, and computer science to develop comprehensive models of social media influence and consumer behavior.

text: Reinforcement learning has achieved great success on many challenging problems. Notable work includes DQN~\cite{mnih2015human}, AlphaGo~\cite{silver2016mastering} and OpenAI Five~\cite{berner2019dota}. However, these successes have primarily been demonstrated in environments with well-defined reward structures and clear objectives. In many real-world scenarios, defining appropriate reward functions remains a significant challenge, often requiring extensive domain expertise and iterative refinement~\cite{ng1999policy}. This limitation has motivated the development of alternative paradigms that can learn from different types of supervision signals. Imitation learning emerges as a promising approach to address this challenge by learning policies directly from expert demonstrations rather than relying on hand-crafted reward functions~\cite{hussein2017imitation}. The fundamental premise is that observing optimal or near-optimal behavior can provide sufficient information to recover effective policies without explicit reward engineering. This paradigm has found applications across diverse domains, including autonomous driving~\cite{bojarski2016end}, robotics~\cite{argall2009survey}, and game playing~\cite{ross2011reduction}. Traditional imitation learning methods can be broadly categorized into two main approaches: behavioral cloning and inverse reinforcement learning. Behavioral cloning treats imitation as a supervised learning problem, directly mapping states to actions using standard regression or classification techniques~\cite{pomerleau1991efficient}. While conceptually simple and computationally efficient, behavioral cloning suffers from distributional shift issues, where the learned policy may encounter states not present in the demonstration data, leading to compounding errors and poor generalization~\cite{ross2010efficient}. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) takes a different approach by first recovering the underlying reward function that explains the expert's behavior, then using conventional reinforcement learning to optimize this recovered reward~\cite{abbeel2004apprenticeship}. Methods such as Maximum Entropy IRL~\cite{ziebart2008maximum} and Guided Cost Learning~\cite{finn2016guided} have shown promising results but often require solving multiple reinforcement learning problems during training, making them computationally expensive and potentially unstable. Recent advances have introduced adversarial approaches to imitation learning, most notably Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL)~\cite{ho2016generative}. GAIL frames imitation learning as a minimax game between a generator (policy) and a discriminator, where the discriminator learns to distinguish between expert and policy trajectories while the policy attempts to fool the discriminator. This approach eliminates the need for explicit reward recovery while addressing some limitations of behavioral cloning. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges persist in imitation learning. First, the quality and quantity of expert demonstrations significantly impact learning performance, yet obtaining high-quality demonstrations can be expensive and time-consuming~\cite{brown2019extrapolating}. Second, most existing methods assume access to complete state-action trajectories, which may not be available in many practical scenarios where only partial observations or outcome data are accessible~\cite{torabi2018behavioral}. Furthermore, the assumption of expert optimality is often violated in practice, as human demonstrators may exhibit suboptimal, inconsistent, or noisy behavior~\cite{brown2020better}. This mismatch between theoretical assumptions and practical realities can lead to poor learning outcomes and highlights the need for more robust imitation learning algorithms that can handle imperfect demonstrations. Another critical limitation lies in the scalability and sample efficiency of current methods. Many state-of-the-art approaches require substantial amounts of demonstration data and computational resources, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional state and action spaces~\cite{kostrikov2018discriminator}. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in domains where collecting demonstrations is expensive or risky, such as medical applications or autonomous vehicle control. The multi-agent setting introduces additional complexity, as agents must learn not only from expert demonstrations but also coordinate their behaviors in environments with multiple learning agents~\cite{le2017coordinated}. Traditional single-agent imitation learning methods may fail to capture the strategic interactions and emergent behaviors that arise in multi-agent scenarios. In this work, we address these challenges by proposing a novel framework that combines the benefits of adversarial imitation learning with improved sample efficiency and robustness to demonstration quality. Our approach introduces several key innovations that advance the state-of-the-art in imitation learning while maintaining computational tractability and practical applicability.

In inverse reinforcement learning, the approach is different: we first estimate the underlying reward function which explains the expert's behavior, and then we apply a standard reinforcement learning technique to optimize this recovered reward, as in Pomerleau, 1991. The basic idea of inverse reinforcement learning is that observing a behavior that is optimal or close to it can provide sufficient information to reconstruct an effective policy, without explicit rewards. This method has been applied to many different domains, such as automatic driving (Bojarski, 2016), robots (Argall, 2009), and games (Ross, 2011). Imitation, though simple in concept and efficient in practice, is subject to the problem of distributional shift, which occurs when the policy meets states not encountered by the demonstration, resulting in errors and bad generalization. Imitation is treated as a supervised learning problem, directly mapping states to actions, using regression or classification techniques. Several methods of imitation learning, such as maximum entropy I-net and guided cost I-net, have yielded promising results, but require the simultaneous solution of several reinforcement learning problems during training, which makes them expensive in terms of computational resources, and in some cases unstable. Recent advances have introduced adversarial approaches to imitation learning, notably generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL). This represents imitation learning as a minimax game between a generator (policy) and a discriminator, where the discriminator learns to distinguish between expert and policy trajectories, and the policy tries to fool the discriminator. In a general way, this approach first eliminates the need for explicit reward reproduction and overcomes some of the limitations of the cloning method. The quality and quantity of the demonstrations are critical for learning performance, but obtaining high-quality demonstrations is expensive and time-consuming. One of the critical limitations of current methods is their scalability and sample efficiency. Many state-of-the-art methods require substantial amounts of demonstration data and computational resources, especially when dealing with high-dimensional state and action spaces. Moreover, the assumption of expert-like optimum performance is often violated in practice, because human demonstrators often exhibit sub-optimal, inconsistent, or noisy behavior. The multi-agent setting adds an additional layer of complexity, as agents not only need to learn from demonstrations but also how to coordinate their actions in environments with multiple learners. This is particularly salient in settings where gathering demonstrations is expensive or risky, such as medical applications or the control of self-driving vehicles. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a new framework that combines the benefits of adversarial imitation learning with improved sample efficiency and robustness to demonstration quality. ... Our method introduces a number of key innovations which simultaneously advance the state-of-the-art in imitation learning while also maintaining tractability and practical applicability.

text: Over the years, \ac{NBR} has received a considerable amount of interest from the research community \citep{fpmc,dream,bai2018attribute}. The fundamental premise of \ac{NBR} lies in leveraging implicit feedback signals, such as user browsing history, click patterns, and purchase sequences, to predict what items users are likely to engage with next \citep{rendle2010factorizing,he2016fusing}. Unlike traditional collaborative filtering approaches that primarily rely on explicit ratings, \ac{NBR} systems must infer user preferences from sequential behavioral data, making them particularly well-suited for modern e-commerce and content recommendation scenarios where explicit feedback is often sparse or unavailable \citep{hidasi2015session,tan2016improved}. The evolution of \ac{NBR} methodologies has been marked by several significant paradigm shifts. Early approaches focused on matrix factorization techniques adapted for sequential data \citep{koren2008factorization,rendle2009bpr}, which decomposed user-item interaction matrices while incorporating temporal dynamics. These methods, while foundational, often struggled to capture complex sequential patterns and long-term dependencies inherent in user behavior \citep{quadrana2018sequence}. The introduction of deep learning architectures revolutionized the field, with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants becoming prominent solutions for modeling sequential user preferences \citep{hidasi2015session,li2017neural}. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) demonstrated superior capability in capturing both short-term and long-term user interests, leading to significant improvements in recommendation accuracy \citep{donkers2017sequential,bogina2017temporal}. More recently, attention mechanisms and transformer-based architectures have emerged as powerful alternatives to recurrent models \citep{kang2018self,sun2019bert4rec}. These approaches excel at modeling complex item relationships and can effectively handle variable-length sequences without the computational bottlenecks associated with sequential processing in RNNs \citep{chen2019behavior,zhou2019deep}. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges continue to plague \ac{NBR} systems. The cold start problem remains particularly acute, as new users with limited interaction history pose significant difficulties for sequential modeling approaches \citep{lam2008addressing,schein2002methods}. Similarly, data sparsity issues become magnified in sequential settings, where the requirement for sufficient historical data to model temporal patterns often conflicts with the reality of sparse user-item interactions \citep{sarwar2001item,su2009survey}. Scalability concerns also present ongoing challenges, particularly as user bases and item catalogs continue to grow exponentially. Traditional sequential models often exhibit quadratic or higher complexity with respect to sequence length, making them computationally prohibitive for real-world applications with extensive user histories \citep{vaswani2017attention,devlin2018bert}. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of user preferences introduces additional complexity, as recommendation systems must adapt to evolving tastes and seasonal patterns while maintaining stability in their predictions \citep{ding2005time,campos2014time}. The balance between exploiting established user preferences and exploring new recommendation opportunities remains a critical consideration in system design \citep{li2010contextual,chapelle2011empirical}. Recent research has also highlighted the importance of incorporating contextual information beyond pure sequential patterns. Factors such as time of day, device type, location, and social context can significantly influence user behavior and recommendation effectiveness \citep{adomavicius2011context,baltrunas2011incarmusic}. However, integrating these diverse contextual signals while maintaining model interpretability and computational efficiency presents ongoing research challenges. The evaluation of \ac{NBR} systems introduces its own set of complexities, as traditional offline metrics may not adequately capture the sequential nature of user interactions or the temporal aspects of recommendation quality \citep{gunawardana2009survey,shani2011evaluating}. The development of appropriate evaluation frameworks that account for temporal dynamics, sequence-aware metrics, and real-world deployment constraints remains an active area of investigation.

text: With the growing complexity of machine learning models, especially those in recommendation systems, how to deal with abundant input features effectively and efficiently becomes a crucial problem. Feature selection and dimensionality reduction have emerged as fundamental challenges in modern machine learning pipelines, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets that are ubiquitous in recommendation systems \cite{chen2016xgboost, he2017neural}. Traditional approaches often struggle to balance computational efficiency with predictive performance, leading to suboptimal model deployment in production environments. The proliferation of deep learning architectures has introduced sophisticated methods for automatic feature extraction and representation learning \cite{goodfellow2016deep}. However, these approaches frequently require substantial computational resources and may not be suitable for real-time applications where latency constraints are paramount. Moreover, the interpretability of learned representations remains a significant concern in many domains where explainable AI is essential \cite{ribeiro2016should, lundberg2017unified}. Recent advances in neural architecture search (NAS) and automated machine learning (AutoML) have shown promising results in automatically discovering optimal feature combinations and model architectures \cite{elsken2019neural, he2021automl}. These methods leverage evolutionary algorithms, reinforcement learning, and gradient-based optimization to explore vast search spaces efficiently. Nevertheless, the computational overhead associated with these techniques often makes them impractical for large-scale industrial applications. Feature interaction modeling represents another critical aspect of handling complex input spaces. Traditional linear models fail to capture non-linear relationships and higher-order interactions between features, while polynomial feature expansion leads to exponential growth in dimensionality \cite{rendle2010factorization}. Factorization machines and their deep learning extensions have addressed some of these limitations by learning low-dimensional embeddings for categorical features \cite{rendle2012factorization, guo2017deepfm}. The challenge becomes even more pronounced in recommendation systems, where the feature space typically includes user profiles, item attributes, contextual information, and historical interactions \cite{koren2009matrix, he2017neural}. The sparse nature of these features, combined with their categorical properties, requires specialized handling techniques. Embedding layers have become the de facto standard for representing categorical features in deep learning models, but determining optimal embedding dimensions and managing the resulting parameter explosion remains an active area of research \cite{kula2015metadata, covington2016deep}. Transfer learning and pre-trained embeddings offer potential solutions for reducing the burden of feature engineering \cite{devlin2018bert, radford2019language}. By leveraging representations learned from large-scale datasets, models can benefit from rich feature encodings without requiring extensive domain-specific feature construction. However, the adaptation of general-purpose embeddings to specific recommendation tasks often requires careful fine-tuning and domain adaptation strategies. Multi-task learning frameworks provide another avenue for efficient feature utilization by sharing representations across related tasks \cite{caruana1997multitask, ruder2017overview}. In recommendation systems, this approach can be particularly effective when dealing with multiple objectives such as click-through rate prediction, conversion rate optimization, and user engagement modeling. The shared feature representations can reduce overfitting and improve generalization, especially when individual tasks have limited training data. The emergence of graph neural networks (GNNs) has introduced new perspectives on feature representation in recommendation systems \cite{hamilton2017inductive, velivckovic2017graph}. By modeling user-item interactions as graph structures, GNNs can capture complex relational patterns and propagate information through the network topology. This approach naturally handles the collaborative filtering aspect of recommendations while incorporating rich feature information at both node and edge levels. Attention mechanisms have revolutionized how models process and weight different features dynamically \cite{vaswani2017attention, chen2019behavior}. Self-attention and cross-attention layers enable models to focus on the most relevant features for each prediction, effectively performing soft feature selection. This capability is particularly valuable in recommendation systems where the importance of different features may vary significantly across users, items, and contexts. The scalability challenges associated with large-scale feature processing have led to the development of distributed computing frameworks and specialized hardware accelerations \cite{dean2012large, jouppi2017datacenter}. Techniques such as feature hashing, quantization, and pruning help reduce memory footprint and computational requirements while maintaining model performance. These optimizations are crucial for deploying recommendation models in production environments with strict latency and resource constraints.

text: {\bf Motivation}. Stack Overflow\footnote{https://stackoverflow.com/} is one of the most popular websites for users to ask and answer questions about topics in software development. Since its launch in 2008, Stack Overflow has grown to become the largest online community for programmers, hosting millions of questions and answers across virtually every programming language, framework, and technology stack. The platform's success stems from its unique combination of gamification elements, community-driven moderation, and sophisticated ranking algorithms that help surface high-quality content \cite{mamykina2011design, bosu2013building}. The collaborative nature of Stack Overflow creates a rich ecosystem where developers can share knowledge, troubleshoot problems, and learn from each other's experiences. However, this vast repository of information also presents significant challenges for both users seeking answers and researchers attempting to understand programming practices and trends. The sheer volume of content—with thousands of new questions posted daily—makes it increasingly difficult to locate relevant, high-quality solutions efficiently \cite{treude2011programmers, yang2016query}. Recent studies have highlighted several key issues within the Stack Overflow ecosystem. First, the problem of question quality and discoverability has become increasingly pronounced as the platform has scaled \cite{calefato2018ask, wang2018much}. Many questions are poorly formulated, lack sufficient context, or duplicate existing content, leading to fragmented knowledge and user frustration. Second, the temporal nature of technology means that highly-ranked answers from several years ago may no longer represent current best practices or may reference deprecated APIs and frameworks \cite{barua2014developers, rosen2016mobile}. Furthermore, the democratized nature of the platform, while being one of its greatest strengths, also introduces challenges related to answer quality and reliability. Unlike traditional documentation or peer-reviewed publications, Stack Overflow answers can be contributed by anyone, regardless of their expertise level. While the community voting system and moderation help filter content, studies have shown that popular answers are not always technically accurate or represent optimal solutions \cite{zhang2019empirical, mondal2019empirical}. The complexity of modern software development has also evolved significantly since Stack Overflow's inception. Today's developers work with increasingly sophisticated toolchains, microservices architectures, cloud platforms, and machine learning frameworks. This evolution has created new categories of questions that often require interdisciplinary knowledge spanning multiple technologies and domains \cite{vasilescu2014social, ahmed2017systematic}. From a research perspective, Stack Overflow represents an unprecedented source of data about real-world programming practices, common pitfalls, and the evolution of software development methodologies. The platform's structured format, with questions, answers, comments, and voting mechanisms, provides rich metadata that enables various forms of analysis \cite{vasilescu2013stackoverflow, allamanis2013mining}. However, extracting meaningful insights from this data requires sophisticated approaches that can handle the platform's scale, diversity, and inherent noise. The motivation for studying Stack Overflow extends beyond academic curiosity. Understanding how developers seek and share knowledge on the platform can inform the design of better development tools, educational curricula, and documentation practices. Additionally, insights derived from Stack Overflow data can help identify emerging trends in technology adoption, common security vulnerabilities, and areas where the developer community struggles most \cite{bajaj2014mining, fischer2013users}. Several research directions have emerged from the study of Stack Overflow data. These include automatic question classification and tagging \cite{stanley2013predicting, xu2008tag}, answer quality prediction \cite{correa2014chaff, shah2019predicting}, duplicate question detection \cite{ahasanuzzaman2016mining, hoogeveen2015automatic}, and the analysis of programming language ecosystems \cite{ray2014large, bissyande2013popularity}. Each of these areas presents unique challenges and opportunities for advancing our understanding of collaborative knowledge sharing in software development. The intersection of natural language processing and software engineering has proven particularly fruitful in the context of Stack Overflow research. The platform's textual content, combined with code snippets and technical discussions, provides an ideal testbed for developing and evaluating techniques that bridge the gap between human communication and technical documentation \cite{ponzanelli2014mining, gu2016deep}. As artificial intelligence and machine learning continue to transform software development practices, Stack Overflow data has become increasingly valuable for training and evaluating AI-powered development tools. From code completion systems to automated bug detection and repair tools, many modern development aids rely on large-scale datasets of real-world programming examples, with Stack Overflow serving as a primary source \cite{allamanis2018survey, chen2019neural}. The platform's global reach and multilingual community also present opportunities for studying cross-cultural aspects of software development and knowledge sharing. While English dominates the platform, the presence of international developers creates interesting dynamics around language barriers, cultural differences in communication styles, and the globalization of programming practices \cite{vasilescu2012continuous, baltes2018usage}.

In addition, insights from Stack Overflow data can be used to identify emerging trends in the use of technology, common security problems, and where the developer community struggles the most. During the evolution of the development practices, the data from StackOverflow have become more and more valuable for the training and testing of AI-driven tools. This is the case for automatic question classification and tagging (citing stanley,2013predicting, xu,2008tag), for quality prediction of answers (citing correa,2014stack, shah,2019predict), for the detection of duplicate questions (citing ahasanuzzaman,2016mining, hoogeveen,2015automated) and the analysis of the language of the questions (citing ray,2014large, bissyande,2013popularity). Each of these fields has its particular challenges and opportunities for advancing our understanding of knowledge development through collaboration. In a largely English-speaking environment, the presence of international users creates interesting dynamics around language barriers, cultural differences in communication styles and the internationalization of development practices. Many modern development tools rely on large-scale collections of real-world programming examples, and Stack Overflow has become one of the primary sources. The textual content of the platform, along with code fragments and technical discussions, constitutes an ideal testbed for developing and evaluating the techniques to bridge the gap between human communication and technical documentation. The platform's international reach and its multilingual community also provide opportunities for examining the cross-cultural aspects of software development and knowledge sharing.

text: A common approach to explanation generation in automated planning has been to treat the problem as one of model reconciliation~\cite{chakraborti2017plan}. In this framework, the explainer assumes that the human has an incomplete or incorrect mental model of the planning domain, and the goal is to provide explanations that help reconcile this model with the ground truth used by the automated planner. This reconciliation process typically involves identifying discrepancies between the human's mental model and the actual domain model, then generating explanations that address these specific gaps in understanding. The model reconciliation approach has proven particularly effective because it provides a principled foundation for determining what information should be included in an explanation. Rather than attempting to explain every aspect of a plan or decision, the explainer can focus specifically on those elements that differ between the human's assumed model and the actual model. This targeted approach helps avoid information overload while ensuring that explanations address the most critical misunderstandings. Several key challenges emerge within the model reconciliation framework. First, the explainer must somehow infer or estimate the human's mental model, which is inherently unobservable and may vary significantly between individuals. Second, the explainer must determine the most effective way to communicate the identified discrepancies, considering factors such as cognitive load, prior knowledge, and the specific context of the interaction. Third, the explanation generation process must be computationally tractable, particularly in time-sensitive applications where delays in providing explanations could undermine their utility. Recent work has extended the basic model reconciliation approach in several important directions. Some researchers have explored interactive explanation methods that allow humans to ask questions and receive targeted responses, enabling a more dynamic reconciliation process~\cite{miller2019explanation}. Others have investigated the use of machine learning techniques to better predict human mental models based on observed behavior or explicit feedback. Additionally, there has been growing interest in developing explanation methods that can handle uncertainty in both the domain model and the human's understanding. Despite these advances, significant limitations remain in current model reconciliation approaches. Many existing methods rely on strong assumptions about the structure and content of human mental models, which may not hold in practice. Furthermore, the effectiveness of explanations generated through model reconciliation has not been thoroughly validated through empirical studies with human subjects. There is also limited understanding of how explanation quality depends on factors such as domain complexity, plan length, and individual differences in cognitive abilities and domain expertise. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a novel approach to explanation generation that extends the model reconciliation framework while incorporating insights from cognitive science and human-computer interaction research. Our contributions include a more flexible representation of human mental models, an adaptive explanation generation algorithm that can handle uncertainty and individual differences, and an empirical evaluation demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach across multiple planning domains and user populations.

text: \IEEEPARstart{C}ivil drones have been a hot topic for a decade. Notably, this interest is shared between industry, academia, business, and civil society. The proliferation of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in civilian applications has fundamentally transformed numerous sectors, ranging from agriculture and logistics to emergency response and environmental monitoring \cite{shakhatreh2019unmanned, mohsan2023unmanned}. This technological revolution has been driven by significant advancements in miniaturization, battery technology, sensor integration, and autonomous navigation systems, making drones more accessible, reliable, and cost-effective than ever before \cite{zhang2020comprehensive}. The commercial drone market has experienced exponential growth, with projections indicating a compound annual growth rate exceeding 15\% through 2030 \cite{grand2023drone}. This surge is attributed to the convergence of several factors: decreasing manufacturing costs, regulatory frameworks becoming more accommodating, and the recognition of drones as viable solutions for complex operational challenges. Industries such as precision agriculture have embraced drone technology for crop monitoring, pesticide application, and yield optimization, demonstrating measurable improvements in efficiency and resource utilization \cite{tsouros2019review}. From an academic perspective, civil drone research has evolved into a multidisciplinary field encompassing aerodynamics, control systems, artificial intelligence, computer vision, and telecommunications. Universities worldwide have established dedicated research centers focusing on UAV technologies, fostering innovation in areas such as swarm intelligence, autonomous path planning, and human-drone interaction \cite{chung2018survey}. The integration of machine learning algorithms with drone platforms has opened new frontiers in data collection and analysis, enabling applications previously considered impractical or impossible. The business sector has witnessed remarkable innovation driven by drone technology adoption. Startups and established corporations alike have developed novel service models, from last-mile delivery systems to infrastructure inspection services. Companies such as Amazon, Google, and UPS have invested billions in developing autonomous delivery networks, while specialized firms offer drone-as-a-service solutions for industries lacking in-house capabilities \cite{kellermann2020drones}. This entrepreneurial ecosystem has created new employment opportunities and sparked venture capital interest, further accelerating technological advancement. Civil society's engagement with drone technology presents both opportunities and challenges. Public safety organizations have integrated drones into search and rescue operations, disaster response, and traffic monitoring, significantly enhancing their operational capabilities \cite{erdelj2017help}. However, concerns regarding privacy, security, and airspace safety have emerged as critical issues requiring careful consideration. The balance between technological benefits and societal implications continues to shape public discourse and regulatory development. Regulatory frameworks have evolved to address the unique challenges posed by civil drone operations. Aviation authorities worldwide have implemented registration requirements, operational limitations, and certification processes to ensure safe integration into existing airspace systems \cite{stolaroff2018energy}. The development of remote identification systems, geofencing technologies, and traffic management protocols represents ongoing efforts to create a sustainable ecosystem for civil drone operations. Environmental applications have demonstrated the potential for drones to contribute to sustainability goals. Wildlife conservation efforts utilize drones for anti-poaching surveillance, habitat monitoring, and species population assessment with minimal ecological disruption \cite{linchant2015wildlife}. Climate research benefits from drone-based atmospheric sampling, glacier monitoring, and oceanographic studies that would be prohibitively expensive or dangerous using traditional methods. The technological convergence of 5G networks, edge computing, and artificial intelligence promises to unlock new capabilities for civil drones. Real-time data processing, enhanced communication reliability, and improved autonomous decision-making will enable more sophisticated applications and broader deployment scenarios \cite{mozaffari20195g}. These developments suggest that the current interest in civil drones represents merely the beginning of a transformative technological era. Despite significant progress, several challenges persist in realizing the full potential of civil drone technology. Battery life limitations continue to constrain operational range and payload capacity, while weather sensitivity affects reliability in adverse conditions. Cybersecurity vulnerabilities pose risks to both individual operators and critical infrastructure, necessitating robust security protocols and continuous monitoring systems \cite{altawy2016security}. The interdisciplinary nature of civil drone research and development has fostered unprecedented collaboration between traditionally separate fields. Engineers, computer scientists, policy makers, and social scientists work together to address technical challenges while considering broader societal implications. This collaborative approach has proven essential for developing solutions that are not only technically feasible but also socially acceptable and economically viable. As civil drone technology continues to mature, the sustained interest across multiple stakeholders reflects its transformative potential and the recognition that UAVs represent a fundamental shift in how we approach aerial operations, data collection, and service delivery in civilian contexts.
