text: COVID-19 has catalyzed rapid adoption of telehealth \cite{Wosik2020} leading to greater than 100\% increase in virtual urgent care visits and greater than 4000\% increase in virtual non-urgent care visits during the initial months of the pandemic \cite{Mehrotra2020}. This unprecedented shift has fundamentally transformed healthcare delivery models, with telehealth utilization rates that previously required decades to achieve being reached within mere weeks \cite{Alexander2021}. While the immediate benefits of telehealth adoption during COVID-19 are well-documented, including maintained access to care during lockdowns and reduced exposure risks \cite{Reed2021}, the long-term implications for healthcare quality, patient outcomes, and system sustainability remain subjects of active investigation. The rapid implementation of telehealth services during the pandemic was facilitated by temporary regulatory changes, including relaxed licensing requirements, expanded reimbursement policies, and modified privacy regulations \cite{Centers2020}. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) significantly broadened telehealth coverage, allowing healthcare providers to deliver services across state lines and receive reimbursement equivalent to in-person visits \cite{CMS2020}. Similarly, the Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily permitted prescribing of controlled substances via telehealth without prior in-person examinations \cite{DEA2020}, fundamentally altering established protocols for medication management. However, this rapid transformation has revealed significant disparities in telehealth access and utilization. Studies have consistently demonstrated that older adults, racial and ethnic minorities, individuals with lower socioeconomic status, and those residing in rural areas face substantial barriers to telehealth adoption \cite{Rodriguez2021, Nouri2020}. These disparities are multifaceted, encompassing technological barriers such as limited internet connectivity and device access, as well as socioeconomic factors including digital literacy and language barriers \cite{Hsueh2021}. The digital divide has thus created a two-tiered healthcare system, where those with greater technological resources have enhanced access to care, while vulnerable populations may experience reduced access compared to pre-pandemic levels \cite{Campos-Castillo2021}. The clinical effectiveness of telehealth across different medical specialties and conditions has become a critical area of research. While telehealth has demonstrated efficacy for certain conditions such as mental health services, chronic disease management, and routine follow-up care \cite{Batsis2021}, questions remain regarding its appropriateness for complex diagnostic procedures, physical examinations requiring tactile assessment, and emergency situations \cite{Dorsey2016}. The inability to perform comprehensive physical examinations through virtual platforms has raised concerns about diagnostic accuracy and the potential for missed or delayed diagnoses \cite{Reed2019}. Furthermore, the economic implications of widespread telehealth adoption extend beyond immediate cost savings from reduced facility utilization and travel expenses. Healthcare systems must consider long-term investments in technological infrastructure, staff training, and cybersecurity measures to maintain sustainable telehealth programs \cite{Whaley2020}. The cost-effectiveness of telehealth varies significantly across different clinical scenarios, patient populations, and healthcare settings, necessitating careful economic evaluation to inform policy decisions \cite{Totten2016}. Patient and provider satisfaction with telehealth services has shown mixed results, with satisfaction levels varying based on factors such as technological proficiency, clinical condition complexity, and prior telehealth experience \cite{Car2017}. While many patients appreciate the convenience and reduced travel burden associated with virtual visits, others express concerns about the quality of care and the absence of physical presence in the patient-provider relationship \cite{Powell2017}. Healthcare providers similarly report both benefits and challenges, including improved scheduling flexibility but concerns about clinical assessment limitations and increased administrative burden \cite{Mehrotra2021}. The regulatory landscape surrounding telehealth continues to evolve as policymakers grapple with balancing access expansion against quality assurance and patient safety considerations. Key regulatory challenges include establishing appropriate standards for provider credentialing across state lines, ensuring adequate cybersecurity and privacy protections, and developing quality metrics specific to virtual care delivery \cite{Lacktman2021}. The temporary nature of many pandemic-era regulatory flexibilities has created uncertainty about the future regulatory framework governing telehealth services \cite{Shachar2020}. As healthcare systems transition from emergency pandemic response to sustainable long-term care models, understanding the optimal integration of telehealth within existing care delivery frameworks becomes paramount. This integration must address not only technological and logistical considerations but also fundamental questions about care quality, equity, and patient outcomes in hybrid care models that combine virtual and in-person services.

text: Enabling autonomous robots to solve diverse and complex manipulation tasks has been a grand challenge for decades. In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for addressing this challenge, demonstrating remarkable success in learning complex motor skills from scratch through trial and error~\cite{lillicrap2015continuous, schulman2017proximal, haarnoja2018soft}. However, despite these advances, current DRL approaches for robotic manipulation face several fundamental limitations that hinder their practical deployment in real-world scenarios. One of the primary challenges is sample efficiency. Traditional DRL methods typically require millions of environment interactions to learn even relatively simple manipulation tasks~\cite{andrychowicz2020learning, rajeswaran2017learning}. This sample complexity becomes prohibitively expensive when training directly on physical robots, where each interaction involves real-time execution and potential safety risks. Consequently, most DRL-based manipulation systems rely heavily on simulation for training, which introduces the well-known sim-to-real transfer problem~\cite{tobin2017domain, peng2018sim}. Another significant limitation is the brittleness of learned policies to variations in task conditions, object properties, and environmental factors~\cite{kumar2021rma, yu2017preparing}. Robots trained on specific object configurations often fail catastrophically when encountering novel objects with different shapes, sizes, or physical properties. This lack of generalization severely limits the applicability of DRL methods in dynamic, unstructured environments where robots must handle diverse objects and adapt to changing conditions. Furthermore, current approaches struggle with complex, multi-step manipulation tasks that require long-horizon planning and coordination of multiple sub-skills~\cite{nachum2018data, levy2019hierarchical}. While DRL has shown success in learning individual manipulation primitives such as grasping or pushing, combining these primitives into coherent, goal-directed behaviors remains challenging. The sparse reward signals typical in manipulation tasks exacerbate this problem, making it difficult for agents to discover effective strategies for complex sequential behaviors. The integration of perception and action learning presents another layer of complexity. Most successful DRL manipulation systems operate with privileged state information or carefully engineered visual features~\cite{kalashnikov2018scalable, zeng2018learning}. Learning robust visuomotor policies that can handle realistic visual inputs, including occlusions, lighting variations, and cluttered scenes, remains an open challenge. The high-dimensional nature of visual observations combined with the continuous control requirements of manipulation tasks creates a particularly difficult learning problem. To address these challenges, researchers have explored various directions including domain randomization~\cite{sadeghi2016cad2rl, tobin2017domain}, meta-learning approaches~\cite{finn2017model, nagabandi2019learning}, hierarchical reinforcement learning~\cite{nachum2018data, levy2019hierarchical}, and imitation learning techniques~\cite{ho2016generative, nair2018overcoming}. Domain randomization attempts to bridge the sim-to-real gap by training policies on diverse simulation conditions, while meta-learning aims to develop algorithms that can quickly adapt to new tasks or environments. Hierarchical approaches decompose complex tasks into simpler sub-problems, and imitation learning leverages expert demonstrations to guide policy learning. Despite these advances, existing methods often address only specific aspects of the broader challenge. Domain randomization, while effective for certain transfer scenarios, can lead to overly conservative policies that sacrifice performance for robustness~\cite{mehta2020active}. Meta-learning approaches typically require extensive offline training on related tasks, which may not be available in many practical scenarios. Hierarchical methods face challenges in learning appropriate decompositions and coordinating between different levels of the hierarchy~\cite{bacon2017option}. Recent work has begun to explore the integration of large-scale pre-training and foundation models for robotic manipulation~\cite{brohan2022rt, shridhar2022cliport}. These approaches leverage vast amounts of internet-scale data to learn general representations that can be fine-tuned for specific manipulation tasks. While promising, these methods are still in their early stages and face challenges in grounding language and visual understanding in physical manipulation skills. The emergence of transformer architectures and attention mechanisms has also opened new possibilities for manipulation learning~\cite{chen2021decision, janner2021offline}. These models excel at capturing long-range dependencies and can potentially address some of the sequential reasoning challenges inherent in complex manipulation tasks. However, adapting these architectures to the continuous control and real-time requirements of robotic manipulation remains an active area of research. In this work, we propose a novel approach that addresses several of these fundamental challenges through a unified framework that combines adaptive skill learning, robust perception, and efficient transfer mechanisms. Our method builds upon recent advances in self-supervised learning and attention-based architectures to develop manipulation policies that can generalize across diverse objects, environments, and task variations while maintaining sample efficiency and real-world applicability.

text: \input{images/figure1} Natural language processing (NLP) systems exist for a small fraction of the world's over 6,000 living languages, the primary reason being the lack of resources required to train such systems. This resource scarcity is particularly acute for low-resource languages, which often lack large-scale annotated datasets, comprehensive dictionaries, and robust computational tools necessary for developing effective NLP applications \cite{joshi2020state}. The digital divide between high-resource languages like English, Chinese, and Spanish, and low-resource languages spoken by millions of people worldwide, continues to widen as technological advancement accelerates \cite{bender2021dangers}. The development of multilingual language models has shown promise in addressing this disparity, with models like mBERT \cite{devlin2018bert}, XLM-R \cite{conneau2020unsupervised}, and more recently, large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 \cite{brown2020language} and PaLM \cite{chowdhery2022palm} demonstrating cross-lingual capabilities. However, these models still exhibit significant performance gaps between high-resource and low-resource languages, often failing to capture the linguistic nuances, cultural context, and domain-specific knowledge inherent in underrepresented languages \cite{wu2020machine}. Recent advances in few-shot and zero-shot learning paradigms have opened new avenues for low-resource NLP \cite{schick2021exploiting}. These approaches leverage the knowledge encoded in pre-trained models to perform tasks with minimal or no task-specific training data. Prompt-based learning, in particular, has emerged as a powerful technique that reformulates downstream tasks as language modeling problems, enabling models to utilize their pre-training knowledge more effectively \cite{liu2023pre}. This paradigm shift has shown remarkable success in various NLP tasks, including text classification, named entity recognition, and machine translation, especially when combined with in-context learning capabilities of large language models. The emergence of instruction-following models has further revolutionized the landscape of low-resource NLP. Models like InstructGPT \cite{ouyang2022training}, ChatGPT, and GPT-4 \cite{openai2023gpt4} have demonstrated the ability to follow natural language instructions and perform complex tasks across multiple languages with varying degrees of proficiency. These models can potentially serve as universal tools for low-resource languages, providing translation services, text generation capabilities, and even serving as educational resources for language preservation efforts. Transfer learning techniques have also proven instrumental in bridging the resource gap. Cross-lingual transfer learning allows models trained on high-resource languages to be adapted for low-resource languages through various strategies, including multilingual pre-training, cross-lingual word embeddings, and parameter sharing architectures \cite{ruder2019neural}. Meta-learning approaches, which enable models to quickly adapt to new tasks and languages with minimal data, have shown particular promise for few-shot learning scenarios common in low-resource settings \cite{finn2017model}. Data augmentation strategies specifically designed for low-resource languages have gained significant attention. Techniques such as back-translation \cite{sennrich2016improving}, paraphrasing, and synthetic data generation using large language models can help alleviate data scarcity issues. Additionally, the utilization of related high-resource languages through techniques like cross-lingual data projection and code-switching augmentation has proven effective in improving model performance for underrepresented languages \cite{hedderich2021survey}. The role of community-driven initiatives and collaborative platforms cannot be understated in addressing the low-resource language challenge. Projects like Common Voice \cite{ardila2020common}, Masakhane \cite{nekoto2020participatory}, and various Wikipedia language editions have demonstrated the power of crowdsourcing in creating valuable linguistic resources. These initiatives not only provide essential training data but also ensure that the development of NLP tools remains culturally sensitive and community-centered. Despite these promising developments, significant challenges remain. The evaluation of NLP systems for low-resource languages often suffers from the lack of standardized benchmarks and evaluation metrics that account for linguistic diversity and cultural specificity \cite{blasi2022systematic}. Furthermore, the computational requirements of state-of-the-art models often exceed the technological infrastructure available in regions where low-resource languages are predominantly spoken, creating additional barriers to adoption and deployment. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a comprehensive framework for developing robust NLP systems for low-resource languages. Our approach combines transfer learning, data augmentation, and community engagement strategies to create sustainable solutions that can be adapted across diverse linguistic contexts while maintaining computational efficiency and cultural sensitivity.

text: Driving in a real-world environment, with ever-changing dynamics, consisting of other actors (i.e., non-player character or NPC) is inherently a risky task. The complexity of autonomous driving systems must account for numerous unpredictable variables, including pedestrian behavior, weather conditions, traffic patterns, and mechanical failures of surrounding vehicles \cite{badue2021self}. Traditional rule-based approaches to autonomous navigation have proven insufficient for handling the full spectrum of real-world scenarios, leading researchers to explore more sophisticated methodologies that can adapt to dynamic environments \cite{grigorescu2020survey}. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have shown promising results in addressing these challenges by enabling autonomous agents to learn optimal driving policies through interaction with their environment \cite{kiran2021deep}. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on pre-programmed rules, DRL-based systems can develop nuanced understanding of complex traffic scenarios through trial and error, potentially discovering strategies that human programmers might not have anticipated \cite{chen2021deep}. However, the application of reinforcement learning to autonomous driving presents several fundamental challenges. First, the safety-critical nature of driving tasks demands that learning algorithms maintain high performance standards while exploring new strategies \cite{garcia2015comprehensive}. The exploration-exploitation trade-off becomes particularly crucial when incorrect actions can result in catastrophic consequences, such as collisions or traffic violations \cite{dulac2019challenges}. Second, the multi-agent nature of traffic environments introduces additional complexity, as the behavior of one vehicle directly influences the decisions and actions of surrounding agents \cite{tampuu2017multiagent}. This interdependency creates a non-stationary learning environment where the optimal policy for one agent continuously evolves based on the policies adopted by other agents \cite{hernandez2019survey}. Furthermore, the vast state and action spaces inherent in driving scenarios pose significant computational challenges. Real-world driving involves continuous sensor inputs from cameras, LiDAR, radar, and other perception systems, generating high-dimensional state representations that must be processed in real-time \cite{yurtsever2020survey}. The action space, encompassing steering angles, acceleration, and braking decisions, requires precise control to ensure smooth and safe vehicle operation \cite{paden2016survey}. Transfer learning has emerged as a potential solution to address the sample efficiency limitations of reinforcement learning in autonomous driving \cite{pan2009survey}. By leveraging knowledge gained from simulated environments or related driving tasks, transfer learning approaches can potentially reduce the amount of real-world training data required while maintaining performance guarantees \cite{taylor2009transfer}. The integration of imitation learning with reinforcement learning has also gained attention as a method to bootstrap the learning process with expert demonstrations \cite{hussein2017imitation}. This hybrid approach allows agents to initialize their policies based on human driving behavior while retaining the ability to improve beyond human performance through continued reinforcement learning \cite{ho2016generative}. Safety considerations remain paramount in the development of learning-based autonomous driving systems. Various approaches have been proposed to ensure safe exploration during the learning process, including the use of safety constraints \cite{achiam2017constrained}, safe policy optimization methods \cite{schulman2017proximal}, and the incorporation of formal verification techniques \cite{katz2017reluplex}. The evaluation of autonomous driving systems presents another significant challenge, as traditional metrics may not adequately capture the nuanced requirements of real-world driving performance \cite{dosovitskiy2017carla}. Simulation environments have become essential tools for testing and validation, offering controlled settings where various scenarios can be systematically evaluated without real-world risks \cite{shah2018airsim}. This work addresses the intersection of these challenges by proposing a novel framework that combines deep reinforcement learning with safety-aware exploration strategies specifically designed for multi-agent driving scenarios. Our approach leverages hierarchical learning structures to decompose complex driving tasks into manageable sub-problems while maintaining coordination between different behavioral modules.

text: Knowledge graphs~(KGs), representing facts in semantic graph structures, have been applied to multiple artificial intelligence tasks, e.g., recommendation~\cite{leiconversational,2021Learning}, dialogue generation~\cite{moon-etal-2019-opendialkg,leiinteractive}, and question answering~\cite{ChristmannRASW19,zhu2021retrieving}. However, real-world knowledge graphs are inherently incomplete, missing numerous facts that exist in reality~\cite{west2014knowledge,ji2021survey}. This incompleteness significantly limits their effectiveness in downstream applications. Knowledge graph completion (KGC), also known as link prediction, aims to address this limitation by predicting missing links between entities in knowledge graphs~\cite{bordes2013translating,wang2017knowledge}. Traditional knowledge graph completion methods primarily focus on learning embeddings for entities and relations to capture the semantic and structural information within KGs~\cite{trouillon2016complex,sun2019rotate,zhang2020learning}. These approaches typically assume that all entities and relations follow similar patterns and can be effectively modeled using uniform embedding spaces. However, this assumption often fails to capture the inherent heterogeneity present in real-world knowledge graphs, where different types of entities and relations exhibit distinct characteristics and interaction patterns~\cite{schlichtkrull2018modeling,vashishth2020composition}. Recent advances in knowledge graph completion have explored various directions to improve prediction accuracy. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a promising approach, leveraging the graph structure to propagate information between neighboring entities and relations~\cite{kipf2016semi,schlichtkrull2018modeling,vashishth2020composition}. These methods can capture multi-hop relationships and complex interaction patterns that traditional embedding-based approaches might miss. Additionally, attention mechanisms have been incorporated to dynamically weight the importance of different neighbors and relations during the learning process~\cite{wang2019kgat,nathani2019learning}. Another significant advancement involves the integration of textual information with structural knowledge. Many knowledge graphs contain rich textual descriptions for entities and relations, which can provide valuable semantic signals for completion tasks~\cite{xie2016representation,zhong2015aligning,toutanova2015representing}. Pre-trained language models, such as BERT and its variants, have been successfully adapted to encode textual descriptions and integrate them with graph structural information~\cite{yao2019kg,wang2021kepler,zhang2019ernie}. Despite these advances, several challenges remain in knowledge graph completion. First, the scalability issue becomes prominent when dealing with large-scale knowledge graphs containing millions of entities and relations~\cite{ruffinelli2020you,ali2021bringing}. Many existing methods suffer from computational complexity that grows quadratically or even exponentially with the graph size, making them impractical for real-world applications. Second, the sparsity problem persists, where many entities have very few connections, making it difficult to learn meaningful representations~\cite{teru2020inductive,chen2020meta}. Furthermore, most existing approaches focus on transductive settings, where all entities are observed during training. However, in practical scenarios, new entities frequently emerge, requiring inductive capabilities to handle previously unseen entities~\cite{teru2020inductive,hamaguchi2017knowledge}. This inductive knowledge graph completion poses additional challenges as models need to generalize to entities not present in the training data. The evaluation of knowledge graph completion methods also presents unique challenges. Traditional metrics such as Mean Rank (MR), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and Hits@K provide useful insights but may not fully capture the practical utility of predictions~\cite{sun2020re,kotnis2017analysis}. Moreover, the filtered evaluation setting, while addressing some biases, may still not reflect real-world performance where multiple correct answers might exist for a given query~\cite{berrendorf2020comprehensive}. Another critical aspect is the handling of temporal dynamics in knowledge graphs. Many facts in real-world KGs are time-dependent, and their validity changes over time~\cite{dasgupta2018hyte,garcia2018learning}. Temporal knowledge graph completion aims to predict not only missing links but also their temporal validity, adding another dimension of complexity to the problem~\cite{jin2020recurrent,wu2020temporal}. The interpretability of knowledge graph completion models has also gained increasing attention. Understanding why a model makes specific predictions is crucial for building trust and ensuring reliability in downstream applications~\cite{rossi2021knowledge,wang2021explainable}. This has led to the development of explainable KGC methods that provide reasoning paths or attention weights to justify their predictions. In this paper, we address several of these challenges by proposing a novel approach that combines the strengths of graph neural networks with efficient attention mechanisms and incorporates both structural and semantic information for improved knowledge graph completion performance.

Second, the sparsity problem persists, where many of the nodes have few connections between them, thus making it difficult to learn meaningful representations. The knowledge graph completion has another problem, which is to generalize to the entities not seen during training. Moreover, most existing approaches focus on transductive settings, where all entities are observed during the training. However, in practical scenarios, new entities often arise, and thus inductive capabilities to handle the previously unknown entities are needed. This type of evaluation is also unique. The metrics used to evaluate methods such as Mean Rank, Mean Reciprocal Rank, and Hits@K provide useful insights, but may not fully capture the practical utility of the predictions. Filtered evaluation settings, although they address some biases, may still not reflect real-world performance, where there might be multiple correct answers to a given query. A critical aspect is the way temporal dynamics are handled in knowledge graphs. Many facts in real-world knowledge graphs are time-dependent, and their validity changes over time. Temporal knowledge graph completion tries to predict not only missing links, but also their temporal validity, adding another dimension of complexity to the problem. Interpretability of knowledge graph completion models is also gaining more and more attention. To understand why a model makes a specific prediction is crucial for building trust and ensuring reliability in downstream applications. This has led to the development of explainable KGC methods, which can provide reasoning paths or attention weights to justify their predictions. In this paper, we tackle several of these problems by proposing a novel approach that combines the strengths of neural networks with an efficient attention mechanism, and combines both structural and semantic information to achieve better performance on the knowledge graph completion task.

text: Trajectory planning for autonomous agents often proceeds in a receding time horizon. At each time step, the agent solves an optimization problem to determine the optimal control sequence over a finite prediction horizon, executes the first control action, and then repeats this process with updated state information. This model predictive control (MPC) framework has proven effective for handling dynamic environments, system constraints, and uncertainty in real-time applications \cite{rawlings2017model, garcia2019comprehensive}. The fundamental challenge in receding horizon trajectory planning lies in balancing computational efficiency with solution optimality. Traditional approaches often rely on convex approximations or simplified models to ensure tractability, potentially sacrificing accuracy in complex scenarios \cite{verscheure2009time, lam2010receding}. Recent advances in nonlinear optimization and computational hardware have enabled more sophisticated formulations, yet the curse of dimensionality and nonconvex constraints continue to pose significant challenges \cite{chen2018obstacle, zhu2019chance}. A critical consideration in receding horizon planning is the prediction horizon length, which directly impacts both computational burden and control performance. Shorter horizons reduce computational complexity but may lead to myopic behavior and suboptimal long-term performance \cite{mayne2000constrained}. Conversely, longer horizons provide better foresight but exponentially increase computational requirements, potentially violating real-time constraints \cite{kouvaritakis2016model}. The integration of safety constraints within the receding horizon framework presents additional complexity. Hard constraints on state and control variables must be satisfied at each time step while maintaining feasibility throughout the prediction horizon \cite{bemporad2002explicit}. This requirement becomes particularly challenging in dynamic environments where obstacle positions and system parameters may change unpredictably \cite{richards2002robust}. Modern autonomous systems often operate in multi-agent environments, necessitating coordination mechanisms within the trajectory planning framework. Distributed MPC approaches have emerged to address scalability concerns while maintaining system-wide performance guarantees \cite{negenborn2014distributed, christofides2013distributed}. These methods typically involve iterative information exchange between agents to converge on compatible trajectory plans. Uncertainty quantification represents another crucial aspect of receding horizon planning. Stochastic MPC formulations explicitly account for process noise and model uncertainties through probabilistic constraints or robust optimization techniques \cite{mesbah2016stochastic, mayne2005robust}. However, these approaches often require conservative approximations that may degrade nominal performance. The choice of cost function significantly influences the resulting trajectories and system behavior. Common objectives include tracking error minimization, energy consumption reduction, and comfort optimization \cite{borrelli2017predictive}. Multi-objective formulations allow simultaneous consideration of competing goals but introduce additional complexity in weight selection and Pareto front exploration \cite{zavala2008interior}. Computational implementation of receding horizon planners requires careful consideration of numerical optimization algorithms and software architectures. Sequential quadratic programming (SQP) and interior-point methods dominate the landscape for nonlinear problems, while specialized solvers exploit problem structure for enhanced efficiency \cite{andersson2019casadi, wachter2006implementation}. Real-time implementation often necessitates warm-starting strategies and early termination criteria to meet strict timing constraints. The emergence of machine learning techniques has introduced new paradigms for receding horizon planning. Learning-based approaches can improve model accuracy, accelerate optimization convergence, or provide intelligent initialization strategies \cite{karg2020efficient, rosolia2017learning}. Neural network approximations of optimal control policies offer potential computational speedups but raise questions about safety guarantees and generalization capabilities. This work addresses several key challenges in receding horizon trajectory planning through novel algorithmic contributions and comprehensive experimental validation.

text: Recognizing multi-party speech from an arbitrary number of speakers with naturally occurring speech overlap in a far-field environment is a challenging research problem that has been extensively studied in recent years \cite{watanabe2018espnet, kanda2021large, raj2021integration}. This problem, commonly referred to as multi-speaker automatic speech recognition (ASR), encompasses several interconnected challenges including speaker diarization, speech separation, and continuous speech recognition in noisy acoustic environments \cite{anguera2012speaker, wang2018alternative}. The complexity of multi-party speech recognition stems from multiple factors that distinguish it from single-speaker scenarios. First, the presence of overlapping speech segments creates significant acoustic interference, where multiple speakers produce simultaneous utterances that must be separated and attributed correctly \cite{boeddeker2018front, zeghidour2021wavesplit}. Second, far-field recording conditions introduce additional complications such as reverberation, background noise, and varying speaker distances from recording devices \cite{yoshioka2012making, nakatani2019speech}. Third, the arbitrary number of speakers requires systems to adapt dynamically to varying conversation dynamics without prior knowledge of participant counts \cite{bullock2020overlap, landini2022bayesian}. Traditional approaches to this problem have evolved through several paradigms. Early methods relied on sequential processing pipelines that first performed speaker diarization to identify "who spoke when," followed by single-speaker ASR on segmented audio regions \cite{tranter2006overview, garcia2017speaker}. However, these cascaded systems suffer from error propagation, where mistakes in early stages compound throughout the pipeline \cite{boakye2011overlapped}. Moreover, they typically handle overlapping speech poorly, either by discarding overlapped regions entirely or by making arbitrary speaker assignment decisions \cite{shum2013unsupervised}. More recent research has focused on end-to-end approaches that jointly optimize speaker separation and recognition objectives \cite{qian2017single, yu2017recognizing}. These methods leverage deep neural networks to learn complex mappings from multi-speaker mixtures to individual speaker transcriptions, often employing techniques such as permutation invariant training (PIT) \cite{yu2017permutation} and deep clustering \cite{hershey2016deep}. The serialized output training (SOT) framework has emerged as a particularly promising approach, where systems learn to generate sequential outputs for multiple speakers using attention-based encoder-decoder architectures \cite{kanda2020serialized, kanda2021investigation}. Speaker-attributed ASR represents another significant advancement, where systems simultaneously produce transcriptions and speaker labels \cite{kanda2019guided, chang2019end}. This approach addresses the fundamental limitation of traditional diarization-then-recognition pipelines by jointly optimizing both tasks. Recent work has demonstrated that incorporating speaker embedding information and multi-task learning objectives can substantially improve performance in challenging acoustic conditions \cite{medennikov2020target, cornell2020overlapped}. The advent of transformer-based architectures has further revolutionized multi-speaker ASR capabilities \cite{chen2020continuous, fujita2021end}. Self-attention mechanisms enable models to capture long-range dependencies and complex speaker interactions more effectively than recurrent architectures \cite{zhang2020transformer}. Additionally, large-scale pre-trained models such as wav2vec 2.0 and Whisper have shown remarkable generalization capabilities when fine-tuned for multi-speaker scenarios \cite{baevski2020wav2vec, radford2023robust}. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges remain unresolved. Handling highly overlapped speech with more than two concurrent speakers continues to pose difficulties for existing methods \cite{raj2021integration}. The computational complexity of joint optimization approaches often makes real-time processing impractical for many applications \cite{yoshioka2019multi}. Furthermore, domain adaptation remains challenging, as models trained on specific acoustic conditions or speaking styles often fail to generalize to new environments \cite{watanabe2020chime}. Recent evaluation campaigns such as CHiME and DIHARD have provided standardized benchmarks for comparing different approaches \cite{barker2018fifth, ryant2020third}. These challenges have highlighted the importance of robust evaluation metrics that capture both transcription accuracy and speaker attribution performance. The development of speaker-agnostic word error rate (SA-WER) and other specialized metrics has enabled more comprehensive assessment of multi-speaker ASR systems \cite{watanabe2020chime}. This paper addresses the multi-party speech recognition problem by proposing a novel architecture that integrates recent advances in transformer-based modeling with improved speaker separation techniques. Our approach aims to overcome current limitations while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for practical deployment scenarios.

text: \vspace{-0.2cm} Embedding models have been the mainstay algorithms for several machine learning applications like Information Retrieval (IR)~\citep{croft2010search,baeza1999modern} and Natural Language Processing (NLP)~\citep{word2vec, glove, attention, bert} . These models learn dense vector representations of discrete objects such as words, sentences, documents, or even entire corpora, capturing semantic relationships and enabling efficient similarity computations. The fundamental principle underlying embedding models is the distributional hypothesis~\citep{harris1954distributional}, which posits that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. In the realm of information retrieval, embedding models have revolutionized how we approach document ranking and relevance assessment. Traditional approaches relied heavily on lexical matching techniques such as TF-IDF~\citep{salton1988term} and BM25~\citep{robertson1995okapi}, which suffer from the vocabulary mismatch problem where semantically similar documents may not share common terms. Embedding-based retrieval systems address this limitation by mapping queries and documents into a shared semantic space where similarity can be computed using vector operations like cosine similarity or dot product~\citep{karpukhin2020dense,reimers2019sentence}. The evolution of embedding models has been marked by several key milestones. Early approaches like Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA)~\citep{deerwester1990indexing} and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)~\citep{blei2003latent} laid the groundwork for learning distributed representations from text corpora. The introduction of neural embedding methods, particularly Word2Vec~\citep{word2vec} and GloVe~\citep{glove}, marked a significant advancement by learning dense, low-dimensional representations that captured both syntactic and semantic relationships between words. These models demonstrated remarkable capabilities in analogical reasoning tasks, famously exemplified by the relationship "king - man + woman = queen." The advent of transformer architectures~\citep{attention} and pre-trained language models like BERT~\citep{bert} has further transformed the embedding landscape. Unlike static word embeddings, these contextual models generate dynamic representations that vary based on the surrounding context, enabling more nuanced understanding of polysemous words and complex linguistic phenomena. The success of these models has led to the development of specialized sentence and document embedding techniques~\citep{reimers2019sentence,ni2021sentence} that can capture semantic information at higher levels of granularity. Despite their widespread adoption and empirical success, embedding models face several fundamental challenges that limit their effectiveness and applicability. One primary concern is the curse of dimensionality, where high-dimensional embeddings can lead to computational inefficiencies and storage requirements that scale poorly with corpus size~\citep{aggarwal2001surprising}. Additionally, the learned representations often lack interpretability, making it difficult to understand what semantic features are being captured or why certain similarities are computed~\citep{rogers2020primer}. Another significant challenge is the domain adaptation problem, where embeddings trained on one domain may not generalize well to others due to vocabulary shifts, semantic drift, or different linguistic patterns~\citep{kenton2019bert}. This is particularly problematic in specialized domains such as biomedical literature~\citep{lee2020biobert} or legal documents~\citep{chalkidis2020legal}, where domain-specific terminology and semantic relationships may not be adequately captured by general-purpose embedding models. The evaluation of embedding quality presents additional complexities. Traditional intrinsic evaluation metrics such as word similarity benchmarks~\citep{finkelstein2001placing,hill2015simlex} may not correlate well with downstream task performance, leading to a gap between what we measure and what we actually care about in practical applications~\citep{schnabel2015evaluation}. Furthermore, the choice of similarity metric and evaluation methodology can significantly impact the perceived quality of embeddings, making fair comparison between different approaches challenging. Recent research has also highlighted issues related to bias and fairness in embedding models. These representations can inadvertently encode and amplify societal biases present in training data, leading to discriminatory outcomes in downstream applications~\citep{bolukbasi2016man,caliskan2017semantics}. This has sparked interest in developing debiasing techniques and fair representation learning methods, though achieving both high utility and fairness remains an active area of investigation. The computational requirements for training and deploying large-scale embedding models present practical limitations, particularly for resource-constrained environments. While techniques like knowledge distillation~\citep{hinton2015distilling} and model compression~\citep{chen2015compressing} have been proposed to address these concerns, there remains a trade-off between model capacity and computational efficiency that practitioners must carefully navigate.

Later, the introduction of neural word embeddings, such as Word2Vec and GloVe, has represented a major development. These methods learn dense, low-dimensional word representations that capture both the syntactic and semantic relationships between words. In particular, such methods, which are based on neural networks, learn word representations by means of the cosine similarity of the word vectors, which is an inverse of the dot product. Despite their general acceptance and the empirical success of their models, embeddings are subject to certain fundamental limitations which limit their effectiveness and applicability. Unlike static word representations, context models generate dynamic word representations which change according to the context and facilitate a more subtle understanding of polysemic words and complex linguistic phenomena. These models also have shown remarkable performance in analogy tasks, such as the famous king-man-woman-queen relation. The success of these models led to the development of sentence and document embedding methods [Reimers, 2019; NI, 2021], which capture semantic information at a finer level of granularity. Another serious problem is domain adaptation, where embeddings trained on one domain fail to generalize well to others, either because of changes in vocabulary, different semantics, or different linguistics. It is also difficult to evaluate the quality of the learned representations, because they are often inexplicable and it is difficult to know what semantic features they have captured and how they are related. This is especially important in specialized domains, such as medical literature (Lee, et al., 2020, Biobert), or legal documents (Chalkidis, et al., et al., et al., et al., et al., 2015, Simlex). This is especially important in specialized domains such as medical literature (Lee, Biobert, 2020) or legal documents (Chalkidis, et al., Legal, et al., et al., 2020), where domain-specific terminology and semantic relations are poorly represented by general-purpose word embeddings. Recent research has also questioned the issue of fairness and bias in these models. The social biases inherent in the training data are inevitably encoded in these representations, which leads to discriminatory results in downstream applications. The choice of similarity metrics and evaluation methodology has a large influence on the perceived quality of embeddings, which makes it difficult to compare the quality of different approaches. The computation necessary to train and deploy large-scale embedding models presents a practical limitation, particularly in resource-constrained environments. Hence the interest in developing debiasing techniques and fair representation learning methods. Obtaining both high utility and fairness is an active area of research. Against these objections distillation and compression of knowledge have been proposed as means of coping with them, but there must be a carefully negotiated balance between the scope of the model and its efficiency.

text: In the knowledge economy, large amounts of data are collected to support decision-making, policy analytics, service delivery etc. However, the proliferation of data collection practices has raised significant concerns about privacy, security, and ethical use of personal information. Organizations across various sectors—from healthcare and education to finance and government—face the challenge of balancing data utility with privacy protection requirements. This tension has become particularly pronounced with the implementation of stringent data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in the United States \cite{voigt2017eu, pardau2018california}. Traditional approaches to data sharing and analysis often require direct access to raw datasets, which inherently poses privacy risks. When multiple organizations need to collaborate on data-driven projects, they typically resort to data sharing agreements, anonymization techniques, or centralized data repositories. However, these methods have proven inadequate in many scenarios due to re-identification risks, loss of data utility, or concerns about data sovereignty \cite{ohm2009broken, sweeney2000uniqueness}. The emergence of privacy-preserving technologies has opened new avenues for enabling data collaboration while maintaining privacy guarantees. Among these technologies, differential privacy has gained significant attention from both academia and industry due to its rigorous mathematical foundation and provable privacy guarantees \cite{dwork2006calibrating}. Differential privacy provides a formal framework for quantifying and limiting the privacy loss that occurs when statistical information is released about a dataset. Federated learning represents another paradigm shift in privacy-preserving data analysis, enabling machine learning models to be trained across decentralized data sources without requiring raw data to leave its original location \cite{mcmahan2017communication}. This approach has shown particular promise in scenarios where data cannot be centralized due to regulatory, technical, or business constraints. Healthcare consortiums, financial institutions, and telecommunications companies have begun adopting federated learning frameworks to leverage collective intelligence while maintaining data locality \cite{li2020federated}. Secure multi-party computation (SMC) offers yet another approach to privacy-preserving computation, allowing multiple parties to jointly compute functions over their private inputs without revealing those inputs to each other \cite{yao1982protocols}. While computationally intensive, recent advances in SMC protocols have made them increasingly practical for real-world applications, particularly in scenarios requiring exact computations rather than approximate results \cite{evans2018pragmatic}. The integration of blockchain technology with privacy-preserving mechanisms has also emerged as a promising research direction. Blockchain's immutable ledger and decentralized architecture can provide transparency and auditability in data sharing scenarios while maintaining privacy through cryptographic techniques \cite{zyskind2015decentralizing}. Smart contracts enable automated enforcement of data usage policies and consent management, creating new possibilities for privacy-preserving data ecosystems. Despite these technological advances, significant challenges remain in the practical deployment of privacy-preserving data analytics systems. The trade-offs between privacy, utility, and computational efficiency must be carefully balanced based on specific application requirements. Organizations must also navigate complex regulatory landscapes that vary across jurisdictions and sectors. Furthermore, the lack of standardized frameworks and interoperability between different privacy-preserving technologies creates barriers to widespread adoption \cite{ji2014differential}. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a comprehensive framework for privacy-preserving data analytics that combines multiple complementary technologies. Our approach leverages the strengths of differential privacy, federated learning, and secure computation while mitigating their individual limitations. We present novel algorithms that optimize the privacy-utility trade-off and demonstrate their effectiveness through extensive empirical evaluation on real-world datasets from healthcare, finance, and telecommunications domains. The contributions of this work are threefold: first, we develop a unified theoretical framework that formally characterizes the privacy guarantees provided by our hybrid approach; second, we design efficient algorithms that enable practical deployment of privacy-preserving analytics at scale; and third, we provide comprehensive experimental validation demonstrating the superior performance of our methods compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our results show that the proposed framework can achieve comparable utility to non-private methods while providing strong privacy guarantees, making it suitable for deployment in privacy-sensitive environments where traditional data sharing approaches are not feasible.

text: The main goal of this work is to design a system for maintaining an \emph{audit trail} for the knowledge representation (KR) system that tracks all changes made to the knowledge base throughout its lifecycle. In knowledge-intensive applications, particularly those deployed in critical domains such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, the ability to trace the evolution of knowledge representations becomes paramount for ensuring accountability, reproducibility, and regulatory compliance. Traditional knowledge representation systems often lack comprehensive tracking mechanisms, making it difficult to understand how and why specific inferences were made at particular points in time. This limitation becomes particularly problematic when dealing with dynamic knowledge bases that undergo frequent updates, corrections, or refinements. Without proper audit trails, system administrators and domain experts cannot effectively debug reasoning processes, validate knowledge integrity, or meet regulatory requirements that mandate detailed documentation of decision-making processes. The challenge of maintaining audit trails in KR systems is multifaceted. First, knowledge representations can be highly interconnected, where a single modification may cascade through multiple inference chains, affecting numerous derived facts and conclusions. Second, the temporal dimension adds complexity, as the same query may yield different results depending on when it is executed relative to knowledge base modifications. Third, the granularity of tracking must be carefully balanced—too coarse and important details are lost, too fine and the system becomes overwhelmed with metadata. Our proposed audit trail system addresses these challenges through a novel combination of \emph{versioned knowledge graphs}, \emph{provenance tracking}, and \emph{temporal reasoning mechanisms}. The system maintains a complete history of all knowledge base modifications while providing efficient querying capabilities that allow users to reconstruct the state of the knowledge base at any point in time. Furthermore, our approach incorporates fine-grained provenance information that traces not only what changes were made, but also who made them, when they occurred, and what reasoning processes led to derived knowledge. The key contributions of this work include: (1) a formal framework for representing temporal knowledge base evolution that preserves both structural and semantic provenance; (2) efficient algorithms for querying historical states and tracking inference chains across time; (3) a practical implementation that demonstrates scalability on real-world knowledge bases; and (4) an empirical evaluation showing the system's effectiveness in supporting debugging, compliance, and knowledge quality assurance tasks. The importance of audit trails in knowledge representation extends beyond mere record-keeping. In many applications, the ability to explain how a particular conclusion was reached is as important as the conclusion itself. For instance, in medical diagnosis systems, clinicians need to understand not only the recommended treatment but also the reasoning path that led to that recommendation, including what knowledge was available at the time and how it was interpreted. Similarly, in financial risk assessment systems, regulatory bodies require detailed documentation of the decision-making process to ensure compliance with industry standards and to facilitate post-hoc analysis of system behavior. Our audit trail system is designed to support multiple types of queries that are essential for knowledge base management and analysis. \emph{Temporal queries} allow users to examine the state of the knowledge base at specific points in time, enabling them to understand how knowledge evolved and to identify when particular facts were introduced or modified. \emph{Provenance queries} trace the origin of derived facts back to their foundational assertions and reasoning rules, providing transparency into the inference process. \emph{Impact analysis queries} identify all knowledge elements that were affected by a particular modification, helping administrators understand the scope of changes and their potential consequences. The system architecture is built around a \emph{temporal knowledge graph} model that extends traditional RDF representations with temporal and provenance annotations. Each assertion in the knowledge base is associated with metadata indicating its validity period, source, and derivation history. This rich metadata structure enables sophisticated reasoning about knowledge evolution while maintaining compatibility with existing semantic web technologies and standards. To ensure practical applicability, our design emphasizes efficiency and scalability. The system employs optimized storage strategies that minimize redundancy while preserving complete historical information. Indexing mechanisms are carefully designed to support fast retrieval of temporal and provenance data, even for large-scale knowledge bases with extensive modification histories. Additionally, the system provides configurable retention policies that allow organizations to balance storage requirements with audit trail completeness based on their specific needs and regulatory obligations. The audit trail system also incorporates mechanisms for handling \emph{knowledge conflicts} and \emph{inconsistencies} that may arise during knowledge base evolution. When contradictory information is introduced, the system maintains records of both the conflicting assertions and the resolution process, providing a complete picture of how knowledge inconsistencies were detected and addressed. This capability is particularly valuable in collaborative knowledge engineering environments where multiple experts may contribute potentially conflicting information. Furthermore, our approach addresses the challenge of \emph{knowledge base synchronization} in distributed environments. The audit trail system supports federated deployments where multiple knowledge bases need to maintain consistency while preserving local autonomy. The provenance tracking mechanisms enable sophisticated conflict resolution strategies that take into account the source credibility, temporal precedence, and domain expertise of different contributors. The practical implications of this work extend to various domains where knowledge-based systems play critical roles. In \emph{regulatory compliance}, the audit trail provides the documentation necessary to demonstrate adherence to industry standards and legal requirements. In \emph{scientific research}, the system enables reproducibility by maintaining complete records of how knowledge bases evolved during the research process. In \emph{collaborative knowledge engineering}, the audit trail facilitates coordination among multiple contributors by providing transparency into each participant's contributions and their impact on the overall knowledge base.

text: Recently, there have been considerable deep-learning-based point cloud generation and completion methods based on the architecture of autoencoder. These methods have demonstrated remarkable success in reconstructing 3D geometries from partial observations and generating novel point cloud structures \cite{yuan2018pcn, tchapmi2019topnet, wang2020cascaded}. However, most existing approaches suffer from fundamental limitations that hinder their practical applicability and theoretical understanding. The primary challenge lies in the inherent unordered nature of point clouds, which differs significantly from structured data representations such as images or voxel grids \cite{qi2017pointnet}. Traditional convolutional neural networks cannot be directly applied to point clouds due to the lack of spatial ordering, necessitating specialized architectures that can handle permutation-invariant operations \cite{qi2017pointnet++}. Early attempts to address this challenge involved converting point clouds to intermediate representations such as voxel grids or multi-view projections \cite{wu20153d, su2015multi}, but these approaches often result in information loss and increased computational overhead. Autoencoder-based architectures have emerged as a dominant paradigm for point cloud processing tasks due to their ability to learn compact latent representations while preserving geometric information \cite{achlioptas2018learning}. The encoder component typically employs hierarchical feature extraction mechanisms to capture both local and global geometric patterns, while the decoder reconstructs the original point cloud from the learned latent code \cite{yang2018foldingnet}. However, several critical issues persist in current methodologies. First, the reconstruction quality often degrades significantly when dealing with complex geometries or fine-grained details \cite{wen2020point}. This limitation stems from the difficulty of capturing intricate surface variations and sharp features within the constrained dimensionality of latent representations. Many existing methods struggle to maintain geometric fidelity, particularly for objects with thin structures, holes, or irregular surfaces \cite{liu2019morphing}. Second, the training stability of autoencoder-based models remains problematic, with many approaches exhibiting convergence issues and mode collapse phenomena \cite{li2018point}. The optimization landscape for point cloud generation is inherently complex due to the discrete nature of point sets and the challenges associated with defining appropriate loss functions that capture both local and global geometric properties \cite{fan2017point}. Third, existing methods often lack theoretical guarantees regarding the quality and diversity of generated point clouds \cite{tree2019learning}. The absence of rigorous mathematical frameworks for analyzing the generative capabilities of these models limits our understanding of their fundamental properties and potential failure modes. This theoretical gap impedes the development of more robust and reliable algorithms. Furthermore, computational efficiency presents another significant challenge, as many state-of-the-art methods require substantial computational resources for both training and inference \cite{zhao2019point}. The quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms commonly used in point cloud processing limits scalability to large-scale datasets and real-time applications \cite{guo2020pct}. The evaluation metrics commonly employed for assessing point cloud generation quality also present limitations \cite{sun2020canonical}. Traditional metrics such as Chamfer distance and Earth Mover's distance, while useful, fail to capture perceptual quality and semantic consistency adequately \cite{luo2021learning}. This evaluation gap makes it challenging to compare different methods objectively and understand their relative strengths and weaknesses. Recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) have shown promise for addressing some of these challenges \cite{valsesia2018learning, shu2019point}. However, adapting these techniques to point clouds requires careful consideration of the unique properties of 3D geometric data and the development of specialized loss functions and training procedures. To address these fundamental limitations, this work proposes a novel approach that combines the representational power of deep autoencoders with principled geometric constraints and improved training strategies. Our method introduces several key innovations that collectively enhance both the quality and efficiency of point cloud generation and completion tasks, while providing theoretical insights into the underlying mechanisms governing these processes.

This decentralized framework addresses critical privacy concerns in applications ranging from healthcare \cite{li2020federated} to financial services \cite{yang2019federated}, where data sharing is restricted by regulatory constraints or competitive considerations. The fundamental challenge in federated learning lies in the substantial communication overhead required for model synchronization. Traditional FL algorithms necessitate frequent exchange of high-dimensional model parameters between the central server and participating clients, creating significant bandwidth bottlenecks. In practical deployments, communication costs can be orders of magnitude higher than local computation costs \cite{konevcny2016federated}, particularly when dealing with modern deep neural networks containing millions of parameters. Gradient quantization has emerged as a promising solution to mitigate these communication challenges by reducing the precision of transmitted gradients. Existing quantization schemes can be broadly categorized into uniform quantization \cite{seide2014compression}, non-uniform quantization \cite{banner2018post}, and stochastic quantization \cite{alistarh2017qsgd}. While uniform quantization divides the gradient range into equal intervals, non-uniform approaches adapt interval sizes based on gradient distributions. Stochastic methods introduce randomization to maintain unbiasedness despite quantization errors. However, conventional quantization techniques face several limitations. First, they often employ fixed quantization levels that fail to adapt to the dynamic nature of gradient distributions during training. Second, many existing methods do not adequately account for the heterogeneous data distributions inherent in federated settings, where different clients may exhibit vastly different gradient characteristics. Third, the trade-off between compression ratio and convergence accuracy remains suboptimal, particularly in scenarios with limited communication budgets. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel adaptive quantization framework that dynamically adjusts quantization parameters based on gradient statistics and training progress. Our approach leverages statistical properties of gradient distributions to optimize quantization intervals, thereby minimizing information loss while maximizing compression efficiency. The key contributions of this work include: \begin{enumerate} \item A theoretical analysis of gradient distribution evolution in federated learning environments, providing insights into optimal quantization strategies. \item An adaptive quantization algorithm that dynamically adjusts compression levels based on local gradient statistics and global convergence metrics. \item Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrating superior performance compared to existing quantization methods across diverse datasets and model architectures. \item Convergence guarantees for the proposed method under standard federated learning assumptions, including non-IID data distributions and partial client participation. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in gradient compression and federated optimization. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our adaptive quantization framework and theoretical analysis. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} provides experimental results on benchmark datasets, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with discussion of future directions.

text: Many scenarios in software transformation and software security require us to analyze or operate on a given program binary. When faced with such analysis tasks, disassembly represents the foundational step that converts machine code back into human-readable assembly instructions. The quality and accuracy of this initial disassembly phase fundamentally determines the success of all subsequent analysis operations, from vulnerability detection to malware reverse engineering \cite{kruegel2004static, miller2019binary}. Traditional disassembly approaches have achieved remarkable success on conventional binaries produced by standard compilation toolchains. Linear sweep disassemblers process instructions sequentially from known entry points, while recursive descent methods follow control flow transfers to discover reachable code segments. These techniques work exceptionally well when applied to binaries that follow predictable patterns and maintain clear separation between code and data sections \cite{roundy2013hybrid}. However, the landscape of binary analysis has evolved significantly with the proliferation of code obfuscation techniques, packing mechanisms, and deliberate anti-analysis measures. Modern adversarial binaries frequently employ sophisticated countermeasures designed specifically to thwart static analysis tools. These include control flow obfuscation that obscures the natural program structure, dynamic code generation that creates instructions at runtime, and anti-disassembly techniques that exploit weaknesses in traditional parsing algorithms \cite{david2016neural, shin2015recognizing}. The challenge becomes particularly acute when dealing with malware samples, which routinely incorporate multiple layers of obfuscation to evade detection and analysis. Packed executables compress or encrypt their payload, revealing the actual code only during execution. Self-modifying programs alter their instruction sequences dynamically, making static analysis inherently incomplete. Control flow flattening transforms natural program structures into opaque dispatcher-based schemes that obscure the original logic flow. These adversarial techniques pose fundamental challenges to traditional disassembly methods. Heuristic-based approaches that rely on statistical patterns and structural assumptions often fail when confronted with deliberately crafted anomalies. The resulting disassembly errors propagate through the entire analysis pipeline, leading to missed vulnerabilities, incorrect malware classifications, and failed reverse engineering attempts \cite{wang2020comprehensive}. Recent research has explored machine learning approaches to address these limitations. Neural network architectures, particularly those based on recurrent and transformer models, demonstrate the ability to learn complex patterns in binary sequences that traditional heuristics cannot capture. These models can potentially identify instruction boundaries and opcodes even in heavily obfuscated code by leveraging learned representations of valid instruction patterns \cite{shin2015recognizing, david2016neural}. Despite their promise, pure machine learning approaches face several practical limitations. They require extensive training datasets that may not adequately represent the diversity of obfuscation techniques encountered in practice. Novel obfuscation methods not present in training data can cause significant performance degradation. Additionally, the black-box nature of neural models makes it difficult to understand and debug their decision-making processes, which is crucial for security-critical applications. This paper presents a hybrid approach that combines the interpretability and domain knowledge of traditional heuristic methods with the pattern recognition capabilities of modern machine learning techniques. Our methodology integrates multiple disassembly strategies through a confidence-based fusion mechanism that dynamically weights different analysis methods based on the characteristics of the input binary. The key contributions of this work include: \begin{itemize} \item A multi-stage disassembly pipeline that employs both linear sweep and recursive descent strategies with enhanced robustness against obfuscation \item A bidirectional LSTM architecture specifically designed for instruction boundary detection in adversarial binaries \item A confidence-based fusion mechanism that intelligently combines predictions from heuristic and neural components \item Comprehensive evaluation on a diverse dataset including standard binaries, obfuscated executables, and real-world malware samples \item Detailed analysis of performance characteristics across different obfuscation techniques and binary types \end{itemize} Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in disassembly accuracy, particularly on obfuscated binaries where traditional methods struggle. The hybrid approach maintains near-perfect performance on standard executables while providing substantial gains on adversarial samples. For control flow obfuscated binaries, we achieve F1-scores of 0.96340\xspace compared to baseline methods that typically fall below 0.8. On packed executables, our approach reaches 0.75949\xspace F1-score, representing a meaningful improvement over existing techniques. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in binary disassembly and machine learning approaches to reverse engineering. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} details our hybrid disassembly methodology, including the multi-stage pipeline design, neural network architecture, and fusion mechanism. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and evaluation methodology. Section~\ref{sec:results} presents comprehensive results and analysis across different binary types and obfuscation techniques. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our findings and limitations of the current approach. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with a summary of contributions and directions for future work. The field of binary disassembly has evolved through several generations of techniques, each addressing specific challenges in reverse engineering and program analysis. Early approaches focused primarily on linear sweep and recursive descent methods, which formed the foundation for most commercial disassemblers \cite{kruegel2004static}. Linear sweep disassembly processes instructions sequentially from known entry points, making the assumption that code sections contain contiguous instruction sequences. While computationally efficient and simple to implement, this approach struggles with variable-length instruction sets and fails when code and data are intermixed. Recursive descent methods address some of these limitations by following control flow transfers to discover reachable code segments, but they can miss code that is only reachable through indirect jumps or dynamically computed addresses. More sophisticated approaches have incorporated probabilistic models and statistical analysis to improve accuracy. Kruegel and Robertson \cite{kruegel2004static} introduced probabilistic disassembly techniques that use statistical models to distinguish between code and data regions. Their approach computes likelihood scores for different interpretations of byte sequences and selects the most probable disassembly. While effective on many binaries, these methods still rely on assumptions about instruction distributions that may not hold for obfuscated code. The emergence of sophisticated obfuscation techniques has driven research toward more robust disassembly methods. Roundy and Miller \cite{roundy2013hybrid} proposed hybrid approaches that combine multiple analysis techniques to improve resilience against anti-disassembly measures. Their work demonstrated that integrating static and dynamic analysis can overcome many limitations of purely static approaches, though at the cost of increased computational overhead. Machine learning approaches to binary analysis have gained significant attention in recent years. Shin et al. \cite{shin2015recognizing} explored the use of neural networks for recognizing functions in binary code, demonstrating that learned features can capture patterns that traditional heuristics miss. David and Yahav \cite{david2016neural} extended this work to instruction-level analysis, showing that recurrent neural networks can effectively model the sequential structure of assembly code.
