text: Phishing websites are a prominent social-engineering threat whose volume has significantly increased over the past few years~\cite{phishincreasing:2020,data-breach:2020}. These malicious websites are designed to deceive users into divulging sensitive information such as login credentials, financial data, or personal details by impersonating legitimate web services \cite{jagatic2007social,dhamija2006phishing}. The sophistication of modern phishing attacks has evolved considerably, with attackers employing advanced techniques to create nearly pixel-perfect replicas of trusted websites, making detection increasingly challenging for both automated systems and human users \cite{hong2012state}. Traditional phishing detection methods have primarily relied on URL analysis, domain reputation, and textual content examination \cite{ma2009beyond,whittaker2010large}. However, these approaches face significant limitations when confronted with sophisticated visual mimicry attacks that employ legitimate-looking domains, SSL certificates, and carefully crafted content \cite{lin2011phishmarket}. Furthermore, the rapid deployment and short lifespan of phishing websites—often lasting only hours or days—necessitate real-time detection capabilities that existing methods struggle to provide \cite{moore2007measuring}. Recent advances in computer vision and deep learning have opened new avenues for addressing these challenges through visual similarity analysis \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,simonyan2014very}. Visual-based detection methods can identify phishing attempts by analyzing the graphical appearance of websites, comparing them against known legitimate sites to detect suspicious similarities \cite{chen2013phishing,abdelnabi2020visualphishnet}. This approach is particularly effective against attacks that rely heavily on visual deception while maintaining distinct URL structures or textual content. The motivation for our work stems from several key observations. First, human users primarily rely on visual cues when assessing website legitimacy, making visual similarity a natural detection criterion \cite{dhamija2006phishing}. Second, while attackers can easily modify URLs and textual content, creating convincing visual replicas requires more sophisticated resources and often results in subtle but detectable differences \cite{marchal2014know}. Third, visual features exhibit greater stability across different phishing campaigns targeting the same legitimate service, enabling more robust detection models \cite{liu2005real}. Phishing detection research has evolved through several distinct phases, each addressing different aspects of the threat landscape. Early approaches focused primarily on blacklist-based methods, maintaining databases of known malicious URLs and domains \cite{sheng2009anti}. While effective against known threats, these methods suffer from poor coverage of zero-day attacks and require constant updates to remain effective. URL-based detection methods emerged as a more proactive approach, analyzing structural and lexical features of web addresses to identify suspicious patterns \cite{ma2009identifying,mcgrath2008phishing}. Features such as URL length, presence of suspicious keywords, domain age, and WHOIS information have been extensively studied \cite{khonji2013phishing}. Machine learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs) \cite{abu2007machine} and Random Forests \cite{ham2007investigation}, have been applied to these feature sets with considerable success. Content-based approaches analyze the textual and structural elements of web pages, employing techniques such as term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) analysis \cite{fette2007learning}, HTML structure comparison \cite{wenyin2005detection}, and natural language processing \cite{basnet2008learning}. These methods can detect attacks that employ legitimate-looking URLs but maintain malicious content. However, they often struggle with multilingual attacks and sophisticated content obfuscation techniques. More recently, researchers have begun exploring visual-based detection methods. Chen et al. \cite{chen2013phishing} proposed one of the first approaches using image processing techniques to compare website screenshots. Their method employed edge detection and color histogram analysis to identify visual similarities. However, the approach was limited by its reliance on handcrafted features and sensitivity to minor visual variations. Abdelnabi et al. \cite{abdelnabi2020visualphishnet} introduced VisualPhishNet, a deep learning framework that uses Siamese networks to learn visual representations of websites. Their approach demonstrated significant improvements over traditional methods, achieving detection accuracies exceeding 90\% on several benchmark datasets. However, the method required extensive training data and computational resources, limiting its practical deployment. Hybrid approaches combining multiple detection modalities have also been proposed. Marchal et al. \cite{marchal2014know} developed a system integrating URL analysis, content examination, and visual comparison. While achieving high detection rates, these methods often suffer from increased complexity and computational overhead. Despite these advances, several challenges remain unaddressed. First, existing visual methods often fail to capture fine-grained similarities that are crucial for detecting sophisticated attacks. Second, most approaches lack real-time processing capabilities required for practical deployment. Third, the evaluation of visual-based methods has been limited by the availability of comprehensive datasets containing both legitimate and phishing website screenshots. To evaluate our proposed VisualGuard framework, we constructed a comprehensive dataset comprising website screenshots from both legitimate and phishing sources. The dataset construction process involved multiple stages to ensure data quality, diversity, and representativeness. \subsection{Data Collection} We collected legitimate website screenshots from the Alexa Top 10,000 websites \cite{alexa2021top}, focusing on commonly targeted categories including banking, e-commerce, social media, and email services. Screenshots were captured using an automated web crawler implemented with Selenium WebDriver \cite{selenium2021}, configured with standardized browser settings (1920×1080 resolution, Chrome browser version 96) to ensure consistency. For phishing websites, we aggregated data from multiple threat intelligence sources, including PhishTank \cite{phishtank2021}, OpenPhish \cite{openphish2021}, and VirusTotal \cite{virustotal2021}. Given the ephemeral nature of phishing sites, we implemented a real-time collection system that captures screenshots within hours of URL discovery. This approach resulted in a dataset of 15,847 legitimate websites and 12,934 phishing websites, spanning a six-month collection period from January to June 2021. \subsection{Data Preprocessing} Raw screenshots underwent several preprocessing steps to standardize the input format and improve model performance. First, images were resized to 224×224 pixels using bilinear interpolation to match the input requirements of our CNN architecture. text: Image classification is a long-standing yet important task with a wide range of applications such as autonomous driving, industrial automation, medical diagnosis, and biometric identification~\cite{autonomous_driving, industrial_automation, medical_diagnosis, biometric_identification}. Traditional image classification approaches rely on the closed-world assumption, where all possible classes are known during training and the model is expected to classify only among these predefined categories~\cite{closed_world_assumption, traditional_classification}. However, this assumption is often violated in real-world scenarios where new classes emerge continuously, making it impractical to retrain models from scratch every time a new category appears~\cite{open_world_challenges}. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) addresses this limitation by enabling models to recognize unseen classes without any visual training examples~\cite{lampert2009learning, palatucci2009zero}. The key insight behind ZSL is to leverage auxiliary information, typically in the form of semantic attributes or word embeddings, to bridge the gap between seen and unseen classes~\cite{semantic_attributes, word_embeddings}. For instance, if a model has learned to recognize ``tiger'' and understands attributes like ``striped'' and ``carnivorous,'' it should be able to identify a ``zebra'' based on the shared ``striped'' attribute, even without seeing zebra images during training. While conventional ZSL focuses on classifying among unseen classes only, Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL) presents a more realistic and challenging scenario where the model must distinguish between both seen and unseen classes during inference~\cite{chao2016empirical, xian2018zero}. This generalized setting better reflects real-world deployment conditions but introduces additional complexities, particularly the bias problem where models tend to favor seen classes due to their familiarity with visual patterns from training data~\cite{bias_problem_gzsl}. Several approaches have been proposed to tackle GZSL challenges. Early methods focused on learning embeddings that map visual features to semantic spaces using linear transformations~\cite{socher2013zero, frome2013devise}. However, these approaches often suffer from the hubness problem and fail to capture complex non-linear relationships between visual and semantic modalities~\cite{hubness_problem}. More recent works have explored generative models that synthesize visual features for unseen classes~\cite{xian2018feature, felix2018multi}, adversarial training schemes~\cite{li2019leveraging, chen2021semantics}, and graph-based methods that exploit class relationships~\cite{kampffmeyer2019rethinking, wang2018zero}. Despite these advances, existing GZSL methods face several persistent challenges. First, the domain shift between seen and unseen classes remains a fundamental issue, as the distribution of visual features for unseen classes may differ significantly from that of seen classes~\cite{domain_shift_gzsl}. Second, most approaches rely on simple concatenation or linear fusion mechanisms to combine visual and semantic information, which may not effectively capture the intricate relationships between different modalities~\cite{multimodal_fusion}. Third, the semantic attributes used in many datasets are often incomplete or noisy, leading to suboptimal performance~\cite{attribute_noise}. Recent developments in attention mechanisms and transformer architectures have shown remarkable success in various computer vision tasks~\cite{vaswani2017attention, dosovitskiy2020image}. These mechanisms allow models to selectively focus on relevant parts of the input, potentially addressing the alignment challenges in cross-modal learning. However, their application to GZSL has been limited, with most existing works still relying on conventional convolutional neural networks and basic fusion strategies~\cite{attention_in_zsl}. Furthermore, the evaluation protocols and metrics used in GZSL research have evolved over time. Early works primarily focused on accuracy on unseen classes, but the community has increasingly adopted more comprehensive metrics that consider performance on both seen and unseen classes, such as harmonic mean accuracy~\cite{xian2017zero}. This shift in evaluation methodology has highlighted the importance of developing balanced approaches that do not sacrifice performance on seen classes while maintaining good generalization to unseen categories. The calibration of classification scores represents another critical aspect often overlooked in existing literature. Many GZSL methods produce biased confidence scores that favor seen classes, necessitating post-processing calibration techniques~\cite{calibration_gzsl}. However, most calibration approaches are applied as separate post-processing steps rather than being integrated into the learning process itself. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing the Semantic-Visual Alignment Network (SVAN), which introduces several novel contributions to the GZSL literature. Our approach leverages advanced attention mechanisms to achieve better cross-modal alignment, incorporates calibration directly into the learning objective, and demonstrates superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets. The following sections detail our methodology, experimental setup, and comprehensive evaluation results.

text: Clique finding is a well-researched topic in the graph community and it has many interesting practical applications for community detection \cite{6249683, palla2005uncovering, 7117352, fang2019efficient} , social network analysis \cite{wasserman1994social, fortunato2010community}, bioinformatics \cite{abu2006finding, spirin2003protein}, and recommendation systems \cite{sarwar2001item, su2009survey}. The fundamental challenge lies in identifying complete subgraphs where every pair of vertices is connected by an edge, representing tight-knit groups or highly correlated entities within complex networks. The practical significance of clique detection extends beyond theoretical computer science. In social networks, cliques correspond to groups of individuals who are all mutually connected, indicating strong social cohesion \cite{wasserman1994social}. In protein-protein interaction networks, cliques may represent functional modules or protein complexes that work together to perform specific biological functions \cite{spirin2003protein, abu2006finding}. Market basket analysis utilizes clique structures to identify sets of items frequently purchased together, enabling more effective cross-selling strategies \cite{sarwar2001item}. Despite decades of research, the computational complexity of clique problems remains a significant barrier to practical applications. The decision version of the clique problem is NP-complete, while the optimization version (maximum clique) and enumeration version (all maximal cliques) are even more challenging \cite{garey1979computers}. For dense graphs with $n$ vertices, the number of maximal cliques can grow exponentially, reaching $3^{n/3}$ in the worst case according to Moon and Moser's theorem \cite{moon1965cliques}. Recent algorithmic advances have focused on exploiting structural properties inherent in real-world networks to achieve better practical performance. Many empirical networks exhibit power-law degree distributions, small-world properties, and community structure that can be leveraged for more efficient clique detection \cite{barabasi1999emergence, watts1998collective}. The concept of graph degeneracy has proven particularly valuable, as it provides tight bounds on clique sizes and enables effective vertex ordering strategies \cite{lick1970k}. Branch-and-bound techniques represent another important class of exact algorithms for maximum clique problems. These methods systematically explore the solution space while maintaining upper and lower bounds to prune infeasible branches early. The MAXSAT formulation of the maximum clique problem allows leveraging sophisticated SAT solvers, though the translation overhead can be substantial for large instances \cite{li2006maxsat}. Heuristic approaches offer practical alternatives when exact solutions are computationally infeasible. Greedy algorithms iteratively select vertices with maximum degree or other local criteria, achieving reasonable approximation ratios in polynomial time \cite{johnson1974approximation}. Metaheuristic methods such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and tabu search have shown promise for large-scale instances, though they sacrifice optimality guarantees for computational tractability \cite{pardalos1998maximum}. The emergence of streaming and dynamic graph scenarios has introduced new challenges for clique detection algorithms. Traditional batch processing methods become inadequate when graphs evolve continuously, requiring incremental algorithms that can efficiently update clique structures as edges are added or removed \cite{zanghi2008clustering}. Memory constraints in streaming environments further complicate the problem, necessitating space-efficient data structures and approximation schemes. Machine learning techniques have recently been applied to clique detection problems, with graph neural networks showing particular promise for learning structural patterns that indicate clique presence \cite{scarselli2008graph, zhou2020graph}. These approaches can potentially overcome some limitations of traditional combinatorial methods by learning from graph topology and node features simultaneously. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of modern clique detection algorithms, evaluating their performance across diverse graph types and application domains. We introduce novel optimization techniques that combine theoretical insights with practical implementation considerations, demonstrating significant improvements in both runtime efficiency and scalability. Our contributions include enhanced pruning strategies, parallel processing frameworks, and hybrid approaches that balance accuracy with computational feasibility.

text: With the proliferation of mobile and edge devices, federated learning~\cite{konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication} has emerged as a framework for training machine learning models over geographically distributed and heterogeneous devices. In federated learning, the central challenge lies in coordinating model training across numerous devices while respecting privacy constraints and minimizing communication overhead. Unlike traditional distributed learning where data can be centralized, federated learning must operate under the constraint that raw data never leaves individual devices, necessitating the exchange of model parameters or gradients instead. The communication bottleneck in federated learning is particularly pronounced due to several factors. First, the sheer number of participating devices can range from hundreds to millions, creating a massive communication burden when aggregating updates. Second, many edge devices operate on limited bandwidth connections, such as mobile networks, where communication costs are both monetary and energy-intensive. Third, the heterogeneous nature of devices means that communication capabilities vary significantly across participants, potentially creating synchronization issues and stragglers. \subsection{Challenges in Federated Communication} The federated learning paradigm introduces unique challenges that distinguish it from traditional distributed optimization settings. \emph{Statistical heterogeneity} arises when data distributions across devices are non-identically distributed (non-IID), leading to gradient diversity that can impede convergence. \emph{System heterogeneity} manifests in varying computational capabilities, memory constraints, and network conditions across devices. \emph{Privacy requirements} necessitate that sensitive user data remains local, constraining the types of information that can be shared. These challenges are further compounded by the intermittent availability of devices, as mobile and edge devices may frequently disconnect from the network due to power constraints, mobility, or network instability. This creates a dynamic participation pattern that algorithms must accommodate while maintaining convergence guarantees. \subsection{Communication Compression in Federated Settings} To address the communication bottleneck, compression techniques have been adapted and extended for federated learning applications. The fundamental idea is to reduce the size of transmitted gradients or model updates while preserving sufficient information for convergence. However, the federated setting introduces additional complexities compared to traditional distributed learning. In the federated context, compression must account for the heterogeneous nature of local updates. Different devices may produce gradients with varying magnitudes and sparsity patterns, making uniform compression strategies suboptimal. Moreover, the aggregation process at the server must be designed to handle compressed updates from multiple sources while maintaining theoretical convergence properties. \subsection{Beyond Traditional Compression Bounds} Recent theoretical developments have begun to address the limitations of classical compression analyses. text: Recently, modern voice-controlled devices with virtual assistants like Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant, have been working their way into every activity of our daily life from playing a song to booking a flight or controlling smart home devices. These systems rely heavily on Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) to interpret user intents and extract relevant information from natural language utterances. However, the majority of these systems are primarily designed and optimized for high-resource languages such as English, leaving speakers of low-resource languages with limited or suboptimal functionality. The challenge of building effective SLU systems for multiple languages is particularly acute given the diversity of linguistic structures, cultural contexts, and domain-specific expressions across different language families. Traditional approaches to multilingual SLU often require substantial amounts of labeled training data for each target language, which is both expensive and time-consuming to obtain. This data scarcity problem is especially pronounced for low-resource languages, where collecting sufficient annotated examples for intent classification and slot filling tasks remains a significant bottleneck. Recent advances in multilingual pre-trained language models, particularly BERT-based architectures \cite{devlin2018bert, conneau2019unsupervised}, have shown promising results in various cross-lingual natural language processing tasks. These models leverage large-scale multilingual corpora during pre-training, potentially enabling knowledge transfer across languages without requiring extensive target-language supervision. However, the effectiveness of such transfer learning approaches in the context of SLU tasks, particularly for languages with limited resources, remains an open research question. In this work, we investigate the cross-lingual transfer capabilities of multilingual BERT models for SLU tasks, focusing on both intent classification and slot filling across a diverse set of languages. Our primary research questions include: (1) How effectively can a multilingual BERT-based SLU model transfer knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in a zero-shot setting? (2) What linguistic factors influence the quality of cross-lingual transfer? (3) How much target-language data is required to achieve satisfactory performance through few-shot learning approaches? To address these questions, we conduct comprehensive experiments using the MultiATIS++ dataset \cite{xu2020end}, which provides parallel annotations for intent classification and slot filling tasks across multiple languages. Our experimental setup includes 12 languages representing different language families, writing systems, and resource availability levels, ranging from high-resource languages like English and German to low-resource languages such as Turkish and Hindi. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: First, we provide a systematic evaluation of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for multilingual BERT-based SLU models, revealing significant performance gaps between high-resource and low-resource languages. Second, we analyze the linguistic factors that influence transfer effectiveness, including language family relatedness, script similarity, and morphological complexity. Third, we demonstrate that few-shot learning with minimal target-language data can substantially bridge the performance gap, requiring as few as 100 labeled examples to achieve meaningful improvements. Finally, we propose practical guidelines for deploying multilingual SLU systems in resource-constrained scenarios. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work on multilingual SLU and cross-lingual transfer learning. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} describes our experimental methodology, including model architecture, training procedures, and evaluation metrics. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents our experimental results and analysis. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our findings and provides practical recommendations. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

text: During the recent years, micro-blogging become a source of current and topical news. Twitter\footnote{www.twitter.com} is one of the most prominent micro-blogging platforms, allowing users to share short messages (tweets) of up to 280 characters. The platform has evolved into a critical communication channel for real-time information dissemination, public discourse, and social interaction \cite{kwak2010twitter}. With over 450 million monthly active users worldwide, Twitter generates approximately 500 million tweets daily, creating an unprecedented volume of user-generated content \cite{statista2023twitter}. The significance of Twitter as a data source extends beyond its scale to encompass its unique characteristics. Unlike traditional media outlets, Twitter provides unfiltered access to public opinion, enabling researchers to observe authentic user reactions and sentiment in real-time \cite{pak2010twitter}. This immediacy makes Twitter particularly valuable for studying breaking news events, political campaigns, natural disasters, and social movements as they unfold. Twitter's influence on information propagation has been extensively documented in academic literature. The platform's retweet mechanism facilitates rapid information diffusion, allowing messages to reach audiences far beyond the original poster's followers \cite{boyd2010tweet}. This viral nature of content sharing has made Twitter a powerful tool for both legitimate information dissemination and the spread of misinformation, necessitating careful analysis of information credibility and source verification \cite{vosoughi2018spread}. The platform's role in crisis communication has proven particularly noteworthy. During emergencies such as natural disasters, terrorist attacks, or public health crises, Twitter serves as both an information source and a coordination platform for relief efforts \cite{vieweg2010microblogging}. Emergency responders, government agencies, and affected individuals use the platform to share critical updates, request assistance, and coordinate response activities. From a research perspective, Twitter data offers unique advantages for computational social science studies. The platform's public nature means that most tweets are accessible for analysis without requiring user consent, subject to Twitter's terms of service and ethical research guidelines \cite{williams2017network}. The structured format of tweets, combined with rich metadata, enables researchers to conduct large-scale quantitative analyses while maintaining the ability to examine qualitative aspects of communication. However, working with Twitter data also presents significant methodological challenges. The platform's user base exhibits demographic biases, with certain populations being overrepresented or underrepresented compared to the general population \cite{mislove2011understanding}. Researchers must carefully consider these sampling biases when drawing conclusions about broader social phenomena. Additionally, the dynamic nature of Twitter data requires sophisticated analytical approaches. Users may delete tweets, change their profiles, or deactivate accounts, leading to data availability issues in longitudinal studies \cite{almuhimedi2013tweets}. The platform's algorithmic timeline and recommendation systems also influence user behavior and content visibility, adding layers of complexity to data interpretation. The temporal aspect of Twitter data provides both opportunities and challenges for researchers. The precise timestamps associated with tweets enable fine-grained temporal analysis, allowing researchers to study the evolution of topics, sentiment changes over time, and the relationship between online discussions and real-world events \cite{sakaki2010earthquake}. This temporal richness is particularly valuable for studying phenomena such as election campaigns, where public opinion may shift rapidly in response to new information or events.

text: Clinicians currently spend more time documenting information in electronic health records (EHRs) than they do providing direct patient care \citep{sinsky2016allocation, arndt2017tethered}. This documentation burden has contributed to widespread physician burnout and decreased job satisfaction across healthcare systems \citep{shanafelt2019changes, west2018interventions}. The challenge is particularly acute given that clinical documentation must be both comprehensive and precise, capturing complex medical information while adhering to regulatory requirements and billing standards. Traditional approaches to reducing documentation burden have included voice recognition software, scribes, and template-based systems. However, these solutions often introduce their own limitations: voice recognition systems struggle with medical terminology and ambient noise, scribes require additional personnel costs, and templates can lead to rigid, checkbox-style documentation that may not capture the nuanced nature of patient encounters \citep{gidwani2017impact, murphy2019impact}. Recent advances in natural language processing and machine learning present new opportunities to address these challenges. Large language models trained on medical corpora have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding clinical context and generating medically relevant text \citep{lee2020biobert, alsentzer2019publicly}. However, most existing applications focus on post-hoc analysis of clinical text rather than real-time assistance during the documentation process itself. Our work addresses this gap by developing an intelligent autocompletion system specifically designed for clinical documentation workflows. The system operates as a writing assistant, providing contextually relevant suggestions as clinicians type their notes. This approach differs from existing autocomplete systems in several key ways: first, it incorporates deep medical knowledge to suggest clinically appropriate terms even when they lack surface-level similarity to the current input; second, it maintains awareness of the broader clinical context within the note to ensure suggestions remain coherent with the overall patient narrative; and third, it adapts to individual clinician preferences and specialty-specific terminology over time. The technical foundation of our system rests on a transformer-based architecture that has been specifically fine-tuned for medical language understanding. We leverage a large corpus of de-identified clinical notes spanning multiple medical specialties to train models that can capture the complex relationships between symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes. The training process incorporates several novel techniques designed to address the unique challenges of medical text, including handling of medical abbreviations, maintaining patient privacy through careful anonymization, and balancing suggestions across different levels of clinical specificity. Our evaluation methodology focuses on both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments from practicing clinicians. We measure traditional information retrieval metrics such as precision, recall, and ranking quality, but also assess more nuanced factors such as clinical appropriateness, documentation completeness, and user satisfaction. The evaluation dataset comprises \num{50000} clinical notes from diverse medical specialties, including internal medicine, cardiology, oncology, and emergency medicine, ensuring that our results generalize across different clinical contexts. The contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we present a novel architecture for medical autocompletion that incorporates domain-specific knowledge and clinical reasoning; (2) we demonstrate significant improvements in documentation efficiency while maintaining clinical accuracy through comprehensive evaluation on real-world data; and (3) we provide detailed analysis of system performance across different medical specialties and documentation types, offering insights for future development of clinical decision support tools. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in clinical natural language processing and documentation assistance systems. Section~\ref{sec:methods} describes our model architecture and training methodology in detail. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents our experimental setup and evaluation metrics. Section~\ref{sec:results} discusses our findings, including performance comparisons with baseline systems and analysis of clinical utility. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our contributions and outlines directions for future research. The intersection of natural language processing and healthcare has seen rapid development in recent years, with particular attention to applications that can directly support clinical workflows \citep{wang2018clinical, kocabas2020medical}. Within this broader field, several distinct research directions are relevant to our work. \subsection{Clinical Text Understanding} Early work in clinical NLP focused primarily on information extraction and named entity recognition tasks \citep{uzuner2011evaluating, suominen2013overview}. Systems like MetaMap \citep{aronson2001effective} and cTAKES \citep{savova2010mayo} established foundational approaches for processing clinical text, but were limited by their reliance on rule-based methods and predefined vocabularies. The introduction of neural approaches marked a significant advancement in clinical text understanding. BioBERT \citep{lee2020biobert} and ClinicalBERT \citep{alsentzer2019publicly} demonstrated that domain-specific pre-training could substantially improve performance on clinical NLP tasks. More recent work has explored even larger models, with systems like GatorTron \citep{yang2022gatortron} showing promising results across multiple clinical benchmarks.

text: Hand dexterity is fundamental to daily human activities, requiring complex and precise control of finger movements. The human hand, with its 27 degrees of freedom and sophisticated sensorimotor control, enables manipulation tasks ranging from delicate threading of needles to powerful grasping of heavy objects \cite{cutkosky1989grasp, feix2016taxonomy}. This remarkable versatility stems from the integration of multiple sensory modalities, adaptive motor control, and learned manipulation strategies that generalize across vastly different object properties and environmental conditions. Replicating such dexterous capabilities in robotic systems remains one of the most challenging problems in robotics. While significant progress has been made in developing sophisticated robotic hands with multiple degrees of freedom \cite{shadow2005design, dollar2013yale}, the control strategies required to fully exploit their potential lag far behind human performance. The fundamental difficulty lies in the complex interplay between perception, planning, and control that must operate seamlessly across diverse manipulation scenarios. Traditional approaches to robotic manipulation have largely relied on analytical models of contact mechanics and rigid body dynamics \cite{murray1994mathematical, siciliano2009robotics}. These methods, while theoretically sound, require precise knowledge of object properties, contact locations, and environmental constraints that are often unavailable or difficult to estimate in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the computational complexity of solving contact-rich manipulation problems analytically often limits their applicability to simplified scenarios with known object geometries and controlled environments. The emergence of deep learning has introduced data-driven alternatives that learn manipulation policies directly from experience \cite{levine2016end, kalashnikov2018scalable}. Reinforcement learning approaches have demonstrated impressive results on specific manipulation tasks, learning to exploit the full dexterity of multi-fingered hands through trial and error \cite{openai2019solving, chen2022system}. However, these methods typically require extensive training for each new task and object category, limiting their practical deployment in scenarios requiring rapid adaptation to novel objects or manipulation requirements. A critical limitation of existing approaches is their treatment of perception and control as separate modules. Traditional pipelines first estimate object pose and properties through vision systems, then plan and execute manipulation strategies based on these estimates \cite{bohg2014data}. This decoupling introduces compounding errors and fails to leverage the rich feedback available during manipulation execution. Recent work has begun to explore end-to-end learning approaches that integrate perception and control \cite{james2017transferring, zeng2018learning}, but these methods often lack the interpretability and generalization capabilities needed for robust real-world deployment. Neural implicit representations have emerged as a powerful paradigm for encoding complex geometries and physical properties in continuous function spaces \cite{sitzmann2020implicit, tancik2020fourier}. Unlike discrete representations such as voxel grids or point clouds, implicit representations can capture fine-grained geometric details while maintaining computational efficiency and enabling smooth interpolation between different object configurations. Recent applications to robotics have demonstrated their potential for shape completion \cite{wu2020multimodal}, grasp planning \cite{lundell2020multi}, and dynamic scene understanding \cite{li2021neural}. Building upon these advances, we propose a unified framework that leverages neural implicit representations to bridge the gap between perception and control in dexterous manipulation. Our approach jointly encodes object geometry, material properties, and manipulation dynamics within a single implicit neural network, enabling seamless integration of sensory feedback and motor control. The hierarchical control architecture decomposes complex manipulation tasks into manageable sub-problems while maintaining global coherence through the shared implicit representation. The proposed framework addresses several key limitations of existing approaches: (1) it provides a unified representation that eliminates the perception-control interface bottleneck, (2) it enables rapid adaptation to novel objects through few-shot learning on the implicit representation, and (3) it maintains interpretability through the hierarchical decomposition of control policies. We validate our approach on a comprehensive suite of manipulation tasks involving objects with diverse geometric and material properties, demonstrating significant improvements in success rates and adaptation speed compared to existing methods.

text: The task of image captioning aims to generate human-readable descriptive text from an image. This fundamental problem in computer vision and natural language processing has garnered significant attention due to its potential applications in accessibility, content indexing, and human-computer interaction. The challenge lies in bridging the semantic gap between visual perception and linguistic expression, requiring models to not only recognize objects and their attributes but also understand spatial relationships, actions, and contextual information. Early approaches to image captioning followed a template-based paradigm, where predefined sentence structures were filled with detected objects and attributes~\cite{farhadi2010every, kulkarni2013babytalk}. While these methods could generate grammatically correct sentences, they lacked flexibility and often produced repetitive descriptions that failed to capture the richness and diversity of natural language. The advent of deep learning revolutionized this field, enabling more sophisticated approaches that could learn complex mappings between visual and textual modalities. The dominant paradigm in modern image captioning has been the encoder-decoder architecture, popularized by \cite{vinyals2015show} and \cite{xu2015show}. These methods typically employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) to encode visual features and a recurrent neural network (RNN) or transformer to decode these features into natural language descriptions. A critical advancement was the introduction of attention mechanisms~\cite{xu2015show}, which allowed models to focus on different image regions while generating each word, leading to more accurate and contextually relevant captions. Most state-of-the-art captioning systems rely heavily on pre-trained object detectors to extract regional visual features~\cite{anderson2018bottom, jiang2018recurrent, huang2019attention}. These detector-based approaches, exemplified by the Bottom-Up Top-Down model~\cite{anderson2018bottom}, use object detection networks like Faster R-CNN~\cite{ren2015faster} to identify salient regions and extract corresponding feature representations. While this paradigm has achieved remarkable success, it introduces several limitations: (1) dependency on large-scale object detection datasets for pre-training, (2) computational overhead from running separate detection models, (3) potential error propagation from detection failures, and (4) limited generalization to novel objects or scenes not covered in the detection training data. Recent advances in vision-language pre-training have opened new possibilities for end-to-end image captioning without explicit object detection~\cite{radford2021learning, li2022blip, wang2022git}. Models like CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning} and ALIGN~\cite{jia2021scaling} have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in learning joint visual-textual representations from large-scale web data. However, when adapted for image captioning, these approaches often struggle with fine-grained visual understanding and spatial reasoning, leading to generic or inaccurate descriptions. The fundamental challenge in detector-free captioning lies in learning to attend to relevant visual regions without explicit supervision. While global image representations can capture overall scene semantics, they often fail to encode the detailed spatial and relational information necessary for generating rich, descriptive captions. This limitation becomes particularly apparent when describing complex scenes with multiple objects, actions, or spatial relationships. Our proposed Visual Attention Refinement Network (VARN) addresses these challenges by introducing a novel multi-scale attention mechanism that progressively refines visual representations. Unlike existing approaches that rely on either global image features or pre-detected regions, VARN learns to dynamically identify and attend to salient image regions through self-supervised learning. The key insight is that effective visual attention for captioning should operate at multiple scales, capturing both coarse scene-level context and fine-grained object details. The multi-scale attention mechanism in VARN operates through a hierarchical refinement process. Starting with global image representations, the model progressively focuses on smaller, more specific regions while maintaining awareness of the broader context. This approach enables the model to generate captions that are both contextually coherent and rich in detail, without requiring explicit object detection supervision. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose VARN, a novel architecture that eliminates the dependency on pre-trained object detectors while maintaining competitive captioning performance. (2) We introduce a multi-scale attention refinement mechanism that progressively focuses on salient visual regions at different granularities. (3) We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance among detector-free methods and remains competitive with detector-based approaches. (4) We provide comprehensive ablation studies and qualitative analyses that validate the effectiveness of each component in our architecture. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in image captioning and visual attention mechanisms. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents the detailed architecture of VARN and its key components. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and presents quantitative and qualitative results. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

A crucial advance was the introduction of attentional mechanisms (Vinyals,2015,Xu,2015), which enabled the model to focus on different parts of the image while generating each word of a caption, thus producing more accurate and relevant captions. The most popular image captioning method is the encoder-decoder architecture, popularized by Vinyals,2015 and Xu, 2015, which uses a convolutional neural network to encode the visual features and a recurrent neural network to decode them into natural language descriptions. As has been mentioned, while global image representations can capture the general meaning of a scene, they often fail to capture the detailed spatial and relational information required to write richly descriptive captions. This is especially evident in complex scenes with many objects, actions, and spatial relations. Detector-based systems, such as the BUD model of Anderson (2018), which uses Faster-RCNN (Ren, 2015) to detect objects in regions, also have several drawbacks: (1) strong reliance on large-scale object detection data for pre-training, (2) high computation costs to run separate object detection models, (3) propagation of errors in the detection, and (4) low generalization ability to novel objects and scenes not covered by the training data. The principal problem of automatic captioning without visual attention markers is learning to pay attention to the relevant visual regions without any explicit guidance. The proposed model, the visual attention refinement neural network, or VARN, addresses these challenges by introducing a novel mechanism that iteratively refines visual representations at various scales. It is the main insight of our system that effective visual attention for captioning should operate at different scales, capturing coarse-grained context and fine-grained object details. This hierarchical attention mechanism in VARN works by progressive refinement: starting from a global representation of the image, the model progressively refines its attention towards smaller and more specific regions, while maintaining an awareness of the context. This allows the model to produce captions which are both context-aware and rich in detail, without needing any supervision on the recognition of objects. Unlike previous methods which rely either on global image features or on the identification of regions, VARN learns, through self-supervision, to dynamically identify and attend to the most salient regions. We review the related work on image captioning and attention mechanisms. (1) We introduce the VARN architecture, which eliminates the need for pre-trained object detectors while maintaining competitive performance for text generation. (2) We propose a multi-scale attention mechanism that gradually focuses on salient visual regions of different granularities. refsec:method describes the detailed architecture of VARN and its main components. refsec:experiments describes the experimental procedure and presents numerical and qualitative results. refsec:analysis gives detailed ablation experiments and qualitative analysis to test the effectiveness of each component of our architecture. Section  refers to the conclusion of the article and the suggestions for further research.

text: Modeling and rendering humans is a core technology needed to enable applications in sports visualization, telepresence, shopping, and many others. Recent advances in neural rendering have shown remarkable progress in reconstructing static scenes from multi-view images \cite{mildenhall2020nerf, barron2021mip}. However, extending these methods to dynamic human subjects presents unique challenges due to the complex interplay between articulated motion, clothing deformation, and appearance variations under different lighting conditions. Traditional approaches to human modeling rely on parametric body models such as SMPL \cite{loper2015smpl} or SMPL-X \cite{pavlakos2019expressive}, which provide a compact representation of human shape and pose but lack the expressiveness needed to capture fine-grained appearance details and clothing geometry. While these models excel at representing the underlying body structure, they struggle to handle loose clothing, hair dynamics, and subject-specific appearance variations that are crucial for photorealistic rendering. Recent work has explored combining neural representations with parametric human models to achieve more detailed reconstructions. Neural Body \cite{peng2021neural} and Animatable NeRF \cite{peng2021animatable} represent humans using neural radiance fields conditioned on SMPL parameters, enabling novel view synthesis of people in different poses. However, these methods typically require multi-view capture setups with carefully controlled lighting conditions, limiting their applicability to casual video recordings. Our approach addresses these limitations by learning from monocular "in-the-wild" videos, which are readily available but pose significant technical challenges. The key insight is to leverage the temporal consistency inherent in video sequences while explicitly modeling the geometric and photometric transformations induced by pose changes. We achieve this through a carefully designed architecture that separates the canonical appearance representation from pose-dependent deformations. The canonical neural field operates in a reference coordinate system where the person is in a T-pose, allowing the network to learn a consistent representation of surface geometry and texture without the confounding effects of articulated motion. The deformation network then maps points from this canonical space to the observed pose space using SMPL-derived transformations, enabling the model to handle complex pose variations while maintaining appearance consistency. To ensure temporal coherence across video frames, we introduce several regularization terms that encourage smooth transitions between adjacent frames and penalize unrealistic deformations. Additionally, we employ a coarse-to-fine training strategy that progressively refines the model resolution, allowing for efficient optimization while capturing fine-scale details.

text: Autoencoders are a powerful type of Neural Networks that can realize compact representations of data, and are often used as a denoising method \cite{autoencoders}. In the quantum computing paradigm, the concept of autoencoders has been extended to quantum systems, giving rise to Quantum Autoencoders (QAEs) \cite{romero2017quantum}. These quantum neural networks leverage the unique properties of quantum mechanics, such as superposition and entanglement, to perform compression and denoising tasks on quantum states. Unlike their classical counterparts, QAEs operate directly on quantum information, making them particularly suitable for quantum error correction and state purification applications \cite{bondarenko2020quantum}. The fundamental principle underlying QAEs is the ability to encode high-dimensional quantum states into lower-dimensional representations while preserving essential quantum correlations. This compression is achieved through a variational quantum circuit that learns to map noisy input states to a latent space of reduced dimensionality. The subsequent decoding process reconstructs the original quantum state from this compressed representation, effectively filtering out noise and decoherence effects \cite{cerezo2021variational}. Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states represent a class of maximally entangled quantum states that play a crucial role in quantum information processing protocols, including quantum cryptography, quantum teleportation, and quantum error correction \cite{greenberger1989going}. These states are particularly fragile under environmental decoherence, making them ideal candidates for demonstrating the effectiveness of quantum denoising techniques. The $n$-qubit GHZ state is defined as: \begin{equation} |\text{GHZ}_n\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle^{\otimes n} + |1\rangle^{\otimes n}) \end{equation} When subjected to noisy quantum channels, GHZ states lose their coherence and entanglement properties, resulting in mixed states that deviate significantly from the ideal pure state. Common noise models include the bit-flip channel, which flips individual qubits with probability $p$, and the depolarizing channel, which replaces the quantum state with the maximally mixed state with probability $p$ \cite{nielsen2010quantum}. The architecture of our QAE consists of two main components: an encoder circuit $U_E(\boldsymbol{\theta}_E)$ and a decoder circuit $U_D(\boldsymbol{\theta}_D)$, where $\boldsymbol{\theta}_E$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_D$ represent the variational parameters of the encoder and decoder, respectively. The encoder compresses the $n$-qubit noisy input state into a $(n-k)$-qubit latent representation by tracing out $k$ ancilla qubits, while the decoder reconstructs the denoised GHZ state from this compressed representation.

text: Environmental sound provides rich perspectives on the physical world. For example, if we hear: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash;} we can infer a scene of people enjoying themselves at a swimming pool or beach. This natural human ability to interpret and describe acoustic environments has inspired the development of automated audio captioning systems that can generate textual descriptions of environmental soundscapes. Audio captioning represents a challenging cross-modal task that requires models to bridge the semantic gap between acoustic signals and natural language descriptions. Unlike speech recognition, which focuses on transcribing spoken words, audio captioning must identify, localize, and describe diverse environmental sounds, often occurring simultaneously in complex acoustic scenes. The task demands not only accurate sound event detection but also the ability to generate coherent, contextually appropriate textual descriptions that capture both the content and temporal dynamics of the audio. The significance of automated audio captioning extends across numerous applications. In assistive technology, such systems can provide audio descriptions for visually impaired users, enhancing their understanding of surrounding environments. Content indexing and retrieval systems benefit from automatic audio annotations, enabling efficient search through large multimedia databases. Additionally, audio captioning can support environmental monitoring, security surveillance, and multimedia content analysis, where automated interpretation of acoustic scenes provides valuable insights. Current approaches to audio captioning primarily fall into two categories: encoder-decoder architectures and contrastive learning methods. Encoder-decoder models, inspired by successful image captioning systems, typically employ convolutional neural networks or transformers to extract audio features, followed by recurrent or attention-based decoders for text generation \cite{drossos2017automated, xu2015show}. These models are trained end-to-end to maximize the likelihood of ground-truth captions given input audio. However, the effectiveness of these supervised approaches is fundamentally limited by the availability of high-quality paired audio-text data. Creating such datasets requires extensive manual annotation efforts, where human annotators must carefully listen to audio clips and provide detailed textual descriptions. This process is not only time-consuming and expensive but also subject to inter-annotator variability and potential inconsistencies in description styles and granularity. The data scarcity problem is further exacerbated by the inherent diversity and complexity of environmental soundscapes. Unlike controlled speech or music datasets, environmental audio exhibits tremendous variability in acoustic properties, recording conditions, and semantic content. Sounds may be overlapping, temporally distributed, or exhibit varying degrees of prominence, making consistent annotation challenging. Moreover, the subjective nature of sound description means that multiple valid captions may exist for the same audio clip, complicating evaluation metrics and training objectives. To address these limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to weakly-supervised and self-supervised learning paradigms. Weakly-supervised approaches leverage readily available but noisy data sources, such as web-scraped audio-text pairs or automatically generated tags from pre-trained models. While such data may contain errors or inconsistencies, its abundance can compensate for quality limitations when appropriate training strategies are employed. Self-supervised pre-training has shown particular promise in learning robust audio representations without requiring manual annotations. Methods such as contrastive predictive coding \cite{oord2018representation} and masked reconstruction \cite{baevski2020wav2vec} enable models to capture meaningful acoustic patterns from unlabeled audio data. These learned representations can then be transferred to downstream captioning tasks, potentially reducing the dependency on large-scale paired datasets. Recent work has also explored the integration of large language models (LLMs) into audio captioning pipelines. By leveraging the extensive world knowledge and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained language models, these approaches can generate more natural and contextually rich descriptions. However, effectively conditioning language generation on audio representations remains an active area of research, with challenges including modality alignment, temporal synchronization, and maintaining semantic consistency. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges persist in audio captioning research. The evaluation of generated captions remains problematic, as traditional metrics like BLEU and ROUGE, borrowed from machine translation and summarization, may not adequately capture the quality of audio descriptions. The temporal nature of audio events, the subjectivity of sound interpretation, and the potential for multiple valid descriptions all contribute to evaluation complexity. Furthermore, current datasets and benchmarks may not fully represent the diversity of real-world acoustic environments. Most existing datasets focus on relatively short audio clips with clear, identifiable sound events, potentially limiting the generalizability of trained models to more complex, naturalistic soundscapes. The development of more comprehensive evaluation frameworks and diverse datasets remains crucial for advancing the field. In this work, we address these challenges by proposing a novel approach that combines the strengths of contrastive learning with efficient utilization of limited paired data. Our method leverages both supervised learning on high-quality annotations and self-supervised pre-training on abundant unlabeled audio, achieving improved performance while reducing dependency on expensive manual annotations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across multiple benchmarks and provide comprehensive analysis of the learned representations.

text: The release of large pre-trained language models like BERT~\cite{bert} has shaken-up Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding natural language semantics and have been successfully adapted for various retrieval tasks \cite{nogueira2019passage, qiao2019understanding}. The transformer architecture underlying these models enables sophisticated contextual understanding that traditional bag-of-words approaches cannot capture \cite{vaswani2017attention}. In the context of information retrieval, BERT and similar models have been employed in multiple ways. Cross-encoders, which process query-document pairs jointly, achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness but suffer from computational inefficiency during inference \cite{nogueira2019passage}. Bi-encoders, which encode queries and documents separately, offer better scalability but often sacrifice some retrieval quality \cite{reimers2019sentence}. This trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency remains a central challenge in neural information retrieval. The advent of large language models has also introduced new paradigms for retrieval. Generative models like T5 and GPT have been explored for document ranking tasks \cite{nogueira2020document, sun2023chatgpt}, while instruction-tuned models demonstrate zero-shot retrieval capabilities across diverse domains \cite{su2022one}. These developments suggest that the traditional boundaries between retrieval and generation are becoming increasingly blurred. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges persist. The computational cost of large language models makes them impractical for real-time retrieval in many applications \cite{lin2021distilling}. Additionally, these models often exhibit biases present in their training data, which can propagate to retrieval systems and affect fairness \cite{rekabsaz2021societal}. The lack of interpretability in neural retrieval models also poses challenges for understanding why certain documents are retrieved over others \cite{singh2021explain}. Furthermore, the evaluation of neural retrieval systems presents unique challenges. Traditional metrics like precision and recall may not fully capture the nuanced improvements that neural models provide \cite{zhang2021evaluating}. The development of more sophisticated evaluation frameworks that account for semantic similarity and user satisfaction remains an active area of research \cite{hofstatter2021efficiently}. Recent work has also focused on making neural retrieval more practical and accessible. Techniques for model compression and knowledge distillation have been developed to reduce the computational requirements while maintaining retrieval quality \cite{lin2021distilling, hofstatter2021efficiently}. Additionally, few-shot and zero-shot learning approaches aim to reduce the dependency on large labeled datasets \cite{ma2021zero, su2022one}. The integration of neural retrieval with traditional IR systems has emerged as a promising direction. Hybrid architectures that combine the strengths of both approaches while mitigating their individual weaknesses show considerable potential \cite{lin2021few}. These systems can leverage the robustness of traditional methods while benefiting from the semantic understanding capabilities of neural approaches.

text: Data sets and statistics about groups of individuals are increasingly collected and released, feeding many optimization and learning algorithms. However, the release of such data raises significant privacy concerns, as statistical information about groups can potentially reveal sensitive information about individual participants. The challenge lies in balancing the utility of data for legitimate research and business purposes while protecting individual privacy rights—a tension that has become increasingly prominent in the era of big data and machine learning \cite{nissim2007smooth}. Differential privacy, introduced by Dwork et al. \cite{dwork2006calibrating}, has emerged as the gold standard for quantifying and achieving privacy in statistical databases. The framework provides a rigorous mathematical definition of privacy that limits the ability of an adversary to infer whether any specific individual's data was included in a dataset, regardless of their auxiliary knowledge. This is formalized through the concept of indistinguishability: a randomized algorithm $\mathcal{M}$ satisfies $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy if for all neighboring datasets $D$ and $D'$ (differing by at most one individual) and all possible outputs $S$: \begin{equation} \Pr[\mathcal{M}(D) \in S] \leq e^{\epsilon} \Pr[\mathcal{M}(D') \in S] + \delta \end{equation} The parameters $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ control the privacy-utility tradeoff: smaller values provide stronger privacy guarantees but typically result in reduced utility of the output. In the context of machine learning, differential privacy has been successfully integrated into various training algorithms, most notably through the differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) algorithm \cite{abadi2016deep}. This approach adds carefully calibrated noise to gradient computations during training, ensuring that the final model parameters satisfy differential privacy with respect to the training dataset. The noise injection is typically performed using the Gaussian mechanism, where noise scaled to the sensitivity of the gradient computation is added at each training step. The application of differential privacy to deep learning presents unique challenges. Deep neural networks often require large amounts of data and numerous training iterations to achieve good performance, making them particularly sensitive to the noise injection required for privacy. Moreover, the high-dimensional parameter spaces of modern neural networks can amplify the effects of noise, leading to significant utility degradation when strong privacy guarantees are required \cite{papernot2021tempered}. Recent advances have focused on improving the privacy-utility tradeoff through various techniques. Privacy amplification by subsampling \cite{li2012sampling} demonstrates that randomly sampling training batches can significantly reduce the effective privacy cost of each gradient update. The moments accountant method \cite{abadi2016deep} provides tighter privacy analysis compared to basic composition theorems, enabling more accurate tracking of privacy budgets throughout training. Additionally, techniques such as private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) \cite{papernot2017semi} offer alternative approaches that can achieve strong privacy guarantees while maintaining competitive utility. The theoretical foundations of differential privacy extend beyond individual algorithms to encompass important properties such as composition and post-processing immunity. Composition theorems allow practitioners to reason about the cumulative privacy cost when multiple differentially private mechanisms are applied sequentially or in parallel. Advanced composition results \cite{dwork2010boosting} show that under certain conditions, the privacy cost grows more slowly than the basic composition bounds would suggest, enabling more sophisticated privacy-preserving workflows. Post-processing immunity, as discussed in the previous section, ensures that any data-independent transformation applied to differentially private outputs preserves the original privacy guarantees. This property has profound implications for practical deployments, as it allows for flexible model manipulation and deployment strategies without requiring additional privacy analysis. Despite these theoretical advances, significant gaps remain between theory and practice in differentially private machine learning. Real-world deployments must contend with issues such as hyperparameter tuning, model selection, and performance evaluation—all of which can potentially leak information about the training data if not handled carefully \cite{jagielski2020auditing}. Furthermore, the choice of privacy parameters $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ often lacks principled guidance, leading to arbitrary selections that may not reflect meaningful privacy guarantees in practice.

text: This work considers a perimeter defense problem in a conical environment in which a single mobile vehicle seeks to intercept mobile intruders before they enter a specified region (referred to as the defended perimeter). The intruders emerge from the boundary of the conical sector at random times and locations, following predetermined trajectories toward the defended perimeter. This problem is motivated by applications in border security, facility protection, and autonomous surveillance systems where the operational environment is naturally constrained to a sector-shaped region. The conical geometry presents unique challenges that distinguish this work from existing perimeter defense literature. Unlike circular or linear perimeter defense problems, the conical environment introduces asymmetric coverage requirements and varying geometric relationships between the defender's position and potential intrusion points. The defender must account for the fact that angular coverage becomes increasingly costly toward the sector boundaries, while the central region offers more efficient positioning for rapid response to multiple threat directions. We formulate this problem within the framework of differential game theory, treating the interaction between the defender and intruders as a zero-sum game where the defender seeks to minimize the probability of successful intrusion. The defender operates under kinematic constraints with maximum speed $v_d$ and has a finite capture radius $\rho$, meaning intruders must come within distance $\rho$ of the defender to be neutralized. Intruders appear according to a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ at the outer boundary and move with constant speed $v_i$ toward the defended perimeter. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Let $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ denote the conical sector defined by \begin{equation} \mathcal{C} = \{(r,\theta) : 0 \leq r \leq R, -\alpha \leq \theta \leq \alpha\} \end{equation} where $R$ is the outer radius, $2\alpha$ is the opening angle, and we use polar coordinates centered at the apex. The defended perimeter $\mathcal{P}$ is a concentric circular arc of radius $r_p < R$: \begin{equation} \mathcal{P} = \{(r_p,\theta) : -\alpha \leq \theta \leq \alpha\} \end{equation} The defender's position at time $t$ is denoted by $\mathbf{p}_d(t) = (r_d(t), \theta_d(t)) \in \mathcal{C}$, and its velocity is constrained by \begin{equation} \|\dot{\mathbf{p}}_d(t)\| \leq v_d \end{equation} Intruders appear at random locations on the outer boundary $\partial\mathcal{C}_{outer} = \{(R,\theta) : -\alpha \leq \theta \leq \alpha\}$ according to a spatial-temporal Poisson process. Each intruder $i$ appears at time $t_i$ and position $\mathbf{p}_i(t_i) = (R, \theta_i)$, then moves radially inward with constant speed $v_i$ along the trajectory \begin{equation} \mathbf{p}_i(t) = (R - v_i(t-t_i), \theta_i), \quad t \geq t_i \end{equation} The defender successfully intercepts intruder $i$ if there exists a time $t^* \geq t_i$ such that \begin{equation} \|\mathbf{p}_d(t^*) - \mathbf{p}_i(t^*)\| \leq \rho \end{equation} before the intruder reaches the defended perimeter, i.e., before $r_i(t) = r_p$. \subsection{Geometric Constraints and Coverage Analysis} The conical geometry imposes several important constraints on the defender's strategy. First, the angular coverage from any position $(r,\theta)$ is limited by the sector boundaries. The maximum angular span that can be effectively covered from position $(r,\theta)$ depends on both the capture radius $\rho$ and the radial distance from the apex. For a defender positioned at $(r_d, \theta_d)$, the angular coverage at the outer boundary can be approximated by \begin{equation} \Delta\theta_{coverage} \approx \frac{2\rho}{R-r_d} \end{equation} when $\rho \ll R-r_d$. This relationship highlights the trade-off between radial positioning and angular coverage: positions closer to the outer boundary provide greater angular coverage but reduce the time available for interception. The time available for interception of an intruder appearing at angle $\theta_i$ when the defender is at position $(r_d, \theta_d)$ is given by \begin{equation} T_{available} = \frac{R - r_p}{v_i} \end{equation} while the time required for the defender to reach an interception point depends on the geometric relationship between the defender's current position, the intruder's trajectory, and the optimal interception location. \subsection{Literature Review} Perimeter defense problems have been extensively studied in various geometric settings. \cite{isaacs1965differential} introduced the fundamental concepts of differential games applied to pursuit-evasion scenarios. More recently, \cite{garcia2020optimal} analyzed circular perimeter defense with multiple defenders, while \cite{shishika2018local} considered linear perimeter defense under sensing constraints. The conical geometry has received limited attention in the perimeter defense literature. \cite{zhou2019sector} studied surveillance coverage in sector-shaped regions but focused on static sensor placement rather than mobile defense. \cite{chen2021angular} examined pursuit games in wedge-shaped domains but did not address the perimeter defense objective. Our work extends these previous studies by incorporating the unique geometric properties of conical environments and analyzing the resulting optimal control problem. The key contributions include: (1) formulation of the conical perimeter defense problem as a differential game, (2) analysis of geometric constraints and coverage relationships, (3) derivation of optimal positioning strategies, and (4) performance evaluation under various system parameters. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the mathematical formulation of the optimal control problem and derives the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function. Section 3 analyzes the geometric properties of the conical environment and their impact on optimal strategies. Section 4 develops numerical solution methods and presents simulation results. Section 5 concludes with a discussion of the results and directions for future work.

text: Semi-VOS tracks an object of interest across all the frames in a video given the ground truth mask of the initial frame. The task requires the model to maintain consistent object identity while adapting to temporal variations in appearance, pose, and environmental conditions. Unlike fully supervised approaches that rely on dense annotations for every frame, Semi-VOS leverages the initial mask as the sole supervisory signal, making it particularly attractive for practical applications where manual annotation is prohibitively expensive. The fundamental challenge in Semi-VOS lies in establishing robust correspondences between the reference frame and subsequent frames while handling various forms of visual ambiguity. Traditional approaches typically employ template matching strategies, where features extracted from the initial frame serve as a reference for identifying the target object in later frames \cite{caelles2017one, maninis2018video}. However, these methods often struggle with appearance variations caused by illumination changes, partial occlusions, or non-rigid deformations. Recent developments have shifted towards more sophisticated propagation mechanisms that exploit temporal coherence in video sequences. Propagation-based methods \cite{oh2019video, yang2021associating} maintain a memory of historical frames and utilize feature matching to establish correspondences between the current frame and relevant memory frames. These approaches have demonstrated significant improvements in handling challenging scenarios, but they face scalability issues as the memory grows with sequence length. The emergence of deep learning has revolutionized Semi-VOS by enabling end-to-end learning of discriminative features and sophisticated matching strategies. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been extensively employed to extract hierarchical representations that capture both low-level visual details and high-level semantic information \cite{caelles2017one, voigtlaender2017online}. More recently, transformer architectures have gained prominence due to their ability to model long-range dependencies and perform flexible attention-based matching \cite{cheng2022xmem, duke2021sstvos}. Despite these advances, several critical challenges remain unresolved. First, the error accumulation problem persists in sequential propagation approaches, where segmentation errors in early frames propagate and amplify throughout the sequence. Second, computational efficiency remains a concern, particularly for real-time applications or processing high-resolution videos. Third, handling complex scenarios involving multiple similar objects, severe occlusions, or rapid motion changes continues to pose significant difficulties. Current evaluation protocols primarily focus on accuracy metrics such as region similarity ($\mathcal{J}$) and contour accuracy ($\mathcal{F}$) \cite{pont2017davis}, but these metrics may not fully capture the temporal consistency and practical usability of segmentation results. Furthermore, existing benchmarks \cite{pont2017davis, xu2018youtube} may not adequately represent the diversity of real-world scenarios, potentially leading to overfitting to specific dataset characteristics. In this work, we propose a novel approach that addresses these limitations through a multi-scale temporal modeling framework. Our method integrates bidirectional information flow with adaptive memory management to achieve robust object tracking while maintaining computational efficiency. The key contributions of our approach include: (1) a hierarchical feature propagation mechanism that operates at multiple temporal scales, (2) an adaptive memory selection strategy that dynamically identifies the most relevant historical frames, and (3) a consistency regularization scheme that enforces temporal coherence across the entire sequence.
