text: Query attribute value extraction is the joint task of detecting named entities in the search queries as the diverse surface form attribute values and normalizing them into a canonical form that can be used by downstream applications. This problem is particularly prevalent in e-commerce and information retrieval systems, where user queries exhibit significant linguistic diversity while referring to the same underlying semantic concepts \cite{zhang2019attribute, li2020query}. The complexity of this task stems from several inherent challenges. First, user queries are typically short and lack sufficient context, making it difficult to disambiguate attribute values that may have multiple interpretations. Second, the same attribute value can be expressed through numerous surface forms, including synonyms, abbreviations, and domain-specific jargon. For example, the color attribute "red" might appear as "crimson," "scarlet," "cherry," or even product-specific terms like "fire engine red." Third, queries often contain implicit attribute references that require domain knowledge to properly identify and extract. Traditional named entity recognition (NER) approaches \cite{lample2016neural, ma2016end} are insufficient for this task because they typically focus on predefined entity categories such as person, location, and organization, rather than the fine-grained attribute-value pairs required in domain-specific applications. Moreover, these methods do not address the normalization challenge, leaving extracted entities in their original surface forms without canonical mapping. Recent work in attribute value extraction has explored various approaches, including rule-based methods \cite{putthividhya2011human}, statistical models \cite{ghani2006text}, and neural architectures \cite{zheng2018learning, xu2019scaling}. Rule-based systems, while interpretable, suffer from limited coverage and require extensive manual effort to maintain. Statistical approaches often struggle with the sparse nature of attribute-value distributions in real-world queries. Neural methods have shown promise but frequently lack the domain-specific knowledge necessary for effective normalization. \subsection{Named Entity Recognition} The foundation of attribute value extraction lies in named entity recognition, which has evolved from rule-based systems to sophisticated neural architectures. Early approaches relied on handcrafted features and conditional random fields (CRFs) \cite{lafferty2001conditional}, while modern methods leverage deep learning techniques such as bidirectional LSTMs \cite{huang2015bidirectional} and transformer-based models \cite{devlin2018bert}. Recent advances in contextualized word representations have significantly improved NER performance across various domains \cite{akbik2018contextual, peters2018deep}. However, these general-purpose models often underperform in specialized domains where entity types and linguistic patterns differ substantially from standard benchmarks. This limitation is particularly pronounced in e-commerce applications, where product attributes exhibit unique characteristics and naming conventions. \subsection{Entity Normalization and Linking} Entity normalization, also known as entity linking or entity resolution, aims to map surface forms to canonical representations in knowledge bases \cite{shen2015entity, ganea2017deep}. Traditional approaches have focused on Wikipedia-based entities, leveraging rich contextual information and link structures to disambiguate mentions \cite{hoffart2011robust, francis2016capturing}. In domain-specific applications, normalization becomes more challenging due to the lack of comprehensive knowledge bases and the dynamic nature of attribute vocabularies. Recent work has explored embedding-based approaches \cite{yamada2016joint, le2018improving} that learn distributed representations of entities and their surface forms, enabling similarity-based matching for normalization tasks. \subsection{Query Understanding in E-commerce} E-commerce query understanding has received considerable attention due to its commercial importance and technical challenges \cite{paolacci2014running, carmel2018estimating}. Key tasks include query intent classification \cite{li2014semantic}, product categorization \cite{kozareva2015multilingual}, and attribute extraction \cite{putthividhya2011human, ghani2006text}. Existing attribute extraction systems often employ pipeline approaches that separate detection and normalization stages \cite{zheng2018learning}. While this modular design offers flexibility, it can propagate errors between stages and fails to leverage joint optimization opportunities. End-to-end approaches \cite{xu2019scaling} have shown promise but require careful design to balance detection accuracy with normalization quality. Our proposed framework addresses the attribute value extraction problem through a unified architecture that jointly optimizes detection and normalization objectives. The system consists of three main components: (1) a neural sequence tagger for attribute value detection, (2) a knowledge-enhanced normalization module, and (3) a joint training procedure that enables end-to-end optimization. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Given a user query $q = \{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n\}$ consisting of $n$ tokens, our goal is to identify attribute-value pairs $\{(a_i, v_i)\}_{i=1}^k$ where $a_i$ represents an attribute type (e.g., color, brand, size) and $v_i$ corresponds to the canonical form of the extracted value. Formally, we define the sequence labeling task as: \begin{equation} \hat{y} = \arg\max_{y} P(y|q; \theta) \end{equation} where $y = \{y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n\}$ represents the tag sequence, and $\theta$ denotes the model parameters. text: Manipulation aims to achieve a relative arrangement of objects, often with a desired set of contacts between them. Manipulation aims to achieve a relative arrangement of objects, often with a desired set of contacts between them. The success of manipulation tasks fundamentally depends on the robot's ability to establish, maintain, and transition between different contact configurations while adapting to environmental uncertainties and disturbances. Contact detection serves as a critical sensing modality that enables robots to understand their interaction with the environment and make informed decisions about task execution. In assembly operations, for instance, detecting the moment when a peg makes contact with a hole allows the robot to transition from position control to compliant insertion strategies \cite{whitney1987historical}. Similarly, in surface following tasks, maintaining consistent contact while avoiding excessive forces requires real-time feedback about contact state changes \cite{siciliano2009robotics}. The challenge of contact detection becomes particularly acute in dynamic manipulation scenarios where the robot must simultaneously handle moving objects, reject disturbances, and maintain precise control. Traditional static analysis methods that assume quasi-static conditions often fail when applied to these dynamic contexts, where inertial effects, vibrations, and rapid state transitions dominate the system behavior \cite{mason2001mechanics}. Current industrial practice predominantly relies on force/torque sensors mounted at the robot's wrist or end-effector to provide direct measurements of contact forces. While these sensors offer high accuracy and bandwidth, they introduce several practical limitations. The additional hardware increases system cost and complexity, creates potential failure points, and may require careful calibration and maintenance. Moreover, external sensors can be sensitive to environmental conditions such as temperature variations, electromagnetic interference, and mechanical shock \cite{dahiya2010tactile}. Alternative approaches based on proprioceptive sensing have gained significant attention due to their potential to eliminate external sensors while leveraging information already available within the robot's control system. Motor current measurements provide insights into the torques being generated at each joint, while encoder feedback reveals kinematic deviations from expected trajectories. These signals contain rich information about contact events, as external forces directly influence the robot's internal dynamics through the kinematic chain \cite{de2016collision}. The fundamental principle underlying proprioceptive contact detection relies on the fact that contact forces create observable changes in the robot's dynamic behavior. When a robot makes contact with the environment, the external forces alter the joint torques required to maintain the desired motion. These changes manifest as deviations in motor currents, unexpected kinematic trajectories, or discrepancies between commanded and actual joint positions \cite{haddadin2008collision}. However, extracting reliable contact information from proprioceptive signals presents significant technical challenges. The relationship between contact forces and internal measurements is mediated by the robot's complex dynamics, including nonlinear friction effects, gear backlash, and structural flexibility. Additionally, the signals are contaminated by various noise sources, including quantization errors, electromagnetic interference, and mechanical vibrations that can mask the subtle signatures of contact events. The problem is further complicated in dynamic manipulation scenarios where the robot operates under time-varying conditions. Payload changes affect the system's inertial properties, while varying operating speeds alter the relative importance of different dynamic effects. Environmental disturbances such as vibrations from nearby machinery can introduce spurious signals that mimic contact signatures, leading to false detections. Machine learning techniques offer a promising avenue for addressing these challenges by learning complex, nonlinear mappings between sensor measurements and contact states. Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of neural networks in recognizing contact patterns from proprioceptive data, achieving detection accuracies that surpass traditional threshold-based methods \cite{kim2021learning}. These approaches can automatically adapt to different operating conditions and learn to distinguish between genuine contact events and noise-induced artifacts. Despite their promise, purely data-driven approaches face limitations in terms of interpretability, generalization, and training requirements. Neural networks often require extensive datasets covering diverse operating conditions, and their black-box nature makes it difficult to understand failure modes or provide theoretical guarantees about performance. Furthermore, the learned models may not generalize well to scenarios significantly different from the training conditions. This work addresses these limitations by developing a hybrid approach that combines the interpretability and theoretical foundation of physics-based models with the adaptability and pattern recognition capabilities of machine learning techniques.

text: Let $T$ be a weighted tree. The tree metric induced by $T$, denoted $M_T$, is the complete graph on the vertices of $T$ where the weight of each edge $(u,v)$ is equal to the distance between $u$ and $v$ in $T$. A fundamental problem in metric embeddings and approximation algorithms is to construct sparse subgraphs that preserve distances in the original metric space. In the context of tree metrics, this leads to the study of tree spanners. A $t$-spanner of a metric space $(X,d)$ is a subgraph $H$ such that for all pairs of vertices $u,v \in X$, we have $d_H(u,v) \leq t \cdot d(u,v)$, where $d_H$ denotes the distance function in $H$ and $t \geq 1$ is called the stretch factor. The primary objectives in spanner construction are to minimize the stretch factor, the number of edges (size), and the total weight of edges (lightness) simultaneously. For general metrics, achieving sublinear stretch with near-linear size is often impossible due to lower bounds established by \cite{thorup2005approximate}. However, tree metrics possess special structural properties that enable the construction of efficient spanners. The hierarchical nature of trees allows for recursive decomposition schemes that can exploit the unique path property: for any two vertices in a tree, there exists exactly one simple path connecting them. \subsection{Previous Work} The study of tree spanners has a rich history in the approximation algorithms literature. Early work by \cite{peleg1989graph} established basic upper and lower bounds for spanners in various graph classes. For tree metrics specifically, several approaches have been developed: \textbf{Clustering-based methods:} These approaches partition the tree into clusters and add inter-cluster shortcuts. The work of \cite{abraham2008nearly} introduced techniques for hierarchical clustering that achieve polylogarithmic stretch with near-linear size. However, their lightness bounds were not optimal. \textbf{Shortcutting schemes:} More recent work has focused on systematic shortcutting procedures. The breakthrough result of Solomon and Elkin \cite{solomon2019light} achieved the first construction with simultaneously logarithmic stretch, logarithmic lightness, and near-linear size for weighted trees. \textbf{Lower bounds:} Several papers have established fundamental limitations on spanner parameters. \cite{elkin2017hopsets} showed that any spanner for tree metrics with stretch $s$ must have size $\Omega(n^{1+1/s})$ in the worst case, providing a trade-off between stretch and size. \subsection{Our Contributions} In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the Solomon-Elkin construction and provide several improvements and extensions: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Refined Analysis:} We provide a tighter analysis of the Solomon-Elkin spanner, improving the constants in the stretch and lightness bounds by a factor of $O(\log \log n)$. \item \textbf{Dynamic Extensions:} We extend the construction to handle dynamic updates (insertions and deletions of edges) while maintaining the same asymptotic guarantees. \item \textbf{Fault-Tolerant Variants:} We show how to modify the construction to obtain fault-tolerant spanners that can handle the failure of up to $k$ edges while preserving connectivity and stretch guarantees. \end{enumerate} The technical core of our improvements lies in a more careful analysis of the cluster hierarchy and the shortcut selection process. We introduce a novel charging argument that allows us to bound the total weight of shortcuts more precisely than previous analyses. \subsection{Technical Overview} The Solomon-Elkin construction proceeds in phases. In each phase $i$, the algorithm partitions the current forest into clusters of diameter roughly $2^i$, then adds shortcuts between cluster boundaries. The key technical challenge is to ensure that the total weight of shortcuts remains bounded while preserving distance approximation guarantees. Our main technical contribution is a refined potential function analysis that tracks the "contribution" of each edge to the final spanner more precisely. We define a potential $\Phi(e)$ for each edge $e$ in the original tree that measures its expected contribution to shortcut weights across all phases. By carefully analyzing how this potential evolves, we obtain improved bounds on both stretch and lightness. The analysis proceeds by induction on the phase number. For phase $i$, we show that the expected weight of shortcuts added is at most $O(1/i^2)$ times the total weight of the remaining tree edges. Summing over all $O(\log n)$ phases yields the logarithmic lightness bound. For the stretch analysis, we use a path decomposition argument similar to the original construction, but with a more refined accounting of how shortcuts are used in shortest paths. This leads to the improved stretch bound of $O(\log n / \log \log n)$.

text: A text index built on a string $T$ of length~$n$ is a data structure that can answer the following queries, for a given pattern~$P$ of length~$m$: \begin{description} \item[\textsc{Count}] Return the number of occurrences of $P$ in $T$. \item[\textsc{Locate}] Return the positions of all occurrences of $P$ in $T$. \item[\textsc{Extract}] Return a substring $T[i..j]$ for given positions $i$ and $j$. \end{description} The classical suffix array~\cite{manber1993suffix} and suffix tree~\cite{weiner1973linear} provide optimal $O(m + \text{occ})$ query time for pattern matching, where $\text{occ}$ denotes the number of occurrences. However, these structures require $O(n \log n)$ bits of space, which becomes prohibitive for large datasets. The FM-index~\cite{ferragina2000opportunistic} revolutionized this field by achieving compressed space while maintaining efficient query capabilities through the use of the Burrows-Wheeler transform (BWT)~\cite{burrows1994block}. The BWT rearranges the characters of the input text to create a permutation that exhibits better compressibility properties. Formally, given a text $T[1..n]$, the BWT is defined as follows: construct the suffix array $SA$ of $T$, then $\text{BWT}[i] = T[SA[i] - 1]$ for $SA[i] > 1$ and $\text{BWT}[i] = T[n]$ for $SA[i] = 1$. This transformation groups together characters that appear in similar contexts, often creating long runs of identical characters, particularly in repetitive texts. The key property that makes the BWT useful for indexing is the \emph{last-first mapping} (LF-mapping), which establishes a correspondence between positions in the BWT and the suffix array. For any position $i$ in the BWT, $\text{LF}(i) = C[c] + \text{rank}_c(\text{BWT}, i)$, where $c = \text{BWT}[i]$, $C[c]$ is the number of characters lexicographically smaller than $c$ in the entire text, and $\text{rank}_c(\text{BWT}, i)$ counts the number of occurrences of character $c$ in $\text{BWT}[1..i]$. The FM-index exploits this property to perform \emph{backward search}, which processes pattern characters from right to left. Starting with the full range $[1, n]$ representing all suffixes, each character narrows down the range to those suffixes that have the processed pattern as a prefix. Specifically, if the current range is $[l, r]$ and we process character $c$, the new range becomes $[C[c] + \text{rank}_c(\text{BWT}, l-1) + 1, C[c] + \text{rank}_c(\text{BWT}, r)]$. For highly repetitive datasets, such as collections of genomic sequences from the same species or versioned software repositories, the BWT exhibits extensive runs of identical characters. A \emph{run} is a maximal sequence of consecutive identical characters. The run-length encoded BWT (RLBWT) represents each run as a pair $(c, \ell)$, where $c$ is the character and $\ell$ is the run length. If the original BWT has $r$ runs, the RLBWT requires only $O(r)$ space instead of $O(n)$. The effectiveness of run-length encoding on repetitive texts stems from the fact that similar substrings in the original text tend to produce similar contexts in the BWT. When multiple copies of a substring exist, their corresponding BWT intervals often contain long runs of the same character. This phenomenon has been formalized through the concept of \emph{string attractors}~\cite{kempa2017string} and \emph{macro schemes}~\cite{belazzougui2015bidirectional}, which provide theoretical foundations for understanding why certain repetitive structures compress well. However, supporting efficient rank queries on the RLBWT presents significant challenges. In the uncompressed case, rank queries can be answered in $O(1)$ time using auxiliary structures of size $o(n)$ bits. For the RLBWT, naive approaches might require $O(r)$ time per query, which can be prohibitive when $r$ is large or when many queries are performed. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. \citet{gagie2012lightweight} introduced a structure that supports rank queries in $O(\log r)$ time using $O(r)$ additional space. \citet{belazzougui2015bidirectional} improved this to $O(\log \log r)$ expected time through the use of exponential search combined with binary search on run boundaries. More recent work by \citet{policriti2016lz77} has explored connections between run-length compression and other compression schemes like LZ77, leading to hybrid approaches. The practical performance of these structures depends heavily on the distribution of run lengths. When runs are highly variable in length, some queries may require examining many short runs, while others benefit from long runs that can be processed efficiently. Understanding this trade-off is crucial for designing indexes that perform well on real-world repetitive datasets. In this paper, we present novel theoretical and practical contributions to the problem of supporting efficient queries on run-length compressed BWTs. Our main contributions include: (1) a new rank data structure that achieves $O(\log \log r)$ worst-case query time using optimal space, (2) theoretical analysis of the relationship between run structure and query performance, and (3) experimental evaluation on diverse repetitive datasets demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods.

text: % \noindent {\bf Motivation and Problem:} Machine learning (ML) systems have found wide adoption in mission-critical applications. However, their deployment in real-world scenarios presents significant challenges related to reliability and trustworthiness. A fundamental issue arises when production data differs from training data, leading to potential performance degradation that often goes undetected until catastrophic failures occur. Traditional approaches to ML deployment assume that test and training distributions remain stationary, an assumption that rarely holds in practice due to concept drift, covariate shift, and evolving data patterns \cite{quinonero2009dataset,storkey2009training}. The absence of ground truth labels in production environments exacerbates this challenge, making it difficult to assess model performance continuously. Existing solutions primarily focus on detecting distribution shifts \cite{rabanser2019failing,liu2020learning} or quantifying prediction uncertainty \cite{abdar2021review,hullermeier2021aleatoric}, but fail to provide a holistic risk assessment framework that combines multiple risk factors into actionable insights. Furthermore, most current approaches lack interpretability, making it challenging for practitioners to understand the sources of risk and take appropriate mitigation actions. \noindent {\bf Contributions:} This paper addresses these limitations by introducing Risk Advisor, a comprehensive post-hoc risk assessment framework that provides interpretable and actionable risk evaluations for deployed ML models. Our key contributions are: \begin{itemize} \item A novel multi-dimensional risk decomposition framework that separates overall model risk into three interpretable components: data drift risk, model uncertainty risk, and prediction confidence risk. \item A unified methodology that combines statistical tests, uncertainty quantification, and calibration metrics to provide comprehensive risk assessments without requiring ground truth labels. \item An interpretable risk scoring system that enables practitioners to identify specific risk sources and prioritize mitigation strategies based on risk component analysis. \item Extensive experimental validation on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrating superior performance compared to existing approaches, with practical case studies showing the framework's effectiveness in real-world deployment scenarios. \end{itemize} \subsection{Distribution Shift Detection} Distribution shift detection has been extensively studied in the machine learning literature, with approaches broadly categorized into statistical tests, learned representations, and adversarial methods. Classical statistical approaches include the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test \cite{massey1951kolmogorov} and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) \cite{gretton2012kernel}, which compare empirical distributions using kernel-based metrics. These methods provide theoretical guarantees but may struggle with high-dimensional data and complex distribution shifts. More recent approaches leverage deep learning techniques to detect shifts in learned feature representations. \citet{liu2020learning} proposed learning-based methods that train classifiers to distinguish between training and test distributions. \citet{rabanser2019failing} introduced adversarial approaches that use domain adaptation techniques to identify distributional differences. While these methods show improved performance on complex datasets, they often lack interpretability and require additional model training. \subsection{Uncertainty Quantification} Uncertainty quantification in ML has gained significant attention, particularly for deep learning models. Bayesian approaches \cite{mackay1992practical,neal2012bayesian} provide principled uncertainty estimates but are computationally expensive for large models. Practical alternatives include Monte Carlo dropout \cite{gal2016dropout}, which approximates Bayesian inference by treating dropout as a Bayesian approximation, and ensemble methods \cite{lakshminarayanan2017simple} that aggregate predictions from multiple models. Deep ensemble approaches \cite{ovadia2019can} have shown promising results in capturing both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. However, these methods require training multiple models, increasing computational overhead. Recent work on single-model uncertainty estimation \cite{malinin2018predictive,sensoy2018evidential} attempts to address this limitation but often sacrifices uncertainty quality for computational efficiency. \subsection{Model Calibration and Confidence} Model calibration ensures that prediction confidence scores accurately reflect the likelihood of correctness. Temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} and Platt scaling \cite{platt1999probabilistic} are popular post-hoc calibration methods that adjust model outputs to improve calibration. However, these approaches require validation data with ground truth labels, limiting their applicability in production scenarios. Confidence estimation without ground truth has been explored through various approaches, including prediction entropy \cite{wang2019aleatoric}, mutual information \cite{smith2018understanding}, and learned confidence functions \cite{devries2018learning}. While these methods provide useful confidence estimates, they typically focus on individual predictions rather than system-level risk assessment. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Let $\mathcal{D}_{train} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ denote the training dataset where $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ represents input features and $y_i \in \mathcal{Y}$ represents labels. Consider a trained model $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ deployed in production with access to unlabeled deployment data $\mathcal{D}_{deploy} = \{x_j\}_{j=1}^{m}$. Our objective is to assess the risk of model $f$ on $\mathcal{D}_{deploy}$ without access to ground truth labels $\{y_j\}_{j=1}^{m}$. We define the overall risk $R_{total}$ as a composite measure that captures different aspects of model reliability: \begin{equation} R_{total} = \alpha R_{drift} + \beta R_{uncertainty} + \gamma R_{confidence} \end{equation} where $R_{drift}$, $R_{uncertainty}$, and $R_{confidence}$ represent data drift risk, model uncertainty risk, and prediction confidence risk, respectively. The weights $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are hyperparameters that can be tuned based on application requirements, with $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$. \subsection{Data Drift Risk Assessment} Data drift risk quantifies the extent to which deployment data differs from training data distributions. We employ a multi-metric approach that combines complementary statistical tests to capture different aspects of distributional shift. \subsubsection{Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)} MMD provides a non-parametric test for comparing distributions by measuring the distance between their embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). For datasets $\mathcal{D}_{train}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{deploy}$, the empirical MMD is computed as: \begin{equation} \text{MMD}^2(\mathcal{D}_{train}, \mathcal{D}_{deploy}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,i'} k(x_i, x_{i'}) + \frac{1}{m^2}\sum_{j,j'} k(x_j, x_{j'}) - \frac{2}{nm}\sum_{i,j} k(x_i, x_j) \end{equation} where $k(\cdot, \cdot)$ is a kernel function, typically a Gaussian RBF kernel. The MMD statistic follows a known distribution under the null hypothesis, enabling statistical significance testing. \subsubsection{Feature-wise Drift Detection} To provide interpretable insights into which features contribute most to distributional shift, we perform feature-wise drift detection using Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistics: \begin{equation} D_{KS}^{(f)} = \sup_x |F_{train}^{(f)}(x) - F_{deploy}^{(f)}(x)| \end{equation} where $F_{train}^{(f)}$ and $F_{deploy}^{(f)}$ are the empirical cumulative distribution functions for feature $f$ in training and deployment data, respectively. The overall data drift risk is computed as: \begin{equation} R_{drift} = w_{mmd} \cdot \text{MMD}_{norm} + w_{ks} \cdot \frac{1}{d}\sum_{f=1}^{d} D_{KS}^{(f)} \end{equation} where $\text{MMD}_{norm}$ is the normalized MMD statistic, $d$ is the number of features, and $w_{mmd}$, $w_{ks}$ are weighting factors. \subsection{Model Uncertainty Risk Assessment} Model uncertainty risk captures the model's epistemic uncertainty about its predictions on deployment data. We employ ensemble-based uncertainty estimation combined with Monte Carlo dropout to provide robust uncertainty quantification. \subsubsection{Ensemble-based Uncertainty} For an ensemble of $K$ models $\{f_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$, the predictive uncertainty for input $x$ is estimated using prediction variance: \begin{equation} \sigma_{ensemble}^2(x) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} (f_k(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2 \end{equation} where $\bar{f}(x) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x)$ is the ensemble mean prediction. \subsubsection{Monte Carlo Dropout} For single models with dropout layers, we approximate Bayesian inference by performing multiple forward passes with dropout enabled during inference: \begin{equation} \sigma_{dropout}^2(x) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (f_t(x) - \bar{f}_{dropout}(x))^2 \end{equation} where $f_t(x)$ represents the $t$-th forward pass with dropout and $T$ is the number of Monte Carlo samples. The model uncertainty risk is computed as: \begin{equation} R_{uncertainty} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m} \max(\sigma_{ensemble}^2(x_j), \sigma_{dropout}^2(x_j)) \end{equation}

text: The quantum community has made significant advances in developing algorithms that hold the promise of speedup over their classical counterparts. However, many of these algorithms rely on fundamental quantum operations that must be efficiently implemented to realize practical quantum advantage. Among these operations, the quantum SWAP test stands out as a crucial primitive for comparing quantum states, with applications ranging from quantum machine learning~\cite{schuld2015introduction} to quantum algorithms for linear systems~\cite{harrow2009quantum}. The standard quantum SWAP test, introduced by Buhrman et al.~\cite{buhrman2001quantum}, provides an elegant method for estimating the overlap between two quantum states $|\psi\rangle$ and $|\phi\rangle$ using a single ancillary qubit and one controlled-SWAP (CSWAP) gate. The test yields the probability $P_0 = \frac{1}{2}(1 + |\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2)$ of measuring the ancilla in the $|0\rangle$ state, directly encoding information about the inner product between the states. Despite its theoretical elegance, extending the quantum SWAP test to multiple states presents significant challenges. The naive approach of performing pairwise comparisons between $m$ states requires $\binom{m}{2} = O(m^2)$ individual SWAP tests, making it prohibitively expensive for large state collections. Alternative direct extensions that attempt to compare all states simultaneously typically require $O(m)$ ancillary qubits, creating substantial overhead in terms of quantum resources. Recent work has explored various generalizations of the SWAP test. Garcia-Escartin and Chamorro-Posada~\cite{garcia2013swap} proposed extensions for multiple qubits, while Lloyd et al.~\cite{lloyd2014quantum} investigated applications in quantum principal component analysis. However, these approaches either maintain the quadratic scaling in the number of comparisons or require extensive ancillary resources. The resource requirements for quantum algorithms become particularly critical in the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era~\cite{preskill2018quantum}, where the number of available qubits is severely limited and gate fidelities impose constraints on circuit depth. Developing resource-efficient implementations of fundamental operations like multi-state SWAP tests is therefore essential for near-term quantum applications. \subsection{Our Contributions} In this work, we present a novel recursive algorithm that generalizes the quantum SWAP test to an arbitrary number $m$ of quantum states while achieving significant improvements in resource efficiency. Our main contributions are: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Resource-efficient algorithm}: We develop a recursive construction that requires only $O(\log m)$ ancillary qubits compared to the $O(m)$ qubits needed by naive implementations, representing an exponential improvement in ancillary qubit requirements. \item \textbf{Optimal gate complexity}: Our algorithm uses exactly $m-1$ CSWAP gates, which is optimal since any algorithm must perform at least $m-1$ comparisons to extract information about $m$ states. \item \textbf{Binary tree structure}: The algorithm employs a hierarchical binary tree architecture where each internal node represents a CSWAP operation between quantum registers, enabling efficient parallel implementation on quantum hardware with appropriate connectivity. \item \textbf{Statistical guarantees}: We prove that the success probability of our algorithm scales as $\prod_{i=1}^{m-1} |\langle\psi_i|\psi_{i+1}\rangle|^2$, providing a direct measure of the collective overlap between consecutive states in the input sequence. \item \textbf{Practical implementation}: We provide explicit quantum circuits for small values of $m$ and analyze the trade-offs between circuit depth and parallelization opportunities. \end{enumerate} \subsection{Technical Overview} Our approach builds upon the observation that the standard SWAP test can be viewed as a special case of a more general recursive structure. Instead of comparing all states simultaneously, we organize them in a binary tree where each leaf corresponds to one of the input states $|\psi_1\rangle, |\psi_2\rangle, \ldots, |\psi_m\rangle$. The algorithm proceeds by recursively applying CSWAP operations at each internal node of the tree. At level $\ell$ of the tree, we have $\lceil m/2^\ell \rceil$ nodes, each managing quantum registers that contain superpositions of the original input states. The key insight is that by carefully managing the quantum registers and ancillary qubits, we can extract global information about all $m$ states using only $\lceil \log_2 m \rceil$ ancillary qubits. The measurement outcome at the root of the tree provides statistical information about the collective behavior of all input states. Specifically, if we denote the input states as $|\psi_1\rangle, |\psi_2\rangle, \ldots, |\psi_m\rangle$, the probability of measuring all ancillary qubits in the $|0\rangle$ state is given by: \begin{equation} P_{\text{success}} = \frac{1}{2^{\lceil \log_2 m \rceil}} \left(1 + \text{Re}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{m-1} \langle\psi_i|\psi_{i+1}\rangle\right]\right) \end{equation} This expression reveals that our algorithm naturally captures the coherent interference between all input states, providing information that goes beyond simple pairwise comparisons. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} reviews the standard quantum SWAP test and establishes notation. Section~\ref{sec:algorithm} presents our recursive algorithm with detailed circuit constructions. Section~\ref{sec:analysis} provides theoretical analysis of the success probability and resource requirements. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} discusses practical implementation considerations and circuit optimizations. Section~\ref{sec:applications} explores potential applications in quantum machine learning and state discrimination. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our results and discusses future directions.

text: With the rapid development of radiological imaging techniques, ophthalmic images are produced in ever-increasing quantities. There are three common ophthalmic image modalities: (1) \textbf{Slit Lamp.} Slit lamp biomicroscopy provides detailed visualization of the anterior segment of the eye, including the cornea, iris, lens, and anterior vitreous. This imaging modality is essential for diagnosing conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, and corneal disorders through high-magnification examination of ocular structures. (2) \textbf{Fundus Photography.} Fundus cameras capture comprehensive images of the posterior segment, including the retina, optic disc, and blood vessels. These images are crucial for detecting and monitoring diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and other retinal pathologies that can lead to vision loss if left untreated. (3) \textbf{Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT).} OCT provides cross-sectional imaging of retinal layers with micrometer-level resolution, enabling precise assessment of macular thickness, retinal layer integrity, and the presence of fluid accumulation or structural abnormalities. The exponential growth in ophthalmic imaging data presents both opportunities and challenges for clinical practice. While the availability of large-scale image databases facilitates comprehensive analysis and comparison studies, it also creates significant computational burdens for storage, transmission, and retrieval operations. Traditional content-based image retrieval (CBIR) systems often struggle with the computational complexity and storage requirements associated with high-dimensional feature representations of medical images \cite{zhang2018medical, liu2019deep}. In this context, deep hashing emerges as a promising solution for efficient large-scale ophthalmic image retrieval. By learning compact binary representations that preserve semantic similarity, hashing methods can dramatically reduce storage requirements while maintaining fast query processing capabilities \cite{wang2018survey, cao2017deep}. However, the application of deep hashing to ophthalmic images presents unique challenges that distinguish it from general-purpose image retrieval tasks. First, ophthalmic images often contain subtle pathological changes that may be localized to specific anatomical regions. For instance, early-stage diabetic retinopathy may manifest as microaneurysms or small hemorrhages that occupy only a fraction of the total image area. Similarly, glaucomatous changes in the optic disc require precise assessment of the cup-to-disc ratio and neuroretinal rim characteristics. Conventional deep hashing methods that rely on global feature representations may fail to capture these fine-grained pathological details, leading to suboptimal retrieval performance for clinically relevant cases. Second, the multi-modal nature of ophthalmic imaging requires robust feature learning approaches that can adapt to different imaging characteristics and pathological presentations. Each imaging modality provides complementary diagnostic information, and the optimal feature representation should account for these modality-specific characteristics while maintaining cross-modal consistency for comprehensive clinical assessment. Third, the class imbalance inherent in medical imaging datasets poses additional challenges for hash code learning. Normal cases typically outnumber pathological cases, and within pathological categories, rare conditions may have limited representation. This imbalance can bias the learned hash functions toward common cases, potentially compromising the retrieval accuracy for rare but clinically important conditions \cite{cheplygina2019not}. To address these challenges, we propose an attention-guided deep hashing framework specifically designed for ophthalmic image retrieval. Our approach builds upon the foundation of spatial attention mechanisms to identify and emphasize diagnostically relevant regions while generating compact binary codes. The key contributions of this work include: \textbf{Attention-Guided Feature Learning:} We introduce a multi-scale spatial attention mechanism that adaptively focuses on pathologically relevant regions in ophthalmic images. Unlike conventional attention models that operate on fixed spatial resolutions, our approach integrates attention computation across multiple scales to capture both fine-grained pathological details and broader anatomical context. The attention weights are learned end-to-end through backpropagation, enabling the model to automatically discover discriminative regions without requiring manual annotation of pathological areas. \textbf{Multi-Modal Consistency Regularization:} To handle the diverse characteristics of different ophthalmic imaging modalities, we incorporate a consistency regularization term that encourages similar attention patterns for semantically related images across different modalities. This regularization helps the model learn modality-invariant representations while maintaining sensitivity to pathological changes that may manifest differently across imaging techniques. \textbf{Balanced Hash Code Generation:} We address the class imbalance problem through a novel balanced sampling strategy during hash code learning. Our approach ensures that rare pathological conditions receive adequate representation in the learned hash space, preventing the dominance of common cases and improving retrieval performance for clinically important but underrepresented conditions. \textbf{Comprehensive Evaluation Framework:} We conduct extensive experiments on three large-scale ophthalmic imaging datasets, including fundus photographs for diabetic retinopathy detection, OCT images for macular degeneration assessment, and slit lamp images for anterior segment evaluation. Our evaluation methodology incorporates both standard retrieval metrics and clinically relevant assessment criteria to provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method's effectiveness. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in deep hashing and medical image retrieval. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents the detailed methodology of our attention-guided deep hashing framework. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes the experimental setup and presents comprehensive results on multiple ophthalmic imaging datasets. Section~\ref{sec:analysis} provides detailed analysis of the attention mechanisms and their impact on retrieval performance. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and discusses future research directions. \subsection{Deep Hashing Methods} Deep hashing has emerged as an effective approach for large-scale image retrieval by learning compact binary representations that preserve semantic similarity \cite{erin2015deep, lai2015simultaneous}. Early deep hashing methods focused on supervised learning scenarios where labeled training data is available to guide the hash function learning process \cite{xia2014supervised, liu2016deep}.

In this context, deep learning methods can offer a promising solution to the large-scale ophthalmic image search. Third, the inherent imbalance of the medical images further hinders the learning of hash functions: normal cases usually outnumber pathological ones, rare pathologies may be underrepresented in the pathological class. Each modality provides complementary diagnostic information, and an ideal representation must be capable of capturing these particular features while preserving consistency between the modalities to ensure a comprehensive clinical assessment. Deep learning methods that rely on a single global representation of features may miss these fine-grained pathological features, resulting in lower recall in clinically relevant cases. We present a multi-scale spatial attention mechanism which adapts to the pathologically relevant regions of the image. This mechanism can bias the learned hash functions towards common cases, which may influence the accuracy of the search for rare, but clinically important conditions. We address the issue of class imbalance by a novel balanced sampling strategy during hash learning. Multi-Modal Consistency Regularization: To deal with the different characteristics of the different ophthalmological image modalities, we introduce a consistency regularization which encourages attention to the same areas of the image in different modalities. Attention weights are learned end-to-end by backpropagation, which enables the model to discover discriminative regions without any manual annotation of pathological regions. Section 2 reviews related work in deep hashing and medical image retrieval. Section 3 conducts extensive experiments on three large-scale ophthalmic image data sets: diabetic retinopathy screening photographs, OCT images for macular degeneration screening, and slit-lamp images for anterior-segment screening, where we employ both standard and clinically relevant metrics to test the effectiveness of the proposed method. The resulting hash space ensures that rare conditions have a proper number of samples, which prevents the common ones from dominating the space and improves the retrieval performance of clinically important but under-represented conditions. text: Robots are increasingly navigating around populous areas and moving along with people. This is true for service robots found in airports, hotels, restaurants, delivery robots on sidewalks, mobile robots in warehouses, and autonomous vehicles on city streets. For these robots to operate safely and effectively in human-populated environments, their motion must be not only collision-free but also interpretable to human observers \cite{sisbot2007human, kruse2013human}. When humans can predict a robot's intended destination, they can better coordinate their own movements, leading to more efficient and comfortable shared spaces \cite{rios2015understanding, truong2016toward}. The concept of \textit{legible motion} has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge. Legible motion refers to robot trajectories that clearly communicate the robot's intended goal through the characteristics of the motion itself, rather than through explicit communication channels \cite{dragan2013legibility}. This approach draws inspiration from human motion, where observers can often infer a person's destination by observing their movement patterns, even without verbal communication \cite{flash1985coordination, giese2003neural}. Traditional legibility frameworks have demonstrated success in scenarios with discrete goal sets, where robots must choose between a small number of predetermined destinations \cite{dragan2015effects, lichtenthaler2012legible}. These methods typically optimize trajectories to maximize the probability that an observer will correctly identify the intended goal from among the available alternatives. The mathematical foundation relies on comparing the likelihood of the observed trajectory under different goal hypotheses, often using inverse optimal control or maximum entropy principles \cite{ziebart2008maximum, ramachandran2007bayesian}. However, this discrete goal assumption severely limits the applicability of existing legibility methods to real-world scenarios. In continuous environments, robots frequently need to navigate to locations that are not predefined but emerge dynamically based on task requirements \cite{chen2017socially}. Consider a mobile robot in a library that must retrieve books from arbitrary shelf locations, or an autonomous wheelchair navigating to any point along a hospital corridor. In such scenarios, the traditional approach of enumerating all possible goals becomes computationally intractable and conceptually inappropriate. The transition from discrete to continuous goal spaces introduces fundamental challenges for legibility computation. First, the probability distributions over goals become continuous, requiring integration over infinite spaces rather than summation over finite sets \cite{vasquez2014inverse}. Second, the notion of "alternative goals" becomes ambiguous when every point in the continuous space could potentially be a destination. Third, the computational complexity of trajectory optimization increases dramatically when considering the infinite set of possible goal locations. Recent work has begun to explore extensions of legibility concepts to more complex scenarios. Some researchers have investigated legibility in the context of social navigation, where robots must consider not only their own goals but also the intentions and comfort of nearby humans \cite{kretzschmar2016socially, mavrogiannis2018social}. Others have examined legibility in multi-robot systems, where individual robots must communicate their intentions to both humans and other robots \cite{huang2019robot}. However, these approaches still primarily rely on discrete goal representations. This paper makes several key contributions to address the gap between discrete legibility frameworks and continuous navigation scenarios. First, we introduce a novel mathematical formulation for legibility in continuous goal spaces that extends traditional probability-based metrics to handle infinite destination sets. Our approach leverages concepts from information theory and optimal transport to define meaningful legibility measures over continuous domains \cite{villani2003topics, cover2012elements}. Second, we develop computationally efficient algorithms for optimizing legible trajectories in continuous environments. Our method combines sampling-based trajectory planning with kernel density estimation to approximate the continuous legibility metrics in a tractable manner \cite{lavalle2006planning, scott2015multivariate}. This allows real-time trajectory generation for mobile robots operating in dynamic environments. Third, we present comprehensive experimental validation of our approach through both simulation studies and human subject experiments. Our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of continuous legibility optimization across various environmental configurations and robot types. The human subject studies provide empirical evidence that trajectories optimized using our continuous legibility framework are indeed more interpretable to human observers compared to traditional path planning approaches. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in legible motion planning, human-robot interaction, and continuous trajectory optimization. Section~\ref{sec:problem} formally defines the problem of legibility in continuous goal spaces and establishes the mathematical foundations for our approach. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our novel continuous legibility framework, including the theoretical formulation and computational algorithms. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental methodology and presents results from both simulation and human subject studies. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} discusses the implications of our findings and outlines directions for future research.

text: Multi-agent motion planning has a wide range of real-world applications, but it is notoriously difficult. The complexity arises from the exponential growth of the joint configuration space with the number of agents, making optimal solutions computationally intractable for large-scale systems \cite{lavalle2006planning, van2008reciprocal}. Traditional approaches often suffer from scalability issues or provide limited safety guarantees, particularly in dynamic environments where obstacles and agent goals may change during execution. Recent advances in multi-agent systems have focused on decentralized approaches that balance computational efficiency with coordination quality \cite{alonso2013multi, zhou2017fast}. However, existing methods typically make strong assumptions about communication reliability, perfect state information, or static environments that may not hold in practice. Furthermore, many approaches lack formal safety guarantees, relying instead on heuristic collision avoidance strategies that may fail in congested scenarios or under system uncertainties. The challenge is further compounded by the need to handle heterogeneous agents with different dynamics, sensing capabilities, and objectives. Real-world applications such as autonomous vehicle coordination \cite{rios2016survey}, warehouse robotics \cite{wurman2008coordinating}, and aerial swarm navigation \cite{chung2018survey} require robust solutions that can adapt to changing conditions while maintaining safety and efficiency. \subsection{Related Work} Multi-agent motion planning approaches can be broadly categorized into centralized, decentralized, and hybrid methods. Centralized approaches \cite{sharon2015conflict, wagner2015subdimensional} provide optimal or near-optimal solutions by reasoning about the joint state space of all agents. While these methods guarantee completeness and optimality, they suffer from exponential computational complexity, limiting their applicability to small-scale systems. Decentralized approaches \cite{van2008reciprocal, snape2011hybrid} distribute the planning burden among individual agents, achieving better scalability at the cost of solution quality. Velocity obstacle methods \cite{fiorini1998motion} and their extensions \cite{berg2008reciprocal} enable agents to avoid collisions by selecting velocities outside predicted collision cones. However, these methods may lead to oscillatory behavior or deadlock situations in dense environments. Recent hybrid approaches \cite{cap2015prioritized, li2019lifelong} attempt to combine the benefits of both paradigms. Priority-based planners \cite{erdmann1987multiple} assign fixed priorities to agents and plan sequentially, while reservation-based methods \cite{dresner2008multiagent} coordinate agent movements through spatial-temporal reservations. These approaches offer reasonable computational complexity but may produce suboptimal solutions due to their greedy nature. Model predictive control has emerged as a promising framework for multi-agent coordination \cite{richards2002robust, dunbar2006distributed}. MPC-based approaches can naturally handle dynamic constraints and uncertainties while providing closed-loop stability guarantees. However, incorporating collision avoidance constraints in the MPC formulation often leads to non-convex optimization problems that are computationally challenging to solve in real-time. Control barrier functions have recently gained attention for safety-critical control applications \cite{ames2019control, cortez2018control}. CBFs provide a systematic framework for encoding safety constraints and can guarantee forward invariance of safe sets. Several works have explored the integration of CBFs with multi-agent systems \cite{wang2017safety, glotfelter2017nonsmooth}, but most focus on simple kinematic models or small-scale scenarios. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Consider a system of $n$ agents operating in a bounded workspace $\mathcal{W} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, where each agent $i$ has state $x_i(t) \in \mathcal{X}_i$ and control input $u_i(t) \in \mathcal{U}_i$. text: Recovering the most significant directions or \emph{principal components} of a matrix from noisy observations is a fundamental problem in both mathematical statistics and applications \cite{Rao-1964-PCA,Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA,Ringner-2008-PCA,AW-2010-PCA}. The classical Principal Component Analysis (PCA) framework assumes that data matrices are fully observed and noise-free, but in many modern applications, observations are corrupted by noise, missing entries, or adversarial perturbations. This has motivated extensive research into robust variants of PCA that can handle such challenging scenarios while maintaining statistical and computational efficiency. One particularly important setting is \emph{sparse PCA}, where the principal components are assumed to have only a small number of non-zero entries \cite{Zou-2006-SparsePCA,dAspremont-2007-SparsePCA,Johnstone-2009-SparsePCA}. This sparsity constraint is motivated by interpretability considerations in high-dimensional data analysis, where identifying a small subset of relevant features is often more valuable than obtaining dense loadings that involve all variables. The sparse PCA problem can be formulated as: \begin{align} \max_{\mathbf{v}} \quad &\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{v} \\ \text{subject to} \quad &\|\mathbf{v}\|_2 = 1, \quad \|\mathbf{v}\|_0 \leq k \end{align} where $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ is the sample covariance matrix and $k$ is the desired sparsity level. Unfortunately, this combinatorial optimization problem is NP-hard in general \cite{Moghaddam-2006-SparsePCA}, leading researchers to develop various approximation schemes and relaxations. Semidefinite programming has emerged as one of the most principled approaches to tackle such non-convex optimization problems with discrete or combinatorial constraints. \subsection{Semidefinite Programming Relaxations} The connection between quadratic optimization over discrete sets and semidefinite programming has been extensively studied in the optimization literature \cite{Goemans-1995-MaxCut,Lasserre-2001-SDP}. The key insight is that many combinatorial optimization problems can be reformulated as rank-constrained semidefinite programs, and relaxing the rank constraint often yields tractable convex approximations. For the Boolean quadratic optimization problem introduced earlier, the SDP relaxation exploits the fact that any rank-one positive semidefinite matrix $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}$ with $x_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ satisfies $X_{ii} = x_i^2 = 1$. By lifting the problem to the space of $n \times n$ matrices and dropping the rank constraint, we obtain a convex relaxation that can be solved efficiently using interior-point methods. The quality of this relaxation depends crucially on the spectral properties of the matrix $\mathbf{W}$. When $\mathbf{W}$ has a dominant eigenvalue that is well-separated from the rest of the spectrum, the SDP relaxation often produces rank-one solutions, making it tight \cite{Montanari-2015-SDP,Bandeira-2016-SDP}. However, when the spectrum is more uniform or when the matrix has certain random structures, the relaxation may be loose, requiring more sophisticated techniques. \subsection{Random Matrix Theory and Phase Transitions} A particularly rich line of research has emerged at the intersection of semidefinite programming and random matrix theory. Consider the case where $\mathbf{W}$ is a random matrix, such as a Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) matrix or a spiked covariance model. In such settings, the performance of SDP relaxations exhibits sharp phase transitions as a function of problem parameters. For instance, in the spiked Wigner model, we have: \begin{equation} \mathbf{W} = \lambda \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top} + \mathbf{G} \end{equation} where $\mathbf{u} \in \{-1,+1\}^n$ is the planted signal, $\lambda > 0$ is the signal strength, and $\mathbf{G}$ is a GOE matrix with entries $G_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/n)$ for $i \neq j$ and $G_{ii} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2/n)$. The fundamental question is: for what values of $\lambda$ can the SDP relaxation successfully recover the planted vector $\mathbf{u}$? This question has deep connections to the theory of spin glasses and statistical physics \cite{Talagrand-2003-SpinGlasses,Guerra-2003-SpinGlasses}. \subsection{Information-Theoretic Limits} From an information-theoretic perspective, there exists a critical threshold $\lambda_{\text{info}}$ below which no polynomial-time algorithm can distinguish between the spiked model and pure noise. This threshold is determined by analyzing the likelihood ratio between the two hypotheses and has been characterized using techniques from statistical physics and concentration of measure \cite{Coja-Oghlan-2010-InfoTheory,Krzakala-2012-InfoTheory}. For the Boolean quadratic optimization problem, the information-theoretic threshold is: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\text{info}} = 1 \end{equation} However, the computational threshold for polynomial-time algorithms is typically higher. The SDP relaxation succeeds when $\lambda > \lambda_{\text{SDP}}$, where: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\text{SDP}} = \sqrt{2 \log 2} \approx 1.177 \end{equation} This gap between information-theoretic and computational thresholds is a manifestation of the fundamental tension between statistical and computational complexity in high-dimensional inference problems. \subsection{Spectral Methods and Their Limitations} Classical spectral methods, such as computing the leading eigenvector of $\mathbf{W}$, provide another natural approach to the Boolean quadratic optimization problem. The spectral threshold is given by: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\text{spectral}} = 2 \end{equation} Above this threshold, the leading eigenvector of $\mathbf{W}$ is correlated with the planted vector $\mathbf{u}$, and simple thresholding can recover the Boolean solution. However, this threshold is significantly higher than both the information-theoretic and SDP thresholds, highlighting the superiority of semidefinite programming approaches in the intermediate regime. The analysis of spectral methods relies heavily on perturbation theory for random matrices. text: Approximating the distribution of a target value $y$ conditioned on an input $x$ is at the core of supervised learning tasks. Most traditional approaches assume that this conditional distribution $p(y|x)$ is unimodal, typically modeling it as a single Gaussian or using point estimates through maximum likelihood or least squares objectives. However, many real-world problems exhibit inherently multimodal target distributions, where multiple plausible outputs exist for a given input. Consider, for example, predicting molecular conformations where a single chemical structure can adopt multiple stable 3D configurations, or forecasting traffic patterns where similar road network conditions can lead to vastly different flow outcomes depending on external factors not captured in the input. Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) \cite{bishop1994mixture} address this limitation by modeling the conditional distribution as a weighted sum of parametric components, typically Gaussians: \begin{equation} p(y|x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k(x) \mathcal{N}(y; \mu_k(x), \sigma_k^2(x)) \end{equation} where $\pi_k(x)$, $\mu_k(x)$, and $\sigma_k(x)$ are the mixing coefficients, means, and standard deviations predicted by neural networks conditioned on input $x$. This framework has proven effective for capturing multimodal distributions in various domains \cite{zen2014statistical, ha2017sketch}. However, existing MDN formulations are primarily designed for vector inputs and fail to leverage the rich structural information present in graph-structured data. Graphs are ubiquitous in many domains, from social networks and biological systems to molecular structures and transportation networks. The challenge lies in extending probabilistic mixture modeling to handle the irregular, non-Euclidean structure of graphs while preserving the ability to capture multimodal output distributions. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) \cite{scarselli2008graph, kipf2016semi, hamilton2017inductive} have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations from graph-structured data. By iteratively aggregating information from local neighborhoods, GNNs can capture both node-level features and global graph topology. Popular variants include Graph Convolutional Networks \cite{kipf2016semi}, GraphSAGE \cite{hamilton2017inductive}, and Graph Attention Networks \cite{veličković2017graph}, each offering different mechanisms for information propagation and aggregation. The key insight of our work is to combine the representational power of GNNs with the probabilistic modeling capabilities of MDNs. This fusion enables us to capture complex, multimodal distributions over outputs while leveraging the structural information encoded in graph inputs. Our Graph Mixture Density Networks (GMDNs) learn graph-aware embeddings that inform the parameters of mixture components, allowing for more nuanced and context-sensitive probabilistic predictions. The architecture consists of three main components: (1) a GNN encoder that processes the input graph to produce node embeddings, (2) a graph-level aggregation mechanism that combines node embeddings into a global graph representation, and (3) mixture parameter networks that predict the mixing coefficients, component means, and covariances based on the graph representation. Formally, given an input graph $\mathbf{G} = (\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{E}, \mathbf{X})$ with nodes $\mathbf{V}$, edges $\mathbf{E}$, and node features $\mathbf{X}$, our model predicts a mixture distribution: \begin{equation} p(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{G}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k(\mathbf{G}) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{y}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_k(\mathbf{G}), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k(\mathbf{G})) \end{equation} where each mixture component parameter is a function of the entire graph structure and features. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We introduce Graph Mixture Density Networks, a novel architecture that extends mixture density networks to handle graph-structured inputs while maintaining the ability to model multimodal output distributions. (2) We develop efficient training procedures and demonstrate theoretical properties of our approach, including consistency guarantees under mild regularity conditions. (3) We provide comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains, showing significant improvements over both traditional MDNs applied to graph data and standard GNN approaches that assume unimodal outputs.

text: From delivery drones to autonomous electrical vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) passenger aircraft, modern unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) require sophisticated obstacle avoidance capabilities to operate safely in complex urban environments \cite{kopardekar2016unmanned}. The rapid proliferation of commercial UAS applications has created an urgent need for reliable, real-time obstacle detection and avoidance systems that can function effectively across diverse operational scenarios while adhering to strict regulatory requirements \cite{johnson2017regulatory}. Current obstacle avoidance methodologies for small UAS can be broadly categorized into three primary approaches: reactive systems that respond to immediate threats, predictive systems that anticipate potential collisions based on trajectory analysis, and hybrid systems that combine both reactive and predictive elements \cite{chen2018hybrid}. Each approach presents distinct advantages and limitations that must be carefully considered in the context of specific mission requirements and operational constraints. Reactive obstacle avoidance systems typically employ real-time sensor data to detect imminent collision threats and execute immediate evasive maneuvers \cite{wang2019reactive}. These systems excel in dynamic environments where obstacles may appear suddenly or change position unpredictably. However, reactive approaches often result in suboptimal flight paths and may struggle with closely spaced obstacles or confined spaces where maneuvering options are limited \cite{patel2020reactive}. Predictive obstacle avoidance systems leverage advanced path planning algorithms and environmental mapping to identify potential collision scenarios before they become critical \cite{martinez2018predictive}. By analyzing obstacle positions, velocities, and predicted trajectories, these systems can generate optimal avoidance paths that minimize deviation from the intended flight plan while maintaining safe separation distances \cite{rodriguez2019predictive}. The computational complexity of predictive systems, however, can be prohibitive for resource-constrained platforms, particularly when operating in highly dynamic environments with multiple moving obstacles. The selection of appropriate sensors for obstacle detection represents a critical design decision that significantly impacts system performance, weight, and power consumption. Optical sensors, including visible light and infrared cameras, provide rich environmental information and can detect a wide range of obstacle types \cite{thompson2020optical}. Monocular camera systems offer the lightest weight solution but require sophisticated computer vision algorithms to extract depth information from two-dimensional imagery \cite{lee2018monocular}. Stereo camera configurations provide direct depth measurement capabilities but increase system complexity and computational requirements \cite{brown2019stereo}. Radar systems excel at detecting metallic objects and can function effectively in adverse weather conditions, but their resolution limitations and difficulty in distinguishing small obstacles make them less suitable for close-proximity navigation \cite{anderson2018radar}. Ultrasonic sensors provide accurate short-range distance measurements at low cost and power consumption, making them attractive for small UAS applications, though their limited range and susceptibility to environmental interference restrict their utility \cite{davis2020ultrasonic}. Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) systems offer exceptional accuracy and resolution for obstacle detection but traditionally carry significant weight and power penalties \cite{wilson2018lidar}. Recent developments in solid-state LiDAR technology have produced lighter, more power-efficient solutions that may be suitable for larger small UAS platforms, though cost considerations remain a limiting factor for widespread adoption \cite{garcia2021solidstate}. The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques has revolutionized obstacle avoidance capabilities for small UAS \cite{kumar2020ai}. Deep neural networks can process complex sensor data streams in real-time, enabling sophisticated obstacle classification and trajectory prediction that surpasses traditional algorithmic approaches \cite{singh2019deep}. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated particular effectiveness in processing visual data for obstacle detection, while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) excel at temporal pattern recognition for predicting obstacle movement \cite{zhang2020cnn}. Reinforcement learning approaches have shown promise for developing adaptive obstacle avoidance behaviors that can improve through experience and handle novel scenarios not encountered during initial training \cite{miller2018reinforcement}. These systems can learn optimal avoidance strategies for specific operational environments, potentially outperforming pre-programmed solutions in complex or dynamic situations \cite{taylor2019adaptive}. The computational requirements of AI-based obstacle avoidance systems present significant challenges for small UAS platforms with limited processing power \cite{roberts2020computational}. Edge computing solutions, including specialized neural processing units and optimized inference engines, have emerged as potential solutions for deploying sophisticated AI algorithms on resource-constrained platforms \cite{johnson2021edge}. Environmental factors significantly impact the performance and reliability of obstacle avoidance systems. Weather conditions such as rain, snow, and fog can degrade sensor performance and reduce detection range, particularly for optical systems \cite{white2019weather}. Lighting conditions present additional challenges, with low-light and high-contrast scenarios potentially compromising computer vision-based approaches \cite{clark2020lighting}. Urban environments introduce unique obstacles including power lines, building structures, and other aircraft that may not be easily detectable with certain sensor modalities \cite{adams2018urban}. The presence of electromagnetic interference in urban areas can also affect radar and communication systems, requiring robust signal processing and filtering techniques \cite{lewis2019interference}. Regulatory considerations play an increasingly important role in obstacle avoidance system design and implementation. Aviation authorities worldwide are developing standards and certification requirements for UAS obstacle avoidance systems, with particular emphasis on reliability, redundancy, and fail-safe operation \cite{federal2020standards}. These requirements often mandate specific performance criteria and testing protocols that must be satisfied before commercial deployment \cite{european2021certification}. The integration of obstacle avoidance systems with broader UAS Traffic Management (UTM) infrastructure represents a critical component of future urban air mobility operations \cite{rios2018utm}. Cooperative obstacle avoidance, where aircraft share position and trajectory information to coordinate avoidance maneuvers, offers the potential for more efficient and safer operations in high-density airspace \cite{mueller2019cooperative}.

text: Frequently-Asked-Questions (FAQ) provide a collection of question-answer pairs that are either manually created or automatically extracted from relevant documents. These collections serve as structured knowledge repositories designed to address common user inquiries efficiently. FAQ systems have evolved from simple static web pages to sophisticated interactive platforms that can understand natural language queries and retrieve the most appropriate responses from extensive databases. The proliferation of FAQ systems across various domains—from customer service chatbots to technical documentation portals—has highlighted the critical importance of accurate query-FAQ matching. Users typically express their information needs in natural language, often using terminology and phrasing that differs significantly from the formal language used in FAQ entries. This semantic gap presents a fundamental challenge that traditional lexical matching approaches struggle to bridge effectively. Modern FAQ retrieval systems must address several key challenges: (1) \textit{Lexical mismatch}, where users employ different vocabulary than FAQ authors; (2) \textit{Semantic ambiguity}, where identical queries may have multiple valid interpretations; (3) \textit{Query complexity}, ranging from simple keyword searches to complex multi-sentence inquiries; and (4) \textit{Domain specificity}, where specialized terminology and context significantly impact retrieval accuracy. The advent of deep learning and transformer architectures has revolutionized the field of information retrieval, offering new opportunities to address these challenges through dense vector representations and contextual understanding. Pre-trained language models such as BERT \cite{devlin2018bert}, RoBERTa \cite{liu2019roberta}, and more recent variants like DeBERTa \cite{he2020deberta} have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in capturing semantic relationships between textual content. However, the direct application of these general-purpose models to FAQ retrieval tasks often yields suboptimal results due to the domain-specific nature of FAQ content and the unique characteristics of user queries. This limitation has motivated researchers to explore domain adaptation techniques, fine-tuning strategies, and specialized architectures tailored specifically for FAQ retrieval scenarios. \subsection{Problem Statement} Given a user query $q$ and a collection of FAQ pairs $\mathcal{F} = \{(f_1^q, f_1^a), (f_2^q, f_2^a), \ldots, (f_n^q, f_n^a)\}$, where $f_i^q$ represents the $i$-th FAQ question and $f_i^a$ represents its corresponding answer, the objective is to identify the most relevant FAQ pair that addresses the user's information need. Formally, this can be expressed as: \begin{equation} \hat{f} = \arg\max_{f_i \in \mathcal{F}} \text{sim}(q, f_i^q) \end{equation} where $\text{sim}(\cdot, \cdot)$ denotes a similarity function that measures the semantic relatedness between the user query and FAQ questions. The challenge lies in designing an effective similarity function that can accurately capture semantic relationships while being computationally efficient for real-time applications. Traditional approaches have relied on surface-level lexical matching, which fails to account for paraphrasing, synonymy, and contextual variations common in natural language queries. \subsection{Contributions} This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into neural approaches for FAQ retrieval, with the following key contributions: \begin{enumerate} \item We propose a novel dual-encoder architecture that leverages pre-trained transformer models to generate dense vector representations for both user queries and FAQ questions, enabling efficient semantic matching through vector similarity operations. \item We introduce a domain-adaptive fine-tuning strategy that specializes general-purpose language models for FAQ retrieval tasks, incorporating both positive and negative sampling techniques to improve discriminative capability. \item We present an extensive empirical evaluation across multiple FAQ datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over traditional baseline methods and providing insights into the effectiveness of different neural architectures for this task. \item We analyze the computational trade-offs between retrieval accuracy and inference speed, offering practical guidelines for deploying neural FAQ retrieval systems in production environments. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:related} reviews related work in information retrieval and neural ranking models; Section \ref{sec:methodology} details our proposed approach; Section \ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results and analysis; and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with future research directions.
