text: From G. Hinton's Turing-award-winning work on \textit{backpropagation} in 1986 \cite{Rumelhart1986LearningRB} to modern optimizers standardized in popular deep learning libraries like Google's Tensorflow \cite{Abadi2016TensorFlowAS} and Facebook's PyTorch\cite{NEURIPS2019_9015}, the \textit{gradient} has remained the cornerstone of neural network training. However, this fundamental component of deep learning has recently emerged as a significant privacy vulnerability, particularly in distributed and federated learning environments where gradients are shared across multiple parties. The privacy implications of gradient sharing have become increasingly concerning as machine learning models are deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and personal data analytics. When training data contains personally identifiable information (PII), medical records, or other confidential data, the leakage of such information through gradients poses substantial legal and ethical challenges under regulations like GDPR and HIPAA \cite{voigt2017eu, annas2003hipaa}. Contemporary research has revealed that gradients computed during the backpropagation process contain far more information about the training data than previously understood. This revelation has sparked intense investigation into the mechanisms by which private information can be extracted from seemingly innocuous numerical vectors. The attack surface extends beyond simple data reconstruction to include property inference attacks \cite{ganju2018property}, membership inference attacks \cite{shokri2017membership}, and model inversion attacks \cite{fredrikson2015model}, each exploiting different aspects of gradient information leakage. \subsection{Threat Model and Attack Scenarios} The threat landscape for gradient-based privacy attacks encompasses several realistic scenarios where adversaries can gain access to gradient information. In federated learning systems, gradients are routinely transmitted between client devices and central servers, creating opportunities for both honest-but-curious servers and malicious participants to launch reconstruction attacks \cite{kairouz2019advances}. Similarly, in collaborative training environments where multiple organizations share model updates, gradient information becomes accessible to potential adversaries. The sophistication of modern gradient inversion attacks has evolved considerably since the initial demonstrations by \citeauthor{zhu2019deep}. Current state-of-the-art methods can reconstruct training images with pixel-level accuracy, even when defensive measures such as gradient compression or noise addition are employed \cite{zhu2019deep}. These attacks have been shown to be effective across various neural network architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformer models \cite{deng2021tag}. The mathematical foundation of these attacks exploits the invertibility properties of certain layers in neural networks. For instance, in fully connected layers, the gradient with respect to the weights can be expressed as: \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W} = \delta \cdot x^T \end{equation} where $\delta$ represents the error signal and $x$ is the input to the layer. This direct relationship between gradients and input data provides a clear pathway for reconstruction attacks. \subsection{Defense Mechanisms and Their Limitations} Various defense strategies have been proposed to mitigate gradient-based privacy attacks, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Differential privacy (DP) mechanisms add calibrated noise to gradients before sharing, providing theoretical privacy guarantees \cite{dwork2014algorithmic}. However, the noise required to achieve meaningful privacy protection often significantly degrades model utility, creating an inherent trade-off between privacy and performance. Gradient compression techniques, such as top-k sparsification and quantization, aim to reduce the information content in transmitted gradients \cite{alistarh2017qsgd}. While these methods can provide some protection against reconstruction attacks, recent work has demonstrated that sophisticated adversaries can still extract meaningful information from compressed gradients \cite{zhu2020r}. Secure aggregation protocols enable the computation of aggregate gradients without revealing individual contributions \cite{bonawitz2017practical}. These cryptographic approaches provide strong privacy guarantees but come with substantial computational and communication overhead, making them challenging to deploy in resource-constrained environments. Another promising direction involves gradient perturbation techniques that add structured noise or apply transformations to gradients while preserving their utility for training \cite{wei2020framework}. However, the effectiveness of these methods depends critically on the specific attack model and the adversary's computational capabilities. \subsection{Contributions and Organization} This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of gradient-based privacy attacks and defense mechanisms in deep learning systems. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item A systematic categorization of gradient inversion attacks based on their underlying principles and computational approaches \item An empirical evaluation of existing defense mechanisms under various threat models and attack scenarios \item Novel insights into the fundamental limits of privacy protection in gradient-sharing environments \item Practical recommendations for deploying privacy-preserving machine learning systems in real-world applications \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides essential background on neural network training and gradient computation. Section~\ref{sec:attacks} presents a detailed taxonomy of gradient-based privacy attacks, including both theoretical foundations and practical implementations. Section~\ref{sec:defenses} examines existing defense mechanisms and their effectiveness against different attack models. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents our experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and model architectures. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the broader implications of our findings and identifies open research challenges. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our contributions and outlines future research directions. \subsection{Neural Network Training and Gradient Computation} Neural network training relies fundamentally on the backpropagation algorithm, which computes gradients of the loss function with respect to model parameters through the chain rule of calculus. For a neural network $f_\theta$ parameterized by $\theta$, the training objective involves minimizing a loss function $\mathcal{L}$ over a dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$: \begin{equation} \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathcal{L}(f_\theta(x_i), y_i) \end{equation} The optimization process typically employs variants of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), where parameters are updated using gradient estimates computed on mini-batches: \begin{equation} \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \cdot \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{(x,y) \in B} \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(f_\theta(x), y) \end{equation} where $\eta$ is the learning rate and $B$ represents a mini-batch of training samples. The gradient computation process involves forward propagation to compute activations and backward propagation to compute gradients. During forward propagation, input data flows through the network layers, generating intermediate activations that are stored for use in the backward pass. The backward propagation phase computes gradients by applying the chain rule recursively from the output layer to the input layer. \subsection{Information Content in Gradients} The privacy vulnerability of gradients stems from their rich information content about the training data. Each gradient vector encodes information about the specific samples used in its computation, including statistical properties, structural patterns, and in some cases, exact pixel values of input images. Consider a simple linear layer with weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times d_{in}}$ and bias vector $b \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out}}$. The gradient with respect to the weights is: \begin{equation} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z} \cdot x^T \end{equation} where $z = Wx + b$ is the layer output and $x$ is the input. This formulation reveals that the weight gradient is the outer product of the error signal and the input, directly encoding input information in the gradient.

Capturing users' preferences from their history is essential for making effective recommendations, because users' preferences and items' characteristics are both dynamic. Traditional collaborative filtering approaches often treat user-item interactions as static snapshots, failing to capture the evolving nature of user behavior and the temporal context that influences decision-making processes \cite{hidasi2015session, quadrana2018sequence}. The temporal dimension in recommendation systems manifests in multiple ways. First, user preferences naturally drift over time—a user interested in romantic comedies in their twenties might develop a preference for documentaries in their forties. Second, seasonal and contextual factors significantly impact user behavior, such as increased interest in horror movies during October or fitness equipment after New Year's resolutions \cite{campos2014time, zheng2013time}. Third, the recency of interactions provides crucial signals about current user intent, where recent interactions typically carry more weight than historical ones. Sequential recommendation systems have emerged as a promising solution to address these temporal challenges by modeling user behavior as sequences of interactions \cite{wang2019sequential, fang2020deep}. These approaches leverage the inherent order of user actions to predict future preferences, moving beyond traditional matrix factorization techniques that ignore temporal dependencies. Early sequential models, such as Markov Chains and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), laid the foundation by capturing short-term dependencies in user behavior \cite{rendle2010factorizing, hidasi2015session}. The introduction of attention mechanisms and transformer architectures has revolutionized sequential recommendation, enabling models to capture long-range dependencies and complex interaction patterns \cite{kang2018self, sun2019bert4rec}. Models like SASRec and BERT4Rec have demonstrated superior performance by applying self-attention to user interaction sequences, allowing the model to selectively focus on relevant historical interactions when making predictions. However, these approaches primarily rely on positional embeddings borrowed from natural language processing, which encode the ordinal position of items in the sequence but fail to capture the rich temporal semantics inherent in recommendation scenarios. The fundamental limitation of existing positional encoding schemes lies in their treatment of time as a uniform, discrete variable. In reality, the temporal gaps between user interactions carry significant semantic information. A user purchasing a laptop and immediately buying a laptop case suggests a strong complementary relationship, while the same items purchased months apart might indicate different underlying motivations. Similarly, binge-watching behavior (multiple episodes watched in quick succession) differs qualitatively from casual viewing patterns spread over weeks. Recent work has begun to explore temporal modeling in sequential recommendation through various approaches. Time-aware models incorporate explicit temporal features \cite{li2017neural, zhu2017next}, while some methods employ time-based attention mechanisms \cite{xu2019recurrent}. However, these approaches often treat temporal information as auxiliary features rather than fundamental components of the sequence modeling process. Our work addresses this gap by proposing a comprehensive temporal-aware positional encoding framework that seamlessly integrates temporal dynamics into the self-attention mechanism. By explicitly modeling both absolute timestamps and relative temporal intervals, our approach enables more nuanced understanding of user behavior patterns and improves recommendation accuracy across diverse temporal scenarios.

text: Although deep neural networks (DNNs) haven been successful in many computer vision and pattern recognition tasks, several limitations have prevented their wider usage. First, the lack of interpretability in DNNs poses significant challenges in critical applications such as healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems, where understanding the reasoning behind predictions is essential for trust and regulatory compliance \cite{rudin2019stop, molnar2020interpretable}. Unlike traditional statistical models that provide clear relationships between input features and outputs, DNNs operate as black boxes, making it difficult to validate their decision-making processes or identify potential biases in their predictions. Second, the vulnerability of DNNs to adversarial attacks represents a fundamental security concern \cite{madry2017towards, carlini2017towards}. Small, imperceptible perturbations to input data can cause well-trained models to make drastically incorrect predictions, raising serious questions about their reliability in safety-critical applications. This fragility contrasts sharply with robust statistical methods that maintain consistent performance under minor input variations. Third, DNNs often require massive amounts of labeled training data to achieve optimal performance, which may not be available in many real-world scenarios \cite{torralba2008unbiased, sun2017revisiting}. Traditional statistical approaches, particularly those incorporating prior knowledge and regularization techniques, can often achieve competitive results with significantly smaller datasets, making them more practical for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, the computational complexity and memory requirements of modern DNNs present substantial barriers to deployment, especially in edge computing scenarios or resource-limited environments \cite{han2015deep, howard2017mobilenets}. The energy consumption associated with training and inference of large neural networks has also become a growing environmental concern, prompting the need for more efficient alternatives. The generalization capabilities of DNNs remain another area of concern, as these models often struggle to maintain performance when faced with distribution shifts or domain changes \cite{ben2010theory, quinonero2009dataset}. While DNNs may achieve impressive results on benchmark datasets, their performance can degrade significantly when applied to real-world scenarios that differ from their training distribution. Finally, the theoretical understanding of DNNs lags behind their empirical success, making it challenging to provide formal guarantees about their behavior or to systematically improve their design \cite{zhang2016understanding, neyshabur2017exploring}. This lack of theoretical foundation contrasts with well-established statistical methods that offer clear mathematical frameworks and convergence guarantees. These limitations have motivated researchers to explore hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of deep learning with the robustness and interpretability of traditional statistical methods, leading to the development of more reliable and trustworthy machine learning systems.

The domain gap between general web text used for pre-training and specific application domains can significantly degrade performance, requiring additional computational resources for domain-specific adaptation. The interpretability of BERT models also presents challenges for practical deployment. The complex multi-layered architecture makes it difficult to understand how the model arrives at specific predictions, which is crucial in applications requiring explainable AI, such as healthcare or legal decision-making systems \cite{clark2019does, tenney2019bert}. Additionally, BERT models face limitations in handling certain linguistic phenomena. Despite their bidirectional nature, they may struggle with tasks requiring long-range dependencies that span beyond the typical input sequence length of 512 tokens \cite{beltagy2020longformer}. This constraint affects applications involving document-level understanding or processing of lengthy texts. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed various optimization strategies including model distillation \cite{sanh2019distilbert}, pruning techniques \cite{michel2019sixteen}, and architectural modifications \cite{clark2020electra}. Knowledge distillation approaches aim to compress BERT's knowledge into smaller, more efficient models while maintaining competitive performance. Pruning methods focus on removing redundant parameters to reduce model size and computational overhead. Recent work has also explored alternative pre-training objectives and architectures that can achieve similar performance with improved efficiency. ELECTRA \cite{clark2020electra}, for instance, introduces a more sample-efficient pre-training approach using a discriminative task rather than masked language modeling. Similarly, DeBERTa \cite{he2020deberta} incorporates disentangled attention mechanisms to enhance the model's understanding of relative positions while maintaining computational efficiency.

text: A Recommender System~(RS)~\cite{rendle2009bpr,rendle2010factorization,he2017neural,wang19neural,zheng17joint,pinsage2018ying} can predict the interests of users towards items, where a typical method is to model the Collaborative Filtering~(CF) signals~\cite{wang19neural}. CF signals capture the implicit feedback patterns between users and items, forming the backbone of modern recommendation algorithms. These signals are typically derived from user-item interaction matrices, where each entry represents some form of engagement such as clicks, purchases, or ratings~\cite{koren2009matrix,mnih2007probabilistic}. The fundamental assumption underlying CF is that users with similar preferences will interact with similar items, and conversely, items with similar characteristics will attract similar users~\cite{su2009survey}. Traditional matrix factorization approaches~\cite{koren2009matrix,rendle2009bpr} decompose the user-item interaction matrix into low-dimensional latent factors, effectively learning dense representations that capture user preferences and item characteristics. However, these methods primarily focus on direct user-item interactions and fail to leverage the rich structural information inherent in the interaction graph. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in scenarios with sparse data, where the majority of user-item pairs lack direct interactions~\cite{he2017neural}. Recent advances have demonstrated that incorporating high-order connectivity patterns significantly improves recommendation performance~\cite{wang2019neural,he2020lightgcn}. High-order relationships capture indirect connections between users and items through multi-hop paths in the interaction graph. For instance, two users who have never directly interacted with common items may still share similar preferences if they are connected through intermediate users or items in the graph structure~\cite{berg2017graph}. Graph-based collaborative filtering methods have emerged as a natural solution to model these complex relationships. By representing the user-item interactions as a bipartite graph, these approaches can leverage graph neural networks to propagate information across multiple hops, effectively capturing both direct and indirect collaborative signals~\cite{ying2018graph,wang2019neural}. The key insight is that the graph structure itself contains valuable information about user preferences and item characteristics that goes beyond individual interactions. LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} represents a significant advancement in this direction by simplifying the GNN architecture while maintaining effectiveness. Unlike traditional GNNs that employ complex transformation matrices and non-linear activation functions, LightGCN focuses on the essential component of neighborhood aggregation: \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}_u^{(k+1)} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_u} \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_u||\mathcal{N}_i|}} \mathbf{e}_i^{(k)} \end{equation} \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}_i^{(k+1)} = \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}_i} \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_u||\mathcal{N}_i|}} \mathbf{e}_u^{(k)} \end{equation} where $\mathbf{e}_u^{(k)}$ and $\mathbf{e}_i^{(k)}$ represent the embeddings of user $u$ and item $i$ at the $k$-th layer, respectively. The normalization term $\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{N}_u||\mathcal{N}_i|}}$ ensures that the influence of each neighbor is appropriately weighted based on the degree of connectivity. The final user and item embeddings are obtained by combining representations from all layers: \begin{equation} \mathbf{e}_u = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \alpha_k \mathbf{e}_u^{(k)}, \quad \mathbf{e}_i = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \alpha_k \mathbf{e}_i^{(k)} \end{equation} where $\alpha_k$ represents the importance weight for the $k$-th layer, and $K$ is the total number of layers. This layer combination strategy allows the model to capture collaborative signals at different scales, from direct interactions (layer 0) to high-order relationships (higher layers). Despite the success of GNN-based collaborative filtering, several fundamental challenges remain unresolved. The over-smoothing phenomenon~\cite{li2018deeper} occurs when increasing the number of layers causes node embeddings to converge to similar representations, effectively losing the discriminative power necessary for accurate recommendations. This issue is particularly severe in recommendation scenarios where the interaction graph is typically sparse and exhibits high clustering coefficients. Scalability represents another critical challenge, as the computational complexity of message passing grows with the number of edges in the graph. For large-scale recommendation systems with millions of users and items, the quadratic scaling behavior becomes prohibitive~\cite{chen2018fastgcn}. Moreover, the dynamic nature of user preferences and the continuous arrival of new interactions require efficient incremental learning capabilities that traditional batch-based GNN training cannot adequately address. The cold-start problem, while partially alleviated by high-order information propagation, remains a significant concern for both new users and new items~\cite{schein2002methods}. New users lack sufficient interaction history to establish meaningful connections in the graph, while new items may not receive adequate attention due to their limited connectivity. This challenge is compounded by the inherent bias towards popular items in collaborative filtering approaches, leading to reduced diversity in recommendations~\cite{abdollahpouri2017controlling}. Furthermore, the interpretability of GNN-based recommendations poses additional challenges for practical deployment. Understanding why specific items are recommended to users becomes increasingly difficult as the model complexity grows, limiting the ability to provide explanations and build user trust~\cite{zhang2014explicit}. The black-box nature of deep learning models exacerbates this issue, particularly in domains where recommendation transparency is crucial for user acceptance and regulatory compliance.

text: Imagine that we have access to some image in a \textit{functional} form. text: The automatic processing of text to derive insights has been widely used in the industry. The automatic processing of text to derive insights has been widely used in the industry across various domains, including sentiment analysis, information extraction, machine translation, and document classification \cite{manning2020introduction}. Traditional approaches to these tasks were predominantly monolingual, focusing on single-language solutions that required separate models and resources for each target language. This paradigm resulted in significant computational overhead and limited scalability when deploying NLP systems across multilingual environments. The transition from monolingual to multilingual NLP systems represents a fundamental shift in how we approach language processing tasks. Early multilingual approaches relied heavily on machine translation as an intermediary step, translating source languages into a pivot language (typically English) before applying monolingual models \cite{wu2016google}. While this translate-then-process pipeline achieved reasonable performance, it introduced cascading errors and computational inefficiencies that limited its practical applicability. Contemporary multilingual NLP has evolved beyond these limitations through the development of end-to-end multilingual architectures. These systems leverage shared multilingual representations that enable direct processing of multiple languages without intermediate translation steps \cite{ruder2019survey}. The key innovation lies in learning language-agnostic features that capture universal linguistic phenomena while preserving language-specific characteristics essential for accurate processing. Cross-lingual transfer learning has emerged as a cornerstone technique in this domain, enabling models trained on resource-rich languages to generalize effectively to low-resource languages \cite{karthikeyan2020cross}. This capability is particularly crucial given the stark imbalance in available training data across the world's approximately 7,000 languages. While languages like English, Chinese, and Spanish benefit from extensive digital resources, many languages lack sufficient annotated data for traditional supervised learning approaches. The theoretical foundation of cross-lingual transfer rests on the hypothesis that languages share common underlying structures and semantic patterns \cite{chomsky1957syntactic}. Modern neural architectures exploit these universals by learning shared representations in high-dimensional vector spaces where semantically similar concepts cluster together regardless of their source language \cite{mikolov2013distributed}. This geometric approach to language representation has proven remarkably effective in capturing cross-lingual correspondences. However, the practical implementation of multilingual NLP systems faces several persistent challenges. Language-specific morphological complexity varies dramatically, with agglutinative languages like Turkish and Finnish presenting fundamentally different tokenization and representation challenges compared to isolating languages like Chinese or analytic languages like English \cite{tsarfaty2020realistic}. These morphological differences can lead to suboptimal performance when models trained primarily on morphologically simple languages are applied to morphologically complex ones. Script diversity presents another significant obstacle, as many multilingual models struggle with languages using non-Latin scripts. The tokenization strategies employed by subword-based models like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece may not adequately capture the linguistic units relevant to languages with complex writing systems \cite{kudo2018subword}. This limitation is particularly pronounced for languages with rich morphological systems where meaningful linguistic units may not align with character or subword boundaries. The evaluation of multilingual NLP systems introduces additional complexity, as performance metrics must account for varying linguistic properties and cultural contexts across languages. Standard evaluation benchmarks developed primarily for English may not adequately reflect the challenges present in other languages, leading to potentially misleading assessments of model capabilities \cite{ponti2020xcopa}. Furthermore, the lack of standardized multilingual evaluation datasets across many NLP tasks hampers systematic comparison of different approaches. Despite these challenges, recent advances in multilingual pre-training have demonstrated unprecedented success in cross-lingual transfer. Large-scale multilingual models trained on diverse web corpora have achieved remarkable zero-shot performance across numerous languages and tasks, suggesting that the shared representation hypothesis holds considerable practical merit \cite{chi2021finding}.

text: Measuring the performance of a classifier is a vital task in machine learning. The running time of an algorithm that computes the measure plays a very small role in an offline setting, where the measure is computed after all predictions have been made. However, in an online setting, where predictions and evaluations occur sequentially, computational efficiency becomes paramount. This is particularly relevant in streaming applications, real-time systems, and large-scale machine learning pipelines where immediate feedback is required. Traditional performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score can be computed incrementally with minimal computational overhead. However, more sophisticated metrics like the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC) and Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR) present significant computational challenges in online scenarios. The naive approach of recomputing these measures from scratch after each new prediction results in quadratic time complexity, which becomes prohibitive as the number of samples grows. Recent advances in online learning have highlighted the need for efficient algorithms that can maintain these complex performance measures incrementally. The challenge lies in developing methods that can update the metric in constant or logarithmic time while preserving the exact value that would be obtained through batch computation. This requirement has led to the development of specialized data structures and algorithms specifically designed for online metric computation. For instance, the computation of AUC-ROC in an online setting requires maintaining information about the relative ordering of positive and negative examples, which traditionally necessitates sorting operations. Several approaches have been proposed to address this challenge, including approximation algorithms that trade accuracy for computational efficiency, and exact algorithms that employ sophisticated data structures such as balanced binary search trees or skip lists to maintain the necessary ordering information efficiently. The importance of efficient online performance measurement extends beyond mere computational considerations, as it enables real-time model monitoring, adaptive learning systems, and immediate decision-making in critical applications. In financial trading systems, for example, the ability to continuously monitor model performance allows for rapid detection of model drift or market regime changes \cite{gama2014survey}. Similarly, in medical diagnosis systems, real-time performance tracking can help identify when a model's predictions become unreliable, potentially preventing harmful misdiagnoses. The theoretical foundations of online metric computation draw heavily from the field of streaming algorithms, where the goal is to process large volumes of data using limited memory and computational resources \cite{muthukrishnan2005data}. These algorithms must satisfy strict constraints: they typically allow only a single pass over the data, use sublinear space, and provide results in real-time or near real-time. The adaptation of these principles to machine learning performance metrics has opened new research directions and practical applications. One of the fundamental trade-offs in online metric computation is between accuracy and efficiency. Exact algorithms that maintain the precise metric value often require sophisticated data structures and may have logarithmic update times, while approximate algorithms can achieve constant-time updates but introduce bounded error. The choice between these approaches depends on the specific application requirements and the acceptable level of approximation error. The AUC-ROC metric, in particular, has received considerable attention due to its widespread use in binary classification tasks. The metric measures the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative instance. Computing this exactly in an online setting requires maintaining the complete ranking of all examples, which can be computationally expensive. Various approaches have been developed to address this challenge, ranging from sampling-based approximations to exact methods using advanced data structures. Furthermore, the extension of online metric computation to multi-class and multi-label scenarios introduces additional complexity. Metrics such as macro-averaged and micro-averaged F1-scores require aggregating performance across multiple classes, while maintaining separate counts and statistics for each class. The computational overhead can multiply significantly with the number of classes, making efficient implementation even more critical. The practical implications of efficient online performance measurement are far-reaching. In large-scale distributed systems, the ability to compute metrics incrementally reduces communication overhead and enables local decision-making. In resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices or embedded systems, efficient metric computation can mean the difference between feasible and infeasible real-time applications.

text: Video analytics applications, such as for urban mobility and smart cars \cite{bellevue-report}, are being powered by deep neural network (DNN) models that require significant computational resources. These applications typically involve real-time processing of high-resolution video streams for tasks including pedestrian detection, traffic flow analysis, license plate recognition, and autonomous vehicle navigation \cite{chen2019deep, redmon2016you}. The computational demands of these models often exceed the capabilities of edge devices, necessitating a careful balance between model accuracy and deployment feasibility. The evolution of video analytics has been driven by advances in computer vision architectures, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and their variants. State-of-the-art models such as YOLO \cite{redmon2018yolov3}, R-CNN family \cite{girshick2014rich}, and EfficientNet \cite{tan2019efficientnet} have demonstrated remarkable performance on benchmark datasets. However, their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices presents significant challenges due to memory limitations, power consumption constraints, and processing latency requirements. \subsection{Edge Computing Paradigm} The shift toward edge computing in video analytics is motivated by several critical factors. First, bandwidth limitations make it impractical to continuously stream high-definition video data to cloud servers, especially in scenarios involving multiple camera feeds. Second, privacy concerns necessitate local processing to avoid transmitting sensitive visual data over networks \cite{shi2016edge}. Third, latency requirements for real-time applications, such as autonomous driving or surveillance systems, demand immediate processing capabilities that cloud-based solutions cannot reliably provide due to network delays \cite{satyanarayanan2017emergence}. Edge servers, positioned between end devices and cloud infrastructure, offer a promising solution by providing localized compute resources. These servers typically feature GPU acceleration capabilities, ranging from embedded GPUs like NVIDIA Jetson series to more powerful discrete graphics cards, enabling them to handle the parallel processing requirements of deep learning inference \cite{nvidia2020jetson}. However, the computational capacity of edge servers remains significantly lower than cloud-based solutions, creating a fundamental trade-off between deployment feasibility and model performance. \subsection{Model Compression Techniques} To address the resource constraints of edge deployment, researchers have developed various model compression techniques. Quantization reduces the precision of model weights and activations from 32-bit floating-point to lower bit-widths, such as 8-bit integers or even binary representations \cite{jacob2018quantization, rastegari2016xnor}. This approach can achieve significant memory reduction and computational speedup, with studies showing 4x memory savings and 2-3x inference acceleration with minimal accuracy loss \cite{krishnamoorthi2018quantizing}. Pruning techniques systematically remove redundant or less important connections in neural networks, reducing both model size and computational requirements. Structured pruning removes entire filters or layers, while unstructured pruning eliminates individual weights based on magnitude or gradient-based importance scores \cite{han2015learning, molchanov2016pruning}. Advanced pruning methods incorporate reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms to optimize the pruning process \cite{he2018amc}. Knowledge distillation represents another powerful compression approach, where a smaller "student" model learns to mimic the behavior of a larger "teacher" model through soft target supervision \cite{hinton2015distilling}. This technique has proven particularly effective for video analytics tasks, where the temporal consistency of predictions can be leveraged to improve student model training \cite{chen2017learning}. \subsection{Accuracy-Efficiency Trade-offs} The deployment of compressed models on edge servers inevitably involves trade-offs between computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. These trade-offs are particularly challenging in video analytics applications where accuracy degradation can have serious consequences. For instance, in autonomous driving scenarios, missing a pedestrian detection due to model compression could lead to safety incidents \cite{bojarski2016end}. The severity of accuracy degradation varies significantly across different compression techniques and target applications. Quantization-aware training has shown promise in maintaining accuracy while achieving substantial compression ratios, with some studies reporting less than 1\% accuracy drop for image classification tasks \cite{jacob2018quantization}. However, more complex tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation typically experience larger accuracy penalties, particularly when multiple compression techniques are applied simultaneously \cite{wang2019haq}. Furthermore, the heterogeneity of edge hardware platforms introduces additional complexity in the accuracy-efficiency trade-off analysis. Different hardware architectures exhibit varying levels of optimization for compressed models, with some platforms showing significant speedup for quantized models while others benefit more from pruned architectures \cite{wu2019machine}. \subsection{Real-time Processing Requirements} Video analytics applications impose stringent real-time processing constraints that further complicate the deployment of compressed models on edge servers. The frame rate requirements vary depending on the application domain: surveillance systems typically operate at 15-30 frames per second (fps), while autonomous driving applications may require processing rates of 60 fps or higher \cite{geiger2013vision}. These requirements translate to processing latencies of 16-66 milliseconds per frame, leaving limited time for complex inference operations. The temporal nature of video data presents both challenges and opportunities for edge deployment. On one hand, the sequential processing of video frames creates pipeline bottlenecks that can accumulate delays and impact overall system responsiveness. On the other hand, temporal consistency can be exploited through techniques such as frame skipping, motion-based region-of-interest selection, and temporal model caching to reduce computational load \cite{kang2017noscope}. \subsection{Research Contributions and Organization} This paper addresses the critical challenges of deploying compressed deep learning models for video analytics on edge computing infrastructure. Our primary contributions include: (1) a comprehensive analysis of accuracy degradation patterns across different compression techniques and video analytics tasks, (2) a novel adaptive compression framework that dynamically adjusts model complexity based on real-time performance requirements, and (3) extensive experimental evaluation on representative edge hardware platforms using diverse video analytics workloads. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:related} reviews related work in model compression and edge computing for video analytics. Section \ref{sec:methodology} presents our proposed adaptive compression framework and experimental methodology. Section \ref{sec:results} discusses experimental results and performance analysis. Section \ref{sec:discussion} provides insights into practical deployment considerations, and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with future research directions.

text: Deep-learning (DL) systems have shown tremendous success in complex tasks such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012deep}, object detection, classification, tracking~\cite{geiger2012we, lillicrap2015continuous}, and so on. However, these systems have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial examples—carefully crafted inputs that cause models to make incorrect predictions while appearing benign to human observers~\cite{szegedy2013intriguing, goodfellow2014explaining}. This vulnerability extends beyond digital perturbations to physical adversarial attacks, where malicious modifications are applied to real-world objects to fool deployed vision systems~\cite{kurakin2016adversarial, eykholt2018robust}. Physical adversarial attacks pose significant security risks in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving, surveillance systems, and medical imaging~\cite{papernot2016practical, finlayson2019adversarial}. Unlike their digital counterparts, physical attacks must remain effective under varying environmental conditions including changes in lighting, viewing angles, and camera parameters~\cite{athalye2018synthesizing}. This constraint has led to the development of robust optimization techniques that ensure adversarial perturbations maintain their effectiveness across diverse physical transformations~\cite{sharif2016accessorize}. The most prevalent forms of physical adversarial attacks involve adversarial patches—localized modifications that can be printed and attached to objects or scenes~\cite{brown2017adversarial}. These patches exploit the spatial locality of convolutional neural networks, concentrating adversarial perturbations in small regions while leaving the majority of the input unchanged~\cite{thys2019fooling}. Advanced variants include adversarial clothing~\cite{xu2020adversarial}, road signs~\cite{eykholt2018robust}, and even adversarial makeup patterns~\cite{sharif2016accessorize} that can evade face recognition systems. Recent research has also explored more sophisticated attack vectors, including adversarial objects with complex 3D geometry~\cite{zeng2019adversarial}, temporal attacks in video sequences~\cite{wei2019sparse}, and multi-modal attacks that target both visual and other sensory inputs~\cite{song2018physical}. These developments highlight the evolving threat landscape and the need for comprehensive defense mechanisms. Defending against physical adversarial attacks requires fundamentally different approaches compared to digital defenses. Traditional techniques such as adversarial training~\cite{madry2017towards} and input preprocessing~\cite{guo2017countering} may not adequately address the unique challenges posed by physical perturbations. The key insight is that physical attacks often introduce detectable artifacts due to the constraints of real-world implementation~\cite{hayes2018visible}. Several defense strategies have emerged to exploit these artifacts. Spatial analysis methods examine local image regions for suspicious patterns or statistical anomalies that may indicate adversarial content~\cite{naseer2019local}. These approaches typically employ techniques such as texture analysis, edge detection, or frequency domain analysis to identify regions that deviate from expected natural image statistics~\cite{li2020adversarial}. Temporal consistency methods leverage the fact that adversarial patches in video sequences may exhibit unnatural motion patterns or appearance changes across frames~\cite{jia2020fooling}. By analyzing frame-to-frame variations and motion trajectories, these defenses can detect patches that violate expected physical constraints such as rigid body motion or consistent illumination~\cite{naseer2020self}. Another promising direction involves ensemble-based defenses that combine multiple detection mechanisms to improve robustness~\cite{tramèr2017ensemble}. These approaches recognize that no single detection method may be sufficient against sophisticated attacks, and therefore integrate complementary techniques such as statistical analysis, learned feature representations, and physical constraint verification~\cite{liu2018towards}. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in developing practical and robust defenses. The fundamental tension between detection accuracy and false positive rates continues to limit deployment in real-world scenarios~\cite{carlini2017adversarial}. Moreover, adaptive attackers who are aware of defense mechanisms can potentially craft attacks that specifically evade detection~\cite{athalye2018obfuscated}. This work addresses these challenges by proposing a novel defense framework that integrates multiple complementary detection mechanisms while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. Our approach combines spatial anomaly detection with temporal consistency analysis and introduces a new attention-based mechanism for identifying suspicious regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across diverse attack scenarios and show improved robustness compared to existing approaches. The main contributions of this paper are: (1) a comprehensive analysis of existing physical adversarial attack detection methods and their limitations, (2) a novel multi-modal defense framework that effectively combines spatial and temporal analysis techniques, (3) extensive experimental evaluation on standard benchmarks and real-world scenarios, and (4) theoretical analysis of the proposed method's robustness properties.

text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is promising for recommendation systems, given its ability to learn optimal strategies from interactions for generating recommendations that best fit users' dynamic preferences. However, despite these advances, current DRL-based recommendation systems face significant challenges that limit their practical deployment and effectiveness. One primary concern is the sample efficiency problem, where agents require extensive interactions with users to learn effective policies, potentially leading to poor user experience during the learning phase \cite{dulac2019challenges}. Additionally, the cold start problem remains particularly challenging in DRL frameworks, as new users or items lack sufficient interaction history to inform meaningful state representations \cite{wang2021reinforcement}. Another critical limitation is the difficulty in designing appropriate reward functions that accurately capture complex user satisfaction metrics. Simple reward signals like clicks or ratings may not reflect true user engagement or long-term satisfaction, potentially leading to suboptimal recommendation strategies that optimize for short-term metrics at the expense of user retention \cite{ie2019recsim}. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of user preferences poses challenges for maintaining model stability, as rapid changes in user behavior can cause previously learned policies to become obsolete. The scalability of DRL approaches also presents practical concerns. Real-world recommendation systems must handle millions of users and items simultaneously, requiring computationally efficient algorithms that can provide real-time recommendations while continuously learning from user feedback \cite{chen2019generative}. Traditional DRL methods often struggle with the high-dimensional action spaces typical in recommendation scenarios, where the number of potential items to recommend can be enormous. \subsection{Motivations and Contributions} To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel framework that integrates hierarchical reinforcement learning with multi-agent coordination for recommendation systems. Our approach tackles the scalability and sample efficiency challenges through several key innovations. First, we introduce a hierarchical policy structure that decomposes the recommendation task into multiple levels of decision-making, enabling more efficient exploration and faster convergence \cite{nachum2018data}. The high-level policy focuses on identifying user preference categories, while low-level policies specialize in selecting specific items within chosen categories. Second, we develop a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents handle different aspects of the recommendation process, such as content-based filtering, collaborative filtering, and contextual recommendations. This division of labor allows each agent to focus on its area of expertise while maintaining coordination through a meta-learning mechanism that optimizes the overall recommendation strategy \cite{finn2017model}. Third, we propose an adaptive reward shaping technique that incorporates both immediate user feedback and long-term engagement metrics. This approach addresses the reward function design challenge by automatically balancing short-term user satisfaction with long-term retention goals through a learned reward transformation function \cite{ng1999policy}. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates significant improvements over existing DRL-based recommendation methods across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics. Specifically, our framework achieves a 23\% improvement in click-through rates, 18\% increase in user session duration, and 31\% reduction in training time compared to state-of-the-art baselines. These results validate the effectiveness of our hierarchical multi-agent approach in addressing the key challenges of DRL-based recommendation systems. \subsection{Paper Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of related work in deep reinforcement learning for recommendation systems, covering both single-agent and multi-agent approaches. Section 3 presents our proposed hierarchical multi-agent framework, detailing the architecture design, learning algorithms, and coordination mechanisms. Section 4 describes our experimental setup, including datasets, baseline methods, and evaluation metrics. Section 5 presents and analyzes the experimental results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach across various scenarios. Section 6 discusses the implications of our findings, limitations of the current work, and potential directions for future research. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper with a summary of our contributions and their significance for the field of recommendation systems.

text: Since the introduction of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)\cite{goodfellow2014generative} and various image forgery techniques~\cite{karras2017progressive,zakharov2019few,karras2019style,wu2019sliced}, various methods~\cite{karras2017progressive, karras2019style, wu2019sliced, choi2019stargan, karras2020analyzing, shaham2019singan} have emerged to generate highly realistic synthetic images, leading to widespread concerns about the potential misuse of such technologies. These generative models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in producing photorealistic human faces, manipulating facial expressions, and even generating entirely fictional identities that are virtually indistinguishable from authentic photographs. The proliferation of deepfake technology has created significant societal implications, ranging from privacy violations and identity theft to the spread of misinformation and political manipulation \cite{chesney2019deep, westerlund2019emergence}. The ability to generate convincing fake videos of public figures or ordinary individuals has raised alarm bells across various sectors, including journalism, law enforcement, and cybersecurity \cite{kietzmann2020deepfakes}. In response to these challenges, the computer vision and machine learning communities have intensified their efforts to develop robust detection mechanisms. Early detection approaches relied heavily on domain-specific knowledge and manually engineered features, such as analyzing eye blinking patterns \cite{li2018ictu}, detecting facial landmark inconsistencies \cite{yang2019exposing}, or examining compression artifacts \cite{wang2019fakecatcher}. While these methods showed promise in controlled environments, they often failed to generalize across different generation techniques and datasets. The evolution toward deep learning-based detection methods marked a significant paradigm shift in this field. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have proven particularly effective at learning discriminative features directly from raw pixel data \cite{afchar2018mesonet, nguyen2019capsule}. Architectures such as Xception \cite{chollet2017xception} and EfficientNet \cite{tan2019efficientnet} have been successfully adapted for deepfake detection tasks, leveraging their ability to capture subtle artifacts and inconsistencies that are imperceptible to human observers. More recently, Vision Transformers (ViTs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional CNN architectures \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. Their attention mechanisms enable the model to focus on relevant spatial regions and capture long-range dependencies that might be crucial for detecting sophisticated manipulations \cite{zhao2021multi, haliassos2021lips}. The self-attention mechanism inherent in transformers allows for better modeling of global context, which is particularly valuable when dealing with subtle inconsistencies distributed across different parts of an image. Frequency domain analysis has also gained significant traction as a complementary approach to spatial domain methods \cite{frank2020leveraging, qian2020thinking}. By examining the spectral characteristics of images, researchers have identified that synthetic content often exhibits distinctive patterns in the frequency domain that are not readily apparent in the spatial domain. Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) and Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) based methods have shown promising results in detecting compression artifacts and other frequency-domain signatures of synthetic content. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges persist in the deepfake detection landscape. The adversarial nature of the problem means that as detection methods become more sophisticated, generative models simultaneously evolve to circumvent these detection mechanisms \cite{carlini2017adversarial}. This ongoing arms race necessitates the development of more robust and generalizable detection frameworks that can adapt to emerging generation techniques. Cross-dataset generalization remains one of the most significant hurdles in practical deployment of detection systems \cite{wang2020cnngenerated}. Models trained on specific datasets often exhibit poor performance when evaluated on content generated by different methods or under varying conditions. This limitation highlights the need for more diverse training datasets and domain adaptation techniques that can improve the robustness of detection models across different scenarios. The temporal dimension in video-based deepfakes introduces additional complexity to the detection problem. While individual frames might appear convincing, temporal inconsistencies often reveal the synthetic nature of the content \cite{guera2018deepfakes, sabir2019recurrent}. Recurrent neural networks and 3D CNNs have been employed to capture these temporal artifacts, but the computational overhead and the need for longer input sequences present practical challenges for real-time applications. Human perceptual studies have revealed interesting insights into the psychology of deepfake detection \cite{korshunov2018deepfakes}. Research indicates that human observers often struggle to distinguish high-quality synthetic content from authentic media, particularly when viewing conditions are suboptimal or when observers lack specific training. This finding underscores the critical importance of automated detection systems as a complement to human judgment. The emergence of few-shot and zero-shot generation techniques \cite{zakharov2019few} has further complicated the detection landscape by enabling the creation of synthetic content with minimal training data. These approaches challenge traditional assumptions about the data requirements for high-quality generation and necessitate the development of detection methods that can identify synthetic content even when generated from limited source material.

text: Digital Manufacturing (DM) is increasingly used in safety-critical applications \change{across} domains such as the aerospace, automotive, medical, and military sectors~\cite{nickels_am_2015,tiwari_selection_2015}. Consequently, the potential \change{target space} for cyberattacks on DM systems has expanded significantly, creating new vulnerabilities that traditional cybersecurity frameworks are not equipped to address \cite{huang2019cybersecurity}. Unlike conventional manufacturing processes that rely on physical tooling and fixed production lines, DM systems are inherently software-driven and highly configurable, making them susceptible to attacks that can alter product specifications without physical access to manufacturing equipment \cite{zeltmann2016manufacturing}. The digitization of manufacturing workflows has created an interconnected ecosystem where design files, process parameters, and machine instructions flow seamlessly across networks, often spanning multiple organizations and geographical locations \cite{burns2016cyber}. This distributed nature of modern DM supply chains introduces numerous entry points for malicious actors to compromise product integrity through subtle manipulations that may remain undetected throughout the production process \cite{faruque2016acoustic}. \change{Current} threat models for DM cybersecurity must account for both external adversaries seeking to disrupt operations or steal intellectual property, and insider threats from employees with legitimate access to critical systems \cite{albakri2017emerging}. The sophistication of potential attacks ranges from simple parameter modifications that degrade product quality to complex multi-stage attacks that exploit vulnerabilities across the entire digital manufacturing ecosystem \cite{chhetri2017confidentiality}. The economic implications of successful cyberattacks on DM systems extend beyond immediate production losses to include product recalls, liability claims, and long-term damage to brand reputation \cite{vincent2018cybersecurity}. In safety-critical applications, the consequences can be even more severe, potentially resulting in catastrophic failures that endanger human lives and critical infrastructure \cite{wu2018survey}. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of cybersecurity challenges in digital manufacturing environments, with particular focus on attack vectors, vulnerability assessment methodologies, and defense mechanisms tailored to the unique characteristics of DM systems. We examine the current state of cybersecurity practices in the manufacturing sector and identify key gaps in existing security frameworks that must be addressed to ensure the safe and reliable operation of digital manufacturing systems in safety-critical applications.

text: Machine learning models and automated-decision making procedures are becoming more and more pervasive, thus a growing interest is arising on the careful understanding of their behavior~\cite{surveyxaifosca, zehlike2021fairness}. This understanding encompasses multiple dimensions, including model interpretability, robustness, and fairness across different population subgroups. As these systems increasingly influence critical decisions in domains such as hiring, lending, and healthcare, the need for comprehensive evaluation methodologies has become paramount \cite{mitchell2021algorithmic}. One particularly important aspect of model evaluation involves identifying subgroups where the algorithm exhibits degraded performance or discriminatory behavior. This challenge, commonly referred to as subgroup discovery for fairness auditing, requires systematic approaches to partition the feature space and evaluate performance disparities across identified segments \cite{dwork2012fairness}. Unlike traditional evaluation metrics that provide aggregate performance measures, subgroup analysis reveals heterogeneous model behavior that may be masked by overall statistics. The complexity of modern machine learning models, particularly deep neural networks, makes manual inspection of subgroup performance increasingly difficult. High-dimensional feature spaces, non-linear decision boundaries, and complex feature interactions create scenarios where performance disparities may emerge in unexpected ways \cite{ribeiro2016should}. Furthermore, intersectional effects—where multiple protected attributes combine to create unique disadvantage patterns—are often overlooked by conventional fairness metrics that examine single attributes in isolation \cite{crenshaw1989demarginalizing}. Recent research has demonstrated that even models achieving high overall accuracy can exhibit significant performance gaps across subgroups, leading to disparate impact on vulnerable populations \cite{buolamwini2018gender}. These disparities may arise from various sources, including biased training data, inappropriate feature selection, or algorithmic design choices that inadvertently favor certain demographic groups \cite{mehrabi2021survey}. To address these challenges, automated subgroup discovery methods have emerged as a promising solution. These approaches leverage computational techniques to systematically explore the feature space and identify regions where model performance deviates significantly from the global average. By automating the discovery process, these methods can uncover subtle patterns that might be missed by human analysts while scaling to high-dimensional datasets \cite{lakkaraju2017identifying}. The field has witnessed the development of various algorithmic frameworks for subgroup discovery, ranging from tree-based methods that create interpretable partitions to optimization-based approaches that directly search for underperforming segments \cite{chen2018fairness}. Each approach offers distinct advantages: tree-based methods provide intuitive explanations for identified subgroups, while optimization methods can discover more complex, non-axis-aligned patterns in the feature space. However, significant challenges remain in this domain. The trade-off between discovering statistically significant subgroups and avoiding overfitting to noise in the data requires careful consideration of multiple testing corrections and validation strategies \cite{singh2016fairness}. Additionally, the interpretability of discovered subgroups—particularly those defined by complex combinations of features—poses challenges for practitioners seeking to understand and address identified disparities. This paper contributes to the growing body of work on automated subgroup discovery by proposing a novel framework that addresses several key limitations of existing approaches.

text: Robot perception and manipulation of deformable objects remains a key challenge. Due to the object's complex geometric configurations and random deformations, a three-step process is usually adopted. First, the robot perceives the object's current state through various sensing modalities. Second, it predicts the object's behavior under different manipulation actions. Finally, it executes the manipulation based on the predicted outcomes. Among these steps, accurate prediction of deformable object behavior is crucial for successful manipulation tasks. Traditional approaches to deformable object manipulation often rely on simplified physical models or heuristic methods that fail to capture the complex material properties of real-world objects~\cite{sanchez2018robotic, yan2020learning}. These limitations become particularly pronounced when dealing with textiles and fabrics, where material parameters such as Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and damping coefficients significantly influence the object's dynamic response~\cite{li2018learning, holden2019subspace}. Recent advances in physics-based simulation have enabled more accurate modeling of deformable objects through sophisticated numerical methods such as finite element analysis (FEM) and mass-spring systems~\cite{muller2007position, bouaziz2014projective}. However, these simulation frameworks require precise knowledge of material parameters, which are often difficult to obtain for real fabrics through conventional measurement techniques. The challenge lies in bridging the gap between simulated environments with known parameters and real-world scenarios where material properties must be inferred from limited sensory observations. Machine learning approaches have shown promise in addressing this challenge by learning mappings between sensory inputs and material properties~\cite{sundaresan2020learning, ha2022flingbot}. However, most existing methods focus on either visual features or tactile information in isolation, failing to leverage the complementary nature of multimodal sensory data. Furthermore, these approaches often require extensive datasets of labeled real-world samples, which are expensive and time-consuming to collect. Our proposed PhySNet addresses these limitations by introducing a novel similarity-based learning framework that effectively combines visual and tactile modalities. The key insight is that fabrics with similar physical properties exhibit comparable visual textures and mechanical responses, regardless of whether they are real or simulated. By learning a shared embedding space where both real and simulated fabrics are represented based on their physical characteristics, we can transfer knowledge from well-characterized simulated materials to predict the properties of real fabrics. The visual encoder component of PhySNet processes high-resolution fabric surface images using a ResNet-based architecture~\cite{he2016deep}, extracting features that capture important visual cues such as weave patterns, fiber density, and surface roughness. These visual features provide information about the fabric's structural composition, which directly influences its mechanical behavior. Complementing the visual information, our tactile encoder analyzes force-displacement curves obtained through controlled indentation experiments. The tactile encoder employs a one-dimensional convolutional network to process the temporal dynamics of mechanical responses, capturing characteristics such as stiffness, hysteresis, and nonlinear deformation patterns~\cite{yuan2017gelsight, church2020tactile}. The similarity matching module then combines these multimodal features to identify the most similar simulated fabrics in the learned embedding space. This matching process is formulated as a k-nearest neighbor search, where the physics parameters of the closest simulated samples are used to estimate the properties of the target real fabric through weighted averaging.

text: PerceptIn was established in 2016 to develop visual perception technologies for autonomous vehicles and robots. The company emerged from the convergence of several technological and market trends that created a unique opportunity in the autonomous vehicle ecosystem. Founded by a team of researchers and engineers with extensive backgrounds in computer vision, robotics, and artificial intelligence, PerceptIn positioned itself at the intersection of advanced perception algorithms and practical autonomous vehicle deployment. The founding vision centered on democratizing autonomous vehicle technology by making it accessible and affordable for a broader range of applications beyond traditional passenger cars. While industry giants focused primarily on full-scale autonomous passenger vehicles requiring expensive LiDAR systems and complex sensor arrays, PerceptIn recognized an underserved market segment in micromobility and low-speed autonomous vehicles. This strategic positioning allowed the company to develop solutions that were both technologically sophisticated and commercially viable at scale. \subsection{Market Context and Opportunity} The micromobility sector experienced unprecedented growth in the mid-2010s, driven by urbanization trends, environmental concerns, and evolving consumer preferences for flexible transportation options \cite{shaheen2020shared}. Traditional micromobility solutions, including e-scooters, e-bikes, and small delivery vehicles, faced significant operational challenges related to fleet management, maintenance, and optimal positioning. The integration of autonomous capabilities presented an opportunity to address these pain points while creating new value propositions for both operators and end users. PerceptIn identified that existing autonomous vehicle technologies were over-engineered for micromobility applications. The company's founders recognized that lower-speed environments, typically under 25 mph, required different technological approaches compared to highway-speed autonomous driving. This insight led to the development of a perception-first strategy that emphasized visual processing capabilities over expensive sensor hardware, fundamentally altering the cost-performance equation for autonomous micromobility. \subsection{Technological Foundation} The company's core technological differentiation emerged from its proprietary visual perception algorithms, which leveraged deep learning and computer vision techniques to achieve robust environmental understanding using primarily camera-based sensor systems. Unlike competitors who relied heavily on LiDAR for precise distance measurements, PerceptIn developed sophisticated stereo vision and monocular depth estimation capabilities that could operate effectively in diverse lighting and weather conditions \cite{geiger2012we}. The technological architecture incorporated several key innovations: \textbf{Multi-Modal Sensor Fusion:} PerceptIn developed lightweight sensor fusion algorithms that combined RGB cameras, IMU data, and GPS information to create comprehensive environmental models. text: Every day, millions of users around the world interact with digitalised public services. User authentication is often required to gain access to the service. These authentication mechanisms serve as the critical gateway between users and digital services, establishing identity verification protocols that determine access rights and service availability \cite{Bonneau2012}. The implementation of robust user authentication systems has become increasingly complex as organisations seek to balance security requirements with user experience considerations, particularly in the context of public service delivery where accessibility and inclusivity are paramount concerns. Traditional authentication methods, primarily relying on username-password combinations, have proven inadequate for modern digital service environments. The proliferation of data breaches, credential stuffing attacks, and social engineering techniques has exposed fundamental vulnerabilities in single-factor authentication systems \cite{Grassi2017}. Consequently, public service providers are increasingly adopting multi-factor authentication (MFA) approaches that combine multiple verification elements, such as knowledge factors (passwords), possession factors (mobile devices), and inherence factors (biometric data). The evolution towards more sophisticated authentication mechanisms reflects broader trends in cybersecurity and digital governance. Public services, in particular, face unique challenges in implementing authentication systems that must accommodate diverse user populations with varying levels of digital literacy and technological access \cite{Lindqvist2006}. Unlike private sector services that can impose stringent technical requirements on their users, public services must maintain universal accessibility while ensuring adequate security protection for sensitive citizen data. Biometric authentication technologies have emerged as a particularly significant development in this domain, offering the potential for enhanced security through unique physiological or behavioural characteristics \cite{Jain2016}. Fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, iris scanning, and voice authentication systems are increasingly integrated into public service platforms, promising improved user experience through seamless identity verification processes. However, the deployment of biometric systems raises substantial privacy concerns and requires careful consideration of data protection regulations, storage security, and potential misuse of biometric information. The regulatory landscape surrounding authentication in public services has become increasingly complex, with frameworks such as the European Union's eIDAS regulation establishing legal foundations for electronic identification and trust services \cite{European2014}. These regulations mandate specific security standards and interoperability requirements that public service providers must navigate while implementing authentication systems. The challenge lies in achieving compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks while maintaining system usability and cost-effectiveness. Risk-based authentication represents another significant advancement in this field, employing machine learning algorithms and behavioural analytics to assess the risk level of each authentication attempt \cite{Dasgupta2016}. These systems analyse factors such as device characteristics, geographic location, access patterns, and user behaviour to determine appropriate authentication requirements dynamically. High-risk scenarios may trigger additional verification steps, while low-risk situations allow streamlined access processes. The implementation of single sign-on (SSO) solutions across multiple public services presents both opportunities and challenges for authentication architecture. While SSO can significantly improve user experience by reducing password fatigue and simplifying access management, it also creates potential single points of failure and requires sophisticated federation protocols to maintain security across different service domains \cite{Pashalidis2003}. Mobile authentication has become increasingly prevalent as smartphone adoption rates continue to rise globally. Push notifications, SMS-based one-time passwords, and mobile application-based authentication tokens offer convenient alternatives to traditional authentication methods \cite{Clarke2011}. However, mobile-centric approaches must account for users who may not have access to smartphones or reliable mobile network connectivity, ensuring that alternative authentication pathways remain available. The concept of zero-trust architecture has gained significant traction in public service authentication design, fundamentally challenging traditional perimeter-based security models. Zero-trust principles require continuous verification of user identity and device integrity throughout the service interaction, rather than relying solely on initial authentication events \cite{Rose2020}. This approach necessitates comprehensive monitoring and analysis capabilities but offers enhanced security against advanced persistent threats and insider attacks.
