text: A projected 276,480 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in the U.S. in 2020, and 42,170 women will die of the disease \cite{Sieg20}. Breast cancer remains the second leading cause of cancer death among women, underscoring the critical importance of accurate diagnostic and prognostic assessment \cite{DeSantis2019}. The histological grading system, particularly the Nottingham grading system, serves as a fundamental component in determining prognosis and guiding treatment decisions \cite{Elston1991, Rakha2010}. This three-tiered system evaluates tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic count to classify tumors as Grade 1 (well-differentiated), Grade 2 (moderately differentiated), or Grade 3 (poorly differentiated). Among these three components, nuclear pleomorphism assessment presents the greatest challenge for standardization due to its inherently subjective nature \cite{Genestie1998, vanDiest2002}. The evaluation requires pathologists to assess nuclear size variation, shape irregularity, chromatin pattern, and nucleolar prominence—features that can be interpreted differently across observers and institutions. Studies have reported inter-observer agreement rates as low as 60-70\% for nuclear pleomorphism grading, significantly lower than the agreement rates observed for tubule formation and mitotic count assessment \cite{Frierson1995, Theissig1990}. The clinical implications of this variability are substantial. Grade 2 tumors, which represent approximately 50-60\% of all invasive breast carcinomas, pose particular challenges as they occupy an intermediate position between the clearly well-differentiated Grade 1 and poorly differentiated Grade 3 tumors \cite{Rakha2010}. Inconsistent nuclear pleomorphism assessment can lead to grade migration, where tumors are inappropriately upgraded or downgraded, potentially affecting treatment recommendations including the use of adjuvant chemotherapy \cite{Colpaert2001}. Digital pathology has emerged as a transformative technology in anatomical pathology, enabling the acquisition of high-resolution whole slide images (WSI) that can be analyzed using sophisticated computational methods \cite{Pantanowitz2011, Madabhushi2016}. The digitization of histopathological specimens provides unprecedented opportunities for quantitative analysis of morphological features that were previously assessed only through qualitative visual inspection. This paradigm shift from subjective interpretation to objective measurement holds particular promise for nuclear pleomorphism assessment. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems have demonstrated significant potential in automating various aspects of histopathological analysis \cite{Gurcan2009, Komura2018}. For nuclear pleomorphism assessment, these systems can extract and quantify numerous morphometric parameters including nuclear area, perimeter, circularity, aspect ratio, and texture features that characterize chromatin distribution \cite{Petushi2006, Doyle2008}. Unlike human observers, computational systems provide consistent, reproducible measurements that are not subject to fatigue, experience variations, or subjective bias. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep learning architectures, have revolutionized medical image analysis by automatically learning discriminative features from large datasets \cite{LeCun2015, Esteva2017}. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown remarkable success in various pathology applications, including breast cancer detection, subtype classification, and prognosis prediction \cite{Cruz-Roa2014, Bejnordi2017}. These networks can learn complex patterns and relationships in histopathological images that may not be apparent to human observers or traditional image analysis methods. The application of deep learning to nuclear pleomorphism assessment represents a natural evolution of these technologies. By training on large datasets of expertly graded nuclear regions, CNN architectures can potentially learn to recognize the subtle morphological patterns that distinguish different grades of nuclear pleomorphism \cite{Wang2016, Spanhol2016}. Furthermore, ensemble methods that combine multiple CNN architectures or integrate deep learning with traditional morphometric features have shown enhanced performance in various classification tasks \cite{Kather2019}. Despite these technological advances, several challenges remain in developing robust automated systems for nuclear pleomorphism assessment. The heterogeneity of nuclear morphology within individual tumors requires sophisticated sampling strategies to ensure representative assessment \cite{Allred1998}. Additionally, variations in tissue processing, staining protocols, and imaging conditions across different laboratories can affect the generalizability of automated systems \cite{Janowczyk2016}. The standardization of nuclear pleomorphism assessment through computational methods could significantly impact breast cancer management by reducing diagnostic variability, improving prognostic accuracy, and enabling more consistent treatment decisions. This standardization is particularly important in the era of personalized medicine, where precise tumor characterization is essential for optimal therapeutic selection \cite{Perou2000, Sorlie2001}. This study aims to address these challenges by developing and validating a comprehensive computational framework for automated nuclear pleomorphism assessment in breast cancer histopathological images. Our approach combines advanced image processing techniques, quantitative morphometric analysis, and state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms to provide objective, reproducible, and clinically relevant nuclear grading. The proposed system is designed to assist pathologists in standardizing nuclear pleomorphism assessment while maintaining compatibility with existing clinical workflows and diagnostic practices.

text: Pose transfer, applying the desired pose of a source mesh to a target mesh, is a promising and challenging task in 3D computer vision, which can be widely applied to various domains including character animation, virtual reality, gaming, and digital content creation. The fundamental challenge lies in transferring pose information while preserving the identity and intrinsic geometric characteristics of the target mesh. Traditional approaches often struggle with maintaining semantic consistency and producing natural-looking deformations, particularly when dealing with complex poses or significant shape variations between source and target meshes. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promising results for pose transfer tasks, with methods ranging from variational autoencoders \cite{tan2018variational} to generative adversarial networks \cite{aberman2020unpaired}. However, most existing approaches either operate on intermediate representations that lose important geometric information or fail to adequately capture the complex relationships between mesh vertices during deformation. Graph neural networks \cite{kipf2016semi} have emerged as a natural choice for mesh processing due to their ability to handle irregular data structures, yet they often lack the global context awareness necessary for semantically meaningful pose transfer. The key insight driving our work is that effective pose transfer requires a deep understanding of both local geometric properties and global structural relationships within 3D meshes. While local information determines how individual vertices should move relative to their immediate neighbors, global context ensures that the overall deformation maintains anatomical plausibility and preserves the target mesh's identity. This dual requirement motivates our design of a multi-scale Transformer architecture that can simultaneously capture fine-grained local details and long-range global dependencies. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose a novel 3D mesh Transformer architecture specifically designed for pose transfer that operates directly on mesh vertices while preserving topological structure throughout the entire pipeline. (2) We introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism that processes mesh information at multiple resolution levels, enabling the model to capture both local surface details and global pose characteristics. (3) We develop an edge-aware attention formulation that incorporates both Euclidean and geodesic distance information, ensuring that the model respects important topological constraints during deformation. (4) We present a graph-based pooling strategy that efficiently handles meshes with varying vertex counts and topologies while maintaining structural coherence. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:related_work} reviews relevant literature on pose transfer and mesh processing techniques. Section \ref{sec:method} provides a detailed description of our proposed architecture, including the multi-scale attention mechanism and edge-aware formulations. Section \ref{sec:experiments} presents comprehensive experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on various datasets and comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper with discussions on limitations and future research directions. \subsection{Traditional Pose Transfer Methods} Early approaches to pose transfer primarily relied on geometric and statistical techniques. Sumner and Popović \cite{sumner2004deformation} introduced deformation transfer, which establishes correspondence between source and target meshes through a set of control vertices and transfers deformation gradients. This method, while effective for similar shapes, often fails when dealing with significant geometric variations between meshes. Baran et al. \cite{baran2007automatic} proposed automatic rigging techniques that extract skeletal structures from meshes and use linear blend skinning for pose transfer. While computationally efficient, these methods are limited by the quality of the extracted skeleton and often produce artifacts in regions with complex deformations. More recent geometric approaches \cite{gao2019sparse, zhou2016sparse} have attempted to address these limitations through sparse representation learning and optimization-based techniques, but they still struggle with capturing complex non-linear deformations. \subsection{Learning-Based Mesh Processing} The advent of deep learning has revolutionized mesh processing tasks. Masci et al. \cite{masci2015geodesic} introduced geodesic convolutional neural networks for shape analysis, extending traditional CNNs to non-Euclidean domains. Subsequent works \cite{defferrard2016convolutional, kipf2016semi} developed various graph neural network architectures for mesh processing, demonstrating their effectiveness in tasks such as shape classification and segmentation.

text: Searcher struggle is the event that a searcher ``makes strenuous efforts in the face of difficulties"\footnote{\url{merriam-webster.com}} during a search process. Identifying and understanding searcher struggle has become increasingly important as search engines strive to provide more personalized and effective search experiences. When users encounter difficulties during their search sessions, it not only affects their immediate task completion but also influences their long-term satisfaction and engagement with search platforms \cite{fox2005evaluating, hassan2014predicting}. Traditional approaches to struggle detection have predominantly focused on behavioral indicators that suggest increased cognitive load or frustration. These include metrics such as query reformulation frequency, time spent on search engine result pages (SERPs), click-through patterns, and session duration \cite{liu2010predicting, guo2009ready}. While these effort-based features provide valuable insights into user behavior, they often fail to distinguish between productive high-effort search activities and genuine struggle scenarios. Consider, for example, a researcher conducting a comprehensive literature review who issues multiple queries, spends considerable time examining results, and reformulates search terms iteratively. Such behavior exhibits many characteristics traditionally associated with struggle—high query volume, extended session duration, and frequent reformulations—yet represents successful, goal-directed search activity rather than difficulty \cite{marchionini2006exploratory}. Conversely, a user who quickly abandons their search after viewing only a few results might be experiencing significant struggle despite exhibiting low effort indicators. This disconnect between effort and struggle highlights a fundamental limitation in current detection methodologies. The assumption that struggle correlates linearly with search effort oversimplifies the complex relationship between user behavior and search difficulty. Users may invest substantial effort in search tasks for various reasons: the inherent complexity of their information need, exploratory search intentions, thoroughness in information gathering, or genuine enjoyment of the search process \cite{white2009exploratory}. Furthermore, individual differences in search expertise, domain knowledge, and personal search strategies introduce additional complexity to struggle detection. Expert searchers may employ sophisticated search strategies that appear effortful to automated systems but represent efficient problem-solving approaches. Novice users, conversely, might struggle significantly while exhibiting seemingly straightforward search behaviors \cite{aula2005how}. The temporal dimension of search behavior also plays a crucial role in understanding struggle. Users experiencing genuine difficulty often exhibit distinct patterns in their behavioral sequences—such as rapid query abandonment followed by reformulation, inconsistent click patterns, or erratic navigation behaviors \cite{hassan2013beyond}. These temporal signatures provide richer context than aggregate effort metrics alone. Recent advances in user modeling and machine learning present opportunities to develop more nuanced struggle detection approaches. By incorporating contextual factors such as query complexity, result quality, user expertise, and task characteristics, we can build more accurate models that distinguish between different types of high-effort search scenarios \cite{kiseleva2016understanding}. Our research addresses these challenges by proposing a multi-faceted framework for struggle detection that moves beyond simple effort-based heuristics. We integrate behavioral analysis with contextual understanding and user satisfaction signals to create a more comprehensive picture of search difficulty. This approach recognizes that struggle is not merely a function of effort expenditure but emerges from the interaction between user capabilities, task demands, and system limitations. The implications of improved struggle detection extend beyond academic interest. Search engines can leverage accurate struggle identification to trigger interventions such as query suggestions, result re-ranking, or alternative search interfaces. Understanding when and why users struggle also informs the design of more intuitive search systems and helps identify areas where search technology can be improved \cite{agichtein2006improving}.

text: The publication of the Bitcoin paper by~\cite{Satoshi2008} in 2008 has motivated the exploration of blockchains and smart contracts in the development of innovative applications. However, the initial enthusiasm surrounding blockchain technology has led to an oversimplified binary view of trust mechanisms, where decentralized solutions are automatically considered superior to centralized alternatives. This perspective has resulted in a systematic undervaluation of Trusted Third Party (TTP) based smart contract implementations, which often provide more practical and efficient solutions for many real-world applications. The fundamental premise of this paper is that the blockchain community has created a false dichotomy between trustless and trusted systems, failing to recognize that trust is not binary but exists on a spectrum. While complete trustlessness may be desirable in certain adversarial environments, many commercial and institutional applications operate within established legal and regulatory frameworks where trusted intermediaries provide valuable services beyond mere transaction processing \cite{wright2021law, zetzsche2017regulating}. \subsection{Problem Statement} The current academic and industrial focus on blockchain-based smart contracts has created several critical gaps in our understanding of optimal contract deployment strategies. First, there is insufficient comparative analysis between on-chain and on-TTP implementations across different application domains. Second, the cost-benefit analysis of trust assumptions versus system performance has been inadequately explored. Third, the regulatory and compliance advantages of TTP-based systems have been largely overlooked in favor of ideological commitments to decentralization. This research addresses these gaps by providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating smart contract deployment options based on application requirements, trust assumptions, and performance constraints. We argue that the choice between on-chain and on-TTP implementations should be driven by practical considerations rather than ideological preferences. \subsection{Research Contributions} This paper makes several key contributions to the smart contract literature: \begin{enumerate} \item We present a systematic comparison of on-chain versus on-TTP smart contract architectures, analyzing their respective advantages and limitations across multiple dimensions including cost, performance, privacy, and regulatory compliance. \item We develop a decision framework that enables practitioners to select appropriate smart contract deployment strategies based on application-specific requirements and constraints. \item We provide empirical evidence demonstrating that TTP-based smart contracts can achieve superior performance characteristics while maintaining adequate security guarantees for many practical applications. \item We identify specific use cases where on-TTP implementations offer clear advantages over blockchain-based alternatives, challenging the prevailing assumption that decentralization is always preferable. \end{enumerate} \subsection{Scope and Limitations} This research focuses primarily on smart contract deployment architectures rather than specific implementation details or programming languages. While we acknowledge the importance of technical implementation considerations, our analysis operates at a higher architectural level to provide broadly applicable insights. The study examines both public and private blockchain implementations as well as various TTP architectures including traditional databases, secure multi-party computation systems, and trusted execution environments. However, we do not extensively cover hybrid approaches that combine blockchain and TTP elements, as these represent a separate research direction requiring dedicated analysis. \subsection{Evolution of Smart Contract Platforms} The concept of smart contracts predates blockchain technology by several decades, with \cite{szabo1997formalizing} introducing the foundational ideas in the 1990s. However, the practical implementation of smart contracts became feasible only with the advent of programmable blockchain platforms, particularly Ethereum \cite{buterin2014ethereum, wood2014ethereum}. Early smart contract implementations focused primarily on simple financial transactions and basic conditional logic. The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) provided the first widely adopted platform for executing arbitrary code on a blockchain, enabling more sophisticated contract logic \cite{antonopoulos2018mastering}. Subsequently, numerous alternative platforms emerged, including Hyperledger Fabric \cite{androulaki2018hyperledger}, Cardano \cite{chakravarty2020extended}, and Solana \cite{yakovenko2018solana}, each offering different trade-offs between decentralization, performance, and functionality. Despite these technological advances, the fundamental limitations of blockchain-based smart contracts have become increasingly apparent. Transaction throughput constraints, high gas fees, and energy consumption issues have limited the practical applicability of on-chain solutions \cite{croman2016scaling, gudgeon2020defi}. \subsection{Trusted Third Party Architectures} Traditional TTP-based systems have long provided secure transaction processing and contract execution capabilities in various domains. Banking systems, electronic payment processors, and enterprise resource planning platforms demonstrate the viability of trusted intermediaries in managing complex business logic and maintaining transaction integrity \cite{evans2014economic}. Modern TTP architectures have evolved to incorporate advanced cryptographic techniques, including secure multi-party computation \cite{yao1982protocols}, homomorphic encryption \cite{gentry2009fully}, and trusted execution environments \cite{costan2016intel}. These technologies enable TTPs to provide enhanced privacy and security guarantees while maintaining the performance advantages of centralized processing. The integration of regulatory compliance mechanisms represents another significant advantage of TTP-based systems. Unlike blockchain networks, which operate according to predetermined protocol rules, TTPs can implement flexible compliance policies, integrate with existing legal frameworks, and provide dispute resolution mechanisms \cite{werbach2018trust, zetzsche2017regulating}. \subsection{Comparative Analysis Literature} Several studies have attempted to compare blockchain and traditional database systems, though most focus on technical performance metrics rather than comprehensive architectural trade-offs. \cite{dinh2017blockbench} provides one of the most systematic performance comparisons, demonstrating significant throughput and latency advantages for traditional databases over blockchain systems. \cite{xu2017taxonomy} offers a broader architectural perspective, categorizing different blockchain applications and identifying scenarios where traditional systems might be more appropriate. However, this work does not specifically address smart contract deployment considerations or provide practical decision-making frameworks. More recent research has begun to acknowledge the limitations of blockchain-first approaches. \cite{wust2018you} presents a decision tree for determining when blockchain technology is necessary, though their analysis focuses on data storage rather than smart contract execution. \cite{fridgen2018don} extends this work by considering additional factors such as regulatory requirements and business model constraints. \subsection{Comparative Framework Development} Our analysis employs a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that systematically compares on-chain and on-TTP smart contract implementations across eight critical dimensions: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Performance Metrics}: Transaction throughput, latency, and scalability characteristics \item \textbf{Economic Factors}: Transaction costs, infrastructure requirements, and total cost of ownership \item \textbf{Security Properties}: Attack resistance, data integrity, and availability guarantees \item \textbf{Privacy Considerations}: Data confidentiality, access control, and regulatory compliance \item \textbf{Governance Mechanisms}: Upgrade procedures, dispute resolution, and regulatory integration \item \textbf{Development Complexity}: Programming model simplicity, debugging capabilities, and maintenance requirements \item \textbf{Interoperability}: Integration with existing systems and cross-platform compatibility \item \textbf{Environmental Impact}: Energy consumption and carbon footprint considerations \end{enumerate} For each dimension, we establish quantitative metrics where possible and qualitative assessment criteria where quantitative measurement is impractical. This approach enables comprehensive comparison while acknowledging the inherent trade-offs between different architectural choices. \subsection{Case Study Selection} We selected four representative application domains to illustrate the practical implications of our comparative framework: \textbf{Supply Chain Management}: Tracking product provenance and authenticity across complex multi-party supply networks, where transparency and auditability are critical but complete decentralization may not be necessary. \textbf{Financial Services}: Processing high-frequency transactions and implementing complex financial instruments, where performance and regulatory compliance are paramount concerns. \textbf{Digital Identity Management}: Managing user credentials and access permissions across multiple services, where privacy protection and regulatory compliance are essential requirements. \textbf{Internet of Things (IoT) Integration}: Coordinating automated transactions between connected devices, where low latency and energy efficiency are critical for practical deployment. These domains represent different points on the trust-performance spectrum and enable us to demonstrate how application requirements should influence architectural decisions. \subsection{Experimental Design} Our experimental evaluation consists of three components: performance benchmarking, cost analysis, and qualitative assessment of non-functional requirements. For performance benchmarking, we implemented equivalent smart contract logic on both Ethereum (representing on-chain deployment) and a custom TTP platform built using PostgreSQL with cryptographic extensions (representing on-TTP deployment). We measured transaction throughput, confirmation latency, and resource utilization under various load conditions. Cost analysis incorporates both direct transaction fees and indirect costs such as development time, infrastructure maintenance, and compliance overhead. We collected data from multiple sources including blockchain explorer APIs, cloud service pricing models, and industry surveys of development costs. Qualitative assessment involves structured evaluation of privacy, governance, and regulatory compliance characteristics based on established frameworks from the information security and regulatory compliance literature.

This has led to a systematic underestimation of the use of trusted third parties (TTPs) in the implementation of smart contracts, which often provide a more efficient and practical solution for many real-world applications. ‘The basic assumption of this paper is that the blockchain community has created a false dichotomy between trustless and trusted systems, not realizing that trust is not a two-state but a spectrum; and although trustlessness may be desirable in certain adversarial environments, many commercial and institutional applications operate in legal and regulatory frameworks where trusted intermediaries can provide valuable services beyond mere transaction processing, as Wright20 and Zetzsche17 describe. In the first place, there has been no sufficient comparison between on-chain and off-chain implementations in various application areas. Second, the cost-benefit analysis of trust assumptions and system performance has not yet been sufficiently explored. The following research paper aims to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating smart contract deployment options, based on application requirements, trust assumptions, and performance constraints. It presents a systematic comparison of smart contract architectures that run on chains and those that run on the TTP, analyzing the respective advantages and disadvantages on various dimensions such as cost, performance, privacy, and regulatory compliance. Third, the regulatory and compliance advantages of the TTP-based systems have been largely overlooked because of the ideological commitment to decentralization. - We provide empirical evidence that TTP-based smart contracts can achieve superior performance characteristics while maintaining sufficient security guarantees for many practical applications. We present use cases where the on-TTP implementation offers a clear advantage over the on-blockchain alternative, challenging the common assumption that decentralization is always better. We propose a decision framework that helps practitioners to select the most appropriate smart contract deployment strategy based on application-specific requirements and constraints. This study focuses primarily on the architectures of smart contracts, not on the specific details of the implementation and the choice of a language. It covers both public and private implementations of the blockchain, and various architectures for processing the trust of transactions such as traditional databases, secure multiparty computation systems, and trustable execution environments. We recognize the importance of the implementation details, but our study proceeds at a higher architectural level, allowing us to derive more general conclusions. This section will give an overview of the relevant research in smart contract platforms and give a brief overview of their evolution. The concept of smart contracts predates the emergence of the blockchain by several decades, with Szabo's paper from the nineties setting out the basic idea, but only with the emergence of a programmable blockchain platform like Ethereum [1,2] [1,3] could a practical implementation be made. Early implementations focused primarily on simple financial transactions and simple conditional logic. With these technological advances, however, the fundamental limitations of the smart contract have become more obvious. The first widely used platform for arbitrary computation on the blockchain was the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), see Androulakis, “Hyperledger”; Chakravarty, “Extended Smart Contracts”; “Silicon Valley”; and the emergence of the so-called Semantic platform, which enabled smart contract execution of arbitrary complexity, see Antonopoulos, “Mastering Smart Contracts”; and the emergence of the so-called “Semantic” platform, which allowed smart contract execution of arbitrary complexity, see Antonopoulos, “Mastering Smart Contracts”; several new platforms have since been developed, including Hyperledger, Cardano, Solana, Solana-Lite, and SOLOON, each offering different tradeoffs between decentralization, performance, and functionality. With the technological progress of smart contract, however, the fundamental limitations of the system have become more apparent. The performance constraints, the high gas fees, and the energy problems have restricted the practical application of on-chain solutions. Modern TTPs have evolved to take advantage of advanced cryptographic techniques such as homomorphic encryption (Yao 1982), secure multi-party computation (Gentry ’09), and trusted execution environments (Costan ’16). These advanced cryptographic tools enable TTPs to offer improved privacy and security guarantees while retaining the performance advantages of a centralized, ephemeral server. Trusted third party (T3P) architectures have long provided secure transaction and smart contract execution services in many different contexts. Our experimental evaluation consists of three parts: performance assessment, cost analysis and qualitative assessment of non-functional requirements. For performance assessment, we implemented the same smart contract in both Ethereum (representing on-chain deployment) and in a custom TTP platform, built on PostgreSQL with cryptographic extensions (representing on-TTP deployment). We collected data from a number of sources, including the Ethereum Block Explorer API, cloud service price models and industry costs. The quality of privacy, security and regulatory compliance features was assessed by means of a standardized assessment framework based on the literature on information security and regulatory compliance. We measured the throughput, confirmation latencies, and resource consumption under various load conditions. The cost analysis includes direct and indirect transaction costs, as well as development time, equipment maintenance costs, and the cost of compliance.

text: In recent years, we have witnessed the great success of deep neural networks (DNNs) in various fields of artificial intelligence including computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{6296526}, and robot control~\cite{levine2018learning}. However, despite their remarkable performance on clean data, DNNs have been shown to be vulnerable to adversarial examples~\cite{szegedy2013intriguing, goodfellow2014explaining}. These are carefully crafted inputs that are imperceptibly different from natural examples but can cause the model to make incorrect predictions with high confidence. The existence of such adversarial examples poses significant security risks in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving~\cite{eykholt2018robust}, medical diagnosis~\cite{finlayson2019adversarial}, and face recognition systems~\cite{sharif2016accessorize}. To defend against adversarial attacks, numerous methods have been proposed, with adversarial training being one of the most effective approaches~\cite{madry2017towards, zhang2019theoretically}. Adversarial training involves augmenting the training data with adversarial examples generated during the training process, thereby improving the model's robustness to such perturbations. However, adversarial training comes with substantial computational overhead, often requiring 5-10 times more training time compared to standard training~\cite{shafahi2019adversarial}. Moreover, adversarially trained models typically exhibit reduced accuracy on clean data, a phenomenon known as the robustness-accuracy trade-off~\cite{tsipras2018robustness, raghunathan2019adversarial}. Given these challenges, there has been growing interest in developing more efficient methods to obtain robust models. One promising direction is the transfer of robustness from pre-trained robust models to new models through knowledge distillation techniques~\cite{papernot2016distillation, wang2019improving}. This approach offers several advantages: (1) it reduces the computational cost of training robust models from scratch, (2) it enables the creation of robust models even when adversarial training data is limited, and (3) it allows for the adaptation of robustness to new domains or architectures. The concept of knowledge distillation was originally introduced by \citet{hinton2015distilling} as a method to transfer knowledge from large, complex teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. In the context of adversarial robustness, the goal shifts to transferring the defensive capabilities learned by a robust teacher model to a student model. This process involves training the student model to mimic not only the predictions of the teacher on clean data but also its behavior under adversarial perturbations. Recent work has demonstrated that robustness can indeed be transferred across different network architectures and even across different datasets~\cite{pang2019improving, goldblum2020adversarially}. \citet{wang2019improving} showed that student models trained with robust teacher guidance achieve better adversarial robustness compared to those trained with standard knowledge distillation. Similarly, \citet{pang2019improving} proposed adversarial knowledge distillation methods that specifically target the transfer of robustness properties. The effectiveness of robustness transfer can be attributed to the nature of adversarially learned representations. \citet{ilyas2019adversarial} provided evidence that adversarial training encourages models to rely on robust, human-interpretable features rather than brittle, non-robust features that are easily manipulated by adversarial perturbations. These robust features tend to be more generalizable and transferable across different models and tasks. Despite the promising results, several challenges remain in the field of robustness transfer. First, the optimal strategies for selecting teacher models and designing transfer objectives are not well understood. Different teacher architectures and training procedures may lead to varying degrees of transferability. Second, the relationship between the similarity of teacher and student architectures and the effectiveness of robustness transfer needs further investigation. Third, most existing work focuses on image classification tasks, and the generalizability to other domains such as natural language processing or reinforcement learning remains largely unexplored. Furthermore, theoretical understanding of why and when robustness transfer works is still limited. While empirical evidence supports the effectiveness of these methods, a deeper theoretical analysis could provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying robustness transfer and guide the development of more principled approaches. In this work, we aim to address some of these challenges by conducting a comprehensive study of robustness transfer mechanisms. Our contributions are threefold: \begin{enumerate} \item We provide a theoretical analysis of the conditions under which robustness can be effectively transferred between neural networks, establishing connections between the geometric properties of learned representations and transferability. \item We propose a novel framework for adaptive robustness transfer that dynamically adjusts the transfer objectives based on the similarity between teacher and student feature spaces, leading to improved transfer efficiency. \item We conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures to validate our theoretical insights and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method compared to existing approaches. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work on adversarial robustness and knowledge distillation. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our theoretical analysis and proposed framework. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and results. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

text: Android increasingly becomes the most popular mobile operating system in the world. Unfortunately, due to its reputation, it has also become the leading target platform for attackers. The widespread adoption of Android devices across diverse demographics and geographical regions has created an attractive ecosystem for cybercriminals seeking to maximize their impact and financial gains. According to recent market analysis, Android holds approximately 71\% of the global mobile operating system market share, representing over 3 billion active devices worldwide \cite{android_market_share_2024}. This extensive user base provides malicious actors with an unprecedented opportunity to deploy large-scale attack campaigns and harvest sensitive data from millions of potential victims. The architecture of the Android operating system, while designed with security principles in mind, presents unique challenges for malware detection and prevention. The Linux-based kernel, combined with the Java application framework and the Dalvik/ART runtime environment, creates a complex multi-layered system where malware can operate at various abstraction levels \cite{android_architecture_security_2023}. Malicious applications can exploit vulnerabilities in native libraries, manipulate the Java runtime, or abuse legitimate system APIs to achieve persistent access and execute unauthorized operations. One of the most significant security challenges in the Android ecosystem stems from its permission-based security model. While this model provides users with granular control over application privileges, research has shown that users frequently grant permissions without fully understanding their implications \cite{permission_study_2023}. Malware authors exploit this behavior by requesting excessive permissions under the guise of legitimate functionality, subsequently using these privileges to access sensitive resources such as contacts, SMS messages, location data, and financial information. The diversity of Android malware families has expanded considerably in recent years, with each category employing distinct attack methodologies and targeting specific user behaviors. Adware remains one of the most prevalent forms of Android malware, generating revenue through aggressive advertisement display and click fraud schemes \cite{adware_analysis_2023}. These applications often masquerade as legitimate utilities or games while secretly collecting user data and displaying intrusive advertisements that degrade device performance and user experience. Spyware applications represent another significant threat vector, designed to covertly monitor user activities and exfiltrate personal information. Modern Android spyware employs sophisticated techniques such as keylogging, screen recording, microphone activation, and camera access to gather comprehensive intelligence about target users \cite{spyware_techniques_2024}. These applications often operate silently in the background, utilizing minimal system resources to avoid detection while continuously transmitting collected data to remote command-and-control servers. The emergence of cryptocurrency-related malware has introduced new dimensions to the Android threat landscape. Cryptojacking applications surreptitiously utilize device computational resources to mine cryptocurrencies, leading to battery drain, device overheating, and reduced performance \cite{cryptojacking_mobile_2023}. Additionally, cryptocurrency wallet targeting malware specifically focuses on stealing private keys and seed phrases, potentially resulting in irreversible financial losses for victims. Ransomware attacks on Android devices have evolved from simple screen lockers to sophisticated encryption-based threats that target both device storage and cloud-synchronized data. Modern Android ransomware variants employ advanced encryption algorithms and implement anti-forensics techniques to complicate recovery efforts \cite{android_ransomware_evolution_2024}. These attacks often combine social engineering elements with technical exploitation, convincing users to grant administrative privileges that enable comprehensive device compromise. The supply chain attacks targeting Android applications have become increasingly sophisticated, with threat actors compromising legitimate development tools, software development kits (SDKs), and third-party libraries to inject malicious code into otherwise benign applications \cite{supply_chain_attacks_2023}. These attacks are particularly dangerous because they can affect applications distributed through official channels, bypassing traditional security screening processes and reaching large user populations. Machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies have revolutionized both malware development and detection in the Android ecosystem. Adversarial machine learning techniques enable malware authors to generate variants that can evade automated detection systems, while security researchers leverage deep learning models to identify previously unknown malware families and predict emerging threat patterns \cite{ai_malware_detection_2024}. This technological arms race continues to drive innovation in both offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities. The economic impact of Android malware extends beyond direct financial theft to include costs associated with incident response, device replacement, productivity loss, and reputation damage. Small and medium-sized enterprises are particularly vulnerable to Android malware attacks, as they often lack comprehensive mobile device management solutions and security awareness training programs \cite{sme_mobile_security_2023}. The cascading effects of successful malware infections can disrupt business operations and compromise sensitive corporate data stored on employee devices. Current research efforts in Android malware detection focus on developing more effective static and dynamic analysis techniques that can identify malicious behavior patterns while minimizing false positive rates. Hybrid analysis approaches that combine multiple detection methodologies show promising results in identifying sophisticated malware variants that employ evasion techniques \cite{hybrid_analysis_2024}. Additionally, collaborative threat intelligence sharing initiatives enable security researchers to rapidly disseminate information about emerging threats and develop coordinated response strategies.

text: Recent advancements in end-to-end neural networks-based approaches have shown wide success in various sequence generation tasks: machine translation~\cite{sutskever2014sequence,luong2015effective}, dialogue systems~\cite{vinyals2015neural,serban2016building}, textual summarization~\cite{rush2015neural,nallapati2016abstractive,see2017get}, image/video captioning~\cite{bahdanau2014neural,venugopalan2015sequence,pasunuru2017multi}, question generation~\cite{du2017learning,du2018harvesting,zhang2019addressing}, etc. These models typically employ maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) during training, which maximizes the probability of the ground truth sequence given the input. While MLE training has proven effective for learning meaningful representations and achieving strong performance on various benchmarks, it suffers from several inherent limitations that become particularly problematic in sequence generation tasks. First, MLE training creates a discrepancy between training and inference procedures, commonly referred to as exposure bias \cite{ranzato2015sequence,bengio2015scheduled}. During training, the model has access to ground truth tokens at each decoding step, whereas during inference, it must rely on its own previously generated tokens. This mismatch can lead to error accumulation, where small mistakes early in the sequence compound over time, resulting in increasingly poor generation quality for longer sequences. Second, MLE optimization does not directly align with the evaluation metrics commonly used to assess generation quality in downstream applications. For instance, machine translation systems are typically evaluated using BLEU scores \cite{papineni2002bleu}, summarization models using ROUGE metrics \cite{lin2004rouge}, and dialogue systems using task-specific measures such as success rate or user satisfaction. The disconnect between training objectives and evaluation criteria can result in suboptimal performance on the metrics that matter most for practical applications. To address these fundamental limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to reinforcement learning (RL) approaches for sequence generation. By formulating text generation as a sequential decision-making process, RL enables direct optimization of non-differentiable evaluation metrics through policy gradient methods \cite{williams1992simple,sutton2018reinforcement}. In this framework, the neural sequence generator acts as a policy that selects actions (tokens) at each time step, and the final evaluation metric serves as a reward signal to guide learning. The REINFORCE algorithm \cite{williams1992simple} has emerged as a particularly popular choice for optimizing sequence generation models. REINFORCE estimates policy gradients using Monte Carlo sampling, allowing optimization of arbitrary reward functions without requiring differentiability. Several successful applications have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach: Ranzato et al. \cite{ranzato2015sequence} applied REINFORCE to improve machine translation and summarization models; Paulus et al. \cite{paulus2017deep} achieved state-of-the-art results in abstractive summarization by combining MLE pre-training with REINFORCE fine-tuning; and Li et al. \cite{li2016deep} used policy gradient methods to optimize dialogue systems for more engaging and diverse conversations. However, the application of REINFORCE to sequence generation introduces new challenges. The high variance of policy gradient estimates can lead to unstable training, requiring careful implementation of variance reduction techniques such as baseline subtraction and reward normalization \cite{greensmith2004variance,tucker2018mirage}. Additionally, the sparse nature of sequence-level rewards provides limited guidance during early stages of training, often necessitating pre-training with MLE to establish a reasonable initialization. More critically, optimizing solely for specific evaluation metrics can result in reward hacking behaviors where models exploit weaknesses in the reward function to achieve high scores without genuinely improving generation quality. For example, a model optimized for BLEU scores might generate repetitive phrases or copy portions of the input to artificially inflate n-gram overlap, leading to fluent but semantically poor outputs \cite{paulus2017deep,wu2018study}. To mitigate these issues, recent work has explored hybrid training approaches that combine MLE and RL objectives. Mixed training schemes alternate between MLE and REINFORCE updates \cite{paulus2017deep}, while others employ weighted combinations of likelihood and reward-based losses \cite{wu2018study}. These approaches aim to maintain the stability and coverage benefits of MLE training while incorporating the direct metric optimization advantages of reinforcement learning. Despite these advances, significant challenges remain in effectively applying reinforcement learning to sequence generation tasks, particularly in developing robust reward functions and training procedures that consistently improve generation quality across diverse evaluation criteria.

text: Object counting has become increasingly important due to its wide range of applications such as crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation and inventory management. In these applications, the ability to accurately count objects without extensive manual annotation or retraining for each new scenario is crucial for practical deployment. Traditional counting methods face significant limitations when encountering novel object categories, as they require substantial labeled data and computational resources for model adaptation. The emergence of one-shot learning paradigms has opened new possibilities for addressing these challenges. By requiring only a single exemplar to specify the target object category, one-shot counting methods can rapidly adapt to new scenarios without the need for extensive retraining. This capability is particularly valuable in dynamic environments where new object types frequently appear, such as manufacturing quality control, ecological monitoring, or emergency response situations. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Formally, the one-shot object counting problem can be defined as follows: Given a query image $I_q \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ and an exemplar bounding box $B_e$ that defines a region of interest containing the target object category, the objective is to predict the total count $N$ of all instances belonging to the same category within $I_q$. Unlike traditional counting methods that operate on pre-defined object categories, this formulation requires the model to understand and generalize from a single visual example. The key challenge lies in developing feature representations that can capture the essential visual characteristics of the exemplar while being robust to variations in appearance, scale, orientation, and occlusion that naturally occur across different instances of the same category. This requires sophisticated similarity matching mechanisms that can distinguish between true positive instances and visually similar but semantically different objects. \subsection{Technical Challenges} Several fundamental challenges make one-shot object counting particularly difficult: \textbf{Intra-class Variation:} Objects within the same category can exhibit significant visual differences due to variations in pose, lighting conditions, partial occlusion, or natural diversity within the category. The model must learn to identify these variations as belonging to the same class while maintaining sensitivity to inter-class differences. \textbf{Scale and Perspective Changes:} Objects may appear at different scales and viewing angles throughout the image, requiring scale-invariant feature representations and robust matching strategies that can handle geometric transformations. \textbf{Background Clutter:} Complex backgrounds with visually similar objects or textures can lead to false positive detections. The model must develop discriminative features that focus on object-specific characteristics rather than contextual information. \textbf{Limited Supervision:} With only a single exemplar available, the model cannot rely on statistical learning from multiple examples. This necessitates strong inductive biases and effective transfer learning from related tasks or domains. \subsection{Related Work} Early approaches to object counting focused on density estimation methods \cite{lempitsky2010learning, fiaschi2012learning}, which predict pixel-wise density maps and integrate over regions to obtain final counts. While effective for specific domains like crowd counting, these methods typically require category-specific training and struggle with novel object types. More recent work has explored few-shot and zero-shot counting scenarios. \citet{lu2018class} introduced class-agnostic counting by learning generic object detection features, while \citet{laradji2018blobs} proposed blob detection methods for biological image analysis. However, these approaches often rely on strong assumptions about object appearance or require additional supervision during training. The development of attention mechanisms has significantly advanced one-shot counting capabilities. \citet{cholakkal2019object} introduced spatial attention for localizing objects based on exemplar similarity, while \citet{wang2020learning} proposed multi-scale attention networks that can handle objects at different scales. These attention-based approaches have shown promising results but often struggle with complex backgrounds and significant appearance variations. Recent advances in contrastive learning have also influenced one-shot counting methods. \citet{hobley2022learning} demonstrated that contrastive pre-training can improve feature representations for counting tasks, while \citet{you2022class} explored prototype-based matching using contrastive embeddings. These methods show promise for learning more robust and generalizable features. \subsection{Our Contributions} In this work, we propose a novel architecture that addresses the key limitations of existing one-shot counting methods through several technical innovations: \begin{enumerate} \item We introduce a multi-scale feature pyramid network with cross-attention mechanisms that enables effective matching between exemplar and query features across different scales and spatial locations. \item We develop a prototype refinement module that iteratively updates exemplar representations based on high-confidence matches within the query image, improving robustness to appearance variations. \item We propose a contrastive learning framework specifically designed for counting tasks, which learns discriminative features by contrasting positive and negative object pairs during training. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across various object categories and challenging scenarios. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our proposed architecture and training methodology, Section~\ref{sec:experiments} provides detailed experimental evaluation and analysis, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with discussion of limitations and future directions.

text: Recommendation systems have been extensively applied in online platforms nowadays, e.g., Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS} and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. These platforms rely heavily on understanding user behavior patterns to deliver personalized content and maintain user engagement. The evolution from simple collaborative filtering approaches to sophisticated deep learning models has transformed how recommendation systems operate, with sequential recommendation emerging as a particularly crucial paradigm \cite{hidasi2015session, tan2016improved}. Sequential recommendation systems aim to predict the next item a user will interact with based on their historical sequence of interactions. Unlike traditional recommendation approaches that treat user preferences as static, sequential methods explicitly model the temporal dynamics of user behavior \cite{rendle2010factorizing}. This temporal modeling capability makes sequential recommendation particularly valuable for applications where user interests evolve over time, such as e-commerce, streaming services, and social media platforms. The fundamental assumption underlying sequential recommendation is that user preferences exhibit both consistency and evolution over time. While users maintain certain long-term interests, their immediate preferences are heavily influenced by recent interactions and contextual factors \cite{quadrana2018sequence}. For instance, a user's music listening behavior might reflect both their general taste for specific genres and their current mood or activity. Capturing this dual nature of user preferences represents one of the core challenges in sequential recommendation. Early sequential recommendation methods primarily relied on Markov chains and matrix factorization techniques \cite{rendle2010factorizing, he2016fusing}. These approaches, while computationally efficient, suffered from limited modeling capacity and struggled to capture complex long-term dependencies in user sequences. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized this field, with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants becoming the dominant paradigm for sequential modeling \cite{hidasi2015session, tan2016improved}. More recently, attention-based models, particularly transformer architectures, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in sequential recommendation tasks \cite{kang2018self, sun2019bert4rec}. These models excel at capturing both local and global patterns in user sequences through self-attention mechanisms. The SASRec model \cite{kang2018self} demonstrated that self-attention could effectively model user behavior sequences without the computational burden of recurrent architectures. Similarly, BERT4Rec \cite{sun2019bert4rec} adapted the bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) framework for recommendation tasks, achieving remarkable improvements in recommendation accuracy. Despite these advances, several critical challenges persist in sequential recommendation research. The cold-start problem remains a significant obstacle, particularly for new users with minimal interaction history or new items with limited user engagement \cite{schein2002methods}. Traditional sequential models require sufficient historical data to learn meaningful user representations, making them ineffective for scenarios with sparse interaction data. The scalability challenge poses another major concern. As user sequences grow longer and datasets become larger, the computational complexity of processing these sequences increases dramatically \cite{hidasi2015session}. This scalability issue is particularly problematic for real-time recommendation systems that must provide instant responses to user queries. The quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms in transformer-based models exacerbates this problem, making them computationally prohibitive for very long sequences. Data sparsity represents an additional fundamental challenge in sequential recommendation. Real-world user-item interaction data is typically highly sparse, with most users interacting with only a small fraction of available items \cite{su2009survey}. This sparsity makes it difficult for models to learn robust representations and often leads to overfitting on limited training data. The problem becomes more severe in domains with large item catalogs, where the majority of items receive minimal user interactions. The temporal dynamics of user preferences add another layer of complexity to sequential recommendation. User interests naturally evolve over time, influenced by factors such as seasonal trends, life events, and changing personal circumstances \cite{tang2018personalized}. However, most existing models struggle to distinguish between temporary interest shifts and permanent preference changes, often treating all temporal variations with equal importance. Moreover, the evaluation of sequential recommendation systems presents unique challenges. Traditional offline evaluation metrics, while useful for model comparison, may not accurately reflect real-world performance \cite{rossetti2016contrasting}. The temporal nature of sequential data requires careful consideration of evaluation protocols, including proper train-test splits that respect temporal ordering and metrics that capture the dynamic aspects of user behavior. The integration of contextual information represents another important consideration in sequential recommendation. User behavior is influenced by various contextual factors, including time of day, device type, location, and social context \cite{adomavicius2011context}. Incorporating these contextual signals into sequential models can significantly improve recommendation quality but also increases model complexity and computational requirements. Recent research has begun addressing these challenges through various innovative approaches. Multi-task learning frameworks have been proposed to jointly optimize for multiple recommendation objectives, potentially improving model robustness and generalization \cite{ma2018entire}. Graph neural networks have shown promise in leveraging auxiliary information and capturing complex user-item relationships beyond sequential interactions \cite{wu2019session, xu2019graph}. Furthermore, the emergence of large language models and foundation models has opened new possibilities for sequential recommendation. These models, pre-trained on vast amounts of textual data, can potentially provide better item representations and handle cold-start scenarios more effectively \cite{geng2022recommendation}. However, adapting these models for recommendation tasks while maintaining computational efficiency remains an active area of research. This paper addresses several of these fundamental challenges in sequential recommendation through a novel approach that combines the strengths of existing methods while mitigating their limitations. Our contributions focus on improving model scalability, handling data sparsity, and better capturing temporal dynamics in user behavior patterns.

In spite of these achievements, there are still some critical problems in the field of recommendation. Recently, attention-based models, especially transformer-based architectures, have achieved outstanding performance in the field of recommendation, such as Kang and Sun's self-referential recommendations (Kang, 2018 and Sun, 2019). These models are good at capturing local and global patterns of sequences of users through attention mechanisms. The cold start problem is a major challenge, especially for new users with few interaction histories and new items with little attention. The scalability problem is another major challenge. For example, the self-attention-based SASRec model [Kang et al., 2018] effectively models the sequential behavior of users without using a recurrent architecture. Similarly, BERT4Rec [Sun et al., 2019] adapted the BERT framework to recommender tasks and achieved remarkable results. The scalability problem is a significant one. As the length of the sequences and the size of the data increases, the computational complexity of processing them increases dramatically. This problem is especially troublesome for real-time recommendation systems, which must answer a query in real time. Real world item-user interactions are sparse, with most users interacting with only a small fraction of available items. This sparsity makes it difficult for models to learn robust representations and often leads to overfitting of the available training data. The quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms in transformer-based models exacerbates this problem, and they become prohibitively complex for long sequences. The dynamic nature of the users’ preferences adds another layer of complexity to the recommendation of subsequent items, because the preferences of the users naturally change with time, influenced by seasonal trends, life events, and personal circumstances. The problem is further complicated in large libraries of items, in which the majority of the items have little or no interaction with each other. The problem is further complicated by the difficulty of evaluating the performance of sequential recommendation systems, where the traditional metrics used for model comparison are not necessarily indicative of real-world performance. Apart from the consideration of temporal data, another important aspect of sequential recommendation is the consideration of context. The behavior of the user is influenced by many contextual factors such as time, device, location, and social context. However, most existing models do not distinguish between temporary interest changes and permanent preference changes, but treat all temporal variations as the same. These contextual signals, if they are incorporated into sequential models, can greatly improve the quality of recommendations, but also increase the complexity of the model and the processing requirements. The temporal nature of the data also requires evaluation of a special kind, with the train-test split observing the temporal order and the metrics capturing the dynamic aspects of behavior. Multi-Task learning frameworks have been proposed to optimize multiple recommendation objectives simultaneously, which may potentially improve model robustness and generalization. These two difficulties have been addressed in recent research through various creative methods. Recent developments in large-scale language models and deep learning have also opened up new horizons for sequential recommendation. These models, which have been pre-trained on a large amount of textual data, may provide more accurate representations of the items and perform better when they start cold. text: Security researchers regularly find serious security flaws in critical components, even those with years of scrutiny and widespread deployment. For example, the Heartbleed vulnerability in OpenSSL~\cite{heartbleed2014} exposed millions of systems to potential data breaches, while the recent discovery of memory safety issues in widely-used C libraries demonstrates that traditional testing and code review are insufficient for ensuring correctness~\cite{miller2019security}. These incidents underscore the critical need for more rigorous approaches to software verification, particularly for security-critical components that form the foundation of modern computing infrastructure. The challenge becomes even more pronounced when considering the increasing complexity of modern software systems. Contemporary applications rely on intricate interactions between multiple layers of abstraction, from hardware interfaces and operating system kernels to network protocols and cryptographic libraries. Each layer introduces potential vulnerabilities, and the composition of these layers can create emergent security properties that are difficult to reason about using conventional analysis techniques~\cite{anderson2020security}. Formal verification offers a principled solution to these challenges by providing mathematical certainty about program behavior. Unlike testing, which can only demonstrate the presence of bugs rather than their absence, formal verification can prove that a program satisfies its specification under all possible execution scenarios. This level of assurance is particularly valuable for security-critical systems where even rare edge cases can have catastrophic consequences~\cite{wing2010trustworthy}. However, the practical application of formal verification to real-world systems faces several fundamental obstacles. First, the specification problem requires developers to precisely articulate what their programs should do, which is often more challenging than implementing the programs themselves~\cite{lamport2019specifying}. Incomplete or incorrect specifications can lead to formally verified programs that nonetheless fail to meet their intended requirements. Second, the scalability problem arises from the exponential growth in verification complexity as system size increases, making it impractical to verify large codebases using current techniques~\cite{clarke2018handbook}. Third, the abstraction gap between mathematical models used in verification and actual implementations running on real hardware can introduce discrepancies that compromise correctness guarantees~\cite{kumar2014cakeml}. Even perfectly verified high-level code may exhibit unexpected behavior when compiled to machine code or executed on processors with complex microarchitectural features such as speculative execution and caching. Recent developments in automated verification techniques show promise for addressing these limitations. Bounded model checking~\cite{biere2009bounded} can efficiently explore finite state spaces to find bugs or prove correctness within specified bounds. Symbolic execution~\cite{king1976symbolic} systematically explores program paths by treating inputs as symbolic variables, enabling the discovery of subtle bugs that traditional testing might miss. Abstract interpretation~\cite{cousot1977abstract} provides a framework for computing safe approximations of program behavior, allowing verification tools to reason about infinite state spaces. Machine learning techniques are also beginning to impact formal verification. Neural networks have shown promise in automatically generating loop invariants~\cite{si2018learning}, predicting proof strategies~\cite{bansal2019holist}, and synthesizing program specifications from examples~\cite{padhi2016data}. These approaches could significantly reduce the manual effort required for verification while improving the quality of specifications and proofs. The integration of verification into the software development lifecycle represents another important research direction. Rather than treating verification as a post-hoc activity, emerging approaches embed formal reasoning directly into programming languages and development tools~\cite{leino2010dafny}. This integration can provide immediate feedback to developers and catch errors early in the development process when they are less expensive to fix. \subsection{Contributions} This paper makes several key contributions to the field of automated software verification: \begin{enumerate} \item We present a novel verification framework that combines symbolic execution with machine learning-guided proof search to automatically verify security properties of cryptographic implementations. \item We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a comprehensive benchmark suite including implementations of AES, RSA, and elliptic curve cryptography, achieving verification times that are orders of magnitude faster than existing approaches. \item We provide a detailed analysis of the trade-offs between verification completeness and computational efficiency, offering practical guidance for applying automated verification to real-world systems. \item We release our verification toolchain as open-source software, enabling researchers and practitioners to reproduce our results and extend our techniques to new domains. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides background on formal verification techniques and their application to cryptographic software. Section~\ref{sec:approach} describes our automated verification framework in detail. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Section~\ref{sec:related} discusses related work, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with directions for future research.

text: Robots are increasingly operating in environments where they must interact with humans, such as collaborative grasping~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} and autonomous driving~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}. As these applications become more prevalent, ensuring safe human-robot interaction has emerged as a fundamental challenge that spans multiple research domains including robotics, machine learning, and human factors engineering \cite{goodrich2007human, steinfeld2006common}. The complexity of this challenge is amplified by the inherent unpredictability of human behavior, the dynamic nature of shared environments, and the need for robots to make real-time decisions under uncertainty \cite{kaber2006issues}. Traditional approaches to robot safety have predominantly focused on physical separation between humans and robots, utilizing safety barriers, light curtains, and emergency stop mechanisms \cite{ISO10218}. While effective in controlled industrial settings, these methods are inadequate for collaborative scenarios where humans and robots must work in close proximity to achieve common goals \cite{bauer2008human}. The paradigm shift towards collaborative robotics necessitates a more nuanced understanding of safety that encompasses not only the prevention of physical harm but also the optimization of task performance and user experience \cite{colgate2003cobots}. One of the primary difficulties in developing safe human-robot interaction systems lies in the multi-modal nature of human communication and behavior. Humans convey intentions through verbal communication, gestures, facial expressions, and body language, creating a rich but complex information space that robots must interpret accurately to ensure safe operation \cite{breazeal2016social, hoffman2019evaluating}. Misinterpretation of human intentions can lead to unsafe situations, ranging from minor inefficiencies to potentially dangerous collisions or system failures \cite{lasota2017survey}. The temporal dynamics of human-robot interaction further complicate safety considerations. Unlike static safety assessments, interactive scenarios require continuous monitoring and adaptation to changing conditions. Human attention levels fluctuate, environmental conditions vary, and task requirements evolve dynamically \cite{admoni2017social}. Consequently, safety mechanisms must be capable of real-time adaptation while maintaining robust performance guarantees across diverse operational scenarios \cite{fisac2018general}. Recent developments in sensor technology and computational capabilities have enabled more sophisticated approaches to safety in human-robot interaction. Vision-based systems can track human pose and predict motion trajectories \cite{rudenko2020human}, while force and torque sensors enable robots to detect and respond to unexpected contact \cite{haddadin2017robot}. However, the integration of multiple sensing modalities introduces new challenges related to sensor fusion, computational complexity, and system reliability \cite{chen2020deep}. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep reinforcement learning and imitation learning, have shown promise in developing adaptive safety behaviors \cite{garcia2015comprehensive, liu2021safe}. These methods can potentially learn complex safety policies from demonstration data or through interaction with simulated environments. However, the black-box nature of many machine learning algorithms raises concerns about interpretability and verification in safety-critical applications \cite{amodei2016concrete}. The verification and validation of learning-based safety systems presents unique challenges compared to traditional control systems. Standard formal verification techniques may not be directly applicable to neural networks and other machine learning models \cite{katz2017reluplex}. New methodologies for safety analysis, including statistical guarantees and distributional robustness, are being developed to address these limitations \cite{berkenkamp2017safe}. Furthermore, the definition of safety itself varies significantly across different application domains and cultural contexts. In healthcare robotics, safety encompasses not only physical harm prevention but also patient privacy, data security, and clinical efficacy \cite{taylor2016medical}. In autonomous driving, safety considerations extend to all road users and must account for complex traffic scenarios and regulatory requirements \cite{koopman2016challenges}. These domain-specific requirements necessitate flexible safety frameworks that can be adapted to diverse operational contexts. The psychological aspects of safety in human-robot interaction are often overlooked but equally important. User acceptance and trust in robotic systems are closely linked to perceived safety, which may not always align with objective safety metrics \cite{hancock2011meta}. Understanding and addressing these perceptual factors is crucial for the successful deployment of interactive robotic systems in real-world applications \cite{schaefer2016meta}. This paper addresses these multifaceted challenges by proposing a comprehensive framework for safe human-robot interaction that integrates adaptive learning mechanisms with formal safety guarantees. Our approach combines real-time human behavior prediction with constrained optimization techniques to ensure both safety and task performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive simulation studies and real-world experiments across multiple application domains, showing significant improvements in both safety metrics and user satisfaction compared to existing approaches.
