text: The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse for a multitude of differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. However, the Gaussian mechanism produces continuous-valued noise, which can be problematic in scenarios requiring discrete outputs or when dealing with integer-valued queries. This limitation has motivated the development of discrete differential privacy mechanisms that preserve the integer nature of the data while providing rigorous privacy guarantees. The discrete Laplace mechanism \cite{ghosh2012universally} was among the first to address this need, but it suffers from several drawbacks including limited tail behavior control and suboptimal utility for certain query types. More recently, researchers have explored alternative discrete mechanisms, including the discrete Gaussian \cite{canonne2020discrete} and geometric mechanisms \cite{ghosh2012universally}, each with their own trade-offs between privacy, utility, and computational efficiency. In this work, we propose the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism as a novel approach to discrete differential privacy. The Skellam distribution, originally introduced by Skellam \cite{skellam1946frequency} as the distribution of the difference between two independent Poisson random variables, offers several attractive properties for privacy-preserving applications. Unlike the discrete Laplace distribution, the Skellam distribution exhibits symmetric behavior around zero and provides natural parameter tuning through its underlying Poisson components. Our main contributions are threefold. First, we develop a comprehensive privacy analysis framework for the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism, deriving exact expressions for the privacy loss function and establishing tight bounds on the privacy parameters $(\varepsilon, \delta)$. Second, we demonstrate that our mechanism achieves superior utility compared to existing discrete mechanisms across a range of query types, particularly for counting queries and histogram releases. Third, we provide efficient sampling algorithms and implementation strategies that make our mechanism practically viable for large-scale applications. The theoretical foundation of our work builds upon recent advances in the analysis of discrete privacy mechanisms. We leverage tools from probability theory, particularly the properties of modified Bessel functions and their asymptotic behavior, to characterize the privacy guarantees of our mechanism. The parameters $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ control the privacy level, with smaller values providing stronger privacy guarantees. text: Given that machine learning has achieved super-human performance in image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and games \citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, the question arises why we do not see similar results in robotics. The answer lies in the fundamental differences between these domains and the unique challenges that robotics presents. Unlike image classification tasks that operate on static datasets with well-defined ground truth labels, or games with deterministic rules and perfect state information, robotics involves continuous interaction with dynamic, unpredictable environments where the cost of failure can be substantial \cite{kober2013reinforcement}. The primary obstacle is the \textit{embodiment problem} -- the fact that robotic systems must physically interact with the world through imperfect sensors and actuators, subject to mechanical constraints, latency, and noise \cite{brooks1991intelligence}. This creates a complex feedback loop where small errors in perception or control can compound rapidly, leading to catastrophic failures. Moreover, the high dimensionality of robotic state and action spaces, combined with the need for real-time decision making, makes direct application of traditional machine learning approaches challenging \cite{deisenroth2013survey}. Data collection represents another critical bottleneck. While computer vision and game-playing algorithms can leverage massive datasets or generate unlimited training examples through simulation, robotics requires expensive hardware, careful experimental setup, and significant human supervision. A single robotic manipulation experiment might take minutes to complete, compared to millions of game states that can be processed in the same timeframe \cite{levine2018learning}. This data scarcity is exacerbated by the fact that robotic tasks often require learning from sparse rewards and dealing with partial observability, making sample-efficient learning essential but difficult to achieve. The \textit{reality gap} further complicates matters. While simulators have become increasingly sophisticated, they still struggle to capture the full complexity of real-world physics, including factors such as friction, deformation, contact dynamics, and sensor characteristics \cite{collins2021review}. Policies trained in simulation often exhibit brittle behavior when deployed on real systems, as they exploit simulator-specific artifacts that do not exist in reality. This phenomenon, known as \textit{simulation optimization bias}, leads to overconfident policies that fail gracefully when confronted with distribution shifts between simulated and real environments \cite{zhang2021learning}. Furthermore, robotics involves safety-critical applications where exploration must be constrained to prevent damage to equipment or harm to humans. This requirement for \textit{safe exploration} fundamentally limits the types of learning algorithms that can be applied, ruling out many of the aggressive exploration strategies that have proven successful in other domains \cite{garcia2015comprehensive}. The need to maintain safety while learning creates a tension between exploitation of known safe behaviors and exploration of potentially better but risky actions. The temporal dimension adds another layer of complexity. Robotic tasks often involve long-horizon planning and sequential decision making, where actions taken early in a trajectory can have consequences that only become apparent much later. This credit assignment problem is particularly challenging in robotics, where the mapping between actions and outcomes may be obscured by complex dynamics and environmental factors \cite{sutton2018reinforcement}. Despite these challenges, recent years have witnessed significant progress in robotic learning through several key innovations. \textit{Sim-to-real transfer} techniques have emerged as a promising approach to leverage simulation for training while ensuring robust deployment in real environments. Domain randomization systematically varies simulation parameters during training to expose policies to a wide range of conditions, promoting generalization \cite{tobin2017domain}. Progressive approaches start with simplified scenarios and gradually increase complexity, allowing policies to build robust foundations before tackling more challenging tasks \cite{florensa2017reverse}. \textit{Meta-learning} and \textit{few-shot adaptation} methods have shown promise in enabling robots to quickly adapt to new tasks or environments with minimal additional data \cite{finn2017model}. By learning general principles that transfer across tasks, these approaches can overcome the sample efficiency limitations that have traditionally plagued robotic learning. The integration of \textit{model-based approaches} with deep learning has also yielded significant advances. By learning explicit models of system dynamics, robots can perform mental simulation and planning, reducing the need for extensive real-world interaction \cite{nagabandi2018neural}. Hybrid approaches that combine model-free and model-based elements have shown particular promise in balancing sample efficiency with asymptotic performance. This work contributes to addressing these fundamental challenges by proposing a novel framework that tackles simulation optimization bias through adaptive domain randomization coupled with uncertainty quantification. Our approach recognizes that the key to successful sim-to-real transfer lies not just in exposing policies to diverse conditions, but in explicitly modeling and managing the uncertainty inherent in the transfer process.

text: We aim to solve a fundamental problem in statistical inference---mean estimation---under minimal assumptions. Formally, we seek the tightest confidence interval (up to constants) for the unknown mean $\mu$ when the underlying distribution has heavy tails and infinite variance. \subsection{Problem Formulation and Motivation} Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables from a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ with mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ and infinite second moment. We consider the following regularity condition on the tail behavior: \begin{assumption}[Heavy-tailed condition] There exist constants $\alpha \in (1, 2)$, $C_1, C_2 > 0$, and $t_0 > 0$ such that for all $t \geq t_0$: \begin{equation} C_1 t^{-\alpha} \leq \mathbb{P}(|X_1 - \mu| > t) \leq C_2 t^{-\alpha}. \end{equation} \end{assumption} This assumption captures the essence of heavy-tailed behavior while being sufficiently general to encompass many important distribution families. The parameter $\alpha$ characterizes the tail decay rate, with smaller values of $\alpha$ corresponding to heavier tails. When $\alpha \in (1, 2)$, the first moment exists but the second moment is infinite, creating a challenging regime for statistical inference. The motivation for studying this problem stems from numerous applications where heavy-tailed phenomena naturally arise. Financial returns often exhibit power-law tails with $\alpha$ close to 2 \cite{mandelbrot1963variation}, while network traffic and web page sizes frequently display even heavier tails with $\alpha$ between 1 and 2 \cite{crovella1997self}. In such contexts, classical statistical methods based on finite variance assumptions can lead to severely misleading conclusions. \subsection{Main Results and Contributions} Our primary theoretical contribution establishes the minimax optimal rate for mean estimation under Assumption \ref{ass:heavy_tail}. We prove both matching upper and lower bounds, thereby completely characterizing the fundamental limits of statistical inference in this heavy-tailed regime. \begin{theorem}[Minimax rate] Under Assumption \ref{ass:heavy_tail}, the minimax risk for mean estimation satisfies \begin{equation} \inf_{\hat{\mu}_n} \sup_{\mathcal{D}} \mathbb{E}[|\hat{\mu}_n - \mu|] \asymp n^{-1/\alpha}, \end{equation} where the infimum is taken over all measurable estimators $\hat{\mu}_n$ and the supremum is over all distributions satisfying Assumption \ref{ass:heavy_tail}. \end{theorem} The proof of the upper bound relies on a carefully constructed truncated mean estimator, while the lower bound employs a sophisticated two-point testing argument that exploits the heavy-tailed nature of the distributions. Beyond establishing the optimal rate, we provide several practical estimators that achieve this rate up to logarithmic factors. Our main algorithmic contribution is the \emph{adaptive truncated mean} (ATM) estimator: \begin{definition}[Adaptive Truncated Mean] Given observations $X_1, \ldots, X_n$, the adaptive truncated mean estimator is defined as \begin{equation} \hat{\mu}_{\text{ATM}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \mathbf{1}_{|X_i| \leq \tau_n}, \end{equation} where the truncation threshold $\tau_n$ is chosen adaptively based on the empirical tail behavior: \begin{equation} \tau_n = \inf\left\{t > 0 : \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}_{|X_i| > t} \leq \frac{(\log n)^2}{n^{1/2}}\right\}. \end{equation} \end{definition} \begin{theorem}[Performance of ATM estimator] Under Assumption \ref{ass:heavy_tail}, the adaptive truncated mean estimator satisfies \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}[|\hat{\mu}_{\text{ATM}} - \mu|] \leq C(\alpha) \cdot (\log n)^{2} \cdot n^{-1/\alpha} \end{equation} for some constant $C(\alpha)$ depending only on $\alpha$. \end{theorem} The ATM estimator is particularly appealing because it does not require prior knowledge of the tail parameter $\alpha$ or the tail constants $C_1, C_2$. The adaptive threshold selection mechanism automatically adjusts to the observed tail behavior, making the method broadly applicable in practice. \subsection{Technical Challenges and Innovations} The heavy-tailed setting presents several fundamental challenges that distinguish our work from classical mean estimation theory: \textbf{Lack of concentration inequalities:} Standard concentration results like Hoeffding's inequality require bounded support or finite moments. In our setting, we must develop new probabilistic tools that can handle the heavy-tailed behavior directly. \textbf{Bias-variance tradeoff:} Truncation-based estimators introduce a systematic bias by discarding extreme observations, but this bias must be carefully balanced against the reduction in variance. Our analysis reveals the precise nature of this tradeoff in the heavy-tailed regime. \textbf{Adaptive parameter selection:} The optimal truncation threshold depends on unknown population parameters. We develop a data-driven selection mechanism that achieves near-optimal performance without prior knowledge of these parameters. To address these challenges, we introduce several novel technical innovations: 1. \emph{Refined tail probability bounds:} We establish sharp concentration inequalities for truncated sums under heavy-tailed conditions, extending classical results to our setting. 2. \emph{Uniform convergence theory:} Our analysis of the adaptive threshold selection requires uniform convergence results for empirical tail probabilities, which we establish using sophisticated empirical process theory. 3. \emph{Two-point testing lower bounds:} The minimax lower bound construction requires a delicate choice of alternative distributions that are both sufficiently separated and satisfy the heavy-tailed assumption. \subsection{Related Work and Positioning} The problem of robust mean estimation has a rich history in statistics, with connections to several related areas: \textbf{Robust statistics:} The field of robust statistics, pioneered by \cite{huber1964robust}, studies estimators that perform well under model misspecification. Our work contributes to this literature by focusing specifically on heavy-tailed deviations from normality. \textbf{Stable distributions:} Symmetric $\alpha$-stable distributions represent a canonical class of heavy-tailed distributions with infinite variance. Previous work by \cite{nolan2020univariate} studied parameter estimation for stable distributions, but did not establish minimax optimality results. \textbf{Extreme value theory:} Our truncation-based approach has connections to extreme value theory and the study of tail behavior. The work of \cite{hill1975simple} on tail index estimation provides important background for our adaptive procedures. \textbf{High-dimensional robust estimation:} Recent advances in high-dimensional robust estimation \cite{lugosi2019mean} have focused on settings with bounded second moments. Our work extends these ideas to the more challenging infinite variance regime. The key distinction of our work is the focus on establishing fundamental limits (minimax rates) rather than just proposing estimators. This theoretical perspective provides important insights into the inherent difficulty of the heavy-tailed mean estimation problem. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:preliminaries} establishes notation and reviews relevant background material. Section \ref{sec:upper_bounds} presents our main algorithmic contributions and establishes upper bounds on the estimation error. Section \ref{sec:lower_bounds} develops the minimax lower bound through a careful information-theoretic analysis. Section \ref{sec:simulations} provides extensive numerical experiments validating our theoretical predictions. Section \ref{sec:extensions} discusses extensions to related problems including confidence interval construction and multi-dimensional settings. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with a discussion of open problems and future directions.

text: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to make predictions on privacy-sensitive data. Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to make predictions on privacy-sensitive data. From healthcare diagnostics to financial risk assessment, ML models are trained on datasets containing personal information that individuals expect to remain confidential. While these applications offer tremendous societal benefits, they also introduce novel privacy risks that extend beyond traditional data protection concerns \cite{fredrikson2015model}. The fundamental challenge lies in the inherent nature of machine learning algorithms, which must extract patterns from training data to make accurate predictions. This learning process inevitably creates a form of "memory" within the model parameters, where information about individual training samples can become embedded in ways that may be recoverable through carefully crafted attacks \cite{carlini2019secret}. Unlike traditional database systems where access controls can provide clear boundaries between authorized and unauthorized data access, ML models present a more complex privacy landscape where the boundary between legitimate inference and privacy violation is often unclear. Membership inference attacks represent one of the most fundamental privacy threats in this landscape. These attacks exploit the observation that ML models typically exhibit higher confidence when making predictions on data points that were part of their training set compared to unseen data \cite{shokri2017membership}. An adversary with access to a trained model can leverage this differential behavior to infer whether a specific individual's data was used during training, even without direct access to the training dataset itself. The implications of successful membership inference attacks extend far beyond academic curiosity. In healthcare settings, determining that a patient's record was used to train a disease prediction model could reveal sensitive medical conditions \cite{homer2008resolving}. In financial applications, membership inference could expose an individual's participation in datasets related to loan defaults or credit assessments. Even in seemingly benign applications like recommendation systems, membership inference can reveal personal preferences and behaviors that individuals prefer to keep private \cite{backstrom2007wherefore}. Recent research has demonstrated that membership inference vulnerabilities are not limited to obviously overfitted models. Even well-regularized models that achieve good generalization performance can still leak membership information through subtle differences in their prediction patterns \cite{yeom2018privacy, nasr2019comprehensive}. This finding challenges the conventional wisdom that good generalization necessarily implies strong privacy protection, highlighting the need for more sophisticated privacy-preserving techniques. The landscape of membership inference attacks has evolved significantly since their initial introduction. Early attacks relied primarily on confidence-based metrics, comparing the model's prediction confidence on target samples against reference distributions \cite{shokri2017membership}. However, more recent work has introduced increasingly sophisticated attack methodologies, including metric-based attacks that leverage multiple statistical properties of model predictions \cite{nasr2019comprehensive}, model-based attacks that train dedicated classifiers to distinguish between member and non-member samples \cite{salem2019ml}, and label-only attacks that require minimal information about the target model \cite{choquette2021label}. The effectiveness of these attacks varies significantly across different model architectures, training procedures, and application domains. Generative models, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs), have shown particular vulnerability to membership inference due to their explicit goal of modeling the training data distribution \cite{hayes2019logan, hilprecht2019monte}. Similarly, models trained on small datasets or those with high-dimensional input spaces often exhibit increased susceptibility to membership inference attacks \cite{song2019auditing}. Defense mechanisms against membership inference attacks have emerged along multiple dimensions. Differential privacy \cite{dwork2006calibrating} provides theoretical guarantees by adding carefully calibrated noise to the training process, ensuring that the presence or absence of any individual record has minimal impact on the model's output. However, achieving meaningful privacy guarantees through differential privacy often requires substantial noise injection, which can significantly degrade model utility \cite{abadi2016deep}. Alternative defense strategies focus on regularization techniques that reduce overfitting and minimize the memorization of individual training samples. These include traditional approaches like dropout and weight decay, as well as more specialized techniques such as knowledge distillation \cite{papernot2016semi} and adversarial regularization \cite{nasr2018machine}. While these methods can provide some protection against membership inference, they typically offer no formal privacy guarantees and their effectiveness can vary unpredictably across different attack scenarios. More recent defensive approaches have explored adversarial training paradigms, where models are explicitly trained to resist membership inference attacks during the learning process \cite{jia2019memguard}. These methods treat privacy protection as an adversarial objective, simultaneously optimizing for prediction accuracy while minimizing the model's vulnerability to membership inference. However, such approaches face the fundamental challenge of defending against unknown future attacks, as adversaries may develop new attack strategies that circumvent existing defenses. The evaluation of both attacks and defenses in the membership inference domain presents significant methodological challenges. Standard evaluation protocols must carefully consider factors such as the adversary's background knowledge, the availability of auxiliary data, and the specific threat model under consideration \cite{jayaraman2019evaluating}. Furthermore, the privacy-utility trade-off inherent in most defense mechanisms requires careful measurement and reporting to enable meaningful comparisons between different approaches. This work contributes to the growing body of research on membership inference attacks and defenses by providing a comprehensive analysis of the fundamental factors that influence membership inference vulnerability. We present novel theoretical insights into the relationship between model memorization and membership inference risk, develop improved attack methodologies that achieve higher accuracy with minimal adversarial knowledge, and propose defense mechanisms that offer better privacy-utility trade-offs than existing approaches. Our contributions are organized as follows: First, we provide a theoretical framework for understanding membership inference vulnerability in terms of the statistical properties of model predictions. Second, we introduce enhanced attack algorithms that leverage ensemble methods and advanced statistical techniques to improve inference accuracy. Third, we develop novel defense mechanisms based on adaptive noise injection and regularization techniques that maintain model utility while providing stronger privacy protection. Finally, we present comprehensive experimental evaluations across multiple datasets and model architectures, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed methods and providing insights into the factors that most significantly influence membership inference risk.

text: Confidence intervals are a common tool to summarize the underlying distribution, and to indicate outlier behaviour. When dealing with time series data, the construction of confidence intervals becomes more complex due to the temporal dependence structure inherent in such data. Traditional pointwise confidence intervals, while useful for individual time points, fail to account for the correlation between observations at different times. This limitation becomes particularly problematic when researchers need to make simultaneous inferences across multiple time points or identify periods where the observed values deviate significantly from expected patterns. The challenge of multiple comparisons in time series analysis has led to the development of simultaneous confidence bands, which provide a unified framework for uncertainty quantification across the entire time domain. These bands are designed to maintain a specified coverage probability for the entire trajectory, rather than at individual points. The distinction between pointwise and simultaneous inference is crucial: while pointwise intervals may suggest significance at individual time points, simultaneous bands provide a more rigorous assessment of whether observed deviations are truly meaningful when considered across the entire time series. Several methodological approaches have been developed to construct simultaneous confidence bands for time series data. The choice of method depends critically on the assumed dependence structure of the underlying process. For stationary Gaussian processes, asymptotic results based on extreme value theory provide a foundation for band construction \cite{adler2007random}. These methods exploit the fact that, under regularity conditions, the maximum of a standardized Gaussian process converges to a Gumbel distribution. For non-stationary processes or when the Gaussian assumption is questionable, bootstrap-based methods offer a more flexible alternative \cite{efron1993introduction}. The bootstrap approach involves resampling the residuals or blocks of observations to generate empirical distributions of the test statistics under the null hypothesis. This resampling framework can accommodate various forms of dependence and non-normality, making it particularly valuable for practical applications where model assumptions may be violated. Another important consideration in confidence band construction is the specification of the null hypothesis. In many applications, researchers are interested in testing whether the mean function follows a particular parametric form, such as a linear trend or periodic pattern. The bands can then be constructed to test deviations from this specified model, providing a visual and statistical tool for model validation. The width of simultaneous confidence bands is necessarily larger than that of pointwise intervals, reflecting the penalty for multiple testing. The magnitude of this penalty depends on several factors, including the length of the time series, the correlation structure of the data, and the desired confidence level. Understanding this trade-off is essential for practitioners who must balance the need for comprehensive coverage against the desire for precise inference. Recent developments in the field have focused on adaptive methods that can automatically adjust the band width based on local characteristics of the data \cite{hall2013methodology}. These approaches recognize that the uncertainty may vary across different regions of the time series, leading to bands that are narrower in periods of high predictability and wider during periods of increased volatility or model uncertainty.

text: As the adoption of autonomous robotic systems increases around us, there is a need for the controllers driving them to exhibit the level of sophistication required to operate in complex, unstructured environments. Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for developing such sophisticated control policies, demonstrating remarkable success in simulated environments across various robotic tasks \cite{schulman2017proximal, haarnoja2018soft}. However, the transition from simulation to real-world deployment remains a significant challenge, particularly when considering the safety and reliability requirements of autonomous systems operating in human-centric environments. The fundamental issue lies in the inherent uncertainty and variability present in real-world scenarios that are difficult to capture accurately in simulation. Physical systems exhibit complex dynamics that may deviate from their modeled counterparts due to manufacturing tolerances, wear and tear, environmental conditions, and unmodeled phenomena \cite{garcia2015comprehensive}. Moreover, sensor measurements are subject to noise, calibration errors, and occasional failures that can significantly impact policy performance \cite{kober2013reinforcement}. Current approaches to address these challenges can be broadly categorized into three main strategies. First, \emph{domain randomization} methods seek to expose the learning agent to a wide variety of simulation conditions during training, with the hope that the resulting policy will generalize to real-world variations \cite{tobin2017domain, peng2018sim}. While effective in certain scenarios, these approaches often suffer from the \emph{reality gap} problem, where the randomization distribution fails to adequately represent real-world conditions, leading to either insufficient robustness or overly conservative policies. Second, \emph{domain adaptation} techniques attempt to bridge the sim-to-real gap by leveraging limited real-world data to adapt simulation-trained policies \cite{tzeng2017adversarial, bousmalis2018using}. These methods typically employ adversarial training or other transfer learning techniques to align the feature representations between simulation and reality. However, they often require substantial amounts of real-world data and may not generalize well to unseen environmental conditions. Third, \emph{robust reinforcement learning} approaches explicitly account for uncertainty and distributional shifts during the learning process \cite{rajeswaran2017epopt, mankowitz2019robust}. These methods formulate the learning problem as a minimax optimization: \begin{equation} \max_{\pi} \min_{P \in \mathcal{U}} \mathbb{E}_{P}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T} \gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)\right] \end{equation} where $\mathcal{U}$ represents an uncertainty set of possible environment dynamics, and the policy $\pi$ is optimized to perform well under the worst-case scenario within this set. While theoretically appealing, these approaches often lead to overly conservative policies that sacrifice nominal performance for robustness. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines the strengths of these existing approaches while addressing their limitations. Our key insight is that rather than treating robustness and performance as competing objectives, we can leverage \emph{adaptive confidence estimation} to dynamically adjust the policy's behavior based on the perceived reliability of the current state estimate and environmental conditions. Specifically, we introduce the concept of \emph{confidence-aware policy execution}, where the policy maintains an estimate of its confidence in the current situation and adapts its behavior accordingly. When confidence is high, the policy can exploit its learned behaviors more aggressively to achieve optimal performance. Conversely, when confidence is low due to unfamiliar states, sensor anomalies, or environmental variations, the policy automatically transitions to more conservative, safety-oriented behaviors. Our framework, termed \emph{Confidence-Aware Robust Reinforcement Learning} (CARRL), makes the following key contributions: \begin{itemize} \item A novel confidence estimation mechanism that quantifies the reliability of policy decisions based on state familiarity, sensor quality, and environmental consistency \item An adaptive policy execution strategy that dynamically balances performance and safety based on real-time confidence assessments \item A training methodology that jointly optimizes for nominal performance and robust behavior under uncertainty \item Extensive experimental validation on both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing robust RL methods \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related_work} provides a comprehensive review of related work in robust reinforcement learning and sim-to-real transfer. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} presents our confidence-aware framework in detail, including the confidence estimation mechanism and adaptive policy execution strategy. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and presents results on various robotic tasks. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with a discussion of limitations and future research directions.

The physical system behaves in a complex way, deviating from the modeled system due to manufacturing tolerances, wear and tear, and external conditions. While effective in certain situations, these methods often suffer from the'reality gap' problem, where the randomization distribution fails to adequately represent the distribution of the real world, resulting in either insufficiently robust or overly conservative policies. The second method, domain adaptation, tries to close the gap between simulation and reality by using the data from the real world to adapt the simulation-trained policy. These methods usually use adversarial training or other transfer learning techniques to align the feature representations between simulation and reality. text: With the growing popularity of open-access academic article repositories, such as arXiv or bioRxiv, disseminating new research findings has become nearly effortless. However, this accessibility paradoxically creates new challenges for researchers attempting to stay current with developments in their fields. The sheer volume of publications—with arXiv alone receiving over 150,000 submissions annually—makes comprehensive literature review increasingly impractical for individual researchers \cite{larsen2010rate}. Traditional approaches to literature management, including manual curation and keyword-based search systems, fail to scale effectively with this exponential growth in scientific output. The problem is further compounded by the interdisciplinary nature of modern research, where breakthrough discoveries often emerge at the intersection of multiple domains \cite{uzzi2013atypical}. Researchers must therefore monitor publications across diverse fields, each with its own specialized terminology, methodological conventions, and publication patterns. This cross-domain complexity makes it difficult to identify relevant work using conventional search strategies, potentially leading to missed opportunities for collaboration or knowledge transfer. Moreover, the quality and relevance of scientific content vary significantly across publications. While peer review processes aim to maintain standards, the proliferation of preprint servers and predatory journals has introduced additional noise into the academic ecosystem \cite{bohannon2013who}. Researchers need sophisticated filtering mechanisms that can distinguish high-quality, relevant contributions from the broader corpus of available literature. Existing solutions for scientific literature management suffer from several limitations. Traditional bibliographic databases rely primarily on metadata-based search, which fails to capture semantic relationships between concepts \cite{chen2019scibert}. Recent advances in automated summarization have shown promise, but most systems focus on single-document processing rather than the multi-document synthesis required for comprehensive literature review \cite{el2021automatic}. Additionally, current approaches lack personalization capabilities, treating all users uniformly despite significant variations in research interests, expertise levels, and information needs. To address these challenges, we present \textsc{SciDigest}, a comprehensive framework for intelligent scientific literature analysis and personalized summarization. Our system combines state-of-the-art natural language processing techniques with domain-specific knowledge to provide researchers with relevant, high-quality summaries tailored to their individual needs. The key contributions of this work include: \begin{enumerate} \item A novel multi-granular summarization architecture that operates simultaneously at sentence, paragraph, and document levels to capture both fine-grained details and high-level concepts. \item An adaptive personalization mechanism that learns user preferences through both explicit feedback and implicit behavioral signals, enabling dynamic content filtering and ranking. \item A comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses summarization quality across multiple dimensions, including factual accuracy, coverage, coherence, and user satisfaction. \item Empirical demonstration of superior performance compared to existing baselines across diverse scientific domains, with particular emphasis on cross-disciplinary knowledge discovery. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews relevant work in automated summarization, scientific text processing, and personalization systems. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} details our proposed framework, including the multi-stage processing pipeline and personalization algorithms. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents comprehensive experimental results, while Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with directions for future research. Our approach represents a significant step toward addressing the information overload problem in scientific research, providing a scalable solution that can adapt to the evolving needs of the research community while maintaining high standards of accuracy and relevance.

text: Advances in deep neural networks over the past decade has allowed models to begin solving new tasks requiring information from more than modality. Visual Question Answering (VQA) represents one of the most prominent examples of such multimodal reasoning tasks, requiring models to comprehend both visual content from images and semantic information from natural language questions to produce accurate answers \cite{antol2015vqa, goyal2017making}. The complexity of VQA lies not merely in processing each modality independently, but in effectively fusing and reasoning over the interactions between visual and textual representations. Traditional approaches to multimodal fusion have relied on simple concatenation or element-wise operations, which often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between different modalities \cite{baltrusaitis2018multimodal}. These limitations become particularly apparent in VQA scenarios where answering questions requires understanding spatial relationships, object attributes, and contextual dependencies that span across visual and linguistic domains. For instance, answering "What color is the car on the left?" necessitates not only object detection and spatial reasoning in the visual domain but also grounding of linguistic concepts like "color," "car," and "left" to specific visual regions. Recent research has increasingly focused on attention mechanisms as a solution to these challenges. Visual attention models \cite{xu2015show, anderson2018bottom} have demonstrated remarkable success in image captioning tasks by learning to focus on relevant image regions when generating each word. Similarly, textual attention mechanisms \cite{bahdanau2014neural, luong2015effective} have proven effective in machine translation and other sequence-to-sequence tasks. The natural extension of these approaches to VQA has led to the development of co-attention mechanisms \cite{lu2016hierarchical, yu2017multi}, which aim to jointly attend to both visual and textual features. However, attention-based approaches, while effective, often treat multimodal fusion as a sequential or hierarchical process rather than capturing the inherent bilinear interactions between modalities. This limitation has motivated the development of bilinear pooling methods, which explicitly model pairwise interactions between all combinations of visual and textual features. The theoretical foundation of bilinear pooling rests on the assumption that meaningful multimodal representations emerge from the comprehensive exploration of feature interactions across modalities. The success of bilinear pooling in VQA has sparked interest in understanding its computational properties and developing more efficient variants. Low-rank bilinear pooling \cite{kim2016hadamard} addresses computational constraints by factorizing the bilinear transformation into lower-dimensional components, while Multimodal Low-rank Bilinear pooling (MLB) \cite{kim2016hadamard} further simplifies the operation through Hadamard products. These methods demonstrate that effective multimodal fusion can be achieved without the full computational overhead of complete bilinear expansions. Beyond computational efficiency, recent work has explored the interpretability and robustness of bilinear pooling methods. Analysis of learned bilinear transformations reveals that different regions of the bilinear space capture distinct types of visual-linguistic relationships \cite{cadene2019murel}. For example, certain bilinear features may specialize in color-object associations, while others focus on spatial or quantitative relationships. This specialization suggests that bilinear pooling not only improves performance but also provides a structured approach to multimodal reasoning. The evolution of bilinear pooling methods reflects broader trends in deep learning toward more sophisticated fusion mechanisms. While early VQA models treated visual and textual features as independent inputs to be combined at the final decision layer, contemporary approaches recognize that effective multimodal reasoning requires dense interactions throughout the network architecture. This shift has implications beyond VQA, influencing research in visual dialog \cite{das2017visual}, multimodal sentiment analysis \cite{zadeh2017tensor}, and embodied AI applications. Despite these advances, several challenges remain in bilinear pooling research. The quadratic scaling of computational complexity continues to limit the applicability of full bilinear methods to very high-dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, the interpretability of bilinear interactions, while improved compared to simple fusion methods, remains an active area of investigation. Understanding which types of visual-linguistic relationships are best captured by bilinear operations, and how these relationships generalize across different datasets and domains, represents an important direction for future research.

text: The task of question answering has benefited largely from the advancements in deep learning, especially from the pre-trained language models(LM)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating human-like text, leading to significant improvements across various NLP tasks including reading comprehension and QA systems \cite{rogers2020primer,qiu2020pre}. However, most existing QA benchmarks and models have been primarily evaluated on factual, encyclopedic content where answers can be directly extracted or inferred from relatively short passages \cite{rajpurkar2016squad,joshi2017triviaqa,kwiatkowski2019natural}. The unique challenges of narrative story comprehension present a different paradigm that requires models to engage with literary devices, understand character psychology, track complex plot developments, and make inferences about implicit story elements \cite{mostafazadeh2016corpus,chaturvedi2017story}. Stories often contain multiple interweaving plotlines, character arcs that span entire books, and subtle thematic elements that require deep contextual understanding to properly interpret. Additionally, the temporal structure of narratives, with flashbacks, foreshadowing, and non-linear storytelling techniques, adds layers of complexity that are rarely encountered in traditional QA tasks \cite{chambers2008unsupervised,modi2017event}. Recent work has begun to address some of these challenges through datasets like NarrativeQA \cite{kocisky2018narrativeqa} and BookTest \cite{bajgar2016embracing}, which focus on longer documents and more complex reasoning patterns. However, these datasets still primarily emphasize extractive or simple inferential questions, leaving significant gaps in evaluating models' abilities to understand deeper narrative elements such as character motivations, thematic development, and symbolic meaning \cite{paperno2016lambada,zhang2020record}. The limitations become even more pronounced when considering that human readers naturally engage with stories on multiple levels simultaneously - tracking plot events, understanding character development, recognizing literary themes, and making connections to broader cultural and social contexts \cite{mar2006bookworms,kidd2013reading}. Current QA models, despite their impressive performance on standard benchmarks, often struggle with these multifaceted aspects of narrative comprehension, particularly when questions require understanding implicit relationships or making complex inferences that span large portions of text \cite{sugar2021textual,sun2019investigating}. To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive framework for evaluating and improving question answering over narrative stories. Our approach focuses on developing models that can better handle the unique characteristics of literary texts, including their length, complexity, and the need for sophisticated reasoning about fictional worlds and characters.

text: Drones have great potential for transforming urban logistics services. By enabling quick, flexible, and efficient delivery, they can help address the rapidly growing logistics and e-commerce needs of urban populations while reducing traffic congestion and environmental impact \cite{murray2015flying, agatz2018optimization}. However, the integration of drones into existing logistics networks faces significant challenges, particularly regarding their limited battery life and payload capacity compared to traditional ground vehicles \cite{dorling2017vehicle}. Recent advances in multi-modal transportation systems have demonstrated the potential for combining aerial and ground vehicles to leverage the complementary strengths of each platform \cite{sacramento2019adaptive, karak2019land}. Trucks provide substantial cargo capacity, extended operational range, and the ability to serve as mobile charging stations, while drones offer rapid point-to-point delivery capabilities and the ability to bypass ground traffic constraints \cite{boysen2018drone, poikonen2017branch}. The coordination of heterogeneous vehicle fleets in urban environments presents a complex optimization challenge that extends beyond traditional Vehicle Routing Problems (VRP). Classical VRP formulations assume homogeneous vehicle capabilities and independent routing decisions \cite{toth2014vehicle}. In contrast, drone-truck collaboration requires sophisticated temporal and spatial coordination mechanisms to enable effective rendezvous operations \cite{murray2020multiple}. Several recent studies have explored various aspects of drone-truck cooperation. \cite{agatz2018optimization} introduced the concept of truck-drone tandem deliveries, where a single truck collaborates with one drone for last-mile delivery optimization. \cite{wang2017vehicle} extended this to consider multiple drones per truck, while \cite{schermer2019branch} developed branch-and-bound algorithms for the flying sidekick traveling salesman problem. However, these approaches typically focus on small-scale problems with simplified operational constraints. The scalability challenge becomes particularly acute in dense urban environments where road networks contain thousands of nodes and edges. Traditional exact optimization methods become computationally intractable for realistic problem instances \cite{choi2020multi}. Furthermore, real-world operations must account for dynamic factors such as traffic conditions, weather constraints, and time-varying energy consumption patterns \cite{raj2020survey}. Our contribution addresses these limitations through several key innovations. First, we develop a comprehensive mathematical formulation that captures the full complexity of multi-drone, multi-truck coordination in large-scale urban networks. This includes detailed modeling of energy consumption patterns, payload-dependent flight characteristics, and temporal synchronization requirements for rendezvous operations. Second, we propose a hierarchical decomposition approach that enables scalable solution methods for realistic problem sizes. The decomposition separates strategic routing decisions from tactical coordination problems, allowing specialized algorithms to be applied at each level while maintaining solution quality guarantees. Third, we introduce adaptive coordination protocols that can respond to real-time operational disruptions while maintaining system-wide performance objectives. These protocols incorporate machine learning techniques to predict optimal rendezvous locations and timing based on historical traffic patterns and operational data \cite{chen2021machine}. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:literature} provides a comprehensive review of related work in drone-truck collaboration and multi-modal routing optimization. Section \ref{sec:formulation} presents our detailed mathematical formulation, including the complete constraint sets and objective functions. Section \ref{sec:algorithm} describes our hierarchical solution approach and adaptive coordination protocols. Section \ref{sec:experiments} presents computational experiments on realistic urban network instances, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach compared to existing methods. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our contributions and discusses future research directions. The practical implications of this work extend beyond academic interest. Major logistics companies are actively exploring drone integration strategies, with companies like Amazon, UPS, and FedEx conducting pilot programs for drone-assisted delivery services \cite{amazon2020prime, ups2019flight}. Our framework provides the theoretical foundation and algorithmic tools necessary to support large-scale deployment of such systems in complex urban environments.

text: In a server system, the Quality of Service (QoS) of a job is normally measured by its response time, which is defined as the amount of time between the job's arrival and its completion. This response time, also known as flow time in scheduling literature, serves as a critical performance metric that directly impacts user experience and system efficiency \cite{pinedo2016scheduling}. Understanding and optimizing flow time has become increasingly important as modern computing systems handle diverse workloads with varying performance requirements and service level expectations. The significance of flow time optimization extends beyond theoretical considerations to practical applications in numerous domains. In cloud computing environments, minimizing response times ensures efficient resource utilization and maintains competitive service offerings \cite{armbrust2010view}. Similarly, in manufacturing systems, reducing job completion times translates to improved throughput and reduced work-in-process inventory \cite{hopp2011factory}. Healthcare scheduling systems also benefit from flow time optimization, where patient waiting times directly correlate with service quality and operational efficiency \cite{cayirli2003outpatient}. \subsection{Problem Formulation and Notation} To establish a formal framework for our analysis, we introduce the following notation. Let $\mathcal{J} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ represent the set of jobs to be processed, where each job $j \in \mathcal{J}$ has an associated processing time $p_j > 0$. The arrival time of job $j$ is denoted by $r_j \geq 0$, and its completion time is represented by $C_j$. Consequently, the flow time of job $j$ is defined as: \begin{equation} F_j = C_j - r_j \end{equation} In scenarios where all jobs are available at time zero (i.e., $r_j = 0$ for all $j \in \mathcal{J}$), the flow time reduces to the completion time: $F_j = C_j$. The scheduling environment significantly influences the complexity and solution approaches for flow time optimization problems. We consider several machine configurations: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Single Machine ($1|\cdot|\cdot$):} All jobs are processed sequentially on a single processing unit. \item \textbf{Parallel Machines ($P_m|\cdot|\cdot$):} Jobs are distributed among $m$ identical parallel machines. \item \textbf{Unrelated Machines ($R_m|\cdot|\cdot$):} Jobs are assigned to $m$ machines with machine-dependent processing times. \end{itemize} \subsection{Algorithmic Approaches and Complexity Analysis} The algorithmic landscape for flow time minimization problems exhibits remarkable diversity in terms of computational complexity and solution methodologies. For the single-machine total flow time minimization problem without release dates, the SPT rule achieves optimality in $O(n \log n)$ time through simple job sorting \cite{smith1956various}. This elegant result demonstrates that prioritizing shorter jobs leads to globally optimal solutions. However, the introduction of release dates fundamentally alters the problem structure. The single-machine problem with release dates, denoted as $1|r_j|\sum F_j$, becomes NP-hard \cite{lenstra1977complexity}, necessitating the development of approximation algorithms and heuristic approaches. Notable contributions include the work of \cite{phillips1998approximation}, who developed polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for this problem variant. The parallel machine setting introduces additional complexity layers. The problem $P|||\sum F_j$ (parallel machines without release dates) remains polynomially solvable through list scheduling algorithms combined with SPT ordering \cite{bruno1974scheduling}. Specifically, the algorithm proceeds as follows: \begin{algorithm}[H] \caption{SPT-List Algorithm for $P|||\sum F_j$} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Sort jobs in non-decreasing order of processing times: $p_1 \leq p_2 \leq \cdots \leq p_n$ \STATE Initialize machine completion times: $T_i = 0$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$ \FOR{$j = 1$ to $n$} \STATE Find machine $k$ with minimum completion time: $k = \arg\min_i T_i$ \STATE Assign job $j$ to machine $k$ \STATE Update machine completion time: $T_k = T_k + p_j$ \ENDFOR \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} The maximum flow time minimization problem presents a contrasting complexity profile. For single machines, the problem $1||\max F_j$ reduces to minimizing the makespan when all jobs have zero release dates, which is trivially solved since the makespan equals the sum of all processing times. However, with release dates, the problem $1|r_j|\max F_j$ becomes more intricate, requiring sophisticated scheduling techniques to balance job priorities and release time constraints. \subsection{Advanced Scheduling Constraints and Extensions} Real-world scheduling scenarios often involve additional constraints that significantly impact the problem structure and solution approaches. Precedence constraints, where certain jobs must be completed before others can begin, introduce dependency relationships that complicate the optimization process. The notation $1|prec|\sum F_j$ represents single-machine scheduling with precedence constraints, which remains NP-hard even for simple precedence structures \cite{lawler1993sequencing}. Resource constraints constitute another important class of extensions. In many practical applications, jobs require specific resources (memory, specialized equipment, skilled personnel) that are available in limited quantities. The resource-constrained project scheduling problem (RCPSP) framework provides a mathematical foundation for modeling such scenarios: \begin{equation} \min \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j F_j \end{equation} subject to: \begin{align} \sum_{j \in A_t^k} r_{jk} &\leq R_k, \quad \forall k, t \\ C_j - C_i &\geq p_j, \quad \forall (i,j) \in E \end{align} where $w_j$ represents the weight or priority of job $j$, $A_t^k$ denotes the set of jobs active at time $t$ requiring resource type $k$, $r_{jk}$ is the amount of resource $k$ required by job $j$, $R_k$ is the total availability of resource $k$, and $E$ represents the set of precedence relationships. Preemption capabilities add another dimension to the scheduling problem. In preemptive scheduling, jobs can be interrupted and resumed later, potentially on different machines. The notation $1|pmtn|\sum F_j$ indicates single-machine preemptive scheduling for total flow time minimization. While preemption can lead to better objective function values, it also introduces implementation complexity and potential overhead costs. The integration of these various constraints and extensions creates a rich taxonomy of scheduling problems, each requiring specialized algorithmic approaches and theoretical analysis. The interplay between problem structure, computational complexity, and practical applicability continues to drive research in this fundamental area of operations research and computer science.

The fundamental challenge in SLAM lies in the simultaneous estimation of robot trajectory and environment structure from sensor observations, creating a chicken-and-egg problem where accurate localization requires a known map, while precise mapping depends on accurate pose estimates~\cite{durrant2006simultaneous}. Traditional visual SLAM approaches can be broadly categorized into feature-based and direct methods~\cite{engel2017direct}. Feature-based methods, exemplified by systems like ORB-SLAM~\cite{mur2015orb} and PTAM~\cite{klein2007parallel}, extract and track distinctive visual features across frames to establish correspondences for pose estimation and mapping. While these methods have demonstrated remarkable success in well-textured environments, they suffer from several limitations: dependency on feature extraction quality, vulnerability to environments with poor texture or repetitive patterns, and computational overhead associated with descriptor computation and matching~\cite{forster2014svo}. Direct methods, on the other hand, bypass explicit feature extraction by directly optimizing photometric consistency across images~\cite{newcombe2011dtam,engel2013semi}. These approaches minimize the photometric error between corresponding pixels, making them particularly suitable for environments where traditional features are scarce. The seminal work of Engel et al.~\cite{engel2017direct} introduced Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO), which combines the advantages of direct methods with sparse reconstruction to achieve real-time performance while maintaining high accuracy. Stereo vision systems offer significant advantages over monocular approaches by providing immediate depth information and resolving scale ambiguity inherent in single-camera systems~\cite{hartley2003multiple}. Classical stereo SLAM systems like STEREO-PTAM~\cite{pire2015s} and ORB-SLAM2~\cite{mur2017orb} extend feature-based monocular methods to stereo configurations. However, these systems inherit the fundamental limitations of feature-based approaches while adding computational complexity associated with stereo feature matching. Recent advances in direct methods have shown promising results in monocular settings, but extending these approaches to stereo vision presents unique challenges. The primary difficulty lies in formulating a coherent optimization framework that effectively exploits the geometric constraints of stereo cameras while maintaining the computational efficiency of sparse direct methods~\cite{wang2017stereo}. text: Due to the exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, use of AI methods in structural engineering, similar to many other disciplines, has seen a reasonable increase in recent years \cite{Sun2019, Flah2021}. The integration of AI techniques in post-disaster reconnaissance represents a paradigm shift from traditional manual inspection methods to automated, data-driven approaches that can process vast amounts of information with unprecedented speed and accuracy \cite{Xu2019, Liang2021}. Machine learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and deep learning architectures, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in image recognition, pattern detection, and damage assessment tasks \cite{Cha2017, Zhang2020}. These methods can automatically identify and classify different types of structural damage, including cracks, spalling, collapse, and deformation, from high-resolution imagery collected through various remote sensing platforms \cite{Gao2018, Ma2019}. The ability to process thousands of images in minutes rather than requiring weeks of manual inspection represents a significant advancement in post-disaster response capabilities. Computer vision techniques have been successfully applied to detect building damage using pre- and post-event satellite imagery, enabling rapid assessment of affected areas and prioritization of emergency response efforts \cite{Sublime2019, Nex2019}. Deep learning models trained on large datasets of damaged structures can achieve accuracy rates exceeding 90\% in damage classification tasks, often surpassing human inspector consistency \cite{Duarte2018, Doshi2018}. The fusion of multiple data sources, including optical imagery, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), and LiDAR point clouds, has further enhanced the robustness and reliability of AI-based damage assessment systems \cite{Plank2014, Dong2020}. Multi-modal approaches leverage the complementary strengths of different sensing technologies, providing comprehensive damage characterization even under challenging conditions such as cloud cover, debris, or limited accessibility \cite{Bai2017, Adriano2021}. Transfer learning techniques have proven particularly valuable in this domain, allowing pre-trained models developed for general image recognition tasks to be fine-tuned for specific damage detection applications with relatively small training datasets \cite{Perez2018, Pi2020}. This approach significantly reduces the computational resources and labeled data requirements typically associated with training deep neural networks from scratch. The implementation of AI-driven reconnaissance systems also enables real-time damage assessment and continuous monitoring throughout the recovery process \cite{Kerle2019, Ghaffarian2018}. Automated change detection algorithms can track the progression of repairs and reconstruction efforts, providing valuable insights for disaster management authorities and urban planners \cite{Contreras2016, Sublime2017}. Despite these technological advances, several challenges remain in the widespread adoption of AI methods for post-disaster reconnaissance. These include the need for high-quality training data representing diverse damage types and geographic conditions, ensuring model generalizability across different disaster scenarios, and addressing computational limitations in resource-constrained environments \cite{Vetrivel2018, Ci2019}. Additionally, the integration of AI outputs with existing emergency response workflows and decision-making processes requires careful consideration of user requirements and system interoperability.

text: A central challenge in machine learning is building models that are reliable and safe in the real world. Traditional approaches to machine learning focus primarily on maximizing predictive accuracy on held-out test sets, often neglecting crucial aspects of model behavior that are essential for deployment in safety-critical applications. These aspects include the ability to detect when the model encounters inputs that are significantly different from its training data, maintaining consistent predictions under minor input perturbations, and providing well-calibrated confidence estimates that accurately reflect the likelihood of correctness. The limitations of deterministic neural networks become particularly apparent when deployed in dynamic environments where the data distribution may shift over time. Such models tend to produce overconfident predictions even when faced with inputs from previously unseen domains or adversarially crafted examples designed to fool the classifier \cite{szegedy2013intriguing, goodfellow2014explaining}. This overconfidence can lead to catastrophic failures in applications such as autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, or financial decision-making, where incorrect predictions with high confidence can have severe consequences. Bayesian neural networks address these fundamental limitations by treating network parameters as random variables with associated probability distributions. This probabilistic treatment allows BNNs to naturally express uncertainty in their predictions, providing a measure of confidence that reflects both the model's knowledge about the underlying function and the inherent noise in the data generating process. When a BNN encounters an input that is dissimilar to its training data, the uncertainty in the parameter distributions translates to increased uncertainty in the output predictions, effectively signaling that the model is operating outside its domain of expertise. The theoretical foundation of BNNs rests on Bayes' theorem, which provides a principled mechanism for updating beliefs about model parameters given observed data. Given a dataset $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ and a neural network with parameters $\theta$, the posterior distribution over parameters is given by: \begin{equation} p(\theta | \mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\mathcal{D} | \theta) p(\theta)}{p(\mathcal{D})} \end{equation} where $p(\mathcal{D} | \theta)$ is the likelihood, $p(\theta)$ is the prior distribution over parameters, and $p(\mathcal{D})$ is the marginal likelihood or evidence. For prediction on a new input $x^*$, the predictive distribution is obtained by marginalizing over the parameter posterior: \begin{equation} p(y^* | x^*, \mathcal{D}) = \int p(y^* | x^*, \theta) p(\theta | \mathcal{D}) d\theta \end{equation} This integration captures the uncertainty in the model parameters and propagates it through to the predictions, resulting in a distribution over possible outputs rather than a single point estimate. Despite their theoretical appeal, the practical implementation of BNNs faces significant computational challenges. The parameter space of modern deep neural networks can contain millions or billions of dimensions, making exact posterior inference computationally prohibitive. The marginal likelihood $p(\mathcal{D})$ requires integration over the entire parameter space, which is generally intractable for non-trivial network architectures.

text: Owing to the great success of deep convolutional networks~\cite{he2016deep, chen2017deeplab, long2015fully}, object recognition tasks, such as object detection and instance segmentation, have achieved impressive progress during the last decade. Instance segmentation, which aims to simultaneously detect and segment individual object instances in images, has become a fundamental task in computer vision with applications ranging from autonomous driving~\cite{caesar2020nuscenes} to medical image analysis~\cite{ronneberger2015u}. The task requires precise localization of object boundaries while maintaining the ability to distinguish between different instances of the same class. Current state-of-the-art approaches for instance segmentation can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: two-stage methods~\cite{he2017mask, cai2018cascade} and single-stage methods~\cite{bolya2019yolact, wang2020solov2}. Two-stage methods, exemplified by Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask}, first generate object proposals and then refine them through region-of-interest (RoI) pooling operations. While these methods achieve high accuracy, they suffer from computational inefficiency due to the sequential nature of proposal generation and refinement. Single-stage methods, on the other hand, directly predict instance masks without explicit proposal generation, offering improved inference speed but often at the cost of segmentation quality. A critical component in both paradigms is the feature refinement process, which transforms coarse initial features into high-quality representations suitable for precise mask prediction. Traditional approaches rely on explicitly stacked convolutional layers~\cite{he2017mask, chen2019hybrid} to progressively refine instance features. For example, Mask R-CNN employs a series of $3 \times 3$ convolutions followed by deconvolution layers to upsample and refine RoI features. Similarly, recent methods like CondInst~\cite{tian2020conditional} and SOLO~\cite{wang2019solo} utilize multiple convolutional layers with varying kernel sizes to capture multi-scale contextual information. However, these explicit refinement strategies face several fundamental limitations. First, the computational overhead scales linearly with the number of refinement layers, leading to increased memory consumption and slower inference times. Second, the fixed receptive fields of convolutional kernels constrain the model's ability to adaptively capture contextual information at different scales. This limitation becomes particularly problematic when dealing with objects of varying sizes within the same image. Third, the sequential nature of stacked convolutions inherently limits parallelization opportunities, preventing efficient utilization of modern GPU architectures. Recent advances in implicit neural representations~\cite{mildenhall2020nerf, sitzmann2020implicit} have demonstrated remarkable success in modeling complex continuous functions across various domains, including 3D scene reconstruction~\cite{mescheder2019occupancy}, image synthesis~\cite{chan2021pi}, and neural rendering~\cite{yu2021pixelnerf}. These methods leverage the universal approximation capabilities of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) to represent continuous functions without explicit spatial discretization. Inspired by these developments, we investigate the potential of implicit function approximation for instance feature refinement. Our approach fundamentally differs from existing explicit refinement methods by formulating the refinement process as a continuous function learning problem. Instead of relying on predefined convolutional architectures, we parameterize the refinement transformation using an implicit function that can adaptively learn the optimal mapping from initial to refined features. This formulation offers several theoretical and practical advantages: (1) it eliminates the need for manually designed refinement architectures, (2) it provides greater flexibility in modeling complex feature transformations, and (3) it enables more efficient parallel processing through vectorized operations. The implicit refinement function $\mathcal{F}$ is designed to capture both local and global contextual information through a carefully constructed architecture. We incorporate positional encodings~\cite{vaswani2017attention} to preserve spatial relationships while allowing the MLP to focus on learning semantic transformations. Additionally, we introduce a multi-scale feature fusion mechanism that enables the implicit function to access information at different resolution levels, addressing the scale variation challenge inherent in instance segmentation. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft} and Cityscapes~\cite{cordts2016cityscapes}. Our method consistently outperforms existing explicit refinement approaches across different backbone architectures and instance segmentation frameworks. Notably, we achieve a $2.1\%$ improvement in mask AP on COCO while reducing computational overhead by $15\%$ compared to traditional stacked convolution approaches. The main contributions of this work are threefold: (1) We introduce a novel implicit feature refinement module that leverages continuous function approximation for instance segmentation, addressing the limitations of explicit refinement approaches. (2) We propose a comprehensive architecture that integrates coordinate encoding, multi-scale feature fusion, and adaptive refinement within the implicit function framework. (3) We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our approach achieves superior performance while maintaining computational efficiency across multiple benchmarks and network architectures. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{related_work} reviews related work in instance segmentation and implicit neural representations. Section~\ref{method} presents our implicit feature refinement module in detail. Section~\ref{experiments} provides comprehensive experimental evaluation and analysis. Finally, Section~\ref{conclusion} concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

text: The state of the art in machine learning has achieved exceptional accuracy on many computer vision tasks solely by training models on images. However, real-world applications often require understanding objects in three-dimensional space, necessitating models that can perceive depth, orientation, and spatial relationships. This fundamental limitation has driven significant interest in 3D object detection, where the goal is to not only identify objects in images but also estimate their precise 3D pose and dimensions in world coordinates. Traditional 2D object detection methods, while highly successful, provide limited information about object geometry and spatial configuration. They can identify what objects are present and where they appear in the image plane, but cannot determine how objects are oriented in 3D space or their actual physical dimensions. This limitation becomes particularly problematic for applications such as augmented reality (AR), robotics, and autonomous navigation, where understanding the 3D structure of the environment is crucial for safe and effective operation. The transition from 2D to 3D object detection introduces several technical challenges. First, the problem becomes significantly more complex as models must estimate additional parameters including 3D orientation (typically represented as rotation matrices or quaternions), 3D translation, and object dimensions. Second, acquiring ground truth annotations for 3D objects is substantially more difficult and expensive than 2D bounding boxes, requiring specialized equipment or manual annotation processes that are both time-consuming and error-prone. Existing approaches to 3D object detection can be broadly categorized into several paradigms. RGB-based methods attempt to infer 3D information from single images or video sequences, leveraging monocular depth cues and learned priors about object geometry~\cite{mousavian20173d, kundu2018object}. Point cloud-based approaches utilize 3D sensor data from LiDAR or depth cameras to directly operate in 3D space~\cite{qi2017pointnet, zhou2018voxelnet}. Hybrid methods combine multiple modalities, such as RGB images with depth information or point clouds, to leverage the complementary strengths of different data types~\cite{frustum2018, imvoxelnet}. Despite these advances, progress in 3D object detection has been hindered by the limited availability of large-scale, diverse datasets with high-quality 3D annotations. Most existing datasets focus on specific domains such as autonomous driving~\cite{geiger2012kitti, caesar2020nuscenes} or indoor scenes~\cite{song2015sun3d, dai2017scannet}, limiting the generalizability of trained models to broader real-world scenarios. Furthermore, many datasets provide synthetic or semi-synthetic data, which may not capture the full complexity and variability of real-world imaging conditions. The Objectron dataset addresses these limitations by providing a large-scale collection of real-world video sequences with precise 3D annotations across diverse object categories and environments. By leveraging mobile AR technology, we capture objects in their natural contexts with varying lighting conditions, backgrounds, and viewpoints, creating a more representative dataset for training robust 3D object detection models.

A new problem arises from the three-dimensionality of objects. Object recognition in three dimensions involves several difficulties. These achievements notwithstanding, progress in 3D object detection has been hampered by the scarcity of large, diverse, and accurate 3D data.
