text: With the explosion of the quantity of scientific papers, it becomes more challenging for researchers to glean papers worth reading from a large amount of literature for a quick understanding of the current state-of-the-art and identify promising research directions \cite{fortunato2018science, wang2019microsoft}. This information overload problem is particularly acute in rapidly evolving fields such as machine learning, artificial intelligence, and computational biology, where thousands of new papers are published monthly across various venues \cite{larsen2010rate, bornmann2015growth}. Traditional academic search engines like Google Scholar, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore primarily rely on keyword matching and citation-based ranking algorithms \cite{harzing2016google, falagas2008comparison}. While these systems have been instrumental in democratizing access to scientific literature, they exhibit several limitations. First, keyword-based retrieval often fails to capture semantic similarity between documents that discuss related concepts using different terminology \cite{manning2008introduction}. Second, the ranking mechanisms heavily favor highly-cited papers, potentially overlooking recent publications or work from emerging research areas that have not yet accumulated substantial citations \cite{waltman2016field}. The challenge becomes even more pronounced when researchers venture into interdisciplinary domains or seek to explore connections between seemingly disparate fields. Traditional search paradigms struggle to identify papers that bridge multiple disciplines or those that apply established techniques from one domain to novel problems in another \cite{porter2007research, wagner2011approaches}. This limitation hinders scientific discovery and innovation, as breakthrough research often emerges at the intersection of different fields \cite{uzzi2013atypical}. To overcome these challenges, the research community has increasingly turned to automated recommendation systems that can intelligently suggest relevant papers based on various signals beyond simple keyword matching \cite{beel2016paper}. These systems aim to understand the semantic content of scientific documents, model user preferences and reading patterns, and leverage the rich network structure inherent in academic literature to provide personalized and contextually relevant recommendations \cite{ekstrand2011collaborative}. Early approaches to paper recommendation were largely inspired by traditional recommender systems used in e-commerce and entertainment domains \cite{ricci2015recommender}. Collaborative filtering techniques, which recommend items based on the preferences of similar users, were adapted to suggest papers based on the reading or citation behavior of researchers with similar interests \cite{mcnee2002being, torres2004recommending}. While these methods showed promise, they suffered from several drawbacks including the cold start problem for new papers or researchers, sparsity issues in user-item interaction matrices, and limited ability to explain why particular papers were recommended \cite{schein2002methods}. Content-based filtering approaches emerged as a complementary solution, focusing on the intrinsic properties of papers rather than user behavior patterns \cite{pazzani2007content}. These methods typically extract features from paper titles, abstracts, keywords, and sometimes full text to compute similarity measures between documents \cite{hassan2018survey}. Early implementations relied on bag-of-words representations and simple similarity metrics such as cosine similarity or Jaccard coefficient \cite{salton1975vector}. While computationally efficient, these approaches often failed to capture the semantic relationships between concepts and were sensitive to vocabulary mismatch problems \cite{furnas1987vocabulary}. The introduction of probabilistic topic models, particularly Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), marked a significant advancement in content-based paper recommendation \cite{blei2003latent}. LDA and its variants can discover latent thematic structures in document collections, enabling the identification of papers that share similar topical distributions even when they use different vocabularies \cite{griffiths2004finding, wallach2009evaluation}. These models have been successfully applied to various academic corpora, demonstrating their ability to uncover meaningful research themes and facilitate paper discovery \cite{hall2008studying, chaney2012visualizing}. The emergence of neural embedding techniques has further transformed the landscape of paper recommendation systems. Word2Vec and its extensions introduced the concept of learning dense vector representations that capture semantic relationships between words based on their co-occurrence patterns in large corpora \cite{mikolov2013distributed, mikolov2013efficient}. Building upon this foundation, Doc2Vec extended the embedding paradigm to entire documents, enabling the learning of fixed-size representations for papers that encode their semantic content \cite{le2014distributed}. More recently, transformer-based models have achieved remarkable success in various natural language processing tasks, including document understanding and similarity computation \cite{vaswani2017attention, devlin2019bert}. Models like BERT, which are pre-trained on large text corpora using self-supervised objectives, have demonstrated superior performance in capturing contextual relationships and semantic nuances in text \cite{rogers2020primer}. Specialized variants such as SciBERT, trained specifically on scientific literature, have shown particular promise for academic paper analysis tasks \cite{beltagy2019scibert}. Despite these advances in content modeling, purely content-based approaches often overlook the rich structural information embedded in academic networks. Citation relationships, author collaborations, and venue affiliations provide valuable signals about paper quality, influence, and topical relevance \cite{fortunato2010community, newman2001structure}. Graph-based methods that can effectively combine textual content with network structure have emerged as particularly promising solutions for paper recommendation \cite{hamilton2017representation}. Node embedding techniques such as DeepWalk, node2vec, and LINE have demonstrated the ability to learn meaningful representations of nodes in networks by modeling random walk patterns or preserving various types of proximity \cite{perozzi2014deepwalk, grover2016node2vec, tang2015line}. When applied to citation networks, these methods can capture both local neighborhood structures and global network properties, enabling the identification of papers that are structurally similar even if they are not directly connected \cite{wang2016structural}. Graph neural networks (GNNs) represent the current state-of-the-art in combining node features with graph structure \cite{wu2020comprehensive}. These models can iteratively aggregate information from local neighborhoods while updating node representations, effectively propagating semantic information through the network structure \cite{kipf2017semi, veličković2018graph}. In the context of paper recommendation, GNNs can leverage both the textual content of papers and their position within the citation network to generate more accurate and contextually relevant recommendations \cite{wang2019heterogeneous}.

text: Learning 3D-aware image synthesis draws wide attention recently~\cite{graf, giraffe, pigan}. An emerging solution is to integrate a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)~\cite{nerf} into a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)~\cite{gan}. This integration enables the generation of photorealistic images with explicit 3D geometry understanding, allowing for controllable viewpoint synthesis and consistent multi-view generation~\cite{eg3d, stylenerf, gram}. However, the computational complexity of volumetric rendering in NeRF-based generators poses substantial challenges for practical deployment and real-time applications. Traditional NeRF-GAN approaches require dense sampling along camera rays to accurately capture fine-grained geometric details and appearance variations~\cite{pigan, giraffe}. This necessitates evaluating the neural network at hundreds of points per ray, resulting in prohibitive computational costs during both training and inference phases. For instance, generating a single $512 \times 512$ image may require processing over 250,000 sample points, making real-time synthesis infeasible on standard hardware configurations. Recent works have attempted to mitigate these computational bottlenecks through various optimization strategies. StyleNeRF~\cite{stylenerf} introduces a two-stage training procedure that first learns coarse geometry before refining appearance details. EG3D~\cite{eg3d} employs a hybrid approach combining volumetric rendering with 2D super-resolution networks to reduce the rendering resolution. However, these methods still suffer from significant computational overhead and often compromise on either generation quality or geometric consistency. Our proposed \textsc{EfficientNeRF-GAN} addresses these fundamental limitations through three key technical contributions. First, we develop an adaptive sampling strategy that dynamically allocates computational resources based on scene complexity. Unlike uniform sampling approaches, our method concentrates samples in regions with high density variations while sparsely sampling empty space areas: \begin{align} N_{\text{samples}}(\mathbf{r}) = N_{\text{base}} + \beta \cdot \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{r}) \end{align} where $N_{\text{base}}$ represents the minimum sampling rate, $\beta$ is a scaling factor, and $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{r})$ quantifies the complexity along ray $\mathbf{r}$ based on density gradient magnitudes. Second, we introduce a hierarchical feature representation that decomposes the 3D scene into multiple resolution levels. This multi-scale approach enables efficient feature extraction by processing coarse structural information at low resolutions while capturing fine details only where necessary. The hierarchical decomposition follows: \begin{align} \sigma(\mathbf{x}) &= \sum_{l=0}^{L-1} w_l \cdot \sigma_l(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) &= \sum_{l=0}^{L-1} w_l \cdot \mathbf{c}_l(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \end{align} where $\sigma_l$ and $\mathbf{c}_l$ represent density and color predictions at resolution level $l$, respectively, and $w_l$ are learnable combination weights that adapt during training. Third, we propose a progressive training curriculum that gradually increases scene complexity and sampling density. text: Data minimisation is a core principle of the European Union's Data Protection Regulation~\citep{regulation2016regulation}, as well as data protection laws in other jurisdictions: \begin{quote} Personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (`data minimisation'). \end{quote} This principle reflects a fundamental tension in modern machine learning: while practitioners often assume that more data leads to better model performance, privacy regulations mandate collecting only the minimum data necessary to achieve specified objectives. The challenge lies in operationalising this principle without compromising the effectiveness of machine learning systems. Traditional approaches to data collection in machine learning have largely ignored this constraint, operating under the assumption that larger datasets invariably yield superior models \cite{halevy2009unreasonable}. However, recent empirical studies suggest that the relationship between data quantity and model performance is more nuanced than previously assumed. \citet{banko2001scaling} demonstrated power-law scaling in natural language processing tasks, while \citet{kaplan2020scaling} revealed logarithmic scaling properties in large language models that exhibit diminishing returns beyond certain thresholds. The implications of excessive data collection extend beyond regulatory compliance. From a technical perspective, larger datasets impose computational burdens that may not be justified by marginal performance gains \cite{strubell2019energy}. From a privacy standpoint, unnecessary data collection increases the attack surface for potential breaches and re-identification attacks \cite{narayanan2008robust, sweeney2000simple}. Furthermore, the storage and processing of superfluous data incurs ongoing costs and maintenance overhead that could be avoided through principled data minimisation strategies. Despite the clear benefits of data minimisation, its implementation in practice remains challenging. Practitioners face uncertainty about the minimum data requirements for achieving acceptable model performance, leading to conservative approaches that favour over-collection. This uncertainty is compounded by the difficulty of predicting model performance from dataset characteristics alone, particularly in novel domains or with evolving data distributions. Our work addresses these challenges by introducing a principled framework for adaptive data collection that respects privacy constraints while maintaining model utility. We propose a performance bound function $\dmBoundFn$ that models the expected relationship between dataset size and model performance, enabling practitioners to make informed decisions about data collection limits. This function takes the form: \begin{equation} \dmBoundFn(n) = \dmBoundParameterA \cdot \log(n + 1) + \dmBoundParameterB \end{equation} where $n$ represents the dataset size, $\dmBoundParameterA$ controls the scaling rate, and $\dmBoundParameterB$ represents the baseline performance. This logarithmic formulation captures the diminishing returns characteristic observed in empirical scaling studies while providing a tractable framework for optimisation. The core contribution of our approach lies in formalising the data minimisation problem as an optimisation task that balances privacy costs against utility gains. We define the optimal data collection strategy as one that maximises model performance subject to privacy budget constraints, expressed as: \begin{equation} \max_{\dmTraining \subseteq \dmPool} \dmPerformance[\dmTraining] \quad \text{subject to} \quad |\dmTraining| \leq \dmBudget \end{equation} where $\dmPool$ represents the available data pool, $\dmTraining$ denotes the selected training subset, $\dmPerformance[\dmTraining]$ quantifies model performance on the selected data, and $\dmBudget$ represents the privacy budget constraint. Our framework incorporates several key innovations. First, we introduce adaptive sampling strategies that dynamically adjust data collection based on observed performance curves. Second, we develop theoretical bounds on the privacy-utility trade-off that guide the selection process. Third, we provide empirical validation across multiple domains, demonstrating that our approach achieves comparable performance to traditional methods while collecting significantly less data. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in privacy-preserving machine learning and data minimisation techniques. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our theoretical framework and algorithmic approach. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} provides empirical evaluation across diverse datasets and model architectures. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our findings for both regulatory compliance and practical machine learning deployment. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarises our contributions and outlines directions for future research. The intersection of privacy and machine learning has generated substantial research interest, with several distinct but related approaches emerging. Differential privacy \cite{dwork2014algorithmic} provides formal guarantees about individual privacy through controlled noise injection, while federated learning \cite{mcmahan2017communication} enables distributed training without centralised data collection. However, these approaches primarily focus on protecting data during processing rather than minimising collection at the source.

text: The \textit{Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch} (SCED) is a fundamental optimization model for Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to clear real-time energy markets while ensuring reliable operations of power grids. In a context where renewable energy sources are increasingly integrated into power systems, the SCED problem becomes more complex due to the inherent uncertainty and variability of wind and solar generation. Traditional deterministic approaches to SCED may lead to suboptimal solutions or even infeasible operations when faced with significant forecast errors or unexpected contingencies \cite{wood2013power, kirschen2018fundamentals}. The stochastic formulation of SCED addresses these challenges by incorporating uncertainty directly into the optimization framework. This approach considers multiple scenarios representing possible realizations of uncertain parameters, such as renewable generation output, load demand, and equipment availability \cite{birge2011introduction, conejo2010decision}. The objective function typically minimizes the expected total cost across all scenarios while ensuring that operational constraints are satisfied with high probability. The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources has fundamentally transformed the operational landscape of modern power systems. Wind and solar generation exhibit significant variability and limited predictability, creating substantial challenges for system operators who must maintain the delicate balance between supply and demand in real-time \cite{milligan2011integration, ela2011evolution}. This paradigm shift necessitates a departure from traditional deterministic dispatch methods toward more sophisticated stochastic optimization approaches that can effectively handle uncertainty. Recent developments in computational methods and scenario generation techniques have made stochastic SCED more tractable for practical implementation. Advanced decomposition algorithms, such as Benders decomposition and progressive hedging, enable the solution of large-scale stochastic programs within reasonable computational timeframes \cite{rahmaniani2017benders, watson2012progressive}. Furthermore, machine learning techniques are increasingly being employed to improve scenario generation and reduce the computational burden associated with solving multi-scenario optimization problems \cite{zhang2018data, khodayar2017machine}. The mathematical formulation of stochastic SCED extends the classical deterministic model by incorporating probability distributions over uncertain parameters. Let $S$ denote the set of scenarios, each with associated probability $\pi_s$ such that $\sum_{s \in S} \pi_s = 1$. The stochastic SCED problem can be formulated as: \begin{equation} \min_{p_g, r_g^+, r_g^-} \sum_{s \in S} \pi_s \left[ \sum_{g \in G} C_g(p_{g,s}) + \sum_{g \in G} (C_g^+ r_{g,s}^+ + C_g^- r_{g,s}^-) \right] \end{equation} subject to: \begin{align} \sum_{g \in G} p_{g,s} + \sum_{g \in G} r_{g,s}^+ - \sum_{g \in G} r_{g,s}^- &= D_s + L_s, \quad \forall s \in S \\ P_g^{\min} \leq p_{g,s} + r_{g,s}^+ - r_{g,s}^- &\leq P_g^{\max}, \quad \forall g \in G, s \in S \\ 0 \leq r_{g,s}^+ &\leq R_g^+, \quad \forall g \in G, s \in S \\ 0 \leq r_{g,s}^- &\leq R_g^-, \quad \forall g \in G, s \in S \\ \sum_{g \in n} (p_{g,s} + r_{g,s}^+ - r_{g,s}^-) - D_{n,s} &= \sum_{l \in L_n} f_{l,s}, \quad \forall n \in N, s \in S \\ |f_{l,s}| &\leq F_l^{\max}, \quad \forall l \in L, s \in S \end{align} where $p_{g,s}$ represents the power output of generator $g$ in scenario $s$, $r_{g,s}^+$ and $r_{g,s}^-$ denote the upward and downward reserve deployments, respectively, $C_g(\cdot)$ is the generation cost function, $C_g^+$ and $C_g^-$ are the reserve deployment costs, $D_s$ represents the system demand, and $L_s$ accounts for transmission losses in scenario $s$. The constraint set includes power balance equations \eqref{eq:power_balance}, generator capacity limits \eqref{eq:gen_limits}, reserve capacity constraints \eqref{eq:up_reserve}-\eqref{eq:down_reserve}, nodal power balance equations \eqref{eq:nodal_balance}, and transmission line flow limits \eqref{eq:line_limits}. The nodal balance constraint ensures that the net injection at each bus equals the sum of power flows on connected transmission lines, where $f_{l,s}$ represents the power flow on line $l$ in scenario $s$. Security constraints play a crucial role in the SCED formulation, ensuring that the system can withstand credible contingencies without violating operational limits. The N-1 security criterion, which requires the system to remain stable after the loss of any single component, is typically incorporated through additional constraints: \begin{align} |f_{l,s}^{(c)}| &\leq F_l^{\max}, \quad \forall l \in L, c \in C, s \in S \\ P_g^{\min} \leq p_{g,s}^{(c)} &\leq P_g^{\max}, \quad \forall g \in G, c \in C, s \in S \end{align} where $f_{l,s}^{(c)}$ and $p_{g,s}^{(c)}$ represent post-contingency power flows and generator outputs, respectively, for contingency $c$ in the set of credible contingencies $C$. The stochastic nature of renewable generation introduces additional complexity through the need for accurate scenario generation. Various approaches have been developed to create representative scenarios that capture the statistical properties of uncertain parameters while maintaining computational tractability. Monte Carlo simulation, moment matching techniques, and copula-based methods are among the most commonly employed approaches \cite{morales2013integrating, papaefthymiou2009using}. Scenario reduction techniques are essential for managing the computational complexity of stochastic SCED problems. The trade-off between solution accuracy and computational efficiency requires careful consideration of the number and selection of scenarios. Advanced reduction algorithms, such as the fast forward selection and backward reduction methods, help identify the most representative subset of scenarios while preserving the statistical characteristics of the original uncertainty distribution \cite{heitsch2003scenario, dupacova2003scenario}. The implementation of stochastic SCED in practice faces several challenges, including the need for robust optimization algorithms, accurate forecasting models, and efficient computational infrastructure. Real-time applications require solutions within tight time constraints, typically on the order of minutes, which places stringent demands on algorithm performance and scalability \cite{capitanescu2011state, gomez2013electric}. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for stochastic SCED that addresses the key challenges associated with renewable energy integration while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time applications. The proposed methodology incorporates advanced scenario generation techniques, robust optimization formulations, and efficient solution algorithms to provide reliable and economically optimal dispatch decisions under uncertainty.

text: DNA-sequencing aims to measure the genetic makeup of individuals. Without going into details about the many different technologies, these processes determine (fragments of) the genetic sequence. However, the reference genome used for alignment is typically a linear representation that may not adequately capture the full spectrum of genetic diversity present in populations. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when dealing with structural variants, complex rearrangements, or regions of high polymorphism where multiple valid sequences exist within the population. Modern sequencing technologies produce millions to billions of short reads that must be computationally assembled or aligned to reconstruct the original genomic sequence. The alignment process inherently introduces ambiguities, especially in repetitive regions, homologous sequences, or areas with high mutation rates. Traditional approaches often rely on a single "best" alignment, potentially discarding valuable information contained in alternative alignments that may be biologically relevant. The challenge of variant calling becomes even more complex when considering that genetic variants do not exist in isolation. Variants can interact through linkage disequilibrium, epistatic effects, or simply through their physical proximity on the chromosome. Understanding these relationships requires a systematic framework that can capture the various ways variants relate to each other across different genomic contexts and alignment scenarios. Current variant calling pipelines typically process variants independently, applying statistical thresholds and quality filters without explicitly considering the relationships between nearby variants. This approach can lead to inconsistent calls, particularly in regions where multiple variants are present within close proximity. For instance, a complex indel might be represented as multiple smaller variants, or a single large variant might be missed due to alignment artifacts. \subsection{Motivation and Objectives} The primary motivation for this work stems from the need to develop more robust and comprehensive methods for variant identification and classification. Traditional approaches often suffer from several limitations: \textbf{Alignment bias:} Most variant callers rely on alignments to a single reference genome, which may not represent the optimal reference for all individuals or populations. This can lead to systematic biases in variant calling, particularly for variants that are common in certain populations but rare in the reference genome. \textbf{Incomplete variant representation:} Complex structural variants, such as inversions, translocations, or large insertions and deletions, are often poorly represented or missed entirely by standard variant calling approaches. These variants can have significant biological impact but are challenging to detect and characterize using conventional methods. \textbf{Lack of systematic relationship modeling:} Current approaches do not provide a formal framework for understanding how variants relate to each other. This limitation hinders downstream analyses that require understanding of variant interactions, such as haplotype reconstruction, population genetics studies, or clinical interpretation of compound variants. Our approach addresses these limitations by introducing a comprehensive framework that considers all minimal alignments and provides a systematic method for classifying variant relationships. By examining multiple alignment possibilities, we can capture variants that might be missed by single-alignment approaches and provide a more complete picture of genetic variation. \subsection{Technical Approach} The foundation of our method lies in the concept of minimal alignments—alignments that cannot be further reduced without losing essential information about the relationship between sequences. Unlike traditional approaches that seek a single optimal alignment based on scoring functions, we systematically enumerate and analyze all minimal alignments between sequences. This comprehensive approach allows us to identify variants that exist in some alignment contexts but not others, providing insights into the ambiguity inherent in sequence alignment and variant calling. By considering all possible minimal alignments, we can: \begin{itemize} \item Detect variants that are only visible under specific alignment conditions \item Identify regions where variant calling is inherently ambiguous \item Provide confidence measures based on the consistency of variants across different alignments \item Establish formal relationships between variants that account for alignment uncertainty \end{itemize} The Boolean relations framework builds upon this foundation by providing a mathematical language for describing how variants relate to each other. These relations are designed to be: \textbf{Complete:} Every pair of variants can be classified using our relation set, ensuring comprehensive coverage of all possible variant relationships. \textbf{Consistent:} The relations are defined formally to avoid ambiguities and ensure reproducible results across different implementations and datasets. \textbf{Biologically meaningful:} Each relation corresponds to a biologically interpretable relationship between variants, facilitating downstream biological interpretation. \textbf{Computationally tractable:} The relations can be computed efficiently, making the approach scalable to genome-wide analyses. \subsection{Applications and Impact} The framework presented in this work has broad applications across genomics and computational biology. In clinical genomics, understanding variant relationships is crucial for interpreting compound heterozygous variants, where the combined effect of multiple variants may be more significant than individual variant effects. Our systematic approach to variant relationship classification can improve the accuracy of clinical variant interpretation. In population genetics, the ability to comprehensively characterize variant relationships enables more sophisticated analyses of linkage patterns, recombination events, and evolutionary processes. By providing a complete picture of genetic variation, including variants that might be missed by traditional approaches, our method can contribute to a better understanding of human genetic diversity. For genome assembly and annotation projects, the framework provides tools for quality assessment and validation. By identifying regions where variant calling is ambiguous or where multiple valid interpretations exist, researchers can focus attention on areas that require additional validation or specialized analysis approaches. The computational methods developed here also contribute to the broader field of sequence analysis by providing new algorithms for alignment analysis and variant detection. The concept of minimal alignments and systematic enumeration of alignment possibilities may have applications beyond variant calling, including comparative genomics, phylogenetic analysis, and structural biology. \subsection{Organization of the Paper} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:methods} provides detailed descriptions of the algorithms for identifying minimal alignments and computing Boolean relations between variants. Section~\ref{sec:results} presents experimental validation using both simulated and real genomic data, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our findings and potential extensions of the framework. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes the key contributions and outlines directions for future work.

text: The Tresillo is a rhythm that originated in Africa and was brought to the Caribbeans during the Atlantic Slave Trade period. The rhythm subsequently spread throughout Latin America and eventually found its way into various genres of popular music worldwide \cite{Floyd2008}. Characterized by its distinctive 3+3+2 subdivision pattern within an 8-beat framework, the Tresillo has become a fundamental building block in numerous musical styles, from Cuban son and salsa to contemporary pop and hip-hop \cite{Washburne2008, Peñalosa2009}. The cultural significance of the Tresillo extends far beyond its rhythmic properties. As noted by \citet{Roberts1999}, this pattern represents one of the most enduring African musical elements to survive the Middle Passage and subsequent cultural assimilation processes. Its persistence across centuries and geographical boundaries speaks to both its inherent musical appeal and its deep cultural resonance within diasporic communities. In contemporary popular music, the Tresillo manifests in various forms and intensities. While some songs feature the pattern prominently in their percussion sections, others incorporate subtle variations or fragments of the rhythm in melodic lines or harmonic accompaniment \cite{Moore2012}. This variability in implementation presents both opportunities and challenges for computational analysis, as traditional binary pattern matching approaches may fail to capture the nuanced ways in which the Tresillo influences modern musical compositions. The quantitative study of rhythmic patterns in popular music has gained considerable attention in recent decades, driven by advances in digital signal processing and machine learning techniques \cite{Gouyon2006, Dixon2007}. However, most existing research has focused on broad tempo analysis or general rhythmic complexity measures, rather than examining the prevalence of specific cultural rhythmic patterns like the Tresillo \cite{Holzapfel2015}. Our computational approach addresses this gap by developing a robust framework for detecting and quantifying Tresillo presence across large musical corpora. Unlike previous studies that rely on manual annotation or simplified pattern matching, our method incorporates probabilistic modeling to account for timing variations, dynamic intensity differences, and partial pattern occurrences that are common in real-world musical performances. The temporal evolution of rhythmic patterns in popular music reflects broader cultural and technological shifts within the music industry. The rise of sampling technology in the 1980s, for instance, facilitated the direct incorporation of Afro-Caribbean rhythmic elements into hip-hop and electronic music \cite{Schloss2004}. Similarly, the globalization of music distribution has enabled cross-cultural rhythmic exchange at an unprecedented scale \cite{Connell2003}. To investigate these temporal dynamics, we compiled a comprehensive dataset spanning seven decades of popular music, from the 1950s to the 2020s. This corpus includes over 10,000 commercially successful songs across multiple genres, providing sufficient statistical power to detect subtle trends in Tresillo usage over time. Each recording underwent automated onset detection using state-of-the-art algorithms, followed by our novel Tresillo quantification procedure. The mathematical foundation of our approach rests on information-theoretic principles, treating rhythmic patterns as discrete symbol sequences and employing cross-correlation techniques to measure pattern similarity. Given the inherent variability in human musical performance, we incorporate Gaussian noise models to account for timing imprecision while maintaining sensitivity to the underlying rhythmic structure.

text: Legged robots are extremely versatile and can be used in wide ranges of applications. Nevertheless, robust locomotion is a complex topic which still needs investigation. {Stability and safety} are paramount concerns when deploying legged robots in real-world environments, where unexpected disturbances and terrain variations are commonplace. Traditional control approaches for legged locomotion have relied heavily on model-based methods, which provide theoretical guarantees but often struggle to adapt to unforeseen circumstances or model uncertainties \cite{bledt2018contact, kim2019highly}. Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep reinforcement learning (DRL), have shown remarkable success in generating agile and robust locomotion behaviors for legged robots \cite{hwangbo2019learning, lee2020learning}. These learning-based approaches can discover complex control policies that exhibit impressive adaptability to various terrains and disturbances. However, they typically operate as black-box systems, making it challenging to provide formal safety guarantees or understand the underlying decision-making process. This lack of interpretability poses significant risks when deploying such systems on expensive hardware platforms. The field of legged robotics has witnessed a growing interest in hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of both classical control theory and modern machine learning techniques \cite{grandia2019feedback, ji2022concurrent}. Model Predictive Control (MPC) has emerged as a particularly attractive classical approach for legged locomotion due to its ability to handle constraints explicitly and provide predictive capabilities \cite{bledt2018contact, di2018dynamic}. MPC formulates the control problem as an optimization over a finite horizon, enabling the incorporation of physical constraints such as friction limits, joint torque bounds, and kinematic restrictions. Despite the success of MPC-based approaches, they are inherently limited by the accuracy of their underlying models and their ability to adapt to unexpected situations. Real-world legged robots must contend with model uncertainties, external disturbances, and environmental variations that are difficult to capture in analytical models. This motivates the development of adaptive control strategies that can learn from experience while maintaining the safety and interpretability benefits of classical approaches. In this work, we propose a novel hybrid framework that integrates a neural network-based policy within an MPC architecture for enhanced disturbance rejection in legged robots. Our approach leverages the predictive capabilities and constraint handling of MPC while incorporating the adaptability of machine learning through a carefully designed neural component. The neural network learns optimal foot placement strategies from extensive simulation data, providing the MPC with enhanced predictions that improve overall system performance. The key innovation of our framework lies in the seamless integration of learned and model-based components. Rather than replacing the classical controller entirely, we augment the MPC with neural network predictions that enhance its decision-making capabilities. This design preserves the interpretability and safety guarantees of the underlying MPC while enabling adaptation to complex disturbance patterns that would be difficult to handle with traditional methods alone. Our hybrid controller operates by using the neural network to predict optimal foot placement modifications based on the current state and estimated disturbances. These predictions are then incorporated into the MPC optimization problem as additional constraints or objectives, allowing the controller to proactively adjust its strategy while maintaining dynamic feasibility. The MPC layer serves as a safety filter, ensuring that the neural network's suggestions are dynamically consistent and satisfy all physical constraints. The training of the neural component is performed offline using extensive simulation data generated from various disturbance scenarios. We employ a diverse set of external perturbations, including impulsive forces, sustained pushes, and terrain irregularities, to create a comprehensive training dataset. The neural network learns to map from robot state and disturbance estimates to optimal foot placement corrections, developing an implicit understanding of effective recovery strategies. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on a quadrupedal robot platform under various perturbation conditions. Our experimental setup includes controlled disturbance injection through external forces applied at different magnitudes and directions. We compare our hybrid controller against baseline MPC implementations and purely learning-based approaches across multiple performance metrics, including recovery time, stability margins, and energy efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in disturbance rejection capabilities. Our hybrid framework achieves a 23\% reduction in recovery time compared to baseline MPC when subjected to lateral pushes of up to 150N. Additionally, we observe an 18\% improvement in overall disturbance rejection capability, measured as the maximum sustainable perturbation before loss of stability. These improvements are consistent across different disturbance types and magnitudes, indicating the robustness of our approach. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the neural component learns interpretable strategies that align with established principles of legged locomotion. The learned foot placement modifications exhibit characteristics such as widening the support polygon during perturbations and adjusting step timing to maintain dynamic balance. This interpretability provides confidence in the system's behavior and facilitates debugging and refinement of the controller. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:related} reviews related work in hybrid control for legged robots and discusses the positioning of our approach within the broader literature. Section \ref{sec:method} presents the detailed methodology of our hybrid framework, including the neural network architecture, MPC formulation, and integration scheme. Section \ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and presents comprehensive results comparing our approach against baseline methods. Section \ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our findings, limitations of the current approach, and future research directions. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper with a summary of contributions and key insights. The development of robust control strategies for legged robots has been an active area of research for several decades. Early approaches focused primarily on static stability criteria and quasi-static gaits, which provided reliable but slow locomotion \cite{hirose1984study}. The introduction of dynamic walking concepts revolutionized the field, enabling more agile and efficient locomotion patterns \cite{mcgeer1990passive, raibert1986legged}. Model Predictive Control has gained significant traction in recent years as a powerful framework for legged locomotion control. The work by \cite{bledt2018contact} demonstrated the effectiveness of MPC for quadrupedal locomotion by formulating the problem as a convex optimization with linearized dynamics. This approach enabled real-time implementation while maintaining good tracking performance and constraint satisfaction.

text: The goal of this paper is to study the Parallel Drone Scheduling Traveling Salesman Problem (PDSTSP) defined as follows. Given a set of $n$ customers located at distinct geographical coordinates, a depot, and a fleet of $k$ identical drones with limited battery capacity, the PDSTSP seeks to determine the minimum-time schedule for visiting all customers exactly once and returning to the depot. Each drone has a maximum flight time $T_{max}$ and travels at constant speed $v$. The problem combines elements of the classical Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) with parallel machine scheduling constraints, where drones operate simultaneously and independently. Formally, let $G = (V, E)$ be a complete graph where $V = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ represents the set of nodes with node $0$ corresponding to the depot and nodes $1, 2, \ldots, n$ representing customers. The edge set $E$ contains all possible connections between nodes, with each edge $(i,j) \in E$ having an associated travel time $t_{ij} = d_{ij}/v$, where $d_{ij}$ denotes the Euclidean distance between nodes $i$ and $j$. The objective is to partition the customer set into at most $k$ subsets and construct a tour for each subset such that: (i) each customer is visited exactly once, (ii) each tour starts and ends at the depot, (iii) the total flight time of each tour does not exceed $T_{max}$, and (iv) the maximum completion time among all tours is minimized. The PDSTSP has emerged as a critical optimization problem in various application domains, particularly in last-mile delivery services, surveillance operations, and emergency response systems \cite{murray2015flying, agatz2018optimization}. The increasing adoption of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in commercial and military applications has intensified research interest in this area. Unlike traditional vehicle routing problems, drone-based systems present unique challenges including limited battery life, payload constraints, and regulatory restrictions on flight paths and altitudes. The problem's complexity stems from its multi-objective nature, combining tour construction decisions with scheduling considerations. Each feasible solution must simultaneously address three interconnected subproblems: (i) customer assignment to drones, (ii) tour sequencing for each drone, and (iii) temporal coordination to minimize the overall makespan. The interdependence of these decisions creates a complex optimization landscape that traditional decomposition approaches struggle to navigate effectively. Previous research on the PDSTSP has primarily focused on heuristic and metaheuristic approaches due to the problem's computational intractability \cite{dorling2017vehicle, kim2017traveling}. Genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and variable neighborhood search methods have shown promising results for medium-sized instances but often fail to guarantee solution optimality. More recently, mathematical programming formulations have been proposed, typically employing mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models with exponential numbers of constraints \cite{ponza2022optimization}. The main contributions of this work are threefold. First, we develop a comprehensive mathematical formulation for the PDSTSP that incorporates both temporal and spatial constraints while maintaining computational tractability. Our formulation introduces novel decision variables that explicitly model the relationship between tour construction and scheduling decisions. Second, we design a sophisticated branch-and-cut algorithm that leverages problem-specific structural properties to generate strong cutting planes and implement intelligent branching strategies. The algorithm incorporates several classes of valid inequalities, including subtour elimination constraints, capacity cuts, and precedence-based inequalities that exploit the problem's temporal structure. Third, we conduct extensive computational experiments on a comprehensive set of benchmark instances, demonstrating the superior performance of our approach compared to existing methods. Our results show that the proposed algorithm can solve instances with up to 100 customers to optimality within reasonable time limits, representing a significant advancement over previous exact approaches that were limited to instances with fewer than 50 customers. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:literature} provides a comprehensive review of related work on drone routing and parallel machine scheduling problems. Section~\ref{sec:formulation} presents our mathematical formulation, including the definition of decision variables, objective function, and constraint sets. Section~\ref{sec:algorithm} details the branch-and-cut algorithm, describing the separation procedures for various constraint classes and the branching strategy. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} reports computational results on benchmark instances and provides detailed performance comparisons with existing methods. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} summarizes our findings and discusses directions for future research. The PDSTSP belongs to the broader family of vehicle routing problems (VRPs) with additional scheduling constraints. The classical VRP, introduced by \cite{dantzig1959truck}, seeks to find minimum-cost routes for a fleet of vehicles serving a set of customers. The problem has spawned numerous variants incorporating capacity constraints, time windows, multiple depots, and heterogeneous vehicle fleets \cite{toth2014vehicle}. The integration of drones into logistics operations has created new research opportunities and challenges. \cite{murray2015flying} were among the first to study the Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone (TSP-D), where a single truck collaborates with a drone to serve customers more efficiently. This seminal work established the foundation for subsequent research on drone-assisted delivery systems. \cite{agatz2018optimization} extended this concept by considering multiple drones operating in coordination with ground vehicles, demonstrating significant potential for cost reduction in last-mile delivery scenarios.

text: In the global efforts towards tackling climate change and transitioning to sustainable energy sources, there has been a significant rise in developments and advancements of wind power systems in recent decades \cite{global2021wind}. Wind energy has emerged as one of the most promising renewable energy technologies, with global installed capacity exceeding 900 GW by 2022 and projections indicating continued exponential growth \cite{irena2023global}. This rapid expansion has been driven by technological improvements, cost reductions, and supportive policy frameworks that recognize wind power as a critical component of the clean energy transition \cite{wiser2021land}. The evolution of wind turbine technology has resulted in increasingly sophisticated systems characterized by larger rotor diameters, higher hub heights, and enhanced power generation capabilities \cite{veers2019grand}. Modern offshore wind turbines can exceed 15 MW in capacity, with rotor diameters approaching 250 meters, representing a significant increase in complexity compared to earlier generations \cite{musial2019offshore}. This technological advancement, while enabling higher energy yields and improved efficiency, has simultaneously introduced new challenges in terms of system reliability, maintenance requirements, and operational complexity \cite{carroll2016failure}. The harsh operating environments encountered by wind turbines, particularly offshore installations, subject these systems to extreme weather conditions, corrosive atmospheres, and variable loading patterns that can accelerate component degradation \cite{henderson2003offshore}. Onshore installations face similar challenges from wind shear, turbulence, and temperature fluctuations that contribute to fatigue loading and premature component failure \cite{nijssen2007fatigue}. The remote locations of many wind farms, combined with limited accessibility during adverse weather conditions, make unplanned maintenance interventions costly and time-consuming \cite{dinwoodie2015reference}. Traditional maintenance strategies in the wind industry have historically relied on time-based or reactive approaches, where components are replaced according to predetermined schedules or after failure occurs \cite{tchakoua2014wind}. However, these strategies often result in either premature component replacement, leading to unnecessary costs, or unexpected failures that cause significant downtime and revenue losses \cite{arabian2019review}. The economic impact of turbine downtime is particularly severe in offshore environments, where daily losses can exceed tens of thousands of dollars per turbine \cite{carroll2017availability}. The limitations of conventional maintenance approaches have driven the development and adoption of more sophisticated monitoring and maintenance strategies. Condition-based maintenance (CBM) represents a paradigm shift from reactive to proactive maintenance philosophy, enabling maintenance decisions based on actual component condition rather than predetermined schedules or failure occurrence \cite{jardine2006review}. This approach has demonstrated significant potential for optimizing maintenance costs while improving system reliability and availability \cite{garcia2006condition}. The implementation of CBM systems in wind turbines involves the integration of multiple sensing technologies, data acquisition systems, and analytical tools to continuously monitor component health and performance \cite{hameed2009condition}. Vibration monitoring remains the cornerstone of mechanical component assessment, utilizing accelerometers and displacement sensors to detect bearing defects, gearbox anomalies, and structural issues \cite{crabtree2013wind}. Oil analysis provides complementary information about gearbox and hydraulic system condition through the detection of wear particles, contamination, and chemical degradation \cite{sheng2011gearbox}. Electrical monitoring techniques have gained prominence with the increasing sophistication of wind turbine electrical systems, including power converters, transformers, and generator components \cite{qiao2015condition}. Current signature analysis, partial discharge monitoring, and insulation resistance testing provide valuable insights into electrical component health and can detect incipient faults before they progress to catastrophic failures \cite{yang2014wind}. Temperature monitoring throughout the turbine system enables the detection of thermal anomalies that may indicate component degradation or operational inefficiencies \cite{watson2010condition}. The proliferation of supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems in modern wind turbines has created unprecedented opportunities for comprehensive performance monitoring and fault detection \cite{schlechtingen2013wind}. SCADA systems typically collect hundreds of operational parameters at regular intervals, including power output, wind conditions, component temperatures, pressures, and control system status information \cite{zaher2009online}. This wealth of data provides a holistic view of turbine operation and enables the identification of subtle performance degradations that may not be detectable through individual sensor measurements \cite{garcia2013scada}. The challenge of extracting meaningful information from large volumes of heterogeneous monitoring data has driven the adoption of advanced data analytics and machine learning techniques in wind turbine CBM applications \cite{liu2012artificial}. Statistical process control methods, such as control charts and statistical hypothesis testing, provide baseline approaches for detecting deviations from normal operating conditions \cite{kusiak2011models}. However, the complex, nonlinear relationships inherent in wind turbine systems often require more sophisticated analytical approaches to achieve reliable fault detection and diagnosis \cite{chen2021deep}. Machine learning algorithms have demonstrated remarkable success in addressing the challenges of wind turbine condition monitoring, offering capabilities for pattern recognition, anomaly detection, and predictive modeling that exceed traditional statistical methods \cite{martinez2018data}. Supervised learning approaches, including support vector machines, decision trees, and neural networks, have been successfully applied to fault classification tasks where historical failure data is available for training \cite{kusiak2011models}. Unsupervised learning techniques, such as clustering algorithms and principal component analysis, enable anomaly detection in scenarios where fault examples are limited or unavailable \cite{pandit2018scada}. Deep learning methodologies have emerged as particularly powerful tools for processing the complex, high-dimensional data generated by modern wind turbine monitoring systems \cite{chen2021deep}. Convolutional neural networks excel at extracting features from vibration signals and other time-series data, while recurrent neural networks and their variants, such as long short-term memory networks, are well-suited for modeling temporal dependencies in turbine operational data \cite{wang2018wind}. Autoencoder architectures have shown promise for unsupervised anomaly detection by learning compact representations of normal operating conditions and identifying deviations from these learned patterns \cite{ahmed2020edge}. The integration of multiple data sources and sensing modalities, known as data fusion, represents a critical advancement in wind turbine CBM systems \cite{martinez2018data}. By combining information from vibration sensors, SCADA systems, weather monitoring equipment, and other sources, data fusion approaches can provide more robust and reliable fault detection capabilities than individual monitoring techniques \cite{pandit2018scada}. Bayesian networks, Dempster-Shafer theory, and other probabilistic frameworks offer principled approaches for combining evidence from multiple sources while accounting for uncertainty and sensor reliability \cite{liu2018data}. The incorporation of environmental and meteorological data into CBM systems has proven essential for distinguishing between equipment-related anomalies and normal variations in turbine behavior due to changing operating conditions \cite{martinez2018data}. Wind speed, wind direction, air density, and turbulence intensity significantly influence turbine performance and loading patterns, making it crucial to account for these factors when assessing component condition \cite{pandit2018scada}. Advanced CBM systems increasingly incorporate weather forecasting data to anticipate changes in operating conditions and adjust monitoring sensitivity accordingly \cite{ahmed2020edge}. The economic justification for CBM implementation in wind energy applications is compelling, with multiple studies demonstrating significant cost savings and availability improvements \cite{garcia2006condition, yang2014wind}. Typical benefits include reductions in unplanned maintenance costs of 20-30%, increases in turbine availability of 2-5%, and extensions in component life of 10-20% \cite{arabian2019review}. These improvements translate to substantial economic returns, particularly for large wind farms where small percentage improvements in availability can generate millions of dollars in additional revenue annually \cite{carroll2017availability}.

text: Video Retrieval is one of the most eminent and challenging problems in the digital world today. With the exponential growth of video content across platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and streaming services, the need for efficient and accurate video retrieval systems has become paramount. The sheer volume of video data—estimated to constitute over 80\% of internet traffic by 2024—presents unprecedented challenges in terms of storage, indexing, and real-time search capabilities \cite{cisco2023visual}. Traditional text-based search methods, while effective for web pages and documents, fall short when applied to video content due to the inherent multimodal nature of videos. Videos contain rich temporal information, visual scenes, audio tracks, and often embedded text, making them significantly more complex than static images or textual documents. This complexity necessitates sophisticated approaches that can effectively capture and represent the multidimensional characteristics of video content. Current video retrieval systems face several critical challenges. First, the temporal dimension introduces computational overhead, as models must process and understand sequences of frames rather than individual images. Second, the semantic gap between low-level visual features and high-level user intentions remains a significant barrier. Users often search for abstract concepts like "emotional scenes" or "action sequences" that are difficult to capture through traditional computer vision techniques \cite{smeulders2000content}. Moreover, scalability concerns arise when dealing with massive video databases. Real-time retrieval requires efficient indexing structures and fast similarity computation methods that can handle millions of videos while maintaining acceptable response times. The trade-off between retrieval accuracy and computational efficiency becomes crucial in practical deployments. Recent developments in deep learning, particularly transformer architectures and attention mechanisms, have opened new avenues for video understanding. Vision transformers (ViTs) \cite{dosovitskiy2020image} and their video extensions have shown promising results in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. Additionally, the emergence of large-scale pre-trained models has enabled transfer learning approaches that leverage knowledge from diverse visual and textual datasets. The integration of multimodal learning frameworks represents another significant advancement. By jointly modeling visual, textual, and audio modalities, these systems can achieve more comprehensive video understanding. However, the computational requirements for training and inference remain substantial, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a novel framework that combines efficient temporal modeling with scalable retrieval mechanisms. Our approach leverages hierarchical feature representations and adaptive attention mechanisms to achieve both high retrieval accuracy and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on large-scale video datasets and provide comprehensive comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches.

text: Next generation cellular communication systems are expected to further drive the diversity of applications provided by 5G systems \cite{yazar6g}. The evolution toward 6G networks promises unprecedented connectivity capabilities, supporting ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC), massive machine-type communications (mMTC), and enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) services with even more stringent requirements than their 5G predecessors \cite{saad2019vision}. These advanced communication systems will serve as the backbone for emerging applications including extended reality (XR), holographic communications, brain-computer interfaces, and fully autonomous vehicular networks \cite{letaief2019roadmap}. However, the proliferation of quantum computing technologies poses an existential threat to the cryptographic foundations underlying these next-generation networks. Current public-key cryptographic systems, including RSA, elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), and Diffie-Hellman key exchange, derive their security from mathematical problems that are computationally intractable for classical computers but can be efficiently solved by sufficiently powerful quantum computers using Shor's algorithm \cite{shor1994algorithms}. The timeline for achieving cryptographically relevant quantum computers remains uncertain, with estimates ranging from 10 to 30 years, necessitating proactive migration strategies to post-quantum cryptographic solutions \cite{mosca2015cybersecurity}. The integration of PQC algorithms into 6G networks introduces multifaceted challenges that extend beyond mere algorithmic substitution. The inherent characteristics of post-quantum algorithms—including increased computational complexity, larger key sizes, and extended signature lengths—directly impact critical network performance metrics such as latency, throughput, and energy consumption \cite{bernstein2019introduction}. For instance, CRYSTALS-Kyber-1024 requires public keys of 1,568 bytes compared to 256 bytes for elliptic curve cryptography, while CRYSTALS-Dilithium signatures can exceed 3,000 bytes, significantly larger than ECDSA signatures of approximately 64 bytes \cite{avanzi2019crystals}. These size increases become particularly problematic in bandwidth-constrained scenarios and resource-limited devices that are expected to proliferate in 6G ecosystems. IoT sensors, edge computing nodes, and vehicular communication units must accommodate these larger cryptographic primitives while maintaining stringent power consumption and processing constraints \cite{garcia2020post}. Furthermore, the heterogeneous nature of 6G networks, encompassing terrestrial, aerial, and satellite communication segments, requires adaptive cryptographic implementations that can dynamically adjust security parameters based on available resources and threat models \cite{giordani2020toward}. The migration timeline presents additional complexity, as network operators must balance security requirements with operational continuity. A hybrid approach, supporting both classical and post-quantum algorithms during the transition period, introduces implementation overhead and potential security vulnerabilities if not carefully managed \cite{bindel2019transitioning}. Moreover, the standardization process for PQC algorithms remains ongoing, with NIST continuing to evaluate additional candidates for specific use cases, creating uncertainty for early adopters \cite{nist2023round4}. Performance optimization strategies for PQC integration must consider the unique characteristics of 6G network architectures, including network slicing, edge computing, and artificial intelligence-driven resource allocation. Machine learning techniques can potentially optimize cryptographic parameter selection and algorithm switching based on real-time network conditions and security requirements \cite{zhang2021ai}. Additionally, hardware acceleration through specialized cryptographic processors and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) may mitigate the computational overhead associated with post-quantum algorithms \cite{howe2019standard}. This paper addresses the critical challenge of efficiently integrating post-quantum cryptography into next-generation cellular networks while maintaining the performance characteristics essential for emerging applications. We present a comprehensive analysis of PQC algorithm characteristics, evaluate their impact on 6G network performance, and propose optimization strategies for seamless deployment in diverse network environments.

text: In recommender systems, the user-item interactions and the side information about them can be represented as a graph composed by a set of objects~(nodes) and their relationships~(edges). Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations in such graph-structured data, enabling recommender systems to capture complex relational patterns and dependencies that traditional collaborative filtering methods often miss \cite{wu2020comprehensive}. The fundamental premise of graph-based recommendation lies in the assumption that users and items can be embedded in a shared latent space where their interactions and similarities are preserved through graph topology. By modeling the recommendation problem as a graph learning task, GNNs can leverage the inherent structural information to propagate signals across the network, allowing for more effective representation learning even in the presence of sparse interactions \cite{wang2019neural}. However, despite the theoretical advantages and empirical successes of graph-based approaches, the data sparsity problem remains a persistent challenge that significantly hampers their performance in real-world applications. The typical user-item interaction matrix in recommender systems exhibits extreme sparsity, often with density rates below 1\%, meaning that the vast majority of potential user-item pairs lack explicit feedback signals \cite{su2009survey}. This sparsity manifests in several critical ways that directly impact the effectiveness of graph neural networks. First, the sparse connectivity in the user-item bipartite graph limits the scope and quality of message passing operations, which are fundamental to GNN architectures. When users have interacted with only a few items, the neighborhood aggregation process becomes constrained, leading to insufficient information propagation and potentially biased representations \cite{hamilton2017inductive}. This limitation is particularly pronounced for cold-start users and items, where the lack of historical interactions makes it nearly impossible to learn meaningful embeddings through standard graph convolution operations. Second, the sparsity issue exacerbates the over-smoothing problem commonly observed in deep graph neural networks. As information is aggregated across multiple layers, node representations tend to become increasingly similar, losing their discriminative power and reducing the model's ability to make accurate recommendations \cite{li2018deeper}. In sparse graphs, this phenomenon is amplified because the limited connectivity patterns provide fewer diverse pathways for information flow, resulting in premature convergence to homogeneous representations. Third, data sparsity introduces significant challenges for model training and optimization. The imbalanced nature of sparse interaction data, where positive interactions are vastly outnumbered by unobserved (potentially negative) interactions, creates difficulties in learning effective loss functions and sampling strategies \cite{rendle2009bpr}. Traditional pointwise or pairwise learning approaches may struggle to capture the true preference patterns when the positive signal is overwhelmingly sparse compared to the implicit negative feedback. To systematically address these challenges, researchers have developed various strategies that can be broadly categorized into several complementary approaches. \textbf{Graph augmentation techniques} focus on enriching the original sparse graph structure through data manipulation and synthetic edge generation. These methods include random edge dropout for creating diverse training views \cite{rong2019dropedge}, node feature masking to encourage robust representation learning \cite{you2020graph}, and subgraph sampling to generate multiple perspectives of the same underlying network structure \cite{chen2018fastgcn}. \textbf{Contrastive learning frameworks} have gained significant attention as a means to leverage the augmented graph views for self-supervised representation learning. By maximizing agreement between different augmented versions of the same user or item while minimizing similarity with negative samples, contrastive methods can learn more discriminative embeddings even from sparse interaction data \cite{you2020graph,wu2021self}. These approaches are particularly effective because they do not rely solely on explicit feedback signals but can extract meaningful patterns from the structural properties of the graph itself. \textbf{Multi-modal integration strategies} represent another important direction for addressing sparsity by incorporating heterogeneous information sources. Modern recommender systems often have access to rich side information, including textual descriptions, visual content, categorical attributes, and temporal patterns \cite{chen2017attentive}. By jointly modeling interaction graphs with these auxiliary modalities, multi-modal GNNs can compensate for the lack of explicit feedback through cross-modal knowledge transfer and feature enrichment \cite{wei2019mmgcn,tao2020mgat}. \textbf{Knowledge graph enhancement} methods leverage external structured knowledge to provide additional semantic relationships and entity connections that are not captured in the original user-item interaction graph \cite{wang2019kgat,wang2020knowledge}. By constructing heterogeneous information networks that incorporate both collaborative signals and knowledge graph triplets, these approaches can significantly enrich the representation learning process and provide better generalization capabilities for sparse scenarios. \textbf{Advanced graph construction techniques} focus on creating more informative and dense graph topologies through sophisticated relationship modeling. These methods include higher-order connectivity analysis to capture indirect relationships \cite{song2019session}, implicit feedback integration to model latent user preferences \cite{he2020lightgcn}, and dynamic graph evolution to account for temporal patterns in user behavior \cite{kumar2019predicting}. Despite these advances, several fundamental questions remain open in the field. How can we effectively balance the trade-off between graph density enhancement and noise introduction when augmenting sparse interaction data? What are the optimal strategies for combining multiple information sources while maintaining computational efficiency? How can we design graph neural network architectures that are inherently robust to varying degrees of sparsity across different domains and datasets? Furthermore, the evaluation of sparsity-aware recommendation methods presents unique challenges. Traditional metrics such as precision, recall, and NDCG may not adequately capture the performance improvements in extremely sparse scenarios, particularly for long-tail items and cold-start users. There is a growing need for more comprehensive evaluation frameworks that can assess the effectiveness of different approaches across various sparsity levels and user segments \cite{cremonesi2010performance}. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the data sparsity challenge in graph-based recommender systems, examining both the theoretical foundations and practical implications of various solution approaches. We present a systematic evaluation of existing methods, identify their strengths and limitations, and propose directions for future research that can lead to more robust and effective recommendation systems capable of handling extreme sparsity conditions. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews the related work on graph neural networks for recommendation and sparsity handling techniques. Section~\ref{sec:problem} formally defines the data sparsity problem in graph-based recommendation. Section~\ref{sec:methods} presents a comprehensive taxonomy of existing approaches for addressing sparsity. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} provides extensive experimental evaluation and analysis. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper with discussions on future research directions.

text: If autonomous vehicles are to serve as traffic management systems \cite{wu2017flow}, safe navigation around human vehicles on highways and in cities is crucial. Traditional approaches to autonomous vehicle safety often rely on simplified models and conservative assumptions that may lead to overly restrictive behavior or fail to capture the complex dynamics of multi-agent interactions. In contrast, reachability analysis provides a principled framework for computing the set of all possible future states under worst-case conditions, enabling the synthesis of provably safe control policies. The car following scenario represents a fundamental building block of highway driving, where maintaining appropriate inter-vehicular spacing is critical for collision avoidance. This problem becomes particularly challenging when considering adversarial behavior from human drivers, who may exhibit unpredictable braking patterns or aggressive maneuvers. By formulating this as a differential game, we can systematically analyze the trade-offs between safety and performance while accounting for the worst-case actions of other traffic participants. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability theory offers a robust mathematical foundation for solving such multi-agent safety problems. The approach computes backward reachable sets that characterize all initial conditions from which the system can be driven to a target set (or conversely, avoid an unsafe set) despite adversarial disturbances. The resulting value function encodes the optimal control policy and provides explicit safety guarantees. Our contribution lies in applying HJ reachability to the car following problem with realistic vehicle dynamics and constraints. We consider longitudinal motion with acceleration limits, reaction delays, and varying road conditions. The framework naturally handles uncertainty in the lead vehicle's intentions while ensuring the ego vehicle maintains collision-free trajectories under all admissible disturbances.
