text: A set of metrics called NILC-Metrix was developed both in funded projects, involving multiple researchers, and in master's and doctoral projects at the Interinstitutional Center for Computational Linguistics (NILC) at the University of São Paulo (USP). This comprehensive system represents a collaborative effort spanning several years of research and development, with contributions from linguists, computer scientists, and educational researchers working together to address the critical need for robust textual complexity assessment tools in Portuguese. The motivation for developing NILC-Metrix emerged from the recognition that existing readability measures for Portuguese were limited in scope and theoretical grounding. Traditional readability formulas, such as adaptations of the Flesch Reading Ease and Fog Index, primarily rely on surface-level features like average sentence length and syllable counts \cite{martins1996readability, scarton2010analysis}. While these measures provide useful baseline assessments, they fail to capture the multifaceted nature of textual complexity that encompasses lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse-level dimensions. The theoretical foundation of NILC-Metrix draws extensively from cognitive models of text comprehension, particularly the Construction-Integration model \cite{kintsch1998comprehension} and the Landscape model of reading \cite{van2007landscape}. These frameworks emphasize that text difficulty emerges from the interaction between reader characteristics and multiple textual properties, including lexical accessibility, syntactic processing demands, semantic coherence, and discourse organization. By incorporating metrics that operationalize these theoretical constructs, NILC-Metrix provides a more comprehensive and psychologically grounded approach to textual complexity assessment. The development process involved systematic adaptation and validation of established metrics from other languages, particularly English, while also creating novel measures specifically designed to capture unique features of Portuguese morphosyntax and discourse patterns. Portuguese presents particular challenges for automatic text analysis due to its rich morphological system, flexible word order, and complex agreement patterns \cite{bick2000parsing, freitas2010automatic}. These linguistic characteristics necessitated careful consideration in metric design and implementation. The field of automatic readability assessment has evolved significantly since the early work of Flesch \cite{flesch1948new} and Gunning \cite{gunning1952technique}. Initial approaches focused primarily on surface-level features, operating under the assumption that shorter sentences and more common words correlate with easier comprehension. While these early measures demonstrated practical utility, subsequent research revealed their limitations in capturing the full complexity of text difficulty \cite{benjamin2012difficulty, mcnamara2014computational}. The emergence of computational linguistics and natural language processing technologies enabled more sophisticated approaches to textual complexity assessment. Coh-Metrix \cite{graesser2004coh, mcnamara2014computational} represented a significant advancement by incorporating multiple dimensions of textual analysis, including lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, and discourse structure. This system demonstrated that comprehensive textual analysis requires consideration of features beyond simple surface statistics. For Portuguese, several initiatives have attempted to address the need for automatic readability assessment tools. The work of Martins et al. \cite{martins1996readability} provided early adaptations of traditional readability formulas, while Scarton and Aluísio \cite{scarton2010analysis} developed more sophisticated measures incorporating syntactic parsing and semantic analysis. However, these efforts remained limited in scope compared to comprehensive systems available for English. Recent advances in Portuguese natural language processing have created new opportunities for textual complexity assessment. The development of robust parsing tools \cite{bick2000parsing, freitas2010automatic}, semantic analysis systems \cite{hartmann2014portuguese}, and large-scale corpora \cite{linguateca2019corpus} has provided the necessary infrastructure for implementing sophisticated textual metrics. Additionally, the availability of word embeddings and distributional semantic models for Portuguese \cite{hartmann2017portuguese} has enabled the incorporation of semantic coherence measures previously unavailable for the language. The educational technology domain has also driven interest in Portuguese readability assessment. Projects focusing on automatic text simplification \cite{aluisio2008towards, scarton2018simples} and reading comprehension support \cite{oliveira2009facilita} have highlighted the need for reliable complexity metrics to guide system development and evaluation. These applications require fine-grained analysis of textual properties that influence comprehension difficulty across different reader populations. The development of NILC-Metrix followed a systematic methodology encompassing metric selection, adaptation, implementation, and validation phases. The initial phase involved comprehensive literature review to identify established textual complexity measures with strong theoretical foundations and empirical validation. Priority was given to metrics that had demonstrated effectiveness in predicting reading difficulty and comprehension performance across diverse text types and reader populations. The metric selection process considered several criteria: theoretical grounding in cognitive models of text comprehension, empirical validation in previous studies, computational feasibility for Portuguese texts, and complementarity with other selected measures. This approach ensured that the final metric set would provide comprehensive coverage of textual complexity dimensions while maintaining computational efficiency and theoretical coherence. Adaptation of existing metrics for Portuguese required careful consideration of language-specific characteristics. Morphological complexity measures, for instance, needed modification to account for Portuguese inflectional patterns and derivational processes \cite{bick2000parsing}. Syntactic complexity metrics required adaptation to Portuguese phrase structure and dependency relations, utilizing the Universal Dependencies framework \cite{nivre2016universal} to ensure consistency with international standards. The implementation phase leveraged state-of-the-art natural language processing tools and resources for Portuguese. Morphological analysis was performed using established parsers and taggers \cite{bick2000parsing, freitas2010automatic}, while syntactic analysis utilized dependency parsing systems trained on Portuguese treebanks. Semantic analysis incorporated word embeddings and distributional semantic models specifically developed for Portuguese \cite{hartmann2017portuguese}. Novel metrics were developed to capture Portuguese-specific linguistic phenomena not adequately addressed by existing measures. These included metrics for clitic placement complexity, subjunctive mood usage patterns, and discourse marker distribution. The development of these metrics involved corpus-based analysis to establish baseline distributions and validation against expert linguistic judgments. Quality assurance procedures were implemented throughout the development process to ensure metric reliability and validity. Each metric underwent extensive testing on diverse text samples to identify potential implementation errors or unexpected behaviors. Cross-validation with established readability measures provided additional confidence in metric performance. The validation methodology incorporated both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation approaches. Intrinsic evaluation examined metric distributions across text types and correlation patterns with established complexity measures. Extrinsic evaluation assessed metric performance in predicting human judgments of text difficulty and reading comprehension outcomes. NILC-Metrix is implemented as a modular system designed for flexibility, extensibility, and computational efficiency. The architecture comprises several interconnected components, each responsible for specific aspects of textual analysis. This modular design facilitates maintenance, updates, and the incorporation of new metrics as research advances. The preprocessing module handles text normalization, tokenization, and basic linguistic annotation. This component ensures consistent input formatting across different text sources and prepares texts for subsequent analysis stages. Preprocessing includes sentence segmentation, word tokenization, and initial part-of-speech tagging using robust tools adapted for Portuguese text processing. The morphological analysis component performs detailed morphological parsing, identifying word stems, affixes, and inflectional features. This analysis is crucial for metrics that depend on morphological complexity, lexical diversity calculations, and semantic analysis. The component integrates multiple morphological analyzers to ensure comprehensive coverage of Portuguese morphological phenomena. Syntactic analysis is handled by a dedicated parsing module that generates both constituency and dependency representations of input texts. This dual representation enables the computation of diverse syntactic complexity metrics, from traditional measures based on phrase structure to more recent dependency-based indicators. The parsing module incorporates error handling and fallback mechanisms to ensure robust performance across varied text types. The semantic analysis component implements various approaches to semantic coherence assessment, including latent semantic analysis, word embedding-based measures, and distributional semantic models. This component is particularly important for metrics that assess conceptual coherence, semantic similarity between sentences, and overall text cohesion.

The adaptation of existing metrics for the Portuguese language demanded close attention to language-related issues. The selection of metrics was based on a number of criteria, including theoretical support from models of text comprehension, empirical validation in previous studies, computational feasibility for Portuguese texts, and complementarity with other metrics, which ensured that the final set of metrics would provide a full coverage of the dimensions of textual complexity, while maintaining both efficiency and consistency. New metrics were developed to take into account the peculiarities of Portuguese which the existing metrics failed to properly address. For example, morphological complexity metrics had to be adapted to take into account the inflections and derivations of Portuguese (Bick, 2000). Syntactic complexity metrics had to be adapted to the syntax and the syntax of Portuguese sentences, as well as to the relations between dependencies, based on the Universal Dependency Framework (Nivre, 2016), so as to be compatible with the international standards. These metrics included the metrics of clitic placement complexity, use of the subjunctive mood, and discourse markers. The morphological analysis was performed using parsers and taggers based on established methods (e.g. Bick (2000) and Freitas (2010)), the syntactic analysis with dependency parsers, and the semantic analysis with word embeddings and distributional semantic models for Portuguese (e.g. Hartmann, 2017). These metrics were then subjected to quality assurance procedures in order to ensure the reliability and validity of these metrics. These metrics were developed by corpus-based methods, which enabled the distribution of their underlying features to be determined, and then tested against expert linguistic judgments. The method used for verification employed both internal and external evaluation methods. The NILC-Metrix has been implemented as a flexible, extensible and computationally efficient system. The metrics were extensively tested on various samples of texts to identify bugs and unexpected behavior. Cross-validation with established readability metrics provided further confidence in the accuracy of the metrics. The architecture consists of a number of interconnected components, each responsible for a particular aspect of the text analysis. Intrinsic evaluations looked at metric distributions on different text types and the correlations with established complexity measures. Extrinsic evaluations looked at the performance of the metrics in predicting human judgments of text difficulty and comprehension. The morphological analysis part does a detailed morphological analysis, identifies stems, affixes and inflectional features. The preprocessing part performs text normalization, tokenization and basic linguistic annotation. This system facilitates the maintenance, update and the introduction of new metrics as research progresses. The morphological analysis of the input text is performed by a morphological analyzer that includes several analyzers that guarantee a complete coverage of the morphological phenomena of Portuguese. The pre-processing is a set of tools for sentence segmentation, tokenization and initial tagging of words, adapted to the Portuguese text. This component is responsible for ensuring a uniform input format from all sources and for preparing the text for the following stages. The parsing component includes error correction and fallback methods for robust performance on a wide range of text types. The semantic analysis component uses various methods for semantic coherence analysis, including latent semantic analysis, word embedding, and distributional semantic models. This analysis is of utmost importance for metrics based on morphological complexity, lexical diversity calculations, and semantic analysis. This component is especially important for metrics that measure the cohesion of ideas and sentences, and the cohesion of the whole text. This dual representation makes it possible to calculate a broad spectrum of syntactic complexity metrics, from the traditional measures based on phrase structure to the newer dependency indicators.

text: This paper presents a method to actively sample individuals in a population as a way to mitigate the spread of pandemics such as COVID-19. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical importance of effective testing strategies in controlling disease spread, particularly when testing resources are limited and must be allocated strategically. Traditional random sampling approaches, while statistically sound for prevalence estimation, may not be optimal for epidemic control when the goal is to identify and isolate infectious individuals before they can transmit the disease to others \cite{hellewell2020feasibility, kretzschmar2020impact}. Our approach addresses this challenge by developing a graph-theoretic framework that leverages contact network structure and epidemiological dynamics to guide testing decisions. Unlike conventional testing strategies that rely primarily on symptom-based screening or random sampling, our method actively seeks to identify high-risk individuals who are most likely to be infected or to cause future infections if left undetected. The key insight underlying our methodology is that disease transmission occurs through a complex network of social contacts, and this network structure contains valuable information that can be exploited to improve testing efficiency. By modeling the population as a contact network and incorporating epidemiological knowledge about disease transmission, we can develop adaptive testing strategies that significantly outperform naive approaches in terms of both case detection and transmission prevention. \subsection{Problem Formulation} We consider a population of $n$ individuals represented as vertices in a contact network $G = (V, E)$, where $V = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ and edges $(i,j) \in E$ represent potential transmission pathways between individuals $i$ and $j$. Each edge is associated with a weight $w_{ij}$ that captures the strength or frequency of contact between individuals $i$ and $j$. At any given time $t$, each individual $i$ can be in one of several epidemiological states: susceptible ($S$), exposed ($E$), infectious ($I$), or recovered ($R$). We denote the state of individual $i$ at time $t$ as $X_i(t) \in \{S, E, I, R\}$. The challenge is that these states are not directly observable, and we must infer them through testing and contact tracing. Let $p_i(t)$ denote our estimate of the probability that individual $i$ is infectious at time $t$, based on all available information up to that point. This probability is updated dynamically as new test results become available and as the epidemic evolves. The testing problem can then be formulated as selecting a subset $T(t) \subseteq V$ of individuals to test at time $t$, subject to a budget constraint $|T(t)| \leq B$, where $B$ represents the testing capacity. The objective function we seek to optimize depends on the specific goals of the testing program. For epidemic control, a natural objective is to minimize the expected number of new infections over a future time horizon. This can be expressed as: \begin{equation} \min_{T(t)} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{s=t}^{t+H} \sum_{i \in V} \mathbf{1}_{X_i(s) = I \text{ and } X_i(s-1) \neq I}\right] \end{equation} where $H$ is the planning horizon and $\mathbf{1}_{(\cdot)}$ is the indicator function. \subsection{Dynamic Risk Assessment} A central component of our framework is the dynamic risk assessment system that maintains and updates infection probability estimates $p_i(t)$ for each individual. These probabilities are computed using a Bayesian approach that incorporates multiple sources of information: \textbf{Prior epidemiological knowledge:} We begin with prior probabilities based on population-level prevalence estimates and individual characteristics such as age, occupation, and health status. \textbf{Contact network structure:} The network topology provides information about each individual's potential exposure risk. Individuals with many contacts or connections to high-risk individuals receive higher risk scores. \textbf{Test results:} Both positive and negative test results provide direct evidence about infection status, though the informativeness depends on test sensitivity and specificity. \textbf{Contact tracing data:} Information about contacts with confirmed cases allows us to identify individuals who may have been exposed. The risk update mechanism follows a Bayesian framework where the posterior probability of infection for individual $i$ at time $t$ is given by: \begin{equation} p_i(t) = \frac{P(\text{observations}|X_i(t) = I) \cdot p_i^{\text{prior}}(t)}{P(\text{observations})} \end{equation} where $p_i^{\text{prior}}(t)$ represents the prior probability based on network structure and epidemiological factors, and the likelihood term captures the probability of observing the current data given the infection status. \subsection{Network-Based Super-spreader Identification} Beyond individual risk assessment, our framework incorporates network-theoretic measures to identify potential super-spreaders—individuals who, if infected, are likely to cause many secondary infections due to their position in the contact network. We define a transmission potential score $\tau_i(t)$ for each individual $i$ that combines their infection probability with their potential to spread the disease: \begin{equation} \tau_i(t) = p_i(t) \cdot \phi_i(t) \end{equation} where $\phi_i(t)$ is a network centrality measure that captures individual $i$'s potential for onward transmission. Several centrality measures can be used for $\phi_i(t)$: \textbf{Degree centrality:} $\phi_i^{\text{deg}}(t) = \sum_{j \in V} w_{ij}$, representing the total contact strength. \textbf{Betweenness centrality:} $\phi_i^{\text{bet}}(t) = \sum_{s,t \in V} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}$, where $\sigma_{st}$ is the number of shortest paths between vertices $s$ and $t$, and $\sigma_{st}(i)$ is the number of those paths passing through vertex $i$. \textbf{Eigenvector centrality:} $\phi_i^{\text{eig}}(t)$ satisfies $\lambda \phi_i^{\text{eig}}(t) = \sum_{j \in V} w_{ij} \phi_j^{\text{eig}}(t)$, where $\lambda$ is the largest eigenvalue of the weighted adjacency matrix. \textbf{PageRank centrality:} A variant of eigenvector centrality that includes a damping factor to ensure convergence in all network types. The choice of centrality measure depends on the specific characteristics of the disease and the contact network. For diseases with short infectious periods, degree centrality may be most appropriate, while for diseases with longer infectious periods, betweenness or eigenvector centrality may better capture transmission potential. \subsection{Adaptive Testing Algorithm} Our adaptive testing algorithm operates in discrete time steps and makes testing decisions based on the current state of knowledge about the epidemic. At each time step $t$, the algorithm performs the following operations: \textbf{Step 1: Update risk probabilities.} For each individual $i$, update the infection probability $p_i(t)$ based on new test results, contact tracing information, and epidemiological model predictions. \textbf{Step 2: Compute transmission potential scores.} Calculate $\tau_i(t) = p_i(t) \cdot \phi_i(t)$ for each individual, where $\phi_i(t)$ is the chosen network centrality measure. \textbf{Step 3: Select individuals for testing.} Choose the subset $T(t) \subseteq V$ of size $|T(t)| \leq B$ that maximizes the expected reduction in future transmission. This can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem: \begin{equation} T^*(t) = \arg\max_{T \subseteq V, |T| \leq B} \sum_{i \in T} \tau_i(t) \cdot \Delta_i(t) \end{equation} where $\Delta_i(t)$ represents the expected reduction in transmission if individual $i$ tests positive and is subsequently isolated. \textbf{Step 4: Update network structure.} Based on test results and contact tracing, update the contact network by removing edges corresponding to isolated individuals and adding new edges as contact patterns evolve. The algorithm continues iteratively, adapting the testing strategy as new information becomes available and as the epidemic evolves. \subsection{Theoretical Properties} Our framework possesses several desirable theoretical properties that make it well-suited for pandemic response: \textbf{Adaptivity:} The algorithm continuously updates its testing strategy based on new information, allowing it to respond to changing epidemic conditions and contact patterns. \textbf{Efficiency:} By focusing testing resources on high-risk individuals, the algorithm maximizes the probability of detecting infectious cases with limited testing capacity. \textbf{Robustness:} The Bayesian update mechanism naturally handles uncertainty in test results and network structure, providing robust performance even when information is incomplete or noisy. \textbf{Scalability:} The computational complexity of the algorithm scales reasonably with network size, making it applicable to large populations. We can establish theoretical bounds on the performance of our algorithm compared to random testing strategies. Under certain assumptions about network structure and disease dynamics, we can show that our approach achieves a constant-factor approximation to the optimal testing strategy, which is computationally intractable for large networks. \begin{theorem} Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote our adaptive testing algorithm and $\mathcal{R}$ denote a random testing strategy with the same budget $B$. Under assumptions of network regularity and disease parameters within typical ranges for respiratory pathogens, the expected number of infections prevented by $\mathcal{A}$ is at least $\alpha$ times the expected number prevented by $\mathcal{R}$, where $\alpha > 1$ is a constant depending on network structure and disease parameters. \end{theorem} The proof of this theorem relies on concentration inequalities for functions of random graphs and properties of epidemic processes on networks. The constant $\alpha$ can be computed explicitly for specific network models and disease parameters.

The goal of a regression model is to learn a mapping $f:\mathcal{X}ightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ from a collection of data points $(x_m,y_m)\in \mathcal{X}	imes \mathcal{Y}, \ m=1,\ldots,M,$ such that $y_m\approx f(x_m)$, while avoiding overfitting and ensuring good generalization to unseen data. Traditional parametric approaches often impose rigid structural assumptions that may not align with the underlying data characteristics, while non-parametric methods can suffer from computational complexity and lack of interpretability. In this work, we address these limitations by developing a unified framework that combines the flexibility of kernel methods with the interpretability benefits of sparse representations. The challenge of balancing model complexity with generalization performance has been a central theme in machine learning and statistical inference. Classical approaches such as ridge regression \cite{hoerl1970ridge} and the LASSO \cite{tibshirani1996regression} have provided foundational insights into regularization strategies, but these methods are typically formulated in finite-dimensional parameter spaces. Our contribution extends these concepts to infinite-dimensional function spaces through the lens of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, enabling more flexible and principled treatment of smoothness constraints. \subsection{Motivation and Related Work} The motivation for continuous-domain sparse regression stems from several key observations about real-world data and modeling requirements. First, many physical phenomena exhibit smooth variations that are naturally captured by functions in RKHS. Second, interpretability often requires identifying the most relevant features or basis functions, which translates to sparsity in the function representation. Third, computational efficiency demands tractable algorithms that can scale to large datasets while maintaining theoretical guarantees. Recent advances in kernel methods have demonstrated their effectiveness in various machine learning tasks \cite{scholkopf2001learning, shawe2004kernel}. The representer theorem \cite{kimeldorf1971some} provides a fundamental result showing that the solution to many regularized learning problems can be expressed as a linear combination of kernel functions evaluated at the training points. However, this representation can become dense and difficult to interpret, particularly when the number of training samples is large. Sparse kernel methods have emerged as a promising direction to address these challenges. Approaches such as the relevance vector machine \cite{tipping2001sparse} and sparse Gaussian processes \cite{snelson2006sparse} have shown that it is possible to maintain predictive performance while significantly reducing model complexity. Our work builds upon these foundations by providing a more general theoretical framework that encompasses various sparsity-inducing penalties and kernel choices. \subsection{Technical Contributions} Our primary contributions can be summarized as follows: 	extbf{Theoretical Framework:} We establish a comprehensive theoretical foundation for continuous-domain sparse regression in RKHS. This includes existence and uniqueness results for the optimization problem, characterization of the solution structure, and convergence guarantees for our proposed algorithms. 	extbf{Algorithmic Development:} We present efficient computational methods for solving the resulting optimization problems. Our algorithms leverage modern optimization techniques such as proximal gradient methods and coordinate descent, adapted to the infinite-dimensional setting through careful discretization strategies. 	extbf{Sparsity Analysis:} We provide detailed analysis of the sparsity-inducing properties of various penalty functions in the continuous domain. This includes characterization of the conditions under which exact sparsity is achieved and the relationship between regularization parameters and solution sparsity. 	extbf{Empirical Validation:} We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing against state-of-the-art methods in terms of predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and interpretability. \subsection{Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces} Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}$. We consider functions $f: \mathcal{X} ightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that belong to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ associated with a positive definite kernel $k: \mathcal{X} 	imes \mathcal{X} ightarrow \mathbb{R}$. The RKHS $\mathcal{H}$ is equipped with an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot angle_{\mathcal{H}}$ and corresponding norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}}$. The reproducing property ensures that for any $f \in \mathcal{H}$ and $x \in \mathcal{X}$:  egin{equation} f(x) = \langle f, k(x, \cdot) angle_{\mathcal{H}} \end{equation} This fundamental property allows us to evaluate functions at specific points through inner products in the Hilbert space, providing a crucial link between the abstract function space and concrete computations. \subsection{Continuous-Domain Sparse Regression Formulation} Building upon the optimization problem introduced earlier, we now provide a more detailed mathematical formulation. Given training data $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ where $x_i \in \mathcal{X}$ and $y_i \in \mathcal{Y}$, we seek to find a function $f^* \in \mathcal{H}$ that solves:  egin{equation} f^* = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \mathcal{L}(f) :=  rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(y_i, f(x_i)) + \lambda_1 \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2 + \lambda_2 R_{	ext{sparse}}(f) \end{equation} where $\ell: \mathcal{Y} 	imes \mathcal{Y} ightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$ is a convex loss function, $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0$ are regularization parameters, and $R_{	ext{sparse}}(f)$ is a sparsity-inducing penalty functional. The choice of the sparsity penalty $R_{	ext{sparse}}(f)$ is crucial for achieving the desired balance between model complexity and interpretability. We consider several options: 	extbf{$\ell_1$-type penalties:} For functions that admit a representation $f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \alpha_j \phi_j(x)$ in terms of basis functions $\{\phi_j\}$, we can define:  egin{equation} R_{	ext{sparse}}(f) = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} |\alpha_j| \end{equation} 	extbf{Total variation penalties:} For functions defined on continuous domains, total variation provides a natural sparsity measure:  egin{equation} R_{	ext{sparse}}(f) = \int_{\mathcal{X}} |
abla f(x)| dx \end{equation} 	extbf{Mixed penalties:} Combinations of different penalty types can capture multiple aspects of sparsity:  egin{equation} R_{	ext{sparse}}(f) = \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} |\alpha_j| +  eta \int_{\mathcal{X}} |
abla f(x)| dx \end{equation} \subsection{Existence and Uniqueness} The well-posedness of the optimization problem \eqref{eq:main_optimization} requires careful analysis due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the function space. We establish the following fundamental result:  egin{theorem} Let $\ell$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous loss function that satisfies the growth condition $\ell(y, t) \geq c|t|^p - C$ for some $c > 0$, $C \geq 0$, and $p \geq 1$. Assume that $R_{	ext{sparse}}$ is a convex, lower semicontinuous functional on $\mathcal{H}$. Then the optimization problem \eqref{eq:main_optimization} admits a unique solution $f^* \in \mathcal{H}$. \end{theorem}  egin{proof} The proof follows from the direct method in the calculus of variations. The functional $\mathcal{L}(f)$ is convex and coercive due to the regularization terms. The lower semicontinuity of all components ensures that the infimum is attained. Uniqueness follows from the strict convexity of the RKHS norm term. \end{proof} \subsection{Representer Theorem Extension} A key computational advantage of our framework stems from an extension of the classical representer theorem to the sparse setting:  egin{theorem} Under the conditions of Theorem ef{thm:existence_uniqueness}, if $R_{	ext{sparse}}$ is translation-invariant with respect to the kernel evaluation functionals, then the solution $f^*$ to problem \eqref{eq:main_optimization} admits the representation:  egin{equation} f^*(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i^* k(x_i, x) + g^*(x) \end{equation} where $\{\alpha_i^*\}_{i=1}^n$ are optimal coefficients and $g^* \in \mathcal{H}$ lies in the null space of the evaluation functionals. \end{theorem} This result shows that despite the infinite-dimensional formulation, the solution can be expressed in terms of a finite number of kernel functions centered at the training points, plus potentially a sparse correction term. While humans can effortlessly adapt their anomaly detection mechanisms across different viewing conditions and camera perspectives, developing computational methods that exhibit similar robustness remains an open challenge. The complexity of video anomaly detection is further amplified when considering real-world deployment scenarios where cameras are not stationary. In applications such as autonomous navigation, drone surveillance, and mobile security systems, the camera's ego-motion creates a constantly changing visual field that traditional anomaly detection methods struggle to handle \cite{kumar2020toward, li2021video}. The fundamental assumption of many existing approaches—that the background remains relatively stable—is violated, leading to numerous false positives and missed detections. Moreover, the definition of what constitutes an anomaly becomes more nuanced in dynamic camera settings. This requires sophisticated understanding of 3D scene geometry, optical flow patterns, and temporal consistency across varying viewpoints. text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable performance improvements in various domains. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable performance improvements in various domains, including computer vision \cite{he2016deep}, natural language processing \cite{vaswani2017attention}, and speech recognition \cite{graves2013speech}. However, designing effective neural architectures typically requires extensive domain expertise and manual tuning of hyperparameters, making it a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. The architecture design space is vast and complex, with numerous choices regarding layer types, connectivity patterns, activation functions, and optimization strategies. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a promising solution to automate this design process. By formulating architecture design as an optimization problem, NAS methods can systematically explore the architecture space and identify high-performing designs without human intervention \cite{elsken2019neural}. The general NAS framework consists of three key components: a search space that defines the set of possible architectures, a search strategy that determines how to explore this space, and a performance estimation strategy that evaluates candidate architectures. Early NAS approaches, such as those proposed by Zoph and Le \cite{zoph2016neural}, employed reinforcement learning to train a controller network that generates architecture descriptions. These methods demonstrated the feasibility of automated architecture design by discovering architectures that matched or exceeded human-designed networks on benchmark datasets. However, the computational requirements were enormous, often requiring thousands of GPU days to complete a single search. The prohibitive computational cost of early NAS methods has driven significant research into more efficient alternatives. One major breakthrough came with the introduction of weight sharing mechanisms. Methods like Efficient Neural Architecture Search (ENAS) \cite{pham2018efficient} maintain a single supernet that encompasses all possible architectures in the search space. By sharing weights among different architectural components, ENAS reduces the computational overhead from thousands to hundreds of GPU hours. This approach treats the search process as training a single large network where different paths correspond to different architectures. Building upon weight sharing, Differentiable Architecture Search (DARTS) \cite{liu2018darts} further revolutionized the field by making the search process fully differentiable. Instead of treating architecture search as a discrete optimization problem, DARTS relaxes the search space to be continuous, allowing gradient-based optimization techniques to be applied directly. This approach represents each edge in the architecture as a weighted combination of all possible operations, with the weights learned through standard backpropagation. The continuous relaxation in DARTS enables efficient search using gradient descent, typically completing searches in just a few GPU days. However, this approach introduces its own challenges, including the discretization gap between the continuous search space and the final discrete architecture, and potential instabilities during the optimization process \cite{zela2020understanding}. Progressive search strategies offer another avenue for improving efficiency. These methods start with simple architectures and gradually increase complexity during the search process \cite{liu2017progressive}. By building upon previously discovered good architectures, progressive methods can guide the search toward promising regions of the architecture space more efficiently than random exploration. Performance prediction methods represent a fundamentally different approach to reducing NAS computational costs. Rather than training architectures to completion, these methods aim to predict final performance from limited information. Surrogate models \cite{white2021powerful} learn mappings from architecture encodings to performance metrics using historical data from previous searches. Once trained, these models can rapidly evaluate new architectures without expensive training procedures. Zero-shot NAS methods \cite{mellor2021neural} push this concept further by predicting architecture performance using only network initialization statistics, completely eliminating the need for training. These approaches analyze properties of the randomly initialized network, such as gradient flow characteristics or activation patterns, to estimate final performance. While promising, zero-shot methods often struggle with accuracy and generalization across different datasets and tasks. Multi-objective optimization has also gained attention in NAS, recognizing that practical deployment scenarios require balancing multiple criteria beyond accuracy \cite{tan2019mnasnet}. Modern NAS methods increasingly consider factors such as inference latency, memory consumption, energy efficiency, and model size. This multi-objective perspective is particularly important for mobile and edge computing applications where resource constraints are critical. The search space design itself significantly impacts both the efficiency and effectiveness of NAS methods. Macro search spaces define entire network architectures from scratch, offering maximum flexibility but requiring extensive exploration. Micro search spaces focus on optimizing smaller components, such as individual cells or blocks, which are then repeated to form complete architectures. This hierarchical approach reduces the search complexity while maintaining architectural diversity. Recent advances have also explored hardware-aware NAS \cite{cai2019once}, which explicitly considers the target deployment platform during the search process. These methods optimize architectures not only for accuracy but also for efficient execution on specific hardware, such as mobile processors or specialized accelerators. This approach is crucial for practical applications where deployment constraints are as important as model performance. Despite significant progress, several challenges remain in NAS research. The transferability of discovered architectures across different datasets and tasks is still limited, often requiring separate searches for each new application. The search spaces used in current methods may not capture all relevant architectural innovations, potentially missing novel design patterns. Additionally, the evaluation protocols and benchmarks used to compare NAS methods vary significantly, making it difficult to assess relative performance objectively. Looking forward, the field continues to evolve toward more efficient, generalizable, and practical NAS methods that can democratize neural architecture design across diverse applications and deployment scenarios.

The Wasserstein barycenter (WB) is a popular method in statistics and machine learning for summarizing data from multiple sources while capturing their underlying geometry~\cite{martial11}. The concept of Wasserstein barycenters extends the classical notion of averaging to the space of probability measures, providing a principled framework for computing representative distributions that preserve geometric structure. Unlike simple pointwise averaging, which can lead to undesirable artifacts such as blurring or loss of support structure, Wasserstein barycenters maintain the geometric properties of the input distributions by minimizing the sum of squared Wasserstein distances. Formally, given a collection of probability measures $\{\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n\}$ on a metric space $(\mathcal{X}, d)$ and associated weights $\{\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n\}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = 1$ and $\lambda_i \geq 0$, the Wasserstein barycenter $\mu^*$ is defined as the solution to the optimization problem:  egin{equation} \mu^* = \arg\min_{\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})} \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i W_2^2(\mu, \mu_i), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ denotes the space of probability measures on $\mathcal{X}$ and $W_2$ is the 2-Wasserstein distance. The theoretical foundations of Wasserstein barycenters were established by \cite{agueh2011barycenters}, who proved existence and uniqueness results under appropriate conditions. Their work demonstrated that when the underlying space has non-positive curvature, the barycenter is unique and can be characterized through the first-order optimality conditions. This theoretical framework has since been extended to various settings, including discrete measures \cite{cuturi2014fast}, continuous distributions \cite{bigot2012characterization}, and measures on manifolds \cite{kim2017wasserstein}. The computational challenges associated with Wasserstein barycenters stem from the inherent complexity of optimal transport problems. For discrete measures supported on $m$ points, computing a single Wasserstein distance requires solving a linear program with $O(m^2)$ variables and constraints, leading to computational complexity of $O(m^3 \log m)$ using interior point methods. This method alternates between updating the barycenter support and recomputing the optimal transport plans, but suffers from slow convergence and high memory requirements. The algorithm's convergence rate is typically linear, requiring hundreds or thousands of iterations for reasonable accuracy. To address these computational bottlenecks, several approximation strategies have been developed. Image processing applications include texture synthesis, color transfer, and morphing operations that maintain structural coherence. In machine learning, barycenters serve as powerful tools for data summarization and prototype learning. They have been applied to clustering problems where traditional centroid-based methods fail to capture the underlying data geometry. Domain adaptation represents another important application area, where barycenters help align distributions from different domains while preserving relevant structure. The field of computational biology has also benefited from Wasserstein barycenter methods, particularly in single-cell genomics where researchers need to integrate data from multiple experimental conditions or time points. The geometric nature of Wasserstein distances makes them well-suited for capturing the continuous nature of biological processes. Financial applications include portfolio optimization and risk assessment, where barycenters can represent typical market behaviors while accounting for the geometric structure of return distributions. The ability to incorporate transportation costs makes these methods particularly relevant for problems involving spatial or temporal constraints. Quantum computing approaches may offer exponential speedups for certain classes of optimal transport problems, though practical implementations remain in early stages. text: Dhrupad is one of the oldest forms of North Indian classical vocal music. Dhrupad is one of the oldest forms of North Indian classical vocal music, tracing its origins to the ancient Vedic chanting traditions and flourishing during the medieval period under the patronage of Mughal courts \cite{Sanyal1987, Dagar2005}. Characterized by its austere melodic structure, profound spiritual content, and sophisticated rhythmic framework, Dhrupad represents the most classical and pure form of Indian vocal music. Unlike other North Indian classical forms such as \emph{khayal}, Dhrupad maintains strict adherence to the \emph{raga} structure while allowing for extensive improvisation within well-defined parameters. The performance structure of Dhrupad follows a distinctive four-part format known as \emph{alap}, \emph{jor}, \emph{jhala}, and \emph{bandish}. The \emph{alap} section begins without rhythmic accompaniment, featuring slow, meditative exploration of the chosen \emph{raga} through systematic elaboration of its characteristic phrases and melodic contours \cite{Widdess2006}. This is followed by the \emph{jor}, where a subtle pulse emerges, and the \emph{jhala}, characterized by rapid rhythmic patterns. The final section, \emph{bandish}, introduces the composed text set to a specific \emph{tala} (rhythmic cycle) with full percussion accompaniment, typically provided by the \emph{pakhawaj} drum. The textual component of Dhrupad holds particular significance, as the lyrics are predominantly devotional, drawing from Sanskrit, Braj Bhasha, and other classical languages. These texts often invoke Hindu deities, philosophical concepts, or descriptions of natural phenomena, requiring the vocalist to maintain perfect diction while navigating complex melodic passages \cite{Neuman1990}. The integration of text, melody, and rhythm creates a multidimensional artistic expression that demands exceptional technical skill and deep cultural understanding. From a computational perspective, the analysis of Dhrupad presents unique challenges due to its microtonal inflections, extensive use of \emph{meend} (gliding between notes), and complex ornamental patterns. Traditional Western music analysis tools, designed primarily for tempered scales and fixed pitch systems, often prove inadequate for capturing the subtle nuances of Indian classical music \cite{Serra2011, Koduri2012}. The present research addresses these limitations by developing specialized algorithms that account for the specific characteristics of Dhrupad vocal performance. The automatic segmentation of Dhrupad audio into its constituent structural components represents a significant advancement in computational musicology. Such segmentation enables detailed analysis of performance practices, pedagogical applications, and preservation of this endangered musical tradition. Current digital archives of Dhrupad recordings lack systematic structural annotations, making it difficult for researchers and students to navigate and study specific aspects of the performance \cite{Chordia2005}. Recent developments in machine learning and signal processing have opened new possibilities for music information retrieval in Indian classical music. Deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks, have shown promise in identifying \emph{raga} characteristics and tracking melodic progression \cite{Dutta2016, Gulati2017}. However, the application of these techniques to Dhrupad-specific analysis remains limited, primarily due to the scarcity of annotated datasets and the complexity of the musical form. The motivation for this research stems from the urgent need to preserve and systematically study Dhrupad, which faces the threat of declining practitioner numbers and limited documentation. Master practitioners of this tradition possess invaluable knowledge that is traditionally transmitted through oral instruction, making computational analysis tools essential for broader accessibility and scholarly investigation \cite{Viswanathan2004}. This thesis presents a comprehensive framework for the automatic structural analysis and segmentation of Dhrupad vocal performances, contributing to both the fields of music information retrieval and Indian classical music research. The proposed methodology combines traditional musicological insights with state-of-the-art computational techniques to achieve accurate identification of performance sections and detailed analysis of rhythmic transformation patterns.

text: Stock market returns and volatility prediction have attracted much attention from academia as well as the financial industry. Traditional approaches to forecasting financial time series have relied primarily on historical price data, trading volumes, and macroeconomic indicators. Classical models such as GARCH \cite{bollerslev1986generalized} and its variants have been extensively used to model volatility clustering and heteroskedasticity in financial returns. Similarly, autoregressive models and vector autoregressions have formed the backbone of return prediction methodologies for decades. The efficient market hypothesis \cite{fama1970efficient} suggests that asset prices fully reflect all available information, making prediction inherently challenging. However, behavioral finance research has documented numerous market anomalies and inefficiencies that create opportunities for enhanced forecasting models. These inefficiencies often stem from investor sentiment, cognitive biases, and information processing limitations that manifest in predictable patterns in asset prices. The proliferation of digital media and real-time information dissemination has fundamentally altered the information landscape in financial markets. News sentiment, social media discussions, and analyst communications now influence market dynamics at unprecedented speed and scale. This information-rich environment presents both opportunities and challenges for quantitative researchers seeking to improve prediction accuracy. Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that incorporating textual sentiment measures can significantly enhance the performance of traditional econometric models. \cite{tetlock2008more} showed that media pessimism predicts downward pressure on market prices, while \cite{garcia2013sentiment} found that news sentiment contains information about daily stock returns beyond that captured by standard financial variables. The challenge lies in effectively extracting and quantifying sentiment signals from unstructured textual data while maintaining statistical rigor in model specification and evaluation. Modern natural language processing techniques offer sophisticated tools for this task, but their application to financial forecasting requires careful consideration of domain-specific characteristics and market microstructure effects. This paper contributes to the growing literature on sentiment-enhanced financial forecasting by developing a comprehensive framework that integrates multiple textual data sources with traditional quantitative models. We propose novel feature engineering techniques specifically designed for financial text analysis and demonstrate their effectiveness in both return and volatility prediction tasks across different market conditions and time horizons.

text: A growing body of work has described tools, employed optimization methods, or proposed new algorithms to help automate the design and/or fabrication of robots (e.g.,~\citep{Luck-RSS-17,Schulz17,HoovFearing08,pervan2018low,zhang2020abstractions}). These automated design approaches span multiple domains, from mechanical structure optimization to control system synthesis, addressing the fundamental challenge of creating robots that are both functionally capable and resource-efficient. The complexity of modern robotic systems, which often integrate sophisticated sensors, actuators, and computational units, necessitates systematic methodologies for design space exploration and optimization. Traditional robot design has relied heavily on human expertise and iterative prototyping, processes that are time-consuming and may not explore the full space of possible solutions. Automated design tools promise to overcome these limitations by leveraging computational optimization techniques to systematically search through design alternatives \cite{lipson2000automatic}. However, the high-dimensional nature of robot design spaces presents significant computational challenges, particularly when considering the combinatorial explosion of possible configurations. The intersection of automated design and combinatorial filter reduction becomes particularly relevant when considering robots that must operate under strict computational or memory constraints. Embedded robotic systems, swarm robotics applications, and resource-limited autonomous vehicles all benefit from minimalist state representations that preserve essential functionality while reducing computational overhead \cite{correll2009design}. This motivates the development of design automation tools that can simultaneously optimize both physical robot parameters and their associated computational architectures. \subsection{Problem Formulation} Consider a robot design problem where we seek to minimize both the physical complexity of the robot and the computational complexity of its state estimation and control systems. Let $\mathcal{R} = \{r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n\}$ represent the set of possible robot configurations, where each configuration $r_i$ is characterized by its mechanical design parameters, sensor suite, and computational architecture. The design optimization problem can be formulated as: \begin{equation} \min_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left[ \alpha \cdot C_{\text{physical}}(r) + \beta \cdot C_{\text{computational}}(r) + \gamma \cdot C_{\text{performance}}(r) \right] \end{equation} where $C_{\text{physical}}(r)$ represents the physical cost (e.g., material usage, manufacturing complexity), $C_{\text{computational}}(r)$ captures the computational requirements, and $C_{\text{performance}}(r)$ quantifies the performance degradation relative to an optimal but potentially resource-intensive baseline. The weighting parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ allow designers to prioritize different aspects of the optimization objective. The computational cost term $C_{\text{computational}}(r)$ is particularly relevant to our discussion of combinatorial filter reduction. For robots employing probabilistic state estimation, this cost is directly related to the size and complexity of the belief state representation. Efficient filter reduction techniques can significantly reduce $C_{\text{computational}}(r)$ while maintaining acceptable performance levels. \subsection{Challenges in Automated Robot Design} Several key challenges emerge when attempting to automate robot design processes. First, the multi-objective nature of the optimization problem requires careful balance between competing objectives. A robot design that minimizes physical complexity may require more sophisticated computational algorithms to achieve the same performance level, illustrating the inherent trade-offs in the design space. Second, the evaluation of candidate designs often requires expensive simulations or physical prototyping. This creates a sample efficiency problem where the optimization algorithm must make informed decisions about which designs to evaluate based on limited data. Surrogate modeling techniques and Bayesian optimization approaches have shown promise in addressing this challenge \cite{shahriari2015taking}. Third, the constraint satisfaction aspect of robot design introduces additional complexity. Robots must satisfy kinematic constraints, dynamic stability requirements, and task-specific performance criteria. These constraints often define non-convex feasible regions in the design space, making optimization particularly challenging. \subsection{Integration with Combinatorial Filter Reduction} The connection between automated robot design and combinatorial filter reduction becomes apparent when considering the computational architecture component of robot design. Many automated design tools focus primarily on mechanical optimization while treating the computational system as a separate concern. However, a more holistic approach recognizes that the choice of sensors, actuators, and mechanical configuration directly impacts the complexity of the required state estimation and control algorithms. For instance, a robot equipped with redundant sensors may have access to richer information about its environment, but this comes at the cost of increased computational complexity in sensor fusion and state estimation. Combinatorial filter reduction techniques can help identify which sensor modalities and state variables are truly necessary for achieving desired performance levels, informing both the sensor selection and mechanical design processes. The structural properties of the robot's task environment also influence the effectiveness of different filter reduction approaches. Robots operating in highly structured environments may benefit from exploiting environmental symmetries and regularities to achieve more aggressive state space compression \cite{toussaint2006probabilistic}. Conversely, robots in unstructured or adversarial environments may require more conservative approaches that preserve robustness at the expense of compression efficiency. \subsection{Contributions and Organization} This paper presents a unified framework for integrating combinatorial filter reduction techniques into automated robot design processes. Our main contributions include: \begin{enumerate} \item A mathematical formulation that explicitly couples physical robot design parameters with computational architecture decisions \item Novel algorithms for jointly optimizing robot morphology and state representation complexity \item Experimental validation demonstrating significant improvements in design efficiency and robot performance \item Analysis of the fundamental trade-offs between physical and computational complexity in robotic systems \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in automated robot design and combinatorial optimization. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} presents our integrated design framework and associated algorithms. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes experimental validation on several robot design problems. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations of our approach, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with directions for future research.

text: Ranking search results that match a user query is a critical component of information retrieval (IR) systems that power many popular websites. Typically, learning to rank (LTR) algorithms are employed to optimize ranking functions based on training data consisting of query-document pairs with associated relevance labels \cite{liu2009learning}. These algorithms can be broadly categorized into three approaches: pointwise, pairwise, and listwise methods, each with distinct advantages and computational trade-offs \cite{li2007learning}. Pointwise approaches treat ranking as a regression or classification problem, predicting relevance scores for individual query-document pairs independently. While computationally efficient, these methods fail to capture the relative ordering relationships that are fundamental to ranking tasks \cite{cossock2006subset}. Pairwise methods address this limitation by learning from document pairs, optimizing the probability that one document should be ranked higher than another given a query. Popular pairwise algorithms include RankNet, RankBoost, and LambdaMART, which have shown strong empirical performance across various domains \cite{burges2005learning, freund2003efficient, burges2010ranknet}. Listwise approaches represent the most sophisticated category, directly optimizing list-level metrics such as NDCG or MAP. These methods consider the entire ranked list structure during training, potentially leading to better alignment between training objectives and evaluation metrics \cite{xia2008listwise, cao2007learning}. However, listwise methods often suffer from increased computational complexity and optimization challenges due to the non-differentiable nature of many ranking metrics. The choice of loss function significantly impacts the performance and behavior of learning-to-rank systems. Traditional approaches often rely on surrogate losses that approximate the desired ranking metrics while maintaining differentiability. For instance, the pairwise hinge loss used in RankSVM provides a convex approximation to the pairwise ranking error \cite{joachims2002optimizing}. More recent work has explored direct optimization of non-differentiable ranking metrics through techniques such as policy gradient methods and differentiable approximations \cite{ai2018unbiased, oosterhuis2020policy}. Feature engineering remains a crucial aspect of effective ranking systems, despite advances in end-to-end neural approaches. Traditional ranking features can be categorized into query-dependent and query-independent signals. Query-dependent features capture the relationship between the query and document content, including term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) scores, BM25 similarity measures, and semantic similarity computed through embedding models \cite{robertson2009probabilistic, mikolov2013distributed}. Query-independent features assess document quality and authority, incorporating signals such as PageRank scores, click-through rates, and content freshness indicators \cite{page1999pagerank}. The integration of neural networks into learning-to-rank frameworks has opened new possibilities for automatic feature learning and representation discovery. Deep neural ranking models can learn complex non-linear relationships between queries and documents, potentially eliminating the need for manual feature engineering \cite{guo2016deep}. Convolutional neural networks have been successfully applied to capture local patterns in text matching, while recurrent neural networks excel at modeling sequential dependencies in query and document text \cite{hu2014convolutional, palangi2016deep}. Attention mechanisms have proven particularly valuable in neural ranking architectures, enabling models to focus on the most relevant portions of documents when processing queries. The BERT-based ranking models, such as MonoBERT and DuoBERT, leverage pre-trained transformer representations to achieve state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks \cite{nogueira2019document, nogueira2020document}. These models benefit from large-scale pre-training on diverse text corpora, allowing them to capture rich semantic relationships that traditional sparse features cannot express. However, the deployment of neural ranking models in production systems presents significant challenges. The computational overhead of deep neural networks can be prohibitive for real-time ranking of large candidate sets, necessitating careful architectural design and optimization strategies \cite{mitra2017neural}. Multi-stage ranking pipelines have emerged as a practical solution, where lightweight models perform initial candidate selection, followed by more sophisticated neural re-ranking of top candidates \cite{nogueira2019multi}. Training data quality and bias represent critical concerns in learning-to-rank systems. Human relevance judgments, which form the foundation of most training datasets, are inherently subjective and may not reflect the diverse preferences of actual users \cite{voorhees2001overview}. Position bias, where users are more likely to click on higher-ranked results regardless of relevance, can lead to feedback loops that reinforce existing ranking patterns \cite{joachims2017accurately}. Techniques such as inverse propensity scoring and unbiased learning-to-rank methods have been developed to address these challenges \cite{joachims2017unbiased}. The evaluation of learning-to-rank systems requires careful consideration of both offline and online metrics. Offline evaluation using held-out test sets provides controlled assessment of ranking quality, but may not capture the full complexity of user behavior and satisfaction \cite{sanderson2010test}. Online evaluation through A/B testing offers more realistic performance assessment but requires careful experimental design to account for factors such as novelty effects and long-term user adaptation \cite{kohavi2009controlled}. Fairness and bias mitigation have become increasingly important considerations in modern ranking systems. Algorithmic bias can manifest in various forms, including demographic bias that disadvantages certain user groups, and exposure bias that unfairly promotes or demotes specific content providers \cite{chen2018measuring}. Fair ranking algorithms aim to balance relevance optimization with equitable treatment across different groups, often requiring explicit constraints or regularization terms in the learning objective \cite{singh2018fairness}. The scalability of learning-to-rank systems to web-scale datasets presents additional technical challenges. Distributed training frameworks and efficient sampling strategies are essential for handling billions of query-document pairs in reasonable time frames \cite{dean2008mapreduce}. Online learning approaches that can adapt to changing user preferences and content distributions without full model retraining have gained attention for their practical advantages in dynamic environments \cite{hofmann2013reusing}.

text: The availability of computation as a resource has been growing exponentially since at least the 1970s, and there is every indication that this resource will continue to become cheaper and more accessible in the coming decades. This computational abundance has fundamentally transformed the landscape of control systems design, enabling the deployment of sophisticated algorithms that were previously computationally prohibitive. Modern control applications can now leverage high-performance computing architectures, including graphics processing units (GPUs), tensor processing units (TPUs), and distributed computing frameworks, to implement complex optimization routines and machine learning algorithms in real-time. The intersection of abundant computation and advanced control theory has given rise to a new paradigm in feedback control design. Model predictive control (MPC), once limited to slow industrial processes due to computational constraints, can now be applied to fast-dynamics systems such as autonomous vehicles and robotic manipulators \cite{rawlings2017model}. Similarly, reinforcement learning algorithms that require extensive online learning and adaptation can now be deployed in real-time control scenarios, opening up possibilities for adaptive and self-improving control systems. However, this computational revolution brings with it a fundamental tension between performance and theoretical guarantees. While machine learning-based controllers can achieve remarkable empirical performance across diverse applications, they often operate as "black boxes" that resist traditional stability analysis. The challenge lies not merely in computational complexity, but in the fundamental mismatch between the probabilistic, data-driven nature of modern learning algorithms and the deterministic, model-based foundations of classical control theory. Consider the case of deep reinforcement learning controllers, which have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex control tasks such as robotic manipulation \cite{levine2016end} and autonomous navigation \cite{kahn2017uncertainty}. These controllers are typically trained using stochastic gradient methods on large datasets, resulting in highly nonlinear policies that map observations to control actions through millions of parameters. The resulting control policies may exhibit excellent performance during training and testing phases, yet their behavior under previously unseen conditions or in the presence of adversarial inputs remains largely unpredictable. This unpredictability becomes particularly concerning in safety-critical applications where control failures can result in catastrophic consequences. Aerospace systems, medical devices, and autonomous vehicles require not only high performance but also rigorous safety guarantees that can be verified before deployment. The traditional approach of extensive testing and simulation, while valuable, cannot provide the mathematical certainty that formal verification methods offer. The gap between empirical performance and theoretical guarantees has motivated a growing body of research at the intersection of control theory and machine learning. One promising direction involves the development of hybrid approaches that combine the expressiveness of neural networks with the analytical tractability of linear controllers. For instance, neural network-based observers can be paired with linear quadratic regulators (LQR) to maintain stability guarantees while improving state estimation accuracy \cite{amos2018differentiable}. Another approach focuses on constraining the learning process itself to ensure that the resulting controllers satisfy certain stability properties by construction. This includes techniques such as control barrier functions \cite{ames2019control}, which can be integrated into the training objective to enforce safety constraints, and Lyapunov-based neural network architectures that guarantee stability through their structural design \cite{chang2019neural}. The challenge of bridging machine learning and control theory also extends to the realm of system identification and adaptive control. Modern data-driven system identification methods, powered by deep learning architectures, can capture complex system dynamics that traditional parametric models cannot represent. However, the resulting models often lack the structural properties required for robust control design, such as controllability, observability, and well-defined uncertainty bounds.

text: Recent deep neural networks (DNNs) make breakthroughs in many areas such as computer vision, speech recognition and so on. The power of DNNs brings people infinite reverie. However, the vulnerability of DNNs to adversarial attacks has raised significant concerns about their deployment in safety-critical applications \cite{szegedy2013intriguing, goodfellow2014explaining}. Adversarial examples are carefully crafted inputs that appear benign to human observers but can fool deep learning models into making incorrect predictions with high confidence. These malicious perturbations, often imperceptible to the human eye, expose fundamental weaknesses in the robustness of neural networks and pose serious security threats in real-world scenarios. The adversarial vulnerability problem has attracted considerable attention from the research community, leading to an arms race between attack methods and defense strategies. On the attack side, various techniques have been developed to generate adversarial examples, ranging from gradient-based methods like Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) \cite{goodfellow2014explaining} and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) \cite{madry2017towards} to more sophisticated approaches such as C\&W attacks \cite{carlini2017towards} and AutoAttack \cite{croce2020reliable}. These methods exploit the high-dimensional nature of input spaces and the non-linear decision boundaries of neural networks to find adversarial directions that maximize prediction errors. Correspondingly, numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed to enhance the adversarial robustness of deep learning models. Adversarial training \cite{madry2017towards} remains one of the most effective approaches, where models are trained on a mixture of clean and adversarial examples to learn robust feature representations. However, adversarial training often comes with significant computational overhead and may lead to reduced accuracy on clean examples. Other defense strategies include input preprocessing techniques \cite{guo2017countering}, certified defenses \cite{cohen2019certified}, and ensemble methods \cite{tramer2017ensemble}. Despite these efforts, achieving robust adversarial defense remains a challenging problem. Many proposed defenses have been shown to be vulnerable to adaptive attacks or fail to generalize across different threat models \cite{athalye2018obfuscated, carlini2019evaluating}. This highlights the need for more principled and effective defense mechanisms that can provide reliable protection against a wide range of adversarial attacks. In this context, our work focuses on exploiting the hierarchical structure of deep neural networks to develop a novel defense strategy. The key insight underlying our approach is that adversarial perturbations, while effective at the input level, may be attenuated or filtered out as information propagates through the network's hidden layers. This observation motivates us to design defense mechanisms that operate on intermediate feature representations rather than solely on input preprocessing. \subsection{Adversarial Attacks} Adversarial attacks can be broadly categorized into white-box and black-box attacks based on the adversary's knowledge of the target model. White-box attacks assume full access to the model parameters and gradients, enabling the generation of highly effective adversarial examples through gradient-based optimization. The FGSM attack \cite{goodfellow2014explaining} represents one of the earliest and most influential methods in this category, generating adversarial examples by taking a single step in the direction of the gradient: \begin{equation} \mathbf{x}_{adv} = \mathbf{x} + \epsilon \cdot \text{sign}(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} J(\mathbf{x}, y)) \end{equation} where $J(\mathbf{x}, y)$ is the loss function, $\epsilon$ controls the perturbation magnitude, and $y$ is the true label. More sophisticated iterative methods like PGD \cite{madry2017towards} and Basic Iterative Method (BIM) \cite{kurakin2016adversarial} apply multiple gradient steps with projection to ensure the perturbations remain within the allowed $\ell_p$ norm ball. The PGD attack, in particular, has become a standard benchmark for evaluating adversarial robustness due to its effectiveness and theoretical foundations. Black-box attacks, on the other hand, operate without direct access to model parameters and rely on query-based methods or transferability properties of adversarial examples \cite{papernot2017practical, chen2017zoo}. These attacks are particularly relevant for real-world scenarios where attackers have limited information about the target system. \subsection{Adversarial Defenses} Existing adversarial defense methods can be classified into several categories. \textit{Adversarial training} approaches \cite{madry2017towards, zhang2019theoretically} augment the training data with adversarial examples, forcing the model to learn robust decision boundaries. While effective, these methods often require significant computational resources and may suffer from reduced clean accuracy. \textit{Input preprocessing} defenses \cite{guo2017countering, xu2017feature} attempt to remove adversarial perturbations before feeding inputs to the model. Common techniques include image denoising, JPEG compression, and bit-depth reduction. However, many preprocessing-based defenses have been shown to be vulnerable to adaptive attacks that account for the preprocessing step. \textit{Certified defenses} \cite{cohen2019certified, lecuyer2019certified} provide theoretical guarantees about the model's robustness within a certain perturbation radius. These methods often rely on randomized smoothing or interval bound propagation to compute certified robust radii. While providing strong theoretical foundations, certified defenses typically come with computational overhead and may not scale well to large networks. \textit{Detection-based defenses} \cite{li2017adversarial, ma2018characterizing} aim to identify adversarial examples rather than classify them correctly. These methods analyze various statistical properties or activation patterns to distinguish between clean and adversarial inputs. However, detection-based approaches are often vulnerable to adaptive attacks designed to evade the detection mechanism. \subsection{Feature-based Defenses} Our work is most closely related to feature-based defense methods that operate on intermediate network representations. Several prior works have explored similar ideas from different perspectives. Feature squeezing \cite{xu2017feature} reduces the search space available to adversaries by applying transformations that eliminate unnecessary input features. However, this approach primarily focuses on input-level transformations rather than hidden layer representations. Dimensionality reduction techniques have been applied to adversarial defense in various forms. Some works \cite{bhagoji2017dimensionality, ma2018dimensionality} explore the use of PCA and other linear dimensionality reduction methods for input preprocessing. Our approach differs by applying dimensionality reduction to intermediate feature representations, which we hypothesize can more effectively preserve semantic information while filtering adversarial noise. The concept of feature compression for adversarial robustness has also been explored in the context of network compression and knowledge distillation \cite{papernot2016distillation, goldblum2020adversarially}. These methods typically focus on transferring knowledge from larger teacher networks to smaller student networks, with robustness emerging as a byproduct of the compression process.
