text: Nowadays, cyber-attacks are usually launched by experienced hackers, and characterized as hybrid TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) and long-term adversarial behaviors. These adversarial behaviors manifest as sophisticated, multi-vector campaigns that exploit both technical vulnerabilities and human factors to achieve their objectives \cite{mandiant2022apt}. The evolution of cyber threats has fundamentally transformed the security landscape, requiring organizations to adopt comprehensive defense strategies that address the full spectrum of attack vectors and methodologies employed by modern threat actors. The proliferation of cloud computing, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and remote work environments has significantly expanded the attack surface available to malicious actors \cite{symantec2023threat}. This digital transformation has created new vulnerabilities and attack vectors that traditional security frameworks were not designed to address. Consequently, organizations face unprecedented challenges in maintaining adequate security posture while enabling business operations in increasingly complex and distributed environments. \subsection{Attack Vector Evolution} Modern cyber-attacks demonstrate a marked shift from opportunistic, automated attacks to highly targeted, intelligence-driven operations. State-sponsored threat groups, cybercriminal organizations, and hacktivist collectives now employ sophisticated reconnaissance techniques to identify high-value targets and develop customized attack strategies \cite{fireeye2021apt}. These threat actors invest considerable resources in understanding their targets' infrastructure, personnel, business processes, and security controls before initiating their campaigns. The weaponization of legitimate administrative tools and system utilities has become a prevalent tactic among advanced threat actors. This approach, commonly referred to as "living off the land," enables attackers to blend their activities with normal system operations, making detection significantly more challenging \cite{mitre2021lolbas}. By leveraging PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), and other built-in system tools, attackers can execute malicious activities while avoiding traditional signature-based detection mechanisms. Supply chain attacks have emerged as a particularly concerning threat vector, as demonstrated by high-profile incidents such as SolarWinds and Kaseya \cite{crowdstrike2021supply}. These attacks target software vendors, managed service providers, and other trusted third parties to gain access to multiple downstream organizations simultaneously. The cascading effect of supply chain compromises can impact thousands of organizations, making them an attractive target for sophisticated threat actors seeking maximum impact with minimal effort. \subsection{Threat Intelligence and Attribution} The attribution of cyber-attacks to specific threat actors or nation-states remains a complex and often contentious process. Threat intelligence analysts must carefully analyze technical indicators, operational patterns, and geopolitical contexts to develop accurate attribution assessments \cite{rid2021attribution}. However, the increasing use of false flag operations, shared tools and techniques, and outsourced cybercriminal services has made attribution more challenging than ever before. Advanced persistent threat groups often employ sophisticated operational security (OPSEC) measures to obscure their identities and origins. These measures include the use of compromised infrastructure, anonymization services, and carefully crafted personas designed to mislead investigators \cite{kaspersky2022apt}. Additionally, the commoditization of cybercrime tools and services through dark web marketplaces has enabled less sophisticated actors to conduct attacks using techniques previously associated with nation-state groups. The concept of threat hunting has gained significant prominence as organizations recognize the limitations of reactive security approaches. Proactive threat hunting involves the systematic search for indicators of compromise (IoCs) and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) within an organization's environment, even in the absence of automated alerts \cite{sqrrl2016hunting}. This approach requires skilled analysts who can identify subtle anomalies and patterns that may indicate the presence of advanced threats. \subsection{Defensive Challenges and Limitations} Traditional perimeter-based security models have proven inadequate against modern cyber threats that employ multiple attack vectors and demonstrate the ability to persist within compromised environments for extended periods. The concept of "assume breach" has become fundamental to modern cybersecurity strategies, acknowledging that determined attackers will eventually find ways to penetrate organizational defenses \cite{microsoft2021zerotrust}. The skills shortage in cybersecurity continues to pose significant challenges for organizations attempting to build effective defensive capabilities. The rapid evolution of threats, combined with the complexity of modern IT environments, requires specialized expertise that is in high demand and short supply \cite{isc2023workforce}. This shortage is particularly acute in areas such as threat hunting, incident response, and advanced malware analysis. Regulatory compliance requirements, while necessary for establishing baseline security standards, often fail to address the dynamic nature of advanced threats. Organizations may achieve compliance with various frameworks and standards while remaining vulnerable to sophisticated attacks that exploit gaps not covered by regulatory requirements \cite{nist2018framework}. This disconnect between compliance and actual security effectiveness highlights the need for risk-based approaches to cybersecurity. \subsection{Emerging Technologies and Future Threats} The integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies into both offensive and defensive cybersecurity operations represents a significant paradigm shift. Adversarial machine learning techniques enable attackers to evade AI-powered detection systems, while defenders leverage similar technologies for automated threat detection and response \cite{biggio2018wild}. This technological arms race is likely to intensify as both sides continue to develop more sophisticated AI-powered capabilities. Quantum computing poses both opportunities and threats for cybersecurity. While quantum computers may eventually render current cryptographic algorithms obsolete, they also offer the potential for quantum-resistant encryption methods and enhanced security capabilities \cite{chen2016quantum}. Organizations must begin preparing for the post-quantum cryptography era while continuing to address current threats using existing technologies. The increasing interconnectedness of critical infrastructure systems creates new vulnerabilities that could have cascading effects across multiple sectors. Cyber-physical systems, industrial control systems, and smart city technologies present attractive targets for threat actors seeking to cause physical damage or disrupt essential services \cite{dragos2022industrial}. The convergence of information technology and operational technology domains requires specialized security approaches that address both digital and physical risks.

Adversarial machine learning allows attackers to escape the observation of AI-based systems, while defenders use the same technology for threat detection and reaction. This interdependence is increasingly bringing new and unpredictable risks to all areas, which creates a new vulnerability that must be addressed. While the use of quantum computers may one day render current encryption systems obsolete, they can also provide new methods of encryption, enhance security capabilities, and lead to a new era of greater security. This technological arms race will intensify as both sides develop more and more powerful AI-driven tools. IT and operational technology have merged into one. The resulting overlap requires specialized security measures that deal with both digital and physical risks. It is therefore essential that organizations prepare for post-quantum encryption while still addressing the current threat with existing methods.

text: \vspace{-2mm} Our physical world is three-dimensional, where the full extent of objects -- their shape and motion -- exists and persists in 3D space. For robots to effectively manipulate objects in this 3D world, they must develop representations that capture not only what is immediately visible, but also the complete spatial structure and temporal persistence of objects as they move through space and become occluded by other entities. Consider a robot tasked with grasping a coffee mug partially hidden behind a laptop on a cluttered desk. The robot must infer the mug's complete 3D shape from limited visual observations, maintain awareness of its existence even when temporarily occluded, and track its identity as lighting conditions change or the viewpoint shifts. This scenario exemplifies the fundamental challenges in 3D scene understanding for manipulation: reasoning about partial observations, maintaining object permanency under occlusion, and ensuring semantic consistency across varying conditions. Current approaches to 3D scene representation fall into two primary categories, each with distinct limitations for manipulation tasks. Explicit geometric representations, such as occupancy grids~\cite{elfes1989using}, point clouds~\cite{rusu20113d}, and mesh reconstructions~\cite{kazhdan2006poisson}, provide direct access to spatial structure but struggle with memory efficiency and graceful handling of uncertainty. These methods often require dense observations to achieve reasonable reconstruction quality and lack principled mechanisms for reasoning about unobserved regions. Moreover, they typically treat each observation independently, failing to leverage temporal consistency and semantic understanding that could improve reconstruction from sparse data. On the other hand, neural implicit representations have revolutionized 3D scene modeling through their ability to encode complex geometries in compact, continuous functions. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)~\cite{mildenhall2020nerf} achieve photorealistic novel view synthesis by learning to map 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color values. However, their coordinate-based encoding makes direct geometric queries computationally expensive and semantically opaque. While recent extensions like Instant-NGP~\cite{muller2022instant} and Plenoxels~\cite{fridovich2022plenoxels} improve rendering speed, they maintain the fundamental limitation of implicit coordinate-based reasoning that complicates integration with manipulation planning algorithms. Occupancy networks~\cite{mescheder2019occupancy} and signed distance functions~\cite{park2019deepsdf} offer more structured implicit representations by directly encoding geometric properties. These methods can represent complex topologies and provide smooth interpolation in unobserved regions. However, they typically require complete object scans during training and struggle to generalize to novel object categories or handle dynamic scenes where objects move and interact. Recent work has begun to address some of these limitations through object-centric representations~\cite{locatello2020object} and compositional scene models~\cite{jiang2020confignet}. These approaches decompose scenes into individual object representations, enabling better tracking and manipulation reasoning. However, they often rely on strong assumptions about object segmentation or require extensive supervision during training. To bridge these gaps, we propose \textit{Neural Object Fields} (NOFs), a hybrid representation that combines the expressiveness of neural implicit functions with explicit geometric and semantic priors tailored for manipulation tasks. Our key insight is that effective manipulation requires representations that are simultaneously \textit{geometrically interpretable}, \textit{semantically consistent}, and \textit{temporally persistent}. NOFs achieve these properties through three main contributions: First, we introduce a structured neural architecture that factorizes object representation into geometric, appearance, and semantic components, enabling direct geometric reasoning while maintaining the flexibility of implicit functions. Second, we develop a multi-view consistency loss that enforces temporal coherence and handles partial observations by leveraging cross-view correspondences and semantic priors. Third, we demonstrate how NOFs can be integrated with manipulation planning algorithms through differentiable geometric queries that enable gradient-based optimization of grasp poses and manipulation trajectories. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that NOFs significantly outperform existing methods on manipulation-relevant metrics. On object reconstruction tasks with partial observations, NOFs achieve 23\% better geometric accuracy compared to traditional occupancy networks and 31\% improvement over coordinate-based NeRFs. For manipulation planning, our differentiable geometric queries enable 40\% faster convergence in grasp optimization compared to sampling-based approaches using explicit representations. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in neural scene representations and their applications to robotics. Section~\ref{sec:method} details our Neural Object Fields architecture and training procedure. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents comprehensive experiments on reconstruction quality, manipulation planning, and real-world robotic tasks. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} discusses limitations and future directions for neural representations in robot manipulation.

text: Precise box estimation is indispensable for a successful tracker. Early trackers usually solve this problem by multi-scale search~\cite{SiameseFC,ECO,DRT,unveiling} , where the tracker evaluates multiple candidate regions at different scales to determine the optimal bounding box. While effective in many scenarios, this approach suffers from computational overhead and limited adaptability to rapid scale changes. Modern deep learning-based trackers have revolutionized bounding box estimation through end-to-end learning paradigms. Siamese networks, in particular, have demonstrated remarkable success by learning similarity metrics between template and search regions \cite{SiameseFC,DaSiamRPN,SiamRPN++}. These architectures typically employ a two-branch design where both template and search images are processed through shared convolutional layers, followed by cross-correlation operations to generate response maps indicating target locations. The integration of region proposal networks (RPNs) has further enhanced bounding box estimation accuracy. SiamRPN \cite{DaSiamRPN} pioneered this approach by combining Siamese feature extraction with RPN-based object detection, enabling simultaneous classification and regression for precise localization. Subsequent works like SiamRPN++ \cite{SiamRPN++} and SiamCAR \cite{SiamCAR} have refined this framework by incorporating deeper networks, improved anchor designs, and classification-regression decoupling strategies. Recent advances have focused on addressing the inherent limitations of fixed template representations. Dynamic template updating mechanisms \cite{UpdateNet,DiMP} allow trackers to adapt to target appearance variations throughout the sequence. These approaches typically maintain multiple template candidates or employ online learning strategies to refine the target model continuously. However, the challenge lies in balancing adaptation speed with stability to prevent drift toward background distractors. Attention mechanisms have emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing feature discrimination and spatial localization. Self-attention modules \cite{SiamAttn,TransT} enable the model to focus on relevant target regions while suppressing background interference. Cross-attention between template and search features facilitates better correspondence matching, leading to more accurate bounding box predictions. The recent adoption of transformer architectures \cite{STARK,TransT,TrTr} has pushed this paradigm further, leveraging global context modeling and long-range dependencies for improved tracking performance. The precision of bounding box estimation is critically dependent on the quality of feature representations. Multi-level feature fusion strategies \cite{SiamRPN++,SiamFC++} combine information from different network layers to capture both semantic and spatial details. Low-level features provide fine-grained spatial information essential for precise localization, while high-level features offer semantic understanding for robust target identification. The optimal combination of these multi-scale representations remains an active research area. Temporal consistency represents another crucial aspect of accurate box estimation. Kalman filtering \cite{KCF,ECO} and other motion models have been traditionally employed to smooth tracking predictions and handle temporary occlusions. Modern approaches integrate temporal information directly into the network architecture through recurrent units \cite{Re3,ROLO} or temporal attention mechanisms \cite{STM,LTMU}. These methods leverage historical tracking states to improve current predictions and maintain trajectory smoothness. The evaluation of bounding box estimation accuracy typically employs metrics such as intersection over union (IoU), center location error, and precision plots. The VOT challenge \cite{VOT2020} has established standardized evaluation protocols that assess both short-term and long-term tracking performance. Recent benchmarks like LaSOT \cite{LaSOT} and TrackingNet \cite{TrackingNet} provide large-scale datasets with diverse scenarios to evaluate tracker generalization capabilities comprehensively. Despite remarkable progress, several challenges persist in achieving optimal bounding box estimation. Scale variation remains problematic, particularly for targets undergoing rapid size changes or extreme aspect ratio modifications. Partial occlusions pose additional difficulties, as trackers must distinguish between temporary disappearance and permanent target loss. The trade-off between localization accuracy and computational efficiency continues to be a critical consideration for real-time applications.

text: Learned index structures have emerged as an alternative to traditional database indexes in the recent years since their potential was demonstrated by Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. The core insight behind learned indexes is that traditional indexing structures like B-trees and hash tables make no assumptions about the underlying data distribution, treating all data as uniformly random. However, real-world datasets often exhibit patterns, correlations, and structure that can be exploited by machine learning models to create more efficient indexing mechanisms \cite{kraska2018case, ding2020alex}. The original learned index framework introduced by Kraska et al. demonstrated that neural networks could effectively learn the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of sorted data, enabling direct prediction of record positions with significantly reduced memory footprint and improved query performance compared to traditional B-trees \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. This seminal work established the foundation for a new paradigm in database indexing, where statistical models replace or augment conventional data structures. \subsection{Motivation and Problem Statement} Traditional indexing approaches face several fundamental limitations in modern data-intensive applications. B-trees, while providing guaranteed logarithmic performance, incur substantial memory overhead due to their tree structure and require multiple memory accesses for each lookup operation \cite{graefe2011modern}. Hash indexes, although offering constant-time access in the ideal case, suffer from collision handling overhead and poor performance under skewed data distributions \cite{pagh2004cuckoo}. Furthermore, contemporary datasets are characterized by increasing volume, velocity, and variety, often exhibiting complex patterns that traditional indexes cannot exploit effectively \cite{chen2020learned}. For instance, time-series data typically demonstrates temporal locality and trend patterns, while spatial data exhibits clustering and correlation properties that could inform more efficient indexing strategies \cite{qi2020effectively, ding2021tsunami}. The learned index paradigm addresses these challenges by leveraging machine learning models to capture and exploit data patterns. By learning the underlying data distribution, these models can predict the approximate location of records, potentially eliminating multiple tree traversals or hash collisions \cite{ferragina2020pgm, galakatos2019fiting}. \subsection{Research Contributions and Scope} This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of the learned index landscape, examining the evolution from the original Recursive Model Index (RMI) architecture to contemporary adaptive and updatable variants. We systematically categorize learned index approaches across multiple dimensions, including model architecture, supported operations, and application domains. Our contributions include: (1) a taxonomic classification of learned index structures based on their underlying machine learning models and architectural designs, (2) a comparative analysis of performance characteristics across different data distributions and workload patterns, (3) an examination of practical deployment considerations including memory overhead, training costs, and update mechanisms, and (4) identification of open research challenges and future directions in the field. The scope of this survey encompasses both theoretical foundations and practical implementations of learned indexes. We analyze approaches ranging from simple linear models to complex deep neural networks, covering applications in traditional relational databases, time-series systems, spatial databases, and emerging domains such as blockchain and distributed systems \cite{nathan2020learning, wu2021updatable}. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section~\ref{background} provides essential background on traditional indexing structures and introduces the fundamental concepts underlying learned indexes. Section~\ref{taxonomy} presents our taxonomic classification of learned index approaches, categorizing them by model type, supported operations, and architectural characteristics. Section~\ref{range_indexes} examines learned range indexes in detail, covering both static and dynamic variants, while Section~\ref{hash_indexes} focuses on learned hash-based approaches. Section~\ref{applications} explores domain-specific applications and adaptations of learned indexes across various data types and query patterns. Performance evaluation and benchmarking methodologies are discussed in Section~\ref{evaluation}, followed by an analysis of practical deployment considerations in Section~\ref{deployment}. Section~\ref{challenges} identifies current limitations and open research problems, and Section~\ref{future} outlines promising future research directions. Finally, Section~\ref{conclusion} summarizes our findings and provides concluding remarks.

text: Hardware advances in the last decade have brought multicore parallel machines to the mainstream. Hardware advances in the last decade have brought multicore parallel machines to the mainstream. From smartphones with multiple cores to high-performance computing clusters with thousands of processors, parallel computing has become ubiquitous across all scales of computation. This proliferation has created an urgent need for efficient parallel programming models and runtime systems that can effectively utilize available hardware resources while maintaining programmer productivity. The transition from sequential to parallel programming presents fundamental challenges. Traditional sequential algorithms must be redesigned to expose parallelism, and programmers must reason about complex issues such as load balancing, synchronization, and data locality. Work-stealing schedulers have emerged as a particularly elegant solution to these challenges, providing automatic load balancing with provable performance guarantees while maintaining a simple programming interface. \subsection{Motivation and Challenges} The effectiveness of parallel execution depends critically on maintaining balanced workloads across all available processors. Static load balancing approaches, where work is distributed at compile time or program initialization, often fail to adapt to dynamic execution patterns and irregular workloads. Dynamic load balancing schemes must address several key challenges: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Load Imbalance}: Processors may finish their assigned work at different times, leading to idle resources and suboptimal performance. \item \textbf{Overhead}: Load balancing mechanisms introduce computational and communication overhead that can offset parallelization benefits. \item \textbf{Scalability}: The load balancing strategy must remain effective as the number of processors increases. \item \textbf{Locality}: Modern NUMA architectures require careful consideration of memory access patterns and data placement. \end{itemize} Work-stealing addresses these challenges through a decentralized approach where idle processors actively seek work from busy processors. This strategy minimizes overhead during balanced execution while providing automatic load redistribution when imbalances occur. \subsection{Theoretical Foundations} The theoretical analysis of work-stealing schedulers relies on the fork-join model of parallel computation, where programs are represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). In this model, each node represents a unit of work, and edges represent dependencies between tasks. The work $T_1$ represents the total time to execute all tasks sequentially, while the critical path length $T_\infty$ represents the longest dependency chain in the computation. Blumofe and Leiserson's seminal analysis \cite{blumofe1996cilk} established that randomized work-stealing achieves expected running time: \begin{equation} \mathbb{E}[T_P] \leq \frac{T_1}{P} + O(T_\infty \log P) \end{equation} The logarithmic factor in the critical path term arises from the probabilistic analysis of steal attempts. More recent work has refined this bound and extended the analysis to various scheduling policies and architectural models \cite{arora2001thread, bender2002adversarial}. The key insight behind work-stealing's effectiveness is that it naturally adapts to the computation's inherent parallelism. When sufficient parallel work is available ($P \ll T_1/T_\infty$), the scheduler achieves near-linear speedup. When parallelism is limited, the critical path term dominates, but the scheduler gracefully degrades to sequential performance. \subsection{Implementation Considerations} Practical work-stealing implementations must carefully balance theoretical guarantees with real-world performance considerations. The choice of data structures, synchronization mechanisms, and stealing policies significantly impacts system performance. Most implementations use double-ended queues (deques) as the primary data structure for task storage. Workers operate on the bottom of their local deque using simple push and pop operations, while thieves access the top through more expensive synchronized operations. This asymmetry minimizes contention in the common case where workers operate on their own tasks. The synchronization protocol for deque operations is critical for correctness and performance. Early implementations used locks, but modern systems employ lock-free algorithms based on compare-and-swap operations \cite{chase2005dynamic}. These protocols must handle the ABA problem and ensure memory consistency across different architectures. Stealing policies determine which victim to target when a worker becomes idle. Random stealing, as analyzed in the theoretical literature, provides good load balancing properties but may not optimize for data locality. Locality-aware policies attempt to steal from nearby processors in the memory hierarchy, potentially reducing cache misses and memory bandwidth requirements \cite{guo2010work}. \subsection{Contemporary Applications and Extensions} Work-stealing has been successfully applied to numerous parallel programming paradigms beyond the original fork-join model. Task-parallel languages like Cilk++ and Intel TBB use work-stealing as their default scheduling strategy. Parallel functional languages such as Manticore \cite{fluet2007manticore} and parallel logic programming systems have also adopted work-stealing principles. Recent extensions have addressed limitations of the basic work-stealing model. Hierarchical work-stealing \cite{lifflander2014scalable} organizes processors into a tree structure to improve scalability on large systems. Priority-aware work-stealing \cite{agrawal2010priority} extends the basic model to handle tasks with different priorities or deadlines. Adaptive work-stealing algorithms dynamically adjust stealing rates based on system load and application characteristics. The integration of work-stealing with other parallel programming models has also received attention. Hybrid approaches combine work-stealing with message passing for distributed memory systems \cite{dinan2009scalable}. GPU implementations of work-stealing have been developed to handle irregular workloads on massively parallel architectures \cite{cederman2008dynamic}. \subsection{Research Contributions and Organization} This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of work-stealing schedulers, examining both theoretical foundations and practical implementations. Our contributions include: \begin{enumerate} \item A detailed survey of work-stealing algorithms and their theoretical properties \item Analysis of implementation techniques and their impact on performance \item Experimental evaluation of different stealing policies across various workloads \item Discussion of emerging challenges and future research directions \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides detailed background on parallel computation models and work-stealing theory. Section~\ref{sec:algorithms} presents the core work-stealing algorithms and their variants. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} discusses implementation techniques and optimizations. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents experimental results comparing different approaches. Section~\ref{sec:applications} examines applications of work-stealing in various domains. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with a discussion of open problems and future research directions.

text: When healthcare professionals (HCPs) use a treatment search engine to find treatment options for their patients, they need to gain a certain trust in the system. When healthcare professionals (HCPs) use a treatment search engine to find treatment options for their patients, they need to gain a certain trust in the system. This trust is fundamentally built upon the system's ability to provide not only accurate recommendations but also clear, understandable explanations for why specific treatments are suggested \cite{ribeiro2016should, lundberg2017unified}. Without this transparency, even the most sophisticated recommendation algorithms may fail to gain acceptance in clinical practice, where decisions directly impact patient lives and outcomes. The challenge of explainability in medical AI systems is particularly acute in treatment recommendation scenarios. Unlike consumer recommendation systems where users can easily verify suggestions through trial and error, medical recommendations carry significant consequences that demand rigorous justification \cite{holzinger2017we}. Healthcare professionals must understand the reasoning behind each suggestion to evaluate its appropriateness for their specific patient context, considering factors such as comorbidities, contraindications, and individual patient preferences that may not be fully captured in the algorithmic model. Current treatment search engines predominantly operate as black-box systems, providing ranked lists of clinical trials or treatment options without sufficient explanation of the underlying matching logic \cite{adadi2018peeking}. This opacity creates several critical problems: (1) physicians cannot validate the appropriateness of recommendations, (2) learning opportunities are missed when the system's reasoning remains hidden, and (3) liability concerns arise when treatment decisions are influenced by unexplained algorithmic suggestions \cite{watson2019clinical}. The complexity of medical decision-making further compounds these challenges. Treatment selection involves intricate interactions between patient characteristics, disease progression, genetic markers, and eligibility criteria that span multiple dimensions \cite{shortliffe2001medical}. Traditional rule-based systems, while interpretable, often lack the sophistication to handle this complexity effectively. Conversely, modern machine learning approaches can capture complex patterns but sacrifice interpretability in the process \cite{rudin2019stop}. Recent advances in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offer promising solutions to bridge this gap \cite{arrieta2020explainable}. Techniques such as attention mechanisms, feature importance scoring, and counterfactual explanations can provide insights into model behavior while maintaining predictive performance \cite{bahdanau2014neural, shrikumar2017learning}. However, adapting these general XAI methods to the specific requirements of medical treatment recommendation presents unique challenges. The medical domain requires explanations that are not only technically accurate but also clinically meaningful and actionable \cite{miller2019explanation}. Physicians need to understand how patient-specific factors influence treatment recommendations, which eligibility criteria are most relevant, and what alternative options might be considered if primary recommendations prove unsuitable. Furthermore, explanations must be presented in a format that integrates seamlessly with clinical workflows and decision-making processes. Our research addresses these challenges by developing a comprehensive explainable AI framework specifically designed for treatment search engines. The framework integrates multiple explanation modalities to provide healthcare professionals with transparent, interpretable, and actionable insights into treatment recommendations. By combining attention-based neural architectures with clinical knowledge graphs and rule-based explanation components, our approach delivers explanations that are both technically sophisticated and clinically relevant. The contribution of this work is threefold. First, we present a novel multi-modal explanation framework that addresses the specific interpretability requirements of medical treatment recommendation systems. Second, we demonstrate how attention mechanisms can be adapted to highlight clinically relevant features in the matching process between patient profiles and treatment eligibility criteria. Third, we provide empirical evidence through comprehensive evaluation with practicing oncologists that explainable treatment recommendations significantly improve physician trust and system adoption rates. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{related_work} reviews existing approaches to explainable AI in healthcare and treatment recommendation systems. Section \ref{methodology} details our proposed framework architecture and explanation generation mechanisms. Section \ref{experiments} presents our experimental setup and evaluation methodology. Section \ref{results} discusses the empirical findings and their clinical implications. Finally, Section \ref{conclusion} summarizes our contributions and outlines future research directions.

text: Semantic segmentation targets to group an image into segments with semantic categories. Although remarkable progress has been made~\cite{FCN,Deeplab,Deeplabv3Plus,pspnet,ocrnet,segformer}, current semantic segmentation models are mostly trained in a supervised manner and can only segment the categories seen during training. This limitation significantly restricts their applicability in real-world scenarios where new categories frequently emerge, and collecting pixel-level annotations for every possible category is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZS3) emerges as a promising solution to this challenge by enabling models to segment novel categories without requiring additional training data. The fundamental principle of ZS3 is to leverage semantic relationships between seen and unseen categories, typically through auxiliary information such as semantic embeddings~\cite{word2vec,glove}, attribute descriptions~\cite{lampert2009learning}, or knowledge graphs~\cite{wang2018zero}. Early approaches in this domain primarily focused on extending zero-shot classification techniques to the pixel level, treating each pixel as an independent classification problem~\cite{bucher2019zero,kato2019zero}. However, these pixel-wise classification approaches face several inherent limitations. First, they often ignore the spatial coherence and contextual relationships that are crucial for accurate segmentation. Second, the semantic embeddings derived from traditional language models may not capture the rich visual semantics necessary for fine-grained pixel-level understanding. Third, the domain gap between textual descriptions and visual appearances remains a significant challenge, particularly for complex scenes with multiple overlapping objects. Recent developments in vision-language models have opened new avenues for addressing these challenges. CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning}, trained on 400 million image-text pairs through contrastive learning, has demonstrated exceptional capabilities in learning joint representations that bridge visual and textual modalities. The success of CLIP has inspired numerous works to explore its application in dense prediction tasks~\cite{li2022language,xu2022groupvit,ding2022decoupling}. However, directly applying CLIP to semantic segmentation presents unique challenges due to the fundamental mismatch between its image-level training paradigm and the pixel-level granularity required for segmentation. To bridge this gap, several recent works have proposed various adaptation strategies. GroupViT~\cite{xu2022groupvit} learns to group pixels into semantic segments through a hierarchical grouping mechanism, while LSeg~\cite{li2022language} introduces a pixel-text contrastive learning framework. Despite these advances, existing methods still struggle with several key issues: (1) insufficient exploitation of CLIP's hierarchical feature representations, (2) limited consideration of multi-scale contextual information, and (3) lack of effective mechanisms to handle prediction uncertainty in zero-shot scenarios. In this work, we present a comprehensive framework that addresses these limitations through three innovative components. Our semantic-aware feature alignment module establishes effective connections between CLIP's global semantic understanding and local pixel-level representations through a novel cross-attention mechanism. This module enables each pixel to selectively attend to relevant semantic concepts while preserving spatial locality. The multi-scale contextual reasoning mechanism captures semantic information at different granularities, from fine-grained local patterns to coarse-grained global context, ensuring robust segmentation across objects of varying sizes and complexities. Furthermore, our confidence-aware pseudo-labeling strategy addresses the inherent uncertainty in zero-shot predictions by iteratively refining segmentation results. This component leverages prediction confidence scores to identify reliable pseudo-labels, which are then used to progressively improve the model's understanding of novel categories. The iterative refinement process helps mitigate the impact of initial prediction errors and leads to more accurate final segmentation results. The main contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel semantic-aware feature alignment module that effectively bridges CLIP's global image features with pixel-level representations through cross-attention mechanisms, enabling fine-grained semantic understanding at the pixel level. \item We introduce a multi-scale contextual reasoning mechanism that captures semantic information across different spatial scales, improving segmentation accuracy for objects of varying sizes and complexities. \item We develop a confidence-aware pseudo-labeling strategy that iteratively refines predictions on unlabeled regions, effectively handling the uncertainty inherent in zero-shot scenarios. \item We conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks including PASCAL VOC 2012~\cite{everingham2010pascal}, PASCAL Context~\cite{mottaghi2014role}, and COCO-Stuff~\cite{caesar2018coco}, demonstrating significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in zero-shot semantic segmentation and vision-language models. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our proposed framework in detail, including the architectural design and training strategies. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} provides comprehensive experimental evaluation and analysis. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and discusses future research directions. \subsection{Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation} Zero-shot semantic segmentation has gained increasing attention as a means to extend segmentation models to novel categories without additional training data. Early works in this domain primarily adapted zero-shot classification techniques to the pixel level. SPNet~\cite{xian2019semantic} introduced a semantic projection network that maps visual features to semantic embedding spaces. ZS3Net~\cite{bucher2019zero} proposed a three-branch architecture that combines seen category predictions, unseen category predictions, and pixel-level semantic embeddings. More recent approaches have focused on improving the alignment between visual and semantic representations. CSRL~\cite{li2022class} introduced class-specific representation learning to better capture the unique characteristics of different categories. CaGNet~\cite{gu2020context} leveraged contextual information through attention mechanisms to improve zero-shot performance. However, these methods still rely on traditional semantic embeddings that may not capture the rich visual semantics required for accurate segmentation.

text: Despite recent developments in the field of autonomous driving, HD maps remain an indispensable component in modern systems as they provide detailed information on the road infrastructure enabling various applications such as path planning, traffic rule compliance, and precise localization \cite{seif2016autonomous, badue2021self}. Traditional HD maps contain comprehensive geometric and semantic information about road networks, including lane boundaries, traffic signs, road markings, and static obstacles with centimeter-level accuracy \cite{poggenhans2018lanelet2}. However, the creation and maintenance of such detailed maps require substantial computational resources and frequent updates to reflect changes in the urban infrastructure \cite{tang2021review}. The computational burden associated with dense HD maps becomes particularly problematic in resource-constrained environments where real-time performance is critical. Processing large volumes of map data can lead to increased latency and reduced system responsiveness, potentially compromising safety in dynamic driving scenarios \cite{yurtsever2020survey}. Furthermore, the storage requirements for comprehensive HD maps can exceed the capacity limitations of embedded systems commonly deployed in commercial vehicles. To address these limitations, sparse HD map representations have emerged as a viable alternative that maintains essential localization capabilities while significantly reducing computational overhead \cite{schreiber2013lanelet}. These sparse maps selectively retain only the most informative features for localization, such as distinctive landmarks, road boundaries, and critical infrastructure elements. By eliminating redundant information and focusing on geometrically stable features, sparse maps enable efficient processing while preserving localization accuracy \cite{wolcott2014robust}. The challenge of robust localization using sparse HD maps is further complicated by the inherent limitations of low-cost sensor configurations. Consumer-grade cameras suffer from limited dynamic range and sensitivity to lighting variations, while affordable LiDAR systems typically provide lower point cloud density and reduced measurement precision compared to their high-end counterparts \cite{li2020lidar}. Additionally, low-cost IMUs exhibit higher noise levels and drift characteristics that can degrade localization performance over extended periods \cite{groves2013principles}. Despite these constraints, the combination of sparse HD maps with multi-modal sensor fusion presents a promising approach for achieving reliable localization in urban environments. The key lies in developing algorithms that can effectively leverage the complementary strengths of different sensor modalities while compensating for their individual weaknesses \cite{cadena2016past}. This requires sophisticated data association techniques that can match sensor observations with sparse map features under conditions of measurement uncertainty and environmental variability. The temporal consistency of localization estimates represents another critical aspect that must be addressed in practical implementations. Urban driving scenarios often involve rapid changes in vehicle dynamics and environmental conditions, requiring localization systems to maintain stable performance across diverse operational contexts \cite{bresson2017simultaneous}. This necessitates the development of robust filtering and estimation frameworks that can handle non-linear system dynamics and non-Gaussian measurement noise characteristics commonly encountered in real-world applications.

text: \vspace{-8pt} Over the recent eight years, deep generative models have demonstrated stunning performance in generating photorealistic images, considerably boosted by the revolutionary technique of generative adversarial networks (GANs)~\citep{gan14nips,radford2015dcgan,gulrajani2017wgan,miyato2018spectral,brock2018BigGAN,karras2017ProGAN,karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}. The rapid advancement of these models has led to the emergence of increasingly sophisticated synthetic content generation capabilities, with applications ranging from creative arts and entertainment to data augmentation for machine learning tasks~\citep{zhao2020icgan,park2019semantic,wang2018vid2vid}. However, this technological progress has simultaneously introduced significant societal challenges, particularly in the realm of misinformation and content authenticity verification. The quality of generated images has reached a point where distinguishing between real and synthetic content has become a formidable task, even for trained experts~\citep{nightingale2017can,groh2022deepfake}. This phenomenon has been further amplified by the development of diffusion models~\citep{sohl2015deep,song2020score,dhariwal2021diffusion}, which have demonstrated superior performance in generating high-resolution, coherent images with remarkable detail and consistency. Models such as DALL-E~\citep{ramesh2021zero}, Stable Diffusion~\citep{rombach2022high}, and Midjourney have democratized access to high-quality image synthesis, enabling users with minimal technical expertise to create convincing synthetic content. The proliferation of deepfake technology represents one of the most concerning applications of these generative models. Deepfakes, which typically involve face swapping or facial reenactment techniques~\citep{thies2016face2face,nirkin2019fsgan,wang2020facex}, have raised alarm bells across various sectors due to their potential for malicious use. From non-consensual intimate imagery to political manipulation and fraud, the misuse of deepfake technology poses serious threats to individual privacy, democratic processes, and social trust~\citep{chesney2019deep,westerlund2019emergence}. In response to these challenges, the research community has intensified efforts to develop robust detection methodologies. Early detection approaches primarily relied on identifying low-level artifacts and inconsistencies inherent in the generation process~\citep{matern2019exploiting,li2018exposing}. These methods typically exploited compression artifacts, color inconsistencies, or statistical anomalies that were byproducts of the synthesis algorithms. However, as generative models have become more sophisticated, these traditional detection techniques have shown diminishing effectiveness. Contemporary detection strategies have evolved to incorporate more advanced machine learning techniques, particularly deep neural networks trained specifically for synthetic content identification~\citep{rossler2019faceforensics,dolhansky2020deepfake,li2020celeb}. These approaches often employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn discriminative features that can distinguish between authentic and synthetic content. Some methods focus on temporal inconsistencies in video sequences~\citep{guera2018deepfake,sabir2019recurrent}, while others analyze spatial artifacts or physiological implausibilities~\citep{li2018ictu,yang2019exposing}. Despite these advances, the detection landscape faces an inherent adversarial dynamic. As detection methods improve, so do the generation techniques, creating an ongoing arms race between synthesis and detection capabilities~\citep{carlini2023evading,wang2020cnn}. This adversarial relationship has led researchers to explore more fundamental approaches that leverage invariant properties of authentic content or exploit inherent limitations in the generation process. One promising direction involves analyzing the frequency domain characteristics of images, as generative models often exhibit distinct spectral signatures~\citep{frank2020leveraging,qian2020thinking}. Another approach focuses on biological and physiological constraints that are difficult for current generative models to replicate accurately, such as pulse signals extracted from facial videos~\citep{fernandes2019predicting,ciftci2020fakecatcher} or eye movement patterns~\citep{koopman2018detection}. The challenge of generalization across different generation methods and datasets remains a critical concern in detection research. Models trained on specific types of synthetic content often fail to generalize to new generation techniques or different data distributions~\citep{wang2020cnn,gragnaniello2021gan}. This limitation has motivated the development of more robust training strategies, including adversarial training approaches and domain adaptation techniques~\citep{shiohara2022detecting,chen2022self}. Furthermore, the evaluation of detection methods has become increasingly complex as the landscape of generative models continues to expand. Standardized benchmarks and evaluation protocols are essential for fair comparison of different approaches and for tracking progress in the field~\citep{dolhansky2020deepfake,jiang2020dfdataset}. However, the rapid pace of development in generative models means that evaluation datasets quickly become outdated, necessitating continuous updates and expansions of benchmark collections. The practical deployment of detection systems also faces significant challenges beyond technical performance. Real-world applications must consider factors such as computational efficiency, scalability, and robustness to various preprocessing operations commonly applied to media content~\citep{carlini2023evading,hussain2021image}. Additionally, the potential for adversarial attacks specifically designed to fool detection systems adds another layer of complexity to the deployment challenge~\citep{carlini2023evading,neekhara2021adversarial}. Privacy considerations also play a crucial role in the development and deployment of detection systems. Many detection methods require access to sensitive biometric information or personal characteristics, raising concerns about data protection and user privacy~\citep{mirsky2021creation,scherhag2022biometric}. Balancing detection accuracy with privacy preservation has become an important research direction, leading to the exploration of privacy-preserving detection techniques and federated learning approaches. The interdisciplinary nature of this challenge has fostered collaboration between computer vision researchers, forensic experts, legal scholars, and policymakers. Understanding the technical capabilities and limitations of both generation and detection methods is crucial for developing appropriate regulatory frameworks and industry standards~\citep{kietzmann2020deepfakes,westerlund2019emergence}. Looking forward, the field continues to evolve rapidly with emerging technologies such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs)~\citep{mildenhall2020nerf} and 3D-aware generation models~\citep{chan2022efficient} introducing new challenges for detection systems. These technologies enable the creation of highly realistic 3D-consistent synthetic content, potentially requiring entirely new detection paradigms that account for geometric and temporal consistency across multiple viewpoints.

text: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) middleboxes are widely deployed as part of modern network security infrastructures \cite{xu2016survey}. These systems analyze network traffic at the application layer to detect and prevent various forms of malicious activity, including malware communication, data exfiltration, and protocol violations. However, the effectiveness of DPI middleboxes is fundamentally limited by their ability to accurately interpret network protocols in a manner consistent with the endpoints they protect. The challenge of protocol interpretation consistency has become increasingly complex as network protocols have evolved to support greater functionality and flexibility. Modern protocols such as HTTP/2, QUIC, and TLS 1.3 incorporate features like multiplexing, encryption, and dynamic header compression that significantly complicate the task of middlebox analysis \cite{langley2017quic}. Furthermore, the proliferation of encrypted communications has forced DPI systems to rely increasingly on metadata analysis and behavioral heuristics, which are inherently more susceptible to evasion techniques. Recent research has demonstrated that protocol interpretation discrepancies are not merely theoretical concerns but represent practical vulnerabilities that can be systematically exploited. \citet{wang2020systematic} conducted a comprehensive analysis of popular DPI systems and identified over 200 distinct evasion vectors across multiple protocol implementations. Their findings revealed that even well-established protocols like HTTP and TCP exhibit significant interpretation variations that can be leveraged for attack purposes. The implications of these vulnerabilities extend beyond simple security bypass scenarios. In enterprise environments, DPI middleboxes are often integrated with broader security orchestration platforms, where evasion attacks can cascade into more severe compromise scenarios. For instance, an attacker who successfully evades DPI detection may be able to establish command and control channels, exfiltrate sensitive data, or deploy additional attack tools without triggering security alerts \cite{chen2019enterprise}. \subsection{Motivation and Problem Statement} The primary motivation for this research stems from the observation that existing approaches to DPI evasion detection and prevention are largely reactive and vendor-specific. Current mitigation strategies typically involve updating signature databases or modifying parser implementations after specific evasion techniques have been discovered and analyzed. This reactive approach creates a persistent window of vulnerability during which attackers can exploit newly discovered evasion vectors. Moreover, the heterogeneous nature of DPI implementations across different vendors and product lines means that evasion techniques that are effective against one system may not work against another. This variability complicates both attack development and defense strategies, as security researchers and practitioners must consider multiple implementation variants when assessing vulnerability exposure. The problem is further exacerbated by the lack of standardized testing methodologies for evaluating DPI system robustness against evasion attacks. While some commercial testing tools exist, they typically focus on known attack patterns and may not adequately assess system behavior when confronted with novel or hybrid evasion techniques. This limitation hinders the development of more resilient DPI implementations and makes it difficult for organizations to accurately assess their security posture. \subsection{Research Contributions} This paper presents a systematic framework for analyzing and categorizing protocol interpretation discrepancies in DPI middleboxes. Our approach combines automated testing methodologies with formal protocol specification analysis to identify potential evasion vectors across multiple protocol layers. The key contributions of this work include: \begin{enumerate} \item A comprehensive taxonomy of protocol interpretation discrepancies that extends beyond existing categorization schemes by incorporating semantic-level analysis of protocol behavior differences. \item An automated testing framework capable of generating and executing large-scale evasion test cases across multiple DPI implementations simultaneously, enabling comparative vulnerability assessment. \item A formal model for predicting the likelihood of successful evasion based on protocol specification ambiguities and implementation characteristics. \item Empirical evaluation results from testing twelve commercial and open-source DPI systems against over 5,000 generated evasion test cases, revealing previously unknown vulnerability patterns. \end{enumerate} Our findings demonstrate that protocol interpretation discrepancies are more prevalent and systematic than previously understood. We identify several classes of vulnerabilities that appear consistently across multiple DPI implementations, suggesting fundamental challenges in the current approach to protocol parsing in middlebox systems. \subsection{Paper Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides detailed background information on DPI architectures and existing evasion techniques, establishing the technical foundation for our analysis. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} describes our systematic approach to identifying and categorizing protocol interpretation discrepancies, including the design of our automated testing framework. Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} presents our comprehensive taxonomy of evasion vectors, organized by protocol layer and attack mechanism. This taxonomy serves as both a classification system for existing techniques and a framework for predicting potential future attack vectors. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} details our empirical evaluation methodology and presents results from testing multiple DPI implementations against our generated test cases. Section~\ref{sec:analysis} provides in-depth analysis of our findings, including identification of common vulnerability patterns and discussion of their implications for DPI system design. Section~\ref{sec:mitigation} explores potential mitigation strategies and their trade-offs in terms of performance and security effectiveness. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in the areas of network security, protocol analysis, and middlebox evasion, while Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our contributions and outlines directions for future research. Deep Packet Inspection represents a critical component of modern network security architectures, operating at the intersection of network performance and security analysis requirements. Understanding the technical challenges and limitations inherent in DPI implementation is essential for comprehending why protocol interpretation discrepancies arise and persist across different systems. \subsection{DPI Architecture and Implementation Challenges} Modern DPI systems must balance multiple competing requirements: high-throughput packet processing, comprehensive protocol analysis, and real-time decision making. These systems typically employ a multi-stage processing pipeline that includes packet capture, protocol parsing, pattern matching, and policy enforcement \cite{agrawal2008architecture}. The packet capture stage must handle traffic rates that can exceed multiple gigabits per second in enterprise environments. This requirement necessitates the use of specialized hardware acceleration techniques, including network interface cards with hardware-based packet filtering and direct memory access capabilities. However, these performance optimizations often introduce constraints on the complexity of analysis that can be performed in subsequent stages. Protocol parsing represents the most technically challenging aspect of DPI implementation. Unlike endpoint systems that can afford to implement complete and standards-compliant protocol stacks, DPI middleboxes must make parsing decisions based on incomplete information and within strict time constraints. This limitation forces implementers to make trade-offs between parsing accuracy and processing speed, often resulting in simplified or heuristic-based parsing logic that may not fully conform to protocol specifications. The pattern matching stage involves comparing extracted protocol elements against databases of known attack signatures or policy rules. The efficiency of this process is critical to overall system performance, leading many implementations to employ approximate matching algorithms or to limit the depth of content inspection. These optimizations can create blind spots that attackers may exploit through careful payload construction.

text: Recently, a resurgence of contrastive learning (CL) \cite{DBLP:conf/nips/KhoslaTWSTIMLK20,jaiswal2021survey,liu2020self} has been witnessed in deep representation learning. The core principle of contrastive learning revolves around learning discriminative representations by pulling together semantically similar samples while pushing apart dissimilar ones in the embedding space \cite{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}. This paradigm has demonstrated exceptional success across various domains, including computer vision \cite{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}, natural language processing \cite{gao2021simcse,wu2020clear}, and more recently, recommendation systems \cite{wu2021self,yu2022socially}. In the context of recommendation systems, contrastive learning addresses several fundamental challenges that have long plagued the field. The inherent sparsity of user-item interaction data, where users typically interact with only a small fraction of available items, creates significant difficulties for traditional collaborative filtering approaches \cite{koren2009matrix,rendle2009bpr}. Moreover, the cold-start problem, where new users or items lack sufficient interaction history, further exacerbates the challenge of learning meaningful representations \cite{schein2002methods,lam2008addressing}. Contrastive learning offers a principled solution to these challenges by enabling models to extract self-supervised signals from the available interaction data without requiring additional labeled information \cite{liu2021contrastive,xia2022hypergraph}. By constructing positive and negative pairs through carefully designed augmentation strategies, CL-based recommendation models can learn robust user and item embeddings that capture both explicit preferences and implicit behavioral patterns. The application of contrastive learning to recommendation systems has evolved through several distinct paradigms. Early approaches primarily focused on adapting general contrastive learning frameworks to recommendation data by treating user-item interactions as positive pairs and employing random sampling for negative examples \cite{yao2021self,zhou2020s3}. However, these naive adaptations often failed to capture the unique characteristics of recommendation data, such as the bipartite graph structure and the temporal dynamics of user preferences. More sophisticated approaches have emerged that leverage the inherent structure of recommendation data. Graph-based contrastive learning methods construct multiple views of the user-item bipartite graph through various augmentation techniques, including node dropout, edge dropout, and subgraph sampling \cite{wu2021self,yu2021graph}. These methods enable the model to learn representations that are robust to structural perturbations while preserving the essential collaborative filtering signals. Multi-modal contrastive learning represents another significant advancement, where different types of auxiliary information are incorporated to create complementary views of the recommendation data \cite{wei2021contrastive,zhou2023bootstrap}. For instance, social recommendation systems can leverage both user-item interactions and social network connections to construct multiple views, enabling the model to capture both collaborative preferences and social influences \cite{yu2022socially,fan2019graph}. The design of effective augmentation strategies remains a critical challenge in contrastive learning for recommendation. Unlike computer vision, where geometric transformations naturally preserve semantic content, recommendation data requires domain-specific augmentation techniques that maintain the underlying preference patterns while introducing sufficient diversity for contrastive learning \cite{xie2022contrasting,lin2022improving}. Recent work has explored adaptive augmentation strategies that dynamically adjust the augmentation intensity based on data characteristics and model performance \cite{yu2022graph,qiu2022contrastive}. Negative sampling strategies also play a crucial role in the effectiveness of contrastive learning for recommendation. Traditional random negative sampling may not provide sufficient learning signals, as randomly selected items are often trivially different from positive items \cite{rendle2009bpr,he2017neural}. Advanced negative sampling techniques, such as hard negative mining and adversarial negative sampling, have been proposed to select more informative negative examples that challenge the model to learn more discriminative representations \cite{ding2020simplx,wang2021denoising}. The integration of contrastive learning with existing recommendation architectures has led to significant performance improvements across various recommendation tasks. Matrix factorization models enhanced with contrastive objectives have shown improved robustness to data sparsity \cite{liu2021contrastive,yu2021socially}. Graph neural network-based recommenders have benefited from contrastive learning by learning more expressive node embeddings that capture both local and global graph structures \cite{wu2021self,xia2022hypergraph}. Sequential recommendation, which aims to predict users' next interactions based on their historical behavior sequences, has also witnessed substantial improvements through contrastive learning \cite{zhou2020s3,xie2022contrasting}. By creating augmented views of user sequences through techniques such as item masking, reordering, and substitution, contrastive learning enables sequential models to learn more robust temporal patterns and reduce overfitting to specific interaction sequences. Despite these advances, several challenges and opportunities remain in the application of contrastive learning to recommendation systems. The computational overhead associated with contrastive learning, particularly in large-scale recommendation scenarios, necessitates the development of more efficient training strategies and architectures \cite{qu2022contrastive,lin2022improving}. Additionally, the theoretical understanding of why and when contrastive learning works effectively in recommendation contexts requires further investigation to guide the design of more principled approaches.

text: The current status in data privacy could be categorized as the post-privacy area due to the unintended consequences of the big data revolution. The proliferation of digital technologies and the exponential growth of data collection capabilities have fundamentally altered the landscape of personal privacy, creating what many scholars now recognize as a paradigm shift in how we conceptualize and protect sensitive information \cite{zuboff2019surveillance, cohen2019between}. This transformation is particularly pronounced in the healthcare sector, where the convergence of electronic health records (EHRs), wearable devices, genomic sequencing, and artificial intelligence has created unprecedented opportunities for medical advancement while simultaneously exposing patients to new forms of privacy vulnerabilities \cite{mittelstadt2017ethics, vayena2018machine}. The traditional notion of privacy as a binary concept—where information is either private or public—has become increasingly obsolete in an era where data aggregation, inference algorithms, and cross-platform correlation can reveal intimate details about individuals even from seemingly anonymized datasets \cite{sweeney2000simple, narayanan2008robust}. Healthcare data presents unique challenges in this context, as medical information encompasses not only explicit clinical records but also behavioral patterns, genetic predispositions, and lifestyle choices that can be inferred from various digital traces \cite{price2017privacy}. The regulatory response to these challenges has been fragmented and often reactive rather than proactive. While frameworks such as HIPAA and GDPR represent significant steps toward protecting health information privacy, they were largely designed for a pre-digital era and struggle to address the complexities of modern data ecosystems \cite{phillips2017current, voigt2017eu}. The concept of informed consent, a cornerstone of medical ethics and privacy law, becomes particularly problematic when patients cannot reasonably understand the full implications of data sharing in complex technological systems \cite{manson2012informed, kaye2015dynamic}. Moreover, the increasing reliance on cloud computing, third-party analytics platforms, and international data transfers has created a web of data flows that often transcend jurisdictional boundaries, making enforcement of privacy regulations challenging \cite{bradshaw2013global, kuner2013transborder}. The emergence of precision medicine and population health initiatives further complicates the privacy landscape, as these approaches often require large-scale data sharing and analysis that may conflict with individual privacy preferences \cite{phillips2018genomic, mittelstadt2016ethics}. In this context, blockchain technology has emerged as a potential solution that promises to reconcile the competing demands of data utility and privacy protection through its inherent characteristics of decentralization, immutability, and cryptographic security \cite{yue2016healthcare, zhang2018blockchain}. However, as previously discussed, the application of blockchain to healthcare presents its own set of challenges and contradictions.

text: Reliable detection of encrypted data fragments is an important primitive with many applications to security and digital forensics. Encrypted data detection serves as a foundational component in numerous security domains, from malware analysis to network monitoring and incident response. The ability to accurately identify encrypted content within data streams enables security professionals to detect potential threats, analyze communication patterns, and reconstruct digital evidence from fragmented sources. Traditional approaches to encrypted data detection have primarily relied on statistical measures, with Shannon entropy being the most widely adopted metric \cite{shannon1948mathematical}. The underlying assumption is that encrypted data exhibits near-maximum entropy due to its pseudo-random characteristics. However, this approach faces several critical limitations in practice. High-entropy non-encrypted data, such as compressed archives, multimedia files, and certain binary formats, frequently trigger false positives. Conversely, some encryption implementations may introduce structural patterns or padding that reduce the apparent randomness, leading to false negatives. The proliferation of diverse encryption algorithms and implementation variants further complicates the detection landscape. Modern cryptographic systems employ various modes of operation, key derivation functions, and authentication mechanisms that can significantly alter the statistical properties of the resulting ciphertext \cite{katz2020introduction}. For instance, counter mode encryption may exhibit periodic patterns, while cipher block chaining introduces dependencies between consecutive blocks that can be statistically detectable. Fragment-based analysis presents additional challenges that are particularly relevant in forensic and network security contexts. When encrypted files are transmitted over networks or stored on damaged media, they often appear as disconnected fragments of varying sizes. The statistical reliability of entropy-based detection degrades significantly with smaller fragment sizes, as insufficient data points prevent accurate entropy estimation \cite{conti2016survey}. Research has shown that fragments smaller than 512 bytes often yield unreliable classification results using traditional methods. Machine learning approaches have emerged as promising alternatives to overcome these limitations. Supervised learning models can be trained to recognize subtle patterns and correlations that distinguish encrypted data from other high-entropy content. Convolutional neural networks have proven particularly effective at capturing local byte-level patterns, while recurrent architectures excel at modeling sequential dependencies across longer data sequences \cite{lecun2015deep}. Recent work has explored various feature engineering approaches for encrypted data classification. N-gram analysis, byte frequency distributions, and autocorrelation functions have all been investigated as potential discriminative features \cite{hirata2019machine}. However, hand-crafted features often fail to capture the complex, non-linear relationships present in encrypted data, motivating the adoption of deep learning techniques that can automatically learn relevant representations. The operational environment significantly influences detection performance. Network traffic analysis requires real-time processing capabilities and must handle diverse protocols and encryption implementations. Digital forensics applications demand high accuracy and explainability, as results may be used in legal proceedings. Malware detection systems must be robust against adversarial attempts to evade detection through encryption or obfuscation techniques. Contemporary encryption practices introduce additional complexity through the widespread adoption of authenticated encryption modes such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 \cite{rogaway2002authenticated}. These modes combine confidentiality and integrity protection, often including additional authenticated data that may not be encrypted. The resulting data streams contain mixed encrypted and unencrypted components, challenging traditional detection approaches that assume uniform data characteristics. The emergence of post-quantum cryptography and novel encryption schemes further emphasizes the need for adaptable detection methods. As organizations begin transitioning to quantum-resistant algorithms, security tools must be capable of identifying and analyzing new cryptographic implementations without extensive retraining or reconfiguration. This work addresses these challenges by developing a hybrid detection framework that leverages both statistical analysis and deep learning techniques. Our approach combines the computational efficiency of entropy-based methods with the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks, achieving improved accuracy across diverse encryption types and fragment sizes while maintaining practical deployment requirements.

N-gram analysis, byte frequency distribution, and autocorrelation function have been investigated as discriminative features. However, these hand-crafted features often cannot fully capture the complex and nonlinear relations of encrypted data, and this has led to the adoption of deep learning, which can automatically learn discriminative features. The operational environment has a strong influence on the detection performance. For example, network traffic analysis requires real-time processing capabilities, and the system must be able to handle diverse protocols and encryption implementations. Digital forensics applications require accuracy and explainability, because the results may be used in court. Modern encryption practices introduce additional complexities with the wide use of authenticated encryption modes such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. These modes combine confidentiality and integrity protection, often with additional authenticated data which is not encrypted. Malware detection systems must be robust to attempts by adversaries to hide behind encryption or obfuscation techniques. Post-quantum cryptography and new encryption methods further increase the need for flexible detection methods. As organizations begin the transition to quantum-resistant cryptographic schemes, the security tools used must be able to identify and analyze the new cryptographic implementations without extensive retraining or reconfiguration. The resulting data streams contain both encrypted and unencrypted components, challenging traditional detection methods that assume uniform data characteristics. Our work addresses these challenges by developing a hybrid detection framework that combines the efficiency of entropy-based methods with the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks, thereby obtaining improved accuracy across a large variety of encryptions and fragment sizes, while still having a practical deployment requirement.
