text: The brain is one of the most complicated and mysterious tissues, controlling the motion, perception, and emotion of animals (including us humans). Understanding its structure and function requires detailed mapping of neural circuits at the cellular level, a field known as connectomics \cite{sporns2005human}. Recent advances in electron microscopy (EM) imaging have enabled the acquisition of neural tissue volumes at nanometer resolution, generating datasets that can span multiple terabytes for even small brain regions \cite{briggman2011wiring, helmstaedter2013connectomic}. The reconstruction of neural circuits from these high-resolution EM volumes presents unprecedented computational challenges. Traditional image segmentation approaches, designed for natural images or medical scans, fail to capture the intricate morphology and dense packing of neural structures \cite{funke2019large}. Neurons exhibit complex branching patterns with processes that can extend across the entire imaging volume, while synaptic connections occur at sub-micrometer scales that demand precise boundary delineation \cite{plaza2014diadem}. Deep learning has emerged as the dominant paradigm for automated neural structure segmentation, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) demonstrating remarkable success in identifying cell boundaries and organelles \cite{ronneberger2015u, lee2017superhuman}. However, the transition from 2D natural image processing to 3D volumetric neural data introduces several critical challenges that existing frameworks inadequately address. First, the sheer scale of connectomics datasets necessitates specialized data handling and memory management strategies. A single cubic millimeter of neural tissue can generate over 1000 terabytes of raw imaging data \cite{kasthuri2015saturated}, requiring efficient streaming, caching, and distributed processing capabilities that standard computer vision frameworks lack. Second, EM imaging protocols often result in anisotropic voxel resolutions, where the z-axis resolution is significantly coarser than the x-y plane resolution \cite{briggman2011wiring}. This anisotropy complicates 3D convolution operations and requires careful consideration of kernel design and data augmentation strategies to prevent directional biases in learned features. Third, the evaluation of segmentation quality in connectomics differs fundamentally from standard computer vision metrics. While pixel-wise accuracy measures like IoU are informative, connectomics applications prioritize topological correctness and the preservation of neural connectivity patterns \cite{funke2019large}. Metrics such as the Adapted Rand Index (ARAND) and Variation of Information (VOI) better capture the biological relevance of segmentation errors \cite{arganda2015crowdsourcing}. Existing deep learning frameworks, while powerful for general computer vision tasks, exhibit several limitations when applied to connectomics research. TensorFlow-based solutions often struggle with the memory requirements of large 3D volumes and lack native support for connectomics-specific data formats such as HDF5 and Zarr \cite{collman2015mapping}. Similarly, general-purpose frameworks provide limited built-in support for the specialized loss functions and evaluation metrics essential for neural circuit reconstruction. To address these challenges, we developed PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC), a comprehensive framework specifically designed for deep learning-based analysis of volumetric neural imaging data. PyTC builds upon the flexibility and dynamic computation graph capabilities of PyTorch while incorporating domain-specific optimizations for connectomics applications. Our framework makes several key contributions to the field: (1) We provide a unified, modular architecture that seamlessly integrates data preprocessing, model training, and post-processing workflows specifically optimized for large-scale EM volumes. (2) We implement state-of-the-art 3D segmentation architectures including residual U-Net variants, Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN), and transformer-based models, all adapted for anisotropic neural data. (3) We introduce efficient memory management and data streaming capabilities that enable processing of terabyte-scale volumes on standard computational hardware. (4) We incorporate connectomics-specific evaluation metrics and visualization tools that facilitate biological interpretation of segmentation results. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in connectomics segmentation and deep learning frameworks. Section~\ref{sec:methods} details the architecture and implementation of PyTC, including our novel approaches to handling anisotropic data and memory-efficient processing. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents comprehensive experimental validation on benchmark datasets, demonstrating both accuracy improvements and computational efficiency gains. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the implications of our results and future directions for the framework. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes our contributions and their impact on connectomics research. The field of connectomics has witnessed rapid evolution in computational approaches, driven by the increasing availability of high-resolution EM datasets and advances in machine learning techniques \cite{helmstaedter2013connectomic, plaza2014diadem}.

text: Assessing the structure of the brain is critical to better understanding its normal and abnormal functioning. Advances in electron microscopy (EM) now allow three-dimensional (3D) imaging of hundreds of micrometers of tissue with nanometer-scale resolution, enabling unprecedented visualization of neural circuits and subcellular organelles \cite{briggman2011wiring, helmstaedter2013cellular}. These technological breakthroughs have revolutionized our ability to map synaptic connectivity patterns, trace individual axons and dendrites across multiple brain regions, and characterize the fine-scale organization of cellular components such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and vesicle populations \cite{kasthuri2015saturated, shapson2021connectomic}. The emergence of serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM), focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM), and transmission electron microscopy tomography (TEM-T) has made it possible to acquire continuous 3D volumes spanning entire cortical columns or hippocampal regions \cite{denk2012serial, xu2017enhanced}. However, these advances come with substantial computational challenges. A single dataset can contain billions of voxels and require petabytes of storage, making traditional image analysis approaches computationally intractable \cite{lichtman2014big}. Manual segmentation of neuronal structures in such datasets is not only time-intensive but also subject to inter-annotator variability and fatigue-induced errors \cite{arganda2015crowdsourcing}. Expert neuroanatomists typically require hundreds of hours to fully annotate even modest tissue volumes, creating a significant bottleneck in connectomic research \cite{plaza2014diadem}. Furthermore, the complexity of neural tissue morphology, including overlapping processes, membrane contact sites, and densely packed neuropil, presents unique challenges for automated analysis methods \cite{funke2019large}. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated remarkable success in medical image segmentation tasks, with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieving human-level performance in various domains \cite{litjens2017survey, shen2017deep}. In the context of EM image analysis, several pioneering studies have shown that deep learning approaches can effectively segment neuronal membranes, identify synaptic connections, and classify organelles with high accuracy \cite{lee2017superhuman, januszewski2018high, meirovitch2016cross}. The U-Net architecture, originally developed for biomedical image segmentation, has been particularly influential in EM applications due to its ability to capture both local and global contextual information through skip connections \cite{ronneberger2015u, cicek20163d}. However, standard U-Net implementations face limitations when processing large-scale 3D volumes, including memory constraints, computational inefficiency, and difficulty in capturing long-range spatial dependencies \cite{isensee2021nnu}. More recently, attention mechanisms and transformer architectures have emerged as powerful alternatives for capturing global context in image analysis tasks \cite{vaswani2017attention, dosovitskiy2020image}. These approaches can potentially address some limitations of purely convolutional architectures by enabling direct modeling of long-range interactions between distant image regions \cite{wang2018non, hu2018squeeze}. Despite these technological advances, several critical challenges remain in automated EM segmentation. First, the extreme variability in imaging conditions across different laboratories, sample preparation protocols, and microscopy platforms creates domain adaptation problems that can significantly impact model performance \cite{wei2018mitoem, heinrich2018automatic}. Second, the anisotropic resolution typical of many EM acquisition protocols, where axial resolution is often 5-10 times lower than lateral resolution, complicates 3D analysis and requires specialized handling \cite{funke2018large}. Third, imaging artifacts such as section compression, charging effects, and staining irregularities can introduce systematic biases that automated methods must learn to handle robustly \cite{cardona2012trakem2}. The development of effective data augmentation strategies is particularly crucial for EM applications, given the limited availability of expertly annotated training data and the high cost of generating new ground truth labels \cite{arganda2015crowdsourcing}. Traditional augmentation techniques such as rotation, scaling, and intensity transformations may not adequately capture the specific types of variability encountered in EM datasets \cite{chen2019med3d}. Furthermore, evaluation metrics for EM segmentation tasks require careful consideration of the specific biological structures being analyzed. Standard pixel-wise accuracy measures may not adequately reflect the biological relevance of segmentation errors, particularly for thin structures like dendritic spines or axonal processes where small misalignments can have significant impact on downstream connectivity analysis \cite{arganda2015crowdsourcing, funke2019large}. In this work, we address these challenges by developing a comprehensive deep learning framework specifically designed for large-scale 3D EM segmentation. Our approach integrates several key innovations: (1) a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture that combines the efficiency of convolutional operations with the global context modeling capabilities of attention mechanisms, (2) a multi-scale training strategy that enables processing of high-resolution volumes while maintaining computational tractability, (3) domain-specific data augmentation techniques that simulate realistic EM imaging variations, and (4) biologically-informed evaluation metrics that better reflect the quality of neuroanatomical reconstructions.

text: Recent advances on Supervised Re-Identification (re-ID) have led to excellent performance on widely used public re-ID datasets (\cite{ye2021deep,ni2021adaptive}). However, these supervised methods heavily rely on large amounts of manually annotated data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain in real-world scenarios \cite{wang2018transferable}. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when deploying re-ID systems across different domains, where the distribution shift between source and target domains significantly degrades model performance \cite{wei2018person}. Consequently, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) for person re-ID has emerged as a critical research direction to bridge this gap by leveraging labeled source domain data and unlabeled target domain data \cite{deng2018image}. The domain gap in person re-ID manifests in various forms, including differences in camera specifications, lighting conditions, background environments, and population demographics \cite{zhong2018generalizing}. Traditional domain adaptation techniques that rely solely on feature alignment often fall short in addressing these complex variations, as they fail to capture the fine-grained identity-specific information crucial for re-ID tasks \cite{song2018mask}. This has motivated the development of specialized UDA approaches tailored for person re-ID that can effectively handle both domain shift and identity discrimination simultaneously. Among the various UDA strategies, pseudo-labeling has demonstrated remarkable success due to its ability to progressively adapt models to target domains while maintaining discriminative capabilities \cite{fu2019self}. The core idea involves generating pseudo-labels for unlabeled target samples through clustering or nearest neighbor search, then iteratively refining the model using these pseudo-labels as supervision signals \cite{lin2019bottom}. This approach has proven particularly effective because it directly addresses the identity classification nature of re-ID tasks, unlike generic domain adaptation methods that focus primarily on feature distribution alignment. However, the success of pseudo-labeling methods critically depends on the quality of generated pseudo-labels. Inaccurate pseudo-labels can lead to error accumulation and model degradation, especially in the early stages of adaptation when the model's predictions on target data are unreliable \cite{yu2019unsupervised}. To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed various strategies including confidence-based filtering \cite{zheng2019joint}, progressive pseudo-label refinement \cite{zhai2020ad}, and multi-model ensemble approaches \cite{chen2021ice}. Recent developments have also explored the integration of contrastive learning principles with pseudo-labeling frameworks \cite{ge2020mutual}. These methods leverage both positive and negative sample pairs to learn more robust feature representations while simultaneously improving pseudo-label quality through iterative refinement. The contrastive learning paradigm has shown particular promise in handling the inherent noise in pseudo-labels by emphasizing the relative relationships between samples rather than absolute label assignments. Another significant advancement in UDA re-ID involves the incorporation of temporal and spatial consistency constraints \cite{li2020unsupervised}. These approaches exploit the natural structure present in surveillance data, where the same person typically appears across multiple cameras with certain temporal and spatial relationships. By enforcing consistency across these dimensions, models can generate more reliable pseudo-labels and achieve better adaptation performance. The clustering-based pseudo-labeling framework has also evolved to incorporate more sophisticated clustering algorithms and distance metrics specifically designed for re-ID tasks \cite{wang2020unsupervised}. Traditional k-means clustering has been replaced by more advanced techniques such as DBSCAN \cite{lin2019bottom} and hierarchical clustering \cite{zhang2019self}, which can better handle the varying cluster sizes and densities typical in person re-ID datasets. Furthermore, recent works have begun to explore the use of auxiliary information to improve pseudo-label generation. Camera-aware clustering \cite{zhong2018camera} leverages camera viewpoint information to constrain the clustering process, ensuring that samples from the same camera are not assigned to the same identity cluster. Similarly, some methods incorporate temporal information from tracklets \cite{li2020unsupervised} or utilize pose and attribute information \cite{chang2019domain} to enhance the reliability of pseudo-labels. The evaluation of UDA re-ID methods has also evolved, with researchers recognizing the importance of comprehensive benchmarking across diverse datasets and domain shift scenarios \cite{ristani2016performance}. Standard evaluation protocols now include multiple source-target domain pairs, such as Market-1501 to DukeMTMC-reID \cite{zheng2015scalable, ristani2016performance}, and more challenging cross-dataset evaluations that better reflect real-world deployment scenarios. Despite these advances, several challenges remain in UDA re-ID. The cold-start problem, where initial pseudo-labels are highly unreliable, continues to pose difficulties for many methods \cite{yu2019unsupervised}. Additionally, the scalability of clustering-based approaches becomes questionable when dealing with large-scale target datasets containing thousands of identities. The computational overhead associated with iterative clustering and model retraining also presents practical limitations for real-time deployment scenarios.

text: This paper describes a policy learning approach that leverages task-and-motion planning (TAMP) to train robot manipulation policies for long-horizon tasks. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenge of learning robust manipulation policies that can handle complex, multi-step tasks requiring both high-level reasoning and low-level control. Traditional reinforcement learning methods excel at learning reactive policies from sensory input but often fail to generalize to tasks with sparse rewards and extended temporal dependencies \cite{andrychowicz2017hindsight, plappert2018multi}. Conversely, classical TAMP systems provide principled solutions for long-horizon planning but rely heavily on symbolic representations and struggle with perception uncertainty and continuous control \cite{kaelbling2011hierarchical, toussaint2018differentiable}. The key insight driving our work is that TAMP can serve as an effective teacher for policy learning by providing structured demonstrations and intermediate goals. Rather than treating TAMP and policy learning as competing paradigms, we propose a synergistic framework where TAMP solutions guide the learning process while learned policies handle the continuous control aspects that are challenging for traditional planners. Our framework, which we call \textit{TAMP-Guided Policy Learning} (TGPL), operates in three phases. First, we use a TAMP solver to generate high-level plans for training tasks, decomposing complex manipulation sequences into semantically meaningful subgoals. Second, we train hierarchical policies that learn to achieve these subgoals through interaction with the environment, using the TAMP solutions as curriculum guidance. Finally, we employ a meta-learning approach to enable rapid adaptation to new task instances and environmental variations. The hierarchical structure of our learned policies mirrors the natural decomposition provided by TAMP, with a high-level policy responsible for subgoal selection and low-level policies handling primitive execution. This design enables effective temporal abstraction while maintaining the flexibility to adapt to dynamic environments and unforeseen situations where the original TAMP assumptions may not hold \cite{konidaris2018skills, bacon2017option}. A critical component of our approach is the integration of geometric and semantic reasoning capabilities. We leverage recent advances in vision-language models to ground natural language task descriptions in visual observations, enabling our system to understand complex manipulation objectives without requiring hand-crafted symbolic representations \cite{huang2022language, ahn2022can}. This grounding mechanism allows the high-level policy to make informed decisions about subgoal sequencing based on the current visual state and task context. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks including multi-object rearrangement, tool use, and assembly operations. Our results demonstrate that TGPL significantly outperforms both pure RL baselines and traditional TAMP approaches in terms of success rate, sample efficiency, and generalization to novel scenarios. Particularly noteworthy is the system's ability to recover from execution failures and adapt to environmental changes that would cause traditional planners to fail. The main contributions of this work are: (1) a novel framework for combining TAMP and policy learning that leverages the strengths of both approaches, (2) a hierarchical policy architecture that enables effective temporal abstraction for long-horizon tasks, (3) an integration mechanism for vision-language models that enables semantic grounding without symbolic preprocessing, and (4) comprehensive experimental validation demonstrating superior performance across diverse manipulation scenarios. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work in hierarchical reinforcement learning, task and motion planning, and vision-language integration for robotics. Section~\ref{sec:method} presents our TGPL framework in detail, including the hierarchical policy architecture and training methodology. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} describes our experimental setup and presents results on benchmark manipulation tasks. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} discusses limitations and future directions for this research.

text: It is a well-studied and understood fact that humans can associate voices and faces of people because the neuro-cognitive pathways for voices and faces share same structure~\cite{kamachi2003putting,belin2004thinking}. This remarkable human ability has inspired researchers to explore whether computational models can learn similar cross-modal associations between facial appearance and vocal characteristics. The task of face-voice association learning has emerged as a fundamental challenge in multimodal machine learning, with applications spanning from speaker verification and audio-visual synchronization to person identification in multimedia content. Early computational approaches to this problem were primarily based on hand-crafted features that attempted to capture correlations between facial geometry and vocal tract characteristics~\cite{wen2003mapping,kamachi2003putting}. These methods relied on explicit modeling of physiological relationships, such as the connection between facial bone structure and vocal resonance properties. However, such approaches were limited by their dependence on domain expertise and struggled to capture the complex, non-linear relationships that exist between visual and auditory modalities. The advent of deep learning has revolutionized this field, enabling end-to-end learning of cross-modal representations without explicit feature engineering. Recent works have demonstrated that convolutional neural networks can learn meaningful associations between faces and voices by optimizing various objective functions~\cite{nagrani2018learnable,oh2019speech2face,wen2021disjoint}. These approaches typically employ siamese or triplet network architectures that learn to embed faces and voices into a shared representation space where matching pairs are closer than non-matching ones. Despite these advances, several fundamental challenges remain unresolved. First, the inherent ambiguity in face-voice associations poses a significant difficulty. Unlike other cross-modal tasks where correspondences are more deterministic, the relationship between facial appearance and vocal characteristics is influenced by numerous factors including age, gender, ethnicity, health conditions, and even emotional state~\cite{smith2016correlation,gonzalez2019demographic}. This ambiguity makes it challenging to define what constitutes a "correct" association, particularly when dealing with individuals who may not conform to typical demographic patterns. Second, existing contrastive learning approaches suffer from the negative sampling problem. The effectiveness of triplet loss and similar formulations heavily depends on the selection of informative negative samples~\cite{schroff2015facenet,hermans2017defense}. Random sampling often leads to trivial negatives that provide little learning signal, while hard negative mining can cause training instability and convergence issues. Moreover, the batch composition significantly affects the learning dynamics, as the availability of diverse negative samples within each batch directly impacts the quality of the learned representations. Third, most current methods operate at a single scale of granularity, typically focusing on global face-voice matching while ignoring fine-grained correspondences that may exist between specific facial regions and vocal characteristics. For instance, lip shape and size may correlate with certain phonetic properties, while facial bone structure might influence vocal resonance patterns~\cite{pisanski2014vocal,feinberg2005masculinity}. Capturing these multi-scale relationships requires sophisticated architectures that can model both global and local correspondences. Furthermore, the evaluation protocols used in existing work often lack standardization, making it difficult to compare different approaches fairly. Many studies use different train-test splits, evaluation metrics, and preprocessing procedures, leading to inconsistent and sometimes contradictory findings~\cite{nagrani2018learnable,oh2019speech2face}. This lack of standardization hinders progress in the field and makes it challenging to identify the most effective approaches. To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive framework that tackles face-voice association learning from multiple perspectives. Our approach introduces several key innovations: a multi-scale contrastive learning mechanism that captures correspondences at different levels of granularity, an adaptive negative sampling strategy that progressively increases training difficulty, and a cross-modal attention mechanism that identifies the most discriminative facial and vocal features for association learning. The multi-scale nature of our approach is particularly important because face-voice associations manifest at different levels of abstraction. At the coarsest level, global demographic characteristics such as age and gender provide strong cues for association. At intermediate levels, facial structure and vocal tract properties may exhibit correlations. At the finest level, specific facial features may correspond to particular vocal characteristics or speaking patterns. Our experimental validation demonstrates the effectiveness of this multi-faceted approach across multiple benchmark datasets, achieving significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods while providing insights into the nature of face-voice associations that can inform future research directions.

text: Edge-aware filters are among the most commonly used image processing operators in a wide range of computational photography applications. Also called \emph{edge-preserving smoothing} filters, these operators aim to reduce noise and small-scale variations while maintaining the structural integrity of prominent edges and boundaries in the image. The fundamental challenge lies in distinguishing between noise or unwanted texture that should be removed and meaningful edges that must be preserved. The mathematical formulation of edge-preserving filters typically involves a trade-off between data fidelity and smoothness constraints. Let $I$ denote the input image and $O$ the filtered output. Most edge-aware filters can be expressed as an optimization problem of the form: \begin{equation} \arg\min_O \sum_{p} \left( (O_p - I_p)^2 + \lambda \sum_{q \in N(p)} w_{pq} (O_p - O_q)^2 \right) \end{equation} where $p$ and $q$ are pixel indices, $N(p)$ represents the neighborhood of pixel $p$, $w_{pq}$ are edge-aware weights that adapt based on local image structure, and $\lambda$ controls the smoothing strength. The key innovation in different edge-preserving filters lies in how these weights $w_{pq}$ are computed and how the optimization is solved efficiently. Classical approaches such as the bilateral filter \cite{tomasi1998bilateral} compute weights based on both spatial proximity and intensity similarity: \begin{equation} w_{pq} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|p-q\|^2}{2\sigma_s^2}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{(I_p-I_q)^2}{2\sigma_r^2}\right) \end{equation} where $\sigma_s$ and $\sigma_r$ control the spatial and range kernels, respectively. While effective, the bilateral filter requires careful parameter tuning and can be computationally expensive for large kernel sizes. The weighted least squares (WLS) approach \cite{farbman2008edge} reformulates edge-preserving smoothing as a sparse linear system, enabling efficient solutions through standard numerical methods. The WLS formulation defines smoothness weights based on image gradients: \begin{equation} w_{pq} = \left(\left|\frac{\partial I}{\partial x}\right|_p^{\alpha} + \left|\frac{\partial I}{\partial y}\right|_p^{\alpha} + \epsilon\right)^{-1} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ controls the sensitivity to gradients and $\epsilon$ prevents division by zero. This approach allows for global optimization while maintaining edge awareness through locally adaptive weights. More recent developments have focused on achieving linear-time complexity without sacrificing quality. The guided filter \cite{he2013guided} assumes a local linear relationship between the guidance image $G$ and the output $O$ within a window $\omega_k$: \begin{equation} O_i = a_k G_i + b_k, \quad \forall i \in \omega_k \end{equation} The coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ are determined by minimizing the cost function: \begin{equation} E(a_k, b_k) = \sum_{i \in \omega_k} \left((a_k G_i + b_k - I_i)^2 + \epsilon a_k^2\right) \end{equation} This leads to closed-form solutions that can be computed efficiently using box filters, resulting in $O(N)$ complexity for an image with $N$ pixels. The domain transform filter \cite{gastal2011domain} introduces another paradigm by transforming the filtering problem into a 1D domain where edge-preserving smoothing becomes separable. This approach achieves real-time performance while maintaining high-quality results comparable to more computationally intensive methods. Recent neural network-based approaches have also emerged, leveraging deep learning to learn optimal edge-preserving transformations directly from data \cite{xu2015deep}. These methods show promise in handling complex textures and patterns that traditional hand-crafted filters may struggle with. The applications of edge-preserving filters extend far beyond basic denoising. In HDR tone mapping, these filters help compress dynamic range while avoiding halo artifacts around high-contrast edges. Detail enhancement techniques rely on edge-aware decomposition to separate fine details from base structures. Computational photography applications such as flash/no-flash denoising, image abstraction, and artistic stylization all benefit from robust edge-preserving smoothing operators.
